# [The Complete Works of St. Bruno of Asti]

[Col. 0009]

# Prolegomenon Divided into Two Parts

The first concerns the manuscript codices from which this collection of the works of St. Bruno was made; the other contains an analysis of the six books of *Sentences*.

[Col. 0009]

## Part One

[Col. 0009A] The extant expositions of St. Bruno of Asti on the books of the Old Testament were included in the first volume, published last year. We now begin the second part with the Commentaries on the Four Gospels; these will be followed by the interpretation of the Apocalypse and the remainder of his works known and accepted up to this point.

We republish those Commentaries on the Gospels by St. Bruno—formerly made public by the most learned Jesuit theologian Peter Lazzari, under the patronage and encouragement of the eminent Cardinal Francis Xavier de Zelada, whose countless praises no age will ever cease to proclaim—because we have been moved by many weighty reasons.

The first is that Lazzari fully attained the matter, or elucidation, of the author. His notes are written so copiously and learnedly that it would be superfluous to add others to them; for no greater clarity in the sacred text would be obtained, but instead there would arise a burdensome mass of authorities and an uncertain understanding produced by a multiplicity of senses.

A second reason is supplied by the certain knowledge that that edition of St. Bruno’s Commentaries on the Gospels, although elegant and accurate, was little distributed in Italy and was still less widely disseminated beyond the Alps.

A third consideration is that the homilies and sermons of the same holy Bishop of Segni are to be printed, and a large portion of them is taken from these same Commentaries. It is therefore necessary to show and place before the eyes of readers the passages in which either fragments of the homilies or entire sermons may be read.

Fourth, no one is unaware how long those homilies were circulated under the name of Eusebius of Emesa [Col. 0009C] and reprinted in many editions.

> [Note: [Col. 0009C] St. Thomas Aquinas himself cites Eusebius’s authorities in various places, for example, *Summa Theologiae*, III, question 75, article 5, and question 75, article 4, from Sermon 3 on Easter, and elsewhere [Col. 0010C]; so firmly had such an opinion taken hold.]

For this reason Lazzari took particular care to expose so deceptive an attribution and establish St. Bruno of Asti as the author of those discourses. We reproduce also the preface of the most learned Lazzari himself, since it abounds in remarkable learning and has gathered many things concerning the country, birth, manner of life, and writings of St. Bruno which especially illuminate and confirm our commentary on the life of the holy bishop.

Those who knew from the witness of writing that St. Bruno had been an interpreter of the Gospels [Col. 0010A] greatly desired to enjoy that work while the manuscript codex containing the interpretation still lay hidden in the library of the Roman College. Their wishes were therefore satisfied, and the distinguished editor gained the approval of learned men. For those devoted to reading the Holy Fathers confess that in this work they find the substance, or compendium, of the most excellent elucidations of ancient expositors, and have in it honey, as it were, made from many flowers. Accordingly, we have called this fruit of such great labor not *Commentary* but *Commentaries on the Gospels*.

One point remains: we must warn readers that we have not followed the old spelling of the manuscript codex—now obsolete and burdensome to readers—as Lazzari did, but have made it conform to modern [Col. 0010B] usage.

For foreign readers it may be added that St. Bruno’s *Commentaries on the Evangelists* were issued from the Roman press of Marcus Palearinus in the Jubilee year 1775, in two octavo volumes. The first contains the exposition on Matthew; the second, those on Mark, Luke, and John.

Stricken with apoplexy in January of the preceding year, 1789, Peter Lazzari died at Rome, advanced in years and piously, as he had lived, deeply engaged in sacred studies, as his many works attest, to the grief of all good people.

It would be our task here to state which manuscript codices we consulted for this edition, lest we seem insufficiently diligent in adorning it. We do not omit this, but reserve it for a more suitable place, [Col. 0010C] when the homilies and sermons of St. Bruno are to be discussed. Meanwhile, we frankly confess that, during the autumn vacation of 1784, when we were at Turin, we were unable, owing to the brevity of our stay in that city, to complete such a collation with the manuscript codex of the Royal Academy mentioned by Lazzari. We did observe, however, that it is a parchment folio, written in Roman script, which more expert judges assign to the twelfth century or the beginning of the thirteenth.

There is added in this volume, after the Commentaries on the Books of the Gospels, an exposition [Col. 0011A] of the Apocalypse. A few preliminary remarks concerning it are needed, since St. Bruno the interpreter himself warned readers what they ought to observe.

These matters concern the objections by which Abauzit, a Genevan Calvinist, sought to weaken the authority of the Book of Revelation—but in vain. Since, a few years ago, the distinguished Vincent Fassini, O.P., professor of Sacred Scripture at the Lyceum of Pisa, most learnedly pleaded the cause of the prophecy of St. John the Evangelist, I shall mention only the principal points necessary for understanding the controversy.

First, Abauzit had said that no one is unaware how many Gospels, revelations, and Acts attributed to apostles existed in the first centuries of the Church, which were afterwards condemned by the Church as apocryphal writings.

Second, he observed that the Apocalypse had by no means been received among the protocanonical books.

Third, the constant obscurity of this book, and the distorted and malicious interpretations attached to it in many places, furnish no slight argument that its author was profane rather than divinely inspired.

Fourth, he challenges us to show the tradition of the Fathers, by whose testimonies it may plainly appear that the Apocalypse rightfully and deservedly held a place among the apostolic Scriptures.

I first premise that it has always been the practice of heretics, when they felt themselves overwhelmed by the authority of the divine Scriptures and had no means of escaping their pronouncements, to remove them from the list of canonical books and count them among inventions. Thus Luther and Calvin called the Epistles of Paul and James spurious because they openly opposed their errors.

The Marcionites, Theodosians, and Alogi therefore rejected the Apocalypse [Col. 0011C] in the first ages of the Church; the Fathers of that age refuted them most conclusively. When Abauzit revived their ashes, his audacity did not go unpunished: his weapons were utterly broken and shattered by a stronger hand.

Thus the force of the first argument is immediately turned back against Abauzit himself. For if, by his own admission, the Church never accepted fabulous and fabricated writings, but refuted and condemned them, then, since she numbered the prophecy of St. John the Evangelist among the canonical books and commended it to the faithful, it must be said that she recognized it as a genuine work of the apostle, written under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

As for his second claim, that the Apocalypse was not immediately admitted together with the other protocanonical books of the New Testament [Col. 0011D], I say that this must be ascribed to the Church’s greatest care and prudence. She wished first to weigh the works of the Latin and Greek Fathers, so that, fortified by their authority, she might declare the Apocalypse a divine book. This was certainly done by Pope Gelasius in the Roman synod, likewise by the Third Council of Carthage, and later the Fathers of Trent confirmed it by solemn decree.

The third objection is to be given no weight. Papias, Justin, Irenaeus, and a few others, who supposed that the righteous would reign with Christ for a thousand years after the first resurrection, according to Revelation chapter 20, were far removed from the heretical Chiliasts or Millenarians. For those heretics, whose leader was Cerinthus, asserted that the righteous would delight in pleasures of the flesh [Col. 0012A] and every worldly gratification; whereas Catholics ascribed to those blessed elect spiritual delights, namely the possession of a more perfect love of God and a fuller knowledge of heavenly goods.

But if sacred writings were to be rejected because of the wicked interpretation of the unjust, then, since from the Church’s beginning, as St. Peter testifies in his Second Epistle, chapter 3, the Epistles of Paul themselves were distorted by certain unlearned and unstable persons, scarcely any divine book would retain authority in the Church.

To the final objection, that tradition does not favor the Apocalypse, I answer first that the heterodox critics Grotius, Flacius Illyricus, and Richard Simon did not think so. They name the more ancient Fathers of the Church—Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Origen, Clement [Col. 0012B] of Alexandria, likewise Theophilus of Alexandria, Cyprian, and many others—who recognized the prophecy of St. John concerning the future state of the world as a divine book.

Secondly, I answer that from the second century of the Church to the ninth, the perpetual agreement of both Greek and Latin Fathers in affirming the divinely inspired Apocalypse is clearly shown and proved. The Church therefore acted with the fullest right in condemning those who opposed her decree.

Moreover, anyone wishing to see more on this controversy should consult Natalis Alexander, vol. III of *Ecclesiastical History*, article 2, §5; Augustin Calmet, in the preface to the *Apocalypse of John*; Lanius, *On Apostolic Learning*, part II, chapter 6; and Vincent Fassini, *On the Authority of the Book of Revelation*.

[Col. 0012C] Having briefly discharged my replies to the heretics’ objections, by which they attempted to weaken the authority of the Book of Revelation, I shall not pass over in silence the materials sought out, and assembled with no small labor, to illustrate this new edition of the same book.

First, I shall say that St. Bruno earned singular praise in being among the few Fathers who expounded the entire Apocalypse.

Second, I shall mention that in this edition I give readers not the mutilated and interpolated interpretation of our bishop on the Apocalypse published by Marchesius, but the complete, whole, and perfect work.

After I had vainly tried in many libraries to compare Marchesius’s text with manuscript codices, I finally discovered from a Vatican codex what is lacking in it and what may restore its sense. No one will deny the authority of that codex after the description which I shall now give. It is a small parchment folio of the twelfth century, written in exceptionally fine Roman script. It once belonged to Queen Christina of Sweden and bears on its front this heading: “Of St. Bruno, Bishop of Segni.” It begins with the preface of the same commentator and displays a division of the Apocalypse, not into chapters as in the Vulgate, but into seven books arranged by Bruno himself.

Third, in speaking of the homilies and sermons of our Bruno, I confess that the greatest thanks are due to the eminent Cardinal Zelada. By his generosity he caused the Commentaries on the Gospels of that holy bishop [Col. 0013A] to be brought to light; by that edition he completely crushed and destroyed the fabrication of some unknown, unskilled copyist who, finding in a manuscript volume a certain series of homilies and sermons attributed to no author, inscribed upon it the name of Eusebius of Emesa.

Such an attribution prevailed for a long time, and three editions were published under that name. Casimir Oudin mentioned the first, and we shall cite his testimony below. The second bears this title:

> *Homilies of the Lord Eusebius of Emesa on the Gospels, customarily read on all Sundays of the whole year and on the weekdays of Lent, now first brought to light; to which we have taken care to append his homilies on the principal festivals of the year.* Antwerp, John Steelsius, A.D. 1555, octavo.

After the index of homilies—142 in all—is added a homily: “On the Repentance of the Ninevites, by the same Eusebius.”

The later edition bears this title:

> *Works of the Divine Bishop Eusebius, namely homilies on the Gospels, customarily read on all Sundays of the whole year and on the weekdays of Lent. In addition, homilies on the principal festivals of the year; finally, homilies to the people, most eloquent and devout, recently brought to light.* Paris, Jerome de Manef and William de Cavallat, under the sign of the Pelican, Mont Sainte-Hilaire, 1575, octavo.

Both editions are in the Chigi Library, and I compared them with the homilies published by Marchesius.

At this point the testimony of Theophilus Raynaud is especially pertinent. In *On Bad and Good Books*, part [Col. 0013C] 1, heresy X, §2, no. 217, *Works*, vol. XI, Lyons, 1665, p. 282, he writes:

> “Sermons *on the seasons* and *on the saints*, which stand first in the work attributed to Eusebius, have through a grave error been ascribed to Eusebius of Emesa. They are the work of Bruno of Segni, the great opponent of Berengar under Gregory VII. This is shown by the Cassinese and Vatican indexes and by Peter the Deacon, librarian, who attributes all these sermons, identifying each by name, to St. Bruno of Segni, whose contemporary he was.”

Casimir Oudin gave an even fuller judgment concerning these homilies in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, fourth century, col. 393:

> “In 1554,” he says, “the Parisian printer Claude Fremy first published under the false name of Eusebius of Emesa 145 homilies [Col. 0013D] *on the seasons* and *on the saints*, printed in octavo [Col. 0014A] and presented to the most distinguished Gabriel Bouvery, Bishop of the Church of Angers, on 19 May. A certain doctor of the Order of Friars Preachers had supplied him with a copy, declaring them worthy of being entrusted to the press. I do not deny that this work is sound and bears with it at least some antiquity and some stylistic conformity pointing to the twelfth century; but that it can be compared with the ancient doctors of the Church and exhibits the elegance and manner of speech of the fourth or fifth century of the Church—no one, I think, would dare assert. This complete collection, so beautifully adapted to the present pontifical usage, cannot possibly antedate even the eleventh or twelfth century of the Church. Therefore, although this work had been attributed to Eusebius, bishop of Emesa, in order that he might thereby appear a greater writer, it was at last rightly and deservedly restored to its parent, St. Bruno, bishop of Segni, as he is called, on the faith of manuscript codices and the authority of Peter the Deacon, librarian of Monte Cassino. This stripping of our Eusebius of Emesa and restoration to Bruno of Segni took place in 1651 through the careful folio edition of this Bruno’s works, which is now readily available. From that time, so far as I know, no one has wished either to ascribe these homilies to Eusebius of Emesa or to take them from Bruno; thus this truth has prevailed among critics.”

Oudin also stated what opinion ought to be held about this Eusebius of Emesa.

> [Note: [Col. 0013D] See the most learned Mamachi on what is to be thought of Oudin’s criticism, vol. IV, *Christian Origins and Antiquities*, pp. 377 and 406.]

“Eusebius,” he says, “bishop of Emesa in Syria or Phoenicia, whom Theodoret calls bishop of Phoenicia, lived during the reign of Emperor Constantius as standard-bearer of the Arian faction. St. Jerome speaks of him in the *Chronicle* under the year of Christ 348, Olympiad 281, and also in the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 101.”

> [Note: [Col. 0013D] (3) Eusebius of Emesa, although undeservedly accused of the Arian heresy, is defended by the distinguished Paolo Antonio Paoli, Regular Cleric of the Mother of God and President of the Ecclesiastical Academy in Rome, in Dissertation 3, “On the Sanctity and Martyrdom of Pope Felix II,” p. 250. There he adduces the testimonies of Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapters 9–10, pp. 74 ff., and Sozomen, book III, chapter 6, pp. 92–93, who maintain that he adhered to Catholic doctrine. Nevertheless, the orthodoxy of Eusebius, bishop of Emesa, is not so certain that it cannot be doubted. The most learned Carlo Sebastiano Berardi, Turinese jurist, while discussing canon 35, *De consecratione*, distinction 2, produced by Gratian under the name of this Eusebius, wrote the following:
>
> “When the Arians, with crafty and cunning design, scattered among the unlearned populace various formulas of faith in which they concealed, so far as possible, the marks and features of their heresy, some of them were commonly believed to be Catholic; indeed, through those formulas they drew many Catholics over to themselves. This explains why Eusebius, bishop of Emesa, a man otherwise exceptionally learned in every kind of literature, received a varying reputation for himself among ancient writers: by some he was regarded as a holy man, illustrious for miracles; by others he was condemned among Arian heretics; nor were there lacking those who called him patron and leader of the Arians. He was substituted for Athanasius after Athanasius had been expelled from the Alexandrian Church by the Arians, perhaps deceived by an error of fact, etc.”
>
> See vol. IV, part 3, p. 43, where he gives his judgment on the homilies published under Eusebius’s name.]

The theft committed by the editors of Eusebius of Emesa is most clearly demonstrated by three chief codices: namely, the Cassinese, the Vallicellian, and the Medicean-Laurentian. I shall show what authority they claim for themselves.

I was informed about the first by the repeatedly commended Dom Thomas Capomatius, superior of the arch-monastery of Monte Cassino. I handled the other two myself and compared them most diligently with Marchesius’s edition.

The Cassinese codex, marked no. 184, a small parchment folio written in Lombard characters in the twelfth century, contains homilies on the Gospels [Col. 0014D] for the entire year and begins with the Gospel: “This is my commandment” [Col. 0015A] (*Hoc est praeceptum meum*). In a later hand the following title is written:

> “Homilies of St. Bruno of Segni and Abbot of Monte Cassino: they are falsely attributed to Lord Eusebius, whereas they are Bruno’s.”

I shall append the judgment of the distinguished Dom Erasmus Gattola, Abbot of Monte Cassino, who says in vol. I of his *History of Monte Cassino*:

> “As Marchesius shows, 140 homilies on the Gospels for the whole year, assigned to Eusebius of Emesa, are to be vindicated for our St. Bruno. Peter the Deacon bears witness to this, for he enumerates them individually; and they are seen described in the same order in a codex of our library written in Lombard characters, apparently marked no. 194. Certainly none of the ancients attributes these homilies to Eusebius, and their style rejects him: it represents not a Greek author but a Latin one, and Bruno himself.”

Then follows a catalogue [Col. 0015B] of the homilies, which we shall give elsewhere.

The second codex, the Vallicellian, is likewise a parchment folio, written in the same Lombard script and not later in date than the Cassinese. It does not preserve the same order, but begins the first homily for Ash Wednesday with these words: “For hypocrites are called sad” (*Tristes enim dicuntur hypocritae*). It bears the name of Bishop Bruno, as do the other homilies inserted in the same codex, although many are absent, and the rest are read as attributed partly to St. Gregory and partly to the Venerable Bede.

Those homilies were derived from an excellent archetype, since in many places they correct and supplement Marchesius’s edition. I know this with certainty from reading the commentary of the same St. Bruno on the Gospels, from which the greater part of the homilies was taken, as I shall show in its proper place.

The third [Col. 0015C] codex is a homiliary, formerly in the library of Santa Croce of the Friars Minor at Florence and transferred to the Laurentian Library. It is a parchment folio, marked no. III, Pluteus XXX, p. 5. In its rubric placed at the end, in the hand of the same scribe, one reads:

> “Here ends this book of Bishop Bruno.”

The time at which it was written is marked thus:

> “From the time of Christ, one thousand, four times ten, and six times ten.”

Then, in a more recent hand, is added:

> “This book is for the use of Brother Thedaldus. After his death it must remain in the bookroom of the Friars Minor of the Florentine convent. It belonged to Dom Philip of Villani of Florence, who granted it on that condition to the said Brother Thedaldus.”

The same is noted in the published catalogue of the Laurentian Library by the distinguished Canon Angelo Maria Bandini, librarian, [Col. 0015D] vol. IV, p. 247.

This codex contains 148 homilies. The greater part bears the name of Bishop St. Bruno; yet I found almost all of them in the Paris edition of the homilies of Eusebius of Emesa, with certain changes or additions at their beginnings and ends. Without doubt, as we have said, they must be attributed to our holy bishop, because they appear to have been excerpted from his Commentaries on the Gospels.

The collector used an excellent exemplar, since he follows the order of the Cassinese codex. He begins with the First Sunday of Advent and continues through the Twenty-Eighth Sunday after Pentecost, including the weekdays of Lent and the principal feasts of the entire year as celebrated by the Church at that time.

To these three complete and very well preserved codices [Col. 0016A] I can add the codex possessed by the chapter of the cathedral church of Segni. It is a parchment folio written in Roman script in the twelfth century, but several pages are missing at the beginning as well as at the end. I observed this when, in the autumn vacation of 1786, I went to Segni to fulfill a vow to my patron saint, the bishop, who had obtained health for me from God when, near the end of the preceding year, I lay mortally ill. It contains homilies arranged throughout the year in the same order described for the above codices.

Finally, there is another manuscript codex in the archive of the Basilica of St. Peter, also parchment and folio, recording the age and name of St. Bruno of Segni and likewise containing his sacred discourses.

By these very clear testimonies of so many manuscript codices, the homilies of St. Bruno of Asti, which we are about to publish again, are not merely vindicated from Eusebius of Emesa; the judgment included in the *Library of the Fathers*, Lyons edition, vol. VI, p. 686, is also confirmed. There those same discourses, once likewise attributed to St. Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, are expressly assigned to our Bruno.

It is superfluous, I think, to speak of the excellence of doctrine and learning with which our author adorned his homilies, since Peter Lazzari has already done this abundantly in the preliminary dissertation to St. Bruno’s Commentaries on the Gospels, noting everything that needed observation.

A catalogue of the homilies and sermons will precede them. Under page numbers it will mark those contained in the same Commentary and therefore omitted; [Col. 0016C] we have not taken care to print them again except those wholly absent from it or those containing clear additions at their beginnings or ends.

After the homilies and sermons, which we have added to the expositions of the holy Bishop of Segni on the Gospels and the Apocalypse, there come fourthly the six books called *Sentences*. Before speaking of them, I declare my profound gratitude to the most distinguished and beneficent Cardinal Stefano Borgia. After I consulted him concerning this edition of St. Bruno’s works, he not only encouraged me to complete it and assisted me with his advice, but most generously gave me everything which he had already gathered about the same holy Bishop of Segni from the Cassinese archive.

Among the many things extracted from those manuscript codices, I shall mention those relating to these books of *Sentences*. Since he knew of the controversy long conducted between Benedictines and Carthusians over whether Bruno of Segni or Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, should be regarded as their author, he examined with the greatest care codex no. 196, formerly 317. He described its Lombard script, its date—namely the twelfth century—and the titles affixed to its individual chapters, and he obtained a full account of this monument of antiquity, which bears the name of St. Bruno, bishop.

Nor did that most learned prelate believe himself satisfied unless he had carefully examined another codex, no. 619, in which, together with several other commentaries and compositions of St. Bruno, the same books of *Sentences* are found, inscribed with the same titles [Col. 0017A].

I have thought it right to establish these points as preliminaries before discussing the controversy just mentioned, which I shall treat in a separate dissertation. I shall also answer a recent anonymous Carthusian author of Naples who, in a letter issued in 1788 to Dom Xavier Mattei, endeavors to vindicate those books of *Sentences* for the renowned patriarch of his order, St. Bruno.

Perhaps someone will ask why works of this kind are called books of *Sentences*. I see no reason at all why Marchesius gives them this title, since all the codices I have consulted announce treatises either on the praises, ornaments, or figures of the Church. Indeed, these titles more truly indicate what St. Bruno proposed to do and the end at which he aimed; and that end is clearly known if all the parts—that is, the chapters and sermons—are compared with one another, particularly with due regard to the time when the holy Bishop of Segni wrote them.

## Part Two

[Col. 0017]

[Col. 0017B] The remnants of the long-lasting and disastrous schism were still vigorous in the Church; simony and audacity increased the calamity; moral corruption had cast off every restraint; and spiritual authority lay oppressed and almost despised. In order, therefore, to meet these evils, A. N. undertook to demonstrate that the Church is one, holy, catholic, and apostolic. Although he had elsewhere asserted these prerogatives, or marks, as we said in the Prolegomena, in these books he treated them more fully and extensively, and vindicated the Church’s glory.

Under elegant figures and images he pursued the argument for the Church’s unity in the first book; in the second he proved the Church holy; he devoted the third to showing that the Church is catholic and apostolic; while the remaining three books, which contain either doctrines of faith or praises of martyrs and other saints, tend toward the same end. The first book is divided into ten chapters, distinguished by their respective titles. Chapter 1 is entitled *On Paradise*; 2, *On Noah’s Ark*; 3, *On the Tabernacle of the Covenant*; 4, *On Solomon’s Temple*; 5, *On the Woman Whom John Saw in the Apocalypse*; 6, *On the City Jerusalem*; 7, *On the Rite of the Consecration of a Church*; 8, *On the Authority of the Gospels*.

Since, then, Holy Scripture relates that one paradise, abounding in every good and delight, was created by God, and that Adam was placed in it to cultivate and guard it, one Church—not several—is to be acknowledged; and whoever divide this unity—heretics, schismatics, or simoniacs—are regarded as outsiders. [Col. 0017D] Saint Bruno the bishop indicates who the laborers in this paradise, or Church, are, maintaining that they are bishops and priests, whom he admonishes thus:

> It is clear that by the garden, that is, by paradise, the Church is signified. But whom should we understand by Adam, if not the guardians of the Church, bishops and priests? Let these, therefore, hear what Scripture says concerning Adam, who was sent into paradise for this purpose: to cultivate and [Col. 0018B] guard it. Let them not be idle, because they are guardians.

By the trees planted in paradise A. N. understands the apostles, who bore manifold fruits, and also the other Christians who follow their precepts and imitate their glorious deeds. Likewise, in the fountain from which the four rivers issued, he says that Christ the Lord is prefigured: from the fullness of whose knowledge all doctrine of faith flowed forth through the four Evangelists.

But after the human race had been corrupted through Adam’s sin and fallen into a worse condition of vice, God commanded Noah, a righteous man, to build an ark, lest the Church should wholly perish. In it, while the whole world was to be destroyed by the waters of the flood, Noah himself and his family might be saved, and from them a new generation of humankind might arise.

[Col. 0018C] Saint Bruno therefore declares the ark to be a symbol of the Church, outside which no one is saved, and in which whoever is found on the day of vengeance shall not perish. Many appear to be in it who will be found outside it, like those to whom the Lord says: “I do not know you” (Matt. XXV.12). No one, says the same holy bishop, enters this ark, or Church, except through the door which Christ said that he himself was: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John X.7).

> For those who do not enter through the door are not saved, says A. N. No animal enters the ark except through the door. But simoniacs and heretics strive to enter the Church by another way.

[Note: [Col. 0017D] The zeal with which Saint Bruno burned against simoniacs has been shown in the *Commentary on Matthew, Luke, and especially John*, no. 28, where he expounds [Col. 0018D] the words: “He who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber.”]

Since the Church is composed, besides the laity, of various ranks of ministers, he finds in it, in some measure, the form of the ark; [Col. 0018D] accordingly he discoursed on it as follows:

> If anyone wishes also to consider the orders of the Church—how clerics sit above the laity, presbyters above clerics, bishops above presbyters, archbishops above bishops, patriarchs in order above them, and finally sees the Roman Pontiff seated above all—he will be able in this way also to understand how [Col. 0019A] the ark of God, broad in its lower parts, gradually narrowing, is brought to an end in one cubit.

Several other analogies and resemblances between the ark and the Church are offered in this second chapter; we omit them for brevity’s sake.

A. N. draws a third argument for the unity of the Church from the tabernacle of the covenant, that is, the ark of the testament. In it, as Saint Paul says (Heb. IX.4), were a golden vessel containing manna, Aaron’s rod which had budded, and the tablets of the Testament. Since the majesty of God present there was represented in it, the building for guarding it was entirely of gold; and before the ark a golden lampstand continually burned, with many lights hanging from one shaft. Moreover, there was a table upon which the loaves of presentation were placed, and a golden censer in which [Col. 0019B] incense was burned before God.

As Moses was the maker of the old tabernacle, so Christ was the institutor and founder of the new one, “not made by hands, nor of this creation”; but, as the Apostle says, “through his own blood he entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption” (ibid., 12). For he gathered to himself a people acquired by his own passion, first from the Jews and then from the Gentiles, and made them participants in his inheritance through one faith and baptism.

The one lampstand signified one teacher of doctrine, namely Christ, enlightened by whom the apostles spread throughout the universal Church all his doctrines and precepts. There is one table, on which the one sacrifice of the body and blood of Christ the Lord is offered; none participate in it except those admitted within the tabernacle, [Col. 0019C] that is, the Church. In the Church, too, as though precious offerings of incense, the unceasing prayers of the faithful are raised to God and obtain his blessing.

Saint Bruno presents to us another image by which our Church may be recognized: Solomon’s Temple. After enumerating in the fourth place the nobler parts of this most splendid structure, he says:

> This temple is the Church; this temple is ourselves. The Apostle says of us: “The holy temple, which you are” (I Cor. III.17).

Indeed, the faithful, who constitute one body of believers, adorn and illuminate this spiritual building all the more as they are more perfect; and because they share with Christ, their perfect head, they receive the fullness [Col. 0019D] of his grace.

But what, asks A. N., do the two columns set before the doors of the temple mean, which seem idle because they support nothing? He answers that nothing in the temple is idle, and that these are the first things encountered by those entering it. In one he understands the patriarchs and prophets, and the other leaders and princes of the Old Testament—such as Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Joshua, David, and Daniel. In the other he says that the apostles, martyrs, confessors, and bishops are represented, who by their courage and steadfastness fearlessly upheld the holy religion against every effort of its opponents. The former righteous persons, justified by faith in the restorer to come, and the latter, justified through Christ’s grace, deserved excellently of the Church because, through love of righteousness, constancy of spirit, and zeal for propagating truth, they not only preserved but spread far and wide the true religion—that is, the knowledge and worship of the supreme Ruler—although worshippers of false gods and teachers of iniquity resisted them in vain.

[Col. 0020A] A. N. applies several further features of Solomon’s Temple to signify the one Church; I pass them over lest I become too lengthy.

When we proceed, however, to chapter 5 of the same first book, which concerns the woman by whom the Church is prefigured, the author makes quite clear what he proposes to do. He begins:

> Blessed John the Evangelist relates that he saw the holy Church in the form of a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon beneath her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars; and she was in travail, suffering in order to give birth.

The distinguishing marks of this woman, therefore, are the brightness and splendor with which she is surrounded like the sun; the crown of twelve stars on her head; the moon beneath her feet; and the pains and labor of childbirth.

> Great is the praise of the Church of God, says A. N., which is said to be clothed with the sun. It is clothed with the sun because it is adorned with every splendor and every brightness. The Church has the moon beneath its feet because it despises the world and counts it as nothing. The world is rightly called the moon, because, like the moon, it is always in motion, always changing and varying.

Is not the most splendid Church clothed with the sun of righteousness, namely Christ the Lord, its founder, who enriched it with such great gifts that he called it wholly beautiful and free from every stain? He draws it away from earthly things—that is, from the world—by the promise of heavenly [Col. 0020C] goods, and refreshes and consoles it with the hope of eternal blessedness.

The same holy bishop continues:

> It also has on its head a crown of twelve stars, by which we understand the twelve apostles. They crowned it; they led it into the bridechamber of the eternal King.

What other Church, then, except the catholic Church shines adorned with this crown of twelve stars, that is, of twelve apostles? Whether we consider the doctrines of faith, it receives from them all truth; or examples of virtues, they made themselves perfect models of Christ their teacher; or testimonies of greatness of soul, the same apostles poured out their life along with their blood for Christ. Certainly none of the ancient or recent sects [Col. 0020D] can claim for itself this crown, so holy, so splendid, and of such divine origin, since all arose at a later time from audacity, error, or impiety.

Saint Bruno offers another most beautiful image signifying the Church in the holy city Jerusalem, as we have it described by the same Evangelist John: namely, situated upon a great and high mountain and built with new workmanship and marvelous art. He saw its walls constructed of precious stone and the city’s street of purest gold, like the clearest glass. It had twelve gates, each made of a single pearl; three looked eastward, three northward, three southward, and [Col. 0021A] three westward.

> This city, says A. N., is the holy Church. These walls and these precious stones are people—people, indeed, noble and illustrious in virtues and endowed with wisdom—such as the apostles, martyrs, and all others who pleased God through faith and holy conduct. This is that Jerusalem which, as it is written, “is built as a city, whose participation is in the same thing” (Matt. IX.22).

For, Saint Bruno explains, those participate “in the same thing” whose heart is one and whose soul is one, among whom there is no discord and the concord is most firm. They all think the same thing, as though he meant, concerning faith, doctrine, mutual sharing in peace, and their bond with the center of unity, the Church’s supreme head, the Roman pontiff.

[Col. 0021B] The same holy doctor continues:

> It should be noted that these same holy apostles are called both the foundations of this city and its gates: foundations, indeed, because in the whole building they are first and bear the rest; gates, because no one is joined to the fellowship of the Church or enters the palace of heaven except through them—that is, through their teaching. To them were given the keys of the kingdom of heaven; they are both gates and gatekeepers.

Those, therefore, who dissent from the Church’s teaching, who spread novelties of opinions and doctrines, and who strive to defend their own inventions, are separated from this holy fellowship and are regarded as branches torn from the tree of life and salvation.

I wish to run through the chief points briefly, lest my discourse be drawn out without measure. Therefore, omitting the rest, I shall turn to chapter 8, entitled *On Basilicas* [Col. 0021C], and be as brief as I can. In it A. N. explains the rite for consecrating a church; since we shall speak of it elsewhere, we refrain for the present from pursuing that subject.

But because Saint Bruno is intent upon impressing the Church’s unity ever more strongly, he explains what is meant by it:

> “Church” is a Greek name; it signifies an assembly of people. But in order to indicate its distinctive properties, he adds: namely, of a people fearing the Lord and serving the Lord. For just as one house is made out of many stones arranged in order and with design, so one Church is constituted from many people united by the love of affection and brotherhood.

Here the holy bishop assigns chiefly two marks to this assembled people, without which it cannot have the form [Col. 0021D] of a Church: namely, that this people fear God and render him honor and obedience, and that they agree perfectly among themselves. Whoever therefore resists the word of God, whoever does not heed but despises the guardians and rulers of the faith appointed by God, demonstrates that he despises God himself and has nothing; consequently, by his disobedience he cuts himself off from the Church. Likewise, those who foster disagreements in doctrine and offend mutual charity renounce its holy fellowship.

Finally, in the last chapter of this first book, entitled *On the Gospels*, he says that, in order that persons outside the Church may be recognized, their fruits—that is, their works—must be examined. If these are contrary to the apostles’ examples, they have no part in the body of the Church. For the apostles did not choose themselves to preach the Gospel; rather, Christ the Lord chose them and sent them into all the world to proclaim and teach the heavenly sacraments and the mysteries of the kingdom of God. Since they wonderfully joined holiness of conduct to the truth of doctrine, they proved themselves sent by God for the conversion of the world and fulfilled their ministry without deceit, without rivalry, but holily and devoutly.

[Col. 0022A] Let Luther and Calvin, and their successors in the chair of pestilence, be ashamed to arrogate to themselves the apostolic name; let them be ashamed to wish to bear themselves as pastors of peoples. Who sent them, if not pride and ambition? What has been reported of their preaching, apart from impious doctrines, except that they stirred up horrible seditions and perpetrated sacrilegious [Col. 0022B] abominations? What deceits did they not employ in order to ensnare the unwary and spread everywhere the plague of their errors? There was never peace and concord among them; rather, they continually disagreed with one another, because amid rivalry and audacity no one wished to yield to another. Their communions, therefore, wholly alien from the catholic Church, are likened to a sea restlessly tossed by waves.

Since the Church’s second mark is holiness, and the holy Church is proposed in the Creed as an object of belief, the entire second book of Sentences concerns the holiness of the Church. For in it he treats of the principal virtues by which Christians become holy and illuminate the Church by their outstanding and glorious deeds. The author divides this book into twelve chapters: the first [Col. 0022C], On Faith; the second, On Hope; the third, On Charity; the fourth, On the Cardinal Virtues; the fifth, On Humility; the sixth, On Mercy; the seventh, On Peace; the eighth, On Patience; the ninth, On Chastity; the tenth, On Obedience; the eleventh, On Abstinence; the twelfth, Where—that is, in what things—the Church is adorned.

He therefore begins, in the opening of chapter 1, by establishing that faith is the Church’s first adornment, or the first degree of holiness, and that it holds primacy in the whole army of virtues. Where it is absent, even though the other virtues are found, they are of no use for eternal salvation, do not establish a person within the body of the Church, and cannot in any way make him a member of Christ.

“For the Gentiles and philosophers,” says St Bruno, “although they shone with many virtues, nevertheless all perished because they did not have faith. Therefore, deservedly, Holy Church [Col. 0022D] receives no one who comes to her unless he has first been clothed with the adornment of faith. Whoever, then, seeks entrance into the Church—that is, baptism—is asked whether he believes, whether he holds the Catholic faith. If he answers that he believes and holds the Catholic faith, he is received, baptized, and joined to the children of the Church. But if he says otherwise, he is by no means received, but is cast out as profane.”

Then, in order to show faith’s excellence, the Lord Himself, as A. N. observes, attributes the power of His mighty works not to Himself but to faith, and declares that faith performs what He Himself does. We read that He healed many men and women and freed them from their infirmities; and He was accustomed merely to say to them: “Your faith has made you whole; go in [Col. 0023A] peace” (Matt. XI, 22).

“The Gospel says,” continues the same St Bruno, “that He once came into His own country; and when the people there doubted His omnipotence and had no faith, ‘He could not perform many mighty works there,’ to use the Gospel’s words, except that He healed sick persons by laying His hands upon them; and He marvelled at their unbelief. Does faith therefore possess such power that He who is able to do all things is, through its absence, hindered from the exercise of His power?”

There are many testimonies of the Evangelists concerning how greatly Christ the Lord urged His disciples to possess this faith. He commended such a virtue to them so strongly that, if they believed perfectly and fully, they would not only heal every infirmity and restore the dead to life, but would even wish to move mountains themselves from one place to another [Col. 0023B]. Thus in Matthew chapter XXI and Mark chapter XI, 23: “Have the faith of God. Amen, I say to you, whoever shall say to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and cast into the sea,’ and shall not hesitate in his heart, but shall believe that whatever he says shall come to pass, it shall be done for him.”

By this most excellent and exalted faith the Catholic Church has deserved always to be glorified, so that it alone ought to be considered holy, since the working of powers within it—which has never been lacking when needed—has furnished proofs of truth and holiness. I am not ignorant of everything advanced by the heterodox in order to weaken miracles, though they have been most conclusively refuted, above all by this argument: such wonders could not have continued to occur through the successive lapse of so many centuries except where the Church was true, and among those whose outstanding merits had obtained from almighty God the power to perform them.

St Bruno proceeds [Col. 0023C] in the second chapter to treat of hope, of which he immediately says:

“Hope is a great adornment of the Church of God. Whoever does not possess it is stripped of every good and is more unhappy than every creature . . . . Hope is the expectation of future goods; and those possess this expectation who most certainly hope that they will someday receive whatever has been promised to them.”

He then continues by recalling the righteous persons who formed the primitive Church: Abraham, Moses, David, Hezekiah, Daniel, the Maccabees, Judith, Esther, and the three youths cast into the furnace. Through the virtue of hope they were not only saved but became illustrious by most glorious deeds. But if we turn our eyes toward our own Church and contemplate the apostles, [Col. 0023D] martyrs, confessors, and virgins who flourished in it, we shall see that, having placed all their hope in God, they emerged victorious from every torment, adversity, and enemy; and that through hope they deserved to tread upon serpents and scorpions and fearlessly overcome every wickedness of malignant spirits. Therefore the prophet David sang most fittingly: “God is wonderful in His saints, the God of Israel; He Himself will give strength and power to His people. Blessed be God” (Ps. LXVII, 36).

Let the founders of the new sects now compare their own heroes with ours. Let them see to what end their boastfulness, false wisdom, contempt for Christian truths, and ambition for worldly [Col. 0024A] glory brought them while they still lived unharmed. How mournfully, how miserably they departed this life! Not a few of them, afflicted by grief and despair, were seized by such madness that they took their own lives.

In the third chapter follows a treatment of charity. Preaching its sublimity and extent, St Paul exalts it so highly that he says that without it the other virtues are absolutely nothing, even though someone might appear, in outward show, to have reached their summit (1 Cor. XIII, 2). Following, therefore, the teaching of so great a master, A. N. explains the properties which he assigns to this most excellent virtue and sets forth most eloquently how much perfection it confers upon those who possess it.

“Charity,” says St Bruno, “is patient, because it is angry with no one and is moved by no injuries, but intercedes even for its own enemies. And [Col. 0024B] because it is kind, it shows kindness and mercy to all whom it can. Therefore, since through patience it forgives all, and through kindness has compassion, what more can it do? Because it is kind, it is not jealous and does not envy. It does not act perversely—that is, it does not do anything rashly or unjustly. It is not puffed up with pride. It is not ambitious, because it does not seek the honours of the world. It does not seek its own interests, but those of all, so that they may be saved. It sets aside its own concerns and attends to those of others. It is not provoked; otherwise it would not be patient. It thinks no evil, which is contrary to kindness. It does not rejoice in iniquity, but rejoices together with truth; and both of these belong to kindness. It believes all things that are to be believed. But what are those things that are to be believed [Col. 0024C]? Do you wish to hear what they are? All those things which both Testaments command us to believe, hope for, and endure. Charity never fails.

“This, then, is the point in which charity is greater than the two virtues mentioned above—that is, faith and hope; hence it is added: ‘The greatest of these is charity.’ It is greater because it never fails, because it is eternal, because it always is and has no end. The other virtues, however, will not be necessary after this life, because they concern only those things which are awaited and have not yet appeared. For hope is the expectation of future things; faith, indeed, is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.”

This lengthy explanation of the properties of charity may perhaps seem excessive; yet it is fitting for confounding those heretics who boast of the mutual love and affection of their [Col. 0024D] own society. For although they take care to render every civil service to their own people, they are not moved by love of God, who commands that one’s neighbour be loved as oneself; nor do they direct their acts toward a supernatural end. Rather, everything they do is earthly and human. Since their charity, therefore, is not heavenly but altogether worldly, it often fails, and is more anxious to seek its own interests than those of others. Consequently, it cannot rise to the level of Christian charity, nor does any adornment of the Church proceed from it.

Having completed these matters, Bruno undertakes in the fourth chapter to expound the four cardinal virtues—prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance—which advance and greatly enlarge the Church’s holiness. On prudence [Col. 0025A] he speaks thus:

“Prudence, which is also called wisdom, is the knowledge of divine and human things. But I do not mean the wisdom of this world, which is foolishness with God, concerning which the Apostle also says that ‘God has made foolish the wisdom of this world’ (1 Cor. I, 20). Rather, I mean that wisdom which pertains to moral uprightness and the salvation of souls—not that which philosophers and orators teach, but that which apostles and doctors preach. These alone have knowledge of divine things, as the Lord Himself says: ‘He who loves Me will be loved by My Father; and I will love him and reveal Myself to him’ (John XIV, 21). This is true knowledge of the Divinity [Col. 0025B], or knowledge of Him who is true wisdom and without whom there is no wisdom.”

To how many most pure souls, revealing Himself, did God disclose the mysteries of His greatness—formerly veiled in mysteries—while He snatched them up and raised them to contemplation of Himself, so that they illuminated the Church by their most learned writings! What teaching did John the Evangelist hand down concerning the divinity of the Word, a doctrine not yet so clearly understood? What instructions of salvation and what knowledge of loftier lights did the Apostle Paul make manifest in his Epistles? How great and noble is the choir of the most holy Fathers, who proved themselves most valiant guardians and propagators of the Catholic faith, crushed the monsters of heretics, and trampled underfoot the ravings of philosophers!

Illuminated, therefore, by these splendours [Col. 0025C], what wonder is it if the Catholic faith, so quickly spread throughout the whole world, triumphed over Jews, idolaters, and all wicked men? Since prudence, or true wisdom, had acquired for itself a kingdom over all nations, it was easy for it to take justice as its companion, justice being second among the cardinal virtues. For the Church, knowing very well the things that are God’s and what human beings owe to her, prescribes the internal and external acts by which her worship is to be exercised; distributes ministries; and causes rules, whether preserved from tradition or newly established according to the exigencies of the times, to be observed. The Church is the defender of justice; and since her rule, unlike all earthly powers, is not subject to change, she maintains a firm and stable administration of law.

Accordingly [Col. 0025D], after St Bruno had discussed wisdom, he continues thus concerning justice:

“Understand, you powerful men of the age, and devote yourselves to wisdom. The imperial laws, canons, and decrees of the saints, made for justice’s preservation, sufficiently show how necessary justice is. Take justice away, and the world perishes. Where justice is absent, iniquity rules: there are frauds, robberies, thefts, murders, fear, distress, and no security. Justice is fear to the wicked and security itself to the good.”

This doctor of the Church speaks on behalf of the Church; his teaching is wholly derived from the divine Scriptures and the holier Fathers. Let us therefore hear him also discoursing on fortitude:

“But what,” he says, “shall I say [Col. 0026A] about fortitude, without which both wisdom and justice seem useless? Fortitude is not strength of body but steadfastness of mind, by which we overcome injuries, endure every adversity, and are not raised up by prosperity. Whoever is overcome by pride, anger, avarice, lust, drunkenness, and such things does not possess this fortitude. Nor are those strong who, placed in adversity, strive for deliverance at the expense of their souls’ salvation. Thus the Lord says: ‘Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul’ (Matt. X, 28). Likewise, those who exalt themselves in prosperity and dissolve into excessive delight cannot be called strong. How are those strong who cannot conceal and restrain the impetuosity of their hearts? Fortitude is not conquered; and if it is conquered, it is not fortitude. The saints possessed this fortitude, for they could be overcome neither by vices, torments, nor blandishments.”

St Bruno then brings forward [Col. 0026B] many examples of saints both of the Old and New Testaments who fought most bravely for truth, justice, and religion, and won glorious palms to the Church’s highest praise.

When A. N. wishes to proceed to temperance, he immediately defines it, saying that it is the virtue which does not exceed due measure in its actions, because it seeks nothing superfluous. This balance in acting rightly and refusal to incline to either side seemed so necessary to the Apostle that, writing to the Romans, he condemned excessive wisdom—that is, excessive ambition for knowledge (Rom. XII, 3): “Do not be wise beyond what it is fitting to be wise, but be wise [Col. 0026C] unto sobriety.” Solomon likewise said that temperance must be observed even in justice: “Do not be excessively just” (Eccl. VII, 17).

For this reason our St Bruno rightly and deservedly commends his patriarch Benedict, who prescribes nothing excessive in his rules, so that those wishing to cultivate holiness may have the means of advancing without oppressing nature or becoming worse in health; mindful certainly of St Paul’s statement that our service should be rational before God (Rom. XII, 1). “For,” A. N. adds, “that service is rational by which not nature itself, but vices, are destroyed.”

After the holy bishop has completed his exposition of the four cardinal virtues, he treats in chapter 5 of humility; in chapter 6, of mercy; in chapter 7, of peace; in chapter 8, of patience; in chapter 9, of [Col. 0026D] chastity; in chapter 10, of obedience; in chapter 11, of abstinence; and finally in chapter 12, of where—that is, in what things—the Church is ordered. Since every one of these virtues contributes, each by its own excellence and property, to the Church’s perfection and adornment, he treats them individually at great length. But for us it is sufficient to learn them briefly gathered together in chapter 12.

He begins therefore:

“We have spoken above concerning the Church and her adornments. It remains for us to see her clothed in her adornments, and to delight most beautifully in her appearance. Concerning her the Psalmist says to the Lord: ‘The queen stood at Thy right hand in a garment of gold, surrounded with variety’ (Ps. XLIV, 10). This queen is the Church of God of which we speak. [Col. 0027A] Her garments are many, her adornments are many; and therefore she is said to be surrounded with variety. Yet she has no adornment which is not either golden or silver.”

Indeed, if we consider humility, who was humbler than Mary, the mother of Christ, from whom the work of redemption began, when she herself confesses that the Lord regarded not her virginity but her humility? Nothing further can be added concerning the humility of Christ her Son after the Apostle, who says that He emptied Himself and offered Himself as the example of this virtue. It is clear that Christ founded the Church in humility, when He made poor, unlearned, and uneducated men the preachers of His word, established them as the foundation of His building, and sent them to enlighten all nations, just as He Himself had been sent by the heavenly Father.

The Church is therefore adorned by this [Col. 0027B] virtue, which is followed by mercy, the disposition of beneficence toward the needy. The Church embraces all believers as children, nourishes and strengthens them with spiritual food, namely the sacraments, protects them, defends them from malignant enemies, and, if they repent from their evil ways, receives and consoles them in her bosom. Nor does she cease diligently to pursue peace, which the angels first announced to the world at Christ’s birth and which the Lord, when about to leave the world, gave and confirmed to the apostles. For, preserving the hierarchical order, maintaining the laws intact, bestowing her offices according to justice, and distributing ministries, the Church obtains and preserves peace by these safeguards.

[Col. 0027C] What shall I say of patience, whose power, steadfastness, and constancy in Christ’s followers were so great that it conquered every power hostile to His name and defeated them with the banner of the Cross raised high? Who can recount the infinite multitude of martyrs of every age and condition, who bore the most savage torments and punishments for faith and justice? The more their blood was shed, the more the Christian people sprang up and flourished. They made themselves worthy of the same commendation with which the Apostle adorned the most valiant Israelites: those who through faith conquered kingdoms, worked righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, recovered strength from weakness, became mighty in battle, [Col. 0027D] and turned to flight the armies of foreigners (Heb. XI, 23), etc.

Besides the eternal and incomprehensible reward which these witnesses and champions of truth gained for themselves, the tokens of victory by which they adorned the Church and sealed her holiness with their own blood will always be most splendid.

But the Church shines most brightly also through chastity, of which A. N. treats in chapter 9. Through purity of life her children become like the angels of God, as they invincibly restrain the impulses of flesh and concupiscence, keep their souls free from every impurity, and make themselves acceptable to God. Although he commends this virtue to all Christians as a kind of badge of religion, he inculcates it much more strongly upon ecclesiastical men, lest, if they despised and violated it, they should [Col. 0028A] wickedly profane the sacred ministry.

For St Bruno says: “Although all Christians ought to possess continence and chastity, it is especially necessary for clerics to maintain and observe this virtue. Hence the Lord commanded Moses (Lev. XVI, 4) to make breeches for Aaron the priest and his sons, without which they were never to approach the altar, lest they die. The breeches signify chastity, because they restrain and keep chaste those members in which lust especially rules. Those priests and clerics do not possess breeches who do not restrain these members but permit them to wander unlawfully. But one must greatly fear the words, ‘lest perhaps they die.’ If you do not wish to die, either preserve chastity or do not approach the altar.”

I omit many other excellent statements by A. N. concerning chastity [Col. 0028B], in order to mention some things about obedience, concerning which in chapter 10 he instructs readers, supported by splendid authorities and examples from both Testaments. He first sets forth that the Lord Himself and our Saviour taught how great is the good of obedience, since the Apostle Paul wrote of Him that Christ “became obedient to the Father unto death” (Phil. II, 8).

“Through the disobedience,” says St Bruno, “of the first man the world perished; through the obedience of the second man, Jesus Christ, the world was saved. The former, disobedient, approached the forbidden tree; the latter showed Himself obedient even unto the tree of the Cross. St Peter likewise gave the same instruction in these words: ‘Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow in His footsteps’ (1 Pet. II, 21).”

To this [Col. 0028C] St Bruno adds: “What does ‘that you should follow in His footsteps’ mean, except that you should learn and observe His obedience?”

Since the Church militant is an active body and perfectly constituted, unless its members render services to one another and are united with the head by which they are governed, they can in no way attain the end for which they are joined together—namely, God’s glory and their own salvation. Therefore the divine Bridegroom, addressing His bride the Church, called her “an army set in array”; by this order she is made terrible to her enemies, and she is like a tower from which a thousand shields hang (Cant. VI, 3): that is, defenders who fight bravely for her and preserve her firm and stable.

[Col. 0028D] But for those contending in this struggle, abstinence is necessary, as St Paul teaches, in order that we may receive not a corruptible but an incorruptible crown.

“There are two abstinences,” says A. N., “one bodily and the other spiritual. Both are great, but the latter is greater, because abstaining from vices is greater than abstaining from food. Yet abstinence from food is also so great that it has been confirmed not only by the prophets but by the Lord Himself.”

What the holy bishop says here briefly, he demonstrates through a long series of examples from the holy Fathers of both the Old and New Testaments, who, pursuing the excellence of every virtue, spent their entire lives in fastings and mortification of the flesh, and therefore shone in the Church as miracles of holiness. He celebrates the great Anthony, Paul the patriarch of hermits, Hilarion, [Col. 0029A] Benedict, and others, whose delight was fasting and whose life was abstinence.

Clothed with this beauty and resplendent with these adornments—that is, virtues—the Church so merits the love of her Bridegroom that, admiring her as wholly immaculate and beautiful, He declares and commends her holiness: “You are altogether beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Cant. IV, 7).

The Church’s third prerogative is that which we confess her to be, namely Catholic. Its adornment is so beautiful and excellent that, in order to set it forth, A. N. devoted the first four chapters of the third book of Sentences to the most fitting figures and comparisons gathered from Sacred Scripture, while in the remaining six he shows the Church to be apostolic.

Considering that Christ the Lord, the teacher of heavenly [Col. 0029B] doctrines, came to earth, he saw that the world had been wholly renewed by Him, so that a new world, a new order, and a new arrangement of things arose and presented another aspect or image. The first four chapters of the third book are: 1. On the New World; 2. On the New Heavens; 3. On the New Clouds; 4. On the New Mountains.

St Bruno first derives how a new world would arise when Christ came to earth from that prophecy of Baruch in which it is written concerning Christ: “This is our God, and no other shall be esteemed in comparison with Him. He found out every way of discipline and gave it to Jacob His servant and to Israel His beloved. After these things He was seen upon earth and conversed with men” (Baruch III, 36).

Thus a new teacher and master was promised to the world—that is, to humankind [Col. 0029C]—who would open every path of knowledge and teach every truth. Before Him, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. X, 1), all the fathers were under the cloud, passed through the sea, and were baptized in cloud and sea. They saw future sacraments in enigma and figures, but did not attain their excellence and truth. Moreover, God had chosen only the Israelite people for this knowledge, though obscure and imperfect, leaving the nations in darkness and the shadow of death.

Christ therefore came—the Word made flesh—and, as the Evangelist John testifies, brought into the world the fullness of grace and truth. Hence, if previously the Law had been received through Moses, it was necessary to acknowledge grace and truth as having been made through Jesus Christ [Col. 0029D]. For the grace of Christ freed the world from sin and from the power of the devil by which it was held, and introduced into it heavenly knowledge and awareness of eternal goods.

Therefore the Lord Himself said that He had come to make all things new: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. XXI, 5). He created a new world, namely His Church, setting apart some and calling to Himself others whom He had chosen for the accomplishment of so great a work. “You have not chosen Me, but I have chosen you,” Jesus said to the apostles, His first followers, “and have appointed you that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John XV, 16). The Apostle Paul testifies to the same, saying that the grace of our Saviour appeared and that, in order to pour out His teaching, He gave Himself [Col. 0030A] so that He might redeem us from iniquity and cleanse for Himself an acceptable people, zealous for good works (Tit. II, 14).

“If,” says St Bruno, “all things in this world have been made new, then the Church has a new heaven, a new sun, a new moon, new stars, clouds, rains, lightning and thunder, mountains, forests, new human beings, and all the rest—things which nevertheless had been signified by the old things and bear a certain likeness to them.”

Having set this out, A. N. begins to treat of the new heavens, which he says are the apostles. For since the heaven which God created in the beginning is the greatest and noblest part of the world and manifests above other created things God’s wisdom and omnipotence, so the apostles, established as princes of peoples, [Col. 0030B] shining with every brilliance of knowledge, chosen for the governance of the Church and propagation of truth, are said to declare the glory of God and the works of His hands: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of His hands” (Ps. XVIII).

“They are,” the holy bishop continues, “those to whom the Lord says: ‘You are the light of the world’ (Matt. V, 14). Thus the whole Church is illuminated by their faith and teaching, as the whole earth is illuminated by the sun’s radiance and splendour; and in them the beauty of every virtue shines like stars.”

The same author explains excellently how the apostles were enlightened in likeness to heaven, taking the image from the illumination of the firmament. The firmament did not receive light immediately upon being created; rather, God merely divided the waters from the waters, [Col. 0030C] the dry land appeared, and the gatherings of waters were formed. But on the third day, when God had made and placed in it the great lights—the sun, moon, and stars—the firmament began to shine and illuminate the earth with its splendours.

“Our heavens also,” says St Bruno, “in likeness to the firmament, were by no means called and enlightened at the same time. Rather, in the third year after their calling they deserved to receive the illumination of the Holy Spirit. For, as blessed Luke says, they did not understand the Scriptures, that Christ had to rise from the dead (Luke XXIV, 46). They were still without light, oppressed by so great a darkness. Therefore, just as the firmament was illuminated on the third day, so the apostles were enlightened in the third year.

“In this also the apostles seem to bear the likeness of the firmament: the waters above the firmament are divided from the waters below [Col. 0030D] it. Placed in a certain middle position, they divide waters from waters because they separate the New Testament from the Old.”

From St Paul, writing to the Galatians and declaring circumcision useless after Christ’s grace, he clearly proves this, as likewise from the abolition of the legal observances, which came to an end at that time. The apostles, then, are those heavens that declare the glory of God, Christ the Lord Himself teaching and instructing them, since He is light and there is no darkness in Him. They were sent into all the world in order to pour forth the light of truth, so that all people might acknowledge the true God, receive His holy law, profess one faith, and, despising earthly goods, strive for eternal blessedness.

[Col. 0031A] To them, therefore, it was given to speak in every tongue the mighty works of God, namely to reveal heavenly mysteries and proclaim what had never been heard before: the salvation of the human race accomplished by the divine man, according to the prophetic oracle: “All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God” (Isa. LII, 10).

And because the divine majesty and nature can in no way be perceived by a created mind, God is seen to have placed darkness around Himself, as the Psalmist sang: “He made darkness His hiding place; dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. XVII, 12). It was therefore necessary that in the renewal of the world—that is, the establishment of the Church—new clouds should appear, not dark but bright and radiant, and should illuminate the whole face of the earth.

“What then,” says A. N. [Col. 0031B], “are these clouds, unless we understand them to be the apostles, of whom it is written: ‘Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?’ (Isa. LX, 5). The holy apostles are called heavens, clouds, mountains, fountains, and by many other names, because of certain significations appropriate to them. But where do they fly? Let the Psalmist say: ‘Their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world’ (Ps. XVIII, 4). Whence do they come? ‘Bringing forth clouds from the uttermost part of the earth, He made lightnings into rain’ (Ps. CXXXIV, 7).

“The apostles, then,” St Bruno continues, “fly like clouds, watering everywhere, making the whole earth fruitful, calling to faith, shining with miracles, and making lightning into rain. For lightning becomes clouds when miracles follow doctrine. Thus the Gospel says [Col. 0031C] concerning the apostles that, having gone forth, they preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark XVI, 20).

Therefore, by clouds let us understand the apostles; by rain, doctrine; by thunder, voices; and by lightning, miracles. In this arrangement the admirable ways of the Lord are displayed: He made the apostles announcers of His word—men trained in heavenly knowledge and outstanding holiness—whom He willed to pour out the same teaching among all nations, and whose precepts and instructions He confirmed by most brilliant signs and wonders. This surely demonstrates that God intended nothing other than that the confession of faith should be one and universal: that all should believe the same things with a sincere heart and preach them with one voice. [Col. 0031D] Thus the Church formed from these believers is rightly and deservedly called not only one and holy, but also Catholic.

Proceeding to adorn the same image of the new world, A. N. urges us to raise our eyes to the new mountains and seek help from them. He explains the words of the royal prophet, “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence help shall come to me” (Ps. XX, 1), thus:

“These mountains also are new and belong to the new world; we must raise our eyes to them and expect help from them. By these mountains are understood patriarchs and prophets, apostles and doctors, who, raised above earthly mountains and made nearer to heaven, despise all worldly things.”

Further below he calls the same mountains eternal, concerning which the Psalmist says: “The foolish of heart were troubled by the eternal mountains” [Col. 0032A] (Ps. LXXV, 6), and adds:

“But all the foolish of heart were troubled by these: namely Jews and Gentiles, wise in speech but foolish in heart, speaking philosophically and understanding nothing. Why were they troubled? Because of the signs which they saw and because they could not resist them. For it was not they who spoke, but the Holy Spirit in them, to whom God had given a mouth and wisdom which all their adversaries could neither resist nor contradict. Some were troubled for good, others for evil; some believing, others raging.”

[Col. 0032B] Faith, therefore, proclaimed everywhere by the apostles and confirmed by prodigies and wonderful signs, led very many to embrace it. And although some attempted to assail and overthrow its truth, the fury of its opponents achieved nothing except that the Christian religion acquired greater glory and splendour through the unconquered fortitude and constancy of the martyrs.

But from what source did the enemies of the faith, while admiring such virtue in the martyrs, prove unable to overcome it? A. N. teaches that Christ the Lord, before making Peter shepherd of His sheep, questioned him three times concerning his love; and when for the third time he answered that he loved Him, then He set him over His flock to feed it. “For,” says St Bruno, “he was first questioned by the Lord concerning charity, first professed charity three times, and thus received the care of feeding the sheep.”

This was intended to signify that, if great love of God were joined to the profession of faith, Christians would never fall away from it, since Peter himself had offered them testimony both of the doctrine of truth [Col. 0032C] and of unconquerable fortitude. A. N. brings forward many other matters most learnedly concerning the height of these mountains—that is, the outstanding holiness of the first propagators of the faith—upon whom the Church is founded. As the Psalmist says: “Her foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI, 1), she shall always enjoy complete safety and firmness. I shall not dwell longer on these points, since I must proceed to expound the Church’s fourth mark, namely that she is apostolic.

The excessive abundance of images and subjects which St Bruno presents on this theme in chapters 7, 8, 9, and 10 of this third book of the *Sentences* does not so much compel me to pass over chapters 5 and 6, entitled “On New Trees,” as to bring forward only the more outstanding matters which, in his usual manner, the holy bishop treated most fully and ingeniously. The title of chapter 7 is “On New Powers,” where he prefaces the passage from Matthew in which Peter said to Christ: “Behold, we have left all things and followed thee: what therefore shall we have?” The Lord replies: “You who have left all things and have followed me shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life. And because you have followed me, you shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:27). From this divine oracle St Bruno argues and establishes that supreme and universal authority in the Church was conferred upon the apostles. Introducing the following words, he says:

> “The new world has a new emperor, new kings, new leaders, new princes, and judges. [Col. 0033A] The new kings, leaders, and judges are the apostles; and they are new indeed in the Lord, for they are and shall be wiser, more powerful, stronger, more righteous, and richer than all the powers of this world, whatever they have been, are, and shall be.”

St Bruno proves the apostles’ wisdom from that promise of Christ the Lord: “But when that Spirit of truth shall come, he will teach you all truth” (John 16:13). He also demonstrates their authority from Matthew, where Christ said to them: “Whatever you shall bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven” (Matt. 18:18). The author’s comment on these words is outstanding; for he says:

> “Earth does not suffice for them: heaven itself is included within their rule and dominion. They have power to shut and to open; they admit whom they will and exclude whom they will. [Col. 0033B] The apostles likewise excel so greatly in strength that evil spirits fear them, obey their command, and cannot endure their presence. And what need is there to speak of riches?”—this is again St Bruno—“when they are so rich that, as the Apostle says, they are ‘as needy, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and possessing all things’” (2 Cor. 10). “He is exceedingly rich to whom all things suffice.”

Since, however, the apostles not only left all things but also followed Jesus, he appointed them princes and leaders for the enlightenment and sanctification of the entire world, and subjected all nations to their judgment. “He left no part of the world,” St Bruno comments, “who commanded that the whole world be preached to. Thus the Lord divided the nations and so separated the sons of Adam [Col. 0033C] that some should be converted to the faith through Peter, others through John, and others through other apostles. This too seems to be signified by what is read of Christ in the Psalms: ‘In place of thy fathers, sons are born to thee; thou shalt appoint them princes over all the earth’” (Ps. 44:17). “For sons were born to our Saviour in place of fathers, because the number of the sons was made according to the number of the fathers. There were, indeed, twelve sons of Jacob, from whom the whole Synagogue sprang; and there are twelve sons of Christ, from whom the multitude of the Church has sprung.”

Thus the Church, which took its origin from Christ, was propagated and multiplied by the apostles as by sons. They showed that the Mosaic law had been given for a time and was, as it were, a preparation for the mysteries to come; hence, once truth had dawned, shadows [Col. 0033D] and enigmas ought to come to an end. They led the people who walked in darkness and served false gods or demons to the knowledge and worship of the true God; and from both peoples—namely, Jewish and Gentile—they gathered one flock under the one shepherd, Christ.
