Therefore the whole flock which was gathered together in the world by the apostles—like a new sea, with the apostles established as new fishermen—may be called apostolic.

Under these images the author continues in chapter 8 to demonstrate the apostolic Church. First he recalls the event when Christ the Lord, walking by the Sea of Galilee, called Peter and Andrew, James and John to himself and said to them: “Come after me; I will make you become fishers of men” [Col. 0034A] (Mark 1:17). On this calling he speaks thus:

> “When I hear men called fish and Christ’s disciples made fishers of men—something which cannot be understood literally—I am necessarily compelled to understand a new sea, new nets, new fishermen, and new fish. The new sea, then, is the new world, of which the Psalmist said: ‘This sea is great and spacious; there are creeping things without number’ (Ps. 103:25). The nets are the Gospels, the fish are human beings, and the fishermen are the apostles.”

These alone are called to this fishing and come to fish in the great and deep sea; nor does the difficulty of the catch frighten them, although they must both fight and fish. Few in number, unarmed, poor, furnished with no equipment of worldly wisdom, they undertake—and accomplish—so great a work, namely the conversion of the world, relying only on the word of their master. And what is more wonderful, the force and firmness of the doctrines they preached were such that all who then and afterward rose up as opponents—namely Gentile philosophers, Jews, and heretics, disseminating contrary doctrine and errors—were found to have raved and to have vanished away in their own discourses. What the apostles committed to writing—the Gospels and Epistles—and what they communicated orally to their churches, which Paul in writing to Timothy called the deposit of faith [Col. 0034B] (1 Tim. 6:20), was preserved so faithfully that, beneath it as beneath an impregnable rampart, all assailants fell prostrate and defeated. No deceit, no tyrannical power, no unstable change of the age prevailed against [Col. 0034C] the foundations of divine doctrine laid by the apostles, because, by Christ’s promise, “I am with you unto the consummation of the world” (Matt. 18:20), none of their efforts could ever prevail.

Therefore our Church is to be called apostolic from its institution, apostolic from its propagation, and apostolic from its firmness. Yet the following two chapters, which treat “On New Birds” and “On New Rivers,” renew and confirm this eminent excellence of the Church.

With the keenness and fertility of intellect which our Bruno possessed, observing that God created fish and birds from the waters and blessed them that they might multiply, he conceived that the same spiritual creation occurs through the waters of baptism:

> “Fish and birds have a new origin, and both were created from waters. The former occupy the depths; the latter are raised toward heavenly things. Both are good, because among all other creatures these deserved to receive the first blessing. By them, therefore, holy men are signified, who have been regenerated from water. For unless one has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5); “they thoroughly search out the depths of the Scriptures, which are signified by waters, and by their virtues raise others to heavenly things.”

Having spoken of new animals in the preceding chapter, he now undertakes to speak of mystical birds. For he observed that the Church is called a dove by God: “My dove is one” (Song 6:8); that John the Evangelist is likened to an eagle; and that David himself called himself like a pelican and a solitary sparrow on a roof. [Col. 0035A]

> “And not only human beings,” he says, “but the angels themselves also seem to assume the appearance and nature of birds. Everywhere we see them winged and feathered. They are described as flying rather than walking, which indeed belongs especially to birds.”

He then recounts Isaiah’s vision, in which he saw winged seraphim above the throne of God, filling the whole earth with his majesty; and he likewise speaks of Ezekiel’s vision, to whom four mystical living creatures appeared. Having mentioned these, he says:

> “All the elements teach us to fly; all summon us upward, to heavenly things. We have already become birds, because we have been regenerated in the waters. Wings alone are lacking: let us seek them, for [Col. 0035B] without wings and feathers we cannot fly. Wings are virtues; wings are understood to be good works. Without them we cannot fly. Let them bear us; let them raise us to heavenly things.”

He then enumerates the virtues which carry us up to God and enable us to enjoy the sight of him. But when he comes to explain the vision of the four living creatures, he wonderfully expounds the mystery hidden in it with the same clarity with which he set forth the rest:

> “It is not without mystery that the first living creature is described as having the face of a man, by which we understand Matthew the apostle and his Gospel. Beginning with Christ’s birth, Matthew shows that Jesus was a perfect man and born of human beings, setting out his entire genealogy from Abraham down to him. Mark seems to have the face of a lion, at the beginning of whose Gospel a voice is described as crying in the wilderness. But blessed Luke has the face of an ox, because he begins to write from the priesthood, which was instituted especially for sacrifices; and among sacrificial victims the ox is the greater offering. Why John has the face of an eagle is shown most plainly by the beginning of his Gospel: ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.’ [Col. 0035C] He who speaks thus flies far more sublimely than an eagle.”

Nevertheless, these four very different faces of the living creatures seem to offer us something, because the human being summons us to reason, the lion to courage, the ox to labour, and the eagle to contemplation. Therefore the Church, which received Christ’s teaching and deeds from the Evangelists, did not learn worldly prudence and respectability, but is raised and stirred up to attain heavenly righteousness and perfection. Since Christ the Lord said to the apostles, “Be perfect as my heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5:48), he wished them to aspire to that height of holiness which would correspond to the fullness of his grace and teaching and produce outstanding fruits.

St Bruno perceived this outpouring of divine gifts upon Christ’s faithful, or upon the Church, in chapter 10 of Book III as a most abundant river of paradise, by which the whole city of God is watered and increased with wonderful fertility:

> “This river is Christ, whose most abundant wisdom and knowledge gladden the holy Church. Hence Solomon says: ‘Wisdom preaches; she cries aloud outside; in the streets she gives her voice’ (Prov. 8:1). She also cries in the temple, saying: ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink, and from his belly shall flow living waters’ (John 7:38). Hence comes that fountain of which it is said: ‘For with thee is the fountain of life’ (Ps. 35:10). He also speaks to the Samaritan woman, saying: ‘Whoever drinks of the water which I shall give him shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life’ (John 4:14). This river, therefore, by which paradise is purified and the Church gladdened, is divided into four heads, by which the four Gospels are signified.” [Col. 0036A]

He then explains the names of these rivers; I shall endeavour to condense his very full exposition into a few words, while leaving readers in the same chapter a great abundance of sacred learning.

[Col. 0036B] The first river, then, is called Phison [Pishon], which is interpreted “change of speech.” For Gospel preaching changed the mouths and tongues of human beings, so that those who praised and proclaimed false gods now praise and proclaim the one God and his wonders. How great a change of speech occurred when the apostles, who scarcely knew how to speak one language, being poor and unlearned men, soon, divinely inflamed, began to speak in all languages! Gyon [Gihon], the second river, is interpreted “breast.” For the heart is in the breast, in which is the seat and fountain of all wisdom and knowledge. John the Evangelist drank from this river when, reclining upon Christ’s breast at the Supper, he saw that which he later wrote: “In the beginning was the Word,” etc. Whenever we desire to drink from the river Gyon, let us look to the breasts of the pontiffs, [Col. 0036C] for this reason they were adorned with the rational [the priestly breastpiece], so that we might understand that a great treasure of wisdom is hidden there.

Tigris is called “arrow,” because this river is most swift like an arrow. But what is of such speed as Gospel preaching, which, running everywhere, filled the whole world in a very short time? It remains now to speak of Euphrates, which is interpreted “fertility.” There is no need here to show at length how great a fertility the Gospels produced, namely in the conversion of peoples to Christ, since all the prophecies concerning this new multiplication of the children of God have been perfectly fulfilled and the Church is seen to have spread throughout the earth.

> “For because the field of God, the vineyard of God, the garden of God—that is, the holy Church—is so fruitful, [Col. 0036D] this is caused by this Euphrates, by whose river it is flooded and watered. These are the four rivers of paradise, proceeding from one fountain and flowing forth from the one breast of Christ, by which the entire world is watered. But from these many other rivers have arisen. For there are as many rivers as there are volumes of books.”

The same author then teaches that the Old Testament has its own rivers, whose waters, unless tempered with the waters of the New Testament, are in themselves unpleasant and deadly, according to the Apostle’s saying: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). Therefore the Church, watered by these rivers, namely the apostolic teachings, daily produces ever more outstanding fruits of holiness and wisdom; and carefully guards against its springs—that is, its doctrines—being infected by the pestilential [Col. 0037A] waters of heretics, so that they may be kept entirely pure and healthful.

The remaining three books of the *Sentences* are as follows: the fourth treats the principal mysteries of faith; the fifth treats the praises of the Blessed Virgin Mary; and the sixth contains several sermons on martyrs, confessors, and virgins, whose praises show the holiness and glory of the Church shining through so great a succession of ages. Since, therefore, such treatises on the praises and ornaments of the Church, by which St Bruno wonderfully defends and illustrates its characteristics or notes, are to be held in the highest esteem, it was altogether right and proper to ascribe them to their author and thereby to present the case so that the empty and frivolous efforts of those contending for Bruno of Carthusian order may appear as they are.

[Col. 0037B] I shall proceed to enumerate the remaining writings of the holy bishop of Segni contained in this volume. After the six books of the *Sentences*, then, come three treatises. The first is “On the Incarnation of the Lord and on His Burial”; the second, “On the Sacrifice in Unleavened Bread against the Greeks”; the third, “On the Mysteries, Sacraments, and Rites of the Church.”

In the first, St Bruno treats of the necessity of the restoration of the human race after Adam’s sin, and of the fittingness that the Son of God, by assuming our flesh and through his passion and death, should rescue us from damnation and save us, the price of his blood having been paid for us. The author further discusses the burial of Christ the Lord, his descent into hell, and his resurrection; but he merely runs through the chief points of the doctrine, omitting [Col. 0037C] many matters which theological authors treat at length.

St Bruno’s second treatise was written to Leo the monk and concerns the sacrifice of the Mass, to be performed with unleavened bread. Since monks of the Latin Order of St Benedict were living at Constantinople and celebrating the sacred rites according to the rite of the Holy Roman Church, the Greeks charged them with not consecrating in leavened bread, while affirming that they themselves preserved a tradition received from the apostles and the first holy Fathers. Asked by the monk Leo, who was living there, the bishop of Segni answered that Latin priests were just as permitted to use unleavened bread made from wheat in consecrating Christ’s body as Greek presbyters were permitted to use leavened bread, since each Church, Latin and Greek alike, could administer the sacrament according to its own custom. St Bruno nevertheless proves that Latin priests conform more closely to the Lord’s institution, since Christ the Lord at the Paschal supper, in accordance with the Mosaic law—which he had not come to abolish but to fulfil—had unleavened bread set before him and consecrated this bread, not leavened bread. The author exhorts Leo and the other monks at Constantinople not to accommodate themselves to the Greeks in the sacrament of the altar, but to hold most firmly the teaching and customs of the Holy Roman Church.

This little work, published by Marchesius, I found in no manuscript codex, although I searched diligently in several libraries. [Col. 0038A] The case was otherwise with the treatise “On the Mysteries, Sacraments, and Sacred Rites,” since several most excellent codices bear witness to it, although under different titles. I shall mention two codices of the Ambrosian Library at Milan, shelf-marks Q. 54 and I. 80. The first codex, written at the end of the twelfth century, and the other in the thirteenth century, are parchment volumes in small folio and bear this heading at the beginning: “Of Bishop Bruno, On the Sacraments.” A Paris manuscript of the Royal Library, likewise parchment and in small folio, shelf-mark 3876, has the title: “On the Sacraments of the Church.” Another codex exists at Florence in the Library of St Mark of the Order of Preachers; I collated it with Marchesius’s printed edition during the autumn vacation. I made the same collation with three other codices: namely, two in the Vatican Library, 994 and 1334, formerly belonging to the Queen of Sweden, and another in the Vatican Archive. These are parchment manuscripts in small folio and, from their Lombardic script, may be assigned to the twelfth or thirteenth century. The Royal Athenaeum Library of Turin possesses another codex of the same little work, shelf-mark no. 1113 and no. 33, with the following inscription: “On the Sacraments of the Church, Mysteries, and Ecclesiastical Rites.” The titles transcribed in the codices cited above do not differ from this.

Several editions of this little work have appeared. The first, as we have said, was prepared by Marchesius; the second was issued by the Lyons printers in the *Bibliotheca Maxima Veterum Sanctorum Patrum* (1677), vol. 20, and in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. 6, among the works of Bruno of Asti; the third was produced at Turin without a year of publication; the fourth was published by Dom Luc d’Achery in the *Spicilegium*, vol. 12, p. 79, at Paris in 1575, [Col. 0038C] under this title: “On the Consecration of a Church and Episcopal Vestments.” But I should prefer to all these the edition by Philip Zazzera, Doctor of Sacred Theology and Canon of St Peter’s [*S. T. D. et C. P. M.*], who published the same treatise at Rome, from the Salomoni press, in octavo, in 1784. Having discovered in the Vatican Library manuscript no. 5046, with the heading, “An explanation of the holy rites of the Church and of the divine offices, composed by an anonymous writer,” he judged it worthy to make public, to illustrate it with notes, and to dedicate it to Pope Pius VI, happily reigning. The anonymous author appears to have compiled his work from various writers on liturgical matters, but especially from Bruno of Segni, whom he copies word for word [Col. 0038D] when he begins to discuss the consecration of a church.

The esteem and authority which that treatise won are evident from the fact that it was proposed for reading as a master of sacred rites, and that its doctrine on the essence and effects of the sacraments, and on the mysteries and ceremonies by which they are performed, is presented as perfectly consonant with the practice of the Roman Church. Hence, since our St Bruno drew many matters in composing this work from the canons of councils and decrees of popes, its editor Zazzera notes every rule and decree established by supreme authority and embellishes his commentary with much learning.

St Bruno’s little work is preceded by a letter to Gualterius, bishop of Maguelonne, at whose request he had written it; and its parts are as follows:

1. An exposition of the rite for consecrating a church, in which the mysteries represented under various symbols are explained.
2. The rules concerning the sacraments of baptism and confirmation are concisely presented, both for those administering and those receiving them.
3. The significance of the individual episcopal vestments is set forth; and because that sacred attire represents the dignity of the high priest, many garments used by the pontiff of the old law seem to have been transferred to adorn the new Church and the new priesthood. [Col. 0039A]

We have assigned the sixth place in this volume to the *Life of Pope St Leo IX*, which our Bruno composed at the command of the same holy pontiff. He added to it a treatise bearing the title “On the Corrupt State of the Church.” [Col. 0039B] The origin of this question was as follows. Since in the eleventh century the stain of simony had spread far and wide, and bishoprics and priesthoods were sold for money, it was doubted whether ordination remained valid in the Church, since according to canonical rulings holy orders, through which the Holy Spirit is bestowed, must be received freely and given freely. Bruno of Segni, who flourished at that time, treated this controversy and proved that the Church was not so corrupted by simony that its priesthood had failed. He condemns and most vigorously rebukes simoniacs, who made use of that shameful profit in sacred ministries, and declares them struck by anathema; nevertheless, he maintains that, however much this plague may have prevailed, the holy Church had not lost the ordination of its ministers.

I seem to have said enough by way of preliminary on this question here, since the most distinguished Pietro Lazzari, in his preface and notes to the *Commentary on the Gospels* [Note: [Col. 0039C] See the *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 21, no. 10.], has treated many points learnedly, and I have other matters to note in my exposition of the same question.

Our Bruno also rendered excellent service in writing the life of St Peter, bishop of Anagni; we have added it to the deeds of St Leo. Yet it is greatly to be regretted that only an abridged account of St Peter’s virtues and deeds survives. [Col. 0040A] At our request, the diligent Dom Giovanni Battista Frederici, prefect of the Cassinese archive, did not spare efforts to produce the complete sequence of the acts of this same St Peter, which we conjectured from several considerations had been written by Bruno; but all labour was spent in vain.

Finally, this collection will be completed by four letters of the author: the first to Pope Paschal II; the second to Peter, cardinal and bishop of Porto; the third to all the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church; the fourth to the monks of the Congregation of Vallombrosa. The first two are found in various editions; the others, transcribed by us from a Riccardian manuscript, we now publish for the first time.

In chapter 5 of the first Prolegomenon we said that in the Vallicellian codex containing St Bruno of Segni’s exposition on the Psalms, there is, at the end of the same volume, a little work bearing the name of that holy bishop, entitled: “Questions on the Books of Kings.” [Col. 0040B] We had already learned that, after the anonymous historian of Segni, several writers—namely Jacques Le Long, Calmet, and Mabillon—had called our Bruno the author of those questions; nor were we unaware that the most learned Cardinal Sirleto agreed with them, since in the proper lessons for this saint he listed this little work also among St Bruno’s writings. Nevertheless, because Johannes Herwagen, printer at Basle, attributed these questions to him in the 1563 edition of the works of the Venerable Bede, vol. 7, col. 357, and because no mention of them occurs in the catalogue of writers of St Bruno of Segni which the eminent Borgia—then secretary of the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith—formerly prepared with the utmost diligence from Cassinese codices, we resolved to omit this work. For no reason drawn from similarity of style, like interpretation of the Scriptures, or connection with the other commentaries of the same holy bishop moves us to list this work even among his doubtful writings. [Col. 0040C]

# COMMENTARIES ON THE GOSPELS

[Col. 0039]

# PREFACE OF PIETRO LAZZARI, FORMERLY THEOLOGIAN OF S. [ABBREVIATION AS PRINTED], TO THE COMMENTARIES ON THE FOUR GOSPELS OF ST BRUNO OF ASTI

[Col. 0039]

[Col. 0039D] This city, chief of all cities, which in the common judgment of humankind surpasses others in many most splendid and distinguished respects, I think yields in this respect to no city, however large and richly adorned: it possesses very many well-furnished libraries, especially abundant in manuscript codices. Thus from this literary storehouse many works of Greeks, Latins, and foreign peoples, and especially many writings of the most learned Fathers of the Church, have either emerged into the light and sight of humankind after being saved from destruction, or, after the stains with which they had appeared defiled were removed, have been restored through the efforts of learned men to the splendour and, as it were, native elegance which they possessed from their authors. [Col. 0040D]

I think this may be inferred not only from its larger and more celebrated libraries, praised even by the most expert foreign scholars in these matters—Mabillon, Montfaucon, and others—and whose exceptional distinction in magnificence of building, abundance of books, and excellence of manuscript codices no one of even modest learning fails to know; but especially from certain smaller libraries which have scarcely entered public report or knowledge. So true is this that there is none which cannot offer something rare and excellent, useful to learned people and to the advancement of letters.

If among these latter I name the library of the Roman College, I shall at the same time recall the munificence, foresight, and generosity of Pope Clement XIV of blessed memory. He ordered it to be well and richly equipped, and increasingly enriched with books of every kind, so that this new academy of his for the liberal arts and sciences might not lack that almost indispensable instrument and ornament. From a manuscript of this library there now appears a complete commentary on the four Gospels. Concerning this commentary—its excellence and usefulness, its author, the manuscript from which it is published, and finally the manner and method of publishing it—I have resolved to speak, not so much in the customary fashion of those who set forth such matters as compelled by a certain necessity; and as briefly as I can, lest in the decline of my age I seem either to be seeking a reputation for learning or [Col. 0041B] to have an abundance of leisure.

As for our manuscript—for it is fitting to begin here—it is an oblong parchment folio, of 223 pages if counted, which, apart from the first page, somewhat worn by use and handling, and a few of the final pages, retains all the rest complete and bright, so that it is evident that it has been preserved with the greatest care. Its letters are rather large and so formed that, in the judgment not only of myself but also of the most knowledgeable men of this city who have seen it, they indicate the twelfth century. The scribe must have been both diligent and skilled. For he almost never makes an error; and when he does, another hand, not very different and not much later, is ready to correct the place.

The commentary is prefaced by a prologue of the author himself, in which he explains the method he used in dividing and distributing the commentary into several parts. He divided Matthew into four parts, Luke into two, John into three; he did not divide Mark into parts, evidently because of the commentary’s brevity. Besides these larger parts, the author made other smaller ones, setting forth both their number and the beginning of each in the words of the Evangelists. There are 106 in Matthew, 9 in Mark, 50 in Luke, and 56 in John. [Col. 0041C]

Further, from this division—now to speak of the author—I thought I had attained something on which to base a conjecture about him. It is very well known to learned men that the divisions of the individual books of Scripture made in ancient times were established at each person’s discretion and were not, as now, fixed and uniform divisions displayed by all books. On these many and various divisions the Venerable Cardinal Thomasius wrote excellently in the preface to his work, in which he presented from old codices some of them and their titles; so too did the most learned editor of that most learned and eminent man’s works, Father Vezzosi, recently. Further, Martianay in Prolegomenon 4 to Jerome’s *Bibliotheca*, Joseph Blanchini in Prolegomenon 2 to the *Evangeliarium*, Richard Simon, Book I, chapter 23, and many others, all agree in what we have said concerning the diversity of divisions.

> “I should first wish it observed,” says Martianay, “that the same must be affirmed of the ancient chapters and sections of the sacred books as Jerome and Augustine taught concerning Latin translations of the Scriptures: namely, that there are as many kinds of such divisions or capitulations as there are codices.” [Col. 0041D]

Indeed, the oldest codices themselves bear witness to differing divisions: the Vercelli manuscript attributed to St Eusebius, the Verona, Corbie, Brescia, Clermont, Cividale, Perugia, and the rest which learned and industrious scholars have hitherto presented to us; likewise the single Jerome translation itself, carefully described by Martianay and Vallarsi. Now the aforementioned Cardinal Thomasius says that he was unable to find this varied and uncertain division, made almost at the discretion of the individual writer, later than the eleventh century; and among the latest persons who mention it he names Pope Leo III and Fulbert of Chartres. Since, therefore, it occurs in our codex, the author of the commentary does not seem capable of being placed later than the age I have named.

I pass over the fact that an argument may be drawn from the rigor of public penance, not yet relaxed, from what is found in the commentary on John, no. 14. The argument provided by the age of the codex is entirely certain: the author cannot be later than the eleventh century or the beginning of the twelfth.

But how long before that age he should be placed—that was what caused me great concern and inquiry. The manuscript did indeed bear a magnificent title, clearly indicating a most ancient and eminent author: “Here begins the prologue of St Jerome.” In publishing the commentary we retained it, lest we depart from the testimony of the book. Yet I readily understood that this title was plainly misleading, both from the author’s manner of speech, so very different from Jerome’s, and from the catalogue of that great doctor’s works prepared by the most diligent and skilled scholars, in addition to the one he himself included in his catalogue; and also from Jerome’s genuine commentary on Matthew.

Indeed, once I had set aside the manuscript’s inscription and turned wholly to finding the true author, I understood that he was much later than Jerome. I drew the following argument from this. In commenting on Matthew, no. 86, Luke, no. 46, and elsewhere, he vehemently attacks simoniacs and the vice of simony, plainly showing that this stain had grown very strong in his own age. Now although it is established that it sometimes stained persons of earlier ages, it invaded Italy and other regions especially in the eleventh century; therefore Clement II and Leo IX laboured with the utmost effort to remove it.

> “Concerning those consecrated by simoniacs,” writes Peter Damian in *Opusculum* VII, which he entitled *Gratissimus*, “how much dispute there has already been for three years in three Roman councils, . . . [Col. 0042C] and that it is debated daily in those regions, I do not think has escaped your Holiness.”

For the very sharp question was being debated whether those ordained by simoniacs should be accepted or ordained again. The writers of the *Life of St John Gualbert*, who lived in the same eleventh century and laboured with all possible effort and zeal to eliminate that plague from the regions of Tuscany, also relate this at length. By observing this fact—an observation also used for their own purpose, that is, to establish the date of the writer of the *Life of St Severus*—the Antwerp editors of the *Acts of the Saints*, who continue Bolland’s work, at 1 February, p. 79, seemed to lead me, as it were by the hand, to the eleventh century in identifying the author of the commentary.

To identify the same man, another fact was added which, as it seemed to me, plainly pointed to him. For in several places in this commentary he mentioned certain other works of his own, and stated that he had written on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, and the Apocalypse. Thus, at no. 104 on Matthew [Col. 0042D], explaining the words, “You know that after two days the Passover will take place,” and discussing the rite by which Passover was celebrated, he says: “We have spoken sufficiently of this in Exodus.” Then, at the following no. 105, on the words, “And very early in the morning, while it was still dark,” after introducing the words of Genesis, “And there was evening and there was morning, one day,” and explaining them, he adds: “Although I have explained this differently in Genesis.” Earlier, at no. 24, treating of the leper cleansed by Jesus Christ in Matthew, and mentioning the offerings which those cleansed of leprosy were required to present under the old Law, he writes: “We pass briefly over these matters, of which we have spoken sufficiently in Leviticus.” He also cites this commentary of his on Leviticus in his commentary on Matthew, no. 76, and on Luke, nos. 2 and 9. Why say more? In the opening words of this commentary he expressly declared that he had explained the entire Pentateuch: “After the Pentateuch of Moses, that we might join the new things to the old, obedient to your wish, we have compressed the books of the four Gospels into this single volume by a sufficiently brief and easy exposition.” Likewise, on Luke, no. 14, he says that he is reconsidering what he had written “with insufficient caution on the Apocalypse.”

Now, among later writers, and in the eleventh century with which we are concerned, I find no one who wrote commentaries on these sacred books except Bruno of Asti. The writers of his Life testify that he commented on the entire Pentateuch and on the Apocalypse; and Maurus Marchesius published those commentaries, which were afterward transferred into the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. Thus I had, as it seemed to me, found sufficiently clear evidence and determined who was the author of this commentary, when I happened upon the catalogue of manuscripts in the Turin library. There I found mentioned a commentary on the four Gospels under the name of Bruno of Asti. This would have been little, had not the distinguished editors, in providing a specimen of it, transcribed there its entire preface. Comparing this with the preface of our manuscript, I found them identical [Col. 0043B]; and accordingly the very same commentary which in our manuscript falsely bore the name of Jerome is there ascribed to Bruno.

Yet after discovering that the matter stood thus, I did not regret my labor and conjectures. For who does not know—and our manuscript itself bears witness—how often titles of manuscripts attribute spurious offspring to whatever authors; how often copyists, having found one work inscribed with a given name, adorn the rest with that same name; or, according as any man loves or hates a particular nation, work, or author, add to or remove from a collection every sort of book? Therefore, apart from the authority of the Turin manuscript, our arguments seem fully to establish the author of this commentary.

Nor do I think that I must investigate here the name of Jerome or the manner in which it was imposed on our manuscript. As I was just saying, copyists have always taken this liberty: when manuscripts did not bear an author’s name [Col. 0043C], they attached to them some especially illustrious person, or even exchanged one name for another. Photius long ago noted this practice in codex 48, when speaking of a certain book entitled *On the Universe*, which he had discovered to be by the presbyter Gaius, who had also written a work *On the Labyrinth*. That book, however, bore certain more illustrious names of others:

> “For, he says, since the book had been left without a title, some, they say, inscribed on it the name of Josephus, others that of Justin Martyr, others that of Irenaeus; just as they wrote the name of Origen over *The Labyrinth*.”

Those shrewd and by no means simple people apparently wished to commend their work in copying such books by the name of great authors; or rather, as is truer, by this splendid advertisement—like Lucian’s Mercury—to attract good purchasers. Thus they employed deceptions for profit.

But if I too may indulge in conjecture—for I do not see a more suitable word—I shall say that the whole error arose from confusion of names [Col. 0043D]. Besides our Bruno, there was another fairly celebrated Bruno of Angers, who was also called Eusebius (from the *Chronicles of Angers* in Labbe, vol. I, *Bibliotheca Manuscriptorum*, pp. 276, 282, 287, 388); Jerome also had Eusebius as a forename, as the very title of his works shows. Copyists, moreover, when writing hastily, often used only one name out of an author’s several names. Thus it was easy to substitute Eusebius for Bruno, and Jerome for Eusebius. What of these things would not be possible for an ignorant scribe?

I say “an ignorant scribe,” since Aubertus Miraeus himself, certainly no unlearned man, confused Bruno of Angers—that is, Eusebius—with our Bruno of Asti in this daylight of scholarship, while writing his work on ecclesiastical authors, p. 57; and thereby himself turned Bruno of Asti into Eusebius. Would that this conjecture of mine were true! [Col. 0044A] For otherwise it may be harder to explain why the homilies of Bruno of Asti, which were drawn from this commentary, as we shall say below, were for so long attributed to Eusebius of Emesa. Nothing can seem more credible than that, when little works of our Bruno carried the name of Eusebius, and some moderately learned person wished to determine which of several Eusebii they belonged to, he turned to Eusebius of Emesa, because he knew that Jerome, in the *Catalogue*, chapter 91, and Honorius of Autun after him, testified that Eusebius had “many brief homilies on the Gospels.” But I wish these remarks to be regarded merely as conjectures, so that I shall not strongly oppose those who disagree with or reject them.

To return to Bruno of Asti, the author of this commentary: I do not wish it to be expected of me here that I should set forth in a lengthy discourse what manner and how great a man he was; with what integrity of character, holiness of life, learning, and eloquence; with what offices he served the Church in most difficult times; and with what highest honors and encomiums he was adorned [Col. 0044B]. There are very many who do this and recount his deeds and praises. Magnoald Ziegelbauer listed them in the *History of the Literary Affairs of the Order of St Benedict*, part III, p. 130. Some of them almost reach Bruno’s own age, namely Leo of Ostia and Peter the Deacon; others can be unknown to no one: Baronius’s *Martyrology*, 18 July; Ferdinando Ughelli; Raffaele Soprani; M. A. Scipio; Hippolyte Maracci; Philippe Labbe; Augustine Oldoinus; and Johann Albert Fabricius. Ziegelbauer names them all.

He could, and should, have named still more: above all Baronius’s *Annals* for the years 1104, 1105, 1107, 1108, 1111, and 1116; Pagi for the year 1125, who at no. 14 calls him “most renowned for piety and learning”; Fleury for the year 1079, who calls him “a learned monk.” Besides those he named, he could have cited very many others who surveyed ecclesiastical writers: Possevino, *Apparatus*, vol. I, p. 253; Cave; Oudin; and Combelis, vol. I of the *Bibliotheca Concionatoria*. But who treated our Bruno more fully than Mabillon and Martène, the authors of the *Benedictine Annals*, vols. V and VI, etc., or the Bollandist Sollier for 18 July? I omit other writers of monastic and Benedictine history—Gabriel Bucelin, Arnold Wion, and others. That he was unaware of Count Giovanni Battista Mazzucchelli, a thoroughly careful author who discussed Bruno and his writings most diligently, vol. II, part IV, p. 227 [Col. 0044C], must be attributed to the more recent date of the latter’s work, not to any negligence on Ziegelbauer’s part.

Still, lest I say absolutely nothing about Bruno, I shall cite what Mabillon reduced, as it were, to the briefest summary under the year 1079:

> “He was born in the village of Soleria in the province of Liguria, to parents Andrew and Willa. Educated in the monastery of St Perpetuus in the diocese of Asti, he afterward went to Bologna for the sake of study, then to Siena, where he was admitted among the canons by the bishop and canons of the cathedral church. From there he went to Rome, where Peter Igneus, bishop of Albano, received him as a guest. When that Roman synod was held, he disputed with Alberic against Berengar. Shortly afterward Gregory VII made him bishop of Segni; and finally, having resigned the bishopric, he became a monk of Cassino.”

Mabillon took this from the anonymous author of the *Life*, whom he judged more trustworthy than Peter the Deacon; Sollier likewise judged so, contrary to the opinion of Philip Malabaila. Mabillon reviewed all this under the year 1079. The same authors of the *Benedictine Annals* subsequently relate that Paschal II recalled Bruno from the monastery, sent him to Gaul as legate of the Apostolic See, entrusted him with other legations, and that he died while again governing the church of Segni. They maintain, from the anonymous author of the *Life*, that he died not in 1125, as Ughelli, Angelo de Nuce, Pagi, and others had asserted, but two years earlier [Col. 0045A]. Sollier, Dupin, and the most illustrious Mansi, in his notes on Baronius under the year 1125, agree with him.

Some have asserted that Bruno was admitted to the College of Cardinals, but have produced no adequate witness. I shall produce what is read in Martène’s *Collection of Ancient Monuments*, vol. I, col. 556, in an old charter, where the following names are found subscribed: “Dobertus of Pisa, John of Porto, Bruno, cardinal of Segni.” If this charter may safely be considered trustworthy—and why should it not?—this distinction too should be added to the other praises and honors of our Bruno.

Yet the greatest and most ample ornaments of a man must be judged to be, first, those arising from his pious and holy deeds—of which we have just spoken in Bruno’s case—and then those made up of monuments of learning, produced for the Church’s defense and for the benefit of Christians. We shall now speak of these in our Bruno. Although many have carefully listed and praised his writings—Peter the Deacon, the anonymous author of the *Life*, Dom Aloysius Squadronus, Maurus Marchesius, and above all the most illustrious Mazzucchelli [Col. 0045B]—I shall avoid doing what has already been done and, omitting the rest, linger only over this commentary of ours.

We have already stated that, besides the library of the Roman College from which we publish it, this commentary exists in the royal library at Turin. It is also in the Royal Library at Paris, manuscript 2510, according to the distinguished Mazzucchelli, who lists among Bruno’s works an “Exposition of the Four Gospels.” Jacques Le Long reports that, besides other commentaries of Bruno preserved in the Parisian library of St Victor, there is this one “on the Four Gospels.” Since sermons or homilies of Bruno were excerpted from this commentary, we shall speak of them too. Montfaucon found them in a manuscript in the archive of St Peter’s Basilica and mentions this in the *Bibliotheca bibliothecarum*, p. 156. He also lists some of them in the Royal Library at Paris, p. 748, and in the Ambrosian Library, p. 511. In the manuscripts of the library at Cassino, he likewise lists Bruno’s “homilies on the Gospels for the entire year,” ibid., p. 218, in an eleventh-century manuscript, and again p. 223 in another manuscript of the same library, whose date he does not give [Col. 0045C].

If I say anything too grandly about the excellence and usefulness of this commentary, I fear that I may seem to imitate dealers in wares, who habitually adorn and extol their merchandise in the most magnificent language in order to sell it. Yet I have one whom I may call as guarantor and name as a most illustrious witness to this commentary’s excellence: the most competent judge in these matters, the most illustrious Mansi, formerly archbishop of Lucca. Speaking of the Turin manuscript we mentioned and Bruno’s commentary, in Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, vol. I, p. 288, he says:

> “The most distinguished Joseph Pasini, librarian of that library, long ago informed me by letter that he was considering publishing that work. I beg and earnestly entreat that most learned man, by the common prayer of all scholars, to carry it out” [Col. 0045D].

That learned man, I think, would have been filled with every joy if he could have seen that what he had sought with the highest wishes had been achieved and completed. And when completed, no learned and Christian person ought not greatly to approve the bringing forth and placing in Christians’ hands of the writings of the ancient Fathers—especially those by which the divine books are expounded and, as our author does, human conduct is shaped toward every holiness—so that Christians may profit by them and more ample testimonies to tradition may survive, especially in the books of bishops. For these bear witness not merely to their own faith but to that of the Church over which they preside; and from individual Churches is formed that tradition of the Catholic and universal Church, in which, besides the written word, the other part of the deposit of our faith is contained.

Leaving these considerations aside, this commentary has praises peculiar to itself. No one is ignorant that many commentaries on the Gospels were written by the ancients [Col. 0046A], and that Le Long and others have compiled catalogues of them. Yet I do not hesitate to affirm that ours deserves a place among the more excellent and outstanding. So great, within its extreme brevity, is its wealth of ideas and matter, joined with no ordinary learning; and all of these are employed to form character and teach every holiness of life. Thus anyone may rejoice to possess in this commentary a most skillfully composed summary of Christian doctrine.

Nor does this writer labor to advance novel interpretations or coin new opinions. Rather, plucking, as it were, flowers from the older Fathers—the most approved explanations, instructions, teachings, and sayings—he seems to have wished for nothing other than that the reader of his commentary might have in his own work whatever useful and excellent things are found in all the others. Thus he transfers here what others had noted admirably; he compresses what they had said more fully; or, if things had been set forth somewhat obscurely and briefly, he expands and adorns them. If difficult Gospel passages occur, he not only does not pass them over, but explains them clearly and solidly. Everywhere he establishes harmony among the Evangelists; observes the order of events, whether preserved or neglected by them; interprets Hebrew; compares and expounds passages from other divine books alongside those in hand. In short, you will find nothing lacking in him that is required in a learned and erudite interpreter.

I shall observe only this: although he very often cites passages of the Old and New Testaments, and although it is certain that he consistently follows the Vulgate, he sometimes changes a few words—either because he trusted his memory too much or because, content to convey the sense, he neglected the exact wording. Those somewhat versed in dealing with the Fathers know perfectly well that this is extremely common among other Fathers as well. For as to the distinguished Ansaldus’s different view—that these are the actual readings of different manuscripts—I do not know whether, in his whole book *On the Authentic Readings of Sacred Scripture in the Holy Fathers* [Col. 0046C], he has achieved this or persuaded learned men of it.

There is also a certain exceptional and principal benefit from this commentary: it wholly uproots from men’s minds the opinion, deeply embedded for many ages, that there was an Eusebius of Emesa, a commendable doctor of the Church and a Catholic bishop, to whom many homilies expounding Gospel passages should be attributed. Thus it became necessary to posit two Eusebii of Emesa, both bishops: besides the wicked and ruined Arian, another Eusebius, a Catholic—upright, learned, and a distinguished teacher of piety and every virtue.

When this Catholic Eusebius had long been sought and was not found in all antiquity, there suddenly appeared, as though introduced onto the stage, some Eusebius Gallicanus: a man whom no one had ever seen, whom no one knew by report, and of whose identity or origin there was no one to give an account. Yet this fabulous man was able to creep into the *Bibliotheca Patrum* published at Lyons, vol. VI [Col. 0046D]. Great thanks are indeed owed to Maurus Marchesius, a learned man and monk of Cassino, who, having found those homilies in manuscripts of the Cassinese library under the name of our Bruno, seemed to expose the entire fable and determined that both Eusebii—the Emesan and the Gallican—should be removed from the company of Catholic Fathers.

Still, the matter could not hitherto be said to have been settled. For how often does a manuscript or two mislead by its title? Nor are domestic witnesses easily accepted, even by fair-minded and prudent men. There was this further point: in the homilies themselves something occasionally occurs that could raise suspicion whether some compiler had altered them after their author. For they sometimes stray into matters which in no way belong to that day’s Gospel reading; and passages that follow in the Evangelist’s text, and were not read in church that day, are appended. Now the matter must plainly be regarded as examined and known, since it clearly appears whence the homilies arose; and, besides the Cassinese manuscripts, all the surviving distinguished and approved manuscript copies of these commentaries attribute them to Bruno: the Parisian manuscripts, the Turin manuscript, and the Roman manuscript [Col. 0047A].

I do not mean the statement I made—that the homilies were drawn from this commentary—to be understood so absolutely as if the commentary contained nothing more than those homilies. Even if this were so, the labor and effort of publishing it could certainly not be rejected. For, as I have said, it would provide a sufficiently clear and manifest argument establishing the author of the homilies; and the whole text of the commentary, arranged in Gospel order, would bring a greater light and usefulness to readers of the sacred books, whereas the homilies present matters in a disjoined and disordered form, according to the days on which they are read in church.

But anyone who formed the opinion that one and the same work, now published under the title *Commentary*, had previously been issued under the title *Homilies*, would be greatly mistaken [Col. 0047B]. A substantial part of the commentary was indeed made into and transferred into homilies, according as that part of the Gospel was customarily read in churches. But besides the fact that certain things are absent from the commentary which are added in the homilies either for a kind of suitability or to accommodate the understanding of the common hearers, the commentary abounds in very many matters—that is, explanations of the Gospels—which found no place in ecclesiastical readings.

But there is no need to pursue this at greater length. Every portion of the commentary transferred into homilies has been marked, to alert the reader; and many such portions will be found without this marking. Moreover, after the author had written and completed the commentary, he himself bears witness that he excerpted his homilies from it. In the homily “For the First Sunday after Epiphany,” on the words, “And on the third day a marriage took place at Cana of Galilee,” when he wished to explain the preceding words, he says: “The Evangelist relates that they occurred on the third day. How this is to be understood literally, we have explained in that commentary from which these things have been taken” [Col. 0047C].

Nor was this the first time an author had done this, nor is it a novelty that those who delivered sermons to the people borrowed them from other works of their own. Those who observe that in Augustine and other Fathers many parts of homilies consist of the same ideas and even the very same words found in their other, more carefully elaborated works will readily be convinced. We must suppose that they did this either to spare themselves a labor not at all necessary; because they doubted whether those things could be said more appropriately than they had already been; or because of the frequency of these homilies and sermons, which left no time for meditation and reflection.

Since others have discussed this frequency of preaching at length—especially Bernardino Ferrario, *On the Rite of Sacred Preaching*, chapter 18, and the author of *Ecclesiastical Origins*, a heterodox but indeed very learned man, vol. VI, book XIV, chapter 4, §§6, 7, etc.—I need not treat it here [Col. 0047D]. In more ancient times this was less necessary, when authors either read out to the people their commentaries on the divine books and their *Tractates*—whence sermons bear the name *Tractates*, and their deliverers that of *Tractators*—or recited their writings from memory. The learned men just praised have shown that this was done in both ways.

In later ages, however, it became necessary for bishops to draw up their homilies from commentaries already composed, perhaps also set aside for this purpose, and to employ labors worked out in vigil for extemporaneous delivery. If they were not the sort who could use their own material, they called in the help of other learned or less occupied men. Hence Gennadius’s statement in chapter 57 of *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers* concerning Cyril: “Cyril, bishop of the church of Alexandria, composed many homilies, which Greek bishops commit to memory for delivery.” They also mention Salvian in chapter 67: “He composed many homilies for bishops”; and Honorius, in *On the Luminaries of the Church*, chapter 67, has nearly the same words. That an address was written by Isidore of Pelusium but delivered by Dorotheus is established by book VII, letter 382 of the former [Col. 0048A].

Sirmond likewise observed this concerning Ennodius: namely, that he wrote what Honoratus, bishop of Novara, was to say; and composed another speech and gave it to the vicar Stephen to deliver before Bishop Maximus. Hence the titles of these compositions: “Address sent to Honoratus, bishop of Novara, for the dedication of the Basilica of the Apostles”; “Address given to Stephen, vicar of distinguished rank, to be delivered before Bishop Maximus.”

Since learned men whose work could be used were not available everywhere or at every time, recourse had to be had to published works of the ancients. These were often interpolated, as though with patches sewn on from the books of various writers, or with something inserted from the compiler himself. Thus good works were often made worse: parts badly joined, with an uneven style and ideas insufficiently fitted together. Hence arose that infinite crop—I had almost said cesspool—of sermons which reflects the style of no ancient author, yet contains much from the sayings and opinions of the ancients. This gave recent critics abundant material for investigating to whom a particular sermon should chiefly be assigned, and produced remarkable disagreement and contention in identifying authors. It is enough to take in hand the so-called Appendix of Augustinian sermons to see my point more than sufficiently demonstrated [Col. 0048B].

Those who wished to extract what they would say from a single author certainly consulted their own convenience, and also the works of the ancients, better. Hence those Ambrosian sermons which, if we heed their Maurist editor, were never delivered by Ambrose, though all were compiled from Ambrose’s works. So too are other works by other men, made in the same fashion, which present a kind of mosaic work from an earlier writer—whom we may readily judge never to have spoken to the people, and, had he spoken, never to have spoken in this patchwork of material and words.

A remedy for this inconvenience was sought and supplied in the discovery and compilation of what are called Homiliaries: books containing the most excellent sermons of the ancients, distributed among the feast days and solemn days of the year. We now possess the most widely published and best-known Homiliary bearing the name of Paul the Deacon, with Paul’s prefixed letter. From this it is clear that the work was completed—or, as I think, restored and renewed—at the command of Charlemagne. For it is wholly certain from manuscripts older than Paul that a Homiliary existed before him; Montfaucon saw and catalogued one of these, older than Paul, in the Cassinese library in his *Bibliotheca bibliothecarum*. Nor should we doubt that manuscripts preserving it exist elsewhere.

Indeed, I myself saw one such manuscript, and had it in my possession to inspect and handle at will, from the exceedingly rich and choice library of the most eminent Cardinal Francesco Saverio de Zelada—such is his kindness, generosity, and liberality toward students of letters [Col. 0048D]. A most certain indication of its earlier date is that the cycle of the year begins not, as in Paul’s Homiliary and later ecclesiastical books, with the First Sunday of Advent, but with the very day of Christ’s birth, as we see in the Gelasian Sacramentary and other earlier books. Yet it has the same blemish as Paul’s Homiliary: it inscribes under the Fathers’ names homilies which are not theirs and which, in the appendices to the Fathers, are rejected by learned critics.

From this book and from Paul’s Homiliary we gain help in confirming what has been said: we see that sermons were excerpted from the Fathers’ own commentaries and even from their letters, so that on each solemn day something might either be delivered by bishops or read aloud to the people. We return to our Bruno [Col. 0049A], and say that no one should be surprised that he transcribed homilies from his commentaries, often without changing a word, so that a large part of the work could be presented in both forms, under the name both of homilies and of commentary—and has been so presented by me.

And thus far it was necessary to speak at some length of the excellence of our Commentary, so that all might understand what sort of work it is. Yet I have not covered everything. For there will certainly be those who think it should be faulted because it contains a great number of allegorical and mystical interpretations and explanations: nearly all, or almost all, are referred to the immortal life to come; to the Church of Christians and the ancient Synagogue of the Jewish people; to bishops, the rulers of churches; to vices which must be condemned, and virtues and chaste morals which must be praised. Thus, as it were, the author seems to dwell in these matters, while scarcely lodging in the so-called literal sense in explaining them. But first, as I have said, Bruno does indeed explain such a literal sense—when [Col. 0049B] it is not so plain and manifest that listeners can understand it without anyone teaching them—and he does so very clearly.

Then those who think that the other explanations, which do not seem intended by the Holy Spirit but drawn, as it were, by those authors from their own storehouse, must be condemned and rejected, ought to consider what they disapprove and whom they take as authors to be condemned and repudiated. For these same explanations occur most frequently in the writings of the Fathers; so that, if you wished to remove them from their writings, works of this kind would almost entirely perish. Nor do I mean only Gregory or Bede, who are known to take the greatest delight in such things; or, among the earlier writers, Origen, whom we know to have borne the charge of excessive frequency in allegories and of neglecting the literal sense; but I mean those ancient Fathers approved and highly praised by the judgment and voices of all—Hilary, Ambrose, Jerome, Chrysostom, Augustine. How often they pursue such interpretations in commentaries on the divine books, [Col. 0049C] I think will easily be evident to anyone from several notes which I have appended.

But I must explain why they did so, since I do not know whether anyone has set it forth clearly and weightily. The first reason is readily conceived: that they might season, with a certain not ungenerous savor, moral precepts which seemed harsh to refined persons unaccustomed to evangelical teaching. They imitated nurses, concerning whom that ancient poet aptly observed that, when they administer something bitter to children, they usually smear honey around the rim of the cup, so that, deceived by this kind of trick, they may not unwillingly swallow what they would otherwise refuse.

But there is, further, another and deeper reason arising from ancient Christian institutions; from these, I believe, that great abundance of allegorical and mystical explanations flowed altogether into the writings of the Fathers. From the earliest times Christians had so great a love and devotion toward the divine books that, in order to keep them away from secular writings, especially those of the pagans, the ancient teachers diligently fostered this devotion [Col. 0049D]: Christians were to wish to read, hear, and learn almost those books alone, while almost rejecting and despising all others. Hence the schools to which young people were sent for education resounded with nothing other than the divine books and their exposition.

Eusebius testifies to this concerning the ancient and celebrated school of Alexandria, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, chapter 10, writing:

> “At the same time, the school of the faithful was governed by a man exceedingly renowned for learning, named Pantaenus. For from ancient times a school of sacred letters had been established in that city; it still continues even in our own age, and is said to be held by men most thoroughly equipped both in eloquence and in devotion to the divine writings.”

Traces of those most ancient schools and teachers of this kind are found in the offices which Codinus Curopalates records in the Church of Constantinople in later ages: “The Quinary I, teacher of the Psalter; teacher of the Gospel; teacher of the Apostle.” Nor can we doubt that there were also schools established at Rome in the Lateran Patriarchate; this may readily be inferred from Anastasius’s accounts of the deeds of the popes.

But if you do not wish to interpret the offices said to exist at Constantinople as referring to schools, but, with Gretser, to addresses delivered to the people and to the office which he calls that of the “preacher,” I have no objection. For that is precisely my point. If Christians were taught nothing in schools except sacred and divine writings, neither ought anything else to have been heard in churches and their sacred assemblies from bishops or other members of the clergy who spoke there. “From this,” writes the learned Jacques Goar on that passage of Codinus, “you perceive why certain homilies of the holy Fathers are on the Gospels, others on the Psalms, and some on the Apostle.” Add others on Genesis, on the entire Pentateuch, and on the prophetic books, such as the homilies and treatises still extant in the works of Basil, Chrysostom, Gregory of Nyssa, and Augustine. For, as we indicated above, Augustine expressly writes in Epistle 224, calling them his “popular treatises,” [Col. 0050B] “which,” he says, “the Greeks call *homilies*.”

Since, therefore, Christian orators for many centuries followed the practice that their sermons, homilies, or treatises should almost all be occupied with the exposition of sacred books, and since they had to address artisans and other people drawn from the dregs of the populace, what, I ask, had to be done in order that such hearers might attend to the speaker, gain some benefit, and not, wearied by boredom, abandon him while he was speaking, except to descend to those exhortations (*paræneses*) which everyone could understand, and to seek these most fitting byways of allegorical and mystical interpretation for shaping morals, censuring vices, and instilling the love of virtues—which was their chief aim?

They would surely have found their hearers drowsy if, while interpreting the days in which Moses teaches that the world was created, or Isaiah, or any one of the prophets, they had cut the matter to the quick, as learned commentators now do. Even many of these, lest their books [Col. 0050C] be neglected, we see frequently intermixing and connecting those very same things.

Gregory of Nyssa begins excellently in his *Hexaemeron*, replying to those who blamed his brother Basil because he had passed over certain lofty matters:

> “These men, it seems to me, do not consider the end proposed by our Father in his teaching, who, speaking in a most crowded church to a very numerous people, adapted his discourse to his hearers’ understanding. For in such a great multitude, although some might have understood even more elevated discussions, the greater number could not grasp the subtlety of the teaching: they were uneducated persons, artisans, people occupied in humble trades, women scarcely trained in disciplines of this kind, a crowd of children, and old men advanced in years. All these had to be instructed and refreshed by an easy discourse.”

It must nevertheless be admitted that this was done not only for the sake of the less educated, but also for the learned—for men plainly scholarly and intellectually gifted. Such matters, if executed with judgment and a certain elegant subtlety, are not usually displeasing to them; indeed, they are greatly and vehemently approved. For that which is the greatest work of ingenuity affords great delight: things which seem far apart and wholly different from one another are brought closer together, and the connection between them which we had not seen is taught and shown. This is precisely what happens in those mystical and allegorical interpretations—that is, in fitting and adapting things wholly diverse and remote to passages of sacred Scripture.

Bruno appears to have addressed such gifted and learned persons, who delighted in these things, in his Commentary on John, no. 5—that is, in the homily for the First Sunday after Epiphany. There, explaining the Gospel account of water changed into wine and offered to the steward, who judged it the very best, and allegorically interpreting the steward as understanding, he adds:

> “The ministers of the holy Scriptures daily offer wine to this Church; and, drinking it, he admires and praises it, although he does not know whence it comes. For when these things are recited here in the churches, they have savor for none but those who understand them. Therefore the Lord rightly commanded that this wine be brought to the steward, so that we too may give wine to those who understand greater things, but offer water to those who do not understand. For those who understand well venerate both the letter and the spirit. . . . But those of lesser understanding should drink water and hear the plainest parts of the Scriptures.”

Thus Bruno here calls “gifted and learned persons” those whom he describes as understanding greater things—or rather, those accustomed to the contemplation of divine matters and skilled in the spirit of things, who take delight in these mystical interpretations. Others, even if gifted and learned, do not do so; of the latter the Apostle also says: “The carnal man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit.” From this it follows that our author can be blamed for the multitude and frequency of allegorical and mystical interpretations only unjustly.

[Col. 0051B] It remains for me to speak of the edition of this Commentary. For it is not our business to discuss editions of our author’s other works; moreover, what could be said has been dealt with by learned men, above all by the celebrated Mazzucchelli in every detail—except perhaps one thing which they seem to have passed over: the fifty-six homilies, different from ours, which were nevertheless first published under the name of Eusebius of Emesa at Paris in 1547, by Nicolas Le Riche, through the efforts of the theologian Jean Gagné. In that edition the bookseller addresses the reader:

> “Lest you think that a deception is being practiced upon you,” etc.;

and at the end:

> “Meanwhile, excellent reader, enjoy this distinguished gift of Master Jean Gagné, and wish him well.”

To this letter is appended what Trithemius says about Eusebius of Emesa.

I have noted these matters concerning that edition because Casimir Oudin, an apostate, who boasts that he has seen nearly everything, had not seen it; he consequently confused many things and sought to correct several matters wholly free from any error, while meanwhile writing much himself that deserved rebuke. In particular, in volume I, column 394, he wrote that Jean Gagné published these homilies under Eusebius of Emesa’s name in 1575, and acknowledged no earlier edition of them. For how could he have been ignorant of the edition which he himself had caused to be made with such care and diligence nearly thirty years earlier? So prudent, cautious, and attentive to everything must a person be who undertakes to criticize and condemn any learned man.

Now, to speak of the edition of this our Commentary: [Col. 0052A] if I had transcribed it from some manuscript mentioned above with the utmost fidelity and diligence, had published that transcription, and had merely noted, as I did, the age of the manuscript and the place where it was preserved, adding nothing else—what could have made me seem worthy of blame, or what further could rightly have been demanded of me? For I see that this, and nothing else, has been done by eminent men who have labored, and still labor, in this field of study to the great praise of the learned.

Yet I shall say what I think. Although I should have spared my own effort and labor by that method, I should never have been fully satisfied with myself, nor should I have thought that the author’s reputation or the reader’s benefit had been sufficiently provided for in the case of a writer who frequently pursues the explanations I have mentioned and occasionally offers some which seem new and unfamiliar to the ears of most people. He might therefore easily be thought to depart from the straight line and to indulge his own ingenuity too much; but the truth is far otherwise. For the author draws almost none of these explanations which he has not borrowed from the caskets of earlier writers, in which they lay stored away, and he has preferred always to follow the footsteps and, as it were, the track of the more celebrated ancient commentators.

Accordingly, I undertook the task of revealing the sources from which he drew them and of transcribing, or at least indicating, similar passages from older interpreters. This can contribute to Bruno’s praise: he has brought almost nothing to the interpretation of the Gospels which was not drawn from the treasure-chambers of the most approved Fathers. It can also bring benefit and delight to the studious reader, who may recognize and possess in one writer the thoughts and painstaking labors of many earlier authors. How much this has cost, I prefer to leave to the judgment of others rather than explain by recounting it.

It remains that, if the reader recognizes anything appropriately noted by me; if in these most excellent and holy studies he derives some benefit; if he judges that in editing this Commentary I have devoted effort neither useless nor fruitless; and that some progress has been made in explaining the Gospel books for the nurturing of piety and for knowing and preserving Christian discipline—then thanks are owed to the most deserving Cardinal Francesco Saverio de Zelada, through whom it was brought about that this book should not lie longer hidden in darkness and in the shelves of this library’s Athenaeum, and that it should be printed in most elegant type, with no expense spared.

[Col. 0051]

## APPENDIX

[Col. 0051]

[Col. 0051D] In the Florentine literary folio entitled *Annali Ecclesiastici*, dated 20 May of the year just past, there appeared a certain review, written courteously and mildly, concerning grace and free will. These were matters which I treated in the third prolegomenon to the works of St Bruno of Asti, whose first volume I had published in that same year. That its authors treated me with much civility and commended my edition, I attribute to their affection: they still remember, perhaps, how each year I spent my efforts in forming Florentine youth in piety and letters, and how I published several small works, favorably received, on theological matters themselves. Since I value highly this expression of benevolent feeling, and render them very many thanks, I ask them to receive kindly some observations upon the doubts and objections proposed to me. It was not the heat of controversy, but love of truth, that led me to write them.

In the first place, my reviewers wish that, when on [Col. 0052D] page XXXV (column 58) I defined free will after Adam’s sin as “the faculty of active indifference which can turn itself, wherever it wills, to either side,” I had instead said that it is “a faculty for opposites.”

**Reply 1.** According to some, such as Bartholomew Camerarius, the faculty or indifference toward opposites is not necessary to constitute free will; rather, human beings are sufficiently constituted free by the freedom they enjoy in choosing their actions. Other theologians have also chosen to define free will as “an active faculty for opposites, determining itself by the judgment of reason”; these words amount to my definition. See Ludwig Habert, *On Grace and Free Will*, p. 21. Free will has also been defined as “the power to act from the knowledge of the intellect.” See vol. II of the *Complexus Augustinianus*, Book III, chapter 3, p. 497.

**Reply 2.** I preferred my definition to the others because it appeared to me more plainly consonant with the Church’s teaching. For it rests upon Canons 5 and 6 of Session VI of the Council of Trent, which read as follows:

> “If anyone says that, after Adam’s sin, the free will of man was lost and extinguished, or that it is a thing of mere title—indeed, a title without a reality, finally a fiction introduced into the Church by Satan—let him be anathema.”

The other says:

> “If anyone says that it is not in man’s power to make his ways evil, but that God works evil deeds in the same way as good ones—not merely permissively but of himself—so that Judas’s betrayal is no less his proper work than Paul’s calling—let him be anathema.”

When, therefore, I said that free will is a faculty of active indifference, I intended to counter the error of the Lutherans, who teach that, after Adam’s sin, human will is deprived of every action proper to itself and is wholly passive. And when I added that it “can turn itself, wherever it wills, to either side,” I considered it necessary to refute the blasphemy of those same heretics, who make God the author of sin and, by taking liberty away from man, deny him the capacity of deserving and of incurring demerit. It is also against Proposition 27 of Michael Baius, condemned by Gregory XIII: “Free will without the aid of God’s grace avails for nothing except sinning”; and against other similar propositions of Quesnel.

To remove the confusion, noted by the reviewers on page 446, between the different wording in the cited exposition of St Bruno on Psalm LXIX and the wording found in the aforementioned prolegomenon, read *mala* (“evils”) for *male* (“badly”); it is a typographical error.

Their second objection is that, on page XXXVII (column 61), I misuse Bruno’s authority, since I have attributed to him the doctrine of sufficient grace.

**Reply.** My reviewers are not ignorant that more obscure or insufficiently explicit passages of the holy Fathers are to be understood according to other passages expressed in clearer and more explicit words. Therefore, even if I grant that St Bruno, in that Commentary on the words of Psalm CXVIII, “Help me, and I shall be safe,” illustrated by these words, “It is God who works in us both willing and being able, and without his help we can do nothing,” has not opened his mind sufficiently for us to understand that by *being able* he teaches sufficient grace, and by *willing* efficacious grace, with reference to the Apostle’s statement, “It is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish” (Philippians 2:13), still, since the same holy doctor elsewhere admitted sufficient grace more clearly, I could indeed know his mind on this matter in the passage previously cited, which can without contradiction be understood of sufficient grace.

For in the same Commentary on Psalms XXII and XLIII, although he does not expressly call it sufficient grace, he nevertheless describes its effect, which is to move and prepare the will toward the good; just as in these and other places he discusses helping and following grace. But I ask the reviewers: what kind of grace does that grace appear to them to be which our commentator, on Psalm LXVII, designated under the allegorical name of voluntary and unforced rain, and of which he said that it is freely given and freely received, but which the Jews refused to receive? It was certainly not efficacious grace, for by its powerful help they would have been converted. Therefore it must be called sufficient grace. “Because the Jews would not receive it,” says St Bruno, “God set it apart for his inheritance.”

> [Note: [Col. 0053D] What St Bruno only briefly indicated here concerning the Jews, he expounded more fully in the Commentary on John, chapter XV, under no. 44: “Christ came to them, spoke to them, opened the Scriptures, revealed the truth, and performed many signs and unheard-of miracles. Yet they would not believe him. Therefore they have no excuse,” etc.]

Moreover, in the Commentary on Psalm LXIX he acknowledges that God provides great assistance to those who resist evil desires, and promises them greater help lest they fall. Therefore he understood that slight assistance is given to those who do not resist temptations and act wrongly.

I readily admit that more recent theologians spoke more explicitly about sufficient grace and explained what is understood by the word *being able*. Let them hear the most learned Thomas Lemos, renowned in the Congregation *de Auxiliis*, who writes as follows in volume IV of the *Panoplia*, Part II, Treatise 3, p. 6:

> “Theologians call that help sufficient, not through which so great an influence is given as is required for the action to occur, but that which gives sufficiency and the possibility of acting well, if one wills—as has often been said from St Augustine—even though, in order that one should will in fact, another and more powerful help is required. Therefore it does not belong to the nature of sufficient help that through it so great an influence be given as is required for the action to occur; for this help belongs to efficacious grace.”

> [Note: [Col. 0053D] “For there are two things, willing and being able. Thus one who wills is not always at once able, nor is one who is able always at once willing. For just as we sometimes cannot do what we will, so we are also sometimes able to do what we do not will. The terms themselves sufficiently echo this: from *willing* comes the name *will*, and from *being able* the name *power*.” After some further words, the holy doctor concludes: “What more do we seek, then, since we call this power the condition in which the ability to act is at hand for the will? Hence each person is said to have in his power that which, if he wills, he does, and, if he does not will, he does not do.” *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 31. Likewise, *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 25: “For God has not only bestowed and helps our ability, but also works willing and working in us.”]

Let them also hear the distinguished Cardinal Lorenzo Lauria, who, discussing actual graces in Opuscule III and accepting the theologians’ distinction of actual grace, teaches:

> “When God, in his goodness, comes before someone—whether by stirring, enlightening, and inspiring an unbeliever to come to faith; or a fallen believer to come to repentance; or a just believer to perform works of precept or counsel—one thing is the passive stirring, enlightenment, and inspiration themselves, which God alone causes in us without us. These are received in the intellect and will; these effects are always produced by God alone; and thus the stirring grace, with respect to its effects of enlightening and stirring, is always efficacious. But another thing that must be observed is the very work concerning which the stirring, enlightenment, or inspiration occurs: in the examples proposed, faith for the unbeliever; repentance for the baptized sinner; and observance of precept or counsel for the just believer. I call these the principal works, because the stirrings are ordered toward them. But these works are not [Col. 0054C] always brought into existence by those who are stirred.”

To these I add the most learned Berti, who sets forth the same doctrine in the *Vindiciae*, Dissertation XII, chapter 2, §2, p. 215, and Book XIV, chapter 8:

> “Thus, in the Thomist sense and in ours, sufficient grace is that which gives the ability but not the willing.”

And below:
