> “We admit that through sufficient grace there is given to us a true and proper power to fulfill the divine commandments; but it is not so strong and ready that efficacious grace is not necessary for the act actually to be performed.”

Again, in Book XVII, chapter 3, he says:

> “Augustine acknowledges in this state not only help by which, but also help without which—that is, purely sufficient help.”

Let my reviewers see chapter 3, “On the Efficacy of Grace and Sufficient Grace,” in the *Expostulation against the Judgment of the Most Reverend Languet, Archbishop of Sens*, published at Livorno in 1756, p. 59 ff.

Since it was most deeply in Augustine’s heart to reconcile God’s gratuitous grace with human free will, and since, by investigating this mystery, he learned that God does not act with human beings in the same manner at all times, but sometimes converts them through external motions and at other times through internal impulses:

> [Note: [Col. 0054D] On the words of John 6, “No one can come to me unless he who sent me draws him,” St Augustine, after some preliminary remarks, says: “Therefore a person is drawn in marvelous ways so as to will by him who knows how to work inwardly in the very hearts of human beings—not so that human beings, which is impossible, believe unwillingly, but so that from unwilling persons they become willing.” *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 19.]

He also discovered the wonderful wisdom of God, by which, having compassion on human weakness, God assists free will by the gratuitous bounty of grace. For God admonishes through hearing the evangelical law, through the examples of believers, through wonders, and through other external gifts. These have more or less force for moving the will, together with inward calling, delight in the commandment, and desire to acquire righteousness; and these are works of God’s acting grace. Whenever, therefore, external persuasions are given and the will, by God’s help, inclines toward them, a disposition toward good then arises in it. If a greater impulse and divine force comes upon it, the will deliberately cleaves to virtue and consents to righteousness. So St Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 34.

The Fathers of Trent seem to have had this teaching before their eyes when, in chapter 6, *On Justification*, they declared that through divine motions of this kind human beings are disposed toward righteousness:

> “They are disposed toward righteousness when, stirred and assisted by divine grace, they conceive faith from hearing and freely move toward God, believing true what has been divinely revealed and promised.”

What, then, prevents us from calling that stirring grace sufficient, or slight, or weak—namely, grace not yet brought to its full effect? The holy doctor discusses both kinds in *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 17. In the martyrs he presents for admiration a strong and great good will, since they gave their lives for Christ, than which love no one can have greater. But he supplies an example of the other kind—of small love, or weak good will—in Peter:

> “The Apostle Peter himself did not yet have that love when, through fear, he denied the Lord three times. For fear is not in love, as John says in his epistle; but perfect love casts out fear. Yet then, though small and imperfect, it was not absent when he said to the Lord, ‘I will lay down my life for you’; for he thought himself able to do what he felt himself willing to do. And who had begun to give him that small love except he who prepares the will and, by cooperating, completes what he begins by working? For he works in us when beginning, that we may will; and, when we will, he cooperates in bringing it to completion.”

Augustine, therefore, recognized in Peter a slight impulse—that is, small grace—when Peter said, “I will lay down my life for you”; nevertheless, it was a good impulse, by which he declared that he would lay down his life for the Lord. But in order actually to lay it down, he did not yet possess great and strong grace.

Therefore the doctrine of sufficient grace remains unshaken among us. We call it a pious motion or affection inspired in human beings, through which they are granted not the execution of the whole work, but a true power—although not so ready as actually to advance to the final act. This comes not from a defect in grace, but from human will itself setting an obstacle against grace. “For,” said the Apostle, “the good which I will, I do not do; but the evil which I do not will, that I do” (Romans 7:19); and he gives the reason from the opposition of the lower part, or perverse concupiscence.

Knowledge of the commandment itself ought to kindle in the righteous the desire to fulfill it; recognizing their own weakness, they are moved by that consideration to implore the help of almighty God.

> [Note: [Col. 0055D] “But when we ask him for his help in doing and completing righteousness, what else do we ask than that he open what was hidden and that what was not pleasing become sweet? For from him this must be asked, by whose grace we have learned; when it was hidden, and by whose grace we have loved, when it was not previously pleasing.” St Augustine, Book II, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 19.]

But if, overcome by sloth or evil desire, they neglect to pray to God, they should blame themselves if, by resisting that small grace, they render it useless and ineffectual. Moreover, whatever grace is given—whether small or weak, in the sense explained—we call it Christ’s grace, and we say that even the smallest grace can resist any concupiscence.

We also acknowledge that no grace, whether small or great, proposes truth to the intellect and good to the will in such a way as to remove the freedom of indifference in judgment and irresistibly compel assent. This is against the second proposition of Jansenius, condemned by Innocent X: “In the state of fallen nature, inward grace is never resisted.” It is also against Quesnel’s propositions 2, 10, 11, 12, and 13, proscribed by Clement XI, all of which affirm that under grace a human being has no liberty and deny that human will can resist it.

The third objection is stated thus: “If the power of acting well were not natural to man, free will would be extinguished.”

**Reply.** I think my reviewers did not speak of the natural power of man with respect to supernatural goods. But because their proposition appears ambiguous, I should like everyone to note that Pelagius’s error was this: that free will does not exist if it needs God’s help, since each person has it within his own will either to do something or not to do it; and that our victory comes not from God’s help but from free will.

Permit me, therefore, to remind them how the holy doctor assailed this heretic in his delusion:

> “What is it,” he says in Book I *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 2, “that this man wishes to attribute to free will—the power of living well—when power is given only by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord? For the Gospel says: ‘But to as many as received him, he gave power to become children of God.’”

He confirms the same in chapter 3 of that book:

> “Unless this power is given by God, it can be nothing from free will; for it will not be free for good unless the Liberator has freed it. But for evil it has free will, when either manifest error has implanted delight in wickedness or it has persuaded itself.”

The same doctrine is further confirmed from another passage of St Augustine, where he reproaches Pelagius because, while striving to exalt the soundness of nature, he detracts from and altogether empties the benefit of grace:

> “In thinking that he is defending God’s grace,” says the holy doctor in *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 33, no. 39, “by defending nature, he does not notice that, in saying that this nature is sound, he rejects the physician’s mercy. We must not therefore praise the Creator in such a way that we are compelled—indeed, convicted—of calling the Savior superfluous.”

Nor, indeed, do we derogate from free will because we refer the human capacity to act well to the restoring grace of Christ. Whatever belongs to the beginning and whatever belongs to the continuation of faith is wholly God’s; for the human being, moved by God, does everything, not by the powers of nature but by the powers of grace, without which he can do no supernatural good. The Fathers of Trent established such teaching as a dogma of faith in Session VI, chapter 5, so that no Catholic may lawfully dissent from it.

> [Note: [Col. 0056D] On the Apostle’s words in Romans 9:16, “It is not of one who wills or runs, but of God who has mercy,” St Augustine adds in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 12: “Human will alone is not sufficient unless God’s mercy is also present.” We do not deny free will deprived of grace, but we do not call it good, as St Fulgentius explains in the synodal letter of the bishops of Africa, §5: “Before the bounty of grace, free will indeed exists in man, but it is not good, because it is not enlightened. Therefore, unless grace is given, good free will itself is not possessed. For human will without the gift of grace is like an eye without light.”]

Against Pfaff, who makes free will act lifelessly under the motion of grace, the distinguished Father Georgius has recently written most learnedly in his exposition of the third Coptic fragment, written in [Col. 0056D] Coptic characters, chapter VI of the Gospel of St John, p. 90.

By the beginning of faith we mean the first dispositions which arise from fear, hope, or initial love; and we affirm that these proceed not from the powers of human will but from the powers of heavenly grace. So far are they from doing violence to liberty that they wonderfully assist liberty itself. Certainly nothing is freer than that which proceeds from the very source of freedom.

[Col. 0057A] In the fourth place, the Florentine reviewers censure the doctrine of grace drawn from Bruno, because in establishing the necessity of grace for every good work of the supernatural order, I seemed to them not to differ from the Pelagians, who admitted a certain general grace; and because St Augustine, they say, attacked them for this error in more than one place.

The reply: The Pelagian heresy had two stages, as Natalis Alexander demonstrates, vol. V of his *Ecclesiastical History*, fifth century, art. 3. At first Pelagius was entirely devoted to praising human nature; he wrote a book in its praise and said that its powers were sufficient for fulfilling all the divine commandments. “Who created man?” he used to say. “God. Who gave him free will? God. Therefore, if God created man and gave man free will, whatever man can do by free will—to whose grace is it due, if not to His who made him with free will?” Thus St Augustine, *Sermon II on the Words of the Apostle*, ch. 7. This [Col. 0057B] is, according to Pelagius, that grace given commonly to all, which the holy Doctor attacked; and he showed that Pelagius did indeed admit a common grace in the gift of nature, but not the grace of Christ. Therefore, when Pelagius had been attacked by Augustine in *On Nature and Grace*, and heard on every side the outcry of Christians that he was leaving man to the powers of nature alone, he said that man had the assistance of another grace, namely one located in the law and doctrine, and also in Christ’s example.

> [Note: [Col. 0058D] “But as to this possibility which Pelagius acknowledges is assisted by the grace of God, it is not clear here either what grace he means, or in what respect he thinks that nature is assisted by it. Yet, as may be understood from other places where he speaks more plainly, he wishes nothing else to be understood than law and doctrine, by which natural possibility is assisted.” St Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ*, ch. 7.]

Although Pelagius granted this kind of grace, he nevertheless did not depart from his earlier doctrine or manner of speaking, but always displayed nature as though it were a sufficient cause of human merit. In order, however, that St Augustine might expose and refute the deceitful heretic’s design of misleading others, he stated Catholic truth in plain words in *On the Grace of Christ*, ch. 10: “But we,” he says, “want him at last to acknowledge that grace by which the greatness of future glory is not merely promised but also hoped for; by which wisdom is not merely [Col. 0057C] revealed but also loved; not merely recommended, etc. … Pelagius must confess this if he wishes not merely to be called, but actually to be, a Christian.” He repeats this in ch. 13, where he discusses the excellence of Christ’s grace: “If this grace,” he says, “is to be called doctrine, it must certainly be called so in such a way that God is believed to pour it in more deeply and more intently, with ineffable sweetness—not only through those who water externally, but also through Him who, hidden, supplies His increase—so that He not merely shows truth, but also imparts love.”

Again, when the Pelagians devised another means of concealing their error, saying that human nature, created by God, is assisted by Him in doing righteousness, and that this assistance is at hand for all, the same St Augustine refutes them, emphatically declaring in *On the Spirit and the Letter*, ch. 3, that God’s assistance must be internal rather than external. “But we say that the will is divinely assisted in doing righteousness, so that, beyond the fact that man was created with free choice [Col. 0057D] of will, and beyond the doctrine by which he is instructed how he ought to live, he receives the Holy Spirit, through whom there comes to be in his mind delight and love of that supreme and unchangeable good.”

Nor should another splendid passage of the holy Doctor from ch. 19 of the same work be omitted. “Therefore,” he says, “let none of the Christians depart from this faith, which alone is Christian; nor, when anyone has been rebuked for saying that we are made righteous through ourselves rather than through God’s grace working within us—since he sees that believers and pious persons cannot do this—let him turn to this and say that we cannot be righteous without God’s operation because He gave the law, established doctrine, and commanded good precepts. For without the assisting Spirit that law is beyond doubt the letter that kills; but when the life-giving Spirit is present, He causes that very thing, inscribed within, to be loved which the law written without had caused to be feared.” From these Augustinian authorities, the difference is sufficiently clear between the general grace which the Pelagians admitted—namely, an external prompting from hearing the law and from the force of commandments—and the general grace which the holy Doctor required of them if they were to think as Catholics: grace inspiring inwardly in the heart. He pressed them to confess an internal assistance, namely that by which love of righteousness and a purpose of good life come to exist in the mind.

When we advance this teaching from St Augustine, we encounter the question whether all human beings are assisted by God’s grace unto salvation. Catholic [Col. 0058B] theologians disagree among themselves on this matter: some affirm it, others deny it. The Florentine censors prefer the negative opinion to the affirmative and, claiming St Augustine as their teacher, assert it as Catholic doctrine: God is not the giver of His grace to all people. They therefore reproved me for holding, along with theologians who affirm a common grace, that it is given to all.

I reply. First, I premise that the doubt concerns sufficient grace, not efficacious grace, concerning which all theologians agree that it is not given to everyone.

Second, I premise that the Fathers of Trent have firmly provided that no opinion upon which many learned and approved theologians agree is to be condemned.

With these points premised, I shall cite the most learned Cardinal Gotti, who resolves this question which he puts to himself in vol. III, q. 2, doubt 3, of his theology as follows: “It is more probable that God not only offers but also confers upon all and every human being—even unbelievers, the blinded, and the hardened—helps sufficient, either proximate or at least remote, for observing the commandments and for the things necessary to salvation; so that no one may excuse himself for not keeping them or not being saved on the ground that this is impossible for him.” Other well-known theologians, whose doctrine is highly esteemed in Catholic schools, think the same.

The resolution of this controversy depends especially upon the interpretation of the Apostle’s passage in 1 Timothy, ch. 2, where he wrote concerning God’s will: “Who wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth: for there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself for all.” Considering this weighty testimony of St Paul, St Prosper, in his *Reply to Vincent’s Objections*, says: “It must be believed and confessed with entire sincerity that God wills all to be saved. For the Apostle, whose statement this is, most earnestly commands that this be observed in all churches, and that prayer be made to God for all people. Among these, [Col. 0058D] the fact that many perish is the merit of those who perish; the fact that many are saved is the gift of Him who saves.”

The author of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, bk. II, ch. 25, agrees with Prosper’s teaching. After stating that God in every age has provided people with sufficient helps by which they might be aided to seek God, he concludes that God was pleased to confer particular grace upon many. “That grace,” he adds, “which proceeds from general benevolence, He withholds from no one, so that from both it may be clear that what is bestowed upon a portion is not denied to the whole; but in some grace has prevailed, while in others nature has recoiled.” [Col. 0059A]

Why, then, are not all human beings in fact saved, although Christ is the true light “which enlightens every man coming into this world,” and although all who died in Adam are said to be made alive in Christ? Some theologians devised the view that a twofold will must be recognized in Christ: an antecedent and a consequent will.

> [Note: [Col. 0059D] “The Catholic opinion is that Christ died sufficiently for all, not merely by the sufficiency of price, because His blood would be enough to redeem all people, but by a sufficiency of will and intention, because He wished it to benefit all by an antecedent and general—though pious and paternal—will, as the scholastic theologians say after Saints John Damascene and Thomas.” Natalis Alexander, cited place, art. 8, no. 4.—“The death of Christ,” says St Thomas, *Against the Gentiles*, bk. VI, ch. 55, “is like a universal cause of salvation, just as the sin of the first man was like a universal cause of condemnation. But a universal cause must be applied particularly to each individual in order that he may share in the effect of the universal cause.” [Col. 0060D]]

They accordingly said that, prior to any distinction among persons, God established a general decree of salvation for all and prepared the means by which, if they made use of them, all would be saved. They thought they had discovered a consequent will in actual salvation, joined to the merits of individuals. But not a few theologians, with St Thomas, oppose this distinction, maintaining that such alternation of His will ought not to be attributed to God, who is utterly simple and supremely wise. Indeed, the Angelic Doctor says of that distinction, *Summa Theologiae*, I, q. 19, art. 6, reply to objection 1: “This distinction is not taken from the side of the divine will, in which there is nothing prior or subsequent, but from the side of the things willed.” [Col. 0059B]

Some have held that God wills not every individual of every class of people to be saved, but certain persons from every class. Others have thought that the Apostle said Christ wills all to be saved because no one will be saved unless He Himself wills that person to be saved. Thus St Prosper, *Letter to Rufinus*, ch. 15: “But whatever may be the cause or rationale of this distinction in the secret counsel of God, it is sought beyond the capacity of human knowledge and is unknown without any diminution of faith, provided we confess that no one is delivered undeservedly, and that the most almighty goodness of God saves all and instructs all in the knowledge of truth whom He wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of truth. Unless He wills, teaches, and saves, no one comes, no one is instructed, no one is saved.” See St Thomas, cited place, and St Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 29. Therefore, anyone who chooses to follow either one or the other [Col. 0059C] of these opinions cannot be accused, since they have the most eminent Fathers and theologians as their authorities.

> [Note: [Col. 0060D] Dionysius Petavius himself agrees in this distinction of the divine will. In *Dogmatic Theology*, vol. I, bk. V, ch. 4, no. 16, he says: “The first will is that by which God, from Himself, wills something without any consideration of surrounding circumstances, as when He is said to will all human beings to be saved. The second, or consequent, will is that by which, in view of certain circumstances, He wills something which otherwise He would not will, as when He wills certain persons to be damned.”]

Fifthly. Since the Florentine censors further object against me that the passages cited in the third Prolegomenon do not sufficiently prove that St Bruno held that all human beings are called by God to salvation, I ask them not to demand rigidly that the bishop-saint should have delivered, in those same words, a doctrine concerning God’s will to save all persons such as theologians were obliged to discuss after heresies had arisen. For when the Fathers of Trent, in ch. 2 on justification, dealt with the dispensation and mystery of Christ’s coming, they judged that they adequately expressed the entire work of divine mercy with these words:

> “When the fullness of time had come, God sent Christ Jesus His Son, that He might redeem both the Jews who were under the law and that the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, might attain righteousness, and that all might receive the adoption of sons. God set Him forth [Col. 0059D] as a propitiator through faith in His blood for our sins—not only for ours, but also for those of the whole world.”

No one fails to see, nor can anyone challenge, that the Council’s intention [Col. 0060A] was to teach the infinite mercy of God, by which, in order to relieve the most wretched condition of humankind, He gave His only-begotten Son, who by the outpouring of all His blood paid the price of redemption for human beings whom, truly and properly, in obedience to His Father, He willed to save.

The holy Fathers who flourished before the controversies of more recent times, firmly holding the same truth—namely that God wills all human beings to be saved—spoke of this will of God through likenesses, figures, and symbols according to Holy Scripture. One of them was St Bruno. In his Commentary on St Matthew, ch. 13, v. 47, “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind,” etc., he says: “This net gathered fish of every kind, because it called the holy Church to faith and gathered into its bosom people of every class. For there are Jews and Greeks, Latins and barbarians, rich and poor, wise and foolish, wheat [Col. 0060B] and tares, grain and chaff, righteous and sinners together.”

Thus according to Bruno, not only the predestined are called to salvation, but also sinners, signified by tares and chaff, who will be damned. Likewise, on the words of the same Gospel, ch. 25, “Teach all nations,” etc., he says: “Teach all; call all; baptize all.” Similarly, in his Commentary on John, ch. 1, “There was the true light, which enlightens every man,” etc., he says: “There was the true light, eternal and unfailing light, which enlightens every person coming into this world. For every person coming into this world is enlightened inwardly and outwardly by this light alone.”

Nor are there lacking commentaries on the Psalms that confirm the same point. Thus, on Psalm 35: “You will save humans and beasts, O Lord; how you have multiplied your mercies, O God,” he says: “What are we to understand by humans, if not the wise, rational, and righteous? But what by beasts, if not the foolish, senseless, lustful, and those devoted to pleasures of the flesh? As much as humans appear to differ from beasts, so greatly do these seem to differ from one another. Yet the Lord saves both these and those, He who did not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.” [Col. 0060C]

Passing over other places, I shall conclude with this one from Psalm 49, where, speaking of the calling of all nations to faith, he says: “All have been called from East to West; but Zion and Jerusalem are in the middle, according to the words: ‘Yet God our King before the ages has worked salvation in the midst of the earth.’ Thus it was excellently said that this city is situated in the middle, from which all things around it were to receive faith and doctrine, splendor and beauty.”

For the holy bishop of Segni to affirm God’s general will to save all human beings, it was enough that he taught the Church to call all nations to herself and receive them into her bosom, and affirmed that no human beings are excluded from salvation by divine goodness and that, through the preaching of the Apostles, an almost innumerable [Col. 0060D] accession of believers to the Church had been made. By these and similar statements, St Bruno seems certainly to have held the same view as the author of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, who, bk. II, ch. 2, testifying to the same truth, says: “Christ excepted no one, separated no one, distinguished no one by race or condition. The Gospel of Christ’s cross was sent to all nations without exception.”

> [Note: [Col. 0061C] By one argument employed by the most distinguished Berti, I shall gather together everything quoted above from St Bruno, so that the doctrine we defend may be established more firmly. “Whatever Sacred Scripture affirms of God,” he says, “if it especially befits His goodness, mercy, and providence by which He directs rational creatures into the way of salvation, must be asserted of God without any hesitation. But in the sacred books we read that God wills all human beings to be saved; and this especially befits His infinite love and His directing of creatures to their last end. Therefore it must be asserted without hesitation that God properly and most sincerely wills the salvation of all.” See the *Expostulation* cited above, p. 6. [Col. 0061D; 0062C–D]]

They object sixthly: infants who either perish in their mother’s womb, or die before being regenerated by baptism, or are born in places where the sacrament is unknown, must be said to be assisted by no grace at all toward salvation.

I reply, first: with the most eminent Gotti, vol. III, q. 2, doubt 3, §6, many hold that, in order to say that God willed the salvation of all infants by a general will, it was sufficient that He instituted baptism also for them, so that, speaking in itself, it can be conferred upon all, although, by a consequent will not to save certain persons, it is not conferred upon them.

I reply, second: St Augustine teaches in *On Original Sin*, ch. 6, that the unhappy condition of infants must be traced back to the infection of original guilt. “Infants,” he says, [Col. 0061B] “are damned because they are born children of wrath from the mass of perdition; and one born from Adam is rightly understood to be condemned by the obligation of the ancient debt, unless he has been delivered from it—not according to debt but according to grace. And what grace, except the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord?” The holy Doctor repeats the same in many other places, as the author of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, bk. II, chs. 1 and 24, treats the matter extensively. Let my censors consult him, and they will attain a purer doctrine from these sources.

As to what is to be thought concerning hardened sinners, theologians have gone into different opinions, as is clear from the aforementioned Cardinal Gotti, from Habert, and from others, who generally agree upon Augustine’s celebrated saying: “No one is forsaken by God unless he first forsakes God.” St Bruno answers this in his Commentary on Psalm 82: “He is always with God who does not depart from His faith and love.” Concerning many indeed abandoned by God, one may apply what St Augustine said of [Col. 0061C] the Jews: “It is easy to charge the Jews with unbelief arising from free will, since they refused to believe despite the great miracles performed among them.” See the most learned Fr George, cited place, p. 109. There he also adduces St Cyril of Alexandria’s authority, likewise condemning the Jews for the guilt of unbelief.

I shall not linger over the remaining objections of the censors, copied from Ludovico Habert; they have already been answered by him. Yet I shall answer one: they say that faith arises from hearing, but that Christ’s Gospel was not heard because it was not preached throughout the whole world.

I reply: since the Apostle Paul made the same objection to himself in Romans, ch. 10, see how he resolves it: [Col. 0062A] “Therefore faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ. But I say: Have they not heard? Indeed, ‘their sound has gone out into all the earth,’ namely that of the Apostles, ‘and their words to the ends of the world.’” Likewise, in Romans, ch. 16, the same Apostle testifies to this divine glorification: “the mystery kept silent through eternal times was made manifest for the obedience of faith among all nations.” The same Apostle uses the same manner of speaking elsewhere. To the Colossians, ch. 1, 6, he says: “In the word of truth of the Gospel, which … is in the whole world and bears fruit and grows.” And again: “The Gospel … has been preached in the whole earth which is under heaven.” Likewise, 1 Timothy, epistle III, 16: “Great,” he says, “is the mystery of godliness, which was preached among the nations and believed in the world.” I pass over the authorities of the earliest Fathers of the Church. Let my critics see Dissertation 11 of the most distinguished Andrea Gallandi, in defense of the two epistles of Pope St Clement I, which Dom Placidus Sprengher, Benedictine monk, reissued, vol. I, p. 54, Würzburg, 1784. [Col. 0062B]

But why is there this dispute among us, who ought to profess and teach orthodox doctrine? I freely admit that the hinge of the disagreement lies in defining the nature of sufficient grace. If we gather the views of all Catholics concerning sufficient grace, they finally come down to this: sufficient grace is that which gives powers sufficiently ready for performing a supernatural work, either immediately or at least mediately through prayer. Yet this grace can not only be resisted, as efficacious grace can also be resisted, but is in fact usually resisted. Since this opinion contradicts the second Jansenist proposition, it must therefore be regarded as Catholic. For under this assisting grace human beings recognize themselves as fully in control of themselves; and consequently they maintain that in that state of grace they are able to merit and demerit—a point which both Augustinians and Thomists establish and demonstrate by many records of argument. [Col. 0062C]

My censors formerly received with the highest praise what the most learned Francesco Cajetano Incontri, Archbishop and one who deserved exceedingly well of the Florentine Church, thought and published concerning efficacious and sufficient grace in his treatise *On Human Acts*. If they keep his excellent and safe doctrine before their eyes, they will show in this matter also that they honor his memory and follow his most approved teachings. Finally, I entreat them to listen to St Bruno himself, if they desire to make themselves worthy of God’s goodness. “How good,” he says, “is the God of Israel—but especially to those who think rightly and Catholicly, and do not pass over to false thoughts and dangerous disputations.” In his Commentary on Psalm 72.

[Col. 0063]

## THE PROLOGUE OF ST JEROME BEGINS

[Col. 0063A] 1 After the Pentateuch of Moses, in order that we might join the new writings to the old, obedient to your wish we have compressed the four books of the Gospels into this one volume, with a sufficiently brief and easy exposition.

> [Note: [Col. 0063C] Thus our manuscript reads, and rightly so, rather than “and in the specimen of the Turin composition.”]

Matthew, who in the order of the others came first, we have expounded wholly in sequence; and wherever it seemed necessary to us, we have established peace and harmony between him and the other Evangelists. In Mark, however, we have taken care to expound only those things that were not expounded in Matthew. For it seemed superfluous to us that what had been expounded in Matthew should again be expounded in Mark. We did the same in Luke and John, expounding in the later writers only those things that had not been expounded in the earlier ones. Thus, while we have expounded all true matters in briefer speech, [Col. 0063B] we have neither said superfluous things nor passed over necessary ones. We have divided Matthew into four parts, Luke into two, and John into three, so that, by looking at the headings, the reader may more easily find what he seeks.

> [Note: [Col. 0063C] Mark is omitted because it is not divided into any parts.]

> [Note: [Col. 0064C] Manuscript: “so that” (*ut*).]

## MATTHEW, THIRD PART

XLVII. Then there was brought to Him a man possessed by a demon, blind and mute; and He healed him, so that he spoke and saw.  
XLVIII. Then some of the scribes answered Him.  
XLIX. When an unclean spirit has gone out from a person.

LIII. He set another parable before them, saying: The kingdom of heaven has become like a man who sowed good seed in his field.  
LIV. He set another parable before them, saying: The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed.

LVI. The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field.  
LVII. The kingdom of heaven is like a merchantman. [Col. 0065C]

LXIII. Then scribes and Pharisees from Jerusalem came to Him, saying: Why do Your disciples transgress the traditions of the elders? For they do not wash their hands. [Col. 0065D]  
LXIV. And Jesus, going out from there, withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon.  
LXV. And when Jesus had passed on from there, He came beside the Sea of Galilee.  
LXVI. But Jesus, having called His disciples together, said: I have compassion on the crowd.  
LXVII. And having dismissed the crowd, He went up into the little boat.  
LXVIII. But Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi.  
LXIX. Then Jesus said to His disciples: If anyone wishes to come after Me, let him deny himself.

# COMMENTARIES ON MATTHEW BY ST BRUNO OF ASTI, BISHOP OF SEGNI

## FIRST PART

[Col. 0071]

### I. [CHAPTER I.] “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.”

[Note: [Col. 0071C] From these opening words has been copied a homily spuriously attributed to Eusebius of Emesa, entitled *On the Nativity of St Mary*, p. 195, Paris edition of 1575, published by Michel Sonnius, and the edition of 1554. It asks, first, why it begins with Christ’s genealogy, and answers: in order to show that Jesus Christ was of the offspring of Abraham and David, as he had long promised would be the case. So too St Ambrose, book III on Luke II: what does Joseph’s genealogy contribute to proving this? That Mary had necessarily to be of the same tribe and stock as Joseph. See also Ambrose, the cited book; St Jerome on this passage; Cornelius Jansen, *Concordia*, chapter 6, [Col. 0072C] Maldonatus on Matthew chapter I, verse 16, and the other interpreters, [Col. 0072D] who almost all repeat substantially the same points.]

[Col. 0071A] Why the blessed Evangelist Matthew begins with Christ’s genealogy, we think that this is the greatest and principal reason: to show that our Saviour descended according to the flesh from David’s line and from the tribe of Judah. Therefore, beginning with Abraham and coming through Judah’s line to David, he weaves in sequence the whole genealogy of those succeeding one another, until he reaches Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ. For our Lord Christ had been promised both to Abraham and to David; and it had been prophesied that he would derive his origin from the tribe of Judah. For the Lord had said to Abraham:

[Note: [Col. 0072D] This passage of Genesis 22:18 is rendered only in sense from Scripture, where it is said, “All the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your seed.” Author of the *Imperfect Work on Matthew* adduces the passage in the same sense. See also Ecclesiasticus 44:23.]

“In your seed I shall make all nations my inheritance.” Explaining this, however, the Apostle [Col. 0071B] says: “He did not say, ‘and to seeds,’ as though of many, but as though of one: ‘and to your seed,’ which is Christ” (Gal. 3:16).

And the patriarch Jacob, blessing his son Judah, said: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hand shall be upon the necks of your enemies; the sons of your father shall bow down before you. Judah is a lion’s whelp; from the prey, my son, you have gone up. Resting, you lay down like a lion, and like a lioness: who shall rouse him? The sceptre shall not be taken from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49:1).

In this Gospel also, as is read in what follows (Matt. 2:5), when Herod asked the chief priests and scribes of the people where Christ was to be born, they answered him: “In Bethlehem [Col. 0071C] of Judah; for thus it has been written through the prophet: ‘And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come forth a leader who will rule my people Israel.’”

You see, then, that our Saviour had been promised to Abraham, and that, according to the sayings of the prophets, he was expected to be born from the tribe of Judah. Let us also see what had been said to King David about the same one. Let David himself say it: “The Lord,” he says, “swore truth to David, and he will not turn away from it: ‘Of the fruit of your womb I shall set one upon my throne’” (Ps. 131:11). And again: “Once I have sworn by my holiness: shall I lie to David? His seed shall remain for ever” (Ps. 88:35).

Behold, [Col. 0072A] not merely is it promised but it is even sworn that Christ should arise according to the flesh from David’s stock. Thus it was not without reason that Christ is called the son of David in many places. For the children also cried: “Hosanna to the son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 21:9). The Canaanite woman too said: “Have mercy on me, son of David” (Matt. 15:22). Hence he himself, questioning the Jews, said: “What do you think about Christ? Whose son is he?” They say to him, “David’s” (Matt. 22:42). Who, then, could believe anyone to be the Christ unless it were first certainly established that he had been born of David’s stock? Matthew was therefore right, when he was about to speak of Christ, to show immediately at the beginning of his discourse that he was born of Abraham’s seed, Judah’s tribe, and David’s line. [Col. 0072B]

[Note: [Col. 0072D] So Jerome on this passage, Bede, and others.]

Having shown the reason why the evangelist adopted such an opening, let us answer the Jews, heretics, and others for whom this same reason seems irrelevant unless we believe Christ to be Joseph’s son. For it is not Mary’s genealogy but Joseph’s which is traced here. What relevance is it to Christ that Joseph is proved to be David’s son, when Christ was born not of Joseph but of Mary? For just as according to divinity our Saviour had no mother, so according to humanity he had no father.

Let such persons, then, hear what is commanded in the Law: namely, that all men should marry wives from their own tribe and kinship, and all women should take husbands from the same tribe, so that inheritance might remain [Col. 0072C] within families and tribes might not intermingle, but might remain as the Lord had separated them.

[Note: [Col. 0072D] See St Jerome on this passage and St John Chrysostom, Homily 2. The passage is expressly found in Scripture, Numbers 36.]

It is therefore proved by the testimony of the Law that the Virgin Mary and Joseph belonged to the same tribe and kinship; for otherwise they could not, according to the Law, have been joined together unless both belonged to the same tribe. If anyone objects to me:

[Note: [Col. 0072D] Chrysostom also raises this objection for himself in the cited passage and resolves it in the same manner.]

that many men took wives from another, and not only from their own, tribe, I answer that the Jews frequently did not only this but many other things contrary to the Law. Joseph, however, could not act contrary to the Law, since he was righteous and feared to offend God in anything. This law, moreover, although perhaps not observed in full by others, [Col. 0073A] nevertheless had necessarily to be observed by those women who, because they had no brothers, succeeded their parents in the inheritance. As Moses—or rather, the Lord through Moses—commands: if anyone dies without sons, his inheritance is to pass to his daughters. If they took husbands from another tribe, the inheritance too would necessarily pass into another tribe. Such women, therefore, must either marry from their own tribe or not marry at all, lest, if they marry from another, possessions and inheritances become intermixed; and this is in no way permitted.

It is therefore evident that the most blessed Virgin Mary, who had succeeded to her parents’ inheritance as their most noble heiress (for she had no brothers, nor is she recorded as having had any), could not have taken as husband anyone from [Col. 0073B] another tribe. But perhaps you say that she had no inheritance. Read, then, Leviticus chapter 25, and you will find that no one could sell his inheritance outright, though he could sell its use. For when the Jubilee came, every inheritance returned to its proper owner. How, then, could she be without an inheritance when she was descended from such exceedingly noble parents?

By these arguments, therefore, it is most clearly established that Joseph and the blessed Virgin Mary belonged to the same tribe. But the evangelist wished to trace the genealogy through Joseph because he followed the practice of the Holy Scriptures: everywhere they set out a genealogical line through men, nowhere through women. Thus all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; from David to the Babylonian deportation, fourteen generations; and from the Babylonian deportation to Christ, fourteen generations. This is true if one and the same person is counted twice, [Col. 0073C] and if the end of one set of generations is the beginning of another; otherwise the count does not work.

[Note: [Col. 0073D] Augustine held the same view, as reported by Bede on this passage, where he also records Jerome’s opinion, which he subsequently follows: that the Jechoniah first mentioned is not the same as he whose son is named after the captivity, but that the former is Jehoiakim and the latter Jehoiachin, confused among Greeks and Latins alike through scribal error and the lapse of time. See St Ambrose, book III on Luke. Among more recent writers, Jansen, Maldonatus, a Lapide, Calmet, etc. St Gregory writes that Jechoniah is named a second time mystically, *Morals*, book XXVIII, chapter 9; Augustine also, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, book II, chapter 4.]

But the generation of Christ was thus:

### II.

[Note: [Col. 0073D] It is a homily attributed to Emesa, *On the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord*, p. 13.]

“When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit.”

The first question, however, is why blessed Mary was betrothed, she who was a virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, a virgin after childbirth, and was never to know a man. Many reasons may be given for this. For if [Col. 0073D] she had had no husband and appeared pregnant, no defence could have been available to prevent her being stoned as an adulteress. Who would have believed that she had conceived without a man? Who would have believed that her womb had swollen by the Holy Spirit? This was unprecedented, unheard of, and without example. It was therefore better that she who was always a virgin should for a time be thought not to be a virgin, than that she should be stoned when accused under the Law. Virginity is not violated by a false opinion; yet an innocent woman is often killed by a false accusation.

The Lord could, if he had wished, have protected his mother in another way, not only from unjust condemnation but even from false [Col. 0074A] suspicion. Why he preferred this course, he knows, not I. It pleased him; let it therefore please us also.

Moreover, the Virgin Mary needed a man’s assistance in many ways, since by God’s ordinance she was to give birth in Bethlehem, and she had to flee with her son into Egypt. Thus it had been ordained by the Lord, thus foretold by the prophets, thus it was to happen and could not be changed. This, therefore, is the reason why she was betrothed.

[Note: [Col. 0074D] Apparently from Jerome on this passage: “Why does she conceive not as an unmarried virgin but as a betrothed woman? (1) That Mary’s origin might be shown through Joseph’s genealogy; (2) that she might not be stoned by the Jews as an adulteress; (3) that, in fleeing to Egypt, she might have support.” See chapter 2 *Against Helvidius*, and Ambrose, *On the Institution of Virgins*, chapters 5 and 6.]

“When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit.” Perhaps you ask: what kind of mother? First ask: what kind of son? Among men the son has no equal; among women the mother has no peer. He is more beautiful than the sons of men; she is beautiful as the dawn rising. He made his mother—a thing no other did; she bore a son and remained a virgin—a thing no other did. He existed before he was born; she did not exist before her son. Which of these seems to you more wonderful? [Col. 0074C] Both are wonderful, because neither happened before nor afterwards.

“Before they came together,” he says, “she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit.” What does “before they came together” mean?

[Note: [Col. 0074D] Thus some understood it with the author, according to Jansen and Calmet; against them, Cornelius a Lapide and others.]

Before they lived together in one house. For they had not yet come together; they did not yet live together. He remained in his own house, and she still remained in hers. Yet she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit. I should ask by whom she was found, if such a condition were difficult to detect. For there are many signs by which pregnant women are recognized. She therefore appeared pregnant to those familiar with her.

[Note: [Col. 0074D] Jerome and Bede say she was discovered by Joseph “as it were through the confidence proper to marriage.”]

Yet nobody suspected her of anything, because they knew that she was betrothed. Joseph eventually understood this also, and realized that [Col. 0074D] his betrothed was pregnant. He was therefore astonished and was stirred by jealousy concerning his betrothed.

[Note: [Col. 0074D] This term is usually understood in a bad sense, as is the very name *zelus* (“jealousy”) among ecclesiastical authors. Hence the title of Cyprian’s treatise *On Jealousy and Envy*, where he speaks of the devil: “After he saw man made in God’s image, he burst forth into jealous, malevolent envy; nor did he cast another down by the prompting of jealousy before he himself had first been cast down by jealousy,” etc. See the remainder. They say that *zelotypia* is derived from Greek ζῆλος (*zēlos*, “jealousy”) and τύπος (*typos*, “impression/image”), because it arises not from true love but from a kind of false image of love. It seems to have the same force among pagan authors also. Hence Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* IV, no. 8: “Detraction, however, is that which I mean to be understood as *zelotypia*: distress because another too obtains what one himself has desired.” Nevertheless, I fully believe that our author takes it in a favourable sense.]

What was he to do? He feared to expose her, lest she should be killed. [Col. 0075A] He thought of dismissing her, judging this easy for himself and not dangerous for her. For he would give her a writ of divorce, as the Law commands. This is what follows: “But Joseph her husband, being righteous and unwilling to expose her publicly, wished to dismiss her secretly.” Since he was righteous and holy, he wished rather to dismiss her secretly than to accuse her. For he did not wish to bring her into his house,

[Note: [Col. 0075D] This meaning of the Gospel word *traducere* is opposed by the Greek text παραδειγματίσαι (*paradeigmatisai*), meaning “to expose with disgrace”; nevertheless, this is another interpretation, and was later that of Abulensis.]

because he saw that she was pregnant, not by him.

While he was considering this, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream and said: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife.” While, he says, he was thinking thus, while he was troubled by these anxieties, while he was uncertain what to do, behold the angel of the Lord, behold the heavenly messenger, behold Gabriel,

[Note: [Col. 0075D] St Bernard later held the same view: Homily 1, *Missus est*.]

the Virgin’s counsellor and witness of [Col. 0075B] her chastity, to whom these secrets had been entrusted and these mysteries revealed, appeared to Joseph in a dream. And appropriately, indeed, in a dream. For if Joseph had not slept, if he had not been outside himself, if he had had the eyes of his mind open; if, through the Holy Spirit’s revelation, he had recognized the sun now rising in Mary, undoubtedly he could have thought nothing of this kind.

Let us hear what the angel said: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife.” Do not fear, he says; do not hesitate. Cast off this jealousy; drive away suspicion. It is not as you think. You do not yet know this Virgin; you have not yet rightly seen Mary your wife. For she is God’s temple; she is heaven’s gate; she is your lady, whom you think to be your betrothed. Take her, then, [Col. 0075C] now as your lady. Receive her, not as one given over to you, but entrusted to you. Be obedient to her as a servant, not commanding as a husband. Why is this so? Do you wish to hear why? “Because what is born in her is from the Holy Spirit.”

Let it suffice to hear and believe this. Let us not inquire how Christ was incarnate from a Virgin and born of the Holy Spirit. For the Virgin believed and conceived. Elizabeth bears witness to this: “Blessed,” she says, “is she who believed, because the things spoken to you by the Lord shall be fulfilled” (Luke 1:45). The Virgin believed, and through the Holy Spirit’s working the Word [Col. 0076A] became flesh. “And she will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.” Why he is called by such a name is immediately added when it says: “For he shall save his people from their sins.” It is evident, therefore, that *Jesus* means “Saviour.”

[Note: [Col. 0075D] See Cornelius Jansen’s extended discussion of this name and its meaning, *Concordia*, chapter 7, and Maldonatus on this passage. Long before them, Chrysostom, Homily [Col. 0076C] 2 on Matthew: “Jesus is not a word of Greek speech, but in the Hebrew language Jesus is called that which in our language is ‘Saviour’”; and St Jerome: “Jesus in the Hebrew tongue is called ‘Saviour’; thus the evangelist has indicated the etymology [Col. 0076D] of his name.”]

Now all this happened in order that what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled: “Behold, a Virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted “God with us.” The Jews, falsely cavilling at this, say that their books contain not “virgin” but “young woman.”

[Note: [Col. 0076D] Ancient and modern interpreters argue against the Jews on Isaiah 7:14. See, among modern writers, Calmet in a particular dissertation, Jansen, Maldonatus, etc. In the Hebrew of Isaiah stands the word עַלְמָה (*ʿalmāh*), concerning which Jerome discusses at length. The homily ends here; for the following material against the Jews, being unsuitable for hearers, has been omitted.]

To them we reply in return: if they wish to understand not a virgin but a young woman, do they think it a sign or a wonderful thing if a young woman gives birth? It would be a sign [Col. 0076B] if an old woman bore a child. Thus the births of Sarah and Elizabeth are considered miraculous. But if a young woman bears a child, no sign is thought to occur; for it is utterly commonplace.

Observe why he said this. For Isaiah, in the passage where he writes these things, speaks thus to Ahaz: “Ask a sign for yourself from the Lord your God, in the depths of hell or in the height above.” And Ahaz said, “I will not ask, and I will not test the Lord.” Then Isaiah said: “Hear therefore, house of Jacob. Is it too little for you to be burdensome to men, that you are burdensome also to my God? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign.” But what sign? “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. 7:14). Therefore, if for a young woman to bear a child is not a sign, it is necessary to understand “virgin.”

Correct, then, [Col. 0076C] your books, Jews, which we do not doubt have been maliciously falsified.

[Note: [Col. 0076D] He says this with certain ancient writers, with whom agree Jean Morin, Pezron, and some others; against them Martianay, Le Quien, Richard Simon, Dupin, and before them Bellarmine deny that the Jews maliciously corrupted the sacred text.]

“His name was called Emmanuel,” that is, “God with us,” because, although according to divinity he is everywhere, he nevertheless dwelt bodily in Judaea for a time. Hence Jeremiah says:

[Note: [Col. 0076D] Baruch 3:37. He has, however, given some words differently from the Vulgate, and names Jeremiah rather than his scribe Baruch, because Baruch was not only formerly, as now also, continuously placed after Jeremiah, but is often found in manuscripts without any title attached.]

“This is our God, and no other shall be accounted against him; he discovered every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and Israel his beloved. After this he was seen upon earth and conversed with men.”

But Joseph, rising from sleep, did as [Col. 0077A] the angel of the Lord had commanded him: he took his wife, and did not know her until she bore her firstborn son; and he called his name Jesus.

Here also we must answer the Jews and heretics, who contend that the blessed Virgin Mary had other sons by Joseph, because it says here: “He did not know her until she bore her firstborn son.” If someone says, “I know that I shall have no children until I take a wife,” does it consequently follow that, after taking a wife, he will have children? Many have wives who have no children. Thus the adverb *until* does not establish any necessary consequence in this passage.

[Note: [Col. 0077D] See Jerome, *Against Helvidius*, and Chrysostom on this passage concerning this and similar particles; also Ambrose, book II on Luke; *On Noah and the Ark*, chapter 17; *On the Institution of Virgins*, chapters 5 and 8; Isidore of Pelusium, book I, letter 4; etc.]

For the evangelist’s entire purpose in saying this was to show that Christ was not Joseph’s son. For Christ was thought to be [Col. 0077B] Joseph’s son, as another evangelist testifies when he says: “Jesus, when he began, was about thirty years of age, being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph” (Luke 3:23). Thus the evangelist Matthew intended to dispel this false opinion in saying, “He did not know her until she bore her firstborn son.”

But he did not notice these arrows of the heretics, which they hurl against these words because of one obscurely used particle and, blinded, understand perversely. They also attempt to prove their case differently, saying that he could not be called “firstborn” unless other brothers followed him, in relation to whom he would be called firstborn. If this were so, no firstborn children could be offered to the Lord. For Moses commands (Exod. 13):

[Note: [Col. 0077D] Jerome here briefly invokes the usage of Scripture: “that it calls firstborn not one whom brothers follow, but one who has been born first”; he nevertheless refers his reader to the little book *Against Helvidius*.]

that every firstborn son, after one month, should be offered to the Lord. [Col. 0077C] Yet he who is offered after one month does not yet have other brothers in relation to whom he is called firstborn. Why, then, is one who has no brother, and concerning whom it is wholly unknown whether he will ever have one, offered as firstborn? It is therefore evident that “firstborn” is not said in relation to brothers who follow, but because one first came forth from the mother’s womb, whether others later follow or do not follow.

But perhaps you quibble not only over “firstborn” but also over “first.” Hear, then, what the Lord says through Moses: “Whatever first breaks forth from the womb of every flesh shall be mine.”

[Note: [Col. 0077D] Numbers 18:15 appears to be the passage to which our author refers, although he quotes the words less exactly: “Whatever first breaks forth from the womb of all flesh which they offer to the Lord, whether of human beings or cattle, shall be yours by right; provided only that you receive a price for the firstborn of a human being, and cause every unclean animal to be redeemed, [Col. 0078D] its redemption being after one month.”]

If, then, “first” in this passage is relative and cannot be said by itself, how was that which was offered immediately after one month offered when it was not yet known whether it was first? [Col. 0077D] [Col. 0078A] What if the mother died immediately after her first delivery? What if no further son was born from her, as we often see happens? It would then follow that those offered to the Lord as if first or firstborn—though we have no names by which to call them—would be called neither first nor firstborn. These considerations therefore plainly show that an only-begotten child can also be called firstborn.

### III. [CHAP. II.]

[Note: [Col. 0078D] This is a homily of St. Bruno, attributed to Emesenus, on the Epiphany of the Lord, edition p. 27.]

When Jesus therefore had been born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the East. It is not without mystery that the blessed Virgin Mary, leaving her native city and home, came to Bethlehem to give birth to her Son. For Bethlehem is interpreted “house of bread.” [Note: [Col. 0078D] See Chrysologus, Sermon 156; Ambrose also mentions this interpretation in *On Jacob*, book II, chapter 7.] But Jesus speaks of himself, saying: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” (John VI, 42). It was fitting, then, that the living bread should be born in the house of bread; Christ’s birth was the reason it bore that name. For Christ was not born there because it was so named; rather, it was so named because Christ was to arise there.

Let us, then, also be Bethlehem; let us be a house of bread. Whoever is not a house of bread will perish through hunger. For the Lord himself says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, you shall not have life in yourselves” (ibid., 54). Let us therefore receive Christ into our house; let us receive him in our mind and breast. Let him arise in us; for he is the way, the truth, and the life; he is wisdom and righteousness. Let him therefore arise in us, since these things are born and built up in us.

It follows: “Behold, Magi came from the East.” Why from the East? [Note: [Col. 0078D] In almost the same manner, the Author of the *Imperfect Work*, Homily 2: “Because they came from the East, whence the day is born, thence proceeded the beginning of faith, because faith is the light of souls,” etc.] Because they had already been inwardly illumined, and the sun of righteousness had already enlightened their minds. But where did they come? To Jerusalem. And what did they say? “Where is he who has been born King of the Jews?” How do you know this? Who told you? They reply: “For we saw his star in the East, and we have come to worship him.”

These are the firstfruits of the Gentiles. [Note: [Col. 0078D] St. Leo, Sermon 2 on the Epiphany, calls them so; likewise St. Augustine, or the Author of Sermon 30 for the season, St. Fulgentius, Sermon 5, etc.] These were the first among the Gentiles to believe in Christ. To them not the earth but the heavens proclaimed Christ’s birth. And in them was fulfilled what is said: “The heavens declare the glory of God.” [Note: [Col. 0078D] Psalm XVIII, 1; St. Leo likewise cites this passage in the sermon mentioned.] Yet they believe, not in a speaking heaven, but in a heaven displaying a new star. The Jews, however, [Col. 0078D] refuse to believe Christ preaching, expounding prophecies, [Col. 0079A] raising the dead, giving sight to the blind, and working other miracles.

But was that star seen by everyone? For if it had been seen by all, they would certainly not have said that they had seen it in the East, when it appeared not only in the East. Thus it happened that, on seeing the star, they immediately understood whatever was signified by it—not through a demonstration of astrological art, [Note: [Col. 0079D] Chrysostom, Homily 6 on the Nativity: “This seems to be not the work of the star alone, but of God, through whom their soul was moved to this.”] but through the illumination of the Holy Spirit. They sought Christ in the star, understanding by divine inspiration that he was signified through the star.

For Balaam had also indicated this, saying: “A star shall arise out of Jacob,” and “a man shall rise from Israel.” [Note: [Col. 0079D] Bede says that prophecy is signified by the star; our author speaks with Ambrose, who says in book II on Luke: “According to the mystery of the Incarnation, Christ is the star.” I believe that he had Ambrose before his eyes here because, although he usually follows the Vulgate, he now gives the passage from Numbers according to the Septuagint, as Ambrose gave it: “And a man shall rise from Israel.” The Vulgate: “And a rod shall rise from Israel.”] Therefore Christ is both man and star: a star in signification, a man in truth; a star for the Gentiles, a man for the Jews. The Gentiles follow him in the star and are enlightened; [Col. 0079B] the Jews think that he is only a man and are blinded. Hence he himself says: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and that those who see may become blind” (John IX, 39).

“But when King Herod heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.” Great indeed were the things that were being said; but because they sounded forth joy and intimated the glory of the whole kingdom, Herod and all Jerusalem should certainly not have been troubled, but rejoiced. Thus weak eyes are accustomed to be disturbed upon seeing light. Such persons are aptly signified in the books of the prophets by those birds which daylight blinds and night illuminates.

But who would not rejoice that our little child still cries in the cradle, while the king of the earth and his whole kingdom are dissolved in fear? Do not be afraid, wretch; for he did not come [Col. 0079C] to take the kingdom from you, but to restore the kingdom to all who have been driven out of it.

It follows: “And gathering together all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he asked them where Christ was to be born.” And they said to him: “In Bethlehem of Judaea; for thus it has been written through the prophet: And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come forth a leader who shall rule my people Israel.”

Troubled, Herod cannot rest. He is distressed; and, lest he be caught unawares, he summons the chief priests and the scribes of the people and asks where Christ is to be born. He is told: “In Bethlehem of Judaea.” Fear is added to fear; and he who had been disturbed by the words of the Magi is again terrified by the answer of the scribes and priests. [Col. 0079D] For how could one who thought only earthly thoughts fail to be afraid of losing his kingdom when he heard that Christ had been born in his own time—Christ whom, on the testimony [Col. 0080A] of the prophets, he believed would come?

“Then Herod, secretly summoning the Magi, carefully learned from them the time when the star had appeared to them.” He did this [Note: [Col. 0079D] See Chrysostom, Homily 7, and Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 158.] so that, if he could not find Christ, he might at least, once the time of his birth was known, have him—who alone could not be killed—slain together with the other boys of the same age.

You do not understand, Herod; you do not understand what the Lord says to you through Moses: [Note: [Col. 0079D] Exodus XXIII, 19. Thus indeed Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, question 90, writes: “How this is to be observed according to the literal propriety of the words is either not clear or does not appear. Yet I approve the understanding concerning Christ: that by this prophecy it was foretold that he would not be killed by the Jews as an infant, when Herod sought him in order that he might be killed but did not find him.”] “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk”—that is, you shall not kill Christ as an infant, hanging upon the breasts of his virgin Mother.

And sending them to Bethlehem, he said: “Go and inquire carefully concerning the child; and when you have found him, report to me, that I too may come and worship him.” You accomplish nothing; you achieve nothing by this cunning of yours. “There is no counsel, no wisdom, [Col. 0080B] no strength against the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0080D] Proverbs XXI, 30: “There is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against the Lord.” St. Gregory likewise cites this passage to the same effect in Homily 10 on the Gospels.]

“And when they had heard the king, they departed; and behold, the star which they had seen in the East went before them, until it came and stood over the place where the child was. And seeing the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy.”

The Magi leave Herod and see the star, because those also who separate themselves from the devil see the light of righteousness. But why does the star go before them, except to show them the way and lead them to the child? They follow it, then; they come to Bethlehem; it stands over that house in which the Virgin Mary was. It stands above a star, for Mary is interpreted “star of the sea.” [Note: [Col. 0080D] St. Bernard, Homily 2 on *Missus est*, on the same name: “which, translated, is called ‘star of the sea’ … she herself is that noble star arisen from Jacob,” etc.] Thus the Son is a star, and the Mother too is a star; a star arises from a star, but the one who arises is greater than she from whom he arises. Therefore it rightly seems to stand above her.

It did not say, “over the child.” But what [Col. 0080C] did it say? “Over where the child was.” For where was the child, except in his Mother’s bosom? The star stood and cried out; for it has its own language. To avoid seeking examples far away: that star spoke to the Magi just as these letters speak to us. It spoke by signifying—but what did it signify? What did it say? Do you wish to hear? “Here is the child; here is the Mother of the child; seek him here; here you will find him. Here, in a little body, lies hidden he who is everywhere and fills all things.”

For this is what it says: “Seeing the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy.” What is “seeing the star” except seeing and understanding what was signified and said to them through the star? For it is no great joy to see stars. We often see the sun and moon, [Col. 0080D] yet we do not greatly rejoice merely in seeing them. They rejoiced, then, not because of the star, but because of what the star signified.

“And entering the house, they found [Col. 0081A] the child with Mary his mother; and falling down, they worshipped him. And opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.” What exultation must then have been yours, most blessed Virgin—who can conceive it? For you saw him whom you had lately borne already worshipped as Lord. Receive the first gifts offered to your Son; receive the tributes paid to him. You who had come to pay tribute with others, first receive tribute from others.

For this was why Joseph, as Luke says (I, 5), had come to Bethlehem: that he too, like the rest, might register himself and bind himself to pay the taxes, because he was of the house and family of David. Hence it is clear that taxes were paid according to families, and that all members of the same family assembled for this obligation. Indeed, Joseph and Mary, [Col. 0081B] because they were of David’s family, needed to come to Bethlehem, where that family lived.

But why did they offer three gifts, [Note: [Col. 0081D] The mystical meanings of these gifts pleased even the most ancient Fathers to a remarkable degree: Irenaeus, book III, chapter 10; Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chapter 9; Nazianzen, Oration 38; Jerome, Ambrose, Fulgentius, etc. But our author treats them very fully and elegantly.] except to reveal the mystery of the Trinity? We offer the first gift by believing in the Father, the second in the Son, the third in the Holy Spirit. These three gifts suffice for us. Whoever does not offer them is not received by Christ. This, then, is why they offered three gifts to the Lord; for if they had offered either more or fewer, they would not have held the catholic faith.

What do we suppose is signified by gold except that royal power which is greater than the rest and shines more widely? We offer gold to Christ because we believe that he is the king of all. We also offer frankincense because we confess that he is God. For even the Gentiles customarily offered frankincense in sacrifices to [Col. 0081C] their gods. We offer myrrh also because we believe him to be God in such a way that we do not doubt that he is man and mortal; for in former times the bodies of the dead were embalmed with myrrh so that they might not decay.

Since, therefore, we have offered Christ what is his, let us offer him what is ours as well. That we believe him to be King, God, and man belongs to him; but ours are the things which have been given to us by him. The Church possesses gold in wisdom, frankincense in holy conduct pleasingly fragrant to God, and myrrh in the bitterness of repentance and the mortification of the flesh. Thus teachers offer gold; martyrs and confessors, frankincense; sinners now repenting, myrrh. In some, therefore, gold shines; in others frankincense gives forth a sweet fragrance; in others myrrh is wisely bitter. What [Col. 0081D] else can we offer God? Our entire offering is contained in these three gifts.

The Magi, then, offered such gifts, in which they signified both the truth of faith and the whole discipline of the Church. “And having received an answer in a dream that they should not return to Herod, they returned by another way to their own country.” [Col. 0082A]

Let us also return by another way to our own country, because we cannot return by the way by which we departed. This too is commanded to the children of Israel as they leave Egypt: that they should not return by the same way. [Note: [Col. 0081D] (52). Deuteronomy XVII, 16: “When the Lord has commanded you that you shall by no means return again by the same way.”] For our country is paradise; our country is the land of the living. [Note: [Col. 0081D] (53). He clearly intended to express the passage from Gregory, Homily 10 on the Gospels: “For our country is paradise, to which, having come to know Jesus, we are forbidden to return by the way by which we came. For from our country we departed through pride, disobedience, following visible things, and tasting forbidden food; but it is necessary that we return to it through weeping, obedience ….” See Ambrose, in the work cited; Fulgentius, Sermon 5; Chrysologus, Sermons 158 and 159, etc.] There our first parents lived; from there they departed. But by what way? Certainly through pride, disobedience, vainglory, and intemperance of appetite. We cannot return to our homeland by this way. Therefore another way must be sought, by which we may return to our homeland.

This way is Christ; for he himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV, 6). We have found [Col. 0082B] the way; let us run by it, if we wish to return to our homeland by the straight path. For he runs by this way who keeps Christ’s commandments: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbour as yourself.” This he commands; this is sufficient for you to keep. Seek no more: this way leads you back to your homeland.

### IV.

“And when they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph, saying: ‘Arise, take the child and his mother, flee into Egypt, and remain there until I tell you; for Herod will seek the child in order to destroy him.’” [Note: [Col. 0082D] This is a homily ascribed to Emesenus, on the Nativity of the Innocents, p. 23, with some additions at the beginning and end.]

For how could Christ have been presented in the Temple at Jerusalem when the days of purification were completed, if he fled into Egypt immediately after the Magi departed? [Note: [Col. 0082D] On this question see Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, book II, chapter 5; among later writers, Jansenius, chapter 11, Maldonatus, à Lapide, etc.] Or perhaps did the Magi remain so long in Bethlehem [Col. 0082C] that Joseph returned from Jerusalem after the purification together with the child and his mother?

But it seems better to me that it should be stated thus: “When they had departed,” after some time had elapsed and all that was required by the Law had been fulfilled, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph, saying: “Arise, take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt.” For everything was still peaceful; Herod, still awaiting the Magi, had not yet disclosed the wickedness of his heart. Therefore they went safely to Jerusalem to fulfil the commands of the Law. Then they were ordered to flee into Egypt, where Abraham, Jacob, and the children of Israel had sojourned.

For the prophet foretold this, saying: “Behold, the Lord shall ascend upon [Col. 0082D] a light cloud and shall enter Egypt” (Isaiah XIX, 1), “and all its idols shall fall.” The light cloud, unburdened by the weight of any corruption, is the Virgin Mary, who carried Christ into Egypt so that light might shine in darkness and the people who sat in [Col. 0083A] darkness might see the light.

“He arose, took the child and his mother by night, departed into Egypt, and remained there until the death of Herod.” Behold, Christ flees, and flees at night, so that flight—which is difficult in itself—might be made more difficult by the darkness of night. If Christ fled Herod, how much more ought we to flee the devil and his members? Let no difficulty of journey frighten us, for it is better to be wearied by hard toil than to be killed by enemies; for narrow and strait is the way that leads to life.

Nevertheless, one must neither always flee nor always resist; rather, according to the nature of the time and circumstance, both must be done. For the saints sometimes fled and sometimes willingly met their enemies. Our Savior himself, who commanded us to flee from city to city, [Col. 0083B] though he could himself have fled if he wished, willingly went out to meet his enemies at the time of his Passion. [Note: [Col. 0083D] A true teaching, handed down in word and examples by the Doctors of the Church and holy men. See Augustine, Letter 228 to Honoratus; Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXI, chapter 28; before them Cyprian, Letter 56 to Thibaris; and Athanasius, *Apology concerning Flight*. They both taught and practised what they taught, contrary to what Tertullian, already a Montanist—as Jerome observes in the *Catalogue*—wrote in *On Flight in Persecution*.]

Therefore we ought to flee visible and invisible enemies, not from fear of death, if we judge that it will be just and beneficial, [12] but from fear of sinning.

Why Christ fled into Egypt, the Evangelist adds in these words: “That what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Out of Egypt I called my son.’” For if he had not gone into Egypt, he could not have been called out of Egypt. Thus both the prophecy and the purpose of the prophecy were fulfilled.

“Then Herod, seeing that he had been mocked by the Magi, was exceedingly angry; and sending, he killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem and in all its borders, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had learned from the Magi.” Because [Col. 0083C] Herod had heard from the oracle of the prophets that Christ was to be born in Bethlehem, he killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem and in all its borders, so that, because he could not find the one, he might kill the one together with the rest.

But why from two years old and under? Because, according to the Magi’s answer, [Note: [Col. 0083D] There are various opinions of authors on this subject, which Jansenius explains in chapter 11 of his *Harmony*, and interpreters commonly discuss. Our author’s view is the third in Jansenius’s order. See also Menochius, *On the Life of Christ*, book I, chapter 14, no. 6.] he knew Christ to be of this age. For, occupied with other affairs, when nearly two years had passed and the Magi had not returned to him, he understood that he had been deceived; in great anger he ordered all these boys to be killed.

“Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, saying: ‘A voice was heard in Ramah, much weeping and wailing: Rachel weeping for her children, and she would not be comforted, because they are not.’” Ramah is interpreted “high place.” [Note: [Col. 0083D] Interpreters discuss this passage of Jeremiah at length. Jerome not only interprets *Ramah* so, but thinks that it is here a common noun rather than the name of a place near Gibeah: “When it is said, ‘in Ramah,’ let us not suppose it to be the name of a place beside Gibeah; rather, *Ramah* is interpreted ‘high,’ so that the sense is: ‘A voice was heard on high,’ [Col. 0084D] that is, scattered far and wide.” The Author of the *Imperfect Work*: “Because the cry over the death of the Innocents was being sent into heaven, it was heard on high.” Maldonatus adopted a different interpretation.]
