Therefore that voice is heard in Ramah which, greatly raised by its magnitude, spreads far and wide. For there was much weeping and much wailing where so many mothers, so many parents, so many persons of both sexes, beholding such cruelty, could not restrain their cries even had they wished to do so.

But why is Rachel said to weep for her children, when all these, in the literal sense, were not Rachel’s children but those of her sister Leah? For Judah was the son not of Rachel but of Leah, and this immense slaughter took place in his tribe. But because Rachel is interpreted “sheep” and signifies the holy Church, which imitates the simplicity of a sheep, those who are slaughtered like innocent and voiceless lambs are not undeservedly called Rachel’s children. [Col. 0084B] For whose children are lambs, if not a sheep’s? They are therefore Rachel’s children, since she is the sheep and they are the lambs.

Rachel—that is, the holy Church—continues to weep for her children even to this day, because, although she understands that they go to rest, she nevertheless grieves because they are bodily separated from her. Thus also those grieved to whom the Lord said: “And you indeed now have sorrow; but I shall see you again, and your heart shall rejoice” (John XVI, 22). And although they are far better off than they were—for they are now with God—yet for a time she receives no consolation, because they are not in this life.

### V.

[Note: [Col. 0084D] Matthew II, 19. This Gospel is read on the vigil of the Epiphany, as is also noted at the final edge of the codex. On this passage is a sermon of St. Bruno, published by Marchesius in volume XX of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 1780.]

“But when Herod was dead, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying: ‘Arise, take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel; [Col. 0084C]

for those who sought the child’s life are dead.’ He arose, took the child and his mother, and came into the land of Israel.”

These matters are plain; if they are explained, they can be made more difficult. Christ’s return to his native land admonishes us too to hasten to our own homeland. “But hearing that Archelaus reigned in Judaea in place of Herod his father, he was afraid to go there.” By Judaea he means Jerusalem and the territory surrounding it which was possessed by the tribe of Judah.

The kingdom, then, had been divided and was now ruled by several persons. [Note: [Col. 0084D] From Josephus, *Antiquities* XVII, 10, we learn that, when Herod was near death, he altered the will he had previously made and divided his kingdom. Herod Antipas, whom in the earlier document he had designated successor to the kingdom, he made tetrarch of Galilee and Peraea; he left the kingdom to Archelaus; and he assigned to his son Philip Gaulanitis, Trachonitis, Batanaea, and Paneas with the title of tetrarchy. But since, even by Herod’s own will, Augustus’ consent was required, Archelaus sailed to him. At last Augustus did not indeed honor Archelaus with the title of king, [Col. 0085C] but granted him half of the dominion which had belonged to Herod and made him ethnarch, [Col. 0085D] promising to declare him king if he showed virtue worthy of a king. Judaea and Idumaea fell to him, and, besides these, Samaria, including the cities of Strato’s Tower, Sebaste, Joppa, and Jerusalem. Augustus detached Gaza, Gadara, and Hippos—cities of Greek constitution—from the kingdom and attached them to Syria. Augustus divided the other half of Herod’s dominion between Herod’s other two sons: Galilee and Peraea fell to Herod Antipas; Batanaea with Trachonitis, Auranitis, and a certain portion of Zenodorus’s domain fell to Philip. So Josephus, chapter 11, no. 4. See Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, book II, chapters 7–8.]

“And being warned in a dream, he withdrew into the parts of Galilee; and coming, he lived in a city called [Col. 0085A] Nazareth, so that what had been spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘For he shall be called a Nazarene.’” Christ was called a Nazarene from Nazareth; but a Nazirite [Note: [Col. 0085D] Jerome on this passage: “Nazirite is interpreted ‘holy.’ But all Scripture declares that the Lord was to be holy.”] because he was consecrated to God from infancy.

Nevertheless, since *Nazaraeus* also means “pure,” and Nazareth “purity,” Christ may appropriately be called both Nazirite and Nazarene from Nazareth. For from what, if not from purity, is the term “pure” derived? Christ is rightly called a Nazirite, because not only is he himself pure, but apart from him nothing is pure.

VI. [Chapter III.] Now in those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judaea, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” “In those days,” he says, in which Jesus was dwelling at Nazareth; not, however, in those in which he had returned from Egypt [Col. 0085B], did John the Baptist begin to preach. For Luke the Evangelist says that John began to preach in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar.

[Note: [Col. 0085D] Chrysostom, Homily 10, and other interpreters generally make the same point.]

But where was he preaching? In the wilderness of Judaea. And what did he say? “Repent.” Why this? Because the kingdom of heaven has drawn near. We see, then, that Judaea is called a wilderness; for the Lord himself, signifying this, said: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXII, 58).

[Note: [Col. 0085D] Bede on this passage: “He says ‘in the wilderness of Judaea,’ because, just as it had been prophesied to them beforehand, ‘Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate’ [Col. 0086C], so in John’s days Judaea was in large measure desolate . . . . Mystically, moreover, John [Col. 0086D] signifies the Saviour, who preached to deserted Judaea, that is, Judaea abandoned by God because of transgression of the law.” The same mystical meaning had been given by St Ambrose, Book II, on Luke chapter 3, who wished it to be called desolate “because it was not yet cultivated by any works of a people gathering together.” Thus Pseudo-Chrysostom, Imperfect Work, Homily 3, etc.]

For a wilderness is not a dwelling-place of human beings, but of wild beasts and irrational animals. For if the Jews had possessed reason, they would not have killed their Lord. Indeed, unless they were beasts, they would not be called lions, dragons, dogs, and unicorns. John therefore preached in the wilderness [Col. 0085C], because he was calling wild beasts and brutes to faith. And he said, “Repent,” so that, released from sins, you may be transferred from an earthly kingdom into the kingdom of heaven. For the kingdom of heaven has drawn near, because the King of angels dwells with you and among you. Repent, therefore; cleanse yourselves from sins, that you may be both the kingdom and the people of so great a King.

But who is this John, who preaches so well? For this is he of whom it was spoken through Isaiah the prophet, saying: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight” (Isa. XL, 3). John is called a voice because Christ is called the Word.

[Note: [Col. 0086D] Thus Bede: “He is named a voice because he preceded the Word.” See Pseudo-Chrysostom, Imperfect Work.]

For just as John precedes Christ [Col. 0086A], so a voice precedes a word. For as soon as any sound whatsoever proceeds from the speaker’s mouth, it is a voice; but it is not yet a word, since every word signifies something. The voice therefore comes first, the word follows; rightly, then, John is called the Lord’s forerunner, since in being born, in preaching, in dying, and in the very designation of his name, he precedes Christ.

Finally, the Word of God that is in my breast cannot be understood or pass to you unless it has the garment of a voice. Thus the Word of God does not need the garment of a voice in order to be understood, just as formerly it needed the garment of flesh in order to be seen. Hence “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us.”

But what is it to prepare the way of the Lord and make his paths straight, except to love, hold fast to, pursue, and embrace with all one’s strength the virtues and good works? John himself wore a garment of camel’s hair and a leather belt around his loins; and his food was locusts and wild honey. By this blessed John shows most plainly how utterly he regarded this world and all its allurements as nothing, since he used such very cheap clothing and food. For he sought only what was necessary for this life, since he had resolved to live in this manner. Those follow his example who say: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these.”

[Note: [Col. 0086D] 1 Tim. VI, 8: “But having food and coverings, with these we are content.”]

Moreover, because he preached repentance, he provided in himself a rule for how penitents ought to live. The locust is a clean animal and is not forbidden by the Law [Col. 0086C], although food of this kind is not now in use.

[Note: [Col. 0086D] See Bochart, *De animalibus sacrae Scripturae*, part 1, book I, chapter 5. Chrysostom discusses John’s food and clothing in Homily 10; St Ambrose, Book III on Luke I.]

Then Jerusalem went out to him, and all Judaea, and the whole region around the Jordan; and they were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins. But seeing many Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come?”

[Note: [Col. 0086D] “From the wrath to come,” Vulgate; “from coming wrath,” Old Latin.]

For this is said to be the nature of vipers:

[Note: [Col. 0086D] On this matter see Pseudo-Chrysostom, Imperfect Work, Homily 3, and Bede on this passage.]

when the female conceives, she kills the male; and when she gives birth, she herself is likewise killed by her young. For they do not wait to emerge according to nature’s accustomed order, but violently burst forth after tearing open their mother’s womb. The viper, therefore, is the Synagogue,

[Note: [Col. 0086D] Bede interprets this concerning the Pharisees and Sadducees.]

which, after her husband—our Saviour, for he too is called a serpent—came to her [Col. 0087A], after he impregnated her with his seed and poured into her the whole seed-field of Gospel preaching, rose up against him like a viper, venomous and impious, and killed him.

[Note: [Col. 0087D] See Num. XXI; John III, 14; and the interpreters on those passages.]

But her children are these persons, who flee their mother’s wickedness, come to repentance, and strive to emerge from her impious womb. Her children also were the Apostles,

[Note: [Col. 0087D] Ambrose also understands this in a favourable sense, in the work cited.]

who, after their mother had been put to death, came forth from her womb and preached the Gospel throughout the world. The Apostle too, coming forth joyfully from this womb, says: “But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace,” and the rest (Gal. I, 15). They, indeed, killed the Synagogue, because they sentenced her to perpetual death [Col. 0087B]. Thus good children arise from an impious mother; to them it is now said, “Brood of vipers,” but now unlike the nature of vipers: “Who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come?”

“Produce therefore fruit worthy of repentance.” For that repentance is without fruit which manifests itself in no good work, whatever its character. Just as good trees are commended by their fruit, so those who repent worthily are commended by good works. For who would say that one repents who still does the very thing for which he pretends to repent?

[Note: [Col. 0087D] Chrysostom discusses repentance of this kind in Homily 10 on this passage.]

“And do not wish to say within yourselves, ‘We have Abraham for our father.’” Such a thought produces false and useless security. For it does not suffice that you are Abraham’s children unless you perform Abraham’s works and keep his faith. “For I tell you that the Lord is able to raise up children to Abraham from these stones” [Col. 0087C]. Thus it is clear that Abraham’s children are called such not according to the flesh,

[Note: [Col. 0087D] See Paul, Romans chapters II, III, etc.]

but according to faith. For if they were called such according to the flesh, those not from his flesh could not be called his children. Children of Abraham are raised up from stones

[Note: [Col. 0087D] This is another interpretation found in Chrysostom, in the work cited, and also in Jerome, Ambrose, Pseudo-Chrysostom, Bede, etc.]

because the Gentiles, formerly stony, hard, and fruitless, were made Abraham’s children by imitating his faith and works.

“For now the axe has been placed at the root of the tree.” The axe is Christ;

[Note: [Col. 0087D] For Jerome, the axe is the preaching of the Gospel.]

the tree is the Synagogue. It is therefore near to being cut down, since the axe has already been placed at its root. Yet he still waits to see whether it will produce good fruit. This was signified by that fig tree

[Note: [Col. 0087D] Ambrose, in the work cited, applies this to the present passage.]

which the Lord cursed because it had no fruit and withered [Col. 0087D]. Therefore, he who did not spare the whole tree, how will he spare one branch? Do not then say within yourself, “I am Abraham’s son”; instead, perform his works, lest you be cut off from his root [Col. 0088A] together with the rest. For every tree that does not produce good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire. What this tree, this fruit, and this fire signify is plain. For of this fire it is said: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. LXIV).

“I indeed baptize you in water unto repentance. But he who is to come after me is stronger than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry; he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.”

[Note: [Col. 0087D] Cyprian, Book I of the *Testimonies*, and manuscript codices cited by Sabatier, have “sandals.” See Jerome and Bede on this passage. See also Du Cange, *Glossarium*, under *Calcia*, *Calciare*, etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0088D] See Calmet’s Dissertation before the commentary on Mark, “On Baptism,” article 2, concerning John’s baptism.]

Blessed John baptized only with water, because his baptism could wash the flesh from filth but could not cleanse the soul from sins. For it was a shadow and figure of a better baptism. He baptized unto repentance—that is, in order that they might repent [Col. 0088B]—so that, as he washed them outwardly with water, they might wash themselves inwardly by repentance, and so be ready, when Christ came, to receive his baptism.

But what are Christ’s sandals, which the holy man says he is unworthy to carry? To carry Christ’s sandals is to preach the mysteries of his Incarnation. In a manner, divinity clothed itself with sandals, because the Son of God assumed the dead flesh of our flesh. For though we have other garments made from various materials, we have sandals only of skin, received from flesh.

Christ baptized in the Holy Spirit and fire—that is, in the power of the Holy Spirit, by which sins are at once removed and burned away. For one and the same power belongs to Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. But because the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, the Lord Jesus is rightly said to baptize in the Holy Spirit, because in this one Person the power of the whole Trinity is briefly displayed. For he who said, “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit” (John III, 5), is the same who said, “Baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19).

If blessed John had said, “He will baptize you in himself,” when he said, “He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit,” it would indeed have been obscure, but it would nevertheless have referred to him. Likewise, if he had said, “He will baptize you in the Father,” this too would again have been obscure, although the operation of all three is one. He therefore rightly said: “He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit” [Col. 0088D], that is, in the power common to Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0088D] Jerome explains the words “he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire”: “either because the Holy Spirit is fire, or because in the present we are baptized in the Spirit and in the future in fire.” Chrysostom interprets baptism in the Holy Spirit as the abundance of grace, and thinks that the mention of fire is added to express the energy of grace. Bede expounds it as grace and remission of sins, or as the fire of tribulations. Others differently.]

“His winnowing-fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing-floor [Col. 0089A] and gather his wheat into the granary; but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire.” For by the winnowing-fan, by which grains are separated from chaff, what else is meant but the balance and examination of his judgment?

[Note: [Col. 0089D] Jerome, Ambrose, and Bede also explain this of the future judgment and eternal punishment or reward; Pseudo-Chrysostom, Imperfect Work, Homily 3, of the temptations and calamities of this life.]

And by the threshing-floor, what but the Church? By the wheat, what but the good? By the chaff, what but the wicked? By the granary, what but the heavenly homeland? Therefore, after our Saviour, by the examination of his judgment, separates the good from the bad and the sheep from the goats, the whole holy Church, freed and cleansed from the fellowship of the unrighteous, will then invite the good into the kingdom, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” But what will he say to the chaff—that is, to the unrighteous? “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire.”

Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan [Col. 0089B], to John, to be baptized by him. When it says “then,”

[Note: [Col. 0089D] See Bede on this passage and Jansenius, chapter 14.]

it must be understood as when John was preaching and baptizing such things, not when he began to preach. For each had already entered his thirtieth year when the Lord came for baptism. Jesus is baptized not for himself but for us.

[Note: [Col. 0089D] “For a threefold reason,” says Jerome on this passage, “the Saviour received baptism from John: first, that because he had been born a man, he might fulfil all righteousness and the humility of the Law; second, that by his baptism he might approve John’s baptism; third, that by sanctifying the waters of the Jordan, the Holy Spirit’s coming upon the washing of believers might be shown through the descent of the dove.” Bede says nearly the same. See Maldonatus, Jansenius, etc.]

He washes the waters and sanctifies them by his touch; he is not himself washed by the waters. There the old circumcision perished; there the renewal of new faith began. There John first learned to baptize, where he came to know, hear, and see the mysteries of the whole Trinity.

Then John, terrified and trembling to approach the Lord, resisted him, saying: “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” But Jesus answered and said: “Allow it now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness.” “You,” he says, “are greater; you are Lord [Col. 0089C]; I am lesser and a servant. I must decrease, but you must increase. Why, then, do you come to me? Rather, I ought to have gone to you. You are pure and cleanse all things. Not you by me, but I by you, ought to be cleansed and baptized.”

But he says: “Allow it now. What I am doing is a mystery. While I am baptized, you too are baptized in me, because you are a member of him who is baptized. For thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness: setting an end and limit to the old things, while giving an example and rule to the new.” Then he allowed him. What does “he allowed him” mean? He resisted no longer, contradicted no longer; rather, he consented and permitted him to act according to his will.

[Note: [Col. 0089D] Here begins the homily attributed to Eusebius of Emesa, First Sunday in Lent [Col. 0090D], p. 52. All the following homilies, as we have said repeatedly, have not Eusebius of Emesa but St Bruno of Asti as their author.]

And when Jesus had been baptized, he immediately came up from the water; and behold, the heavens were opened to him [Col. 0089D], and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him; and behold, a voice from heaven saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

Why are the heavens opened when the Lord has been baptized? This is a great mystery, and it prefigures great joy for those who are baptized. They had formerly been closed; before baptism no one entered there. But now they are opened—yet opened to the baptized. For the Lord himself says (John III, 5): “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

[Note: [Col. 0090D] Chrysostom and Bede explain this in the same way, concerning the effect of baptism.]

He saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, not because the Holy Spirit was incarnate in a dove; for the Son alone was incarnate. Rather, the Spirit of God chose to show himself in a dove. For the Holy Spirit is also in us; the Apostle says (1 Cor. III, 16): “Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Holy Spirit [Col. 0090B] dwells in you?”

[Note: [Col. 0090D] The Vulgate reads “Spirit of God.”]

Yet the Holy Spirit is not incarnate in us. But that voice heard from heaven—whose could it have been but the Father’s? For who else could say, “This is my beloved Son”? Yet let him who can explain how a bodily and perceptible voice proceeds from the invisible and incorporeal one.

God the Father is pleased in his beloved Son because he begot such a Son ineffably and without beginning before the ages. For, if it is fitting to say so, we too are pleased with ourselves in our works when we do something that appears worthy of praise. Most plainly in this passage the Trinity is shown and is wholly perceived personally: the Son is manifested in the man, the Holy Spirit in the dove, and the Father in the testimony of his voice.

[Note: [Col. 0090D] “The mystery of the Trinity is displayed in the baptism: the Lord is baptized; the Spirit descends . . . . the Father’s voice is heard,” Jerome.]

VII. [CHAPTER IV.] Then Jesus was led into the wilderness by the Spirit, to be tempted by the devil. And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry. [Col. 0090C]

The chief holy doctors of the Church explain that the Lord Jesus was led into the wilderness by his own Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0090D] Jerome: “There is no doubt that it was by the Holy Spirit.” So Chrysostom, Gregory, Homily 16 on the Gospels, Bede, etc. See Maldonatus.]

Yet if they had explained that he was led also by another spirit, this would not have been unfitting, since Luke the Evangelist plainly says that he was not merely taken up but led by the devil into Jerusalem and onto a very high mountain. If it is not unfitting that there and there he was led by another spirit, why should it seem unfitting that he was also led by another into the wilderness?

[Note: [Col. 0090D] See Calmet on this passage.]

But whether he was led by his own spirit or by another, we must consider why he allowed himself to be tempted by the devil. For our Saviour does nothing without usefulness [Col. 0090D] and reason; and especially there we must seek the reason, where he does something—if indeed he does such a thing—that appears unworthy of his majesty. For who would not shudder to hear [Col. 0091A] that divine power is either led or tempted by the devil?

Yet if he is led of his own accord—or rather, led at his own command, since for him to will is to command—this is not so much dreadful as it is to be wondered at and investigated for what it signifies. For who does not know that Pilate and the Jews who killed him were not only members of the devil, but also his servants? And indeed, an injury suffered from someone’s servants seems to us greater than one suffered from their master himself. Therefore, it is no more dreadful that our Saviour is led and tempted by the devil than that he is killed and scourged by the Jews.

For as Christ is killed not for himself but for us, so he is tempted not for himself but for us. He died for us because his death was necessary for us; for unless he himself had died, we would not live. He died, therefore, that we might live. Likewise, he was tempted for us, because his temptation provides us with a twofold benefit. First, that we may know how we ought to answer our tempters and those who wrong us. Second, that we may place confidence in none of our own strength or wisdom; because our enemy the devil, who presumed to tempt our Lord himself, continually prowls about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour.

[Note: [Col. 0091D] See Chrysostom, Homily 13, and among later writers Cornelius a Lapide.]

Having given the reason for the temptation, let us also consider the mystery of its meaning. Although the devil tempts human beings in many ways, he attacks them chiefly by these three temptations: appetite for food, vain glory, and the exaltation of honour and riches. He strives [Col. 0091C] to lead those whom he tempts to high places and raise them aloft, so that, just as he fell when raised up, he may cause others to fall by exalting them. For he is the one who says:

[Note: [Col. 0091D] Isa. XIV, 15: “I will ascend into heaven,” etc.]

“I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I will exalt my throne; I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the North, and I will be like the Most High.”

He therefore leads some into the wilderness;

[Note: [Col. 0091D] See St Gregory, *Morals*, Book XIV, chapter 7; Ambrose, Book III on Luke; Chrysostom, Homily 13; Pseudo-Chrysostom, Imperfect Work, Homily 5.]

he places others upon the pinnacle of the Temple; and still others he raises onto a very high mountain. He leads them into the wilderness when he turns human minds away from love of the heavenly homeland and divine contemplation, and makes them think of earthly and transitory things; for whatever is far from God is a wilderness.

But because merely to think such things is not a great sin unless delight follows the thought [Col. 0091D], he places before the mind varied delicacies of food, so that, just as he deceived the first human being through intemperance of appetite, he may likewise deceive the rest. For all kinds of food are signified by bread, according to the saying:

[Note: [Col. 0091D] Luke XIV, 1: “And it came to pass when he entered,” [Col. 0092D] etc. See Calmet on this passage in Luke.]

“Jesus entered on the Sabbath into the house of a certain ruler of the Pharisees to eat bread.”

Therefore, when these things come into your mind and, forgetting what belongs to the soul, you begin to think only of things in which the flesh delights, grows fat, and becomes proud [Col. 0092A], remember that you are in the wilderness, that the enemy is tempting you, and that he sets his breads before you. Answer, therefore, as your Lord answered when he too was tempted by him: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.” The body is nourished by bread; the soul is refreshed by the word of God.

[Note: [Col. 0092D] “Therefore, if anyone does not feed upon the word of God, that person does not live,” as Jerome infers from this. On these temptations of Jesus Christ, see St Leo, Sermon 3 on Lent; Ambrose, Book I, *On Cain and Abel*, chapter 5, etc.]

Both, therefore, are good; but to desire one excessively, to seek it too delightfully, and to have no moderation in receiving it, is evil. From this arise all luxury and every wantonness of the flesh. For this reason that rich man who feasted splendidly every day, because he had received his good things in his life, now suffers every evil after his death.

Let us now consider those whom the devil places upon the pinnacle of the Temple, in whom the order of clerics seems to me especially to be signified [Col. 0092B].

[Note: [Col. 0092D] An especially elegant and noteworthy passage.]

For those are raised by the devil above the pinnacle of the Temple who, thinking themselves fit to govern the Church of God, strive by payment, petitions, and every means they can to become prelates and bishops in the Church. Nor would Christ otherwise have allowed himself to be led there by the devil, except because by this action he wished to signify such Christians marked with his name. And rightly, indeed, when he permitted himself to be tempted by the devil, he assumed in himself the persons of all, both good and evil, by signifying them.

When he says, “If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down,” what else does he seem to say but this: “You have already been counted among God’s sons; you have already been ordained bishop; you already appear to those who do not know you to be what you are not. Therefore do something [Col. 0092C] by which you may be praised, deemed glorious, and appear great before men. Cast yourself down.” For persons of this kind always cast themselves down, because, seeking only riches, glory, and dignities, they become worse every day.

Yet the most gracious Lord does not disdain to teach even these how they ought to answer their tempter—if only they are willing to hear not the tempting devil, but themselves giving saving counsel. For he says: “Again it is written: You shall not tempt the Lord your God.” The Lord gave this answer when the devil led him above the pinnacle of the Temple and said to him: “If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down.”

Likewise, therefore, since you understand that you have been improperly ordained over the Church of God, and placed there not by God but by the devil, and set above others [Col. 0092D]—he who also daily says to you, “Cast yourself down,” and strives daily to cast you headlong and destroy you—remember this testimony, which the Lord says not to the devil but to you and all people. Answer, therefore: “I will not believe you; I will not cast myself down. Instead, I will obey the Scripture that says to me: ‘You shall not tempt the Lord your God.’”

For how does one not tempt the Lord who retains and possesses, against the ordinances of the canons and the will of God, the Church which he has invaded secretly and by robbery [Col. 0093A]? He greatly tempts God who persists in the sin through which he does not doubt that he is perishing.

With these matters thus set forth, let us also consider those who are led by the devil onto a very high mountain, to whom he shows all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and promises them what he has shown if they fall down and worship him. Whom else should we understand by these but emperors, kings, dukes, princes, and the other powerful persons of this world,

[Note: [Col. 0093D] So too St Gregory, *Morals*, Book XVIII, chapter 36, and Book XXX, chapter 26.]

whom the devil leads and raises onto a high mountain—that is, to the exaltation of these very offices—through murders, perjuries, thefts, robberies, betrayals, frauds, and other such things? These, indeed, worship, serve, and venerate him; they follow him as if he were God [Col. 0093B], and after him they plunge into darkness. For they do not hear what the Lord Jesus says: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.”

Since, then, we have spoken of those led into the wilderness, those placed above the pinnacle of the Temple, and those raised very high above the mountain, let us return to the beginning and explain why our Saviour fasted forty days and forty nights.

[Note: [Col. 0093D] On this matter see Cornelius a Lapide at length, and other interpreters. See St John Chrysostom, Homily 1 on Genesis, no. 3.]

For it may be asked why he fasted neither more nor less, and why it pleased him to fast for this number of days. For we read that Moses and Elijah fasted just as long.

[Note: [Col. 0093D] See in St Basil, in the homily on the Forty Martyrs, their prayer. St Augustine, Sermon 51, no. 32; Sermon 125, no. 9; Sermon 205, no. 1; Sermon 264, no. 5; Sermon 270, no. 3, etc. In Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 16, he also expounds certain mysteries of this number. See St Gregory, Homily 12 on the Gospels, no. 5. Peter Bongo wrote on the mysteries of numbers.]

For the number forty consists of four and ten: four tens, or ten fours, make forty. By four [Col. 0093C] the New Testament is signified, because it consists in four Gospels. By ten the Old is signified, which is contained in the ten commandments of the Law. Thus to fast forty days is to keep the precepts of both Testaments. For one fasts forty days who keeps himself free and fasting from all things which both Testaments forbid one to do; so that, just as the flesh fasts outwardly from foods, the mind may fast inwardly from vices.

For Scripture says: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not covet your neighbour’s property,” and similar things. These are the foods from which both Testaments command us to abstain. Therefore, one who mortifies the flesh by fasts does not fast well unless he inwardly keeps himself fasting from these foods [Col. 0093D]. Let us therefore fast with the flesh, and let us fast also with the mind. We know the foods from which we ought to abstain.

The Lord Jesus therefore fasted forty days [Col. 0094A] and forty nights, so that in fasting from food he might signify for us the fast of the body, and in the number of days show the fast of the heart.

VIII.

[Note: [Col. 0093D] This is a homily falsely attributed to Eusebius of Emesa, for the feast of St Andrew [Col. 0094D], p. 199, this section 8 and the following section 9.]

But when Jesus heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee; and, leaving the city of Nazareth, he came and dwelt in maritime Capernaum, in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali, that what had been spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: “The land of Zebulun and Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles: the people who sat in darkness saw a great light; and upon those sitting in the region of the shadow of death light arose.”

It is clear, therefore, that the Lord withdrew into Galilee, leaving his own city Nazareth, not from fear of anything, but that the prophecy might be fulfilled which had foretold that he would come into the territories of Zebulun and Naphtali. For Isaiah says thus (Isa. IX, 1): “At the first time the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali was lightened.” But why “at the first time”? Because, immediately at the beginning of his preaching [Col. 0094B], before he had chosen the Apostles, he came there, called Peter and Andrew, James and John from their fishing, and commanded them to come after him. Thus, at the first time, the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali was lightened from the burden of its sins.

[Note: [Col. 0094D] St Jerome explains the prophet’s passage in almost the same words, Book III on Isaiah.]

It is called the way of the sea because it had harbours and was exposed to shipwrecks.

[Note: [Col. 0094D] Jerome, in the same place: “Here he calls the Sea of Gennesaret a lake, formed by the inflow of the Jordan; on its shore are situated Capernaum, Tiberias, Bethsaida, and Chorazin, in which region the Lord dwelt especially.”]

Hence Jacob also says in his blessings:

[Note: [Col. 0094D] Gen. LIX, 13. See St Ambrose, *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*, chapter 5.]

“Zebulun shall dwell on the shore of the sea, at the station of ships, extending as far as Sidon.”

But why is he said to have withdrawn into Galilee, when Luke the Evangelist [Col. 0094C] shows Nazareth to be in Galilee, saying: “The angel Gabriel was sent from God into a city of Galilee called Nazareth” (Luke I, 26)? Earlier in this Gospel it is likewise read that Joseph, warned in a dream, “came into the parts of Galilee and dwelt in the city Nazareth” (Matt. II, 22). From this it is understood that Nazareth was situated not in the heart of the province of Galilee but on its outer borders.

[Note: [Col. 0094D] See Jerome, *On Places*; Bonfrerius, *Onomasticon*; Reland, *Palestine*, p. 905.]

He withdrew into Galilee, therefore—that is, into the interior of the province itself. The people of those Gentiles who dwelt there in darkness and did not possess the light of truth, because they did not understand the Law spiritually, then saw a great light. Truly a great light; for it is that light which illumines every person coming into this world [Col. 0094D], and whoever follows it does not walk in darkness but shall have the light of life.

“And upon those sitting in the region of the shadow of death light arose.” Those sit beneath the shadow of death who do not know the tree of life [Col. 0095A]. It is an evil shadow, cooling in such a way as to kill; so dark that it wholly removes light. Unless this light had shone upon them, they would alike have lacked life and light, because both the shadow removed their light and death took away their life. The light therefore came; the Lord Jesus came, who at once enlightened and healed them.

Hence it follows: “From that time Jesus began to preach and say: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.’” By these words our Saviour both enlightens and heals his hearers; for Christ’s preaching is both light and life. But where is it necessary to kindle light except in darkness? To whom is medicine necessary except to the sick? A soul in sins is both sick and without light. Repentance, therefore, is given to it, by whose remedy it is healed [Col. 0095B] and enlightened.

The Lord rightly begins his preaching with repentance, since he came to heal and enlighten by this one singular remedy the minds of human beings, weak and blinded by the mists of error. John the Baptist also took the same beginning for his preaching. Unless this medicine comes first, no other remedy can avail to help sick minds. For although little children cannot know repentance, the faith and repentance of those presenting them is accepted on their behalf.

IX. But as He was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, He saw two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen; and He said to them: “Come after Me, and I will make you become fishers of men.” But they, leaving their nets, followed Him. [Note: On the repeated calling of these men, see Chrysostom, Homily 14, and Bede.]

Behold, the Lord calls His first disciples from the sea, because through them He had purposed to call many others from the stormy bitterness of this world to faith. Thus, since they are called by the Lord from the sea, they too may learn to rescue endangered souls from the shipwreck of this world and from the rising storms of vices. And just as they were brothers according to the flesh, so they may teach others also to be brothers in faith and love. For we are all brothers, born from one mother, the Church, and children of one Father. Hence we all say together: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. 6:9). For since He is the common Father of all, He is invoked in common by all.

Moreover, the Lord calls fishermen because He needed such men—accustomed to waters and skilled both in fishing and in baptizing. Therefore He does not command them to change their trade, but promises that they will be fishers in a far better fishery and of another kind of fish. [Col. 0095D] [Note: Hence, no doubt, Chrysostom calls bringing human beings over to piety *sagēneuein*, “to catch with a dragnet”; and Cyril calls the multitude of nations not yet brought to God *tōn ethnōn hē plēthys asagēneutos*, “the multitude of nations not caught with the dragnet.”]

He says to them: “Come after Me, and I will make you become fishers of men.” For unless human beings were fish, the apostles could not become fishers of men. [Col. 0096A] [Note: It is well known that Christians were called fishes and little fishes. Thus Tertullian, *On Baptism*, ch. 1: “We little fishes are born in water according to our Jesus Christ.” And the word *ichthys*, “fish,” was a kind of Christian token inscribed on so many monuments of ancient Christians. There is an erudite dissertation in Italian by the distinguished Anselmo Costadoni, *On the Fish as a Symbol of Jesus Christ*.] Such fish are worthy of God’s banquet. Such fish swim in the river of baptism. Such fish are caught by the hook of faith and by the nets of holy preaching.

They are therefore transferred from sea to sea, because from the Sea of Galilee they are sent into “this great and wide sea, where are creeping things without number, small and great animals” [Ps. 103:25], by which all classes of human beings are signified.

But what does it mean to say, “Come after Me”? For to go after Christ is to follow His footsteps, imitate His works, and retain the same patience and humility. It is not enough for us to go after Jesus merely with our feet, unless we also follow Him with mind and love. It is worthwhile, moreover, to consider [Col. 0096B] how great was the obedience of these blessed brothers, who immediately left their nets and followed Him. Hence Simon is not undeservedly interpreted as “obedient” [Note: See here Cornelius a Lapide.], while Andrew is interpreted as “answering” [Note: See Andrew of Sarrassey, *On the Glory of St Andrew*, ch. 1, p. 5. Bede also gives an interpretation of these names.] or “handsome.”

And going on from there, He saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in a boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and He called them. But they immediately, leaving their nets and their father, followed Him. Their obedience is found to be no less than that of the former two [Note: Chrysostom, Homily 14, praises their faith and obedience.], because at the sound of a single command they left not only their nets but also their father, and followed Christ the Lord. These too, like the others, were not only fishermen but brothers.

O blessed fellowship of service, gathered from brothers, all of whom have one heart and one soul; concerning whom it had also been said through the Prophet: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 32:1).

But what is it to mend nets, except to explain and restore by sound understanding the sayings of the holy Scriptures, torn apart and corrupted by the violence of heretics? For these four Gospels are like four fishing nets; likewise the five books of Moses and all the books of the prophets. In short, there are as many nets as there are volumes. By these nets Christians are caught; by them all believers are gathered in the Church. “Go,” says the Lord, “into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature. He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16:16). You see, therefore, the fishermen, to whom it is said, “Go into all [Col. 0096D] the world”; you see also the nets—that is, the Gospel—of which it is said, “Preach the Gospel to every creature”; you see also the waters in which the fish are caught—that is, baptism; and you see the fish themselves, namely those who are baptized and believe. It follows:

X. Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom of God, and healing every sickness and every infirmity among the people. This is what we explained above: that in the first period not only was the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali relieved of the burden of sins, but also of bodily sickness. And His fame went throughout all Syria; and they brought to Him all who were ill, and those afflicted [Note: The Vulgate does not have “those afflicted,” nor does the ancient Old Latin version.] with various diseases and seized by torments, those who had demons, lunatics, and paralytics; and He healed them.

Behold how suddenly Christ is made known; behold how suddenly the report and fame of His power fills the land. From every side all the sick and those in ill health are brought to Him, and He, as the true physician, heals every infirmity, inward and [Col. 0097B] outward. For this the prophet foretold, saying [Note: Isaiah 53:4. But A. does not refer this passage of Isaiah to the present matter; rather, Matthew does so at 8:17, after recounting the cures, “that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘He Himself took our infirmities and bore our diseases.’” See Cornelius a Lapide on the passage from Isaiah.]: “Surely He Himself bore our sicknesses, and He Himself carried our infirmities.” And great crowds followed Him from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and from beyond the Jordan.

XI. [CHAPTER V.] [Note: There is a homily attributed to Eusebius of Emesa for the feast of many martyrs, p. 217, with some preliminary material inserted into the text of the preceding section.]

When Jesus saw the crowds, He went up onto the mountain; and when He had sat down, His disciples came to Him. And opening His mouth, He taught them, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

Christ’s ascent onto the mountain signifies that He was about to speak something great. Thus the prophet also says [Note: Isaiah 40:9. On the various meanings of “mountain” in Scripture, see St Gregory, beginning of Book 33 of the *Morals*; St Ambrose, Book 8 on Luke, ch. 4; St Bernard, Homily 1 for the feast of All Saints; Jerome: “The Lord ascends the mountains in order to draw the crowds with Him to higher things”; and St Ambrose, Book 5 on Luke 6:17.]: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion.” There He teaches the disciples, whom He knew to possess greater understanding. But what does He say? [Note: On these matters see St Augustine, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*; St Bernard, *Various Sermons*, 66; and others.] “Blessed are the poor in spirit.”

He does not say simply, “Blessed are the poor,” because neither are all poor persons blessed nor all rich persons unhappy. For we see many poor persons who are thieves, murderers, adulterers, perjurers, and traitors; they are miserable in this life and will be unhappy after this life. Yet we read that many rich persons pleased the Lord by holy conduct.

Blessed, therefore, are the poor in spirit—but not poor in every spirit; for there is a good spirit and also an evil spirit. Just as those who are poor in an evil spirit are blessed, so those who are rich in a good spirit are also blessed. Blessed, then, are the poor in spirit, and blessed are the rich in spirit. There is a spirit of pride, [Col. 0097D] a spirit of fornication, a spirit of discord, and many other spirits; all who are poor in these are blessed. Blessed also are those who are rich in the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord [Col. 0098A].

But why are they blessed? Because theirs is the kingdom of heaven. “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.” For who are the meek but the patient and humble? Every virtue perishes without patience. Hence the Lord says: “By your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21:19). Therefore, whoever is impatient can possess neither his own soul nor his own earth. How can one possess one’s soul who is unable to restrain the rage and anger of one’s own mind? And how can one possess one’s earth who cannot restrain his eyes from unlawful sight, his ears from unlawful hearing, his nostrils from unlawful smell, his mouth from unlawful taste, or his hands from unlawful touch?

Yet by this earth we may understand the land of the living; and thus the meek possess no less than the poor in spirit possess, because, although the latter possess heaven and the former earth, nevertheless the same thing is signified by heaven and by earth. When Christ our Lord promises such things to His faithful, does He not seem to you to be seated upon a mountain and in royal exaltation?

It follows: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” What if they mourn over the loss of temporal possessions? What if they mourn over injuries inflicted upon them? For we see some weeping because they cannot avenge injuries done to them; yet when they avenge them, they become not blessed but miserable. Thus it should be said: Blessed are those who mourn the sins that they have committed; blessed are those who weep over their own sins and those of others. Thus Samuel mourned for Saul all the days of his life [Col. 0098C] (1 Sam. 15:35). David too was blessed because he repented and wept; for he says: “My tears were my bread day and night” (Ps. 41:3). Our Savior Himself also wept at the death of Lazarus (John 11:35). Seeing likewise that Jerusalem was to perish, He wept over its miseries (Luke 19:41). The apostle Peter also wept and did not lose blessedness. Blessed, therefore, are those who mourn in this way, because they shall be comforted with eternal joy.

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness.” Those hunger and thirst for righteousness who delight so greatly in observing righteousness as though they were refreshed by splendid banquets. Hence the Psalmist says: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at every time” (Ps. 105:3). Let kings and princes hear this; let the powerful and judges hear it; and let us too hear it—I mean we bishops and priests. Let us always remember this chapter, without which we cannot properly treat the remaining chapters.

But note that not only those who do righteousness, but also those who hunger and thirst for it—that is, who desire to do it—are blessed, even if they cannot do what they desire; for, so far as lies within them, they do what they desire. And these shall be filled when all their desires are fulfilled; for as the body is filled with food, so the soul is filled with its desire.

“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” Immediately after righteousness He placed mercy. Thus the Psalmist says: “I will sing to You, O Lord, of mercy and judgment” (Ps. 100:1). Righteousness is good, and mercy is good also. The one has its place, and the other has its place. Nor does righteousness perish if it is moderated by mercy in certain cases. Mercy is [Note: St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, II–II, q. 30, art. 1, from Augustine: “Mercy is compassion in our heart for another’s misery, by which, certainly, we are compelled, if we can, to give aid.”] an affection of the mind by which we are grieved [Col. 0099B] at another’s evils; envy is its opposite, through which a person is grieved at another’s good things. Whether, then, we spare those who sin against us, assist the miserable and needy, or bring those who err back to the way of truth, it is mercy. But whoever has no mercy shall find no mercy: “for with the same measure with which we have measured, it shall be measured back to us” (Luke 6:38).

It follows: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” For “from the heart,” as the Lord says, “come evil thoughts, thefts, murders, perjuries, adulteries, false testimonies” (Matt. 15:19), and the like; these are what defile a human being. Such a heart, however, is not pure. For if it were pure, it would not defile the whole person with its filth. Therefore that heart is pure [Col. 0099C] from which such things do not proceed. Hence David asks the Lord, saying: “Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within my inward parts” (Ps. 50:11). For if the heart is pure from wicked thoughts, the whole person will be pure from iniquities. For sins arise there and take root there; if they are cut off there, there is nowhere for them to grow.

Hence it is written: “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash your little ones against the rock” (Ps. 136:12). For this reason priests are forbidden to let their hair grow. But how the pure in heart see God, or with what eyes they see Him, may be questioned, and is not easily resolved. Nevertheless, the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face [Col. 0099D] to face. Now I know in part; but then I shall know even as I am known” (1 Cor. 13:12). And the apostle John says: “We know that when He appears, we shall be like Him, because we shall see Him as He is” (1 John 3:2). Great will be that eye which, by the clarity of its sight, shall be able to comprehend Him [Col. 0100A] who contains all things.

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” Peacemakers are those who reconcile the discordant, reconcile the world to God, and sow peace and concord among others. For the Apostle says: “Pursue peace with all, without which no one shall see God” (Heb. 12:14). And again: “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Rom. 12:18). And the Psalmist: “With those who hate peace, I was peaceable” (Ps. 109:7). Peacemakers are rightly called sons of God, because “He Himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2:14). He is the peaceful King, who, joining two walls in Himself as the cornerstone, made peace for those who were far off and those who were near.

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution [Col. 0100B] for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” He said, “for righteousness’ sake,” [Note: Jerome also observes this at the passage: “He expressly adds, ‘for righteousness’ sake’; for many suffer persecution because of their sins and are not righteous.” Chrysostom explains “for righteousness” as for virtue and piety, for the defense of others; for he commonly calls every virtue of the soul “righteousness.” See also A., *Imperfect Work*, Homily 9.] not for worldly honors, not for riches, not for pride and wrongdoing. For we see many who for these and similar reasons persecute others and are persecuted by others. The apostles and martyrs suffered persecution from the ungodly for righteousness’ sake. For if they had wished to cease preaching righteousness, they would not have suffered persecution. Even to this day, all who strive to preach and uphold righteousness suffer persecution in the holy Church. Therefore not all who suffer persecution are blessed, since the wicked persecute one another; but only those are blessed because of persecution who suffer it for righteousness’ sake.

Let everyone who hears these things see whether he is included in any of these beatitudes. If he finds himself in any of them, let him be assured that he shall be blessed; for Truth has said this, and Truth cannot lie.

“Blessed are you when people curse you, persecute you, and, lying, say every evil thing against you for My sake. Rejoice and exult, because your reward is abundant in heaven.” “Blessed,” He says, “are you when people curse you.” Do not fear their curses, but rather rejoice and exult, [Note: Jerome: “I do not know who among us can fulfill this: that our reputation should be torn to pieces by reproaches and that we should exult in the Lord.” One who pursues vain glory cannot fulfill this. Bede copied these final words. Chrysostom, however, says splendidly in Homily 15 on Jesus Christ: “Not only did He say this, but He also readily persuaded—not two or ten, but now almost the entire world.”] because their curses, their persecutions, their slanders, and their lies prepare for you joy in heaven, exultation, and a great reward and recompense. “For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.” [Col. 0100D] This is not new; it is not unprecedented. Thus they persecuted Isaiah, thus Jeremiah, and thus the other prophets. Therefore let their example teach you, if their blessedness delights you.

XII. [Note: There is a homily of Eusebius of Emesa for the feast of a confessor and doctor, p. 227—namely St Bruno—as are the remaining homilies attributed to Eusebius of Emesa.]

“You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt loses its savor, with what shall it be salted?” [Col. 0101A] “You,” He says, “are the salt of the earth; you are the seasoning of humankind.” [Note: Chrysostom’s words in Homily 15 are very well known, though he has much more in his book *On the Priesthood*. Both ancient and modern writers eagerly bring forward admonitions and precepts on this passage. There is a work entitled *Priestly Trumpets, Compiled from the Fathers and Ancient Writers*, from which anyone may easily draw whatever he wishes. Here we shall offer one statement from A., *Imperfect Work*, Homily 10: “It is better to do and not teach than to teach and not do; for one who acts, even if he keeps silent, corrects some by his example; but one who teaches and does not act not only corrects no one, but even causes many to stumble. For who would not be moved to sin when he sees the very teachers of piety sinning?” See the rest.]

Others ought to be instructed by your example, taught by your wisdom, and disciplined by your humility and patience. But if the salt loses its savor—if the preacher loses his strength, if the bishop gives himself over to luxury and vanity—with what shall it be salted, with what shall the people be seasoned? It is good for nothing any longer except to be cast out and trampled underfoot by people. For such salt, because it has become foolish, is cast out; so too the false preacher and his teaching, which is empty, tasteless, and useless, are expelled from the Church. It is trampled underfoot by people because it is worthy of being despised by all.

“You are the light of the world.” What the sun and moon provide for the body, the apostles and teachers provide for the soul. The former illuminate [Col. 0101B] the eyes of the body; the latter illuminate the eyes of the mind. Therefore those are the light of the world who illuminate the greater and better part of the world. “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden.” For apostles and bishops are over the Church as a city is above a mountain. They cannot be hidden: they sit higher, and everyone’s eyes look to them. If they are beautiful and preserve the dignity and honor of their order, they are revered, admired, and praised by all.

“Nor do they light a lamp and place it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, that it may shine upon all who are in the house.” For this purpose a lamp is lit: that it may give light; for this purpose a bishop is ordained: that he may enlighten others. For the bishop is a lamp [Col. 0101C]; the light is the grace of the Holy Spirit or the preaching of the Gospel; the lampstand is the Church. Therefore let him who has been placed upon the Church’s lampstand take care not to place under a bushel the grace of the Holy Spirit by which he has been enlightened. Let him take care not to bury in the earth the talent entrusted to him; for it is written: [Note: The passage in Ecclesiasticus 41:17, in the Vulgate, is: “For what profit is there in hidden wisdom and unseen treasure?” In the Sixtine version: “But hidden wisdom and concealed treasure—what profit is there in either?”] “Hidden wisdom and concealed treasure: what profit is there in either?” Likewise, one who hides grain is cursed among the people.

“Let your light so shine before people that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” “You are light,” He says; you must shine both in speech and in deed. For you profit more by acting than by speaking, because the splendor of a deed is greater than that of speech. Hence He does not say, “That those hearing your good discourse may glorify [Col. 0101D] your Father.” But what does He say? “That, seeing your [Col. 0102A] good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

“Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish, but to fulfill.” For the Lord had come not merely to interpret and explain what the Law and the Prophets commanded, but also to do it. Moreover, the Lord had come not merely to interpret and explain the Law and the Prophets, but to fulfill what they lacked. [Note: Jerome likewise: “Either because He fulfilled in Himself what had been prophesied concerning Him by others; or because by His preaching He completed those things which formerly, owing to the weakness of the hearers, had been rudimentary and imperfect.”]

For in many ways the Law and the Prophets could not be fulfilled unless He Himself came. They had foretold His birth, passion, resurrection, ascension, and the miracles which He performed as a human being; these could in no way be fulfilled unless He Himself came. Therefore the Law and the Prophets lacked much—namely spiritual understanding—which could not be fulfilled except through Christ. This is attested by John the Evangelist. When he wept greatly because no one could be found able to open the book sealed with seven seals, he was told not to weep: “Behold, the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, to open the book and loose its seven seals. For truly I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, one iota or one stroke shall not pass from the Law until all things are done” (Rev. 5:5; Matt. 5:18).

For how could those things not come to pass which God Himself foretold would come? Otherwise, He who cannot lie would be lying. The iota and the stroke, which are the smallest things in letters, [Note: From the form of the letter it is shown that even those matters considered least in the Law are full of spiritual mysteries. Jerome. In addition, this passage is discussed in many different ways by those who treat of ancient Hebrew letters.] signify even the smallest saying of the Law and the Prophets.

But when He says that, until heaven and earth pass away, none of these things shall pass away until all things are fulfilled, He plainly shows that in saying “until” He looks only to what precedes. For the Law and the Prophets speak much concerning the blessedness of the saints which will occur after, and not before, heaven and earth pass away. Thus also should be understood what He had said above concerning Joseph and Mary: [Note: See what he said in no. 3 concerning Matt. 1:24, “And he did not know her,” etc., which he here repeats.] “He did not know her until she bore her firstborn son.” For “until” properly determines what precedes, but imposes no necessity upon what follows. For if it imposed necessity upon what follows, then, after heaven and earth had passed away, none of those things could happen which the Law and the Prophets had foretold would happen later.

It follows: “For whoever shall abolish one of these least commandments [Col. 0102D] and teach people accordingly shall be called least in the kingdom [Col. 0103A] of heaven; but whoever shall do and teach them shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.” “I have not come,” He says, “to interpret and set forth the Law, but I have come to do and fulfill what the Law commands.” Why is this? Do you wish to hear why? Because whoever merely interprets and explains the Scriptures, yet does not do what the Scriptures command, shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever both does and teaches them shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven. [Note: Jerome interprets it in the same way: “That the learning of a teacher, even if liable to a slight sin, brings him down from the highest rank; teaching righteousness does not profit him when a small fault destroys it; and perfect blessedness consists in fulfilling by deeds what you have taught in speech.”]

In which kingdom of heaven? For not only the heavenly homeland but also the Church is called the kingdom of heaven. [Note: The well-known statement of St Gregory, Homily 12 on the Gospels, is familiar to everyone: “We should know that in sacred discourse the Church of the present time is often called the kingdom of heaven.”] But how shall he be called least there, when he shall be neither great nor least there? Therefore this must be understood of the Church, which in many places is called the kingdom of heaven. In it the holy apostles, martyrs, and confessors, who both fulfilled and taught the commandments of the Law, are greatly [Col. 0103B] honored and esteemed. But what need is there to speak of the rest, because they are least, when they are neither remembered among people nor numbered among the saints in heaven?

Indeed, we see many such persons in the Church, and have no doubt that there have been still more, who know how to preach well but do not know how to act well. These, therefore, are deservedly both called and are least in the kingdom of heaven, because although they seem great to some, they are nevertheless despised by others in whom the Lord of heaven reigns and dwells.

But let us see what is meant by “whoever shall abolish one of these least commandments.” [Note: Either he had Bede before his eyes, or by chance he fell into nearly the same words: “Whoever does not fulfill God’s commandment in himself abolishes it and becomes most despised in the Church of the saints.”] Which commandments are these? Surely those contained in the Law, which He had declared that He came not to abolish but to perform. Yet how can we understand any commandment to be least, when one who does not observe it is called least and one who observes it is called great? Such a commandment seems not least but greatest.

For my part, I think that these words signify that all the commandments of the Law are least to those who do not perform them, but greatest to those who do perform them, since they make the former least and the latter greatest. Moreover, there are least things among the least and great things among the great, because the former regard them as least and the latter as greatest.

It follows: “But I say to you that unless your righteousness exceeds [Note: In my judgment, A., *Imperfect Work*, rightly interprets “least” here as that which seems least in appearance or reality—for example, what follows concerning the insult, ‘raca,’ ‘fool,’ and so forth.] that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.” For the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees consisted in preaching well and admonishing the people well, while not doing what they preached and admonished. Hence the Lord says elsewhere: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat in Moses’ seat. Therefore do everything that they tell you, but do not act according to their works” (Matt. 23:2). Why? “For they say and do not do.” Their righteousness, then, was to speak and not to act, to interpret the Law and not fulfill it; but these things are insufficient for those hastening toward the kingdom of heaven.

XIII. [Note: [Col. 0104D] Thus far, the material is found both in the homily attributed to Emisenus and in the commentary. From the exposition of the following words, “Unless your righteousness exceeds,” etc., another homily is attributed to Emisenus, for the sixth Sunday after Pentecost, p. 464; it comprises the whole of the following section.] “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not kill; but whoever kills shall be liable to judgment.’ But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment. Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ shall be liable to the council. Whoever says, ‘You fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna.”

He does not say: “Those things which the Scribes and Pharisees wrongly thought sufficient for themselves are sufficient for your righteousness.” Greater precepts [Col. 0104B] are given to the new people than to the ancients. To them it is said not to kill; to these, not to be angry. They are restrained from homicide; these from anger and hatred.

But what is this which the Lord says: “Whoever kills shall be liable to judgment”? For not everyone who kills is judged guilty of death in a court; nor indeed does the law condemn all who kill, since it itself commands many to be killed. This passage must therefore be defined, as must other statements that, being briefly expressed, appear to lack something. For the law says: whoever knowingly, or through hatred and ambush, kills a human being, shall himself also be put to death (Num. XXXV, 13). [Note: [Col. 0104D] It may be asked what law A. means which prescribes this. I think it is what is laid down in Num. XXXV, 20: “If anyone through hatred pushes a man, or throws something at him by ambush, or, being his enemy, strikes him with his hand, and he dies, he shall be guilty of homicide.”] But for the others it appointed three cities to which they might flee, lest they die. What this signifies is not to be explained here.

Let us see what follows. “But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” [Col. 0104C]. In what judgment? For this is not so held in the judgment conducted in the Church. But in that strict judgment, if everyone who is angry is to be condemned, either none or few can be saved. For who is so calmly gentle as never at any time to be angry? This too must therefore be defined, so that it is understood not of every anger, but of anger that is present and persistent, which is now called by another name: hatred. For inveterate anger is called hatred. [Note: [Col. 0104D] Cicero too says that hatred is inveterate anger, *Tusculan Disputations* IV, no. 9.] Hence he appropriately uses neither the past nor the future but the present tense, saying: “Everyone who is angry.”

And this is indeed clear: the person who hates his brother is condemned just as is the one who kills, since each is called a murderer. For John the Apostle says: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer; and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him” [Col. 0104D–0105A] (1 John III, 15). Thus everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment. “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ shall be liable to the council.” For *raca* signifies an attitude of mind marked by indignation and mockery: as when, in derision and with puffed cheeks, we blow at someone. Yet it is said that *raca* means “empty” or “vain.” But is it so great a sin to say *raca*—that is, to mock someone by whatever sound of voice—that whoever says it should be held liable before the council?

Every insult is indeed a great sin. Therefore let it be said thus: if someone says *raca* to his brother and, by mocking one who does not deserve mockery, provokes him to indignation and anger, he shall be judged liable and guilty before a council of bishops. For great quarrels are often stirred up from a small insult. All these [Col. 0105B] recoil upon the head of the person who was their chief cause, according to that saying: “He who lets loose water is the source of strife.” [Note: [Col. 0105D] Prov. XVII, 14: “He who releases water is the source of quarrels.”] Hence the law also commands: “If a fire that has broken out finds ears of grain [Note: [Col. 0105D] A. expressly writes “ears of grain,” which Calmet testifies that not a few Latin manuscripts contain, and which would seem highly suitable to the sense; but the Hebrew [Col. 0106D] and the Greek Septuagint, ἀκάνθας, “thorns,” stand in the way.] and consumes stacks of grain or standing crops in the fields, the one who kindled the fire shall make restitution for the loss” (Exod. XXII, 6). The Lord himself also says: “Woe to the one through whom scandal comes” (Matt. XVIII, 7). For if we are to render an account for an idle word, how much more for injuries and insults?

“But whoever says, ‘You fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna.” What is this, O Lord? What is this, O teacher of truth? What if he says it and repents? For we know that many saints were not afraid to call others not only fools but heretics, and, having accused them [Col. 0105C] of heresies and defeated them, condemned them. Thus the Apostle Paul, writing to the Galatians, called them “senseless” and “foolish,” which is no less insulting than if he had called them fools. For he says: “O senseless Galatians, who has bewitched you not to obey the truth?” (Gal. III, 1). And shortly afterward: “Have you become so foolish that, having begun with the Spirit, you are now brought to completion by the flesh?” (*ibid.*).

Therefore let us say thus: whoever, puffed up by a spirit of pride, calls his brother a fool not for the purpose of correction but enviously and maliciously, and does not fear to provoke him against himself to indignation and hatred, shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna until, led by repentance, he reconciles to himself, in whatever way lies within his power, the person whom he had unjustly provoked. To understand that the Lord himself meant this [Col. 0105D], hear what follows: “If therefore you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and first go to be reconciled with your brother; then, when you come, you will offer your gift.”

It is as though he said: “You called your brother a fool; he is angry with you; he has a just complaint against you. His indignation is your sin. I do not receive you: first go and be reconciled to your brother.” Perhaps this is why the Lord specifically set down the insults already mentioned [Col. 0106A]: at that time they were more commonly used and seemed to be either a slight sin or no sin at all. He therefore gave us a rule and established a new law: that we should neglect no sin, because even those things thought least, unless they are cut off, destroy and condemn souls. Nor should those things be neglected as if they were small, when God, offended by them, deigns not to receive gifts already laid before the altar.

It follows: “Be quickly agreed with your adversary while you are on the way with him, lest perhaps your adversary hand you over to the judge, the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be cast into prison.” This is as though he said: “Have you heard what I have said? These are words of life and salvation; therefore agree with them, for this is your adversary.” For what [Col. 0106B] opposes a human being as the divine word does? One wishes to kill; it says: “You shall not kill.” One wishes to commit adultery; it says: “You shall not commit adultery.” One wishes to steal; it says: “You shall not steal.” Finally, comprehending nearly everything in a single saying, it declares: “What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another.”

Therefore agree with this adversary of yours, and do so quickly, while you are on the way with him; for this way ends quickly, and its miles are few. This way is as long as the life of each individual. Although it is longer for some and shorter for others, it is not very long for anyone. [Note: [Col. 0106D] Jerome likewise says: “From what precedes and follows, the sense is clear: our Lord and Savior exhorts us to peace and concord while we run along the way of this present world.”] But once the way has been completed and life ended, it will no longer profit one to wish to agree.

What then? Your adversary will accuse you and hand you over to the judge. Why do you not say, “and hand you over to me,” most excellent Lord? For you are he whom God appointed judge of the living and the dead. But what follows? “The judge hand you over to the officer.” O, to what an unjust officer for torment is the person handed over who refused to agree with a good counselor! And what will happen afterward? “And you be cast into prison.” This prison is hell. Such as the officer is, such also is the prison. For that officer is more cruel than all others; this prison more fearful and horrible than all things, in which darkness never fails, fire is never extinguished, and the worm never dies. “Amen, I say to you, you shall not depart from there until you pay the last farthing.” This is a great debt, and this sum is boundless and innumerable: its last farthing is never reached; it is always being paid and never finished.

XIII*. “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”

By these words not only bodily but also mental fornication is removed; for not only to act with the bodily members, but also mentally to desire, is called fornication. And, as though someone might blame the eyes, which draw the mind after unlawful things, he added, saying: [Col. 0107A] “But if your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it away from you.” For what purpose? “For it is expedient for you that one of your members should perish rather than your whole body be cast into Gehenna.” Do likewise, if your hand causes you to stumble in anything.

The councils of the holy Fathers forbid this to be understood literally [Note: [Col. 0107D] This, I think, refers to canon 22, otherwise 17, of those called Apostolic, and canon 1 of Nicaea—on which see Morinus, book IV, chapter 9, *On Penance*. Although they seem to speak only of that mutilation which is castration, and this appears to be supported by the answer given to Ammonius in Sozomen, book VI, chapter 30, nevertheless Ammonius himself understood it in another and universal sense; and Innocent I decided the matter in epistle 37 to Felix of Nuceria, according to the recension of Constant, where he explains the law generally, even concerning one who voluntarily cuts off part of any finger.], and they do not admit to holy orders those found to have done any such thing.

Yet we pluck out our eyes and cast them away from ourselves when we remove from them the freedom, within our body, to wander after unlawful things. Hence the Psalmist says: “Turn away my eyes, lest they behold vanity” (Ps. CXVIII, 37). But there is another way of plucking out an eye that causes stumbling: when we forcefully cast away and cut off from ourselves a brother, son, or another friend whom we love as an eye or hand [Col. 0107B], if they cause us to stumble in the faith of Christ and in the salvation of our soul. For we ought to love no one in opposition to these things. Thus Eli the priest is severely rebuked because he tolerated the stumbling-block caused by his sons. Let us therefore remove and pluck away from ourselves anyone who invites us to fornication of body or soul, even if they have been dear and necessary to us as eyes and hands. For it is expedient that they alone perish rather than that we too perish with them.

It follows: “It was also said: ‘Whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce.’” [Note: [Col. 0107D] “Everyone who dismisses [his wife], let him give her a certificate of divorce.”] “But I say to you that everyone who dismisses his wife, except for the cause of fornication, makes her commit adultery; and whoever marries a dismissed woman commits adultery.”

In these words [Col. 0107C] it is clearly shown that no one may dismiss his wife except for the cause of fornication. On account of fornication, a man may dismiss his wife; but he may not marry another. Another Evangelist shows this, saying: “Everyone who dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery.” [Note: [Col. 0107D] Luke XVI, 18: “Everyone who dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery.”] For who is the one who dismisses his wife except the man whose wife has committed fornication? Others are not permitted to dismiss their wives. Likewise, a woman commits adultery if she dismisses her husband and marries another.

But someone says: “See, he who dismisses her commits adultery.
