Does she who is dismissed likewise commit adultery?” Hear the Evangelist: “Whoever marries a dismissed woman commits adultery.” Why does the man who marries the dismissed woman commit adultery? Because he marries one whom he is not permitted to marry; for if he married another woman, he would not commit adultery. If, therefore, he commits adultery who marries her, much more does she commit adultery who is married.

If, therefore, a wife may not be dismissed except on account of fornication [Col. 0107D–0108A], what does the Apostle mean when he says: “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart; for a brother or sister is not subject to bondage in such cases” (1 Cor. VII, 15)? It is as though he said: if a believer wishes to dismiss an unbeliever, he is no longer bound by any marital bond so as not to dismiss her. Yet it is better to retain her, so that perhaps in this way he may convert her. Therefore he is not constrained by necessity to retain her, but by charity alone, in order to convert her. Hence, if the unbeliever departs and cannot be retained by the believer, the believer should not be troubled by it: let the unbeliever depart.

And this divorce is indeed effected only by fornication. For what fornication is greater or more intolerable than that the husband should cleave to God while the wife commits fornication with idols? The Apostle therefore heard Christ saying that a man cannot dismiss his wife except for the cause of fornication, and understood this [Col. 0108B] as referring to both kinds of fornication: that of the body, namely, and that of the soul. Nor should we doubt that the Lord also understood it in this way.

“Again, you have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not swear falsely, but you shall render your oaths to the Lord.’ But I say to you: do not swear at all—neither by heaven, because it is God’s throne; nor by earth, because it is the footstool of his feet; nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King; nor shall you swear by your head,” [Note: [Col. 0108D] “You shall have sworn.”] because you cannot make one hair white or black. “But let your speech be: yes, yes; no, no. Whatever exceeds this is from evil.”

The Apostle James included this in his Epistle: “But above all, my brothers, do not swear, neither by heaven nor by earth nor by any other oath. But let your speech be yes, yes; no, no, lest you fall under judgment” [Col. 0108C] [Note: [Col. 0108D] “Lest you fall away under judgment.”] (James V, 12). For perhaps someone could have understood that the Lord, having listed a few things by which it is not permitted to swear, approved the rest by passing over them in silence, had not the Apostle James added to all these, “nor any other oath whatsoever.”

Why, then, did he forbid every oath? Immediately adding, he says: “Lest you fall under judgment.” For one who never swears never incurs perjury; and one who does not commit perjury is never judged for perjury. This, then, is why both the Lord and blessed James forbid swearing. For the same Spirit spoke in both; thus each signified the same thing.

Yet it must be asked why we are forbidden to swear by a creature. [Col. 0108D] What obligation is incurred in this case, such that we should fear [Col. 0109A] to swear by heaven and earth and other similar things? [Note: [Col. 0108D] Jerome answers the question aptly with reference to Christ’s Jewish hearers: “The Jews, swearing by angels, the city of Jerusalem, the temple, and the elements, worshiped creatures and earthly things with the honor and service due to God.” Chrysostom says nearly the same in Homily 17. Saint Hilary had said precisely the same on this passage: “For it was a religious practice among the Jews to swear by these names of the elements—by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, and even their own head—to which, to God’s dishonor, they gave the reverence of an oath.” Maldonatus, as usual, treats Christ’s teaching on this passage excellently.]

When we invoke God or his words in an oath, we make him in some way a mediator and renounce his assistance unless we keep our agreement with the person who trusted us under such a pledge. But by what obligation are we bound in other cases? If I say, “I swear to you by my head,” what is meant? Perhaps this: “May my head remain sound.” But if I say, “I swear to you by heaven and earth and by the city of Jerusalem,” it may be understood: “May heaven give me rain; may earth give me its fruit; and may I dwell in this city.” These are not slight obligations, especially if understood allegorically: if by heaven [Note: [Col. 0109D] Bede is not very different: “More specifically, he signifies holy souls by the name of heaven, and sinful persons by earth,” etc.] we signify the Apostles, by earth the Church, and by the city Jerusalem the heavenly homeland.

For the Lord himself seems to signify this [Col. 0109B], when he says of heaven that it is God’s seat; of earth, that it is his footstool; and of Jerusalem, that it is the city of the great King. It is greatly to be feared to introduce these things into an oath if they are so understood. Nor should anyone swear by his own head, since he cannot restore health that has been divinely taken away; indeed, he cannot do the lesser thing, make one hair white or black. For no one can cause black and white hairs not to arise in their due time.

How, then, shall we speak? How shall we make our words firm? “Let your speech,” he says, “be yes, yes; no, no.” This is as though he said: say that what is, is; say that what is not, is not. Speak thus; answer thus. If you do this, you will not sin or lie. Add nothing to these: let your speech be simple. For what exceeds these is from evil. What is it that exceeds these except falsehood? Whoever says that what is not, is; or that what is, is not—such speech exceeds these and is from evil, from sin, and from the devil. For it is said of him that he was a liar from the beginning, “and did not stand in the truth.” [Note: [Col. 0109D] John VIII, 44: “He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth”; Chrysostom also cites this passage here, Homily 17.]

XIV. You have heard that it was said: “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth.” But I say to you, do not resist evil. But if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also; and to one who wishes to contend with you in court and take your tunic, yield to him your cloak as well. [Note: [Col. 0109D] “Release” (*dimitte*).] And whoever compels you to go a thousand paces, go with him another two thousand paces. And give to one who asks you; [Col. 0110A] and do not turn away from one who wishes to borrow from you. [Note: [Col. 0109D] Everyone sees that the preceding words signify what was written in Exodus XX, 24; Leviticus XXIV, 20; Deuteronomy XIX, 21. Jerome says well here: “Our Lord, removing retaliation, cuts off the beginnings of sins; in the Law there is recompense, in the Gospel grace; there the offence is corrected, here the beginnings of sins are removed.” Chrysostom discusses that Old Testament law at length at the beginning of Homily 18; and Bede’s judgment on the words “you shall hate your enemy” is elegant: namely, the voice is not to be understood as that of one commanding the righteous, but of one permitting the weak.]

For these few words are sufficient for the perfection of all people: in them every form of patience and the virtue of generosity are openly commended. All these things look to and are connected with that passage which says: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.” For the Pharisees were full of greed and had no patience.

You have heard that it was said: “You shall love your neighbour and hate your enemy.” But I say to you: love your enemies; do good to those who hate you. The other things stated above [Note: [Col. 0110D] The words which follow in the commentary may be read in Homily 6 after Ash Wednesday, p. 99 of the spurious Emisenian homiliary.] seem not contrary to the Law, but rather to be a certain fulfilment of it, according to what he had said: “I came not to abolish the Law, but to fulfil it.” [Col. 0110B] But what is now said seems contrary to it; for these are opposed: “you shall hate your enemy,” and “love your enemies.” How, then, shall we understand the words of truth so that they are not contrary to the Law? Who is this enemy whom he commands us both to hate and to love?

This enemy [Note: [Col. 0110D] So, almost, St Augustine also, *Sermon on the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, book I, chapter 41: “In the one person who is evil, you have both a neighbour and an enemy. For insofar as he is human, he is your neighbour; insofar as he is evil, he is an enemy not only of you but also of himself. Therefore love in him the flesh and soul—that is, your neighbour—which God made; and hate the wickedness which, with his own consent, the devil introduced.”] is a human being: an enemy because a sinner; a friend because human. You have heard two things: “human being” and “sinner.” Love, therefore, the human being; hate the sinner. Love nature, not vice; hate vice, not nature. In this way Christ will agree with the Law, and the Law with Christ.

For one and the same person is both friend and enemy to you; one and the same person persecutes you and does not persecute you. What God made in the human being is your friend and does not lie in wait for you; [Col. 0110C] but what the devil made in the human being is your enemy and lies in wait for you. Thus, in one and the same human being, we love the friend and hate the enemy.

Therefore, when the Law says, “You shall love your neighbour,” understand the nature of the human being, which is near to you because you were made from the same mass. But when it continues, “and you shall hate your enemy,” understand vice, which is the cause of all enmities. For there would be no enmities among human beings if this alone were removed from them.

It follows: “Do good to those who hate you.” For the Lord himself both taught and did this. Speaking to the Jews, he said: “I have done many good works among you; for which of these do you wish to kill me? And pray for those persecuting [Col. 0110D] and slandering you.” [Note: [Col. 0110D] John X, 32: “I have shown you many good works from my Father; for which of those works do you stone me?”] He himself fulfilled this when he prayed [Col. 0111A] for his persecutors, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing. That you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven.” [Note: [Col. 0111D] Luke XXIII, 34: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”]

This is understood as follows: just as you are children of God by creation, so you may also be his children by imitation. For he does good not only to friends, but also to enemies. This is what he says: “He makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust.” Thus he nourishes enemies as friends; he illumines both alike with the radiance of his sun, and fertilizes the possessions of each by the cleansing of his rains.

But these things are small; hear greater things. He makes his sun [Note: [Col. 0111D] Ambrose, book V on Luke, gives a mystical explanation on a not dissimilar principle: “The Lord watered the Jewish people with prophetic rains, and made the rays of the eternal Sun shine even upon those who did not deserve it,” etc.]—his Son, the Sun of righteousness, the light which enlightens every person coming into this world—now rise, now appear, now shine in darkness, now shine upon the good and [Col. 0111B] evil. And he rains upon the just and unjust. For the almighty Lord sent down rains of faith and teaching first through the prophets, then through the Son, and afterwards through the apostles and teachers. Great are these clouds: by them the Church is made fruitful; by them the seeds of good works are nourished; whoever has not been watered by them will be wholly dry and burned in the fire.

“For if you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even tax collectors do this? And if you greet only your brothers, what more do you do? Do not even the Gentiles do this?” We must not understand this to mean that we ought not to love those who love us; otherwise we would love neither God nor neighbour, which are the two greatest commandments of the Law. What then? That we should not love only those [Col. 0111C] who love us, but also those who do not love us; and not merely because they love us—for that is returning favour—but because we are members of the same body and children of the same Father.

For such love is spiritual, and therefore unfailing; carnal love quickly dissolves, like the flesh itself. Tax collectors and Gentiles, that is, love one another with such carnal love: as soon as they perceive that they are not loved by others, they too cease to love others. Therefore we must love all, seek the salvation of all, and show to all the affection of charity. For what else is greeting someone than showing the affection of charity and love? In this way love grows and concord increases.

“Therefore be you also perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.” [Col. 0111D] He does not say that we should be perfect to the same degree as our heavenly Father is perfect; this is impossible. Rather, he says that we should be perfect as he is. Thus a child is a human being just as a young man is, although he is not a human being as complete as the young man in strength and knowledge. Let us therefore be perfect according to our measure; [Col. 0112A] for the perfect Lord wishes to have good and perfect believers.

But what this perfection is, hear what the Lord himself says: “If you wish,” he says, “to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor” (Matt. XIX, 21). [Note: [Col. 0111D] Bede briefly says: “provided that God is understood as perfect as God, [Col. 0112D] and the soul as perfect as a soul.”] These words, however, are said especially to the apostles, and through them commanded to their successors.

[CHAPTER VI.] “Take heed not to do your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them; otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.” For if we ought not to do our righteousness before people, what is the meaning of his earlier statement: “Let your light so shine before people that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven”? How will they see our good works if we do not dare to do them before them and [Col. 0112B] while they see? For if we do them, we shall have no reward.

Let us therefore see what “in order to be seen by them” means; for in this the whole question is resolved. It is not the person who performs his righteousness before people who loses his reward, as the words might seem to say, but the person who does so in order to be seen by people. For the one who acts in order to be seen by people does not seek the reward of righteousness, but human praise, vain glory, and popular favour. Therefore he has no reward with God, because he receives among people the empty reward of praise.

“When, therefore, you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before yourself, as hypocrites do in synagogues and streets, in order that they may be honoured by people. Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward.” I ask, therefore: why have they received [Col. 0112C] their reward? Is it because they gathered the poor by the sound of a trumpet, whom perhaps they could not otherwise have assembled so readily? Or because they did this in synagogues [Note: [Col. 0112D] Chrysostom, Homily 19, denies that they did this and wishes the words to be understood of display in these good works. The author of the *Imperfect Work* and more recent writers who investigate ancient Hebrew rites, such as Lightfoot in his *Hebrew Hours*, also deny it.] and streets, where it seemed more suitable because the place was more spacious? Certainly not. Why, then? Do you wish to hear why? Because they acted thus in order to receive reward not from God, but to be honoured by people. So much did their love of praise and glory profit them that they gave alms and yet had no reward.

How, then, ought we to give alms? It follows: “But when you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand does, so that your alms may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.” What, then, should we understand by the right hand and the left? [Col. 0112D] If we wish to understand our actual hands, I do not know how one hand can understand the other’s action; understanding lies not in the hands but in the mind. Besides, why should the right hand hide its work from the left, which agrees with it so closely and assists it so faithfully in all things? We must therefore understand something else by [Col. 0113A] right and left.

Our right hand is love of God; our left [Note: [Col. 0113C] Bede reasons in precisely the same way: “The declaration of human praise seems to be signified by the left hand; by the right hand, the intention of fulfilling the divine commandments.” Augustine, *Exposition of Psalm* CXX, §8, explains it otherwise, though mystically: “Our left hand is called whatever we possess temporally. Our right hand is called whatever eternal and unchangeable thing the Lord promises us”; and he adds in §10: “When you do a [Col. 0113D] good work, do it for eternal life. For if … you do it in order that earthly things may abound for you, your left hand knows what your right hand does.” Much the same occurs in his exposition of Psalm CXLV, §22, and Sermon 149, §15.] is love of praise; for the former leads to the lambs, the latter to the goats. Recall that Gospel in which the lambs are placed at the right and the goats at the left. If, therefore, you give alms, do so from love of God, who commanded you to do it; this is your right hand. Let the left hand—that is, love of praise—not know it. Do not seek popular favour from the same act through which you seek to please God. For although you may be able to have both at once, you will not have them if you desire to have them.

Thus, in every work we do, the left hand does not know what the right hand does if we perform it not from love of praise but from love of God and righteousness. Hence it is also said here: “that your alms may be in secret.” Whether you give alms in a synagogue, in streets, or in public squares, [Col. 0113B] you nevertheless do it in secret if, in doing it, you desire to be seen not by people but by God. Conversely, one who acts in secret but desires to be seen, seeking praise and glory from this, does not in fact act in secret, because he does not wish what he does to be hidden; it counts for him just as though he acted publicly.

But God, who sees in secret, and to whom nothing hidden is hidden, who searches hearts and sees thoughts, will repay each one according to his works.

“And when you pray, you shall not be like the hypocrites, who love to stand praying in synagogues and at the corners of streets so that they may be seen by people. Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you pray, enter into your chamber; and, having shut the door, pray to your Father in secret, and your Father, [Col. 0113C] who sees in secret, will repay you.”

For all these comparisons almost signify the same thing and can be explained and understood in one way. No one sins because he prays in a synagogue, which is a house of prayer; nor is it sinful to pray in streets. Why, then, is it forbidden? Hear what follows, and you will understand: “so that they may be seen by people.” [Col. 0114A] What it means to wish to be seen by people has already been stated above. This is why your prayer is not accepted: because you wish to be seen by people. Wherever you pray, if you pray in order to be seen by people, your prayer is not accepted.

But if you wish to pray well, [Note: [Col. 0113D] Chrysostom treats all this most elegantly in Homily 8 on the First Epistle to Timothy: “What then does Paul mean when he says: ‘I wish men to pray in every place’ …? For certainly it would be absurd if we took this simply, as though prayer were not permitted in every place and in church. What, then, is meant? Christ plainly warned us to avoid vain glory, when he commanded that vows and prayers be offered not only secretly but in the more hidden part of the house. For just as, when he says, ‘Let not your left hand know,’ etc., he is not speaking simply about hands, but strives to destroy the greatness of vanity, so in this passage by the name of the chamber he expressed the secrecy of the innermost heart.”] enter into your chamber; return to the heart, for this is the chamber in which prayer is contained, the chamber in which God himself rests. Pray there; speak there, where both what you say and the one to whom you speak are present. Shut the door: the one to whom you pray has no need of the sound of the mouth or of a loud voice. For he looks to the heart, sees in secret, and attends not to the arrangement of words but to the contrition of the heart. Hence the Psalmist says: “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” [Note: [Col. 0113D] Thus far the homily.] (Ps. [Col. 0114B] L, 19).

It follows: “But when praying, do not speak much, as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard because of their many words. Therefore do not be like them, for your Father knows [29] what you need before you ask him.”

For the Gentiles, whether they are called from *ethna*, [Note: [Col. 0114C] I regret that our author gives such a far-fetched and false derivation of this name. Even schoolchildren are taught that *pagani* (“pagans”) were so called from *pagi* (“districts” or “villages”), when the superstition of idols had been almost abolished and expelled from cities, but had withdrawn into hamlets and rural districts, though it had once prevailed widely and embraced almost the whole world. In Latin they were called *gentiles* from *gentes* (“nations”), whom in Greek they called *ethnici*, ἐθνικοί, [Col. 0114D] from ἔθνος, “nation.” Indeed, in Scripture they are very frequently called “nations” in the same sense; Arnobius’s books *Against the Nations* survive. The meaning of both *pagani* and *gentiles* is indeed manifold and sometimes bears no relation to religion, as is evident even from title XIV, book III, of the Theodosian Code, *On Marriages of Gentiles*. Perhaps for this reason Jerome distinguished *gentiles* from *ethnici* in his commentary on Ephesians, chapter VIII, 20. Among ecclesiastical writers, however, the sense we have stated is customary, as it is also for Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VIII, chapter 10.] or, as seems more likely, from the valley of Ennon, from which *Gehenna* is named, signify hypocrites and sinners. These people, deceived by I know not what error, thought they would be heard through much speaking and prolonged prayer. For prayer is heard not because it is long, but because it is made with the devout disposition of the mind, from a contrite heart and a distressed spirit.

But what then is meant by the Apostle’s saying, “Pray without ceasing,” [Note: [Col. 0114D] I Thessalonians V, 17. Chrysostom raised the same question in Homily 19 and answered it thus: “Here he called *battologia* loquacity, which we use whenever we ask the Lord for things that are not beneficial to us, such as power, glory,” etc. More recent writers, especially Jansenius, chapter 41, and Maldonatus on this passage, observe that the Greek has βατταλογεῖν, meaning the empty repetition of the same words, [Col. 0115C] and that the Gentiles believed such *battologia* highly effective for obtaining requests; this seems confirmed by the example of the priests of Baal in III Kings XVIII, 37.] when the Lord forbids us to speak much in prayer? Perhaps it should be defined thus: pray without ceasing while you pray, so that we may either cease quickly from prayer, or, while we pray, pray with the utmost attentiveness and with the whole intention of the heart?

Yet it can also be understood in this way: the Lord spoke of loud vocal prayer, whereas the Apostle spoke of the hidden petition of the mind. The former, therefore, must be shortened because it wanders; the latter must be continued [Col. 0115A] because it is steadfast and firm. The former is heard by people; the latter is heard only by God. The former is moved by modulation; the latter is tempered by tears. Let the former, therefore, be brief so that it may be heard by people; let the latter be long so that it may be heard by the Lord.

For whether we eat, drink, or do anything else, we can nevertheless keep our mind directed toward God; but we cannot always speak or pray aloud. And because the best God knows what we need even before it is requested, there is no need to make vocal prayer lengthy, since it is very often interrupted in its continuance by many impediments. Therefore let that prayer be prolonged and made without ceasing which seeks no praise, desires no favour, is not commended for its melody, and is not criticized for being tuneless; which is not heard by human beings but is heard by [Col. 0115B] the Lord.

It follows: “Thus, therefore, you shall pray:

XV. Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.” [Note: [Col. 0115C] Very many of the ancient Fathers explained the Lord’s Prayer: besides Jerome, Chrysostom, and other interpreters, Tertullian and Cyprian in separate books, whom St Hilary cites in his commentary on Matthew; Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis 23; Augustine, Epistle 130, Sermon 56, *Sermon on the Mount*, the author of Sermon 65 among Augustine’s works, etc.; and among theologians St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, II–II, question 83, article 9, and his commentators, Cardinal de Lauræa, *On Christian Prayer*, chapter 9; Suárez, *On Religion*, vol. II, book III, chapter 8; etc.]

It is a great honour and immeasurable nobility that we call Father one whose servants we are not worthy to be called. [Note: [Col. 0115C] Tertullian, who says of it, “this title is one both of filial affection and authority,” and Cyprian, who calls this designation that “of those who believe, and of him who began to be called ours and ceased to belong to the Jews who forsook him,” treat this as a kind of preface to the Lord’s Prayer. [Col. 0115D] Augustine, in the *Sermon on the Mount*, says that Father is addressed as “our,” not “my,” so that we may acknowledge that we are all brothers; and Chrysostom, Homily 20, says that “he wishes us to pour out prayers for the common crown, seeking not so much our own advantage as that of our neighbours.” See Cyprian’s most elegant passage.]

For, having been made adopted children, we say together with the only Son of God: “Our Father.” Yet it is not those who wish, but those who are chosen, who are made worthy by adoption. For “he chose us before the foundation of the world, that we might be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. VIII, 29): these are the Apostle’s words.

Let no one henceforth boast of nobility: we are all brothers; the nobler person is the better. For a servant is often nobler than a master, because the former is a servant of a human being, the latter [Col. 0115C] a servant of the devil.

Although God is everywhere, he is said specially to be in heaven [Col. 0116A] because he dwells in the saints, who are called heavens. [Note: [Col. 0115D] Thus St Augustine, in the *Sermon on the Mount*, explains this as “who art in the saints.” So too Bede, and Cyril not differently. Elsewhere Augustine (*Epistle* 186 to Dardanus, §16) adds another, more literal explanation; after teaching that “God is everywhere by the presence of divinity, but not everywhere by the grace of indwelling,” he adds: “Because of this indwelling, where the grace of his love is undoubtedly recognized, we do not say, ‘Our Father, who art everywhere,’ although that is true, but ‘Our Father, who art in heaven,’ so that in prayer we may rather commemorate his temple, which we ourselves ought to be, and insofar as we are so, insofar do we belong to his fellowship and to the household of adoption.” Chrysostom excellently says in the cited passage: “When he says that God is in heaven, he does not thereby confine him there, but draws the person praying away from earthly things.” Nearly the same is said by the author of the *Imperfect Work*, Homily 14.]

The saints are called heavens because, raised higher, they love not earth but heaven. But how can the name of God be hallowed, when it is always and naturally holy? What does “hallowed be thy name” mean? Formerly, “God was known in Judah; his name was great in Israel” (Ps. LXXV, 1). Therefore God’s name had not yet been hallowed among the nations. For among the nations the names of Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, and Saturn were held holy. Now, therefore, the name of God has been hallowed in the Church, and the names of false gods have become accursed and profane. Moreover, God’s name is not hallowed among those who do not fear to abjure it.

What, then, does “hallowed be thy name” mean [Col. 0116B] except that it may be held holy, terrible, and greatly to be feared by all? “Thy kingdom come.” [Note: [Col. 0116C] Chrysostom observes that “hallowed” here is the same as “glorified”—ἁγιασθήτω, that is, δοξασθήτω—and that it signifies: “Grant that we may keep our lives in such purity of conduct that through us all may altogether glorify thee.” Tertullian: “We ask that he may be hallowed in us, who are in him, and in the rest, whom the grace of God still awaits.” Most others—Cyprian, Cyril, Augustine, Sermon 56—explain it of our own sanctification, although Augustine in the *Sermon on the Mount*, §19, explains it as “that it may be held holy by people.”]

This can be understood both of the ecclesiastical kingdom, which is ruled and governed by God, and of the eternal kingdom which will have no end. This kingdom comes daily, grows daily, and daily people are born who are joined to it by faith. For the kingdom is enlarged by those being born and is not diminished by those dying; thus it always comes until it is completed in full. When it has been completed, it will then begin to be much better. This, indeed, is what we pray for: that it may be completed and transferred. For whoever does not pray thus does not desire to be blessed.

“Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.” [Note: [Col. 0116D] The author’s first explanation seems to concern the ecclesiastical kingdom, or the expansion of the Church, so that this petition is almost identical with the preceding one. Yet many Fathers, such as Jerome, after explaining the preceding petition as a request that God’s name be hallowed in us, expound this one as a request “either generally for the kingdom of the whole world, that the devil may cease to reign in the world, or that God may reign in each person and sin may not reign in the mortal body of human beings.” Augustine, Sermon 111: “Let ‘thy kingdom come,’ therefore, be understood as ‘let it be made manifest to people.’” The author of Sermon 65: that is, “let it be manifested to the world.” Yet almost all of them, together with our author, understand it also of the eternal kingdom, especially when the body, after the resurrection, shall attain its blessedness and “the blessed life shall be perfected in every respect,” as Augustine says in *Sermon on the Mount*.]

“Let thy will,” he says, “be done and fulfilled on earth [Col. 0116C] by human beings, as it is done and [Col. 0117A] fulfilled in heaven by angels.” [Note: [Col. 0117B] “May your commandments be obeyed by human beings as by angels,” Augustine, in the cited work and in Epistle 130. [Col. 0117C] Augustine nonetheless adds other interpretations in the *Sermon on the Mount*: first, “may sinners as well as righteous people do your will”; he takes “heaven” to signify the righteous and “earth” sinners. Second, “may reward be rendered to the righteous and condemnation to sinners.” Third, “as the spirit does not resist God, so may the body not resist the spirit”; Tertullian and Cyprian had also offered this interpretation, followed later by Bede. Fourth, that the will perfected “in the Lord Jesus Christ himself” may likewise be perfected “in the Church.” Cyril has the first interpretation, and elsewhere Augustine himself gives almost that alone.]

For there peace alone reigns; there are no disputes, no discord, no wars, and no anger.

“Give us this day our supersubstantial bread.” This is the bread which came down from heaven; the soul is nourished by this bread. It is rightly called “supersubstantial,” because Christ’s flesh has been exalted above the substance both of angels and of human beings. This bread is also the divine word, which another Evangelist calls “daily,” [Note: [Col. 0117C] It is well known that the Greek text, both here, where the Vulgate renders “supersubstantial,” and at Luke II, 3, where it renders “daily,” has τὸν ἐπιούσιον; indeed, the more frequent patristic reading in Matthew also is “daily” (see Sabatier, vol. III, p. 33). Jerome discusses both interpretations here and in book II of his commentary on the Epistle to Titus, where he proposes another excellent and distinctive interpretation. Augustine, in the *Sermon on the Mount*, summarizes what these terms mean or may mean: “Daily bread is said either of all things which sustain the necessities of this life … or of the sacrament of Christ’s body, which we receive daily, or of spiritual food.” Yet, because “very many in eastern regions do not daily partake of the Lord’s supper,” he ultimately prefers the last explanation to the second: “namely, the divine commandments which we ought daily to meditate upon and practise.” Cyril, however, proposes only the second interpretation, that ordinary bread is not ἐπιούσιος. Chrysostom, on the contrary, explains it of ordinary bread or daily sustenance, since mention is made of ἄρτου τοῦ ἐφημέρου, “bread for the day.” Tertullian, though more inclined toward the Eucharistic explanation, nevertheless admits the interpretation of daily sustenance; Cyprian likewise approves both, so that “daily bread may be understood spiritually and simply.” All [Col. 0118B] who in some way accept the last interpretation recall Christ’s command against anxiety [Col. 0118C] concerning tomorrow. Maldonatus discusses this entire question at length and is well worth reading.]

For it is received daily by the Church. Although it is not individually received daily by everyone, it is received daily by her who is the mother of all and whose members are all people. We ask that this bread be given to us only today, because we exist only today. Why should I ask that it be given to me tomorrow, when I do not know whether [Col. 0117B] I shall reach tomorrow? For the Lord himself says: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow.” [Note: [Col. 0118C] Matt. VI, 54: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow.”] You exist today; seek today. If you arrive at tomorrow, seek tomorrow too. Once you have arrived at tomorrow, tomorrow will no longer be tomorrow for you, but today. Therefore you ask only for today, because you never possess anything except today. For there are three times, of which we possess only one. [Note: [Col. 0118C] “Since you do not know what span of a day you will see, why should you torment yourself with anxiety about it?” Chrysostom.]

“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” For he himself explains this immediately afterwards, saying: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins.” [Note: [Col. 0118C] “And your heavenly Father will forgive you your offences,” Vulgate, Matt. VI, 14.] “But if you do not forgive people, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins.”

[Col. 0118A] You have heard the condition: what do you think? If you forgive, you will be forgiven; [Note: [Col. 0118C] See Chrysostom, Augustine, etc. Bede: “Binding us by a certain promise, so that we seek forgiveness from God, to whom we are debtors, only as we forgive our debtors.”] if you do not forgive, you will not be forgiven. Therefore either forgive, or do not say these words; for by saying them you bind yourself and pray against yourself. It is as if you said: “Do not forgive me my sins, Lord, because I too am unwilling to forgive others.” [Note: [Col. 0118C] See St Thomas, question 83, article 16, reply to objection 3.] It is therefore better to forgive than to say such things against oneself and lose so great a benefit.

“And lead us not into temptation.” Thus the Lord leads us into temptation just as he hardened Pharaoh’s heart. Since nothing occurs without his permission, he seems himself to do what he permits to occur. Therefore he leads us into temptation because our enemy would have had no power to tempt us unless this had been granted him from above. [Note: [Col. 0118C] Tertullian: “That is, do not allow us to be led in by him who tempts.”] This can be proved from the fact that, unless he had been permitted, he could not tempt blessed Job. [Col. 0118B] We pray, therefore, not that we may never be tempted at all, but that we may not be led into temptation [Note: [Col. 0118C] See Augustine, *Sermon on the Mount*, etc., where he distinguishes “being tempted” from “being brought into temptation”; for he reads, “do not bring us [Col. 0118D] into temptation.” And in Epistle 130: “We are admonished to ask this, lest, abandoned by his help, we either consent to some temptation through deception or yield under affliction.” See St Cyril.] in such a way that we are held fast and overcome when ensnared by it. For one who is led into temptation, as though already surrounded and entangled, is freed either with difficulty or not at all.

“But deliver us from evil.” Deliver us, he says, from evil; deliver us from sin; deliver us from the devil, [Note: [Col. 0118D] Augustine, *Sermon on the Mount*: “For we must pray that we may not only fail to be led into the evil from which we are free, which is requested in the sixth place, but also be delivered from that into which we have already been led.”] who is the author of evil, [Note: [Col. 0118D] Cyril, Chrysostom, and almost all the Greeks here interpret “the evil one” as the devil.] lest he lead us into temptation; lest, attacking us, he overcome us; lest he conquer us in temptation and swallow us up. [Note: [Col. 0118D] Tertullian: “The closing clause answers it, explaining what ‘do not lead us into temptation’ means: namely, ‘but lift us away from evil.’” Bede: “that we may stand secure and safe from all that the devil and the world bring about.”]

XVI. But when you fast, do not become gloomy like the hypocrites. [Note: [Col. 0118D] It is a homily attributed in error to the Emesan, for the fourth day at the beginning of the fast, p. 47.] For hypocrites are called gloomy [Col. 0119A] because, in order to appear religious, they display a certain sadness and severity in their faces, as though they had been exhausted by much fasting. Hence it is added: *For they disfigure their faces, so that they may appear to men to be fasting.* They disfigure their faces because they allow them, beyond the bounds and natural character of their beauty, to become rough and hideous through neglect. For if deformity had pleased God, he would not have formed man with so beautiful a face. But why do they do this? *So that they may appear to men to be fasting.* For if they had wished to commend their fasting to God alone, they would have displayed it not in their face but in their heart; for it is written: *Man sees the face, but God looks upon hearts.* [Note: [Col. 0119D] 1 Sam. 16:7: “For man sees the things which appear, but the Lord looks upon the heart.”] Therefore those who wish to please not God but men disfigure [Note: [Col. 0119D] Jerome discusses here the word “they disfigure” (*exterminant*) and its use in ecclesiastical writings; Bede copies him. The word occurs in Hilary, Augustine, and others. In Greek: ἀφανίζουσι, “they make unrecognizable” or “disfigure.”] that which is seen by men. Thus, because [Col. 0119B] they seek praise from men, they receive no reward from God. And this is what he says: *Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward.*

But you say: “How, then, shall I fast?” Hear what follows: *But you, when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that you may not appear to men to be fasting, but to your Father, who sees in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.* The hypocrite, he says, when he fasts, disfigures his face, because he has in his heart the destroyer and prince of sadness. But you, who bear in the dwelling-place of your heart the Lord of all consolation and joy, show a cheerful and beautiful face. Let the face outwardly show how great a good of joy is possessed inwardly in the mind; and, through the efficacy of fasting, let the head and face of the soul be anointed [Note: [Col. 0119D] What is said concerning anointing has this meaning. For the Evangelist speaks “according to the custom of the region of Palestine, where on feast days they usually anoint their heads”: Jerome and Bede; and Chrysostom says generally of the ancients: “This was the custom among the ancients: in times of joy they were often anointed.”] and washed inwardly [Col. 0119C], so that outwardly too the beauty not of sorrow but of joy may be revealed.

For fasting duly observed accomplishes this in us: our mind is anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit, and the face of the soul is cleansed of the stains of sins. But the holy joy of the spiritual face removes hypocrisy and suspicion of it. Whatever the face may be, God nevertheless does not look upon the face but upon hearts. Act openly whatever you wish; feign and pretend whatever you wish: nevertheless he sees in secret, and will repay you according to what he sees there.

*Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and [Col. 0120A] where thieves do not break in or steal.* For to one storing up treasure on earth it is said: “He stores up, and does not know for whom he will gather these things” (Ps. 38:6). Likewise: “O fool, this night your soul will be taken from you [Note: [Col. 0119D] Luke 12:20: “they demand your soul from you,” Vulgate.]; and whose will be the things you have prepared?” But what is said of one who stores up treasure in heaven? “He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness remains for ever and ever; his horn shall be exalted in glory” (Ps. 111). And the Lord says to the rich man: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and follow me, and you will have treasures [Note: [Col. 0119D] Matt. 19:21: “you will have treasure,” Vulgate.] in heaven.” But one who deposits his treasures in this manner is secure and does not fear losing them. Therefore, whoever you are who desire your soul to dwell and to be in heaven, deposit your treasures there. For where your treasure is, there also is [Col. 0120B] your heart. If the treasure is in heaven, the soul too will be there; if it is on earth, it will be on earth—on that earth, indeed, of which blessed Job says to the Lord: “Let me go, that I may mourn my sorrow a little, before I go and do not return, to a dark land covered by the gloom of death; a land of misery and darkness, where there is the shadow of death, and no order, and everlasting horror dwelling there [Note: [Col. 0119D] But the Vulgate reads: “dwells there.”]” (Job 10:20).

Finally, where the treasure is, there also is the heart, because each person desires to arrive where he knows his riches to be stored. Blessed, therefore, is the one who has deposited his riches in heaven, so that he may always have his mind there and always strive thither with all his strength and desire.

XVII. *The lamp of the body is the eye. If your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if [Col. 0120C] your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark. Therefore, if the light that is in you is darkness, how great will that darkness itself be?* [Note: [Col. 0119D] “The lamp of your body is your eye: if [Col. 0120D] your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark.”]

The purpose for which he introduced this comparison is not plainly evident, unless perhaps it was because he was speaking to the disciples, to whom at the beginning of this discourse he had said: “You are the salt of the earth, and you are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:13). By this they might understand what they ought to be in the body of the Church. It is as though he said: As the eye is the lamp of the body, so you are the lamp of the Church. If you are sound [Note: [Col. 0120D] Thus, almost, St. Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*: “The lamp of the body is the eye; that is, the bishop is the light of the Church. … For when the priest preaches the true faith, darkness is driven from every heart,” etc. More closely, *On the Dignity of the Priesthood*, ch. 6—which Mabillon, vol. II of the *Annals*, thought to be by Pope Sylvester II, though formerly attributed to Ambrose: “If your eye is sound,” etc., that is, if the bishop, who has deserved to preside in the body as a light, is adorned with holy simplicity and innocence, the whole Church is illumined by the radiance of light; “but if your eye is evil,” etc., that is, if the bishop, who seemed to furnish light to the body subject to him, is clouded by the blindness of wickedness, what will the other members do, when the light of their eyes has been taken away?] and without stain, the whole body will be full of light; but if you are evil and without light, the whole body will be dark. For neither the hands will know whither to stretch, nor the feet whither [Col. 0121A] to walk, nor will the other members know in what direction they ought to go.

Therefore, if the light that is in you is darkness, and itself lacks light within itself and cannot illumine even itself—without which the other members have no light—consider how great that darkness will be. It will be as great, certainly, as the members themselves. For just as all are illumined by the light of one, so all are blinded by the darkness of one. It is necessary, therefore, that the eye of the Church—the priest and bishop—be sound, without stain, without error, so that all the members may be illumined by his life, his doctrine, his conduct, and his holy manner of life. But if, God forbid, he is evil—if he is a heretic, if he is a fornicator and [Col. 0122A] adulterer—the whole body will be dark. He did not say that the whole body will be evil, but that the whole body will be dark, because not all imitate his wickedness, though all are enveloped in his darkness. For all are enveloped in darkness because the lamp of light has been extinguished in them. Light does not arise from darkness, nor truth from falsehood. Therefore, if the light of the whole body is turned into darkness, how great will that darkness itself be?

This can also be understood of the soul, whose eye is the intellect. [Note: [Col. 0121D] Chrysostom, and many ancient and modern writers, interpret it of the intellect, as Lapide notes. See Jansenius, who expounds this fully, *Concordia*, ch. 42.] If the intellect loses the light of true light, the whole soul will immediately be enveloped in the gloom of error and darkness. But if it is sound and pure, the soul too will be bright and full of light.

## PART TWO

[Col. 0121]

XVIII. [Note: [Col. 0121D] It is a homily of the Emesan for the fifteenth Sunday after Pentecost, p. 167. We have already said who ought to be recognized as the author of these homilies.] *No one can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will uphold the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and mammon.* [Col. 0121B]

Our Savior has just above spoken of treasure, and has shown in what place we ought to deposit it, saying: *Store up for yourselves treasure in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal.* Now he says that we cannot serve two masters, namely God and mammon; for mammon means riches. [Note: [Col. 0121D] The well-known statement of St. Augustine, *Sermon on the Mount*, ch. 14: “Among the Hebrews, mammon is said to mean riches. The Punic word also agrees; for in Punic Mammon means profit.” Jerome is more precise: “In the Syriac language mammon is called riches”; Bede copies him. See Lapide.] Therefore, let the one who desires to serve God in familiar devotion deposit his riches in heaven. For God does not accept the service of one who serves riches. “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person [Col. 0121C] to enter the kingdom of heaven.”

To serve riches is to render them a kind of subjection, and to fear spending them when necessity or usefulness requires it. Therefore it is one thing to serve riches and another to possess riches. [Note: [Col. 0121D] Chrysostom, Homily 22, adducing the examples of Abraham, Job, and others who were rich: “Do not set rich men before me in opposition to this saying, but those who serve riches,” etc.] The rich person who does not place his hope in riches, but distributes them generously and usefully, differs little from the poor.

But if this is understood literally, as the plain words seem to say, it is impossible to serve not only two masters but also many masters. Therefore he immediately added, to show of which masters this should be understood: *You cannot serve God and mammon.* No one can serve these two together. For who serves mammon except the greedy person? The greedy person, therefore, despises and hates God. Why so? Because he serves idols; for the Apostle says: “Know and understand this: that every fornicator, or unclean person, or greedy person—which is idolatry—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Eph. 5:5).

It follows: *Therefore I say to you: do not be anxious for your soul, what you shall eat, nor for your body, what you shall wear.* These words are especially addressed to the apostles and their successors [Note: [Col. 0122D] See St. Augustine, *On the Work of Monks*, ch. 26.], and to all others who wish to attain the highest summit of perfection. Such persons have no concern for earthly goods, because, having food and clothing, they are content with these. They readily possess these things, and without all anxiety, when they place their entire hope in God. Hence the Psalmist says: “Cast your thought [Col. 0122C] upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you.” [Note: [Col. 0122D] Ps. 53:25: “Cast your care upon the Lord,” etc., Vulgate.] And again: “I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread.” [Note: [Col. 0122D] Ps. 36:26: “His seed seeking bread,” Vulgate.]

*Is not the soul more than food, and the body more than clothing?* Whoever you are, he says, who have despised worldly glory and chosen to serve God and devote yourself to contemplation, do not be anxious for your soul—that is, for your life—because he who gave life will provide also what sustains life. For the soul is greater than food and life greater than the means of maintaining life. [Note: [Col. 0122D] “In this saying,” Bede says, “he admonishes us to remember that God, who made us, has given us much more than any food or covering.”] Therefore he who gave the greater thing will certainly give the lesser as well.

These words were especially necessary for the apostles, who were about to travel throughout the world without purse or bag. To them the Lord also said: “Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves.” [Note: [Col. 0122D] “As sheep in the midst of wolves,” Matt. 10:16; “as lambs among wolves,” Luke 10:3.] Of them, as the Apostle says, the Lord ordained that they should live by the Gospel: “For the laborer is worthy of his reward” [OCR: *wercede*, “reward”] (Luke 10:7).

*Look at the birds of heaven: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth more than they?* For God created no animal in this world that is of greater love and affection, greater value and honor before God, than the human being. Therefore, if the almighty Lord feeds without labor and anxiety those things made for humanity, which by comparison with humanity are either small or nothing, how much more will he not abandon those who were made in his image and reconciled by his grace? [Note: [Col. 0123C] Jerome: “If birds are nourished by God’s providence without care and toil—birds which are today and tomorrow will not be—how much more are human beings, to whom eternity is promised, governed by God’s will?” Bede says nearly the same in almost the same words. “If God shows himself to have such care even for those far inferior beings, how,” he asks, “will he not grant you these necessary things?” See Chrysostom, Homily 22.]

*Which of you, by thinking, can add one cubit to his stature?* [Col. 0123B] This is as if he said: What you cannot accomplish by anxiety, thought, skill, intelligence, or labor—namely, adding a single cubit to your stature—God accomplishes in you without your thought and anxiety. From your emergence so small from your mother’s womb, he has brought you to the full measure of a perfect human being. [Note: [Col. 0123D] As though he said: “Then leave to him the care of clothing the body, by whose care you see it has come about that you have a body of such stature”: Bede. “From this he also shows,” Chrysostom says in the cited place, “that the body itself grows not so much by nourishment as by the providence of its Creator.”] Will he then be unable to feed you, who was able to create, give life, and bestow such growth?

*And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they do not labor or spin. But I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.* Do you suppose, he says, that he cannot clothe you without labor and anxiety, when he clothes the fields with flowers and distinguishes lilies by their colors? For how do lilies grow? How are they clothed with coverings so beautiful? They do not know how to work or spin [Note: [Col. 0123D] You see a wholly vernacular expression, which may be added to the others discussed by Muratori, Dissertation 32, *Antiquitates Italicae Medii Aevi*.], for they are without sensation; yet they are clothed more splendidly even than Solomon himself, who surpassed the other kings of that people both in wealth and in wisdom. No one can imitate by art or wisdom the beauty of God’s work. [Note: [Col. 0123D] “And truly, what silk, what royal purple, what embroidery of weavers can be compared with flowers? What is as red as the rose? What is as white as [Col. 0124C] the lily?” etc. See Jerome and Chrysostom, Homily 23.]

*But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is cast into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, you of little faith?* If he has such care for things beneath you, what care do you think he has for you? *Do not be anxious, saying: What shall we eat? or what [Col. 0124A] shall we drink? or with what shall we be covered?* For the one who lacks nothing will sufficiently provide you with all things, if you have faith. *For the Gentiles seek all these things;* but it is not necessary for you to seek them—that is, to seek them with labor and anxiety. Therefore the Lord does not say, “Do not seek,” but, “Do not be anxious”; for your Father knows that you need all these things.

Hence the apostle Peter says in his Epistle: “Casting all your anxiety upon him, because he cares for you.” [Note: [Col. 0124D] “Labor must be performed; anxiety must be removed”: Jerome.] *Seek first the kingdom of God,* he says; seek eternal life; seek the growth of the Church; pray that the kingdom of God may come and grant you his righteousness, so that you who have been made judges of all may be able to judge all in justice and equity [Col. 0124B]. *And all these things will be added to you.* This is what he says elsewhere: “You will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. 19:29).

*Do not be anxious about tomorrow,* for he uses “tomorrow” to mean the future. [Note: [Col. 0124D] Jerome: “In the Scriptures ‘tomorrow’ is understood as future time, as Jacob says: ‘And tomorrow my righteousness will answer for me,’” etc. See St. Augustine, *Against Adimantus*, ch. 24.] For the Lord does not wish us to be anxious about the future when we are not even certain and secure about the present. Yet in forbidding us to be anxious about tomorrow, he seems in some manner to permit concern for present things. [Note: [Col. 0124D] Jerome expresses this at this passage: “Therefore, in forbidding consideration of the future, he granted that there ought to be concern for the present”; whence the Apostle also says (1 Thess. 11:9 [sic]): “Night and day, working with our hands, lest we burden any of you.”] Hence blessed Paul, as though concerned for the present, labored with his hands so that he might have enough for his daily sustenance. Such concern removes idleness, yet does not serve riches.

Why we should not be anxious about tomorrow he adds: *For tomorrow will be anxious for itself.* It is as though he said: Just as I do not forbid today’s concern, so neither do I forbid tomorrow’s once tomorrow has arrived. Let the present day, therefore, be concerned for itself and not for another; and likewise tomorrow, and the rest in succession. *For sufficient for the day is its own evil.* It is enough for you if you can endure the hardship of this present day. Why, then, should you wish to add hardship to hardship, labor to labor, distress to distress, and weariness to weariness?

For in this place *malitia*, “evil,” is not used for moral evil but for weariness and labor. [Note: [Col. 0124D] This too is from Jerome, on this passage: “Here he used *malitia* not for that which is contrary to virtue, but for labor, affliction, and the distresses of the world; just as Sarah afflicted Hagar.” In Greek this is expressed significantly by ἐκάκωσεν αὐτήν, “she afflicted her.” Writers of Latin’s golden age furnish examples of this sense, such as Virgil, *Georgics* 2.168: *Assuetumque malo Ligurum*—“the Ligurian accustomed to hardship.” See Henri Estienne, *Schediasmata*, bk. I, ch. 6.] Thus we commonly say, “Today we have suffered many evils,” when we are wearied by some great labor.

But this may seem unsuitable to some unless it is understood only of the apostles and persons like them. For why should we keep and guard sheep, oxen, and other animals that we needed today, once the day is over, if we are to have no concern whatever for tomorrow? Why moreover do we cultivate fields and vineyards and store their fruits in granaries? Many other objections of the same kind can plainly be raised against this. Therefore let these words be understood of those who are pleased to possess nothing in this world beyond bodily necessities. [Note: [Col. 0125D] See St. Augustine, *On the Work of Monks*, chs. 26 and 34.] Such were the prophets and apostles, and we read that many others were such. For if all people wished to be such, God would not lack the means to feed them. [Note: [Col. 0125D] Thus far the homily.]

XIX. [CHAPTER VII.] [Note: [Col. 0125D] “Do not judge, that you may not be judged,” Luke 6:37. “Do not judge and you will not be judged.”] *Do not judge, and you will not be judged.*

Let no one suppose that just judgments are forbidden by these words, provided that they are rendered by those who ought to render them. For what does “Do not judge, and you will not be judged” mean? Many do not judge and yet will be judged. Therefore let it be said: Do not judge anyone unjustly and contrary to the command of the law, and you will not be judged for unjust judgment. For the judge who does not judge unjustly, although he may be judged for other sins, is not judged for his just judgment, because he did not sin in judging. [Note: [Col. 0125D] “Therefore he did not forbid judging, but taught how to judge”: Jerome.]

Hence it follows: *For with what judgment you have judged, you will be judged; and with what measure you have measured, it will be measured back to you.* This is not to be understood [Note: [Col. 0125D] Bede: “Will God then judge us rashly as we judge others, or measure back with an unjust measure? This is by no means so with God,” etc.] as though someone who has judged another badly and unjustly will himself also be judged unjustly by the Lord. For God is a [Col. 0125C] just judge and judges nothing unjustly. Therefore, in a certain manner, they will be judged by the same judgment by which they judge others, yet not by the same judgment. It is the same because they too will be condemned; it is not the same because they will not be condemned unjustly.

Whether, therefore, anyone knowingly judges another unjustly, or accuses and condemns in matters hidden and doubtful, let him know most certainly and not doubt at all that he too will be judged by the same judgment and that the same measure will be measured back to him. The Apostle forbids judging hidden matters, saying: “Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” (1 Cor. 4:5). Of doubtful matters he says: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? Before his own Lord [Col. 0125D] he stands or falls. But he shall stand, for God is able to make him stand. Let each person abound in his own conviction” (Rom. 14:4).

It should be noted, as is plainly evident here, that those too are said to judge who rebuke or accuse the deeds of others. Hence the Apostle, after saying, “Here [Col. 0126A] it is required among stewards that one be found faithful,” [Note: [Col. 0126D] 1 Cor. 4:2. Chrysostom, Homily 50, in the cited place: “Here he did not forbid all sins generally to be judged, nor take this authority away from everyone, but only from those who, though abounding in innumerable crimes, condemn others with all rashness for the slightest offenses.” Jerome: “He speaks of those who themselves are liable to a mortal crime yet do not pardon lesser sins in their brethren.”] immediately added: “But to me it is a very small matter that I should be judged by you or by a human day” (1 Cor. 4:2 [as printed]).

There are also others who gladly spread abroad, accuse, and condemn the small offenses of others, while refusing to see the crimes that oppress themselves. Though they do not see themselves, they always keep their eyes open upon others. These try to draw the speck from another’s eye, but do not consider the beams fixed in their own. Of them it follows: *Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not see the beam in your own eye?* You are burdened with crimes and yet rebuke others for sins? For the difference between sin and crime is that between a speck and a beam.

*Or how do you say [Col. 0126B] to your brother, “Allow me to remove the speck from your eye,” when behold, there is a beam in your own eye? Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.* If you are so diligent in correcting the sins of others, he says, why do you not first correct your own? If compassion moves you so kindly toward others, why do you not rather have compassion on yourself? For it is written: *You shall love your neighbor as yourself* (Matt. 19:19). But, as you pretend, you love your brother more than yourself: you care for him and neglect yourself. Perhaps, however, you do this skillfully, so that you may first try on him how afterward to heal yourself, and prefer to test the skill of your art in another rather than in yourself. If you do it for this reason, it is cunning, not compassion.

But this is not why you do it. Why then? Because you are a hypocrite [Col. 0126C]: because you do not wish to be good but to appear good. It is enough for you if you are seen by the people and if others say of you: “Behold a righteous man; behold one who spares no one; behold one who rebukes everyone’s sins; behold one who wishes to heal everyone and illumine everyone’s eyes.” This is what the people say; but you understand it differently. For you know that it is false, though you rejoice in their falsehood.

XX. *Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine, lest perhaps they trample them under their feet and turn and tear you to pieces.*

What should we understand by what is holy and by pearls, except the divine sacraments? And what by dogs except unbelieving and wicked people, who bark at the truth and refuse to assent to it, and who often return to their accustomed evils as a dog to its vomit? For the Lord says concerning dogs: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and cast it to dogs to eat” (Matt. 15:26), when he spoke of the Canaanite woman. Swine are those who delight, as though in a wallow of mud, in the stench of vices. Therefore we are forbidden to give divine sacraments to such persons, [Col. 0127A] because, while a person persists in sins and returns to them as a dog to vomit, or delights in them like a filthy swine, we ought not to give that person the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood. For they trample them underfoot and, regarding them as nothing, do not receive them with the reverence they ought. They immediately return to their customary wicked conduct, and inwardly rend and tear us with grief and sadness, since we grieve for their destruction even more than they themselves do.

It may also be understood of unbelievers in this way: so long as they do not assent to the truth, bark against the Gospel in contradiction, and do not separate themselves from the mud and stench of their error, the greater mysteries should not be revealed to them, lest by blaspheming and mocking they trample them underfoot and, turning against [Col. 0127B] the preachers themselves, inflict upon them not only the pain of insults but also of blows, and tear them to pieces. [Note: [Col. 0127D] Many Fathers understand “what is holy” to mean the word of God and the proclamation of the mysteries of faith: Hilary and Jerome here; St. Leo, Epistle 78; Chrysostom, Bede, and others; and before them Origen, Homily 1 on Psalm 37; likewise the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book III, ch. 5. But St. Cyril of Jerusalem interprets “what is holy” as baptism, *Catechesis* 1, no. 3, and *Catechesis* 17, no. 36. Closer to the present interpretation, St. Athanasius, *Apology against the Arians*, no. 11, speaks of the Eucharist being addressed to the uninitiated; and St. Gregory, book XXXV of the *Moralia*, no. 13, understands the Eucharist itself.]

XXI. Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; and whoever seeks finds; and to him who knocks it shall be opened. For, according to Luke, these words are joined to the Lord’s Prayer previously mentioned (Luke 11:9), which we ought indeed to recite persistently, so that the desires expressed in our petitions may be fulfilled. But how is it true that everyone who asks receives? For many ask and do not receive what they ask. This, therefore, is to be understood of that petition concerning which he said above: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all things shall be added unto you.” For he does not grant his faithful followers foolish requests, since he himself knows what we need.

> [Note: Col. 0127D] Jerome: “After he had forbidden the asking of earthly things above, he shows what we ought to seek.” Relevant here is that saying of St James 4:3: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, in order to spend it upon your desires.” See the Bishop of Ávila on this passage, perhaps no one has explained the matter more clearly or called readers back more effectively to perseverance in asking—a subject also treated by Chrysostom, Bede, and others.

[Col. 0127C] He therefore hears us in those matters which he knows to be salutary for us. Thus, everyone who asks receives—provided that his request is worthy to be heard; but God does not hear another kind of request. Hence he adds: Or what man among you, if his son asks him for bread, will offer him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will offer him a serpent? Therefore, if you, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father, who is in heaven, give good things to those who ask him.

It is as though he said: You, who are evil, nevertheless give not evil but good gifts to your children; and will God, who is good by nature, not give good gifts to his faithful? Certainly he will give good gifts, and he will give them nothing but good things, even if they ask for what is useless, while supposing that they seek what will benefit them. [Col. 0128A] For sometimes the saints, by not receiving what they ask, are heard more fully than they would be if they received it. Blessed Paul was heard more fully by not receiving than he would have been had he received that for which, as he himself says, he had asked the Lord three times. He was therefore heard in order that he might not be heard. For the Apostle sought only what was good, although he did not understand that it was not good for him. Thus he was heard by receiving what was good, lest he be heard by receiving what was not good.

For one who does not seek what is good for himself, while believing that he does seek it, is not heard if he receives what he asks; if he does not receive it, he is heard. Therefore God, who considers nothing but the intention of the petitioner, gives good to one who believes that he seeks good for himself, even though what he asks is not good for him.

Let us see, [Col. 0128B] then, what is signified by bread and fish, and what by stone and serpent.

> [Note: Col. 0128D] In pouring himself out here into mystical explanations, he follows the tendency of his own age, indeed of earlier centuries as well. For Bede explains it in no dissimilar way—perhaps he even wished to emulate Bede: “Bread signifies charity . . . to which the hardness of heart, compared with a stone, is contrary. Fish signify faith in invisible things, whether because of the water of baptism, or because they are caught from what is invisible, or because they are not broken by the waves of this world. To this he opposed the serpent, because of the poisons of deceit which it first sowed in the first man. But in the Gospel according to Luke, the comparison of an egg and a scorpion follows these two. The egg indicates hope, in which the offspring is not yet complete but is hoped for through incubation; or because it is contrary to hope to look backward—whereas hope stretches itself toward the things ahead—and therefore he set against it the scorpion, whose poisonous sting is to be feared behind; by this is meant the deadly despair to be dreaded at the end.”

For my part, I think that bread signifies the spiritual understanding of the holy Scriptures, while the stone signifies the letter, because it was written upon tablets of stone. But by the fish I understand Christ our Lord, who first swam in the stream of baptism and, like a fish, was born of the Virgin without intercourse. And who else is meant by the serpent but he who deceived the first man in the serpent?

Luke the Evangelist, however, adds an egg and a scorpion after these. By the egg, therefore, let us understand the resurrection, in which, like chicks from eggs, all the saints rising from their tombs will fly upward to heavenly things. By the scorpion, however, let us understand the devil or Antichrist, who, [Col. 0128C] while secretly deceiving people, strike them as it were with their tail; for the scorpion strikes only with its tail.

Thus good sons—that is, Christians—ask for bread, because in the Law and the Prophets they seek spiritual understanding. They also ask for a fish, because they desire to be filled with Christ’s flesh. Likewise they ask for an egg, because with most steadfast hope they await the resurrection of the flesh. But evil sons—that is, Jews—ask for a stone, because in the sacred books they seek the letter alone. They also ask for a serpent, because in poison and crookedness they imitate the devil. Likewise they ask for a scorpion, awaiting Antichrist, whom they call the Messiah: so that, having been slain by the dragon in the first man at the beginning of the world, they may be struck by the scorpion near the world’s end.

[Col. 0129A] Thus the good Father grants good gifts to good sons asking for good gifts. But evil sons, asking for evil gifts, receive evil gifts from an evil father.

Therefore, whatever you wish people to do for you, do also to them; for this is the Law and the Prophets. “Because,” he says, “you wish your petitions to be heard by the Lord, willingly hear the petitions of others also. But lest perhaps you suppose that you ought to assent to evil requests, do to others what you wish to be done to you. Aid others in their needs, if you wish others to aid you in yours.”

And elsewhere indeed it is said: “What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to others”; but here it is said: “What you wish done to yourself, do to others.”

> [Note: Col. 0129D] Where is this said in Scripture? One might think of Tobit 4:16: “What you hate to have done to you by another, take care that you never do to another.” On this matter see Augustine, *City of God*, XIV.8; Chrysostom, homily on Psalm 5; Fulgentius, *On the Remission of Sins*, I.17; Gregory the Great, *Morals*, book [uncertain], ch. 23, book X, ch. 6, and book XIX, ch. 18. In the first of these passages: “Hence a certain wise man says: What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another.” A recent annotator thinks that the book of Tobit is denoted by the name of “a certain wise man.” But Gregory would not have called an author whom he knew and regarded as canonical by those words; and in *Pastoral Rule*, III.20, he introduces it with his customary formula for citing canonical writers: “it is written.” Indeed, he presents this very saying from Tobit in book X, epistle 51. Although the Fathers remember this maxim—as Augustine does in *On Christian Doctrine*, III.14—they do not identify its author.  
>   
> [Col. 0130D] Lampridius, in his *Alexander*, ch. 51, indicates that this saying was common among Jews and Christians. But its author need not be sought, since “God implanted it in our conscience from the beginning,” as Chrysostom says in Homily 13 to the People of Antioch, no. 3.

There we are forbidden to do evil; here we are also commanded to do good even to the evil. [Col. 0129B] For this is the Law and the Prophets; this is perfect charity: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. 5:43), because you desire your neighbour to love you as himself. What you ask from him, you ought to do for him. This, then, is the Law and the Prophets, because the Law and the Prophets command this. Yet he does not say that the whole Law and the Prophets depend upon this single commandment.

And as though someone might say: “This way is narrow; these commandments are exceedingly difficult to observe,” he added: Therefore enter through the narrow gate, because wide is the gate and spacious the way that leads to destruction, and many enter through it. How narrow is the gate and constricted the way that leads to life, and few find it! The way, he says, is constricted and the gate narrow, and therefore few find it; [Col. 0129C] nevertheless, this is that way and that gate through which eternal life is attained. For those who are saved are few in comparison with those who are condemned. Hence elsewhere the Lord says: “For many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 22:14).

But the way and gate which lead to destruction are very wide and spacious, and therefore many enter through them. For to fast, to keep vigil, to abstain from the desires of the flesh and from every pleasure, not to do one’s own will—who would not find this narrow and constricted? But to eat and drink abundantly and luxuriously, to obey every desire and pleasure of the flesh, and in no respect to oppose one’s own will—who would not find this broad and spacious? Many therefore walk by this way; many enter through this gate. But [Col. 0129D] where do they enter? Certainly, into the city of destruction, the fellowship [Col. 0130A] of death, the prison of distress, and the pit of every misery.

XXII.

> [Note: Col. 0130D] It is a homily spuriously attributed to Emesenus, for the Sunday after Pentecost, p. 156.

Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves. Beware, he says, and guard yourselves against false prophets, evil priests and bishops; beware of false preachers; beware of simoniacs and heretics.

> [Note: Col. 0130D] St Jerome understands the false prophets here to mean heretics; Bede, copying Jerome, does likewise. Chrysostom denies that the context permits this interpretation, and wishes it to be taken of “those who, though corrupted by depravity of life, nevertheless put on the appearance of virtue”—those commonly called impostors, under the designation τῶν ἐπιθετῶν προσιγορίᾳ (“the appellation ‘impostors’”).

Who come to you in sheep’s clothing. They pretend the simplicity of sheep, feign the innocence of sheep, and counterfeit the patience of sheep. If indeed you saw them within, if beneath the garments you perceived them, you would recognize that there was something other than a sheep there. For a wolf lies hidden beneath a sheep’s skin, and those whom you think outwardly to be sheep are inwardly ravening wolves. They are ravening wolves because they came not to guard the flock, [Col. 0130B] but to steal and plunder, slaughter and destroy.

But hear how you may recognize them: You shall know them by their fruits. For just as every tree is known by its fruit, so every person can be known by his deeds. Therefore he did not say, “You shall know them by their leaves,” but, “by their fruits.” For if we attend to words, good persons are not easily distinguished from bad. Hence elsewhere the Lord says: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat: therefore do whatever they tell you, but do not act according to their works.”

> [Note: Col. 0130D] Matthew 23:2: “upon the seat, etc., observe and do.” Vulgate.

By this he very clearly shows that they speak well but act badly. Those, therefore, who are not distinguished by their words are apprehended in their deeds. Let them preach whatever they wish; but you, consider their works. [Col. 0130C] If they are faithful, gentle, patient, merciful, humble, peaceable, chaste, benevolent; if they hate greed and do not hoard money; and if they have the other qualities which would take too long to enumerate—these are the fruits of a good tree, while the praises of these qualities are its leaves. For those who praise these things but do not practise them display leaves only, not fruits. Thus you shall know them by their fruits.

For thorns and thistles too are known by their fruits, since neither grapes are gathered from thorns nor figs from thistles. So every good tree produces good fruit, but a bad tree produces bad fruit. A good tree cannot produce bad fruit, nor a bad tree good fruit.
