For it is true that every good tree produces good fruit and every bad tree produces bad fruit; but how is that true—which Truth says is true—that no good tree produces evil and no bad tree produces good? For no one is so righteous that he does not sometimes sin. John the Apostle says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”

> [Note: Col. 0131D] First Epistle 1:8: “If we say that we have no sin, we ourselves . . . ,” etc., Vulgate.

But every sin is bad fruit. Therefore bad fruit is found even on a good tree. Similarly, no one is so wicked that he does not sometimes do good; for it cannot happen that he does not at least sometimes speak the truth. Yet to speak truth is good; therefore good fruit is found on a bad tree. What then? How shall we prove true what we do not doubt to be true? For Truth could not lie.

It is therefore true that no good tree produces bad fruit, and no [Col. 0131B] bad tree produces good fruit. It is certainly true, but true with a qualification. Let it therefore be said: No good tree, insofar as it is good, produces bad fruit.

> [Note: Col. 0131D] Jerome here: “We shall object that Judas, once a good tree, produced bad fruit after betraying the Saviour; and that Saul, a bad tree . . . afterwards produced good fruit when he was transformed from a persecutor into a vessel of election. Thus a good tree produces no bad fruits so long as it perseveres in the pursuit of goodness; and a bad tree remains in the fruits of sins so long as it does not turn to repentance. For no one, while remaining what he was, begins to be what he has not yet begun to be.” Chrysostom says the same in Homily 24: good fruit is not produced by a person “so long as he is fixed in wickedness.”

For no opposite produces its opposite: sweetness does not produce bitterness, health does not produce sickness, cold does not produce heat, nor truth falsehood. Good therefore does not produce evil, nor evil good, for they are contraries. Every tree is good according to its nature and produces good fruit; but according to corruption it is bad and produces bad fruit. You understand what is signified by this tree: this tree is a human being.

> [Note: Col. 0131D] Bede explains it in a similar way: “By the tree we understand either a good or an evil will; by its fruits, deeds,” etc.  
>   
> [Col. 0132D]

But do you wish to see that it is not human nature, which is certainly good, that produces bad fruit, but rather its corruption and sin? Hear what [Col. 0131C] the Apostle says: “For I do not do the good that I will, but the evil which I do not will, that I do. But if I do what I do not will, it is no longer I who do it, but sin which dwells in me.”

> [Note: Col. 0132D] Romans 5:1–15: “For I do not do the good that I will, but the evil that I hate,” etc.

Thus it is called a bad tree, not because it is bad in itself, but because it has the corruption of evil. If it is only slightly corrupted, being as it were still sound despite its corruption, it is called not bad but good; but if it is greatly corrupted, it is called bad and not good. For it receives its name from what is more abundant in it.

False prophets, then, are known by their fruits, because, even if they sometimes appear to do some good, nevertheless, since they act either for gain or for praise, their pretence cannot remain hidden for long. Since they do all their works to be seen by people, even that which appears good [Col. 0131D] is not good.

It follows: [Col. 0132A] Every tree that does not produce good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire. Trees are cut down when human beings die; they shall be cast into the fire when it is said to them: “Go, you cursed, into everlasting fire.”

Not everyone who says to me, “Lord, Lord,” shall enter the kingdom of heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven—he shall enter the kingdom of heaven. What does this mean? Do we not do the Father’s will when we call his Son “Lord”? For he himself said to the disciples: “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am” (John 13:13).

I say, therefore: If the Father and Son have one will, how does one who does the Son’s will fail to do the Father’s will? For it is the Son’s will to be called Lord; therefore it is also the Father’s will. [Col. 0132B] But this one act of will is not enough. It will suffice, however, if you possess as Lord him whom you call Lord, and serve him as Lord.

> [Note: Col. 0132D] Hilary on this passage: “The kingdom of heaven is not gained by the service of words alone.”

For if you serve him as Lord, you will be a faithful and good servant, and the good Lord will say to you: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many; enter into the joy of your Lord.”

It follows: Many will say to me on that day: “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons in your name, and perform many miracles in your name?” And then I shall declare to them: “I never knew you; depart from me, you who work iniquity.” Who are these many, if not those whom a little earlier he called false prophets? This great multitude will say these things on that day. On what day? Do not [Col. 0132C] ask its name, for it is very well known.

What will they say? “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name?” Balaam prophesied.

> [Note: Col. 0132D] Jerome: “For Saul, Balaam, and Caiaphas also prophesied,” etc.

Caiaphas too prophesied, as the Evangelist says: “Since he was high priest that year, he prophesied, saying: ‘It is expedient for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish’” (John 11:51).

They even cast out demons and perform many other miracles—those who baptize and those who preach. For as many sins as there are, so many demons are in each person. Thus Mary Magdalene is said to have had seven demons cast out of her, because, as is said elsewhere, “many sins were forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47).

> [Note: Col. 0132D] St Augustine, Sermon 1, exposition of Psalm 88, no. 6, on the words, “The heavens shall confess thy wonders, O Lord,” writes: “The heavens shall not confess their own merits, but the heavens shall confess thy wonders, O Lord. For in every act of mercy toward the lost, in the justification of the ungodly, what do we praise but God’s wonders? You praise the fact that the dead rose again; praise still more the fact that the lost were redeemed,” etc.

These demons are cast out when sinners repent and are converted through evangelical preaching, by whomever [Col. 0132D] it is proclaimed. [Col. 0133A] They also perform many other miracles, because they enlighten the blind, cure lepers, and raise the dead. Some preachers performed these miracles in the body; all perform them in the soul. Nor is healing a soul any less than healing a body. The body is healed and dies; the soul is healed and never dies.

Do you wish to know what soul is blind? The unbelieving soul, which does not see God and does not understand truth, is blind. The leprous soul is that which is defiled by the stains of vices. The dead soul is that which persists in sin. Thus preachers enlighten the blind, cure lepers, and raise the dead as often as wicked people are converted by their admonitions and preaching; led by repentance, they renounce the devil and all [Col. 0133B] his works, and receive from them the medicine of their salvation.

But what does this profit them, when the Lord says to them: “I never knew you; I never loved you; your works never pleased me”? For the Lord knows and loves them according to the nature which he created in them. But he does not know or love them according to the corruption by which the devil has spoiled them.

Therefore every person who hears these words of mine and does them shall be likened to a wise man who built his house upon a rock. It is not enough, therefore, to hear God’s words. The Apostle too says: “For not the hearers of the Law are righteous before God, but the doers” (Rom. 2:13). Hearing belongs to all; doing, to few.

The house which is founded upon the rock has a firm and stable foundation. [Col. 0133C] The person who builds in this way is wise. The foundation must first be sought. But let us see what this rock signifies. The Apostle says that “the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4); likewise: “For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus.”

> [Note: Col. 0133D] 2 Corinthians 3:11. Jerome gives the same explanation here of the house’s foundation: “The foundation laid by the Apostle, the architect, is one: our Lord Jesus Christ. Upon this stable and firm foundation, founded by a mass strong in itself, the Church of Christ is built,” etc.

You have found the foundation; build the house here. For you will build the house here if you keep these commandments. Believe and do what Christ commands, and you will be founded upon Christ the foundation. He himself will be your foundation; therefore you will not fear rain and wind. This is what he says: And the rain came down, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they rushed upon that house, and it did not fall, for it was founded upon the rock.

[Col. 0133D] Do you wish to see how the house founded upon the rock [Col. 0134A] fears neither rains, rivers, nor winds? “I am certain,” says the Apostle, “that neither death nor life, nor principalities nor powers, nor any persecution, can separate me from the charity of God which is in Christ Jesus.”

> [Note: Col. 0133D] Romans 8:38: “Neither angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things to come, nor strength, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature shall be able to separate us.”

Although tyrants raging against the saints might rush upon them with fury and terror, scourges and threats, and every kind of torture—as with great storms of winds and tempests—they could in no way separate them from faith in Christ. This happened because they were firmly founded upon the rock.

Let us also consider the house which is founded not upon the rock but upon sand. “And everyone,” he says, “who hears these words of mine and does not do them shall be like a foolish man who built [Col. 0134B] his house upon sand. The rain came down, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they rushed upon that house, and it fell; and its fall was great.”

For those who delight in hearing God’s words but take no care to keep them build the house of their faith—and themselves—upon sand, because they are cast down by the lightest breeze of persecution. Their fall will indeed be great when they are hurled down into Tartarus by the fury and wrath of evil spirits, as by some great assault of storms.

XXIII. And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these words, that the crowds marvelled at his teaching. For he was teaching them as one having authority, and not as the scribes and Pharisees.

For he teaches with authority who does not conceal the truth out of fear. In this respect, although the scribes and Pharisees may have taught many things well, [Col. 0134C] they may nevertheless be understood to have omitted very many things, either because they feared to say them, or because they did not observe them and therefore were ashamed to speak of them.

> [Note: Col. 0133D] Jerome and Bede explain this “authority” to mean that Jesus Christ did not merely set forth what had been written in Moses and the Prophets, as the scribes and Pharisees did, but by the freedom of his own will added certain things and changed certain things, as is clear from the preceding discourse. Chrysostom, Homily 26, explains it by the fact that, when establishing the commandments themselves, he often used the formula, “But I say to you,” and, in mentioning the terrible judgment, “showed himself to be judge by rewards and punishments.”  
>   
> [Col. 0134D]

Our Saviour delivered this very lengthy discourse on the mountain according to Matthew, but in a level place according to Luke. How this may be resolved, I do not see unless we understand that he gave the same discourse twice.

> [Note: Col. 0134D] It is scarcely possible that this opinion of our author can be proved. Nevertheless, he rightly identified it as a difficult passage, which ancient and modern writers have attempted to explain. It depends on what is said in Matthew at the beginning of chapter 5 (above, no. 11) and in Luke 6:17. Modern learned interpreters—Maldonatus, a Lapide, Calmet, and others—hold not that the discourse was repeated or delivered twice, but that it was delivered once; Matthew, however, did not follow the order of events, but set forth events separated in time. Nonetheless, almost all the ancient writers will be found to agree with our author: Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, II.19; Gregory, Homily 9 on Ezekiel; and the Author of the *Imperfect Work*.

And this was not unsuitable, because as some departed, others arrived, for whom the same words were necessary. Therefore, when those to whom he had spoken these words departed, he remained on the mountain that night, “spending the night,” as Luke says, “in the prayer of God. And when day came, he called his disciples and chose twelve from among them, whom he also named apostles. And [Col. 0134D] coming down with them, he stood in a level place; and a crowd of disciples and a great multitude, which had flocked there from every direction [Col. 0135A] (Luke 6:12), stood with him.” There he delivered this same discourse, although not everything related here is contained in that discourse, just as not everything said there is found in this one.

Moreover, it should be understood that the Evangelists do not write the history in the same order in which everything was done by the Saviour.

> [Note: Col. 0135C] This is canon 2 in Cornelius a Lapide, drawn from the principles he established before his commentary, and applied to this passage. See Maldonatus on this passage, etc.  
>   
> [Col. 0135D]

Hence in this respect they seem to disagree greatly. Read them, and you will see that this is so. For I think that they devoted attention not to chronological order but to narration.

## XXIV. [CHAPTER VIII.]

Now when he had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. The Lord, it says, came down from the mountain with his disciples and found there [Col. 0135B] many crowds of people waiting for him. After he had spoken to them the things which Luke the Evangelist relates (chapter 6), they followed him. And behold, a leper came and worshipped him, saying: “Lord, if you will, you can heal me.”

This miracle, however, did not take place at the time when the Evangelist appears to say that it did; as Luke testifies when he says: “And it came to pass, when he was in one of the cities, behold, a man full of leprosy; and seeing Jesus, he fell upon his face and begged him, saying: Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me” (Luke 5:12). Therefore let no one suppose that this happened on the plain, when he hears that it happened in one city. Thus these things are not connected with what precedes. For in saying, “Now when he had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him,” [Col. 0135C] he brings the preceding discourse to an end. Then, passing over the sequence of events, place, and time, he begins to write from this miracle. It therefore seems necessary that we should say a few things about that sequence, lest the Evangelists be found contradictory to one another. [Note: [Col. 0135D] Nearly all recent interpreters agree in holding that the events of Jesus Christ were not narrated in chronological order. See Jansenius, *Harmony*, chapter 43; Maldonatus on this passage and on chapter 6; a Lapide; Calmet; John de la Haye, *Arrangement of the Gospel*, chapter 53. Chrysostom, however, Homily 26, and the *Imperfect Work* seem to interpret almost all the matters narrated by Matthew in these three chapters as having occurred on the mountain.]

For after the Lord Jesus had called Peter and Andrew, James and John, he came with them to Capernaum, where both he and they lived. He entered the synagogue and preached, and all marvelled at his teaching. Then, leaving there, he came to Peter’s house, healed his mother-in-law, performed other mighty works there, left Capernaum, and crossed the water. After some days had passed, [Col. 0136A] he returned again to Capernaum; and then he healed the paralytic and called Matthew, the apostle and evangelist. In those same days he went up on the mountain, and there delivered the discourse of which we have spoken above, when he proclaimed the eight Beatitudes. When everyone had departed and he himself had remained there that same night, at daybreak he called his disciples and chose twelve of them, whom he also named apostles. Then, coming down, he delivered almost the same discourse on a plain. But when he came to the nearby city of Capernaum, he healed the centurion’s servant. Such, then, is the sequence.

But when or where this leper was cleansed is uncertain. It may nevertheless suitably be understood that he was cleansed in the aforesaid city, because [Col. 0136B] this miracle is written among the other miracles which the Lord performed there. The other Evangelists indeed write of Peter’s mother-in-law and of the centurion’s servant before writing of the cleansing of this leper.

But now let us come to the matter. “Behold,” he says, “a leper came and worshipped him, saying: Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me.” [Note: [Col. 0135D] Here begins the homily ascribed to Eusebius of Emesa, for the Third Sunday after Epiphany, p. 34; it also comprises the following section.]

41 See how great is the leper’s faith: he sees a man, worships God, and does not doubt his omnipotence. But what does he say? “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me.” You are Lord; you are almighty; your will is accomplishment; every creature obeys you. I have not deserved your benefit; I am not worthy of converse with you. Yet I believe that, if you will, you can cleanse me.

And the Lord, in response, stretched out his hand and touched him, saying: “I will; be cleansed.” The Lord [Col. 0136C] stretches out his hand: he makes his power manifest and does not conceal his might; he touches the man, and the leprosy flees. Indeed, the leprosy fled before his hand reached the man, [Note: [Col. 0135D] Jerome seems to hold the same view. Having observed that the leper met the Lord as he came down from the mountain—“for, while he had leprosy, he could not yet hear the Saviour’s very extensive discourse on the mountain”—he writes: “When the Lord stretched out his hand, the leprosy immediately fled.” He further gives two timely cautions: first, on the order of the healings: “It should be noted that this man was the first specially healed; second, the centurion’s servant; third, Peter’s mother-in-law; fourth, those brought to him afflicted by demons.” The second concerns the reading of this passage: the two words should not be joined; nor, as most Latin writers think, should it be read, “I will cleanse,” but separately: first he says, “I will,” then, as a command, “Be cleansed.” Bede also says elegantly here: “He says, ‘I will,’ against Photinus; he commands, against Arius; he touches, against Manichaeus.” Chrysostom and the *Imperfect Work*, however, hold that he did touch him and wished to show that the law concerning not touching a leper (Leviticus 13) had not been imposed upon him.] lest, if he had touched the leper, he might seem to act contrary to the law. For the law judges a person of this kind unclean, and forbids the touching of anything unclean.

But what does he say? “I will; be cleansed.” You believe that I can; I will because you believe. Put your faith to the test; recognize my power. I will that you be cleansed, and therefore be cleansed. And immediately his leprosy was cleansed, so that both the power of faith and the omnipotence of the healer might appear.

And Jesus said to him: “See that you tell no one, but go, show yourself to the priest.” [Note: [Col. 0136D] Interpreters give several reasons for the command to silence. Jerome: because there was no need to proclaim in words “what he openly displayed in his body.” Bede: “to teach us to abstain not only from the reward of money, but also from that of grace.” Chrysostom: that he might command the avoidance of boasting and vainglory. The *Imperfect Work* reasonably judges that silence was requested until he had shown himself to the priest.]

He would not have said this if he had performed this miracle [Col. 0137A] among the crowds which followed him down from the mountain; for one man could not conceal what so many thousands had seen. Yet it must be asked why the Lord commands him to tell no one. For it belongs to priests to preach and announce God’s miracles to the peoples. But the leper, even though cleansed, ought not to become a priest; for those are chosen for this office who, as the Apostle says, are without reproach. [Note: [Col. 0137D] This refers to Paul’s words at Titus 1:7: “A bishop must be without reproach,” and “If anyone is without reproach,” etc.]

In this too we are taught that, in the things which we do well and commendably, we ought not to seek human praise and vain glory. But why do you send him to the priest, Lord Jesus? Why do you command him to show himself to the priest, when you, the greatest of all priests, heal him? Who will dare to judge one who returns cleansed [Col. 0137B] by your judgment? You do this, then, so that you may be recognized as assenting to the mysteries of the law. For that person is clean whom the judgment of the priests declares clean: it belongs to them to distinguish good from evil, just from unjust, and clean from unclean. You therefore confirm this privilege for them by referring this man to their judgment.

It follows: “And offer the gift which Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.” But first let us say what this leper signifies—for he does signify something—and then what the gift signifies which Moses commands him to offer. This leper may be understood as the whole human race, and as every sinner individually. For this is leprosy not of the body but of the soul. That soul is leprous which is defiled by pride, anger, avarice, discord, hatred, and lust. [Col. 0137C] Let such a leper run to Jesus, hasten to the physician, not despair, repent, and desire cleansing. Let him say: “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me.” Certainly you can, because I too am repentant and you are almighty. For you have said that, at whatever hour a sinner turns and groans, he shall live and not die (Ezekiel 21:28). If he says this and does this, let him be assured of mercy and not despair of pardon, because the Lord is kind and repels no one who comes to him.

Then let him offer the gift which Moses commanded. Moses commanded, [Note: [Col. 0138D] Leviticus 14:4 ff. The *Imperfect Work*, Homily 21, gives similar allegorical and mystical interpretations here.] when a leper is cleansed, that he should offer for himself two living sparrows which may lawfully be eaten, cedar wood, scarlet yarn, and hyssop; and that he should sacrifice one of the sparrows in an earthen vessel over [Col. 0137D] living water, but release the other to fly away into the open country. This would seem vain and useless unless it had been commanded by him to whom nothing vain or useless is pleasing.

Therefore let the person cleansed offer two sparrows, and render body and soul to the Lord, so that they may now serve God rather than the pleasures of the world. They are rightly said to be offered alive, because they pass from death to life; and because they may lawfully be eaten, this shows that they are clean and free from sin, since the law commands nothing but what is clean to be eaten. Let him offer with them cedar wood as well, so that, because he has rendered [Col. 0138A] his body and soul to God, he may promise to maintain incorrupt faith and sincere conduct; for cedar is imperishable and fragrant in nature. Let him add scarlet also, so that, kindled by the fire of charity, he may love God and his neighbour; for scarlet is the colour of fire. Let him moreover offer hyssop, so that, rooted and founded on the rock, he may never be able to be separated from the faith of Christ; for hyssop naturally grows on rock, and the rock was Christ.

After he has thus rendered his whole self to God, let him sacrifice one of the sparrows in an earthen vessel over living waters. This sparrow is the body, and for that reason is sacrificed in an earthen vessel, because our bodies are earthen and clay vessels. It is sacrificed over living waters—that is, as the Holy Scriptures command us to sacrifice. [Col. 0138B] Hence the Apostle says: “I beseech you, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God, your rational service” (Romans 12:1). For this is the living water which teaches you rightly to sacrifice your sparrow. The Jews do not sacrifice rightly because they do not come to this water.

But let him release the other sparrow—that is, the soul—to fly into the open country, so that now free and no longer weighed down by the burden of earthly corruption, it may learn to fly by the wings of virtues to heavenly things. Because the other sparrow has now been sacrificed, this one flies freely and is held back by no one: “For the body which is corruptible weighs down the soul” (Wisdom 9:15).

This, then, is the proper order of repentance: whoever comes to God to be cleansed should first offer his whole self to the Lord, promise faith, charity, and perseverance in good works; reduce and afflict the flesh which has sinned into servitude; and let the soul, now endowed with freedom, fly away to contemplate heavenly things.

Moses further commands that the person who is to be cleansed should offer other gifts: namely, two unblemished lambs, a year-old ewe without blemish, three tenths of fine flour mixed with oil, and separately a sextary of oil. Moses commanded this offering, and the Lord himself commanded it to be offered. But what do these two lambs signify except the two greatest commandments of charity? Since they do no evil, they are not improperly called unblemished lambs. Hence the Apostle says: “Love of neighbour does no evil” (Romans 12:10). [Col. 0138D] Let him therefore offer these two lambs: let the one who desires cleansing from the stains of his sins promise that he will keep and observe these two commandments.

Let him also offer an unblemished year-old ewe, by which whole and perfect innocence is signified. Let him offer also the three tenths of fine flour: that is, faith, which wholly consists in the Trinity. For this is our fine flour; this is the life of our soul. Hence the Apostle says: “But the righteous lives by faith” (Romans 1:17). Yet this fine flour is made not from just anywhere, but from tithes, because we ought to receive our faith only from the sanctuary and from the priests. [Col. 0139A] For there all tithes are deposited, by which the priests and Levites are supported. And this fine flour is suitably mixed, because our faith is sanctified by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Beyond these things let him offer also a sextary of oil: namely, a whole and perfect measure of mercy. For to offer is to vow and promise. He therefore offers oil who promises to maintain mercy. For as oil excels among liquids, so mercy excels among works. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Psalm 144:9).

Here too the proper order of repentance is observed: whoever comes to repentance should offer and promise charity and innocence, faith and mercy. For he offers charity in the lambs, [Col. 0139B] innocence in the ewe, faith in the three tenths, and mercy in the sextary of oil. But this sextary of oil is set apart because it will be needed for what follows.

For Moses commands that the priest should set all these things, together with the person being cleansed, before the Lord at the entrance of the tabernacle; and then offer one lamb and the sextary of oil. From the lamb’s blood he is to touch the tip of the right ear, the thumb of the right hand, and the great toe of the right foot; and he is to do the same with the oil for the one being cleansed.

This lamb is Christ, who, like a lamb led to sacrifice, did not open his mouth (Isaiah 53). He is offered at the entrance of the tabernacle when his passion is preached in the hearing of the Church. For if the tabernacle is human beings, what is the entrance of the tabernacle except the ears, through which [Col. 0139C] divine words enter the secret chamber of the heart? Therefore the one being cleansed is touched with the lamb’s blood on ear, hand, and foot, because he is commanded not merely to hear Christ’s passion but also to imitate it. For hearing resides in the ear, just as action resides in hand and foot; and he is touched on the right side, which is both stronger and more faithful. “Let not your left hand,” says the Lord, “know what your right hand does” (Matthew 6:3).

Likewise he is touched with oil on the same parts, because he is admonished both to hear and to observe the good of piety and mercy. We pass briefly over these matters, of which we have said enough in Leviticus. [Note: [Col. 0139D] See the author on Leviticus 14:4, Roman edition, vol. I of St Bruno, p. 154 ff.]

## XXV

[Note: [Col. 0139D] This is the homily falsely attributed to Eusebius of Emesa, the same one assigned to the Third Sunday after Epiphany.]

Now when he had entered Capernaum, a centurion came to him, beseeching him and saying: “Lord, my boy lies at home paralysed and grievously tormented.” And Jesus said to him: “I will come and heal him.”

How the centurion approached Jesus is shown by Luke the Evangelist, who relates that he approached him not in person but through the elders of Israel (Luke 7:3), 43 in order that they might intercede for his boy and, because [Col. 0140A] they were more familiar with the Lord, might petition for him. When they came to Jesus, they earnestly begged him, saying: “He is worthy that you should grant this to him, for he loves our nation and himself built us the synagogue.”

Thus the centurion approached Jesus not in person, but through the elders of Israel, [Note: [Col. 0139D] Bede raises the same question on this passage; before Bede, St Augustine, *Against Faustus*, book 33, chapter 7, and *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, book 2, chapter 20; and before both, Chrysostom, Homily 27. Chrysostom explains the matter by saying that the Jewish elders were first sent to announce that the centurion was coming, and then the centurion himself came. Augustine says that, in customary speech, one is said to have done what one does through others. Bede similarly holds that Matthew, for the sake of brevity, said that the man himself approached whose wish had been conveyed to the Lord by others. Our author follows Augustine.] namely, in order to teach us what we should do in such a matter when we perceive that our servant lies paralysed in our house and is grievously tormented.

For who is this child except the soul, innocent and pure in itself? For *puer* (“boy” or “child”) is so called from purity. Luke, however, calls him a servant because we cannot live without the soul’s service. This child of ours, this servant of ours—our spirit, unjustly subjected and oppressed by the service of the flesh—lies paralysed in [Col. 0140B] the house; it lies weak in the body; it lies in the dwelling-place of flesh, overcome by the disease of vices, and is grievously tormented. Here it is troubled by lust; here it is constricted by avarice; here it is wearied by pride.

What then? Let us send to the physician; let us send to Jesus. But whom shall we send, and who will go for us? Let us send the elders of Israel—that is, bishops and priests. For they ought to intercede for others; they ought to pray for the sick and for sinners. They come quickly to Jesus; they can move him, bend him, and incline him to mercy, especially if we wish to be healed, if we grieve that we have sinned, and if we have done some good by which they may commend us before the judge. For priests readily obtain pardon from the Lord for the penitent person who is ashamed of sins and with all the effort of the mind turns himself [Col. 0140C] to repentance.

And indeed we see many who, although they are tormented in themselves by some vice, nevertheless love good people and in many ways build up the holy Church. Of these, then, we may say: “They are worthy to be heard, because they love our nation and have built us a synagogue.” But what follows? “I will come and heal him”: Matthew says this. But what does Luke say? “And Jesus was going with them.” For Jesus comes to the sick person; he comes with bishops and priests to the penitent, because he is moved by their petitions and led by their prayers.

And when he was already not far from the house, the centurion sent friends to him, saying: “Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; therefore I did not judge myself worthy even to come to you.” [Col. 0140D] Matthew omitted these things, but the rest is common to both. These two therefore agree well in this passage, if only this is understood in Matthew: that the centurion approached Jesus not in person, but first through the elders of Israel and then through friends.

But who are these friends of ours, whom we send to meet Christ as he comes and now draws near to our house? They are, I think, understanding, mind, and a contrite spirit. For they perceive Christ’s coming; they dare to speak with him; they commend us to God and reconcile us to his grace. For when we act inwardly, when in our heart we consider with ourselves what great and manifold kindness our Saviour displayed in taking flesh for us and enduring the insults of the world, then these our aforesaid friends speak with the Lord and in a certain manner say to him: “Lord, do not trouble yourself.” For they marvel and tremble at his trouble and weariness. This is what John the Baptist did when he said: “I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” (Matthew 3:14).

But when we approach Christ’s sacraments and [Col. 0141B] consider our frailty, what else does each of us say but: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; I am not worthy to receive your flesh and blood in my mouth”? [Note: [Col. 0141D] The author applies the centurion’s words, as though on his own authority, to one receiving the Eucharist. Was this not, in his time, a practice in his church whereby they were said by the priest? Cardinal Bona testifies that they are absent from most manuscript missals: *On the Liturgy*, book 2, chapter 17, no. 1.]

“Lord, speak the word, and my boy shall be healed. For you spoke and all things were made; you commanded and all things were created. The same power is yours; the same might remains. Therefore speak the word, command that it happen, and my boy shall be healed; for to heal is no greater thing than to create. For I too am a man set under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”

“I,” he says, “am a man; you are God. I am under authority; you are above all authorities. I have soldiers; you have angels. These obey me; those [Col. 0141C] do your will. Therefore send whom you will, command health to come, and order sickness to depart.”

This pleased the Lord, and he praised the centurion’s faith. For the Lord delayed mercy in order that the centurion’s exceedingly great faith might be shown more clearly. Therefore it is added: “When Jesus heard this, he marvelled and said to those following him: Amen, I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel.” Jesus marvels at the centurion’s faith; he marvels at the faith of a Gentile man. Even then he marvelled at the faith of the Gentiles, which he saw would surpass 44 the faith of the Jews.

Accordingly he immediately adds: “I say to you that many shall come from East and West and shall recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven; but the children [Col. 0141D] of the kingdom shall be cast into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” In these few words he foretells that the Church will be gathered from all parts of the world; that, after hell has been despoiled, the souls of the saints will be transferred to the kingdoms of heaven; and the unbelief and condemnation of the Jews.

But outer darkness is that beyond which no other darkness exists. [Col. 0142A] There are also inner darknesses, from which one comes to these outer darknesses, which unbelieving people suffer in their minds. Of them the Apostle says: “Blindness has happened in part to Israel” (Romans 11:24).

And he said to the centurion: “Go, and as you have believed, let it be done to you.” And the servant was healed in that hour. [Note: [Col. 0141D] Thus far the homily.]

In this Gospel John the Evangelist differs so greatly from the others that the accounts just given cannot in any way agree with his, [Note: [Col. 0141D] Maldonatus demonstrates this, and nearly all other interpreters agree.] if they are understood to concern the same centurion’s servant. For here the centurion is praised for faith and declares himself unworthy for Jesus to come to his house; there he is rebuked for unbelief, as one who does not believe unless he sees signs and wonders, and he urgently invites Christ to come to his house. Here it is related that all these things happened [Col. 0142B] within the city of Capernaum; there it is said that the centurion went out to meet Christ as he came from Judaea, and, because of the length of the journey, servants met him not on the same day but on the following day and said: “Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him.” It is therefore clear that they do not speak of the same person.

We must understand, then, that before Jesus healed this centurion’s servant, of whom Matthew and Luke write, he had already healed that same man’s son, of whom John the Evangelist relates. And because the centurion had first experienced his power in his son, he now has no doubt about his omnipotence in healing the servant. For we readily run for help to the physician whose skill we have already experienced.

## XXVI

And when Jesus came into Peter’s house, he saw his mother-in-law lying sick with a fever. He touched her hand, the fever left her, and she arose and ministered to them.

We must know who Peter’s wife is, in order that we may know who his mother-in-law is. Peter’s wife is the Church, because she was specially entrusted to him by the Lord, who said: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John 21:18). Her mother is therefore the Synagogue, because it is the mother of the Church. [Note: [Col. 0141D] Bede interprets this not very differently [Col. 0142D]: “Peter’s house is circumcision; his mother-in-law is the synagogue, because it is in a sense the mother of the Church,” etc. Peter Chrysologus says elegantly in Sermon 18, “He saw his mother-in-law lying”: “He saw the synagogue lying prostrate in the darkness of its unbelief, weighed down by the burden of its sins,” etc. The same interpretation occurs in Theophilus of Antioch, *Allegories*, book 3, etc.]

Thus the Lord says to it in the Song of Songs: “Under the apple tree I raised you up; there your mother was corrupted; there she who bore you was violated” (Song of Songs 8:5). But it lies in Peter’s house and is feverish, because to this day the Synagogue remains and dwells infirm among Christians. For wherever [Col. 0142D] the Church is, there also is Peter’s house. But near the end of the world the Lord will touch its hand; then, when the fever has fled, it will rise and minister to the Lord. For he will then touch its hand when he approves its works.

But when evening came, they brought to him many who had demons, and he cast out the spirits by a word and healed all who were ill, so that what was spoken by Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: “He took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses.” [Col. 0143A] He casts out spirits by the Word of whom it is written: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1); by a word, indeed, because by his own power. But why at evening, except because he had come to heal, cure, and drive out demons in this last age, this final hour? For that people ought not to have been healed except at evening, since it does not return to the physician until evening. Hence the Psalmist says: “They shall return at evening and suffer hunger like dogs, and shall go round about the city” (Psalm 58:15).

Then they will come, then they will turn; then the Jews will bring to the Lord their sick people, their souls worn out by much weakness; and he will heal them and cast out demons [Col. 0143B] from them. [Note: [Col. 0143C] On Romans 11:25–26: “Blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter.”] “For when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then Israel shall be saved” (Romans 11:25–26); [Note: [Col. 0143C] On Romans 9:27: “But Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, the remnant shall be saved.”] “and though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, the remnant shall turn to the Lord” (Isaiah 10:22).

—But when Jesus saw many crowds around him, he commanded them to go across the water. I think that Jesus commanded the crossing because, unless we cross through the waters of baptism, we could not escape the crowds of vices and the hosts of evil spirits.

And one scribe came to him and said: “Master, I will follow you wherever you go.” Jesus said to him: “Foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” Nothing is hidden from God; no pretence is concealed from his eyes. He sees all things and answers thought. The scribe says: [Col. 0143C] “Master, I will follow you wherever you go.” Jesus says: “It is not so. You do not wish to follow me; you do not wish to keep my commandments. I do not see in you a place where I may lay my head.” Christ’s head is God; and God dwells in the humble, the quiet, and those who tremble at his words. But in you, he says as it were, foxes have dens, and therefore you speak with cunning and pretence. [Note: [Col. 0143C] Chrysostom, Sermon 19: “Christ did not reject the scribe because he wished to follow, but exposed him because he was pretending.”]

Foxes are called evil spirits because of their cunning; [Col. 0144A] they are also called birds of the air because they hold dominion in this air. [Note: [Col. 0143D] St Hilary, chapter 7, no. 10, similarly says: “The fox is a deceitful animal, hiding about the dens of houses and lying in wait for domestic birds; and in several passages we read that false prophets are called by this name. We have often learned that birds of the air are likewise called unclean spirits.” Hilary later interprets him as distrustful and as not having firmly resolved within himself to follow Christ; Titus of Bostra says the same still more expressly on Luke chapter 6 (*Auctarium Ducaeanum*, vol. II, p. 791). Jerome too, from whom this is copied, says that he was “not seeking a master, but profit from a master.” See Chrysologus, Sermon 19.]

These indeed make nests and dens in sinful and wicked people, because in their hearts they give birth to evil thoughts and the offspring of iniquities.

But another of his disciples said to him: “Master, I will follow you.” He said to him: “Follow me.” But he said: “Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father.” Jesus said to him: “Follow me, and let the dead bury their dead.”

This man spoke in another spirit; and therefore he is rightly called not a scribe but a disciple. Nor is he forbidden to follow the Lord; rather, he is commanded to follow and imitate him. Yet he wished first to go and bury his father. He wished to perform a work of piety; yet his piety was not pleasing to his Father and Lord. Why [Col. 0144B] was this? Because it signified something else and, in this act, gave us examples. It was as though he were saying: “You have come to life and wish to return to death. I am life; I am your Father and Creator. Follow me, and let the dead bury their dead.”

For the dead bury the dead when sinners [Note: [Col. 0143D] Hilary, chapter 7, no. 11, and Jerome write that unbelievers are meant by “the dead.” Augustine too, Sermon 62, no. 2, though later more generally: “For as the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul. As the body expires when it gives up the soul, so the soul expires when it loses God. God lost is the death of the soul; the soul lost is the death of the body.” Chrysologus has very similar words in Sermon 19. Augustine also, *City of God*, book 20, chapter 6: “Souls have their own death in impiety and sins; according to that death are dead those of whom the same Lord said: ‘Let the dead bury [Col. 0144D] their dead,’” etc. See Chrysostom, Homily 29.] who are dead to God—for they are dead because the life of which we have just spoken is not in them—hide and conceal within themselves mortal works and criminal sins. Nor only this: they also bury in the grave of their breast their father, the devil, of whom the Lord said to the Jews: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44), and preserve and conceal him as though he were some good thing. The Lord therefore forbids the burial, and this kind of burial, of such a father. [Note: [Col. 0144D] On the latter disciple of Jesus Christ, see Gregory, *Morals*, book 7, chapter 17; on both, Basil, or the author of the *Monastic Constitutions*, chapter 20, no. 3, and the Chrysologus cited above.]

XXVII. [Note: [Col. 0144D] This is a homily attributed to Eusebius of Emesa, for the Fifth Sunday after Epiphany, p. 38.] And when he entered the boat, his disciples followed him; and behold, a great disturbance arose in the sea, so that the boat was covered by the waves. But he was asleep. For what is the boat but the Church? What is the sea but the world? What is the agitation of the sea but the raging fury of persecutors and tyrants? [Note: [Col. 0144D] See Alexander Junius’s dissertation entitled *The Ship as a Symbol of the Church*, etc., where he adduces witnesses to this allegory: Augustine, Ambrose, Jerome, and Bede. Above all, this is done by the author of the *Opus Imperfectum*, Homily 23, and by Chrysologus—whom he passed over. The latter, Sermon 20: “When Christ boarded the ship of his Church in order to cross the sea of this age, the gusts of the Gentiles, the whirlwinds of the Jews, the storms of persecutors . . . so rushed upon it that one storm arose out of the whole world,” etc. See the remainder and the following sermon. Earlier still, Tertullian, *On Baptism*, ch. 12. [Col. 0145D] “Moreover, that boat prefigured the Church, because on the sea—that is, in the world—it is troubled by waves—that is, by persecutions and temptations—while the Lord, through patience, is as though asleep, until, awakened in the last times by the prayers of the saints, he restrains the world and restores tranquillity to his own.”]

Behold, the Lord sleeps in the boat, and the boat is covered by waves. The disciples are afraid and are not yet delivered from danger. They cry out and awaken the Savior. He rises from sleep who never sleeps: “For he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” (Ps. 120:4). He commands the winds and the sea, and a great calm arises.

These things happen for us, brothers; for us Jesus sleeps, for us he rises from sleep. This is a sign and an instruction concerning our weakness: he dies for us. For he would not sleep unless he understood that his sleep would benefit us. The shepherd seems to sleep when wolves rage against the sheep, when thieves seize them, and there is none to rescue them. Thus Jesus, though he does not sleep, nevertheless appears to sleep when tyrants rage, when evil people rise against good people, when the good are overcome and the wicked prevail. He does not sleep, however: he watches the battle and at the same time awaits [Col. 0145B] both the end of the struggle and the faithfulness of those who fight. Because he does not immediately help, because he does not swiftly come to the aid of those in distress, he is thought to sleep.

But if we consider the character of that contest and the manner of its victory, then the saints prove victorious precisely when they are believed to have been conquered by the wicked. For the saints unquestionably conquer when they do not lose humility and patience. Let Jesus therefore appear to sleep, so that the cruelty of the wicked and the patience of the saints may become known, and so that Christ’s disciples may learn to lay the storms of this sea to rest not by arms but by cries and prayers. But if they can no longer endure them, if they are unable to withstand such great turmoil, 46 let them come to Jesus and awaken him, saying, “Lord, save us; we are perishing.” Thus let them defend themselves; let them take up these weapons, [Col. 0145C] protect themselves by this aid, and fortify themselves with this shield.

Nor should they suppose themselves unheard because persecution does not cease. They are no less heard when patience to endure adversity is given them than if all persecution were removed from them. He himself knows what we need; nevertheless let us always say, “Lord, save us; we are perishing.” For whoever says this seeks nothing other than salvation. Yet perhaps he speaks of bodily salvation, whereas Christ understands salvation of the soul. No saint desires bodily salvation against the salvation of the soul, even if he perhaps sometimes asks for it. God therefore hears not words but intention.

And he says to them: “Why are you fearful, you of little faith?” I am here, and yet you are afraid? But why are you afraid, except because you have little faith? Then, rising, he commanded [Col. 0145D] the winds and the sea, and a great calm came about. Indeed, every day he rises; every day he calms wars; every day he commands visible and invisible things. At his command battles and disputes cease, and there comes great peace and tranquillity.

But the people were astonished, saying: “What sort of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?” They are rightly called people, [Col. 0146A] since they marvel as people do. For they did not yet believe him to be God, whom they saw sleeping as a man at one time and awake at another. Therefore they said, “What sort of man is this?” Let us also say: “What god is great like our God? You are the God who works wonders,” whom winds and sea obey, whom all creatures serve; whom the sea saw and fled, whose voice it heard and feared (Ps. 76). [Note: [Col. 0145D] Other material follows in the homily mentioned above, p. 39.]

XXVIII. And when he had crossed over into the region of the Gerasenes, two men possessed by demons met him, coming out from the tombs, exceedingly fierce, so that no one could pass along that road. Mark and Luke, however, write not of two but of one. Why, then, does Matthew relate that they were two? [Note: [Col. 0145D] The literal solution of the difficulty is given by Chrysostom [Col. 0146D] on this passage, Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, book II, ch. 24, etc.: either because one was better known than the other, or because he was more savagely afflicted by the demon. Ambrose, book VI, on Luke, also refers the matter allegorically to the Gentile people, both one and many, descended from Noah’s two sons, Ham and Japheth. Bede includes both explanations, writing that there was one person of greater notoriety, and two Gentile peoples occupied by idols.]

Perhaps they indeed speak about the man, whereas Matthew speaks about what the man signifies. For although the man was personally one, he nevertheless represented two peoples. Likewise, although all the other Evangelists relate that only the colt was brought to Jesus, Matthew describes both the colt and the she-ass as brought to him, attending more to the signification than to the history. This one man, therefore, is the human race, which has been possessed by demons ever since the time when it first committed original sin. But because it is divided into two peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles, the others narrate the whole, while this Evangelist narrates the parts.

They are rightly said to come out of the tombs, because they are transferred from death to life. And they cried out, saying: [Col. 0146C] “What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?” “What,” they say, “have we in common with you? Let heaven suffice you; allow us to possess the earth. You did not expel us from heaven; you ought not again to expel us from the earth. For where shall we go from your Spirit, and where shall we flee from your face? You have come here to torment us before the time. The time prepared for us and for our angels has not yet arrived, and already we are tormented. Your presence torments us; your face burns us.”

O wretched Jews! Why do you not observe that the demons call Jesus the Son of God—he of whom you, worse and more wicked than they, say: “According to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John 19:7)? Believe at least the demons, since you refuse to believe the prophets and apostles. Let those teach you in [Col. 0146D] what is good whom you are not afraid to imitate in evil.

Now the demons begged him, saying: “If you cast us out, send us into the herd of swine.” There was not far from them a large herd of swine feeding. “If,” they say, “you cast us out—for we know that you will cast us out, and will no longer permit us to remain in a human being—you who were made in the likeness [Col. 0147A] of human beings and appear to human beings to be man and not God: but you appear otherwise to us, because at some time we recognized you in another form. For we know that you are the Son of God, though the Jews neither believe nor understand this. Send us into the herd of swine.”

Whence comes this terrible desire in unclean spirits, that they seek unclean animals as places to dwell? This, indeed, is a signification. For what had the swine sinned, that they should be handed over to demons? He who is creator of swine is also creator of angels. Finally, no animal is evil except angel and human being; and therefore no other is condemned and no other made blessed. What, then, do the swine mean? I ask not about their nature, but about their signification. [Note: [Col. 0147D] Chrysostom also, Homily 29, describes “many people who live like swine rather than human beings; if they become wholly swine, they will not only be driven about by demons, but will also be hurled over precipices.” See Ambrose, book VI, on Luke.]

For swine are all who delight in the filth of vices, [Col. 0147B] all who delight in the rot of sins. Every fornicator, every adulterer, every voluptuary is a swine—outwardly speaking. Inwardly, however, every heretic, every Jew, and every idolater is a swine. These, then, are the persons sought by demons; these are those in whom demons dwell; these are those whom the Lord 47 hands over to the devil. For the Apostle also handed over a certain fornicator “to Satan for the destruction of the flesh.”

And Jesus said to them, “Go”; and, coming out, they went into the swine. You see, therefore, that evil spirits have no power even over swine without God’s permission. [Note: [Col. 0147D] Gregory, *Dialogues*, book III, ch. 21: “From this matter it is also inferred that without the permission of almighty God an evil spirit has no power against a human being, since it could not enter the swine unless permitted.” Chrysostom, Homily 29: “Thus they seem not even to have power over swine unless the Creator of all, God, grants it.”] They dare not approach them unless permitted; they dare not attack them unless power has been granted by God. Yet unless they were swine, they would not be handed over; and if they were handed over, they would not be utterly conquered.

And behold, the whole herd rushed [Col. 0147C] violently down a precipice into the sea, and they died in the waters. Whoever is possessed by the devil is not governed by order or reason, but is hurled and falls headlong in violence and madness: one into adultery, another into perjury, another into murder, another into theft; but all are hurled and fall into eternal death and condemnation.

But the herdsmen fled, and coming into the city reported everything, including what had happened to those who had had demons. And behold, the whole city came out to meet Jesus; and when they saw him, they begged him to depart from their territory. These herdsmen are bishops and priests. For bishops do not tend sheep alone; often more swine than sheep are found in their flocks. They flee—and rightly flee. For who would not flee demons? Who would not flee mad swine? We ought not to associate with such persons, especially when we openly recognize their wickedness. “For what agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what share has a believer with an unbeliever?” (2 Cor. 6:15.)

This they ought to report in the city, that is, in the Church, so that the others may beware lest they perish by their example. Swine perish; human beings are saved. Those who flee to Christ are saved; those who lie in filth and do not withdraw from the stench of vices perish. But what are you doing, foolish city? You see Jesus; you see also a man healed by Jesus; and you ask him to depart from your borders. For this city is the synagogue of the wicked, which saw and heard Christ and beheld his works and miracles, yet refused [Col. 0148B] to believe in him.

XXIX. [CHAPTER IX.] And, entering the boat, he crossed over and came to his own city. In this place we must understand his own city not as Nazareth but as Capernaum. Both are called his city: the former because he was brought up there; the latter because he lived there for a time. For it is said above that, leaving the city of Nazareth, he came and lived in maritime Capernaum. [Note: [Col. 0147D] Jerome here disagrees: “We understand his city to be none other than Nazareth, from which he is called Nazarene.” But Augustine, agreeing with our author, observes in *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, part II, ch. 25, that St. Mark expressly names Capernaum when he appears to narrate the same event, and concludes: “Who could doubt that Jesus did this in his own city, since he did it [Col. 0148D] in Capernaum, a city of Galilee?” Bede copies Augustine. Some wish it to be called Christ’s city because it was the chief city in Galilee and because he was born in Galilee. Chrysostom more conveniently says at the beginning of the homily, followed by almost all modern writers—Jansenius, Maldonatus, a Lapide, Calmet, etc.: “Here he called Capernaum his own city: Bethlehem bore him, Nazareth brought him up, but Capernaum was his permanent dwelling.”]

And behold, they brought to him a paralytic lying on a bed. Mark says that this paralytic was carried by four men. This paralytic is the human spirit, also called the soul. [Note: [Col. 0148D] Jerome: “According to the tropological interpretation, the soul sometimes lies in its body, with all the powers of its members loosened, and is brought by a perfect teacher to the Lord to be healed,” etc. Bede is even closer to our author: “The healing of this paralytic . . . signifies the salvation of the soul, which first needs ministers—that is, good teachers—to bring it to Christ. These are fittingly found to be four, as Mark relates, either because all the strength of preachers is established by the four books of the Gospel, or because of the four virtues,” etc.]

But he lies on a bed, that is, in the body, and is burdened by that from which he ought to have received rest: “For the corruptible body [Col. 0148C] weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15). The spirit is weak because it does not lie well. For a paralytic spirit is one that is not in its own power; paralysis, wherever it seizes a limb, makes it in some manner insensible, as though dead, and useless. A paralysed soul has neither eyes for seeing nor ears for hearing.

But who are these four who carry this paralytic and offer him to the Lord? No persons seem capable of being understood more fittingly by them than these four Evangelists. For no soul is offered to the Lord except through these, and no soul is healed except through their faith. Therefore it is said here: “And Jesus, seeing their faith, said to the paralytic, ‘Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you.’” [Col. 0149A] It is as if he said: “You are indeed weak, but those who carry you are sound. Their faith heals you, if you take courage in their faith. Take courage, therefore, son, made my son through faith: your sins are forgiven you.”

Do you see how the Lord himself expounds his Gospel? How, in those things which are done outwardly—if one has eyes and does not lie wholly paralysed—he teaches us otherwise inwardly by the Spirit? For in saying, “Your sins are forgiven you,” he shows that the inner human being, that is, the spirit, is paralysed. For what is the weakness of the soul but sins? Let these be removed, let this disease be taken away, and the soul will be healed. He would not have said this had he been referring to bodily weakness. For the body is not healed merely because the soul is freed from sins. 48

The Apostle says: “When I am weak, then I am stronger,” [Note: [Col. 0149D] 2 Cor. 12:10: “Then I am powerful.”] signifying that the spirit is strengthened through weakness of the flesh. But the scribes present there, misunderstanding this and attending not to paralysis of the soul but of the body, said that Christ the Lord had blasphemed. Hence it follows: “And behold, some of the scribes said within themselves, ‘This man blasphemes.’” And when Jesus saw their thoughts, he said: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” For they too were inwardly paralysed, although they did not perceive their weakness, since they said that the Lord had blasphemed. Jesus regarded their wicked thoughts no less than that man’s weakness.

He therefore said: “Why do you think evil in your hearts? You know neither the physician nor recognize the power of the remedy. [Col. 0149C] For a good physician looks to the vein and root of the disease; once he has cut this away, he considers the rest easy to heal. For which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? If we attend only to the saying, I do not know which of the two is easier, for both are very easy. But to forgive sins, or to provide a paralytic with strength to rise and walk, is difficult. Yet because one was invisible and the other visible, he proves the invisible through the visible, so that, seeing him possess authority in the body, they may not doubt that he also possesses authority in the soul.”

For they said: “No one can forgive sins except God alone.” They spoke rightly, indeed. Although the Church forgives sins—for the Lord showed this when he said, “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20:23)—nevertheless he alone forgives sins who says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). He was God; [Col. 0150A] he was also man—indeed, he is God and man. But as God he forgives sins through himself; as man he possesses the authority to forgive sins through the Lord’s power.

And this is what he says: “But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”: see what you can see, that you may believe what you could not see. You believe that no one can forgive sins except God alone; now you will know that the Son of Man too has authority to forgive sins. Then he said to the paralytic: “Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house.” And he rose and went to his house.

What they sought has therefore been proved; they ought no longer to doubt. Let them believe that the soul has been loosed from sins when they see the body healed from paralysis. But what does he mean by saying, “Rise, take up your bed”? We have said [Col. 0150B] that the bed signifies the body, on which the weak soul lay. Thus the soul is told to rise. For what is rising but awakening to a good work? Hence the Apostle: “Rise, he says, you who sleep; rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14). “Rise, take up your bed”: have authority over your flesh; rule your body. You carry it, govern it, direct it; let it serve you, obey you, and henceforth be wholly subject to you. “And go to your house”: return to your homeland; bring your flesh back to your homeland, because it expelled you from your homeland. [Note: [Col. 0149D] St. Gregory, Homily 12 on Ezekiel, aptly says: “By the bed, in which the flesh takes its rest, the flesh itself is signified; but by the house conscience is figured. And because, when dead in mind, we lie in vices, we rest in carnal pleasure and, being weak, are carried on a bed. But when we have been healed in mind, so that we now resist the assaults of fleshly vices, it is necessary that we also bear the reproaches of temptations arising from our flesh. Therefore, after the sick man has been restored to health, he is commanded: ‘Take up your bed,’” etc.] And when the crowds saw it, they were afraid and glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings.

XXX. And as Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man named Matthew sitting at the tax office, and said to him: “Follow me.” And rising, he followed him. Blessed Matthew speaks about himself as though of another person. We read that Moses and certain others did the same, teaching humility and cutting off vain glory. [Note: [Col. 0150D] Jerome: “The other Evangelists, out of reverence and honor for Matthew, did not wish to call him by his common name, but called him Levi; for he had two names. Matthew himself, following Solomon’s precept that ‘the righteous man is his own accuser,’ etc., calls himself Matthew and a tax collector.” Bede copies Jerome.]

He is also called Levi, a name with nearly the same meaning: *Matthew* means “given,” and *Levi*, “added.” [Note: [Col. 0150D] These points, I think, are from Jesus. Bede on this passage: “Matthew in Hebrew is called ‘given’ in Latin . . . Levi means ‘added’ or ‘assumed.’”] For, added to the order of the apostles, he was given as a great gift to the holy Church. And he is rightly called from the tax office, so that he who collected public taxes may teach us too to pay tribute. For what else does he teach us in this Gospel except what tribute we should render to the Lord, of what kind, and in what manner? In everything we do at the Lord’s command, we do nothing other than pay [Col. 0150D] tribute.

And it came to pass, as he reclined at table in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and reclined with Jesus and his disciples. Luke says (ch. 5:29) that Levi made him a great feast [Col. 0151A] in his house; hence, I think, it happened that tax collectors and other people of the same rank assembled there for the feast. Nevertheless, we must understand that neither that feast nor that gathering of tax collectors was without some signification. For the feast which Levi then prepared for the Lord signified this Gospel, 49 which he afterwards wrote and by whose delights our souls are now refreshed in Christ.

The Jews refused to come to this feast; tax collectors and sinners were compelled to enter. Hence elsewhere the Lord says: “None of those who were invited shall taste my supper.” And when the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples: “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” (Luke 11:24.) Likewise, [Col. 0151B] some believers later took offence at blessed Peter because he had associated with the uncircumcised Cornelius (Acts 11:2); and he gave them an explanation, just as the Lord did not disdain to give an explanation to these people.

For he says: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill.” It is as though he said: “I came to heal, not to eat; I am a physician, not a guest—indeed, I am a guest precisely because I am a physician.” [Note: [Col. 0151D] “The Lord went to the feasts of sinners in order to have an opportunity to teach, and to offer spiritual food to those who invited him.” Jerome.] This kind of illness is nowhere healed as well as at a feast. Hence the Apostle says: “I became as weak to the weak, that I might gain the weak” (1 Cor. 9:22). Christ does not disdain to receive at a feast those whose mortality he did not disdain to assume. Outwardly he refreshes bodies; inwardly he refreshes minds. There can be no hunger [Col. 0151C] where the living bread which came down from heaven is present.

Let bread, then, be given to the hungry, of whom it is said: “And the hungry were filled” (1 Sam. 2:5). Let the physician help the sick, who cannot otherwise be healed. “But go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice.’” This is written in Hosea. [Note: [Col. 0151D] Hosea 6:6: “For he desired mercy, not sacrifice.” See Chrysologus, Sermon 31, who also discusses Matthew’s calling in the preceding Sermons 28, 29, and 30.] Had the Pharisees understood it, they would never have reproached the Father of mercy for mercy. What this mercy is, he then explained, saying: “For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.” That sinners are called and saved is mercy; but that those are rejected who unjustly suppose themselves righteous is justice. The world could not be saved [Col. 0151D] through sacrifice; it was saved through mercy, because Christ’s sacrifice was mercy.

XXXI. Then John’s disciples came to him, saying: “Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but your disciples do not fast?” And Jesus said [Col. 0152A] to them: “Can the children of the bridegroom mourn while the bridegroom is with them? But days will come when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then they will fast.”

“You do well,” he says, “in fasting; nor do I condemn fasting, by which the flesh is subdued, lust overcome, and demons driven away. Since, therefore, my disciples do not now fast, there is a great mystery and sacrament.” [Note: [Col. 0151D] Jerome—whom Bede, as often elsewhere, copies—expounds this mystery on this passage: “The bridegroom is Christ; the bride is the Church. From this holy and spiritual marriage the apostles have been begotten; they cannot mourn while they see the bride in the bridal chamber [Col. 0152D] and know that the bridegroom is with the bride.” See the remainder.]

These are wedding days: the bridegroom is present, banquets are prepared, joy is everywhere, instruments sound everywhere, and the pleasant psaltery is heard with the harp. For that rejoicing of the banqueters signified the rejoicing of that eternal banquet by which all the saints will at last be refreshed through the presence of the supreme Good himself. “But days will come when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them”—that is, the days on which he will be received [Col. 0152B] into heaven—and then they will fast.

And as though someone were to say: “If these are wedding days, if new and spiritual banquets have been prepared, if what you do are sacraments, why do you not also compel these men? Why do you not make them also participants in such great sacraments?” To this he replies: “Because they are unwilling; because they came not to learn but to criticize; because they are clothed in old garments; because they have no wedding garments; because they are old wineskins, unable to contain new wine; because, intoxicated by old wine, they abhor new wine, saying, ‘The old is better.’”

And this is what he says: “No one puts a patch of unshrunk cloth upon an old garment, for it takes away its fullness from the garment and the tear becomes worse. Nor do they put new wine [Col. 0152C] into old wineskins; otherwise the wineskins burst, the wine is spilled, and the wineskins perish. But they put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved.”

We are therefore taught by this that we must adapt our speech and teaching to the capacity of our hearers. For the Pharisees to whom the Lord then spoke could still be saved under the teaching and observance of the old law. If the Lord had immediately disclosed the new sacraments to them, they would have departed scandalized rather than edified. [Note: [Col. 0152D] Jerome: “He set forth two examples, that of old and new wineskins and that of a garment. By old wineskins we must understand the scribes and Pharisees; by the patch of new garment and new wine, the Gospel precepts, which the Jews cannot bear, lest the tear become greater.”] Therefore they first had to be renewed gradually, and only then at last called to the wedding feast of the Lamb.

### XXXII.

While he was speaking these things to them, behold, one ruler came and worshipped him, saying [Note: [Col. 0152D] There is a homily attributed to Emesenus for the twenty-fourth Sunday after Pentecost, p. 178.]: “Lord, my daughter has just died; but come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live.”

For what are we to understand by this ruler except Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, Moses and Aaron, and the other rulers of that people, who always come to the Lord and intercede for the death and blindness of their daughter—that is, the Synagogue [Note: [Col. 0152D] Bede: “For the Synagogue is the daughter, who was Moses’ only one,” etc. Jerome had preceded Bede in explaining what is added below: “When Jesus came into the house,” etc.: “To this day,” he says, “the girl lies dead in the ruler’s house, and those who appear to be teachers are flute-players, singing a funeral song. The crowd of Jews also is not a crowd of believers, but a crowd of tumult-makers.” Hilary had preceded them both, writing on this passage: “This ruler is understood to be the Law, which entreats the Lord for the people whom it had itself nourished for Christ through the preaching of the expectation of his coming, that he might restore life to the dead woman.”]? [Col. 0153A]

Therefore they ask the Lord to come, lay his hand upon her, and she will live. For all the patriarchs and prophets prayed for this; all awaited and longed for Christ’s coming. At last the Lord Jesus came; but because of the length of the journey, he has not yet reached the girl, has not yet laid his hand upon her: she still lies dead. Yet he is going to her, and his disciples are with him. For every day we draw nearer to this girl’s resurrection, every day nearer to the conversion of the Synagogue. Yet another woman must first be healed before we reach this one, because “when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in, then all Israel shall be saved” (Rom. IX, 26).

But what does “my daughter has just died” mean? What is “just”? “Just now,” he says, “you came; just now you began to preach; just now my daughter died.” The physician came; health and life came; and at the very time when my daughter ought to have been healed, she died. “For if you had not come and spoken to her, she would not have had sin; but now she has no excuse for her sin” (John XV, 22). Thus my daughter is dead; but come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live.

And Jesus arose and followed him, together with his disciples. Rightly indeed this ruler is called Jairus, whom Jesus and his disciples follow; for Jairus is interpreted “enlightened” [Note: [Col. 0153D] This is from Bede: “Mystically Jairus, whose name is interpreted ‘Enlightened’ or ‘Enlightening,’ is understood as Moses, who, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, had received words of life, in order through them to enlighten others.”]. Therefore he fittingly signifies the patriarchs and prophets, whose eyes he enlightened, and to whom he revealed the mysteries, “the uncertain and hidden things of his wisdom” (Ps. L, 8). Jesus and his disciples follow these, because all walk the same way of mercy and justice: what those men foretold, these strive to do and fulfil. They go before by speech and prophecy; these follow by action and confirmation.

And behold, a woman who had suffered from an issue of blood for twelve years came behind him and touched the fringe of his garment. Who is this woman except the Church of the Gentiles [Note: [Col. 0154D] Jerome likewise: “Observe, therefore, that this woman—that is, the people of the Gentiles—began to be sick at the time when the Jewish nation had believed,” etc. Bede expands Jerome’s point still further. See also Hilary, who understands in the type of this woman the multitude of sinners healed before the Jews either were healed or are to be healed.]? The Lord had come to heal the Synagogue; for he himself says: “I was not sent except to the sheep that have perished of the house of Israel” (Matt. X, 6). And behold, the woman who suffered from an issue of blood, and who was called unclean according to the Law, came behind him, touched the fringe of his garment, and was healed.

For she suffered an issue of blood because she dwelt in the blood of her own sins; because she was nourished by bloodshed, robbery, and murder. She came from behind; she did not stand before his face, but came with fear and shame. Hence the Apostle says: “What fruit, then, did you have in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. VI, 21.) [Col. 0154A]

She touched the garment: she believed the mystery of his incarnation. For Christ’s garment is his humanity, with which divinity was clothed and thereby could not be seen. But she said within herself: “If I only touch his garments, I shall be healed.” This woman, as the other Evangelists say, had spent all her substance on physicians and had gained nothing, but had grown worse. By these physicians we may understand diviners and philosophers. Those who believed their persuasions and wandered from the truth of faith could not attain health of soul, because salvation is far from sinners. The substance and riches of the soul are virtues and honorable habits; these are indeed lost by those who place their faith and hope in vanities.

But Jesus turned and, seeing her, said [Col. 0154B]: “Take courage, daughter; your faith has made you whole.” And the woman was made whole from that hour [Note: [Col. 0154D] Heb. XI, 6; Rom. IV, 3; I, 17; Heb. XI, 33; Matt. XVII, 17; Mark IX, 12.]. “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI, 6).—“Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Jas. II, 23).—“The righteous person lives by faith” (Heb. X, 38).—“The saints conquered kingdoms through faith” (Heb. XI, 33).—“If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed” (Matt. XVII, 19), you will be able to move mountains. “All things are possible to one who believes” (Mark IX, 22).

Great, therefore, is faith, which the Lord thus commends everywhere, granting to each according to his faith.

And when Jesus came into the house of the ruler of the Pharisees, and saw the flute-players and the tumultuous crowd, he said: “Depart, for the girl is not dead but asleep.” And many mocked him. What then happened at that time in one girl will happen at the end of time in the whole Synagogue. For then the Lord Jesus will come with his disciples into the house of the ruler of the Pharisees, because then the entire multitude of Jews will receive Christ’s faith and the apostles’ teaching.

Then, at the Lord’s command, the flute-players and the tumultuous crowd will depart, since then the letter—which sweetly, yet fruitlessly and uselessly, charms human ears—and its lovers will cease.
