For what were the scribes and Pharisees except flute-players, expounding the Law and the Prophets according to the letter, while not understanding what they said? A flute produces a sweet sound [Col. 0154C] without understanding. Let the flute-players therefore depart; let every tumultuous crowd depart; let the chattering and clamorous depart, roaring with their voices and understanding nothing.

“For the girl is not dead, but asleep.” This is the song of the dead. So long as the Synagogue listened to these flutes, it was dead; indeed, these flutes killed it: “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (II Cor. II, 6). [Col. 0155A] Let the letter therefore depart; let the Spirit come, awaken the sleeper, make her understanding, and console both parents.

But who are those foolish people who mocked the Lord, except those who did not believe in the resurrection? We do not doubt that many such have existed, still exist, and will exist. And when the crowd had been put out, he entered, took her hand, and the girl arose. The crowd therefore has not yet been put out; the Synagogue has not yet arisen. It is still disturbed; it still delights in the letter. But it will arise when Jesus comes, when he enters to her and takes her hand. For then Jesus will enter to her when the oldness of the letter has been driven away and the words of the new sacred Gospel are written on her heart. Then indeed she will be able to say: “You have held my right hand; in your counsel you have guided me, and with glory you have received me” (Ps. LXXII, 24). [Col. 0155B]

### XXXIII.

And as Jesus passed on from there, two blind men followed him, crying out and saying: “Have mercy on us, Lord, Son of David.” When he had come into the house, the blind men came to him; and Jesus said to them: “Do you believe that I can do this for you?” They said to him: “Certainly, Lord.” Then he touched their eyes, saying: “According to your faith, let it be done to you.” And their eyes were opened.

The blind men cry out and are not yet enlightened. They follow Jesus as far as the house; they are questioned about faith; they answer that they believe; Jesus touches their eyes, and they are enlightened. For every unbeliever is blind; the two blind men are Gentile and Jew [Note: [Col. 0155D] “For both peoples were blind,” says Jerome here, “while the Lord was passing through this age and desiring to return to his house.” Bede likewise: “The two blind men are the two peoples, blinded by observance of the letter and by Gentile rite, ignorant of things to come. While the Lord was passing through this age and desiring to return to his house, the two blind men followed him, because, when the Gospel was preached through the apostles, many among Jews and Gentiles began to follow the Redeemer.”].

But if, having heard of Christ’s power, they already begin to believe, this very believing [Col. 0155C] is crying out. Already in a certain manner they cry through faith; already with the cry of the heart they say: “Have mercy on us, Son of David. If what we have heard of you is true, have mercy on us; make us understand the truth and enlighten our eyes.”

They cry well, pray well, and begin well to follow Jesus. It remains, then, that they should come to the house and hasten to the Church. There the blind are enlightened; there true light is found; there Christ our Lord is heard. But what does he say? It follows: “Do you believe that I can do this for you?” What Jesus then said in person, he also says now through his members in the Church. A catechumen comes to the Church; the Creed is read to him; the catholic faith is read to him; he is asked whether he believes thus; he answers that he believes. Then indeed [Col. 0155D] Jesus touches his eyes, enlightens his mind, and he is baptized and enlightened. For unless he had answered, “I believe,” he would not be baptized; and unless he were baptized, he would not be enlightened.

Thus in these two blind men our Savior taught us what we ought to do in all others: how we ought to receive them, question them, and enlighten them. [Col. 0156A] In saying, “According to your faith let it be done to you,” he plainly signifies that no one is saved except through faith. Hence he also says elsewhere: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark XVI, 16). He did not say simply that whoever is baptized shall be saved, but “he who believes and is baptized.” Infants are saved by the faith of those baptizing them; after they understand faith, they are no longer saved except by their own faith. Prayers and almsgiving, sacrifices and other good works are beneficial—but for believers.

And Jesus charged them, saying: “See that no one knows.” But they, going out, spread word of him throughout that whole region. The Lord seems to command something virtually impossible. For how could they conceal it unless they concealed their eyes? But if they had concealed their eyes, what benefit would the light newly restored to them have given them? What then? Shall we call disobedient those who, preaching Christ’s glory, commendably made him known throughout that whole region [Note: [Col. 0156D] Jerome: “The Lord, fleeing the glory of boastfulness through humility, had given this command; but they, because they remembered the grace bestowed, could not keep silent about the benefit.” Bede likewise.]?

First, this defends them: they praised not themselves but the Lord, nor did they boast of the light they had received. Thus the Apostle also says: “We do not preach ourselves, but the Lord Jesus” (II Cor. IV, 5). Moreover, it signified something else: the Lord does not wish us to perform good deeds in order that they may be seen by people. Those who do this have received their reward. This, therefore, is the reason why he commands that the deeds he gloriously performs in many places be concealed.

### XXXIV.

When they had gone out, behold, they brought to him a dumb man possessed by a demon; and when the demon had been cast out [Note: [Col. 0156D] “A demon,” etc., Vulgate.], the dumb man spoke. And the crowds marveled, saying: “Never has anything like this appeared in Israel.” But the Pharisees said: “By the prince of demons he casts out demons.”

Some depart healed; others come to be healed. There are never lacking persons in whom the Lord may display the power of his virtue. “And behold,” he says, “they brought to him a dumb man possessed by a demon.” Christ’s works never lack meaning; they are always fortified with a twofold power, since in one person many are enlightened and in one many are healed.

Who is this dumb man? Is he only one person? In this dumb man many dumb people are signified. Every person possessed by a demon is dumb. This is shown by the fact that, after the demon was expelled, the dumb man spoke [Col. 0156D] [Note: [Col. 0156D] St. Hilary: “First the demon is expelled, and then the remaining functions of the body follow. For once, through knowledge of God, the madness of all superstitions has been driven away, sight, hearing, and the speech of salvation are brought in.”].

This dumb man is called dumb not because he does not speak at all, but because he speaks badly rather than well. He does not know how to speak good things; he does not know how to open his lips in the praises of God. But if he is converted, if he returns to repentance, you will immediately see the dumb man speaking, praising God, accusing himself, and proclaiming the truth. Who would not marvel at this? For this is “the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. LXXVI, 11). [Col. 0157A] Miserable Pharisees, who suppose this is done by the prince of demons—as though the prince of demons could do more than the prince of men and angels.

### XXXV.

And Jesus went about all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom, and healing every sickness and every infirmity.

This, therefore, was the work of our Savior: for this he had come—to teach, to preach the Gospel of the kingdom of God, to turn those who had gone astray to the way of truth, and to heal every sickness and infirmity inwardly and outwardly. But seeing the crowds, he had compassion on them, because they were troubled and lying down like sheep without a shepherd. This is what the Apostle Peter says [Col. 0157B]: “For you were like wandering sheep; but now you have been converted to the shepherd and bishop of your souls” (I Pet. II, 25).

### XXXVI.

Then he said to his disciples: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray therefore the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest.”

For the field is as great as the world [Note: [Col. 0157D] Jerome likewise: “The plentiful harvest signifies the multitude of peoples; the few laborers, the scarcity of teachers”; and then: “The plentiful harvest is the whole multitude of believers; the laborers are few, both the apostles and their imitators who are sent to the harvest.” Bede copies these latter words.]. The harvest is plentiful because people are many; the laborers are few because preachers are few. Yet the Lord wishes to be asked to send laborers into his harvest, so that his faithful may be rewarded not only for their labor but also for their affection and will.

### [CHAPTER X.]

And having called his twelve disciples, he gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out and to heal every sickness and every infirmity. [Col. 0157C] It is no wonder that Christ’s disciples could overcome kings, rulers, tyrants, and powerful men, since they received power over the evil spirits themselves, their rulers and lords.

Even now bishops and priests perform in souls what the apostles then performed in bodies [Note: [Col. 0157D] Bede: “The holy Church does this daily when it heals those weak in good works by exhortation; calls back through repentance those dead in unbelief or sins; heals lepers needing correction from the various stains of error; and expels demons from people through the grace of exorcism.”]. For they cast out unclean spirits, heal human minds of every ailment, and raise souls already dead to life. Why indeed did the Lord and his disciples heal bodies destined soon to die, except that through this the soul, destined to live forever, might be healed? They would not have believed unless they had seen signs and wonders. For the Lord himself says: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe” (John IV, 48). But if they had not believed, they could not have attained salvation of soul.

It is therefore greater to heal a soul than a body, because that which is done through itself is greater than that which is done through another. The names of the twelve apostles are these: first Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James of Zebedee and John his brother; Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and [Col. 0158A] Matthew the tax collector; James of Alphaeus and Thaddaeus; Simon the Cananean; and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him.

Jesus sent these twelve, commanding them and saying: “Do not go into the ways of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” For this reason the Lord says: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel”: because he had come to preach to the Jews personally and in the presence of his body, but to the Gentiles through the apostles and teachers. Therefore, after he had now forbidden his disciples to go into the ways of the Gentiles and enter Samaritan cities, he later commanded them, saying: “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature” [Note: [Col. 0158D] Mark XVI, 15: “Going into the whole world.”].

He wished to call the Jews first and the Gentiles afterward. The Samaritans, however, following Jeroboam [Col. 0158B], worshipped idols; hence they are not improperly grouped here with the Gentiles. “As you go, preach, saying: ‘The kingdom of heaven has drawn near.’” Let the kingdom of evil therefore be removed; let the kingdom of demons be destroyed and perish, because now on earth the kingdom of the saints is being built, because now the King of Angels dwells among us.

This will be the proof of this proclamation: “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons; freely you received, freely give.” These things are not human but divine, not earthly but heavenly. Who, then, can doubt that the kingdom of heaven and its King and Lord are present, when in Jesus’ name sickness flees, death perishes, life and health return, leprosy departs, and evil spirits that ruled human beings are driven from them? [Col. 0158C]

“Freely you received, freely give.” Let the Simoniacs hear this; let those hear it who do not fear to buy and sell the gifts of the Holy Spirit. But the Simoniac says: “I did not receive freely; I cannot give freely.” If you did not receive freely, you did not receive from the Lord, for the Lord gives to no one except freely. Therefore do not give, whether freely or not freely; for these words are not addressed to you: “Do not possess gold, silver, or money in your belts; no bag for the journey, nor two tunics, nor footwear, nor a staff: for the laborer is worthy of his reward” [Note: [Col. 0158D] “For the laborer is worthy of his food,” here and Luke X, 7: “For the laborer is worthy of his reward.”].

By these words every occasion for greed and avarice is removed, every superfluity cut away, and only necessities allowed. Thus the way is made easy, fear flees, and confidence grows. Hence one writer rightly says: “The traveler, unburdened, will sing before the robber.” Why should they carry a bag or purse when they may not think about tomorrow? For in these are stored and kept what is reserved for the future. But what can one store who reserves nothing for himself? Nor should they carry two tunics, so that they may run more readily and not be weighed down by a useless and superfluous burden. By one tunic is understood only as much clothing as may suffice each person to ward off the cold.

The staff and footwear seem to be permitted in Mark but forbidden in Matthew and Luke. Yet because he said, “nor two tunics,” and immediately added footwear, we may understand that they are not to carry duplicate footwear [Note: [Col. 0159D] Thus St. Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, book II, ch. 30: “When Matthew says that footwear is not to be carried on the road, he forbids the carrying of a spare pair, which one might think should be taken lest it be lacking. The same must be understood concerning two tunics: no one among them should think he ought to carry another besides the one he was wearing, out of anxiety lest there be need.” Thus St. Thomas, Cajetan, Maldonatus, Calmet, and, according to his testimony, most interpreters of better note.]; or they may not carry the sort of shoes other people used, but another kind of footwear suitable for travelers, by which the foot is not constricted [Note: [Col. 0159D] This view also has its defenders: Euthymius, Jansenius, ch. 55, the Council of Toledo, and à Lapide.] and the sole is kept safe.

Mark appears to signify this when he says: “But shod with sandals” (Mark XVI, 15); for he would not have added this unless he had wished them to differ in some respect from others in their footwear [Col. 0159B]. But if anyone wishes to interpret this otherwise, let him do so; nevertheless, no one should suppose the Evangelists contradictory.

For my part, I would not believe that the Lord entirely forbade footwear when he allowed coverings for the other limbs of the body, which do not endure as much hardship as the feet—especially since the Apostle says: “Feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace” (Eph. VI, 15).

But what shall we say concerning the staff? Some say, “not even a staff”; Mark says, “except a staff.” This cannot be resolved unless it is distinguished according to different times, provided that the same staff is meant [Note: [Col. 0160D] See Maldonatus, who thinks that the Lord spoke of two kinds of staff. See other interpreters after Augustine, in the work cited.]. For the staff belongs to shepherds, and the apostles were not yet shepherds. Peter had not yet been told: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI, 17); the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified. The Lord had not yet opened their understanding to understand the Scriptures. Therefore they were not yet shepherds, because they did not yet know how to feed sheep. Therefore they did not yet carry the staff. It was not fitting for them to carry staffs while that greatest Shepherd of all still dwelt bodily among them.

They received the staff and the shepherd’s office at the time when the Lord said to them: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI, 15). It is therefore not incongruous that they are said to carry and not carry a staff, since these statements are understood with reference to different times.

When he says, “The laborer is worthy of his reward,” it is as though he said: “Carry nothing but the Gospel; labor in it; live from it; for the laborer is worthy of his reward.” Hence the Apostle says: “If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?” (I Cor. IX, 11). And likewise: [Col. 0160A] “You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain” (II Tim. V, 8; XXV, 5).

### XXXVII.

“Into whatever city or village you enter, inquire who in it is worthy, and remain there until you leave.”

“Remain there,” he says. Where? In the house of the person who is worthy. By this the liberty of wandering is removed, and moving from house to house is forbidden [Note: [Col. 0160D] See Chrysostom, Homily 33; Victor of Antioch on Mark, ch. 6: “Lest they come under suspicion among the inhabitants of the city of having an unsettled and fickle disposition, he commands that they not go from house to house.”]. Remain in one house; there let the person who wishes to minister to you minister.

“And when you enter into a house, greet it, saying: ‘Peace to this house.’ And if the house is worthy, your peace shall come upon it; but if it is not worthy, your peace shall return to you.” Those who preach Christ rightly offer peace, for “he is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II, 24). Where there is no peace and concord, Christ cannot remain and dwell. Hence it is written: “His place has been made in peace” (Ps. LXXV, 3). [Col. 0160B]

Therefore that house is worthy of peace [Note: [Col. 0160D] See Chrysostom, Homily 33, who discusses peace at length here.] which is worthy for Christ to dwell in. But if it is not worthy, your peace shall return to you. How does that return to them which never left them? It returns because it becomes greater and, as it were, doubled, while they desire the good they perceive to be in themselves to be greater still. Thus they receive a reward not only for the peace they possessed, but also for that which they offered to others. Thus the peace they preach returns to them fruitful and doubled.

“And whoever shall not receive you or hear your words, as you go out of that house or city, shake the dust from your feet.” Whoever, he says, does not receive you, does not open to you the inward parts of charity and mercy, and neither hears nor believes your words and the faith you preach: leave them, separate yourselves from them, go out from their midst, and shake the dust from your feet, [Col. 0160C] so that nothing from their unbelief and impiety, their filth and uncleanness, their wicked conduct and earthly way of life may cling to you and defile your feet and holy journeys [Note: [Col. 0160D] See Jansenius, ch. 55, and Maldonatus on this passage.].

For this reason it is said: “He who has bathed does not need anything except to wash his feet” (John XIII, 10). This shall be a testimony against them that they were wicked and reprobate, and that they are cast out from the fellowship of the saints, “like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth” (Ps. I, 4). [Col. 0160D]

“Amen I say to you: it shall be more tolerable for the land of the Sodomites and Gomorrheans on the day of judgment than for that city.” By this it is certainly understood that those who, having heard the truth, refused to accept it are subjected to a more severe punishment [Col. 0161A] than those to whom the truth was not proclaimed [Note: [Col. 0161D] Hilary: “For those who erred without knowing Christ, the error is lighter; but for these it is inexpiable either not to have received what was preached, or, having received it, not to have preached it holily and catholically.”].

### XXXVIII.

“Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves.” You know, and know well, the nature of both. You go to suffer; preserve patience and innocence. Do not defend yourselves, because you are sheep; let them rage, because they are wolves. “Be therefore prudent as serpents and simple as doves.”

For Moses says of the serpent that it “was more cunning than all the animals of the earth” (Gen. III, 1). [Note: [Col. 0161D] See Hilary, who adduces this very passage from Genesis.] Serpents are called both evil spirits and wicked people, because they are venomous and do not walk on the straight path. Therefore, just as they are prudent in evil, so you, the Lord says, be prudent in good. See that they do not deceive you through their cunning, because “the children of this age are more prudent in their generation than the children of light” (Luke XVI, 8). [Col. 0161B] Be prudent, therefore, but prudent in such a way that you do not lose simplicity [Note: [Col. 0161D] Jerome: “By prudence let them avoid snares; by simplicity let them do no evil.”].

“Be simple as doves”: let your prudence, he says, be simple—without fraud, without venom, without deceit, without gall, and without every bitterness. “But beware of people; for they will hand you over in councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you; and you will be led before kings and governors for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles.”

“Beware of people,” he says. There prudence will be necessary, lest they deceive or mislead you, lest through threats and scourges, through flatteries and persuasions, they make you depart from the truth [Note: [Col. 0161D] Bede admirably: “As if he openly says to his weak members: Do not be afraid; you approach the contest, but I fight; you utter words, but I am the one who speaks.” See also Chrysostom, Homily 34.]. They will try to deceive you in many ways, by many arguments and many snares. [Col. 0161C]

“For they will hand you over, scourge you, and lead you before kings and governors”; and this will be for my sake, so that you may give testimony concerning me to them and to all nations. “But when they hand you over, do not be anxious how or what you shall speak; for in that hour what you should speak will be given to you. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.”

The person goes securely into battle who fights with such weapons and under such a leader. And he also goes securely before the council who has such an advocate defending his cause. For when we read the triumphs of the saints, we often hear that philosophers and wise men were overcome by young women and unlettered people. Who accomplished this except the Holy Spirit speaking in them?

“Brother will hand brother over to death, and father son; children will rise against parents and put them to death; and you will be hated by all because of my name.” [Col. 0161D] This prophecy needs no exposition, since it has already been fulfilled; its fulfilment itself has been its exposition.

“But whoever perseveres to the end, this person shall be saved.” [Col. 0162A] Every person is judged in the condition in which he is found. At whatever hour he turns, he shall live and shall not die. But perhaps you expect to turn in the final hour. Hear what the Lord says: “Watch, for you know neither the day nor the hour” (Matt. XXV, 13). Therefore those who await the final hour in this manner may be deceived; but those who persevere in good cannot be deceived. For those who are always found in good are never judged except in good.

XXXIX. But when they persecute you in this city, flee to another. Amen I say to you, you will not have gone through the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes. Everywhere the Lord teaches patience and innocence: he warns them not to resist, but to flee. “Flee,” he says, “the wicked; flee persecutors; flee to another city [Col. 0162B]; for cities to which you may flee will not fail you.” [Note: [Col. 0162D] Thus Chrysostom, Homily 35: “For lest they should say, ‘If we flee from one city to another, what are we to do if the persecutors arrive even there?’ freeing them from this fear, he says: ‘You will not be able to traverse Palestine before I come to you.’”] For the Son of Man will come first; he will return first for judgment, before you have gone through all the cities of Israel and converted them to the faith. Let my examples teach you; look to me: what you see being done to me, fear the same being done to yourselves. For a disciple is not above his master, nor a servant above his lord. Those who do not fear to offend and persecute me will not fear to offend and persecute you also. It is enough for the disciple to be like his master, and for the servant to be like his lord.

But he says this of himself: he calls himself master and lord. For if the master is unlearned, the master’s ignorance is not enough for the disciple; and if the lord is poor and wretched, the lord’s misery is not enough for the servant [Col. 0162C]: for if it were enough, he would seek nothing further. That he says this of himself and not of another is also made clear by what follows. For he says: “If they have called the master of the household Beelzebub, how much more his household?” He himself is the householder, whose household is the whole Church; yet the Jews did not fear to say of him: “By Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Luke 11:15). Therefore do not fear them: for neither did I fear, but patiently endured all things.

These things that I say are covered over; they are not yet seen; I speak of future things. Yet all will be revealed in their own time: “For there is nothing covered that shall not be revealed, and hidden that shall not be known.” Hence the Apostle says: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also bring to light the hidden things of darkness [Col. 0162D], and will reveal the counsels of hearts” (1 Cor. 4:5). “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light.” What you hear in mystery and figure, what I make known to you in private counsels, speak plainly and openly. [Note: [Col. 0162D] Bede: “What you have learned mystically and secretly, proclaim publicly; and what I taught in the small region of Judaea, declare boldly throughout the whole world. In the Palestinian manner he teaches them to preach from roofs raised high above the houses; these they make level, not by our custom, but according to a flat plan.” The preceding words were copied from Jerome.] “And what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops.” For one hears in the ear what is said secretly and, as it were, under silence; but what is beneath a roof lies concealed. To preach from the housetops, therefore, is to speak openly and for all to hear.

“And do not fear those who kill the body.” Preach, he says; proclaim the Gospel; fulfill your office. Many indeed will persecute you, afflict you, and kill you; but do not fear those who kill the body. For they kill what was mortal; even if they did not kill it, it would nevertheless die. But they cannot kill the soul. For the soul is immortal; when it sins, it dies and is separated from the true life, which is Christ, yet it cannot be killed by swords. “But rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.” They have power over the body alone; he has power over body and soul [Col. 0163B]. Their punishment quickly passes; his never ends. Nor would they have had power even over the body itself unless it had been given them by the Lord.

“Are not two sparrows sold for an assarion, and not one small one falls to the ground without your Father?” If, therefore, those sold at so cheap a price cannot fall without God’s will or permission, how much more you, who have been bought at a great price and redeemed by Christ’s blood? “But even all the hairs of your head are numbered.” Let tyrants rage as much as they wish; nevertheless they will not be able to destroy and consume you by any form of torture. Nor is it difficult for him to number hairs, to whom it was not difficult to create them. [Note: [Col. 0163D] Bede aptly says: “This numbering is not an act of comparison, but a capacity of knowledge.” This he took from Chrysostom, Homily 35. See Jerome, who discusses this passage at length.]

In saying that their hairs are numbered, he signifies that the whole substance of the human being will rise again [Col. 0163C], and that none of it will perish. For if all hairs are numbered and all will rise again, why should not the whole person rise? Who would believe that a hair rises in part and perishes in part? But perhaps it seems unsuitable to you that such long hair should rise again in a human being. It is indeed necessary that the whole person rise, but it is not necessary that the whole human substance rise in that part in which it was formerly in the body. For as in gold and silver vessels which are melted down again, all the material is preserved, but the arrangement of the parts is not preserved in the same way—so that what was in the bottom or at the top of the former vessel may form other parts of the vessel that follows—so also in the human being, the whole substance [Col. 0163D] will indeed rise again, but it will not necessarily all rise again in the same parts. Accordingly, nothing superfluous, nothing deficient, nothing unbecoming or unsuitable will rise again in the human being; for what abounds in some parts will provide a supplement to other parts.

“Therefore do not fear; you are of greater value and better than many sparrows” [Col. 0164A]. He who cares for them will much more not abandon or forsake you. “Therefore everyone who confesses me before men, I also will confess him before my Father who is in heaven; but whoever denies me before men, I also will deny him before my Father who is in heaven.” The words of our Savior must be defined; for the Lord will neither confess all who confess him, nor deny all who deny him. [Note: [Col. 0163D] Our author interpreted this passage thus, as did St. Cyril of Alexandria, *On the Right Faith to the Empresses*, book 1; Ambrose, *On Repentance*, book 1, chapter 3, takes the word “everyone” [Col. 0164D] in reference to the classes of individuals: “Everyone who has confessed me,” he says, “that is, from whatever manner of life and whatever condition.” Bede explains it thus: “A good Christian confesses the Lord by the faith that works through love . . . To deny Christ before men is to refuse obedience to his commands.”] For he himself says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter into the kingdom of heaven.” And blessed Peter, who denied him, will by no means be denied by him. Therefore this should be understood of those who, placed under tortures, firmly and faithfully persist to death in confession of his name. Those who deny God through fear of death, unless they make satisfaction by worthy repentance [Col. 0164B], will without doubt perish eternally. For all these things are said to those who suffer persecution for Christ’s name.

XL. Therefore do not suppose that I have come to bring peace upon the earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. What then is meant by the Psalmist’s statement: “In his days righteousness shall arise, and an abundance of peace” (Ps. 71:7), when the Lord himself says, “I have not come to bring peace”? For the Lord came to bring peace, and he came also to destroy peace: he came to bring peace among the good, and a sword between the wicked and the good. For those of whom it is said, “The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32), had peace; thus among such people an abundance of peace arose [Col. 0164C].

But what does the Apostle mean when he says: “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all” (Rom. 12:18)? For if we ought to have peace with all people, among whom did our Savior come to send a sword? We must indeed have peace with the wicked: we are to love them, invite them to the salvation of their souls, and intend them no evil. Yet there must be a sword and discord between them and us, so that we do not imitate them, follow their faith and deeds, or consent to their wicked counsels. [Note: [Col. 0164D] Thus almost St. Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, part 3, adding: “For when we heedlessly join ourselves to the friendships of evil persons, we are bound by faults.”] The Lord therefore came to bring peace—but that peace by which good people agree with one another. He did not come to bring that peace by which evil people agree among themselves in evil.

Hence it is added: “For I came to separate [Col. 0164D] a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s household shall be his enemies.” All these were united in evil; all had peace and agreement in evil. The Lord did not come to bring this peace; Jesus does not approve this agreement [Col. 0165A]. These are those among whom he sends not peace but a sword—the sword, certainly, of separation—so that, while some persist in unbelief, others may be converted to faith. Thus those who had formerly been members of a person’s household become afterward his enemies and persecute him as though he were an enemy. [Note: [Col. 0165D] Chrysostom excellently, *Second Oration against the Jews*: “He was not declaring what he himself desired, but predicting the event of the matter . . . namely, that in the same house one would be faithful and another unbelieving, and then the father would wish to drag his son into impiety.”]

And lest anyone perhaps should say, “O Lord, you command a matter exceedingly difficult and, in some sense, intolerable—that we should be so greatly separated from brothers, children, and parents,” he added: “He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and he who loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me.” And further, as though saying in addition to this: “He who does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me.” For one who takes up his cross and follows Christ loves Christ not merely more than father [Col. 0165B] and mother, son and daughter, but even more than himself. By “himself” I mean his life: one who does not fear to lay down his life for Christ plainly loves Christ more than his own life.

By taking up the cross he does not mean carrying the wood of the cross, but imitating Christ’s Passion; or also subduing and crucifying the flesh through abstinence. For in the cross every kind of torment is denoted. Hence someone is said to be “crucified” when afflicted in any manner. The Apostle bore the cross when he said: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14).

“He who finds his soul shall lose it, and he who loses his soul for my sake shall find it.” Here he uses *soul* for life, because all our life is in the soul [Col. 0165C]. Some, then, find their life in this age, because through love of this life they seek no other life; and these will lose both lives together. Others, however, willingly lose this life because, through love of another life, they regard this life as nothing; and these, because they have lost this life, will preserve it unto eternal life and possess eternal life. For what does “unto eternal life” mean except “for eternity”?

“He who receives you receives me.” Above he said that it would be more tolerable for the land of the Sodomites or Gomorrhites on the day of judgment than for the city which had not received them. Now he shows how great a favor those who receive them obtain from the Lord [Col. 0165D], because, he says, you are my members and I am in you: “He who receives you receives me.” Likewise, because the Father and I are one, and I am in the Father and the Father in me: he who receives me receives him who sent me. It is thus manifest that one who reveres and receives God’s messenger [Col. 0166A] receives the Father, the Son, and the whole Trinity; but whoever injures God’s minister injures God almighty, the inseparable Trinity. The Son is sent by the Father because the whole holy and undivided Trinity has one and the same will, by which the Son of God was sent into the world and made incarnate.

“He who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward.” He receives a prophet in the name of a prophet who receives him not from carnal affection, but because he prophesies and proclaims Christ’s faith; therefore he shall receive a prophet’s reward, because the recipient will have the same reward for receiving him that the prophet has for prophesying. [Note: [Col. 0165D] Thus nearly Euthymius; for St. Gregory says elegantly in Homily 20 on the Gospels: “Although the elm bears no fruit, yet, carrying a vine laden with fruit, it makes its own what it well bears for another.”] Therefore, whoever reveres and receives God’s priests for Christ’s name will not be deprived of the priests’ reward.

“And he who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man”—that is, because he is righteous—“shall receive a righteous man’s reward.” For he will deservedly receive righteousness’ reward who loves righteousness so greatly that he serves all persons from affection in whom he recognizes righteousness. “And whoever gives one of these little ones only a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple, amen I say to you, he shall not lose his reward.” Not only, he says, for a greater service, but also for the smallest, whoever serves you in the name of a disciple will receive a reward. For many serve bishops and priests, not because they are bishops and priests, but because they expect some temporal recompense from them. Such persons do not serve in the name of a disciple. If, therefore, they lack reward here, they will not have reward there on this account.

[CHAPTER XI.] And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished [Col. 0166C] instructing his twelve disciples, that he departed from there to teach and preach in their cities. He calls theirs the cities in which the apostles had formerly lived: that is, Capernaum, Chorazin, and Bethsaida, of which he speaks later.

XLI. [Note: [Col. 0166D] This is a homily falsely attributed to Emesenus, assigned to the Third Sunday of Advent.] But when John, in prison, had heard of the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples and said to him: “Are you he who is to come, or are we to await another?” John the Baptist, placed in chains and prison, heard of the miracles which the Lord performed. Understanding that the day of his death was now approaching, he wished, as it were, to ask him as a master concerning matters which still seemed uncertain to him. He therefore sent two of his disciples [Col. 0166D] to convey his words to Christ. Let us hear what they said: “John the Baptist sent us to you, saying: ‘Are you he who is to come, or are we to await another?’”

I do not think that John’s disciples understood what was signified by this question of their master, [Note: [Col. 0166D] I think he drew this solution to the difficulty from St. Gregory, who writes in Homily 6 on the Gospels: “Sent into prison, he asks whether he himself is to come, not because he doubts that Christ is the Redeemer of the world, but so that he may know whether he who had come into the world by himself would also descend by himself to the gates of hell. For he whom, as forerunner, he had announced to the world, he was also to precede by dying [Col. 0167D] and descending to the dead. Therefore he says: ‘Are you he who is to come, or are we to await another?’—as though plainly saying: ‘Since you deigned to be born for human beings, tell me whether you will also deign to die for human beings and descend to the dead, so that, having been the forerunner of your birth, I may also become the forerunner of your descent, and announce in hell that you are to come, whom I have already proclaimed to have come into the world.’ The same idea is found in his Homily 1 on Ezekiel. Jerome also held it before Gregory, at this passage. The sense is: Tell me, since I am about to descend to the dead, whether I ought to announce you also to those in the lower world, as I announced you to those above; or whether it does not befit the Son of God to taste death, and you will send another for these mysteries?”] just as they did not understand that the question had been answered in Christ’s reply [Col. 0167A].

“Are you he who is to come?” he says. “I indeed am going; I am descending to the patriarchs and prophets in hell; but will you also come there? Must I announce to them that you will come there, just as I have already announced to the world that you have come? Will you descend there yourself, or are we to await another sent by you? For I fear to believe this concerning you unless you make it certain to me yourself. You have humbled yourself greatly indeed—will you perhaps humble yourself yet more? What shall I tell them? What shall I announce?”

And Jesus answered and said to them: “Go and report to John what you have heard and seen: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, and the poor receive the Gospel. And blessed is he who is not offended in me.” What else did the Lord signify in this answer except that he would not shrink from fulfilling in himself [Col. 0167B] this oracle of the prophets, just as he did not shrink from fulfilling the other things which the prophets had foretold of him? “Go,” he says; “tell John what you have heard and seen.” For in that very hour, and before their eyes, as Luke testifies, the Lord performed many mighty works. It was as though he said: “I came into the world, took flesh, and chose to be baptized. But now I preach; now I convert the poor to faith; I give light to the blind; I raise the dead; and I do the other things which the prophets proclaimed that I would do. Therefore, I who confirm and fulfill the prophets’ testimonies in all other things—far be it from me to make them false in this one matter.”

“Blessed is he who is not offended in me.” Blessed is he who faithfully and steadfastly believes whatever has been written and prophesied concerning me. For I who did not shrink from the womb of a virgin will certainly not shrink from undergoing the cross, nor will I shrink from descending to the dead [Col. 0167C]. Hell is the sewer of the world; nevertheless light is not defiled by filth. I pass pure through impurity; pure, I fill the whole world. Descend, therefore, in confidence. You are my Forerunner: go and precede me; announce joy to my faithful ones. I shall quickly follow and shall free them.

Consider now with what great joy that place of darkness, that place of pain and sorrow—consider, I say—with what great delight and rejoicing it exulted when blessed John began there to tell these words. But as they were departing, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John. It was right that they should depart; for if he spoke such things about John in their presence [Col. 0167D], perhaps he could have been accused of flattery by those who believed him to be a man, not God.

“What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” John is not a reed; he is a pillar. He is not moved by wind [Col. 0168A], not shaken by fear, not bent by flattery. With one and the same expression he looks upon both those who praise him and those who blame him. He loves enemies as friends; he rebukes the powerful as he rebukes the powerless. See, therefore, how cautiously our Savior both commends John’s righteousness and protects himself against the fault of flattery, by saying that the one whom he praises takes pleasure in no praise.

“But what did you go out to see? A man clothed in soft garments?” For John, as is written, was clothed in camel hair; by this he showed most plainly that he counted this world and its desires as nothing. Moreover, because he preached repentance, as a good teacher he gave penitents in himself both an example and a rule of repentance. Hence someone not without reason said:

> . . . . . . If you would have me weep,  
> You yourself must first feel grief.

“Behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses.” For one clothed softly seeks gatherings of people and desires to be seen; and therefore he is found not in a wilderness or solitary place, but in a royal house. [Note: [Col. 0168D] Jerome: “A covering of camel hair is his garment. A prison’s hospitality receives such food and clothing, and the preaching of truth has such a dwelling-place. But those who are flatterers, pursue gain, seek riches, abound in luxuries, and wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses. From this it is shown that a rigorous life and austere preaching ought to avoid royal courts and decline the palaces of effeminate persons.”] Thus one who clothes himself softly for this purpose is weighed down by vain glory.

“But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. For this is he of whom it is written: ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare the way before you.’” Thus John is an angel, and John is more than a prophet. For before he was born he prophesied; and unlike the other prophets, who foretold Christ’s coming after a long time, he stood before Christ’s face [Col. 0168C], baptized and touched him, and, through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” He would not have said this unless he had been a prophet. How, indeed, could he have known him unless he had been a prophet? But he was also more than a prophet, because he pointed with his finger to the very one whom he prophesied. [Note: [Col. 0168D] Jerome: “In this John is greater than the other prophets: what they had proclaimed as still to come, he showed to others as having come.”]

And in that respect in which he is called more than a prophet, he may be called not a prophet: for by doing more than a prophet, he showed himself also to be something other than a prophet. It belongs to prophets to foretell future things, but not to prophets to point out present realities. Hence the same John, when asked whether he was a prophet, answered that he was not a prophet.

It follows: “Amen I say to you, among those born of women none has arisen greater than John the Baptist.” John had equals and peers, but no superiors. Moses, Job, Elijah, Jeremiah, and many others were his equals, but they were not greater. [Note: [Col. 0168D] Jerome: “He did not set John above the other prophets and patriarchs, but made the others equal to John.”] Therefore none among those born of women was greater than John the Baptist, except he who is lesser in the kingdom of heaven; of whom it is then added: “But he who is lesser in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.” Who is this one who is greater than John and lesser in the kingdom of heaven, if not our Savior [Col. 0169A]? [Note: [Col. 0169D] Many wish this to be understood of the Savior: he who is lesser in time is greater in dignity. Bede copied both this and the preceding passage from Jerome. Chrysostom, Homily 38; Isidore of Pelusium, Letter 68; and Ambrose on Psalm 34 understand it of the Savior. See Caesarius, *Dialogue* 3.] Of him it is written: “You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor and set him over the works of your hands” (Heb. 2:7). The Apostle, explaining this, says: “But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death” (ibid. 2:9). Jesus is lower than the angels insofar as he was made mortal and capable of suffering; yet he is greater than all, insofar as he is God and Creator of all things.

“From the days [Col. 0169B] of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.” [Note: [Col. 0169D] Jerome: “If John first proclaimed repentance to the people, then consequently from his days the kingdom of heaven suffers violence.” Hilary gives another interpretation: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence because Israel’s glory, due to the patriarchs, announced by the prophets, and offered by Christ, is taken and seized by the faith of the Gentiles.”] From the time when John the Baptist began to preach and say, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near,” the kingdom of God, which is the Church, began to increase, as many flowed into it from every side. And because it is violently seized by the violent, it is rightly said to suffer violence.

This is a good violence by which the kingdom of God is obtained. This was the violence possessed by the person whose friend, although unwilling to lend him three loaves, nevertheless gave him as many as he needed because of his importunity. Do you wish, therefore, to enter the kingdom of heaven? Do you wish to be enrolled in the army and service of the saints? Be violent and importunate. Hear what the Lord says: “Ask, and it shall be given you; seek [Col. 0169C], and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; and he who seeks finds; and to him who knocks it shall be opened” (Matt. 7:7). This, then, is the violence by which the kingdom of heaven is seized.

“For all the prophets and the law prophesied until John.” John, therefore, is the end of the law, just as Christ is. For John, the last of all the prophets of the Old Testament, pointed with his finger to him whom the other prophets had foretold in words. [Note: [Col. 0170D] Chrysostom admirably shows the consequence of these words: “For if those things were fulfilled until John, I am he who was to come.”] Thus the prophecies extending down to him were finally fulfilled in him, when he showed that they had been fulfilled. For every prophecy ends where that which it prophesied is fulfilled.

For when Christ was born, the prophecy was fulfilled which said: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive [Col. 0169D] and bear a son” (Isa. 7:14). Yet the prophecies were also fulfilled in another way, because they are now understood otherwise: not according to the letter but according to the Spirit. Therefore the law prophesied until John because it spoke in cloud and darkness; afterward Christ prophesied because he taught the same law to be understood spiritually [Col. 0170A]. For a prophet is called both one who prophesies and one who expounds prophecies. At that time repentance and mercy displaced sacrifice, and baptism circumcision; for the Lord had come not to abolish the law, but to fulfill it.

It follows: “And if you are willing to receive it, John himself is Elijah who is to come.” When John was asked whether he was Elijah, he answered, “I am not.” What, then, does it mean that the Lord calls him Elijah, while he himself denies that he is Elijah? John was not Elijah in person, but he was Elijah in spirit and power; for thus the angel had foretold of him: “He himself shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah.” Thus John was Elijah and was not Elijah. Therefore it is added: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” For one has no ears for hearing who, understanding this literally, imagines that John was Elijah [Col. 0170B].

XLII. [Note: [Col. 0170D] See Jerome’s fine comparison of John and Elijah which he makes here.] “But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplace, who call to their companions and say: ‘We sang to you, and you did not dance; we sang a lament, and you did not mourn.’” For John came neither eating nor drinking, but clothed in haircloth and preaching repentance; in all that he does, he displays mourning and sadness. Although they ought to have imitated him by mourning and fasting and followed him in repentance, they say instead that “he has a demon.” The Son of Man came eating and drinking, singing and preaching; although they ought to have danced and rejoiced with him, they say: “Behold, a gluttonous man, a drinker of wine, a friend of tax collectors and sinners” [Col. 0170C]. [Note: [Col. 0170D] Thus nearly the interpreters. Some of them hold that the passage speaks of a game customary among the Jews, and that Christ’s rebuke was drawn from it; Theophylact is among them. Maldonatus, Jansenius, and other more learned interpreters deny this.]

Therefore they wish neither to sing nor to mourn; neither fasting nor eating pleases them. What then will happen? What medicine, or what kind of medicine, will help them? The sick person who does not listen to the physician and loathes every food is near to death and despair. “And wisdom has been justified by her children.” Because they are foolish, he says, because they are children, because they do not understand the truth, they speak ill of me, calling me a glutton and a friend of sinners. Yet it is enough for me that the children of wisdom justify me, and that my children, my disciples, friends of truth and righteousness, bear witness to me. For it is not fitting that wisdom should be praised or justified by anyone except her children, except the wise, except [Col. 0170D] those who know her.

Then he began to reproach the cities in which most of his mighty works had been done, because they had not repented: “Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida. For if the mighty works done among you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in ashes and haircloth. Nevertheless [Col. 0171A] I say to you, Tyre and Sidon shall fare more leniently on the day of judgment than you.” Why is this? Because very many mighty works were done among you; because you both heard and saw Truth itself speaking in person, yet would not believe it. But none of these things was done among them; if it had been, they would long ago have believed and repented. This was afterward proved, because, while the Jews persisted in unbelief and persevered in malice, not only Tyre and Sidon, but also the other cities of the Gentiles, were converted to faith.

“And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall descend to hell; for if the mighty works done in you had been done in Sodom, perhaps it would have remained until this day. Nevertheless I say to you that the land of the Sodomites [Col. 0171B] shall fare more leniently on the day of judgment than you.” In this city the Lord healed the centurion’s servant, Peter’s mother-in-law, the paralytic, and countless others; yet it remained in its unbelief, like the other cities of the Jews. It will therefore deservedly descend to hell, though it might certainly have been raised to heaven had it wished to believe the King of heaven, who chose it as his dwelling-place.

But the Lord, to whom nothing is uncertain, used in his speech *perhaps*, [Note: [Col. 0171D] Maldonatus, Jansenius, and especially Cornelius a Lapide observe this, noting that the Greek has ἄν, which is not properly a particle of doubt; therefore it was omitted by our translator in verse 21, even though it occurs in the Greek.] an adverb of doubt, in order to accommodate his speech to human words as a true man. Those cities were overthrown for their sins; if such great mighty works as were done in Capernaum had been done in them, perhaps, like the Ninevites, they would have turned to repentance and remained [Col. 0171C] until this day. Therefore they will have a lesser punishment and a greater excuse at judgment.

XLIII. At that time Jesus answered and said: “I confess to thee, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, for so it pleased thee.” And rightly indeed does he say, “Jesus answered,” although at that moment he seemed to be questioned by no one; for all his speech is an answer and a resolution of questions. [Note: [Col. 0171D] See Maldonatus on this passage.] For when he said these things, he was answering me and thee and all who doubt concerning this most weighty question. For the greatest question is: why has the Lord chosen some and rejected others? But the greatest answer is: because so it pleased him. This answer must be given in all questions in which no other solution is found. “I confess,” he says, “to thee,” that is, I praise thee, [Note: [Col. 0171D] So also St Augustine, *Questions on Matthew*, ch. 9.] I bless thee, and I magnify thee, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, who rulest in heaven and on earth. Or likewise, as other manuscripts have it: “Father of the Lord of heaven and earth” (*Pater, Domini coeli et terrae*), by which the Son too is shown to be Lord of heaven and earth. Hence he immediately adds: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father.” But for what reason [Col. 0172A] do I praise thee? “Because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones.” For the Lord has hidden the secrets of his power and redemption from the wise and prudent of this age, since the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God; and he has revealed them to little ones—to those to whom the Apostle says: “Do not become little children in understanding, but be little children in malice” (1 Cor. XIV, 20). [Note: [Col. 0172D] Hilary: “For the mysteries and powers of heavenly words are hidden from the wise and revealed to little ones: little ones in malice, not in understanding; while the wise are so through the presumption of their own folly, not for reasons of pride.” See Maldonatus on this passage.] For, as the same Apostle says: “God chose the foolish things of the world in order to destroy the wise; and God chose the weak things of the world in order to confound the strong; and things which are not, that he might destroy things which are” (1 Cor. I, 27). But why is this so? Because so it pleased him. For he has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills: he chose Jacob because he willed; he rejected Esau because he willed. Neither willing [Col. 0172B] belongs to the one who wills, nor running to the one who runs. If we will well, it is God’s doing; if we run well, it is likewise his doing.

It follows: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father”; and therefore there can be no doubt that I too am Lord of heaven and earth. For according to that whereby he is man, he is inferior not only to the Father but also to the angels. Therefore, speaking according to that whereby he is man, he says: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father.” But someone says: Who art thou, or who is thy Father? To him he himself replies: “No one,” he says, “knows the Son except the Father; neither does anyone know the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son shall have willed to reveal him.” And that person says: If no one knows the Son except the Father, then neither does the Holy Spirit know the Son, nor does the Son himself know himself. Likewise, neither does the Father know himself, nor does the Holy Spirit know him, if the Son alone knows the Father [Col. 0172C]. But it is not so. [Note: [Col. 0172D] See Cornelius à Lapide on this passage. On similar passages of Scripture, see St Augustine, *On the Trinity*, VI, ch. 9.] For because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the same, whatever the Father knows the Son and the Holy Spirit know; whatever the Son knows the Father and the Holy Spirit know; and whatever the Holy Spirit knows the Father and the Son know. It is therefore plain that “no one knows the Son except the Father,” that is, except the power and divinity which are in the Father; and “no one knows the Father except the Son,” that is, except the power and divinity which are in the Son. Likewise concerning the Holy Spirit: for the power and divinity of the three are one, because the three are one. Thus the Trinity itself knows itself essentially; but no one else knows it except the one to whom the Son of God wills to reveal it. For he is the one who reveals mysteries and opens the sacraments. For he is the Word, the light, the wisdom [Col. 0172D], and the truth. What is heard except through the Word? What is seen except through the light? What is understood except through wisdom? What is known except through truth?

Let us therefore approach him that we may be enlightened; let us hear him saying: “Come to me, all who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you.” For this refreshment excludes every want and brings in every sufficiency. The Apostles had not yet received this refreshment [Col. 0173A] when they said: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John XIV, 9). Moses too, desiring it, said: “If I have found grace in thy sight, show me thy face” (Exod. XXXIII, 5, 13), that I may know thee. Hence also the Psalmist: “My soul thirsted,” he says, “for the living God: when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. XLI, 13). And the Apostle: “I desire [Note: [Col. 0173D] Phil. I, 23: “having a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.”] to be dissolved and to be with Christ.” Those, therefore, who are thus refreshed have all their desires fulfilled.

But he calls those who labour under sickness of soul and are burdened with the weight of sins, [Note: [Col. 0173D] Hilary: “He calls to himself those labouring under the difficulties of the Law and burdened with the sins of the world, promising to remove their labour and burden.”] because he came not to call the just, but sinners to repentance. “Take,” he says, “my yoke upon you, and learn of me, because I am meek and humble of heart.” Put off the yoke [Col. 0173B] of the devil under which you are burdened, and do not draw the yoke with unbelievers, nor choose to labour with them in the field of vanity; but take my yoke upon you, humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, and learn of me because I am meek and humble of heart; for “God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace to the humble” (1 Pet. V, 6). The humility of the heart is true; but that which appears in the countenance often lies. “And you shall find rest for your souls. For my yoke is sweet, and my burden light.” What, indeed, is lighter than to believe and be baptized? “But he that shall believe and be baptized shall be saved” (Mark XVI, 16).

The Apostle Peter likewise said to those who preached that circumcision and the Law of Moses must be observed: “Why tempt ye God, to put a yoke upon the necks [Col. 0173C] of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But through the grace of the Lord Jesus we believe that we shall be saved” (Acts XV, 10). And again: “It hath seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose no further burden upon you, except that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, and blood, and what is strangled, and fornication” (ibid., 28).

XLIV. [CHAPTER XII.] At that time Jesus went through the cornfields on the Sabbath; and his disciples, being hungry, began to pluck ears of grain and eat. For Moses commands (Lev. XXIII, 25) that if you enter your friend’s field of grain, you may break off ears and rub them in your hand, but you shall not reap with a sickle. Therefore, what Moses commands and what the Apostles do signify the same thing. Let us also, passing through this harvest of the Gospel by reading and exposition [Col. 0173D], break ears of grain, open up meanings, and, rubbing them with the hand of understanding, refresh the hungry soul with such food. [Note: [Col. 0173D] St Hilary, §2: “Because hunger is the hunger for human salvation, the disciples hasten to pluck and strip ears of grain—that is, to satisfy themselves with the salvation of the saints. For an ear of grain is not a food suited to man, nor is the eating of plucked ears useful; but the image follows forth the faith of the future event, and the power of the intervening words completes the mystery both of hunger and of satisfaction. See Bede.” [Col. 0174D]]

But those reap this harvest with a sickle who hurry through this and other books by rapid reading, and understand while gathering little or nothing. But when the Pharisees saw it, they said to him: “Behold, thy disciples do that which it is not lawful for them [Col. 0174A] to do on Sabbaths.” As though the Pharisees said: It is indeed lawful for thy disciples to pluck ears and eat, because Moses said this; but it is not lawful to do it on the Sabbath, because Moses forbids this. For Moses forbids servile work to be done on the Sabbath. But servile work, if rightly understood, is not what slaves do, but what makes a person a slave: “For he who committeth sin is the slave of sin” (John VIII, 34). Sin, therefore, is servile work because it makes a person a slave. It is not lawful to do this on the Sabbath; but it is lawful every day both to pluck ears and to eat them. For if it were not lawful, the Lord would have forbidden it. Therefore he keeps the Sabbath well, not who abstains from work, but who abstains from sins.

But he said to them: “Have you not read what David did when he [Col. 0174B] was hungry, and those who were with him: how he entered into the house of God and ate the loaves of the presentation, which it was not lawful for him to eat, nor for those who were with him, but for priests alone?” What are we to think that our Saviour accomplished by this answer, in which the Apostles do not seem to be defended from violating the Sabbath, and David with his companions is said to have acted against the Law? For an accused person is not defended because another is found equally guilty. What defence, indeed, is it for Christ’s disciples that David ate the loaves of presentation contrary to the command of the Law? Or perhaps he had nothing else to answer, and, as the saying goes, drove out one stake with another, setting objection against objection? It is not so. Rather, because the Pharisees attended only to the letter of the Law, the Lord did not wish to reveal to them the secrets of spiritual understanding [Col. 0174C], for they would not have received them. He therefore gave them this testimony, that they might cease from reproaching his disciples, or else censure David as well with them—which seemed unfitting to them. For the loaves which priests alone were allowed to eat signified the greater mysteries of the holy Scriptures, which are to be revealed only to those who have the faith and understanding of priests. David therefore acted contrary to the Law according to the letter, not according to the spiritual meaning. [Note: [Col. 0174D] See the commentators on 1 Kings, ch. XXI.] For he himself was spiritually a priest. Hence it is said of his sons: “Now the sons of David were priests”—not because they exercised the office of priest, for this was permitted only to Aaron’s sons, but because they were close to the king and knew his secrets and counsels.

It follows: “Or have you not read in the Law that on Sabbaths the priests violate the Sabbath and are without guilt?” For those who served the temple could not avoid violating the Sabbath, since they had necessarily to do and prepare so many things on the Sabbath for the adornment and maintenance of the temple itself. Why, then, were they without guilt? Because whatever pertains to God’s service is not sin [Col. 0175A]. [Note: [Col. 0175D] See Maldonatus here.] “But I tell you that one greater than the temple is here;” and that the Son of Man is Lord [62] even of the Sabbath. If, therefore, the temple and the temple service could free priests from guilt, how much more can I free my disciples? Especially since I am Lord of that very Sabbath which you charge with having been violated. The disciples are mine, and the Sabbath is mine; I am Lord of both. It is mine, therefore, to make peace between them. “But if you knew what this means, ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice,’ you would never have condemned the innocent.” For the world was saved not by sacrifice but by mercy. For all the sacrifices of the Law were fulfilled in that sacrifice in which, and through which, the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord. Therefore, as at this appointed time the Lord does not desire sacrifice [Col. 0175B], so he does not desire new moons and Sabbath observance, or the other observances of the Law according to the letter; for Christ is the end of the Law. Let the Pharisees, then, cease to defend the Sabbath and to condemn Christ’s disciples—or rather Christ himself—on account of the Sabbath, of whom they themselves said: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath.” For not only the Sabbath, but also the sacrifice itself which was offered every Sabbath, was fulfilled in Christ and may no longer be performed.

XLV. And when he had passed on from there, he came into their synagogue. And behold, there was a man with a withered hand; and they asked him, saying, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?” that they might accuse him. The wretched Pharisees did not understand what the Lord had just said above. For had they understood, there was nothing further concerning the Sabbath for them to ask. Every person has a withered hand who cannot extend it to a good work. [Note: [Col. 0175D] Theophylact on Luke, ch. VI: “He has a withered hand who performs no works of virtue; for the hand is the organ of action.”] The avaricious have a withered hand, as do all those unwilling to give alms. [Note: [Col. 0175D] Bede on this passage: “This man is the Gentile people, who according to Luke had his right hand withered and his left healthy, because he did not stretch out his right hand to the poor, and while labouring in earthly things was idle in divine matters.” [Col. 0176D]]

But he himself said to them: “Which of you, having one sheep, if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out? How much more valuable is a man than a sheep? Therefore it is lawful to do good on Sabbaths.” Then he said to the man: “Stretch forth thy hand.” And he stretched it forth, and it was restored whole like the other. This is an excellent comparison and an unanswerable argument: what holds in the lesser necessarily holds in the greater. A human being, however, is greater and better than a sheep. Therefore let what holds for the sheep hold for the human being. If it is lawful, then, to rescue a sheep from danger on the Sabbath [Col. 0175D], why is it not lawful to heal a person on the Sabbath? It is thus manifest that it is lawful to do good on Sabbaths; and immediately, by doing good, he healed the man on the Sabbath.

XLVI. But the Pharisees, going out, took counsel against him, how they might destroy him. But Jesus, knowing it, withdrew from there; and many followed him, and he healed them all. How could he fail to know the wicked counsel of the Pharisees, he who knows human thoughts and all hidden secrets? He withdrew from there not because he feared them, but in order to teach us. For the Lord wills that we withdraw from those whom we see growing continually worse through good admonitions. And many followed him. But with what result? “And he healed them all.” If thou desirest to be cured, if thou desirest to be made whole, if thou desirest to be delivered from the danger of death, follow and imitate Jesus. For he drives no one away; he heals all who follow him. And he charged them not to make him known.

Why he gave this command and withdrew from there, the Evangelist explains in what follows [Col. 0176B]: “That it might be fulfilled which was spoken through Isaiah the prophet, saying” (Isa. XLII, 3): “Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul is well pleased; I will put my Spirit upon him, and he shall declare judgment to the Gentiles. He shall not contend, nor cry out, nor shall anyone hear his voice in the streets. A bruised reed he shall not break, and smoking flax he shall not quench, until he brings forth judgment unto victory; and in his name the Gentiles shall hope.” For the Lord had come to declare judgment to the Gentiles and to give counsel as to how they might flee death and receive life. But he had not come in order to contend, cry out, quarrel, fight with arms, and conquer by strength. Therefore he withdrew from there; and he not only withdrew [Col. 0176C], but also wished to remain hidden. Yet his voice is heard in the streets when he humbly speaks words of life to all. But it is not heard in the sense that he proudly threatens anyone. And although he could destroy all his adversaries with one word, he nevertheless did not break the bruised reed or quench the smoking flax. By these things [Note: [Col. 0176D] Bede interprets the bruised reed as the Israelite people, the smoking flax as the Gentiles.] he signifies the Pharisees, whom the Lord could as easily break and extinguish as we easily break a bruised and almost broken reed, or extinguish flax already nearly burned out, which begins to smoke because the fire within it is failing. Yet the Lord will not display this power of his might until he casts forth and brings judgment unto victory—that is, until, in the last judgment, he reveals himself to be the victor. And in his name the Gentiles [Col. 0176D] shall hope—he in whom the Jews refused to place their hope.

63. PART THREE

[Col. 0177]

XLVII. Then there was brought to him a man possessed by a demon, blind and mute; and he healed him, so that he spoke and saw. Every person has a demon who perseveres in some grave sin. [Note: [Col. 0177D] Jerome and Bede interpret this of unbelievers who, after the demon has been cast out, first behold the light of faith and then open mouths formerly silent to the praises of God.] Therefore the Apostle exhorts us, saying: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. VI, 12). For as long as sin reigns in a person, that person is both blind and mute: blind, indeed, because he does not follow the light—“I,” he says, “am the light of the world; he who follows me does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” (John VIII, 12)—and mute because he does not know how to confess his sin. But if this blind and mute man is offered to the Lord, if he is converted to repentance, Jesus will immediately heal him, so that, the demon having been cast out, he speaks and sees. Let him speak, indeed, not empty and useless things as formerly, but holy and religious things, such as it befits a Christian to speak. Let him see, moreover, not the vanities before the eyes of the body, but the light of life and truth with the eyes of the heart.

And all the crowds were amazed. At what were they amazed? Because the mute man spoke. Thus all marvelled when blessed Paul, who formerly, full of a demon and blind and mute, persecuted the Church of God, afterwards being more beneficially blinded, converted to the faith, reborn through the water of baptism, and enlightened by the Lord, entered the synagogue and, opening his mouth in Christ’s praises, began to preach with a clear voice the one whom he had persecuted: “And all who heard him were amazed and said: Is not this the man who ravaged in Jerusalem those who invoked this name, and who came here for this purpose, to lead them bound to the chief priests?” (Acts IX, 21). Thus all the crowds were then amazed and said: “Is this perhaps the Son of David?” For the Jews knew that Christ was to come from David’s seed and perform the mighty works which they now saw being done; therefore some doubted, while others believed that he was the Christ.

But the Pharisees, hearing it, said: “This man does not cast out demons [Note: [Col. 0177D] *Daemonia*, the common reading.] except by Beelzebub, the prince of demons.” Who, Pharisees, taught you these things? Unless you were disciples of Beelzebub, you would not speak such things in his praise. You see Jesus raising the dead, giving sight to the blind, cleansing lepers, healing every ailment and every infirmity, and you say that he casts out demons by Beelzebub. Could Beelzebub, the god of flies, [Note: [Col. 0177D] See Calmet, *Dissertation on the Deities of the Philistines*.] ever do such things?

But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said to them: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste, and every [Col. 0178A] city or house divided against itself shall not stand; and if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. How, then, shall his kingdom stand?” [Note: [Col. 0178D] Bede aptly observes on Luke XI: “He answered not their words but their thoughts, so that even thus they might be compelled to believe in the power of one who saw the hidden things of the heart.”] For if matters were as they say, Beelzebub would already have completely lost his strength, dominion, and kingdom. For if demons waged war against themselves, they would have little or no power against human beings. Yet, what is worse, scarcely are any people found who have as great a concord in good as evil spirits have in evil. Although they are infinite and innumerable, they all agree in this: that they desire to do nothing but evil. If, then, they had not possessed this concord in wickedness, and had wished and been able to turn to repentance, Beelzebub’s kingdom would already have been laid waste. For we see this happen in other kingdoms. It is therefore not as they say: Satan does not cast out Satan; rather, all assist one another in everything.

Hence the Lord also says concerning the devil through blessed Job (Job XLI, 6): “His body is like cast shields, compacted with scales that press upon one another: one is joined to another, and not even a breath passes between them; one clings to another, and, holding fast together, they are by no means separated.” By these words he indicates that evil spirits possess such great concord among themselves that they can in no way be separated from one another. For the devil’s body is understood to be that whole army of evil spirits. Evil spirits are called cast shields on account of their strength. They are also called scales pressing one another, holding one another mutually, and cleaving to each other [Col. 0178C], on account of their mutual concord and unity in every wickedness and desire to harm. Would that, if it could be done, this great peace and concord of theirs might be broken and that kingdom of wickedness dissolved.

It follows: “And if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out?” If, he says, you think such things about me, what do you say also about my disciples? [Note: [Col. 0178D] Jerome: “By ‘the sons of the Jews’ he means either the exorcists of that nation, according to their custom, or the Apostles born from their stock.”] For I know that you do not think well even of the disciples, since you think such abominable things of the Master. This is what he said above: “If they have called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more his household?” The Apostles are called sons of the Pharisees [64] because they themselves, and all others who believed in the resurrection which the Pharisees preached, regarded the Pharisees as fathers and teachers. Hence it may also be understood that they belonged to that sect. For this sect was better than the others, although in many respects it too was not good.
