Thus in the Acts of the Apostles, the Apostle Paul is recorded as crying out: “I am a Pharisee; I am judged concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead” (Acts XIV, 6). This, therefore, is the reason why Christ’s disciples are called sons of the Pharisees.

It follows: “Therefore they shall be your judges.” [Note: [Col. 0179D] Jerome again: “But if this was said of the Apostles, as we ought rather to understand it, they themselves will be their judges, because they will sit upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”] For they shall sit on twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. “But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God”—which is certainly true and must not be doubted—“then the kingdom of God has come upon you.” For where the Spirit of God is, there also is the kingdom of God. Another Evangelist, however, said, “by the finger of God”; and what this means is explained in this place. [Note: [Col. 0179D] Jerome, followed by Bede on Luke, ch. XXI: “In Luke we read this passage thus: ‘But if I by the finger of God,’ etc. Therefore, if the hand and arm of God are the Son, and his finger the Holy Spirit, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one substance.”] The Holy Spirit is called the finger of God because of the manifold division of graces; for in no part of the body is there as great a division as in the fingers.

This is as though he said: I indeed cast out demons by the Spirit of God and by the power of divinity, because they are subject to me, because they are in my power, because they cannot resist me, because I hold them bound and captive. And this is what he says: “Or how can anyone enter the house of a strong man and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? Then he will plunder his house.” The devil was strong, but I am stronger. I entered his house; I came into this world, which he possessed as his own house. But the ruler of this world is soon to be cast out. I bound him, plundered his goods, and freed from his slavery the wretched people whom he had seized. Therefore he is not with me [Col. 0179C], does not gather with me, does not cast out demons with me, does not heal people as I do, does not set free as I do, does not gather sheep or lead them to the pastures of life as I do. What, then, does he do? Do you wish to hear what? He scatters, disperses, kills, and draws with himself to death and eternal condemnation all whom he can. This is what he says: “He who is not with me is against me; and he who does not gather with me scatters.”

“Therefore I say to you: Every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven to men; but the blasphemy of the spirit shall not be forgiven.” You have blasphemed, he says, and spoken against the truth, because you say that what I do by the Spirit of God I do by Beelzebub. Repent, therefore, if you wish this sin and this blasphemy to be forgiven you. For every sin and every [Col. 0179D] blasphemy shall be forgiven to people if they acknowledge that they have sinned and repent; but the blasphemy of the spirit shall not be forgiven to people. For that blasphemy is not forgiven which, puffed up, enlivened, and strengthened by the spirit of pride, does not bow and humble itself to repentance [Col. 0180A]. But blasphemy is saying something against God. If, therefore, thou hast blasphemed, let blasphemy die in thee. It dies when it loses its spirit—that is, the spirit of pride which does not permit thee to humble thyself and return to repentance. For sin is never forgiven as long as it is enlivened by this spirit.

“And whoever shall speak a word against the Son of Man, it shall be forgiven him; but whoever shall speak against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this age nor in the age to come.” For Christ our Lord is both the Son of God and the Son of Man. But the Pharisees spoke a word against him, saying: “This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, the prince of demons.” It is therefore as though he said: If you speak against the Son of Man and believe that I, according to that [Col. 0180B] whereby I am man and the Son of Man, do not possess the power to cast out demons, it shall be forgiven you. [Note: [Col. 0179D] So Jerome: “He who speaks a word against [Col. 0180D] the Son of Man, scandalized at my flesh … such an opinion and blasphemy, although it is not without the fault of error, nevertheless receives pardon because of the lowliness of the body. But whoever manifestly understands God’s works, and, though unable to deny their power, yet prompted by envy slanders them and says that Christ, God’s Word, and the works of the Holy Spirit are Beelzebub—for him there is forgiveness neither in the present age nor in the age to come.” See Augustine, Sermon 11 on the Words of the Lord. St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, II–II, q. 14, should be read.] But if you do not believe that, according to that whereby I am God and by the power of the Holy Spirit, I am able to cast out demons and do all else whatsoever I will, and if you persist in this unbelief, it shall not be forgiven you, either in this age or in the age to come. For many sins are discharged and forgiven after this life by purgatorial fire. Lesser sins, therefore, are easily discharged; but greater sins are not forgiven without worthy repentance. Worthy repentance, however, is measured not so much by mortification of the flesh or length of time as by contrition of heart.

It follows: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree evil and its fruit evil; for the tree is known by its fruit.” He explains this: “Brood of vipers, how can you speak good things, when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” Because, he says, you are evil and wicked, it is no wonder that you speak evil. Foul waters flow from a foul spring. The stench of the mouth reveals the dung of the heart: for what abounds in the heart is disclosed by the mouth. And this is fitting; for as the tree is, so is its fruit, since the tree is known by its fruit. It is fitting, therefore, that you speak evil, lest you appear to be good trees. A good person brings forth good things from a good treasure, and an evil person brings forth evil things from an evil treasure. A person’s treasure is his heart; for there both good and evil things are stored. From it burst forth words of honour and disgrace, blessing and curse. The evil Pharisees therefore, drawing evil things from the evil treasure of their hearts, said of Christ our Lord that he cast out demons by Beelzebub. All these words answer to this one saying. Why they are called a brood of vipers [Col. 0181A] has been explained above, where they are also called “a brood of vipers” by blessed John.

“But I say to you that for every idle word which people shall have spoken, they shall render an account of it on the day of judgment.” Consider, therefore, what answer you will make concerning this great blasphemy which you have spoken with an impious mouth against the Holy Spirit. [Note: [Col. 0181C] Jerome: “If an idle word, which does not edify those who hear it, is not without danger to its speaker, and if on the day of judgment each person must render an account of his words [Col. 0181D], how much more will you, who slander the works of the Holy Spirit … render an account of your slander?” And he adds: “An idle word is one spoken without benefit to speaker or hearer.” St Gregory, Homily 6 on the Gospels: “An idle word is one lacking either the benefit of uprightness or the just reason of necessity.” St Bernard, *On the Threefold Guard*: “An idle word is one that has no reasonable cause.” See St Thomas, I–II, q. 4, art. 9.] An idle word is one that lacks either reason or usefulness. They shall indeed render an account of it, unless they repent of it; there is no sin which repentance cannot erase. “For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned.” Thus a person is justified by good words and condemned by evil ones, just as he is justified by good deeds and condemned by evil deeds. For it is written: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. XVIII, 21). And the Psalmist says: “I said: I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue” (Ps. XXXVIII, 2). Therefore let both be guarded against, because in both there is sin.

XLVIII. Then some of the scribes and Pharisees answered him, saying: “Master, we wish to see a sign from you.” [Note: [Col. 0181D] This is a homily attributed to Eusebius of Emesa, sermon 4 after the First Sunday in Lent, p. 57, as far as no. 51.] How great is the pride of the scribes and Pharisees—how great their folly and unbelief! They do not ask; they do not make a humble request; but with puffed-up breast and raised neck they say: “We wish to see a sign from you.” They want to see signs, but they do not wish to believe. But why do they seek signs, when they have already seen so many signs?

[Note: [Col. 0181D] Jerome: “They ask for a sign as though the things they had seen were not signs.” But another Evangelist explains more fully what they ask for (Mark VIII, 11): “We wish to see a sign from you from heaven.” “Either they wished fire to come down from above, after the manner of Elijah, or thunder to roar in summertime contrary to the nature of the place, in imitation of Samuel,” etc.]

For are these not signs: that the dead rise, the blind receive sight, lepers are cleansed, paralytics are healed, and demons are cast out? All these are signs. Hence, when the Lord was about to heal the centurion’s boy, he said: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe” (John IV, 48).

And he answered and said to them: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign; and no sign shall be given it except the sign of Jonah the prophet.” For while the Pharisees wish to see signs, they hear, not undeservedly, what they do not wish to hear: an evil and adulterous generation, which has so often prostituted itself to idols and followed the gods of the nations, seeks a sign. “For the Jews ask for signs, and the Greeks seek wisdom.” And no sign shall be given it except the sign of Jonah the prophet.

For great is the sign of Jonah the prophet, in which Christ’s death, burial, and resurrection [Col. 0182A] are signified, and in which the destruction of the Jews and the praise of the nations are signified.

[Note: [Col. 0182C] Thus Chrysostom, Homily 8 on Matthew: concerning the sign of Jonah the prophet, “It signified the cross, death, tomb, and resurrection.”]

“For as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster three days and three nights, so shall the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights.” For who could know how Jonah had been in the belly of the sea-monster for three days and three nights, unless the Lord had given this comparison? If Jonah was thus in the belly of the sea-monster as Christ was in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights, it is clear that he completed there one whole day, and the end of another day and the beginning of another. For Christ was in the heart of the earth for precisely so long.

But what is “in the heart of the earth” but in the tomb?

[Note: [Col. 0182D] Chrysostom: “He did not say ‘in the earth,’ but ‘in the heart of the earth,’ so as both to denote the tomb and prevent anyone from suspecting that it was merely an appearance.”]

For Christ’s tomb, because it is of stone, is not undeservedly compared to the heart. For a stone is in the earth as the heart is in the body. [Col. 0182B] Therefore, because our Savior lay in the tomb for three days and three nights according to his humanity, he is rightly said to have been in the heart of the earth for the same period. For Christ’s body was placed in the tomb on the sixth day, Friday. Thus he was in the tomb on Friday; on the Lord’s Day he rose from the tomb: therefore he was in the tomb then as well. It is clear, then, that he was in the heart of the earth for three days, since he was in the tomb on Friday, throughout the Sabbath, and on the first day.

For no one says that the eye is not in the body because it is not in the whole body. Let no one therefore say that Christ was not in the tomb for three days because he was not there for three entire, complete days.

[Note: [Col. 0182D] St Augustine, *Questions on the Gospels*, book II, ch. 7: “Take the portion of the sixth day on which he was buried, together with the preceding night, as night and day—that is, as a whole day; take the Sabbath night and day; and the Lord’s-Day night with that dawning day. Thus, by taking the part for the whole, you have three days and three nights. For when ten months are attributed to a pregnant woman, nine are complete; the beginning of the tenth is taken for the whole.” He says the same in *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, book III, ch. 24, and *On the Trinity*, book IV, ch. 6. Jerome, on this passage: “By synecdoche the whole is to be understood from the part—not that the Lord remained in hell throughout all three days and three nights, but that the part of Preparation Day and of the Lord’s Day, together with the whole Sabbath day, are understood as three days and as many nights.” See the same author on Jonah II, 2.]

For neither was Christ whole and entire there for this period of time; yet Christ was there, because his flesh was there. Let us now see in what manner [Col. 0182C] he was there also for three nights. Christ’s body was in the tomb throughout the whole night following Friday, and throughout the whole night following the Sabbath; of the third night, however, we have nothing. Let us therefore seek it, if perhaps we can find it. Yet even if I could not find it, I should nevertheless not doubt that there were three, because Truth said that there were three, and Truth could not lie.

I think that this third night is not so called by the measurement of time, but by a certain likeness to night. Thus we say that blind persons, because they are in darkness, are always in night. Thus it is said of the holy city Jerusalem that “there shall be no night in it,” because there shall be no darkness there. [Col. 0183A] Therefore we call not only the measured duration of time and hours “night,” but darkness as well.

[Note: [Col. 0183D] This question has occupied both ancient and modern writers. Among the ancients, Isidore of Pelusium, book I, epistle 114: “The Lord was led to the cross at the sixth hour of Preparation Day. From that hour until the ninth there was darkness. Understand this as night.” Modern writers seem to agree that “three days and three nights” has the force of “three natural days,” since this was Hebrew idiom. Therefore, as it is sufficient for Christ to be said to have been in the tomb for three natural days if he was there during some part of the three days, so it is sufficient for him to be said to have been there for three days and three nights. Maldonatus therefore rightly said that this passage has seemed far more difficult to many than it is, because they wished to separate the nights from the days. See Maldonatus; Jansenius, ch. 49; a Lapide; Calmet; etc.]

Hence it is said in Genesis that God called the light day, and the darkness night (Gen. I, 5). Jonah therefore had this third night, and it was continuous, in the belly of the sea-monster, because as long as he was there he was always in darkness. Let us add to it those two which are called nights not figuratively but properly, and there will be three.

Jonah was therefore in the belly of the sea-monster for three nights: one with respect to himself, since he felt no daylight there; two with respect to the revolution of the heavens. Conversely, with respect to himself he was there for no day, but with respect to the revolution of the heavens he was there for three days. The same should be understood of Christ. With respect to itself, Christ’s body was in the tomb for one [Col. 0183B] night, because it lay in darkness and death until the Lord’s Day, when, the soul having returned and light having been received, he rose from the dead. But it was there during two other nights according to the span and measurement of time; joined together, these make three nights.

It follows: “The men of Nineveh shall rise in judgment with this generation and shall condemn it, because they repented at Jonah’s preaching; and behold, one greater than Jonah is here.” He rightly says “with this generation,” because, as the Apostle says, “We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed” (I Cor. XV, 51). For all of us, good and evil alike, shall stand before Christ’s tribunal. But the Ninevites shall condemn the Jews, because by their example the Jews shall be condemned: they did not repent at Christ’s preaching as the Ninevites did at Jonah’s, though Jonah was not merely lesser than Christ but also Christ’s servant.

Likewise, “The Queen of the South shall rise in judgment with this generation and shall condemn it, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom; and behold, one greater than Solomon is here.” The Queen of the South signifies the Church of the nations, which has come from all parts of the world to hear and receive Christ’s faith and wisdom.

XLIX. “When an unclean spirit has gone out of a man, it walks through dry places, seeking rest and finding none. Then it says: ‘I shall return to my house from which I went out.’ And when it comes, it finds it vacant, swept with brooms, and adorned. Then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits [Col. 0184A] more wicked than itself, and they enter and dwell there; and the last state of that man becomes worse than the first. So it shall be for this most wicked generation.”

The Lord gave this comparison in order to show that the evil and adulterous generation of the Jews, because of its hardness and unrepentant heart, deserved to be condemned not only by the Ninevites but also by the other nations.

[Note: [Col. 0183D] Jerome: “From the fact that, at the end of the parable or narrative, there follows: ‘So it shall be also for this most wicked generation,’ [Col. 0184D] we are compelled to refer the parable not to heretics or to any persons whatsoever, but to the Jewish people.”]

For this impious generation does not know how to repent, but daily makes itself worse; its last state shall become worse than its first. They themselves signified this when they said of our Savior: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 25). Thus it shall be for this most wicked generation as for that man possessed by an unclean spirit.

For when an unclean spirit has gone out of a man, it walks [Col. 0184B] through dry places seeking rest and finds none. The malignant spirit easily both enters a person and departs from one: whenever a person commits some abominable deed in thought or act, the devil is present; but if he begins to repent from the heart, the devil departs. When it has departed, it walks through dry and waterless places, namely by tempting those who lack the moisture of wickedness and pleasure; in them it finds no rest, because it seeks what is flowing and moist. Hence it is said of it: “It sleeps under the shade in the secret place of the reed and in moist places.”

[Note: [Col. 0184D] Job XL. See the Roman edition of St Bruno, vol. I, p. 293, ch. 1.]

By these are signified the sexual organs.

[Note: [Col. 0184D] St Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXIII, ch. 3: “The ancient enemy, therefore, pressing the human race chiefly either through pride or through lust, sleeps in the secret place of the reed and in moist places; for under the stench of his dominion he holds the condemned person either through pride of spirit or through corruption of the flesh.” Bede: “Dry places are the hearts of believers, which do not possess the moisture of lust; wandering about in them, he will not find assent to his wicked suggestion.”]

Then it says: “I shall return to my house from which I went out.” Since it cannot have rest among the good, it returns to the wicked. For the devil can tempt the good, but cannot have rest [Col. 0184C] in them, because he is troubled, moved, and driven away now by their prayers, now by their tears, now by their almsgiving, and by other such things.

But when it comes to its house, it finds it vacant—vacant indeed, because it finds there neither charity, nor right faith, nor humility, nor patience, nor justice, nor mercy, nor the other things by which the souls of the saints are fortified.

[Note: [Col. 0184D] Bede: “He will find the house vacant, that is, idle in respect of good works.”]

What, then, does it find it like? Swept with brooms and adorned: it finds it as it desires to find it. For it finds it swept with evil brooms and adorned with evil ornaments: evil brooms which drive out virtues and leave vices behind; evil brooms which scatter the floors and do not cast out the dust. [Col. 0185A] Luxury, fornication, pleasure, pride, avarice, discord, and every impurity are the devil’s ornaments; and it finds the house adorned with these ornaments.

“Then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they enter and dwell there.” It is not enough for it to possess such a house alone; it seeks companions. The place is spacious; it needs many inhabitants. But who are these seven spirits? Why seven? Why more wicked? Because there are seven graces of the Holy Spirit, by which every soul is converted to faith and, once converted, defended: therefore this wicked one took with itself seven spirits opposed to those graces, by which it might defend its house against them.

It opposes the spirit of folly to the spirit of wisdom; to the spirit [Col. 0185B] of understanding, the spirit of dizziness and madness; to the spirit of counsel, the spirit of rashness; to the spirit of fortitude, the spirit of instability and fear; to the spirit of knowledge, the spirit of ignorance; to the spirit of piety, the spirit of impiety; and to the spirit of fear of the Lord, the spirit of contempt and hatred.

Unhappy is the soul in which these spirits reign and over which they rule. In a sense they are more wicked than the one who brought them in: they corrupt the soul in this life, whereas he torments the soul after this life; he tempts, they kill; he opens the doors, they enter and destroy and lay waste everything. He can tempt and afflict a person, but he cannot kill the soul except through these. Thus they are more wicked than he, because [Col. 0185C] they do more harm than he. He is more wicked in counseling and tempting; they are more wicked in acting and corrupting. The Apostle delivered a man “for the destruction of the flesh” (I Cor. V, 5); but of these spirits he says: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. VI, 12). It is therefore no wonder if that man’s last state becomes worse than his first, when he was previously oppressed by one demon and afterwards by seven.

L. While he was still speaking to the crowds, behold, his mother and brothers stood outside, seeking to speak with him. By his brothers he means the nephews of blessed Mary:

[Note: [Col. 0185D] Jerome: “We … understand the Lord’s brothers not as Joseph’s sons, but as the Savior’s cousins—the children of Mary’s sister, the Lord’s maternal aunt, who is said to be the mother of James the Less, Joseph, and Judas, whom elsewhere in the Gospel we read to be called the Lord’s brothers.”]

That is, James, Joseph, Judas, and Simon; for it is the custom of Holy Scripture to call all relatives brothers. And someone said to him: “Behold, your mother and your brothers stand outside seeking you.” [Col. 0185D] But he answered the one speaking to him and said: “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said: “Behold, my mother and my brothers. For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother and sister [Col. 0186A] and mother.”

While Jesus speaks with outsiders, his mother and brothers stand outside. These sit with him in the house; those wait for him outside. This is not said without mystery; it signifies something. For even now we see Jesus speaking with outsiders. Jesus speaks with outsiders when this Gospel is read to the people of the Gentiles; but his mother, the Synagogue, and his brothers, the Jews, stand outside.

[Note: [Col. 0185D] Jerome: “His mother and brothers—that is, the Synagogue and the Jewish people—stand outside and desire to enter, and are judged unworthy of his discourse.”]

They are outside because they are not in the Church; yet they wait for him and desire to speak with him. For, as the Apostle says, “They have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. X, 2). Nevertheless, they will not speak with him nor see him unless they enter his house and are baptized in the Church.

The Lord says that none are his relatives [Col. 0186B] except those who do his Father’s will. He calls them both mother and brothers because he loves them as mother and brothers. These words show most plainly that spiritual love ought to be preferred to carnal love. For we ought to love our brothers and all our relatives with that love by which Christ loved his mother and brothers. He loved them not because they were more closely related according to the flesh, but because they did his Father’s will more fully. Therefore the one who is better is closer to Christ.

LI. [CHAPTER XIII.] “On that day Jesus, going out of the house, sat beside the sea; and great crowds gathered to him, so that he went aboard a boat and sat down, while the whole crowd stood on the shore.” On that day, he says, [Col. 0186C] when his mother and brothers stood outside, Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea. This day is long; it has not yet ended, because his mother and brothers still stand outside.

But every day Jesus goes out from the house in order to be seen, heard, and known by those who are outside; for all who have not been baptized are outside.

[Note: [Col. 0185D] St Hilary: “By the nature of this event he signifies [Col. 0186D] that those who are placed outside the Church can receive no understanding of the divine word. For the ship bears the type of the Church, within which the word of life is set forth and preached; those who are outside … cannot understand it.” Bede: “The little boat signifies the Church … while those standing on the shore … signify those newly coming to faith, stripped of the error of unbelief but who have not yet entered the Church through the washing of baptism.”]

The Lord sits beside the sea, that is, beside the waters of baptism. There great crowds gather to him, for daily many and countless people come to baptism. But where does he sit? In the little boat. This little boat is to be understood as each priest and bishop. Through them he now speaks; through them he baptizes and teaches the crowds. Through them he is carried outside the house; through them he is revealed to outsiders who do not know him. The whole crowd stands [Col. 0186D] on the shore. For the whole crowd remains standing on the shore until, having heard the preaching, it believes in Christ, goes down to the sea, and rises after being washed in the waters of baptism.

LII. And he spoke many things to them in parables, saying: “Behold, the sower went out to sow his seed. And while he sowed, some fell by the way; and birds came and ate it. Other seed fell upon rocky ground, where it did not have much earth, and immediately sprang up because it had no depth of earth; but when the sun had risen, it was scorched, and because it had no root, it withered. Other seed fell among thorns; and the thorns grew up and choked it. Other seed fell into good soil and yielded fruit: some a hundredfold, some sixtyfold, and some thirtyfold. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

We have set down the entire parable. Since the Lord himself stated it and explained it, let us hear his explanation and not seek another in it, which indeed is not permitted. And the disciples approached and said to him: “Why do you speak to them in parables?” He answered and said to them: “Because it has been given to you to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, but it has not been given to them.” To you, he says—who believe; to you who have faith; to you who love truth; to you who seek not carnal things but spiritual things—it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven; but to them [Col. 0187B] it has not been given. Why? Because they do not believe; because they do not seek spiritual things. For it is written: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand.” “For whoever has, to him shall be given, and he shall abound; but whoever does not have, even what he has shall be taken from him.”

For whoever has faith, as you have it, will be given also knowledge of the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, and will abound in knowledge and every good thing. But whoever does not have faith, even what he has will be taken from him, so that, unhappy and naked as he goes out from this world, nothing may remain to him except sin [Col. 0187C] and the punishment of sin.

[Note: [Col. 0187D] See Hilary, Jerome, and Bede.]

“Therefore I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear or understand.” The Lord rightly speaks to them in parables, for though they see outwardly the works of power and miracles which he himself performs, they do not see with the eyes of the heart, nor do they believe him to be the Christ. Hence he himself says: “If I had not done among them works which no other has done, they would not have sin” (John XV, 24). And although they hear the words of life and salvation which he announces to them, they do not hear with the ears of the heart or understand, so as to repent, turn, and be healed; for they do not have ears to hear.

This happens so that Isaiah’s prophecy may be fulfilled in them, saying: “By hearing you shall hear and shall not understand; and seeing you shall see and shall not see” (Isa. VI, 9). For they hear [Col. 0187D] and do not understand; they see and do not see, as we have just explained. “For the heart of this people has grown fat, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and they have closed their eyes, lest at any time they should see with their eyes, hear with their ears, turn, and I should heal them.”

A bad fatness, by which knowledge is taken away and folly nourished. Of this fatness the Psalmist says: “Their iniquity came forth as though from fat” (Ps. LXVII, 7). Hence Moses commands all the fat which covers the vital parts to be offered and burned. They hear heavily when, because they do not believe, what they hear seems burdensome and difficult to them. For those heard heavily who said: “This saying is hard; and who can hear it?” (John VI, 61). They close their eyes who refuse to open the eyes of the mind for knowing truth. The result is that they do not turn and are not healed; therefore they shall die in their sins.

“But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear.” If this were understood of bodily eyes and ears, only the blind and deaf would be wretched, and not merely people but even beasts and other animals would be blessed. In saying this, therefore, [Col. 0188A] he requires the eyes and ears of the mind.

[Note: [Col. 0187D] Jerome: “Had we not read above that the hearers were summoned to understanding … we might suppose that the eyes and ears which receive blessedness [Col. 0188D] are those of the flesh. But it seems to me that blessed are those eyes which can know Christ’s mysteries,” etc.]

“For amen I say to you: many prophets and righteous persons desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it.” By these words he shows that the prophets and righteous people awaited his coming [Col. 0188B] and desired to hear his words and see his deeds. Though they had seen and understood these things spiritually, this joy and blessedness was given only to the apostles and other believers then living: that they might bodily enjoy Christ’s conversation. Thus the righteous Simeon, seeing him and filled with great joy, said: “Now, Lord, you dismiss your servant in peace according to your word, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke II, 29).

“Therefore hear the parable of the sower. Everyone who hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what was sown in his heart: this is the one sown by the way. But the one sown on rocky ground is he [Col. 0188C] who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy; yet he has no root in himself but is temporary; and when tribulation and persecution arise because of the word, he is immediately offended. The one sown among thorns is he who hears the word, but the anxiety of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it becomes fruitless. But the one sown in good soil is he who hears the word and understands it and bears fruit, producing some a hundredfold, some sixtyfold, and some thirtyfold.”

This explanation is very brief and plain. Grammarians might perhaps judge it artless and confused, because it intermingles the seed and the person in whom it is sown, so that it now calls the seed sown and now the person himself [Col. 0188D] sown. In this also it appears that the Evangelists served, in simple speech, not so much the rules of grammatical art as the truths they expressed.

Although the same one God is the sower both of human beings and of the word: first almighty God sowed human beings; afterwards he sowed the words of the Gospel in human beings. The person sown by the way is the one who hears the word and does not understand it—that is, who scorns to understand. But what wonder if such persons scorn to understand and perform God’s words, when, seated beside the way of destruction and death, they serve and obey malignant [Col. 0189A] spirits? The word sown in them is therefore easily snatched away by the devil and trampled down by vices passing through there along their customary path.

The person sown upon rocky ground is one who easily perishes and is so quickly cut off because he is not established by the roots of faith and charity. The seed which falls into him therefore sprouts quickly and quickly dries up, because it lacks the moisture of faith and virtues by which it might be nourished.

The person sown among thorns is one over whom riches and pleasures rule.

[Note: [Col. 0189D] See Jerome here; Basil on Psalm XLV; Chrysostom, Homily 59 on Genesis; Gregory, *Morals*, I, 4; etc.]

The seed sown in him becomes fruitless because it is choked by those very riches and pleasures. These are thorns not of the body but of the soul, because, although they delight the flesh for a time, they prick and torment the soul forever. [Col. 0189B] The rich and pleasure-loving also seem to lie among thorns because they are always pressed and pricked by care and anxiety.

But the person sown in good soil is one who constantly bears fruit in faith, knowledge, and good action. Therefore the seed falling into him yields fruit both a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold. The Evangelist did not explain this; he left it for us to explain. Some assign the hundredfold fruit to virgins, the sixtyfold to the continent, and the thirtyfold to good married persons.

[Note: [Col. 0189D] Jerome: “As in bad soil there were three kinds—by the way, rocky places, and thorny places—so in good soil there is a threefold variety: fruit a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold … assigning the hundredfold fruit to virgins, the sixtyfold to widows and continent persons, and the thirtyfold to chaste marriage.” The same author discusses this more fully in his letter to Pammachius and in *Against Jovinian*. Isidore of Pelusium, book I, epistle 144: “One a hundred, another sixty, another thirty, may signify virginity, continence, and marriage.”]

Marriage, then, is good; continence is better; virginity is best. But they also bear a hundredfold fruit who, despising all worldly things, devote themselves solely to divine contemplation. Those bear sixtyfold fruit who serve the Lord by [Col. 0189C] preaching and baptizing. Those bear thirtyfold who obey faith by hearing and believing. Great, then, is the fruit of obeying and believing; greater is that of preaching and baptizing; greatest is that of devoting oneself to heavenly contemplation.

[Note: [Col. 0190D] Gregory, Homily 17 on Ezekiel: “Good soil yields thirtyfold fruit when the mind has conceived the perfection of faith which is in the Trinity; sixtyfold when it has perfectly brought forth works of good life; but a hundredfold when it has advanced to the contemplation of eternal life.”]

Because all people who come into the vast field of this world are handed over to be tempted by vices, malignant spirits, pleasures of the flesh, and every kind of desire, they are rightly said to be sown by the way, upon rocky ground, and among thorns. The soil is good, but corrupted from elsewhere it has lost the name of goodness. It retains its proper name in those who do not serve vice and corruption. Therefore the soil bears good fruit which persists [Col. 0189D] in goodness while good; but that which departs from goodness either lies by the way and is trampled by passers-by, or is rocky and has no moisture, or is thorny and bristles with the stings of pleasures.

LIII. He put another parable before them, saying:

[Note: [Col. 0190D] This parable and the two following, explained by the author, are contained in a single homily ascribed to Eusebius of Emesa, for the twenty-fifth Sunday after Pentecost, p. 180.]

“The kingdom of heaven has become like a man who sowed good seed in his field. But while people were asleep, his enemy came and oversowed tares in the midst of the wheat and went away. When the blade [Note: [Col. 0190D] “But when the blade had grown,” etc., Vulgate.] grew and bore fruit, then the tares also appeared. And the servants of the householder came and said to him: ‘Lord, did you not sow good seed in your field? Where, then, did it get tares?’ He said to them: ‘An enemy has done this.’ And the servants said: ‘Do you wish us to go and gather them?’ But he said: ‘No, lest perhaps in gathering the tares you uproot the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest; and at harvest time I shall say to the reapers: Gather the tares first and bind them in bundles to burn them, [Col. 0190B] but gather the wheat into my barn.’”

Then, having dismissed the crowds, he came into the house; and his disciples approached him, saying: “Explain to us the parable of the tares of the field.” He answered and said: “The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man; the field is the world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom; the tares are the children of the evil one; the enemy who sowed them is the devil; the harvest is the consummation of the age; and the reapers are angels. Therefore, as the tares are gathered and burned, so it shall be at the consummation of the age. The Son of Man shall send his angels, and they shall gather out of his kingdom all stumbling-blocks and those who do iniquity, and shall cast them into a furnace of fire; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Then the righteous shall shine as the sun in the kingdom of their Father. He who [Col. 0190C] has ears to hear, let him hear.”

I myself fear to add anything further to this, lest, while wishing to illuminate the light, I instead darken it. But this ought to be considered very carefully: before the time of harvest the Lord forbids the tares to be separated from the wheat, lest the wheat be uprooted with them. The wicked are to be endured where, if they are disturbed, the good are exposed to grave danger. Where faith is not lost, it is better to tolerate their corrupt habits and actions than, by provoking them, to disrupt the Church’s peace and tranquility. Let them therefore be admonished, not expelled; for some are more readily overcome by warnings than by threats. Those tares should remain among the wheat which cannot be pulled up without uprooting the wheat. In all things [Col. 0190D] discernment must be exercised; nor should all be treated in one manner.

[Note: [Col. 0190D] Bede on this passage: “From this we are taught the long-suffering of patience: that in long-suffering we may practice justice, and in judgment may not neglect patience.” [Col. 0191D]]

LIV. He put another parable before them, saying: “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field. It is indeed the least of all seeds; but when it has grown, it is greater than all herbs and becomes a tree, so that the birds of heaven come and dwell in its branches.”

Such from the beginning was the Church, now called the kingdom of heaven by comparison with other kingdoms, as the mustard seed is in comparison with other grains. For it is the least of all seeds commonly sown by people; but when it grows, it becomes greater than the other herbs, as can be proved by sight. Likewise the Church, [Note: [Col. 0191D] Jerome: “The kingdom of heaven is the preaching of the Gospel … This preaching, which seemed small at the beginning … does not grow into herbs, but grows into a great tree.” Bede gives the same from Jerome.] beginning from one or from a few, has grown into an innumerable multitude. Hence the Lord says through the Psalmist: “I have declared and spoken; they have multiplied beyond number” (Ps. XXXIX, 6). And again: “But to me your friends have been exceedingly honored, O God; their dominion has been greatly strengthened. [Col. 0191B] I shall count them, and they shall be multiplied beyond the sand” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 17).

LV. He spoke another parable to them: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until the whole was leavened.” This parable is the same as the preceding one. For as the smallest mustard seed grows into a tree, so a little leaven enlivens and causes a great mass of flour to rise. Here leaven produces not corruption but enlivening. The kingdom of heaven is the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0191D] Jerome and Bede: “The woman is the aforesaid apostolic preaching, or the Church gathered from diverse nations,” etc.]

The woman is the wisdom of God; the three measures of flour are the three parts of the world: Asia, Africa, and Europe. The woman, that is, the wisdom of God, took [Col. 0191C] the leaven, that is, the primitive Church, and hid it in the three measures of flour, saying to her disciples: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI, 15). For from these we see that almost the whole world has now been leavened and enlivened, and has grown into the body of the Church.

“Jesus spoke all these things to the crowds in parables, and without parables he did not speak to them, so that what had been spoken through the Prophet might be fulfilled: ‘I shall open my mouth in parables; I shall utter things hidden from the foundation of the world’” (Ps. LXXVII, 2). A parable is a comparison in which one thing is said and another is reasonably understood.

71. LVI. “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field, which a man who finds it hides; and, because of his joy over it, goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.” [Note: [Col. 0191D] Matt. XIII, 44. You may read an explanation of this and the following two parables in a homily published under the name of Eusebius of Emesa, for the feast of the birth of a virgin, p. 230.]

Here “the kingdom of heaven” means the heavenly homeland [Note: [Col. 0192D] Bede, from Homily 2 of St Gregory on the Gospels: “The hidden treasure is heavenly desire . . . . . and indeed he buys that field, having sold all things, who tramples all his desires underfoot in keeping heavenly desire.”], rightly compared to a treasure hidden in a field, because its riches do not yet appear openly to all. Yet it is found, though not in its fullness, because the teaching and preaching of the saints reveal to a great extent what and how great it is. The holy apostles found this treasure when Christ the Lord preached, and, selling everything because of their joy over it, bought it. “If you wish,” says the Lord, “to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, follow me, and you shall have treasure in heaven” (Matt. XIX, 21).

Thus this field with its treasure is bought most perfectly. But the person hides this treasure who, once he has learned what it is like, keeps it in his heart, loves it in his mind, and by no means forgets it; for we hide what we hold dear and fear to lose.

LVII. “Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls; but, having found one precious pearl, he went away, sold everything that he had, and bought it.”

This comparison and the one stated above mean almost the same thing [Note: [Col. 0192D] Jerome also says here: “The same thing that was said above is expressed in other words.”], except that here the kingdom of heaven is understood not, as there, as the heavenly homeland, but as the holy Church; and what there is called treasure is here called a pearl. The kingdom of heaven, that is, the holy Church, is therefore like a merchant, because as that man sold all things out of desire for a single pearl and bought it, so the Church, for love of the heavenly homeland and eternal blessedness, has not only sold what she possessed, but has even subjected herself to servitude, so that she might be able to buy and possess it. For a shrewd merchant is one who, from things which he cannot possess for long, buys something such that he need never fear losing it and in which he possesses all things.

LVIII. “Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a dragnet cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind. When it was filled, they drew it out and, sitting beside the shore, chose the good fish into vessels but threw the bad outside.”

The kingdom of heaven, that is, the holy Church, is rightly said to be like a dragnet [Note: [Col. 0192D] Matt., final chapter, 19: “Go therefore, teach,” etc.], because it was entrusted to fishermen and daily encloses and catches innumerable fish in the waters of baptism. Of these the Lord himself says to his disciples: “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of men” (Matt. IV, 19). The Lord cast this net into the sea when he commanded these same disciples, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” [Note: [Col. 0192D] Bede, from Jerome: “The dragnet signifies the Church, which invites all alike to forgiveness of sins; it is drawn to the shore, that is, to the end of the age, through the teaching of preachers; and at the end of the age the righteous are received into heavenly dwellings, while the ungodly are sent into the outer darkness.”]

This world is called the sea; of it the Psalmist says: “This sea is great and wide; there are creeping things there without number” (Ps. CIII, 25). This net gathered fish of every kind, because the holy Church called to faith and collected in her bosom persons of every sort. There are together Jews and Greeks, Latins and barbarians, rich and poor, wise and foolish, wheat and tares, grain and chaff, righteous persons and sinners alike.

But it is not yet full: fish still enter, people are still baptized. It will be filled when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered it and when Israel is saved. Then those who draw it out, sitting beside the shore, will choose the good fish and cast out the bad. For the seashore is the end of the age. Explaining this himself, the Lord says: “So shall it be at the consummation of the age: the angels shall go out and separate the evil from among the righteous, and shall cast them into the furnace of fire; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” This furnace is hell, where neither the worm dies nor the fire is extinguished. By weeping and gnashing of teeth he signifies the extremity of pain and the intolerability of punishments.

“Have you understood all these things?” They say to him, “Yes.” He says to them: “Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old.” It is as though he said: “I spoke to them in parables, and they did not understand; but to you I have explained the parables themselves, and you have understood. To them, because they are still old, I brought forth old things; but to you, because you are new, both new and old things. To them I spoke according to the custom of the prophets; to you after the manner of a teacher and master. Speak and teach in this way; maintain this rule of speech. For one must speak differently in the kingdom of heaven, differently in the assembly of the Scribes and Pharisees, differently in the Church, and differently in the Synagogue.”

72. “Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven.” Every teacher and preacher of the Church, if he is wise and learned, is like a householder who brings forth new and old things from his treasure—from the riches of his breast and the knowledge of his heart. The scribes of the Synagogue, because they are not instructed, bring forth old things; but the scribes of the Church, because they are instructed, bring forth both new and old things. [Note: [Col. 0193D] Cyril, Book III on John: “Human beings are strengthened in faith by a twofold grace, namely legal and evangelical grace; this the Lord taught through the parable: ‘Every scribe,’ etc.”] Those follow the letter alone; these follow both letter and spirit. To these, finally, it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to those it has not been given, so that seeing they may not see and hearing they may not understand. [Note: [Col. 0193D] In another homily there follows material from Isaiah, the Psalms, and elsewhere; since it does not pertain to the explanation of Matthew, we omit it here.]

LIX. “And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these parables, that he departed from there. And, coming into his own country, he taught them in their synagogues, so that they were astonished and said: ‘Whence has this man this wisdom and these mighty works?’”

By “his own country” he means the city of Nazareth, where his mother lived and where he himself had been raised. All who heard him and saw his mighty works were astonished, remembering that he had lived among them and had neither learned letters nor ever done anything of the kind. They therefore said: “Whence has this man this wisdom and these mighty works?” They say this because they do not know that he is the power of God and the wisdom of God. Yet it is not readily apparent whence Wisdom has wisdom, or Power has power.

“Is this not the carpenter’s son?” He is indeed the son of a carpenter, but not of the one whom you suppose. Joseph is a good carpenter, but better is he who made the dawn and the sun, whose son this one is. [Note: [Col. 0193D] St Ambrose, Book III on Luke, beginning: “Nor does it seem irrelevant to explain in what sense he had a carpenter as father. By this type he shows that he has as his Father him who, being the maker of all things, created the world.” See Sermon 36, *On Time*, among the sermons of Augustine.] “Is not his mother called Mary?” You know his mother, indeed, but you do not know his Father. For whoever does not know the Son does not know the Father either. Hence he himself says: “Whoever sees me sees the Father” (John XIV, 9).

But neither do you properly know his mother, while you suppose him to be Joseph’s son; for his mother is a virgin. Say, therefore: “Is not his mother called the Virgin Mary?” For this is what we call her. “And are not his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas, and are not all his sisters among us? Whence, then, has he all these things?” And they were scandalized by him. By his brothers and sisters they mean the children of his mother’s sisters, that is, his cousins; for it is the custom of Holy Scripture to call the children of brothers or sisters “brothers.” [Note: [Col. 0194D] See Augustine, *Questions from Matthew*, chapter XVII.]

But Jesus said to them: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country and in his own house.” For Christ is honored everywhere that he has deigned to reveal his virtue and power in signs and miracles; only the Jews dishonor him, among whom he lived for a time. “And he did not perform many mighty works there, because of their unbelief.” Hence Mark also says: “And he could not perform many mighty works there.” [Note: [Col. 0194D] Mark VI, 5: “And he could perform no mighty work there.” See St Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 4, and Euthymius on Mark VI.]

Why could he not? Because he did not will to. Why did he not will to? Because of their unbelief. For the Lord could, if he had wished, have healed even unbelievers; but in bodily health he signified the health of the soul. The soul, unless through faith, can neither be healed nor saved, because God has established its salvation in faith, saying: “Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved; but whoever does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark XVI, 16). For the unchangeable Lord has established certain things in such a way that they can no longer be changed at all.

LX. [CHAPTER XIV.] “At that time Herod the tetrarch heard the report concerning Jesus and said to his servants: ‘This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead, and therefore mighty works are performed in him.’” [Note: [Col. 0194D] There is a homily among the others falsely said to be by Eusebius of Emesa, on the beheading of St John the Baptist, p. 194.]

These words clearly show what reputation blessed John the Baptist had and how holy he was considered by all. For, as is read in another Gospel, everyone was wondering about John whether perhaps he himself might be the Christ. Therefore, when Herod heard of the miracles performed by the Lord, and did not believe that anyone besides John could perform such things, he thought that John had risen from the dead and was therefore performing them with greater powers.

The Evangelist then relates how the impious Herod killed the holy man. “For Herod seized John, bound him, and put him in prison because of Herodias, the wife of his brother.” John had said to him: “It is not lawful for you to have her.” For, as the law says, it is not lawful for a brother to take his brother’s wife except to raise up offspring for his brother, if he has died without children. But this man took the wife of his brother Philip—who, it is said, was still alive—not to raise up his brother’s offspring but to gratify lust. Therefore, because blessed John forbade this great crime, he was seized, bound, and put in prison.

Herod wished to kill him but did not dare, both because he knew him to be a holy and righteous man and because he feared the people, who regarded him as a prophet. For this reason his death was delayed for some time. But on Herod’s birthday the daughter of Herodias danced in the midst, 73 and pleased Herod. For what can please a foolish and lustful man except empty glory, feasting, and a woman’s dancing—indeed, incentives and instruments of lust? The fact that the girl is called not Herod’s daughter but Herodias’s daughter shows that she was Philip’s daughter. [Note: [Col. 0195D] Josephus, *Antiquities* XVIII.6, relates that Philip died leaving no children. Calmet infers from this that this daughter, named Salome, followed her mother and lived with Herod Antipas as with a parent.]

Her dancing pleased Herod—indeed, pleased him exceedingly. Therefore he promised her on oath that he would give her whatever she asked of him. For drunkenness, joined to folly and vanity, casts a man down so far that he does not consider what he says. What if the girl had asked Herod for his eyes? Would he have torn them out and given them to her? For if he had not given them, she could have accused him of perjury. He had sworn that he would give her, without exception, whatever she asked. And she asks for more than Herod’s eyes—not she herself, however, but through her the impious and adulterous mother. For, instructed beforehand by her mother, she said: “Give me here on a platter the head of John the Baptist.”

It is rightly written of an evil woman: “There is no wickedness greater than the wickedness of a woman” (Ecclus. XXV). She could have had half the kingdom had she wished; but she considers that nothing and asks for John’s head. “And the king was grieved; but because of the oath” [Note: [Col. 0195D] Jerome: “He excuses his crime by the oath, so that under a pretext of piety he might become impious.”] “and those who reclined with him, he commanded it to be given.” He regretted having sworn; he feared to lie; shame prevailed, he blushed before human faces, and he forgot justice.

Lying is evil, certainly; but murder is worse. David acted much better: though he had sworn to kill Nabal, he was nevertheless overcome by Abigail’s entreaties and did not kill him (1 Sam. XXV). Therefore, where someone cannot escape a lesser sin without a greater sin, let him do what is lesser, lest he incur the greater sin. [Note: [Col. 0196D] Euthymius: “Because you swore rashly, it was better to commit perjury; for from two evils the lighter must be chosen.”] For if you say that today you will kill an innocent person: if you kill him, you speak truth; if you do not kill him, you lie. But it is better not to kill him and to lie than to kill him and speak truth. Thus it would have been better for Herod to be judged guilty of perjury than to be condemned for such a murder.

“He sent and beheaded him in prison. And his head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and the girl brought it to her mother.” O impiety! O cruelty! A righteous man is beheaded; his head becomes the price of dancing; it is brought on a platter and set before the diners: a great dish indeed, but horrible to behold. “And his disciples came, took his body, and buried it; and coming, they told Jesus.” [Note: [Col. 0196D] The homily ends here.]

When Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there by boat into a deserted place apart. And when the crowds heard, they followed him on foot from the towns. Going out, he saw a great crowd, had compassion on them, and healed their sick. We pass quickly over what is plain, in order to dwell on the more difficult matters.

LXI. “And when evening had come, his disciples approached him, saying: ‘The place is deserted and the hour is already past. Dismiss the crowds, so that they may go into the villages and buy food for themselves.’ But Jesus said to them: ‘They have no need to go away; give them something to eat yourselves.’”

The Lord refreshes the crowds in the evening because he began to preach in the final hour and final age. Hence John says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John II, 18); and the Apostle: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. X, 11). He does this in the desert—that is, among a wild and untamed, undisciplined and unlearned people. Of this the Psalmist says: “In a desert land, trackless and waterless, so I appeared to you in the sanctuary, that I might see your power and your glory” (Ps. LXXII, 3). John the Baptist also preached in this desert, saying: “I am the voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord” (Matt. III, 3).

If his disciples had known what the Lord was about to do, as his mother did when she had been invited to the wedding, they would never have said to him: “Dismiss the crowds, so that they may go into the villages and buy food.” For she, filled with the Spirit of God and already foreknowing what was to come, said: “They have no wine” (John II, 3), because she knew that her son would give new wine there. But what does the Lord say? “Give them something to eat yourselves.” They answered: “We have here only five loaves and two fish.”

You see, then, that Christ’s disciples did not yet understand what the two fish and five loaves signified. Therefore they thought that what was sufficient for the whole world could not suffice such a great crowd. The five loaves are the five books of Moses [Note: [Col. 0197D] St Augustine, Tractate 24 on John: “The five loaves are understood as the five books of Moses, appropriately not of wheat but of barley, because they belong to the Old Testament.” The same is said by Bede on this passage. Before them Hilary says of the disciples: “They answered that they had only five loaves, because they were still contained under the five loaves, that is, the five books of the Law.”]; if spiritually understood, the whole of both New and Old Testament is most fully contained in them. Their riches suffice for all people to eat, for they always increase like these loaves, and whoever eats more has more abundance.

The two fish are understanding and memory. Without these, these loaves can neither be eaten nor retained in the stomach of the soul. Such food is eaten by understanding and retained by memory. Therefore neither loaves without fish nor fish without loaves have savor. What can you read if you do not understand? And what can you understand if you do not entrust to memory what you understand? Let us therefore eat the loaves and eat the fish: let us read, understand, and retain in memory what we understand. For when people act otherwise, the devil comes and takes the word from their hearts, lest, believing, they should be saved.

The Lord therefore commanded that those loaves be brought to him; and, having made the crowd recline upon the grass, he took the five loaves and two fish, looked up to heaven, blessed, broke, and gave the loaves to the disciples, and the disciples to the crowds. Behold, our Savior makes the crowd recline upon grass, so that whoever has not yet reclined upon the grass may understand that he is unworthy of this food. For the Prophet says: “Truly the people are grass; the grass has dried up and the flower has fallen” (Isa. XL, 7).

Whoever you are, if you wish to be filled with Christ’s loaves, first recline upon the grass—indeed, first recognize yourself to be grass. Let the verdure of the flesh no longer luxuriate within you. Hear the Apostle saying: “Put to death your members which are upon the earth” (Col. III, 5). Understand that the flower and beauty of this life quickly wither. [Note: [Col. 0197D] Bede, from Jerome: “To recline is to trample underfoot, with the mind’s contempt, the flowers, pleasures of this age, and enticements of the flesh.”]

Taking the five loaves and two fish, the Lord looked up to heaven, blessed them, broke them, and gave them to his disciples. Since he was about to give great gifts to his disciples, the Lord first looked to heaven, so that we might understand that “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. I, 17). “For all wisdom is from the Lord God, and has always been with him and is before the age” (Ecclus. I, 1). Hence the Lord says also of himself: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” (John VI, 41). Thus the Lord looks to the place from which all good things come.

He blesses the loaves so that they may multiply by his blessing. For so too, in the beginning, the Lord blessed the first seeds; and, having received his blessing once, they have not ceased to bear fruit even to this day. And he broke them, which was very necessary. For what is breaking the loaves except revealing the mysteries of the Scriptures? He himself opened the disciples’ understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures; he taught them to break loaves and expound the Scriptures. This is what is meant by “he gave them to his disciples, and the disciples to the crowds”: he taught his disciples, and the disciples taught us. Hence the Apostle says: “For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you” (1 Cor. XI, 23).

We too break these loaves for others, having received them broken from Christ’s disciples, and set them daily before the crowds as we expound these words of the holy Gospel. “And they all ate and were filled.” The number of those eating was five thousand men, besides women and children. There are only five loaves, but more than five thousand eat. They eat, and the loaves increase; there is a contest between loaves and people. The loaves suffice; the people fail. Indeed, if people had not ceased eating, perhaps the loaves would have increased without end. So too spiritual food, the bread of both Testaments: the more it is eaten, the more it increases.

Do you not see how this bread increases even in my own mouth? The words being expounded are few; yet if someone eager to eat and strong in chewing, with stronger teeth and a healthier stomach, wished to chew them further and break them more, he could still prepare innumerable delights for himself from them. It follows: “And they took up twelve baskets full of the fragments left over.” The remnants of the loaves were far more numerous than the loaves themselves had been. There were twelve baskets of remnants, whereas all the loaves before they were eaten could have been placed in less than one basket.

If anyone wonders at this, let him wonder also at all the other things which the Lord does. What has God done that is not wonderful? He made heaven and earth: that is wonderful. He created human beings and all animals: that too is wonderful. But is this not also wonderful—that from a little seed he fills so many granaries for us every year? Or that, though the moisture of the earth is the same, it changes taste in every tree or herb? Though in itself it is perceived as neither sweet nor bitter, in some plants it is found sweet and in others bitter. Search through things one by one, then, and you will find nothing that is not wonderful. Do not, however, wonder at these things, but rather wonder at him who created these and all other things so admirable. [Note: [Col. 0198D] Hilary: “Do not marvel that springs flow, that vines contain grapes, that wines pour forth from grapes, and that all the resources of the world flow out in an unceasing channel; for so great an increase of loaves reveals the author of this universe.”]

This also deserves consideration: there are as many baskets as apostles. Each apostle filled the basket of his mind from the fragments of these five loaves, so that he might have the means to refresh the people entrusted to him. [Note: [Col. 0198D] Hilary: “When the people have been fed, such an abundance thereafter accumulates as corresponded to the number of the believing people and of the apostles destined to be filled with heavenly grace.” Jerome: “Each apostle fills his own basket from the Savior’s remnants, either that he may have the means afterward to provide food to the nations, or that from the remnants he may teach that the loaves later multiplied were true loaves.” Bede: “The twelve baskets are the twelve apostles, who gathered from them the sacraments; for what cannot be understood by the unlearned must be investigated by the perfect.”]

See now in this one basket of the blessed evangelist Matthew, which he has poured out before the eyes of our mind, what great delights it contains. Nor can we doubt that he received much also from the fish, since he understood all these things so well and entrusted what he understood to memory. Likewise blessed John filled his basket from these loaves; he records that they were barley loaves. They were indeed barley loaves, coarse and difficult to eat. Therefore the Lord broke them and added the fish to them, so that with the fish they might be eaten more easily.

LXII. [Note: [Col. 0199D] “And immediately he compelled.” Vulgate.] And immediately he ordered the disciples to embark in the boat and go before him across the strait, until he had dismissed the crowds. In this he seems to have signified his Passion: when he was left behind and the disciples fled, he himself would remain alone among the crowds of Jews. For he said [Note: [Col. 0199D] John XVIII.9. Hilary: “That he is alone in the evening [Col. 0200D] shows his solitude at the time of the Passion, when the rest had scattered in terror.”]: “If you seek me, let these go.” But because he orders the disciples to enter the boat and travel by the perilous way of the sea, it is shown that they too were not secure amid that great disturbance.

“And, having dismissed the crowd, he went up alone onto the mountain to pray.” The Lord dismissed the crowd and ascended the mountain when, leaving the Jews, he returned to heaven; and he was alone indeed, because no one went bodily with him. There he prays because, as the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0200D] Hebrews VII.25: “Ever living to make intercession for us.”], he intercedes with the Father for us.

“Now when evening had come, he was alone there; but the boat was being tossed by the waves in the midst of the sea, for the wind was contrary.” From the time when Christ, the Sun of righteousness, departed this world, evening fell upon the people of the Jews. For at his birth [Col. 0199C] light rose for them, but at his death darkness came upon them. That the boat was tossed by waves in the midst of the sea signified that, after Christ’s Ascension, the holy Church would suffer many adversities in this world. Hence it is rightly said that the wind was contrary. For what is a contrary wind but the raging persecution of tyrants?

“But in the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking upon the sea.” The fourth watch has been in progress from the time when our Savior came into the world. The first watch was from Adam to Moses; the second from Moses to David; the third from David to Christ [Note: [Col. 0200D] Hilary: “But the Lord comes in the fourth watch; for then, in the fourth, he will return to the wandering and shipwrecked Church. . . . The first watch was that of the Law; the second, of the prophets; the third, of the bodily advent; and the fourth, of the return in glory.”]. The first watch, oppressed by excessive sleep, was without the Law; the second had the Law; the third the prophets; the fourth the Gospel. Therefore he comes to them in the fourth watch, because [Col. 0199D] in this more than in all the others the Lord deigns to visit his servants.

He walks upon the sea because the whole world is subject to him. “And when they saw him walking upon the sea, they were troubled, saying that it was [Col. 0200A] a phantom; and from fear they cried out.” Their confused and disorderly cry shows that they were troubled by extreme fear. And immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying: “Take courage; it is I; do not be afraid.” Thus the Lord also said to Moses: “I am who I am. Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: He Who Is has sent me to you” (Exod. III.14).

Or perhaps he said, “It is I,” so that they might recognize who he was by hearing the voice which they knew. For we often immediately recognize a person by hearing his voice at a distance, even if we do not see him.

Peter answered and said: “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters.” But he said: “Come.” For blessed Peter is everywhere shown to have possessed most ardent faith [Note: [Col. 0200D] Jerome: “Peter is found in all places to possess most ardent faith”; Bede copies this. See Hilary.]. He would not have entrusted himself to the deepest sea unless he had possessed the most certain faith [Col. 0200B] in the Lord. For he knew that our Savior could do all things and believed that he had no less power upon the sea than upon land.

Yet Peter’s walking upon the sea shows that this world is subject not only to the Master but also to the disciples. This necessarily happened on account of the heretics who later said that Christ the Lord, because he walked upon the sea, possessed not a true body but a phantom body. These people are refuted when they hear that blessed Peter also walked upon the sea, though they surely do not doubt that he possessed a real body.

“And Peter, descending from the boat, walked upon the water in order to come to Jesus. But seeing the strong wind, he was afraid; and when he began to sink, he cried, saying: ‘Lord, save me.’ And immediately [Col. 0200C] Jesus stretched out his hand and caught him; and he said to him: ‘O you of little faith, why did you doubt?’” By this deed blessed Peter already signified what would happen to him. In Christ’s Passion he walked, as it were, confidently upon the waters when he said: “Even if all are scandalized, I shall never be scandalized” (Matt. XXVI.33). But he saw the strong wind and was afraid because, when the Lord was seized by the Jews, he too fled with the other disciples. He sank when he denied him. Then he cried, “Lord, save me,” when he went out and wept bitterly; for his weeping atoned for his crying out.

But immediately Jesus stretched out his hand and caught him when, by the voice of the angel, he was consoled and in a sense drawn back to himself, as the women were told: “Go, tell [Col. 0200D] his disciples and Peter that he goes before you into Galilee” (Mark XVI.7). For by calling him by his own name, he raised him, as it were caught by the hand—trembling and already afraid of perishing—to the hope of grace [Col. 0201A].

In these things the Church’s prosperity and adversity may also be signified. It sometimes seems to sink, and at other times to rise again.

“And when they had gone up into the boat, the wind ceased.” It must not be understood that Jesus then entered the boat [Note: [Col. 0201D] See St. Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, book II, ch. 47, and St. Hilary here, v. 19.]. For he first came to Capernaum, and there spoke many things in the synagogue, which John records but Matthew and Mark omit. John says that the disciples wished to take him into the boat, but immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going, namely Capernaum. Hence it is plain that he did not then enter the boat.

For, as was said above, the Lord had commanded his disciples to go ahead of him. When they came to Capernaum and did not find him there, [Col. 0201B] they were turning back again to return to him; and then indeed the Lord appeared to them walking upon the sea. After all the matters now related in this Gospel had been completed, after he had spoken the things which John recounts down to the place where it is said, “Jesus said these things while teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum,” they returned to the boat; and when they had gone up into the boat, the wind ceased.

For the wind had not yet ceased, nor had the sea rested from its turbulence; but, as at night, so also by day they were still agitated by the same waves. But when Jesus entered the boat, the wind at once ceased. Those who were in the boat, astonished at so great a miracle, came and worshipped him, saying: “Truly you are the Son of God.” Mark, however, rebukes them, calling them forgetful and blinded [Col. 0201C], because they were amazed at this, although on the preceding day they had known that the Lord had performed so great a miracle with the five loaves. Therefore he says [Note: [Col. 0201D] Mark VI.52–53: “For their heart was blinded.”]: “For they had not understood about the loaves.” For if they had remembered the miracle of the loaves, they would no longer have had reason to marvel at the miracle of the calmed sea.

“And when they had crossed over, they came into the land of Gennesaret and landed. And when they had come out of the boat, immediately they recognized him.” Matthew states this more clearly. Mark seems to say that the disciples did not recognize him until they came out of the boat. But this is not so. The statement is not about the disciples, but about the people of that region, who immediately recognized him and brought their sick to him from every quarter to be healed. This is what Matthew says: “And when the men of that place recognized [Col. 0201D] him, they sent throughout that whole region and brought to him all who were ill; and they begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment; and all who touched it were made well.”

Let us also pray that the Lord may deign to enter the boat of our breast [Col. 0202A], and make the windiness of pride and the storms of rising vices cease [Note: [Col. 0201D] Bede: “For into whatever heart God comes through the grace of his love, immediately all the battles of the world, of vices, and of evil spirits are subdued and cease.”]. Let him also enter his own boat, that is, the holy Church [Note: [Col. 0201D] Hilary: “By his ascent into the boat, the calming of wind and sea signifies the eternal peace and tranquility of the Church after the return of his glory.”], and make himself manifest there—he who in a sense seems not to be there while he permits it to be shaken by so great a storm of persecutions. Let him command the winds, and let there be a great calm.

But when he says: “And when the men of that place recognized him, they sent throughout that whole region and brought to him all who were ill,” in order that he might heal them, what else does this signify except that holy men, who have deserved to know God, ought to pray for the sins of others and commend and offer others to God?

But what is it to touch the fringe of Christ’s garment [Note: [Col. 0202D] Matthew here, v. 36: “And they brought to him all who were ill, and begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. And all who touched it were made well.”]? It is one thing to touch Christ, another to touch Christ’s garments. Thomas [Col. 0202B], touching Christ, said: “My Lord and my God” (John XX.28). Philip, however, touched the garments and not Christ when he said: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John XIV.8). Thomas therefore touched Christ more closely than Philip. Hence the former is told: “Because you have seen me, you have believed”; but the latter: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? He who sees me sees the Father.”

The one, therefore, is said already to have seen and believed; the other not yet to have seen or believed well. Those touch Christ who, believing perfectly in him, know the truth of the catholic faith. But those touch Christ’s garments who, although unable to understand, nevertheless believe what is preached to them by catholic men. Thus each touches Christ at a greater distance [Col. 0202C] to the extent that he understands and knows Christ less. Yet all are healed who touch even the fringe of his garment, since “everyone who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark XVI.16).

LXIII. [CHAPTER XV.] Then scribes and Pharisees from Jerusalem came to him, saying: “Why do your disciples transgress the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread.” The traditions of the elders are called not the sayings of the prophets but the customs of forefathers. By them they are taught to wash hands, jars, cups, and all vessels frequently, and always keep them clean and bright [Note: [Col. 0202D] Euthymius: “For the divine Law did not command that they should not eat before washing, but the elders of the people did.”]. The Jews obeyed these more than the Law and the prophets.

They also had many other [Col. 0202D] traditions and customs which were contrary even to the Law and the prophets. Rebuking them for these immediately afterward, the Lord said: “Why do you also transgress the commandment of God because of your tradition?
