For God said: ‘Honor your father and mother’; and, ‘He who curses father or mother shall surely die.’ But you say: ‘Whoever says to father or mother: Whatever gift there is from me will benefit you,’ and he shall not honor his father or mother; and you have made void the commandment of God because of your tradition.”

Mark the evangelist appears to state this somewhat more plainly. For he says (Mark VII.11): “But you say: If a man says to father or mother, ‘Whatever gift there is from me may benefit you,’ then you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother, nullifying the word of God.” This is as though he said: God commands parents to be honored; but you, interpreting honor wrongly, teach children to dishonor their parents. For you say that this is sufficient honor for parents: that they should be honored by their children in words and intention [Col. 0203B], since Moses commands that they be honored but does not prescribe how they are to be honored. By doing this, you permit them to do nothing further for their parents, because, wrongly instructed by you, they console them with empty words so that they may seem to honor them.

For honor in Holy Scripture is understood more in services than in words, according to the saying: “Honor the Lord from your substance” (Prov. III.9); and the Apostle: “Honor widows who are truly widows” (1 Tim. V.2). Thus people commonly say, “So-and-so honored me well,” if he received one into his home, gladly served him, and generously supplied what was necessary. Therefore we ought to honor our parents with such honor.

By these things it is made clear that the scribes and [Col. 0203C] Pharisees, providing for their own advantage, drew children away from the service of their parents and invited them to the services of the Temple and to offerings and sacrifices. When they replied that they could by no means do this because they needed to support their poor parents from their own means, the scribes and Pharisees said that God should be obeyed rather than human beings. But the parents said in return: Why then did God command that parents be honored? To this they answered: No one honors his parents better than one who offers gifts to the Lord for himself and for them. Therefore, whoever wishes rightly to honor his parents should say to his father and mother: “Whatever gift there is from me will benefit not myself only, but you also. As I offer gifts for myself, so I offer them for you; every offering of mine is not mine only, but yours also.”

When the parents heard this, they preferred to be tortured by hunger rather than hinder such offerings. By this device, therefore, the scribes and Pharisees both tormented parents with hunger and stripped children of their resources. This is what he means when he says: “You no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother, nullifying the word of God.” For they nullify God’s word who interpret it so wrongly. [Col. 0204A] By an evil interpretation, a person is deceived, mercy is removed, and greed is nourished. They do nothing further for their parents: they offer up everything that they ought to have given their parents. Those who so honor their parents certainly sin, but those who teach them to honor them in this way sin more grievously.

[Note: [Col. 0203D] Modern interpreters—Jansenius, *Harmony*, ch. 60; Maldonatus; Cornelius a Lapide; and others—following the judgment of Origen and Euthymius, explain this difficult passage as our author has done: namely, as though children, when appealed to by needy parents, had replied: “Whatever gift I contribute to the worship of God will also benefit you, because I shall contribute it with the intention of helping you no less than myself and rendering God favorable to you.” By this teaching the scribes and Pharisees, under the pretext of religion, pursued their own gain. See Jerome and Bede on this passage; Victor of Antioch on Mark VII; Augustine, *Questions on the Gospels*, book I, ch. 16.]

“Hypocrites, Isaiah prophesied well concerning you, saying: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. But in vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men.’” These are those of whom it is said: “They speak peace with their neighbor, but evils are in their hearts” (Ps. XXVII.3). They worship God in vain because they will receive no reward for their service; for God attends not to words but to hearts.

He rebuked them because, abandoning the commandments of the Law and the prophets [Col. 0204B], they taught human doctrines and commandments—namely, those which they called traditions of the elders. “And having called the crowds to him, he said to them: Hear and understand: not what enters the mouth defiles a person, but what proceeds from the mouth, that defiles a person.” “You,” he says, “hear and understand, since these men indeed wish to hear but refuse to understand; for their wickedness has blinded them.”

Then his disciples came and said to him: “Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?” But he answered and said: “Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be uprooted.” Therefore every planting of philosophers, every planting of heretics, every planting of scribes and Pharisees—whatever is against God, against truth, [Col. 0204C] against justice—shall be uprooted. For any planting which is not against these things, even if it is done by them, is nevertheless not theirs.

God plants his own planting not only through the good [78] but also through the evil. Hence the Lord elsewhere commends even the planting of these same scribes and Pharisees when he says: “The scribes and Pharisees sit upon Moses’ seat; therefore do whatever they tell you” (Matt. XXIII.2). Yet not absolutely everything, but only all those things that accord with the teaching and chair of Moses. Such teaching and planting is theirs because it is done through them; and it is not theirs because it is not their tradition. For every doctrine, if it is good, belongs to God, by whomever it is taught.

“Leave them alone: they are blind, and guides of the blind. But if a blind man gives guidance to a blind man, [Col. 0204D] both fall into a pit.” This blindness is not of the body but of the heart. For one is blind who follows error and does not understand truth, since the light of the mind is understanding. Those fall into a pit who descend into hell.

Peter answered and said to him: “Explain this parable to us.” But he said: “Are you still without understanding?” The apostles were without understanding because they thought that matters had been spoken in parables which the Lord had spoken not in parables but in plain speech. Therefore those too are rightly rebuked who attempt to interpret allegorically matters which ought to be understood literally.

“Do you not understand that everything which enters the mouth goes into the belly and is discharged into the privy?” It is clear that food is digested in the belly, and one part of it is distributed through the limbs for the nourishment of the body [Note: [Col. 0205D] Jerome: “From this brief saying some maliciously allege that the Lord, ignorant of physical inquiry, supposes that all foods go into the belly and are discharged into the privy, whereas food immediately after being taken in is dispersed through the limbs, veins, marrow, and sinews.” Jerome answers this objection in the same place.]; while another part, which is not necessary to the body, is discharged into the privy.

Hence it was carefully said, “everything,” and not “the whole.” If he had said “the whole,” it would not have been true, for not the whole of what goes into the belly is discharged into the privy. “Whole” is one thing, “every” another. If you say, “Every human being is bodily,” you speak truly; but if you say, “The whole human being is bodily,” you do not speak truly, since the soul, though part of a human being, is incorporeal. Thus everything which goes into the belly is discharged into the privy, yet not the whole of what goes into the belly is discharged into the privy. For all things that enter the belly to nourish the body, even though very small, undergo both digestion and excretion.

“But the things which proceed from the mouth come from the heart, and they defile the person.” Let philosophers, then, be silent, who maintain that mind and reason, memory and understanding, are in the brain. He who made the human being knows what he placed in every part of a human being; for he searches the kidneys and hearts.

But they say: If these things are in the heart and not in the head, why are they lost through an illness of the head [Col. 0205C] and recovered through its good health? Why, so that mad and frantic persons may return to their right mind, is a remedy applied to the head rather than to the heart? For almost every treatment of those who suffer such things is directed not to the heart but to the head.

Let them know, however, that mind and reason, memory and understanding have their chief and proper seat in the heart [Note: [Col. 0205D] Jerome, in the same place: “Therefore the ruling faculty of the soul is not, according to Plato, in the brain, but, according to Christ, in the heart; and from this saying those are to be reproved who think that thoughts are implanted by the devil.” Jerome says nearly the same in Letter 64 to Fabiola and in *Against Jovinian*, book I. Origen likewise, Homily 9 on Exodus, and Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 15, maintain this by many testimonies of Scripture. Philo also, in the treatise *On the Worse Thing Lying in Wait for the Better*; Gregory of Nyssa, Oration I *On the Resurrection*; and Theodoret, Discourse 3 *On Providence*. Lactantius, however, *On the Workmanship of God*, book I, leaves the question undecided as to whether it is in the brain or in the heart.]. These faculties are sometimes hindered by the weakness of the head, just as they are strengthened by its health.

We know that sight is in the eye. If you place your hand over it, sight is immediately removed; if you remove your hand, sight returns. But do you therefore say that sight is not in the eyes but in the hand, because sight is removed when the hand obstructs it? So reason, although it is removed by an impediment in the head, should nevertheless be believed to reside not in the head but in the heart. For the natural heat, which is diffused from the heart throughout the entire body by the channel of the pulses, is sometimes corrupted in a sick head, for some cause unknown to us. When the heart is affected by this corruption, the mind and reason in it are darkened. Hence, when the head is cured, the corruption is removed and mind and reason return.

It follows: “For [Col. 0206A] evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies come from the heart. These are what defile a person.” They come from the heart because they are generated there and have their seat there. Whether they arise through human invention or diabolical persuasion, there can nevertheless be no doubt that they proceed from the heart. These are what defile a person; these separate a person from God and make him abominable. “But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile a person.” Eating with unwashed hands is uncouthness, not sin.

LXIV. [Note: [Col. 0206D] This is ascribed to Bruno, its author, as Homily for Thursday after the First Sunday in Lent.] “And Jesus, going out from there, withdrew into the regions of Tyre and Sidon. And behold, a Canaanite woman, coming out from those borders, cried, saying: ‘Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David; my daughter is grievously tormented by a demon.’” [Col. 0206B] “But he answered her not a word. And his disciples came and begged him, saying: ‘Send her away, for she cries after us.’ But he answered and said: ‘I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.’”

This, therefore, is the reason why God does not hear the crying woman; this is the reason why Mercy does not show mercy; this is the reason why he who in the beginning was the Word, although the woman multiplies many words, nevertheless does not answer her a word. “I was not sent,” he says, “except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”

What then does the Prophet mean when he says: “There shall be a root of Jesse, and he who rises to rule the nations; in him the nations shall hope” (Rom. XV.12)? If you were not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, why is it said to you by the Father: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession” (Ps. II.8)? Again, if you were not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, why does the Father speak to you in Isaiah, saying: “It is too small a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and turn back the dregs of Israel. Behold, I have given you as a light of the nations, that you may be my salvation unto [Col. 0206D] the end of the earth” (Isa. XLIX.6)?

By this testimony you seem to have been sent more to the nations than to Israel. For it seems too small to the Father—and rightly indeed too small—that you, who are equal to him, should be his servant at so cheap a price, should become human, should take the form of a servant, if you came only to turn back and call the tribes of Jacob and the dregs of Israel. The Father says: “Behold, I have given you as a light of the nations, that you may be my salvation unto the end of the earth”; and you say: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” These statements appear contrary, yet they are not contrary.

For the Lord was sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel in order to call them, heal them, preach to them, and convert them to faith—and this in person. He was also sent [Col. 0207A] to call, heal, preach to, and convert the nations to faith, but this through his disciples and not in person. Finally, he was sent first to preach to the Jews [Note: [Col. 0207D] Jerome: “Not that he was not also sent to the nations, but that he was sent first to Israel, so that, when they did not receive the Gospel, the transfer to the nations might be just.” Hilary: “Not that salvation was not also to be imparted to the nations; but the Lord had come to his own and among his own. Therefore he expected the firstfruits of faith from those among whom he had arisen, while the rest were afterward to be saved through the preaching of the apostles.”], and then to the Gentiles. Thus the Apostle says to those same Jews [Note: [Col. 0207D] Acts XIII.46: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life,” etc.]: “It was necessary that the word of God be preached first to you; because you rejected it and made yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII.46).

Thus the Lord was both sent and not sent. We have heard what the Canaanite woman said; we have heard what Christ answered his disciples, who interceded for her while on the road. Now let us see what he did after coming into the house. For Mark the evangelist, who omits all the things said on the road, describes the following events as occurring not [Col. 0207B] on the way but in the house. For he says [Note: [Col. 0207D] Mark VII.24: “See St. Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, ch. 49.”]: “And rising from there, he went into the borders of Tyre and Sidon; and entering a house, he wished no one to know, yet he could not remain hidden. For a woman, as soon as she heard of him—whose daughter had an unclean spirit—entered and fell at his feet. For the woman was a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by race.”

Because he was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, he answered nothing to the woman who cried out along the road. Moreover, after entering the house, he wished no one to know, yet he could not remain hidden. But why did he wish no one to know? Because all of them were Gentiles; and he did not yet wish to be revealed to the Gentiles. Why, then, could he not remain hidden? It seems inappropriate that he who can do all things should wish to remain hidden and be unable to do so.

It must not, therefore, be understood [Col. 0207C] as though he wished to remain hidden and could not. For the evangelist uses simple language here. What does “he wished no one to know” mean except that he commanded the disciples to tell no one that he was there? The disciples could not have understood this otherwise unless he commanded them not to reveal him. Therefore he wished to be known, and because he wished it, he could not remain hidden.

Likewise it is said elsewhere of this same one that he pretended to be going farther (Luke XXIV.28), though he certainly did not wish to go farther. Thus he did not wish to remain hidden, but, having entered the house, he showed that he wished to be hidden, because the time had not yet come when he was to be preached to the Gentile people.

The woman who had cried after him on the road, after she did not find him among the disciples, asked where he was; and, as soon as she heard of him, [Col. 0207D] she entered the house and fell at his feet. But what did she say? “Lord, help me.” He answered and said: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs.” The wretched woman follows Mercy; though repulsed, she is not ashamed; she enters the house, cries insistently, worships the Savior, and at last deserves to hear an answer.

The Lord tests whether she has patience and maintains humility. He calls her a dog; she confesses that she is a dog. “It is not good,” he says, “to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs.” She says: “Yes, Lord; I am a dog, from the Gentile people, of Canaanite descent. I am unworthy of the children’s bread; I am unworthy of the benefit of the saints. But because I am a dog, give me the crumbs; for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table.”

This woman teaches us how we ought to pray. She had not read the Gospel, yet she prays as the Gospel commands [Note: [Col. 0208D] Jerome: “Under the figure of the Canaanite, the Church’s faith, patience, and humility are wonderfully proclaimed: faith, by which she believed that her daughter could be healed; patience, by which, though despised so often, she persists in prayer; humility, by which she compares herself not to dogs but to little dogs.”]. For it is written [Note: [Col. 0208D] Matthew VII.7: “Ask and it shall be given to you,” etc.]: “Ask and you shall receive; seek and you shall find; knock, [Col. 0208B] and it shall be opened to you.”

Then Jesus answered and said to her: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish.” You asked for bread with importunity; because of your importunity you shall be given as many loaves as you need. “Go, for your daughter is well”; and her daughter was healed from that hour.

Let us therefore pray to the Lord that he may heal our daughters; let us pray that he may heal and free our souls from sins. For that soul is tormented by a demon which does not cease to sin and perseveres in crime. If it is well converted and does not despair of Christ’s mercy, the most merciful Lord will say to it: “Let it be done for you as you wish,” and it will be healed from that hour; because the sinner, in whatever hour he turns and groans, shall live and shall not die.

LXV. “And when Jesus had passed on from there, he came beside the Sea of Galilee; and, ascending the mountain, he sat there. And great crowds came to him, bringing with them the mute, the blind, the lame, the weak, and many others; and they laid them at his feet, and he healed them, so that the crowds wondered as they saw the mute speaking, the lame walking, and the blind seeing; and they glorified the God of Israel.”

Jesus rightly ascended the mountain when he was about to perform so many and such great miracles, so that on the mountain the height of his authority, and in his miracles the power of his divinity, might appear.

LXVI. But Jesus, having called his disciples, said: “I have compassion on the crowd, because they have now remained with me for three days and have nothing to eat.” For the three days are the three ages of the world: namely, before the Law, under the Law, [Col. 0208D] and under grace. [Note: “The Lord does not wish to dismiss fasting the crowd which has remained with him for three days—that is, in faith in the Holy Trinity, or before the Law, under the Law, and under grace.” Bede, on this passage.] Therefore the crowds remain with the Lord for three days, because throughout all these three periods holy men, filled with the Spirit of God, believe in Christ, await Christ, and long with great desire to be refreshed by his loaves and teaching. [Col. 0209A] And they had nothing to eat, because the living bread that came down from heaven had not yet been set before them; the Lion from the tribe of Judah had not yet opened the book or unsealed its seven seals.

Therefore on the third day—that is, in this third age of his Incarnation—he refreshes the crowds and no longer allows them to perish from hunger. Hence he says: “And I do not wish to send them away fasting, lest they fail on the way.” For we are all on the way; we are all striving toward our homeland. Of this way the Psalmist says: “I ran in the way of thy commandments” (Ps. CXVIII [119]:32); and again: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. V [119]:1). But on this way those who fast grow faint; those who have not been refreshed by Christ’s bread cannot run along this way—especially if they have come from [Col. 0209B] afar. For salvation is far from sinners (Ps. CXVIII [119]); just as this way is short and easy for the good, so it is long and difficult for the wicked.

And the disciples say to him: “Whence then shall we have so many loaves in the wilderness as to satisfy so great a crowd?” Perhaps Christ’s disciples had forgotten that the Lord had already above satisfied five thousand men from five loaves. And Jesus said to them: “How many loaves have you?” But they said, “Seven, and a few little fishes.” For the seven loaves are the seven graces of the Holy Spirit; but the few little fishes are the few books of the New Testament. [Note: St Hilary: “Seven loaves, therefore, are offered: for no salvation is drawn for the Gentiles from the Law and the Prophets, but they live through the grace of the Spirit, whose gift, as grace teaches, is sevenfold.” St Ambrose, Book VI on Luke: “Many have thought that the grace of the sevenfold Spirit is signified by the loaves, and that the figure of the twofold Testament is to be understood also in the fishes.”]

For the books of the New Testament are indeed very few in comparison with the Old Testament. Yet these few, if joined to those seven loaves, suffice for the refreshment of the souls of all people; for without [Col. 0209C] those loaves they can neither be eaten nor give satiety or strength to those who eat them. For those seven loaves are wisdom and understanding, counsel and fortitude, knowledge and piety and the fear of the Lord. But who is wise without wisdom? Who understands without understanding? Who is provident without counsel? Who is strong without fortitude? Finally, who is knowing without knowledge, devout without piety, and faithful without the fear of God? Therefore these fishes cannot be eaten without those loaves.

And these books are rightly called fishes because they swim in the living fountain, of which it is written: “For with thee is the fountain of life, and in thy light we shall see light. And he commanded the crowd to recline upon the ground” (Ps. XXXV [36]:10). For all recline upon the ground who recognize that they are earth and dust. [Col. 0209D] Hence it is also said: [Note: Eccles. X [Sirach 10]:9: “Why is earth and ashes proud?”] “Why are you proud, dust and ashes?”

And Jesus, taking the seven loaves and the fishes, giving thanks, broke them and gave them to his disciples. The Lord breaks both the loaves and the fishes because, as he wills, he grants to each person the graces of the Holy Spirit and unfolds the deep mysteries of the Holy Scriptures. [Col. 0210A] But to whom does he give them, if not to his disciples? To whom does he entrust their proclamation, if not to bishops and priests? For these are those whom “the Lord appointed over his household, that they might give them food in due season.” They feed the others; they refresh the whole multitude of the Church with the bread of the divine word.

“And they all ate and were satisfied.” Therefore let us too eat, that we may be satisfied; let us read, that we may understand. For the more one eats this food, the more one desires to eat. This food cheers the mind and does not burden the stomach. The more it is eaten, the more abundantly it grows. Hence it is added: “And they took up seven baskets full of what remained of the fragments.” There are more fragments than loaves, because more people now receive the fragments than those who then [Col. 0210B] ate the loaves and fishes. [Note: St Hilary: “For, as a figure of the future, the people are counted as healed in so many thousands of parts as it is believed that thousands of believers from the parts would gather to receive the gift of heavenly food.”]

Do you not see how many volumes of books have been multiplied from these four Gospels? But what is signified by the seven baskets, except the seven Churches, through which all the other Churches are understood? Thus John the Evangelist writes to seven Churches. Thus also Isaiah says: “Seven women shall take hold of one man in that day, saying: ‘We shall eat our own bread’” (Isa. IV:1)—the bread now given to us, the bread by which we have been filled and refreshed. As though they were saying: We are those seven baskets which the apostles of old took up in the wilderness, full of fragments; therefore, because we have bread, we shall eat our own bread.

Now those who ate were four thousand men, apart from little children and women. Why are little children and [Col. 0210C] women not counted, except because those are not worthy to be reckoned among God’s people who imitate either children in foolishness and silliness, or women in softness and weakness? Hence the Apostle says: “Do not become children in understanding; but in malice be children” (1 Cor. XIV:20).

LXVII. [Note: “Magedan,” Vulgate.] “And, having dismissed the crowd, he went up into the boat and came into the borders of Magedda.” For Mark says that “having entered the boat with his disciples, he came into the region of Dalmanutha” (Mark VIII:10). We must therefore understand either places close to one another, or two names of the same place, [Note: Thus Bede and Euthymius.] or one name as general for the province and the other as proper to the place itself. [Note: See Jansenius, chapter 64; Maldonatus; Cornelius a Lapide, who almost agrees with our author. See also Calmet on this passage and Bonfrerius in the Onomasticon.]

[CHAPTER XVI.] And Pharisees and Sadducees came to him, testing him, and asked him to show them a sign from heaven. [Col. 0210D] What is it, then, that these men wish to see—a sign from heaven? Perhaps they do not believe that our Saviour has power in heaven, though he works so many and such great signs on earth? For he could not do this on earth if he did not have power in heaven.

But he answered and said to them: “When evening comes, you say: [Col. 0211A] ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red’; and in the morning: ‘Today there will be a storm, for the sky is red and gloomy.’ You know, then, how to discern the face of the sky, but you cannot know the signs of the times?” As though he said: In other matters your eyes are open, but in regard to me you are blind. For what are “the signs of the times” except signs that occur in time? In your own times you see signs being done which were done in no other times; yet you still seek signs, and seeing, do not see.

But Luke says this: “When you see a cloud rising from the west, immediately you say, ‘A rainstorm is coming,’ and so it happens; and when the south wind blows, you say that heat will come, and it happens. Hypocrites, you know how to test the face of sky and earth” (Luke XII:54); how then do you not test this time? “And why do you not even judge from yourselves what is [Col. 0211B] right?” For if they judged what was right, they would certainly say that this was the Son of God, in whose time they saw all things happen that the prophets had foretold concerning Christ.

It is no wonder if the Evangelists do not say the same things, because not all write everything. Luke writes what Matthew omits, and Matthew writes what Luke omits; and so likewise with the others. Yet no one should doubt that Christ our Lord said all the things that either all or individual Evangelists recount.

It follows: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given it except the sign of Jonah.” Enough has been said above about the sign of Jonah. “And he left them and went away. And when his disciples had come across the sea, they forgot to take bread.” He said to them: “Look and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and [Col. 0211C] Sadducees.” But they reasoned among themselves, saying: “Because we have not taken bread.” He said to them: “Why do you reason among yourselves, O you of little faith, because you have no bread? Do you not yet understand, nor remember the five loaves for the five thousand men, and how many baskets you took up? Nor the seven loaves for the four thousand men, and how many baskets you took up? Why do you not understand that I did not speak to you of bread? Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.”

For to rebuke them in this manner was to teach them. Hence it is added: “Then they understood that he had not told them to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” For teaching is called leaven because, just as a little leaven corrupts the whole lump, so a little heretical [Col. 0211D] teaching defiles the whole faith. [Note: Jerome: “This is the leaven of which the Apostle also speaks: ‘A little leaven corrupts the whole lump.’ Marcion and Valentinus, and all heretics, possessed this sort of leaven, which must be avoided by every means. Leaven has this power: if it is mixed with flour, what seemed small grows greater and draws the whole mass to its own taste. So too heretical teaching, if it casts even a small spark into your breast, soon grows into a vast flame and draws to itself the whole possession of the person.”]

LXVIII. Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi and questioned his disciples, saying: “Whom do people [82] say that the Son of Man is?” The Lord asks his disciples what opinion people [Col. 0212A] have of him and whom they think him to be—not because he is ignorant of the various opinions of the crowd, but in order to instruct and teach them in the truth.

But they said: “Some say John the Baptist; others Elijah; others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.” John had already died; while he was still alive, all thought perhaps that he himself was Christ. Herod too, hearing Jesus’ report, said to his servants: “This is John the Baptist; he himself has risen from the dead” (Matt. XIV:2). Most foolish was the people that now thought John to be Christ and now Christ to be John. Most foolish, I say: when it sees prophets, it persecutes and reviles them; but after their death it venerates them and builds monuments to them, and thinks that no others like those [Col. 0212B] whom it had killed can thereafter be born.

Thus, seeing John, they thought him not John but Christ, Elijah, or some other one of the prophets who had gone before. Likewise, seeing Christ, they believed him not to be Christ. They knew that he would come, but because they saw him, they could not believe. For if these people had seen Elijah or Jeremiah, would they have believed them? Certainly not: their fathers had seen them, yet had refused to believe them.

Jesus said to them: “But whom do you say that I am?” This, he says, is the judgment of the people: thus those who do not know me speak of me; they do not say that I am what I am, but say that I am what I am not. First they say that John is Christ; now they think neither I nor John to be Christ. But whom do you say that I am? [Col. 0212C] Do you too hold the same opinion?

Simon Peter answered and said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” It was fitting for Peter to make this answer, inasmuch as he was to be the chief of the apostles. [Note: St Augustine, Sermon XIII, *On the Words of the Lord*, etc.: “For Peter himself, first in the order of the apostles and most prompt in love for Christ, often answered alone for all.” The same, Sermon XXXIII, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] But let us see what Peter answered. Christ says: “Whom do people say that the Son of Man is?” Peter says: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” The one asks about a man; the other says that the Son of God is the son of man. Therefore he who is the Son of the living God is himself also the son of man.

Hence the Blessed Virgin Mary is called *Theotokos*, that is, “she who bears God and man.” [Note: The Latins translate it *Deipara*, “God-bearer.” In the *Synodicon against the Tragedy of Irenaeus*, chapter 15, in Baluzius, *Collectio nova*, etc.: “she who gave birth to God”; by Greeks, as by Ephrem cited in Photius, Codex 228, she is called in other words μήτηρ Θεοῦ, “Mother of God.” See Allatius, *On the Liturgy of St James*; Suicer; Du Cange; etc.] Since Nestorius refused to confess this, he was expelled from and condemned by the Church.

Jesus answered and said to him: “Blessed are you, Simon Barjona, because flesh and [Col. 0212D] blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” “Blessed,” he says, “are you, Simon Barjona”: Simon, son of the dove; for *Barjona* is interpreted “son of the dove.” [Note: St Jerome: “Therefore from his confession he receives a name implying that he has received revelation from the Holy Spirit, whose son he is to be called. For *Barjona* in our language means ‘son of the dove.’”]

But why is Peter called the son of the dove? What is this dove? For we read that the Holy Spirit appeared over Christ the Lord in the form [Col. 0213A] of a dove. Therefore he is the son of this dove who has so sound and so spiritual an understanding. For, as the Lord says: “That which is born of flesh is flesh, and that which is born of Spirit is spirit” (John III:6). Hence it is added: “Because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” This knowledge is not carnal; this faith is not of flesh and blood. Neither your parents nor your own flesh taught you these things, but my Father who is in heaven. [Note: St Leo, Sermon 4, Ballerini edition, chapter 2: “Therefore you are blessed because my Father taught you; no earthly opinion deceived you, but heavenly inspiration instructed you. And not flesh nor blood, but he whose only-begotten Son I am, made me known to you.”]

Thus the Apostle too says, in Galatians I:16, that he did not confer with flesh and blood, but came to Jerusalem to see Peter. “And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.” You say—and you speak truly—that I am Christ, the Son of the living God; [Col. 0213B] and I say to you that you are Peter, strong in faith and steadfast in teaching. For unless Christ had understood strength and steadfastness in this name, he would not immediately have added what follows, saying: “And upon this rock I will build my Church.”

If you do not understand Peter, look to the rock; and the rock was Christ. Thus Peter is from the rock, just as Christian is from Christ. [Note: St Augustine, Sermon 270, no. 2: “Peter, one for the rest, one for all: ‘You are,’ etc.; deservedly he merited to receive such an answer. ‘Blessed,’ etc., because I am the rock and you are Peter; for the rock is not from Peter, but Christian from Christ.” Nearly the same in Sermon 76, no. 1.]

Let us therefore see what “upon this rock I will build my Church” means. Upon this rock, which you have just laid as the foundation of faith; upon this faith, which you have just taught, saying: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God”; upon this rock and upon this faith I will build my Church. For the Apostle, agreeing with this statement, [Col. 0213C] says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. III:11). As though he said: There is no other foundation but that rock which Peter laid as a foundation when he said: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God.” Upon this rock, moreover, the whole Church of God is built.

[Note: Our author shares this interpretation of the Gospel saying with other Fathers, whom the most eminent Orsi enumerates in *De irreformabili Romani Pontificis judicio*, vol. II, p. 310, and explains at length what should be determined about it. On the same saying, Charles du Plessis d’Argentré, among French theologians, writes in *Elementa Theologiae*, p. 260: “It is manifest that these words, ‘You are Peter,’ etc., were spoken by Christ concerning the person of Peter, whom he wished to be the principal foundation of his Church and, as it were, the centre of the Church’s unity; as is evident from the perpetual tradition of the Church and from six hundred testimonies of the ancients, who explicitly asserted that Peter and his successors in the Roman see are that most firm Rock upon which Christ founded his Church. But since the same passages of Scripture can very often admit various meanings, you should not be surprised if certain holy Fathers sometimes understood, in another sense more suited to their own purpose, the passage cited by us. Thus St Hilary, with certain others, sometimes asserts that the rock upon which Christ founded the Church is Peter’s confession of Christ’s divinity. But this interpretation does not exclude, indeed confirms, the former sense already given: for the confession made by Peter is Peter himself, insofar as he made that confession. Nor do those differ greatly from this exposition who interpret the rock as Christ, whom Peter had confessed. For they do not understand Christ considered simply in himself to be that rock of which Christ speaks in the famous passage, ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock,’ etc.; rather, they understand Christ insofar as Peter confessed him, or Peter himself insofar as he confessed Christ’s divinity. St Augustine, who often employed this interpretation against the Donatists because it was more suited to his purpose, also approves the other in Book I of the *Retractations*, chapter 11.”]

“And the gates of hell shall not prevail [83] against it.” “For whoever falls upon this stone shall be broken; but upon whomever this stone falls, [Col. 0214A] it shall crush him.” For this rock moves with such force and strength that it breaks down walls, shatters gates, and no power or strength can withstand it.

But if you wish to understand “the gates of hell” differently, first recognize the gates of heaven. For the gates of heaven are the apostles, bishops, priests, and others through whose teaching and examples the souls of the faithful enter the heavenly palace. Conversely, the gates of hell are Jews, heretics, all deceivers, and corrupters of the Catholic faith; through these the souls of unbelievers enter hell and are plunged into darkness. And these indeed will not be able to prevail against this rock and against the Church built upon it.

“And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” What is said principally to Peter [Col. 0214B] must be understood as having been said also to the other apostles—and not only to the apostles, but also to bishops and priests. For to these the keys and power have been given by the Lord, that they may open not only the Church but also heaven to others. “And whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven.”

Let bishops hear this: let them rejoice in the gift, but not be proud of their power. For if they bind as Peter did, whatever they bind shall be bound, and whatever they loose shall be loosed. Therefore let them imitate him in discernment and justice whose power of binding and loosing they wish to imitate. For if they act otherwise, what they have done shall not be ratified. [Note: See Jerome on this passage.] Therefore [Col. 0214C] these things were said to Peter alone, because there was no one more faithful, more just, more discerning, or better to whom these words could have been spoken. They were said to him alone so that all others might see themselves in him as in a mirror: living, acting, binding, and loosing in this way, and not departing from peace and concord.

Nevertheless, just as prelates deprive themselves of the power of binding if they bind unjustly, so subjects also, even if they are bound unjustly, bind themselves more tightly by their own pride if they make light of being bound. [Col. 0215A] Therefore even those who are bound in this way should desire to be loosed and pledge satisfaction; if the prelate refuses to accept it, then they should know that they are loosed.

Then he commanded his disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ. For the Lord wishes all things to be said and done in their proper time: the time had not yet come when he was to be made known by the preaching of the disciples. [Note: Jerome: “It may be that before the Passion and Resurrection he did not wish himself to be preached, in order that, after the sacrament of blood was completed, he might more fittingly say to the Apostles: ‘Go, teach all nations.’”]

From that time Jesus began to tell his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things from the elders, scribes, and chief priests, be killed, and rise on the third day. By foretelling future things to his disciples and showing that he suffers willingly, the Lord confirms their faith, according to what he says elsewhere: “And now I have told you before it happens, so that when [Col. 0215B] it has happened, you may believe” (John XIV:29).

And Peter, taking him aside, began to rebuke him, saying: “Far be it from thee, Lord; this shall not happen to thee.” But he turned and said to Peter: “Go behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me, because you do not savour the things of God, but those of men.” “Go,” he says, “behind me; follow and imitate me, so that as I die for you, you too may die for me.” [Note: This interpretation is St Hilary’s, chapter 16, no. 10. He says to Peter: “Go back behind me,” that is, “follow him by the example of his Passion.” The Maurist editor notes that Origen, in Huet’s edition, p. 285; Ambrose, Book I, *On Abraham*, no. 55; and Eusebius, Book I, *Against Marcellus*, chapter 2, explained the same words in this manner.]

Do not oppose me; do not resist my will; do not stand against the divine counsels. For so it must be, because it was predestined before the ages and foretold by the prophets. This is what he says elsewhere: “O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary for Christ so to suffer and rise from the dead, and thus enter into his glory?” (Matt. [Col. 0215C] XXIV:25). Therefore Peter savoured the things of men because he gave human counsel; but he did not savour the things of God because he did not know these secrets of the divine counsel by which humanity would be redeemed.

LXIX. Then Jesus said to his disciples: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny [84] himself.” For every person must deny himself—not that he is a human being, or that he is faithful and Christian—but if he has been an idolater, an unbeliever, an adulterer and fornicator, greedy and avaricious, he must deny being such and show that he is no longer such. But let him show it not by voice, but by deed; let him say with the Apostle: “Yet now I live, not I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II:20). For the Apostle lived, but not himself: not Saul lived, but Paul. Therefore he had denied himself, [Col. 0215D] being now greatly different from himself.

It follows: “And let him take up his cross and follow me.” For one takes up one’s cross who crucifies and afflicts one’s flesh with its vices and lusts. [Col. 0216A] But because it is not enough to take up the cross, he immediately added, saying: “And follow me.” [Note: Chrysostom, Homily 56, distinguishes three things: denying oneself, taking up one’s cross, and following Christ. “For,” he says, “someone might suffer such things and yet not follow Christ, if he suffered nothing for Christ himself.”]

For it does not profit one who does not follow God either to take up the cross or to afflict the flesh. Hence the Apostle says: “If I should deliver my body so that I might burn, but have not charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. XIII:3). And of those who perform all their works in order to be seen by people, though they fast greatly and crucify and afflict the flesh, the Lord nevertheless says that they have received their reward (Matt. VI:2). Therefore it does not profit the Jew, the hypocrite, or the heretic to bear the cross. Why? Because they do not follow Christ; for the person who imitates Christ follows him.

Do you wish to follow Christ? Be humble, patient, and merciful; [Col. 0216B] be without hatred or pretense; be obedient to God and love your neighbour. For Christ walks this way; therefore walk in it if you wish to follow him. Unless you walk in this way, you do not follow him, even if you seem to do so. For many follow the devil who appear to follow Christ.

“For whoever wishes to save his life shall lose it.” Who then will save his life, if the person who strives to save it loses it? What is this life which we must lose? This life is the present life. Therefore one who, forgetful of the other life, loves this present life alone will lose it and will have no other. “But whoever loses his life for my sake shall find it.” Blessed, then, are the martyrs who have lost this life and did not love their lives even unto death; for they shall find life—not merely any life, but eternal life.

“For what does it profit a man if he gain the whole world but suffer loss to his own soul?” What did it profit the rulers of the Romans to possess the world for a time and to do nothing for the salvation of their souls, when their bodies return to dust and their souls are tormented in hell? For if it were said to you: Be rich and powerful throughout this whole month; do whatever you wish; enjoy bodily pleasures as you please—but on the condition that your eyes be torn out, every consolation removed, and that throughout the whole time of your life you live in hunger and thirst, in every torment and every misery—would you accept such a good on these terms?

Yet this whole present life is not even the span of a month, or of one [Col. 0216D] day, or hour, in comparison with that eternal wretchedness, whose misery has neither end nor any comparable punishment. [Note: Hilary: “For what profit is there in having seized the world and in brooding over the riches of this age with complete dominion of earthly power, if the soul must be lost and the loss of life undergone? . . . What shall we bring to life? Treasures of earthly riches, I suppose, prepared for future transactions; ambitious titles of rank and fame; or old portraits of luxurious nobility? All these things must be denied, that we may abound in better things; by contempt for all things Christ must be followed, and eternity must be purchased at the loss of earthly things for spiritual things.”]

“Or what exchange shall a man give [Col. 0217A] for his soul?” For there is no exchange and no price by which the soul can be saved except faith and repentance. If it leaves this life without these, it can thereafter be redeemed by no price. Hence the Psalmist says: “Those who trust in their own strength and glory in the multitude of their riches: a brother shall not redeem; shall a man redeem? He shall not give his propitiation to God, nor the price for the redemption of his soul” (Ps. XLVIII [49]:7). Therefore he shall labour forever and live in torments without end.

“For the Son of Man shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he shall render to each one [Note: [Col. 0217D] “According to his works.”] according to his work.” For he first came humble, that the Son of Man might be judged; but he will come again exalted and sublime, in the glory, honour, and majesty [Col. 0217B] of the Father, to judge the world and render to each according to his works. “For God shall come manifestly, our God, and shall not keep silence” (Ps. XLIX [50]:3).

And as though someone said, “Would that we might someday see that glory,” he added: “Amen I say to you: there are some standing here who shall not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.” If we understand this to refer to that kingdom and glory in which he has just promised that he will come with his angels to judge, it cannot stand: for no one was present when the Lord said these things who has not now tasted death, yet he has not come to judgment. The following words make clear how these things should be understood.

LXX. [CHAP. XVII.] [Note: [Col. 0217D] This is a homily attributed to Eusebius of Emesa, Saturday after the First Sunday of Lent, p. 62.] “And after six days Jesus took Peter and James and John his brother, and led them apart up a high mountain, and he was transfigured before them.” These, therefore, are those of whom he had just said: “who shall not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom” (Matt. XVI, 28); that is, appearing in the power and glory of his kingdom. For when the Lord was transfigured, he appeared on the mountain to these three disciples of his in such a form as he will appear after this life [Note: [Col. 0217D] Bede: “As he then appeared to the apostles, so after the judgment he will appear to all the elect.”] to all his faithful in his kingdom.

But why did our Savior choose to transfigure himself into that appearance of his brightness, except that he might make us more certain of that glory which he preached? Accordingly, he wished his three disciples to be present—those who elsewhere are called pillars of the Church (Gal. II, 9)—so that they might be witnesses of so great a vision. For these three suffice for bearing this testimony, because, as it is written, “By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Matt. XVIII, 16). For who would not believe what Peter, James, and John testify?

It was fitting, moreover, that these things should take place upon a high mountain, which were afterwards to take place in heaven. They take place after six days because, as the Apostle says, when the labor of this life, which is carried on in six days, has ended, there remains “a sabbath-rest, and rest for the people of God” (Heb. IV, 9). Therefore we ought greatly to desire that these six days may pass, so that we may see our King in his beauty and in the glory of his majesty. “For we know,” John says, “that when he shall appear, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John III, 2).

“And his face shone like the sun, and his garments became white as snow.” The Evangelist could find nothing brighter than the sun, nothing whiter than snow, to which he might compare Christ’s face and garments [Note: [Col. 0217D] Bede: “Since we know that nothing is seen brighter than the sun, therefore not only the glory of the Lord but also that of the saints in the resurrection is compared with the appearance of the sun.”]. Yet we do not doubt that he is brighter than the sun; for a creature cannot be fully like the Creator.

“And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, speaking with him.” But why Moses and Elijah? For in Moses we see the Law, and in Elijah the prophets [Note: [Col. 0218D] Jerome: “The Law and the prophets are displayed, who with repeated voices announced both the Lord’s passion and his resurrection.”]. Thus the apostles see Moses and Elijah speaking with Christ; they see the Law and the prophets bearing testimony to him. Hence also the prophet Habakkuk: “In the midst of two living creatures you shall be known” [Note: [Col. 0218D] Chap. III, 2, from the Septuagint version, also cited by Jerome on Habakkuk; the Church likewise uses it in the tract for the First Prophecy on Good Friday: “In the midst of two living creatures you shall become known.”].

For even to this day Christ is known and seen in the midst of the two living creatures, in the midst of Moses and Elijah—that is, in the Law and the prophets. Read the books of Moses; read the books of the prophets: there you will find Christ, there you will know and see him. For there he is transfigured; there the glory of his majesty is revealed to his faithful.

These two men, as Luke says (chap. IX, 31), were speaking with Jesus together about his death, which he was soon to suffer in Jerusalem; and perhaps they were glad because they saw the day of their redemption and that of the whole human race drawing near.

Then Peter answered and said to Jesus: “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you will, let us make three tabernacles here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” Peter, therefore, recognized Moses and Elijah, whom he had never seen before, although, as the other Evangelists say, he did not know what he was saying.

While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them; and behold, a voice from the cloud saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him.” For God appeared in a cloud because he cannot be seen by human beings in his majesty, as he himself says: “No man shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII, 20).

We may also understand this cloud to signify the divine Scripture, which, full of the water of wisdom, appears bright to those who understand and obscure to those who do not understand. In this cloud almighty God can indeed be heard, but he cannot at all be seen and understood as he is. For everywhere we hear him speaking, but nowhere do we see him except through a mirror and in an enigma; for he himself speaks in the prophets, he himself in the apostles. Hence the Lord himself says: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X, 20).

We can therefore see the cloud, but we cannot see him who speaks in the cloud. For even now, in this cloud of the sacred Gospel [Note: [Col. 0219D] In a similar way Gregory, *Morals*, book XVII, chap. 14: “By the name of clouds he teaches that the preachers of the Gospel are meant. For, lest unlearned hearers be flooded by an inundation of knowledge rather than nourished by the measured sprinkling of preaching, God binds up the waters in the clouds,” etc.], we hear him speaking, but do not see him. For whose voice is this which these letters sound, if not his: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased”?

For he was rightly well pleased in his Son, whereas he was displeased in the creation of man. Hence he himself says: “It repents me that I have made man” (Gen. VI, 7). He admonishes us to hear this Son, and to believe and obey him. For in whom ought we to believe but Wisdom, Righteousness, and Truth? For he is the power of God and the wisdom of God; he is the way, the truth, and the life.

“And when the disciples heard this, they fell upon their faces and were greatly afraid.” For what if they had seen his appearance, when they could not bear his voice? “And Jesus came and touched them, and said to them: Arise; do not be afraid.” Blessed are those whom Jesus touches; blessed are those whom salvation and life touch. For they rise; they become fearless and secure [Note: [Col. 0219D] Jerome: “Because they lay prostrate and could not rise, he mercifully approaches and touches them, so that by his touch he may drive away fear and strengthen their weakened limbs. Those whom he had healed by his hand, he heals by command: ‘Do not be afraid.’ First fear is expelled, so that instruction may afterwards be given.”].

Therefore let us ask him to touch us also, to awaken us from the sleep of stupefaction and folly, and to open our eyes to see him. “But when they lifted up their eyes, they saw no one but Jesus alone.” For it is enough to see Jesus; it is enough to see that light, for whoever follows it does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.

“And as they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, saying: Tell the vision to no one, until the Son of Man rises from the dead.” For it was fitting that his great glory should first be proclaimed when he had put off the mortality of the flesh and was clothed in the glory and beauty of the new resurrection.

LXXI. [Note: [Col. 0219D] Chrysostom, Homily 58: “They did not know this from the Scriptures, but because the scribes explained it to them, this opinion was commonly circulated. … For the divine Scriptures bear witness to two comings of Christ, one of which has already taken place and the other is yet future. … But the scribes, confusing these matters and misleading the people, remembered only the second coming and said to the people: If Christ were here, Elijah would already have come. … For this reason the Pharisees sent to John and asked: Are you Elijah?—making no mention of the first coming. Christ supplied the solution: namely, that Elijah will then come, before my second coming; and that Elijah has already now come, calling John himself by that name,” etc. See Origen, *Tractate 3 on Matthew*; Jerome here and in the letter to Algasia, and on Malachi, chaps. 3 and 4.] “And his disciples asked him, saying: Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?”

For when the disciples heard of the resurrection of the Son of Man, they understood it to mean the final and universal resurrection, which, because of these words, they thought was already near. Yet the sayings of the scribes opposed this, since they proclaimed that it could not occur unless Elijah came first.

But he answered them: “Elijah indeed will come and restore all things.” What the scribes say is true, he says: Elijah will come before the resurrection which you understand takes place; and when he comes, he will restore all things, because through his preaching the Jewish people, persisting in unbelief until that time, will be converted to the Church and restored to faith. For then the fullness of the Gentiles will enter and Israel will be saved.

“But I say to you that Elijah has already come, and they did not know him, but did to him whatever they wished. So also the Son of Man is to suffer at their hands.” Elijah, he says, will come, and has already come. The one who has already come preceded my resurrection; the one who will come shall precede the general resurrection of all. Then the disciples understood from these words that he had spoken to them about John the Baptist; for John was called Elijah because he went before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah.

LXXII. [Note: [Col. 0220D] “Falling down before him on his knees … he falls into the fire.”] “And when he had come to the crowd, a man approached him, falling down before him on his knees and saying: Lord, have mercy on my son, for he is moon-struck and suffers grievously.”

Such persons are called “moon-struck” (*lunatici*) because they are more severely afflicted according to the waxing of the moon [Note: [Col. 0220D] See Francisco Valles, *Sacred Philosophy*, chap. 71.]. “For he often falls into the fire, and frequently into the water; and I brought him to your disciples, and they could not heal him.”

Jesus answered: “O unbelieving and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I bear with you?” The Lord is now weary of dwelling with the unbelieving race of the Jews. Hence elsewhere he says: “Your house shall be left to you desolate.” “Bring him here to me.” And Jesus rebuked him, and the demon went out of him, and the boy was healed from that hour (Matt. XXIII, 38).

But perhaps someone will ask what these things signify, since Christ’s miracles are rarely found without some signification. This man, therefore, may be understood as the Jewish people, whose son is the spirit, which is also called the soul; in accordance with what is said of the Lord himself, that “bowing his head, he gave up the spirit,” that is, the soul. This man therefore prays for his son; this people prays for its spirit and soul. Why? Because he is moon-struck. “The fool,” someone says, “changes like the moon” (Ecclus. XXVII, 12).

For if the Jews had not been moon-struck, the Lord would never have said to them: “You are of your father the devil” (John VIII, 44). Thus, tormented by the devil, they were often plunged into the fire of envy and rage, and often into the water of depraved doctrine and error. Whoever wishes to understand how this generation was always unbelieving and perverse should read the books of Moses and the prophets. And because neither priest nor Levite could heal this people, it is said here: “I brought him to your disciples, and they could not heal him.” It was necessary, therefore, that the Samaritan should heal him.

The Lord also asked the boy’s father, as Mark says, how long this had been happening to him; and he answered, “From childhood.” By this it is understood that this people has always been unbelieving and faithless from its earliest age. Hence Moses says to the same people: “While I am still alive and going among you, you have always acted contentiously against the Lord; how much more after I am dead?” (Deut. XXXI, 27).

Then the disciples came to Jesus and said: “Why could we not cast it out?” He said to them: “Because of your unbelief.” For the apostles did not yet have perfect faith [Note: [Col. 0221D] Hilary, no. 6: “The apostles did indeed believe, but they were not yet of perfect faith. For while the Lord remained on the mountain and they sat with the crowd, a certain lukewarmness had slackened their faith.”]. Hence elsewhere they say: “Lord, increase our faith” (Luke XVII, 5) [Note: [Col. 0221D] Vulgate: “increase.”]; and again: “For neither did his brethren believe in him” (John VII, 5); hence they are called by the Lord, “Foolish and slow of heart to believe” (Luke XXIV, 25).

“For amen I say to you, if you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain: Move from here, and it shall move; and nothing shall be impossible to you.” For above he said of the mustard seed that “it is the least of all seeds; but when it has grown, it is greater than all herbs and becomes a tree, so that the birds of heaven come and dwell in its branches” (Matt. XIII, 32). This seed, moreover, not only grows into a tree, but also yields seed a hundredfold and a thousandfold. Therefore whoever has such faith, which grows and multiplies in this way and perseveres always strong and unfailing, will find nothing impossible.

Hence the Apostle says: “The saints, through faith, conquered kingdoms, worked righteousness, obtained the promise, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the violence of fire, recovered strength from weakness, and became mighty in war” (Heb. XI, 33). But if you wish to know what faith can accomplish, read also the rest contained in the same Epistle.

But what does he mean by saying: “You will say to this mountain: Move from here, and it shall move”? What is “this mountain” except that evil one, whom the apostles could neither cast out nor move from the aforesaid man? Although the devil may be called a mountain because of the height of his pride [Note: [Col. 0221D] Hilary: “He called the devil a mountain, because in him are spiritual wickednesses, and heavenly powers are to cast them out into the height of the sea, as into the depth of hell.”], yet in this passage he is very fittingly called a mountain because of the weight with which he oppressed this wretched man and could not be moved by such and so great men.

“But this kind is not cast out except by prayer and fasting.” Although this mountain and this kind of demons are moved and cast out by faith, he says, prayers and fasts are nevertheless necessary for accomplishing this. This, then, is a great and singular defense for all believers: in great temptations they should flee to prayer and fasting, since those kinds of malignant spirits are conquered and cast out by these means, though in no other way can they be moved even by Christ’s own disciples.

Let us therefore note this carefully, commit it carefully to memory, and always remember the conclusion of this saying in every temptation. Let those especially hear it who are thrown by the devil into fire and water—that is, [Note: [Col. 0221D] Bede, from Jerome: “The moon-struck person who does not persist in what he has begun signifies those who are now carried into the fire of lust, now into the water of covetousness.”] those who are afflicted by the spirit of fornication, by the flame and pleasure of concupiscence. For lust is both fire and water: fire, indeed, because it inflames; hence through Hosea it is said: “All who commit adultery are inflamed like an oven heated by the baker” (Hos. VII, 4). But it is water because it effeminates the whole person and dissolves him into softness.

LXXIII. “And while they were in Galilee, Jesus said to them: The Son of Man is to be delivered into the hands of men, and they shall kill him, and on the third day he shall rise again.” And they were greatly grieved.

But, as the other Evangelists say, the disciples did not understand this, and were afraid to ask what it meant. Therefore they were greatly grieved afterwards, from which we understand that at first they did not understand, but later, when they did understand, they were greatly grieved.

“And when they had come to Capernaum, those who received the didrachma approached Peter and said to him: Does not your master pay the didrachma?” He said, “Yes.” And when he had entered the house, Jesus anticipated him, saying: “What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute and tax: from their sons or from strangers?” And he said, “From strangers.” Jesus said to him: “Then the sons are free.”

If earthly kings receive taxes not from their sons but from strangers, he says, it is evident that the sons of kings are free from every payment of tribute. But if the sons of kings do not pay tribute, how much more ought I not to pay tribute, who am the Son of that King who is King of kings and Lord of lords [Note: [Col. 0222D] St. Hilary: “To show that he was not subject to the Law, and to attest in himself the glory of his Father’s dignity, he set forth the example of an earthly privilege: that the sons of kings are not bound by census-tax or tribute; and that he is rather the Redeemer of our soul and body than one from whom anything should be demanded for his own redemption, because the king’s son must be outside the common condition of the rest. Yet, to prevent scandal, he concedes payment; otherwise he is free from the obligation of the Law.”]?

“But lest we scandalize them, go to the sea, cast in a hook, take the first fish that comes up, and when you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater; take it and give it to them for me and for yourself.” Behold, our Savior, who ought not to have paid tribute, nevertheless paid tribute so that no scandal might arise. “Woe therefore to him through whom scandal comes” (Matt. XVIII, 7), provided that he can avoid scandal without sin. For one does not sin who gives what is his own; but one sins who seizes what belongs to another. “To whom tribute, tribute; to whom tax, tax; to whom fear, fear; to whom honor, honor” (Rom. XIII, 7). These are the Apostle’s words.

It is better for Catholic and ecclesiastical men to give even what is not due than to stir up the weapons of the wicked against the Church and to scandalize the impious and tyrants. It should also be considered that our Savior, in one respect, receives tribute from others, and in another respect pays tribute to others. For the King’s Son receives tribute, but the Son of Man pays tribute. For to whom, if not to the King’s Son, do the fish of the sea pay tribute? One fish was summoned, and immediately came with the tribute. If all were summoned, all would likewise hasten [Note: [Col. 0223D] Hilary: “When he is instructed to seek the first fish, those about to come up are shown to be many.”] and all would pay their tribute; and indeed fish are far more numerous than human beings. See, then, how much tribute the Lord could have received from his tributaries, had he wished.

LXXIV. [CHAP. XVIII.] “At that hour the disciples came to Jesus, saying: Who do you think is greater in the kingdom of heaven?”

The disciples came to Jesus, certainly, not by speaking but by thinking. For the Lord heard their thoughts no less than their words, since both sounded in his ears in the same manner; and so he often answers thoughts. I have said this beforehand because the other Evangelists say not that the disciples came to Jesus, but that they thought and discussed among themselves on the way which of them seemed to be greater [Note: [Col. 0223D] Chrysostom resolves this differently, Homily 59 on Matthew: “If Mark writes not that they asked but that they thought this among themselves, there is no contradiction; I would suppose that they thought this not once, but twice and a third time, and only then asked.”].

“And Jesus, calling a little child, set him in the midst of them and said: Unless you are converted and become like little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.” The Lord rightly calls a little child, so that those who wish to appear greater may be instructed by his example. “Do you see this little child?” he says. “Unless you are turned away from this foolish exaltation which disturbs your minds, to this child’s patience and humility, and become like little children—without envy, without hatred, without pride, without ambition—you shall not only fail to be greater in the kingdom of heaven; you shall not even enter it.”

For the devil was cast out from there because he wished to be greater there. “For the Lord puts down the mighty from their seat and exalts the humble” (Luke I, 52). “Whoever, therefore, humbles himself like this little child, he is greater in the kingdom of heaven.” Whoever among you humbles himself more, he says, shall be exalted more and become greater; and if all of you humble yourselves in the likeness of this little child, all of you will there be among the greatest [Note: [Col. 0223D] Hilary: “We must therefore return to the simplicity of children, because when we are established in it, we shall bear about the form of the Lord’s humility.”].

Therefore it is not ambition but humility that makes persons greater: the greater person is the humbler one. “And whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me.” Such a one, namely, not in age but in conversion, so that what age gives to this child, holiness and humility may give to the other. Let him therefore be humble and patient; let him be without hatred and envy, without deceit and pretense, without pride and ambition. For children are without these things, and the apostles were without them as well. Whatever they may have been before, nevertheless, receiving their teacher’s admonitions with ears not deaf, they afterwards became what he had instructed them to become.

Of these little children, therefore, the Lord says: “Whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me.” What does “in my name” mean except for my name’s sake: because he is a Christian, because he is my disciple, because he is marked with my name [Note: [Col. 0224D] Jerome: “Whoever is such as to imitate Christ’s humility and innocence, in him Christ is received.”]? But whoever receives him in Christ’s name receives not only that person, but Christ dwelling in that person as well.

“But whoever scandalizes one of these little ones who believe in me, it is better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea.” For people are scandalized in many ways, and scandals are spoken of in many ways. Whenever you offend someone in any manner and move him to anger and indignation, it is scandal; but such scandal is not unto death. To scandalize someone in faith, however—as Jews and heretics often scandalize the Church—is unto death. Of this the Lord says: “Blessed is he who shall not be scandalized in me” (Luke VII, 23).

It is better for a person to die—and not by just any death, but by that which seems more dreadful, namely, to be drowned with a great stone in the depth of the sea—than to scandalize some simple and little one who believes in Christ and cause him to depart from the Catholic faith [Note: [Col. 0224D] Jerome: “He speaks according to the custom of the province, in which this was the ancient Jews’ punishment for greater crimes: that the guilty person should be drowned in the deep with a stone bound to him.”].

For it is better to be killed than to kill, since the person who is killed is not thereby deprived of blessedness. We read that some holy martyrs were drowned in the depth of the sea with stones bound around their necks; nevertheless, we do not believe that they were deprived of that blessedness of which those are deprived who scandalize someone. It is better, therefore, for a person to be killed in body than to scandalize someone in faith.

“Woe to the world because of scandals.” Woe to those who stir up scandals, and to those who believe those who scandalize: woe to heretics and schismatics, and to those who follow their errors. “For scandals must come.” Hence the Apostle says: “There must be heresies, that those who are approved may be made manifest” (1 Cor. XI, 19).

What was woe to heretics and schismatics, then, was necessary and useful to Catholic men. For through this the Church’s faith shone forth more clearly, and those persons would have done far greater harm if they had always remained hidden. Thus scandals needed to come for the good. “Nevertheless, woe to that man through whom scandal comes.” Although many good things followed from this evil, woe nevertheless to the one through whom scandal came. For the evil person did not do evil so that good might come; and even if he had done so, he would have acted not for himself but against himself, like those of whom the Apostle says: “Let us do evil that good may come, whose condemnation is just” (Rom. III, 8).

“But if your hand or your foot scandalizes you, cut it off and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter life maimed or lame than, having two hands or two feet, to be cast into eternal fire.” What are we to understand by hand and foot except our friends and relatives [Note: [Col. 0225C] Hilary, chap. 4, no. 21: “We are admonished to cast off from ourselves—or rather to tear out—the ties of most dearly loved names, if we perceive anything of this sort in them, lest through familiar association we become partners in their crime.” Jerome on this passage: “If someone is joined to you as hand, foot, or eye, and is useful, diligent, and sharp in discernment, but causes you scandal and through a discordance of morals draws you to Gehenna, it is better to be deprived both of his kinship and of carnal advantages, lest, while you wish to gain relatives and dependents, you have cause for ruin. Therefore neither brother, nor wife, nor children, nor friends, nor any affection capable of excluding us from the kingdom of heaven, should be preferred to love for the Lord.”], whom we love as our own members and who are also necessary to us as hands and feet?

But if these scandalize us in faith and we perceive our souls to be perishing through their wicked manner of life, let us cut them off from ourselves and separate them from our fellowship. For there is nothing that we ought to love against the soul: not father, not mother, not brother, nor wife or children. It is better for us to enter life without them than to be led together with them into eternal punishments and death.

The same thing is also signified by the eye. For we are accustomed to say of people who take from us someone very dear and necessary: “He has torn out my eye; he has cut off my foot; he has taken away my hand.” Yet we do not say this literally, but by a certain likeness of the thing.

“See that you do not despise one of these little ones.” He speaks of those little ones who, humbling themselves from proud loftiness, willingly become little and small through patience and humility. Such persons are not to be despised, concerning whom he further says: “For I say to you that their angels in heaven always behold the face of my Father who is in heaven.” For of angels the Apostle says that they are ministering spirits, sent for service on account of those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation (Heb. I, 14). “For the Son of Man came to save what was lost.”

Therefore one should be greatly afraid of scandalizing or leading into error those for whom the Son of God, coming into the world and assuming flesh, humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death.

LXXV. “What do you think? If a man has a hundred sheep, and one of them goes astray, does he not leave the ninety-nine upon the mountains and go seek the one that has gone astray? And if it happens that he finds it, amen I say to you, he rejoices over it more than over the ninety-nine that did not go astray” [Note: [Col. 0225D] Vulgate: “leaves … goes … rejoices.”]. “Thus it is not the will before your Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish.”

Who is this man who has a hundred sheep, except he himself who speaks, Jesus Christ our Lord [Note: [Col. 0225D] Chrysologus, Sermon 168: “This is not an earthly shepherd, but a heavenly one. … The man who has a hundred sheep is Christ.” So also Hilary on this passage, Ambrose, book VII on Luke V, and others cited by Jerome on this passage.]? By the hundred sheep is understood the whole multitude of angels and human beings. For the hundredth sheep is man, who is often called by Moses not only a tenth, but even a tenth of a tenth [Note: [Col. 0226C] See Num. chap. XXVIII, vv. 13, 21, 29; chap. XXIX, [Col. 0226D] vv. 10, 15, etc.].

This sheep went astray when, transgressing God’s command, it ate the forbidden fruit. Therefore, for this one sheep, the Lord left the ninety-nine—that is, that whole multitude of angels—upon the other mountains of heaven [Note: [Col. 0226D] Ambrose, book VII on Luke, on chap. XV: “Thus the rich Shepherd, of whom all of us are the hundredth portion, has innumerable flocks of Angels, Dominions, Powers, Thrones, and others, whom he left upon the mountains.” See Jerome.] and came to seek this one which had gone astray. Once it was found and redeemed by Christ’s blood, there was such exultation in heaven over it as there had not previously been over all the rest.

This did not occur because this one is loved more than the others, but because no other returned from the danger of death to life, in which the others could have displayed the joy of their love. Although the number of the faithful is believed to be added to the number of angels, man nevertheless was like one sheep among a hundred when there was only one man with his wife and no more.
