This one went astray; for this one Christ descended from heaven [Note: [Col. 0226D] Hilary: “In order to show that there is immense joy in heaven at the return of human salvation, he presented an example by comparison, etc. In the error of the one Adam the whole human race went astray; therefore the ninety-nine that did not go astray must be understood as the multitude of heavenly angels. … Christ is the seeker of man, and the ninety-nine left behind are the multitude of heavenly glory, to which the wandering man has been restored in the Lord’s body with the greatest joy.”].

LXXVI. [Note: [Col. 0226D] On this passage. See Sermon 82 of St Augustine.] “But if your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between yourself and him alone. If he listens to you, you will have gained your brother.”

That the Lord said this especially to the apostles and their successors—namely, bishops and priests—may chiefly be understood from what he himself says immediately afterwards: [Col. 0226C] “Amen I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be [p. 90] loosed also in heaven.” Hence it is rightly said: “If your brother sins against you.” For he sins against a shepherd who afflicts the sheep; he sins against a bishop who injures the people entrusted to him. It belongs to these persons to rebuke; it belongs to them to excommunicate and drive out of the Church. And the Lord himself has taught us the order in which we must do this, saying: “Go, and rebuke him between yourself and him alone.” For if we do this, there is no reason why our brother should deservedly be offended, especially when, [Col. 0227A] in urging what is good, we speak the truth to him.

[Note: [Col. 0226D] Jerome: “A brother must be rebuked apart, lest, if he has once lost shame and modesty, he remain in sin.” Bede: “He therefore indicates in what order we may avoid offences: if we take heed that we ourselves injure no one; if we rebuke the sinner out of zeal for justice; if we open from the heart the inward bowels of mercy and compassion to one who repents.”]

If he listens to us, by our humble address he will be reconciled to the Lord. But if he does not listen, “take with you yet one or two, that every word may stand in the mouth of two or three witnesses.” The Lord commands that only a few more be brought in, lest the person being corrected, offended by the rebuke of many, become worse. Yet these are sufficient for testimony if he should ever wish to proceed against a bishop or priest, whether alleging an unjust summons or claiming that he did not answer them as is said.

“But if he does not listen to them, tell it to the Church,” so that he may at least blush before the rebuke of all, since he refused to make satisfaction at the humble address of a few. Hence the Apostle says: “Sufficient for such a one is this rebuke which is by many. But if he does not listen to the Church, let him be [Col. 0227B] to you as a Gentile and a publican” (I Cor. XI, 6): that is, excommunicated and separated from the Church. Let no individual member of the Church communicate with one who refused to believe the Church and scorned to obey her counsels; and let the rest, hearing this, fear and let many be corrected by the example of one.

“Amen I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.” Let bishops hear this and observe this order of binding and loosing:

[Note: [Col. 0227D] Hilary: “The Lord has imposed upon us the order of preserving charity which he himself observed in preserving Israel.” See the remainder in the same author.]

First, let them approach sinners individually, either personally or through another; then with a few; afterwards with the whole Church. If they scorn to listen to the Church, then let them not hesitate to bind them. For those who are so bound are bound both in heaven and on earth.

“Again I say to you: if two [Col. 0227C] of you agree on earth concerning anything whatsoever which they ask, it shall be done for them by my Father who is in heaven. For where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.” How we ought to understand his words, “concerning anything whatsoever,” is defined by the phrase, “in my name.” Those who are gathered in his name, and in whose midst he is, cannot make an evil request; that is, he presides in their hearts, for he is there in order to govern their hearts, direct their counsels, order their requests, and make them agree with one another in what is good.

This seems applicable to what is said elsewhere: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John XVI, 23). For [Col. 0227D] those agree with one another in good, are gathered and ask in the name of Jesus, who seek those things which belong to salvation. For what is sought in the name of the Saviour except salvation?

[Note: [Col. 0227D] St Augustine, Tractate 73 on John, no. 3: “Jesus signifies Saviour … and therefore, whatever we ask contrary to the usefulness of salvation, we do not ask in the name of the Saviour.” Likewise Tractate 102, no. 1. And, apparently from Augustine, Gregory, Homily 27 on the Gospels: “But because the name of the Son is Jesus, and Jesus means Saviour, or also Saving One, he asks in the name of the Saviour who asks what pertains to true salvation. For if that which is not expedient is asked, the Father is not asked in the name of Jesus.”]

[Col. 0228A] For Jesus is interpreted “Saviour.” Whoever therefore does not ask for salvation, even though he invokes Jesus, does not ask in the name of Jesus, because he does not ask for that which “Jesus” means. Let it therefore be said: if two of you agree on earth concerning anything whatever which they ask with faith and without hesitation in my name, it shall be done for them. Why is this so? Because where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them.

But if two or three who agree in good and ask in Christ’s name are thus heard, how much more will God hear many, how much more the whole Church? But you say: What if they ask in the name of Jesus for the salvation of those who are condemned? Are they heard? For the Church prays daily for Jews, schismatics, and heretics, and is not heard. The [Col. 0228B] Lord also prayed for the Jews, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.” Thus saints pray for the salvation of many and are not heard.

This too must therefore be qualified, so that it may be said: If two of you agree on earth in good concerning anything whatever which they ask in my name, provided that it be such as accords with God’s order and disposition, it shall be done for them by my Father who is in heaven. Otherwise they are not heard, even though they agree with one another and ask in Jesus’ name. Whenever therefore we pray and are not heard, this happens either because we do not ask in Jesus’ name, or because we ask contrary to his order and disposition. For he knows whom he has chosen; he knows what we need before we ask.

Then Peter came to him and said: “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me [Col. 0228C] and I forgive him? Up to seven times?” Jesus said to him: “I do not say to you, up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.”

This is as though he said: As often as he sins, so often forgive.

[Note: [Col. 0228D] St Augustine, Sermon 83, no. 7: “For he meant all sins when he said seventy times seven … therefore he wished all sins to be forgiven, who prefigured them by the number seventy-seven.” See also Sermon 114, where he explains the same and the whole passage more fully.]

If seven times, forgive seven times; if ten times, ten times; if a hundred times, a hundred times; if a thousand times, a thousand times—so that he cannot sin against you more than you can forgive him. Otherwise you too will not be forgiven. Hence he said above: “Unless you forgive people their sins, neither will your Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. VI, 15).

But blessed Peter thought it sufficient for himself if he forgave seven times, because the scribes and Pharisees, expounding but not understanding the Law and the Prophets, greatly commended this number in their discourses.

[Note: [Col. 0228D] On this Gospel passage concerning the number seven, see Chrysologus, Sermon 137, besides Origen, Book XIII on Matthew; Ambrose, Book VIII on Luke, II.23; Augustine; and others.]

They thought it could suffice for satisfaction and amendment. Hence they eat unleavened bread for seven days; hence, when the leper is cleansed, and when a man suffers a flow of semen, [Col. 0229A] he is separated for seven days. A menstruating woman is likewise separated for seven days; similarly, when she gave birth, she was unclean for seven days. Naaman too, at Elisha’s command, immersed himself seven times in the Jordan; and the priest, offering sacrifice, dips his finger in blood and sprinkles it seven times before the Lord. The Psalmist likewise says: “Seven times a day I have spoken praise to you.”

For these reasons, and many others which the Jews understood literally about this number, blessed Peter said, “up to seven times.” But the teacher of the Law and the Prophets, understanding all things more deeply, added to this, “up to seventy times seven.” Nevertheless, if “seven times” is rightly understood, it is no less than “seventy times seven.” On this we have spoken sufficiently in Leviticus.

[Note: [Col. 0229D] On chapter 4 of the Roman edition, p. 132, and on chapter 14, p. 153.]

LXXVII. “Therefore the kingdom of heaven has been likened to a man, a king, who wished to settle accounts with his servants. And when he began to settle accounts, one was brought before him who owed him ten thousand talents.”

This king is he who speaks, God and man, Jesus Christ our Lord. He settles accounts daily with his servants:

[Note: [Col. 0229D] Origen discusses at length the time here indicated for rendering an account, vol. I of Huet’s Origen, p. 350, and vol. III of the MM edition, p. 630. There, p. 343 and MM, p. 622: “Who can be called the king except the Son of God, etc.?”]

For through bishops and priests he judges human sins, when each person who comes to repentance confesses to the Lord how much he owes and in what matters he has sinned. But who is the one who owed ten thousand talents, except all those who sin more than others in every respect?

But why did the Lord first wish to settle accounts with this man, except that by his example the others might understand what they ought to answer in their own reckonings [Col. 0229C] and how great a hope they might have? For if the Lord forgave the whole debt of one who owed more than all others because he humbled himself, how much more will he forgive all sins to others who have not sinned so much, if they repent worthily?

He set down ten thousand talents because no debt is greater than this debt. All numbers are contained in this number, because it is multiplied from the number ten; and every part of it is so complete that it can indeed be repeated but cannot be increased.

[Note: [Col. 0229D] See St Augustine, Sermon 51, no. 34, and Sermon [Col. 0230D] 231, no. 6; Book II of the Questions to Januarius, Epistle 55, no. 28; etc.]

For when we count up to ten, unless we begin again from one, we have nothing more to say. The same occurs when we reach one hundred, and likewise when we reach one thousand, and likewise when [Col. 0229D] we reach ten thousand; for ten times ten make one hundred, ten times one hundred make one thousand, and ten times one thousand make ten thousand. Therefore there is no debt greater than this debt.

But let us see what follows. “And when he had nothing with which to repay, his lord commanded him to be sold, and his wife and children, and all that he had, and payment to be made.” For when a sinner comes to repentance, [Col. 0230A] he does not at first have the means to pay the debt, until, completely humbled, he promises to obey in all things according to the counsel of the priests.

Therefore priests say to him: Unless you pay the debt and do penance, you and your wife, your children, and all that you possess will perish eternally. By this it is understood that he himself, wholly carnal, together with his soul and all the senses of his body, will be delivered to eternal fires. For one who is tormented with all these has rest in no part of himself. But if, hearing this, he trembles and promises from the heart to make satisfaction and obey, what follows will happen to him.

“But that servant fell down and begged him, saying: Have patience with me, and I will repay you all. And the lord of that servant, moved with compassion, released him and forgave him the [Col. 0230B] debt.” Behold, your debt has been forgiven. Take care to persevere in good. You too must forgive your debtors, just as your debt has been forgiven to you. But if you refuse to do this, hear and await what follows:

“But that servant went out and found one of his fellow servants, who owed him a hundred denarii. Seizing him, he choked him, saying: Pay what you owe.” A debt of a hundred denarii is very small [p. 92] compared with ten thousand talents. He is therefore most foolish who does not wish to forgive one hundred denarii, on the condition that ten thousand talents are forgiven him.

“And his fellow servant fell down and begged him, saying: Have patience with me, and I will repay you all. But he would not; rather, he went and put him in prison until he should repay the debt.” Perhaps this man did not hear; [Col. 0230C] or, if he heard, he did not understand; or, if he understood, he disregarded through contempt what the Lord says elsewhere: “For with the same measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” (Luke VI, 38).

“When his fellow servants saw what had happened, they were greatly distressed, and came and reported to their lord all that had been done.” These fellow servants are understood to be both angels and human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0230D] See Origen, in the place cited, who denies that it is possible to explain who these fellow servants should be understood to be. Theophylact, however: “These fellow servants seem to be angels, haters of evil and lovers of good.” See Augustine, Questions on Matthew.]

For all are fellow servants who are servants of one Lord. These report to the Lord the oppression of the wicked and the affliction of the miserable, because they continually cry to God on their behalf.

“Then his lord called him and said to him: Wicked servant, I forgave you all your debt because you begged me. Ought you not therefore also to have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had mercy on you? [Col. 0230D] And his lord, angered, delivered him to the torturers until he should repay the whole debt.”

These torturers are evil spirits:

[Note: [Col. 0230D] Origen, there: “Who are these, except those to whom the charge of punishments has been assigned?”]

To them the miserable man is handed over for punishment, and he is not rescued from their power until he repays the entire debt. Therefore he is never rescued from their power, because this debt is always being paid, yet is never fully discharged.

[Col. 0231A] The Lord immediately explains why he set forth this whole parable, saying: “So also will my heavenly Father do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts.” Notice that he says, “from your hearts”; for it is not enough to forgive with the lips unless the [Col. 0232A] hearts also agree.

[CHAPTER XIX.] “And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these sayings, that he departed from Galilee and came into the borders of Judaea beyond the Jordan. And great crowds followed him, and he healed them there.”

## PART FOUR

[Col. 0231]

LXXVIII. “And Pharisees came to him, testing him and saying: Is it lawful for a man to put away his wife for any cause?”

What he says, “for any cause,” is as if he said, “for some cause,” not, as it seems to sound, “for every cause.”

[Note: [Col. 0231D] Jerome seems opposed: “They ask him whether it is lawful for a man to put away his wife for any cause”; and Origen, vol. I of Huet’s revised edition, p. 355, κατὰ πᾶσαν αἰτίαν, “for every cause.” On this entire passage of Matthew, see at length Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 36; Ambrose, Book VIII on Luke; Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*; also Irenaeus, Book IV, ch. 15, and Chrysostom, Homily 10 against the Anomoeans.]

He answered them: “Have you not read that he who made [Col. 0231B] mankind from the beginning made them male and female? And he said: For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and shall cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined, let no human being separate.”

God is the one who speaks and says that husband and wife are one flesh. Although they are personally two, yet because both are from one flesh, they ought so to love one another, to be joined by the bond of charity, and never to separate from one another, as if they were wholly not two but one flesh.

They say to him: “Why then did Moses command a certificate of divorce to be given and her to be put away?” If, they say, they are one flesh, if they are inseparable and ought to be joined by so great a bond of love, why did Moses command that they be put away?

He said to them: “Because of the hardness of your hearts Moses permitted [Col. 0231C] you to put away your wives; but from the beginning it was not so.” How was it not so? That a man should put away his wife for any cause. But Moses says that one who puts away his wife because of some disgraceful matter should give her a certificate of divorce.

But Moses—or rather, the Lord through Moses—speaks in one way here and another way there. For this wife who is put away because of some disgraceful matter signifies any heresy whatsoever. She ought to be put away not by mere words, but by a written document, oath, and firm stipulation, so that the man who puts her away may not return to her thereafter.

Therefore the Jews were permitted to understand and observe literally that which ought to be understood spiritually, but this was because of the hardness [p. 93] [Col. 0231D] of their hearts: namely, lest they kill their wives or afflict them excessively when they hated them because of some disgraceful matter.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] Jerome says the same on this passage.]

We have spoken sufficiently concerning these matters in Deuteronomy.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] On chapter 24 of the Roman edition, p. 208.]

“But I say to you that whoever puts away his wife [Col. 0232A] except on account of fornication and marries another commits adultery.” We have expounded this above in this same book.

His disciples say to him: “If the case of a man with his wife is thus, it is not expedient to marry.” That is, if they are joined by such a bond and must preserve this fidelity to one another, it is not expedient either to marry or to take a [Col. 0232B] wife.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] Bernard excellently says in *On Precept and Dispensation*, “These are truly great straits: if he keeps a wife he hates, nothing is more burdensome; if he puts away one unwilling to leave, nothing is more unchristian.”]

Likewise the Apostle says: “Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife”; and again: “I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain thus, as I also do. But if they cannot exercise self-control, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn” (I Cor. VII, 27).

And the Lord said: “Not all receive this word, but those to whom it is given.” This word, he says, which you speak—namely, that it is not expedient to marry—this commandment of chastity and continence is not received, kept, or accepted by all, but only by those to whom it has been given by God.

“For there are eunuchs who were born so from their mother’s womb.” These are, namely, those of cold temperament who endure the stirrings of the flesh very easily. “And there are eunuchs who were made by men.” By these we understand not only those whose testicles were crushed, but also [Col. 0232C] those whom the most careful supervision of their superiors makes celibate, even unwillingly. “And there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven.” These are better than the rest: they are made so not by iron, but by mortification of the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0232D] See Epiphanius, Heresy 58.]

“He who can receive this, let him receive it.” Let him who can keep continence keep it; but let him who cannot, marry whom he wishes, only in the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0232D] Jerome on this passage: “Let each person consider his own strength, whether he can fulfil the commands of virginity and chastity. For chastity is attractive in itself and draws anyone to itself. But one’s strength must be considered, so that he who can receive it may receive it. It is as though the Lord were exhorting and stirring up his soldiers to the reward of chastity: ‘He who can receive it, let him receive it’; he who can fight, let him fight, conquer, and triumph.”]

But this permission is not given to those who have vowed chastity or undertaken an order of stricter religious life.

LXXIX. “Then little children were brought to him, that he might lay hands on them and pray”; that is, that he might touch and bless them. But the disciples rebuked them.

For the disciples were still carnal and [Col. 0232D] represented those who think carnally. There are many in the Church who think that they please God by attempting to remove little and simple people from his governance, wishing to choose the powerful and shrewd, so that the Church may grow temporally through their strength [Col. 0233A] and prudence. They do not attend to the fact that “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.”

But let us see what follows. Jesus said to them: “Allow the little children, and do not forbid them to come to me; for of such is the kingdom of heaven.” Choose such persons, he says; do not forbid such persons; establish such persons in the Church; and lay hands on such persons. “And when he had laid hands on them, he departed from there.”

The laying on of hands is spoken of in many ways:

[Note: [Col. 0233D] See Morinus, *On the Sacrament of Ordination*, Exercise V, ch. 11, no. 9; Albaspinaeus, Book II of *Observations*, ch. 31; Habert, *Observations on the Greek Pontifical*, no. 2 on Part VIII; etc.]

Here, however, it signifies consecration, of which the Apostle says: “Lay hands suddenly on no man” (I Tim. V, 22).

LXXX. “And behold, one came to him and said: Good Master, what good thing shall I do that I may have eternal life?” He said to him: “Why do you ask me concerning the good? One is good, [Col. 0233B] God.”

What then is meant by the statement: “God saw all that he had made, and behold, it was very good”? For if God made all things, and everything that he made is not only good but very good, how is God alone and the only good?

[Note: [Col. 0233D] Ambrose, Book VIII on Luke, no. 65: “By adding ‘good Master,’ he called him good in part, not in universality; for God is good universally, a human being in part … For what is good except that which is full of goodness?”]

He alone is good by nature, because he is good through himself and not from another. All other things, however, are not good from themselves but from him by whom they were created good in the beginning.

[Note: [Col. 0233D] Here begins Homily 4, published under the name of Emisenus, *On the Nativity of the Apostles*, which includes this and the following section.]

“But if you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.” He says to him: “Which?” Jesus said: “You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; honour your father and mother; and love your neighbour as yourself.” The young man says to him: “I have kept all these from my youth. What do I still lack?”

For, as the Apostle says, love is the fulfilment [Col. 0233C] of the Law. Either this man did not rightly understand, “Love your neighbour as yourself,” or, if he understood it, he did not answer correctly.

[Note: [Col. 0233D] “The young man lies,” says Jerome here. “For if he had fulfilled in deed the commandment, ‘Love your neighbour,’ etc., how could he afterwards have gone away sorrowful?” etc.]

For what can be lacking to one who keeps the whole Law? He thought, it seems, that he loved his neighbour well because he did not kill him, take away his goods, or inflict other injuries upon him. Therefore the Lord, adding how he ought to understand this, says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; then come and follow me.”

This is the true measure [p. 94] of perfection: the person who observes these things fulfils the Law. He does not fail in love of God who follows Christ, nor in love of neighbour who gives everything generously to those in need. Yet let no one despair to whom it is not granted to attain this perfection. Many are saved who neither leave everything nor give everything to the poor [Col. 0234A]; nevertheless, they do not attain the summit of perfection.

“But when the young man heard the saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had many possessions.” Behold how he was shown to be young: he was good because he did no harm to others, but he was not good because he gave no help to others. He knew neither how to distribute his own goods nor how to seize another’s. He was speaking with God, who showed him true riches; nevertheless, he placed more hope in earthly possession than in the promise of heavenly treasure.

Of such persons the Apostle says: “Command the rich of this world not to hope in the uncertainty of riches” (I Tim. VI, 17). For it is one thing to be rich; another to place one’s hope in riches. Those who place their hope in riches can be saved only with great difficulty.

[Note: [Col. 0234D] St Augustine, *Questions on the Gospels*, Book II, ch. 47: “Here he calls rich the person greedy for temporal things and proud of such things.”]

Hence the Lord adds: “Amen [Col. 0234B] I say to you that a rich person shall enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty. And again I say to you: It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven.”

First he said “with difficulty,” then “impossible.” For it is impossible that rich persons who place their hope in riches should enter the kingdom of heaven; it is of them that this is understood. For Mark the Evangelist reports that the Lord said: “Children, how difficult it is for those who trust in money to enter the kingdom of God!”

[Note: [Col. 0234D] Ch. 10, 24. Jerome: “Because riches are abandoned with difficulty, he did not say, ‘It is impossible for rich persons to enter the kingdom of heaven,’ but ‘difficult.’ Where ‘difficult’ is used, impossibility is not asserted, but rarity is shown.”]

But by the camel, whose sole and peculiar office is to bear burdens, what are we to understand except those weighed down by the burden of sins? The Psalmist counts himself among them, saying: “For my iniquities have gone over my head; as a heavy burden they have weighed me down” (Ps. XXXVI, 5).

[Col. 0234C] And what does he say of rich persons? “Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but trusted in the multitude of his riches and prevailed in his vanity” (Ps. LI, 9). It is therefore easier for a camel—that is, for someone who is a very great sinner—to pass through the eye of a needle, that is, through the narrow and confined way which leads to life, than for such a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0234D] Jerome again: “We shall see how even these camels, to whom rich persons are compared, when they have laid down the heavy burden of sins and the weight of the whole body, can enter through the narrow gate and the confined way which leads to life.”]

For the former can more easily be separated from sins than the latter from hope in riches. When they heard this, the disciples were greatly astonished, saying: “Who then can be saved?” They would not have said this if they had understood the kind of rich person about whom the Lord was speaking.

But Jesus, looking at them, said: “With human beings this is impossible; but with God all things are possible.” What he says, “with human beings,” means according to human understanding; but what he says, “with God,” means according to [Col. 0235A] spiritual and divine understanding. For it is not impossible for God to turn any rich person whatsoever to the way of his will.

[Note: [Col. 0235D] See St Augustine, Letter to Hilary, Question 4, and Letter to Proba, ch. 1.]

Yet it is very difficult for someone who has always been rich to be willing to become poor. If, therefore, this is understood literally, it is impossible; but spiritually, as we have just expounded it, it is not impossible. Literally, indeed, it is impossible for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle; but according to spiritual understanding it is not impossible.

LXXXI. Then Peter answered and said to him: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you. What then shall there be for us?”

That rich man, he says, of whom you spoke above, was unwilling either to leave all things or to follow you; we also heard what answer you gave him. But what do you say of us [Col. 0235B] who have left all things and followed you?

Peter had left all things, because he had left not only what he possessed but also what he could have possessed, in order that thereafter he might possess nothing of his own in this world and desire to possess nothing.

[Note: [Col. 0235D] St Augustine on Psalm CIII: “He left not only whatever he had, but also whatever he desired to have.”]

Hence he himself also admonishes us, saying: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (I John XI, 15). The will to possess is indeed greater than leaving behind what one actually possesses.

But Jesus said to them: “Amen I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

Peter had put forward two things, but Christ took up only one. He did not say, “You who have left [Col. 0235C] all things.” But what did he say? “You who have followed me.”

[Note: [Col. 0235D] See Jerome on this passage.]

For whoever follows Jesus perfectly leaves all things. It was sufficient, therefore, to mention one, because both were contained in one. “You,” he says, “who have followed me; who walk with me in the same way; who hasten toward heavenly things; who despise all earthly things; who love justice and truth, peace and mercy—you shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

Certainly the apostles will sit upon twelve thrones; but others also will sit upon their own thrones, those who lived by the apostles’ example [p. 95] [Col. 0235D] and followed Christ the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0235D] Bede here: “Since universality is often signified by the number twelve, the twelve thrones of the judging apostles show the multitude of all, and the twelve tribes of Israel show all those who are to be judged.” Augustine develops the same point more fully [Col. 0236D] on Psalm XLIX.]

For there are more than twelve thrones there, and more judges will be there. Not only bishops and priests will judge there, but also, as was said above, the Queen of the South and the Ninevites will rise in judgment with this generation and condemn it.

But what are these thrones upon which these judges sit? These thrones are the individual churches. Hence bishops customarily call the churches over which they preside [Col. 0236A] their “sees.” Each, therefore, will sit in his own see, because each will appear greater and more exalted among the people whom he governed and preached to. The Lord too will sit on the throne of his majesty, because the Lord, exalted above all nations, will preside over all angels and human beings.

Therefore the Lord will judge; the apostles will judge; moreover bishops and priests will judge; and all those by whose example others are condemned will judge there.

“And everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands for my name’s sake, shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life.” But the other evangelists say: “He shall receive a hundredfold in this life; after this life, eternal life.” Mark [Col. 0236B] adds:

[Note: [Col. 0236D] Ch. X, 29–30: “No one has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or children, or lands for my sake and for the Gospel, who shall not receive a hundredfold now in this present time—houses, and brothers, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and lands—with persecutions; and in the world to come, eternal life.”]

“with persecutions.” For the saints receive a hundredfold with persecutions in this life, because all who love God and do his will become brothers and sisters, fathers and mothers, friends and relatives of the saints. Thus the Lord says of himself: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. XII, 31).

Those called brothers and sisters, fathers and mothers, wives and children are so called not by nature, but by office and affection; for we customarily call by these names those whom we love greatly.

LXXXII. “But many who are first will be last, and the last first.” [Note: [Col. 0236D] This section and the following one contain the homily of the Emesene preacher for Septuagesima, that is, of St Bruno.]

The following words will show for what purpose he introduced this proposition; for the entire ensuing parable pertains to it. Hence it is also said in the conclusion: “Thus the last shall be first, and the first last.” If this is understood of the ages of the world, I do not see how the first are last, or the last first. For the patriarchs and prophets, and the rest of those of the former Testament, predestined to life, were first; but we are last. Of us John says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18); and the Apostle: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11). And just as they were first in time, so they were also the first to receive the denarius. For Christ the Lord, delivering them from punishments immediately after his Passion, brought them into glory. The Apostle likewise says: “For we who are alive, who remain, shall not precede [Col. 0236D] those who have fallen asleep; because the Lord himself, at the command, at the voice of the archangel, and at the trumpet of God, shall descend from heaven, and the dead who are in Christ shall rise first. Then we who are alive, who are left, shall together be caught up with them in the clouds to meet the Lord” (1 Thess. 4:14–16). How, then, are the last first?

But now let us hear the parable itself. [CHAPTER 20.] “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire labourers for his vineyard.” This is as though he said: Thus it comes about in the kingdom of heaven, as it came about in the householder’s vineyard, into which he went out early in the morning and hired labourers. The kingdom of heaven is the Church; the householder is Christ our Lord. For his household consists both of angels and human beings; it is indeed a great household, because the householder too is great.

This householder came to hire labourers for his vineyard. “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel”; the vineyard is God’s Church. Whoever labours outside it receives no reward; whoever labours in it receives the denarius. For that denarius [Col. 0237B] is the recompense of eternal blessedness; therefore one denarius is given to all: one to the first and one to the last. Some begin to labour early in the morning; others about the third hour; others about the sixth and ninth hour; and others again about the eleventh hour.

For this is what he says: “After agreeing with the labourers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard. And going out about the third hour, he saw others standing idle in the marketplace, and said to them: Go yourselves also into my vineyard, and I will give you whatever is just. And they went. Again he went out about the sixth and ninth hour, and did likewise. But about the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing idle in the marketplace, and said to them: Why do you stand here idle all day? They say to him: Because no one has hired us. He said [Col. 0237C] to them: Go yourselves also into my vineyard.”

Those begin to labour in God’s vineyard early in the morning who, from their earliest age—that is, from childhood—serve the Lord in God’s Church. [Note: [Col. 0237D] Jerome, on this passage, gives two explanations: the first, concerning the ages of a human being, which is our author’s; Chrysostom, Homily 65, etc.; and the other, concerning the ages of the world, which is that of St Augustine, Sermon 59, *On the Words of the Lord*, Ambrose, Book VII on Luke, Bede, etc. Gregory [Col. 0238D], Homily 19 on the Gospels, has both.] But those come to labour about the third hour who begin to serve in adolescence; and those come about the sixth and ninth hour who are converted to repentance either in youth or in old age. The eleventh hour is that which, at any age, approaches the end and is near to death. Not only the young and the old have this hour, but children too. At this hour, therefore, both the person who in decrepit old age and the person who in grave illness turns to the Lord with all the heart begin to labour.

Thus there is no place for despair, no room left [Col. 0237D] for excuse; since at every age and every hour the sinner is received. “For at whatever hour the sinner is converted and groans, he shall live and shall not die.” [Note: [Col. 0238D] See Ezekiel, chapter 23.] Let him therefore be converted even at the eleventh hour; let him be converted even at the very end of life, who previously was idle in good and diligent in evil. For if he wishes and is converted, even if he begins to labour only for an hour, he too will receive the reward and the denarius together with the others.

Hence it continues: “And when evening had come, the lord [Col. 0238A] of the vineyard said to his steward: Call the labourers and pay them their wages, beginning from the last even to the first.” Evening comes for each person when he ends his final day with life. But God’s stewards are the angels, who present the souls of the saints to God and lead them into rest. Of them the Apostle says: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Heb. 1:14).

It often happens that those who came later receive the denarius and reward first, because it frequently occurs that those who begin to labour and serve God later depart this life first. For the first to receive the denarius is the first to depart this life. Many saints departed this world through martyrdom on the very day on which they believed. Thus, labouring in God’s vineyard during one and the last hour, they received the denarius before those who, serving the Lord from their earliest age and departing this world after them, received the denarius after them, just as they had begun labouring before them.

Therefore, sometimes—though not always—in God’s Church there occurs what is said to have occurred in the householder’s vineyard: namely, that the first are last and the last first. Because this does not always happen, the Lord says at the beginning of this comparison: “But many shall be first who are last, and last who are first.” For if it always happened, he would have said not “many” but “all.” Thus many who are last are honoured also in receiving the reward, and are not diminished in worth.

Hence the others, murmuring, say: “These last have worked one hour [Col. 0238C], and you have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden and heat of the day.” The Lord quite rightly rebukes them when he replies to one of them: “Friend, I do you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what is yours and go. But I wish to give to this last one as to you also. Or is your eye evil because I am good?”

These things are not said in order that we should understand the saints to murmur at the prosperity of others, or to have evil [Note: [Col. 0238D] See Chrysostom and Gregory in the places cited. See also Augustine, *On Calling*, Book I, chapter 7.] and envious eyes; but rather that we may understand how great the evil of murmuring and envy is, and guard against it. For it is a great fault, so severely rebuked by the Lord. All who receive this denarius are holy and good; and both the first and the last receive it. Thus both [Col. 0238D] the first and the last are good. How then can they murmur? How can they have evil and envious eyes? Such, therefore, they are not; and lest they become such, they are warned by the example of those others.

For it is good to labour in this vineyard, but evil to murmur. Let us therefore labour and not murmur; let their rebuke be our correction. One group invites us to good; the other dissuades us from evil. Their labour and reward invite us, while the rebuke of their murmuring restrains us from murmuring. [Col. 0239A] Therefore in both cases the Lord gives us counsel: in the one he exhorts us to labour, in the other he dissuades us from murmuring.

What follows—“For many are called, but few are chosen”—shows that very few are saved in comparison with those who are called at the several hours. [Note: [Col. 0238D] The question of the number of adult Christians who are saved has again been raised in our age. This passage of our author, which seems to speak of adult believers, may perhaps be added to the other testimonies collected by the distinguished author of the book published at Rome in 1752, *PP. Ec. On the Agreement concerning the Fewness of Adult Believers to Be Saved*.] Both the first and the last, therefore, receive the denarius; but not all the first, nor all the last. For many are called and invited to labour in the vineyard who are counted neither among the first nor among the last.

LXXXIII. “And as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took his twelve disciples aside privately and said to them: Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man shall be delivered to the chief priests and scribes; and they shall condemn him to death, and shall deliver him to the Gentiles to be mocked, scourged, and crucified; and on the third day he shall rise again.”

In these few words the Lord foretold the whole sequence of his Passion, so that we may understand that he came to the Passion of his own will. [Note: [Col. 0239D] So also Chrysostom, Homily 66: “That afterwards, remembering, they might believe that he underwent the Passion willingly, not in ignorance nor under compulsion.”]

Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came to him with her sons, worshipping him and asking something of him. This woman was devout and familiar with Christ; therefore she asked for a great thing and approached the Lord confidently. For she had very high expectations of Christ when she prayed for her sons what the sons themselves were afraid to ask for on their own. [Note: [Col. 0239D] “Overcome by shame, they took up the advocacy of their mother,” says Chrysostom there.]

But what does she say? “Command that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom.” The mother speaks ambitiously and, through carnal affection, seeks the chief seats in heaven for her ambitious sons. Hence they are rightly told by the Lord: “You do not know what you ask.” It is fitting neither to ask for nor to grant the chief seats in that manner. “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” They say to him: “We can.”

The Lord speaks obscurely to them, and perhaps they did not yet understand of what cup he spoke. For he spoke of the cup of the Passion, concerning which he says elsewhere to the apostle Peter: “The cup which the Father has given me, do you not wish me to drink it?” (John 18:11). And the Psalmist says: “I will receive the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115:13).

And he said to them: “Indeed, you shall drink my cup.” For James and John drank Christ’s cup, not because both ended their lives in martyrdom, but because both endured many persecutions, distresses, [Col. 0239D] and tribulations. Herod killed James, as it is written: “He killed James, the brother of John, with the sword” (Acts [Col. 0240A] 12:2). John, however, was not killed, but was cast into a vat of boiling oil and banished into exile on the island of Patmos; he drank the cup of great affliction and bitterness. [Note: [Col. 0239D] All this appears to derive from Jerome on this passage, where he also speaks of the vat of boiling oil and the banishment to [Col. 0240D] the island of Patmos. Whoever considers these things, he says, will see “that his spirit did not lack martyrdom, and that John drank the cup of confession.”]

“But to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to give to you, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.” It is as if he said: What you now ask has already been given; it is not mine to give now. It does not belong to me now to ordain and determine who ought to sit at my right hand or at my left in my kingdom. This disposition is not of man, nor of this time; what you now ask to be done was done from eternity. Together with the Father, before the ages, I disposed it; nor have I to dispose anew what seat each person is to receive.

Therefore, for those for whom it has been prepared to sit at my right hand or [Col. 0240B] at my left—whether for you or for others—it shall be theirs. What has been prepared and ordained cannot be changed. [Note: [Col. 0240D] Chrysostom, in the place cited, expounded this Gospel passage exceedingly well and wonderfully.]

“And when the ten heard it, they were indignant at the two brothers.” For they too were still carnal and no less ambitious than the others; therefore they were indignant and begrudged others what each desired for himself. [Note: [Col. 0240D] Chrysostom says likewise: “You see how all were still imperfect: the two were trying to seize the first seat against the ten, and the ten, envying the two, were indignant.”]

But Jesus called them to himself and said: “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who are great exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you. But whoever wishes to become great among you shall be your minister; and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your servant.”

“It shall not be so among you,” he says, as it is among the powers of this world, so that the one who appears greater than the rest rules over the rest. Rather, he who wishes to be more exalted shall be lower than all; and he who humbles himself more shall be established greater by God. He demonstrates this by his own example, saying: “Just as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

Just as the Son of Man humbled himself, he says, so let the person who wishes to be greater humble himself. “Though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. 2:6). And, as a servant and minister, he did not disdain to wash the feet of his disciples. [Note: [Col. 0240D] Chrysostom rightly warns here: “Do not therefore fear that by humility you will lose, as it were, your honour; for you can never display as much humility as the Lord undertook for you.”]

LXXXIV. “And as they were going out from Jericho, a great crowd followed him. And behold, two blind men sitting by the road heard that Jesus was passing by, and cried out [Col. 0241A], saying: Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David.”

In some places the blessed evangelist Matthew is found to give attention not so much to the narrative as to its meaning; hence he says that there were two blind men, whereas the other evangelists relate that there was one. Mark also says that this blind man was [Note: [Col. 0241C] Chapter 10:46: “The son of Timaeus, blind Bartimaeus, was sitting beside the road begging.”] the son of Timaeus.

Likewise, in the region of the Gerasenes, he says that Christ our Lord freed two men from a legion of demons and sent the demons into swine, while the others write of only one, not two. [Note: [Col. 0241D] St Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, Book II, chapter 65: “This question is resolved in the same way as that concerning the two who suffered from the legion of demons in the region of the Gerasenes. For that one of the two blind men whom he has just mentioned was especially well known and famous in that city is also apparent from the fact that Mark records both his name and his father’s name. . . . Beyond doubt, therefore, this Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus, having been cast down from some great prosperity, was a case of most well-known and famous misery, since he was not only blind but also sat begging.”]

He also writes that, when Jesus came to Jerusalem, he sat upon a donkey and a colt, whereas the other evangelists say that only the colt was brought to him. It is therefore clear that Matthew attends not so much to the event itself as to its meaning. This blind man [Col. 0241B] is one in himself, but two in meaning: in meaning, because he signifies two peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles. [Note: [Col. 0241D] Jerome: “He calls blind those who were not yet able to see . . . beside the road, because they seemed indeed to have knowledge of the Law, but did not know the way which is Christ. Many understand them as Pharisees and Sadducees; others, however, as both peoples, of the Old Testament and the New: the one following the written law, the other the natural law, and both blind without Christ.” Bede copied these words of Jerome and the foregoing words of Augustine; [Col. 0242C] Jerome, in the *Epitaph of Paula*, and Augustine, Sermon 88, *On the Words of the Gospel*, Matthew 10, interpret the two peoples more explicitly.]

The Lord enlightened them when he approached Jericho—that is, when he assumed the mutability of our flesh. For Jericho is interpreted “moon,” which is so mutable that it never remains in the same condition. What Matthew says, “as they were going out from Jericho,” is as if he said, “as they were passing through the region of Jericho”; hence Luke also says: “And it came to pass, as he drew near to Jericho” [Note: [Col. 0242D] See Augustine, Book II, *Questions on the Gospels*, chapter 48.] (Luke 18:35).

They sit beside the road who are now ready both to believe and to run; you understand what this road is and what this running is. Far from it are those who do not perceive Christ’s coming and passing. Those cry more loudly who pray more earnestly; this cry is of the heart, not of the mouth. But what do they cry? “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David,” so that we too may sing your mercies forever together with David.

But the crowd rebuked them, telling them to be silent; yet they cried out all the more: “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David.” If the blind men had fallen silent and believed the rebuking crowd, they would not yet have been enlightened. It is an evil crowd that drives a person away from such a cry. This crowd is understood as the host of vices and evil spirits, who always strive to hinder us when we cry to God and ask for mercy. [Col. 0242A] Let us therefore imitate these blind men. [Note: [Col. 0242D] St Augustine excellently exhorts us to do the same, Sermon 18, *On the Words [of the Lord]*, no. 13: “Those who love the world object: ‘Why are you mad? You are excessive. Are not others Christians? This is folly, this is madness,’ and other such things: the crowd cries out. . . . Evil and lukewarm Christians hinder good Christians, truly earnest ones, who wish to fulfil God’s commandments. . . . Let them cry out; let them not fail nor be led away, as though by the authority of crowds,” etc.] For these are not among those whom whoever follows falls into a pit. Let us not be overcome by the crowd; let us cry out, persist, and pray, so that we too may be enlightened by the Lord.

Let us say with the Psalmist: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death; lest my enemy should say: I have prevailed against him” (Ps. 12:4). “And Jesus stood still, called them, and said: What do you wish me to do for you? They say to him: Lord, that our eyes may be opened.” See how much prayer can do; see how powerful the cry of the mind is: it conquers the crowd, stops Christ, and holds him by a cry whom strength could not have held. Jesus stands still, calls them and waits for them; he asks what they want, and they seek nothing but light. They speak with light; they seek light, that they may see light. They could seek nothing better: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

But Jesus, moved with compassion, touched their eyes; and immediately they saw and followed him. They were blind, but, touched by light, they receive light, see, and follow Jesus. For whoever follows him does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life; and no one follows him unless touched and enlightened by him.

LXXXV. [CHAPTER 21.] “And when they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two of his disciples, saying to them: Go into the village opposite you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them [Col. 0242C] and bring them to me.”

The Lord sends his two disciples before him, by whom we understand the two Testaments. [Note: [Col. 0242D] Origen does not explain it very differently. Origen, Huet, vol. I, p. 436: “If you interpret the two disciples anagogically, you will say that one is the order of those who minister to the circumcised, the other of those who minister to the Gentiles.”] He himself taught these disciples; he himself issued these two Testaments, and filled them with all fullness of wisdom and knowledge. These disciples are wise, instructed by the wisest teacher; without their teaching no one is found wise.

The Lord sends them before himself. They untie the colt and the donkey and bring them, once untied, to him. But what is signified by the donkey except the Synagogue? What by the colt except the Gentile people? [Note: [Col. 0242D] Jerome: “Let this donkey, which had been yoked and tamed and had borne the yoke of the Law, be understood as the Synagogue; and the playful, free colt of the donkey as the people of the Gentiles. Jesus sat upon them, having sent to them his two disciples, one to the circumcision and the other to the Gentiles.” Bede gives the same from Jerome.] The former had been tamed by the prophets and burdened with the weight of the Law; the latter was playful and untamed, and no human being had ever [Col. 0243A] sat upon it. Yet both were bound, and both needed untying. They could not be untied by one, but are untied by two. For no one is untied except by the hands of both Testaments; no one is freed from the bonds of sins except by the faith and teaching of both Testaments.

It follows: “And if anyone says anything to you, say that the Lord has need of them, and immediately he will let them go.” “The Lord,” he says, “has need of them”—and not just any lord, but their Lord also, and the Lord of all. Hence he is called simply “the Lord,” without addition; for in being called “the Lord” without saying whose Lord he is, he is shown to be Lord of all. Who, then, would dare hold those whom the Lord of all commands to be released?

This happened in order that what was written [Col. 0243B] through the prophet might be fulfilled: “Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, meek, sitting upon a donkey and a colt, the foal of a beast under the yoke.” The evangelist explains why the Lord wished to do all this, lest someone perhaps think it unfitting and unbecoming that, in so short a distance of travel, the Lord should sit upon a donkey as though weary.

The other evangelists relate that Christ the Lord sat not upon the donkey and the colt, but upon the colt alone. Matthew, however, according to his custom, following not the event itself but its meaning, says together with the prophet that he sat upon both. Bodily, indeed, the Lord sat upon the colt; spiritually, however, upon both. Whoever understands what each signifies also understands how the Lord sits upon each; for the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.

“And the disciples went and did as Jesus commanded them, and brought the donkey and the colt; and they placed their garments upon them, and made him sit above them.” If, as was said above, these two disciples signify the two Testaments, what are their garments but the individual sayings by which they are adorned and clothed? If therefore you wish to bear Christ and to be his donkey, you must be clothed with these sayings and adorned with this teaching and faith. For by these garments the soul is clothed, ornamented, and made beautiful; naked and poor indeed is the soul that is not clothed and adorned with them. [Note: [Col. 0243D] Jerome: “This colt and donkey . . . before the Saviour’s coming were naked. . . . The garment may be understood as apostolic teaching, the doctrine of virtues, an exposition of the Scriptures, or the varied doctrines of the Church. Unless the soul is instructed and adorned with these, it does not deserve to have the Lord as rider.” Bede says the same in Jerome’s very words. Ambrose, Book IX on Luke, treats extensively the allegory of the garments and the branches spread beneath; among other things he warns: “Take care not to walk with muddy feet; take care not to abandon, by wandering steps, the paths of the prophetic ways spread out for you.”]

“But a very great crowd spread their garments on the road.” The Testaments are two; but the books of the Testaments are many. [Col. 0244A] Therefore the very great crowd—that is, the whole multitude of patriarchs and prophets—spread their garments on the road: they prepared the way for the Lord and taught others their faith.

“Others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road.” These others are the apostles and teachers. From the individual books of the prophets, as from certain trees, they cut branches, expound the sayings, and prepare and spread the road by which Christ’s animals ought to proceed. They are rightly said to cut branches from trees because they expound and preach not their own faith and teaching but that of others.

“And the crowds that went before and those that followed cried out, saying: Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest.” The crowds going before and following are the peoples of both Testaments. Both therefore cry out, because each people proclaims and blesses Christ. For what else does “Hosanna to the Son of David” signify except glory, praise, and honour to the Son of David—or also, “May salvation come to us from the Son of David”?

Although this word has no fixed meaning, [Note: [Col. 0243D] That this is true is clear from Jerome’s Letter 20 to Damasus, Vallarsi edition, where he gives Hilary’s and other ancient explanations, and then his own. He mentions that letter here in his commentary and explains more briefly what he had said there more fully: namely, “that Christ’s coming is the salvation of the world.” Bede, commending Jerome, mentions and follows his explanation on Mark chapter 11: “Hosanna,” that is, salvation; “Hosanna” means, “Save, I beseech you.” See Jerome for the other explanations mentioned by the author. Others have supposed that Hosanna means glory, etc. Modern writers also discuss this word at length: Jansenius, *Harmony*, chapter 110; Maldonado; a Lapide; etc. See also Macri, *Dictionary*, etc. Anastasius, following Vignoli’s reading, no. 10, mentions an oratory of Hosanna in the patriarchal palace adorned in the name of the blessed apostle Peter in Gregory II.] yet it seems rather to signify praise, which resounded from the mouth of the whole people in praise and glory of Christ.

LXXXVI. And when he had entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred, saying: “Who is this?” But the crowds said: “This is Jesus the prophet, from Nazareth of Galilee.” For the Lord was about to wage war and triumph over his enemies; therefore he came with triumph and glory to the impious city and to the place of contest. [Col. 0244C] Certain of victory even before the battle—a thing which does not ordinarily happen—he assumed the triumph. Therefore, entering the city with such great glory, the whole city was stirred, saying: “Who is this?” All rush to meet him; all desire to see him and to recognize by his very face the one whom they had already known from the report of his miracles. For in those days the Lord had raised Lazarus, and all were astonished at the greatness of that miracle.

And Jesus entered the temple of God, and cast out all who were selling and buying in the temple; and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves. Hear this, you Simoniacs; hear it, you wicked merchants: either cease trading or leave the temple. For the Lord cast not merely one or two, but without distinction all buyers and sellers, [Col. 0244D] out of the temple of the Lord. [Col. 0245A] He overturned both the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves. You are money-changers; you sell doves; you do nothing without money and a price. For those sell doves who confer churches or the graces of the Holy Spirit for a price; and the Lord overturns their seats, so that by this we may understand that they are not bishops.

> [Note: [Col. 0245C] See the preface to this work, and observe the author’s vehemence in attacking Simoniacs, as though directed against a vice infecting his own age. [Col. 0245D] We do not deny that the Fathers said something against this very plague in connection with this passage. Jerome—whom Bede, in his usual manner, almost copies—writes: “Every day Jesus enters the temple of his Father and casts out from his Church all alike, bishops, presbyters, deacons, laypersons, and the whole multitude; and he regards buyers and sellers as guilty of a single crime. For it is written: ‘Freely you received; freely give.’”]

And he said to them: “It is written: My house shall be called a house of prayer; but you have made it a den of thieves.” For you are thieves: “He who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold is a thief and a robber” (John 10:1). Christ is the door; and because you did not enter through him, he overturned your seats. For those enter through this door who are appointed according to the ordinances of the canons. [Col. 0245B] Therefore leave the house of prayer, which, because you dwell in it, has become a den of thieves.

And blind and lame people came to him in the temple, and he healed them. Therefore whoever is blind and does not understand the truth, whoever is lame and does not walk in the straight way, let him hasten to the temple. There he will find Jesus; there he will be enlightened and healed.

But when the chief priests and scribes saw the wonders he had done, and the children crying in the temple and saying, “Hosanna to the Son of David,” they were indignant and said to him: “Do you hear what these are saying?” And Jesus said to them: “Certainly. Have you never read: ‘Out of the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise’?” The indignation of the chief priests and scribes is envy; the praise offered to God by the children is the fulfillment of prophecy. For David himself had thus prophesied [Col. 0245C] that the Lord would be proclaimed and praised from the mouths of infants and nursing children.

And leaving them, he went out of the city to Bethany, and stayed there. For the Lord remains in Bethany even now; Bethany is interpreted “house of obedience.”

> [Note: [Col. 0245D] Origen interprets it thus at this passage, and Jerome: “He went to Bethany, which is interpreted ‘house of obedience,’ already then prefiguring the calling of the Gentiles.” So too St Bernard, *Sermon to the Knights Templar*, chapter 13, draws from this an exhortation to the virtue of obedience. “Therefore,” he says, “this has been briefly indicated in this place. Let it suffice that neither the zeal of good action, nor the repose of holy contemplation, nor the tear of the penitent can be acceptable outside Bethany to him who possessed such obedience that he preferred to lose his very life, becoming obedient to the Father [Col. 0246C] even unto death.”]

For, having left the Synagogue, he dwells in the Church, which is obedient to his will. But in the morning, as he returned to the city, he was hungry; and seeing one fig tree beside the road, he came to it and found nothing upon it except leaves alone; and he said to it: “May fruit never grow from you again for ever.” For the Lord, [Col. 0246A] who never does anything without reason, when he seems to do something without reason, gives a sign of some great matter. Who could think it reasonable that he should seek fruit on a tree at a time when trees are without fruit? Does the Creator of fruits, trees, and seasons not know the season of fruit?

Therefore the Lord hungers not for figs but for faith; he seeks not the fruit of a tree but the fruit of work. For this fig tree is the Synagogue.

> [Note: [Col. 0246C] St Augustine, *Sermon* 89, no. 1: “It is the Synagogue—not called, but rejected.” St Gregory, book VIII, question 42, cites Augustine: “In the sense you have mentioned, blessed Augustine properly speaks concerning the fig tree, because when the Evangelist adds, ‘For it was not yet the season for figs,’ it is clearly understood that the Lord had sought fruit through the fig tree in the Synagogue, which possessed the leaves of the Law but did not possess the fruit of works.” Jerome, Ambrose, book VII on Luke, Chrysologus, *Sermon* 106, and especially Origen, p. 446, Huet, also interpret it as the Synagogue.]

It was planted beside the road and offers no comfort to passers-by. The Lord came to it and found nothing on it except leaves. For leaves are words; leaves are the letter. The Synagogue possesses these: it speaks well, indeed, but does not do what it says. Yet all this must be understood of that part of the Synagogue which persists in its [Col. 0246B] unbelief, shaded by the leaves of verbosity and producing no fruit of spiritual understanding.

> [Note: [Col. 0246D] St Augustine, ibid.: “For from it also the people of God was called which truly and sincerely awaited in the prophets the salvation of God, Jesus Christ.”]

It is this part that the Lord cursed. But for the other part of the Synagogue he prayed, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Therefore those who are cursed and who bear no fruit for ever are the scribes and Pharisees, who burned with excessive envy at the death of our Savior.

And immediately the fig tree withered; and the disciples, seeing it, marveled and said: “How did it wither immediately?” But on the following day, as Mark says, when they passed that way in the morning—

> [Note: [Col. 0246D] Chapter 11:12: “And when evening came, they went out of the city; and when they passed by in the morning,” etc.]

—Peter said to Jesus: “Rabbi, behold, the fig tree which you cursed has withered.” Every day the Lord curses fruitless trees and wicked persons; [Col. 0246C] every day those whom he curses wither and are consigned to fire. He curses both in person and through his servants. Hence it follows: And Jesus answered and said to them: “Amen, I say to you: if you have faith and do not waver, not only shall you do this to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and cast into the sea,’ it shall be done.”

For afterward Christ’s disciples possessed this faith, because, enlightening the blind, cleansing lepers, raising the dead, and performing other miracles, they learned by experience itself that what the Lord had promised was true.

> [Note: [Col. 0246D] See Jerome rebuking those who denied that the apostles had performed miracles because they did not possess faith.]

“And whatever you ask in prayer, believing, you shall receive.” How this should be understood [Col. 0247A] we explained above, namely where it says: “For if two of you agree upon earth concerning anything whatever that they ask, it shall be done for them by my Father who is in heaven.”

And when he had come into the temple, the chief priests and elders of the people came to him as he was teaching and said: “By what authority do you do these things? And who gave you this authority?” Foolish chief priests! They see the dead rise, and say to Christ: “By what authority do you do these things?” By what authority do the dead rise? Who besides God has ever given anyone this authority? This is that madness by which elsewhere, blaspheming, they say: “By Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Matt. 9:34). Understanding their madness, Jesus answered and said to them: “I also will ask you [Col. 0247B] one question; if you tell me this, I too will tell you by what authority I do these things. Whence was John’s baptism—from heaven or from men?” That is: do you believe John’s baptism to have been performed by God’s command or devised by man?

> [Note: [Col. 0247D] See Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 10.]

For if they had answered this question truthfully, they themselves would have resolved their own question. For whoever believes John certainly believes Christ also, since John bore witness to Christ. Understanding this, they deliberated among themselves, saying: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’” For John had preached Christ and announced that he was the Son of God. “But if we say, ‘From men,’ we fear the crowd; for all regarded John as a prophet.” And answering Jesus, they said: [Col. 0247C] “We do not know.” They do not wish to tell the truth; they fear to lie; yet they lie in saying, “We do not know.”

> [Note: [Col. 0247D] “They lied in answering that they did not know,” Jerome.]

And he said to them: “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.”

LXXXVII. “What do you think? A certain man had two sons. Going to the first, he said: ‘Son, go today and work in my vineyard.’ But he answered and said: ‘I will not’; yet afterward, moved by repentance, he went. Going to the other, he spoke likewise. But he answered and said: ‘I am going, sir,’ and did not go. Which of the two did the will of the father?” They said to him: “The first.” Jesus said to them: “Amen, I say to you that tax collectors and prostitutes shall go before you into the kingdom of God. For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him; [Col. 0247D] but tax collectors and prostitutes believed him. And you, seeing this, did not afterward repent so as to believe him.”

The two sons are two parts of the people: one, the scribes, Pharisees, and the rest who pretended [Col. 0248A] to be righteous; the other, tax collectors and prostitutes.

> [Note: [Col. 0247D] Origen, p. 456, Huet; Jerome; Chrysostom, *Homily* 68; Bede; and others interpret the two sons as the Gentile and Jewish peoples. Hilary is very close to the author: “The first son is the people of the Pharisees … This son was insolent, disobedient, and obstinately opposed to the words then spoken, having confidence in the Law … but the younger son is the people of tax collectors and sinners, latter in the condition of sin in which it then remained,” etc. Jerome too, on verse 31, “Tax collectors and sinners shall go before,” etc., writes: [Col. 0248D] “because those who by evil works had denied that they served God afterward received from John the baptism of repentance; but the Pharisees,” etc.]

Thus it is also said elsewhere: “Two men went up into the temple to pray: one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector” (Luke 18:10). For this parable and that one seem to signify the same thing.

The Lord came to the first—that is, to tax collectors and sinners, who are called first because they are more numerous. But how did he come? Through his messengers, through John the Baptist. For in the wilderness John admonished these two sons, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” At first tax collectors and sinners would not believe him; but afterwards, moved by repentance, they flocked to him from every side and were baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins. But the chief priests, elders of the people, and [Col. 0248B] others of that kind, who continually pretended and promised that they served and obeyed God, saw him yet neither repented nor wished to believe him. Thus, when some of them came for baptism, John said, as though in astonishment: “Brood of vipers, who taught you to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore produce fruit worthy of repentance” (Matt. 3:7). Thus tax collectors and prostitutes go before them into the kingdom of God.

LXXXVIII. “Hear another parable. There was a man, a householder, who planted a vineyard, set a hedge around it, dug a winepress in it, built a tower in its midst, leased it to cultivators, and went abroad.”

> [Note: [Col. 0248D] Origen, p. 458, Huet: “The people who preceded us and was God’s portion was the vineyard … God’s protection, by which it was safe, was the hedge; the temple was the tower; the winepress was the place of libations; the cultivators were the priests and wise men of the people; and the departure was when the Lord no longer appeared so manifestly.” Jerome interprets “hedge” in nearly the same sense as either the city wall or the aid of angels; “winepress” as the altar; and of the tower he says, “There is no doubt that it is the temple.”]

In the figurative sense, this man, the householder, signifies God the Father, who transplanted the vineyard [Col. 0248C] *Sorec* from Egypt and planted it in the mountains of Israel. Hence the Psalmist says: “You transplanted a vine from Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it” (Ps. 69:9). And the prophet says of it: “A vineyard was made for the beloved on a horn, the son of oil” (Isa. 5:1); and a little later: “For the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts is the house of Israel.”

He set a hedge around it because he fortified it with the protection of his power; and he dug a winepress in it, by which the altar is understood, where, as wine in a winepress, the blood of victims was poured out daily. He built a tower in its midst, namely the temple, in which the Jewish people especially trusted. And he leased it to cultivators, because he gave that land flowing with milk and honey to the Jews [Col. 0248D] to inhabit. And he went abroad, because salvation is far from sinners.

“But when the season of fruits drew near, he sent his servants to the cultivators to receive its fruits. And the cultivators, seizing [Col. 0249A] his servants, beat one, killed another, and stoned another.” This is what the prophet says: “He expected it to produce grapes, and it produced wild grapes” (Isa. 5:2). These servants were holy men and prophets.

> [Note: [Col. 0249D] Jerome likewise interprets them as prophets. Hilary also writes: “In the servants sent to receive the fruits is represented the varied and often repeated succession of the prophets.”]

The Lord sent them to correct that people and invite it to his service. “Again he sent other servants, more than the first, and they treated them likewise.” Hence blessed Stephen says: “Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who foretold the coming of the Just One, of whom you have now been betrayers and murderers. But last of all he sent his son to them, saying: ‘They will respect my son.’ But the cultivators, seeing the son, said among themselves: ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and we shall have [Col. 0249B] his inheritance’” (Acts 7:52).

These things are plain, in which the Lord foretold his passion; and we see and believe that all has now been fulfilled. For the cultivators—that is, the chief priests—feared that, unless they killed Christ, they would lose their place and their nation. Therefore they counseled the people to kill him. “And having seized him, they cast him outside the vineyard and killed him.” What does “outside the vineyard” mean except outside the city? This is what the Apostle says: “For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the sanctuary by the high priest are burned outside the camp” (Heb. 13:11). Thus Jesus too, “that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate.”

> [Note: [Col. 0249D] Jerome on this passage: “The Apostle says that Jesus was crucified outside the gate.”]

Thus, to their own harm, these people fulfilled what those sacrificial rites signified. “When therefore the lord of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those cultivators?” The Lord asks them for the sentence of judgment so that, by their own judgment, they may condemn themselves.

> [Note: [Col. 0249D] Here also the author seems to have had blessed Jerome before his eyes: “The Lord questions them, not because he does not know what they will answer, but so that they may be condemned by their own answer.”]

They say to him: “He will miserably destroy those wicked men and lease his vineyard to other cultivators, who will render him fruit in its seasons.” Why is it, O chief priests, that now you do not answer, “We do not know,” as above when the Lord questioned you concerning John’s baptism? It is because you do not yet understand this parable. If you understood it, you would either give no answer or a different one. Luke, however, says that, hearing the saying, the Pharisees answered: “May it never be!” (Luke 20:17), which was as if they said: “May it never be that we kill you and therefore perish!”

Jesus said to them: [Col. 0249D] “Have you never read in the Scriptures: ‘The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This was done by the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?” For this and the preceding parable signify the same thing.

> [Note: [Col. 0249D] Jerome observed the same on this passage: “By varied and different [Col. 0250D] parables, the same matters are woven together.”]

For the chief priests, [Col. 0250A] scribes, and Pharisees, who expounded the Law, taught the people, and built the Synagogue, not only rejected Christ our Lord, the cornerstone, but also killed him by a most shameful death. Yet he became the head of the corner, joining two walls: one coming from circumcision and the other from uncircumcision. This was done by the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes. For to whom would it not seem marvelous that he who only recently hung with robbers should now be acknowledged as head and Lord by both peoples, reigning everywhere and worshiped by all?
