“Therefore I say to you that the kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.” Because they did these things, because they rejected this stone and killed the Son of God, [Col. 0250B] the kingdom of God shall be taken from them and given to the Gentile people, which is better than they. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “I shall call ‘my people’ that which was not my people, and ‘having obtained mercy’ that which had not obtained mercy” (Rom. 9:25).

“And whoever falls upon this stone shall be broken; but upon whomever it falls, it shall crush him.” Those fall upon this stone who think wrongly concerning Christ and, departing from the Catholic faith, stumble against him.

> [Note: [Col. 0250D] Jerome: “It is one thing to offend Christ through evil works, another to deny him. The person who is a sinner and yet believes in him … is broken, but not utterly crushed … But whoever has completely denied Christ, him it will crush so that not even a potsherd remains from which a little water may be drawn.”]

Hence the Apostle says: “They stumbled at the stone of stumbling, as it is written: ‘Behold, I place in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense; and everyone who believes in him shall not be put to shame’” (Rom. 9:33). The Lord himself also says: “Blessed is he who shall not be offended in me” [Col. 0250C] (Luke 7:23).

“But upon whomever it falls, it shall crush him.” Upon whom does the Lord fall except those with whom he is angry and indignant? For he is that stone which in Daniel was “cut from the mountain without hands” (Dan. 2:34) and crushed that most famous statue entire, through which all the multitude of the wicked is figured.

And when the chief priests and Pharisees heard his parables, they recognized that he was speaking of them. And seeking to seize him, they feared the crowds, because the crowds regarded him as a prophet. It is clear, therefore, that at first they did not understand his words, and so condemned themselves by their own answer.

103. LXXXIX. [CHAPTER 22.] [Col. 0250D] And Jesus answered and spoke to them again in parables, saying: “The kingdom of heaven has become like a man, a king, who made a wedding for his son.” For then God the Father, King and Lord of all, made a wedding for his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord,

> [Note: [Col. 0250D] Origen, p. 472: “The man who is a king is figuratively called God and Father of Christ; the wedding of the king’s son is the restoration of Christ’s Church, his bride, to Christ himself, her bridegroom; and the servants sent to summon [Col. 0251D] those invited to the wedding are the prophets.” Jerome: “This king who made a wedding for his son is almighty God; he makes the wedding of our Lord Jesus Christ and the Church.” “And he sent his servant”: undoubtedly Moses, through whom he gave the Law to those invited. But if we read “servants,” as most copies have it, it must be referred to the prophets … “The servants sent a second time are better understood as prophets than as apostles.” He seems, I think, to have had Hilary in view, who writes: “The servants sent to call those invited are the apostles.”]

when he sent him into the world to assume [Col. 0251A] our flesh. For he, fair in form beyond the children of men, joined to our flesh, went forth from his chamber as a bridegroom. He chose for himself, as the Apostle says, “a glorious Church as bride, not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5:27). For the entire book called the *Song of Songs* was composed in the manner of a wedding song.

“And he sent his servants to call those invited to the wedding, but they would not come.” All the patriarchs and prophets invited the Jews to Christ’s wedding; all foretold his coming; all praised the delights of the New Testament; yet they themselves would not come and receive them.

“Again he sent other servants, saying: ‘Tell those invited: Behold, I have prepared my banquet; my oxen and fattened fowl have been slaughtered, and all [Col. 0251B] things are ready. Come to the wedding.’ But they neglected it.” These other servants are the apostles and teachers, sent by the Lord, once the wedding had been prepared and the Scriptures opened for understanding, to preach and invite the Jews to the wedding. What else is this entire banquet but the spiritual understanding of both Testaments? Here you will find bulls, lambs, birds, and every delightful thing for nourishment and food. By these foods the soul is refreshed; by these delights the understanding is filled and made rich.

> [Note: [Col. 0251D] Jerome: “The prepared banquet, the oxen, and the fattened fowl that have been slaughtered either describe royal riches metaphorically, [Col. 0252D] so that spiritual things may be understood from bodily ones; or certainly the greatness of doctrines and the teaching of God, most fully present in the Law, may be perceived.”]

The bulls are the greater sayings, more difficult to retain and understand; the birds or winged creatures are those which, flying higher and speaking of spiritual matters, raise our minds to heavenly things. These were slaughtered and prepared when, overcome by understanding and reason and committed to memory, they can no longer flee or resist understanding.

For concerning bulls or calves Hosea says: “Take away all iniquity, receive what is good, and we shall render the calves of our lips” (Hos. 14:3). What are the calves of the lips but the sayings of the Scriptures and the praises of God contained in them? That sacred Scripture is also called a bird, hear what the Lord says through Moses: “If, walking along the road, you find a bird’s nest in a tree or on the ground, and the bird brooding above its young or eggs, let the bird go, while keeping the young you have taken, that it may go well with you and that you may live for a long time” (Deut. 22:6).

For this bird is the letter, which has enclosed its young or eggs—that is, spiritual understanding—[Col. 0251D] under the covering of its wings. It nests in a tree where the passages are more difficult, and on the ground where they are easier. Therefore, walking along the road of this book, [Col. 0252A] we sometimes find the nest of this bird in a tree and sometimes on the ground. Therefore, that we may live long, let us release the bird and the letter that kills, but retain the young and eggs—that is, the spiritual understanding that gives life. These, then, are the bulls; these are the birds; these are the fattened fowl which God has prepared for us at the wedding of his Son.

But the Jews neglected these delights; they would not receive and eat them. Therefore they went away: one to his farm, another to his business. We eat the delights of this wedding in the city of God, in the holy Church; but they remain on the farm, delighting in the coarse bread of the letter and rustic fare. For all who are outside the Church are on the farm. The individual books of the Law and Prophets may also be understood as the farms of the Jews. And because Jews throughout the world live by fraud, commerce, usury, and deception, they are not without reason said to have gone to their business.

“But the rest seized his servants and, having treated them shamefully, killed them.” By these we understand those who persecuted the primitive Church. Hence it is said of the apostles: “They went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been judged worthy to suffer insults for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41).

“But when the king heard of it, he was angry; and sending his armies, he destroyed those murderers and burned their city.” Because these things occurred according to the letter, there seems no need to explain them allegorically. For forty-two years afterward,

> [Note: [Col. 0252D] Since Jerusalem is known to have been captured and destroyed in A.D. 70, counting back forty-two years brings us to A.D. 28. According to the most widely received opinion of chronologers, this preceded the year of Christ’s death, when we may readily establish that the Lord uttered this prediction. Thus the accuracy of our author in these chronological matters is remarkable for that age.]

the Lord sent his armies—that is, the Roman leaders—[Col. 0252C] against the Jews. They killed and sold them, and burned not only their cities but also the most famous and distinguished temple itself.

“Then he said to his servants: ‘The wedding is indeed prepared, but those who were invited were not worthy.’” We have said above what the wedding signifies. Since the Jews proved unworthy of it, the Gentile people is summoned to eat at it. What is the preparation of the wedding except the exposition of the holy Scriptures?

> [Note: [Col. 0252D] See Gregory, *Homily* 38 on the Gospels.]

“Therefore go to the ends of the roads, and summon to the wedding whomever you find. For God is no respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts 10:34). Everywhere he sends his disciples; he calls all to faith and invites everyone to the glory of his kingdom. And his servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found, bad and good; and the wedding was filled with guests reclining at table.

[Col. 0253A] For in this threshing floor grain and chaff, wheat and tares, good and bad, are found together.

> [Note: [Col. 0253C] See Jerome explaining this from the Apostle’s Epistle to the Romans, and Augustine.]

The wedding was filled; the nations came together; the apostles proclaimed and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number. But the king entered to see the guests reclining at table, and saw there a man not clothed in a wedding garment. How can one enter somewhere who is everywhere? Because almighty God does not punish immediately and, bearing with us in much patience, seems to disregard the sight of our sins, he seems as though absent. But he is present when he begins to punish and afflict us.

The person not clothed in the wedding garment is one who does not have faith and does not imitate Christ. Hence the Apostle says: “Put off the old man and put on the new” (Eph. 4:22). “For all of you who have been baptized into Christ [Col. 0253B] Jesus have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27).

> [Note: [Col. 0253C] Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 22: “In the Gospel, the wedding garment can be understood as holiness of the flesh.” Chapter 35: “If anyone at the wedding has been clothed in works less worthy, he must immediately be bound hand and foot,” etc. Origen, p. 480, Huet: “But he saw one not clothed in a wedding garment, comprehending all who retained the wickedness adhering to them before faith.” Hilary: “The wedding garment is … the brightness of heavenly attire, received through the confession of a good examination and kept unstained and whole even to the assembly of the kingdom of heaven.” St Augustine, *Sermon* 90, explains the whole parable: “Charity from a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith—this is the wedding garment.” The same, *Sermon* 114, no. 7, and *Against the Donatists after the Conference*, no. 27: “These are clothed in the wedding garment for the honor of the bridegroom, seeking not their own interests but those of Jesus Christ; the others do not have the wedding garment, that is, the bridegroom’s most faithful charity, seeking their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ.” St Leo, *Sermon* 12 on Lent, 50, in the Ballarini recension: “Whoever understands the sacrament [Col. 0254C] of his restoration ought to put off the vices of the flesh and cast away every filth of sins, so that, about to enter the wedding banquet, he may shine in the garment of virtues.” Jerome and Bede: “The wedding garment [Col. 0254D] is the commandments of the Lord and works fulfilled from the Law and the Gospel, which make the clothing of the new man.” St Bernard, *Sermon* 2, on the beginning of the fast: “Our garments are virtues; charity is a good garment, obedience is a good garment.” Hence interpreters—Jansenius, *Concordance*, chapter 115; Maldonado; Cornelius a Lapide; and others—warn, against recent heretics, that the Fathers did not at all understand the wedding garment as faith alone. Therefore our author rightly adds imitation of Christ to faith.]

And he said to him: “Friend, how did you enter here without having a wedding garment?” But he was speechless. This seems especially to be said to those who approach unworthily the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood. For this man could have answered that he had come to the banquet wearing a wedding garment, but had afterward lost it; yet, overwhelmed by astonishment and fear, he was speechless.

Then the king says to the attendants: “Bind his feet and hands, and cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” This sentence is passed upon those who have no word of excuse to give in answer to God. For God is always present at this wedding; he always sees those properly and improperly clothed; and though he is seen by no one, he nonetheless continually prepares and judges some for [Col. 0253C] punishment and others for glory. That they are bound hand and foot shows that they are without strength and power. Outer darkness is that beyond which there is no further darkness. In weeping and gnashing of teeth the immensity of pain is signified. “For many are called, but few are chosen.” Many are called to the wedding, but few are brought into the king’s chamber and glory.

XC. Then the Pharisees went away and took counsel how they might ensnare him in his speech. [Note: [Col. 0254D] “Then the Pharisees went away,” etc. This is a homily attributed to St Bruno, Eusebius of Emesa.] Foolish Pharisees, who think that they can catch the Word of God in speech [Col. 0254A] and deceive wisdom by their schemes. And they send their disciples to him. With whom? With the Herodians—that is, with Herod’s officials, who collected the taxes. [Note: [Col. 0254D] Origen, p. 482: “It is indeed likely that those who wished tribute to be paid to Caesar among the people were called Herodians by those who held that this ought by no means to be done; while those who, under the appearance of liberty, hindered payment of tax to Caesar seem to have been the Pharisees.” St Jerome also, on this passage, explains “with the Herodians” as [Col. 0255D] “with Herod’s soldiers, or those whom the Pharisees mockingly called Herodians because they paid tribute to the Romans and were not devoted to divine worship”; and adds: “Some Latins absurdly suppose that the Herodians were those who believed Herod to be Christ; but we read this nowhere at all.” Among these Latins were Philastrius, *Heresies* 28, and the author of the appendix to Tertullian’s *On Prescriptions*. See Huet, Baronius, and the commentators.]

This, then, is the church of the malicious, this the council of truth! Evil teachers, evil disciples, are joined with evil officials. They come with deceit; they speak with cunning. But what do they say? “Teacher, we know that you are truthful, that you teach the way of God in truth, and that you care for no one; for you do not regard the person of men.” The Pharisees speak very well; but their mouths say one thing and their hearts another. Sweet words break forth from a poisonous spring. To such great pretence the Psalmist replies: “If indeed you speak righteousness, judge uprightly, sons of men” [Col. 0254B] (Ps. 57:2). You call him teacher and say that he is truthful: then love, honour, and follow him as teacher and truthful one.

“Tell us therefore what you think: is it lawful to pay the poll-tax to Caesar, or not?” For they thought that our Lord Christ, whom they had recognized as a friend of piety and justice, would answer that they ought rather to make offerings to the Temple and to God than pay taxes to Caesar, an unrighteous man; and so the Herodians, provoked by this occasion, might seize him, drag him before a judge, and accuse him as a criminal. But if it were unlawful to pay the tax, and if paying tribute were a sin, he himself certainly would not have commanded that tribute be paid for him. For above he said: “What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute or tax—from their own sons or from strangers?” [Col. 0254C] And he said, “From strangers.” Jesus answered: “Then the sons are free. But lest we give them offence, go to the sea, cast in a hook, take the first fish that comes up; and when you open its mouth, you will find a stater. Take it and give it to them for me and for yourself” (Matt. 17:24).

Therefore he who, lest scandal should arise, paid tribute although he was not obliged to do so, could not fittingly forbid others to pay the tax in order to stir up disputes and scandals. But Jesus, knowing their malice, said: “Why do you tempt me, hypocrites?” [Col. 0255A] For it is foolish to address with hypocrisy and pretence one whom hidden things do not deceive, who sees hearts and considers thoughts. “Show me the coin of the tax.” And they offered him a denarius. On the denarius were inscribed Caesar’s name and image. Jesus said to them: “Whose image is this, and whose inscription?” They said to him, “Caesar’s.” [Note: [Col. 0255D] Not because there was a fixed and established coin—that is, a particular kind of coin—in which the tax was paid, but because this was the sort of denarius which they foolishly offered Christ. So Fucher, *On the Tax Coin*; Valesius, *On Hebrew Coins*, book II, ch. 20; and the more learned commentators.]

See how he binds them by their own answer; see how God’s wisdom catches the wise of this world in their own craftiness! They themselves testify that what they show belongs to Caesar. If it belongs to Caesar, why should it not be returned to Caesar? Indeed, why should they take from Caesar what they admit to be Caesar’s? Then he said to them: “Render therefore the things that are Caesar’s to Caesar.” Do not wrong Caesar; do not take away what is his, lest, if you wish to take away what is his, he [Col. 0255B] who is stronger than you should take both his own things and yours from you. How fitting to this passage is the saying: “He who denies what is just gives everything to one who bears arms.” And render to God the things that are God’s.

For there is nothing that is not God’s; yet that is said especially to be his which he loves more particularly. For he loves all his creation, according to the words: “You have mercy on all things, Lord, and hate none of the things which you have made” (Wis. 11:24–25); but he especially loves that through which he made the other creatures. Let Caesar’s image therefore be returned to Caesar, and God’s image be returned to God; for man was made in God’s image. Let us render his image to God. [Note: [Col. 0255D] See the author of the *Imperfect Work*, Homily 42.] Let us render our souls to God: we have nothing dearer; therefore we ought to pay this tribute. When they heard this they marvelled; and, leaving [Col. 0255C] him, they went away. The Pharisees marvel that they have so easily been trapped; and those who had come to catch Christ in his speech discover that they themselves have been caught in their own words.

XCI. On that day the Sadducees, who say that there is no resurrection, came to him. On that day, he says, on which the Pharisees withdrew defeated, the Sadducees came to be defeated. They questioned him, saying: “Teacher, Moses said: If a man dies without a son, his brother shall marry his wife and raise up offspring for his brother. Now there were among us seven brothers. The first married a wife and died; and, having no offspring, he left his wife to his brother. Likewise the second and the third, down to the seventh. Last of all the woman also died. Therefore, in the resurrection, whose wife of the seven will she be? For [Col. 0256A] they all had her.”

Certainly Moses said this: that a brother should marry his brother’s wife in order to raise up his brother’s offspring. But this tale, in which they say that seven brothers had one wife, is an invention of the Sadducees. [Note: [Col. 0255D] Jerome: “They set before him the indecency of the tale [Col. 0256D] in order to deny the truth of the resurrection.” Chrysostom, Homily 71: “Their audacity is so full of rashness, shamelessness, and obstinacy that they do not fear even to attack impossibilities … They invent, as I think, an event that never happened, believing that they can catch him in uncertainty and afterwards ridicule the mysteries of the resurrection.”]

Yet I know that some have understood the seven brothers to mean the seven books—that is, the Heptateuch. [Note: [Col. 0256D] For the Heptateuch, that is, the collection consisting of the Pentateuch and the following two books, Joshua and Judges. Alcuin uses the name *Eptaticus* in the poem prefixed to the sacred books:

> “For the Heptateuch runs through this book,  
> Which Ruth, a woman sufficiently renowned, follows.”

The learned Lambecius thought the word corrupt, though he could have seen that it was not so from Jerome, *Questions on 1 Chronicles*; Arator, book I, ch. 17; Gregory, book XII, epistle 30; and others.] The Sadducees brought this invention of theirs to the Lord in order to prove by it that there is no resurrection of the dead, saying: either all will have her at once, or none. For if one has her, he will wrong the others; and no one ought to claim as his own what is common.

The teacher of truth answered this great error: “You err, not knowing the Scriptures or [Col. 0256B] the power of God.” And immediately he shows the very error in which they were mistaken, saying: “For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage.” By this he indicates that they wished to prove that, if men rose again, husbands would have intercourse with their wives in the future world just as in this present age. But why were they so mistaken? Because they knew neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. For they neither understood what Moses had said nor believed in God’s power and omnipotence; therefore they despaired that so great a resurrection of all could take place. For it will not be there as it is here; nor will they then devote themselves to pleasure as they now do. “But they will be like the angels of God in heaven.” For angels are by nature chaste and virginal; such therefore men too will be.

Then, immediately supporting this with the testimony of Scripture, he says: “Have you not read concerning the resurrection of the dead what was said by God speaking to you: ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead but of the living.” [Col. 0256C] As though he said: If, as you wrongly suppose, a man did not exist after death, God would by no means call himself the God of the patriarchs, since he is God and Lord not of those who are not, but of those who are. And the crowds, hearing this, marvelled at his teaching.

But since the Sadducees err, understanding neither the Scriptures nor the power of God, let us now see what that Scripture means which the Sadducees proposed to the Lord concerning raising up a brother’s offspring. For this is not observed in the Church according to the letter; indeed, its observance is altogether forbidden. Therefore it must be understood otherwise. Let it then be said: [Col. 0257A] “When brothers dwell together, and one of them dies without children, the wife of the deceased shall not marry another, but his brother shall take her and raise up his brother’s offspring; and he shall call the firstborn son from her by that man’s name, so that his name may not be blotted out from Israel.”

These are the brothers of whom it is said: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 133:1). Although not in body, they all dwell together in mind and spirit. One of them dies without children when some bishop departs this life and leaves among all his subjects in his Church no one worthy to hold his chair. [Note: [Col. 0257D] The same author had explained it thus in his commentary on this passage of Deuteronomy, in the Roman edition, ch. 25, p. 210, col. 2.]

A man is therefore sought from another Church to be joined to the deceased’s wife. And indeed no other is chosen except one who has been the deceased man’s brother: brother not by nature, certainly, but by character—of the same goodness and humanity, of the same faith and charity, like a brother similar to his brother. “This man shall raise up his brother’s offspring” [Col. 0257B] (Deut. 25:5), so that those whom he finds dead in sins or weighed down by evil sleep he may awaken to good work. “And he shall call the firstborn by that man’s name.” The firstborn is not he who was born first, but he who is held first and greatest among all those begotten by him because of the merit of holiness. This man will be called bishop; for that is the deceased man’s name. Why? “So that his name may not be blotted out from Israel”: so that the Church may never lack a bishop, and this name may never fail within her.

“But if he is unwilling to take the wife of his [Col. 0257C] brother, who is due to him by law, the woman shall go to the gate of the city and appeal to the elders, and shall say: ‘My husband’s brother refuses to raise up his brother’s offspring in Israel and to take me in marriage.’ At once they shall summon him and question him. If he answers, ‘I do not wish to take her as my wife,’ the woman shall approach him before the elders, remove the sandal from his foot, spit in his face, and say: ‘Thus shall it be done to the man who does not build up his brother’s house.’ And his name shall be called in Israel, the house of the unsandalled” (Deut. 25:7).

Why is judgment sought before the city gate, unless because the judges sit there? For the Lord speaks of himself, saying: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” (John 10:9). Before this door and this gate, therefore, [Col. 0257D] bishops sit, so that, illumined by his light, they may nowhere depart from truth. All cases ought to be brought before them and decided by their judgment. In their presence the woman therefore approaches her husband’s brother, and, because he has refused to take her in marriage, removes the sandal from his foot. What does removing a sandal from the feet mean, except taking away the licence to evangelize? [Col. 0258A] Thus the Apostle says: “Your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace” (Eph. 6:13). Moreover she spits in his face, because she openly and manifestly shows that he is contemptible and unworthy of so great an honour.

This may most rightly be understood of those who seek larger Churches and disdain to attach themselves to a smaller Church. There is no doubt that they seek not the salvation of souls but the glory of honour. It would therefore be just that they should always be judged unsandalled and spat upon, never worthy of such a marriage. For this is what is said: “And his name shall be called in Israel, the house of the unsandalled.” [Col. 0258B] For who would dare to shoe him? Who would assign to him the office of one shod, when by the very title of his name he shows himself to be unsandalled? Thus, then, what was formerly observed according to the letter in the Synagogue is now observed spiritually in the Church. [Note: [Col. 0257D] See several other allegorical explanations in Origen from p. 489; Huet.]

XCII. But when the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. As the Pharisees withdraw, the Sadducees come; and again, as the Sadducees withdraw, the Pharisees come. Now these, now those, tempt him; and because they cannot catch and hold him by arguments, they try by repeated encounters to unsettle and weary him. [Note: [Col. 0257D] “What we read that Herod and Pontius Pilate did—making peace with one another in the Lord’s death—we now see also in the Pharisees and Sadducees, who are opposed to one another [Col. 0258D] but agree in one mind to tempt Jesus.” Jerome.] Yet he answers them all: he satisfies some and confutes others.

And one of them, a doctor of the law, questioned him in order to tempt him: “Teacher, which is the great commandment in the law?” All tempt him; all call him teacher. Yet they do not wish, as from a teacher, to learn truth from him, but rather desire, if possible, to catch him as unwary [Col. 0258C] in some statement. [Note: [Col. 0258D] Jerome again: “One of the doctors of the law asks, not desiring to know, but tempting him—whether, when questioned, he knew what was being asked.”] But what does this profit them? Wisdom is ignorant of nothing.

Let us hear what the Lord answered: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and with your whole mind. This is the greatest and first commandment. The second is like it: You shall love your neighbour as yourself. On these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets.” Therefore these two commandments are called first and greatest because these two can accomplish as much as all the rest. [Note: [Col. 0258D] See St Augustine, *Enchiridion on Faith, Hope, and Charity*, near the end.] Otherwise they are neither first nor second commandments, since they were not written on the tablets of stone. For the words of the law are ten, of which the first is: “You shall have no strange gods before me” (Exod. 20:3).

This commandment is therefore called first, not because it is first in the order of Scripture, but because in force and meaning it is chief and greatest. The second, like it, is: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself,” because after the former it has a second and similar force. Hence the Apostle John says: “For one who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love [Col. 0259A] God whom he does not see? And we have this commandment from God: whoever loves God must also love his brother” (1 John 4:20). For whoever does not love God loves neither himself nor his brother.

The first thing, then, is that he should love God; next, himself; and afterwards his brother as himself. [Note: [Col. 0259D] St Augustine, *City of God*, book XIX, ch. 14: “Since God, our teacher, teaches the two chief commandments—that is, love of God and love of neighbour—in these man finds three things to love: God, himself, and his neighbour.”] For whoever hates himself, if he loves his brother as himself, hates his brother also. For everyone “who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10:6); therefore he hates his brother’s soul as well, if he loves his brother as himself. Thus no one is told to love his brother as himself except one who loves himself; and no one loves himself except one who loves God. Therefore the first commandment is to love God, and afterwards to love [Col. 0259B] one’s neighbour for God’s sake.

The measure of love is this: that we love God with all our heart, all our soul, all our mind, and all our strength; but our neighbour as ourselves. [Note: [Col. 0259D] St Augustine treats these two commandments at length in his entire sermon *On Christian Discipline*, and Bernard in his treatise *On Loving God*.] For it is more to love someone with one’s whole heart than to love him as oneself. It can happen that one does not love oneself; but it cannot happen that one does not love the person whom one loves with one’s whole heart and whole soul. If therefore you wish to love yourself, first love God with all your heart; then, since you already love yourself, love your neighbour as yourself.

The holy apostles and martyrs loved God with their whole heart, whole mind, and all their strength. Although they could be killed, they could in no way be separated from his love and affection. These therefore loved [Col. 0259C] themselves well, because they attained eternal life, glory, honour, and every blessedness for themselves; and they loved their neighbours as themselves, because they desired for them the same glory and blessedness as for themselves.

On these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets, for everyone who sins sins either against God, against himself, or against his neighbour. But how can one who loves God and neighbour in the aforesaid manner of love offend those whom he loves so greatly? For he fears to sin even against himself, lest in this too he offend God. Therefore, if charity is fulfilled in these two commandments and all sins are removed, it is evident that the whole law and the prophets hang upon them. For what else do the law and prophets command, except that we love God and [Col. 0259D] our neighbour and refrain from vices, sins, and every offence?

XCIII. But when the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus questioned them, saying: “What do you 108 think concerning Christ? Whose son is he?” They said to him, “David’s.” He said to them: “How then does David [Col. 0260A] in the Spirit call him Lord, saying: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet’? If David therefore calls him Lord, how is he his son?”

For he is both David’s son and David’s Lord: his son according to humanity, but Lord according to divinity. For Christ was born of David’s stock according to the flesh. But the Pharisees did not understand this. Like the rest, they believed that Christ—whom they themselves call Messiah—would be merely a man and not God. [Note: [Col. 0259D] Jerome: “Jesus’ question benefits us even today against the Jews. For those also who confess that Christ is to come maintain that he will be a mere man and a holy man of David’s family.”] By this question, therefore, he shows himself to be both God and man, and king and ruler of all creatures. [Note: [Col. 0260D] Chrysostom, Homily 72: “Thus in every way he invited them to faith. Observe how humbly he set forth the prophet’s opinion and pronouncement concerning himself.”]

Since he is David’s son, he is man; but he is God because he is David’s Lord and sits at the Father’s [Col. 0260B] right hand. Since all his enemies are subject beneath his feet, he is shown to be Lord of all. For David, seeing in the Holy Spirit our Lord Christ returning to the Father after his resurrection, and understanding the hidden things done there, says: “‘The Lord’—the Father—‘said to my Lord’—his Son—‘Sit at my right hand’” (Ps. 109:1), so that, as we sit upon one seat, we may be believed equal by all. Sit, I say, until you return for judgment and all your enemies are subjected beneath your feet. Since the Pharisees did not understand this, none of them could answer him a word; nor did anyone dare from that day onward to question him any further.

XCIV. [CH. XXIII.] Then Jesus spoke to [Col. 0260C] the crowds and to his disciples, saying: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat in Moses’ seat. Therefore keep and do whatever they tell you; but do not act according to their works, for they say and do not do.” What is it to sit in Moses’ seat except to preach Moses’ teaching and law [Note: [Col. 0260D] Jerome: “By the seat he indicates the teaching of the law.” Bede uses the same words here.] and to govern and admonish the people? This was the office of the scribes and Pharisees; hence they are said to sit in Moses’ seat.

But why does the Lord elsewhere command, saying: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy” (Luke 12:1), while here he says: “Keep and do whatever they tell you”? [Note: [Col. 0260D] See Chrysostom, Homily 73, who resolves this in precisely the same manner: namely, that they should keep “everything by which men’s morals are corrected and we are made better,” etc.] The teaching of the Pharisees is called leaven, but not that teaching which they give when sitting in Moses’ seat. For they sit in Moses’ seat when they preach nothing but what Moses commands; and this must be kept and done. But when, through fraud and hypocrisy, they teach not the words of the law but their own traditions, then they ought not to be obeyed or believed, [Col. 0261A] because they do not sit in Moses’ seat.

Whatever sort of preacher he may be, therefore, if he proclaims not his own words but God’s, the people ought to obey and believe him. Let them follow him in what he says, not in what he does; for what he says is God’s, but what he does is his own. [Note: [Col. 0261C] Chrysostom, Homily 37 *To the People of Antioch*, showing “that even if you have a wicked teacher, this cannot harm you if you attend to his words. For God will pronounce judgment upon you not for what the priest does, but for what you heard and neglected.”]

“But they bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them upon men’s shoulders, but are unwilling to move them with their finger.” By these words the most merciful Lord seems to admonish us that we should have compassion and mercy toward sinners converted to repentance, and bear their burdens with them rather than burdening them beyond their strength. Thus the priests in the law are commanded to bear the iniquity of the sanctuary. [Note: [Col. 0261C] Num. 18:1: “And the Lord said to Aaron: You, your sons, and your father’s house with you shall bear the iniquity of the sanctuary.”] Thus too the Lord says through Moses: “Whoever strikes his male or female slave with a rod, and they die in his hands, shall be guilty of the crime” [Col. 0261B] (Exod. 21:20).

For it often happens that a shepherd of the Church, by exaggerating the crimes of a sinful male or female servant—that is, men and women subject to him—by threatening future torments and declaring the harsh penance of the canons, strikes too severely with the rod of correction. If they die in his hands—that is, if, because of the enormity of their crime and the unbearable burden of penance, he sees that they despair of pardon, and does not strengthen them by gentler words and the medicine of compassion—then, like a person who kills the sick man by treating him badly, he will be guilty. Let penance therefore have due measure, and let burdens be imposed reasonably upon each person. [Note: [Col. 0261D] Bede here, on the Pharisees: “Those now imitate their example in the Church who teach their subjects what they themselves neglect to fulfil, yet aggravate the burden of penance for sinners, so that the sinner must either reject penance or, accepting it but unable to bear it, be scandalized and sin still more; as though it were not better to give account because of mercy than because of cruelty.”]

For God looks more to contrition of heart than to fasting [Col. 0261C] and mortification of the flesh. Great mercy can be shown to one who already repents in heart and ceases to sin; but one who acts otherwise accomplishes nothing, even if he fasts much. “But they do all their works to be seen by men.” Therefore the scribes and Pharisees receive no reward for their works, because they do all their works not [Col. 0262A] for righteousness or the salvation of souls, but for empty glory, so that they may be seen and praised by men.

“For they enlarge their phylacteries and magnify their fringes.” By phylacteries he means certain little sheets which they wore suspended from their hands or about their necks, in which words of the law were written, so that, always looking at them, they might not depart from righteousness. They seem to have taken this custom from the passage where it is said: “It shall therefore be as a sign upon your hand and as something hung for remembrance before your eyes.” [Note: [Col. 0261D] Jerome says they derived the custom from another passage, Deut. 6:8: “You shall bind them on your hand, and they shall be fixed before your eyes.” He adds: “The Pharisees, wrongly interpreting this, wrote the Decalogue of Moses—that is, the ten words of the law—on little parchments, folding them and binding them on the forehead, making as it were a crown for the head, so that they might always be moved before their eyes; which Indians, Persians, and Babylonians do even to this day.” He writes the same on Ezekiel ch. 24. Yet, if any trust is to be put in the Rabbis and if later custom may bear witness to ancient custom, they wrote in phylacteries not the Decalogue, as Jerome says, nor all the words of the law, but only certain passages from the Pentateuch. See Leon of Modena, *Jewish Ceremonies*, part I, ch. 11. Calmet supplies an illustrated form of phylacteries in his *Dictionary of Holy Scripture*. See Chrysostom, Homily 73, where he calls them βιβλίους μικρούς, “little books.”] (Exod. 13:16).

If they had done this with a good and sincere mind, it would not have seemed greatly blameworthy. Concerning the use of fringes, Moses is likewise instructed by the Lord: “Speak to the children of Israel and tell them to make fringes for themselves at the corners of their garments, placing in them cords of hyacinth-blue; when they see them, [Col. 0262B] they shall remember all the commandments of the Lord, not following their own thoughts and their eyes in fornication through various things, but rather, mindful of the Lord’s commands, doing them.” [Note: [Col. 0262C] Num. 15:38–40. See the Roman edition, *Exposition on This Passage*, p. 181.]

This needs little explanation, since the writer himself has explained it. For he commanded that hyacinth-blue cords be placed in the fringes so that they might be a sign by which, remembering heavenly commandments, they would not think vain and useless things. [Note: [Col. 0262D] Jerome also explains this passage: “Moses had also commanded that they make hyacinth-blue fringes at the four corners of their garments, in order that the people of Israel might be recognized … Superstitious teachers … made large fringes and fastened very sharp thorns to them, so that while walking and sitting they might sometimes be pricked and, as it were by this reminder, be drawn back to the duties of the Lord.”] The fringes, then, are the commandments of the law; the hyacinth-blue cords are holy thoughts. If these are bound together, they turn the eyes away from all vanity and direct the whole mind to heavenly things. For when we see hyacinth-blue, we remember heaven, because heaven and hyacinth-blue are of one colour.

The Lord would not have rebuked these things in the Pharisees [Col. 0262C] [Note: [Col. 0262D] Jerome reproves the customs of his own age in imitating phylacteries: “Among us superstitious little women do this even today with small Gospels, with the wood of the cross, and with things of that kind …” Chrysostom at times speaks more gently of this practice, Homily 73: “They called these phylacteries, just as many little women do now, hanging Gospels from their necks; and, in order that they may be reminded by something else, being forgetful and often doing so, they bind a finger more tightly with a thread. God commanded this for them as though for little children.”] if they had not done all their works so as to be seen by men. Of them it is further said: “They love the first places at feasts, the first seats in the synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by men.”

By these words the scribes and Pharisees are marked out for empty glory, [Col. 0263A] pride, and ambition; and we too are warned not to imitate them in such things. [Note: [Col. 0263C] The author rightly explains this passage not of the simple use of the title, but of that which is done through pride. [Col. 0263D] Jerome asks: “Why, against this commandment, did the Apostle call himself ‘teacher of the Gentiles’? Or how is it that in common speech, especially in Palestine and in the monasteries of Egypt, they call one another Fathers?” He resolves it thus: “It is one thing to be father or teacher by nature, another by indulgent usage. If we call a man father, we show honour to his age; we do not declare him the author of our life. A man is also called teacher by association with the true teacher; and … just as the one God by nature and the one Son do not prejudice others from being called gods and sons by adoption, so the one Father and Teacher do not prevent others from being called fathers and teachers by customary usage.” Bede abbreviates Jerome; Chrysostom is briefer still, Homily 73: “Not that they should call no one father, but that they should not fail to know whom they ought principally to call father … just as no one is principally teacher.”]

The first seats belong to ambition; the rest to pride and empty glory. “But do not be called Rabbi, for one is your teacher.” Since all empty glory is sin, the person who desires to be called thus for empty glory sins; and the disciple too does not escape fault when he arrogates to himself the title of teacher. “But you are all brothers, and call no one your father on earth; for one is your Father, who is in heaven. Nor be called teachers, because one is your teacher, Christ.” One is Father, and one is Teacher. Thus James says: “Do not become many teachers, my brothers” (Jas. 3:1). For where there are many teachers, there are many opinions; [Col. 0263B] where there are many opinions, there is schism. Therefore the Apostle exhorts us all “to say the same thing” (1 Cor. 1:10).

We have a good teacher: let us follow him; let his judgment be our one and universal judgment. We ought not to seek a father on earth, because we are all brothers and have one Father in heaven. We must believe and obey him, for love of whom we ought to cast aside and renounce fathers and mothers, brothers and sisters, teachers and instructors, and whatever exists in the world and is found upon earth. “He who is greater among you shall be your servant.” This the Lord says of himself, who deigned to humble himself even to washing the disciples’ feet, giving us an example of humility. Hence it follows: “Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted.” [Note: [Col. 0263D] 1 Pet. 5:5. See here Chrysostom, discoursing at length on [Col. 0264C] the virtue of humility.] [Col. 0263C] For God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. He casts down the mighty from their seat and exalts the humble.

XCV. But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of heaven before men. For you yourselves do not enter, nor do you allow those entering to enter. For others follow their example and teaching. [Note: [Col. 0264C] Christ. Bede: “He rebukes every teacher [Col. 0264D] who, by evil deeds, shuts before his disciples the entrance to the kingdom of heaven.” Chrysostom, Homily 74, admirably: “For we can scarcely imitate upright teachers; but wicked ones, since we are more inclined to evils, we even surpass.”] Therefore, just as they enlighten and save others if they are good, so they blind and destroy them if they are evil.

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who devour widows’ houses while making long prayers: therefore you shall receive a greater judgment. For by long prayers and [Col. 0264A] other pretences the scribes and Pharisees devoured widows’ houses, because the holy women, considering them religious and righteous, bestowed upon them what they possessed. Thus they first supplied these men because of their pretence, just as later they supplied the apostles because of their religion. [Note: [Col. 0264D] Hence I Cor. IX, 5: “Have we not power to lead about a woman, a sister, as also the other apostles, and the brethren of the Lord, and Cephas?” See also Matt. XXVII, 55, and Jerome, Book I against Jovinian, ch. 14.]

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who traverse sea and land to make one proselyte; and when he has been made, you make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as yourselves. For the scribes and Pharisees strove to convert to Judaism such persons as they could from the Gentile people; after their conversion, taking no care for them, they compelled them to fall into worse things. [Note: [Col. 0264D] Chrysostom, Homily 74: “He accuses them on two great counts: first, because, being useless for the salvation of many, they can scarcely attract anyone even with great exertion; secondly, because they are negligent in guarding those whom they have attracted—indeed, they are betrayers, since by the evil example of their lives they make them worse.”] In this we too are warned not to neglect those whom we convert to the faith.

Woe to you, blind guides, who say: Whoever swears by the [Col. 0264B] temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is bound. Fools and blind! For which is greater, the gold or the temple which sanctifies the gold? And whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the offering which is upon it is bound. Blind! For which is greater, the offering or the altar which sanctifies the offering? But whence the scribes and Pharisees acquired this most foolish opinion is uncertain. [Note: [Col. 0264D] Jerome refers it to their foolish traditions; see V.] For all these things are holy; yet the altar is holier than the temple, and the temple holier than the gold of the temple. The former is so because of sacrifice, the latter because of consecration. For although the whole temple had been sanctified, sacrifice was nevertheless permitted nowhere but upon the altar; therefore the altar is holier.

It follows: Therefore he who swears by the altar swears by it and by all things which are [Col. 0264C] upon it; and he who swears by the temple swears by it and by Him who dwells therein; and he who swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by Him who sits upon it. For he who swears by the altar does not attend to the stones, but to the altar’s consecration and to Him in whose name it was consecrated; and therefore he binds himself not by the stones but by God and His sacred ordinances. The same is to be understood concerning the temple and heaven. We too, when we swear upon the Gospels, consider not the parchment and ink, but Christ and His words; for each person swears by that to which he has regard in swearing.

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who tithe mint [Col. 0265A] and dill and cumin, and have left aside the weightier matters of the Law: judgment, mercy, and faith. Woe, he says, to you who tithe these things—not because you tithe them, but because, in tithing these, you leave aside the greater matters. [Note: [Col. 0265C] Jerome explains it thus, and Bede after Jerome: “He rebukes them for avarice, because, for the maintenance of the priests and Levites, whose portion was the Lord, they zealously demand tithes even of worthless vegetables, while they neglect judgment in the settlement of disputes, mercy toward the poor, orphans, and widows, and faith in God—the weightier matters.” Gregory, [Col. 0265D] Pastoral Rule, admonition 34: “Nor should it be heard carelessly that, when He spoke of the tithing of the smallest things, He chose indeed the least vegetables, yet mentioned fragrant ones; undoubtedly to show that hypocrites, while observing small things, seek to emit from themselves the fragrance of holy conduct; and although they neglect to fulfil the greatest things, nevertheless they observe those small matters which diffuse their scent far and wide in human judgment.”]

For these things ought to have been done, and those not omitted. Hence it is clear that it profits little to observe the lesser commandments of the Law if we abandon the greater. For whatever is built upon it falls unless the foundation is firm. Blind guides, straining out a gnat but swallowing a camel. For such is the difference between the lesser and greater commandments of the Law as between a gnat and a camel. Those strain out the gnat who fear to offend in lesser matters; but those swallow the camel who do not fear to act against the greater matters. [Note: [Col. 0265D] Jerome: “I think that, according to the sense of the present passage, the camel is the magnitude of the commandments, mercy, and faith; while the gnat is the tithes of mint, and so forth. Contrary to God’s commandment, we devour and neglect these great matters, while we display a reputation for religion through diligence in small matters that yield profit.” See Augustine, Book I, Questions on the Gospels, ch. 35; Gregory, Book I of the Morals, ch. 14.] The expression, however, is drawn from those who strain water lest they drink something [Col. 0265B] filthy. Hypocrites therefore perceive the gnat in their throat while drinking, but do not perceive the camel: through a kind of pretence they fear to commit lesser sins, but do not fear to commit greater ones.

XCVI. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who cleanse the outside of the cup and dish, but within are full of robbery and uncleanness. By the cup and dish he metaphorically means those same scribes and Pharisees, who, although inwardly full of robbery, uncleanness, and every iniquity, displayed themselves outwardly as righteous and clean. [Note: [Col. 0265D] Jerome: “In different words but with the same meaning as [Col. 0266C] above, he rebukes the Pharisees for pretence and falsehood: because they display one thing to men outwardly and do another at home; not because their superstition resided in cup and dish.” See Chrysostom, Homily 74.]

Of them he further says: Blind Pharisee, first cleanse that which is within the cup and dish, that that which is outside may become clean. For if the heart within is clean, everything [Col. 0265C] which appears outwardly will be clean. Hence the Psalmist: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Ps. L, 12); and the Apostle: “For I am conscious of nothing to myself; for from the heart proceed evil thoughts” (I Cor. IV, 4).—Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to men, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and of all uncleanness; so you also [Col. 0266A] outwardly indeed appear righteous to men, but inwardly are full of hypocrisy and iniquity. This is an exposition of what was said above and requires no exposition. [Note: [Col. 0266C] So also Jerome: “What he had demonstrated in the cup and dish . . . he now [Col. 0266D] explains by the example of tombs.”]

XCVII. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who build the tombs of the prophets and adorn the monuments of the righteous, and say: If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been their companions in the blood of the prophets. [Note: [Col. 0266] (533) There is a homily published under the name of Eusebius of Emesa, on the nativity of St Stephen, p. 19.] Thus you bear witness [Note: [Col. 0266D] “By a most prudent syllogism he convicts them of being sons of murderers.” Jerome.] against yourselves that you are the sons of those who killed the prophets.

Woe, he says, to you, [Note: [Col. 0266D] “He did not say woe to them because they build,” says Chrysostom, at the beginning of Homily 75, “nor because they accuse their fathers, but because, while doing and saying these things, they pretended to condemn their fathers, though they themselves committed worse deeds.” Likewise Bede.] not because you build and adorn the tombs of the prophets—for this is a work of piety—but because you are the sons of those who killed the prophets: sons not so much by nature as by imitation and wickedness. For just as all are called sons of Abraham because they imitate Abraham, so all wicked men are called sons of the wicked because they imitate the wicked. Hence the Lord also says to such persons: “If you were the children of Abraham, you would surely do the works of Abraham” (John VIII, 39). Woe therefore to them, because they are not sons of Abraham, of the prophets, or of the righteous, since they do not imitate them; indeed, they are sons of those who killed the prophets, imitating them in every malice and iniquity.

Moreover, they say that, had they been in their fathers’ days, they would not have been their companions in the blood of the prophets; although, being far more wicked than their fathers, they killed not only the prophets but even the Lord of the prophets Himself. Hence it follows: And you therefore fill up the measure of your fathers: run, hasten, until you reach the full and perfect [Col. 0266C] measure of their iniquity; for it would be shameful for you to degenerate from your fathers and be found less wicked than they. He says this because He saw that, in envy, they were already excessively inflamed against His own death and that of His disciples. [Note: [Col. 0266D] Jerome: “Having proved by the foregoing statements that they were sons of murderers, he now concludes what he had intended, and sets forth, as it were, the final part of the syllogism: ‘And you fill up,’ etc. ‘What was lacking to them, you complete: they killed the servants; you crucify the Lord.’”] This manner of speech is called irony by grammarians. [Note: [Col. 0266D] Chrysostom, cited above, aptly observes—and Bede after him—that He speaks “not in command, but foretelling what was to happen.”]

Serpents, brood of vipers, how shall you escape the judgment of Gehenna? For they are serpents, [Col. 0267A] because they are cunning and venomous; and a brood of vipers, [Note: [Col. 0267D] Jerome: “Just as vipers are born from vipers, so you, he says, born from murderous fathers, are murderers,” etc. Bede uses the same words.] because they are more wicked than all wicked persons, since neither wife spares husband nor children their parents. They certainly cannot otherwise escape Gehenna’s judgment unless they kill their mother, just as she too killed their father. For vipers are said to have this nature: when the female conceives, she kills the male; and when she gives birth, she is likewise killed by her offspring. [Note: [Col. 0267D] See on ch. III, v. 7, Bede, who has the same account perhaps from Aristotle, *History of Animals*, Book V, ch. 34; Pliny, Book X, ch. 62—whom Gesner and modern writers contradict—or rather from our Jerome, Letter to Praesidius; Chrysostom, Homily 11 on Matthew; Isidore of Pelusium, Book I, Letter 105; Augustine, Sermon 83 *On the Seasons*, among Augustine’s works; Gregory, *Morals*, Book XV, ch. 9, etc.] For they do not wait to emerge in the customary order of nature, but violently burst forth by rupturing their mother’s womb.

The viper, therefore, is the Synagogue; her husband is Christ. Christ came to the Synagogue, He came to His wife; after impregnating her with His seed and pouring into her the whole seed-field of evangelical preaching, she, like a venomous [Col. 0267B] and impious viper, rose against Him and killed Him. Her children, bursting forth from her impious womb, kill her, because Jews coming to the faith excommunicate and condemn her. Hence the Apostle says: “But when it pleased Him who separated me from my mother’s womb and called me by His grace” (Gal. I, 15), and so forth. For all who come from heresies to the Church condemn all heresies. It follows:

XCVIII. Therefore, behold, I send to you prophets and wise men and scribes; and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues, and persecute from city to city, that upon you may come all the righteous blood that has been shed upon the earth. For the apostles were martyrs and teachers, prophets, wise men, and scribes, whom the Lord sent to preach to the Jews and to all the [Col. 0267C] nations of the world. But the Jews killed, crucified, scourged, and persecuted them from city to city. For no Christian has anywhere been killed whom they did not kill either by their hands or in desire; hence they are said to be guilty of all, and the Lord Himself testifies that the blood of all the righteous shall come upon them.

He explains from whom and up to whom this blood extends, saying: From the blood of righteous Abel unto the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar. Since elsewhere it is written that “the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, but each shall die in his own sin” (Ezek. XVIII, 20; Jer. XXXI, 30), what does it mean that here it is now said that all righteous blood shall come upon this generation? By these [Col. 0267D] words our Saviour seems to say that this impious generation shall suffer for its own crime as great a punishment as it would suffer if it had shed the blood of all the righteous, from Abel’s blood down to [Col. 0268A] Zechariah’s. [Note: [Col. 0267D] Chrysostom, Homily 75, here adduces that passage of Exodus II, 9: “Repaying the sins of the parents upon the children unto the third and [Col. 0268D] fourth generation,” adding: “Not because anyone pays penalties for another’s sin, but because he who knows that many have been afflicted for their sins, yet has not thereby become better but commits the same things without concern, will justly bear their punishments also.” See Jansenius, *Concordance*, ch. 84, and Maldonatus on this passage.]

And this deservedly; for it was a greater crime to kill Christ and to persecute with wicked hatred His body, which is the Church, than if they had shed the blood of all preceding righteous persons. Now Zechariah son of Barachiah is nowhere recorded as having been killed; but Zechariah son of Jehoiada is recorded as having been slain in the court of the temple—namely, between the temple and the altar, which stood in the open air, where the blood of victims was poured out. Therefore, since these facts do not fit the history, a spiritual interpretation must be sought. [Note: [Col. 0268D] See Jerome on this passage; Maldonatus; à Lapide.]

For I think that our Lord calls Himself Zechariah and uses the past for the future; for Zechariah is interpreted “memory of the Lord.” Just as Christ Jesus is called the Word of the Lord, the utterance of the Lord, the power and wisdom of the Lord, so He is indeed the son of Barachiah, [Col. 0268B] which is interpreted “the blessed Lord.” Hence, when questioned by the chief priest whether He was Christ, the Son of the Blessed One, He replied, “I am.” The Jews killed Him between the temple and the altar, because there they took counsel among themselves concerning Christ’s death. For the Jews killed Christ the Lord in no other way than by taking counsel, accusing, and condemning Him; hence they themselves also said: “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death” (John XVIII, 31). But that counsel concerning His death was held in the court of the temple, He Himself shows through the Psalmist, saying: “Those who sat in the gate spoke against me, and those who drank wine sang of me” (Ps. LXVIII, 13). Thus Zechariah son of Barachiah was killed between the temple and the altar.

Jerusalem, Jerusalem, [Col. 0268C] who killest the prophets and stonest those sent to thee: how often I wished to gather thy children together, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and thou wouldst not. I, He says, wished many times to gather your children together and defend them from the assault of evil spirits flying above and around them, just as a hen gathers her chicks and hides them beneath her wings, lest troublesome birds snatch them away from her. [Note: [Col. 0268D] See Augustine, Book I, *Questions on the Gospels*, ch. 36, and Tractate 15 on John.] But you would not. Therefore I willed it, but on the condition that you too should will it. Since, therefore, you would not be gathered together and saved, I too now no longer will to gather and save them. Hence I say: “Scatter them in thy power, and destroy them, O Lord, my protector” (Ps. LVIII, 12). For the Lord, who can do whatsoever He wills, wills to save no one except him [Col. 0268D] who wills to be saved by Him. [Note: [Col. 0268D] More is inserted in the homily, p. 21.]

Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate; likewise in the Psalms: “Behold, I fled far away and remained in solitude” (Ps. LIV, 8). For, having left the Jews, the Lord dwells among the Gentiles. [Col. 0269A] For I say to you, you shall not see me henceforth until you say: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. After, He says, I leave you in this bodily presence in which I have lived among you for a time, you shall not see Me henceforth until you more fully recognize Me when I come again for judgment, and all together, with one harmonious voice, say: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0269D] Isaiah XLIX, 18 and XLV, 24. Bede: “We are certainly compelled to understand this mystically of that coming of His in which He will come in glory.” Perhaps from Chrysostom—for Bede copies the rest from Jerome—who in Homily 75 says: “For in this place He signifies the future day of the second coming.”] For this is what He says elsewhere: “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess.” [Note: [Col. 0269D] Thus far the homily falsely attributed to Eusebius of Emesa.]

XCIX. [CHAPTER XXIV.] And Jesus, going out from the temple, was departing; and His disciples came to show Him the buildings of the [Col. 0269B] temple. But He answered and said to them: Do you see all these things? Amen I say to you, not one stone shall be left here upon another which shall not be thrown down. For these things were fulfilled under Titus and Vespasian.

And as He sat upon the Mount of Olives, His disciples came to Him privately, saying: Tell us when these things shall be, and what shall be the sign of Thy coming and of the consummation of the age? Their very question teaches what Christ’s disciples understood. For when they heard of the destruction of the temple, they thought the consummation of the age would immediately follow. [Note: [Col. 0269D] So Chrysostom, Homily 76: “For they thought that His coming would occur immediately then as well.”]

And Jesus answered and said to them: See that no one deceives you; for many shall come in my name, saying, I am Christ, and shall deceive many. For we have heard that Simon Magus did this, [Note: [Col. 0269D] Jerome and Bede also name Simon Magus here: “The first of them,” he says, “was Simon Magus; but the last, greater than the rest, is Antichrist.”] and we read that Antichrist will do it as well. For he, as the Apostle says, “shall exalt himself above everything which is called God or is worshipped, so that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God” (II Thess. XXI, 4).

—[Col. 0269C] But you shall hear of wars and reports of wars: see that you are not troubled. For these things must happen, but the end is not yet. For from Christ’s birth, when the angels sang, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will” (Luke II, 14), throughout the time in which our Lord, the Prince of Peace, lived in this world, there was great peace and concord everywhere among the nations. [Note: [Col. 0269D] By way of excuse or some charitable interpretation, this must concern a particular kind of warfare. For from Florus, Velleius Paterculus, and others, the Armenian war followed shortly after Christ’s birth, to which Gaius Caesar was sent; and the Parthians [Col. 0270D] were allied with the Armenians. Add the Jews in revolt. The Varian disaster in Germany in A.D. 9 and the revolt of the Dalmatians were also notable; Germanicus’ triumph in A.D. 17 over the Cherusci, Chatti, and others; the Gauls revolted from the Roman commander; Tacfarinas in Africa; the Thracians were subdued by Sabinus; and the Frisians, although at Christ’s death they inflicted a defeat on the Romans. But in truth these wars were not of such grave consequence as were certain others in earlier times.]

After His departure, wars gradually began to occur, seditions to arise, and reports of wars to be heard everywhere. But these were not signs of the end and consummation of the age; for those things which will precede the end of the world shall be far greater and more terrible. Of them it follows: For nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom; and there shall be pestilences, [Col. 0270A] famines, and great earthquakes in various places. But all these things are the beginnings of sorrows.

For all these things have already occurred; yet in comparison with what is to come, they were so small that, when those things come, they will be taken as a sign and will plainly declare that the world can no longer stand, linger, or endure much longer. For, as is said in what follows, there will then be tribulation such as has not been nor shall be. [Note: [Col. 0270D] “For there shall then be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor shall be.”] Since then the son of perdition and discord will be born, wars, quarrels, disputes, and every evil must occur everywhere. For as peace preceded Christ, so discord will precede Antichrist.

Then they shall hand you over to tribulation and kill you, and you shall be hated by all nations because of my name. Although these things happened to the apostles, they must nevertheless be referred to the end, [Col. 0270B] since we do not read that signs such as these occurred in the apostles’ time. And then many shall be offended, and shall betray one another, and shall hate one another. And many false prophets shall arise and deceive many. For these will be the greatest and principal cause of all offence, hatred, and tribulation: acting according to Satan’s power, they will give many signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error. [Note: [Col. 0270D] Jerome: “He did not deny the faith of all, but of many; for love will remain in the apostles and those like them.”] Hence it follows: And because iniquity shall abound, the charity of many shall grow cold. For the charity of many will fail and grow cold from the fire of divine love, because iniquity will abound in many ways.

But he who perseveres unto the end, he shall be saved. He, He says, who perseveres in goodness and does not depart from the Catholic faith either through threats, flatteries, signs, [Col. 0270C] or wonders—he, and no other, shall be saved. And the Gospel of the kingdom shall be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations. For just as in the primitive Church the sound of the apostles went forth into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world, so in the last days the Gospel of God’s kingdom shall be preached throughout the whole world to all nations, so that no one may have any excuse.

And then shall the consummation come. For after, through this preaching, the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in and Israel is saved, then the world too will end. [Note: [Col. 0270D] Hilary interprets this of the time preceding Jerusalem’s overthrow: “And when knowledge of the heavenly mystery has been brought to all, then Jerusalem’s downfall and end shall come upon her.” Victor of Antioch likewise, on Mark ch. XIII, and Chrysostom, [Col. 0271C] Homily 76: “It is the greatest proof of Christ’s omnipotence. For within twenty years, or at most thirty, the Gospel traversed all the regions of the world; [Col. 0271D] after this the end of Jerusalem shall arrive.” But Bede, with our author, interprets it of the world’s end: “He plainly signifies that the end of the world will not come before the Gospel is preached throughout the whole world.” Jerome too, although he seems to have thought the end of the world near to his own age: “The sign of the Lord’s coming is that the Gospel is preached throughout the whole world, so that none may be excusable. This we see either already accomplished or about shortly to be accomplished; for I do not think that any nation remains which does not know Christ’s name. And although it has not had a preacher, it cannot be ignorant of the report of the faith from neighbouring nations.” But above all Augustine, Letters 197 and 199 to Hesychius; in one of these, §49: “How, therefore, was this preaching completed by the apostles, when there are still nations, as is most certain to us, among whom it has now begun to be fulfilled, and among whom it has not yet begun?”] And the Church shall be brought to completion and shall rejoice in the fullness of her children.

C. “Therefore, when you see the abomination of desolation, [Col. 0271A] spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place—let the reader understand” [Note: [Col. 0271D] In the homily attributed to Eusebius of Emesa, for the twenty-seventh Sunday after Pentecost [Col. 0272C], there are first set forth the passages in Daniel concerning the seventy weeks; then follows the exposition of Matthew, p. 183, in the form found here.].

“When,” he says, “you see the abomination of desolation”: when you see the abominable and desolating Antichrist [Note: [Col. 0272D] Although many Fathers, such as Chrysostom, Homily 76, interpret this of Caesar’s statue placed in the Temple—a view mentioned by Jerome, Victor, and Bede—yet they think that Antichrist also may be understood with our author: “as the Apostle Paul most plainly preached,” says Bede after Jerome, who cites the Apostle’s passage at 2 Thessalonians II, 4.], who will cause great abomination and desolation among God’s people, so lifted up and exalted that he sits in God’s Temple, displaying himself as though he were God—then let whoever reads these and other things understand that the end is now at hand.

For he shall reign, as it is written in Daniel, “for a time and times and half a time” (Dan. XII, 7), that is, for one year, two years, and half a year. During these there will be such persecution that every previous persecution, however great, will be consigned to oblivion. Then those who are in Judaea must flee to the mountains; and whoever is on the roof must not come down to take anything from his house; [Col. 0271B] and whoever is in the field must not turn back to take his cloak.

These words seem to indicate great terror: people are described as forgetting everything, with flight alone pleasing them above all things. Allegorically, those flee from Judaea to the mountains who, leaving Judaism—or the letter in which the Jews trusted—pass over to spiritual understanding or to the churches [Note: [Col. 0272D] Jerome: “We must flee from Judaea to the mountains; that is, leaving the killing letter, we must draw near to the eternal mountains, from which God wonderfully gives light; and we must be on the roof and the housetop, where the devil’s fiery darts cannot reach; nor must we descend to take anything from the house of our former manner of life,” etc. The same in Bede.].

Those who are on the roof, in the height of faith—or also those who are greater persons and preside over churches—must not descend or bend themselves toward fleeting goods and contemptible possessions. Rather, leaving everything behind, they must hasten to meet Christ, who is now drawing near. But those in the field, who sow among the people the new seed of the Gospel, must not turn back or remember their former cloak. They must run, since the time is near when, stripped of the old garments, they will put on the new garment of immortality [Col. 0271C].

“But woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days” [Note: [Col. 0272D] Bede: “The soul found occupied with carnal desires in that final persecution is necessarily crushed under everlasting woe.”].

The pregnant are those souls which wish through hypocrisy to conceal their sins, yet cannot conceal them because of the swelling of pride. Thus their sins are hidden within, yet in some way shine forth without. Those who nurse are souls that have already brought forth evil deeds and, persisting in them, are not ashamed to do them. Would that they were still only pregnant and had not, by their example, given others an occasion for sinning. It is evil, then, to hide sins [Col. 0272A], but worse to reveal them in this way: for otherwise one harms oneself, but in this way both oneself and others.

“Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath.” Perhaps you may begin to flee when you are unable to flee. Flight is hindered in winter by the harshness of the weather; but on the Sabbath it is not permitted to flee, because the Law forbids it.

“For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor ever shall be.” There will then, he says, be great tribulation. When? Do you wish to hear when? When the abomination of desolation stands in the holy place. “And unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved; but for the elect’s sake those days shall be shortened.”

Those days will not be shortened with respect to God’s ordering; nevertheless, they will be shortened with respect to the hope and expectation [Col. 0272B] of the wicked, because Antichrist will not reign for as long as he himself and his followers hope that he will reign. This will happen for the sake of the elect: for if he lived as long as unbelievers hope that he will live, very few could be saved. For what would he do, if he lived forever, when in three years he will make such devastation?

“Then if anyone says to you, ‘Behold, here is Christ,’ or, ‘There,’ do not believe it.” By these words he signifies that not only Antichrist but also many others will then arise, whom miserable people, because of their various pretences, will think to be Christ. Hence he adds: “For false Christs and false prophets will arise and give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led astray. Behold, I have told you beforehand.”

But why have I told you beforehand? So that you may be on guard [Col. 0272C] and not be deceived by them. “Therefore, if they say to you, ‘Behold, he is in the wilderness,’ do not go out; ‘Behold, he is in the inner rooms,’ do not believe it.” For some will preach in the wilderness, like Elijah and John the Baptist; others in synagogues and houses, like Christ. They will feign everything that they hear people have done.

“For as [115] lightning comes out of the east and appears even to the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.” This is what the Psalmist says: “God will come manifestly; our God, and he will not keep silence” (Ps. XLIX, 3). He will not [Col. 0273A] come hidden as before; rather, shining like the sun in its majesty, he will appear everywhere and shine everywhere. He will be revealed even to all who are unwilling.

“Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered.” The eagles are the souls of the saints, which both fly higher and see more clearly [Note: [Col. 0273C] Bede: “He indicates the zeal of the saints: [Col. 0273D] because the eagle, surpassing other birds in flight, delights to fix its eyes upon the very ray of the sun.”]. Then, coming to their own bodies, wherever and however these have been scattered, they will put them on again, so that the whole, complete, immortal human being may rise. It may also be understood thus: wherever Christ’s body is, there too the souls gather, ready to obey his commands.

“Immediately after the tribulation of those days, the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, the stars will fall from heaven, the powers of heaven will be shaken, and then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven. And [Col. 0273B] then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty.”

For when Christ our Lord, the Sun of righteousness, brighter than every light, descends from heaven, this sun which we see will be darkened, and this moon will not give its light, being obscured by the immeasurable splendour of the greater light [Note: [Col. 0273D] “The sun and moon will be darkened, and the other stars will fall from heaven, not by a diminution of their light, but because, in comparison with the true Light, all things visible will seem dark,” etc. JEROME.].
