For just as the moon and stars grow pale before the splendour of this sun, so by his indescribable radiance the sun itself will be turned into darkness.

When he says that the stars will fall, he means either that the souls of the saints descend to their bodies, or that the stars themselves, literally, as though falling and passing away, lose their customary light. The powers of heaven will be shaken because that entire host of angels will follow Christ our Lord to judgment. [Col. 0273C]

“And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven,” by which we may understand either his cross or another sign of victory [Note: [Col. 0273D] Jerome and Bede say almost the same: “By the sign here, let us understand either the cross or the banner of triumphant victory.”]. “And then all the tribes of the earth will mourn.” Therefore it is written in the prophet Zechariah: “They shall mourn for him as for an only-begotten son, and grieve over him as people grieve at the death of a firstborn. In that day there shall be a great mourning in Jerusalem, like the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the plain of Megiddo. And the families of the land shall mourn, each family separately” (Zech. XII, 10). For how could they fail to mourn over him when they see him in such glory, whom they crucified with such great reproach?

It follows: “And he will send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice, and [Col. 0274A] they will gather his elect from the four winds, from the highest parts of heaven to their limits.” By the ministry of angels, God’s saints will be gathered and raised from all parts of the world: souls descending from the heights of heaven and coming even to its bounds. For when he says “with a trumpet,” he himself explains it by saying, “and with a loud voice.” For the loud voice that raises the dead will fill the whole world.

“Learn the parable from the fig tree: when its branch has already become tender and its leaves have sprung forth, you know that summer is near. So also you, when you see all these things, know that he is near, at the doors.” For just as the fig tree, when new branches and leaves arise, announces that summer is near, so all these great and unprecedented things will most plainly announce Christ’s coming.

“Amen I say to you: this generation shall not pass away until all these things come to pass.” This is understood of the generation of scribes and Pharisees, upon whom he had previously said that all righteous blood would come. Therefore that generation will not pass away first; it will not perish first, nor wholly cease from its wickedness, before all these things are fulfilled [Col. 0274B] [Note: [Col. 0273D] Jerome here and on ch. XXIII, 36: “It is the rule of Scripture to set forth two generations, one of the good and one of the wicked.”].

“Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.” For what Truth says is unchangeable and cannot pass away; otherwise it would not be Truth. Heaven and earth, then, shall pass away, because they will be changed for the better from the state in which they presently are; but the words of Truth cannot be changed from their condition [Note: [Col. 0273D] Thus far the homily.].

“But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, but the Father alone.” Another Evangelist adds, “not even the Son” [Col. 0274C] (Mark XIII, 32). Great, then, is this mystery, which no one knows but the Father—that is, the power and wisdom of the Father, which is simultaneously one and the same as that of the Son and the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Trinity alone, one God, knows this mystery, which the Son himself also does not know insofar as he is man and Son of Man.

For if, insofar as he is man, he knew everything, it would never have been said [Note: [Col. 0273D] Luke II, 52 [printed “XXXI,” evidently an OCR error]. And Jesus increased in wisdom and age and favour with God and human beings.], “But Jesus increased in wisdom and age before God and human beings” [Note: [Col. 0273D] The question arising from these passages in Matthew and Mark is famous. Adding the third passage which our author here supplies from Luke, the Arians—or descendants of the Arians, from whom there also arose a new kind of heretics, called Agnoetae because they attributed this ignorance to Christ—raised it against Catholics. On them see Leontius, *On Sects*; Eulogius and Basil of Cilicia in Photius; Nicephorus Callistus; and, among more recent writers, Petavius, *De Trinitate*, book XI, ch. 3, and *De Incarnatione*, book I, ch. 16; book XI, ch. 1.

Our author’s opinion was the same as that of certain Fathers “of great and most celebrated name in the Church,” as Petavius says in the cited book XI, whom he himself names, as does Maldonatus on this passage. Petavius says that, although at first hearing this opinion seems shocking, it has a true meaning once interpreted—namely, if it signifies “the reason,” and Jesus Christ is said not to know that day “because he is man,” but nevertheless knows it because he is God-man. This is also Menochius’s interpretation, and seems to be Gregory’s in his letter to Eulogius, book X, epistle 39: Christ knows the day and hour of judgment “in the nature of divinity,” but not “from the nature of humanity.”

Others, such as a Lapide and Tirinus, say that Christ, as man, does not know the day of judgment insofar as he spoke to human beings [Col. 0275C]. This interpretation coincides with another in Jansen, *Concordia*, ch. 123, and is nearly the common one: he is said not to know because he makes us ignorant, as Augustine says in book LXXXIII, question 60, and book I, *On the Trinity*, ch. 12, and Bede on this passage—that is, because he does not reveal it to us and received from the Father that it was not to be communicated to human beings. Or the statement must be referred to him, not “according to that by which he is the head, but according to his body,” as Gregory says in the cited book.

Hilary’s explanation, who discusses this matter at length in book IX of *On the Trinity*, no. 63, differs very little—indeed not at all—from this explanation. He writes that God then professes ignorance when “either it is not the time for speaking or it is an economy for not acting.” The latter words, moreover, supply another explanation, that of Epiphanius, *Heresy* 69, no. 44: the day of judgment is said to be unknown because the day for instituting the judgment has not yet arrived. This they call experimental knowledge. By this also they explain Luke’s passage about Christ’s progress and wisdom, insofar as “according to the progress of his age he performed more perfect works,” as St Thomas says, *Summa Theologiae*, III, question 7, article 12, reply to objection 3; he also treats Christ’s experimental knowledge there, [Col. 0276C] question 15, article 8. Others, such as Tirinus, explain in another way the experimental wisdom in which Christ advanced, namely wisdom acquired by practice, etc.

What if we say that Christ as man did not know that day by experimental knowledge—that is, in respect of the particular moment of time when it would occur, so that no experience of affairs, knowledge of times, or conjecture drawn from human experience could attain foreknowledge of it? This certainly would be most appropriate to the entire context and to the Lord’s discourse.].

“As it was in the days of Noah, so shall the coming of the Son of Man be.” And he explains this. [116] “For as in the days before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day [Col. 0275A] Noah entered the ark, and did not know until the flood came and took them all away, so shall be the coming of the Son of Man.”

For after Antichrist has died and peace has been restored to the earth, while all the saints await the last day because of signs which they will not see, unbelievers and sinners, thinking only of earthly and transitory things, will devote themselves, as before, to every pleasure: selling and buying, eating and drinking, contracting marriages, and doing similar things. But behold: when they say, “Peace and security,” “then sudden destruction will come upon them” (1 Thess. V, 3).

“Then two will be in the field; one will be taken and one left.” The field is the world, as the Lord himself says in explaining the parable which says, “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good [Col. 0275B] seed in his field” (Matt. XIII, 24). In this field are two, namely the faithful and the unbeliever: the faithful will be taken into glory, but the unbeliever will be left for punishment.

“Two women grinding at the mill: one will be taken and one left.” This mill seems to be the holy Church, in which, while we grind the grain of sayings, expound the Scriptures, and turn everything into flour, we prepare the bread of God’s word by which souls are nourished. Yet not all who grind, but only the good, will be taken into glory. Rightly they are called not two but two women, because such grinding pertains to souls. Nevertheless, this may quite fittingly be understood of the Synagogue and the Church [Note: [Col. 0276D] Jerome: “In the two who remain in the field and in the two women who grind together, understand either the Synagogue and the Church, because they seem to grind together in the Law and from the same Scriptures to produce the flour of God’s commandments; or the other heresies, which seem from both Testaments, or from one of them, to grind the flour of their doctrines . . . yet they do not receive the same reward: some are taken and others left.” See Hilary, ch. 26, no. 5.]. Both grind; both expound the Scriptures [Col. 0275C]; yet one, and not both, is taken.

“Watch therefore, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come.” Why is this so? Because, as we have just said, no one knows the day or hour. “But know this: if the master of the house knew at what hour the thief would come, he would surely watch and would not allow his house to be broken into.” Because he does not know, because in sleeping he is negligent, the house is often broken into, and whatever is best in it becomes the plunder of thieves.

But you, be ready; be diligent; and because you do not know that one hour, watch at every hour, lest you be found heedless and sleeping in that hour. This is what he says: “Therefore you also be [Col. 0276A] ready, because you do not know at what hour the Son of Man will come.”

“Who do you suppose is the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord appointed over his household, to give them food in due season?” Who, he says, except each one of you and others like you? Who are the faithful and prudent servants whom the Lord has appointed over his household, over his house and Church, so that you may govern, teach, and feed it, and do everything according to time and measure, order and reason?

“Blessed is that servant whom his lord, when he comes, finds so doing.” But why is he blessed? Do you wish to hear why? “Amen I say to you, he will appoint him over all his goods.” For who will be happier than the person appointed over all things? In that very respect in which [Col. 0276B] he humbled himself more and served everyone, the faithful servant will be greater and superior to all.

“But if that evil servant says in his heart, ‘My lord delays his coming,’ and begins to strike his fellow servants, and eats and drinks with the drunken, the lord of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour which he does not know, and will divide him, and assign his portion with the hypocrites; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

For whoever, hoping to live long in this life, [117] loving only perishable and transitory things, and subjecting himself to all fleshly pleasures, eats and drinks not soberly with the sober but intemperately with the drunken, strikes servants, oppresses the household, and despises those subject to him—such a man, though not in speech, nevertheless in heart and deed cries: “My lord delays his coming; I am safe; I fear nothing now; [Col. 0276C] therefore I shall obey my own will.”

When his lord comes on the day he does not expect and at the hour he does not know, compelling him suddenly to leave this life, he divides him. For what is death but the division and separation of body and soul? Thus a human being is divided when the body is separated from the soul. He assigns his portion with the hypocrites: now he afflicts the soul for the time being, but afterwards both body and soul.

CI. [CHAPTER XXV.] [Note: [Col. 0276D] This is a homily of Eusebius of Emesa for the feast of Virgins, p. 232. Always understand St Bruno of Asti.] “Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom and bride.”

What does “then” mean [Col. 0277A]? Is it not also like this now? It is indeed so even now, but this likeness does not yet appear openly. It will be so “then,” therefore, when this likeness is manifest; for it does not yet appear which virgins are foolish and which prudent. Many appear outwardly prudent who are inwardly foolish. For all who perform their works in order to be seen by others are foolish, although they may seem prudent. It is great folly to fast, keep vigil, afflict and mortify the flesh, and thereby expect no reward other than empty glory. Of such people the Lord says: “Amen I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 2).

Hence all are called virgins because they appear good to everyone. Thus they are virgins in action [Col. 0277B], but corrupt in intention, because they do not perform their good deeds with a chaste and sincere intention. But why are these virgins called ten? This number signifies all, because it contains all numbers within itself [Note: [Col. 0277C] Jerome: “The ten virgins encompass all human beings who appear to believe in God.” Hilary: “In the five prudent and five foolish virgins there is established, without qualification, a division of believers and unbelievers.” Augustine, Sermon 93, no. 2: “These five and five virgins are absolutely all the souls of Christians.”].

Therefore, when he says, “The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins,” it is as though he said, “The holy Church is like all virgins.” He immediately explains the likeness itself: “They took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom and bride.” Since we daily draw near to death, we daily go out to meet the bridegroom and bride—that is, Christ and the Church—for this way ends together with life.

We take lamps if we carry good works with us [Note: [Col. 0277D] Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, 59: “They are lamps because works done according to this continence are carried in the hands.” The same author, Epistle 104, no. 75: “The lamps that are lit are good works, of course.” And St Gregory, book IX, epistle 39: “Our lamps, indeed, are good works.”]. For the Lord himself shows that good works are called lamps, saying: “So [Col. 0277C] let your light shine before human beings, so that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16).

“Five of them were foolish and five prudent.” This signifies that some in the Church are vain and foolish, while others are prudent and just. Something may also be understood from the number itself: there are five bodily senses through which people become either prudent or foolish.

But “the five foolish, having taken their lamps, did not take oil with them; whereas the prudent took oil in their vessels with their lamps” [Note: [Col. 0277D] Jerome: “We can interpret the five wise virgins and the five foolish ones as the five senses: some hasten toward heavenly things and desire what is above, while others, longing for earthly dregs, lack the fuel of truth by which they may illuminate their hearts.” See Augustine, the cited *Eighty-Three Questions*, and Epistle 140, no. 33.].

The lamps of the foolish are as though without oil: although their works may seem to shine for a time, they are extinguished together with them, because after this life they supply them with no light. But the lamps of the prudent, because they are nourished by the sincere oil of piety and mercy, shine more brightly when they pass from these darknesses into life. Therefore the Apostle says: “Do not therefore judge before the time, until the Lord comes; he will both illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts; and then praise will come to each from God” (1 Cor. IV, 5).

For then it will be revealed to all which lamps have oil and which do not. Then will be fulfilled the saying written concerning the Church: “Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates” [Col. 0278B] (Prov. XXXI, 31).

“But while the bridegroom delayed, they all became drowsy and slept.” The bridegroom delays and postpones his coming until the Lord comes for judgment. This delay is as long as the span of the present age. In the meantime all grow drowsy and sleep, because after many infirmities they finally close their eyes in the sleep of death [Note: [Col. 0277D] “They all became drowsy, that is, they died, because the death of saints is called sleep.” Jerome. Gregory, Homily 12 on the Gospels: “While the Judge delays his coming [Col. 0278C] for the final judgment, the elect and reprobate are lulled in the sleep of death. For to sleep is to die. But to become drowsy before sleep is to languish from health before death.”].

For just as becoming drowsy before sleep is to languish and become sick before death, so “at midnight a cry was made: ‘Behold, the bridegroom comes; go out [118] to meet him.’” Of this cry the Apostle says: “For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise incorruptible” [Note: [Col. 0278D] 1 Corinthians XV, 52. Jerome likewise: “Suddenly, as in the dead of night and while all are secure, when sleep is deepest, Christ’s coming will resound through the cries of angels and the trumpets of the powers going before.” St Augustine, in the cited work: “Clearly this cry is that trumpet which the Apostle mentions when he says, ‘It will sound,’” etc.].

This cry will occur at midnight, because, while all are ignorant, the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night [Note: [Col. 0278D] Gregory, Homily 12: “The cry concerning the bridegroom’s coming is at midnight because the day of judgment steals upon us in such a way that its coming cannot be foreseen; hence it is written: ‘The day of the Lord like a thief,’ etc.”]. It occurs in the night [Col. 0278C] because it occurs in the darkness of ignorance.

“Then all those virgins arose and trimmed their lamps.” For, as the Apostle says, “We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed” [Note: [Col. 0278D] 1 Corinthians XV, 53. See Augustine, Epistle 140.]. They trim their lamps when they review their works within themselves and consider what words of answer they may find worthy [Note: [Col. 0278D] St Augustine, cited *Eighty-Three Questions*: “They trimmed their lamps, that is, the accounts to be rendered for their deeds.” And in the cited epistle, ch. 34: “They trim their lamps, that is, they prepare to render an account of their works.”].

When the foolish cannot find such an answer, they begin to show this, and distrustful of their own testimony, themselves demand the testimony of others. This is what he says: “But the foolish said to the wise, ‘Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out.’”

The foolish seek oil because they need mercy; it is as though they said: “Because our works fail to shine, illuminate them by your testimony” [Note: [Col. 0279C] Gregory, *Morals*, book VIII, ch. 31: “To ask for oil from one’s neighbours is to beg for the glory of a good work from the testimony of another’s lips.”].

“The wise answered, saying: ‘Perhaps there will not be enough for us and you; go rather to the sellers and buy for yourselves.’” Do not seek oil from us, they say, nor urge us to imitate you. Go instead to the sellers; go to flatterers, who for the cheap price of praise and favour robbed you of all your good works. For you did everything in order to be seen by them [Note: [Col. 0279C] The same author, ibid.: “The foolish virgins, who had not taken oil in their vessels, had glory in the voices of others, not in their own consciences”; and Homily 12 on the Gospels: “The sellers of oil are flatterers.” St Augustine, Sermon 93, no. 12: “What is the oil of the sinner except the flatterer’s blandishments?” He says the same in his exposition of Psalm CXL, no. 13, and Psalm CXLVII, no. 11, where he speaks of this parable; and in Epistle 140, no. 70: “To carry one’s own oil is not to depend upon another’s praise.”].

For we ourselves are not yet wholly secure concerning ourselves [Note: [Col. 0279D] St Augustine, Epistle 140, ch. 31: “‘Perhaps there will not be enough for us and you’ was said not despairingly but humbly. For who can so presume upon his or her conscience as to be certain that it will suffice at God’s judgment, unless the merciful Judge judges mercifully?” And ch. 34: “In answering, they say that they do not know whether the conscience by which they expect mercy will suffice for them under that Judge. When he sits upon the throne, who will boast that he has a chaste heart, or who will boast that he is clean from sin?” etc.]. Hence the blessed apostle Peter says: “And if the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and sinner appear?” (1 Pet. IV, 18 [printed “8,” evidently an OCR error].)

“But while they went to buy, the bridegroom came; and those who were ready entered with him into the wedding feast; and the door was shut” [Col. 0279B]. “While they went to buy,” he says, that is, while they returned in mind to the things they had done in this age; while they considered with what intention they had done their works; while they recalled that they had already received for them the reward of praise—the bridegroom came. For buying then will be nothing other than considering the manner of buying and selling.

“Finally, the remaining virgins also come, saying, ‘Lord, Lord, open to us.’ But he answered and said, ‘Amen I say to you, I do not know you.’” The Lord, who knows all things, says that he does not know the foolish virgins [Note: [Col. 0279D] St Augustine, Sermon 93, no. 16: “Does he who knows all things not know them? What then does ‘I do not know you’ mean? ‘I disapprove of you; I reject you.’”], because their names are not written in the book of life. For the Lord’s not knowing is his rejecting.

CII. “For it is like a man going abroad, who called his servants and entrusted his goods to them” [Note: [Col. 0280C] Matt. 25:14. This is a homily falsely attributed to Emisenus, *On the Feast of a Confessor*, 1, p. 222, beginning: “This man is understood to be our Lord and Savior, who, returning from this world to the Father,” etc.]; and what follows. [Col. 0279C] For just as a man going abroad [Note: [Col. 0280C] Jerome: “This man, the master of the household, is undoubtedly Christ, who, ascending victorious to the Father after the resurrection, called the apostles and entrusted to them the teaching of the Gospel,” etc.] entrusted his goods to his servants, so too our Savior, returning from this world to the Father, first bestowed his goods upon his faithful ones. And to one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one, to each according to his own ability; and he departed at once.

The five talents [Note: [Col. 0280D] This whole interpretation is from Gregory, Homily 9 on the Gospels, though the author expands and embellishes it further. St. Ambrose also, explaining a similar parable in Book VIII on Luke, writes: “Finally, one made ten minas from one mina, another five; perhaps the former represents moral teaching, because there are five bodily senses, while the latter represents the twofold—that is, the mystical teaching of the Law and the moral teaching of uprightness. Hence Matthew sets down five talents and two.”] are the five senses of the body; the two are understanding and action; the one, however, is understanding alone. Although these were naturally given to human beings from the beginning, the Lord nevertheless gave them anew to his faithful ones, and in some manner renewed them, by showing that they should be possessed more inwardly than outwardly. For the soul too has sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—and these are far more excellent than those in the body. The senses of the body are shared with other animals; the senses of the soul, however, we share with angels.

Now he who had received five talents went away, worked with them, and gained another five. Likewise he who had received two gained another two. But he who had received one went away, dug into the earth, and hid his master’s money. We shall explain all these things below.

But after a long time [Col. 0280B] the master of those servants came and settled accounts with them. He comes after a long time, because there is a long interval between Christ’s first and second coming [Note: [Col. 0280D] Jerome: “There is a great interval between the Savior’s ascension and his second coming.”]. Then the Lord will settle accounts with his servants, because, as the Apostle says, “We shall all stand before the judgment-seat of Christ [Note: [Col. 0280D] Rom. 14:10 and 2 Cor. 5:10: “For we shall all stand,” etc., “so that each may receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.”],” so that each may render an account of the things he has done, whether they were good or evil.

And the one who had received five talents came forward and offered another five talents, saying: “Lord, you entrusted five talents to me; behold, I have gained another five. You gave me sight: I worked with it and enlightened many. What I saw I showed; what I understood I taught. I did not conceal or hide what you deigned to reveal to my eyes” [Note: [Col. 0280D] St. Gregory, On the Song of Songs, ch. 2, speaking of the bride’s eyes, teaches that through tears she enlightens peoples: “They wash themselves with tears, so that through them peoples may fittingly be cleansed before God.”]. “Therefore I have this talent multiplied.

[Col. 0280C] You also gave me hearing. In this too I labored, and opened the ears of many others, teaching them to hear and understand the words of your mysteries. For this is the talent the Lord required when he said: ‘He who has ears to hear, let him hear’ (Matt. 13:43; Mark 4:9); and again: ‘To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not [Col. 0281A] understand’ (Luke 8:10).

“You also gave me taste, by which, understanding the flavor of your sweetness, I say: ‘How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth’ (Ps. 118:103). And in this too I labored, inviting others with me to taste, saying: ‘Taste and see how gracious the Lord is; blessed is the man who hopes in him’ (Ps. 31:9).

“But what shall I say of smell, by which I instructed your faithful people how they might discern between Catholic teaching and the foul stench of heretical perversity? Drawn by this, your servants follow you, saying: ‘Draw us after you, and we shall run after the fragrance of your ointments’ (Song 1:3). For this reason the holy Church is also praised for its nose, where it is said: ‘Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward [Col. 0281B] Damascus’ [Note: [Col. 0281C] Gregory I, explaining this passage of the Song: “In the nose,” he says, “there is discernment of smell. [Col. 0281D] Therefore through the nose is signified the discernment of preachers, because through them the fragrances of virtues and the stenches of vices are shown to us.”] (Song 7:3).

“Moreover, I also labored with touch, and gained no less through it than through the other talents. The touch of the soul is faith: by it the Lord is held and touched” [Note: [Col. 0281D] Bede on Mark, ch. 8: “We touch the Lord when we cleave to him with whole and sincere faith.”]. “For the more faithful anyone is, the more familiarly and closely he touches the Lord. Some touch him himself; others the fringe of his garment. We double this talent when we preach our faith to others.”

But let us hear what the Lord answered him who offered the five talents doubled: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a few things, I shall set you over many; enter into the joy of your Lord.” For *euge* is the utterance of one rejoicing [Note: [Col. 0281D] Bede: “‘Euge’ is an exclamation of one who is glad; and the Lord, rejoicing rightly, commands the good and faithful servant to enter into his joy.”].

But observe that the Lord considers even the best things we possess in this world to be few. In this he shows the riches of that kingdom to be beyond estimation [Col. 0281C], concerning which the Apostle says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9). These talents, therefore, are small in comparison with those riches, since through them we can neither see nor hear, nor fully conceive what those riches are like [Note: [Col. 0281D] Jerome: “It must be noted that all things which we possess in the present, though they seem great and numerous, are nevertheless small and few in comparison with future things. ‘Enter,’ he says, ‘into the joy of your Lord, and receive what neither eye,’ etc.]. For who can conceive what has not entered into the human heart?

“Enter into the joy of your Lord.” Of these joys the Psalmist says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83:5); and again: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26:4).

These things have been said concerning the five talents. Now let us hear about the two, by which, as we said, understanding and action are signified [Note: [Col. 0281D] Jerome: “And this man … understood knowledge and the works of the present life as types of future blessedness.”]. Though they are fewer in number, they are not inferior in worth or significance. For one who understands rightly and does what he understands lacks nothing of sight and hearing, nothing of taste, smell, and touch. Those five are most fully contained in these two, which are joined to one another, and neither can prevail without the other. For understanding without action is useless, and action without understanding is useless. Hence it is well said: “Good understanding belongs to all who do it; his praise endures for ever and ever [Col. 0282B] [Note: [Col. 0281D] Ps. 110:115 [sic]. St. Prosper, on this Psalm: “He has good understanding who does what he rightly understands ought to be done.” Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 15, [Col. 0282C] p. 226: “Wisdom shown through deeds is superior to that which shines in speech. For good [Col. 0282D] understanding,” etc.].”

Therefore the one who had received two talents also came forward and said: “Lord, you entrusted two talents to me; behold, I have gained another [120] two. You gave me understanding and action; for you give understanding to those who understand [Note: [Col. 0282D] See Augustine, *City of God*, Book XIX, ch. 14; Sermon 365, §3; Sermon 18 on Psalm 118; etc.]. You also grant both good will and the power to act well. Hence the Apostle says: ‘It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy’ (Rom. 9:16). For willing is not from the one who wills, nor running from the one who runs, but from God who shows mercy, who first grants the will to act rightly and then the capacity to run rightly. Therefore you entrusted two talents to me; behold, I have gained another two, because I was not lazy in teaching others what they should understand and how, once they understand, they ought to act.”

The Lord therefore answered him and rejoiced with him, granting gifts no smaller [Col. 0282C] than those he had just bestowed above upon the other. Let us now consider the one who went away, dug into the earth, and hid his master’s money. By him, of course, we understand those to whom the Lord gave natural ability and understanding, which they bury and hide in an earthly and carnal heart, neither using it for their own salvation nor for that of others. We see many such people, who, if they had wished, could have benefited many others [Note: [Col. 0282D] On this subject at length, St. Augustine, in his explanation of this parable, Sermon 114: “We therefore are stewards; we seek gain. Live rightly, for this is the gain from our distribution. But do not think that distribution does not concern you as well. You cannot distribute from this higher place, but you can do so wherever you are. Where Christ is reproached, defend him; answer complainers, rebuke blasphemers, separate yourselves from their company. Thus you distribute, if you gain anyone. Do your part in your homes,” etc. See also Gregory, Homily 6 on the Gospels.].

And these men, quite deservedly, having lost the understanding which they had used badly [Note: [Col. 0282D] Jerome here: “Many, though naturally wise and possessing keenness of intellect, if they become negligent … lose the good of nature.”], while thinking to excuse themselves, provoke the judge’s anger against themselves, saying: “Lord, I knew that you are a hard man [Col. 0283A]: you reap where you have not sown, and gather where you have not scattered. Being afraid, I went away and hid your talent in the earth. Behold, you have what is yours.”

For if they had understanding and had not lost their discernment, they would never call hard and unjust the one whose favor they were seeking. The Lord himself shows how vain, useless, and devoid of all intelligence and reason such an excuse is, saying: “Wicked and lazy servant, you knew that I reap where I do not sow and gather where I have not scattered. Therefore you ought to have entrusted my money to bankers, and when I came I should at least have received what is mine with interest.”

It is as though he said: “It was not fitting for you to be afraid to entrust my money to bankers, when you knew me to be so powerful that I can claim for myself everywhere not only what is mine but also what belongs to others [Col. 0283B] [Note: [Col. 0283C] Jerome: “What he thought he had said in excuse is turned into his own guilt. If, he says, [Col. 0283D] you knew me to be hard and cruel … why did such a thought not strike fear into you, so that you would know that I would seek my property more carefully, and would give my money, or silver, to bankers?”]. In this matter it is evident that you have no excuse.”

This money is the words of eternal life; the bankers are those to whom those words are proclaimed [Note: [Col. 0283D] Jerome again: “Therefore the money and silver are the preaching of the Gospel and the divine word, which ought to have been given to bankers and money-changers—that is, either to the other teachers … or to all believers, who can double the money and return it with interest, so that they may fulfill in deed whatever they have learned by speech.” Bede abbreviated these and the preceding words of Jerome.], provided that, by trading in them, they do not allow them to remain idle. The Lord receives this money with interest when through it he gains many faithful persons bearing the fruit of good works.

There is nowhere where the Lord has not sown; nowhere where he has not scattered the seed of his grace. For besides the fact that the sound of the apostles has gone out into all the earth, he has bestowed reason and understanding, memory and natural ability upon all human beings [Note: [Col. 0283D] St. Gregory, Homily 6 on the Gospels: “Let no one say, ‘I am unable to admonish; I am not fit to exhort.’ Offer what you can, lest you be required to pay in torments for the talent you received and kept badly.” And Homily 9: “One has indeed received understanding for preaching: from his talent he owes ministry; another, earthly substance, etc. Therefore one who has understanding must take care not to remain silent; one who has abundance of possessions must be watchful lest he grow sluggish in generous mercy; one who has influence with a rich man must fear condemnation for a talent withheld [Col. 0284C],” etc.]. It is therefore clear that this wicked servant lied against him.

Of him the Lord goes on to say: “Take therefore the talent from him, and give it to the one who has [Col. 0283C] five talents.” By this we may understand that only the good possess that blessedness which the evil would also have possessed together with them, had they persevered in goodness. For the talent—that is, the reward and merit of the talent—will belong only to the good. Hence it follows: “For to everyone who has, more shall be given, and he shall abound; but from him who does not have, even what he seems to have shall be taken away from him.”

Whoever has doubled these talents shall receive also the reward of the talents and abound in the fullness of all riches. But from him who has not doubled his talent, but has allowed it to remain idle and fruitless, even what he seems [Col. 0284A] to have shall be taken away, since he will appear foolish and without sense or understanding. Then the useless servant shall be cast into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

CIII. “But when the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he shall sit upon the throne of his majesty; and all nations shall be gathered before him, and he shall separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats; and he shall place the [121] sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left” [Note: [Col. 0284D] Hence the homily of St. Bruno, Sermon 2, after the first Sunday of Lent.].

For the Lord, who first came humble and in the form of a servant, will come again exalted and sublime in his majesty and in the glory of the Father [Note: [Col. 0284D] Chrysostom, Homily 80: “For now he comes in dishonor, in insults, in reproaches; but then he shall sit upon the throne of his glory. And he frequently mentions glory, because the cross was near, a thing that seemed especially shameful; therefore he raises the hearer’s mind, places the judgment before his eyes, and summons the whole world.” See Jerome.]. All the angels will come with him, so that from the very multitude of his host his strength and all his power [Col. 0284B] may be made manifest. Then indeed he shall sit upon the throne of his majesty, because then he shall be revealed as equal and like to the Father, coeternal with him. For nowhere is royal dignity displayed better than upon a royal throne.

“And all nations shall be gathered before him,” according to the saying: “‘As I live,’ says the Lord (Isa. 49:18), ‘every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall confess’ (Isa. 45:24).” Nor will it be difficult to gather all nations, since it was not difficult to create and raise them.

And he himself, the good shepherd who knows his sheep well, shall separate the good from the evil, and set the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left. The good are called sheep because of their simplicity and innocence; the evil are called goats because of their vanity and wantonness [Note: [Col. 0284D] This is approximately from the more recent Cornelius a Lapide. Chrysostom, however: “Calling those goats and these sheep, he indicates the barrenness of the former: for no fruit comes from goats; but the sheep produce abundant yield—wool, milk, and offspring—all of which the goat lacks.” St. Bernard, Epistle 229, §5, calls sheep the name of innocence. Proprius, on Jerome: “He did not say she-goats, which can bear offspring … but kids, a wanton and unruly animal.”]. In the very placing [Col. 0284C] at right and left, each party will from that moment be able to recognize whether mercy or punishment hangs over it.

Then the King shall say to those at his right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” Why is this so? Do you wish to hear why? “For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you took me in; naked, and you clothed me; I was in prison, and you came to me.”

If the kingdom was prepared for them before the foundation of the world, it is clear that before they came into being they were predestined to life; and those predestined to life can by no means perish [Col. 0285A]. But God’s predestination is conditional; nothing is predestined without some condition. It was predestined that the world should be saved, but through the water of baptism and the death of the Son of God. All the good are predestined to glory, but on the condition that they retain faith, possess charity, humility, patience, mercy, and piety, and such things as these.

For the Lord foresaw that those whom he predestined to life would be such persons; and it is as though, in predestining them, he said: “I indeed predestine you to life, provided that you are such and such persons, that you keep my commandments, that you possess faith and mercy, and that you are finally found in goodness.” Therefore one who does not wish to be such, who does not strive to keep God’s commandments, does not come [Col. 0285B] to predestination because he does not fulfill the condition.

Then the righteous shall answer him, saying: “Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you? Thirsty and give you drink? When did we see you a stranger and take you in? Or when did we see you sick or in prison and come to you?” They are astounded in amazement [Note: [Col. 0285C] Bede: “Either they say this in wonder at Christ’s glory, or because then every good thing they did seems small to them in comparison with the greatness of the terror and [Col. 0285D] the abundance of the reward.”], when they hear that he was at some time hungry or thirsty, a stranger, sick, or in prison—he whom they then behold in such great glory and sublimity. Thus they rightly ask him when they saw him in such a state or ministered to him in such a way.

And the King answers them: “Amen, amen, I say to you: insofar as you did it to one of these least brothers of mine, you did it to me.” Christ is received in his members [Note: [Col. 0285D] Hilary: “For he is so poured into the bodies and minds of all the faithful that these offices of humanity, if bestowed, deserve his favor, and if withheld, provoke his offense.”]. For all Christians are his members [Col. 0285C]; indeed, they are called Christians because they are members of Christ. Hence the Apostle says: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Far be it!” (1 Cor. 6:15).

Therefore Christ hungers in those who hunger [Note: [Col. 0285D] St. Leo, Sermon 7 on Lent, ch. 3: “Let us not doubt that what is given to one in need is given to God … What is more fruitful than this work? What is happier than this humanity? It would indeed not be deprived of its own praise if help were given by one human being to another merely because of their common nature; but because what does not proceed from the fountain of faith does not attain eternal rewards, the condition of heavenly works is one thing, that of earthly works another … Christian devotion passes to its own author when we are said to be kind to him whom we confess to be at work in us.” See Sermon 2 on the fast of the seventh month, ch. 4; Gregory, Homily 39 on the Gospels; etc.], thirsts in those who thirst, is sick in the sick, and suffers likewise in others. Therefore Christ’s poor must be received with great reverence and served with great veneration, since Christ is received in them and honored in them.

Then he shall say also to those at his left [Col. 0286A]: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” He adds the reason why he commands this: “For I was hungry and you did not give me food; I was thirsty and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger and you did not take me in; sick and in [122] prison, and you did not visit me.”

If, therefore, eternal fire is prepared for the devil and his angels, it is clear that the evil are thus predestined to death on account of their wickedness, just as the good are predestined to life on account of their goodness. What punishments, then, will those suffer who seize what belongs to others, if these suffer such things because they do not give what is their own [Note: [Col. 0285D] St. Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, Book 3, ch. 21: “Behold, they are not consigned to the eternal fires of Gehenna because they committed robberies or any other acts of violence, yet they are consigned there. From this it must be inferred [Col. 0286C] with how great a condemnation those who seize what belongs to others are to be punished, if those who held their own possessions without discernment are struck with such punishment [Col. 0286D].” See Chrysostom, Homily on Psalm 4 and Homily 5 on Repentance; Basil in the prologue to *On the Judgment of God*; etc.]? If the merciless endure such things, what do we think the cruel will suffer?

“And these shall go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.” [CHAPTER XXVI.] And it came to pass [Col. 0286B], when Jesus had finished all these sayings, that he said to his disciples [Note: [Col. 0286D] These words are joined with what follows in the Gospel.].

CIV. “You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified” [Note: [Col. 0286D] There is a homily attributed to St Bruno for Palm Sunday, p. 105, wrongly ascribed to Emisenus.].

The Lord announces the Passover after two days, and also announces his passion, so that he may be slain at the Passover, he who was signified by the Passover. For that entire feast, celebrated for so many years beforehand, signified nothing other than Christ’s passion [Note: [Col. 0286D] Because of this signification, some supposed that the name itself was Greek and derived from πάσχω, “I suffer”; but this is false, as Jansenius, ch. 128, and many others observe, especially Pererius, in Exodus, ch. XII, disputation 8. Yet the signification is certain, since St Paul himself applies the name to Jesus Christ in 1 Corinthians V: “Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed.”].

It is therefore fitting that the sign and the thing signified should coincide. Fittingly, he is at last handed over to death on that day and no other: each year, on that day, he had been sacrificed in the signification of this event. For Pascha, or Phase [Note: [Col. 0286D] Pascha is a Hebrew word, rendered thus by the Septuagint translators in Exodus XII: πάσχα ἐστὶ Κυρίῳ, “It is the Passover of the Lord.” Jerome reads the Hebrew word Pesah, Phase.], means “passing over”: either because at that time the Lord, passing through the camps of the Egyptians, slew all their firstborn; [Col. 0286C] or also because at that time our Saviour passed from this world to the Father. Hence John says: “Jesus, knowing that his hour had come, that he should pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own, loved them unto the end” (John XIII, 1).

This feast is celebrated for seven days; concerning it we have said enough in Exodus [Note: [Col. 0286D] See the Roman edition of St Bruno, vol. I, p. 60.]. Then the chief priests and elders of the people assembled in the courtyard of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas; and they took counsel to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him. For just as every year all the Jews used to gather, so that [Col. 0287A] at this feast they might sacrifice one kid: so now they all gather into one body, in order to seize and kill Christ by deceit—the one whom that kid signified. Of this it is written: “According to this rite you shall take also a kid, and the whole multitude of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it in the evening” [Note: [Col. 0287B] Exodus XII, 6. Pererius discusses this passage at length in disputation 5, explaining it to mean that not both animals—the lamb and the kid—were sacrificed together, but one or the other, as Theodoret, Questions on Exodus 54, maintains. Cornelius a Lapide, Tirinus, Calmet, and many others follow this opinion. Nor is there any difficulty in the fact that one kid sufficed for very many: “Just as,” says Pererius, “one blessed loaf, divided into small pieces, suffices for all who are in the temple, each receiving a small fragment.” For it was used not to satisfy hunger but for a mystery; and that this mystery was such that, as the lamb, so also a kid sacrificed in its place signified Christ’s sacrifice, is too well known to require witnesses or the authority of the Fathers—though commentators do not omit them here.].

For who would not think it ridiculous that six hundred thousand persons and more should gather together to kill a single kid, unless so great a sacrament was signified in that act? But they said: “Not on the feast-day, lest perhaps a disturbance arise among the people.” For they feared that Christ might be taken from their hands by an uprising of the people, who had gathered there from every quarter for the feast-day.

Now when Jesus was at Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came to him [Col. 0287B] with an alabaster flask of precious ointment and poured it upon the head of Jesus as he reclined. This Simon had been a leper, whom the Lord had already healed [Note: [Col. 0287C] Jerome: “Not that he remained a leper at that time, but that he who had formerly been a leper was afterward cleansed by the Saviour, while his former name remained, so that the power of the healer might be evident.” Bede says the same; among more recent writers, Maldonatus, and others.].

Whether this woman was the same one who washed his feet with tears, or another, I do not contend [Note: [Col. 0287C] If we listen to Jansenius, *Harmony*, ch. 48: after this question, raised among the ancients, especially [Col. 0287D] among the Greeks—some of whom, including Origen, thought there were three distinct women—had been settled or laid to rest in St Augustine’s age, Jodocus Clichtoveus and Jacques Lefèvre revived it; and it still flourishes in our own age. On this question see the Bollandists, vol. V, *Acts of July*, from p. 187.]. Yet it does not seem inappropriate to me that the one whom the Lord had already forgiven of her sins, saying, “Woman, your sins are forgiven” (Luke VII, 48), should have come to anoint Christ’s head.

One Evangelist calls this ointment “spikenard” (Mark XIV, 3); another, “pistic” [Note: [Col. 0287D] Learned interpreters, ancient and modern, agree greatly in explaining the spikenard and costly ointment: Pliny, Galen, Dioscorides, and others distinguish two kinds of nard ointment—spikenard, made from the ear or spike of nard (for Pliny, XII, 12, says: “The tops of nard spread into awns; therefore they celebrate the spikes and leaves of nard for their twofold excellence”), which is the best and hence is called precious; and leaf-nard, made from nard leaves. Yet disagreement is equally, indeed more, extensive concerning “pistic” ointment.

Some derive it from a place-name, as Augustine in Tractate 50 on John and Theophylact on Mark. Following them, some name Bista or Pista, the capital of Carmania, or a province of Kabul among [Col. 0288B] the Indians; others read *opistic*, referring it to the city of Opis near Babylon. Some consider *pistic* either a scribal error or a metathesis: Erasmus, Castalio, and Grotius; Cornelius a Lapide discusses this metathesis at length, and Bede may be added to their number, since he reads “spikenard” in both Evangelists. Some prefer to derive πιστικόν from πιεῖν, “to drink,” meaning that it was not thick and solid, as another kind of ointment of the same sort was, but liquid, so that it could readily be poured for anointing; it might even be mixed with drink, as Hirtius seems to report in *The Spanish War*. Thus Aeschylus uses πιστόν for πότιμον, “drinkable”; Maldonatus, Casaubon, Stephanus, and others held this view.

Finally, some derive *pistic* from πίστις, “faith,” meaning genuine, sound, pure, unadulterated ointment. This is the view of Euthymius, Theophylact, Vatablus, Lorenzo Valla, Isidore Clarius, Toletus, Erasmus Zeger, Cappel, de Dieu, Clericus, and others. Thus Maldonatus’s statement concerning his own age—that this was the commoner and more accepted opinion—is true also of later ages. Our author adopted this view.].

It is called spikenard from the species called the spike [Col. 0288A] of nard. But *pistic* is interpreted as “genuine” or “faithful” [Note: [Col. 0288C] I believe he followed Bede, who writes that the Evangelists call this ointment “pistic, that is, faithful or genuine, because certain physicians customarily adulterate ointments with similar herbs: for πίστις in Greek means ‘faith’ . . . Mystically, it signifies the faith of the Church,” etc. The author also indicates that mystical interpretation here. See Nicolaus Graber and Friedrich Bucher, *On the Anointing at Bethany*.]. Its opposite is that of which it is said: “Let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head” (Psalm CXL, 5). It is clear, therefore, that both meanings are indicated.

When the disciples saw this, they were indignant and said: “Why this waste? For it could have been sold for much and given to the poor.” The Evangelist John reports that Judas alone said this (John XII, 5); perhaps because he spoke more than the others, although the same thing displeased the others as well—indeed, the others because of the poor, but Judas because he was a thief and kept the money-box [Note: [Col. 0288D] Jerome: “The apostles were truly indignant because of the poor, but Judas because of his own gain. Therefore his muttering is recorded together with his guilt: not because he cared for the poor, but because he wished to provide for his own theft.” Augustine says much the same in *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, book II, ch. 79: this may be explained by supposing that “the other disciples either thought this or said it, or had been persuaded when Judas spoke; and that Matthew and Mark expressed the will of all even in their words; but Judas said it because he was a thief, whereas the rest did so from care for the poor, while John wished to mention it of Judas alone, because he believed the opportunity revealed Judas’s habitual theft.” [Col. 0289C]].

Since they did not understand what this act signified, it seemed useless to them. But Jesus, knowing this, said to them: “Why do you trouble this woman? For she has done [Col. 0288B] a good work toward me.” Since Jesus knew what it signified, he defended and praised the woman for her good work. “For you will always have the poor with you; but you will not always have me.” He says this concerning the presence of his body, which they would have with them only a little while.

“For in pouring this ointment upon my body, she has done it for my burial.” “It is a sign,” he says, “not a waste. For I am soon to suffer; therefore this woman offered me this ointment for burial.” For it was an ancient custom that the bodies of nobles to be buried should be anointed with precious [Col. 0289A] ointments [Note: [Col. 0289D] See Gutherius, *On the Law of the Manes*, book I, ch. 15; Kirchranus, *On Funerals*, book I, ch. 8; Spencer, *Funeral Rites*, ch. 1, §3; Blasius Ugolini, *Hebrew Priesthood*, ch. 4; and the interpreters on Genesis I, 2.].

“Amen, I say to you: wherever this Gospel is preached in the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.” “You,” he says, “rebuke her as foolish for the very deed for which she ought to be praised throughout the world” [Note: [Col. 0289D] This is evident even from the homilies of the Fathers. Peter Chrysologus alone has three sermons, 93, 94, and 95. One sermon of Gregory of Nyssa or Asterius is listed, as are homilies of Gregory, etc.].

Then one of the twelve, who was called Judas Scharioth [Note: [Col. 0289D] This is the reading of old manuscript codices. The Colbertine manuscript, from which Sabatier represented the Old Latin version, has *Scariotha*. The two Sangermanensis manuscripts, the two Corbeiensis manuscripts, R. Sat., Maj.-Mon., Claramontanus, and others in the same Sabatier have *Scarioth*.], went to the chief priests and said to them: “What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” And they fixed for him thirty pieces of silver. From then on he sought an opportunity to hand him over.

For all this had been foretold by the prophets: both that he would be betrayed by a disciple and that he would be sold for thirty pieces of silver. Hence the Psalmist says: “The man of my peace, in whom I hoped, who ate my bread, has greatly lifted up his treachery against me” (Psalm XL, 10); and elsewhere: [Col. 0289B] “They weighed out my wage as thirty pieces of silver, the fine price at which I was valued by the children of Israel” (Zechariah XI, 12). He called it a “fine price” ironically [Note: [Col. 0289D] Jerome, on Zechariah: εἰρωνικῶς, “ironically”: “seeing his price—that is, the price of the divine majesty—in thirty pieces of silver, and himself sold for so cheap a payment: ‘Fine,’ etc.” This must be read more sharply, with the speaker’s mockery and derision. Lyra, Ribera, Cornelius a Lapide, Menochius, and others likewise judge that this is said ironically.], because it was shameful and unfitting for the Saviour of the world to be sold at so low a price.

On the first day of unleavened bread, the disciples came to Jesus and said: “Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” Here *Passover* means the lamb sacrificed at Passover, which they ate that night with unleavened bread and wild lettuces. But Jesus said: “Go into the city to a certain man and say to him: ‘The Master says: My time is near; I keep the Passover at your house with my disciples.’” This certain man must be thought to have been of no small merit: at his house the Lord not only keeps the Passover, but also reveals the mystery of his passion [Col. 0289C] to him, saying, “My time is near.”

And the disciples did as Jesus commanded them, and prepared the Passover. When evening came, he reclined with his twelve disciples. And while they were eating, he said: “Amen, I say to you that one of you will betray me.” They were greatly grieved, and each began to say: “Is it I, Lord?” 124 But he answered and said: “He who dips his hand with me [Note: [Col. 0290C] It is consistently written thus, and occurs in the editions under the name of Emisenus, p. 107: *paropside*. Indeed, according to Du Cange [Col. 0290D] in the *Latin Glossary*, it appears in other manuscripts of other writers as well. The derivation of the name supports this spelling, if Isidore’s explanation in *Origins*, book XX, ch. 4, is correct: “A *paropsis* is a square, four-sided vessel—that is, with equal recesses.”] in the dish will betray me.”

First he says, “One of you will betray me”; then, as all doubted and each feared for himself—for they knew that he could not lie [Col. 0290A]—he identifies him more plainly, saying: “He who dips his hand with me in the dish will betray me.”

“The Son of Man indeed goes as it is written of him; but woe to that man through whom the Son of Man is betrayed.” For both were prophesied: that the Son of Man should be betrayed, and that woe should come upon the one by whom he was betrayed. The Lord foresaw both his own death and the wickedness of his betrayer; and he wished to foretell both, so that he might the more take heed for himself and his own, and fear to commit the betrayal.

“It would have been good for that man if he had not been born.” He speaks in ordinary and common language [Note: [Col. 0290D] Jerome: “He should not therefore be thought to have existed before he was born, because no one can be well except one who has existed. Rather, it is simply said that it is far better not to subsist than to subsist miserably.” Bede says nearly the same in nearly the same words.]: not that what does not exist at all can be good or bad for him, unless one wishes to understand this more subtly: if Judas, having been formed in body and received a soul, had died in [Col. 0290B] his mother’s womb before being born, it would have been better for him than to have reached so great a crime. For although he would not have had the glory of blessedness, he would nevertheless not have endured the punishment of betrayal. For we believe that all human beings, even those not born, will rise again, if they have been granted life for however brief a time [Note: [Col. 0290D] See St Thomas, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 43, and *Supplement*, question 75, article 2, reply to objection 5.].

Then Judas, who betrayed him, answered and said: “Is it I, Rabbi?” He said to him: “You have said it.” See, wretch, that the Lord knows all things and that not even your conscience lies hidden from him; cease, therefore, and confess.

While they were at supper, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: “Take and eat; this is my body.” Here the Lord explains what he had meant when elsewhere he said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man [Col. 0290C] and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John VI, 54). Behold the priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek: by ineffable power he changes bread and wine into the substance of his body and blood.

For just as then he lived and spoke, and yet was eaten and drunk by his disciples [Note: [Col. 0290D] See St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, III, question 81. See also Augustine, *Exposition of Psalm XXXIII*, exposition 2, §10: “He was carried in his own hands. How this is to be understood literally in David himself we shall not find; we find it in Christ. For Christ was carried in his own hands when, commending his own body, he said: ‘This is …’” etc. See Jerome, Letter 120 to Hedibia, question 2.], so now he remains whole and incorruptible, and is daily drunk and eaten by his faithful in the sacrament of bread and wine. For unless bread and wine were changed into his flesh and blood, he himself would never be bodily eaten [Col. 0291A] or drunk. These are changed into those; those are eaten and drunk in these. How this happens is known only by him who can do all things and knows all things. Then he spoke in person; now he speaks through his ministers. “For this is my body”; and so great is the power and efficacy of his word that what is said comes to be immediately.

Likewise, when he says, “This is my blood,” the wine is immediately changed into his blood [Note: [Col. 0291C] The author indicates the view that is almost common [Col. 0291D] among theologians concerning the essential words of consecration. Bellarmine discusses these in *On the Eucharist*, book IV, chs. 12–13, maintaining that this is the common view of theologians and of the ancient Fathers. See Estius, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 8, §11; Suárez, *Third Part*, disputations 59–60. Though there is some question concerning St Thomas’s view, Silvius, *Third Part*, question 78, question 3; Drovet, book IV, ch. 3; and Billuart, vol. XVII, defend the same view. See also Bougeant, *Refutation of Le Brun’s Dissertation*, and *Theological Treatise on the Form of the Eucharist*.].

And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: “Drink from this, all of you; for this is my blood of the new covenant, which will be poured out for many for the remission of sins.” “This,” he says, “is my blood which is to be poured out—not one blood here and another there, but one and the same, this and that. Therefore tomorrow it will be poured out from this side of mine, which you now drink and see in the cup.” [Col. 0291B]

For the new covenant cannot otherwise be confirmed; and this is what the Apostle says: “For where there is a testament, the death of the testator must necessarily intervene. For a testament is confirmed in the dead; otherwise it is not yet valid while the testator lives. Hence not even the first covenant was dedicated without blood” (Hebrews IX, 16). Thus the old covenant was dedicated with blood, and the new also with blood; but that one with the blood of goats, this one with Christ’s blood.

“But I say to you: I will not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father.” The kingdom of God is the Church, in which old wine is not drunk and old teaching is not received, because Scripture is understood not according to the letter but spiritually [Note: [Col. 0291D] In a manner not very different, Bede says: “That is, I shall no longer delight in the carnal ceremonies of the Synagogue . . . That day will come when, established in the kingdom of God, I shall be filled with new joy together with you over the salvation of that same people, regenerated from the fountain of spiritual grace.” Jerome, in the letter to Hedibia: “We drink new wine from the kingdom of the Father, not at all in the oldness of the letter, but in the newness of the Spirit,” etc.].

Therefore Christ drinks new wine with us [Col. 0291C] in this Church; for, remaining with us, he hungers and thirsts in us, 125 and in us he is fed and given drink. For he himself says: “I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink” (Matthew XXV, 35). Yet according to himself he now neither hungers nor thirsts, neither eats nor drinks. Therefore, having rejected old wine, he drinks new wine with us in the Church; because, once the faith and teaching of the Jews have been rejected, he receives our faith and teaching. For we drink as it were from one wine when we hold one end and one teaching.

But Luke sets forth two cups [Note: [Col. 0291D] Luke XXII, 18 and 20: “And having taken the cup, [Col. 0292C] he gave thanks and said: Take and divide it among yourselves . . . [Col. 0292D] And having taken bread, he gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying: This is,” etc. “Likewise also the cup after supper.” On this passage in Luke Jerome made the same observation: “In Luke we read of two cups from which he gave the disciples drink: one of the first month and the other of the second.” Fulgentius examines and explains at length what these cups were, Question 5 to Ferrandus, where, p. 261, he says: “It seems . . . that in each cup each covenant should be understood.”], signifying the two covenants. [Col. 0292A] Of the first cup it is said: “I will not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine,” so that we may understand that the old covenant according to the letter has been completed. Hence it is immediately added: “Until I drink it new with you in the kingdom of God.”

And after a hymn had been sung, they went out to the Mount of Olives. Fittingly, after such refreshment they sing a hymn and ascend the Mount of Olives: those who are refreshed by Christ’s flesh and blood are worthy to praise God and ascend the mount of peace.

Then Jesus said to them: “All of you will suffer scandal because of me this night.” For they suffered the scandal of doubt when they saw him, as though powerless, seized, bound, and scourged. “For it is written: ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered’” (Zechariah XIII, 7). He proves by the testimony of Scripture [Col. 0292B] what he had said. For the Psalmist says: “For they persecuted him whom you struck” (Psalm LXVIII, 27). The Father struck the Son, because, as he himself says: “They would have no power over him unless it had been given them from above” (John XIX, 11).

“But after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee.” This prophecy is full of consolation. He goes before them into Galilee—that is, into their homeland, for all were Galileans—signifying that he would at last lead them to a better homeland.

But Peter answered and said to him: “Even if all are scandalized because of you, I shall never be scandalized.” Blessed Peter did not think that the flame of his faith and love could be extinguished by fear of any persecution. Jesus said to him: “Amen, I say to you that this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” [Col. 0292C] Peter said to him: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.” And all the disciples said likewise.

Therefore no one can trust in himself or in his own strength [Note: [Col. 0292D] Ambrose, *On Faith in the Resurrection*, §27: “Peter also, though full of the faith of devotion, nevertheless, because he was not yet aware of our weakness . . . underwent the temptation of presumption before the cock crowed a third time. Yet that temptation was an instruction unto salvation, that we may learn not to despise the weakness of the flesh . . . If Peter was tempted, who may presume?”]. All steadfastness, all strength and fortitude, belong not to man but to God.

Then Jesus came with them to the estate called Gethsemane, and said to his disciples: “Sit here, while I go there and pray.” Since Gethsemane [Note: [Col. 0292D] Jerome here: “Gethsemane is interpreted ‘a most fertile valley.’” Bonfrère, *Onomasticon*: “This word signifies a valley of oil or richness.”] is interpreted “valley of rich abundance,” the Lord came there to pray, so that by the very name of the place he might show how abundant he was in the richness of piety and mercy, since he prayed to the Father even for his enemies.

And taking [Col. 0293A] Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and distressed. The Lord’s prayer, sorrow, and distress must all be referred to his humanity [Note: [Col. 0293C] Cyril, *Treasury*, p. 232: “Whenever you hear that he wept and was affected by grief and emotion, understand that, in addition to being God, he was also man; and attribute to his human nature what belongs to it.”].

He did this before three disciples as witnesses, either to teach us to pray for enemies, or also to show that he wished to save the Jews if they had been willing. Thus he addresses Jerusalem, saying: “How often I wished to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matthew XXIII, 37). For no one who does not wish to be saved will be saved.

“My soul is sorrowful unto death; remain here and watch with me.” The Lord is sorrowful over the destruction of the Jews [Note: [Col. 0293C] Jerome: “He was sorrowful not through fear of suffering . . . but because of most unhappy Judas, the scandal of all the apostles, the rejection of the Jewish people, and the overthrow of wretched Jerusalem.” Ambrose, book X on Luke, II, 56: “Nowhere do I admire his compassion and majesty more; for he would have bestowed less upon me had he not taken up my feeling. Therefore he grieved for me—he who has nothing in himself over which to grieve—and, setting aside the delight of eternal divinity, is affected by the weariness of my weakness. For he took up my sorrow in order to bestow his joy upon me,” [Col. 0293D] etc.]. But this sorrow soon ends, because death is near [Note: [Col. 0293D] Lyra on this passage: “‘Unto’ may be understood in two ways. First, intensively, because it was as intense as it could be. Secondly, extensively, because it lasted until the hour of death.” Our author takes it in the latter sense; and St Jerome had preceded him: “The soul that is sorrowful is sorrowful not because of death, but unto death, until by his passion he frees the apostles.” Hilary likewise: “Did he say, ‘My soul is sorrowful because of death’? Certainly not . . . But it is one thing to fear up to a thing, another to fear on account of a thing . . . Therefore he is sorrowful unto death. Thus death is not feared, but the time of death, because after it the faith of believers was to be strengthened by the power of the resurrection.”].

He is sorrowful, therefore, until death, because after death he is subject to no such [Col. 0293B] suffering. Indeed, to say nothing of the Lord, no saint after the resurrection will be subject to sorrow or pain; otherwise they would not be blessed. For one who lacks something, or has not attained what he desires, cannot be called blessed. But the sorrowful person needs joy 126 and desires to be without sorrow. Therefore the sorrowful person is not blessed.

“Remain here and watch with me.” “Watch with me,” he says; “bear this burden with me. What you see me doing for my enemies, do this also for your enemies. Otherwise you will not be here”—that is, in the estate of Gethsemane, the place of richness and mercy.

And going forward a little, he fell upon his face, praying and saying: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” He withdraws a little from the disciples and falls upon his face, in order to teach us what we ought to do in our [Col. 0293C] prayers [Note: [Col. 0293D] Euthymius: “He went alone to pray, teaching that one who is to pray fervently ought to stand apart.”].

But let no one think that he prayed from fear of death for the cup of suffering [Col. 0294A] to be taken away from him, when he said to Peter, who tried to dissuade him from the passion: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling-block to me, for you do not savour the things that are of God” (Matthew XVI, 23). For he does not pray absolutely [Note: [Col. 0294C] Jerome: “He asks not from fear of suffering but from mercy toward the former people, that he might not drink the cup offered by them. Hence he pointedly did not say, ‘Let the cup pass from me,’ but ‘this cup’: that is, the cup of the Jewish people, who cannot plead ignorance if they kill me.” Bede copied these words.] that the cup be taken from him, but “this cup”; for although he had come to die for the salvation of the world, he did not wish, if it could be done, to be killed by the Jews.

The Father, however, on the contrary, wished him to be killed by them, because they were more wicked than all others; so that they might add this to the full measure of their condemnation, although they were certainly to be condemned even if they had not killed Christ. “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” By these words he plainly shows that he said all this from the affection of his humanity, not of his divinity; for according to his divinity his will is one and the same with the Father’s [Note: [Col. 0294C] Cyril, book IV on John, ch. 1: “Do you see how human nature suffers and fears even in Christ himself? Yet it is restored by the Word united to it to strength and steadfastness fitting for God, and is taught to follow not what seems good to itself but the divine will.” And in *Thess.* [materially uncertain citation], book X, ch. 3: “When, therefore, he said as man that he feared death: ‘Father, let this cup pass from me; yet not as I will,’ etc., although as man he shrank from death, he did not refuse as man to accomplish the will of the Father and his own will as the Word . . . When he adds, ‘But as you, Father, will,’ we must understand this also of himself: for all that the Father wills, the Son wills,” etc. Epiphanius, *Heresies* 69, §58: “Nor was the will of the Son different from that of the Father. But he showed this in order that he might refer all singularity to the Father as to the source, lest that unity and economy be divided in any respect.”].

And he came to [Col. 0294B] the disciples and found them sleeping. He said to Peter: “So, could you not watch with me one hour?” “Is this,” he says, “how you act, how you remember me, how you keep watch with me? Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation.” For he enters into temptation who, already as though defeated, is held and ensnared by the temptation itself. It is one thing, therefore, to be tempted, and another to enter into temptation [Note: [Col. 0294D] Jerome: “At present he does not say, ‘Watch and pray that you may not be tempted,’ but ‘that you may not enter into temptation’; that is, lest temptation overcome and conquer you.”].

“The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” Although the soul may powerfully resist temptations, the flesh that weighs it down is weak and frail unless it is strengthened by prayer and attentive vigilance.

Again, a second time, he went away and prayed, saying: “My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done.” “If,” he says, “it cannot happen that the Jews do not kill me, and if this lies within your will, [Col. 0294C] your will be done.” Therefore it was the Father’s will that the Jews should kill Christ [Note: [Col. 0294D] Epiphanius, in the work cited: “The will of the Father was that the economy should thus be fulfilled, while the Israelites were betrayers of the Son to themselves and were not compelled by God.”].

For since he was to die for the salvation [Col. 0295A] of the world, some nation had to kill him: “For Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead, and thus enter into his glory” (Luke XXIV, 26). But what other nation ought to kill Christ but that which was more wicked and thirsted more than the rest for his blood? God compels no one to sin; nevertheless, he permits those to sin who intensely desire to sin. God therefore wills that such persons, whose whole will inclines to evil, should kill his saints, so that a greater punishment may grow for them and a fuller glory for the saints.

Thus in the death of martyrs a double good occurs: the wicked, who would have perished even if they had not killed them, acquire greater punishment for themselves through their death; while the good, when slain for Christ’s faith, are [Col. 0295B] enriched with greater glory. Accordingly God the Father willed that the Jews should kill his Son; and because they were most wicked, that they should perpetrate the greatest crime, so that they might have no excuse and be subjected to greater punishment: “that upon them may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth.”

And he came again and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy. This sleep of the disciples signified the sleep and torpor of the Church [Note: [Col. 0295D] Hilary: “That when he returned again he found them sleeping shows that, during the time of his absence, many were to be held in a kind of sleep of faith.”], which often languishes and fails amid great temptations unless it is awakened by Christ’s frequent visitation.

Leaving them again, he went away and prayed a third time, saying the same words. Then he came to the disciples and said to them: “Sleep now and rest. Behold, the hour is at hand, and the Son of Man is handed over into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us go; [Col. 0295C] behold, he who betrays me is at hand.” He says this not as a command, 127 but as a rebuke. For in great disturbances one ought not to sleep or rest, but rather to watch and persist in prayer. Therefore he immediately rouses them, saying: “Rise, let us go.” He certainly would not have said this if he had wished them to sleep and rest.

While he was still speaking, Judas, one of the twelve, came, and with him a great crowd with swords and clubs, sent by the chief priests and elders of the people. Where the person being attacked does not wish to defend himself, clubs and swords are unnecessary [Note: [Col. 0295D] “It is foolish,” Jerome says on this passage, “to seek with swords and clubs one who voluntarily hands himself over into your hands.”]. For if the Lord had wished to defend himself, neither clubs nor swords could have withstood him [Note: [Col. 0295D] Chrysostom: “Unless he had voluntarily handed himself over, they could have done nothing even then.
