For when they had him in their hands and had found him in their midst, they still could not hold or overcome him; surely they could not have done so at that time either unless he had willed it.”]. He himself showed this when, by a single answer, he struck them down (John XVIII, 6).

[Col. 0296A] For when he said, “I am he,” they drew back and fell upon their faces. Now his betrayer gave them a sign, saying: “Whomever I shall kiss, he is the one; seize him.” And immediately approaching Jesus, he said: “Hail, Rabbi,” and kissed him. Judas the betrayer seems to have given this sign because the Roman soldiers did not know Christ.

Jesus said to him: “Friend, for what have you come?” He calls him “friend” by contrariety [Note: [Col. 0295D] Jerome: “The word ‘friend’ must be understood either κατὰ ἀντίφρασιν, ‘by antiphrasis,’ or certainly in accordance with what we read above: ‘Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?’”], though he was his enemy. So also blessed Job uses “bless” in place of “curse,” saying: “Perhaps my sons have sinned and have blessed God in their hearts” [Note: [Col. 0295D] Job I, 5. See St Gregory, *Exposition on Job*, book I, ch. IX.].

Then they came up, laid hands on Jesus, and seized him. And behold, one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand, drew his sword, and, striking [Col. 0296B] the servant of the high priest, cut off his ear. This one was the blessed apostle Peter, who, when he saw his Lord being seized, was so moved by grief that he could no longer restrain himself [Note: [Col. 0296D]

Jerome: “In another Evangelist (John XVIII, 10) it is written that Peter did this, with the same fervour of mind as in the other things.”]. He therefore cut off the ear of the servant of the high priest, which had not yet been circumcised [Note: [Col. 0296D] Hilary: “By the apostle the ear of the high priest’s servant is cut off: that is, from the people serving the priesthood, through Christ’s disciple, the disobedient hearing is removed, and what had been incapable of hearing is cut away so as to receive the truth.”], and therefore it had obeyed evil counsels. This servant was called Malchus, which is interpreted “one who will reign” [Note: [Col. 0296D] Jerome: “It should be said in passing that Malchus, that is, king,” etc.]. For only those will reign and live who have circumcised ears. Hence another Evangelist says that the Lord touched and healed this man’s ears (Luke XXII, 51). For the ears which are circumcised by the apostles and teachers, those the Lord touches and heals.

Then Jesus said to him: “Put your sword back in its place; for all who take the sword shall perish by the sword.” The Lord disapproves [Col. 0296C] of Peter’s deed; for although it signified something good, it was nevertheless not done in a good spirit. For all who take the sword—that is, who kill someone through an unjust stirring of mind—unless perhaps they repent worthily, shall perish by the sword: namely, by the sword of everlasting vengeance [Note: [Col. 0296D] Jerome: “By what sword? Surely that flaming sword which turns before Paradise, and the sword of the Spirit, which is described in the armour of God.” Bede: “That is, those who desire to avenge themselves in the present life, according to the law of retaliation, die by the very sin of their souls.”]. For every punishment is called a sword. Blessed Peter, however, had a just cause. Yet the Lord did not wish to be defended by arms, whether just or unjust. Hence he adds: “Do you suppose that I cannot ask my Father, and that he will at once provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” You, he says, are twelve men striving somehow to fight for me; but I, if I wish, can immediately have more than twelve legions of angels. Therefore, my not defending myself is not inability but will. [Col. 0297A] For if I defended myself, they could do nothing against me. But if they could do nothing, how then would the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen thus?

At that hour Jesus said to the crowds: “Have you come out with swords and clubs to seize me as though I were a robber? Day after day I sat among you teaching in the Temple, and you did not arrest me.” The Evangelist explains that this happened neither without reason nor apart from God’s ordinance, saying: “But all this happened in order that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled.” Then all the disciples left him and fled. And those who had seized Jesus led him to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and elders had assembled. But Peter followed at a distance as far as the high priest’s courtyard; and, going inside, he sat with the attendants in order to see the outcome.

Peter, he says, was still [Col. 0297B] following the Lord, but now from a distance; for he was close to denial [Note: [Col. 0297D] Jerome, on this passage: “He followed from a distance, who was about to deny the Lord.”]. Hence not without reason he sat with the attendants, wishing to see the end of the matter. For where does one who denies Christ sit, if not among the Jews and the attendants of the Jews?

But the chief priests and the whole council sought false testimony against Jesus in order to deliver him to death, and they found none, though many false witnesses had come forward. They wish to condemn Christ according to the Law, and seek false testimony, although the Law itself does not accept false testimony. In this matter the Jews’ utmost injustice, and their cruel and execrable hatred, is proved. At last two false witnesses came and said: “This man said: I can destroy the Temple of God and rebuild it after three days.” Christ [Col. 0297C] had not said this. Yet if he had said it, he certainly could have done it. For he had said: “Destroy this Temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” Explaining what this meant, the Evangelist says: “But he spoke of the temple of his body” [Note: [Col. 0297D] Jerome: “The Lord had spoken of the temple of his body. But they slander him even in the very words, and, by adding or changing a few things, manufacture what seems a just accusation. The Saviour had said: ‘Destroy this Temple’; they alter it and say: ‘I can destroy the Temple of God.’ ‘You,’ he says, ‘destroy it, not I, because it is unlawful for us ourselves to lay hands upon ourselves.’ Then they change: ‘and rebuild it after three days,’ so that he may appear to have spoken specifically of the Jewish Temple. But the Lord, to show that it was a living, breathing temple, had said: ‘And I will raise it up in three days.’ It is one thing to build, another to raise.” Bede says the same on this passage.].

And the high priest rose and said to him: “Do you give no answer to what these men testify against you?” But Jesus was silent. Christ is silent and unwilling to answer, both because he hears vain and useless things and because it is written: “From the mouth of the Most High there proceed neither good things nor evil things” (Lamentations III, 38).—And the high priest said to him: “I adjure you by the living God to tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Jesus said to him: “You have said it.” For the Lord answers those things which he sees worthy of an answer. For if, when thus adjured by the high priest, whom all revered by reason of the dignity [Col. 0297D] of his office, he had not answered, he would have seemed not to fear God and to make light of him.

It follows: “Nevertheless I say to you: From now on [Col. 0298A] you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the power of God and coming upon the clouds of heaven.” This will occur at the judgment, when every eye shall see him. Then the high priest tore his garments, saying: “He has blasphemed. What further need have we of witnesses? Behold, you have now heard the blasphemy. What do you think?” And they answered: “He is deserving of death.” The high priest tears his garments, signifying that he himself is the chief and principal cause why the Jewish priesthood should be torn apart and destroyed [Note: [Col. 0298D] Jerome: “He tore his garments to show that the Jews had lost the glory of the priesthood and that the high priests possessed an empty seat.”].

Then they spat in his face and struck him with their fists. For thus it had been prophesied. Others struck his face with the palms of their hands, saying: “Prophesy to us, Christ: who is it that struck you?” The Lord answers nowhere except where [Col. 0298B] his answer is necessary and useful.

But Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard, and a maidservant came to him and said: “You too were with Jesus the Galilean.” But he denied it before all, saying: “I do not know what you are saying.” Peter denies in order that his Master’s prophecy may be fulfilled. As he went out through the gateway, another maidservant saw him and said to those who were there: “This man too was with Jesus the Nazarene.” And again he denied it with an oath, that he did not know the man. A little later those standing there came and said to Peter: “Truly you are one of them, for your speech makes it evident.” Then he began to invoke curses and to swear that he did not know the man. Behold, the shepherd of the Church is compelled to deny the Lord not only by men but even by women; and this not once, but twice and three times. In this matter a rule for granting pardon is also given to them [Note: [Col. 0298D] St Leo, Sermon 9, *On the Passion of the Lord*, ch. 4: “Peter, terrified by the accusation of the priest’s maidservant, incurred through weakness the danger of denial. He was therefore, as appears, permitted to waver, so that in the prince of the Church the remedy of repentance might be established.” Euthymius, on this passage: “Peter was allowed to fall … so that, learning from his own experience the weakness of those who fall, he might learn to forgive them.”]: [Col. 0298C] recognizing in oneself the frailty of others, one should have mercy on others; and we too are permitted to hope for forgiveness even in the gravest transgressions of sins.

And immediately the cock crowed. Peter remembered the word of Jesus, who had said: “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times”; and he went outside and wept bitterly. In another Evangelist, however, we read that the Lord looked at Peter [Note: [Col. 0298D] Jerome, on this passage: “In another Gospel we read that, after Peter’s denial and the cockcrow, the Saviour looked at Peter, and by his look drew him forth into bitter tears [Col. 0299C]. Nor could he remain in the darkness of denial upon whom the Light of the world had looked.”] (Luke XXII, 61). The Lord was held by crowds, dragged away, and scourged; yet mindful of his disciple—whom he was afraid to comfort by words, lest he be betrayed and seized—he comforts and heals him by a look alone, and by the radiance of his countenance invites him to hope for pardon.

Peter therefore recognizes his guilt and also recognizes the will of his Lord; he grieves and repents; he goes outside; he leaves the council of evildoers; he seeks a secluded place [Col. 0298D] suited to tears and repentance; he weeps bitterly, fully understanding that “a contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God; a broken and humbled heart God [Col. 0299A] does not despise.” This is the manner of repentance: have you sinned? Be still, grieve, and weep; and learn with the Apostle to weep bitterly [Note: [Col. 0299C] Chrysostom, Homily 41 to the Antiochenes: “Do you wish to learn perfect repentance? Hear of Peter’s repentance after his denial. For the Evangelist, recounting to us what was done by him, says: ‘He went out and wept bitterly,’ etc.” Ambrose, Book X, *On Luke*: “Look, Lord Jesus, so that we may know how to mourn our sin and wash away our offence … Peter therefore wept most bitterly, that he might wash away his offence with tears. And you, if you wish to deserve pardon, wash your guilt away with tears; at that same instant, at that same time, Christ looks upon you … imitate [Col. 0299D] Peter,” etc.].

[CHAPTER XXVII.]

When morning came, all the chief priests and elders of the people took counsel against Jesus in order to deliver him to death; and, having bound him, they brought him and handed him over to Pontius [129] Pilate the governor. The Jews assemble together, hold a council, and conspire against Jesus; they fear lest some good man and defender of justice be found among them. They hand Jesus, bound, over to Pilate, so that by this he may be thought guilty of death and undeserving of pardon.

Then Judas, who had betrayed him, seeing that he had been condemned, moved by repentance returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying: “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood.” Judas recognized that he had sinned; [Col. 0299B] he returns the silver, as though by the same price for which he had sold him he could redeem Christ the Lord. But they said: “What is that to us? See to it yourself.” That is, “You see what you have done; it does not concern us whether you have sinned and delivered innocent blood.” Having thrown the silver into the Temple, he departed; and he went away and hanged himself.

Unhappy Judas! You had begun to return to the life of salvation; but the devil, who incited you to betray your teacher and Lord, himself gave you the counsel to kill yourself [Note: [Col. 0299D] Chrysostom, Homily 86: “But consider when he repented: when the crime had already wholly reached its consummation. Such indeed is the devil: unless a person keeps watch, he does not allow him to foresee the enormity of the sin before its final completion, lest, moved by repentance, he recoil from sin … That he hanged himself was the devil’s destructive counsel, excluding him from every pardon.”]. This alone would have been enough for your ruin, even had you not betrayed the Lord. How much better it would have been for you to humble yourself at Christ’s feet and seek pardon from him who rejects no one who comes to him [Note: [Col. 0299D] Fulgentius, Letter 7, ch. 5: “Judas repented of his sin, but lost salvation because he did not hope for pardon … therefore he denied himself the fruit of repentance, because he did not hope that the sin of his betrayal would be washed away by the blood of him whom he betrayed.” See St Leo, Sermon 1, *On the Passion of the Lord*, ch. 5.].

But the chief priests, having received the silver, said: “It is not lawful [Col. 0299C] to put it into the corban” [Note: [Col. 0299D] Thus the Greek κορβανᾶν, and the manuscript codices in Sabatier.], “because it is the price of blood.” I say: If it was unlawful to put it into the corban because it was the price of blood, neither was it lawful to take it out of the corban so that it might become the price of blood. Having taken counsel, they bought with it the potter’s field [Col. 0300A] as a burial place for strangers. This potter formed us [Note: [Col. 0299D] Jerome: “We who were strangers to the Law and the prophets received their perverse efforts unto salvation, [Col. 0300C] and rest in the price of his blood. It is called the potter’s field because Christ is our potter.” A sermon numbered 114, *On the Seasons*, among Augustine’s works, copied its material from Jerome. Ambrose, Book X, *On Luke*: “While the price of blood is separated from the Jewish treasuries, and the potter’s field is purchased with the money for which Christ is sold, while that place is designated for burying the remains of strangers, both the oracle of prophecy is fulfilled and the mystery of the rising Church is revealed. For the field … is this whole world; and the potter is he who formed us from the clay of earth … the price of blood is also the price of the Lord’s Passion; [Col. 0300D] therefore the world is bought by Christ with the price of blood,” etc. See also Sermon 128, *On the Seasons*, among Augustine’s works. But above all Hilary: “There is a great mystery of prophecy in this,” etc.]. His field is bought with Christ’s price, and in it his strangers are buried and rest.

For this reason that field was called Achel demach [Note: [Col. 0300D] Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, II, ch. 38, and the Old Latin read thus.], that is, “field of blood,” even to the present day. It is rightly called a field of blood, since it is purchased with Christ’s blood. For this field is the land of the living, in which those who are buried do not die.

Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, saying: “And they received thirty pieces of silver, the price of the one appraised, whom they appraised from the children of Israel; and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord appointed me.” You hear that the Lord appointed this, that he ordained before the ages that Christ the Lord should be sold for thirty pieces of silver, with which the potter’s field should be bought. But this [Col. 0300B] passage is found not in Jeremiah but in Zechariah [Note: [Col. 0300D] See Jerome here and in his letter to Pammachius, *On the Best Method of Translating*; Eusebius, Book X, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, ch. 4; Augustine, Book III, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, ch. 7; Bede; etc.] (Zechariah XI, 13). Yet it is said to be found in certain copies of Jeremiah which we use.

But Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor questioned him, saying: “Are you the King of the Jews?” Jesus said to him: “You say so.” What the governor said interrogatively, Christ accepted affirmatively. And when he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he gave no answer. He answered the governor, he says, but did not answer the chief priests and elders, because the former questioned him simply, whereas the latter spoke maliciously against him. For in every respect prepared to contradict, they were unworthy of an answer from the Lord [Note: [Col. 0300D] Jerome here: “Observe that he answered in some measure to Pilate, who uttered his sentence unwillingly, but refused to answer the priests and rulers, judging them unworthy of his speech.” Chrysostom, Homily 87: “Because, though they had from the facts themselves a thousand proofs of his extraordinary power and greatness, they acted maliciously, voluntarily blinding themselves, and the judgment itself was plainly corrupt; therefore he is silent.” See also Ambrose, Book X, *On Luke*.].

Then Pilate said to him: “Do you not hear how much testimony they are giving against you?” [Col. 0300C] And he did not answer him a single word, so that the governor was greatly astonished. For it was not fitting for the Lord then to answer Pilate when he was provoking him to contend against false and envious accusers. For it is nothing but labour to answer those who are unwilling to hear the truth [Note: [Col. 0301C] Chrysostom: “To the charges brought against him, since he knew that he would by no means persuade them, he gave no answer at all.”].

Now at the feast the governor was accustomed to release to the people one prisoner whom they wished. At that time he had a notorious prisoner called Barabbas. Therefore, when they had assembled, Pilate said: “Whom do you want me to release to you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?” For he knew that they had handed him over out of envy [130]. While he was seated on the tribunal, his wife sent to him, saying: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man; for today I have suffered much in a dream because of him.” Although even evil people foresee many things in visions, I nevertheless believe that this woman had a good spirit [Note: [Col. 0301C] This is plainly the opinion of many ancient Fathers and nearly the common opinion of modern interpreters. Jerome: “Note that dreams are often revealed by God to Gentiles, and that in Pilate and his wife, who confess the Lord righteous, there is the testimony of the Gentile people.” Hilary had written much the same, and Ambrose, Book X, *On Luke*, ch. 23: “His wife warned him; grace shone in the night, divinity stood forth; yet not even so did he refrain from the sacrilegious sentence.” Maldonatus denies that the contrary opinion is probable; nevertheless [Col. 0301D] Jansenius, *Harmony*, ch. 142; Lucas of Bruges; and Menochius support it; finally Estius thinks it conflicts with the Apostle’s statement in 1 Corinthians II, “If they had known,” etc.].

But the chief priests and elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to destroy Jesus. Pilate wishes to release Christ; the Jews insist that he not be released. [Col. 0301B] Hence they themselves are rightly said to have crucified him [Note: [Col. 0301D] Thus Augustine wrote, Book III, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, ch. 13: “It is understood, therefore, that it was the third hour when the Jews cried out that the Lord should be crucified, and it is most truly shown that they crucified him when they cried out.” He says the same in Tractate 116 on John.], although he was crucified not by them but by the Gentiles.

The governor answered and said to them: “Which of the two do you want released to you?” They said: “Barabbas.” Pilate said to them: “What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” They all said: “Let him be crucified.” The Jews kill their Lord; they condemn and command their Saviour to be crucified; they ask for Barabbas, whose name is interpreted “son of their teacher” [Note: [Col. 0301D] Jerome: “In the Gospel written according to the Hebrews, he is interpreted ‘son of their teacher.’” From Jerome, as I think, Bede states it still more precisely: “Luke reports that Barabbas, the son of their teacher, was put into prison for sedition made in the city and for murder.” And even Hilary, who preceded Jerome: “The interpretation of the name Barabbas is ‘son of the father.’”]. For their teacher is the devil, who taught them to cry out thus and make this choice: that they should choose the son of the devil for themselves and crucify the Son of God.

The governor said to them: “What evil, then, has he done?” But they cried out all the more: “Let him be crucified.” Now the Jews strive to kill Christ not by accusation but by clamour, not by judgment but by violence. [Col. 0301C] Pilate asks what evil he has done; they answer nothing to this question, because they have nothing to answer. Therefore they shout, rage, and go mad, so that the Scripture may be fulfilled which says: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers assembled together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Psalm II, 1).

But Pilate, seeing that he accomplished nothing and that rather a disturbance was arising among the people, took water and washed his hands before the people, saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man; see to it yourselves.” Pilate washes his hands so that, just as his hands are clean of filth, he may show himself innocent of Christ’s death [Note: [Col. 0301D] St Leo, Sermon 8, ch. 2: “Hands that have been washed do not cleanse a polluted mind, nor is what is committed by an impious mind expiated by water sprinkled [Col. 0302C] upon the fingers.”]. But it is not so. Although he himself did not judge or condemn him, he is nevertheless guilty, because he handed over for judgment by others one whom he knew was being condemned without cause and through envy.

And the whole people answered and said: “His blood be upon us and upon [Col. 0302B] our children.” For the Jews transmitted this hereditary curse to their descendants [Note: [Col. 0302C] Jerome: “This imprecation persists upon the Jews to the present day, and the Lord’s blood shall not be removed from them, etc.; hence he speaks through Isaiah (I, 15): ‘If you lift up your hands to me,’ etc. The Jews left their children a very fine inheritance, saying, ‘His blood,’ etc.” Bede says somewhat differently: “Their request clings to the Jews to this day … and hitherto they have not deserved to recover the freedom, whether of soul or body, which they sold.”]: all are subject to it who imitate them and whom this deed of theirs does not displease.

Then he released Barabbas to them [Note: [Col. 0302C] In our manuscript Barabbas is consistently read. So too in MS St-Germain 2 in Sabatier.], but Jesus, having scourged him, he handed over to them to be crucified. Pilate scourged Jesus, either so that the Jews, satisfied by such punishment, might relent and thus release him as corrected; or because Roman laws ordered that a man to be crucified should first be scourged [Note: [Col. 0302D] Chrysostom also appears uncertain on this point, Homily 87: “Why does he scourge him? Either as condemned, or as giving the proceedings some semblance of judgment, or to do something pleasing to the Jews.” But Jerome: “One must know that he observed the Roman laws, by which it was ordained that one who is crucified should first be beaten with scourges.” Bede departs from Jerome—rarely: “Pilate himself first scourged him, then handed him over to the soldiers to be mocked, so that the Jews, sated with his punishments and insults, might cease further to thirst for his death.”].

Then the governor’s soldiers took Jesus into the praetorium and gathered the whole cohort around him. Having stripped him, they put a scarlet cloak around him; and, plaiting a crown of thorns, they placed it on his head, and a reed in his right hand; and kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying: [Col. 0302C] “Hail, King of the Jews.” They did all these things, as is said here, in mockery; but for us they are signs of a great mystery [Note: [Col. 0302D] Hilary: “The Lord, having been scourged, is clothed in a scarlet cloak and purple garment, with a crown of thorns and a reed in his right hand; and, after a knee has been bent, he is mocked in adoration. Thus, having assumed all the infirmities of our body, he is next steeped in the scarlet blossom by the blood of all the martyrs, to whom the kingdom was due with him; and he is clothed in purple with the precious honour of the prophets and patriarchs; he is crowned with thorns, that is, with the sins of the Gentiles which once pricked [Col. 0303C] … for there is a sting in thorns, from which Christ’s crown of victory is woven; in the reed, moreover, the weakness and emptiness of those same Gentiles, grasped in his hand, are strengthened, etc. In all these things, while Christ is mocked, he is adored.” Jerome: “Whatever these men did, though they did it with another intent, nevertheless they bestowed mysteries upon us who believe. In the scarlet cloak he bears the bloody deeds of the Gentiles; in the crown of thorns he dissolves the ancient curse,” etc. See Bede, etc.]: and we receive [Col. 0303A] and venerate all these things not as sport but in truth.

That the crown was of thorns signified that a kingdom was to be gathered from sinners. A reed is given to him as a sceptre, that he may write the righteous in heaven and sinners on earth, according to the saying: “Lord, all who hate you shall be confounded; those who depart from you shall be written in the earth” [Note: [Col. 0303D] Jeremiah XVII, 13: “All who forsake you,” etc.]. But to the good the Lord says: “Because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X, 20). For the Jews used to write with a reed. In the scarlet or purple garment, such as other kings also wore, whatever their intent in doing this, they nevertheless most plainly proclaimed him to be king.

And spitting upon him, they took the reed and struck his head. For as the Apostle says: “The head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians XI, 3). Therefore he strikes Christ’s head with a reed who composes Scripture against [Col. 0303B] his divinity, or argues by the authority of some Scripture that the Lord himself is not God [Note: [Col. 0303D] Hilary: “A typological meaning is maintained in this: that the weakness of the Gentile bodies, formerly grasped in Christ’s hand, should rest even upon God the Father, who is his head.”].

And after they had mocked him, they stripped him of the cloak, dressed him in his own garments, and led him away to crucify him. For it was not fitting that he should be crucified in royal array, but that he should appear humble in dress, he who had humbled himself in majesty.

As they went out, they found a man of Cyrene named Simon; they compelled him to carry Christ’s cross. *Cyrenaeus* means “heir,” Simon “obedient” [Note: [Col. 0303D] Bede: “The cross was laid upon Simon, whose name is interpreted ‘obedient,’ coming from the city of Cyrene in Libya, which is interpreted ‘heir’ … when the people of the nations, abandoning pagan rites, obediently embrace the footsteps of the Lord’s Passion.” Jerome likewise: “According to the anagogical sense, the nations take up Jesus’ cross, and the obedient stranger bears the Saviour’s shame.” See also Hilary.]. Thus the Gentile man, heir of the heavenly country and obedient to God, carries Christ’s cross. Of him the Lord himself says elsewhere: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew XVI, 24; Luke [Col. 0303C] IX, 23).—And they came to the place called Golgotha, which is the place of the Skull.

This place was so called because those condemned were beheaded there, and there lost the skulls of their heads [Note: [Col. 0303D] Jerome, on this passage: “I have heard someone explain that the place of the Skull was where Adam was buried, and that it was so called because the head of the old man was laid there; and that this is what the Apostle says: ‘Awake, you who sleep,’ etc. This interpretation is pleasing and delights the people’s ear, but it is not true. For outside the city and beyond the gate are places where the heads of the condemned are cut off; and the skulls—that is, the place of the beheaded—took their name from this.” Some think that Jerome intended to refer to St Ambrose, writing in his commentary on Luke: “The place of the cross was either in the middle of the earth, so as to be visible to all, or above Adam’s burial-place, as the Hebrews maintain.” Yet it is inferred from the commentary on Ephesians [Col. 0304D] V, 14 that he had in mind not Ambrose but another. That Paula and Eustochium held this opinion is evident from Letter 46 to Marcella among Jerome’s letters.]. Yet some thought that this place had been so named from the skull of the first man.

And they gave him wine [Col. 0304A] mixed with gall to drink; and when he had tasted it, he would not drink. Hence the Psalmist says: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Psalm LXVIII, 22). He tasted it but would not drink, signifying that the bitterness of death which he was to taste was momentary and soon to be changed into sweetness.

After they had crucified him, they divided his garments, casting lots, that what had been spoken through the Prophet might be fulfilled: “They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots” (Psalm XXI, 19). But this better garment, which is neither torn nor divided but is allotted by lot, signifies the holy Church, having neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of the kind.

And sitting down, they kept watch over him. And they placed above [Col. 0304B] his head the written charge against him: “This is Jesus, King of the Jews.” Another Evangelist relates that this title was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin [Note: [Col. 0304D] Jerome: “Whether you wish it or not, Jews, the whole multitude of nations answers you: Jesus, King of the Jews—that is, ruler of those who believe and confess.” St Augustine, Tractate 117 on John: “These three languages stood forth there above the rest: Hebrew, because of the Jews who gloried in God’s Law; Greek, because of the wise among the nations; Latin, because of the Romans, who then ruled many—indeed almost all—nations.” Bede says the same in almost the same words from Augustine.] (Luke XXIII, 38; John XIX, 20), so that every language may confess by reading what the Jews refused to believe and confess.

Then they crucified with him two robbers, one at the right and one at the left. Here too we see fulfilled: “And he was numbered among the wicked” (Isaiah LIII, 12; Mark XV, 28); and “You shall be known in the midst of two living creatures” (Habakkuk III, 2, according to the Septuagint).—Those passing by blasphemed him, shaking their heads and saying: “Ha! You who destroy the Temple of God and rebuild it in three days!” Like madmen they shake their heads, mock Christ, and insult him in gesture and speech, saying: “Save yourself [Col. 0304C] and us. If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.” Thus their teacher the devil also said: “If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down” (Matthew IV, 6). For it is no greater thing to come down from the cross than to raise the dead. Jesus did this; why therefore do the Jews not believe that he is the Son of God [Note: [Col. 0304D] Jerome, on this passage: “Which is greater: to come down alive from the cross, or to rise dead from the tomb? He rose, and you did not believe. Therefore, even if he had come down from the cross, you would not have believed. But demons seem to me to be suggesting this.” Augustine likewise, Tractate 37 on John: “What great thing was it for him to come down from the cross, who could rise from the tomb?” [Col. 0305C] St Gregory, Homily 21 on the Gospels: “He who would not come down from the cross rose from the tomb. Was it greater, then, to rise from the tomb than to come down from the cross? It was greater to destroy death by rising than to save life by coming down.”]?

The Jews spoke these words not of themselves but under diabolical inspiration [132] [Note: [Col. 0305C] Jerome, speaking of the demons: “As soon as the Lord was crucified, they sensed the power of the cross and understood that their strength had been broken; and this is what they seek, that he should come down from the cross. But the Lord, knowing the snares of his adversaries, remains upon the cross in order to destroy the devil.”]. For now the devil felt himself conquered and could not bear the power of the cross; therefore he tried to prevent Christ’s Passion.

Likewise the chief priests, mocking him together with the scribes and elders, said: “He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we shall believe him. He trusts in God; let him deliver him now, if he wants him. For he said: ‘I am the Son of God.’” The robbers who had been crucified with him also reproached him with the same thing. All say the same because all speak by the same spirit. They promise that they will believe if he comes down from the cross; yet if he had come down from the cross, he would not have delivered us from death. From where death came, life returns: through wood death came; through wood [Col. 0305B] life returns. Therefore the Lord did not wish to come down from the cross, because he wished to redeem the world through the cross.

Now from the sixth hour darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour. Darkness comes everywhere when the Sun of righteousness sets. Just as at his birth the world was enlightened and the people who sat in darkness saw a great light, so at his death it was darkened and inwardly wrapped in the darkness of ignorance, because “hardening has come upon Israel in part” (Romans XI, 25).

At the sight of this miracle, one of the robbers believed; though he had earlier despised Christ along with his companion, later he began to defend him, saying to the other, as another Evangelist reports: “Do you not fear God, since you are under the same condemnation?” (Luke XXIII, 40). Thus at first both, but afterward one and not both, reproached [Col. 0305C] him [Note: [Col. 0305D] Jerome, on this passage: “Here, by the trope called σύλληψις (*syllepsis*), both are represented as having blasphemed, though only one did. But Luke maintains that, while one blasphemed, the other confessed and on the contrary rebuked the blasphemer. The Gospels do not disagree: at first both blasphemed; then, when the sun fled … one believed in Jesus and corrected his earlier denial by his later confession.” St Ambrose, Book X on Luke: “Perhaps this man too first reviled him, but was suddenly converted.” Augustine, however, Book III, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, ch. 16, holds that only one blasphemed Christ, and that Matthew and Mark, “briefly touching on this passage, used the plural number for the singular.”].

And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying: “Heli, heli, lama sabachthani”—that is: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” It is the man who speaks and says that he has been forsaken. According to some, he laments that his body, which is the Church, has been forsaken by God [Note: [Col. 0305D] St Leo, Sermon 16, *On the Passion of the Lord*, ch. 7: “The Lord Jesus, transforming into himself all the members of his body, cried out in the voice of his redeemed ones under the suffering of the cross what he had formerly uttered in the Psalm: ‘My God, my God,’ etc. ‘The voice is teaching, not complaint.’”]. For in himself he is never forsaken by God; for no one is forsaken by God except one who sins. As often [Col. 0306A] as we sin, so often are we forsaken by God. The Lord himself indicates this when, immediately adding from the Psalm, he says: “Far from my salvation” (Psalm XXI, 2). The words “these are the words” are to be understood. Whose words, then, are they? Do you wish to hear whose? “The words of my offences”; as though he said: “I would not have said these words unless I grieved for the offences of my faithful [Note: [Col. 0306C] St Ambrose, Sermon 3 on Psalm CXVIII: “Christ declares that he has been forsaken on account of
“Us, whose sins he was bearing.”].” I grieve, moreover, because I see that those whom I reconcile to God by so harsh and bitter a death are, because of the sins they commit, again abandoned by God and tending toward death.

But some of those standing there and hearing said, “This man is calling Elijah.” Not all, but certain persons said this—namely, those who did not understand these words.

> [Note: Col. 0306C] St Jerome: “Not all, but some, whom I suppose to have been Roman soldiers, not understanding the particular character of the Hebrew language.” Bede says the same.

And immediately one of them ran, took a sponge, filled it with vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave him drink. “Immediately,” he says, when the Lord said, “I thirst,” as John the Evangelist writes (John 19:29), one of them ran, filled a sponge with vinegar, and gave him drink. For Christ thirsted not for vinegar but for faith. Yet the Synagogue gave what it possessed.

> [Note: Col. 0306D] Jerome: “Even today the Jews and all who disbelieve the Lord’s resurrection give Jesus vinegar and gall to drink.” Bede: “They gave what they themselves were. The Jews themselves were vinegar, having degenerated from the wine of the prophets and patriarchs; as though from a full vessel, filled with the iniquity of this world; having a heart, like a sponge, deceitful in its cavernous and, as it were, winding hiding-places.”

For what is vinegar except their bitter, sour, erroneous, and poisonous doctrine? And what is the sponge except their deceitful and secretive hearts? But the reed with which writing is done signifies Scripture itself. What, then, did that act signify except that the Synagogue, even to this day, does not cease to devise and write perverse doctrine and a heretical draught, and to utter and pour it forth against Christ?

But others said, “Leave him; let us see whether Elijah comes to free him.” Those who had not understood what Christ’s words meant said this—those to whom he had just said above, “Eli, Eli.”

---

But Jesus, again crying with a loud voice, gave up the spirit.

> [Note: Col. 0306D] Bede: “In saying, ‘He gave up the spirit,’ he shows that it belongs to divine power to give up the spirit; as he himself also said, ‘No one can take away my soul,’ etc.” This Bede, as usual, takes from Jerome, who likewise says on this passage: “It is a proof of divine power to give up the spirit, as he himself also said: ‘No one can take my soul from me,’ etc.” Jerome says almost the same in his Letter to Hedibia, question 8.

For he had in his own power both to live and to die, as he willed. Hence elsewhere he says: “No one takes my life from me; rather, I lay it down, and take it up again” (John 10:18).

---

And behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom;

> [Note: Col. 0307C] Jerome: “The veil of the temple was torn, and all the mysteries of the Law which had formerly been kept hidden were disclosed, and passed over to the people of the Gentiles.” See the Letter to Hedibia, cited above.

and the earth was shaken; and the rocks were split; and the tombs were opened; and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose; and, coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they came into the holy city and appeared to many.

At Christ’s voice the elements are moved; and with him all creation wills to be dissolved and brought to an end. The veil of the temple is torn; the Holy of Holies appears; and, when the old covering is removed, the foundations of the Scriptures are revealed. The earth is shaken and the rocks split, so that, since the Jews persisted unmoved in their unbelief, the Gentiles may be moved from unbelief and run to faith; and, in order to draw in the rain of evangelical teaching, may first open hearts that were hard and stony.

> [Note: Col. 0307C] Hilary: “The rocks were split; for the word of God, penetrating then all things firm and strong, and the power of eternal might, had burst forth.” Jerome: “It seems to me that the earthquake and the remaining events bear the figure of believers: having abandoned the former vices of error and had the hardness of their hearts softened, those formerly like the tombs of the dead afterward acknowledged the Creator.” Bede says the same. See St Leo, Sermons 2, 8, and 10, *On the Passion*.

But the bodies that rise bear witness to Christ’s true resurrection.

Now the centurion and those who were with him guarding Jesus, when they saw the earthquake and the things that were happening, were greatly afraid, saying, “Truly this was the Son of God.” The Gentiles believe; the Jews perish. The Jews say, “According to the Law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.” The Gentiles say, “Truly this was the Son of God.” Great was this centurion, who guarded Jesus as he died.

Now many women were there at a distance, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him. Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee. For these women, who had followed Christ in devout love, did not leave him even in death. This is that Mary Magdalene from whom the Lord had cast out seven demons; but that other Mary was his aunt—that is, the sister of his mother.

> [Note: Cols. 0307C–D] Jerome, on verses 55 and 61: “It was a Jewish custom, and was not counted blameworthy under the ancient usage of the nation, that women should provide food and clothing for teachers from their own resources. … They ministered to the Lord from their own substance. … Let us see what companions he had: Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons; Mary, the mother of James and Joseph, his aunt, the sister of Mary the Lord’s mother; and the mother of the sons of Zebedee. … When the others left the Lord, the women persevered in their service, awaiting what Jesus had promised; and therefore they deserved to be the first to see him risen.” See Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, book 3, chapter 21.

When evening had come, a certain rich man from Arimathea came, named Joseph, who was himself also a disciple of Jesus. He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then Pilate ordered the body to be given over. Since this Joseph was rich and noble, he was therefore able to obtain Christ’s body from Pilate so readily.

> [Note: Col. 0307D] Jerome: “He is called rich, not from the writer’s ostentation … but in order to show why he was able to obtain Jesus’ body from Pilate: for it was not open to a poor and unknown person to approach Pilate, governor of the Roman authority, and request the body of one crucified.” Bede has these same words from Jerome.

And Joseph, having received the body, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth and placed it in his own new tomb, which he had cut out in the rock; and he rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb and went away. Joseph teaches us how we ought to receive Christ’s body; he teaches us to receive it with a clean heart and pure conscience—he who himself wrapped it in a clean linen cloth and placed it in a new tomb.

> [Note: Cols. 0307D–0308C] Jerome: “According to the spiritual understanding, we may also take this to mean that the Lord’s body ought to be wrapped not in gold, jewels, and silk, but in pure linen; although it also signifies that the person who wrapped Jesus in a clean linen cloth is one who receives him with a pure mind.” Bede says the same.

But Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb. Rightly the Lord appeared first to them after his resurrection, for they guarded him so faithfully and desired so greatly to see him; and because they could no longer see him, they sat before his tomb. They marked the place which they wished to visit often, and from which, if it could be done, they did not wish to depart.

It now wearies one to hear the blasphemies of the Jews. They assemble again and ask Pilate to guard the tomb, as though he who is everywhere and contains all things could be held in a tomb. But he, already weary and disdaining further to hear them, says: “Go and guard it as you know how.” They go, fortify the tomb, post guards, and seal the stone. They do everything so carefully that, although unwillingly, they themselves become witnesses that the Lord rose, and that it was in no way possible for him, thus laid there, to have been stolen.

> [Note: Cols. 0308C–D] Hilary: “The fear that the body might be stolen, the guarding and sealing of the tomb, are testimony to folly and unbelief: they wished to seal the tomb of him at whose command they had seen a dead man raised from a tomb.” Jerome: “It was not enough for the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees to have crucified the Lord and Saviour, unless they also guarded the tomb, obtained a military guard, sealed the stone, and, so far as lay in them, set their hand against him as he rose, so that their diligence might advance our faith. For the more carefully he was guarded, the more clearly the power of the resurrection was displayed. Hence he was laid in a new tomb cut out in the rock, lest, if it had been built from many stones, it might be said that he was stolen away by undermining the foundations of the tomb.” Bede has this, but in a mutilated form.

CV. (CHAP. XXVIII.) But late on the Sabbath, which [Col. 0308C] dawns into the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb. [Note: [Col. 0308D] This is a homily of Saint Bruno, like the others attributed to Eusebius of Emesa, for Holy Saturday.]

“Evening” [Note: [Col. 0308D] Baronius, at the year 34, no. 167, calls this passage exceedingly difficult, “and one which demands diligent and exact study; since the talents of very learned men have been greatly wearied over it.” A Lapide calls the apparent contradiction difficult here; but, before all other interpreters, Maldonatus writes on this passage: “This passage is judged by all interpreters to be the most difficult, because the words themselves are obscure, and because neither do the other Evangelists seem to agree with Matthew, nor Matthew with himself, nor the others with one another, nor Mark [Col. 0309C] himself with himself.” He later explains this by citing the words of the Evangelists.]—which is also called the evening star—is the star which by another name is called Lucifer, 134 the morning star. Hesperus, or Vesper, is so called at the end of the day; Lucifer, however, at its beginning. For when it rises, it often precedes the sun by a very small interval. That the Evangelist understood this of the star is apparent from the fact that he used the feminine gender: “which dawns into the first day of the week.” To what other thing could the pronoun “which” refer except the star? Now they called every day a sabbath. Let it therefore be said: “With the evening star of the Sabbath appearing,” that is, with that star called both Vesper and Lucifer, now announcing the following day. I do not mean the one appearing at the day’s end, but the one seen at its beginning, that is, the one which dawns into the first day of the week; namely, which begins to shine in the first part of the first day, which is now called the Lord’s Day.

[Col. 0309B] Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb. Travelers customarily observe this star because it is brighter than the rest. Thus, guided by its sign, these holy women began to come to the tomb: “And very early, while it was still dark” (John 20:1), as John says; yet with the sun already rising [Note: [Col. 0309C] Mark 16:2: “And very early on the first day of the week they come to the tomb, the sun having already risen.”], as Mark says, they come to the tomb. For the sun rises before darkness has departed. It may also be said otherwise, so that this is understood not of the evening of the day but of the evening of the night. For night too has its own evening, called dawn or twilight. Of this evening Moses says: “And there was evening and there was morning, one day” (Gen. 1:5). But if it is understood of the evening of the day, the entire night is left out. Hence some interpreters reckon the whole day together [Col. 0309C] with its night as one day; and so the evening of the night together with the morning of the day makes one day. And although I have explained this differently in Genesis [Note: [Col. 0309C] In the Roman edition of Saint Bruno, p. 2, ch. 1.], nevertheless this interpretation now pleases me more because of these words of the Gospel.

Let it therefore be said: “Late on the Sabbath,” that is, at the evening of the Sabbath night, [Col. 0310A] Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb—at that hour, namely, which dawns into the first day of the week, that is, into the first part of the day. [Note: [Col. 0309C] Chrysostom mystically explains everything here, sermons 74, 75, etc. In the literal sense, the question concerns reconciling these Gospel passages: 1. “Late on the Sabbath, which dawned into the first day of the week.” 2. “When the Sabbath had passed, very early on the first day of the week, the sun having already risen.” 3. “But on the first day of the week, at early dawn.” 4. “Very early, while it was still dark.” The author offers two explanations: first, that evening signifies a star which also appears in the morning, and thus denotes the early-morning time here; second, that just as the day has its evening, that is, the end of the day, so the night has its evening, that is, the end of the night and likewise the beginning of the day. Baronius proposed both explanations in the cited passage. When an objection was raised against the first—that in Greek the word is ὄψε, which cannot mean “star”—he disparages the Greek text and concludes: “If this does not please, we propose that Maldonatus be followed before other interpreters in these matters”; thus in the latest edition. Maldonatus’s view scarcely differs from our author’s second explanation, except that he develops and confirms it more fully. Menochius also adopts it, Book VIII, *V. C.*, ch. 1, no. 3, as do others. For since the Greek reads ὄψε σαββάτων, “late on the Sabbaths,” that is, properly after the Sabbath [Col. 0310C] and when the week was ended, Matthew says the same as Mark, “when the Sabbath had passed”: “early on the first day of the week,” that is, as the first day of the week following dawned, the sun having already risen and its rays having somewhat illuminated the sky, as A Lapide explains from Euthymius; or, the sun having risen and become visible by the time they reached the tomb after completing their journey, as Dionysius of Alexandria interprets in his letter to Basilides. See also Jansenius, *Harmony*, ch. 145, and other interpreters.]

Both are called Mary, because the name means “star of the sea.” [Note: [Col. 0310C] Isidore, *Origins*, Book VII, ch. 10, interprets Mary as “illuminator” or “star of the sea.” [Col. 0310D] Thus Saint Bernard later does in Homily 3 on the *Missus est*.] Therefore two stars follow the third, and come together seeking the Sun of righteousness. The two stars, however, are the two Churches, namely that of the Jews and that of the Gentiles. Enlightened from heaven, they proclaim the resurrection of the dead.

“And behold, there was a great earthquake.” A great earthquake [Note: [Col. 0310D] Bede: “The earthquake signifies that the hearts of the carnal are to be shaken into repentance by faith in the Passion and Resurrection.”] occurs when so great a multitude from each people runs to Christ in these two women. “For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and came and rolled away the stone, and sat upon it.” This angel signifies the preachers of the Church; at their voices earthquakes [Col. 0310B] occur, because sinners, who are called earth, pass from unbelief to faith through their preaching. They roll away the stone, expound the Scriptures, open the tablets, and reveal to all the law written upon them. They sit upon the stone because they understand, and hold in their power, what is contained in the writing on the stone tablets.

“His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow.” Thus in the one respect he terrified the wicked, and in the other comforted the good. [Note: [Col. 0310D] Bede: “He was both terrible for condemning the reprobate and kindly and gentle for comforting the elect.”] Preachers imitate him when they promise fire to the wicked, but eternal happiness to the good. Hence the guards are said to have been terrified and become as dead men; but to the women it is said: “Do not be afraid.” [Note: [Col. 0310D] Hilary speaks excellently: “The angel of the Lord descending from heaven … is the mark of the mercy of God the Father, who sends the ministries of the heavenly powers to his Son rising from the underworld.” Gregory, Homily 21 on the Gospels: “In lightning there is the terror of fear, but in snow the gentleness of brightness. Since almighty God is both terrible to sinners and gentle to the righteous, rightly the angel, witness of his resurrection, is displayed in the flashing of his face and the whiteness of his garment, so that by his very appearance he might terrify the reprobate and comfort the devout.”] Let those fear for whom fire and wrath are prepared; but why [Col. 0310C] 135 should you fear, who see your companions and friends? “For I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified”; and therefore you ought not to fear his servants. “He is not here”—that is, in the bodily presence of him who is everywhere in the power of his divinity.

But where do we believe that he then was? I myself would readily believe that he then [Col. 0311A] visited his mother, who, more afflicted by grief than the rest, awaited his resurrection. What then, if the Evangelists do not say this? For, as John says, not all his deeds were written down. Returning thence, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, rather than to the apostles themselves or to any others. Let whoever wishes accept this; I compel no one to believe it. [Note: [Col. 0311D] Suarez argues this at length from the Fathers, vol. II, on Part III, disputation 49, section 1, on the authority of Ambrose, Sedulius, etc. On the others see sections 2 and 3.]

It follows: “For he has risen, as he said. Come and see the place where the Lord lay.” For doctors of the Church often show us the place where the Lord had lain, when, expounding examples from the holy Scriptures, they teach us where his birth, Passion, and resurrection were prophesied. Do you wish to see the place where the Lord had lain? Read in the Psalms: “I lay down and slept; and I rose again, because [Col. 0311B] the Lord sustained me.” [Note: [Col. 0311D] Psalm 3:6. Chrysologus, Sermon 75: “They bear to the Lord’s tomb not the forms of women, but a type of Churches.” And Sermon 76: “We have said that Mary and the other Mary bore the figure of the Church coming from two peoples,” etc.]

“And go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen; and behold, he will go before you into Galilee. There you will see him. Behold, I have told you beforehand.” Behold, the woman who had been the gate of death is the first to proclaim the resurrection [Note: [Col. 0311D] Hilary: “That women first see the Lord, are greeted, fall at his knees, and are ordered to announce it to the apostles, restores in reverse order the principal cause: so that, because death had begun from this sex, to it should first be restored the sight, fruit, and announcement of resurrection glory.” Ambrose, Book XIX on Luke: “By Jesus not only is woman’s guilt loosed, but grace too is multiplied, so that she who had once deceived one might persuade many.” See Chrysologus, Sermon 77, etc., and Gregory, Homily 25 on the Gospels.], and displays the gate of life. The Lord goes before them into Galilee and there awaits the disciples, because the saints will see God when they have returned to their homeland. For Galilee was the homeland of the apostles; hence they are called “men of Galilee” (Acts 1:11).

“And they departed quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, running to tell his disciples.” But Mark says that, fleeing from the tomb (Mark 16:8), because terror had seized them, they said nothing to anyone. From this it is understood that at first they said nothing about the vision of angels, [Col. 0311C] but only reported that the Lord had been removed from the tomb. The sequence, therefore, is as follows. [Note: [Col. 0312D] See Saint Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, Book III, no. 69, whom the author nearly follows; Maldonatus on Matthew ch. 28; Barradas, vol. IV of the *Commentaries on the Harmony*, Book VII, ch. 3; Jansenius, *Harmony*, ch. 145; Francis Lucas, A Lapide, etc.]

The women came to the tomb and saw an angel, whom they nevertheless thought to be not an angel but a young man. They ran to the apostles. About the angel and his words, by which they had heard that the Lord had risen, they said nothing to anyone, announcing only that the Lord was not in the tomb. Peter and John therefore ran together and found only the linen cloths. When they departed, the women remained there. Then Mary Magdalene bent down and looked into the tomb, and saw two angels seated there. While they comforted her, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, [Col. 0312A] whom she thought not to be Jesus but the gardener. When she recognized him by his voice, she approached him; and although he said to her, “Do not touch me,” she nevertheless held him and kissed his feet.

Then the other women came, for Luke records that there were several (Luke 24:10). When the Lord had graciously greeted them, they too held his feet. Hence it is added here: “And behold, Jesus met them, saying: Hail. And they came and held his feet, and worshiped him.” Then Jesus said to them: “Do not be afraid. Go, tell my brothers to go into Galilee; there they will see me.” Thus, certain of the resurrection, they now announce not, as before, that the Lord had been removed from the tomb, but affirm both that they had seen him and had spoken with him. They tell the disciples to go [Col. 0312B] into Galilee, and that there they will see him, as he had foretold.

“And when they had departed, behold, some of the guards came into the city and announced to the chief priests all that had happened. And having assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave much money to the soldiers, saying: ‘Say that his disciples came by night and stole him while we slept. And if this comes to the governor’s ears, we will persuade him and keep you safe.’ And they, having received the money, did as they had been instructed; and this report was spread among the Jews to this very day.”

Can greed, then, do so much? Can love of money do so much? It first sold Christ; now 136 it compels men once again to deny his resurrection. [Note: [Col. 0312D] Chrysologus, Sermon 80: “The Jews, when Judas sold him, bought Christ in order to destroy him; now they poured out much money in order to destroy themselves, the Law, their country, and the Temple. Men of blood and deceit fix the price of falsehood, draw up the instrument of faithlessness, and in a cruel transaction barter the fraud of faith and the robbery of truth,” etc.] O wretched Jews! It had sufficed you once to kill Christ; it had sufficed you once to buy him. Again you buy him with money, and purchase him at a greater price than before; and behold, so far as lies in you, you kill him again, when you deny that he has risen and lives.

CVI. But the eleven disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them; and when they saw him, they worshiped him, though some doubted. [Note: [Col. 0312D] This is part of the homily listed among the spurious works of Eusebius of Emesa for the Friday after Easter, p. 126. For in that homily much is inserted concerning the place—Galilee, namely, and the mountain where Jesus had appointed them—and concerning their mystical meanings, throughout p. 127, section 1. But from the words, “And Jesus came and spoke to them,” etc., the remainder is the same in both places.]

When this vision occurred, I do not know, because Thomas, who was one of these, is said not to have seen the Lord before eight days had passed. “And Jesus came and spoke to them, saying: All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.” He who according to his divinity always possessed, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0313A] authority over all things, has now also received authority over all things according to his humanity. [Note: [Col. 0313A] Cyril, Book on John, ch. 73: “Because authority was given, he will not therefore appear lesser when the Father gives it; [Col. 0313B] for he received as man … Do you not see that in these things the Father, as God, gives, while the Son, as man, receives those things which he possessed as God?” Jerome, on this passage: “Authority was given to him who shortly before had been crucified, had been buried in the tomb, had lain dead, and afterward rose again. Authority in heaven and on earth was given so that he who formerly reigned in heaven might reign upon earth through the faith of believers.”]

Thus may that man who lately suffered be lord of both heaven and earth, and be believed to be God and Lord not merely of the Jews but also of all nations. For he has authority in heaven to crown whom he wills; and he has authority on earth to choose whomever he wills, because here and there he does whatever he wills.

“Go therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” Now, he says, there is no distinction: “Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16:16). Teach all, call all, and baptize all, [Col. 0314A] whether Jews or Gentiles. [Note: [Col. 0313B] Author of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, Book II, ch. 2: “Was any distinction made by this command among any nations or any human beings? He excluded no one, separated no one by race, distinguished no one by condition. The Gospel of Christ’s cross was sent to absolutely all human beings.”] “Teach them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you.” Whoever thinks this impossible should hold and preserve charity alone. [Note: [Col. 0313B] Chrysostom, Homily 91, no. 3: “For what is difficult [Col. 0314A] in Christ’s commandments? Have no enemy, hate no one, curse no one.” See Augustine, [Col. 0314B] Sermon 358, no. 4; exposition of Psalm 89, no. 17, etc.]

“And behold, I am with you all days, even to the end of the age.” A great promise, and a great and invincible shield of security. “I,” he says, “am with you; I fight in you; I defend you. Fear nothing; go in confidence.” [Note: [Col. 0314B] Chrysostom, on this passage: “Do not, he says, tell me of the difficulty of things; for I am with you, who make all things easy,” etc. Author of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, Book II, ch. 2: “‘Behold, I am with you,’ etc.: that is, when you enter as sheep into the midst of wolves, do not tremble at your own weakness, but trust in my power. I shall not abandon you in all this work until the end of the age—not in order that you suffer nothing, but in order to grant what is far greater: that you may be overcome by no cruelty of raging men. For you will preach in my power, and through me it will happen that, among opponents and madmen, children of Abraham will be raised from stones. I shall instill what I taught; I shall accomplish what I promised.”] For if God is for you, who is against you? Therefore say: “In God we shall do valiantly, and he himself will bring our enemies to nothing” (Ps. 107:14), to whom be honor and glory unto ages of ages.

Amen.

HERE ENDS THE COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW.

[Col. 0313]

COMMENTARIES OF SAINT BRUNO OF ASTI, BISHOP OF SEGNI, ON MARK.

[Col. 0313]

[Col. 0313C] Having expounded the Gospel of Matthew, let us now proceed in order to Mark. We shall not need to labor very much in it, since very few things are said there which have not been expounded in Matthew. Since there are four Evangelists, and sometimes two, sometimes three, and sometimes all say the same thing, it is unnecessary to explain individually what we have expounded in one. For it is easier for you to turn back the pages than for me to write the same things in each. Therefore, whatever we do not expound in Mark, [Col. 0314C] we do not expound either because it is clear in itself or because it has already been expounded above in Matthew. Likewise in Luke and John, if life accompanies us, [Note: [Col. 0313C] This formula was customary, both among pagans of old and, still more, among Christians later, from the teaching of Saint James 4:13: “Come now, you who say, ‘Today or tomorrow we shall go,’” etc.; instead one should say, “If the Lord wills [Col. 0313D] and if we live.” Our author seems to have wished to use the words by which, with a similar qualification inserted, the angel used in promising Abraham a son to be born: Gen. 18:10: “Returning I shall come to you at this time, with life accompanying me, and Sarah your wife shall have a son.” Similar are Elisha’s words to the Shunammite woman, 4 Kings 4:16: “At this time, and at this same hour, if life is your companion, you shall have a son in your womb.”] we hope to do the same. Namely, in what follows we shall expound those things that have not been explained in what went before. Now let us come to the words of the Gospel.

THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK BEGINS.

I. [CHAP. I.] “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. As it is written in Isaiah the prophet: Behold, I send [Note: [Col. 0314D] The Vulgate reads *Ecce ego mitto* (“Behold, I send”); nevertheless, *ego* (“I”) is absent from the Old Latin in Sabatier and from Bede, etc. It is present in Greek, ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ ἀποστέλλω (“Behold, I send”), and in certain Latin texts.] my angel before your face, who [Col. 0315A] shall prepare your way before you. The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.”

Thus, he says, I make this beginning in the Gospel of Jesus Christ, Son of God, and begin to write from John the Baptist, who was his forerunner and was sent to announce his coming. “As it is written in Isaiah the prophet: Behold, I send my angel before your face; and, The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord.” This, however, is not all written in Isaiah, but partly in Isaiah and partly in Malachi. [Note: [Col. 0315B] The preceding words are from Malachi, where one reads, 3:1: “Behold, I send my angel, and he shall prepare the way before my face”; the latter words are from Isaiah 40:3: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord.”] Unless perhaps someone wishes to understand it in terms of equivalent force. For the angel sent before Christ’s face in Malachi is called in Isaiah the voice crying in the wilderness; and of him of whom it is said there, “He shall prepare your way before you,” it is said here, “Prepare the way of the Lord.” Therefore, as to the letter, one passage is written in Malachi and the other in Isaiah; but as to the meaning, both are found both in Malachi and in Isaiah. [Note: [Col. 0315C] The question why Isaiah alone is named here is as ancient as it is arduous and difficult. Jerome, on Malachi 3, acknowledged that this testimony was woven together from Isaiah and Malachi; but he neither resolved the question there nor regarded it in *On the Best Kind of Translation* as soluble. It could easily be resolved—indeed, there would be no question—if we followed the Greek manuscripts. For Maldonatus testifies that in most of them there is no name of a single prophet, but the general phrase ἐν τοῖς προφήταις, “in the prophets”; and this reading is also alleged as Irenaeus’s. Yet Irenaeus himself, Book III, ch. 11, no. 8, reads “in Isaiah”; as do Origen, Porphyry in Origen’s Book II *Against Celsus*, Saint Athanasius, Jerome, etc., and many manuscripts in Mill. Add the Old Latin and all Latin manuscripts; add the Syriac, Gothic, Coptic, Armenian, Persian, and Arabic versions. Therefore Jansenius, *Harmony*, ch. 13, and Maldonatus regard the reading “in the prophets” as substituted for the genuine reading by those to whom this passage, objected by enemies of the Gospel, was troublesome. Saint Augustine, whose words Jansenius cites, thought that the two prophetic testimonies were joined under Isaiah’s name because Isaiah had previously indicated that same thing which Malachi prophesied, and because both alike proceeded from one and the same Holy Spirit. More recent writers have adopted other views. First, it seems established that it is not new, and has often been done elsewhere, for one composite testimony to be woven, as it were, from several passages of different canonical writers; Cornelius proves this here with cited examples. Second, one of these is often regarded as principal, while the other is brought in as a kind of interpretation and explanation. Third, Isaiah’s passage is especially pertinent to explaining John’s preaching and office, since John himself applied it to himself. These considerations seem to resolve the question.]

What follows and is not expounded is to be sought in Matthew.

II. [CHAP. III.] “Jesus went up the mountain and called to himself those whom he himself wished; and they came to him. And he appointed twelve to be with him and to send them to preach the Gospel. And he gave them power to heal infirmities and cast out demons.” Jesus went up the mountain, wishing to choose the leaders of his army, 138 [Col. 0316A] that by the elevation of the place itself they might understand to how great a glory they were chosen, and that they were preferred above all others. [Note: [Col. 0315D] The Fathers teach that many things are signified in Scripture by the name “mountains.” Hence Jerome, Homily 9 on Jeremiah—that is, Origen translated into Latin by him—says: “Some [Col. 0316B] mountains are dark, others bright. Yet because both kinds are great mountains, the bright mountains are angels of God and prophets … apostles of Jesus Christ … The dark mountains are those which rise against the knowledge [Col. 0316C] of God. The devil is a dark mountain.” Thus a mountain always signifies something great. Therefore Augustine, on Psalm 45, no. 7, interprets mountains as the powers of this world, and in the same place makes some mountains good and others evil. Hilary, on Psalm 120, no. 4: “We understand mountains as prophetic books raised from earth on high, through which ascent to higher things is made … We may also understand mountains as angelic ministries and the powers and authorities of heaven,” etc.]

But why are twelve chosen, unless because he was the day and had twelve [Note: [Col. 0316C] This the author derives from Augustine, who, in his exposition of Psalm 55, no. 5, says: “Perhaps they became far from the saints because they could not penetrate the height of the day, whose apostles are twelve shining hours.” Augustine says more fully in Tractate 44 on John, no. 8: “To what then does this pertain: ‘Are there not twelve hours in the day?’ Because, in order to show that he himself was the day, he chose twelve disciples. ‘If I am the day,’ he says, ‘and you are the hours, do the hours of the day give advice? The hours follow the day,’” etc.] hours? For he himself says: “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” (John 11:9). “Whoever walks in the light does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” (John 8:12). They are the gates of the Church, of whom it is said: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion” (Ps. 86:2). Therefore, since there are twelve gates of the Church, it was fitting that there be twelve [Note: [Col. 0316C] Bede on Matthew ch. 10: “Rightly are twelve called by divine grace to the apostleship … For these [Col. 0316D] are the three gates of the heavenly Jerusalem from the east, from the north, south, and west.” And both passages of Saint Augustine. For in his exposition of Psalm 86, explaining, “Its foundations are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion,” he writes: “Do not suppose that the foundations are one thing and the gates another. Why are the apostles and prophets foundations? Because their authority bears our weakness. Why are they gates? Because through them we enter the kingdom of God: for they preach to us. And when we enter through them, we enter through Christ; for he himself is the gate. The twelve gates of Jerusalem are called Christ, and the one gate Christ, and the twelve gates Christ, because Christ is in the twelve gates. Therefore the number twelve belongs to the apostles. Great is the sacrament of this number twelve.”]—three gates from the east, three from the west, three from the south, and three from the north.

The Lord sends these to preach the Gospel, [Col. 0316B] heal the sick, and drive out demons, so that, because they are hours, they may shine everywhere; and because they are gates, they may bring peoples from every direction into the Church through faith. “And he gave Simon the name Peter; and James the son of Zebedee, and John the brother of James; and he gave them the names Boanerges, which is, Sons of Thunder; and Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Cananean, and Judas Scarioth, [Note: [Col. 0316D] Bede too reads “Scarioth,” and conjectures that he was so called from the village in which he was born; he interprets it as “memory of death.” It is also read in the Cambridge manuscript, in the Saint-Germain manuscripts, [Col. 0317C] and in two Colbert manuscripts in Sabatier. The Old Latin, which Sabatier likewise presents from a Colbert manuscript, has “Scariotha.”] who betrayed him.”

The Lord gave some disciples other names, yet did not take away their first names. [Col. 0317A] [Note: [Col. 0317C] See Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho*, no. 106; Tertullian, Book IV *Against Marcion*, ch. 13; John Chrysostom, Homily 19 on John, no. 2; and, among more recent writers, Cardinal Baronius at the year 33, no. 19, etc.] Hence Peter, who was first called Simon, was afterward called Simon Peter. Thus he gave Simon the name Peter, so that from him from whom he received strength, he might receive also the name denoting strength. “For the rock,” says the Apostle, “was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). From this rock, therefore, Peter is called Peter. [Note: [Col. 0317C] Saint Augustine, Sermon 76: “He was formerly called Simon. But this name, that he should be called Peter, was given to him by the Lord; and this in such a figure as to signify the Church. For since Christ is the rock, Peter is the Christian people. ‘Rock’ is the principal name. Thus Peter comes from rock, not rock from Peter; just as Christ is not called from Christian, but Christian from Christ.” The same, Sermon 204, no. 1; Sermon 170, no. 2; and Sermon 295, no. 1.]

He also called the sons of Zebedee Bonaerges, or, as it is more correctly written, Banereem, [Note: [Col. 0317D] This name is found written in various ways: *Boanges* in the Cambridge manuscript in Sabatier; elsewhere otherwise. Saint Jerome, on Daniel ch. 1, v. 7: “In the Gospel … the sons of Zebedee were called not, as most suppose, *Boanerges*, but, more correctly, *Benereem*.” Vallarsi notes that the Vatican manuscript reads *Baneraem*, the Palatine *Banarehem*.] that is, sons of thunder, because, speaking magnificently and terribly, they imitated heavenly and celestial voices in their sermons. For whose voice is that, if not thunder’s, which says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1)?

III. [CHAP. IV.] [Col. 0317B] And Jesus said: “So is the kingdom of God: as if a man should cast seed into the earth, and sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should sprout and grow while he does not know it. For the earth bears fruit of itself: first the blade, then the ear, then full grain in the ear; and when the fruit has brought itself forth [Note: [Col. 0317D] The Vulgate has *cum produxerit*, “when it has brought forth.” But Corbie manuscript 1 and Saint-Germain manuscript 2 in Sabatier read *cum se produxerit*, “when it has produced itself.”] fruit, he immediately puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.”

The kingdom of God is the Church. It is both called the field and the earth in which the seed of God’s Word is sown. The sowers are apostles and teachers; the seed is evangelical 139 preaching. This first grows and sprouts into a blade, then into an ear, and afterward into full grain. For the beginning of a good work is like a blade, [Note: [Col. 0317D] Saint Gregory, Book XIX of the *Morals*, no. 52, teaches that five things are signified in Scripture by “grass,” namely: [Col. 0318C] “the flourishing of temporal glory, the refreshment of the devil, support for preachers, good action, and the knowledge and teaching of eternal life.”] because the end it will attain is not yet plainly known. For grass easily dries up and perishes. It becomes an ear while it grows daily [Col. 0317C] and advances for the better by successive increases; yet whether it will attain perfection is still unknown. Then it becomes full grain in the ear when, having overcome the temptations of the flesh, a person wholly subjects himself to God and is found perfect in all things, insofar as human frailty permits.

But not even then is full security present, unless he is quickly harvested and stored in the granary. [Note: [Col. 0318C] Hence Saint Augustine, Sermon 40, no. 7: “What security is there, brothers, whether mine or yours, except that we attentively and diligently hear the Lord’s commands and faithfully await his promises?”] Hence it is said here: “And when the fruit has brought itself forth [Col. 0318A], he immediately puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.” For the Lord sends the sickle when, through bodily death, he summons to himself the souls of his faithful.

IV. [CHAP.
