VII.] Jesus, going out from the region of Tyre [Note: [Col. 0318C] “And again going out from the region of Tyre.” This is a homily of St Bruno for the twelfth Sunday after Pentecost, falsely attributed to Eusebius of Emesa.], came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, through the midst of the territory of the Decapolis. The Evangelist describes by what route the Lord returned to Galilee. And just as Pentapolis is named from five cities, so Decapolis [Note: [Col. 0318D] Jerome: “Decapolis, as we read in the Gospel, is a region of ten cities beyond the Jordan, around Hippos, Pella, and Gadara.” Bede copied Jerome’s words; see Bonfrerius’s extensive discussion in Jerome’s *Onomasticon*.] is named from ten cities. And they bring to Him one who was deaf and mute, and they begged Him to lay His hand upon him.

Who are these who bring the deaf and mute man to the Lord? They are the apostles and teachers; they are bishops and priests; they are all who desire to heal others and persuade them to come to faith. [Col. 0318B] For every person is deaf who does not have ears for hearing and disdains to hear the words of the Gospel. Those were deaf to whom the Lord said: “Whoever is of God hears the words of God; therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John 8:47). Of such persons the Psalmist also says: “Their fury is like that of a serpent, like that of a deaf asp which stops up its ears, which does not listen to the voice of charmers, nor to charms skilfully uttered by the wise man” [Note: [Col. 0318D] “And of the enchanter who charms wisely.”] (Ps. 57:5).

But mute is the person who does not praise the Lord, does not confess Christ, does not defend justice, and does not condemn injustice [Note: [Col. 0318D] Bede: “Deaf and mute is one who neither opens his ears to hear God’s words nor his mouth to speak them. Such a person should be offered to the Lord for healing by those who have long since learned through practice both to speak and to hear the divine sayings, so that He Himself may save by the right hand of His grace those whom human frailty cannot save.”]. Such are those of whom it is said: “Mute dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. 56:10). We therefore ought to lead these to Jesus and pray for them, that He may lay [Col. 0318C] His hand upon them. For he whom Jesus touches is healed; he whom the Saviour touches is healed [Note: [Col. 0318D] The same, on Mark chap. 8: “The Lord touches us when He enlightens our mind by the breath of the Holy Spirit and kindles us to recognize our own weakness and to pursue good action.”]; for He Himself is salvation and life. He does not seek herbs from elsewhere: He is both physician and medicine; He touches and heals; He looks upon and cures.

Therefore it follows: “And taking him aside from the crowd, He put His fingers into his ears; and spitting, He touched his tongue; and looking up to heaven, He groaned, and said to him, *Effeta*” [Note: [Col. 0318D] Thus Bede writes it. In the ancient Italian version from the Colbert manuscript, cited by Sabatier: *Effeta*; in the Vulgate, *Ephphetha*, as also in Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book I; Greek: ἐφφαθά (*ephphatha*). Ambrose: “It is a Hebrew word, which in Latin is said to mean ‘be opened.’” See Maldonatus and others on this word.], “which is, ‘Be opened.’” [Col. 0319A]

Here we recognize the sacraments of the Church [Note: [Col. 0319C] St Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book I, chap. 1, no. 2: “What then did we do on Saturday? The opening, certainly. What mysteries of opening were celebrated? When the priest touched your ears and nostrils. This is signified in the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, when a deaf and mute man was brought to Him.... Therefore the priest touched your ears, that your ears might be opened to the priest’s speech and address.” The same, *On the Mysteries*, chap. 1, no. 3: “Open therefore your ears, and receive the sweet fragrance of eternal life breathed upon you through the gift of the sacraments; this is what we signified to you when, celebrating the mystery of opening, we said: *Ephphatha*, that is, ‘Be opened,’ so that each person coming to grace might know what was asked and remember what ought to be answered. Christ celebrated this mystery in the Gospel, as we read, when He healed the mute and deaf man,” etc.]. We see priests perform these things for those newly coming to faith. They say, *Effeta*, that is, “Be opened”: not so that the senses of the outward person, which are not shut, may be opened, but rather so that the ears of the inward person may be opened and the tongue loosed, in order that they may both carefully understand the words of life and faithfully proclaim to others what they have understood.

For unless it signified something else, the Lord would not have undertaken so much effort in healing this man. He could have healed him by a word alone [Note: [Col. 0319D] Victor of Antioch, in Corderius’s *Catena*, p. 150: “Although He could have wrought the miracle by speech, He showed that the body, united to Him by a mysterious bond and animated by a rational and intelligent soul, also abounds in the riches of divine power.” See also Tolosanus there.], as He was accustomed to heal many others; but He did not do this. What, then, did He do? He drew him away from the crowd; He put His fingers into his ears; He spat and touched his tongue; looking up to heaven, He groaned and said to him: “*Effeta*, that is, ‘Be opened.’”

For this crowd, from which the man is drawn by the Lord, [Col. 0319B] is the multitude of vices and the turbulent host of evil spirits [Note: [Col. 0319D] Bede: “The first gateway of salvation is for the sick man to be taken by the Lord and led apart from the crowd. For the Lord takes the sick man from the crowd and leads him apart when, enlightening by the visitation of His mercy a mind weakened by sins, He calls it away from the customary habits of human life.”]. Whoever is not drawn from this crowd is not healed by the Lord. Rightly, therefore, He drew from the crowd the man He wished to heal, and put His fingers into his ears, because He poured the graces of the Holy Spirit into his hearing [Note: [Col. 0319D] The same Bede: “He puts His fingers into the ears [Col. 0320C] when, through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, He opens the ears of the heart to understand and receive the words of salvation. For the Lord Himself testifies that the Holy Spirit is called the finger of God, when He says to the Jews: ‘If I cast out demons by the finger of God,’ etc.” This, I believe, comes from Gregory, who in Homily 10 on Ezekiel, where he expounds the whole order of the healing mystically, no. 20, says: “What, I ask, are signified by the Redeemer’s fingers except the gifts of the Holy Spirit? Thus, when He had cast out a demon elsewhere, He said: ‘If by the finger of God,’ etc.; and another Evangelist records that He said: ‘If by the Spirit of God,’ etc. From these two passages it is gathered that the finger of God is called the Spirit. To put fingers into the ears, therefore, is by the gifts of the Spirit to open the mind of the deaf person for hearing.”], so that he might possess the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, without whom the ears of the heart are not opened. Of this finger He Himself also says elsewhere: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke 1:20). Matthew, explaining this, says: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then [Note: [Col. 0320D] “Therefore,” Vulgate.] the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matt. 12:28).

Moreover, He spat and touched his tongue, in order thereby to teach him to cast away everything superfluous if he wished to have a loosed tongue, fit for speech. [Col. 0319C] For saliva often hinders the tongue in speaking. Saliva is a kind of excess, a discharge from the stomach and head. Therefore, whoever [Col. 0320A] wishes to speak well, whoever wishes his words to please God and men, must relieve both his stomach and the mind—which we understand through the head—of every superfluous moisture and every impediment.

But by Christ’s saliva, which descends indeed from the head, we may also understand the sweetness of His divinity [Note: [Col. 0320D] Bede: “The Lord’s saliva signifies the savour of wisdom.... For the saliva descending from the Lord’s head signifies His divine nature, which is from God; the portion of earth with which He mixed that saliva signifies His human nature, assumed from human beings.” St Gregory, in the passage cited: “What does it mean that, spitting, He touched his tongue? Saliva for us is wisdom received from the Redeemer’s mouth in divine speech. Saliva flows from the head into the mouth. Therefore, when our tongue is touched by that wisdom which He Himself is, it is immediately formed for the words of preaching.”]. “For,” says the Apostle, “the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11:3). This sweetness, this saliva of our Redeemer, made eloquent the tongues of infants, which the bitterness of the old apple had once bound. Of this sweetness the Psalmist says: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet; blessed is the man who hopes in Him” (Ps. 33:9). And again: “The Lord is sweet and upright” (Ps. 24:8). And the Apostle Peter says: “Putting away all malice and all deceit, [Col. 0320B] and hypocrisy and envy and every kind of detraction, like newborn infants desire the rational milk without deceit, that by it you may grow into salvation—if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet” (1 Pet. 2:1).

This sweetness, therefore, this saliva of Christ, drives the ancient poison and every bitterness from the tongues of believers. But this saliva did not touch the tongues of those who do not confess Christ and who, when questioned about their faith, do not answer that they believe.

“And looking up to heaven, He groaned.” For the Lord looked up to heaven because, according to His humanity, He intercedes for us with the Father [Note: [Col. 0320D] In the Marchant edition, vol. II, p. 97: “He does not cease to pray to the Father.” Anonymous, in Corderius’s *Catena*: “To look up to heaven in prayer is something that teaches man; but since He was man, He ought not to disdain the manner fitting for man.” Victor of Antioch, there: “At once assigning to the Father the causes of the things done by Himself, [Col. 0321C] and at once pitying human nature, which the devil’s envy and the shamelessness of the first-created humans had brought down to such degradation.” See St Gregory and Bede, cited above.]. But why did He groan, unless because He saw that the man whom He had created in His image and likeness was now deaf and mute, and wretched in every respect; and that he had to return to his former dignity [Col. 0320C] through many tribulations and distresses?

After all these things He said to him: “*Effeta*, that is, ‘Be opened,’” because our senses are not first [Col. 0321A] opened by the Lord, nor are they first made fruitful by the rains of His teaching, until we are drawn by Christ from the crowd, touched by His hand, and cleansed and healed from every bitterness by the sweetness of His saliva. Hence it is said here: “And immediately his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was loosed, and he spoke rightly.” For he could speak only rightly whom divine power and wisdom had healed by such touching and curing [Note: [Col. 0321D] Tolosanus, in Corderius’s *Catena*: “Why should he not be restored to a perfect condition, having gained access to his own Creator, who makes good the defect of nature?” Bede: “For he alone speaks rightly ... whose hearing divine grace opens, that he may listen and obey the heavenly commands, and whose tongue the Lord instructs for speech by the touch of that wisdom which He Himself is.”].

“And He commanded him to tell no one; but the more He commanded them, the more abundantly they proclaimed it, and the more exceedingly they marvelled, saying: ‘He has done all things well; He makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.’”

What is this? Why did the Lord command them concerning that in which He knew they would be disobedient? These things are done for us, brothers; they concern us and humble our boastfulness. If at any time we have done something worthy [Col. 0321B] of praise, we ought not to exalt and advertise it for popular favour, but rather humbly conceal and hide it [Note: [Col. 0321D] Tolosanus, in Corderius’s *Catena*: “Again, teaching us moderation here also, He commanded those who had received the benefit to conceal the miracle.”]. Yet the opposite occurs: those who wish to conceal their deeds are more praised than those who strive to make them known through vainglory. Hence blessed Job said: “The praise of the hypocrite [Note: [Col. 0321D] Vulgate, 20:5: “The praise of the wicked is brief, and the joy of the hypocrite,” etc.] is like a point” (Job 20:5). But of the saints it is said: “The king shall rejoice in Him; all who swear by Him shall be praised, because the mouth of those who speak iniquity has been stopped” [Note: [Col. 0321D] Thus far the homily.] (Ps. 62:12).

V. [CHAP. VIII.] And they come to Bethsaida, and bring to Him a blind man, and beg Him to touch him. And taking the blind man by the hand, He led him outside the village; [Col. 0321C] and spitting into his eyes, He laid His hands upon him and asked him whether he saw anything.

By this blind man the same thing is signified as we said just above was signified by the deaf and mute man [Note: [Col. 0321D] Bede speaks here still more generally of all those healed by Christ: “All infirmities healed by the Lord are signs of spiritual infirmities, through which the soul approaches eternal death by sin. Just as [Col. 0322C] in the deaf and mute man healed by the Lord is suggested the healing of the minds of those who had known neither how to hear the word of God nor how to speak it ... so in this blind man gradually healed by the Lord is signified the enlightenment of the hearts [Col. 0322D] of foolish persons who have wandered far from the way of truth.”]. For every person is blind who does not follow the true light, which is Christ, and does not understand the truth of faith. Those, however, who bring the blind man to the Lord and pray for him are understood, as above, to be bishops, presbyters, and the rest of the faithful.

And what is said here—that, taking the blind man by the hand, He led him outside the village—is what is said there: that, taking him, He led him apart from the crowd. By the saliva here and there the same one thing is signified. Let those who do not understand this read what was said there. The Lord asks the blind man whether he sees anything, because at His first touch not all people are immediately enlightened sufficiently. Yet they see something as soon as they begin to understand and believe something about the Lord. Therefore each person sees more clearly in proportion as he believes and understands the truth better [Note: [Col. 0322D] Victor of Antioch, in Corderius: “It signifies that the faith was imperfect both of those who brought this blind man and of the blind man himself.” Bede explains it otherwise, but admirably: “The Lord therefore heals him gradually and not suddenly at once ... in order to show the magnitude of human blindness, which commonly reaches the light of divine vision only little by little and through certain stages of progress; or in order that He might give us frequent signs of His grace, by which He assists every increase of our perfection, so that it may make some progress and not fail.”].

It follows: “And looking up, he said: ‘I see men as trees walking.’ Then again He laid His hands upon his eyes, and he began to see. And he was restored, so that he saw all things clearly.” For as often as the Lord lays His hands upon the eyes of the blind man, so often does He enlighten the eyes of our mind, so that we may understand what we did not understand before. Hence the Psalmist says: “For You, O Lord, enlighten [Col. 0322B] my lamp; my God, enlighten my darkness” (Ps. 17:31): that is, because You have enlightened me in what I know, enlighten me also in what I do not yet know.

For this reason it is plainly apparent that, although the Lord had already laid His hands upon his eyes, he still needed Him to lay them on again, because he did not yet see everything perfectly. Let us therefore ask the Lord to lay His hand upon the eyes of our mind not once or twice, but many times, so that, with every mist wiped away and the darkness of all errors driven off, we may be worthy to see each thing in its proper form and see all things clearly.

And the Lord sent him to his home, saying: “Go into your home, and if you enter the village, tell no one.” [Col. 0322C] For our home is that from which, not well enlightened but rather miserably blinded, we were expelled in the first man. But we cannot return to it unless we are again enlightened by the Lord and feel His hand and power applied to our eyes [Note: [Col. 0322D] Bede understands another mystical meaning here: “Mystically, He admonishes all who are enlightened by the knowledge of truth to return to their own heart and carefully consider in mind how much has been granted them.”]. Why He commands him to tell no one, and commands His works to be concealed and hidden, we have already sufficiently explained. Yet those who do all their works in order to be seen by men do not yet understand this; of them the Lord says: “They have received their reward” (Matt. 6:2). Therefore the Lord teaches us [Col. 0323A] to conceal our works, lest we receive our reward here and, by receiving it, lose our reward [Note: [Col. 0323C] Bede: “He gives His followers an example, that they may not seek popular favour for the marvellous things they do, but be content to please only the divine gaze, where the reward for works remains.”].

VI. [CHAP. IX.] “Everyone shall be salted with fire, and every sacrifice shall be salted. Salt is good. But if salt has become insipid, with what will you season it? Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” [Note: [Col. 0323C] This is one of the more difficult Gospel passages, if we wish to understand both how these words cohere with what precedes and what their meaning is. These two questions are so joined together that one cannot be separated from the other. There are therefore three principal interpretations.

1. Since above, at vv. 44–45, He had spoken of the unquenchable fire of Gehenna, this gives the cause or explains the manner in which it is unquenchable: just as salt preserves things from corruption, so the wicked person is, as it were, salted with fire and preserved incorruptible by divine omnipotence; [Col. 0323D] the fire torments him, indeed, but does not consume him. Thus these words contain two statements seemingly contrary to one another: every sinner shall be salted with fire; but, conversely, every sacrifice pleasing to God, seasoned with the salt of wisdom, shall be preserved from eternal corruption.

2. It refers to what had preceded a little earlier concerning scandal: because great wisdom, caution, and discernment are needed if someone is to avoid scandals, neither causing scandal nor being scandalized. Just as every sacrifice was formerly offered with salt, so now every work must be undertaken with great discernment and wisdom.

3. It speaks of the fire of tribulation, in relation to the good, or even to the good and bad together; so that the good are preserved from corruptions by the fire of tribulation. This does not occur without pain, just as hands and feet—of which He had spoken above—are not cut off without pain. All likewise must be salted with fire, though not in the same manner or by the same fire: either beneficially by the fire of tribulation [Col. 0324C] in the present life, or by everlasting tribulation and torment in the other. See Jansenius, *Harmony*, chap. 71; Noël Alexandre on Mark chap. 9; Lamy, book IV, chap. 32; Maldonatus; à Lapide; and others. Our author follows the second explanation, which seems best, namely because it fits what follows, concerning John; John of Antioch also appears to adopt it, explaining it as concerning the means of preserving peace and avoiding dissension.].

For these words seem to answer what the Apostle John had just introduced into the Lord’s discourse, saying: “Master, we saw someone casting out demons in Your name who does not follow us, and we forbade him.” Jesus said to them: “Do not forbid him. For no one who performs a miracle in My name can soon speak evil of Me. For whoever is not against you is for you.”

Therefore the Lord wishes us to do all things wisely and with discernment, and to forbid not good things but evil things. [Col. 0323B] For one who works miracles in Christ’s name is already closer to Christ, since he reveres His name, whose great power and efficacy he has proved; and so he begins already to be their defender. Because he has known Christ’s power through miracles, he fears to speak evil of Him. Therefore we must not take from him what he possesses, but add to him what he does not possess. Let us tell him to believe in Christ and be faithful to Him.

Therefore the Lord adds: “For everyone shall be salted with fire, and every sacrifice shall be salted.” This is as though He said: Every ruler and teacher of the Church ought to be such as is seasoned with salt, wise and discerning, providing usefully for all things and doing all things according to reason and order. This indeed is signified by the Law itself, which commands every sacrifice [Col. 0323C] to be salted. For it says: “Whatever sacrifice you offer, season with salt; nor shall you take away the salt of the covenant [Col. 0324A] of the Lord from your sacrifice. In every offering you shall offer salt” (Lev. 3:13).

For salt stands for wisdom, which seasons all our words and actions. This salt, therefore, is good, unless it has been made insipid by foolish and stupid people. Heretics, hypocrites, and schismatics make it insipid, because they do not use it with the purity they ought. “But if salt has become tasteless, with what will you season it?” If wisdom itself, without which no one becomes wise, has become foolish, what else can restore it to the condition proper to its dignity?

“Have salt in yourselves”: season everything you do with salt; do everything wisely and discerningly. But in order to be able to do this, have peace among yourselves. For those who do not have peace cannot possess such salt. They do not indeed have such salt, even if at times [Col. 0324B] they possess salt that is tasteless and made insipid.

But what does He mean when He says, “Everyone shall be salted with fire”? Is fire salt, that something should be salted with it? Just as wisdom is called salt because our minds are seasoned by it, so it is also called fire because our minds are illuminated by it. Therefore, if wisdom is fire, and wisdom is salt, then fire also is salt. What is salted with wisdom, then, is salted with fire.

VII. [CHAP. XVI.] When the Sabbath had passed, Mary Magdalene, and Mary of James, and Salome bought spices, so that they might come and anoint Jesus. [Note: [Col. 0324C] The women who had followed him from Galilee saw the tomb . . . and, returning, prepared spices and ointments; but on the Sabbath they kept silence according to the commandment; and on the first day of the week, very early in the morning, they came to the tomb, carrying the spices which they had prepared. Comparing the Gospel passages, some interpreters think that they prepared the spices before the Sabbath began, but rested and “kept silence” on the Sabbath—that is, did not anoint Christ. Thus Jansenius, *Harmony*, chap. 16. Others, such as Lamy, Maldonatus, and others, understand “kept silence” to mean that they did not buy the spices until after sunset on the Sabbath, when the Sabbath festival ended. Others, following Bede, such as Menochius, maintain that the women bought spices twice: before the Sabbath began and after it had ended.]

For on the Sabbath it was permitted neither to sell nor to buy anything, since the Law forbade such a thing to be done on the Sabbath (Lev. XXIII, 31). These holy women come, then, to anoint Jesus. But how do they come? With spices. [Note: [Col. 0324D] St Bernard explains at length the mystical meanings of the spices in his second sermon on this Gospel passage, for the season of the Resurrection, p. 906: “Let the mind seek its spices: before all things, the disposition of compassion; then zeal for uprightness; and amid these let it not omit the spirit of discernment . . . The tongue also has three spices: restraint in rebuking, abundance in exhorting, effectiveness in persuading,” etc. Bede says here: “And so we too, believing in him who died, if, filled with the fragrance of virtues, we seek the Lord with the reputation of good works, certainly come to his tomb with spices”; in these words he copied Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, Homily 21, no. 2: “And so we too, believing in him who died, if, filled with the fragrance of virtues, we seek the Lord with the reputation of good works, certainly come to his tomb with spices.”]

For it is not permitted to come to Jesus otherwise. These spices are faith, hope, charity, peace, patience, humility, gentleness, concord, mercy, and the like; for these smell sweetly to the Lord, just as, conversely, vices stink. Hence the Psalmist says: “My sores have putrefied and been corrupted because of my foolishness” (Ps. XXXVII, 6).

Blessed, therefore, are those women; blessed are those souls which, like Mary Magdalene, always come to the Lord with ointments, always with spices. For this is she who says elsewhere: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song 1). This woman signified the Church of the Gentiles, [Note: [Col. 0325C] Bede gave the same mystical interpretation of the two women in his commentary on Matthew, chap. XXVIII: “The two women, of one name and of the same love and devotion, who came to see the Lord’s tomb, signify the two peoples of believers, namely the Jewish and the Gentile, who desire with one and like zeal to celebrate the passion and resurrection of their Redeemer.”] from whom the Lord cast out seven demons; and because she loved much, many sins were forgiven her.

But Mary of James, who was Christ’s maternal aunt, [Note: [Col. 0325D] Jerome calls her his maternal aunt in his commentary on Matthew, chap. XII, v. 46, as does Bede, who also says on Luke XXIV: “Mary of James is the mother of James the Less and Joseph, as the Evangelist Mark says, the sister of the Lord’s Mother; and therefore James himself deserved to be called the Lord’s brother.” The opinion that Mary of James was the Blessed Virgin’s sister rests upon John XIX, 25: “But there stood by the cross of Jesus his Mother, and his Mother’s sister, Mary of Cleophas.” Modern interpreters generally agree that Mary of James, so called from her son, and Mary of Cleophas, so called from her husband, are one and the same woman, although Baronius held otherwise in the *Appendix*, no. 67. Cornelius and certain others, however, call her not a sister but a cousin. For, as Jerome says in the cited place, all Scripture shows that cousins are called brothers—the same must hold for sisters. See Baronius, cited place; Jansenius, *Harmony*, chap. 19; Maldonatus and other interpreters on Matthew XII, v. 46.] signified the Jewish people, from whom our Savior drew his origin according to his humanity. But Salome, whose name means “peaceful,” [Note: [Col. 0325D] Correctly, as Hure also noted: for Solomon, “peaceful,” comes from the same root, as Jerome relates in Epistle 53 to Paulinus, Augustine in his exposition of Psalm LXXI, no. 1, etc. Moreover, interpreters establish from a comparison of the Gospel passages that Salome is the same as the mother of the sons of Zebedee.] signifies the entire multitude of saints gathered from both peoples. Thus, in her the whole Church is figured; in the other women, parts of the Church. Yet these three women may signify the three regions of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe—in which the whole Church consists. And these anoint Jesus, these delight him, these proclaim his passion and make manifest to all nations the fragrance of the knowledge of him.

Behold, women who until this day blushed and grieved that they were the gate of death and the ruin of the entire human race now rejoice, now preach, now declare that original sin has been blotted out; and they announce the glory of the resurrection even to the apostles themselves.

[Col. 0325C] “And very early on the first day of the week they came to the tomb, the sun having now risen.” This is not contrary to what he says, “very early,” and “the sun having now risen.” Hence another Evangelist says: “While it was still dark” [Note: [Col. 0326C] The time at which the women came to the tomb of Jesus Christ, or set out on their journey, has long and extensively been debated by interpreters, so much so that, as Jansenius relates in his *Harmony*, chap. 165, some have imagined four approaches to the tomb at different times and have held that the Evangelists describe different women on different occasions. On this question see Jansenius himself, all interpreters, and, fully and clearly, Cardinal Baronius under the year 34, no. 169; Menochius, *Life of Jesus Christ*, book VIII, chap. 1, no. 3. Bede, and with Bede our Author, disposes of it briefly. Bede: “But that the women come to the tomb very early, the sun having now risen, means that the sky was already whitening on its eastern side; and this certainly does not happen without the nearness of the rising sun,” etc.] (John XX, 1). Therefore, by the rising of the sun one must understand the time from which its brightness illuminates the sky, though it has not yet appeared upon the earth, while the darkness is still faint. What, then, is “very early,” except when dawn is already reddening? For the Evangelist did not say simply “early,” but “very early,” without reason.

“And they said to one another: Who will roll away for us the stone from the entrance of the tomb? And looking, they saw the stone rolled away; for it was very large.” For the Evangelist Matthew relates that, when Christ rose, “an angel of the Lord came down from heaven and, approaching, rolled away the stone and sat upon it . . . And through fear of him the guards were terrified and became as dead men.” Going into the city, they “reported to the chief priests all that had happened.” [Note: [Col. 0326D] “And when they had gone, behold, some of the guards came into the city and reported,” etc. Perhaps a copyist inadvertently omitted these preceding words.] But the chief priests gave them “a large sum of money, saying: [Note: [Col. 0326D] In the same place: “And having assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave a large sum of money to the soldiers, saying,” etc.] Say that, while you were sleeping at night, his disciples came and stole him away” (Matt. XXVIII, 2).

It follows: “And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right, clothed in a white robe, and they were astonished.” But the angel is seated on the right, clothed in a white robe, because he proclaims joy and prosperity, and announces the glory of the resurrection and the renewal of the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0326D] Bede: “We should note what it means that the angel is seen sitting on the right. For what is signified by the left but the present life, and what by the right but everlasting life? . . . Since our Redeemer had already passed beyond the corruption of this present life, the angel who came to announce his eternal life rightly sat on the right.” This is taken from Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, Homily 21, no. 2, who had said the same.]

Consider with what fire of love they burned inwardly: forgetting feminine fear and frailty, they came not only at night, but even entered the tomb confidently. Thus they deserved to hear words of consolation, when the angel said: “Do not be afraid. You seek Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. Behold the place where they laid him.” You can see the place, he says, but you cannot now see him himself. For he has risen and is not here; but wait a little, and you will see him. For he was not there in the presence of his body, he who is everywhere in the presence of his divinity.

But where do we think he was then? I indeed fear to say what the Evangelists do not say. Perhaps he had gone to his mother, who was afflicted more than all others by longing born of her love for him. [Note: [Col. 0327C] This is the opinion of some devout and learned interpreters, indeed also of theologians. Estius seems to oppose this opinion. Yet Jansenius, *Harmony*, chap. 146, says: “Although the Lord is said first to have appeared to Magdalene, nevertheless devotion strongly persuades us to believe that the Lord first appeared to his most beloved Mother, although the Evangelists passed her over, because the testimony of the Mother would have been ineffective for confirming the resurrection of her Son.” He adds that Mark’s statement that he “appeared first to Mary Magdalene” must be understood as meaning that she was first among all the disciples; for here in Mark and in the other Evangelists the discourse concerns appearances made to disciples.]

As to why the most blessed Virgin herself, among all the women, did not come with the others to the tomb: the cause, I think, was that, after seeing her only-begotten Son seized, scourged, and crucified, beating her tender breast with tender hands and afflicting herself with excessive grief, vigils, and fasts, she had become weakened alike in body and spirit; she sat somewhere alone in seclusion, lamenting and weeping over the calamities that had happened to her. [Note: [Col. 0327D] What our Author expounds here does not seem consistent with the outstanding strength and steadfastness of soul with which the Blessed Virgin was endowed. Ancient and approved Fathers also teach that she experienced the greatest grief of soul. Among them St John Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book IV, chap. 14 (vol. I, p. 277, ed. Le Quien): “This blessed woman, enriched with such benefits as exceed the measure of nature, endured at the time of the Passion the pains she had escaped in childbirth, feeling her inward parts torn and her inmost thoughts, as it were, pierced by a sword, when she saw him whom she had known to be God in bearing him subjected to death as though he were some criminal.” On this point he adduces, with greatest force, the words in Luke: “And a sword of sorrow shall pierce your own soul also.” Yet the same Fathers teach her wondrous strength in bearing these sorrows. Thus St Ambrose, *On the Education of Virgins*, chap. 7, no. 49: “The Mother stood before the cross, and, while the men fled, she stood fearless . . . With devout eyes she gazed upon her Son’s wounds, through whom she knew redemption would come to all. The Mother stood before no unworthy spectacle, she who did not fear the slayer. Her Son hung upon the cross; his Mother offered herself to the persecutors,” etc. Nevertheless, the medieval writers have many supporters for the view of our Author; hence the opinion concerning the Blessed Virgin’s spasm or swoon, which they transmitted, as recounted by Consalvus Durantus on book IV, chap. 7, of the *Revelations of St Bridget*. Yet he acknowledges that almost all recent theologians denied that Mary’s strength failed during her Son’s passion, in connection with the church built near Mount Calvary at the place of the Blessed Virgin’s swoon.]

But let us leave these words, full of devotion and worthy of reflection, for the moment, and listen to what the angels teach: “Go,” he says, “tell his disciples, and Peter, that he will go before you into Galilee. There you will see him, as he told you.” Unless he had called the blessed apostle Peter by name, perhaps he would have feared to come with the others, because he had denied both the Lord and the Master.

But what does it signify that the Lord is seen by his disciples in Galilee, the homeland of the apostles, except that, when he has led us back to our ancient homeland, we shall then see face to face him whom we now see through a mirror and in an enigma? Hence Galilee is interpreted as “completed migration.” [Note: [Col. 0328D] St Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, book III, no. 86: “For Galilee is interpreted either as migration or as revelation.” Bede on Mark XVI: “For Galilee is interpreted as completed migration.” From Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, Homily 21, no. 5: “For Galilee is interpreted as completed migration.”] For after that migration no further migration takes place.

It should be known that, at the hour when our Savior bowed his head and gave up his spirit, leaving his body upon the cross, his soul, together with his divinity, descended to despoil hell. Then was fulfilled the Psalmist’s saying: “Lift up [Note: [Col. 0328D] Psalm XXIII, 7: “Lift up,” etc.] your gates, O princes, and be raised up, O everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter in.” When they asked, “Who is this King of glory?” the answer was made: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle.”

The Lord entered the places of darkness and illuminated all things around with his splendor. A mingled cry arose: the good exulting with joy, the wicked desiring to flee in fear. Then the first parents came to meet him, and, seeing their Creator, cried in joyful voices:

> At last, O Christ, you come to release us from great punishments.

[Note: [Col. 0328D] I can scarcely believe that this Leonine verse escaped our Author unintentionally, when he was thinking of nothing of the kind; rather, I suppose that he borrowed it from some poet, or that he himself, a man surely not ignorant of such refinements, chose to compose it in this place. Whatever the case, it may perhaps refute the opinion of those who wish these verses to have been invented by Leo or Leoninus, the Parisian poet and Benedictine monk. For this man flourished at the end of the twelfth century, about the year 1190, whereas Bruno is thought to have died well before 1125. On this kind of verse see the learned Muratori, *Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, Dissertation 40.]

Then the patriarchs and prophets rush to meet him; then the whole host of saints prostrates itself at his feet. “O long-desired one!” they say. “O one awaited for so long a time! What delays have held you back so long!”

Then David the harpist says: “This is what I used to say: ‘You will give joy and gladness to my hearing, and the humbled bones shall rejoice’” (Ps. L, 10). Behold, now they see; behold, now they hear, the things which the Lord himself said they had desired to see and hear. For he said: “Many prophets and kings wished to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke X, 24).

Then John the Baptist also says: “Behold, this is he of whom I spoke to you. You see him whose coming I announced to you.” But who could recount in detail how great the joy was there when Christ, the sun of righteousness, appeared to them? Then, with the devil bound and a great host of saints accompanying him, the joyful Lord returned in glory and triumph to the heights, [Note: [Col. 0329C] Here the Author appears to exert all his eloquence in the service of his subject’s joy. You will find similar passages in other ecclesiastical writers, especially those of the later age. Certainly not unlike is the passage in Sermon 137, *On the Seasons*, among the works attributed to Augustine, now Appendix 160, where, among other things, it says: “And behold, suddenly innumerable peoples of saints, who were held captive in death, falling at the knees of their Savior, beseech him with tearful voice and prayer, saying: You have come, whom the Law and Prophets foretold would come for us. You have come, granting in the flesh forgiveness to the living sinners of the world . . . You have come after long tears, etc. Ascend, Lord Jesus, hell having been despoiled,” etc.] saying: “For you will not leave my soul in hell, nor give your Holy One to see corruption. You have made known to me the ways of life; you will fill me with joy in your presence; delights,” my Father, “are at your right hand” (Ps. XV, 10), where I sit for ages of ages.

145 VIII. “And they,” [Note: [Col. 0329D] Mark XVI, 8: “But they.”] going out, fled from the tomb; for fear and trembling had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.” They were afraid, he says, to announce that the Lord had risen; and so they told no one anything about his resurrection. For they did not yet perfectly believe what the angel had said, since they thought him to be not an angel but a young man.

Coming, therefore, to the apostles, and keeping the rest in silence to themselves, they reported only this: that Christ the Lord had been removed from the tomb. [Note: [Col. 0329D] Here Bede and the interpreters raise a question by comparing Mark’s words, “they said nothing to anyone,” with Luke XXIV, 9: “And returning from the tomb, they reported all these things to the eleven and to all the rest”; similar words occur in Matthew XXVIII, 8. Bede resolves it by saying that “they said nothing to anyone” means that they gave no answer to the angels or told nothing to the guards “whom they saw lying there.” Jansenius, *Harmony*, chap. 145, says they told no one “whom they met on the way, because they feared the Jews”; this is Euthymius’s answer, followed also by Tirinus and Calmet. Lyra follows Bede. Our Author’s answer is also plausible: they told what they had seen, namely that the body was not found in the tomb, but kept silent about the angel’s words; thus both statements which appear contradictory are true.]

But, returning again to the sepulchre, as Matthew says, they saw the Lord “and held his feet” (Matt. XXVIII, 9). “But Jesus, rising early on the first day of the week, appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. She went and reported it to those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. And they, hearing that he was alive and had been seen by her, did not believe.”

These matters are written most fully in John, and have been sufficiently determined by us in Matthew. “After these things he appeared in another form to two of them walking and going into the country; and they went and reported it to the rest, nor did they believe them.” But because Luke relates these things more fully, we reserve their exposition for that place.

IX. [Note: [Col. 0330D] Mark XVI, 14: “Finally, as the eleven reclined, he appeared.”] As the eleven disciples reclined, Jesus appeared to them and reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him risen. Although Simon Peter, Mary Magdalene, and the two disciples to whom the Lord had appeared in the form of a traveler reported most certainly and firmly that the Lord had risen and that they had seen him, the others did not believe them. And, wonderfully, they believed neither themselves nor their own eyes; seeing him, they did not see him.

For the Evangelist Matthew relates that Christ’s disciples “went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them; and seeing him, they worshipped him; but some doubted” (Matt. XXVIII, 16). For they thought that they saw not a true body but a spirit. Hence he himself said: “Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke XXIV, 39). And perhaps their great doubt arose from intense love; for we do not easily believe what we greatly desire; likewise, we readily believe that what we fear may happen.

And he said to them: “Going into the whole world, preach the Gospel to every creature.” For previously he had said: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; for I am sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. X, 5). But now he commands them to go into the whole world. In this the rejection of the Jews and the election of the Gentiles are most plainly shown. Hence the Father says to him: “Ask of me, and I will give you the Gentiles for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession” (Ps. II, 8).

But when he says, “Preach the Gospel to every creature,” another Evangelist explains it, saying: “Go, teach all nations” (Matt. XXVIII, 19). For “every creature” and “all nations” signify the same thing. Thus the Apostle says of charity that it “believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (I Cor. XIII, 7); yet this is not true unless it is otherwise qualified. For if charity believes all things, it certainly believes both Pharisees and Sadducees—the one affirming, the other denying, the resurrection—which cannot be. Therefore charity does not believe all things. It must be qualified thus: it believes all things which ought to be believed.

Likewise, then, the saying, “Preach the Gospel to every creature,” must be qualified so as to say: preach the Gospel to every creature to which the Gospel ought to be preached. [Note: [Col. 0330D] Bede on this passage: “Was the holy Gospel to be preached to senseless things or to brute animals, so that the disciples are told: ‘Preach to every creature’? But by the name of every creature the whole nation of the Gentiles may be designated. For previously it had been said: ‘Do not go into the way of the Gentiles’; but now it is said: ‘Preach to every creature,’ so that the preaching of the apostles, first rejected by Judaea, might then come to our aid when proud Judaea had rejected it as a testimony to its own condemnation.” St Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, Homily 29, no. 2: “My brethren, was the holy Gospel to be preached to senseless things or brute animals, so that the disciples are told: ‘Preach to every creature’? But by the name of every creature, man is signified . . . For man has something in common with every creature: he shares being with stones, life with trees, sensation with animals, understanding with angels. Therefore, since man has something in common with every creature in some respect, man is in some respect every creature. Thus the Gospel is preached to every creature when it is preached to man alone, because he is taught for whose sake all things on earth were created, and from whom all things are not alien through a certain likeness. By the name of every creature the whole nation of the Gentiles may also be designated. Previously it had been said: ‘Do not go into the way of the Gentiles.’ But now it is said: ‘Preach to every creature,’ so that the preaching of the apostles, first rejected by Judaea, might then come to our aid when proud Judaea had rejected it as a testimony to its own condemnation.” It is evident, therefore, that Bede borrowed this from Gregory; Lyra does the same among later writers. Estius supplies “human,” a word expressed in I Peter II: “Certainly,” he says, “the qualification is suitable, so that the sense is: the Gospel is to be preached, or has been preached, to every creature to which it can be preached.” This is our Author’s explanation.]

For the Gospel is not to be preached to stones and to any other things lacking sense and reason. There are some, however, who, understanding these things too subtly, make difficult what is plain. Many things are found in the Prophets, the Apostles, and the Lord’s words to which this one qualification can suffice. Such is: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John XII, 32). If one adds, “all things which are to be drawn,” there will be no difficulty. But otherwise, who does not see how much absurdity follows? For very few are drawn there, in comparison with those whom the Lord does not draw to himself. Indeed, he will draw only human beings, and not even all of them, to himself.

By these and similar examples it is readily understood what is signified in the saying, “Preach the Gospel to every creature”: namely, that whoever believes the Gospel and is baptized shall be saved. The Gospel says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself.” If you believe and do this, you shall be saved. It also says many other things which bring about salvation and eternal life. But whoever does not believe shall be condemned. For even though a person has been baptized and all sins have been forgiven in baptism, that person too will be condemned if he has not believed the Gospel and given assent to its counsels.

“But these signs shall follow those who believe: In my name they shall cast out demons; they shall speak with new tongues; they shall take up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it shall not harm them; they shall lay hands upon the sick, and they shall recover.” We read that all these things were done in the early Church not only by the apostles but also by other saints. For unbelieving people would not otherwise have been converted from the worship of idols unless the Gospel preaching had been confirmed by such great signs and miracles.

For, as the Apostle says, Christ’s disciples preached Christ Jesus crucified, “a stumbling block indeed to the Jews, and foolishness to the Gentiles” (I Cor. I, 23). But when they suddenly cast out demons, spoke in new tongues, killed or put serpents to flight by a word alone, drank poison without injury, and healed the sick not only by touch but even by the shadow of their bodies, the Gentiles, at once converted to amazement, cried: “One is he whom the apostles preach, one Lord Jesus Christ, who does such things.”

But signs and miracles are no longer necessary for us now; it is enough for us merely to read and hear of those which were done. [Note: [Col. 0332D] See Gregory, cited homily.] For we believe the Gospel, and we believe the Scriptures which recount these things. No one now says in the Church: “I do not believe you unless you raise the dead, give sight to the blind, and do similar things.” Yet signs occur daily in the Church; if anyone is willing to attend to them, he will recognize that they are much greater than those which were then physically performed by those men.

For every day priests, by baptizing the people and calling them to repentance, cast out demons. Every day they speak with new tongues when, expounding the Scriptures, they transform the oldness of the letter into the newness of spiritual understanding. They take up serpents because by gentle admonition they turn evil desires, vices, and sins away from the hearts of sinners. They drink deadly things, but they do not harm them, because, reading the books of pagans and heretics and often hearing bitter, poisonous insults directed against themselves, they pass them by with a deaf ear and account them as nothing. They lay hands upon the sick, and they recover, because they heal infirm souls by their prayers and reconcile them to the Lord.

Therefore the saints of the Lord even now perform the same signs which the Lord then promised they would perform. But the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God. The book of the Acts of the Apostles shows how he was taken up, saying: “And when he had said these things, while they watched, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their sight. But they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Acts I, 9). And then the prophecy was fulfilled which says: “Their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII, 5).

**HERE ENDS THE COMMENTARY ON MARK.**

[Col. 0333]

**COMMENTARIES OF ST BRUNO, BISHOP OF ASTI AND SIGNI, ON LUKE**

[Col. 0333]

[Part One]

[Col. 0333A] 147 Having disposed of these matters, let us come to Luke; and, as we have already said, let us explain only those things which we have explained neither in Mark nor in Matthew. [Note: [Col. 0333A] This is what our author Augustine professed himself to do when he came to Luke, Book IV of *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, ch. 8, no. 9: “Now therefore, henceforth,” he says, “let us treat the Gospel of Luke in order, excepting those matters which he has in common with Matthew and Mark, since all those have already been treated.” He had done the same, after Matthew, when explaining Mark, Book IV, no. 1. But, as Augustine himself adds, “this beginning does not yet belong to the narrative of the Gospel.” For it is a kind of preface; and since it was judged to agree with the other Gospels as well, Ammonius placed it before his entire harmony. The more recent writers Cornelius Jansenius, John de la Haye, Bernard Lamy, and others do the same. All interpreters observe that Luke alone among the Evangelists did this; he likewise investigates why Luke alone did so. The chief reason seems to be this: that Luke, as Ambrose says in no. 4, “maintained, as it were, a historical order,” and, as Jerome says at the beginning of his Commentary on Matthew, wished to trace certain matters back more deeply. Thus he did what historians commonly do. For the same reason, in imitation of the most ancient writers, he named another of his works at its beginning—namely, the book of the Acts of the Apostles. Moreover, in order to win confidence for himself, he relates how he was able to know or attain the matters which he writes. Thus Ambrose, on these words, no. 2: “No one will doubt that this book of the Gospel is more extensive than the others. And therefore he claims for himself not those things which are false, but those which are true.” From Luke’s saying, “as they delivered them to us, who from the beginning themselves saw them and were ministers of the word,” Estius infers against Theophylact that Luke was not one of Christ’s seventy disciples, but received the faith from Christ’s apostles and disciples after His Ascension, and received from them the matters which he writes. Thus Jerome spoke most truly: Luke wrote the Gospel as he had heard it, but composed the Acts of the Apostles as he had seen it. Yet he attained a particular and outstanding praise in writing the Gospel. For, as Ambrose says, no. 2, he deserved even the testimony of the holy Apostle Paul for his diligence; for Paul praises Luke thus: “whose praise,” he says, “is in the Gospel throughout all the churches.” And Jerome, in the *Catalogue*, ch. 7: “Some,” he says, “suppose that whenever Paul says in his epistles, ‘according to my Gospel,’ he means the volume of Luke; and that Luke learned the Gospel not only from the Apostle Paul, who had not been with the Lord in the flesh, but also from the other apostles”; and he adduces the quoted words, “as they delivered them to us,” etc. Origen should also be added, who, in Homily 1 on Luke, in Jerome’s translation, says: “Luke indicates his conviction by the expression in which he says: ‘have been most surely accomplished among us,’ that is, πεπληροφορημένων [fully assured or brought to complete certainty]—which Latin speech cannot express in one word; for he had learned with certain faith and reasoning, and wavered in nothing.” On the force of that Greek word, see Estius here.] “Since many have undertaken to set in order a narrative of the things completed among us, as those who from the beginning themselves saw them and were ministers of the word delivered them to us, it seemed good also to me, having diligently traced everything from the beginning, to write to you in order, most excellent Theophilus, that you may know the truth of those words in which you have been instructed.” [Note: [Col. 0334B] “Having traced everything”: so the Vulgate. But where our author has “having traced everything from the beginning,” the Old Latin, from the Colbert manuscripts in Sabatier, and St Ambrose, Book I on Luke, no. 11, etc., read similarly.]

[Note: [Col. 0334B] Origen, in the passage cited: “Just as formerly among the people of the Jews many professed prophecy, and some were false prophets . . . so now also in the New Testament many have undertaken to write Gospels, but not all have been received. And that you may know that not only four Gospels, but many more, were written, from which those that we possess were selected and handed down to the churches, this is clear from Luke’s very preface, which runs thus: ‘Since many have undertaken,’ etc. His saying ‘have undertaken’ contains a hidden accusation against those who rushed into writing Gospels without the grace of the Holy Spirit. Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John did not undertake to write, but, filled with the Holy Spirit, wrote Gospels,” etc. He then names the Gospel of Basilides and others. Augustine likewise, Book IV of *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, no. 9: “In saying that many undertook,” etc., “he seems to indicate certain persons who were unable to fulfil the task they had undertaken . . . We ought not to understand these as those whose authority has any standing in the Church, because they were quite unable to fulfil what they had undertaken.” Ambrose also, almost to the same effect, no. 5: “Those, then, undertook who were unable to fulfil it. Therefore St Luke, by weightier testimony, declares that many began but did not fulfil it, saying that very many had undertaken . . . For the gifts and grace of God are without undertaking . . . Matthew did not undertake; Mark did not undertake,” etc. He appears to have drawn this from Origen. Therefore our author rightly understands this, with nearly all the ancient and modern writers, of apocryphal works.]

For what reason is there for blessed Luke to wish to write those things which he mentions as already written by many others, unless he had learned that they had said something inadequately and had not rightly held to the truth? For many besides the four Evangelists wrote; and all these writings are counted among the apocrypha. For the Church accepts no Gospels except the four. [Note: [Col. 0334D] Origen, in the passage cited: “But among all these we approve nothing else than what the Church—that is, only the four Gospels—receives.” Bede and all other ancient and modern interpreters profess the same, and it is now established from the mind of the Church.]

148 I. [CHAPTER I.] “There was in the days of Herod, king of Judaea, a certain priest named Zechariah, of the course of Abijah; and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth.” For we read that David divided the families of priests into twenty-four parts and commanded that each should serve the Lord in the ministries assigned to them according to their respective courses. [Note: [Col. 0335C] I Chronicles 24:3: “And David divided them . . . He divided, that is, among the sons of Eleazar sixteen chiefs by families, and among the sons of Ithamar eight by their families and houses; moreover, he divided both families among themselves by lots . . . The first lot came out to Jehoiarib . . . the eighth to Abijah.”]

From these twenty-four men, persons who succeeded one another in turn were always chosen, called chief priests; one of them presided, and was called the high priest. Now Abijah is found placed in the eighth lot; Zechariah, who now performs his course, sprang from his lineage. His wife too is said to have been of the daughters of Aaron, so that we may know them to have been rightly and lawfully joined. For the law commands that each person take a wife from his own tribe (Num. 36:6–7), and that each woman be joined to a man of her own tribe.

“But they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord.” In saying that they were righteous before God, he clears them of every fault of hypocrisy. [Note: [Col. 0335C] St Ambrose on this passage: “And rightly, righteous before God; for not everyone who is righteous before men is righteous before God. Men see one way; God sees another: men see the face, God the heart. Therefore it can happen that someone, through a popular and affected display of goodness, appears righteous to me, yet is not righteous before God . . . Perfect praise, therefore, is to be righteous before God.” Bede transcribes these words almost exactly.]

For they are not righteous before God who do all their works in order to be seen by men. But they walked blamelessly in all the Lord’s commandments and ordinances, because freely and without murmuring they kept all the commands of the law. What is not done freely and from the heart is not free from complaint. For the Lord attends, not to what we do, but to the disposition with which we do something. Hence the Apostle says that the Lord loves, not a giver merely, but “a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7). [Note: [Col. 0335D] This passage has been extensively discussed by the Fathers, especially by Jerome, Dialogue 1 against the Pelagians, no. 12, and Dialogue 2, no. 15. Since St Ambrose seemed to contradict it in Book I on Luke, nos. 17–18, and Pelagius abused Ambrose’s authority, St Augustine answers him in *On the Grace of Christ*, ch. 48, no. 53. See also Augustine, Book II on the Merits of Sins, ch. 13, nos. 19–20, and *On Perfection in Righteousness*, ch. 16, no. 38.]

“And they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren; and both had advanced in their days.” Elizabeth was barren so that she might give birth not by nature, but by power and miracle. Had she borne in youth, she would have been regarded not as barren but as fruitful. [Col. 0335C] Therefore she bears in old age; and, wonderful to say, in that age this one barren woman becomes fruitful, when all fruitful women become barren. John is born from elderly parents; Christ from a young woman, because John is the end of the old things, while Christ is the beginning of the new. “For the Law and the Prophets were until John.” [Note: [Col. 0335D] Matthew 11:13: “For all the prophets and the law prophesied until John.”] But Christ says: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. 21:5).

“And it came to pass, when Zechariah was performing the priestly office before God in the order of his course, that, according to the custom of the priesthood, he was chosen by lot to offer incense.” For this was the custom of the priesthood: that, succeeding one another in order, each of the chief priests—for there were many—should in his own time offer incense and sacrifice victims. Nor is it without significance that he is said to perform the priesthood “before God.” That person performs the priestly office before God upon whose offerings God looks favourably. Hence it is written: “The Lord looked upon Abel and his gifts; but upon Cain and his gifts He did not look” (Gen. 4:4–5).

“And having entered the temple of the Lord, all the multitude of the people was praying outside at the hour of incense.” This solemnity was observed on the tenth day of the seventh month, when the high priest alone entered the Holy of Holies once yearly, not without blood, and no one else was allowed to be in the temple. [Note: [Col. 0335D] From this passage it appears that our author follows the opinion of those who believed Zechariah to have been high priest. Some ancient and highly learned Fathers held this view: St Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 86; Augustine, Tractate 46 on John; St John Chrysostom, Homily 10 on Matthew, no. 3, where he says: “Consider, then, how great a thing it was to see a man coming from the desert after thirty years, the son of the chief priest.” St Ambrose, Book I on Luke, no. 22: “St Zechariah seems here to be designated high priest, because, as has been read concerning the first tabernacle, into which priests always entered to complete the ministries, they did not enter the temple at one time of the year only; but into the second, the one high priest entered once yearly, not without blood, which he offered for himself and for the people’s offences.” Our author, I think, derives this from Bede, whose words on this passage are: “It was commanded that incense be carried by the high priest into the Holy of Holies, while all the people waited outside the temple, on the tenth day of the seventh month. This day is called that of expiation or presentation; among us, owing to the varying course of the moon, by which the Hebrews reckon their months, it falls now in September, now in October . . . The Apostle, writing to the Hebrews, recalls this day thus: ‘Into the first tabernacle priests always entered, completing the offices of sacrifices; but into the second, the high priest alone once yearly, not without blood,’” etc.]

What this signifies the Apostle explains in the Epistle to the Hebrews (Heb. 9:6). We too have said enough on this solemnity in Leviticus. [Note: [Col. 0336D] On chapter 16. Roman edition, 1789, p. 157, col. 1.]

II. “And an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right of the altar of incense.” 149 The angel stood, and stood at the right, because he announced things strong and favourable. [Note: [Col. 0336D] Bede: “The angel fittingly appears both in the temple, beside the altar, and at the right, because he proclaims the coming of the true priest, the mystery of the universal sacrifice, and the joy of the heavenly gift.” St Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 87: “That you may understand that there is nothing sinister in the holy angels, Scripture says: ‘The Lord knows the ways which are at the right.’”]

“And Zechariah was troubled at the sight, and fear fell upon him. But the angel said to him: ‘Do not fear, Zechariah, because your prayer has been heard.’” This is a customary mark of angels, by which they are also distinguished from those who transform themselves into an angel of light: at the beginning of their speech they comfort those to whom they speak and urge them not to fear. [Note: [Col. 0336D] Likewise Bede: “The angel strengthens trembling Zechariah; for as it belongs to human frailty to be troubled at the sight of a spiritual creature, so it belongs to angelic kindness immediately to soothe, by gentle encouragement, mortals who fear at its appearance. But it belongs to demonic ferocity always to shake with greater terror those whom it finds frightened by its presence; this is overcome by nothing more effectively than fearless faith.” Before Bede, St Athanasius in the *Life of St Antony*, St Jerome on Matthew 28, etc.]

But when he says, “because your prayer has been heard,” let no one suppose that Zechariah had prayed to the Lord for a son, especially since he despaired on account of his own age and that of his wife, and did not believe even when the angel reminded him of this very matter. What, then, was he praying for, except what the law commanded him to pray for? For it says: “This shall be an everlasting ordinance for you: that you pray for the children of Israel and for all their sins once in the year” (Lev. 16:34). This, then, was what he prayed; and the angel said that this prayer had been heard. [Note: [Col. 0337C] Thus St Augustine, Book II, *Questions on the Gospels*, question 1: “It is not likely that, when he offered for the sins, health, or redemption of the people . . . this elderly man, having an aged wife, could have prayed in the public vows to receive children, especially since no one prays to receive what he despairs of receiving,” etc. St Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 88: “Do you think so great a priest had forgotten the people and the whole community, so as to ask concerning the conception of his aged wife, the childbirth of a barren woman despaired of? Was he then present as the delegate of all merely for himself? Did the advocate of all pray individually for himself? Did he confine so great an office of high priesthood within domestic concerns?” etc. So also Chrysostom, Homily 2 *On the Incomprehensible*, Bede, etc. See Maldonatus on this passage.]

“And Elizabeth, your wife, shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name John.” The angel did not give him this name without cause. For John means “the grace of God.” [Note: [Col. 0337D] “John, therefore, is interpreted ‘in whom is grace,’ or ‘the grace of the Lord.’” Bede.] Let us see, then, how the name suits him. Let the Lord Himself say: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you and gave you as a prophet among the nations” (Jer. 1:5). Great indeed is the grace of God bestowed upon one sanctified before he is born. The Lord’s further saying, “Among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen” (Matt. 11:11), and other such words which He proclaims in John’s praise, show how great also was the grace which John possessed.

“And there shall be joy and gladness to you, and many shall rejoice at his birth.” For who would not rejoice in and over the birth of him who came to announce the joy of the world? Who would not be glad on hearing Zechariah, mute for so long, at last prophesying at this birth and announcing so great a joy for the entire people? [Note: [Col. 0337D] Bede: “The father rightly rejoices because he has received in old age a son of such grace; others also rejoice, to whom he proclaims an entrance into the kingdom of heaven unheard of until then.”] “Blessed,” he says, “be the Lord God of Israel, because He has visited and wrought redemption for His people” (Luke 1:68). Read this psalm to the end, and you will see that it is wholly full of joy and gladness.

It follows: “For he shall be great before the Lord, and shall drink neither wine nor strong drink.” The things said above sufficiently show how great John was before the Lord. He drank neither wine nor strong drink because, like a Nazirite and one consecrated to the Lord from infancy, he abstained from every thing that could intoxicate either body or soul and overthrow the mind from its settled condition. [Note: [Col. 0337D] Bede: “*Sicera* means ‘intoxication’; by this word the Hebrews signify every drink capable of intoxicating, whether made from fruits, grain, or any other material. It was specifically required in the law of Nazirites that they abstain from wine and strong drink during the time of consecration . . . For it is fitting that a vessel devoted to heavenly grace be disciplined against worldly enticements; nor should one who desires to be filled with the new wine of the Holy Spirit be intoxicated with wine, in which is excess.”]

“And he shall be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb.” Unless he had been filled with the Holy Spirit while still in his mother’s womb, he would by no means have leapt for joy at the Virgin’s greeting. Elizabeth testifies to this when she says: “Whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? For behold, as the sound of your greeting came to my ears, the infant leapt for joy in my womb” (Luke 1:43).

“And he shall turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God. And he himself shall go before Him in the spirit and power of Elijah.” “He himself,” he says, “shall go before Him.” Before whom? Before the Lord their God. Therefore Christ is God and Lord of the Jews. [Note: [Col. 0338C] Bede rightly argues from this against heretics: “The Father plainly calls Christ the Lord God of Israel. But if Christ is—or rather, because Christ is—the Lord God of Israel, let the Arians cease to deny that Christ is Lord God; let the Photinians blush to assign Christ a beginning from the Virgin; let the Manichaeans cease to believe that the God of Israel’s people is one God and the God of Christians another.” See also St Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 88.]

But how will he go before Him? “In the spirit and power of Elijah.” Thus the Lord also says: “If you are willing to receive it, John himself is Elijah.” [Note: [Col. 0338D] Matthew 11:14: “If you are willing to receive it, he himself is Elijah.”] Not, however, in person, but in spirit and power. 150 Hence it is also said that there was one spirit in both. [Note: [Col. 0338D] Ambrose makes an elegant comparison between Elijah and John. Bede: “For as the former was the herald of the coming Judge, so the latter became the herald of the Redeemer.”]

“To turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the unbelieving to the prudence of the righteous, to prepare for the Lord a perfect people.” John turned the hearts of the fathers to the children, because what the patriarchs and prophets believed, he caused their children to understand and believe. [Note: [Col. 0338D] “To turn the hearts of the fathers to the children is to instil, by preaching, the spiritual knowledge of the holy ancients into the peoples.” BEDE. St Ambrose, Book I on Luke, no. 35: “We need no testimony that St John turned the hearts of very many, for the prophetic and evangelical Scriptures bear witness to it. For ‘the voice of one crying in the wilderness’ . . . and the baptisms frequently received by the people declare that the progress of the converted people was not slight; because, while John is believed, Christ is believed.”]

He also turned the unbelieving to the prudence of the righteous because he taught the faithless and unbelieving to walk in the way of the righteous. In doing this, he prepared for the Lord a perfect people.

“And Zechariah said to the angel: ‘How shall I know this? For I am old, and my wife has advanced in her days.’” Perhaps Zechariah did not remember that Abraham and Sarah begot children in old age. For nothing is impossible to the Lord; and all things are possible to one who believes. The angel promises, and the priest seeks a sign, as though he ought to have trusted the sign more than the angel. [Note: [Col. 0339C] Bede excellently says: “Hesitating because of the greatness of the promise, he asks for a sign by which he may be able to believe; but the vision or speech of an angel alone ought to have been sufficient to him as a sign. Therefore he paid the deserved penalty for his distrust by silence, so that this same silence might be both the sign of faith which he asked for and the punishment for unbelief which he deserved.”]

“And the angel answered and said to him: ‘I am Gabriel, who stand before God; and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you these good tidings.’” Why then do you doubt? Why do you not believe? Neither He who sent me nor I can lie to you. Do you seek a sign? The Jews also ask for signs. You say: “How shall I know this?” A sign will be given you, and perhaps after receiving it you will repent. This, then, will be your sign: “Behold, you shall be silent and unable to speak until the day when these things shall take place, because you did not believe my words, which shall be fulfilled in their own time.” Because, I say, you refused to believe the word, believe at least the sign. [Note: [Col. 0339C] Ambrose, Book I on Luke, no. 39: “The priest’s unbelief is condemned by silence . . . Because he did not believe, he was unable to speak.”]

“Behold, you shall be silent until the voice begotten from you arises; and, because you are to beget a voice, do not regret having been silent for a while. For from you will arise one who says: ‘I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness’” (Matt. 3:3).

“And the people were waiting for Zechariah and wondered that he delayed in the temple. But when he came out, he could not speak to them; and they realized that he had seen a vision in the temple. And he continued making signs to them and remained mute.” We may understand the aged Zechariah as the Old Testament and John the child as the New. For at that time the Old Testament lost its voice. [Note: [Col. 0339D] St Ambrose, Book I, no. 40: “It is not the mystery or silence of one man only. The priest is silent; the prophet is silent . . . It is the cessation of sacred rites and the silence of prophets—the silence of prophets and the silence of the priest. ‘I will take away,’ He says, ‘the strong man, the prophet, and the counsellor.’ And truly He took away the prophets when He took away the Word which was accustomed to speak in the prophets . . . For the Word of God passed to us, and in us He is not silent. Finally, the Jew can no longer say what the Christian can say,” etc. Isidore of Pelusium, Book I, Epistle 131: “By the very type of Zechariah’s silence, the silence of the Law was signified”; and Epistle 257: “When the morning light rises, darkness departs; when the bright sun rises, the choir of stars is obscured. When clear and pure day shines forth, the shadows of dawn come to an end. When the wisdom of the Gospel shone forth, the childlike instruction of the Law ceased to exercise its office. Thus Zechariah loses the use of speech after he heard the joyful message of a new and wondrous greeting.” Chrysologus, Sermon 86: “At the hour of incense, the sun was already setting in the Jewish temple, so that the morning sun might rise in the Church; evening pressed upon Jewish teaching because the dawn of the Gospel was imminent; the day of the Law was darkened so that it might shine wholly in grace,” etc.]

This happened when the New began to arise from the Old, because after the apostles and teachers began to preach and expound the new law, the old understanding of the law ceased. But the voice which it had lost was at length restored when, after the New Testament had been born and proclaimed everywhere, it learned from it what it should say. For the Old Testament speaks, but no longer in its own and proper sense.

“And it came to pass, when the days of his service were completed, that he went to his house. And after those days Elizabeth his wife conceived; and she hid herself for five months, saying: ‘Thus the Lord has dealt with me in the days in which He looked upon me, to take away my reproach among men.’”

The days of his service were completed on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [24 September], since the Feast of Tabernacles began on the fifteenth day of the seventh month and lasted seven days, and the eighth day after them was most solemn. Therefore he returned home on the twenty-third day of the seventh month. [Note: [Col. 0340D] This is indeed based on what was said above. For he affirms it because he supposed Zechariah to have been the high priest; concerning this opinion we have already spoken, and it is opposed by certain other Fathers and by modern writers generally: Jansenius, ch. 2 of the *Concordance*; Baronius; Natalis Alexander; Hamelius; Lamy; Tillemont; Calmet; and others.]

How then is it true that, when the angel came on the eighth day before the Kalends of April [25 March] to the Virgin Mary, he said of this same Elizabeth: “This is the sixth month for her” (Luke 1:36), when it was not the sixth but the seventh? It was indeed the seventh; but if we place the seven days of the seventh month at the end of March, we find six months and no more. For seven days of that month still remained when the angel spoke these things to Mary. 151 If seven other days are set in their place, the number of six months, and no more, is completed. “But in the sixth month …”

### III. The Angel Gabriel Is Sent

The angel Gabriel was sent by God into a city of Galilee called Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary.

> [Note: Col. 0340D. This is a homily of Emesenus for Wednesday after the Fourth Sunday of Advent, p. 10.]

“The angel Gabriel,” he says, “was sent.”

> [Note: Col. 0340D. Jerome, on Daniel, ch. IX, v. 16: “Gabriel is translated in our language as ‘the strength’ or ‘the mighty one of God.’ Therefore, at the time when the Lord was about to be born, to declare war upon the demons and to triumph over the world, Gabriel came to Zacharias and to Mary. And afterwards we read in the Psalms concerning the triumphant Lord: ‘Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty,’” etc. Bede here copied all this from Jerome in the same words.]
