Gabriel is interpreted “the Strength of God,” in order that he might announce that the power of God and the wisdom of God would assume flesh. But where was he sent? To Nazareth, a city of Galilee. To whom? To a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David—of a royal family, of noble descent, and more devout than others.

[Col. 0340C] For where ought the mother of chastity and purity to dwell except in Nazareth, which is interpreted “flower” or “purity”?

> [Note: Col. 0340D. Jerome again, Epistle 46, no. 12: “We shall go [Col. 0341C] to Nazareth, and, according to the interpretation of its name, [Col. 0341D] we shall see the flower of Galilee.” The Nazarenes were so called because they were pure, holy, and separated from others. Epiphanius, Heresy 29, no. 5: “For this reason they give themselves this name, so that they may be called Nazarenes, not Nazirites; the latter word means ‘sanctified.’”]

And the virgin’s name was Mary. For Mary is called “star of the sea”—of that sea, namely, concerning which it is written: “This sea is great and wide; there are creeping things there without number” (Ps. 103:25). Heaven has many stars; the sea has one, brighter and better than all the rest. [Col. 0341A] For from this one arose the Sun of righteousness, by whose radiance all things are illumined. Whoever follows him “does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” (John 8:7). Of what brightness, then, do we think that star is which bore into the world so great and such a Sun?

And the angel, entering in to her, said: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women.” For she was not in the streets and did not remain in public. She was within, sitting alone in her private chamber; yet she was not alone, being surrounded by so great an army of virtues.

> [Note: Col. 0341D. Well known are the words of Ambrose, Book II on Luke, no. 8: “Alone in her private chamber, where no man might see her and only the angel might find her; alone without a companion, alone without a witness, lest she be corrupted by any base conversation, she is greeted by the angel.”]

“Hail,” says the angel, “full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women.” It was not enough to say “Hail”: he added, “The Lord is with you,” and then blessed her, as though greeting her three times in one utterance. In this, diligent service, the affection of charity, and reverence are shown.

But who ever possessed so great a grace as the Virgin Mary? To others, grace is given by measure; but she is called full of grace. Consider how many women and virgins there were before her and how many after her. Yet she alone deserved to become the Mother of the Lord.

> [Note: Col. 0341D. Bede: “Mary is called in Hebrew ‘star of the sea,’ and in Syriac ‘lady’; and rightly so, because she deserved to bring forth both the Lord of the whole world and the everlasting light for the ages. She is rightly called full of grace, since she unquestionably obtained the grace which no other had deserved: namely, that she should conceive and bear the very author of grace.” He then copies the preceding words of Ambrose.]

For it is a great and ineffable grace that one should be chosen out of so many thousands. Since she is full of grace even before conceiving, who can imagine how much of God’s grace she abounds in after conception? She alone, moreover, among all women is blessed, while women were still held under the ancient curse arising from transgression, ever since the Lord had said to the first woman: “I will multiply your sorrows, and in pain you shall bear children” (Gen. 3:16).

[Col. 0341C] The Virgin Mary is not bound by this law: as a virgin she conceived, as a virgin she gave birth, and, giving birth without pain, did not lose the glory of virginity. She is therefore deservedly blessed among women, through whom blessing is given to women and the world is freed from the curse.

When she heard this, she was troubled at his saying, and considered what manner of greeting this might be. “She was troubled,” he says, not at his appearance but at his words.

> [Note: Col. 0341D. Eucherius, in the cited work: “She was troubled not at his appearance [Col. 0342C] but at his saying. For she attended not to the angel, but to the angel’s words, [Col. 0342D] and considered what that very respectful greeting meant for her.”]

For she attended not to the angel but to the angel’s words, and considered what that very respectful greeting meant for her. Perceiving this, the angel said: “Do not fear, Mary, for you have found grace with God.” But do you wish to hear what grace? “Behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call [Col. 0342A] his name Jesus.” This is the reason for that greeting. This is what I was sent to announce to you. Let fear depart, let your questioning cease; be secure, and be moved by no anxiety. These words are words not of fear but of joy. For you shall bear a son—none other, indeed, than the Creator and Lord of all things. Your Creator shall be your son, who will be perfectly born of you.

“And you shall call his name Jesus.” Whoever calls upon this name shall be saved. At this name every knee in heaven, on earth, and under the earth shall bend. The Lord himself says concerning it: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John 16:23). Therefore we must use this name in all prayers. He does not ask in this name who asks contrary to God’s ordinance and contrary to his own salvation or that of others.

> [Note: Col. 0342D. See the remarks on Matthew.]

[Col. 0342B] Indeed, there is no doubt that one who asks in this fashion asks against this name.

It follows: “He shall be great and shall be called the Son of the Most High.” He who in himself is always great then became great among men when he was known by men. The Apostle Peter, speaking in the person of the whole Church, called him Son of the Most High when he said: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:17).

“And the Lord God shall give him the throne of David his father, and he shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever; and of his kingdom there shall be no end.” The Lord receives from the Lord the throne of David, insofar as he is David’s son. Yet he reigns not only in the house of David—that is, in the tribe of Judah—but also in the house of Jacob, that is, in the whole people of Israel. By this it is understood that all those who imitate the faith and righteousness of David and Jacob are numbered in the host of his kingdom.

> [Note: Col. 0342D. Bede says that the house of Jacob is the whole Church.]

This kingdom exists even now; this dominion shall not fail, because the Lord shall reign for ever and unto ages of ages.

Mary said to the angel: “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?” She does not doubt that what the angel promises will happen. She asks only how it will happen.

> [Note: Col. 0342D. St Ambrose, Book II, On Abraham, ch. 8: “One who asks how she may know does not doubt that, when God reveals it, she can know; rather, she wishes to understand the manner in which the knowledge is to be obtained. … ‘How shall this be?’ etc. She rightly answered thus: since what belongs to nature is unavailable, since a virgin who has not been joined to a man does not ordinarily bear a child, I ask how she can give birth contrary to the ordinances of nature.” And in Book II on Luke, no. 17: “When Mary says, ‘How?’ etc., she does not appear to have doubted the fact, but to have asked concerning the nature of the fact. For it is clear that she believed it would be done, since she asked how it would be done; and therefore she deserved to hear: ‘Blessed are you who believed.’” See also his preceding remarks, no. 14.]

For although she had heard that a virgin would one day give birth, she had not heard how she would give birth. Isaiah says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. 7:14); but he does not say how she shall give birth. Therefore, because she is a virgin and does not know a man, she asks how she may [Col. 0343A] give birth and remain a virgin—a matter not yet revealed to anyone.

And the angel answered and said to her: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you.” This is the manner of your bearing. Thus you shall conceive; thus you shall give birth. There is now nothing further that you need ask. For the Holy Spirit who shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High which shall overshadow and embrace you and defend you completely within and without, shall do in you what it wills and as it wills.

When he says, “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you,” he explains this by saying, “and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you.” For this power belongs in common to the whole Trinity.

> [Note: Col. 0343D. Rufinus, Commentary on the Apostles’ Creed, in Vallarsi’s edition, no. 10: “See, then, the Trinity cooperating with itself. The Holy Spirit is said to come upon the Virgin, and the power of the Most High to overshadow her. But what is the power of the Most High, except Christ himself, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God? And whose power is this? ‘Of the Most High,’ he says. Therefore the Most High is present, the power of the Most High is present, and the Holy Spirit is present. This is the Trinity,” etc.]

For the whole Trinity is one God, and is itself the Most High. Thus Christ was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary—that is, by the power [Col. 0343B] of the Holy Spirit, which is one and common to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For the Spirit himself is the Spirit both of the Father and of the Son. But the Son is Son of the Father alone, and the Father is Father of the Son alone.

This power, then, coming upon Mary, effected Christ the Lord from two natures: “For as the rational soul and flesh are one human being, so God and man are one Christ.”

> [Note: Col. 0343D. In the Creed bearing Athanasius’s name.]

According to his humanity, therefore, the Son was not only made and created by the Father and the Holy Spirit but also by himself; according to his divinity, however, he was neither made nor created, but begotten by the Father alone.

“And behold, Elizabeth your kinswoman has herself also conceived a son in her old age.” Not only in you, he says, shall God work miracles of his power in these times, [Col. 0343C] but also in Elizabeth your kinswoman, whom you yourself know very well both to be elderly and to have been barren from infancy. “And this is the sixth month for her who is called barren,” so that the whole world may know that no word shall be impossible with God.

What more shall unbelieving Jews say? They deny that a virgin gave birth and refuse to believe the Gospel. Yet they cannot deny that Elizabeth, already old and barren, gave birth. Both are wondrous; both were done contrary to nature. Neither could happen unless he who has nothing impossible changed nature.

For God has done many things contrary to nature which the Jew does not dare deny: he changed a rod into a serpent and a serpent into a rod [Col. 0344A] (Exod. 7:10); he turned waters into blood and blood into waters (ibid., 20); the sea is opened (Exod. 14:21); manna rains down (Exod. 16:15); a she-ass speaks (Num. 22:28); a rock pours out waters (Exod. 17:6); and the Jordan turns backward (Josh. 3; Ps. 113:3). But why should I speak of Aaron’s rod, which, though dry, in one night put forth leaves, flowers, and fruit (Num. 17:8)? Could a dry rod bear nuts, and could a virgin not give birth? God certainly does whatever he wills; did he lose his power in the mother alone?

But Mary said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.” Having heard the reasons, she assented, and by assenting conceived.

> [Note: Col. 0343D. Ambrose, Book II on Luke, no. 16: “See her humility; see her devotion. She calls herself the Lord’s handmaid though chosen as his mother, nor was she lifted up by the sudden promise. In calling herself a handmaid, she claimed no prerogative for herself from so great a grace, but did what she was commanded. … ‘Behold the handmaid of the Lord,’ etc.: here you have obedience; you see the vow. ‘Behold the handmaid of the Lord’ is readiness for service; ‘let it happen to me according to your word’ is the conception of the vow.”]

“I am,” she says, “the Lord’s handmaid; I belong not to my own power but to his. Let it be done to me according to [Col. 0344B] your word.” And the angel departed from her.

> [Note: Col. 0344D. Thus far the homily.]

### IV. Mary Visits Elizabeth

But Mary, rising up in those days, went with haste into the hill country, into a city of Judea; and she entered the house of Zacharias and greeted Elizabeth.

> [Note: Col. 0344D. Luke 1:39. This is a homily of Emesenus for Friday after the Fourth Sunday of Advent, p. 11. We have said enough concerning the homilies falsely attributed to St Bruno which belong to Emesenus. Concerning this one in particular, we warn readers that it was copied by the most distinguished bishop Stephen Borgia from a Cassinese manuscript, no. 34, formerly 217, and bears this title: “On the octave of the Visitation, sermon of St Bruno, bishop.” The vulgate text has “in a city of Judah.”]

The Virgin, full of God, ascends into the hill country and seeks the things above.

> [Note: Col. 0344D. Ambrose, cited above, no. 19: “She went into the hill country not as though unbelieving the oracle, uncertain of the announcement, or doubting the example, but as joyful because of her desire, devout because of duty, and swift because of joy. For being now full of God, where should she hasten except toward things above?”]

She now dwells in mind not on earth but in heaven, and lives in the Spirit. She hastens and presses on, doing nothing negligently. She enters a devout household, desires to see a righteous couple walking blamelessly, and manifests signs of her humility and gentleness. Mary comes to Elizabeth; Christ to John; the Lady to her handmaid; the Lord does not disdain to come to his servant. What else is this but an example of humility?

And it came to pass, when Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, [Col. 0344C] that the infant leaped in her womb. Speak, infant, speak—greatest of all prophets, who will deservedly be called not merely a prophet but more than a prophet: whence comes this leaping of yours? You are not yet born, and already you prophesy, recognizing in the voice the Mother of the Lord. Since you cannot return her greeting, you do what you can by leaping. How joyfully you would have run to meet her if, being already born, you had seen her, when, having heard her voice, you strive by your leap to go forth to meet her!

And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit and cried out with a loud voice: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.” First the son, then the mother through the son, is filled with the Holy Spirit.

> [Note: Col. 0344D. Ambrose, no. 23: “The infant leaped; the mother was filled. The mother was not filled before the son; rather, when the son had been filled, he filled his mother also with the Holy Spirit.”]

The son, hidden within, teaches what [Col. 0345A] the mother should do outwardly. As though inwardly shaken by great force, Elizabeth not only returned the Virgin’s greeting, but even cried aloud: “Blessed are you among women.” The angel said the same thing. She is blessed by all, since she is held worthy of every blessing.

“And blessed is the fruit of your womb.” Blessed is the tree, and blessed also the fruit of the tree. Blessed is the rod from the root of Jesse, and blessed is the flower which springs from such a root.

> [Note: Col. 0345D. The same, no. 24: “The fruit of the womb itself is the flower of the root, concerning which Isaiah rightly prophesied, saying: ‘A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse,’ etc. The root is the family of the Jews; the rod, Mary; the flower of Mary, Christ,” etc.]

Blessed is such a mother, and blessed also is such a son.

“And whence is this to me, that the Mother of my Lord should come to me?” No holiness, devotion, or nobility in me has obtained this for me—that I should be deemed worthy of so great an honor and blessedness. I ought rather to have come to you; but your humility and that of your Son compelled you to come to me.

“For behold, as soon as the voice of your greeting came [Col. 0345B] into my ears, the infant leaped for joy in my womb.” At your coming, she says, not I alone but also my son rejoices; he delights in your greeting and accomplishes by joy what he cannot do by speech.

“And blessed is she who believed, because those things which were spoken to her by the Lord shall be fulfilled.” For what are the things spoken to her by the Lord except those which the angel said above: “Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus”? And a little later: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you.”

And Mary said: “My soul magnifies the Lord.” My soul, she says—my mind, my strength, all my understanding and my conscience—magnifies the Lord, praises, blesses, and proclaims him. And he also magnifies the Lord [Col. 0345C] in whose goodness the Lord is magnified and praised.

> [Note: Col. 0345D. The same St Ambrose: “For the Lord is magnified … not because anything can be added to the Lord by a human voice, but because he is magnified in us. For Christ is the image of God; and therefore, if a soul does anything righteous and devout, it magnifies the image in whose likeness it was created. And while it magnifies that image, it becomes higher through a certain participation in its greatness, so that it seems to express that image in itself by the radiant color of good deeds and a certain imitation of virtue.” Origen says likewise. See Jansenius, *Concordia*, ch. 4. Yet Augustine on Psalm 71, no. 19, must not be omitted. Explaining “All nations shall magnify him,” he writes: “They shall magnify him, not by making great [Col. 0346D] one who is great through himself, but by praising him and confessing him to be great. Thus we magnify God; thus we also say, ‘Hallowed be thy name,’ which is always, certainly, holy.”]

Thus teachers are praised and magnified in their disciples, and individual craftsmen in their works.

“And my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior.” Now, she says, my soul magnifies God. Now it makes known to all nations his majesty, of which it is written: “Your majesty, O God, is exalted above the heavens” (Ps. 8:2). In him it has always rejoiced, always delighted, always loved; to him it has clung with all its inward being and subjected itself in every respect to his service. And rightly so: “Because he has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid.” He regarded it and did not despise it.

> [Note: Col. 0346D. Jerome, Book XVI Against the Pelagians, no. 16: “Observe that she calls herself blessed, not through her own merit and virtue, but through the mercy of God dwelling in her.” See Bernard, Sermon 42 on the Song of Songs; Sermon 45, Homily 1 on *Missus est*, etc.]

For upon whom does God look except upon one who is humble, quiet, and trembles at his words?

“Behold, from henceforth [Col. 0346A] all generations shall call me blessed.” True is the prophecy which the Mother of Truth prophesied concerning herself. For from that time there has been no generation which has not proclaimed her blessedness. The Church always sings of her blessedness, and all generations are contained together in the Church.

“Because he who is mighty has done great things to me.” Indeed, he who is almighty. Truly these are great things—so great that he has never done, nor ever will do, such things for anyone else. He assumed flesh from her and appointed her Lady and Queen of heaven and earth. Great indeed are these things.

“And holy is his name.” He himself is mighty, and his name is holy; no one may take it in vain. In this name we are baptized and sealed, sanctified and called Christians.

“And his mercy is from generation [Col. 0346B] unto generations to those who fear him.” His mercy is not confined to one generation. For he is not God of the Jews alone, but is extended and increased from generation to generation, helping all who fear him.

“He has shown strength with his arm.”

> [Note: Col. 0346D. Bede explains it thus: “By ‘his arm’ he signifies the very Son of God … For as your arm, with which you work, so God’s arm has been called his Word, because through the Word he made the world.” This is the interpretation of other Fathers, as Jansenius has shown in the cited work. Others, comprehending the future and the past, interpret “arm” as God’s power. See Jansenius, ch. 4, and other interpreters.]

She uses the past for the future. For the Lord has shown strength with his arm—that is, with his power and might—because he conquered the devil, despoiled hell, and carried the souls of the saints with him to heavenly places.

“He has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts.” In the imagination of their hearts—that is, according to his own will—the Lord scattered proud Jews throughout all lands and subjected them to all nations. Hence the Psalmist says: “Scatter them in your strength, and destroy them, O Lord, our protector” (Ps. 58:12).

Of them it is further said: “He has cast down [Col. 0346C] the mighty from their thrones and exalted the humble,” namely by exalting the Gentiles to the glory promised to the Jews.

> [Note: Col. 0346D. See Gregory, ch. 2, Book VI on I Kings.]

For this is what the Lord always does: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 18:14).

“He has filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty.” The Gentiles were hungry because they had not tasted the sweetness of heavenly commandments; the Jews were rich because they abounded in the riches of the Law and the prophets. The former he filled with spiritual goods; the latter he allowed to depart empty and devoid of spiritual understanding. Relevant here also are the Lord’s words elsewhere: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6); and: “Woe to you who are rich, [Col. 0347A] for you have received your consolation” (Luke 6:24).

“He has received Israel his servant, remembering his mercy; as he spoke to our fathers, Abraham and his seed for ever.” This is what is said in the Psalms: “He has remembered his covenant for ever, the word which he commanded for a thousand generations, which he made with Abraham and his oath to Isaac” (Ps. 104:8).

For, remembering his mercy, as he had spoken to our fathers—that is, to Abraham and his seed—he received Israel his servant. He received him: he reconciled him, held him, and brought him into the inheritance promised in the fathers. Israel as a servant, certainly—

> [Note: Col. 0347C. Bede: “He beautifully calls Israel the Lord’s servant, since he was received by him for salvation, being obedient and humble.”]

—not Israel as an old man; that is, not followers of the Old Testament but followers of the New.

Mary remained with her about three months, [Col. 0347B] and returned to her own house. For it was fitting that they should remain together, so that in that short span of time Elizabeth might be taught by Mary and John by Christ.

> [Note: Col. 0347C. Origen, Homily 9 on Luke (*Works*, vol. III, p. 942): “For if, merely because Mary came to Elizabeth … in one hour such great progress took place, it is left to our conjecture what progress John made in three months while Mary remained with Elizabeth. It would indeed be very unfitting that the infant should leap and, as it were, frolic with joy in a point and moment of an hour, and Elizabeth be filled with the Holy Spirit, yet that for three months neither John nor Elizabeth should make progress from the neighboring presence of the Mother of the Lord and of the Savior himself [Col. 0347D]. Therefore John was trained and, as it were, anointed for athletic contest by the holy mother during three months, and prepared in his mother’s womb so that, being born wonderfully, he might be nourished wonderfully.” Ambrose seems to have had Origen before his eyes when he wrote, Book II on Luke, no. 29: “Her long stay was not only for the sake of family affection but also for the progress of so great a prophet. For if at her first entrance such advancement occurred … how much, do we think, did the presence of St Mary add through the use of so long a time? … Therefore the prophet was anointed and trained like a good athlete in his mother’s womb; for his very great strength was being prepared for contest.”]

It is pleasant now to consider how many tears Zacharias and Elizabeth then shed when the Virgin Mary—when the joy of the world and star of the sea—returned from there to her own house. John also, though still shut up in his mother’s womb—

> [Note: Col. 0347D. This shows that the author belongs to the opinion of those who held that the Blessed Mary did not wait for Elizabeth’s delivery. This view is defended by Balthasar Corderius in his notes on the *Catena on Luke*, p. 21; by Jansenius, *Concordia*, ch. 4; and by most writers, according to Maldonatus. Maldonatus himself, Cornelius a Lapide, Estius, [Col. 0348C] Menochius, Tirinus, Calmet, and others think that she remained until Elizabeth’s delivery.]

—grieved not a little at her departure, he who had leaped with such great joy at her arrival.

> [Note: Col. 0348C. Thus far the homily.]

### V.

Now Elizabeth’s time to give birth was fulfilled, and she bore a son. [Note: [Col. 0348C] Luke 1:57. This is the homily, like the others wrongly attributed to Emisenus, on the Nativity of St. John, p. 187, no. 2.]

Today John the Baptist is born, greater than the prophets, less than the angels—indeed, less than Him who was made a little lower than the angels. Hence the Lord himself says: “Among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen; yet he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he” (Matt. 11:11). The Apostle explained this when he said: “But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honor” (Heb. 2:9). Thus John is less only than Him than whom no one else born of woman has arisen greater.

Accordingly John himself says: “He must increase, but I must decrease. He who comes after me has been made before me, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to untie” (John 3:30). John decreases when his head is cut off; Jesus increases when he is lifted up upon the cross. And his neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had magnified his mercy toward her, and they rejoiced with her. For barren women were a reproach in Israel, although this signified something else as well. Barrenness of body is not a sin; but those barren in mind are a reproach before God. Therefore, in the literal sense, the Lord showed her great mercy by making her fruitful with so great a pledge. Hence she herself had said above: “Thus has God dealt with me in the days in which he looked upon me, to take away my reproach among men” (Luke 1:25).

And it came to pass on the eighth day that they came to circumcise the child, and they called him Zacharias after his father. Neither Christ nor John needed this circumcision; nevertheless they were circumcised, lest they cause offense and in order that they might fulfill the Law. [Note: [Col. 0348C] St. Thomas, III, question 37, article 1, assigns seven reasons why Christ ought to have been circumcised. The fifth is: “that by his example he might commend to us the virtue of obedience; hence he was circumcised on the eighth day, as the Law commanded.” There is, moreover, another reason given by St. Leo, Sermon 22, chapter 4: “That he might conceal, beneath the veil of our weakness, the power of the Deity inseparable from his humanity”; [Col. 0348D] and thereby the devil’s cunning might be deceived, “which thought the birth of the child begotten for the salvation of the human race to be subject, no differently from that of all who are born.”]

“For the Law and the Prophets were until John.” The Apostle writes much concerning circumcision in the Epistle to the Romans, and commends not circumcision of the flesh but that of the spirit. [Note: [Col. 0348D] Especially chapter 3, verse 28: “For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly; nor is that circumcision which is outwardly in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is that of the heart in the Spirit, not in the letter; whose praise is not from men but from God.” Expounding these words, St. Jerome, Book II of his Commentary on Galatians 5:5, adds: “Therefore circumcision of the flesh profits nothing in Christ, but circumcision of heart and ears, which removes that reproach of the Jews: ‘Behold, your ears are uncircumcised, and you cannot hear.’ Circumcision of the lips is profitable—the circumcision which, in humility, Moses complained that he did not yet possess, as it is written in Hebrew: ‘But I have uncircumcised lips,’” etc. See St. Augustine, Tractate 30 on John, no. 5.]

For spiritual circumcision ought to take place not in one member only, but in all the members [Col. 0348C]: so that the hands may not work evil, the eyes may not behold vanity, the feet may not run to shed blood, and the ears may not be open to slanders. Thus all the members are circumcised. By such [Col. 0349A] circumcision all vices and sins are removed. Hence it was fittingly performed on the eighth day, on which the final resurrection too will occur. [Note: [Col. 0349D] St. Augustine, Book XVI Against Faustus, chapter 29: “He who had power over the times of his passion and resurrection so arranged matters that his flesh rested in the tomb on the Sabbath . . . so that, rising on the third day—which we shall call the Lord’s Day, and which, after the Sabbath, is counted as the eighth—he might declare that the circumcision of the eighth day also pertained to the prophecy of himself. For what does circumcision of the flesh signify, except the putting off of mortality which we bear from carnal generation?” etc. See Sermon 189, no. 3; Book IV of the Unfinished Work against Julian, no. 134, etc.]

Then, with all the members circumcised—that is, with vices and sins cut away—and with the whole human being renewed completely and cleansed of every superfluity, man will rise to immortality.

And his mother answered and said: “By no means; rather, he shall be called John.” “By no means,” she says, “shall he be called Zacharias,” although this too is a name worthy of reverence. “Rather, he shall be called John,” which is interpreted “the grace of God,” because no one among those born of women will possess God’s grace more intimately than he.

And they said to her: “There is no one in your kindred who is called by this name.” For the angel imposed this name; the family did not give it. But how could Elizabeth have known the name? For it had been said not to Elizabeth but to Zacharias: “You shall call his name John.” In this matter we must believe, although it is not written, that she learned this name through an angelic revelation or some other divinely given inspiration. [Note: [Col. 0349D] Bede: “Do not wonder that the woman asserted a name which she had not heard, when the Holy Spirit, who had commanded it to the angel, revealed it to her; nor could she who had prophesied Christ be ignorant of the Lord’s forerunner.”]

Then they made signs to his father, asking what he wished him to be called. Since he could not indicate this to them by speech, he asked for a writing-tablet and wrote, saying: “John is his name.” And all were amazed. For they wondered why it pleased both parents to give this name to the child. Since no one in their family was called thus, they understood that this was done by God’s will.

Immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed, and he spoke, blessing God. For thus the angel had promised: “Because you did not believe my words, which shall be fulfilled in their time, you shall be silent and unable to speak until the day when these things come to pass” (Luke 1:20). When Zacharias spoke, fear came upon all their neighbors, and throughout all the hill-country of Judea all these sayings were spread abroad. And all who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying: “What do you suppose this child will be?”—he who was born contrary to nature, at whose birth a mouth long shut is opened, a mute man speaks, and such miracles occur? For the hand of the Lord was with him. That hand itself, then, wrought all these things in him.

And Zacharias his father was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and wrought redemption for his people.” He visited [Col. 0350A] through the herald, he visited through the Son; [Note: [Col. 0349D] Bede: “The Lord visited his people, wasting away through long infirmity and, as it were, sold under sin, and redeemed them by the blood of his only Son. [Col. 0350D] Because blessed Zacharias knew that this was shortly to be done, he narrates it in the prophetic manner as though already accomplished.”] he preached through both, but accomplished it through one. Both summoned the people to baptism; but one alone redeemed the people and baptized in the Holy Spirit. Hence it is said to John himself: “He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1:33).

“And he has raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant.” [Note: [Col. 0350D] Thus far, the homily.]

The house of David is the Church, a faithful and militant people, whom no adversaries can resist. In this house the Lord raised up the horn of salvation—namely John, who went before by preaching Christ. For David himself speaks of this horn of salvation, saying: “There will I bring forth the horn of David; I have prepared a lamp for my Christ.” [Note: [Col. 0350D] St. Jerome on Isaiah, chapter 5: “We often read that a horn signifies a kingdom and power, as in that passage of the Gospel: ‘He has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David his servant.’” St. Augustine, explaining Psalm 131, “There will I raise up the horn of David”: “A horn signifies height—and what kind of height? Not a carnal one. Therefore all bones are covered with flesh; the horn rises above the flesh. Spiritual height is the horn. And what is spiritual height but that which is of Christ? . . . And that you may know that there is the horn of David, consider what follows: ‘I have prepared a lamp for my Christ.’ What is the lamp? You already know the Lord’s words about John: ‘He was a burning and shining lamp.’” Bede almost transcribes these words of Augustine at this passage.] (Ps. [Col. 0350B] 131:17).

Therefore John is both a horn and a lamp: a horn by crying aloud, a lamp by giving light. For he is the voice crying in the wilderness; he is the burning and shining lamp. “As he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets who have been from of old.” “As,” he says, “we heard it foretold through the prophets, so now we see it taking place in this child: whom the Lord sent to bring us salvation and vengeance against our enemies, and to deliver us from the hand of all who hate us.” This is what he said above: “For he shall turn the hearts of fathers to their children, and the unbelieving to the wisdom of the righteous, to prepare for the Lord a perfect people” (Luke 1:17).

“To perform mercy with our fathers and to remember his holy covenant.” [Col. 0350C] For this purpose, he says, the Lord raised up this horn of our salvation: that he might show mercy to our fathers and, not forgetful of his covenant, fulfill in us the oath which he swore to Abraham our father—that he would give himself to us. Therefore, in fulfilling the covenant in us, he showed mercy to our fathers. For the Lord had sworn this to Abraham, saying: “To your seed I will give this land” (Gen. 15:18). By this he signified the land of the living, which he would give not to Abraham’s carnal but to his spiritual children.

“That, delivered from the hand of our enemies without fear, we may serve him.” Therefore, he says, the Lord gave us salvation from our enemies, so that, delivered without fear from the hand [Col. 0351A] of our enemies—by whom we understand vices and malignant spirits—we may serve not them but him. But how shall we serve him? “In holiness and righteousness before him.” Otherwise God does not regard our service, nor is it before him unless we serve him in holiness and righteousness. And this is not for a time, but for all our days. “For he who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

“And you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High; for you shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways.” John is called not only a prophet but even more than a prophet, and this indeed not by just anyone, but by Truth himself. Concerning John’s going before the face of Christ the Lord to prepare his ways, the Lord himself speaks through the prophet, saying [Col. 0351B]: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way before you.” [Note: [Col. 0351D] Malachi 3:1: “Behold, I send my angel, and he shall prepare the way before my face.”] Hence John himself says: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight’” (John 1:23).

He went before the face of the Lord. But why? “To give knowledge of salvation to his people in the remission of their sins.” And this he did when he said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 4:17). These blessings were given to us through the bowels of mercy of our God, who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all. Through these bowels of mercy and love, the Son of God himself, the Dayspring from on high, visited us: “To give light to those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death,” according to the passage [Col. 0351C]: “The people who sat in darkness saw a great light;” upon those walking “in the region of the shadow of death, light has risen.” [Note: [Col. 0351D] Gregory, Morals, Book IV, chapter 20, explains the various senses in which “the shadow of death” is used in Scripture.] (Isa. 9:2).

“To direct our feet into the way of peace.” For those feet are directed into the way of peace which run not to war but to peace. Of them it is said [Note: [Col. 0351D] Rom. 10:15: “How beautiful are the feet,” etc.]: “Blessed are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things.” [Note: [Col. 0351D] An exposition of this Canticle of Zacharias, separately presented under the name of Bishop Bruno, is found in the Cassinese manuscript no. 251, alternatively 330, in Lombardic script, eleventh century, folio 135.]

### VI. [CHAPTER II.]

Now it came to pass in those days that an edict went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled. This first enrollment was made under Quirinius, governor of Syria. That the whole world was enrolled and brought under tribute to a single power was a sign of great peace. For if the world had still been resisting and fighting against the Roman Empire, it could by no means have been enrolled by his edict or brought under [Col. 0351D] tribute. Concerning this peace the prophet had foretold: “They shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into sickles; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, nor shall they train any longer for war” (Isa. 2:4). And the Psalmist: “In his days righteousness shall arise, and abundance of peace” (Ps. 71:7). For since the Prince of Peace was being born, peace had to be established everywhere. [Note: [Col. 0351D] That the world was at peace at Christ’s birth is inferred by Jerome, Eusebius, Orosius, and other Fathers from the oracles of the prophets; they are cited by Estius, D. E., proposition 9, chapter 8. Maldonatus, at this passage, states that all ecclesiastical authors testify to this. Norisius, Dissertation 2 on the Pisan Cenotaph, chapter 10, refutes Kepler, who denied it. See St. Leo, sermon, chapter 5.]

And all went to be enrolled, each to his own city. Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, into Judea, to the city of David which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David, in order to be enrolled with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was pregnant. These words aptly show that this enrollment had been made according to families. Hence each person had to return, wherever they might be, to their own cities and families, so that, by common agreement, all together might promise to pay tribute and, once the enrollment had been made according to each [Col. 0352B] family, the total sum of the tribute might be collected. [Note: [Col. 0352D] Modern learned men maintain that this enrollment was not of the kind by which tribute was levied. See Norisius, Pagi, Tillemont, etc.]

Accordingly Joseph came with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was pregnant, to Bethlehem, the city of David, where their family lived, so that he too, like the others, might make the same declaration. And it came to pass, while they were there, that the days were fulfilled for her to give birth, and she bore her firstborn Son. For Christ had to be born there, since it had been announced through the prophet: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, shall not be least among the rulers of Judah; for out of you shall come a leader who shall rule my people Israel.” [Note: [Col. 0352D] Micah 5:2: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, are little among the thousands of Judah; from you shall come forth for me one who shall be ruler in Israel.”]

Now under the Law, the son who first proceeds from his mother’s womb is called firstborn, whether other sons follow or do not follow. For since the Law commands every firstborn to be offered to the Lord immediately after one month, who does not understand that one is called firstborn without reference to any other child, when there is as yet no child to which this firstborn could be related? What if the mother should die immediately, or bear no further son? Would that child therefore not be firstborn, though he has already been born from her and, after one month, was offered to God and called firstborn by the Law itself? Therefore either the Law lies, or “firstborn” is sometimes said without relation to another.

Thus the most blessed Virgin gave birth: virgin in conceiving, virgin in giving birth, and remaining virgin forever—closed before childbirth, closed in childbirth, and closed after childbirth. “She bore,” he says, “her firstborn Son, wrapped him in swaddling-clothes, and laid him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn.” O immeasurable mercy! [Col. 0352D] O ineffable humility! O mystery beyond words! God becomes man; the eternal becomes temporal; the immeasurable and immortal becomes capable of suffering; he who, because of his greatness, is not contained by the compass of heaven is wrapped in small swaddling-clothes. [Note: [Col. 0352D] A similar exclamation occurs in Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 38, p. 620: “O new mingling! O wondrous union! He who is, comes to be; he who was not created is created; he who cannot be contained in any place is contained, through the intervention of a rational soul between the Godhead and the grossness of flesh,” etc.]

Who has ever heard such a thing? Who has seen anything like it? He is laid in a manger, and the living bread which came down from heaven is set before not human beings but cattle—that is, revealed not to Jews but to Gentiles. [Note: [Col. 0353D] Ambrose, Book II on Luke, no. 34: “This is the Lord; this is the manger in which the divine mystery has been revealed to us: the irrational Gentiles, who formerly lived like cattle in their mangers, are to be fed with the abundance of sacred nourishment. Therefore the she-ass, the figure and form of the Gentiles, recognized the manger of her Lord.”] Then “the ox knew its owner, and the donkey the manger of its Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0353D] Isaiah 1:3. See Ambrose, who cites this same passage of Isaiah in Book II on Luke, no. 42.]

But what shall I say of the fact that the Creator of heaven and earth, the King of kings and Lord of lords, had no place in the inn? For the Apostle says: “Though he was rich in all things, for our sakes he became poor.” [Note: [Col. 0353D] 2 Cor. 8:9: “For your sakes he became needy, though he was rich.”]

And there were shepherds in the same region, keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock. And behold, an angel of the Lord stood beside them, and the glory of God shone around them, and they feared with great fear. And the angel said to them: “Do not fear. For behold, I announce to you [Col. 0353B] great joy, which shall be for all the people: for today a Savior has been born to you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David.”

In the literal sense, the reason why the angel first announced these words to the shepherds seems to have been that they might not, as though unaware, enter the stable and attempt to approach the manger in which the child had been laid. Spiritually, however, the stable is understood as the Church, the manger as divine Scripture, and the shepherds as bishops and teachers. [Note: [Col. 0353D] The words of St. Ambrose, Book II on Luke, no. 50, are well known: “See the beginning of the Church as it rises: Christ is born, and the shepherds begin to keep watch, so that they might gather into the Lord’s fold the flocks of the Gentiles, who had formerly lived after the manner of cattle, lest they suffer assaults from spiritual beasts through the spreading darkness of the nights. And the shepherds fittingly keep watch, since the Good Shepherd instructs them. The flock, therefore, is the people; the night is the world; the shepherds are priests.” See also Cyril in Corderius’s *Catena*, p. 41.]

For the Church is called a stable, to which God’s animals stream from every side; there they stand and dwell. Hence it is written: “Your animals, O Lord, shall dwell therein” (Ps. 67:11). These animals are nourished, as in a manger, with spiritual food in divine Scripture. There they find Christ laid, and there [Col. 0353C] they eat the living bread. Blessed are those who are fed with the food of this manger and refreshed by the delights laid there.

But you, shepherds of the Church—you bishops and priests—listen and understand. The angel speaks to you. To you he proclaims this great joy, because it has been given to you to know the mystery of the kingdom of God. [Note: [Col. 0354D] Bede: “For a most beautiful reason, when the Lord is born the shepherds keep watch and defend their flock by guarding it against the snares of the night. . . . Therefore, at the Lord’s birth, let shepherds keep watch over their flock of sheep. . . . Fittingly, the angel appears to watchful shepherds and God’s glory shines around them, because those who know how to preside diligently over faithful flocks deserve, above others, to behold sublime things; and while they themselves devoutly watch over the flock, divine grace shines more richly upon them.”]

It has been given to you to hear and understand the secrets of heaven. Therefore proclaim what you have heard, preach what you have seen; do not conceal what you have learned. For Christ is born in the stable as often as you preach these things in the Church; as often as you announce to others the Virgin’s childbirth and Christ’s birth, he is laid there as a little child in the manger. Hence today’s feast is called the Nativity of the Lord, not because the Lord is born today, nor because he now comes forth from the Virgin, but because today the memory of his birth is renewed, celebrated in its commemoration, and preached.

“And this shall be a sign to you: you shall find the infant wrapped in swaddling-clothes and laid in a manger.” Would that the Jews received this sign and sought Christ with us in the manger! [Note: [Col. 0354D] Bernard, Sermon 3 on the Canticle, treats this sign.] Although he is wrapped in swaddling-clothes and lies hidden beneath the veil of the letter, they would nevertheless find him if they sought him, and understand him if they believed. Therefore whoever you are who wish to see Jesus, come to this manger; search the Scriptures; remove the swaddling-clothes, strip away the letter: “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). Then you shall see what you could not see. Thus the shepherds of the Church seek him; seeking, they find him; finding, [Col. 0354B] they venerate and believe.

And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising the Lord and saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

### VII.

And it came to pass, when the angels departed from them into heaven, that the shepherds said to one another: “Let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this Word which has come to pass, which the Lord has shown us.”

The shepherds, he says, spoke to one another; and, discussing among themselves the things which they had heard and seen, they said: “Wonderful are the things we have heard; astounding are the things we have seen. Glory is promised to heaven, peace to earth. Today a Savior has been born to us; today a new king has been given to us, who is Christ the Lord in the city of David. What, then, shall we do? Why do we delay? Let us go [Col. 0354C] as far as Bethlehem; for it is the city of David, and let us see this Word and believe, because ‘in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.’

“Which has come to pass.” In itself, the Word was neither made nor created. Yet it was in a certain manner made, because the Word was made flesh. “Which the Lord has shown us.” Let us see bodily what the Lord has shown us spiritually; what we have conceived in mind and hold by faith, it remains for us to behold with our eyes.

And they came in haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the child laid in the manger. In the stable they found the star; in the manger, the sun: for Mary is called the Star of the Sea, and Christ the Sun of righteousness. [Col. 0355A] Therefore let darkness depart and gloom flee, because the star shines in the stable and the sun in the manger. Nor can there be stench where the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys are, by whose most sweet fragrance the Church, exceedingly delighted, says: “Draw me after you, and we shall run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:3).

But what shall I say of the Mother of the Lord, whose fragrance King Solomon, most wise of men, admiringly described: “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness like a little rod of smoke, from spices of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer?” (Song 3:6.) For where the smoke of every aromatic substance gives forth fragrance, there can be no trace of stench.

And when they saw, they recognized the saying which had been told them concerning this child. For this is the child of whom it is written [Col. 0355B]: “A child has been born to us; a Son has been given to us; and dominion has been placed upon his shoulder. His name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace. His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace. He shall sit upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish it and strengthen it in judgment and righteousness, from now until eternity. The zeal of the Lord of hosts accomplishes this” (Isa. 9:6).

For in these words of peace are described the birth and nobility, power and strength, dominion and righteousness, and the other things which belong to the praise and glory of this child. And all who heard wondered at the things told them by the shepherds. But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart.

O [Col. 0355C] most wise Mother, and alone most worthy of such a Son! She pondered all these words in her heart and therefore preserved them for us and commended them to memory, so that later, as she taught, narrated, and proclaimed them, they might be written down, preached throughout the whole world, and announced to all nations. For the Apostles heard these things from her. The Evangelists learned them in her school; at her dictation they wrote them down and handed them on to us to be read. [Note: [Col. 0355D] Bede: “Because she had read the Holy Scriptures and knew the prophets, she compared the things which had occurred to her concerning the Lord with those which she knew had been written concerning the Lord by the prophets; and, comparing them with one another, she recognized their agreement, like the companion Cherubim, in harmony with the light of his countenance.” St. Ambrose: “She compared the evidences of faith in her heart. If Mary learns from shepherds, why do you refuse to learn from priests? If Mary is silent before the apostolic commands, why, after the apostolic commands, do you desire more to teach than to learn?”]

Who, then, would not believe the Gospels? Who would dare contradict accounts supported by the authority either of the Mother or of the Son? For the Apostles and Evangelists heard some things from the Mother of the Lord, such as these and the other matters written concerning the Savior’s infancy. But they learned very many things through sight and hearing from the Lord himself.

And the shepherds returned [Col. 0356A] glorifying and praising God for all the things which they had heard and seen, as had been told them. Blessed are these shepherds, who merited to see Christ the Lord and, praising and glorifying God, believed the things which they had heard and seen. Blessed are those shepherds who even today seek Christ in the manger of the Church—that is, in the sacred books—and faithfully believe in him, announcing his birth, preaching his faith, and everywhere praising and glorifying him. [Note: [Col. 0355D] Thus far, the homily.]

### VIII.

And when the eight days were completed for the child to be circumcised, his name was called Jesus, as it had been called by the angel before he was conceived in the womb. [Note: [Col. 0355D] This is the homily attributed to Emisenus for the Octave of the Nativity, p. 26.]

The Lord was circumcised for us, not for himself. For just as he was born, baptized, [Col. 0356B] and suffered for us, so also he was circumcised for us. [Note: [Col. 0355D] Bede, at this passage: “Our Redeemer, who came into the world without sin in order to take away the sins of the world, just as by his baptism he procured remedies for us . . . so too by the circumcision which he received he did not cleanse sins of his own, since none had been committed, but taught that the oldness of our nature in himself must be renewed,” etc. See St. Thomas, III, question 37, article 3. Bede also says: “The rite and religion of circumcision took its beginning from the blessed patriarch Abraham.” See St. Ambrose, Book II, *On Abraham*, chapter 2. Johannes Meyer, *On Sacred Times*, chapter 7, and Christian Worm, *On Corrupted Traces of Hebrew Antiquities*, chapter 13, refute Marsham and Spencer, who maintained that the Hebrews borrowed the rite of circumcision from the Egyptians.]

Abraham was the first to be circumcised; of him the Apostle says: “He received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith” (Rom. 4:11). Circumcision was given, [Note: [Col. 0356D] See St. Thomas, I–II, question 102, article 5, reply to objection 1; and commentators on Paul’s statement at Romans 3:1, “What profit is there in circumcision? Much in every way,” etc.] not to take away sins—which is the principal work of baptism—but to signify something and to separate, by a certain distinction, the people of the Jews from other nations.

Therefore, although formerly whoever was not circumcised was condemned because of transgressing the commandment, no one was justified through circumcision. For, as the Apostle says: “Circumcision indeed profits if you keep the Law; but if you are a transgressor of the Law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision. For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh; [Col. 0356C] but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is that of the heart in the spirit, not in the letter” (Rom. 2:25).

Circumcision, therefore, signifies something great—and something so great that whoever has not been circumcised in this manner cannot be saved, leaving aside for the present the question of infants. For of this circumcision it is written: “Circumcise your hearts, and not your bodies.” [Note: [Col. 0356D] Deut. 10:16: “Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart.”] But the Apostle says of circumcision of the flesh: “Behold, I Paul say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2).

This circumcision was fulfilled in Christ, in whom the other ceremonies of the Law were also consummated. “For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4). Therefore he himself was circumcised, in order to fulfill the Law, show that it was good, [Col. 0357A] and commend its meaning to us. Hence, on the night on which he was betrayed, he ate the lamb with his disciples and immediately showed what it signified, when, blessing bread and wine, he said: “Take and eat: this is my body”; and, “Drink of this, all of you: for this is the cup of the new covenant, which shall be shed for you and for many” (Matt. 26:26).

He immediately showed that this sacrament had then been fulfilled by him and in him, and that thereafter it ought neither to be performed nor understood according to the letter, saying: “Amen, I say to you, I shall drink no more henceforth of this fruit of the vine until I drink it new with you in the kingdom of God” (Matt. 26:28). Thus the Lord fulfilled and confirmed the old covenant, put an end to the letter, and granted primacy to spiritual and new understanding. Therefore the Law was consummated and passed away according to the letter; but it remains and always will remain according to spiritual understanding.

Hence the Lord himself says: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Mark 13:31). And again: “Amen, I say to you, not one iota or one stroke shall pass from the Law until all things are fulfilled” (Matt. 5:18).

The Jews indeed are circumcised in one member, but they do not understand why they are circumcised. Christians, however, understanding what circumcision signifies, [Col. 0357B] circumcise not one member only but all the members—not by cutting the skin, but by casting away every superfluity. [Note: [Col. 0357D] St. Gregory, *Morals*, Book XXVIII, chapter 3: “Circumcise the foreskins of your hearts; that is, after you extinguish lust from the flesh, cut away even superfluous thoughts.”]

For whoever does not kill, commit adultery, covet [Col. 0357C] his neighbor’s property, lie, or steal; whoever harms no one, wrongs no one, and does not desire to see, hear, or think vain things—such a person is perfectly circumcised inwardly and outwardly. This is what the circumcision of the Jews signifies. Without this signification it is useless. For if they understood what “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35) signifies—for this is the explanation of that circumcision—they perhaps would not further wound themselves uselessly.

Many things may be said about circumcision, but it is enough that we have said these few things as certain seeds or first principles. [Note: [Col. 0357D] Many other matters are added in the homily, p. 26, no. 2.]

IX. And when the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were fulfilled, they brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord [Col. 0358A]: “Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord.” For it is written in the law of Moses that a woman who “having received seed bears a male child, shall be unclean for seven days, and on the eighth day the little child shall be circumcised. But she herself shall remain thirty days in the blood of her purification. She shall touch no holy thing, nor enter the sanctuary, until the days of her purification are fulfilled” [Note: Vulgate: “purification.”] (Lev. 12:2).

The blessed Virgin Mary was not bound by this law; for, having received no seed, she conceived as a virgin, gave birth as a virgin, was closed before childbirth, closed in childbirth, and remained closed after childbirth. To distinguish her case, Moses did not simply say, “A woman who bears a male,” but added, “who, having received seed, bears a male, shall be unclean for seven days” [Col. 0358B] (ibid.). What these things signify we have explained in Leviticus.

[Note: See the Roman edition of St Bruno, vol. I, p. 147, col. 1. St Bernard, Sermon 3 on the Purification of the Blessed Mary (col. 968, 2nd Mabillon edition): “Do you suppose that Moses, when about to say that a woman who bore a daughter would be unclean, was not afraid of incurring the charge of blasphemy against the Mother of the Lord, and therefore prefaced it with ‘having received seed’? Otherwise, unless he had foreseen that a virgin would bear without seed, what need was there to mention received seed? It is therefore evident that this law does not include the Mother of the Lord, who bore a son without receiving seed,” etc. And Sermon 51, ibid., col. 1191: “What do we mean when we say that Blessed Mary was purified? Or when we say that Jesus himself was circumcised? Truly she no more needed purification than he needed circumcision. Yet for us he is circumcised and she purified: that she may provide an example to penitents, so that, abstaining from vices, we may first be circumcised through that very continence, and then purified from sins committed through repentance.”]

Nevertheless, the Virgin Mary waited until all the days of purification were completed—days which the law had prescribed, not for her, but for other women. For it was not said of her, “She shall touch no holy thing,” she who held in her womb the very Holy of Holies, cherished him in her bosom, and nourished him with virginal milk.

When the days were complete, they brought the child to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord: “Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord.” For from the time when the Lord slew the firstborn of the Egyptians, he claimed all the firstborn of the children of Israel for himself and commanded that they be offered to him [Col. 0358C]. But why was this so? Unless it was that all first and greatest things, all better and dearer things, should be offered to the Lord. Let us therefore offer him our faith; let us offer our souls, which have their origin not from earth but from heaven, and which are the first, chief, and greatest things in us.

“And to offer a sacrifice, according to what is said in the law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.” For the turtledove is a most chaste creature, while the dove is free from gall and bitterness. Those, therefore, who preserve chastity and innocence of body and soul truly offer the Lord a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons. Such a sacrifice pleases the Lord: one in which we offer ourselves to him and, living innocently and chastely in body and soul, dedicate ourselves to him.

[Note: St Ambrose, Book V on the *Hexaemeron*, ch. 19, no. 62: “The law of God chose the turtledove as the gift of a chaste sacrifice. . . . When the Lord was offered in the temple, it was offered. . . . This is the true sacrifice of Christ: bodily chastity and spiritual grace. Chastity belongs to the turtledove, grace to the dove.” See also a certain story in Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, ch. 34. Bede on this passage: “Whoever wishes lawfully to be consecrated to the Lord must offer a lamb of innocence, and likewise a turtledove or a dove of union” [Col. 0359C].]

Such a sacrifice [Col. 0359A] it was fitting for the Mother of the Lord to offer, for her whole life was chastity and innocence.

X. And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon; and this man was righteous and God-fearing, awaiting the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was in him. The Evangelist briefly shows what kind of man and how great this Simeon was, when he says that he was righteous, feared the Lord, awaited and longed for the consolation of the people, and that the Holy Spirit, who was in him, had revealed and promised to him the coming of the Son of God.

[Note: On the praises of this Simeon, see at length Homily on the Meeting of the Lord, among the spurious works of St Athanasius, vol. II, p. 419.]

This is what he says: “And he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had first seen the Christ of the Lord.” With what longing this most blessed old man burned to see the Lord—he whom age was already compelling to depart from this world [Col. 0359B], but whom God’s answer held back! For though he desired to die, he could not die because he had not yet seen the Christ of the Lord, concerning whom he had heard the promise: “He shall not see death before he has first seen the Christ of the Lord.” This, then, was his desire; this he pondered in his mind; this he thought of always, saying: “I know that he will come; when shall I see him? Come, Lord Jesus; loose my bonds, and now let me depart in peace.”

[Note: Ambrose, Book II on Luke, no. 58: “And fittingly is he righteous, since he sought not his own favour but that of the people, desiring himself to be released from the bodily bonds of frailty, yet waiting to see the promised one; for he knew that blessed are the eyes that see him. See the righteous man, as though confined in the prison of a heavy body, wishing to be dissolved that he may begin to be with Christ. . . . But let him who wishes to be dismissed come into the temple, come to Jerusalem, await the Christ of the Lord, receive the Word of God in his hands, embrace him with, as it were, the arms of faith,” etc. St Augustine, Sermon 163: “For what is his salvation but his Christ? . . . The righteous men of old desired this salvation. . . . They said: Give us your salvation; let us see your Christ while we live in this flesh. Let us see in the flesh him who frees us from the flesh; let flesh come that cleanses flesh. . . . In this longing was that holy old man Simeon, that holy old man Simeon, well deserving of God; without doubt he too said: ‘Show us, Lord, your mercy, and give us your salvation.’ In this longing and in prayers such as these he received an answer,” etc. See also his Sermon 277, no. 17; Sermon 288, no. 2; Sermon 370, no. 3, etc.]

While he said these things to himself and burned with this longing, the Holy Spirit said to him: “[lacuna] the one whom you seek; now him [lacuna]; hasten; go to the temple.”

[Note: Here a torn page of our manuscript leaves out some words, though their sense is clear: “You shall see him whom you seek; now they are offering him to God—hasten,” etc.] And he came in the Spirit to the temple—that is, he came at the Spirit’s command. And when his parents brought in the child Jesus, that they might do for him according to the custom [Col. 0359C] of the law, he himself took him into his arms. When, he says, his parents brought the child Jesus into the temple in order to do for him according to the custom of the law, the old man met them, stretched out his arms, and said to the parents: “Give him to me; he is due to me; it is my office; I was sent for this; I was reserved for this service.” Then, joyful and exultant, he took him into his arms.

At once old age fled, and youthful vigour and strength came upon him. He who had previously scarcely been able to carry himself now exults as he lightly carries the child. Thus it was aptly said: “The old man bore the child [Col. 0360A], but the child guided the old man; the Virgin who bore him and remained a Virgin after childbirth worshipped him whom she had borne.”

And he blessed the Lord and said: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace; because my eyes have seen your salvation, which you prepared before the face of all peoples: a light for the revelation of the Gentiles, and for the glory of your people Israel.”

[Note: This is Responsory 2 for the feast of the Purification, among the responsories of St Gregory published by Cardinal Thomasius, 1st edition, p. 75; now in his works, vol. IV, p. 63.]

“I bless you,” he says; “your promise is fulfilled. My desire too is fulfilled, because I see your Christ, my Lord. Therefore dismiss your servant in peace, because I have seen your salvation.” For Jesus is interpreted “Saviour” or “Salvation,” concerning whom it is written: “The Lord has made known his salvation; before the sight of the Gentiles he has revealed his righteousness” (Ps. 97:2).

For you prepared and sent before the face of all peoples this light, this radiance, this sun, this surpassing splendour [Col. 0360B]. For what purpose? For the revelation and illumination of the Gentiles, and for the glory of your people Israel. By this light the Gentiles are illumined and the Jews glorified. For it is a great glory to them that such a light has arisen from their nation.

[Note: Theophylact on this passage: “This saving light is for the illumination of darkened Gentiles and for the glory of Israelites. For Christ is the glory of the people that is truly Israel, since he arose from it.”]

XI. And his father and mother were wondering at the things said concerning him. Why Joseph is called his father, the Evangelist explains in what follows, saying: “Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years old, being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph” (Luke 3:23). Thus Jesus was Joseph’s son not in fact, but in human opinion.

And Simeon blessed them and said to Mary [Col. 0360C], his mother: “Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign that shall be contradicted.” This is what the Lord himself says of himself: “For judgment I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and that those who see may become blind” (John 9:39). The Lord is set for the fall of those who contradict his sign; but for the rising again of those who venerate and believe his signs and wonders. For the former rush to destruction, whereas the latter rise to glory.

[Note: St Gregory of Nyssa, *On the Meeting of the Lord*, vol. II, p. 382: “Thus he is indeed a fall to those who are offended, because of unbelief, at his flesh; but a resurrection to those who have acknowledged the firmness of the divine dispensation and governance” [Col. 0361D].]

For his birth from a Virgin is a great and unprecedented sign [Col. 0361A]. We believe this sign; the Jews contradict it. He rose again and ascended into heaven; that too is a sign. There are also many other signs which the Lord Jesus performed: unbelievers contradict them and are blinded; believers believe and are illumined. Thus he is set for the fall of some and the rising again of others.

“And a sword shall pierce your own soul also, that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.” “A sword,” he says, “shall pierce your own soul”: namely, the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God, so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed to you—thoughts which no one can know unless the Holy Spirit reveals them.

[Note: Ambrose on this passage, no. 61: “Neither the letter nor history teaches that Mary departed this life by suffering bodily death. . . . And therefore he shows Mary’s prudence not to have been ignorant of the heavenly mystery:”—“For the word of God is living and powerful, and sharper than every two-edged sword,” etc.]

To pass over other examples, we may understand that she knew even the thoughts of her own Son from this: when invited to the wedding, she urged him to do what he intended to do, saying, “They have no wine” [Col. 0361B] (John 2:3). When he answered her, “What is that to me and to you, woman? My hour has not yet come” (ibid., v. 4), she, the sword of the Spirit passing through her and knowing beforehand what was to happen, said to the servants: “Whatever he tells you, do” (ibid., v. 5). She would not have said this had she not known his thoughts.

We may also understand by this sword, which wounds not the body but the soul, that immeasurable grief by which the most blessed Virgin was wounded and pierced at the death of her only-begotten Son.

[Note: Nyssenus, in the passage cited: “He plainly foretells that the soul of the Mother of God herself would be pierced by a sword, referring to the suffering that occurred at the cross.” See Augustine, Letter 149 to Paulinus, no. 32, and St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, III, q. 17, art. 4, ad 2.]

“That the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.” For Christ’s Passion revealed the thoughts and hidden mysteries of many hearts, because there the sayings, thoughts, and writings of the prophets [Col. 0361C] were revealed and fulfilled. For who, unless Christ had suffered, could have understood what the prophet had thought when he said: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones” (Ps. 12:17). And again: “I lay down and slept; I rose again, because the Lord sustained me” (Ps. 3:6).

There are many other matters revealed to us which the Jews cannot understand precisely because they do not believe that they were spoken concerning Christ. Hence, in the Apocalypse, when blessed John saw the book of all the prophets sealed and wept greatly because no one could open it, he was told: “Do not weep: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered to open the book and loose its seven seals” [Col. 0362A] (Rev. 5:5). In this it is evident that the thoughts and hidden mysteries of all the prophets were revealed by Christ’s Passion. This too was signified by the veil of the temple, which was torn when he died, so that the Holy of Holies might appear to all.

[Note: Cornelius a Lapide collects mystical interpretations on Matthew 27:51; see Jansenius, *Harmony*, ch. 143; Maldonatus, etc.]

And Anna, a prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher, was advanced in many days. She had lived with her husband seven years from her virginity, and she had been a widow until eighty-four years of age. She did not depart from the temple, serving with fasts and supplications night and day. Coming up at that very hour, she gave thanks to the Lord and spoke of him to all who awaited redemption in Israel.

This venerable woman, whose noble birth is extolled, continence [Col. 0362B] praised, age commended, and devotion proclaimed, was highly fit and worthy to bear witness to the Son of God.

[Note: Bede: “According to the historical sense, Anna is shown to have been of devout manner of life [Col. 0362D], venerable age, and in every respect worthy to bear witness to the incarnate Lord.”]

For women such as these are accepted in giving testimony no less than men. And when they had performed all things according to the law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own city Nazareth.

At this point the Evangelist Matthew writes many things which Luke passes over, just as Matthew omits these things which Luke records here. For Joseph, warned in a dream, as Matthew says, “withdrew with the child into Egypt and remained there until the death of Herod” (Matt. 2:14). But after Herod’s death he returned to Galilee and, as is written here, dwelt in the city of Nazareth.

And the child grew and was strengthened, full of wisdom; and the grace of God was in him [Col. 0362C]. He grew according to his humanity, because according to his humanity he was a child. But divinity could not grow, because wherever it is, it contains all things. Therefore, whenever Christ grows, is strengthened, or does anything of this kind, all such things must be referred to his human nature.

[Note: Thus far, Augustine, Book II against Maximinus, no. 7: “We indeed read that Jesus advanced in age and wisdom, and that the grace of God was in him; but this was according to the form of man which he took from us for our sake, not according to the form of God, in which he did not judge equality with God to be something alien to himself. Nevertheless, even in that form of man we read that he advanced in age and wisdom, yet not as though he became good from not being good, or had earned this by believing.” Theophylact: “By displaying himself according to his physical capacity, he fulfilled the dispensation, not acquiring wisdom—for what could be more perfect than he who was perfect from the beginning?—but gradually unveiling it.”]

XII. And his parents went every year to Jerusalem on the solemn day of Passover. And when he was twelve years old, as they went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast day, and when the days were completed, as they returned, the child Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it.

His devout parents went year by year to Jerusalem [Col. 0363A], that they might hear the law, share in the sacrifices, attend the solemnities, and serve the shadow of him whose truth they already possessed.

[Note: Bede, in his homily on this passage: “That the Lord came to Jerusalem with his parents every year at Passover is surely a sign of human humility. . . . He himself kept the law which he gave, in order to show us, who are mere human beings, that whatever God commands must in every respect be observed.”]

For that whole solemnity signified Christ’s Passion, resurrection, and the other things written concerning him. Thus Jesus, who was the cause of the entire solemnity, was present in the celebration with the rest. Mingled with the crowds, he was seen by all; praised by all, proclaimed in the law and prophets, signified in the sacrifices—and recognized by no one, because he was veiled twice over: on one side by the veil of the letter, on the other by the wall of flesh. Hence it is written: “Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, peering through the lattices” (Song 2:9). He was slaughtered in the lambs, sacrificed in the calves, and offered in all the sacrifices [Col. 0363B].

[Note: St Augustine, Book XXII against Faustus, ch. 17: “These things were rightly celebrated among that people, whose kingdom, priesthood, and prophecy were themselves a prophecy of the coming King and Priest, who would rule and consecrate believers among all nations, introduce them into the kingdom of heaven, the sanctuary of angels, and eternal life.”]

His mother too heard many things sung there in the law and prophets which she understood to be said of herself and knew already to have been fulfilled in her. Such were: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7:14); and again, “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. 11:1); and many others. Rightly, therefore, did they come there every year, where they heard their own praises proclaimed by all the people.

But at last, when the days had been completed and the solemnity fulfilled, as they were returning, the child Jesus remained in Jerusalem. For the solemnities of the Jews were completed when, as Christ our Lord rose from the dead, all old things passed away and all things became new. Then the child Jesus remained in Jerusalem, which is interpreted “vision of peace” [Col. 0363C], by which we understand the holy Church.
