Hence it is also said: “His place is made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. 75:3).

[Note: The same St Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm 9*, no. 12: “Jerusalem bears the image of the Church . . . because Jerusalem is interpreted ‘vision of peace.’” See also his *Exposition on Psalm 50*, no. 22; Psalm 61, no. 7, etc.]

But his parents—that is, the Synagogue and the Jewish people—did not know this. Thinking him to be in the company, they travelled a day’s journey. Foolish Jews, who thought that he was still with them though they had already killed him and heard him say: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Luke 13:35); and in the Psalms: “Behold, I fled far away and remained in the wilderness” (Ps. 54:8).

But seeking him among relatives and acquaintances and not finding him, they returned to Jerusalem seeking him [Col. 0364A]. This was spiritually fulfilled when, after Christ’s Passion, certain Jews pierced in heart came to the apostles—for this was to seek Christ and return to Jerusalem—and said: “What shall we do, brethren?” (Acts 2:31). To them the apostle Peter said: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized” (ibid., v. 38). Jesus’ parents therefore signified these and the others who believed at that time, because, just as the former had lost him through ignorance, so the latter had killed him in ignorance. Hence blessed Peter said: “And now, brethren, I know that you did this through ignorance, as did also your rulers” (Acts 3:17).

Jesus’ parents appropriately signify the Synagogue and the Jews here, when they are said to have brought him to Jerusalem, so that those things might already be seen in symbolic form which he would later suffer on the cross. And it came to pass that after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the teachers, hearing them and asking them questions. Jesus is found in the temple after three days because, after the resurrection that occurred on the third day, he is found in the Church by those who seek him.

[Note: Metaphrastes in Corderius’s *Catena*: “Why is he sought by his parents and found not on the first or second, but on the third day? Perhaps in order thereby to signify his burial and resurrection on the third day” [Col. 0364D].]

Before the third day he was not found because people thought him not God but only a man. But where is he found? In the temple, in the Church, in the assembly of the faithful, among the teachers, and in the company of bishops. Whoever, then, seeks Jesus, let him come to the temple, come to the Church, come to bishops and priests, and listen to what they say; for there he will see Jesus.

[Note: Origen, Homily 19 on Luke: “Where, then, do they find him? In the temple. For there the Son of God is found. Whenever you too seek the Son of God, seek him first in the temple; hurry there. There you will find Christ, the Word and Wisdom, that is, the Son of God.” And Homily 20: “They sought him in the temple, but found him among the masters and in the midst of teachers. Wherever teachers are, Jesus is found in their midst, provided that the teacher sits in the temple and never goes out from it.”]

There he sits in the midst of the teachers, in their hearts [Col. 0364C]. There, by hearing them, he teaches them; by questioning them, he instructs them. All our actions and thoughts answer him. Nothing is hidden from him: he sees everything, and all things speak to him.

And all who heard him were astonished at his wisdom and his answers. Thus he questioned, he answered, and he resolved both his own questions and theirs, acting in the manner of a most accomplished teacher, who instructs disciples now by questioning and now by answering.

[Note: Bede aptly says: “Because he is God and man, he now displays the sublime things of divinity, now the weak things of human frailty. As a man he questions the elders; as God he answers in a way that astonishes elders and learned men; as the Son of God he remains in the temple of God; and as the son of man he returns with his parents where they command” [Col. 0365C].]

And when they saw him, they were amazed. His parents, he says, were amazed when they saw him sitting in the temple in the midst of the teachers. To this day, whatever Jews come to the Church and are converted to the faith are amazed when there they see Christ—whom they call the Messiah [Col. 0365A]—whom they could neither see nor understand in the Synagogue or among relatives and acquaintances, through any explanation of theirs.

And his mother said to him: “Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I have sought you sorrowing.” We have already said that by the Lord’s mother the Synagogue is signified, from which the Lord derived his origin according to the flesh. Whenever it comes to the Church and understands the truth there, it marvels at its own ignorance and Christ’s absence and says in wonder: “Son, why have you done this to us? Why have you left us and passed over to the Church of the Gentiles? Behold, your father, the Jewish people, and I have sought you sorrowing.”

This is what the Apostle says: “I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” [Col. 0365B] (Rom. 10:2). They seek Jesus and do not find him because they have not yet come to the temple and the Church.

And he said to them: “Why did you seek me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that are my Father’s?” “Why,” he says, “did you seek me? Why did you think that I was among the company of unbelievers and outside the Church? I was here; whoever wishes to seek me, let him seek me here. Did you not know that I must be in the things of my Father and among those who do my Father’s will?” But they did not understand the word which he spoke to them. Why did they not understand? Because he signified them.

And he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them. Let subjects hear this and not disdain to be subject, since he who is set over all did not disdain to become subject [Col. 0365C].

[Note: Bernard, Homily 1 on *Missus est*: “He was subject to them. Who was subject, and to whom? God to human beings—God, I say, to whom angels are subject and principalities and powers obedient. He was subject to Mary; and not only to Mary but also to Joseph, because of Mary. Wonder, then, at either thing, and choose which you admire the more: the most gracious condescension of the Son or the surpassing dignity of the mother. On both sides is astonishment, on both sides a miracle: that God obeys a woman is humility without precedent; that a woman rules over God is sublimity without equal. . . . Learn, O man, to obey; learn, O earth, to submit; learn, O dust, to comply. . . . God humbles himself, and do you exalt yourself? God subjects himself to human beings, and you, eager to rule over human beings, set yourself above your Creator? . . . If, O human being, you disdain to imitate the example of a human being, surely it will not be beneath you to follow your Creator.”]

Let rulers also not be proud. In Joseph the superior and Christ the subject, let them understand that subjects are often of greater merit than their superiors. And his mother kept all these words in her heart. Unless she had preserved them, we would not have them. For we have received these things from her treasures.

And Jesus advanced in wisdom, age, and grace before God and men. He advanced, not according to divinity, which can neither increase nor decrease in any respect [Col. 0366A], but according to humanity, by which he was made like us.

XIII. Next follows the time at which John the Baptist began to preach a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins. Since this has been explained in Matthew, it is not necessary to explain it here. But it should be noted that not only water but repentance too is called baptism.

[Note: St Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 39, p. 634, enumerating several kinds of baptism, calls repentance the fifth baptism: “The baptism of tears holds fifth place” [Col. 0366D].]

John therefore preached a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, but did not grant remission of sins. Hence he said to those whom he baptized: “I indeed baptize you in water; but he who comes after me is mightier than I: he will baptize you in the Spirit and fire” (Luke 3:16). Thus for them baptism was a sign and a certain preparation for the baptism to come.

[Col. 0366B] [CHAPTER III.] And the crowds asked him, saying: “What, then, shall we do?” And he answered them: “Let him who has two tunics give to him who has none; and let him who has food do likewise.” By one tunic is meant only as much clothing as can suffice each person for bodily necessities. Therefore, whoever has an abundance beyond these things should give to the one who has none.

[Note: Bede explains differently: “Because a tunic is more necessary to our use than a cloak, to bear fruit worthy of repentance means that we should share with our neighbours not merely outward things and things less necessary, but even those things that are very necessary to ourselves.”]

By these words greed and avarice are removed, while piety and mercy are commended.

[Note: Ambrose, Book II on Luke, no. 77: “St John the Baptist gives an answer appropriate to each class of persons. . . . These and other precepts of duty belong specifically to individuals; but mercy is of common use. Therefore it is a common precept, necessary for every duty and every age, and to be practised by all. . . . For mercy is the fullness of virtues; therefore the perfect pattern of virtue is proposed to all, lest they spare their garments and food. Yet the measure of mercy itself must be observed according to the capacity of the human condition: no one should take everything away from himself, but should share what he has with the poor.”]

Tax collectors also came to be baptized [Col. 0366C], and said to him: “Teacher, what shall we do?” And he said to them: “Exact nothing more than what has been appointed for you.” For what had been prescribed for them had also been prescribed for all the rest. One law had been given to all through Moses. Hence the Lord himself said: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat; therefore do whatever they tell you” (Matt. 23:2). This one ordinance, if properly understood, suffices for everyone’s salvation.

Soldiers also asked him, saying: “And what shall we do?” And he said to them: “Extort from no one; make no false accusation against anyone; but be content with your pay.” By this we are taught that those whom we cannot convert to perfection of life should at least be admonished to restrain themselves from evil. This benefits others and does them no harm [Col. 0367A]. For these men were Gentiles and would not have believed one who urged greater things.

[Note: See St Maximus, or another author, Sermon 82 among Augustine’s sermons [Col. 0367D], and Ferrandus, *Paraeneticus to Count Reginus*.]

XIV. And Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years old, being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph, who was the son of Heli, who was the son of Mathat, who was the son of Levi. But according to Matthew Joseph is the son of Jacob (Matt. 1:15), who was the son of Mathat, who was the son of Eleazar. Joseph, therefore, is the son of two men, namely Heli and Jacob: of one according to the flesh, and of the other according to the Law. [Note: On the genealogy of Jesus Christ in Luke as compared with that found in Matthew, many writers have said many things. See Papebroch’s dissertation on the genealogy of Christ in the *Propylaeum*, and Calmet’s dissertation *On the Reconciliation of the Genealogies*, etc.]

For the Law commands that, if a brother dies without seed, his brother should take the dead man’s wife in order to raise up seed for his brother. Thus Heli died without seed; Jacob took his wife and begot Joseph by her. Joseph, therefore, was the son of two fathers: of one according to the flesh, and of the other according to the Law. Brothers, moreover, are called not only those born of the same parents, but also all who belong to the same tribe. Thus Boaz, although he was not the son of Elimelech and Naomi, nevertheless took Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of Mahlon, because he was of the tribe of Judah, as Mahlon also was; and he begot by her a son whom he named Obed. Obed, therefore, was the son of Boaz and Mahlon, just as Joseph was the son of Heli and Jacob.

[CHAP. IV.] But Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan; and he was led by the Spirit into the wilderness for forty days. And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee, and report of him went out through all the surrounding region; and he taught in their synagogues and was glorified by all.

It must not be understood that the Lord, immediately after the fast, returned from the wilderness and began to preach in the synagogues and perform miracles. [Note: See the Gospel Harmony published under the name of Ammonius of Alexandria, vol. III of the Lyons edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, p. 269; and among more recent writers, Jansenius, in the Gospel History prefixed to his *Harmony*; Tirinus, *Sacred Chronicle*, ch. 49; John de la Haye, *Summary of the Gospel Arrangement*; Calmet, *Harmony of the Four Gospels*, etc. They generally agree on this order of events: after the fast and John’s baptism, Jesus Christ received John’s testimony concerning him; then Andrew and Peter, Philip and Nathanael are thought to have come to Christ; the wedding at Cana of Galilee followed; from there they bring him to Capernaum; afterward, at the Paschal season, to Jerusalem, etc. Bede likewise gave this warning at the beginning of Book II on Luke: “Lest any reader should suppose that the events to be expounded in sequence occurred immediately after the forty days’ fast, he should rather observe that they followed after some miracles performed by the Lord either in Judaea or in Galilee.”]

Otherwise John’s statement concerning the miracle of the wine would not be true: “This Jesus did as the beginning of his signs in Cana of Galilee, and manifested his glory” (John 2:11). It must therefore be understood that throughout the entire year in which our Saviour was baptized, he neither preached publicly in the synagogues nor performed any miracles. Yet he had a few disciples, as John also had, who followed and heard him.

But when the year was nearly completed, and John again saw him walking, he said, “Behold the Lamb of God” (John 1:36). Two of his disciples heard him; one was Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother. They followed Jesus and remained with him that day—on that day, I say, and no longer. Then Andrew brought his brother Simon to Jesus. The Lord said to him: “You are Simon, son of Jonah; you shall be called Cephas,” which is interpreted Peter. “On the next day he wished to go out into Galilee; and he found Philip and said to him, Follow me” (John 1:42).

“But on the third day there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee, and Jesus’ mother was there. Jesus and his disciples were also invited to the wedding” (John 2:1). These were, of course, the disciples whom he then had; for he had not yet called the apostles. Later, as the other evangelists write, he called Peter and Andrew—who had come to him the day before—and James and John from their fishing by the Sea of Galilee (Matt. 10:1; Mark 3:13; Luke 6:13). After these things, “when the Lord heard that John had been delivered up,” as Matthew the Evangelist writes, “he went down to maritime Capernaum and dwelt there” (Matt. 4:13). From there he began to preach publicly, and his fame spread through that whole land.

[CHAP. V.] But when crowds pressed upon him from every side, to hear the word of God, he stood beside the Lake of Gennesaret. Going up into one of the boats, which belonged to Simon, he asked him to put out a little from the land; and, sitting down, he taught the crowds from the boat. When he had ceased speaking, he said to Simon: “Put out into the deep, and let down the net for a catch.” When they had done this, they enclosed a great multitude of fish. And their partners, who were in the other boat, came and filled both boats, so that they were beginning to sink.

When he saw this miracle, Simon, terrified, said: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man.” To him he said: “Do not be afraid. From now on you will be catching men.” When they had gone, each to his own station, he remained a little while and called Peter and Andrew, saying: “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of men.” But they left everything and followed him. Going on a little farther, he called James and John, and they followed him (Matt. 4:19; Mark 1:17).

Thus the order stands. It is therefore clear that what follows here does not preserve chronological order. But since it is established that our Saviour preached for only two years and three months [Note: This is the opinion of many modern writers, especially Petavius, both in *The Doctrine of Times*, Book XII, ch. 17, and in his annotations on Epiphanius, p. 203. Monelia also, *On the Years of Christ*, ch. 5, no. 37, maintains that this opinion rests on irresistible arguments. It must nevertheless be admitted that Grotius calls what are here described as irresistible arguments exceedingly uncertain conjectures, and perhaps many more defend the contrary opinion. Eusebius, both in the *Chronicle* and in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book I, ch. 9, and in the *Evangelical Demonstration*, Book VIII, assigns to Christ’s preaching **three and a half years** (*tria kai hēmisy etē*, Τρία καὶ ἥμισυ ἔτη). Theodoret does the same in his commentary on Daniel 9, as does Jerome. Among more recent writers are Jansenius, Toletus, Emmanuel Sa, a Lapide, John de la Haye, Calmet, etc.; the last of these cites Grotius, Lightfoot, and other heterodox writers of the same opinion.]—if indeed he refrained from preaching during the year in which he was baptized—I wish here briefly to retract and correct certain things which I remember having said less cautiously in my commentary on the Apocalypse.

For when I was expounding the passage in which the woman is said to have fled from the dragon’s face into the wilderness, where she was fed for a time, times, and half a time—that is, for 1,260 days—I said that Christ preached for three and a half years. But this was to be referred not to Christ, but to the times of Antichrist, who will reign for three and a half years. During those years our Saviour will feed and nourish the holy Church with spiritual food, consolations from the Scriptures, and examples of the saints, lest, exhausted in so immense a disturbance, she fail altogether. But enough on these matters.

XV. And Jesus went out in the power of the Spirit into Galilee, and report of him went out through all the surrounding region. [Note: The same exposition is found in Homily 4 after Epiphany, published under the name of Emesene.]

For the Lord Jesus had preached in Judaea and displayed the power of his might in signs and miracles; then he returned into Galilee. But how did he return? In the power of the Spirit. For the Son is always in the Father, and the Father in the Son, and the Holy Spirit in both. Therefore, although Jesus always went in the power of the Spirit, yet at that time he especially seemed to do so, when in word and deed he displayed the power of his might.

Hence it is added: And he taught in their synagogues and was glorified by all. For this reason he was glorified by all: because he preached in the power of the Spirit. And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up; and according to his custom, on the Sabbath day, he entered the synagogue and stood up to read. The book of the prophecy of Isaiah was handed to him.

He had been brought up at Nazareth, but he had not learned letters at Nazareth. Yet he stood up to read, so that by reading he might perform a miracle among those among whom he had been brought up; for we never read that he did this elsewhere. If he had done it elsewhere, it might have been supposed that he had learned letters from a teacher. But these people could not suppose this: they had known him from infancy, had never seen him in schools, and had never heard him read before or afterward.

But note what is said: He entered the synagogue according to his custom. Christians ought to have this custom: to come daily to church, daily either to read themselves or, if they are unable to do this, to hear others reading.

And when he unrolled the book, he found the place where it was written:

> The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me;  
> he sent me to bring good news to the poor,  
> to heal the brokenhearted,  
> to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind,  
> to send forth the crushed into release,  
> to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense.

When he had folded the book, he gave it back to the attendant and sat down. The eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed upon him. And he began to say to them: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” And they all bore witness to him and marvelled at the words of grace that came from his mouth.

They did not marvel merely because he read—unless perhaps because he had not learned letters—but because he expounded wonderfully the things he read. For his words were full of grace and sweet to all who heard them, according to the saying: “You are fairer in form than the children of men; grace is poured out upon your lips” (Ps. 44:3). And again: “How sweet are your utterances to my palate, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. 118:103). This grace and sweetness came not so much from the reading as from the exposition of what was read.

Let us therefore see what this reading of Isaiah the prophet—indeed, of our Saviour himself—signifies. [Note: This is Isaiah 61, on which Jerome, in Book XVII on Isaiah, is especially relevant.] For he understood it of himself and declared it fulfilled in himself. “The Spirit of the Lord,” he says, “is upon me.” For he is the flower from the root of Jesse, “upon whom rests the Spirit of the Lord: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. 11:1). [Note: Jerome on this passage in Isaiah: “His anointing was fulfilled at the time when he was baptized in the Jordan, and the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove and remained upon him. Of him this same prophet had also said here: ‘A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him,’ etc.”]

He is the one of whom it is written: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44:8). It is fitting, and very appropriate, that one be chosen and anointed king who both hates iniquity and loves righteousness.

Therefore let him say: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he sent me to bring good news to the poor”—that is, to those poor of whom it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5:3). [Note: Matt. 5:3. Jerome: “He was therefore anointed with the Holy Spirit in order to announce good news to the poor, or meek, saying to them in the Gospel: ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit,’” etc.] One rich man came to him and, having heard his words, went away sorrowful because he had many possessions. Rightly, therefore, does the Lord preach not to the rich but to the poor. [Note: Hence the homily, to which some things have been added, after which the same words occur.]

He heals the brokenhearted, because his medicine readily comes to the aid of such persons. Of them the Psalmist says: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. 50:19). [Note: Jerome: “And he was sent to heal those who are broken in heart and say: ‘A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise.’”] Let him therefore have a contrite heart who desires to be healed by God.

He also proclaims release to captives: not release from the Babylonians, [Note: Although Hugh and some others think that the literal sense concerns the Babylonians, a Lapide and others refute them.] but release from demons. He proclaims sight also to the blind, who have been blinded in their inward light. Of this blindness the Apostle says: “Blindness in part has happened to Israel” (Rom. 11:25). He sends the crushed forth into release, because those whom the devil had crushed by injuring them, he himself calls to pardon by healing them and forgiving their sins.

He proclaims the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3:2). And again: “Many prophets and kings wished to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Matt. 13:17). Of this acceptable year and this day of recompense the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (1 Cor. 6:2).

And they said: “Is this not Joseph’s son?” This alone, therefore, seemed to diminish him in their eyes: that he was not a stranger, that they knew his parents, and that he had been brought up there. [Note: Bede: “How great is the blindness of the Nazarenes, who, though they recognize him as Christ in words and deeds, despise him solely because of their acquaintance with his family.”] For if he had come from elsewhere and had been wholly unknown to them, he would then have been regarded in every respect as venerable and worthy of all reverence. [Note: Homily of St Bruno, sermon 2 after the Third Sunday in Lent.]

“Surely you will say to me this proverb: ‘Physician, heal yourself. Do here also in your own country what great things we have heard were done in Capernaum.’” They said this disparagingly and did not believe the things they had heard about him. It is as though they said: If you are a physician, if you can heal the sick and drive away maladies—which we do not believe—heal yourself first; heal your own flesh, namely your parents, neighbours, relatives, and your native country. Perform here in your own country what we have heard that you have done at Capernaum and in other cities, so that we may see it.

But he said: “Amen, I say to you: no prophet is accepted in his own country.” “This is why,” he says, “I do not heal my own country: because I am not accepted in it, because I find no faith in it, and because, as do the others, they do not believe me in my own country.” [Note: Ambrose, no. 46, refers this to the citizens’ envy: “Envy is plainly exposed, no slight envy, which, forgetful of civic love, turns causes of love into bitter hatreds,” etc.] It delights in my words, admires my discourses, and takes offence at my parents; and it knows me so much the less because it has known me more than others.

“Truly I say to you: there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when heaven was shut for three years and six months and a great famine came upon all the land; and Elijah was sent to none of them except to Zarephath of Sidon, to a widow woman.” “I was not sent to you,” he says; “I did not come to heal and cure you, because Elijah was not sent to every widow.” For Elijah signified this; and what I do in truth, he did in shadow.

I came to heal and satisfy with spiritual food that widow, and to deliver her from every famine and want, of whom it is written: “Blessing I will bless her widow; I will satisfy her poor with bread” (Ps. 131:15). This widow is the holy Church universally, [Note: The same Ambrose, no. 50: “For we said in another book (*On Widows*, ch. 3) that in that widow to whom Elijah was sent a type of the Church was set forth beforehand . . . That people gathered from foreigners, that people previously leprous,” etc. Before Ambrose, Origen, Homily 33 on Luke: “I think that this saying is truer according to the mystery than according to the letter. Although Jeremiah was not accepted at Anathoth, his own country, nor Isaiah—whatever his country was—nor the remaining prophets, yet it seems to me that it should rather be understood thus: we should say that the country of all the prophets was the people of the circumcision; and that this people did not receive the prophets and their prophecies, whereas the nations, which had been far from the prophets and had no knowledge of them, received the prophecy of Jesus Christ.” Therefore no prophet is accepted in his own country, “that is, among the Jewish people. But we, who were strangers to the covenant and aliens from the promises, received the prophets with our whole heart.”] and each individual faithful soul may also be understood by her.

For the Lord came to call all and to preach to all, but he did not come to heal all and deliver all from famine. For unless he had come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sins. Therefore, when the Lord preaches, heaven is opened, famine is taken away, and faithful souls are intoxicated with heavenly nectar. Conversely, he threatens the unbelieving and wicked: “Behold, I will send among you not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God” (Amos 8:11).

It follows: “And there were many lepers in Israel under Elisha the prophet, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.” The comparison is the same as before. For many lepers are many sinners. The one Naaman signifies the one people of the Gentiles, or each individual faithful person. Coming to the Lord and finally believing his words, he was baptized, healed, and cleansed.

And all in the synagogue were filled with anger when they heard these things. They were filled with anger because they understood that these things had been said against them and perceived that they were judged unworthy of a visit from such and so great a prophet. They rose, drove him out of the city, and brought him to the brow of the hill on which their city was built, so that they might cast him down. But he passed through their midst and went away.

Let people rage as much as they wish; let them roar and be angry. The Lord is secure, fears nothing, has all things in his power, and cannot be seized unless he himself wills it. [Note: Bede: “Understand at the same time that the passion of his body was not necessary but voluntary; that he was not captured by the Jews but offered himself. For when he wills, he is seized; when he wills, he slips away; when he wills, he is suspended; when he wills, he is not held.”] Yet he does not resist, but, passing through the midst of his enemies, despises the dogs barking on either side. [Note: Thus far the homily.]

And he went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee, and taught them there on the Sabbaths; and they were astonished at his teaching, because his word was with authority. His word was with authority because he neither devised what he should say nor spoke to please anyone; rather, as one having authority, he commanded the greater and the lesser, diseases and demons.

And in the synagogue there was a man having an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice, saying: “Leave us alone!” In crying “Leave us alone,” he indicated that he was already being held. He was therefore saying: Do not drive us out. Do not trouble us. Leave us and let us alone. [Note: Bede explains: “Cease for a little while from tormenting me.” In Greek, Luke has ἔα (*ea*) here, which the translator rendered by the imperative *sine*, “leave.” The same Greek word occurs at Mark 1:24, where the same story is narrated, though the Latin translator did not render the Greek particle, but instead gives: “What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us?” The Old Latin version likewise omits it here. Erasmus thinks that ἔα is more properly taken as a Greek adverb, and for us an interjection of one crying out. Grotius likewise declares that he does not agree with those who consider it either a verb or an interjection derived from a verb, but regards it as Hebrew, from which the Greeks formed ἔα; in Aeschylus’ *Prometheus*, ἄ ἄ ἔα ἔα, for which Latin has “ah.” On the same Greek expression, see George Raphelius, *Annotations*, vol. I, p. 364, from Arrian. Since the sense is clear, such matters may be disregarded.]

“What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Why do you not follow? You have heaven; let us have earth. You have the righteous; let us have sinners. We have nothing in common. What pleases you displeases us; what pleases us displeases you. Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God.”

For the Lord destroys demons as often as he takes from them their strength and power to harm. But how do demons know Christ, except through his power, which they cannot endure? For what do we suppose the evil spirits felt when he was present and speaking, when in his disciples they could not bear his name?

Jesus rebuked him, saying: “Be silent, and come out of him.” When the demon had thrown him down in their midst, it came out of him and did him no harm. It is evident with what violence and indignation it left the man, since it threw him down as it left him in the midst. Yet it did him no harm, because it could not harm him. [Note: For reconciling Luke with Mark 1:26, which says, “And the unclean spirit, tearing him and crying out with a loud voice, came out of him,” see Bede and the interpreters.]

XVI. But when the crowds pressed upon him to hear the Word of God, he stood beside the Lake of Gennesaret. [Note: Bonfrerius, in the *Onomasticon*: “Gennesar and Gennesaret are names for the lake or Sea of Galilee; the adjoining region is also called the land of Gennesaret.” See St Jerome on Matthew 14 and Bede here, from whom, I think, he took this. Bede says: “They call the Lake of Gennesaret the same as the Sea of Galilee, or the Sea of Tiberias . . . In Hebrew usage every collection of waters, whether fresh or salt, is called a sea. This lake, through which the Jordan flows, extends 140 stadia in length and 40 in breadth.”]

The Lake of Gennesaret is the same as the Sea of Galilee. Hence Matthew, writing of these same events, says: “Jesus, walking beside the Sea of Galilee, saw two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen; and he called them” (Matt. 4:18). Matthew, therefore, passing over all the other things narrated in this Gospel, records only the calling of the apostles. Luke, however, narrates more fully not only the calling of the apostles but also the other things which the Lord did at that time. No one should seek the order of the narrative here, where things written later are found to have occurred earlier in time.

And he saw two boats standing by the lake, but the fishermen had gone down and were washing their nets. The two boats are the two peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles. [Note: Likewise Bede: “The fishermen are teachers of the Church, who bring us, caught in the net of faith, to the land of the living. The interconnected utterances of preachers are like fishermen’s nets.” Before Bede, Ambrose, Book IV on Luke, no. 71: “What are the nets of the apostles, which are commanded to be let down, except combinations of words, as it were the folds of speech and recesses of arguments, so that they do not lose those whom they have caught?”] The fishermen of the two peoples signify their teachers and rulers: in one, pontiffs and priests used to fish; in the other, philosophers and poets. To wash the nets is to expound and clarify the meanings of one’s preaching. [Note: Bede: “The two boats placed beside the lake figure circumcision and uncircumcision.”]

Going up into one boat, which belonged to Simon, he asked him to put out a little from the land; and, sitting down, he taught the crowds from the boat. The Lord entered Simon’s boat because he came to preach to the synagogue and the Jewish people. Hence he himself says: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24). Of this boat of Simon the Apostle says: “He who worked through Peter in the apostleship of the circumcision worked also through me among the Gentiles” (Gal. 2:8).

Simon’s boat, therefore, is the synagogue, in which the Lord, sitting, taught the crowds, because there he preached the Gospels by which all nations are taught and called to faith. But when he had ceased speaking, he said to Simon: “Put out into the deep, and let down your nets for a catch.” The Lord ceased speaking when, after his passion, he rested from preaching. [Note: Bede: “What he likewise says to Peter, ‘Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch,’ pertains to the more distant nations to whom the Gospel was later preached.”]

Then indeed he commanded Simon and all the other apostles to put the boat out into the deep and let down their nets for a catch, saying: “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Matt. 28:19). And again: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (ibid.).

The sea, therefore, is the world. Hence the Psalmist says: “This great and spacious sea—there are creeping things there without number” (Ps. 103:25). Of its height and depth he says: “Our God is refuge and strength, a helper in tribulations that have found us exceedingly. Therefore we shall not fear though the earth is shaken and the mountains are carried into the heart of the sea” (Ps. 45:2–3).

The nets, however, are the Gospels, by whose meanings faithful souls are caught and entangled. For the Church has many nets and many fishers. Simon answered and said to him: “Master, though we have laboured all night, we have caught nothing.” Thus the synagogue also, although it had laboured much, cast its nets, expounded the Scriptures, and preached the Law and the Prophets, nevertheless, because it did this at night—that is, in the darkness of ignorance, since it did not understand what it said—it was able to catch and convert to itself very few from the Gentile people.

“But at your word I will let down the net.” When they had done this, they enclosed a great multitude of fish. This is what is said through the Psalmist: “I proclaimed and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number” (Ps. 39:6). And again: “But to me your friends have been exceedingly honoured, O God; their rule has been exceedingly strengthened. I shall number them, and they shall be multiplied beyond the sand” (Ps. 138:17–18).

But their net was breaking, and they signalled to the partners who were in the other boat, that they should come and help them. They came and filled both boats, so that they began to sink. The apostles’ net of the Church is broken when Jews, heretics, and unbelievers contradict evangelical preaching by violent arguments. [Note: Augustine, *Questions on the Gospels*, Book II, question 2: “That the nets were also breaking . . . signifies that so great a multitude of carnal people would be in the Church that, even when peace was ruptured and heresies and schisms went out from it, such a multitude would remain, and so great a loss of faith and good morals would befall it, that such a Church might seem to say to Christ: ‘Depart from me,’ etc.” Bede likewise: “The net was broken through the multitude of fish, because now, together with the elect, so many reprobate persons enter into confession of faith that they even divide the Church itself by heresies.”]

Hence the Apostle says: “A great and evident door has been opened to me, and there are many adversaries” (1 Cor. 16:9). Therefore partners from the other boat come to their help, because bishops and priests from all the other churches assemble from every quarter, make the truth clear, condemn heretics, and bring back to faith and the Church those whom the heretics had deceitfully led astray.

When Simon Peter saw this, he fell at Jesus’ knees, saying: “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord.” For amazement had seized him and all who were with him at the catch of fish which they had made, and likewise James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were Simon’s partners.

For the Apostle says: “God chose the foolish things of the world, that he might destroy the wise; God chose the weak things of the world, that he might confound the strong; and the things that are not, that he might destroy the things that are” (ibid. 1:27). And again: “Since the world did not know the Lord through wisdom, it pleased God through foolish preachers to save those who believe” (ibid. 1:21).

Who then would not be amazed? Who would not marvel that through such preachers the world was converted, philosophers overcome, the wisdom of the world destroyed, and the entire multitude of faithful fish gathered within the nets of faith and into the boat of the Church—especially when they preached Christ crucified, a stumbling-block to Jews and folly to Gentiles? [Note: St Maximus of Turin has an excellent homily on the Gospel catch of fish; see the Roman edition of 1784, p. 643.]

But what does Simon Peter’s saying, “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man,” signify, except what the Church says in the Song of Songs: “Flee, my beloved; be like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of spices” (Song 9:14)? Hence the Lord himself speaks to the Jews, saying: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23:38).

For we say that Simon’s boat signifies the synagogue. Peter therefore signified that the Lord would leave this synagogue when he asked him to depart from him. Jesus said to Simon: “Do not be afraid. From now on you will be catching men.” Do not fear, he says, nor be amazed; rather rejoice and believe, because you have been predestined for a greater catch. Until now you have caught fish; henceforth you will catch people. Another boat and other nets will be given you. [Note: Bede, on these Gospel words: “They pertain especially to Peter himself. The Lord explains to him what this catch of fish signifies: namely, that as he now catches fish by nets, so one day he will catch people by words; and that the entire order of this event shows what is done daily in the Church, of which he bears the type.”] And when they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him.

XVII. [CHAP. VI.] And it came to pass on the second-first Sabbath, when he was passing through the grainfields, that his disciples plucked ears of grain and ate them, rubbing them in their hands.

Since all the other matters have been expounded in Matthew, it remains only to say what “the second-first Sabbath” signifies. For the Jews had three first—that is, principal and greatest—Sabbaths, because they celebrated three principal and greatest festivals in the year. The first and principal Sabbath was in March, that is, Passover. The second was when they offered sheaves of ears of grain. The third was observed in the seventh month. The second-first Sabbath—that is, the second principal and greatest Sabbath—was therefore that on which they offered sheaves of ears of grain. [Note: The question of the second-first Sabbath is obscure and very intricate. Nazianzen wonderfully evaded Jerome when Jerome questioned him about it, as Jerome relates here in his letter to Nepotian. What Nazianzen would not or could not do, others have attempted to do and explain. Leaving aside the obscure opinion of Epiphanius, *Heresies* 30: Chrysostom, Homily 39 on Matthew, in Petavius’s and Erasmus’s translation, thought that it was called the Sabbath preceding a festival; Theophylact, by contrast, the Sabbath following one—an interpretation which Maldonatus and Montfaucon regard as Chrysostom’s own view. Isidore, following Petavius, understands the first day of Unleavened Bread; Euthymius, the second; Vatablus, the last. Jansenius, Toletus, Francis Lucas, Emmanuel Sa understand the Sabbath on which the New Moon or another festival fell, as a double or twice solemn Sabbath. Le Moine holds that the Jews called two Sabbaths great: first, that in the month Tishri, at the beginning of the civil year; second, that in the month Nisan, at the beginning of the sacred year. The former was called the first great Sabbath, the latter second-first. Hugo Grotius holds that Pentecost was so called when it fell on a Sabbath, just as a Sabbath falling at Passover was the first Sabbath. Maldonatus understands the very day of Pentecost. Not far from this is our author, who held the second-first Sabbath to be the day on which the sheaves of ears were offered, concerning which rite see Leviticus 23. The explanation of Scaliger, Book VI, *On the Emendation of Times*, is judged best and has been embraced by Petavius, Pagius, Calmet, Casaubon, Lightfoot, Clericus, and others. Since Leviticus 23:15 says, “You shall count from the day after the Sabbath on which you offered the sheaf of firstfruits seven weeks,” or, as it is in Hebrew, seven Sabbaths, each Sabbath occurring from the second day of Passover until Pentecost took its name from the second day of Passover and was called the first Sabbath after the second day, the second Sabbath after the second day, and so forth. The first Sabbath after the second day was more briefly called the second-first Sabbath.]

And concerning these things we have said enough in Leviticus. [Note: See vol. I of the Roman edition of St Bruno, p. 165, col. 1. Thus far the homily.]

[CHAPTER VII.] Jesus was going into a town called Nain, and his disciples and a large crowd were going with him. When he approached the gate of the town, behold, a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow; and a large crowd from the town was with her. [Note: [Col. 0377D] This is from the homily of St Bruno for Thursday after the Fourth Sunday of Lent.]

For this widow, followed by a great crowd, is the holy Church. Of her it is said: “Blessing, I will bless her widow” (Ps. 131:15). She is indeed a widow, not because she has no husband, but because she cannot see him whom she still awaits to come after a long time. [Note: [Col. 0377D] He interprets the widow as the Church; but Bede does so for another reason: the Church is a widow because every soul remembers and acknowledges that it has been redeemed by the death of its Bridegroom and Lord.] For she is called a widow, as though separated from her husband. [Note: [Col. 0378C] Latin writers explain the name *vidua* in quite the same way. Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, I.15: as though *a viro idua* (“divided from a man”); for *iduare* formerly meant the same as “to divide.”] The same thing, moreover, is represented both by the widowed woman and by this town.

The Lord approaches this town because he never ceases daily to visit his Church. From this town a dead man is carried out as often as someone dead in sin is separated from her. Yet his loving mother follows him with tears, because the Church does not forget even her fleeing son: “For, as the Apostle says, she mourns daily over all those who have sinned and have not repented of their sins.” [Note: [Col. 0378C] 2 Corinthians 12:21: “And I shall mourn for many of those who previously sinned and did not repent,” etc.]

When the Lord saw her, moved with compassion for her, he said to her, “Do not weep.” And he came near and touched the bier. Those carrying it stopped; and he said to him, “Young man, I say to you, arise.” And he who had been dead sat up and began to speak. And he gave him to his mother.

God, the comforter of those who mourn, especially regards the tears of those who weep for others’ sins. He touches the bier, stops the bearers, and raises the dead, when by the touch of his visitation he brings a person back to repentance. Those are evil bearers who carry a person to burial; those are good who bring a person back from the graves to life. These bearers are understood to be vices, evil spirits, heretics, and deceivers. [Note: [Col. 0378D] Bede: “Those who carry him for burial are either unclean desires which seize a person and drag him to destruction, or the poisonous enticements of flattering companions.”] Unless the Lord stopped them, they would consign to burial and eternal condemnation all whom they had once seized.

The young man, therefore, is raised, sits up, speaks, and is restored to his mother, because the sinner converted to repentance no longer rushes toward crimes and death, but rests in the peace of the Church, speaks of God’s mighty works, confesses his sins, and is wholly reconciled both to God and to the Church.

Nor is it without mystery that, although the Lord raised many dead persons, the Evangelists wrote that he raised only three. [Note: [Col. 0378D] St Augustine, *Tractates on John*, 40, no. 3, also observed this and found a mystery: “We rightly understand that those three dead persons whom he raised bodily signify and foreshadow resurrections of souls. … Sometimes one sins in thought. … That consent kills you; but the death is inward, because the evil thought has not yet proceeded into action. Signifying that he raises such a soul, the Lord raised the girl who had not yet been carried outside but lay dead in the house. … But if you have not merely consented to evil pleasure, but have actually done the evil itself, you have, as it were, carried the dead person outside the gate: you are now outside, and the dead person has been carried out. Yet the Lord raised even this person and gave him back to his widowed mother. If you have sinned, repent, and he will restore you to your mother the Church [Col. 0379D]. The third dead person is Lazarus. There is a dreadful kind of death: it is called evil habit. For it is one thing to sin, another to make a habit of sinning. … One accustomed to sin is buried, and it is well said of him: ‘He stinks.’ … Yet Christ’s power was not less sufficient to raise even him.”]

For he raised the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue while she was still inside the house, lying in its hidden inner rooms. He also raised this son of the widowed woman, already carried outside the gates of the town but not yet buried. Further, he raised Lazarus not merely buried, but already stinking after four days. These three dead persons therefore signify three kinds of death. A person dies in thought, dies in action, and dies also through the habit of sinning. But this third death is worse than the other two, just as the second is much worse than the first. For a person sins by thinking evil things; he sins more by doing evil; and still more by persisting in sin.

The one who desires unlawful and wicked things in thought is dead, but is still remaining in the house, concealing sin inwardly, and has not yet been carried out to the grave. Such a one is easily raised if Jesus visits, calls, and touches him. For the Lord regards such a soul, because it is easily awakened, not as wholly dead but as though asleep, saying: “The girl is not dead but asleep” (Matt. 9:24).

But if he displays outwardly the evil which he thinks inwardly and carries it into effect, he is not only dead but has been carried outside the house—indeed, outside the town—has become far removed from the Church, and is now near to the grave and perdition. For such a person it is necessary that the Church, his mother, should mourn, shed tears, and pray, so that Jesus may meet him as he rushes to destruction, raise him, restore him to life, stop the bearers, give him back to his mother, and reconcile him to the Church.

But if he is dead in thought, action, and long habit of sinning, he already stinks, like Lazarus four days dead. Yet even he is raised, though not as easily as the others. For the longer one persists in sin, the more difficult it is to be separated from it. This is shown by the fact that at Lazarus’s death Jesus wept, and called him not in any ordinary manner but with a loud voice: “Lazarus, come out” (John 11:43). He is reported to have come forth with hands and feet bound, as though entangled in the long cords of a perverse habit. [Note: [Col. 0379D] Thus far the homily.]

XVIII. A Pharisee asked Jesus to eat with him. And entering the Pharisee’s house, he reclined at table. And behold, a woman in the town, a sinner, when she learned that he had reclined in the Pharisee’s house, brought an alabaster vessel of ointment; and, standing behind him at his feet, she began to wet his feet with tears, wiped them with the hair of her head, kissed his feet, and anointed them with ointment. [Note: [Col. 0379D] This is from St Bruno’s homily for Thursday after Passion Sunday; excerpted above.]

In this Gospel the pride of the Pharisee is rebuked and the humility of the sinful woman commended. [Note: [Col. 0379D] Besides St Ambrose, *On Luke*, VI, from no. 37, and other interpreters, this section of the Gospel was expounded by St Gregory of Nyssa, or Asterius—for Combefis assigned it to the latter—Amphilochius, according to the same Combefis; St Ephrem the Syrian; St Peter Chrysologus, sermons 93, 94, 95; St Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, 33; Peter Damian, sermon 31; St Lawrence Justinian; and others.]

This Pharisee is the Jewish people. This sinful woman signifies the Gentiles. [Note: [Col. 0380D] St Gregory: “Whom does the Pharisee, presumptuously relying on false righteousness, signify but the Jewish people? And whom does the sinful woman, coming and weeping at the Lord’s feet, signify but the converted Gentile world?”] The Lord healed him of leprosy; he forgave her many sins. Therefore there is none who does good, not even one. “For, as the Apostle says, all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3:23).

Jesus came into the Pharisee’s house: he came to the Jewish people. Hence he himself says: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24). But why did he come? To eat with him: to partake with him of bodily and spiritual food and to accomplish the Father’s will in him. For he himself said: “My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven” (John 4:34). For while he lived for a time among the Jews, he received with them the food of the Law and Prophets and supplied them with the nourishment of the divine word.

This the woman who was a sinner in the town understood. This the Gentile world understood, which lived in the very great city of this world. And what did it do? Do you wish to hear what? It brought an alabaster vessel of ointment. By this nothing can be understood better than the breast and inner chamber of the heart, full of faith and charity. [Note: [Col. 0380D] St Bernard, sermon 10 on the Song of Songs, discusses at length the symbolism of ointment: “There is an ointment of contrition, an ointment of devotion, and also one of loving-kindness,” etc. See also sermon 12.] For such an alabaster vessel is accustomed to preserve ointment of this kind. The queen of the South signified the same thing when, coming from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom, she brought him most precious spices. No ointment and no spices smell as sweetly to God as faith, charity, and the other virtues.

“And standing behind him at his feet, she began to wet his feet with tears.” In the woman’s standing behind him, devotion and humility are recognized. In wetting his feet with tears, true repentance and compunction of heart are shown. And because she wipes those same tears with her hair, hides them while wiping them away lest they be seen, and grieves over them, she shows herself not to be among those who do all their works in order to be seen by people, of whom the Lord says: “They have received their reward” (Matt. 6:5).

“And she kissed his feet and anointed them with ointment.” In the kiss she showed peace, love, and affection. [Note: [Col. 0380D] St Gregory: “The woman kisses the feet which she wipes. We too fully do this if we earnestly love those whom we sustain from our abundance.”] But in the ointment she signified the inward tenderness of the heart and the affection of devoted service. Opposed to this ointment is that oil of which it is said: “Let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head” (Ps. 140:5).

How like this Pharisee is that other one of whom it is elsewhere said: “Two men went up to the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector” (Luke 18:10). Confident in his own righteousness, he arrogantly “stood and prayed thus to himself: God, I thank you that I am not like other people—robbers, unjust persons, adulterers—or even like this tax collector.” Just as that Pharisee abhorred and despised the tax collector, so this one abhorred and despised this sinful woman.

Hence it follows: “But the Pharisee who had invited him, seeing this, said within himself: If this man were a prophet, he would surely know who and what sort of woman this is who touches him, because she is a sinner.” Foolish Pharisee, you do not know; you do not know. He recently cleansed you from leprosy, yet now you do not believe him to be a prophet. He is indeed a prophet, and he knows perfectly who and what kind of woman touches him, and that she is a sinner. For this he came; for this he descended from heaven. “For he did not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance” (Matt. 9:13). He himself bears witness to this. These are his words. Therefore he does not abhor sinners, since for sinners he became man.

And Jesus answered and said to him: “Simon, I have something to say to you.” And he said: “Master, speak.” “Two debtors owed a certain moneylender. One owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty. Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both. Which of them, therefore, loves him more?” Simon answered: “I suppose the one to whom he forgave more.” And he said to him: “You have judged rightly.”

For it is very just and reasonable that the person forgiven more should love more. It also seems fair that the one who loves more should be loved more greatly. Rightly, therefore, did the Lord love this sinful woman, from whom he knew himself to be much loved. For this reason many sins were forgiven her, because she loved much.

See, therefore, what a beautiful parable this is about the one who owed more and the one who owed less, in which, from his own answer, the Pharisee could understand that he loved Christ less than Mary did: for he believed that he neither owed as much nor had been forgiven as much as she.

Therefore it follows: And turning toward the woman, he said to Simon: “Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you did not give water for my feet, but she anointed my feet with ointment. Therefore I say to you: many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much. But the one to whom less is forgiven loves less.”

The Lord turned toward the woman because he was about to speak about the woman. But what does he say? “Do you see this woman?” he says. She is not such as you suppose her to be. She appears one way to me and another way to you. You see outwardly; I inwardly. You see the face; I see the heart. Her faith and love are not hidden from me. “I entered your house; you did not give water for my feet, but she wet my feet with tears.” As great as the difference between water and tears, so great is the difference between your love and hers.

But these things seem to signify something besides their literal sense. For it is not believable that one who had invited Christ to a meal would have refused to give water for his feet. We have said that the Pharisee signifies the Jews and the woman the Gentiles; Christ’s feet signify his humanity, as his head signifies his divinity. [Note: [Col. 0381D] St Gregory, no. 6: “His feet can also signify the mystery of his Incarnation itself, by which divinity touched the earth because he took flesh. … We therefore kiss the Redeemer’s feet when we love the mystery of his Incarnation with all our heart; we anoint his feet with ointment when we proclaim, with a good testimony, the power of his humanity in sacred discourse. … If we understand the Lord’s feet as the mystery of his Incarnation, the head fittingly signifies divinity itself. Hence Paul also says: ‘The head of Christ is God.’”] For the Apostle says: “The head of every man is Christ; the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11:3).

Therefore the Jews do not give water to Christ’s feet or wash them; indeed, so far as they can, they soil and defile them, because, reckoning our Savior among the wicked, they judge him stained by the dust of vices and earthly contamination. [Note: [Col. 0381D] St Gregory, in the same place: “The Pharisee is told: ‘You did not anoint my head with oil,’ because he neglected to proclaim with fitting praise the power of Christ’s divinity, in which the Jewish people had promised that it would believe.”] But the Apostle Peter washed Christ’s feet when he said of him: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22). For none is so washed, none so clean, as he who is without sin. Hence the Church, already baptized and cleansed from sins, says: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song 5:3).

But we give not only water but tears to Christ’s feet, because we humbly bow ourselves to his humanity and from it await forgiveness of sins; we adore and venerate it, and implore it with tears.

It follows: “You did not give me a kiss; but she, since she came in, has not ceased to kiss my feet.” A kiss is a sign of peace and affection. Therefore the Jews did not give the Lord Christ a kiss: hating him freely and without cause, they persecuted him even to death. Hence he himself says: “They hated me without cause” (John 15:25). But the Gentiles do not cease to kiss his feet, because they do not separate themselves from his love [Note: [Col. 0382D] St Gregory: “That unbelieving people did not give God a kiss, because it would not love in charity the one whom it served from fear. But the Gentile world, once called, does not cease to kiss the footsteps of its Redeemer, because it continually longs in his love.”] and do not fear to die in confessing his name. In a manner of speaking, Christ’s martyrs kissed him when, confessing him and speaking well of him, they died for him.

“You did not anoint my head with oil; but she anointed my feet with ointment.” The Gentiles, therefore, render greater reverence to Christ’s humanity than the Jews ever rendered to his divinity. The latter believe neither that he is God nor that he was anointed with the grace of the Holy Spirit. But we confess that even according to his humanity he is full of every virtue and grace, saying with the Psalmist: “You loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44:8). “For, as the Apostle says, in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2:9). Surely she anointed his body, his humanity, and his feet.

Let us then hear what the Lord says to this most blessed woman; let us hear what he says, in her figure, to the Church of the Gentiles, for the service of so great a devotion: “And he said to her: Woman, your sins are forgiven.” See, then, what tears can accomplish. See what faith and love achieve. In a short space of time the woman was justified and cleansed from every sin, though she had been such a sinner that the Pharisee disdained even to look at her. Let no one, therefore, despair; let no one distrust the Lord’s mercy. The Lord is merciful and readily takes pity on those converted from the heart. [Note: [Col. 0382D] Thus far the homily. And here St Ambrose, no. 35: “From this woman, then, we understand what that apostolic statement means: ‘Sin abounded, so that grace might abound still more.’ For if sin had not abounded in this woman, grace would not have abounded: for she acknowledged sin and brought grace.”]

XIX. [CHAPTER IX.] [Col. 0383A] Now it came to pass, when the days of his assumption were being fulfilled, that he himself set his face steadfastly to go to Jerusalem. And he sent messengers before him.

“It came to pass,” he says, “when the days of his assumption were now being fulfilled,” and when the time of his passion, resurrection, ascension, or assumption was drawing near, “he set his face steadfastly to go to Jerusalem,” as was clearly apparent in his countenance and face. For the will is easily recognized in the face. “And he sent messengers before him. And going, they entered a town of the Samaritans to prepare for him. But they did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem.”

For, as is said elsewhere, Jews do not associate with Samaritans. Therefore the Samaritans would not receive Jesus because he showed that he wished to go to Jerusalem, now reckoning him almost as an enemy, like one who loved their enemies. [Note: [Col. 0383D] St Jerome, Letter 121 to Algasia, question 5: “Samaritans and Jews are divided by hostile hatred. … Seeing, therefore, that the Lord was going to Jerusalem—that is, to their enemies—they refused to receive him as a Jew, a stranger, and one going to enemies.”]

Even today all the wicked do not receive Jesus, his messengers, or his Gospel for this reason: they recognize that these are moving and hastening toward Jerusalem—toward peace, mercy, and loving-kindness. For Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace.”

But when the disciples James and John saw this, they said: “Lord, do you wish us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them, as Elijah did?” And he rebuked them, saying: “You do not know whose spirit you are. The Son of Man did not come to destroy human souls but to save them.” And they went to another village.

For the Apostles did not know whose spirit they were when they so greatly wished to avenge themselves. If they had known themselves to be servants and disciples of the spirit of mercy, patience, and gentleness, they would never, in any stirring of their own spirit, have wished in anger to kill so many people. [Note: [Col. 0383D] Jerome, cited above: “The Lord, who had come not to judge but to save, not in power but in humility, not in the Father’s glory but in the lowliness of man, rebukes them because they did not remember his teaching and the goodness of the Gospel, in which he had said: ‘Whoever strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other also,’ and ‘Love your enemies.’” St Ambrose, *On Luke*, VII, no. 28: “Perfect virtue has no eagerness for revenge; where charity is complete, there is no anger; weakness is not to be excluded but helped. Indignation is far from the religious; desire for vengeance, far from the great-hearted; rash joining of causes and incautious simplicity, far even from the prudent.”] This was proved afterward when they prayed for their enemies and persecutors.

XX. [CHAPTER X.] “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me; but whoever rejects me rejects him who sent me.” [Note: [Col. 0384D] This is a homily attributed to Emesenus, likewise affected by the same doubtful attribution, *On the Nativity of Several Martyrs*, p. 109.]

The Lord spoke these words to his disciples and their successors, namely bishops and priests. [Note: [Col. 0384D] St Augustine, Sermon 109, no. 1: “If he said only to the Apostles, ‘Whoever rejects you rejects me,’ then reject us. But if his word reached us, called us, and placed us in their position, see that you do not reject us, lest the injury you do us reach him.” See St Gregory, *Homilies on Ezekiel*, 10, no. 15, comparing these words with other words of Ezekiel: “They will not listen to you because they will not listen to me”; and especially St Basil, *Monastic Constitutions*, on obedience, ch. 22, vol. II of his works, p. 571.]

Whoever you are, therefore, who despise hearing bishops and priests and scorn to comply with their words and exhortations, at least do not make light of God himself and do not disdain to hear him. You despise hearing the priest; but this is no wonder, because he is poor, weak, humble, lowly, and contemptible, born among the poor. Hear, rather, the Lord speaking in him, admonishing you through him and restoring you to life. For the Apostle says: “Do you seek proof of Christ, who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3). Thus Christ speaks in bishops and priests, and in them is honored by some and rejected by others.

For now he endures and does not easily avenge his injuries. But hear him say: “I have kept silent. Shall I always keep silent?” Let the Psalmist say: “O God, who is like you? Do not be silent, nor be still, O God. For behold, your enemies have made a noise, and those who hate you have lifted up their head” (Ps. 82:2–3). Therefore do not reject Christ’s disciples and messengers; indeed, do not reject God himself in his disciples. For unless he himself were rejected in his disciples, he would never have said: “Whoever rejects you rejects me; and whoever rejects me rejects him who sent me.”

Let the Jews hear this and, hearing, fear, so that at least in this way they may be able to appease him whom they did not fear to offend. For they not only rejected but even crucified the Lord Christ.

The seventy-two returned with joy, saying: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name.” For, as was said above, the Lord had sent them two by two before him into every town and place where he himself was about to come. Now, on returning, they joyfully reported to the Lord, who knows all things, what he—not they—had worked in them. For they rejoiced in Christ’s name, whose power they had experienced. They also rejoiced in the immense grace bestowed upon them by the Lord: not only did they heal infirmities, but they commanded demons and saw them subject to themselves—demons to whom they knew the kings and rulers of this world, and all wicked people, were subject.

Therefore they said: “Lord, not only illnesses and infirmities, not only wicked people, but even the demons themselves are subject to us in your name”—those beings to whom all things far from fellowship with you are subject.

And he said to them: “I was seeing Satan fall from heaven like lightning. Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions.”

Heaven may be understood as the Church or the souls of the saints. Therefore the Lord saw Satan falling from heaven. He saw the devil fleeing the Church and the dwellings of the saints, and confirmed that he had already foreseen and known what the disciples were telling him. [Note: [Col. 0385C] Bede: “I was not merely seeing it now, but had seen it before, when he fell.”] Thus he says elsewhere: “Now is the judgment of the world; now the ruler of this world will be cast out” (John 12:31). For unless he had foreseen this, why would he have come into the world? Why would he have taken flesh? [Note: [Col. 0385C] Cyril, in Corderius’s *Catena*: “Certainly,” he says, “I did not fail to know this: armed with my favor, you overcame Satan. I saw him fall like lightning from heaven—that is, cast down from the height to the earth, from honor to disgrace, from great power to utter weakness; and this is entirely true. For before the Savior’s coming, he was worshipped everywhere by all with divine honor; everywhere he had temples, altars, and sacrifices. But after the Word of God descended from heaven, he himself fell like lightning. He who held all his worshippers deceived is placed beneath the feet of those who worshipped him.”]

For this purpose the Lord came into the world: to put the devil to flight and free human souls from his impious power. What was now beginning to happen, therefore, he foresaw before it occurred and ordained to occur in its proper time. We too see even today Satan falling from heaven like lightning and, with great fury and indignation, leaving the holy Church. For as often as a criminal person returns to repentance, Satan falls from heaven. There are many adulterers, perjurers, and murderers in the Church, which is called the kingdom of heaven; when they are converted, they are immediately forsaken by the devil, and lightning does not fall from heaven more swiftly than the devil falls from their minds.

“Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over every power of the enemy, and nothing shall harm you.” Serpents and scorpions may be understood not only as evil spirits but also as tyrants and all persecutors of the Church, because they are venomous and never travel in the straight way. What better can “the power of the enemy” be understood to mean than Nero, Simon Magus, Diocletian, Maximian, and Antichrist himself, the son of perdition? Moreover, pride, avarice, and every kind of lust are the power of the enemy: many are conquered by them and made subject to the devil. Hence Job, speaking of him, says: “His strength is in his loins, and his power is in the navel of his belly” (Job 40:11). But these things will not harm Christ’s disciples, with the Lord protecting and defending them everywhere. They will certainly not harm them if they resist and do not consent to them. [Note: [Col. 0385D] Elias of Crete, on Nazianzen’s Oration 4: “Here serpents perhaps mean sins which are manifestly grave and atrocious; scorpions, however, those vices which, though they seem small in human estimation, nevertheless wound and kill the soul with the sting of death.”]

It follows: “Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that spirits are subject to you; rather rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” For there are many to whom demons are subject, yet not joy but grief and sorrow await them. [Note: [Col. 0385D] Bede: “To cast out spirits, like performing other miracles, is sometimes not the merit of the person acting, but the invocation of Christ’s name accomplishes it either for the condemnation of those who invoke it or for the benefit of those who see and hear. … For in the Acts of the Apostles the sons of Sceva seemed to cast out demons, and Judas the Apostle, though of a traitor’s mind, is reported to have performed many signs among the other Apostles.”]

When some say at the judgment, “Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons, and perform many mighty works?” the Lord will say: “Depart, workers of iniquity. Truly I say to you, I do not know you.” [Note: [Col. 0386C] Luke 13:27: “And he will say to you: ‘I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity.’”] Christ’s disciples should not, therefore, rejoice because demons are subject to them, but because their names are written in heaven. The former joy is empty and temporary; the latter profitable and eternal. The former looks to vain glory; the latter to glory itself. [Note: [Col. 0386D] St Gregory, Book II, Letter 28: “Those who rejoiced in miracles had fixed their minds upon a private and temporary joy. But they are called back from private to common, from temporary to eternal joy, when they are told: ‘Rejoice in this,’ etc. … For the disciples of Truth ought to have joy only in that good which they possess in common with all and in which their joy has no end.”] The former may be possessed alike by evil and good people; the latter only by the good. [Note: [Col. 0386D] Thus far the homily.]

XXI. A certain lawyer stood up, testing him, and saying: “Teacher, by doing what shall I obtain eternal life?” [Note: [Col. 0386D] It is in the homily of St Bruno for the Thirteenth Sunday after Pentecost.] For in saying, “testing him,” he plainly shows that he questioned him not in order to obtain eternal life, but in order to find some ground on which he might reproach him, if he could. But he said to him: “What is written in the Law? How do you read it?” If, he says, you are a lawyer and know the Law, you surely understand what the Law says concerning eternal life. Say, therefore, what is written in the Law on this matter.

He answered and said: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, and with your whole soul, and with all your strength, and with your whole mind; and your neighbour as yourself.” And he said to him: “You have answered rightly; do this and you shall live.” See how the Lord catches the wise in their own craftiness. The lawyer himself discloses his own intention [Col. 0386C] and makes clear why he had questioned the Lord. He asks; he answers; he becomes both teacher and disciple of himself. For he knew what was written in the Law. The Lord compelled him to acknowledge this. Why, then, did he ask what he knew? Certainly because he wished to reproach the Lord. Yet the Lord did not reproach him, but said that he had answered rightly.

But he, wishing to justify himself, said to Jesus: “And who is my neighbour?” For when he had heard that loving God and one’s neighbour could suffice for righteousness and for obtaining eternal life, he immediately wished to show himself righteous, as though he had loved God and his neighbour—unless perhaps the Lord understood otherwise than he did who his neighbour was. Hence he says: “And who is my neighbour?” For perhaps he thought that only the person nearer to him than others, either through affection or through kinship of the flesh, was his neighbour. But it is not so. For the Lord says: “If you love those who love you, what reward shall you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same?” (Matt. V, 46.)

[Note: [Col. 0387C] Isidore of Pelusium, book IV, epistle 123: “That lawyer supposed that only a righteous man was neighbour to a righteous man, and one eminent in virtue to another eminent person. … But the Saviour, as the one who had made man—for he himself made both the small [Col. 0387D] and the great—defined neighbour not by actions or ranks, but by nature alone. … For nearness is measured by nature, not virtue; by substance, not rank; by compassion, not locality; by the manner of healing, not proximity of place.”]

But Jesus, taking up the matter, said: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers. They also stripped him, inflicted wounds upon him, and went away, leaving him half-dead” [Col. 0387B]. For what is this man but the human race? What is Jerusalem but Paradise? What is Jericho but this world? For Jericho is interpreted “moon.”

[Note: [Col. 0387D] So indeed Bede, on this passage: “This man is understood as Adam in the human race. Jerusalem is that heavenly city of peace, from whose blessedness he fell into this mortal and miserable life, which Jericho—interpreted ‘moon’—aptly signifies, since it is ever uncertain through the varying afflictions of decline and error. … Understand the robbers as the devil and his angels, who also stripped him—namely, they deprived him of the glory of immortality and the garment of innocence. … The wounds are sins, by which, injuring the integrity of human nature, etc. The priest and Levite who passed by the wounded man are the priesthood and ministry of the Old Testament, where through the decrees of the Law the wounds of a sick world could only be shown, [Col. 0388C] not healed. The Samaritan, interpreted ‘keeper,’ signifies the Lord. … The beast is his flesh, in which he deigned to come to us. The inn is the present Church [Col. 0388D], etc.” Therefore our author draws from Bede; Bede, I think, from Augustine, who in book II of *Questions on the Gospels*, question 19, says: “A certain man is Adam himself, understood in the human race. Jerusalem is that heavenly city of peace, from whose blessedness he fell. Jericho is interpreted ‘moon’ and signifies our mortality. … The robbers are the devil and angels who stripped him of immortality and, having inflicted wounds by persuading him to sin, left him half-dead, etc. The priest and Levite who saw him and passed by signify the priesthood and ministry of the Old Testament, which could not avail for salvation.
