Samaritan is interpreted ‘keeper’; and therefore the Lord himself is signified by this name. … The beast is his flesh, in which he deigned to come to us. The inn is the Church,” etc. See also Origen, Homily 34 on Luke, p. 972, vol. III of his works, and Ambrose, book II on Luke, no. 73.]

It is subject to such great changeability that it never remains [176] in the same state, now increasing and now diminishing. Hence it not inappropriately signifies this world. Its changeability is perpetual, and it cannot remain without changes. For, not to speak of heaven and time, of days, months, and the year, which always revolve and recur upon themselves, neither air, nor earth, nor sea, nor human beings themselves permanently preserve one form. It would take too long to recount in detail the changes of all these things.

Therefore the human race went down from Jerusalem to Jericho when the first man was cast out of Paradise into this world [Col. 0387C]. For the whole human race was in him together. Therefore all descended together with him and fell among robbers. These robbers are malignant spirits, who stealthily and by robbery take from us the treasure of souls, more excellent than all riches—namely, virtue and good works. Indeed, they also stripped him. Certainly, this was that garment of immortality which the first man lost; realizing that he was naked, he answered the Lord when asked where he was: “I heard your voice, Lord, and hid myself, because I was naked” (Gen. III, 10).

[Col. 0388A] “And having inflicted wounds, they went away, leaving him half-dead.” For the devil inflicts as many wounds upon each person as he compels that person to serve vices. He wounds and kills some through pride, others through avarice, others through lust, and others in other ways.

“Now it happened that a certain priest was going down by the same way, and, seeing him, passed by.” Who is this priest but Aaron with his sons and that entire priestly order whom the Lord commanded to pray for the rest? He was going down by the same way because he too was subject to death and corruption. Hence, seeing him, he passed by, because he could not free him. Likewise a Levite, when he was near the place and saw him, passed on. By the Levite is understood not Moses alone, but the whole tribe of Levi. For although only the sons of Aaron performed priestly office [Col. 0388B], the whole tribe of Levi devoted itself to prayer, since it lived from tithes and alms. Thus the Levite also passed by, because neither could these rescue the human race from the peril of death.

“But a certain Samaritan, travelling, came near him; and seeing him, was moved with compassion.” The Lord calls himself a Samaritan, a name which his Jewish enemies applied to him, saying: “Do we not rightly say that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” (John VIII, 48.) Samaritan, however, is interpreted “keeper.” He is surely worthy of this name, to whom it is said through the prophet: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” (Isa. XXXI, 11.) And the Psalmist says: “Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it watch in vain” [Col. 0388C] (Ps. CXXVI, 1).

He, travelling and, like other men, tending toward an end, by his compassion freed man and redeemed him by his blood. Hence it follows: “And drawing near, he bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine.” In this the Lord teaches us how we ought to treat those who are infirm and come to repentance. For we bind up wounds when we command the sinner to cease from sin. For as long as a person persists in sin, so long are his wounds loose and open. We pour in oil—

[Note: [Col. 0388D] Augustine, in the work cited: “Oil is the consolation of good hope, because pardon has been granted for reconciliation to peace [Col. 0389C]; wine is exhortation to act with most fervent spirit.” See Bede. Origen, in the work cited: “One of the presbyters, wishing to interpret the parable, used to say that the man who went down was Adam; Jerusalem, Paradise; Jericho, the world; the robbers, hostile powers; [Col. 0389D] the priest, the Law; the Levite, the prophets; the Samaritan, Christ; the wounds, disobedience; the animal, the Lord’s body; and the inn—that is, the lodging which receives all who wish to enter—the Church. … The robbers are no others than those of whom the Saviour said: ‘All who came before me were thieves and robbers.’ What are the wounds? Vices and sins. … He had oil, of which it is written: ‘That he may make the face cheerful with oil.’ But he also cleanses the wounds with wine, mixing in something harsh; and he set the wounded man upon the animal, that is, his own body, in accordance with the saying that he deigned to assume humanity,” etc. St Ambrose has the same interpretation in the passage cited.]

—when, by merciful consolation [Col. 0389A], we promise pardon to the sinner. Moreover, we pour in wine when, sternly reproving, we command fasting and the mortification of the flesh. Therefore let there not be oil without wine, nor wine without oil. Hence the Apostle says: “Reprove, entreat, insist, in season and out of season” (II Tim. IV, 2). For by entreating we pour oil into the wounds, and by reproving we pour wine.

“And setting him upon his own beast, he brought him to an inn and took care of him.” Christ’s beast is his humanity. By this we are borne; by this we are led to the inn and to the Church. Of it he himself says: “I became as a beast before you” (Ps. LXXII, 23). And the prophet says: “Surely he himself bore our labours and carried our sorrows” (Isa. LIII, 4). For Christ’s humanity taught us, redeemed us [Col. 0389B], and gathered us into one faith and one Church. There he cares for us; there he heals and feeds us daily.

“And on the next day he brought out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, and said: ‘Take care of him; and whatever you spend beyond this, I will repay you when I return.’” The two days are two periods. The first day extends from Adam to Christ; the second, to the end of the age.

[Note: [Col. 0389D] St Augustine, in the work cited: “The next day is after the Lord’s resurrection.” Bede says the same in the same words. Ambrose: “What is this next day, if not perhaps that of the Lord’s resurrection?”]

Thus on this second day—that is, after the Lord came into the world—he brought out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper. The two denarii are the two Testaments.

[Note: [Col. 0389D] St Ambrose, in the work cited: “What are these two denarii, if not perhaps the two Testaments, which bear the expressed image of the eternal King, by whose price our wounds are healed?” [Col. 0390C]]

At first only one denarius was given [177], because the other denarius had not yet been composed. But now two denarii are given, and they can suffice for every expense for all who are sick and come to the Church. [Col. 0389C] For the inn is the Church. Hence the Lord too was born in an inn. The innkeeper is the bishop. He guards the inn, governs the Church, and refreshes God’s animals with the fodder of the divine word.

Blessed Paul is a good innkeeper.

[Note: [Col. 0390C] St Augustine, in the work cited: “Therefore the innkeeper is the Apostle; and what he spends beyond this is the counsel *On Virgins*, etc.; or also that he worked with his own hands, lest he burden any of the weak at the beginning of the Gospel, although he was entitled to be supported by the Gospel.”]

He both faithfully distributed the two denarii entrusted to him by the Lord and spent a great thing beyond them from his own resources. For he says:

[Note: [Col. 0390D] I Corinthians VII, 25. St Ambrose: “That innkeeper, therefore, is he who said: ‘Christ sent me to preach the Gospel.’ The innkeepers are those to whom it is said: ‘Go into all the world and preach the Gospel,’ etc. A good steward is one who also spends beyond what is required. Paul is a good steward,” etc.]

“Now concerning virgins, I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel” (I Cor. VII, 25). Let us therefore hear this counsel which the Apostle gives as something beyond his charge [Col. 0390A]: “I think, he says, that this is good because of the present necessity: that it is good for a man to remain so. Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she will not sin” (ibid., 26). This is what the Apostle spent beyond his charge. He did not receive this in the two denarii. He also spent much else beyond it. For though he had the right to live by the Gospel, he nevertheless did not wish to live by the Gospel, but added labour to labour.

We may also understand by this additional expenditure the actual performance of good works. For one who expounds the words of the Testaments spends the denarii. But one who does what he expounds also expends something beyond the denarii. The Lord promises to repay the reward of this expenditure [Col. 0390B] when he returns for judgment.

It follows: “Which of these three seems to you to have been neighbour to him who fell among robbers?” He said: “The one who showed mercy to him.” And Jesus said to him: “Go, and do likewise.” For that person is your neighbour whom you approach with mercy. But one who has mercy on no one has no neighbour. Great, therefore, is mercy, which makes us neighbours even to strangers and unknown persons. Great is mercy, through which eternal life is obtained.

[Note: [Col. 0390D] Thus far the homily.]

XXII. Jesus entered a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house. And she had a sister named Mary, who also, sitting at the Lord’s feet, listened to his word.

[Note: [Col. 0390D] It is in the homily of St Bruno on the Assumption of St Mary.]

All the works of our Saviour are full of mysteries. [Col. 0390C] Whatever he does anywhere, he does in signification. What he then did bodily in a certain village, he does daily in the holy Church. The Church is a village-fortress—

[Note: [Col. 0390D] There is another elegant interpretation by Bernard, Sermon 5 on the Assumption: “What is this village-fortress but the human heart, which before the Lord comes to it is encircled by the ditch of desire, shut in by the wall of obstinacy, and in its inner spaciousness raised up in a Babylonian tower?” etc.]

—and not an ordinary one, but strong and impregnable: set upon a mountain, surrounded by a wall, fortified with towers, and armed with an army of angels and the protections of virtues. Into this fortress, therefore, the Lord Jesus enters daily. He does not disdain continually to visit it. Here he is received by Martha and brought into her house.

Let us therefore see [Col. 0391A] what Martha signifies. Let us see what Mary signifies. For each signifies something great. The whole Church consists in these two. The one signifies the active life; the other, the contemplative life.

[Note: [Col. 0391D] This very celebrated interpretation of the twofold life, active and contemplative, represented by Martha and Mary: Ambrose, book II on Luke; Basil, *Constitutions for Monks*, no. 85, chapter 1; Augustine, Sermon 27 on the Words of the Lord; Gregory, book VI of the *Morals*, chapter 28; Homilies 3, 4, and 14 on Ezekiel; Bede, etc.]

Martha signifies the active life, Mary the contemplative. Hence it is said that Martha, not Mary, received Christ into the house. For Mary has no house, because the contemplative life despises possessing any property of this world. It is enough for it to sit at the Lord’s feet; enough always to read, pray, and devote itself to the contemplation of God. It is enough besides always to hear the word of God and to nourish the mind rather than the belly. Such were the prophets, such the apostles, and such many others: leaving everything, fleeing the world, clinging to the Lord, [Col. 0391B] as having nothing and yet possessing everything.

But only the good have this life. The active life, however, is shared alike by evil and good people. It is called active because it is always in action, always in toil and labour, and can scarcely ever be at rest. But we are not speaking of that active life which employs robbers, rouses tyrants, troubles the avaricious, agitates adulterers, and incites all wicked persons to works of wickedness. For as we speak not of any Martha except the sister of Mary, so we speak not of any active life except one neighbouring upon the contemplative. For that active life which is pure and without sin is close to the contemplative life.

The Apostle preaches, baptizes, labours with his own hands for his living, travels through cities, and bears concern for all the Churches: to what life does this belong but the active? Hence it is said here of Martha that she was busy with much service. We see [178] even today that the rulers and ministers of the Churches busily go about, labour, toil, and exert themselves in many ways for the needs of their brethren. Thus we may rightly say that they too are busy with much service [Col. 0391C].

Although, therefore, the contemplative life is better than the active, because it is without anxiety and never fails, the active life is nevertheless so necessary that even the contemplative life cannot exist without it in this present life.

[Note: [Col. 0391D] St Ambrose, book II on Luke, no. 85: “Both offices belong to wisdom. For Stephen too, full of wisdom, was chosen as a minister. … For the Church is one body; though its members differ, one needs another. The eye cannot say to the hand: ‘I do not need your works’; nor again can the head deny the feet or [Col. 0392D] the ear to be of the body. For even though some are principal, others are necessary.” St Bernard, Sermon 3 on the Assumption: “They are sisters and ought to dwell together. Let not bodily exercise alone, which profits little, be found in us; but let godliness, profitable for all things, and spiritual exercise be found.”]

Therefore each needs the other. One prays; the other labours. One fills the mind, the other the stomach. Hence the Apostle says: “If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?” [Col. 0391D] (I Cor. IX, 11). For one who sows in this way raises the minds of the hearers to the contemplation of heavenly blessedness.

Therefore let it be said: “But Martha was busy with much service.” She came and said: “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her, then, to help me.” The active life often stands and, if one may say so, envies the contemplative. Therefore one who desires to devote oneself to contemplation alone should choose a solitary life, lest, while unwilling to rise from contemplation amid a gathering of many, one cause the others to stand idle and hinder work necessary to all.

For though he praises Mary’s portion, in churches and communities of many people Martha is more useful than Mary. Martha benefits everyone; Mary benefits herself. Martha is anxious; Mary at rest. Thus the Lord answered: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things. Yet one thing is necessary.” But what is that one thing? Would you hear [Col. 0392B] what it is? “Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her.” Therefore that is necessary which will not be taken away and is eternal.

Nevertheless, the Lord neither commanded Martha to cease her care nor instructed Mary not to help her. Rather, he showed them what is necessary and to what end the purpose of each should tend. For care for all the Churches is good, as the Apostle also says that he possessed it; but not that care which utterly tears the mind away from the contemplation of eternal sweetness. For one is anxious in vain who is anxious not for the love of God, but for vain glory, temporal gain, and dignities of this world. Of such persons the Lord says: “They have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 2). But to one who is rightly solicitous, what is said? [Col. 0392C] “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV, 21–23).

Martha’s care, therefore, is good, provided that it serves not the world but the Lord. Yet Mary ought sometimes to rise and help her busy sister. But when she rises, she should take care not wholly to forget her accustomed contemplation, lest perhaps, while wishing to benefit others, she cause harm to herself. Thus, when religious men, solitary and quiet, devoted to divine contemplation, undertake ecclesiastical governance at the request of many, Mary rises and comes to help her busy sister. Thus it comes about that she who had formerly been quiet, barren, and unfruitful now begins to labour, bears many children for God, and nourishes them.

[Col. 0392D] This was signified by Rachel, who was at first barren while her sister was fruitful and gloried in the progeny of many children. But afterwards Rachel too conceived and began to bear children.

[Note: [Col. 0392D] Innocent III, in the letter to the Bishop of Aecle, reported in the chapter *Nisi cum pridem*, *On Resignation*: “Do not suppose that Martha chose an evil part because she was busy about many things, while Mary chose the best part, which shall not be taken away from her. For although the latter is safer, the former is more fruitful; [Col. 0393D] since in fruitfulness of offspring Leah’s weak eyes were preferred to Rachel’s beauty. Therefore it is more readily permitted for a monk to ascend to the episcopate than for a bishop to descend to monastic life.”]

XXIII. [CHAP. XI.] [Col. 0393A] And it came to pass, when he was praying in a certain place, that when he ceased, one of his disciples said to him: “Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples.” And he said to him: “When you pray, say: Father, hallowed be your name; your kingdom come,” and the rest.

These matters have been explained in Matthew. But Luke omitted the one petition which says: “Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.” If rightly understood, this is wholly contained in the petition, “Your kingdom come.” For what is “Your kingdom come” but that the kingdom which is in heaven may come, be established, and be built upon earth? So that, since the King is one, the kingdom here and there may likewise be alike. And if this happens, his will will surely be done as in heaven, so also on earth.

XXIV. And he said to them: “Which of you will have a friend, and will go to him at midnight and say to him: ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, because a friend of mine has come to me from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’; and he, answering from within, will say: ‘Do not trouble me; the door is already shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give you anything’? Yet if he persists in knocking, I tell you, even if he will not rise and give to him because he is his friend, nevertheless because of his importunity [179] he will rise and give him as many as he needs.”

[Note: [Col. 0393D] It is in a homily on the Greater Litanies, formerly ascribed to Emisenus.]

By these words we are admonished to seek from him the spirit of wisdom and understanding—from him from whom is all wisdom, and with whom it always was and is before the ages—so that we may be able to set spiritual food before our friends who come from a journey and ask for the bread of Holy Scripture.

For the Apostle James says of this: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask it of God, who gives abundantly to all and does not reproach, and it shall be given him. But let him ask in faith, doubting nothing” [Col. 0393C] (Jas. I, 5). For when those subject to us question us about the Scriptures, then our friends come to us from a journey; and their journey is the longer in proportion as they are farther from understanding. Therefore we must have something to set before them, so that we may refresh their hungry minds from it.

But if we do not have it, let us rise at midnight. This night is ignorance. Let us read and search the Scriptures. Let us ask the Lord to open the eyes of our minds and deign to lend us those three most noble loaves, sweeter than all delights [Col. 0393D].

[Note: [Col. 0393D] Our author’s mystical interpretation is not inelegant. Ambrose’s interpretation, book VII on Luke, no. 8, may be related to it: “Who are these three loaves, but the nourishment of the heavenly mystery?” And Augustine, book II of *Questions on the Gospels*, question 21: “That he is told from within that the door is already shut and his children are with him in bed signifies the time of famine of the word, when understanding is closed; and for those who proclaimed through the world Evangelical wisdom, as though distributing bread [Col. 0394D] … through prayer it comes about that the person who desires it receives understanding from God himself, even if no human being is available through whom wisdom may be preached.” But Augustine more frequently—there, and in Sermon 105, no. 4, and Letter 130 to Proba, *On Prayer to God*, chapter 8, no. 15, etc.—followed by Isidore, or the author of the *Book of Allegories*, Bede on this passage, etc., explains them individually as understanding of the Trinity. In Sermon 105 he adds another explanation: Faith, Hope, and Charity. St Bernard, Sermon on the Rogation Days, interprets the loaves as those of truth, charity, and fortitude; Sermon 37 on the lesser virtues, as continence, humility, and charity.]

We understand these three loaves to be the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospels. Concerning them Moses says metaphorically: “The Lord came from Sinai [Col. 0394A] and rose from Seir; he appeared to us from Mount Paran, and with him were thousands of saints” (Deut. XXXIII, 2). These three mountains are the three loaves and the three volumes of Holy Scripture just mentioned. Sinai signifies the Law, because the Law was given there. Seir signifies the Prophets, because it is interpreted “hairy.” For the Prophets are very rough, difficult, and austere. But Mount Paran, which is called fruitful, truly designates the Gospels, whose seeds, we know, have borne fruit among all nations beyond all other seeds.

Therefore the Lord came from Sinai because his coming is announced in many places in the Law, that is, in the books of Moses, according to the saying: “The Lord will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren; you shall hear him as myself” (Deut. XV, 18; Acts III, 22). He rose in Seir because his arising and birth are found most plainly in the Prophets. Hence Isaiah says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” [Col. 0394B] (Isa. VII, 14). He appeared from Mount Paran because the Gospels declare his birth, passion, and resurrection—what he did and how he lived.

Let us therefore seek these three loaves, without which the soul does not live, which can suffice for all who hunger. Let us seek and not fail; let us knock and persevere, even if that friend of ours says to each of us: “Do not trouble me; the door is already shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give to you.” Our friend—that is, God and our Lord, who loved us so greatly that he did not hesitate to die for us—does not himself say this to us [Col. 0394C], yet he seems to say it when, after much labour, many prayers, and great desire for understanding, he does not answer us.

For what prays as holy desires do? Unless desire prayed, the Psalmist would not say: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor” (Ps. X, 17). Therefore we pray well when we desire some good thing. Yet there is no one who does not desire to understand the Holy Scriptures. Therefore no one fails to pray for these loaves.

But because the Lord has now ascended into heaven and shut the door—that is, ceased from preaching—and because he has already gathered his children, namely the holy Apostles, with himself into the bedchamber of eternal rest—

[Note: [Col. 0394D] Bede on this passage: “The friend’s door is understanding of the divine word … [Col. 0395C] and it is shut when those [Col. 0395D] who proclaimed through the world Evangelical wisdom, as though distributing bread, the children of the householder, are now in secret rest with the Lord.”]

—neither he nor they can any longer return bodily here to teach us. This is what he says: “Do not trouble me; the door is shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give to you” [Col. 0394D].

Yet let us not cease from this trouble, importunity [Col. 0395A], and force. For the Lord himself says: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. XI, 12). This violence, therefore, is good; this trouble and importunity are good—and so good that the Lord, though unwilling to give us the loaves for friendship’s sake, nevertheless rises because of importunity and gives them to us sufficiently for our need. For this is what he says: “And if he persists in knocking, I tell you, even if he will not rise and give to him because he is his friend, nevertheless because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needs.”

Hence he further adds: “And I say to you: Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; and whoever seeks finds; and to the one who knocks it shall be opened.” By this great repetition of words [180] [Col. 0395B], the Lord plainly shows how earnest, troublesome, importunate, forceful, and persistent he wishes us to be in asking. Hence someone has said: “Persistent labour conquers all.”

[Note: [Col. 0395D] Thus far the homily.]

These matters, and the rest that follows in this Gospel, have been explained in Matthew.

XXV. “Woe to you who build the tombs of the prophets.” But not because you build tombs for the prophets; rather, because you build them with an evil intention, and because your fathers killed them—that is, because you are sons of those who killed the prophets. They are sons not by nature alone, but by imitation. For by nature the Apostles too were their sons. But by imitation everyone is the child of the one whom he imitates. Thus [Col. 0395C] the good are called sons of Abraham. But to the wicked it is said: “You are of your father the devil” (John VIII, 44).

“Surely you testify that you consent to the works of your fathers: for they killed them, and you build their tombs.”

[Note: [Col. 0395D] Chrysostom, Homily 74 on Matthew, no. 1: “He says ‘Woe,’ not because they build, nor because they accuse their fathers; but because, while doing this and pretending in words to accuse their fathers, they commit worse deeds. Luke teaches that they accused their fathers only hypocritically, etc. Here he condemns the intention with which they built: not to honour those who had been killed, but as though displaying the murders with pomp, and fearing lest, when the tombs had been destroyed by the injury of time, the memory and monument of so great an act of daring should perish. Thus they constructed magnificent tombs, as though erecting a trophy and glorying in their fathers’ crimes.”]

For this shows that they built the monuments of the prophets not from piety or reverence, but rather in memory of the victory and audacity of their fathers: men who had been such that they did not fear to kill the prophets themselves. Thus all who saw this might be afraid, and no one might presume to prophesy against the city and the Temple. For this was why the Lord was accused, as one who had said that he could destroy the Temple of God [Col. 0396A]. For this reason false witnesses also said against blessed Stephen: “This man does not cease to speak against the holy place and the Law. For we heard him say that Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place” (Acts VI, 13). But these points are clearer in Matthew.

XXVI. [CHAP. XII.] But someone from the crowd said to him: “Master, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” But he said to him: “Man, who appointed me judge or divider over you?” For the Lord had not come to divide lands or decide disputes over possessions, but to restrain greed, recommend patience, and teach contempt for the world. [Note: [Col. 0395D] Ambrose, Book VII on Luke, no. 122: “He rightly declines earthly matters, having descended for divine ones. . . . Therefore this brother is not unjustly rebuffed, since he wished to occupy with corruptible concerns the dispenser of heavenly things; [Col. 0396C] [Col. 0396D] whereas between brothers an inheritance ought to be divided not by the intervention of a judge, but by piety acting as mediator.” In nearly the same words Bede, on this passage: “This brother is rightly rebuffed, since he wishes to impose the annoyance of an earthly division upon the teacher who commends the joys of unity and heavenly peace.”]

Therefore elsewhere he says: “Do not resist evil. But if anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also; and to him who wishes to contend with you in court [Col. 0396B] and take your tunic, yield him your cloak also”; and he said to them: “See to it, and guard yourselves against every kind of greed, because a person’s life does not consist in the abundance of what he possesses” (Matt. V, 39). By these words he summoned both the person inflicting injury and the person enduring it to fairness and patience. For human life does not consist in abundance, and all riches are possessed together with life itself only for a short time.

And he told them a parable, saying: “The land of a certain rich man brought forth abundant crops; and he thought within himself, saying: ‘What shall I do, because I have nowhere to store my fruits?’ And he said: ‘This I shall do: I shall tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I shall gather all that has grown for me, and my goods; and I shall say to my soul: Soul, you have many [Col. 0396C] goods laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, and feast.’ But the Lord said to him: ‘Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you. And the things you have prepared—whose will they be?’ Thus is the person who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.”

How beautiful a parable, and how necessary for the greedy and covetous! For who, understanding this, will place his hope in riches, when riches can so easily be lost and a human being can die so suddenly? [Note: [Col. 0396D] Ambrose, in the work cited: “He gathers wealth in vain who does not know that he himself will not use it; like that man whose barns, filled with new harvests, were bursting, and who prepared receptacles for his overflowing produce, not knowing for whom he was gathering it. For all things that belong to the age remain in the age, and whatever is gathered passes away from us to heirs. For those things are not ours which we cannot take with us. Virtue alone accompanies the dead; mercy alone follows us, and, as the guide leading before us to heavenly dwellings, through the interest yielded by paltry money obtains eternal tabernacles for the departed.”] Thus, he says, it will be with every person who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God. For he gathers, yet does not know for whom he will gather these things. But that person is rich toward God who places all his hope not in riches but in God.

181 PART TWO

[Col. 0397]

XXVII. [Col. 0397A] “Let your loins be girded, and your lamps burning; and be yourselves like people waiting for their master when he returns from the wedding, so that, when he comes and knocks, they may open to him at once.” [Note: [Col. 0397C] This is a homily of Emisenus for the Nativity of a Confessor, p. 216, which we shall more correctly call Saint Bruno’s.]

In commanding us to gird our loins, the Lord commends the glory and observance of chastity. For lust holds sway in the loins. Thus it is said of the devil: “His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly” (Job XL, 11). Of the Church likewise it is said: “She girded her loins with strength and strengthened her arm” (Prov. XXXI, 17). And again: “She made fine linen and sold it, and delivered a girdle to the Canaanite” (ibid., 34). Hence the priests under the Law are commanded to have belts and breeches (Lev. XXVIII, 42), without which they may not approach [Col. 0397B] the altar or enter the tabernacle. By these and similar passages it is established how greatly God approves the observance of chastity.

It follows: “And lamps burning in your hands.” Our lamps burn when they shine well in every direction and enlighten others by both our teaching and our deeds. Thus the Lord also says: “So let your light shine before people, that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16). Their lamps are extinguished who enlighten no one either by teaching or by action. [Note: [Col. 0397C] Saint Augustine, Sermon 108, otherwise 39, On the Words of the Lord, chap. 2, no. 2: “It pertains to continence: Let your loins be girded; it pertains to righteousness: and your lamps burning.” Saint Fulgentius, Sermon 1 on Stewardships, [Col. 0397D] no. 9: “Thus in the loins carnal desire is indicated, but in the lamps Christian faith and charity are shown. Therefore, in commanding our loins to be girded, the Lord undoubtedly commands that the desires of the flesh be restrained. But in ordering us to have burning lamps, he commands precisely this: that we may shine from the light of true faith and burn fervently in works of holy charity. In commanding our loins to be girded, he directs us to flee evil desires and deeds; in commanding our lamps to burn, he urges us to love and do what is good.”]

We ought, moreover, to be like persons waiting for their master when he returns from the wedding, lest he find us unprepared and asleep. For our Lord will then return from the wedding when he brings his bride—our mother, namely the holy Church—free from every corruption, in chaste embraces into the bridal chamber of eternal blessedness. [Note: [Col. 0398C] Saint Augustine, in the work cited, no. 1: “You have just heard what the Gospel has warned us: making us watchful and desiring us to be unencumbered and prepared for the expectation of the last things, so that after the last things that are to be feared in this age there may follow rest without end. . . . For this expectation and this hope we have become Christians. Is not our hope other than this age? Let us not love the age.”]

But even now he comes to the wedding every day, when he calls to himself the souls of the saints, which themselves too belong to that bride, and places them with himself in the chamber of eternal blessedness. [Note: [Col. 0398D] Familiar words of Saint Gregory, Homily 15 on the Gospels, no. 3.] Therefore our Savior celebrates weddings every day. Every day he serves to the souls of saints who come to him the delights of the highest good [Col. 0398A] and the banquets of ineffable sweetness.

Therefore it is added: “Blessed are those servants whom the master, when he comes, finds awake. Amen I say to you that he will gird himself, make them recline at table, and, passing by, will serve them.” Of this watchfulness the Apostle says: “Keep watch, you righteous, and do not sin” (I Cor. XV, 34). And again: “Keep watch and pray; stand firm in the faith; act manfully; be strengthened in the Lord; let all your things be done in charity” (I Cor. XVI, 13). Those who keep watch in this way will be blessed. The Lord will make them recline with himself, and, passing among them, will minister to them. Thus, consoling his disciples, he says: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations; and I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom.”

But in saying that he will gird himself and, passing by, minister to them, he shows most clearly with what affection, what love, and what bowels of charity he will receive them and bring them into the glory prepared for them. [Note: [Col. 0398D] Saint Gregory, in the work cited, no. 4: “He will gird himself—that is, he will prepare himself for recompense—and he will make them recline—that is, he will refresh them in eternal rest.”] This should not be understood literally; rather, the inward intention is declared through the outward arrangement.

“And if he comes in the second watch, and if he comes in the third watch, and finds them thus, blessed are those servants.” The three watches are the three periods: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. [Note: [Col. 0398D] Saint Gregory understands it otherwise, no. 5: “The first watch is the guardianship of the first age . . . childhood. The second is adolescence or youth . . . the third, however, is understood as old age.”] Since in the first watch the Lord did not visit the world either through the Law or through the prophets, nothing is here said of the first watch. But in the second watch he deigned to visit the world not only through the Law and the prophets, but also in his own person. Hence the Apostle says: “God, who at many times [Col. 0398C] and in many ways formerly spoke to the fathers through the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us in the Son” (Heb. I, 1). The third watch, however, is this present time, in which he testifies not merely that he will come but that he is always present, saying: “Behold, I am with you all days, even unto the 182 consummation of the age of ages” (Matt. XXVIII, 20).

It follows: “But know this: if the householder knew at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly keep watch and would not allow his house to be broken into.” [Col. 0399A] Therefore, because he does not know, because in sleep he is negligent, the house is often broken into, and whatever is best in it becomes the thieves’ plunder. But you, be prepared; be watchful; and because you do not know that one hour, keep watch at every hour, lest in that one hour you be found heedless and asleep. And this is what he says: “Therefore you also be prepared, because at an hour when you do not expect it, the Son of Man will come.”

But Peter said to him: “Lord, do you speak this parable to us, or also to everyone?” By these words we may understand that the Lord said some things especially to the disciples and some things generally to all people—for example: “Do not think about tomorrow” (Matt. VI, 34); and: “Do not be anxious for your soul, what you shall eat, nor for your body, what you shall put on” (Luke XII, 22), along with many other things.

But the Lord said: “Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord appointed over his household, to give them their measure of wheat in due season? Blessed is that servant whom the Lord, when he comes, finds doing so.” It is thus clear that these things are said not only to the apostles but also to the other ministers and stewards of the Church, namely bishops and priests. [Note: [Col. 0399C] Saint Fulgentius, Sermon 1 on Stewardships, no. 3: “Lest any of us suppose that only the apostles were made stewards . . . [Col. 0399D] the blessed Apostle himself, showing that bishops too are stewards, says: ‘A bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward.’ Therefore we are servants of the householder; we are the Lord’s stewards; we have received the measure of wheat which we are to distribute to you.”]

For the Lord appointed them over his household. He appointed them over the Church and his house, to govern it, teach it, supply it with necessities, and give the measure of wheat in season. By this wheat is understood evangelical teaching, which ought to be given not only in a measured amount but also at its proper time. For not every time is suitable for teaching; nor is the same teaching suitable equally for everyone, nor is it fitting to preach everything to everyone. [Col. 0399C] [Note: [Col. 0399D] Saint Gregory, Book II, Homily 8 on Ezekiel, explaining why the apostles are called inner and outer gates: “They are gates that are at once outer and inner to us. For when they preach to beginners not lofty and mystical matters, but things they are able to grasp, they are outer gates; but when they speak profound and mystical things to the perfect, they are inner gates.” The same, Pastoral Rule, Part III, chap. 39: “A preacher should understand that he must not draw his hearer’s mind beyond its strength, lest, so to speak, while it is stretched beyond what it can bear, the heart of the mind be ruptured. Things that are lofty ought to be veiled for many hearers and scarcely disclosed to a few. Hence Truth himself says: ‘Who, do you suppose, is the faithful and prudent steward . . . to give them in due season [Col. 0400C] [Col. 0400D] their measure of wheat?’ For by the measure of wheat the proportion of the word is expressed, lest, when something incapable of being received is offered to a narrow heart, it be poured out beyond it,” etc.]

Therefore the faithful and prudent steward must consider with the greatest care when, what, and how much he should give to each person. Thus, under the Law, it was lawful for priests alone to eat certain sacrifices, while others might be eaten by others also. Places and times were likewise appointed in which it was lawful to offer them. Blessed therefore is the servant whom the Lord, when he comes, finds doing so. But let us hear why he is blessed: “Truly I say to you that he will appoint him over all that he possesses.” Each person is indeed set over all things, because all things obey him and do all that he wills. [Col. 0400A] For there will be such harmony there that each person will be honored by all as though greater, and will honor all as though lesser. It is therefore not unfitting that each person there should be appointed over all things. [Note: [Col. 0400D] Thus far the homily.]

XXVIII. “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire but that it be kindled?” He explains this as follows: “But I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished!” Of this fire and baptism John the Baptist says: “He who comes after me is stronger than I, and he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. III, 11). Thus, coming into the world, the Lord sent the fire of the Holy Spirit, kindled it, and illumined the hearts of believers; he baptized and cleansed us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood. [Note: [Col. 0400D] Saint Ambrose, Book VII on Luke, no. 131: “‘I came to cast fire upon the earth’: certainly not the fire that consumes good things, but the author of good will, which improves the golden vessels of the Lord’s house but consumes hay and stubble. That divine fire burns up everything secular that is clotted with the pleasure of the world, and the perishable work of the flesh; it was that fire which flamed in the bones of the prophets,” etc. See Saint John Chrysostom, Homily 4 on Acts, no. 2; Saint Gregory, Homily 30 on the Gospels, no. 6.]

The intensity of his desire for this is evident [Col. 0400B] from his saying that he is constrained until it is accomplished: “Do you suppose that I came to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but division.” “I came,” he says, “not only to kindle the earth, but also to divide and separate it against itself.” For from this there will be five persons in one household divided: three against two and two against three. Namely, father against son and son against his father; mother against daughter and daughter against mother; mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. These appear to be six persons, but they are only five, because mother and mother-in-law are one and the same person. [Note: [Col. 0400D] Saint Ambrose, no. 137: “For who are the five, when the subjection of six persons seems to be stated—father and son, mother and daughter, mother-in-law and daughter-in-law? Yet the same mother may be understood as the mother-in-law: for she who is the mother of the son is the mother-in-law of his wife,” etc.]

In the primitive Church it often happened that all these five, dwelling in one household, were divided, three against two and two against [183] three: some defending the faith of Christ [Col. 0400C] and others opposing it.

XXIX. [CHAP. XIII.] At that very time some were present who reported to him concerning the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. And answering, he said to them: “Do you suppose that these Galileans were sinners beyond all Galileans, because they suffered such things? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all perish in the same way. Or those eighteen upon whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: do you suppose that they too were debtors beyond all the people dwelling in Jerusalem? No, I tell you; but if you do not repent, you will all perish in the same way.”

[Col. 0401A] We have no accounts of these events. [Note: [Col. 0401D] A. properly and cautiously touches upon this history, concerning which we have no certainty, as Calmet and others observe. Some refer it to the sedition mentioned in Acts V, 37. Others, to whom this event appears earlier—indeed too early for the Gospel words, “reporting to him concerning the Galileans,” to fit it—prefer to interpret it of the rioting Samaritans, many of whom Pilate killed, as Josephus relates, *Antiquities*, Book XVIII, chap. 4. They say that they were called Galileans by sect and heresy, but Samaritans by origin and homeland. See Baronius, under the year 1, no. 61, and the interpreters, who admit regarding the quite different history of the collapse of the tower of Siloam that it is wholly unknown and is known only from this passage.]

Nevertheless, it should be understood that Pilate killed certain Galileans as they were sacrificing, in the midst of their sacrifices, and thus mingled their blood with their sacrifices themselves. Likewise, some tower in Siloam fell and by its collapse crushed the people just mentioned by the Lord. But people thought, as usually happens, that these were more wicked than others because they happened to perish so extraordinarily. But this is not so. For death, whatever its nature, neither condemns the righteous nor justifies the sinner. But when he says, “Unless you repent, you will all perish in the same way,” this should be understood not of the death of the body but of the death of the soul. For not all who neglect repentance perish amid sacrifices or through the fall of a tower.

XXX. And he spoke this parable: “A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none. Then he said to the keeper of the vineyard: ‘Behold, for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree and find none. Cut it down, therefore: why does it also occupy the ground?’” [Note: [Col. 0401D] This is a homily of Emisenus for a vacant Sunday, p. 185, to be numbered among those taken over by Saint Bruno.]

This parable reveals how great is God’s patience and how great also is human negligence. For God’s field and vineyard is called the world; its trees and vines are human beings, some fruitful and others unfruitful. The cultivators of this vineyard are bishops and priests. The three years are the three periods: before the Law, under the Law, [Note: [Col. 0401D] Bede, on this passage: “This fig tree can signify the nature of the human race, which was well planted—that is, created in the likeness of its Maker. But though God sought fruit for three years, it refused to bear it, because it despised obedience before the Law, under the Law, and under grace.” Others—Saint Ambrose, no. 160; Saint Jerome on Matthew XXI, etc.—interpret it as the Synagogue. Of the former interpretation, which must therefore have been ancient, Saint Ambrose says, no. 172: “Those who interpret it in that way differ in nothing except that they choose the genus in place of the species.”] and under grace. For as often as the Lord deigns to look upon and visit humanity, so often he comes to his vineyard and seeks fruit in its trees.

Thus the unfruitful fig tree is human nature in the persons of the wicked—that is, every unjust and unbelieving person. Therefore, during three years the Lord comes to this fig tree and finds no fruit in it, because such trees have not been lacking in this vineyard either before the Law, under the Law, or under grace. Indeed, this vineyard of the world often seems to abound more in unfruitful fig trees than in fruitful trees. For the good are few in comparison with the wicked. “For many,” as the Lord says, “are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XXII, 14).

It follows: “Cut it down, therefore.” Since, he says, it is unfruitful, useless, and does not yield the fruit of good works, cut it down. [Col. 0401D] “For every tree that does not bear good fruit [Col. 0402A] will be cut down and cast into the fire” (Luke III, 9). “Why does it also occupy the ground?” Such trees occupy the ground uselessly, obstruct others, and the surrounding trees are harmed by their noxious shade. For, as the saying goes, one grape draws discoloration from another; one diseased sheep scatters the whole flock; a little leaven corrupts the whole mass; and “Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it” (Ecclus. XIII, 1).

But he answered and said to him: “Lord, leave it this year also, until I dig around it and put manure on it; and if indeed it bears fruit—but if not, in the future you will cut it down.” Thus Samuel too prayed for the unfruitful tree, lest it be cut down, mourning Saul all his days (I Kings XI, 35). A bishop digs around the fig tree [Col. 0402B] when, through the sinner’s confession, he investigates most diligently that sinner’s deeds, whole life, and depravity. Then he puts manure around it when he shows how shameful, dishonorable, and foul-smelling the sinner’s sins have been. [Note: [Col. 0402D] Bede: “‘I will put manure on it’: that is, I will bring back to the mind the abomination of the evils which it has done, and awaken the grace of compunction as though from the rot of manure.”]

The Apostle had put manure around the fig tree when he said: “What fruit, then, did you have at that time in things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. VI, 21). Hence David, smelling the stench of this manure, said: “My scars have putrefied and become corrupt [184] because of my foolishness” (Ps. XXXVII, 6). For a sinner cannot otherwise be healed unless he first perceives the stench of his own wounds and, perceiving it, recoils from it.

Now he was teaching in their synagogue on the sabbaths, and behold, there was a woman who had had a spirit of infirmity [Col. 0402C] for eighteen years. She was bent over and could not at all look upward. When Jesus saw her, he called her to himself and said to her: “Woman, you are released from your infirmity.” And he laid his hand upon her, and immediately she was made straight and glorified God.

What the Lord did in the bent woman is an exposition of what was said concerning the unfruitful fig tree. For the bent woman and the unfruitful fig tree signify one and the same thing. The bent person is the one who, given over to earthly pleasures, loves only earthly and passing things, does not raise the eyes of the mind to contemplate heavenly things, and does not seek the riches of eternal blessedness. [Note: [Col. 0402D] Ambrose, Book III on the *Hexaemeron*, chap. 12, no. 50: “Nothing weighs down the mind more than the care of this world and the desire either for money or for power. This is shown to you in the Gospel when [Col. 0403C] you read that the woman who had a spirit of infirmity was bent over, so that she could not [Col. 0403D] look upward. For her soul was bent, because it was inclined toward earthly advantages and did not see heavenly grace. Jesus looked upon her and called her, and immediately the woman laid aside her earthly burdens.” Saint Gregory, Homily 31 on the Gospels, no. 6: “Every sinner who thinks of earthly things and does not seek heavenly things cannot look upward. For while he follows inward desires, he is bent away from the uprightness of his mind; and he always sees what he thinks of without ceasing. . . . And because he does not rise to heavenly desire, like the bent woman he cannot look upward at all.”]

But if the Lord touches such a person and lays upon him the hand of his mercy, he is immediately [Col. 0402D] made straight; forgetting earthly things, he contemplates heavenly things.

[Col. 0403A] But the ruler of the synagogue, answering indignantly because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the crowd: “There are six days in which one ought to work. Come therefore on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day.” The ruler of the synagogue understood the Law wrongly, for he did not wish works of piety and mercy to be done on the Sabbath. For the Law prohibited not liberal work on the Sabbath, but servile work. A good work may be done on every day, [Note: [Col. 0403D] Saint Ambrose, on this passage, no. 174: “The Sabbath days are holidays not from good work, but from evil.”] but an evil work on none.

The Lord answered him and said: “Hypocrite, does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or ass from the manger and lead it away to water it?” “If,” he says, “it is not lawful to work on the Sabbath, why then do you lead ox and ass to drink on the Sabbath?” This is a servile work, which, if understood literally, the Law entirely prohibits on the Sabbath. [Col. 0403B] He is therefore rightly called a hypocrite who reveres the Sabbath not in the things in which he ought, but in the things in which he ought not—assenting to evil and reproving good.

“To you hypocrites,” he says, “it is permitted on the Sabbath to untie your ox and ass from the manger and give them water; but was I not permitted to loose from this bond this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound, behold, for eighteen years?” For what applies in the lesser case applies in the greater. Even if it did not apply in the lesser case, it could not be reproved in the greater. For who can reprove what the Lord does?

The same thing is signified by these eighteen years and by the three years mentioned above. For six, that is, three times six, makes eighteen. Let us therefore posit six years before [Col. 0403C] the Law, six under the Law, and six under grace; and there will be eighteen. [Note: [Col. 0403D] Bede: “She was well bent over for eighteen years, a number completed by six multiplied by three, because it shows that she languished in weak works in the witness of the Law, the prophecy of the prophets, and the revelation of grace.” See the mysteries of this number in Saint Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book IV, [Col. 0404C] chap. 4; Sermon 110, no. 2.] In all these periods, neither the unfruitful fig tree nor the bent woman whom Jesus might heal has been absent.

Since Satan is said to have bound this woman, we may understand that she incurred this infirmity because of her sins, just as did the man to whom the Lord said: “Go, and sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John VIII, 11).

And when he said these things, all his adversaries were ashamed, while all the people rejoiced at all the glorious things done by him. The former were ashamed [Col. 0404A] because they saw themselves defeated; the latter rejoiced because in both Christ’s words and his miracles they recognized his power and glory. [Note: [Col. 0404C] Thus far the homily.]

XXXI. On that day certain Pharisees approached him, saying: “Go out and depart from here, because Herod wants to kill you.” And he said to them: “Tell that fox: ‘Behold, I cast out demons and perform healings today and tomorrow; and on the third day I am brought to completion. Yet I must walk today, tomorrow, and the following day, because it is not possible for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem.’”

For the fox is a very crafty animal, always lying in wait for harmless birds. Thus Herod is not without reason called a fox: he had killed John the Baptist and was attempting to kill Christ our Lord. “Behold,” he says, “I cast out demons, which are much [Col. 0404B] stronger and more powerful than Herod himself, and I perform healings”—both of which are signs of power and might. Therefore it is clear that it lies in my power both to live and to die.

But what is meant by “tomorrow” except all future time? The Lord was brought to completion on the third day because on the day of his resurrection, which is the third from the day of his passion, [185] he clothed himself with beauty; the Lord clothed himself with strength and girded himself with power, so that, wholly intact and complete, he might thereafter experience in himself no diminution or mutability and be subject, as before, to no sufferings.

But because he said, “On the third day I am brought to completion,” lest anyone perhaps suppose that he would die immediately on the third day, he added: “Yet I must walk today, tomorrow, and the following day.” Hence it is clear that “tomorrow” signifies, not the next day, but rather [Col. 0404C] future time indefinitely. [Note: [Col. 0404D] Saint Augustine, Book VI against Julian, chap. 19: “The Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Behold, I cast out demons and perform healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am brought to completion.’ The Lord suffered long after this was said. He could not lie. Therefore it is understood thus. The casting out of demons is the remission of sins; and certainly, since the devil is the father and origin of sins, by what is effected the one who effects it is dealt with. Thus the casting out of demons is the remission of sins. . . . The completion of healings occurs while the Church progresses from day to day, and by daily renewal the suffering of corruption, whose guilt has been removed, is diminished. On the third day it is brought to completion when he showed to the Church the resurrection which was to be inaugurated in himself, by which it might attain the consummation of incorruption and the highest healing. Yet he said that he himself was brought to completion. He himself is beginning and end; he himself is head and fullness of the body; he himself is perfected in his members.” In nearly the same sense, see Venerable Bede writing.]

It follows: “Because it is not possible for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem.” This he says not of every prophet but of that prophet of whom he says elsewhere: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country” (Matt. XIII, 57), calling himself, namely, a prophet. It is not possible—that is, the providence of God, the ordinance of God, and the saying of the prophets do not receive, admit, or permit—that this prophet perish and die outside Jerusalem. For it had been predetermined and ordained before the ages, and it could not happen otherwise: he had to be killed only in Jerusalem and nowhere else. [Col. 0405A] In vain, therefore, does Herod strive to kill him, because the time, day, and place where and when the Lord is to be killed have been ordained and cannot be changed.

### XXXII. [CHAPTER XIV.]

“And it came to pass, when he entered on the sabbath into the house of a certain ruler of the Pharisees to eat bread, that they watched him.” [Note: [Col. 0405D] This is a homily falsely attributed to Eusebius of Emesa, for the seventeenth Sunday after Pentecost, p. 169.]

In writing that the Lord entered the Pharisees’ ruler’s house to eat bread, the Evangelist shows that he was content with necessities alone and did not seek luxurious foods—especially since he is not said to have eaten anything else in that ruler’s house. Yet in bread, which holds first place among all foods, we may understand every kind of food. Thus it is said also of the Church: “She does not eat the bread of idleness” [Col. 0405B] (Prov. 31:27).

[Note: [Col. 0405D] St Jerome, Book III on Isaiah, explaining the words of chapter 3, “The Lord will take away from Jerusalem every support of bread and every support of water,” writes: “The strength of bread and the strength of water are taken for every food and drink”; and in confirmation he adduces these Scriptures: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread,” and, “Man does not live by bread alone.”]

“And they watched him,” that is, they lay in wait for him, so that they might either hear something in his words or see something in his actions from which they could rebuke and accuse him.

[Note: [Col. 0405D] The ancient Commentary on the Epistle to the Philippians, among the works of St Jerome, explaining the words, “And observe those who walk thus,” says: “To observe is said in two ways: either in order to imitate, as here; or in order to beware, as when the Apostle says in Romans 14: [Col. 0406D] ‘Observe those who cause dissensions and offences.’”]

Knowing their purpose, the Lord himself gave them material in which they might disclose the wickedness of their intention. What follows makes this clear: “And behold, a certain man suffering from dropsy was before him.” This is the occasion by which both Christ’s power and the Pharisees’ faithlessness are made manifest.

“And Jesus, answering the lawyers and Pharisees, said: Is it lawful to heal on the sabbath? But they were silent. And he took him, healed him, and dismissed him.”

Jesus answered, certainly—but he answered their thoughts. For the Pharisees thought and said within themselves [Col. 0405C]: “Behold, a dropsical man is present, and it is the sabbath; let us see what he does.” Answering these thoughts, the Lord said: “Is it lawful to heal on the sabbath?” But, fearing on either side, they were silent. For if they had said that it was lawful, there would no longer have been anything by which they could rebuke him; but if they had said that it was not lawful, they feared for themselves, because they too did many works on sabbaths. Therefore they were silent.

“But he healed him and dismissed him.” And because they were already thinking of insulting and rebuking him as one who had acted against the law, he forestalled them and answered: “Which of you, if his ass or ox falls into a pit, will not immediately draw it out on the sabbath day?” And they could not answer him in reply. For what could those answer who saw themselves caught by so evident a syllogism? But let us see what this dropsical man signifies; for he does signify something.

Dropsy is a sickness named from water. But the dropsical man, although full of water, is nevertheless always thirsty and cannot be satisfied by drinking. Thus he quite fittingly represents the avaricious, who desire to have more in proportion as they have more. Nor are they satisfied by having, because avarice is defined as an insatiable desire of possessing. [186]

[Note: [Col. 0406D] St Gregory, Morals, Book XIV, ch. 5: “What, then, is signified by the fact that the dropsical man is healed before the Pharisee’s house, except that through one person’s bodily sickness the sickness of another’s heart is expressed? For the more the dropsical man drinks, the more he thirsts; and every miser multiplies thirst by drinking, because, when he has obtained the things he desires, he pants still more after other things to be desired.” Bede copies Gregory’s words here.]

If such persons come to Christ’s banquet and learn there self-restraint, so that they may understand what they ought to seek and what they ought to reject, Jesus heals them.

He also spoke a parable to those invited, observing how they chose the first places at table, saying to them: “When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the first place, lest perhaps one more honourable than you has been invited by him; and he who invited you and him may come and say to you: Give this man place; and then you begin with shame to occupy the last [Col. 0406B] place. But when you are invited, go and recline in the lowest place; and when he who invited you comes, he may say to you: Friend, go up higher. Then you will have honour before those reclining at table.”

He explains what he has just added by saying: “For everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted.” Invited to the banquet, the Lord observed how all chose the more distinguished and first places at table, and how each desired to put and exalt himself before the others. He therefore spoke this parable to them. Taken literally, it is very useful and necessary for all who cultivate propriety and fear shame. It gives favour to those of lower rank and reverence to those of higher rank.

[Note: [Col. 0406D] Hence Proverbs 25:6–7: “Do not appear glorious before the king, and do not stand in the place of the great; for it is better that it be said to you, ‘Come up here,’ than that you be humbled before a prince.”]

But because it is called a parable, it signifies something besides the literal sense [Col. 0406C]. Let us therefore see what these weddings are and who those invited to the wedding are. These weddings take place daily in the Church. Daily the Lord makes weddings, because daily he joins faithful souls to himself: some come to baptism; others pass hence to the heavenly kingdoms. All of us who have received Christ’s faith and seal have been invited to these weddings.

Here is set before us that table of which it is said: “You have prepared before me a table against those who afflict me” (Ps. 22:5). Here are the loaves of offering; here the fattened calf; here the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world; here the living bread which came down from heaven; here the cup of the New Testament. Here the Gospels and the [Col. 0406D] Epistles of the Apostles, and here the books of Moses and the prophets, are set before us like dishes filled with every delight. What more, then, do we seek? [Col. 0407A] Why do we choose the first places? Wherever we sit, we abound in everything and lack nothing.

Nevertheless, whoever you are who seek the first places here, go and recline in the lowest place. Let not pride raise you up, knowledge puff you up, or nobility exalt you; but the greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you shall find favour before God, so that in his own time it may be said to you: “Friend, go up higher”; and then you will have honour before those reclining with you.

[Note: [Col. 0407C] Bede on this passage: “The Savior’s admonition is plainly clear according to the letter, teaching that humility is praiseworthy [Col. 0407D] not only before God but also before men. But because the Evangelist does not without reason call this a parable, we should briefly consider what it signifies mystically as well. That the union of Christ and the Church is called a wedding appears in many places. … Therefore whoever approaches these weddings when invited—that is, joins himself by the grace of faith to the members of the Church—should not recline in the first place: that is, he should not exalt himself as higher than others by glorying in his merits.”]

Moses reclined in the lowest place so far as he himself was concerned. When the Lord invited him to a higher place and wished to send him to the children of Israel, he answered: “I beseech you, Lord, send whom you will send; for I am not eloquent” (Exod. 4:13)—nor worthy, as though he said, of so great an office. Saul likewise, when he was humble in his own eyes, was established king by the Lord. So too Jeremiah, fearing to ascend to the first place, said: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God! Behold, I do not know how to speak, because I am a child” (Jer. 1:6).

Therefore the first place at table—the first place in the Church—is to be sought not by ambition but by humility, not by money [Note: [Col. 0407D] A. also adduces this against the Simoniacs.], but by virtues. Thus children, those unable to speak, and those still untaught and undisciplined should fear to ascend to it, lest perhaps it be said to them: “Give this man place,” and then you begin with disgrace to occupy the lowest place. “For everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted.”

[Note: [Col. 0407D] The homily ends here.]

### XXXIII.

“A certain man made a great supper and invited many.” [Note: [Col. 0407D] This is a homily falsely attributed to Eusebius of Emesa, for the second Sunday after Pentecost, p. 149.]

For this man is he himself who speaks these things, Jesus Christ our Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0407D] St Augustine, Sermon 12: “Who is this man but the man Christ Jesus, mediator between God and men?” Bede: “Who is this man but he of whom it is said through the prophet: ‘And he is a man; and who shall know him?’”]

[Col. 0407C] His great supper is these Gospels, which he himself prepared for us. We read them daily; in reading we eat, and our minds are refreshed. Great indeed is this supper, full of every delight, abundantly supplying everything to all. To this supper the Lord invited many: Jews, namely, and Gentiles—but the Jews first, then the Gentiles. Because the Jews would not come, the Gentiles were called.

Thus it is added: “And he sent his servants at the hour of supper to say to those invited that they should come, because now all things are ready. And they all began together to make excuses.” The Lord first sent his servants when [Col. 0408A] he said to his disciples: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, nor enter into the cities of the Samaritans; but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. As you go [187], preach, saying: The kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 10:5–7).

This is what is here said, “Because now all things are ready”: “Raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons; freely you have received, freely give” (ibid., 8 ff.). The servants went, therefore, and told those invited to come. But they all began together to make excuses.

Before Christ’s incarnation all the Jews had already been invited to this supper. The patriarchs and prophets also invited them to it. But they would not come.

[Note: [Col. 0408C] St Augustine, Sermon 112: “Who are the invited, except those called through the prophets sent beforehand? When? Long ago, from the time prophets were sent: they invite to Christ’s supper; they are therefore sent to the people of Israel. They were often sent; they often called them to come at the hour of supper. But those invited accepted. What does it mean, ‘the invited accepted’? They rejected the supper. They read the prophets and killed Christ.”]

Instead, all began together to make excuses. The first said: “I have bought a farm, and I must go out [Col. 0408B] and see it; I beg you, hold me excused.” Another said: “I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to try them; I beg you, hold me excused.” Another said: “I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.”

In the one who bought a farm we recognize avarice; in the one who bought five yoke of oxen, false religion; and in the one who married a wife, luxury and carnal pleasures.

[Note: [Col. 0408D] St Augustine, in the work cited: “There were three excuses. … In the purchased farm, dominion is denoted. … Oxen turn the earth; there are persons remote from faith … who do not wish to believe anything except what they attain through the fivefold sense of their body: ‘I do not wish,’ he says, ‘to believe except what I see.’ … ‘I have married a wife’: this is the pleasure of the flesh, which hinders many. … There are people who say: ‘It is not well for a man unless he has the delights of the flesh.’” See St Gregory, Homily 36 on the Gospels, and Bede.]

These three things separate many from the kingdom of God. He buys a farm who seeks this world’s possessions, riches, honours, and dignities. He desires to go out to this farm and always to look upon it who takes great pleasure in these things and places all his hope in them. If bishops and priests at some time urge better things upon such persons, they promise to do what is commanded them, but they raise impediments, [Col. 0408C] offer excuses, and ask that the clergy pray to God for them. What else is this but to say: “I beg you, hold me excused”?

The five yoke of oxen are the five books of Moses.

[Note: [Col. 0408D] St Ambrose, Book VII on Luke, no. 119: “The five yoke are the ten words, or the five books of the old law.”]

The Jews bought these; for their sake they were circumcised, and for their sake they offer tithes, firstfruits, and sacrifices. Yet they do not yet have them tested, because they do not yet understand them. For had they understood them, they would have had no excuse for not coming to this supper. But because they do not understand them, while pretending to venerate them, seeking to establish their own righteousness, they are not subject to the righteousness of God. For, as [Col. 0409A] the Apostle says: “They have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. 10:2).

Though they seek an excuse, they shall have none. For the Lord says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have had sin.”

[Note: [Col. 0409C] John 15:22: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin.”]

Those marry a wife who wholly subject themselves to luxury and carnal pleasures. Among them should not be counted those to whom the Apostle says: “Let those who have wives be as though they had none” (1 Cor. 7:29). Such persons indeed do not seek to be excused, because, loving this life alone, they regard another as nothing.

“And the servant returned and reported these things to his master.” Hence Isaiah: “Lord, who has believed our report?” (Isa. 53:1). Then the master of the house, angered, said to his servant: “Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor, the weak, [Col. 0409B] the blind, and the lame.”

Because the Jews would not come to the supper and would not believe, the Apostles are sent to the Gentiles. Hence the Apostle says: “It was necessary that the word of God be preached to you first; but because you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

The Gentiles were poor, weak, blind, and lame, because they had neither the riches of the law, the strength of virtues, nor the light of knowledge, and did not walk with straight feet in the way of God’s commandments.

[Note: [Col. 0409C] St Augustine, Questions on the Gospels, Book II, ch. 50: “In bringing to the supper those invited from the city, he signifies those from the Jewish people itself who believed. … But in commanding others to be brought from the hedges and roads, when there was still room, he signifies the Gentiles, because of the various paths of sects and the thorns of sins.” Bede on this passage: “When the Lord invites to supper from the lanes and streets, he denotes that people who had learned to hold the law amid urban life. But when he commands his guests to be gathered from roads and hedges, he seeks, plainly, to gather the rustic people—that is, the Gentiles.” These are Bede’s very words from St Gregory, Homily 36, no. 8.]

Yet when invited to Christ’s banquet they became rich and strong, were enlightened on earth, and now do not wander on the way but walk on a straight path.

“And the servant said: Lord, what you commanded has been done, and there is still room.” This place will be filled when this life [Col. 0409C] ends. For servants are still being sent daily, and believers still come to the supper: some hasten through baptism, others through repentance. No road, hedge, or place, whether hidden or open, has now been left to which Christ’s servants have not come in searching. Therefore those absent from this supper should ascribe it not to their servants’ negligence but to their own disobedience.

It follows: “But I say to you that none of those men [188] who were invited shall taste my supper.” None of those invited who would not come shall taste Christ’s supper. No one [Col. 0410A] shall enter with the saints into the fare of the eternal banquet.

### XXXIV.

“If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, wives and children, brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple; and whoever does not carry his cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.”

Since elsewhere the Lord says: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. 22:39; Mark 12:31), and not only this but also: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Luke 6:27), what does he mean now when he says that we must hate father and mother, wives and children, brothers and sisters, and our very lives? The Apostle John also says: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). And the Psalmist says: “He who loves [Col. 0410B] iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10:6).

It would follow, then, that only the wicked and murderers could be Christ’s disciples, since only those are his disciples who hate both their parents and themselves. This is unsuitable. Therefore let it be said: if father or mother, or any of your relatives, should wish to separate you from Christ’s faith, flee such a person; fear such a person as an enemy; hate such a person as a member of Satan. Thus Matthew says more plainly: “He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 18:9). And elsewhere: “If your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it away from you.”

[Note: [Col. 0409D] St Ambrose discusses and resolves the same objection more fully in the same manner, Sermon 15 on Psalm 118, introducing Christ as speaking thus, no. 18: “Therefore I did not command civil war among family ties, but I considered their enticement suspect. And was I not rightly suspicious, when that cunning and crafty serpent, in constructing the devices of his wickedness by which he might unsettle the affection of Adam, the first-born, founded upon the endowment of an uncorrupted and unspoiled nature, entrusted his work more to feminine allurements [Col. 0410C] than to his own poisons? … We have often known that a man whom the fearful display of executioners did not terrify, whom the furrow of his riven side did not break, whom burning plates could not draw away from the steadfastness of triumphant courage, was deceived when already set amid sacred rewards by a wife’s presentation of tender children, by the pitiable appeal of one tear. … Therefore there is a time to love and a time to hate: this is the time of martyrdom, when divine things must be preferred to every affection of family ties. It is a time of war, when we must even wage war for Christ’s name against faithless pledges. … Then he himself plainly explained in the Gospel on what ground we must hate our own people, saying: ‘He who loves father or mother more than me,’ etc.” The well-known words of St Gregory, Homily 37 on the Gospels, no. 2, are: “If we weigh the force of the command, we can do both things with discernment: so that we love those joined to us by kinship of the flesh, and whom we know as neighbours; and hate and flee those whom we suffer as adversaries in the way of God,” etc.]

He uses “life” for the bodily life. They hate their life who desire to die for righteousness and Christ’s faith, and who, crucifying their flesh with its vices and desires [Col. 0410C], pursue none of this life’s pleasures. Such persons also carry their cross after Christ, because, having left all things, they bear in their bodies only the mortification of the flesh and follow him with the whole desire of heart and mind.

But it is especially to be noted that he says: if anyone does not do this or that, “he cannot be my disciple.” For it is one thing to be a Christian and another to be Christ’s disciple. The Lord chose seventy-two disciples besides those whom he called apostles. These men, despising the world, leaving all things, and cleaving to the Lord, were specially called Christ’s disciples.
