Therefore those hold their name and place who imitate them in life and conduct.

Thus at the conclusion of this Gospel it is said: “So therefore every one of you who does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple.” Whoever, therefore, wishes to be and to be called Christ’s disciple should first sit down and calculate whether he can maintain the disciples’ life, possess patience, endure labour, build the tower with them, fight against enemies, and do the other things that follow. This is what he says: “For which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the necessary costs, whether he has enough to complete it, lest, after laying the foundation and being unable to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, saying, [Col. 0411B] ‘This man began to build and could not finish’?”

[Note: [Col. 0411D] See St Augustine, Epistle 243, and Questions on the Gospels, Book II, ch. 31.]

He begins to build a great tower who, despising the honours, riches, and dignities of the world, leaves all things and promises the life of the Apostles and the monastic way of life. But before entering upon so narrow and laborious a life, and beginning so great and difficult a work, he ought first to calculate.

[Note: [Col. 0411D] St Gregory, Homily 37, no. 6: “We ought to anticipate by careful reflection everything that we do.” See St Bernard, Treatise on Precept and Dispensation.]

He should also consider whether he has the resources necessary to finish: that is, whether he can maintain and preserve humility, patience, and obedience, without which the building cannot be built. For if he acts otherwise and begins to depart from his good purpose, all will begin to mock him, saying: “This man began to build and could not finish.” But what good did it do him to have begun? For not he who begins, but he who perseveres, shall be saved.

It follows: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, does not first sit down and consider whether he can meet with ten thousand the one who comes against him with twenty thousand? Otherwise, [189] while he is still far away, he sends an embassy and asks for terms of peace.”

This comparison is the same as the preceding one. We are warned by these words of nothing other than not to extend ourselves beyond our powers. Hence the Apostle says: “If he cannot control himself, let him marry; for it is better to marry than to burn. Each has his own gift from God” (1 Cor. 7:9). Let a person therefore first test himself, and so ascend to higher things. Let him be a servant if he cannot be a disciple. Not all are bishops, not all priests, not all [Col. 0411D] monks. For although, as the Apostle says, “We are all one body in Christ, yet all members do not have the same function” (Rom. 12:4–5).

Every faithful person is a king who knows how to govern himself and the army of virtues within him well. He makes war against another king, by whom we understand the devil. Although the devil has a larger army, we nevertheless overcome him easily if we trust not in our own strength but in God’s power. But [Col. 0412A] it should be known that the devil attacks more fiercely those whom he knows to be hastening toward greater things and nearer to God. Hence it is written: “My son, when you come to the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1). For this reason his food is said to be choice; for this reason he is said to have confidence that the Jordan flows into his mouth.

To send an embassy to him and make peace with him is to consent to his temptations. If a person yields to the first temptation, he makes peace while the enemy is still far away. There are many who do not make peace with him, although he is near and violently attacks them for a long time.

Therefore, just as those of whom we have spoken can neither build the tower nor fight against the enemy unless they first carefully consider with themselves whether they have resources for building and strength for fighting, so anyone who does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be Christ’s disciple. For a person renounces all things who, though possessing some things, nevertheless regards the loss of all things for Christ’s name, if necessary, as a small matter. The Apostles themselves had clothes and whatever footwear they possessed, but had already renounced them, because if necessary they did not fear to lose them together with life itself.

[Note: [Col. 0411D] St Gregory, Homily 37, no. 10: “Therefore let him leave all things who can. But he who cannot leave all things, while the king is still far off, should send an embassy of tears and offer gifts of alms. … For if you now possess nothing in this world by loving it, even while possessing, you have left all things.”]

### XXXV. [CHAPTER XV.]

“Now tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to him to hear him. And the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying: This man receives sinners and eats with them.”

For the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, says: “If anyone who is named a brother is a fornicator, or greedy, or an idolater, or abusive, or a drunkard, or a robber, do not even eat with such a person” [Col. 0412C] (1 Cor. 5:11). The Lord does so in order to convert; the Apostle, in order to terrify. The one terrifies his own people; the other calls outsiders. Both, therefore, are good: to terrify neighbours and to soften outsiders. We soften the latter so that they may convert; we terrify the former so that they may be ashamed and cease from evil.

Thus the Pharisees utterly abhorred sinners. But sinners are not to be abhorred; they are to be called. They are to be called either by gentleness or by threats. The Lord calls them by gentleness and by eating with them; the Apostle calls them by frightening them, refusing to eat with them.

It follows: “And he spoke this parable to them, saying: [Col. 0412D] Which of you, having a hundred sheep, if he loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after that which was lost until he finds it? And when he has found it, he lays it upon his shoulders rejoicing; and, coming home, he calls together his friends and neighbours, saying to them: Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep which was lost.”

What this signifies he himself subsequently says: “I tell you that there shall likewise be joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who do not need [Col. 0413A] repentance.”

We must therefore say what this man, the hundred sheep, the one lost sheep, and the wilderness signify, so that we may immediately know also what the ninety-nine righteous persons and the one sinner who repents signify. The hundred sheep signify the whole multitude of angels and human beings. One of these strayed when the first man sinned. Thus the Psalmist says: “I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant, Lord, for I have not forgotten your commandments” (Ps. 118:176).

The ninety-nine remained, by which the nine orders of angels are signified, since this whole number is composed of nines.

[Note: [Col. 0413C] St Hilary, On Matthew, ch. 18: “The one sheep must be understood as humanity, and under the one human being the whole race must be understood. But in Adam’s one error the entire human race went astray; therefore the ninety-nine that did not go astray must be understood as the multitude of heavenly angels, among whom there is joy in heaven and care for human salvation. Thus Christ is the one seeking humanity, and the ninety-nine left behind are the multitude of heavenly glory. Rightly, therefore, this number is added through the letter to Abraham and completed in Sarah,” etc. St Ambrose, Book VII on Luke, no. 208: “Is not Christ the shepherd? … Rich therefore is the shepherd, of whom all of us are the hundredth portion. He has countless flocks of angels, archangels, dominions, powers, thrones, and others, whom he left in the mountains.” St Peter Chrysologus teaches almost the same in Sermon 168.]

For this one, then, our Savior descended from heaven, leaving there the ninety-nine [190] of whom we have just spoken [Col. 0413B]. I say, leaving them there; and hence heaven is in this place called a wilderness. In a sense the Lord seemed to have left heaven when he dwelt bodily among human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0413D] Bede explains it somewhat differently here: “Because the number one hundred is perfect, he had one hundred sheep when he created the substance of angels and of human beings. But one sheep was lost when humanity, by sinning, left the pastures of life. He left the ninety-nine in the wilderness because he left the highest choirs of angels in heaven. But why is heaven called wilderness, except because ‘wilderness’ means something abandoned? Yet humanity left heaven when it sinned.”]

Laying this one sheep upon his shoulders—where burdens are carried—the Lord returned home rejoicing, ascended to heaven, made joy among his neighbours and friends, that is, the angels and archangels, and made joy as great as they had never had for all righteous persons who had never sinned. For it is very customary that, although we do not love him more, we nevertheless rejoice more greatly over one whom we have seen divinely rescued from a greater danger.

It follows: “Or what woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does not light a lamp, overturn the house, and search carefully [Col. 0413C] until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbours, saying: Rejoice with me, because I have found the drachma which I had lost.”

This comparison is the same as the preceding. The ten [Col. 0414A] drachmas signify the same thing as the hundred sheep; likewise, the one drachma and the one lost sheep signify the same thing. The nine remaining drachmas are the nine orders of angels. Since the king’s image is stamped upon a drachma, the human being is fittingly represented by the drachma, since humanity was made in the image of its King.

[Note: [Col. 0413D] St Gregory Nazianzen explains both parables as concerning Christ, Oration 42, p. 694: “Because that good shepherd came to the wandering sheep, laying down his life for the sheep, and went to the mountains and hills on which he sacrificed; he found the wandering sheep, and having found it, took it upon the same shoulders on which he bore the wood of the cross, restored it to the life above, and, having carried it there, placed it in the same number and order as those which had not strayed at all. Because he lit the lamp, that is, his flesh; overturned the house, namely cleansing the world from sin; sought the drachma, that is, the royal image buried beneath foul affections; and called to himself the friendly virtues because of the found drachma, making them sharers in his joy, as he had made them aware also of the Incarnation.” St Gregory, Homily 34 on the Gospels, no. 6: “He who is signified by the shepherd is also signified by the woman. For he is God and the wisdom of God. And because an image is stamped [Col. 0414D] upon a drachma, the woman lost the drachma when humanity, which had been made in God’s image, departed by sinning from the likeness of its Creator. But the woman lit a lamp because the wisdom of God appeared in humanity.” Bede copies these words of Gregory. St Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 169, explains otherwise: “The woman, that is, the Church, lights her lamp, that is, the inward gaze of her heart,” etc.]

Therefore the wisdom of God—for Christ is so called—came to seek this drachma and lit the lamp of his body. For divinity in flesh is light in a lamp. And he overturned the exceedingly spacious house of this world, as he himself says: “Do not think that I came to bring peace upon earth; I did not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10:34). For from this time there shall be five in one house: two shall be divided against three, and three against two.

Thus, in order to find this drachma, the Lord overturned this [Col. 0414B] house—that is, this world—setting discord between son and father, mother and daughter, mother-in-law and daughter-in-law, as some attacked faith and righteousness while others defended them. For previously no one fought for the faith.

[Note: [Col. 0414D] This statement of A. must be understood in the general sense called an appropriate distribution, as in not a few Scriptural statements: “All have turned aside”; “All who came before me are thieves and robbers,” etc. Otherwise, on this passage one should consult St Hilary, On Matthew, ch. 10, nos. 22 and 25; St Augustine, Questions on Matthew, Question 17, no. 3; St Jerome, etc.]

All had agreed in error. The Lord broke up this evil agreement, overturned the house, and found the drachma. Hence the Apostle says: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Cor. 11:19).

Therefore, over the finding of this drachma, all neighbours and friends—all virtues and dominions—rejoice together with the wisdom of God in heaven. Let the scribes and Pharisees then cease murmuring. Let them neither say nor reproach enviously that he receives sinners and eats with them. For the Lord came [Col. 0414C] to seek and save what was lost; and he came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.

### XXXVI.

[Note: [Col. 0414D] Luke XV, 12. This is Homily *Emis.* for the Saturday after the Second Sunday of Lent, p. 69, 2. From the exposition of the Gospel itself, its spurious attribution is recognizable.]

“A certain man had two sons; and the younger of them said to his father: Father, give me the portion of my estate which falls to me. And he divided his estate between them.”

The man here is understood to be God himself. Since man was made in his image and likeness, he does not disdain to be called a man. These two sons are two peoples, namely the Jewish people and the Gentiles.

[Note: [Col. 0415C] Everyone knows Jerome’s letter to Damasus (now Vallarsi edition, 21), in which he answers the question proposed by him: “Who is this father in the Gospel who divided his estate between two sons? Who are the two sons? Who is the elder, and who the younger?” and so forth. In that letter Jerome also discusses the two preceding parables, of the shepherd and of the lost drachma. Thus, at no. 4: “That God is called a man is established by many testimonies . . . But when he says ‘two sons,’ nearly all the Scriptures are full of mysteries concerning the calling of the two peoples.” Augustine, *Questions on the Gospels*, Book II, chap. 33: “The man having two sons is understood as God in relation to two peoples, as though two stocks of the human race: one, of those who remained in the worship of the one God; the other, of those who abandoned God so far as to worship idols.” See the first sermon of St Peter Chrysologus, entitled *On the Two Sons, the Prodigal and the Frugal*, and sermon 3, entitled *On the Same Sons, Representing the Jew and the Gentile*.]

Of these, the younger is the Gentile people, though younger not in age but in knowledge. Thus a child of a hundred years is cursed. Thus the Apostle says: “Do not become children in understanding; but be little children in malice” (I Cor. XIV, 20). Therefore they are called children and youths not only with regard to age, but with regard to knowledge and wickedness. For wisdom is more mature in understanding. The Jewish people, therefore, was the elder, since it was wiser and better.

Now this estate, which God—the Creator and Father of all things—divided to the younger and foolish son, that is, to the Gentile people, is understanding, memory, reason, perception, knowledge, and every capacity and possession of the soul.

[Note: [Col. 0415D] Jerome: “God’s estate is all that by which we live, understand, think, and burst forth into speech.” Augustine: “That by which the soul lives, understands, remembers, and excels in lively intelligence.”]

There is no estate like this; no riches can be compared with these riches. The Father divided them among both good and evil sons.

“And not many days later, after gathering everything together, the younger son went abroad into a far country; and there he squandered his estate in luxurious living.” Every country is far away if it is far from God; and one is far from God if one is far from faith, piety, mercy, and justice. Whoever approaches vices becomes far from these things.

[Note: [Col. 0415D] Augustine: “The far country, therefore, is forgetfulness of God.” Jerome: “It must therefore be understood that we are with God, or depart from him, not through distances of place but through disposition.”]

Thus anyone can quickly, and within not many days, set out for a far country. There the wretched man squanders his estate; there he loses the riches of his soul by living luxuriously amid vices and sins.

“And after he had consumed everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need.” When the virtues have been driven away, the soul is needy and perishes from hunger.

[Note: [Col. 0415D] Augustine: “The famine in that country is a lack of the word of truth.” Jerome: “He who holds back the truth in unrighteousness . . . has consumed all the goods of nature; and, when all have been consumed, he began to lack virtues, having abandoned the fountain of virtues.”]

Of this famine it is said through the prophet: “I shall send among you not a hunger for bread nor a thirst for water, but for hearing the word of God” (Amos VIII, 11). Great, therefore, is the famine in that country; great is the want in that breast in which no remembrance of God’s word is retained. And when this happens, the entire person is now handed over to the devil and wholly possessed by him.

Therefore it is added: “And he went and attached himself to one of the citizens of that country; and he sent him into his field to feed swine.” This citizen is understood to be the devil, the prince and head of all wicked persons. For there are many evil spirits; great is their city and assembly.

[Note: [Col. 0416C] Jerome: “Having abandoned his nourisher, who at the first word had lavishly bestowed every good upon him, he joined himself to such a prince, that is, to the devil, ruler of darkness . . . But when it says, ‘to one of the princes,’ it must be understood that there are many who fly about through this air and, by the deception of various vices, subject humankind to their service.”]

Wherever evil spirits dwell, there is the devil’s farm. The swine too are evil spirits, because they always delight in filth and in the dung of vices. Those who obey their will and fulfill their desires feed these swine. Therefore all who commit adultery, fornication, and other works of iniquity prepare abundant refreshment for these swine.

[Note: [Col. 0416D] Ambrose, Book VII on Luke, no. 216: “And he feeds swine: those, surely, into whom the devil asks to enter, whom he directs into the sea of this world, living amid dirt and stench.”]

“And he desired to fill his belly with the husks which the swine ate, and no one gave him any.” Pride, luxury, avarice, and such things are the husks by which evil spirits are nourished.

[Note: [Col. 0416D] The same, no. 217: “For those given to luxury have no other concern than to fill their belly; their god is their belly.” St Peter Chrysologus, sermon 1: “The food of demons is drunkenness, luxury, fornication, and every vice. These are alluring and wanton, and caress the senses with pleasure . . . The luxurious youth could not be satisfied by them, because pleasure is always hungry for itself and what has passed does not satisfy.”]

Sinners desire to fill their own bellies with these things because, through their excessive desire to sin, they cannot be satisfied with them. The more they sin, the more they desire to sin. This can be demonstrated in fornicators, the avaricious, and robbers, whose wicked desires never attain satisfaction. Hence it is said: “And no one gave him any.” Since they are not given as much as they wish to receive, it is said that no one gave them anything. They are therefore given what they want, but not as much as they want.

“But he came to himself and said: How many hired servants in my father’s house abound in bread, while I perish here from hunger!” Had he not been outside himself, he would not have been said to have returned to himself.

[Note: [Col. 0416D] Ambrose, no. 220: “He fittingly returns to himself, because he had departed from himself. For one who returns to the Lord restores himself to himself; and one who withdraws from Christ renounces himself.” St Peter Chrysologus, sermon 2: “He returned to himself: first he returned into himself in order that he might return to the father, since he had first departed from himself when he departed from the father.”]

He returned to himself, then, when he recovered his memory and remembered his father’s house. The hired servants in this place are called the scribes and Pharisees, who served the Lord more for the wages of tithes and offerings than from love.

[Note: [Col. 0417D] Ambrose, ibid.: “And who are the hired servants, unless they are those who serve for wages, who are from Israel, pursuing what is good not from zeal for uprightness or for virtue’s sake, but drawn by concern for profit?”]

They already then abounded in both spiritual and bodily bread in the Lord’s house, while the Gentile people, still standing outside, was perishing from hunger for spiritual nourishment. At length, returning to himself and led by repentance, he says: “I shall arise and go to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants.” And rising, he came to his father.

The Apostle says: “Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will give you light” (Ephes. III, 14). Thus this man arose, who had previously lain dead in sins, and came to his father. But how did he come except through repentance, a contrite heart, and a crushed spirit? By this way sinners return to the Lord.

“And while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion.” The most merciful Father, as soon as the son is pierced with remorse and begins to repent, though he is still far off, though he is still in sins, is moved with compassion and deigns to look upon his repentant son with a glad countenance.

[Note: [Col. 0417D] St Jerome: “And while he was still far off: before he had returned to the ancient Father through worthy works and true repentance.”]

“And running, he fell upon his neck and kissed him.” What else is signified here but peace and perfect reconciliation?

And the son said to him: “Father, I have sinned against heaven,” loving earth more than heaven; “and before you,” who are everywhere and see all things. “I am no longer worthy to be called your son,” having associated for so long a time with your enemies. “Make me as one of your hired servants.” I do not seek the seats of prophets, the crowns of saints, or the glory of virgins. Let me only be in your household, that I may be least in your kingdom, because your hired servants lack nothing.

Of these hired servants blessed Job speaks, saying: “As a stag desires the shade, and as a hired servant awaits the end of his work, so I too have had empty months and have counted laborious nights for myself” (Job VII, 2, 3).

“But the father said to his servants: Quickly bring forth the first robe and clothe him; put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet.” The first robe is immortality, which the first man lost by sinning; and, having lost it, he immediately realized that he was naked. This garment is recovered through baptism and repentance. Then a ring is given to the person, along with the pledge of faith: that is, a sign by which he is numbered in God’s army. Next sandals are given, that is, strength and authority, so that he may safely tread upon serpents and scorpions and upon every power of the enemy.

[Note: [Col. 0417D] St Jerome: “Bring forth the robe—the robe which Adam had lost by sinning . . . Give him the ring, the seal of Christ’s likeness, according to that saying: ‘Believing in him, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise’; and sandals upon his feet, so that the lurking serpent might not attack the sole of the foot as it stepped, and that he might walk more safely over scorpions and serpents.”]

Only then does he approach his father’s banquet, so as to deserve to receive Christ’s flesh and blood.

“And bring the fatted calf and kill it, that we may eat and feast; for this my son was dead and has come to life, was lost and has been found.” This fatted calf is Christ, full of every virtue and grace, taken from the herd of patriarchs and prophets. Although, as the Apostle says, he died once for us and “dies no more, and death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI, 9), nevertheless he is killed and eaten by the faithful as often as he is sacrificed in this sacrament of the altar.

[Note: [Col. 0417D] Jerome: “The fatted calf, sacrificed for the salvation of the repentant, is the Savior himself, upon whose flesh we are fed daily and whose blood we drink.” See also Augustine, the work cited above, no. 5.]

We eat this calf both bodily and mentally: mentally, indeed, by hearing and commemorating his passion. Through him we have been redeemed from death; through him we are daily reconciled to God.

It follows: “Now his elder son was in the field; and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. And he said to him: Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fatted calf because he has received him safe and sound.”

The Jewish people, returning from the field—from labor and the service of the Law—

[Note: [Col. 0418D] St Augustine, no. 6: “Meanwhile the elder son, the people of Israel according to the flesh, has not indeed gone into a far country, but he is nevertheless not in the house: he is in the field, that is, in the inherited abundance itself of the Law and the prophets, working rather earthly things . . . Coming from the field, he began to draw near to the house. That is, having rejected the labor of servile work, he began from those same Scriptures to contemplate the freedom of the Church. He hears music and dancing: namely, people full of the Spirit preaching the Gospel in harmonious voices.” St Jerome: “And now Israel asks: Why does God rejoice at the admission of the Gentiles? . . . The cause of joy is that, throughout the whole world, a single voice sings in harmony in praise of God: it is the salvation of the Gentiles, the salvation of sinners.”]

—when it was already drawing near to the house and the Church through faith, heard the music, dancing, and preaching of the apostles. When it asked what these things meant, it was told that the Gentile people, having come to know the truth and been redeemed by Christ’s blood, had been converted to the faith, and that God was now not only the God of the Jews but also of the Gentiles.

“Therefore he became angry and would not go in.” This is what is read in the Acts of the Apostles: when “Peter had come to Jerusalem, those who were of the circumcision disputed with him, saying: Why did you go in to men who have the foreskin and eat with them?” (Acts XI, 23). Peter recounted to them everything that had occurred and how the Gentiles had believed. This elder brother therefore signifies that portion of the Jews which, in the primitive Church, was scandalized against the apostles at the conversion of the Gentile people. Much is said about them in the Acts of the Apostles and in Paul’s Epistles.

“Then his father went out and began to entreat him.” For all the arguments which the apostles gave to the Jews concerning the conversion of the Gentiles—what else were they but, in a sense, proclamations and entreaties of almighty God? Such is the Apostle’s statement: “For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, for the same Lord of all is rich toward all who call upon him” (Rom. X, 12)—“for all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. III, 23).

“But he answered and said to his father: Behold, for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your command; yet you have never given me even a kid, that I might feast with my friends. But when this son of yours, who has devoured his estate with harlots, came, you killed the fatted calf for him.”

The elder son partly lies and partly tells the truth. In saying that the father killed the fatted calf for the son who returned, he tells the truth. But he lies in boasting that he has never transgressed God’s command.

[Note: [Col. 0419D] Ambrose, no. 240: “He is shameless, and like that Pharisee who justified himself in an arrogant prayer and thought that he had never transgressed God’s command because he kept the Law in its letter; he is impious because he accused his brother,” etc. Jerome: “The father humbly entreats him toward concord; but he, pursuing the righteousness which is in the Law, does not submit to God’s righteousness . . . as though it were not itself a transgression of the command to envy another’s salvation and to boast before God of one’s righteousness, since no one is clean before him. Thus this may also be said in the person of one who, according to the same Apostle, had lived blamelessly in the righteousness which is in the Law; though it seems to me that the Jew is boasting rather than speaking the truth, after the example of that Pharisee who said: ‘God, I thank you,’ etc.” Chrysologus, sermon 4, on this passage: “The envious person always pretends; the envious person always lies.” See Augustine, the work cited above, no. 8.]

Moreover, he seems ungrateful when, forgetting the many sacrifices by which he was daily cleansed, he complains that he has never received even one kid from his father.

[Note: [Col. 0420D] Ambrose, ibid.: “It seems that the kid is also sought because the Jews have lost the rite of the old sacrifice.”]

These things are set forth as though he had said them because that Jewish people, converted to faith, could think them when it saw Jews rejected and Gentiles chosen. For who would not wonder that so great a change had occurred: that the Lord should permit the Jews, whom he had loved so greatly, to perish in their blindness, and should surrender his only-begotten Son to death for the Gentile people, whom he had hated? But in thinking these things, we too speak, as it were indignant together with the elder son, against God’s ordering.

Nor is it especially surprising if Jews newly converted to the faith had been unwilling to associate with Gentiles, when the Law had utterly forbidden them such association. Therefore he is not reproved here for this indignation; rather, after giving the reason, the father seeks to calm him, saying: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But we had to feast and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.”

For according to some, that people was always with God; and according to others, it was not with God.

[Note: [Col. 0420D] Augustine, on the words “I have never transgressed your command,” no. 8, writes: “This son is not to be understood as representing all Israelites, but those who never turned away from the one God to idols.”]

Hence the Apostle says: “Blindness has happened in part to Israel” (Rom. XI, 25). Likewise, when Elijah said: “They have killed your prophets and undermined your altars, and I alone remain, and they seek my life,” the Lord said to him: “I have reserved for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal” (III Kings XIX, 20).

Of these and such persons the Lord therefore says: “Son, you are always with me.” It is of persons such as these that it is said concerning the Church that she has neither spot nor wrinkle. For if one considers her universality, the Church has many spots. Such sons are said to possess an inheritance, and to such persons every possession of the Father is due—sufficient and necessary for blessedness. Finally, all that belongs to God is in some sense ours, if we ought to possess it in such a way that we do not wish to possess it otherwise.

[Note: [Col. 0420D] See St Augustine, the work cited above, no. 10. And here the homily ends.]

But he also said to his disciples:

### XXXVII. [CHAPTER XVI.]

“A certain man was rich and had a steward; and this man was accused before him of having squandered his goods. And the master called him and said to him: What is this that I hear about you? Render an account of your stewardship, for you can no longer be steward. But the steward said within himself: What shall I do, since my master is taking the stewardship from me? I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg. I know what I shall do, so that, when I have been removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses. Therefore, having summoned each of his master’s debtors, he said to the first: How much do you owe my master? And he said: A hundred measures of oil. And he said to him: Take your bond, sit down quickly, and write fifty. Then he said to another: And you, how much do you owe? He said: A hundred cors of wheat. He said to him: Take your documents and write eighty. And the master praised the steward of unrighteousness because he had acted shrewdly.”

These matters are plain according to the letter, and it is unnecessary to expound them one by one. Let the Lord himself, however, say for what purpose he gave this parable.

[Note: [Col. 0420D] This parable was explained by St Jerome, Letter 121, in the recension of Vallarsi, question 6; St Peter Chrysologus, sermons 125, 126, etc.]

“For the children of this age are shrewder in their generation than the children of light.” The Lord praises not the unrighteousness of the steward but his shrewdness. He praises him not for the fraud he committed, but for the ingenuity by which he provided for himself for the future.

[Note: [Col. 0420D] St Augustine, *Questions on the Gospels*, Book II, chap. 34: “In the steward whom his master was ejecting from the stewardship, and whom he praised because he had provided for himself for the future, we must not take everything as an object of imitation. For we must not commit fraud against our Lord in any respect, so as to make alms from that fraud; nor is it right to understand as debtors of God and our Lord those by whom we wish to be received into eternal dwellings . . . Yet these parables are also spoken by contrast, so that we may understand that, if he who committed fraud could be praised by his master, how much more will those who perform such works according to God’s command please the Lord God.” St Ambrose, no. 245: “Although he sinned, yet because through his master’s indulgence he sought help for himself in the future, he is commended.”]

For, not knowing how he would live, since he could not dig and was ashamed to beg, he found this singular expedient: he who had previously squandered his master’s goods would commit this final fraud. He is praised, therefore, not for any goodness but for cunning and the craft of defrauding: since he could no longer seize and carry off his master’s goods by stealing, he took them away by concealing and hiding them.

Not only the steward’s master, but the Lord of all, seems to applaud this shrewdness when he says: “The children of this age are shrewder in their generation than the children of light.” They are shrewder in evil than these are in good. For scarcely any saints are found who possess as much prudence in acquiring eternal goods as these persons possess cunning in acquiring temporal and fleeting goods. Day and night they keep watch, labor, distress themselves, and through frauds, robberies, thefts, betrayals, perjuries, murders, and such things never cease to heap up riches of this kind. Indeed, who could say how much shrewdness and cunning the children of this age display in mutually deceiving one another?

Let the children of light, then, hear these things and be ashamed to be outdone by the children of this age. These things were written so that they might become wiser by hearing, not so that, by imitating the steward of unrighteousness, they might perpetrate fraud or injustice in any matter.

Hence it follows: “And I say to you: Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness”—but not in the way in which the steward of unrighteousness made friends for himself: not by defrauding others of their possessions, but by giving away your own. For all riches are unrighteous which, kept avariciously, harm their own possessors, or which are not distributed equitably. You distribute them equitably when you retain only as much as can suffice for you, and give the rest to those in need.

Hence the Apostle says: “For it is not that there should be relief for others and affliction for you, but by equality: in the present time let your abundance supply their lack, that their abundance also may be a supply for your lack” (II Cor. VII, 13). In this it is plainly shown that we are commanded to give not what is necessary, but what is superfluous. The Apostle does not wish us to be so prodigal in giving that we ourselves afterward suffer want.

Thus, riches that are in themselves unrighteous, if distributed in this manner, produce for us eternal friends and eternal dwellings. Riches are in themselves unrighteous because, unless distributed, they are not equitable; but once distributed, they are no longer so. They are unrighteous, therefore, as long as they remain riches. For things reserved not for excess but for necessity are not called riches. If, therefore, you remove their superfluity, you also remove the name of unrighteousness.

It follows: “He who is faithful in what is least is faithful also in what is greater; and he who is unrighteous in a little is unrighteous also in a greater thing.” These words are specifically spoken of the apostles and, through them, of the other stewards and prelates of the Church. Hence at the beginning of this Gospel it is said that the Lord spoke these things to his disciples.

Greater affairs of the Church, therefore, ought not to be entrusted and committed to persons who have not proved faithful in private life and have not displayed works of piety and mercy from the little that they possessed. But we need not doubt that those whom we see willingly helping others from the little they possess will be faithful in a priorship. For this reason the Apostle commands that bishops be not covetous nor pursuers of shameful gain. Thus, in electing superiors, one must consider carefully what they have been like in small matters and what piety and mercy they have possessed, since those who are not faithful in little matters are not faithful in great ones either.

Hence it is added: “If, therefore, you have not been faithful in unrighteous mammon, who will entrust to you that which is true?” If you have not exercised mercy from riches which are fleeting, deceptive, and passing, who would dare to entrust and commit to you the stewardship and governance of the Church—which are true, just, holy, and must be administered without deceit?

“And if you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is your own?” Those things are alien and not ours which we possess in such a way that we always fear losing them. But ours are the things of which we are secure and never fear to lose. Temporal riches, therefore, are alien, but eternal riches are ours if we are good and have not placed our hope in temporal things. Yet those things that are ours and have been predestined for us will not be given to us if we have not been faithful in this alien thing.

[Note: [Col. 0422D] St Irenaeus, Book II, chap. 34, no. 3: “Therefore the Lord said to those who were ungrateful toward him: ‘If you have not been faithful in what is little, who will give you what is great?’ signifying that those who have proved ungrateful in the small matter of temporal life toward him who bestowed it will justly not receive from him, unto ages of ages, length of days.”]

For they were given and predestined for us on this condition: that the virtue of this faithfulness should be found in us.

XXXVIII. [Note: [Col. 0422D] This parable (or history, as St Ambrose judges) is also explained by Chrysostom, Homily 65, and likewise by St Gregory, Homily 40.] “There was a certain rich man, and he was clothed in purple and fine linen, and feasted splendidly every day.”

These words are very necessary both for the rich and for the poor, because they give fear to the former and consolation to the latter. Here the rich hear their punishments; the poor too hear their joys. “And there was a certain beggar, named Lazarus, who lay at his gate, full of sores, desiring to be filled with the crumbs which fell from the rich man’s table; and no one gave to him.” For the names of the saints are written in heaven; but the names of the wicked are not written in the book of life. Hence in this passage the rich man’s name is not stated [Col. 0422D], but the beggar’s is. This man is called Lazarus; what the other was called we do not know. For to such persons the Lord will say: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you.” What wonder, then, if we do not know him whom He who knows all things does not know? [Note: [Col. 0422D] Bede, on this passage, Homily 40, etc.: “Certainly, among the people the names of rich men are usually better known than those of the poor. Why then is it that, speaking of the poor man and the rich man, the Lord gives the poor man’s name but does not give the rich man’s name? … It is as though He were plainly saying: I know the humble poor man; I do not know the proud rich man. I acknowledge the one by approval; I am ignorant of the other through the judgment of reprobation.” These are the words of St Gregory, Homily 40, no. 3.]

Each sees the other in turn [Col. 0423A], so that the ungodliness of the one may be made manifest and the patience of the other may increase. The latter sees the former abounding in delights; the former sees the poor man wasting away in want. The one feasts; the other is tormented. Nor would the former have sinned so greatly had he not seen the latter; nor would the latter have been so greatly tormented had he not looked upon the former’s luxuries. [Note: [Col. 0423D] Bruno took this from Bede, as Bede had taken it from St Gregory’s same homily, no. 4.] Thus each was an evil to the other: the one a temporal evil, the other an eternal one.

Yet the poor man had this one consolation: dogs came and licked his sores. For a dog’s tongue is a kind of medicine, and by licking it heals wounds. “And it came to pass that the beggar died, and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died and was buried in hell.” For Abraham, like the other patriarchs and prophets, was in hell [Col. 0423B], though he did not suffer hell’s punishments. Abraham’s bosom, therefore, is understood to be that place in which the saints rested gathered together; hell is the place of punishments, where the souls of the wicked are tormented.

“And lifting up his eyes, when he was in torments, he saw Abraham afar off, and Lazarus in his bosom.” This is what the Lord says: “For with the same measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured to you again” (Matt. VII.2; Luke VII.28; Mark IV.34). Yet the rich man’s torments are greater than Lazarus’s sores would have been. Behold: the rich man now begins to see Lazarus above him—and so far above him that he cannot see him unless he raises his eyes. He sees Abraham; he also sees Lazarus in Abraham’s bosom; and though he is set far away, he nevertheless sees all the riches laid before them. He sees, and desires; he is tormented, and there is no one to pity him [Col. 0423C]. Indeed, he is tormented all the more as he contemplates greater delights. For sight often produces desire, and we are accustomed to desire less those things which we do not see.

Therefore he says: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame.” Lazarus desired crumbs of bread from the rich man’s table; the rich man sought a drop of water from Lazarus’s finger. [Note: [Col. 0423D] Bede: “In this life Lazarus sought the crumbs falling from the rich man’s table … now, concerning the rich man’s punishment, it is said that he desires water to be distilled into his mouth from the tip of Lazarus’s finger. He who would not give even the least thing from his table has, being placed in hell, come to seek even the least things.” This is nearly taken from St Gregory, Homily 40, no. 5.]

But why from Lazarus’s finger? Perhaps because he feared that Lazarus would accuse him, and hoped by such words to incline toward mercy the one whom he had offended; or because he is permitted to see no one but that very man on whose account he is tormented. For the wicked are not allowed to see what they wish, though the good are allowed to see, hear, and possess whatever they wish. In vain, however, does he seek mercy who did not show mercy.

Therefore it continues: “And Abraham said to him: Son, remember that thou didst receive good things in thy lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted, and thou art tormented.” Hence the Lord says: “Woe to you rich, who have your consolation” (Luke VII.24); and, “Blessed are the poor, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (ibid., 20). Riches, therefore, lead to misery; poverty to blessedness. Heaven is opened to the poor, hell to the rich. [Note: [Col. 0423D] Bede: “Abraham’s bosom is the rest of blessed poor persons [Col. 0424D], whose is the kingdom of heaven, into which they are received after this life; the burial of hell is the depth of punishments, which devours the proud and merciless after this life.”] That is, to the rich who use such riches badly.

[Col. 0424B] “And in all these things a great chasm is fixed between us and you, so that those who wish to pass from here to you cannot; nor can they cross from there to here.” This great chasm is God’s ordinance, so firm and stable that it cannot at all be changed contrary to God’s will. Therefore the good cannot pass to the wicked in pity, nor do the wicked wish to cross over to the good. The good do, however, wish through compassion to pass to them, if God wills it; but because God does not will this, such compassion itself fails in them. [Note: [Col. 0424D] St Gregory, Homily 40 on the Gospels, no. 7: “Just as the reprobate desire to pass over to the elect—that is, to depart from the affliction of their punishments—so it belongs to the minds of the righteous to pass over through mercy to the afflicted and tormented, and to wish to free them. But those who wish to pass from the seat of the blessed to the afflicted and tormented cannot do so, because the souls of the righteous, though they have mercy in the goodness of their nature, are then joined to the justice of their Creator and constrained by such uprightness that they are moved by no compassion toward the reprobate. For they agree with that Judge to whom they cling; and toward those whom they cannot rescue, they do not condescend even through mercy.”] For their whole will rests in God’s will.

“And he said: Therefore I ask thee, father, to send him to my father’s house. For I have five brethren, that he may testify to them, lest they also come into this place of torments.” This conversation between Abraham and the rich man was carried on not by sound of voice but by the mere knowledge of the mind [Col. 0424C]. The good indeed know all things; but to the wicked it is granted to know only those things by which their punishment may grow and increase. Thus this rich man is more tormented by concern for his brothers, fearing that they too may suffer the like. Had he wholly forgotten them, he would have had somewhat less torment.

“And Abraham said to him: They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them.” It is sufficient for them to hear these, if they are willing to believe them; for the books of Moses and the Prophets alone suffice for everyone’s salvation, provided they are rightly understood. But he said: “No, father Abraham; but if one should go to them from the dead, they will repent.” And he said to him [Col. 0425A]: “If they do not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe if one rises from the dead.”

For this reason the Jews refuse to believe in Christ the Lord risen from the dead even to this day: because they do not hear Moses and the prophets. Hence the Lord Himself says: “If you believed Moses, you would indeed believe me; for he wrote of me” (John V.46).

If these things are understood allegorically, this rich man signifies the Jewish people. [Note: [Col. 0425D] St Gregory, cited above, no. 2: “Whom, dearest brethren, does this rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day signify, if not the Jewish people, who had an outward observance of life, who used the delights received from the Law for display rather than for profit?” Bede copies these words of Gregory.] For the Jewish people alone, enriched by the wealth and delights of the Law and the Prophets, despised all others and would share with no one the spiritual food in which they abounded. This is the vice under which that people labours even now: it conceals everything as though revealing it would cause its loss. It was clothed in purple in its kings and in fine linen in its priests.

[Col. 0425B] Its five brothers are understood as the five divisions of the people: namely kings, priests, scribes, Pharisees, and the remaining multitude of the people. But the beggar—that is, Lazarus, whose name means “helped” [Note: [Col. 0425D] St Gregory, cited above, and Bede: “Hence Lazarus is rightly interpreted ‘helped.’”]—whom the Lord helped and delivered from the danger of death, is the Gentile people. [Note: [Col. 0425D] St Gregory and Bede: “Whom does Lazarus, full of sores, figuratively represent if not the Gentile people? … Wounded Lazarus desired to be filled with the crumbs falling from the rich man’s table, and no one gave to him, because that proud people despised admitting any Gentile to knowledge of the Law [Col. 0426D]. Since it held the teaching of the Law not for charity but for self-exaltation, it swelled, as it were, over its received wealth. And because words flowed from it through knowledge, crumbs, as it were, fell from its table.”]

Formerly needy and poor in heavenly goods, it desired to know the truth and understand God. But no one gave to it: no one revealed to it the mysteries of truth. Yet at last dogs came—at last Christ’s apostles came—and licked its sores and healed them by licking. For, like dogs, apostles and teachers bear medicine in their tongues, because they heal by preaching. [Note: [Col. 0426D] St Gregory and Bede: “Dogs licked the wounds of the poor man lying there. In sacred discourse, dogs are sometimes understood as preachers. For a dog’s tongue, while it licks a wound, heals it,” etc.]

Let us see what follows: “And it came to pass that the beggar died [Col. 0425C] and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died and was buried in hell.” For Jews and Gentiles die daily; Christians are daily carried to heaven; Jews are daily buried in hell. There, while sensing their torments, they reflect upon the sins they committed, how foolish and unbelieving they were, how greatly they departed from the faith and righteousness of Abraham their father. And while they desire, if possible, to be helped by the Gentile people; and while Abraham considers their vain and useless desires and their late repentance, Abraham in some sense speaks with them, is asked by them, and answers them. For knowledge alone suffices for them to converse concerning whatever they wish. But because they despair of their own salvation [Col. 0425D], they fear for their brothers and pray that they may not be deceived and suffer the same things.

XXXIX. [CHAPTER XVII.] [Col. 0426A] “But which of you, having a servant ploughing or feeding cattle, will say to him when he has returned from the field, ‘Come at once, sit down at table’; and will not say to him, ‘Prepare what I may eat, gird thyself, and serve me until I eat and drink, and afterward thou shalt eat and drink’? Does he thank that servant because he did what he commanded him? I think not. So you also, when you have done all that is commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done.’”

How necessary this comparison was for the man who said: “God, I thank thee that I am not like other men—extortioners, unjust, adulterers—or even like this publican. I fast twice in the Sabbath; I give tithes of all that I possess” (Luke XVIII.11–12). How much better it would have been for him humbly to say [Col. 0426B]: “Lord, I am thy unprofitable servant; I have done what I ought to have done.” For when a servant serves his master from obligation and necessity, the master owes him no thanks if he does what he commanded.

So also when we have done all that has been commanded us, let pride flee, vain glory cease, and arrogance of mind be removed; and let us humbly prostrate ourselves among the unprofitable servants. [Note: [Col. 0426D] St Ambrose, Book VIII, no. 31: “Let no one glory in works, because we rightly owe service to the Lord. … Let us not demand praise from ourselves, nor forestall God’s judgment and anticipate the Judge’s sentence.”] Thus did the man who said: “My soul is as land without water before thee” (Ps. CXLII.6). For land without water is dry, barren, fruitless, and useless.

Yet he had done all that had been commanded him, according as he himself says: “I have not departed from thy commandments” [Note: [Col. 0426D] Ps. CXVIII.51: “I have not departed from thy law.”]; and: “I have not forgotten thy statutes” (Ps. CXVIII.141).

XL. “And it came to pass, while he was going to Jerusalem, that he passed through the midst of Samaria and Galilee. And as he entered a certain village, ten leprous men met him.”

For what are the ten leprous men but all sinners? Because this number contains all numbers within itself, ten is frequently used for all. Thus it is said of the saints in the Apocalypse: “Behold, the devil is about to cast some of you into prison, that you may be tried and may have tribulation for ten days” (Apoc. II.10), that is, for all days. For every person who counts, after he has reached ten, has nothing further to say unless he begins again from the beginning. [Note: [Col. 0426D] St Augustine, Sermon 270, no. 3: “A certain perfection seems to be represented in this number ten. For the person counting proceeds as far as that number, and then returns from one to ten, again to the beginning.” On this same number see Sermon 51, no. 34; Sermon 83; Sermon 251, p. 253; etc.] Therefore it is evident that ten and all are the same.

As regards the soul, all human beings were leprous when Christ the Lord came [Col. 0426D]; as regards the body, not all were so. Every fornicator, adulterer, murderer, perjurer, and sacrilegious person is leprous in soul. [Note: [Col. 0427D] St Augustine, Book II, Questions on the Gospels, ch. 40, and St Gregory, Book V of the Morals, ch. 11, etc., interpret these lepers especially as heretics.] Moses commands that lepers be cast out beyond the camp. “But with adulterers and fornicators,” says the Apostle, “do not even take food” (I Cor. V.11). Those whom we excommunicate on account of their wickedness, we cast out beyond the camp as lepers. For leprosy of the soul is far worse than leprosy of the body.

But let us see what follows: “They stood afar off and lifted up their voice, saying: Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.” They stood afar off because men such as these did not dare approach nearer. Likewise, we stand afar off so long as we persist in sins. Therefore, that we may be healed and cured of the leprosy of our sins, let us cry with a loud voice and say: “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.”

[Col. 0427B] Yet let us cry not with the mouth but with the heart; for the heart’s voice is louder. The cry of the heart pierces the heavens and rises more loftily before God’s throne. “When he saw them, he said: Go, show yourselves to the priests.” God’s looking upon them is His having mercy. He sees them and immediately, having pity upon them, commands them to go to the priests—not that the priests might cleanse them, but that they might judge them to be clean. For the Law commands (Lev. XIII) that if a leprous mark appears on a person, he be brought to the priest and, by the priest’s judgment, be separated for seven days. Then the priest examines him; and if he sees that the leprosy has not increased, he shall judge him clean.

“But all these things,” as the Apostle says, “happened to them in a figure; but they were written for our correction” [Col. 0427C] (I Cor. X.11). For we also separate sinners in many ways. Some from foods which they had previously lawfully used; others from Christ’s body and blood; others from entry into the church; and others from our communion. We separate some for seven days, some for more or fewer days or years; and if in them we see that the leprosy has not increased, that vices have failed and sins have died away, we judge them clean and reconcile them to the Church. This, therefore, is the reason why the Lord commanded these lepers to go to the priests. [Note: [Col. 0427D] See Augustine, cited above.]

“And it came to pass, while they went, they were cleansed.” Let sinners hear this and understand it carefully. It is easy for the Lord to forgive sins. For often a sinner’s debts are remitted before he comes to the priest. In one and the same hour he repents and is healed. For a sinner, in whatever hour he is converted, shall live and shall not die. Yet let him see how he repents; let him see how he is converted. Let him hear what the Lord says: “Turn to me with all your heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning; and rend your hearts and not your garments” (Joel II.12).

Therefore let everyone who is converted be converted inwardly [Col. 0428A], in the heart. [Note: [Col. 0428D] Augustine, *On True and False Repentance*, ch. 10, among Augustine’s works; collected in *On Repentance*, Distinction 1: “Whoever repents, then, let him repent wholly and show his sorrow by tears; let him present his life to God through the priest; let him forestall God’s judgment by confession. For the Lord commanded those who had been cleansed to show their faces to the priests,” etc.] For God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart.

But see how obedient these lepers were. The Lord commanded them to go to the priests. They still saw themselves to be leprous; they still felt their sickness; nevertheless they went to the priests because they believed that the Lord had not commanded this to them without purpose. Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Syria, was not so obedient. When Elisha commanded him to wash himself seven times in the Jordan, he would not comply, but went away indignant—until, taking better counsel, he did what the prophet had commanded. He washed and was cleansed. Perhaps these lepers had heard this and, warned by his example, understood what faith and obedience can accomplish.

But one of them [Col. 0428B], when he saw that he was cleansed, returned with a loud voice glorifying God; and he fell upon his face at Christ’s feet, giving thanks; and he was a Samaritan. By him are figured all those who, after they have been cleansed by baptismal water or healed through repentance, no longer follow the devil but imitate Christ: they follow Him, glorify Him, worship Him, give Him thanks, and do not depart from His service.

And Jesus answered: “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner?” This is what He says elsewhere: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XXX.16). For many are baptized, many are cleansed from the leprosy of sins; but because they do not follow Christ and return again to sins, they will not be reckoned among the elect. The good are indeed very few in comparison with the wicked. But because this man was a foreigner, he signifies that more will be saved from the Gentiles than from the Jews.

“And he said to him: Arise, go thy way; for thy faith has made thee whole.” Great, therefore, is the power of faith, without which, as the Apostle says, it is impossible to please God (Heb. XI.6). For Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness. Faith therefore saves; faith justifies; faith heals the human being inwardly and outwardly. [Note: [Col. 0428D] Thus far the homily.]

XLI. “And when he was asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them and said: The kingdom of God does not come with observation. Neither shall they say: Behold here, or behold there.”

Those things come to us with such observation whose coming has been so determined for us that we can foresee, guard against, and observe them. But no one knows the day and hour when the Lord will come for judgment. He will come suddenly, seize all things at once, and in a single moment be here, there, and everywhere. [Note: [Col. 0428D] Bede, on this passage: “Because when it comes can be observed neither by angels nor by human beings; whereas the time of the Lord’s Incarnation, fixed beforehand by the most certain prophecies, was made known by angelic proclamations.”]

“For behold, the kingdom [Col. 0429A] of God is within you.” Do not seek it, then, because it is unknown to all. Let this suffice you: the kingdom of God is within you; it reigns among you, and God your Lord dwells among you.

And He said to His disciples: “Days will come when you will desire to see one day of the Son of Man, and you shall not see it.” For in the person of the apostles He speaks to those who shall live in the time of Antichrist. Such calamity will come upon them that they will desire to die and long for the last day. This one day is called the day of the Son of Man, concerning which it is written: “For one day in thy courts is better than thousands” (Ps. LXXXIII.11). For there shall then be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor shall be. The saints will desire to see this day, but will not see it until it is revealed in its proper time.

[Col. 0429B] “And they will say to you: Behold here, behold there. Do not go, nor follow them.” If, He says, they tell you, “Behold, Christ is present; He is in this or that place,” do not believe them. Why? Do you wish to hear why? “For as lightning flashing from under heaven shines unto the regions under heaven, so shall the Son of Man be in his day.” As the sun’s brightness is seen and shines not in one part only but throughout all that is under heaven, so also the Son of Man in His day shall appear not here or there, but everywhere at once.

XLII. [CHAPTER XVIII.] “And he spoke a parable to them, because it is necessary always to pray and never to grow weary.”

For the person who perseveres in good always prays. One prays not only with the tongue but also with heart, thought, understanding, hands, eyes, and every good work. [Note: [Col. 0429D] Bede, on this passage: “Either we must say that one always prays and does not grow weary when, at the canonical hours each day, according to the rite of ecclesiastical tradition, one does not cease to praise and petition the Lord with the customary psalmody and prayers; … or certainly that all things which a righteous person does and says according to God are to be reckoned as prayer.” See St Augustine, Letter 130 to Proba, ch. 9, no. 18; and Sermon 115.] If these cease to pray [Col. 0429C], every prayer of the tongue is useless.

He said: “There was a certain judge in a city who did not fear God and did not respect man. There was a widow in that city, and she came to him saying, ‘Avenge me of my adversary.’ And he would not for a long time. But afterward he said within himself: ‘Although I do not fear God or respect man, yet because this widow troubles me, I will avenge her.’”

This, therefore, is the reason why we should always pray and never grow weary. You prayed once and were not heard: pray again and again; indeed, pray continually—provided that you pray rightly—until your prayer is heard. For in many matters our prayer is heard in this life, and in many after this life. [Col. 0429D]

This comparison, however, is drawn from opposites [Col. 0430A], that is, from the just and the unjust. [Note: [Col. 0429D] St Augustine, Book II, *Questions on the Gospels*, ch. 45—whose words Bede here copies: “The Lord presents parables either according to some similarity … or proves something from the very dissimilarity. … Thus this unjust judge is employed not from similarity but from dissimilarity, so that the Lord might show how much more assured those ought to be who persevere in asking God, the fountain of justice and mercy—or if anything more excellent can be said or heard—when the persistence of a petitioner has prevailed even with the most unjust judge until the effect of fulfilling his desire.”] For if an iniquitous and unjust judge, wearied by the widow’s many petitions, finally avenged her against her adversary, much more will God, who is most just, hear the prayers of His saints and take vengeance on their enemies.

This is what follows: “Hear what the judge of injustice says. And shall not God avenge his elect, who cry to him day and night, and shall he have patience with them? I say to you that he will avenge them speedily.” Although this vengeance is sometimes not carried out in this life, it is nevertheless carried out speedily, because this life passes quickly.

But how did the judge of injustice, who fears neither God nor man, show that he feared the woman’s accusation? In a certain manner he both feared and did not fear. [Col. 0430B] He feared God because of punishments, but did not fear through love. Of this fear it is written: “The holy fear of the Lord endures for ever and ever” (Ps. XVIII.10). The unjust judge did not have this fear; he feared only future punishments.

It follows: “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you think that he will find faith on the earth?” I have spoken, He says, of one judge of injustice; yet the followers of injustice are far more numerous than the followers of faith and righteousness—so much more numerous that, in comparison with them, the latter seem scarcely to exist. [Note: [Col. 0430D] St Augustine, *On the Unity of the Church*, ch. 13, on “the Son of Man,” etc.: “We understand this to have been said either because of the perfection of faith itself, which is so difficult among human beings that even in its wondrous saints, as in Moses himself, something may be found in which they trembled or could have trembled; or because of that abundance of the wicked and scarcity of the good.”] “For because iniquity has abounded, the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. XXIV.11). But these things refer chiefly to Christ’s coming, when Antichrist reigns: unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved [Col. 0430C].

XLIII. “And he spoke this parable to certain persons who trusted in themselves as righteous and despised others.”

Arrogance has never pleased God; pride has never been justified. Hence the Lord says elsewhere of those who do all their works to be seen by men: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI.2). Such were also those to whom the Lord spoke these words: justifying themselves before men, they rejected and despised others as sinners. But the Lord, who came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance, rejected no one, but ate with publicans and sinners.

“Two men,” He says, [Col. 0430D] “went up into the temple to pray: one a Pharisee and [Col. 0431A] the other a publican.” The Lord was speaking to Pharisees, who are called Pharisees—that is, “separated.” [Note: [Col. 0431D] St Jerome, *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, no. 23: “The Pharisees, separated from the Jews because of certain superfluous observances, also took their name from the division.”] For they thought themselves better than all others. To them He opposed one Pharisee, in whom, as in a mirror, the rest might have seen what sort of people they were. Perhaps this was the very man of whom the Lord was speaking there:

“But the Pharisee, standing, prayed thus with himself: God, I thank thee that I am not like other men—extortioners, unjust, adulterers—or even like this publican. I fast twice in the Sabbath; I give tithes of all that I possess.”

None of these things is blameworthy. To give God thanks for benefits, to fast twice in the week, and to give tithes of everything are very good and praiseworthy acts. There is, therefore, another reason for which this Pharisee is condemned. It lies within [Col. 0431B], in the heart, in the intention; and this cannot be seen except by God. For God considers not what we say, but with what intention we say something. [Note: [Col. 0431D] St John Chrysostom, Homily 5, *On the Incomprehensible Nature of God*, no. 7, on this parable: “For God heard not the words only, but saw the mind with which they were uttered.”] He attends not to the voice of the mouth but to that of the heart; He looks not at streams but at the fountain.

It is clear, therefore, that this Pharisee said all these things out of pride and arrogance, and that in the things he did he desired to please men more than God. Foolish man, who received nothing but vain glory as the reward for so great and such service.

It follows: “And the publican, standing afar off, would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but struck his breast, saying: God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” The publican stood afar off, as a sinner and publican. He showed himself to be what he was. They are called publicans either because they were not ashamed to sin publicly [Col. 0431C], or because they collected public revenues. [Note: [Col. 0431D] Ulpian, Law 39, Digest, *On Publicans and Taxes*: “Publicans are those who enjoy public revenues. For from this they have their name, whether they pay a tax to the treasury or collect tribute; and all who lease anything from the treasury are properly called publicans.”] Matthew the publican, whom the Lord called from the tax-office, was one of these. Rightly, therefore, the Lord said to the Pharisees concerning publicans: “Publicans and sinners shall go before you into the kingdom of God” (Matt. XXI.31).

The publican stood afar off and, knowing himself to be a sinner, was afraid to draw nearer. He would not even lift his eyes to heaven, lest he offend God in this very thing: that he should presume to look upward, toward God’s seat, from the mire of the deep and from so great a gulf of sins. [Note: [Col. 0431D] St Augustine, Sermon 115, no. 2: “It is little that he stood at a distance; he did not raise his eyes to heaven. In order that he might be looked upon, he did not look.”] “But he struck his breast, saying: God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”

He rightly struck his breast because there [Col. 0432A] he had sinned, there was the wellspring, pit, and origin of evil. For there is the heart, the repository of all good and evil. From it proceed all good things, and from it all evil things. “For,” says the Lord, “from the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, thefts, perjuries, adulteries” (Matt. XV.19), and similar things. Thus the publican struck this, and by striking it in some manner took vengeance upon himself.

Therefore the Psalmist says: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Ps. L.12), because if the heart is clean—the counsellor from which we receive all our counsels—we cannot do evil, except perhaps something imputed to ignorance; though it is questionable whether a heart stained by ignorance can be called clean.

For this reason the breast-piece from sacrifices is always given only to priests [Col. 0432B]. [Note: [Col. 0431D] Origen, Homily 5 on Leviticus, no. 12, somewhat differently: “The breast-piece and the right arm become the priest’s portion, as a sign that the person who formerly thought evil things, converted by the priest’s labour, has received good thoughts.” St Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, Part II, ch. 3, nearer to the author: “By the divine law the priest receives as sacrifice the right and separated shoulder … and the breast-piece is also given with the shoulder for food, so that, in what he is commanded to receive from the sacrifice, he may learn to offer to the Creator that same thing from himself: and not only think what is right in his heart, but invite his hearers to higher things by the shoulder of his work.”] For in them are contained the heart, counsel, all doctrine, and all knowledge of the whole people, so that, being sound in heart and strong in understanding, they may always have enough to answer every person who asks.

The publican therefore struck his breast and said: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner. Do not heed the perverse counsels of this heart; blot out my sins and be merciful. There is nothing in me by which I can please thee or obtain pardon, because I have sinned against thee in heart and body, in thoughts and works. I am more wicked than all others, and I cannot be saved except through thy mercy. Therefore be merciful to me, a sinner.”

Thus he accused himself no less than the Pharisee justified himself. But with what result? With what reward? It follows: “Amen, I say to you [Col. 0432C], this man went down justified to his house rather than that other.” But from where did he go down—from the temple or from God? Certainly from the temple, and by God. For he went down from the temple, but was justified by God. [Note: [Col. 0432D] St Jerome, Letter 122, no. 3: “The Pharisee’s righteousness perishes through pride, and the publican’s humility is saved through confession.” See St Gregory, Homily 7 on Ezekiel.]

Why was this so? “Because everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted.” Therefore, as the publican was exalted by humbling himself, so the Pharisee was humbled by exalting himself. Pride is the root of all evils; humility is the guardian of virtues.

XLIV. [Note: [Col. 0432D] See St. Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 54; Augustine, Sermon 174, §3.] [CHAP. XIX.] And having entered, he was passing through Jericho. And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus; and he was a chief tax-collector, and himself wealthy.

All of us who inhabit this world walk through Jericho. For Jericho is interpreted as “moon” [Note: [Col. 0432D] He had said the same on Matthew, chap. XX, p. 383. Thus Bede, Questions on Joshua, chap. VII: “Jericho is called moon by interpretation . . . because, just as the moon wanes with its monthly completions, so this world, running toward the completion of the ages, falls by daily diminutions:” he repeats this in Psalm LXXXVI.], whose [Col. 0433A] mutability is so great that it never remains in the same condition. It therefore fittingly signifies the world, which is always wholly in motion. Since our Savior assumed this mutability according to his humanity, he is rightly said to have passed through Jericho.

And behold, a man named Zacchaeus, whose name is quite fittingly interpreted “justified” [Note: [Col. 0433D] From the Hebrew: “pure, just.” Bede, on this passage: “Zacchaeus, whose name means justified.”], since he was called and justified by God. This man was not merely a tax-collector, but chief of the tax-collectors. Moreover, he was rich, and it is difficult for such a man to enter the kingdom of heaven. Difficult indeed, and impossible with men. But what is impossible with men is possible with God. And though he was such a man, he nevertheless sought to see Jesus. He sought indeed, but could not see him. But why could he not? Because of the [Col. 0433B] crowd, and because he was small in stature.

These two things greatly hinder a man from being able to see Jesus: an evil crowd, which drives a man away from so great and excellent a good. This crowd is the crowd of vices; whoever is surrounded by it cannot see Christ [Note: [Col. 0433D] Bede on this passage: “He sought to see the Savior entering Jericho, but could not because of the crowd, since . . . an ingrained habit of vices had hindered him from attaining his desire.”]. He is small in stature who has not yet reached the maturity and perfection of knowledge [Note: [Col. 0434D] Ambrose, Book VIII on Luke, §87: “What is meant by the fact that Scripture expressly mentions no one else’s stature except this man’s? See whether perhaps he was small in malice, or still small in faith.”]. Hence the Apostle admonishes us, saying: “Do not become children in understanding; but be little children in malice” (1 Cor. XIV, 20). And again: “As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food. For you were not yet able; indeed, not even now are you able, for you are still carnal” (1 Cor. III, 2).

Therefore, whoever wishes to see Jesus must leave the crowd, flee vices and sins, avoid the company of the wicked; [Col. 0433C] he must raise and stretch himself upward, grow in faith and knowledge, and advance in every goodness. This is what Zacchaeus signified when, running on ahead, he climbed a sycamore tree. He climbed the tree so that from it he might see him whom he could not otherwise see.

This tree is faith. Many, coming to it and climbing it, though still small in stature and not yet greatly advanced in knowledge, nevertheless deserved from it to see and know Jesus. Thus it is also said here that he was to pass that way [Note: [Col. 0434D] Ambrose, cited book, §89: “The Lord was to pass by that place where the sycamore was, or where someone was to believe . . . Thus he saw Zacchaeus above: for already, by the loftiness of faith amid the fruits of new works, he stood out as though by the height of a second tree.”]. For Jesus passes along this road and beside this tree of faith. From there he is seen, and sees; from there he is known, and knows. For the Lord deigns to look upon and call to himself those who climb this tree, whose fruit is blood-red. By it are signified the martyrs [Col. 0433D] who, clinging to the tree of faith, were stained with their own blood because of their steadfastness in faith.

Passing by, therefore, the Lord looked up, saw Zacchaeus, and said to him: “Zacchaeus, make haste and come down; [Col. 0434A] for today I must stay in your house.” “Today,” he says, “you have begun to seek me; you have come to faith; you have climbed the tree; today I must stay in your house.” True, therefore, is what is said through the prophet: “Whenever the sinner is converted and groans, he shall live in life and shall not die” (Ezek. XXXIII, 12, 15). What was done in Zacchaeus is undoubtedly done daily in other sinners also, provided that they are converted from the heart, seek Christ, and hold fast to faith.

It follows: and he made haste, came down, and received him joyfully. For he was already burning inwardly with the fire of faith, who thus outwardly showed obedience and service. He had already grown greatly in faith, though he was small in stature. And when all saw it, they murmured, saying that he had turned in to lodge with a sinful man [Col. 0434B]. For all knew Zacchaeus to be a sinner, since he was chief of the tax-collectors. But this sinner was much better than those who murmured and pretended themselves righteous.
