The following words make this plain, when it is said: But Zacchaeus stood and said to Jesus: “Behold, Lord, I give half my goods to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.” By this one utterance all immediately ceased murmuring, marveling at the tax-collector’s sudden repentance and conversion; and perhaps no one there would have wished, even under compulsion, to make so great a profession. For he was very rich, as the Evangelist himself testifies; yet he promises to give half of all his goods [Col. 0434C] to the poor and to restore fourfold whatever he had defrauded from anyone.

See, then, from what great perfection he began, he who had then for the first time seen the Lord Christ and heard him preaching. It is indeed true that men see the outward appearance, but God looks upon hearts. The Lord saw what this man was to become in a short time, and how righteous he was to be, whereas men judged him so sinful. Jesus said to him: “Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham.” “Today,” he says, “salvation has come to this house; all weakness, every illness, and every contagion of vices has been driven out; it has been healed and wholly sanctified, inwardly and outwardly. For he who dwells in this house is no longer a tax-collector, but a son of Abraham.”

For the sons of Abraham are all those [Col. 0434D] who imitate Abraham and do Abraham’s works. Abraham received angels as guests; Zacchaeus, however, received the Lord of angels. “For the Son of Man came to seek and save what had perished. He did not come [Col. 0435A] to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” [Note: [Col. 0435D] See St. Fulgentius on this saying, Book I, To Trasimund.], “because those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick do” [Note: [Col. 0435D] Thus far, the homily.].

XLV. A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom, and to return. Having called his ten servants, he gave them ten minas.

This nobleman is he who speaks: our Savior. He is noble not only according to his divinity, by which he is Creator and Lord of angels and men, but also according to his humanity, having been born of a noble lineage. For the Lord was born of the tribe of Judah and the lineage of David, which, nobler than the other tribes, held the kingdom and the sovereignty. He went into a far country when, ascending into heaven, he returned to the Father [Note: [Col. 0435D] St. Ambrose, Book V, On the Faith, chap. 6: “He therefore aptly introduced the parable of the rich man who went into a far country to receive a kingdom and return, describing himself according to the substance of divinity and incarnation. For he is rich according to the fullness of divinity, who for our sake became poor though he was rich; he went abroad according to his assumption of a body, because he came into this world, entering, as it were, upon the ways of man as an alien journey, in order to prepare for himself a kingdom from us. Therefore the Son of Man came to receive a kingdom and return.” [Col. 0436D] See also Augustine, Book II, Questions on the Gospels, chap. 46.]. Hence he himself says: “I went out from the Father and [Col. 0435B] came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John XVI, 28).

This country is far away because it is reached with much labor. “For through many tribulations,” says the Lord, “we must enter the kingdom of heaven” (Acts XIV, 21). Each person is farther from it in proportion as he is more wicked than others. The Lord therefore returned to it to receive for himself a kingdom and to return. For the Lord received his kingdom when his humanity was exalted above the heavens and the Father said to him: “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. CIX, 1, 2). It remains, therefore, that he should return, and, returning for judgment, settle accounts with his servants.

Before he ascended there, he called his servants and gave them ten minas, which another Evangelist calls talents (Matt. XXV, 15). There are ten servants, and there are ten talents. Do not say they are few. Consider first what ten signifies. No other number is greater than this, since all numbers are contained in this number [Note: [Col. 0436D] See what was said above on no. 40, Luke XVII.]. Thus ten sometimes signifies many, sometimes all. He called ten, that is, all his servants, and gave them ten minas, that is, all his talents. Elsewhere it is said: “And he gave them his goods” (Matt. XXV, 13). And he said to them: “Do business until I come.”

Blessed Paul was a good merchant, who became all things to all men so that he might gain all. For every day a market is held in the Church. Every day God’s treasure is sold in [Col. 0435D] the Church. For desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise. All servants are God’s merchants, and they buy nothing but servants. [Col. 0436A] For the Lord desires nothing from the riches of the world except their servants. Hence he also drove out of the Temple those who, trading wickedly, sold and bought unlawful things there.

This was said concerning the servants. Now let us hear about the citizens. “But his citizens hated him, and sent an embassy after him, saying: ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’” These citizens are the Jews, who refused to have Jesus Christ, King and Lord of all, reign over them, saying: “We have no king but Caesar.” They send this perverse embassy after him because, since he departed from them, they have persisted in this evil will. Since Christ knows and hears this will, it sounds continually in his ears as though it were an embassy.

“And it came to pass, when he returned, having received the kingdom, [Col. 0436B] that he commanded the servants to whom he had given the money to be called, that he might know how much each had gained by trading.” This will occur at the judgment, when both good and evil alike shall all stand before Christ’s tribunal, that each may render an account for himself.

Then the first came, saying: “Lord, your mina has gained ten minas.” One talent gains ten when some grace granted us by God grows into many virtues, or converts many sinners to faith and righteousness [Note: [Col. 0436D] St. Gregory, Book II, Epistle 47: “The burden of priesthood is heavy. For it is first necessary for a priest to live as an example to others; and then to take care that he does not destroy minds by the examples he displays . . . considering in the most attentive fear that the Lord, who will return to receive his kingdom and who distributes talents to his servants, says: ‘Do business until I come’ . . . We truly carry on that business if by living and speaking we gain the souls of our neighbors.”].

And he said to him: “Well done, good servant; because you have been faithful in a little thing, you shall have authority over ten cities.” Another Evangelist expressed this more clearly, saying: “I will set you over many things; enter into the joy of your lord” (Matt. XXX, 21). Likewise: “Blessed is that servant whom, when the [Col. 0436C] Lord comes, he finds watchful. Amen I say to you: he will set him over all the goods that he possesses” (Matt. XXIV, 46). Thus to give him authority over ten cities [Note: [Col. 0436D] See St. Ambrose, Book VIII on Luke, §96.] is to set him over all that he possesses. For we have said that ten signifies all.

Each person is indeed set over all that the Lord possesses, because all things obey him and do his will. For such harmony will be there that each will be honored by all as though greater, and will honor all as though lesser. Another came, saying: “Lord, your mina has made five minas.” This man too worked well with the talent entrusted to him; but he did not gain from it as much as the one of whom we have just spoken [Col. 0436D]. For even though all work well, not all work equally. Hence the Apostle says: “I labored more abundantly than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. XV, 10). In this respect he shows that he had labored more than the others with the talent and grace given him.

And to this man he says: “And you, be over five cities.” For just as they are not equal in labor, so neither are they equal in reward. Whoever labors more will receive more reward. “For star differs from star in glory,” as the Apostle says; “so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. XV, 41). Though all will be blessed, they will not all be equal. This is signified by the statement that some are set over ten cities and others over five.

Another came, saying: “Lord, behold your mina, which I kept laid away in a napkin. For I feared you, because you are an austere man: you take up what you did not lay down, and reap what you did not sow.” He lays up the talent in a napkin [Col. 0437B] who allows the grace given him to grow sluggish in this flesh, delivered over to labors and weariness [Note: [Col. 0437D] Bede on this passage: “The servant who, commanded to trade, laid the money received from his lord away in a napkin, represents those who are fit to preach but, when the Lord commands through the Church, refuse either to undertake the office of preaching or at least to carry it out worthily once undertaken. For to bind money in a napkin is to hide gifts received beneath the idleness of sluggish torpor.” The final words are St. Gregory’s, Pastoral Rule, Part I, chap. 9.].

But this evil servant lies in calling him austere, though the Psalmist speaks of his sweetness, saying: “The Lord is sweet and upright; therefore he establishes a law for sinners in the way” (Ps. XXIV, 8). The Lord himself shows how vain and useless such an excuse is, saying: “Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant. You knew, as you yourself pretend, that I am an austere man, taking up what I did not lay down and reaping what I did not sow; why then did you not give my money to the bank, so that when I came I might certainly have demanded it with interest?”

As though he said: It was not fitting for you to fear to entrust my money to the table of money-changers, when you knew me to be so strong [Col. 0437C] and powerful that I can lay claim everywhere not only to my own things but even to another’s. In this matter it is manifest that you have no excuse.

This money is the words of eternal life; the table is the Church; the money-changers are the hearers, to whom all this money is proclaimed and entrusted. The Lord receives it with interest because through it he gains many believers along with the fruit of good works. Nowhere is there a place where the Lord has not sown; nowhere has he not scattered the seed of his grace. For because the sound of the Apostles went forth into all the earth, he bestowed upon all men reason and understanding, memory and natural ability. It is clear, then, that this wicked servant [Col. 0437D] lied against him.

The Lord goes on to say of him: “Take the mina from him and give it to him who has ten minas.” From this we may understand that only the good possess that blessedness which the evil too would have possessed with them had they remained in goodness. And they said to him: “Lord, he has ten [Col. 0438A] minas.” He already had ten, certainly; with one added they become eleven. Why then is he said to have not eleven but only ten, unless because, as we said above, ten signifies the same as all? According to this meaning, it was more fitting to say ten than eleven. For eleven signifies only eleven; ten signifies all.

It follows: “But I say to you that to everyone who has, more shall be given; but from him who has not, even what he has shall be taken away from him” [Note: [Col. 0437D] See St. Bernard, Sermon 72 on the Song of Songs.]. For everyone who has faith and works worthy of faith—like this man who thus multiplied his talents—will receive the recompense of eternal blessedness. But from him who does not have this, even that which he has in the opinion of men, that is, what he “seems to have,” as another Evangelist [Col. 0438B] writes, “shall be taken away from him” (Matt. XXV, 29).

“Nevertheless, bring here those enemies of mine who did not want me to reign over them, and kill them before me.” Wretched Jews, against whom these words are spoken! Of them he had said above: “His citizens hated him.” They will then be killed when it is said to them: “Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41). Then the good also will hear: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid., 34).

XLVI. And when he drew near, seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: “If you too had known.”

After Lazarus had been raised, the Lord came to Jerusalem sitting upon the foal of an ass; and when he had drawn near [Col. 0438C] to the descent of the Mount of Olives, all the crowds of disciples began joyfully to praise him with a loud voice, saying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” And some Pharisees from the crowd said to him: “Master, rebuke your disciples.” To them he said: “I tell you that if these are silent, the stones will cry out.”

The stones mean the Gentiles [Note: [Col. 0437D] Titus of Bostra, p. 726, vol. II, *Auct. Duc.* [Col. 0438D]: “And who are these stones? Certainly those who formerly worshiped stones: namely, the deceived nations, led into error by the devil’s deception.” Jerome mentions this interpretation on Habakkuk, chap. II, and writes of it: “Although most people think it should be understood thus, ‘If the Jews are silent, the multitude of the Gentiles will confess me,’ nevertheless this is the more explicit and truer interpretation: even if men should be silent and an envious tongue should not speak of the multitude of my signs, the stones themselves, the foundations of the walls, and the construction of their walls [Col. 0439C] will be able to proclaim my greatness [Col. 0439D]. To make this more significant, let us also set forth examples from secular literature,” etc. He adduces a passage from Sallust and Cicero.], who had been hard, barren, and unfruitful, and worshiped wood and stones. But now they cry out and do not cease to praise Christ’s mighty works.

When, therefore, he drew near and saw the impious city conspiring toward its own destruction, he wept not for his own death, which it was plotting, but for its ruin and perdition: “If you too had known.” “Just as I,” he says, [Col. 0438D] “weep, who see all things and know all future events, so you too would weep if you now saw the things to come.” Brothers, these tears were for us, so that we might imitate the Master and learn from this great Teacher of ours what we ought to do concerning the death and ruin of our enemies. Hence he himself says: [Col. 0439A] “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Luke VI, 27).

“And indeed, in this your day, the things that make for your peace; but now they are hidden from your eyes.” “In this day,” he says, “in this present time, the things that make for your peace have been given you for a short time. But now the evils which will suddenly come upon you in your days are hidden from your eyes.” And he explains: “For days shall come upon you when your enemies shall surround you with a rampart, encompass you, and press you in on every side; they shall cast you and your children who are within you to the ground, and shall not leave in you one stone upon another, because you did not know the time of your visitation.”

All these things were fulfilled under Vespasian and his son Titus, as Josephus most fully [Col. 0439B] relates: when, during the long siege, such calamity oppressed the Jews that mothers themselves devoured their children [Note: [Col. 0439D] Josephus recounts this of a certain noble woman, Mary, in Book VI of *The Jewish War*, chap. 3, §4.]. This happened because they did not know the time of their visitation, when the Dayspring from on high visited them. Of this visitation Zechariah says: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and wrought redemption for his people” (Luke I, 68).

But when he says, “They shall not leave in you one stone upon another,” this is said hyperbolically. Or else no stone was left upon another by which either the city itself, or any person in the whole city, could have been defended [Note: [Col. 0439D] Josephus, Book VII, chap. 1, relates that Titus ordered his soldiers to raze the entire city and Temple to the ground, leaving the towers Phasael, Hippicus, and Mariamne, and that part of the wall which enclosed the city on the west. Victor of Antioch himself testifies, on Mark, chap. 13, that some remains of the Temple existed in his day. There is a notable passage in Chrysostom, Homily *That Christ Is God* (vol. I of the works, ed. Montfaucon, p. 580), §16, where he affirms that “only so much remains of the Temple as is enough to show where the Temple once stood.” There also, concerning fire leaping from the foundations when the Emperor Julian the Apostate wished in his own age to restore the Temple, Jerome, certainly an excellent witness, says on Isaiah, chap. I: “Therefore almighty God also abandoned the Temple and made [Col. 0440C] the city [Col. 0440D] deserted; this need not be proved by words, especially for us who see Zion deserted, Jerusalem overthrown, and the Temple destroyed to its very foundation.” In Book X on Isaiah, at chap. XXXIV, he describes the overthrow and devastation foretold by the prophets. On its restoration by Hadrian, see Epistle 108, §9, ed. Vallarsi. See also Bede on this passage, Theophylact on Matthew XXVI and Mark XIII, etc.].

First the city itself, then the tower called Antonia [Note: [Col. 0440D] Josephus describes the Temple and the tower Antonia in *The Jewish War*, Book V, chap. 5. On the same tower Antonia being taken by the Romans, see Book VI, chap. 1; on the burning of the Temple, ibid., chap. 4, §5; the same Josephus, Book VI, chap. 8; on the city’s capture by the Romans.], and afterwards that most famous Temple, above which some had fled for refuge, were captured and destroyed by great force. If they had surrendered to the enemy, the Temple would not have been destroyed. Titus is said to have entered it while it was already burning and to have praised it greatly [Col. 0439C; Note: [Col. 0440D] See the same Josephus, Book VI, chap. 4, §7.].

The destruction of this city can signify the perdition of any soul. When faith in it has been corrupted and the people of virtues have failed, an army of malignant spirits and vices attacks it, burns it, and lays it waste. Jerusalem was taken forty-two years after Christ’s Passion [Note: [Col. 0440D] So also Jerome, Book III on Isaiah, chap. VI, v. 4. See our author, who said the same at Matthew, no. 89.]. This was aptly signified by Elisha, who, going up to Bethel, was mocked by boys of that place, who said to him: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead.” He cursed them in the name of the Lord, and immediately [Col. 0440A] two bears came out of the forest and killed forty-two of them (4 Kings II, 23). For this reason, forty-two years later, the Jews were slain by two bears, namely Titus and Vespasian: because they mocked Christ, led him to Mount Calvary, and crucified him there.

It follows: And having entered the Temple, he began to cast out those selling and buying in it. Hence Matthew also says: “And Jesus entered the Temple and drove out all those selling and buying in the Temple; and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves” (Matt. XXI, 12).

Hear this, Simonists; hear it [Note: [Col. 0440D] Here again our author inveighs against Simonists, as he had done at the similar passage in Matthew, no. 85. [Col. 0441D] See the Preface. Jerome treats this subject at length on Matthew, chap. XXI.], abominable merchants. Either cease your trading or leave the Temple. For the Lord of the Temple drove not one or two but, without distinction, all sellers and buyers [Col. 0440B] out of the Temple. He also overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves. For you are money-changers; you have sold doves; you do nothing without money and payment. They sell doves who grant, for a price, either churches or the graces of the Holy Spirit. The Lord overturns their seats, so that it may thereby be understood that they are not bishops.

And he says to them: “It is written: ‘My house is a house of prayer’; but you have made it a den of robbers.” For you are robbers because you did not enter through the door. Whoever does not enter through the door into the sheepfold is a thief and a robber. Christ is the door; and because you did not enter through him, he overturns your seats. Only those enter through this door who are appointed bishops according to the ordinances of the canons [Col. 0440C]. Therefore leave the house of prayer, which, because you dwell in it, has become a den of robbers.

Nowhere else is the Lord recorded to have done this; nowhere else is he said physically to have resisted, pushed, or driven out others. Therefore, if we too wish to imitate him in this matter, we must, if we cannot do otherwise, drive Simonists forcibly from the Church—provided, however, that we have strength sufficient to do so without harm to the Church.

XLVII. [CHAP. XXI.] [Col. 0441A] There shall be signs in the sun, moon, and stars; and upon the earth distress of nations because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves, men withering away from fear and expectation of the things coming upon the whole world.

When certain people asked Jesus, “When will the kingdom of God come, and what will be the sign of his coming?” (Matt. XXIV, 3), he answered that first nation would rise against nation, kingdom against kingdom; there would be great earthquakes in various places, plagues and famines, terrors from heaven, and great signs. Hence the Apostle says to certain persons who feared this event and wished to know: “We beseech you, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together unto him, not to be quickly shaken from your understanding or terrified, whether by spirit, speech, or letter as if sent by us, as though the day of the Lord were at hand; because unless the falling away comes first and the man of sin, the son of perdition, is revealed—he who opposes and exalts himself [Col. 0441B] above everything called God or worshiped, so that he sits in the Temple of God, showing himself as though he were God” (2 Thess. II, 1, 2, 3, 4, etc.).

These, then, will be the first signs of Christ’s coming. Afterwards will follow those of which he has just spoken: “There shall be signs in the sun, moon, and stars,” and the rest. For as Christ’s birth was preceded by peace and rejoicing, while the angels sang: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will” (Luke II, 14),

“And behold, I announce to you great joy, which shall be for all the people, because today there is born to you a Savior, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David” (ibid., 10);

so this son of perdition will be preceded by disputes, conflicts, dissensions, earthquakes, plagues, famines, and other similar signs of terror. Then [Col. 0441C] at last he himself will be revealed, and worse evils will follow [Note: [Col. 0441D] On these signs see St. Augustine, *City of God*, Book XX, chaps. 5 and 24; St. Gregory, Homily 1 on the Gospels, and *Morals*, Book XIV, chap. 12; Homily 9 on Ezekiel; etc.]. “For then there shall be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor shall be; and unless the Lord had shortened those days, no flesh would be saved. But for the sake of the elect those days shall be shortened” (Matt. XXIV, 21–23), so that he may not live as long as he hoped to live. For he will reign “for a time, and times, and half a time” (Rev. XII, 14)—“whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of his mouth and abolish by the manifestation of his coming” (2 Thess. II, 8).

But perhaps someone will say that these are not signs, since they commonly happen; for nothing is usually called a sign unless it is something new and unusual. Therefore one must believe that those wars, earthquakes, plagues, famines, and terrors will occur in an unusual manner and with far greater violence at that time. Hence that tribulation is not without reason said to be such as no other has ever been. And, beyond all these things, to complete the sum of evil, “false Christs and false prophets shall arise and give other signs and many wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error” (Matt. XXIX, 24).

Concerning signs in the sun, moon, and stars, another Evangelist says: “The sun shall be darkened, [Col. 0442A] the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall” (Mark XIII, 24). Certain things reported as written in the annals of the Jews seem to agree with these. In them it is related that the sea will rise fifteen cubits higher than all mountains, its waters standing still and flowing in no direction. Then it will sink by the same amount into the abyss, so that it can scarcely be seen by onlookers. Afterwards it will return to its own place. Then perhaps that confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and waves will occur, of which the Lord is now speaking. For so great a disturbance of sea and waves cannot occur without great confusion and noise.

The earth too will give its signs: earthquakes so great will occur that almost all human constructions will collapse and all stones, even small ones, will be split apart. [Col. 0442B] Wild beasts will descend from the mountains and remain among men, harming no one. Men themselves also, as though mad and withering away from fear, will waste away as they run here and there. These things seem to agree with the words of the Gospel, in which the Lord says: “Men withering away from fear and expectation of the things coming upon the whole world.”

It is related that each of these signs, and others not mentioned here, will occur on one day and no longer. We, however, do not endorse their authority; we have written them only because they seemed to agree with the words of the Gospel.

It follows: For the powers of heaven shall be moved. By the powers of heaven we understand the armies of angels [Note: [Col. 0442D] St. Jerome on Matthew, chap. XXIV: “By the powers of heaven we understand the multitude of angels.”], who will accompany our Savior when he comes for judgment. Hence it is added: [Col. 0442C] “And then they shall see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty.” For the Lord will descend as he ascended, as it is written: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, shall so come as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I, 11).

Who can say or even conceive what joy there will then be for the good, and what sorrow for the wicked? “But when these things begin to happen, look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption draws near.” “You have heard,” he says, “the most certain signs of the coming judgment. When they begin to happen, look up and open the eyes of your mind; believe and refuse to doubt; lift up your heads, raise your mind from earthly to [Col. 0442D] heavenly things, because your redemption draws near.” Although no one knows that day, it cannot be doubted that it is near once such great and such extraordinary signs begin to occur.

For this reason he added this very fitting comparison, saying: “Look at the fig tree and all the trees: when they now produce fruit from themselves, you know that summer is near. So also you, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near.” Just as newly appearing fruit and leaves on [Col. 0443A] trees announce the approach of summer, so the signs mentioned above, as soon as they appear, will most certainly announce that the kingdom of God is near [Note: [Col. 0443D] Jerome, cited work: “Under the example of a tree he taught the coming of the consummation. Just as, he says, when the tender shoots of the fig tree arise and its bud bursts into flower and its bark brings forth leaves, you understand the coming of summer and the arrival of the west wind and spring, so, when you see all these things that have been written, think that the consummation of the world is now at hand; yet that they come as prizes and as certain forerunners, showing that it is near and at the doors.” See Victor of Antioch on Mark, chap. XIII, and Augustine, *Questions on the Gospels*, Book I, chap. 39.].

“Amen I say to you, this generation shall not pass away until all these things happen.” Unless these signs appear first, therefore, the generation of humankind cannot end and the last day cannot come. “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.” Heaven and earth shall indeed pass away because they will be changed for the better. But Christ’s words will not pass away; they will always remain firm in their truth. For they would pass away if what they affirm could fail to occur, or if what they deny could come to pass.

XLVIII. Now he was teaching in the temple by day; but at night he went out and lodged on the mountain called Olivet. And all the people came early in the morning to him in the temple to hear him. “All the people,” he says, “came early in the morning to him in the temple,” that is, gathering at the temple at first light, they waited to hear him. For *manicare* is said from *mane*, “morning.”

> [Note: Col. 0443D. On this word, St Augustine, Question 46 on Judges: “I do not recall that *manicabis* is a Latin word.” The old translator of Juvenal used it, and many writers in the Middle Ages did so; see Chrysologus, Sermon 82. It is explained in the manner given by the author, by the Greek glosses, Ugutio, and others.]

What follows concerning Christ’s Passion has been explained in Matthew; therefore it need not be explained here, except for the few points which Matthew omitted. The Lord sends Peter and John to prepare the Passover. As they enter the city, a man carrying a jar of water meets them; they follow him into the house which he enters. And the householder shows them a large furnished upper room.

For these two disciples of Christ are the two Testaments. When they are sent by divine inspiration to the city of our heart, they prepare the Passover there, because they teach us, and enable us to understand, what that lamb sacrificed according to the Law signifies, and in what manner Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed.

> [Col. 0443C]

Our inner person meets them; and because he has been baptized, he is not improperly said to carry a jar of water.

> [Note: Col. 0443D. St Ambrose, Book X on Luke, on this passage, no. 48: “For what shall I say concerning water? … O water, which deserved to become Christ’s sacrament, which washes all things and is not washed! You begin the first mysteries; you bring the perfect mysteries to completion. From you is the beginning; in you is the end—or rather, you cause us not to know an end,” etc.  
>   
> Bede: “It is fitting that a man carrying a jar of water should meet the disciples preparing the Passover, in order to show that the mystery of this Passover is to be celebrated for the perfect cleansing of the whole world. For water is the washing of grace.”]

For no unbaptized person carries this jar. Therefore they follow him into the house, even into the innermost chamber of the heart; and there they find the householder, that is, the understanding, by which our inward household is ruled and governed. And he shows them a large furnished upper room, by which we understand faith

> [Note: Col. 0444D. Bede: “The large upper room is the spiritual Law, which, emerging from the narrow confines of the letter, receives the Savior in a lofty place.”]

adorned with other virtues. For this supper is prepared there because it is revealed through faith. Hence it is rightly said: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand.” The unbelieving do not possess this upper room.

[CHAPTER XXII.] And when the hour had come, he reclined at table, and the twelve with him. And he said to them: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.” “I have greatly desired,” he says, “to eat this Passover with you, in order that I might fulfill the old things and pass on to the new. For I tell you that from this time I shall not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God”: that is, until it is spiritually understood and enacted in the Church.

“You are those who have remained with me in my temptations; and I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” Thus, he says, I hand over and appoint to you the kingdom of the Church,

> [Col. 0444B]

as my Father also appointed it to me, so that you may govern it in my stead; that you may eat at my table the living bread that came down from heaven, and drink the cup of the New Testament. Yet this may also be understood of that heavenly table

> [Note: Col. 0444D. St Ambrose, Book X, no. 49, understood these words in this way. Bede writes: “This table, set before all the saints for their enjoyment, is the heavenly glory of life.” See St Augustine, Book I, *Questions on the Gospels*, chapter 43; St Jerome, Question 2 to Hedibia.]

at which the saints are refreshed solely by contemplation of the highest good. Of it the Psalmist says: “As for me, I shall appear in righteousness before your presence; I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Psalm 16:15).

But the Lord said to Simon: “Simon, behold, Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat.” For as formerly he sifted blessed Job by God’s permission, so he sifted the apostles, to see whether perhaps he might find in them any tares or corruption.

And he said to them: “When I sent you without purse, bag, or sandals, did you lack anything?” But they said:

> [Col. 0444C]

“Nothing.” For nothing could be lacking to those whom the Lord himself guided. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord guides me, and I shall lack nothing” (Psalm 22:1). For the Lord had sent them, not to preach, but to heal the sick, saying to them: “Go, heal all diseases and every infirmity.”

> [Note: Col. 0444D. Luke 9:1: “He gave them power … to cure diseases,” etc.]

And therefore they needed neither purse nor bag nor sandals. For they were not yet shod with the preparation of the Gospel of peace.

Therefore he said to them: “But now, let him who has a purse take it, and likewise a bag.” “Now,” he says, “I permit you to carry both purse and bag, not in order to gather, but to distribute; not in order to heap up another’s goods in them, but in order to draw from them what you may give to others.” For these two things, besides signifying mercy

> [Col. 0445A]

and generosity, also signify both Testaments.

> [Note: Col. 0445D. See St Ambrose, nos. 54–55.]

From them, as from a purse and bag full of every kind of wealth, the apostles drew that by which they might refresh hungry and thirsty minds. Therefore let the apostles be secure and fear nothing, since nothing will be lacking to those who carry purse and bag, to whom nothing was lacking even before, without purse and bag.

“And let him who does not have one sell his tunic and buy a sword.” He who does not have the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, should sell his tunic and buy it, so that, stripped of all things and naked, he may follow the naked cross. These words therefore openly show that only those ought to preach and carry the sword of the Spirit who can say with the apostles: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you”

> [Col. 0445B]

(Matthew 19:27). For one who possesses nothing is rightly called naked and without a tunic.

“For I tell you that what is written must still be fulfilled in me: ‘And he was reckoned among the wicked.’ For the things concerning me are coming to an end.” “There still remains,” he says, “a little that must be fulfilled in me. For the things written concerning me according to the flesh are now nearly completed. But this still remains: that the Jews, reckoning me among the wicked, should crucify me. Then at last I myself shall cease from preaching; but you, having sold all things, buy the sword, gird yourselves, and prepare to preach.”

But they said: “Lord, behold, here are two swords.” And he said to them: “It is enough.” For the swords of the two Testaments are sufficient to carry out the whole work of preaching. See

> [Col. 0445C]

how well all things fit together, although the apostles did not understand what the Lord’s words signified.

And an angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him. And he entered into an agony and prayed more earnestly. And his sweat became like drops of blood running down upon the ground. For this struggle of our Savior signified the agonies and contests of the martyrs.

> [Note: Col. 0445D. Bede: “Let no one attribute this sweat to weakness … Rather, let him understand that by the earth watered and consecrated with his blood, it was openly declared, not for him who knew it, but for us, that he was already obtaining the effect of his prayer: namely, that he might cleanse by his blood the faith of the disciples, which earthly frailty still exposed to accusation.”]

That bloody sweat showed forth the blood of those who would everywhere be shed from his whole body, which is the Church. He prayed more earnestly in order to show us what we ought to do in such a struggle, that we may deserve to receive the consolation of angels. The remaining matters which follow have been explained in Matthew.

XLIX. [CHAPTER XXIV.] Two of the disciples were going that same day to a village called Emmaus, which was sixty stadia from Jerusalem, and they were speaking with one another about all these things which had happened. One of these, the very person who writes these things, is thought to have been the blessed Luke.

> [Note: Col. 0445D. Since the Evangelist names only one of them, Cleophas, there has been a long controversy about the name of the other. St Ambrose, Book X on Luke, no. 173, writing that Christ showed himself to the eleven, just as he had already shown himself separately, toward evening, to Ammaon and Cleophas, seems to have given the name Ammaon to that man. Petavius, however, in his discussion of Epiphanius, *Heresy* 21, considers this passage corrupt, and thinks that something was omitted through a copyist’s fault; he holds that Ambrose did not give this name to the disciple, but called the village Ammaon, that is, Emmaus. Against Petavius, Le Nourry, Ambrose’s scholiast on this passage, argues that Ambrose says the same in many other places: on Luke chapter 17; in *Apology of David*, Book II, chapter 8; in the treatise on the Creed; and elsewhere; and that Origen also gives the disciple the same name in the Preface to the Gospel of John. But in that preface of Origen, vol. II, p. 7, in Huet’s recension, Cologne edition, 1685, I read “Simon,” not “Ammaon.” He likewise has the name Simon in Book II *Against Celsus*, no. 62: “While Simon and Cleophas were speaking of the things which had happened to them, Jesus came among them,” etc. St Basil also names Simon in his commentary on Isaiah chapter 6, no. 186. The Maurist editors of both Origen and Basil hold that this was drawn from apocryphal writings. Whatever may be the case, our author’s statement is true: Luke is the one whom some suppose to be meant—Gregory, *Morals*, Book I, chapter 1; Theophylact on this passage; Nicephorus, Book I, chapter 34; and others. Gregory indeed, no. 3, says that this is characteristic of the writers of sacred discourse: moved by the impulse of the Holy Spirit, they give testimony concerning themselves in it as though concerning others.]

For it was the custom of the ancients to speak of themselves in their writings as though of others. Thus Moses frequently says: “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying” (Exodus 6:2, 10, 1, etc.). And Matthew says: “As Jesus was passing by, he saw a man sitting at the tax booth, Matthew by name” (Matthew 9:9). And there are many such instances.

And it came to pass, while they were conversing and discussing together, that Jesus himself drew near and went with them. It is good, therefore, to speak of Jesus. It is good always to hold in the mind

> [Col. 0446B]

that he does not forget those who remember him. Thus here too, because these two were speaking about him, he himself drew near and went with them. Blessed are those with whom Jesus walks. Blessed are those with whom salvation and life walk, who, because they go with the light, cannot go astray.

It follows: “But their eyes were kept from recognizing him.” Because they doubted, because they did not yet believe perfectly, they saw him but did not recognize him. And he said to them: “What are these words that you are exchanging with one another as you walk, and why are you sad?” And one of them, whose name was Cleophas, answered and said to him: “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem, and do you not know the things that have happened there in these days?” As though he said: So great a crime has newly been committed in Jerusalem that, because of its enormity, it cannot possibly be concealed; and how is it that you alone do not know what has happened there in these days?

> [Col. 0446C]

He said to them: “What things?” And they said: “Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people, and how our chief priests and rulers handed him over to a sentence of death and crucified him. But we had hoped that he was the one who was to redeem Israel.”

These men were gravely ill, and it was very necessary that the physician and Savior should appear to them. For by saying, “We had hoped,” they show that they had in some measure already fallen away from hope.

> [Note: Col. 0446D. St Augustine, Sermon 235, no. 2: “You had hoped? You no longer hope? Is this the whole of your discipleship? On the cross the thief surpassed you … What did you hope? ‘That he was the one who would redeem Israel.’ What you hoped for, and lost when he was crucified, the crucified thief recognized.” See also Sermon 232.]

“And now, besides all this, today is the third day since these things happened.”

> [Col. 0447A]

Therefore today, according to his promise, he ought to have risen. Yet we do not know whether he has risen. “But certain women of our company astonished us; they were at the tomb before daybreak, and, not finding his body, they came saying that they had also seen a vision of angels, who say that he lives. And some of our people went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said; but him they did not find.”

Having heard these things, the knower of all secrets, seeing that they both loved and doubted, answered their unbelief and said: “O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer these things, rise from the dead, and thus enter into his glory?” And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them

> [Col. 0447B]

in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.

For Moses, signifying Christ’s Passion and Resurrection, writes how Jacob blessed his son Judah, from whose lineage the Lord was born, saying to him: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hand shall be upon the necks of your enemies. The sons of your father shall bow down to you. Judah is a lion’s cub; from the prey, my son, you have gone up. Resting, you lay down like a lion, and like a lioness: who shall rouse him?” (Genesis 49:8–9).

For Christ ascended to the cross for prey, because by his death he snatched the world from the devil’s power. But he lay down like a lion, because he did not lose his strength even in death itself. And who raised him up except God the Father, and the very divinity which was in him?

> [Note: Col. 0447D. St Augustine explains this passage concerning the Resurrection of Jesus Christ in Sermon 37, no. 2, and Sermon 218, no. 12. Bede, *Exposition on Genesis*, on this passage. See also St Jerome on Micah chapter 1.]

Likewise David, signifying Christ’s Passion

> [Col. 0447C]

and Resurrection, says: “I slept and took my rest, and I rose again, because the Lord sustained me” (Psalm 3:6).

> [Note: Col. 0447D. Origen also interpreted this passage in this way and referred it to the Resurrection of Jesus Christ: on this passage, vol. II of his works, Delarue’s recension, p. 552; Eusebius, vol. I of Montfaucon’s *Collectanea*, p. 20; Didymus; and our ecclesiastical books.]

And again: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones; they divided my garments among themselves, and cast lots over my clothing” (Psalm 12:17–18).

> [Note: Col. 0448D. This passage of the Psalm is very well known because of the diversity of its reading in Hebrew; all interpret it concerning Christ, as they do also the following passages of Isaiah.]

And Isaiah says that he gave his body to those who struck him, and his cheeks to those who plucked them; he did not turn his face away from those who reproached him and spat upon him (Isaiah 50:6).

> [Note: Col. 0448D. Isaiah 50:6: “I gave my body to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who plucked them; I did not turn my face away from those who reproached me and spat upon me.”]

“Surely he himself bore our infirmities and carried our pains” (Isaiah 53:4). — “He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open his mouth” (ibid., v. 7). — “For the crime of my people I struck him, and he shall give the wicked man for his burial, and the rich man for his death” (ibid., vv. 8–9).

> [Col. 0447D]

While the Lord was saying these and similar things to them and interpreting the testimonies of the prophets, they drew near to the village to which they were going. Then he showed himself as though he would go farther, not merely by the disposition of his body, but even by his very expression, although he did not wish to go farther.

> [Col. 0448A]

For so it is also said above that the Samaritans would not receive him, “because his face was set toward going to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:53). In this manner, then, the Lord was testing them: with what disposition and charity they received strangers, so that we too might learn from them how we ought to receive such persons. For if we cannot otherwise detain them, we ought to use a devout compulsion upon them.

Hence it is said here: “And they compelled him, saying: ‘Stay with us, because evening is drawing near and the day is already declining.’ And he entered in with them. And it came to pass, while he reclined with them, that he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them.” For he used to do this when he still lived among them. “And their eyes were opened,” when they saw his familiar manner.

> [Col. 0448B]

“And they recognized him; and he vanished from their sight.” Then, moved at once by joy and grief, they said to one another: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke on the way and opened the Scriptures to us? Why did we not hold him? Why did we not even fall at his feet? Why did we not believe ourselves and our own hearts? Where shall we seek him? Where shall we find him?”

Rising in that same hour, they returned to Jerusalem and found the eleven gathered together, and those who were with them, saying that the Lord had truly risen and had appeared to Simon. And they themselves recounted what had happened on the way and how they recognized him in the breaking of bread. Consider now how great the joy there must have been, while each party in turn announced its own glad tidings to the other.

L. But while they were speaking of these things, Jesus stood in their midst and said to them: “Peace to you.” The disciples were speaking about Jesus and recounting together the things they had seen. Immediately he himself was present and made them more certain by his presence. For Jesus is always in the midst of those who speak devoutly of him and gather in his name. Hence he himself says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst” (Matthew 18:20).

He commends peace to them. He urges them to possess peace, because without peace it is impossible to please God. For the Lord dwells in those who love peace and concord.

> [Note: Col. 0448D. St Gregory speaks almost thus in Homily 10 on Ezekiel: “God dwells where true peace is sought.”]

Hence the Psalmist says: “His dwelling has been made in peace” (Psalm 75:2). It follows: “It is I; do not be afraid.” “It is I,” he says.

> [Col. 0448D]

Recognize my voice. You see me bodily, not as a spirit, as you suppose. For troubled and terrified, they thought they were seeing not the Lord himself, whom they beheld, but a spirit.

And he said to them: “Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts?” What you imagine is nothing, for you see not some phantom

> [Col. 0449A]

but reality. Then, showing them his hands and feet, he said: “See my hands and my feet, that I myself am he. Recognize the scars of my wounds, if you do not recognize me either by my appearance or by my voice. Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have.”

For this reason the Lord retained the scars of his wounds: that through them he might heal the hearts of his disciples, and, by showing in himself the wounds of the flesh, heal in them the wounds of the mind. For he knew that the apostle Thomas would one day say: “Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I shall not believe” (John 20:25). Therefore he did not wish to erase the scars, though, had he wished, he could have wholly erased them.

> [Col. 0449B]  
> [Note: Col. 0449C. Another reason is given by St Ambrose on this passage, Book X on Luke, no. 170: “He preferred to carry into heaven the wounds received for us, in order to show God the Father the price of our freedom.” But the Fathers also give this reason of our author, especially Augustine: Sermon 88, no. 2: “Could the Lord not have risen without scars? But he knew the wounds in the hearts of the disciples; and in order to heal them, he retained scars in his body.” And Sermon 112, no. 4: “The Lord, who could have risen without any trace of a wound, retained scars to be touched by the doubting, and to heal the wounds of the heart.” And Sermon 116 on this Gospel passage, no. 1: “He rose from the tomb with his wounds healed but his scars retained. He judged this expedient for his disciples: that his scars should be retained, by which the wounds of their hearts might be healed.” He has almost the same words in Sermon 2 on Psalm 88, no. 5: “He retained scars in his body in order to heal in the heart the wound of doubt.” See St Thomas, Third Part, question 54, article 4, reply to objection 3.]

But let no one infer from this that we shall rise with all the scars of our bodies, since nothing will rise in the bodies of the saints which appears unsuitable or unbecoming.

> [Note: Col. 0449D. St Augustine, Sermon 242, nos. 2–3: “Let men therefore ask whether this corruption of the body, which they feel in their flesh, will exist in the resurrection of the dead. We say that it will not exist … Again they ask: Will the defects which were in the human body, with which a person dies, rise again? We answer: Defects will not rise again.” See the same Augustine, Book XXII, *City of God*.  
>   
> Augustine seems to conjecture otherwise concerning the scars of martyrs in the work cited, chapter 23, no. 3: “By some manner of affection we are so moved by love for the blessed martyrs that we wish to see, in that kingdom, in their bodies, the scars of the wounds which they endured for Christ’s name. And perhaps we shall see them. For there will be in them not deformity but dignity; and a certain beauty—though in the body, yet not of the body but of virtue—will shine forth. Nor, however, if any limbs have been cut off or taken away from martyrs, will they be without those limbs in the resurrection of the dead, to whom it was said: ‘Not a hair of your head shall perish.’ But if it is fitting in that new age that the marks of glorious wounds should be seen in that immortal flesh, then, where limbs were struck or cut in order to be severed, scars will appear, yet with the same limbs restored, not lost. Although, therefore, all bodily defects that occurred will not then exist, the signs of virtue must nevertheless not be reckoned or called defects.”]

But while they still did not believe, and wondered for joy, he said: “Do you have here anything to eat?” They offered him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb. Let us also offer this. May this offering always be found in us; for he delights in this food, because our faith is contained in this food, in which Christ’s Passion and Resurrection, and also the perfect pattern of our life, are signified.

For because we grieve at his Passion and in turn rejoice at his Resurrection, we indeed offer him broiled fish through the Passion and a honeycomb

> [Col. 0449C]

through the Resurrection.

> [Note: Col. 0450D. St Gregory, Homily 24 on the Gospels, no. 5: “What do we believe the broiled fish signifies, except the mediator of God and human beings in his Passion? But he who deigned to become broiled fish in his Passion became for us a honeycomb in his Resurrection.”]

Blessed Paul too offered him broiled fish when he said: “I chastise my body and bring it into bondage, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected” (1 Corinthians 9:27). And again: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?”

> [Col. 0450A]

(2 Corinthians 11:29). For that fish is greatly broiled who burns for all. For we are all fish, whoever have swum in baptism.

We also offer the Lord a honeycomb when, filled with the sweetness of his love, we say together with the Psalmist: “How sweet are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (Psalm 118:103). Jesus is refreshed with us by this food, in which he himself delights and by which our minds are made rich.

Hence it is added: “And when he had eaten before them, taking the remains, he gave them to them.” We receive Christ’s remains if we imitate him and keep his words. For his remains are these Gospels, which he left to us for eating and doing. By them the mind is nourished, the soul refreshed, and the understanding made rich. Hence it is added:

> [Col. 0450B]

“These are the words which I spoke to you while I was still with you: that all things written concerning me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms must be fulfilled.” Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures.

Therefore he gave them the remains. He also gave them teeth with which they could eat them. For those whose understanding is not opened by God cannot eat them. And he said to them: “For thus it is written”—because you, who until now did not understand the Scriptures, did not know that it was thus written—“and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. But you are witnesses of these things.”

By your preaching and testimony, all these things will be confirmed everywhere.

> [Col. 0450C]

“And I will send upon you the promise of my Father,” concerning whom the prophet says: “It shall be in those days, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and they shall prophesy. But remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Joel 2:28).

Therefore let no one depart from the Church who desires to be clothed with this power.

> [Col. 0451A]

For this power is given to no one found outside this city. Hence the sacred canons deny that heretics can give the Holy Spirit;

> [Col. 0452A]

and therefore command that those baptized by them be sealed by Catholics.

**HERE ENDS THE COMMENTARY ON LUKE.**

> [Col. 0451]

**COMMENTARY ON JOHN BY ST BRUNO OF ASTI, BISHOP OF SEGNI**

> [Col. 0451]

**PART ONE.**
## The Beginning of the Holy Gospel according to John

### I. [Chapter I.]

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

[Col. 0451B] Jesus Christ our Lord, just as he is called the Son of God, is also called the Word of God, and likewise the Power and Wisdom of God. For Son, Word, Power, and Wisdom signify one and the same thing and are one and the same. Of this Word the Psalmist says: “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. 32:6). And, to show that Word and Wisdom are the same, he says: “You have made all things in Wisdom” (Ps. 103:24).

Therefore the Father was never without the Son, because he could never be without the Word, never without Power, never without Wisdom. This Wisdom, this Power, this Son of God, although born in time from the Virgin, [Col. 0451C] nevertheless existed in the beginning and before time. This is what he says: “In the beginning was the Word.”

> [Note: Col. 0451D. St Ambrose, *On Faith*, I.8.56: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God: this was in the beginning. ‘Was,’ he says, ‘with God’: was, was, was, was—behold, four times, ‘was.’ Where does the impious man find ‘was not’?”]

Let all, therefore, be silent who maintain that our Savior did not exist before he was born from the Virgin. For Jews and Gentiles, and certain heretics, are accustomed to say this. The Evangelist destroys their errors when he says that he was in the beginning.

But where was he? “And the Word was with God.” For the Son is always in the Father, and the Father always in the Son. Thus he himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 10:38). Indeed, where ought the Power and Wisdom of God to be, except in God? For where are your power and wisdom except in yourself and in your mind? Thus the Word of God—that is, the Power and Wisdom of God—was in the beginning with God.

And what was it? “And the Word was God.” [Col. 0451D] For there is nothing in God which is not God. For he is wholly the same and substantially the same. But this Word does not consist of syllables, nor is it uttered by a voice. Rather, always remaining in the bosom and heart of the Father, it orders, governs, and works all things. “This was in the beginning with God.” This is a confirmation.

“All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” Therefore, if all things were made through the Word, and the Lord made all things in Wisdom, it is clear that Word and Wisdom are the same. Therefore, where Wisdom is, there is the Word. But this is not so in us, because we have speech in the mouth and wisdom in the heart.

> [Note: Col. 0451D. See St Augustine, *Tractates on John*, 1.8; *On the Trinity*, XV.10.]

Nevertheless, just as our wisdom is clothed in a voice and becomes speech in order that it may be heard, so God’s Wisdom was clothed in flesh, and “the Word was made flesh,” in order that it might be seen by human beings. Therefore, whether the Son of God is called Word or Wisdom makes no difference. For God accomplishes all things not by speaking, but by knowing and willing.

For what is written—“He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and [Col. 0452C] they were created” (Ps. 32:9)—must not be understood as though a sound had rung out from his mouth by a movement of the tongue and some striking of the air. Rather, God’s speaking is his willing.

> [Note: Col. 0451D–0452D. St Basil, *Hexaemeron*, Homily 2.7: “When we speak of voice, word, and command in God, we do not mean a sound emitted through common bodily organs, nor air shaped by the tongue; rather, we understand the divine utterance as an indication of the will. So that the matter might be set before the eyes of learners, we judge it to be framed in the form of a command.” See St Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*.]

All things were brought to completion through him. For all things whatsoever were made by the Father were made through him, and without him nothing was made by the Father.

> [Note: Col. 0452D. See St Athanasius, *Second Oration against the Arians*.]

For God made nothing without Wisdom. Therefore God is one, who has worked all things in his Wisdom and in his Spirit. His Wisdom assumed flesh; his Spirit appeared in fire. But how he himself begot his Wisdom, his Word, and his Son must not be investigated, since it cannot be resolved.

“What was made in him was life, and the life was the light of human beings; and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.”

There are, indeed, two natures in [Col. 0452D] Christ: the divine and the human. One of these was made; the other was not made. For the humanity which is in him was both made and created. He himself made his own humanity; he himself made his own mother, [Col. 0453A] he through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made. Therefore this alone is in him—and nothing else is—that was made in him. But this was life.

Although the Jews did not believe this, Christ’s humanity is both the salvation and life of all who believe in him. Hence he says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). And again: “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25). “And the life was the light of human beings.” For if Christ’s humanity was life, and life was the light of human beings, then Christ’s humanity was the light of human beings. But why light? Because it shone, taught, preached, and enlightened the people sitting in darkness. Hence the Prophet says: “The people who sat in darkness saw a great light; light arose for those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death” (Isa. 9:2).

[Col. 0453B] Thus the Lord himself also says: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” (John 8:12). Of this it is then added: “And the light shines in the darkness.” For the light shone in darkness when Christ the Lord preached among sinners. Yet the darkness did not comprehend this light, because “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22). He alone could live without sin among sinners. This light alone was obscured by no darkness, blackened by no gloom, stained by no vices.

Others, however, punctuate this passage so that they first say “what was made,” and then add, “in him was life.” But let them see how the following words can be connected under that reading. For all things that happen or have happened in time [Col. 0453C] were in him before they came to be; in him they also lived and flourished. For all things that are within God’s ordering live, since, as they have been ordered, they cannot fail to come to pass.

> [Note: Col. 0453D–0454D. St Ambrose, on Psalm 36, §35: “The Alexandrians and Egyptians indeed read: ‘All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made’; and, inserting a punctuation, they add: ‘In him was life.’ Let that punctuation be preserved for believers; I am not afraid to read, ‘What was made in him was life’; and the Arian has nothing on which to seize. For I do not consider his poisons, but recognize the customary reading of Holy Scripture,” etc. See also Ambrose, *On Faith*, III.3.]

“There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. He came as a witness, to bear witness concerning the light, that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but came to bear witness concerning the light.”

For all, as Luke says, supposed concerning John “that perhaps he was the Christ” (Luke 3:15). For he was “a burning and shining lamp.” But he was not himself the light, because he had come only to bear witness concerning the light.

But the true light was the eternal and unfailing light, “which enlightens every person coming into this world.” Every [Col. 0453D] person coming into this world is enlightened inwardly and outwardly by this light alone. It grants sight to the eyes and understanding to the heart. Whoever is not enlightened by this light is blind and remains in darkness.

A person comes into this world when he is born, because then he first appears in this world. Thus the Lord says of himself: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John 16:28). For God, who is everywhere, is said to come when he manifests himself to us, and to depart when he conceals himself. Thus he came into the world because, according to the flesh which he assumed, he appeared visibly to the world.

This is what is meant by: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him.” For what does “he was in the world” mean except that he lived visibly among people in this world? The world knew him in some persons and did not know him in others. For lovers of the world refused to follow and know Christ; and because they love only this world’s pleasure and glory, they are rightly called “the world.” Thus the Lord says to his disciples: “Because you are not of this world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you. He came into his own, and his own did not receive him” [Col. 0454B] (John 15:19).

Although all things are his, the Jews were nevertheless called his own. They did not receive him, but despising him said: “We do not want this man to reign over us.” “But as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (Luke 19:14). What greater gift could have been given them than to become children of God? “For if children,” says the Apostle, “then heirs: heirs indeed of God, and fellow-heirs with Christ” (Rom. 8:17). And if they are fellow-heirs, they possess the same blessedness and inheritance.

“Who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God.” With regard to this second birth, by which people become children of God, they are regenerated and reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, not according to a man’s will nor according to the will [Col. 0454C] of flesh and blood, but according to God’s will. With regard to the first birth, however, both good and evil persons are born in one and the same manner.

“And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us.” The Word was indeed made flesh, not because the Word was changed into flesh, but because, by assuming flesh, one person was made from divinity and humanity.

> [Note: Col. 0454D. St Fulgentius, *To Thrasamund*, I.18: “The Word was indeed made flesh in that there is one person in Christ, of God and of man.”]

“And he dwelt among us,” as Jeremiah says: “This is our God, and no other shall be accounted beside him; he found out the whole way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he was seen upon earth and conversed with human beings” (Baruch 3:37–38).

“And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.” For those who were with Christ saw this glory when he was transfigured upon the mountain, when his face shone like the sun and his garments became white as snow; when the Father’s voice was also heard: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17:5).

He was full of grace and truth, according to what the Psalmist says: “You are fairer in beauty than the children [Col. 0455A] of men; grace has been poured upon your lips” (Ps. 44:3). And: “Because of truth and meekness and righteousness, your right hand shall lead you wondrously” (ibid., v. 5).

### II.

“John bears witness concerning him and cries out, saying: This is he of whom I said: He who is to come after me has been made before me, because he was before me.”

For the Lord came after John, because he was both born after him and began to preach after him. Yet he was made before John, because he was prior to him.

> [Note: Col. 0455D. St Ambrose, *Commentary on Luke*, II: “‘He who comes after me has been made before me,’ because the inferior voice goes before; the surpassing Word follows.” Bede, on this passage: “‘Before me’ refers not to an order of time, but to a difference in dignity.”]

For it is fitting and entirely appropriate that those who are prior should always be placed first and preferred to their inferiors. This is like saying of someone: “He was once my equal, but now he has been made before me; now he goes before me; now he has been set over me.”

“And from his fullness we all receive [Col. 0455B] grace for grace.” “We saw him,” he says, “full of grace and truth, from whose fullness we all received the grace of salvation and reconciliation in return for the grace of faith by which we believe in him.” Moses could not give us this grace, because “the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.” For through Christ heaven is opened; the faith and truth of the Law and Prophets are understood; and the world is reconciled to God.

For we were, “as it is written, like wandering sheep”; but, having come to know the truth, “we have now turned to the shepherd and bishop of our souls” (1 Pet. 2:25).

“No one has ever seen God. The Only-Begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him.” Since he had said, “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father,” [Col. 0455C] lest anyone understand this of the divinity—which is, of course, invisible—he therefore says: “No one has ever seen God.” He proves this by the authority of the Son of God when he says: “The Only-Begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him.”

For he declared this when he said: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27). What this signifies has been expounded in Matthew.

### III.

“And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to him, to ask him: Who are you? And he confessed and did not deny, and confessed: I am not the Christ.”

For all supposed that John was the Christ, since in life and character, dress and [Col. 0455D] holy conduct, he differed from all others. Yet he fled worldly glory and, declaring that he was not Christ, humbled himself so greatly that he said himself unworthy to unfasten Christ’s sandals.

“And they asked him: What then? Are you Elijah? And he said: I am not.”

When the Lord was asked concerning Elijah, he answered: “Elijah indeed will come and restore all things; and, if you wish to know it, John himself is Elijah” (Matt. 17:11). Why, then, does John deny that he is Elijah, when the Lord himself affirms that he is Elijah? John says: “I am not Elijah.” Jesus says: “John himself is Elijah.” Neither can lie: the one because he is Truth, the other because he is the disciple of Truth. Therefore each speaks truly. One speaks of the person, the other of the spirit. John was Elijah in spirit, but he was not Elijah in person.

> [Note: Col. 0455D–0456D. St Gregory, Homily 7 on the Gospels, §2, in exactly the same way: “What is this: that what Truth affirms, the prophet of truth denies? For ‘he is’ and ‘I am not’ are very different from one another. How, then, is he a prophet of truth if he does not agree with the utterances of Truth itself? But if truth itself is sought carefully, it is found how what sounds contrary is not contrary. For the angel says to Zechariah concerning John: ‘He shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah.’ He is said to be coming in the spirit and power of Elijah because, just as Elijah will precede the Lord’s second coming, so John preceded his first. … Therefore John was Elijah in spirit; he was not Elijah in person. What the Lord affirms concerning the spirit, John denies concerning the person.”]

Concerning him the angel said to Zechariah: “He shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17).

[Col. 0456B] But they said: “Are you the Prophet?” And he answered: “No.” For John was not merely a prophet, but more than a prophet. Hence the Lord says: “What did you go out to see? A prophet? I tell you, and more than a prophet” (Matt. 11:9). John was more than a prophet because he not only announced things to come, which is the work of prophets, but also pointed with his finger to that which the prophets do not do.

Therefore they said to him: “Who are you, that we may give an answer to those who sent us? What do you say of yourself?” He said: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Make straight the way of the Lord, as Isaiah the prophet said.”

John is the voice; Christ, the Word. Just as John [Col. 0456C] precedes Christ, so the voice precedes the word. For as soon as any sound proceeds from the speaker’s mouth, it is a voice; but it is not yet a word, because every word signifies something. Therefore the voice precedes, and the word follows. John is rightly called the voice and Christ the Word, because in being born, preaching, dying, and in the very meaning of his name, John preceded Christ.

> [Note: Col. 0456D. The same St Gregory, in the passage cited: “From your very manner of speaking you recognize that a voice first sounds, in order that the word may afterwards be heard. Therefore John declares himself to be the voice, because he precedes the Word,” etc. The same occurs in Homily 20.]

This voice cried in the wilderness because it called cruel and impious people to faith—people who imitated not human beings in piety but beasts in cruelty. For the wilderness is the habitation not of human beings but of wild animals.

But what did it say? “Make straight the way of the Lord,” as Isaiah the prophet says. “Make straight,” he says, “the way of the Lord, so that he may deign to come to you and dwell in you; for he does not know how to walk except by a straight way.” Faith, hope, and charity, piety, righteousness, and mercy are the ways [Col. 0456D] by which the Lord comes to us, if we possess them and direct them toward God. These ways are not straight for those who walk in them not truthfully, but hypocritically.

“And those who had been sent were of the Pharisees.” [Col. 0457A] The Pharisees considered themselves more righteous than the rest. The Lord said to them: “Tax collectors and prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of God” (Matt. 21:31). John too called them a brood of vipers, saying: “Serpents, brood of vipers, how will you escape the judgments of Gehenna?” (Matt. 23:33).

“And they questioned him and said to him: Why then do you baptize, if you are neither the Christ nor Elijah nor the Prophet? John answered them, saying: I baptize in water; but one stands in your midst whom you do not know.”

For John baptized in water and not in the Spirit, because he did not remit sins, but washed bodies only; and by baptizing he signified Christ’s baptism.

> [Note: Col. 0457D. St Gregory, Homily 8: “John baptizes not in the Spirit but in water, because, being unable to remit sins, he washes the bodies of the baptized with water but does not wash the mind by forgiveness. … Thus, having become Christ’s forerunner in preaching, he might also become his forerunner in baptism, by the imitation of the sacrament.”]

Therefore his baptism was a kind of shadow and signification of a better baptism. “I,” he says, “baptize you in water; but one stands in your midst—and you have seen and heard him, he lives among you and dwells with you—whom you do not know. He is the one who is to come after me, who has been made before me.”

For Christ came after him in being born, preaching, baptizing, and dying. But he was made before him because blessed John follows him as his Lord and goes after him.

> [Note: Col. 0457D. Bede on this passage: “‘He has been made before me’ is said as though one said, ‘He has been placed before me.’ Therefore he comes after me because he was born later; but he has been made before me because he has been preferred to me.”]

For “before” here signifies not time but rank.

“Whose sandal strap I am not worthy to unfasten.” To unfasten Christ’s sandal strap is to preach the mystery of his humanity and mortality. For a sandal, because it is made from the skins of dead animals, signifies the mortal condition of flesh.

> [Note: Col. 0457D–0458D. St Gregory, in the passage cited, §3: “Who does not know that sandals are made from dead animals? But when the incarnate Lord came, he appeared, as it were, shod, because in his divinity he assumed the mortality of our corruption.” Bede has the same words on this passage.]

Our other garments are made from various materials. [Col. 0457C] Sandals, however, are only of flesh; hence they are rightly used to signify flesh. See, then, how greatly the forerunner of the Lord humbled himself: before he had even begun to praise him, as though he were not fit to proclaim his praises, he at once said himself unworthy to announce not only the mystery of his divinity but even that of his humanity.

“These things happened in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.”

### IV.

“On the next day John saw Jesus coming to him and said: Behold the Lamb of God; behold, he who takes away the sins of the world.”

Christ is called a Lamb because of his innocence and simplicity, because “as a lamb he was led to sacrifice, and he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7). He indeed took away the sins of the world—not, however, of that world of which it was said above, “and the world did not know him,” but of the world [Col. 0457D] that followed his faith and teaching.

“This is he of whom I said: After me comes a man who has been made before me, because he was before me.” This has already been expounded above.

“And I did not know him.” What does “I did not know him” mean except: I did not yet know him by appearance and face, since I had not yet seen him bodily? “But that he might be manifested in Israel, for this reason I came baptizing in water.” “Therefore,” he says, “I left solitude and wilderness, came down to the plain, and began to baptize, so that I might reveal him to the Israelite people gathering to me from every side.”

“And John bore witness, saying: I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and he remained upon him. And I did not know him; but he who sent me to baptize said to me: He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.”

For the Holy Spirit descended upon our Savior in the form of a dove, in order to show him gentle and simple, without [Col. 0458B] gall and every bitterness. He remained upon him because he is not in him merely for an hour or temporarily, but always and essentially remains in him.

> [Note: Col. 0458D–0459D. St Basil, *Against Eunomius*, V: “The Spirit remained upon him, so that when you hear ‘remaining,’ you may recognize the freedom proper to his nature.” Jerome, on Ezekiel 35, concerning “He who sent me to baptize, he said,” etc.: “For what is added, ‘and remaining upon him,’ would never be proper to Christ unless he sometimes departed from others,” etc. St Gregory, *Moralia*, II.42: “Although he rightly remains in holy preachers, he is said to remain uniquely in the Mediator; for in these he remains by grace for a particular purpose, but in him he remains by substance for all things.” See also Bede on this passage.]
