Although he came from above, he was nevertheless always in him. But unless he had come in that manner, John would not have seen him. For this had been divinely said to John: “He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.”

For the Lord baptized in the Holy Spirit, that is, in the power of the Holy Spirit, which is common to the whole Trinity. To baptize in the Holy Spirit is the same as to baptize in the name and power of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For there are three persons, one of whom is the Holy Spirit; and no one is baptized in that person alone. Therefore the Lord said to the disciples: [Col. 0458C] “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

But because John did not baptize in the Holy Spirit, those whom he baptized were baptized again. For if he had baptized in the Holy Spirit, his baptism would no longer have been a figure but the reality.

It follows: “I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God.”

Immediately after he was baptized, as the other Evangelists write (Matt. 4:1; Mark 1:12; Luke 4:1), Jesus went into the wilderness and fasted forty days and forty nights. Then, when the end of that year was already approaching, while he had not yet preached openly and in synagogues and had only a few disciples with him, whom he taught privately, he came again to where John was.

[Col. 0458D] Hence it is added: “On another day John was again standing, and two of his disciples; and looking at Jesus as he walked, he said: Behold the Lamb of God.” Here “another” does not refer to yesterday, but is used for “a different [day].”

> [Note: Col. 0459D. See St Augustine, *Harmony of the Gospels*, II.17–18.]

For, properly speaking, that day which follows after so many days is not called “the next day.” Concerning these matters we have spoken sufficiently in Luke.

“And the two disciples heard him speaking and followed Jesus.” They believed their teacher as he spoke and bore witness to Christ the Lord; they followed Jesus, rejoicing that they had at last found him of whom they had so often heard John speak. Leaving John, they followed him whom they had learned, by John’s own testimony, to be the master even of John himself.

“Then Jesus turned, and seeing them following him, said to them: What do you seek? They said to him: Rabbi, where do you dwell?” The Evangelist explained what *Rabbi* means when he said: “which, translated, means Teacher.”

[Col. 0459B] The Lord’s turning toward them, looking upon them, and speaking with them are signs of his mercy and good will. For he knew what kind of men they were, what they would later become, and with what intention they were following him. For Jesus loves all who follow him and repels no one who comes to him.

Therefore, when they asked, “Where do you dwell?” he answered: “Come and see.” He did not say, “In this place” or “that place”; had he done so, he would seem rather to point out a location than to invite them. “They came and saw where he remained, and remained with him that day,” destined to remain with him all their days. “Now it was about the tenth hour.”

“Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, was one of the two who had heard from John and followed him. He first found his own brother [Col. 0459C] Simon and said to him: We have found the Messiah.” The Evangelist explains what Messiah means: “which, translated, is Christ.” For the Jews expected the Messiah, and still expect him, but in vain. Hence the Lord says: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and him you will receive” (John 5:43).

“And he brought him to Jesus.” Good brothers, who so desire to see Jesus.

“Jesus looked at him and said: You are Simon, son of Jonah; you shall be called Cephas.” The Evangelist also explains this: “which is translated Peter.” “You are,” he says, “Simon,” which means obedient,

> [Note: Col. 0459D. So also Bede on Matthew 4; but he gives another interpretation on Matthew 10.]

“whom Jonah begot,” that is, “the Great.”

> [Note: Col. 0459D–0460D. Jerome, on Matthew 16, concerning Peter: “Therefore he receives his name from his confession, because he has a revelation from the Holy Spirit, whose son he is also to be called. For *Barjona* in our language means ‘son of the dove.’ Others take it simply that Simon—that is, Peter—was the son of John … and maintain that the text has been corrupted through a scribal fault, so that *Barjona* was written instead of *Bar Joanna*, that is, ‘son of John,’ with one syllable omitted. *Joanna* means ‘the Lord’s grace.’” Bede almost copies the earlier words on Matthew 16, as does our author in his commentary on Matthew.]

“You shall be called Cephas,” that is, Peter, named from the rock and strengthened by Christ—though the name means “recognizing.” For he, recognizing the Lord before the rest, says: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16). To him the Lord says: “And I say to you that you are Peter” (ibid., v. 18), answering well and recognizing well.

[Col. 0460A] It must not be understood that the Lord chose Peter and Andrew at that time, since, as the other Evangelists write (Matt. 4:18; Mark 1:16; Luke 5:2), Christ called them away from fishing.

> [Note: Col. 0460D. On the twofold calling of these apostles, see Chrysostom, Homily 14 on Matthew, and commentators generally.]

Thus it is said here that they remained with him that day. For after he chose them, they remained with him not for one day but for all their days.

“On the following day he wished to go into Galilee; and he found Philip, and Jesus said to him: Follow me. Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.” According to these words of blessed John, Philip appears to have been the first of the apostles called. He is rightly called first, since his name is interpreted “mouth of a lamp,” so that he and the rest after him might understand to what office they were chosen.

> [Note: Col. 0460B–0460D. Bede on Matthew 10: “Philip is interpreted ‘mouth of a lamp,’ and rightly so, because, when called by the Lord, he at once proclaimed to Nathanael the light which he had recognized.”]

For they all received such a mouth when the Holy Spirit descended upon them in tongues of fire. We read when Peter and Andrew, James and John, and Matthew the Evangelist were called; but we do not read concerning the others. Yet Jesus already had disciples at that time, with whom, as is read in what follows, he was invited to the wedding. But who they were, we do not know.

“Philip found Nathanael and said to him: We have found him of whom Moses wrote in the Law, and the Prophets: Jesus, son of Joseph, from Nazareth.” Philip was still untrained: he wished to preach, but did not know how. He says that he had found Jesus, of whom both Moses and the other prophets wrote. What he says is true.

“Nathanael said to him: Can anything good come from Nazareth?” As though he said: Something good may indeed come [Col. 0460C] from Nazareth, but Christ Jesus is to be born in Bethlehem. Philip said to him: “Come and see.” “Come,” he says, “and see. Speak with him; listen to his words, so that you may be able to understand who and what he is.” Nathanael believed and followed him.

“Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him, and said of him: Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit.” This Nathanael was a great man, to whom the Lord himself gives such testimony. Surely great is the person in whom there is no deceit. But why is he called an Israelite, unless because he was already beginning to see God and believe in him?

> [Note: Col. 0460D. Bede: “He declared him a true Israelite—that is, a man able to see God—because he had no deceit.”]

For *Israelite* is interpreted “a man seeing God.”

“Nathanael said to him: How do you know me? Jesus answered and said to him: Before Philip called you, when you were [Col. 0460D] under the fig tree, I saw you.” Although this should be understood literally—that Nathanael really was under a fig tree when Philip called him—it can nevertheless be understood in a higher sense.

> [Note: Col. 0460D–0461D. Bede on this passage: “Because our first parents, ashamed by the guilt of transgression, made themselves girdles from fig leaves, this fig tree may not unfittingly signify the sweet-but-evil custom of sinning in the human race. Under it the Lord saw Nathanael—one of his elect, though not yet knowing the grace of his election—as if set beneath the fig tree and not yet seeing him. For the Lord knows those who are his.”]

For after our first parents sinned, realizing that they were naked, they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves coverings (Gen. 3:7). They covered those bodily parts in which generation occurs and from which the entire human race came forth; and Nathanael was there among the others. This is perhaps what he meant when he said: “When you were under the fig tree,” that is, under the fig leaves, “I saw you.” For the Lord saw Nathanael even then, he who knows and sees all things before they happen.

“Nathanael answered him and said: Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel.” How could Nathanael have recognized him so quickly, unless the Holy Spirit, who “breathes where he wills” (John 3:8), had enlightened his mind?

Jesus answered and said: “Because I said to you, I saw you under the fig tree, do you believe? You shall see greater things than these.” “Because,” he says, “you believed through one word of prophecy, divinely enlightened, you shall see much greater things for the strengthening of your faith.”

[Col. 0461B] And Jesus said to them: “Amen, amen, I say to you, you shall see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending above the Son of Man.” These things are clear if they are referred to that day on which the Lord will come to judge upon the throne of his majesty, with all the angels with him. For then the saints will see heaven opened and the angels ascending and descending. Then Nathanael also, who believed so readily, shall see greater things, when Christ the Lord appears in his majesty.

V. [CHAP. II.] And on the third day a wedding took place at Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. The first day was before the Law; the second, under the Law; the third, under grace. On this third day—that is, in this third period of the Incarnation—[Note: [Col. 0461D] Bede, on this passage: “Nor is it without mystery that, on the third day after the events described by the preceding discourse of the Gospel, a wedding is reported to have taken place; rather, it signifies that in the third age of the world the Lord came to take the Church as his bride. For the first age of the world was before the Law, under the examples of the patriarchs; the second, under the Law, in the writings of the prophets; the third, under grace, through the preaching of the evangelists,” etc.] [Col. 0461C] 217 the Lord deigned to come to the wedding, in order to destroy the errors of those who oppose marriage. [Note: [Col. 0461D] Many Fathers take the same view, such as St Jerome, Homily 1 on Psalm 50, and Homily 42 on Acts; Cyril, Book II on John, chapter 22, etc.] For Jesus does not reject married persons, even though virgins and the continent are better.

And when the wine failed, the mother of Jesus said to him: “They have no wine.” For the Virgin Mary, full of the Holy Spirit, already foresaw at that time the miracle which her Son was going to perform. What Jesus was intending to do, she urged him to do. And Jesus said to her: “What is there between me and you, woman?” “What do you and I have in common,” he says, “except this mortal flesh and this humanity which I bear, which knows how to suffer hunger, thirst, and death, [Col. 0462A] but does not know how to perform miracles? For water being changed into wine belongs not to humanity but to divinity.” [Note: [Col. 0461D] St Gregory, in nearly the same way, explains this passage in Book X, Epistle 39 to Eulogius: “Because the Virgin Mother, when the wine failed, wished a miracle to be performed through him, she was immediately answered: ‘What is there between me and you, woman?’ as though he plainly said: ‘That by which I can perform a miracle is mine from the Father, not from the mother. From the mother he could die, who performed miracles from the nature of the Father. Hence, too, when set upon the cross, dying, he acknowledged that same mother whom he commended to the disciple, saying: “Behold your mother.” Therefore he says: “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.” That is: “In the miracle which I do not have from your nature, I by no means acknowledge you. When the hour of death comes, I acknowledge you as mother; for that whereby I can die, I have from you.”’” From Gregory, I suppose, Bede on this passage; from Bede, A.]

“My hour has not yet come.” The hour of my Passion has not yet come, in which what you and I have in common will become known to all. For then you will see that the flesh which I received from you does not perform powers and miracles, but hangs upon the cross and dies. And then indeed I shall make new wine; then I shall make all things new; then, leaving behind the oldness of the letter, I shall transform all things into a new and spiritual understanding. For he himself signified this when he said: “I shall not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of God” (Matt. 26:29).

His mother said to the servants: “Whatever he tells you, do it.” [Col. 0462B] Mother and son were speaking with one another. They understood one another. They knew their own secrets. They knew what ought then to be done and what would afterward come to pass. [Note: [Col. 0462D] See St Bernard, Sermons 1 and 2 for the Sunday after the Octave of Epiphany.] But the others did not know what they were saying.

Now six stone water-jars had been placed there, according to the purification of the Jews, each holding two or three measures. For the six water-jars are the six ages of the world: the first, from Adam to Noah; the second, from Noah to Abraham; the third, from Abraham to David; the fourth, from David to the Babylonian deportation; the fifth, from the Babylonian deportation to Christ; the sixth, to the end of the age. [Note: [Col. 0462D] Bede: “The six vessels in which water was kept are the devout hearts of the saints, whose perfection of life and faith was set before humankind, through the six passing ages of the world, as an example of right belief and life—that is, until the time of the Lord’s preaching.”]

Jesus said to them: “Fill the jars with water.” And they filled them to the brim. For what are we to understand by these servants, who at the Lord’s command fill [Col. 0462C] the jars with water, except the apostles and teachers? Whenever we recount and preach what was done in each age, we fill these jars with water. For in many places Holy Scripture is called water.

In the first age, “God made heaven, earth, seas, and all things that are in them” (Ps. 145:6), and then made “man in his image and likeness” (Gen. 1:27). And he said: “It is not good for man to be alone; let us make for him a helper like himself” (ibid., 2:18).—“He therefore cast Adam into a deep sleep, and took one of his ribs” (ibid., v. 21), from which woman was made [Col. 0463A]. In saying these things we fill the first jar with water. For all this, understood according to the letter, what else is it but water? Yet this water is turned into wine if it is understood spiritually.

Thus, by Adam, because he was made in the image of God, we understand him of whom the Apostle says: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized” (Phil. 2:6). By Eve, however, the mother of all the living, let us understand the holy Church. For as Eve was made from one rib taken from the side of sleeping Adam, so too the Church was made from the side of Christ dying upon the cross, when blood was shed. [Note: [Col. 0463D] St Augustine, *City of God*, Book XXII, chapter 17: “For just as at the beginning of the human race a rib was taken from the side of the sleeping man so that a woman might be made, so it was fitting that Christ and the Church should already then be prophesied by such an event. For that sleep of the man was Christ’s death, whose lifeless body, hanging on the cross, was pierced in the side by a lance, and blood and water flowed from it; these we know to be the sacraments by which the Church is built.” See the same author, Book XIX, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 19, and Tractate 9 on John; St Bernard, Sermon 2 on Septuagesima, etc.] Hence the Apostle says to us: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood.” [Note: [Col. 0463D] That is, John, Apocalypse, chapter 5.]

Let us now come to the second [Col. 0463B] jar, not to fill it, but to pour into it a little water. For in the second age an ark was made of smoothed timbers, in which were gathered the kinds of all animals, so that the seed of all flesh might be saved in it and not perish. This, then, is water, which is indeed turned into wine if understood spiritually. For the ark made of smoothed timbers signifies the holy Church, [Note: [Col. 0464D] Thus St Augustine, *City of God*, Book XV, chapter 26; St Gregory, Homily 16 on Ezekiel, etc.] which, built from holy and perfect human beings, has neither stain nor wrinkle. 218 In it all races of humankind are gathered, so that that seed may be saved and not perish, which the Lord blessed. Of it the prophet says: “Unless the Lord God of hosts had left us a seed, we would have been like Sodom and made like Gomorrah” [Col. 0463C] (Isa. 1:9). For no one found outside this ark shall be saved.

Let us now speak also of the third jar, which is certainly so great that its water can abundantly suffice for all living beings and all who wish to drink. In this age were Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the twelve patriarchs. In it were Moses and Aaron, who, delivering the people of God from Egypt and leading them through the Red Sea, deserved to receive the Law. On their account the Lord scourged the Egyptians and drowned Pharaoh with all his army in the depths of the sea.

But the water of this jar likewise is turned into wine if understood spiritually: so that in Moses we signify Christ, and in Aaron the order of bishops and priests. For these lead the people of God through the waters of baptism [Col. 0463D], kill Pharaoh—that is, the devil—with the whole army of vices, and bring God’s saints into the land of the living and into the inheritance promised them. [Note: [Col. 0464D] That the crossing of the Red Sea signifies the passage to life and glory through baptism is taught by Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 9; Cyprian, Epistle to Magnus; Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, Book II, chapter 6. Origen confirms the same in Homily 5 on Exodus, no. 1, citing the Apostle’s words in 1 Cor. 10: “We know that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all crossed the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,” etc.]

Let us now come to the fourth [Col. 0464A] jar, in which are contained the books of David and Solomon, and of all the prophets down to Jeremiah. In it Isaiah also cries out: “You who thirst, come to the waters; and you who have no money, hasten, buy, and eat” (Isa. 55:1). Many days are needed—not one alone—to fill and expound this jar. If this jar alone had been turned into wine for the Jews, all would today be Christians with us. For in it Christ’s birth, Passion, resurrection, and ascension are most fully contained. Anyone who reads the expositions of the prophets understands how its water has been changed into wine.

Let us pass also to the fifth jar, in which the people, led away into captivity because of their sins, weep, saying: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and [Col. 0464B] wept, when we remembered you, Zion. On the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments” (Ps. 136:1–2). Yet, converted to God through repentance, they later returned joyfully to their homeland under Jesus the great Priest. And whoever understands these things spiritually will perceive water changed into wine.

For that captivity signified this captivity which we suffer in the world. When God’s saints see in it peoples sinning and always, like waters, flowing downward—for “many waters” are many peoples—they weep and grieve, remembering that heavenly blessedness. And because there are either few or none who wish to yield to their admonitions, they hang the instruments of holy preaching upon the willows; that is, they commit them to memory as though to certain very tenacious bonds, [Col. 0464C] saying with the Psalmist: “I have hidden your words in my heart, that I may not sin against you” (Ps. 118:11). For memory, because it firmly binds and holds what it understands, is not undeservedly called a willow. Preachers are often silent and cease from preaching when they see both their words despised and themselves held in contempt. But as then, so now, through repentance and satisfaction, under the leadership of Jesus the great Priest—who was signified then by that Jesus—all sinners return to their homeland.

It remains for us now to speak of the sixth jar, which is nobler than all the others and from which all the others also receive their flavour. For it contains the books of the four Gospels and all the sayings of the apostles. The Lord himself [Col. 0464D] filled this jar in his own person. He gave it to his disciples, that all nations might be satisfied from it, saying to them: “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15).

Its water is exceedingly sweet. [Col. 0465A] Its wine is most delightful. But do you wish to drink of its water? Hear the Lord himself: “The kingdom of heaven,” he says, “has become like a man who sowed good seed in his field. But while people slept, his enemy came and sowed tares over it” (Matt. 13:24). When his servants wished to gather them, he said: “Let both grow until the harvest; and at harvest-time I shall say to the reapers: First gather the tares and bind them into bundles to be burned; but store the wheat in my barn” (ibid., v. 30). This, then, is the water of this jar.

That it may be turned into wine, let us say with the apostles: “Lord, explain this parable to us.” “The field,” says the Lord, “is the world. The good seed are the children of the kingdom; but the tares are the children of [Col. 0465B] wickedness. The enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the consummation of the age; and the reapers are angels. Therefore, just as the tares are gathered and burned with fire, so it will be at the consummation of the age. The angels will go out and separate the wicked from among the righteous, and cast them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (ibid., vv. 36–43).

Thus water is turned into wine; thus the letter is changed into spiritual understanding. [Note: [Col. 0465D] I believe our author wished in this mystical explanation of the six water-jars to emulate Bede, who at length offers his own exposition at this point, one scarcely differing from Bruno’s. Allegorically, he interprets the first jar as Abel’s death and the murder committed by Cain, referring these to the death of Jesus Christ and the Jews’ killing of God; for the second jar, the second age, he adduces the Flood, much as A. does; for the third, Isaac’s sacrifice; for the fourth, David’s replacement of Saul; for the fifth, captivity, as A. does; for the sixth, the circumcision of Jesus Christ, which signifies baptism and resurrection. St Gregory, writing Homily 6 on Ezekiel, no. 7, opened and led the way in devising mystical explanations of this event: “Whom does not the Gospel narrative itself refresh in the performance of the miracle, when the Lord commanded empty jars to be filled with water and immediately changed that water into wine? But when those more alert in intellect hear these things, they both venerate the sacred history in faith and seek what it intimates inwardly. For he who was able to change water into wine was also able immediately to fill the empty jars with wine. Yet he commands the jars to be filled with water because our hearts must first be filled through the history of sacred reading. And he changes water into wine for us when that same history is transformed for us, through the mystery of allegory, into spiritual understanding.”]

It has been stated what the six jars signify. [219] They were rightly placed there according to the purification of the Jews, because whatever they contain is a kind of baptism and purification of souls. Each held two or three measures; this signifies that the measure of love of God and neighbour, and of faith in the Trinity, suffices for everyone to drink, retain, and believe.

It follows: And Jesus said to them: “Draw now, and carry it to the master of the feast.” And they carried it. When the master of the feast tasted the water made wine and did not know whence it came—though the servants who had drawn the water knew—the master of the feast called the bridegroom and said to him: “Every man first sets out the good wine, and when they have become drunk, then that which is inferior. But you have kept the good wine until now.”

Who is this master of the feast, to whom this new and wonderful wine is first brought? This master of the feast seems to me to be understanding, by which alone good wine is known and praised. For every person has [Col. 0465D] this master of the feast in the palace of the heart. He [Col. 0466A] is the ruler of the house; he governs and orders everything. To him the ministers of the Church daily offer the wine of the holy Scriptures. Drinking it, he admires and praises it, although he does not know whence it comes. For when these things are read in churches, they impart flavour to no others than those who understand them.

The Lord therefore rightly commanded that this wine be carried to the master of the feast, so that we too may give wine to those who understand greater things, but bring water to those who do not understand. For those who understand well reverence both the letter and the spirit. Hence this master of the feast says: “But you have kept the good wine until now,” praising both the first and the last. But those of lesser understanding should drink water and hear the plainest matters of the Scriptures.

Jesus performed this beginning of signs at Cana [Col. 0466B] of Galilee, manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him. For in the spiritual exposition of the holy Scriptures, which is signified by this wine, Christ’s glory is manifested and the faith of believers is increased.

After this, he went down to Capernaum, he and his mother and his brothers and his disciples; and they remained there not many days. How his brothers ought to be understood, we explained in Matthew.

VI. And the Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. He found in the temple those selling oxen, sheep, and doves, and money-changers seated there; and, having made something like a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple. These matters, indeed, have been explained in Matthew. The other evangelists relate that the Lord did this [Col. 0466C] when he came to Jerusalem seated upon a young donkey (Matt. 21; Mark 11; Luke 19). It is therefore clear that blessed John does not everywhere preserve the chronological order of the narrative. [Note: [Col. 0466D] St Augustine, *Harmony of the Gospels*, Book II, chapter 67, holds that Christ drove these sellers from the temple twice: first now, when St John narrates it, in the first year of his preaching; and then near the time of the Passion, when it is described by the other evangelists. So St John Chrysostom, Homily 22 on John.]

The Jews therefore answered and said to him: “What sign do you show us, since you do these things?” Jesus answered and said to them: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall raise it up.” But the Jews did not understand this; thinking that he spoke of the stone temple made by hands, they said: “This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it in three days?” But he, says the evangelist, spoke of the temple of his body, which the Jews were going to destroy in those days by the torment of the cross.

Yet it would not have been a greater miracle to rebuild that temple [Col. 0466D] in three days than to raise himself [Col. 0467A] on the third day after death. For he who, as Moses writes, created heaven and earth in one day (Gen. 1:1) could easily rebuild one house in three days. Therefore, when he had risen from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this. From this it appears that Christ’s disciples themselves also did not understand this saying. And they believed the Scripture and the word which Jesus had spoken. They believed, he says, the Scripture of the prophets speaking of Christ’s resurrection. They also believed this saying of Jesus, prophesying his own resurrection. Christ’s resurrection, therefore, was the reason why the apostles believed both the Scriptures of the prophets and Jesus’ word.

Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover, on the feast day, many believed in his name, seeing the signs which he performed. Here again [Col. 0467B] the evangelist seems to alter the order of his narrative, so that he is not speaking of the Passover about which he has been speaking until now. For at the Passover when the Lord was crucified, we read neither that he performed many signs nor that many believed in him; rather, even the apostles themselves doubted. It is therefore established that either he speaks of another Passover, or the Lord did not drive sellers and buyers out of the temple only once. [Note: [Col. 0467D] Besides the Augustine and Chrysostom cited above, Bede also takes this latter view on this passage: “Indeed, we read twice in the Holy Gospel that, coming into the temple, the Lord drove out traders of this sort: now, that is, in the third year before his Passion, as we learn from the following writings of this Evangelist; and in the very year in which he suffered, when five days before Passover he had come seated on a donkey into Jerusalem.”]

But Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people and had no need that anyone should bear witness concerning a human being. For he himself knew what was in a human being. If this is understood of those who believed in his name, it seems incongruous that Jesus should not entrust himself to them. It should therefore be understood of others. In a certain manner [Col. 0467C] Jesus both entrusted himself to them and did not entrust himself to them. He entrusted himself to them because he associated with them and daily preached to them in synagogues and in the temple. But he did not entrust himself to them—that is, he did not trust that he himself was among them securely and free from their snares. Why was this? Because he knew all people, and knew what deceit and wickedness was in each human being.

VII. [CHAP. III.] Now there was a man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. He came to him by night and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher.” This Nicodemus was a good man, already believing indeed, but not yet perfect in charity. For perfect charity casts out fear. He came by night [Col. 0468A], because he feared the Jews, yet wished to be enlightened. But what does he say? “We know,” he says, “that you have come from God as a teacher.” He adds the ground on which he received this faith: “For no one can do these signs which you do, unless God be with him.” Nathanael spoke much better, when he said: “You are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel” (John 1:49). For Nicodemus did not yet confess Christ to be God, although he confessed that God was with him.

[Note: [Col. 0467D] Bede observes this also: “From the miracles he wisely understood that the Lord was with him; nevertheless, he did not know that he himself was God.”]

Jesus answered and said to him: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” He invites him to baptism, in which, when a person is baptized in the Trinity, he comes perfectly to know what he ought to believe. But because he speaks obscurely, Nicodemus does not yet understand him. Hence he says: “How can a man be born [Col. 0468B] when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born again?” Seeing, therefore, that he could not come by himself to an understanding of this sacrament, the Lord says more plainly: “Amen, I say to you, unless a man be born of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.”

For the Apostle says: “All of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death. For we have been buried with him through baptism into death, so that, as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6:3). By these words he shows what baptism signifies. For when we are baptized in the faith of Christ and immersed beneath the waters, in a certain way we both die with him and are buried with him, so that, washed and wholly renewed, we may rise again [Col. 0468C] and thereafter walk in newness of life, just as the Son of God did not lose the glory of the Father.

So great is the power of this sacrament that it immediately cleanses a person from every sin.

[Note: [Col. 0467D] On this power of baptism and spiritual death, Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 40, p. 641: “Such is the grace and efficacy of baptism: it does not overwhelm the whole world with waters as of old, but cleanses the sin of each individual person and utterly wipes away the obstructions and stains contracted through vices … [Col. 0468D] Therefore let us be buried with Christ through baptism, that we may also rise with him; let us descend with him, that we may likewise be exalted with him.”

Chrysostom, Homily 25 on John, no. 2: “In this sacrament divine symbols are enacted: burial, mortification, resurrection, life; and all these take place together. For when we immerse our heads in the water, as in a tomb, the old man is buried and wholly submerged; then, when we emerge, the new man rises.”

And Homily 10 on the Epistle to the Romans, no. 4: “What does this mean: ‘We have been baptized into his death’? That we may die as he also died. For baptism is a cross. Therefore what the cross and tomb were for Christ, baptism has been for us, though not in the same respects. For he died and was buried in the flesh; we, however, in sin,” etc. He says almost the same in Homily 9 on the Epistle to the Hebrews, no. 3. See St John Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, 54, chap. 9.]

Hence it is added: “That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.” As, he says, flesh resembling itself is born from corrupt and sinful flesh—wholly corrupted, that is, and full of sins—so what is born of water and the Holy Spirit is holy, spiritual, and clean from every sin.

“Do not marvel that I said to you: You must be born again.” For I did not say this of carnal but of spiritual birth. Carnal birth occurs only once. But one who is born once from the flesh, unless he is born again from the Spirit, is born not to life [Col. 0469A] but to death.

“The Spirit breathes where he wills.” Therefore, he says, what is born of the Spirit is spirit, because the Spirit breathes where he wills: whom he wills he enlightens; whom he wills he sanctifies; and he makes spiritual and clean. “And you hear his voice, but do not know whence he comes or whither he goes.” As though he said: That Spirit who thus sanctifies all things, who breathes where he wills—that Spirit, I say, is he whose voice you now hear, and who now speaks to you in me and through me. Yet although you can hear his voice both in me and in my disciples, you nevertheless do not know whence he comes or whither he goes. For who can know whence he comes and whither he goes, when he is everywhere and fills all things? “For the Spirit of the Lord fills the whole world” (Wisdom 1:7). No one knows how he proceeds from the Father and the Son.

“So is every one who is born of the Spirit” [Col. 0469B]. As, he says, the Spirit breathes where he wills, so also does everyone born of the Spirit, provided that he is not separated from the Spirit. For if he is separated from the Spirit, he becomes carnal and natural.

[Note: [Col. 0469C] The author follows the explanation of those who take the first occurrence of “the Spirit breathes where he wills” [Col. 0469D] in this passage of John in the same sense as its second occurrence, referring it to the Holy Spirit. Calmet asserts that most of the ancient Fathers did so; although, according to the same witness, most modern writers understand “wind” in the first instance, such as Lyra, Estius himself, Calmet, and others. Toletus, Calmet, and Natalis Alexander cite the ancients on this passage.]

“But the natural man,” says the Apostle, “does not receive the things of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:14). But the spiritual man examines all things, even the deep things of God. Therefore he breathes where he wills, since he examines all things. For although perhaps at present he does not fully see, breathe, and understand whatever he wishes, nor is admitted to investigate every secret, still after this life the holy and spiritual person will see and possess whatever he wishes.

Nicodemus answered and said to him: “How can these things be?” Jesus answered and said to him: “Are you a teacher in Israel and do not know these things? [Col. 0469C] Amen, amen, I say to you: what we know we speak, and what we have seen we testify; yet you do not receive our testimony.” Our Savior affirms the truth of what he says, as one who speaks what he knows and here testifies to what he has seen. For ignorance produces falsehood, and a witness is not accepted unless he testifies that he has both seen and been present. It is as though he said: Only believe, and do not doubt. Do not ask how these things happen. For they are heavenly, and cannot be grasped by earthly understanding.

Hence it is added: “If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” Nevertheless, I shall tell you something [Col. 0470A] of heavenly things: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.” For these are heavenly things.

For Christ Jesus is one and the same: both Son of God and son of man; naturally Son of God and temporally son of man. And he, as son of man according to the other nature, that is, according to divinity, descended from heaven, according to which he is always both on earth and in heaven. For he descended not by changing place, but by humbling himself and assuming flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0469D] Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book X, no. 16: “Thus the Lord himself shows that greatest and most beautiful mystery of the assumed humanity, saying: ‘No one has ascended into heaven,’ etc. That he descended from heaven belongs to the origin conceived from the Spirit. For Mary did not give bodily origin from herself, although she contributed all that is natural to her sex for the growth and birth of the body. But that he is the Son of Man belongs to the birth of the flesh assumed in the Virgin. And that he is in heaven belongs to the power of his ever-abiding nature, which, having initiated and formed flesh through itself, did not confine itself by the power of its infinity [Col. 0470C] within the region of a limited body. By the power of the Spirit and the might of the Word of God [Col. 0470D], while remaining in the form of a servant, the Lord of heaven and world was not absent from any circles within or without heaven and world. Thus he descended from heaven, is the Son of Man, and is in heaven, because the Word made flesh had not ceased to remain what the Word is.”

See Fulgentius explaining the same passage, book II to Trasimund, chap. 17; Augustine, book I, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chap. 31; Gregory, book XXVII of the *Morals*, chap. 11. The latter two interpret this passage of Christ’s members, that is, Christians.]

But he ascended, as regards his humanity, by changing place also; as regards divinity, by manifesting his proper glory. Hence the Psalmist: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth” (Ps. 107 [Col. 0470B]:6). For God, because he is everywhere, cannot otherwise either ascend or descend.

And he alone and entire ascended into heaven, drawing all his members with him into heaven. For all believers are his members, and he is the head of the whole Church. Hence elsewhere he says: “What you have done to one of the least of mine, you have done to me” (Matt. 25:40). Therefore no one ascends into heaven except he and his members together with him. Or rather, he alone ascends through himself, while others ascend through him and not through themselves.

The Son of Man therefore descended from heaven so that, lifted up from the earth, he might draw all things after him into heaven. And this is what he says: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

[Col. 0470C] Moses lifted up the bronze serpent in the wilderness so that those bitten by serpents might look upon it and be healed. Christ too was lifted up upon the cross, so that everyone who sees him with the eyes of the mind, everyone who believes in him, may not perish but have eternal life.

[Note: [Col. 0470D] St Augustine, Sermon 26 on Psalm 118, no. 4: “Moses, by God’s merciful command, raised in the wilderness the likeness of a serpent upon wood, so that the likeness of sinful flesh to be crucified might be prefigured in Christ. Looking upon this saving cross, we drive out every poison of slanderous and proud persons.” See Sermon 353, no. 2; *City of God*, book X, chap. 8, etc.]

For there is no other medicine by which a human being can be healed of the poison of the first serpent. The Lord rightly chose to signify himself in that serpent: as it had the likeness of a serpent but not the serpent’s poison or malice, so our Savior, though reckoned among the wicked and crucified between robbers, had the likeness of sinful flesh [Col. 0471A], as the Apostle says (Rom. 8:3), but had no sin at all. For he appeared “in the likeness of sinful flesh, that through sin he might condemn sin in the flesh” (ibid.).

See, therefore, how greatly God loved humankind, for whom he delivered his Son to death, lest humankind should perish. This is what he says: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.” For God did not then send his Son into the world to judge—that is, to condemn and destroy—the world, but that the world might be saved through him. He came first to save; he will come again to judge.

“He who believes in him is not judged,” that is, is not condemned. For “judgment” is often used [Col. 0471B] for condemnation.

[Note: [Col. 0471D] On this passage, St Hilary on Psalm 1 says that it “troubles the negligence of hearers and the heedless facility of readers.” And St Augustine, *On the Christian Combat*, chap. 27, no. 29, reports that there were persons who, from this text, denied that a day of judgment would occur.

Hence many Fathers undertook to explain this passage. Though their explanations appear varied, most come nearly to this: judgment of examination is one thing, judgment of condemnation another, or there are two acts of judgment. They deny that those whose case is wholly manifest will be judged by a judgment of examination; they do not deny that they will be judged by a judgment of condemnation.

Thus Basil, explaining “the ungodly shall not rise in judgment” in Psalm 1, writes: “They do not come in order to be convicted, but to bear condemnation.” Nearly the same is said by St Ambrose, Sermon 20 on Psalm 118, and at length by St Gregory, *Morals*, book XXV, chap. 20.

Jerome explains differently, on Jeremiah 25: the nations will not be judged—regarding condemnation universally—because by their very unbelief they have been judged; yet they will be judged as to the manner and, as it were, the degree of condemnation. Chrysostom explains differently, Homily 27: evil persons will not be judged insofar as it need not be determined whether their works are good or evil; yet they will be judged, that is, sentence will be given and pronounced against them.

Our author’s explanation appears to be Augustine’s in the cited book: “For judgment is used for condemnation.” In support of this sense he adduces the Apostle’s statement, “Let not him who does not eat judge him who eats,” and the other passage, Matthew 7: “Do not judge, lest you be judged.”]

According to that saying: “Judge, O Lord, those who harm me” (Ps. 34:1). For God will judge both good and evil persons. But because he will not condemn all, therefore he who believes in him is not judged. “But he who does not believe has already been judged.” Why? “Because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.”

But someone may say: Then no judgment remains, since neither are the good judged, nor have the evil already been judged. In God’s disposition the evil have already been judged and condemned; his sentence is certainly unchangeable. Nevertheless, they still are to be judged—not that the sentence may be altered, but that they may openly hear and understand what has been decreed concerning them, as the Lord says: “Go, you cursed, into everlasting fire” (Matt. 25:41).

“And this is the judgment: light came [Col. 0471C] into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light.” This, he says, is the judgment for which the wicked will be condemned. If anyone asks why they are condemned, this is the judgment and this reason is given: because light came into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light. For if he had not come and spoken to them, they would not have had sin; but now they have no excuse for their sins. They love darkness rather than light because they imitate not Christ but the devil. For Christ is called the light of the world (John 9:5); the devil is called the prince of darkness.

“For their works were evil.” Therefore, he says, they loved darkness because their works were evil. Evil works seek not light but darkness [Col. 0471D]. Thus robbers and adulterers love night [Col. 0472A] and cherish darkness. This is what he says: “For everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved.” This is why adulterers, perjurers, murderers, thieves, traitors, and sacrilegious persons refuse to present themselves to bishops and to hear the words of God.

“But he who does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be manifested, because they are done in God.” He, he says, who does truth—that is, works of truth, works that are true and uncorrupted—because he does not fear being seen, willingly comes to the light. He willingly presents himself to Christ and his disciples. That Christ’s disciples are called light, hear the Lord himself: “You,” he says, “are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14). Therefore he comes to the light who does not fear to come to them.

VIII. After these things Jesus and his disciples came into the land of Judaea [Col. 0472B], and he remained there with them and baptized. Now John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there; and they came and were baptized. For John had not yet been sent to prison.

After the Lord had changed water into wine and spoken the things written above, he came with his disciples into the land of Judaea—with those disciples, of course, whom he then had; for he had not yet chosen the apostles. For, as Matthew says, after Jesus was delivered up, “leaving the city of Nazareth, the Lord came to Capernaum and dwelt there” (Matt. 4:13). Then indeed he called Peter and Andrew, James and John from fishing.

That John was baptizing signified Christ’s baptism. Hence he ceased [Col. 0472C] baptizing after he recognized that Christ was now baptizing.

IX. Therefore a question arose between John’s disciples and the Jews concerning purification. And they came to John and said to him: “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you bore witness—behold, he baptizes, and all are coming to him.” John answered and said: “A man cannot receive anything unless it has been given him from heaven.”

It is as if he said: All come to him; nevertheless, not all receive his testimony, since a person can receive nothing good unless it has been given to him from heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0472D] St John Chrysostom, Homily 28, refers the words “A man cannot receive anything,” etc., to Christ, in this sense: “Christ could not have received authority to baptize and be preferred to me unless it had been given him by God.” St Cyril, book II, chap. 60, thinks John said it of himself, in this sense: “I am a man, one among the rest; what I have has been bestowed upon me from heaven.”]

Hence the Lord himself says: “No one comes to me unless my Father draws him” (John 6:44). “For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” [Col. 0472D] (James 1:17).

“You yourselves will bear witness to me that I said: I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him.” He, he says, is the Christ, and not I. I bore witness to him, not to myself. You yourselves will be my witnesses that I said this, that I bore this testimony, exalting him as was fitting and humbling myself as was proper. For I was sent before him, like a herald before a judge and like a friend before the bridegroom.

And this is what he says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice.” He, he says, is the bridegroom to whom the holy Church is joined in chaste embraces, redeemed by his blood, fashioned from his side, and betrothed by the ring of his faith [Col. 0473B]. But I am the bridegroom’s friend, standing before him to serve, listening in order to obey, and exulting with great joy at his delightful voice.

This is what he says: “Therefore this my joy is fulfilled.” Behold, he says, he now preaches, he now baptizes; my joy is fulfilled; my prophecy is fulfilled. This I was awaiting; this I desired to see. Let the shadow cease: Truth is present. “He must increase, but I must decrease.”

For Christ increased because he was now believed to be what he was. John decreased because he ceased to be thought what he was not. For all thought John to be Christ. But concerning Christ, “some said, ‘He is good’; others, ‘No, but he deceives the crowds’” (John [Col. 0473C] 6:41, 13). Thus Christ increased; thus John decreased.

[Note: [Col. 0473D] This is the pre-eminently literal explanation. Ambrose, *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*, book VI, chap. 11, refers “increase” to the Christian people and “decrease” to the Jewish people, as though John assumed the person of the latter. St Gregory proposes it in Homily 20 on the Gospels:

“We must ask in what Christ increased and John decreased, unless it was that the people, seeing John’s abstinence and observing that he was then withdrawn from men, thought him to be Christ; but seeing Christ eating with publicans and walking among sinners, they believed that he was not Christ but a prophet. Yet as time advanced, Christ, who was thought to be a prophet, was recognized as Christ; and John, who was believed to be Christ, became known as a prophet. Thus was fulfilled what Christ’s forerunner foretold concerning him.”

See St Augustine, Tractate 16, no. 4; and St Bernard, Sermon on the Nativity of St John.]

And this fittingly: “He who comes from above is above all.” For Christ came from above, because he came from heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0474D] St Cyril explains “from above” as from the heavenly root, *ho tēs anōthen rhizēs*—“he of the root from above,” that is, the divine substance; and thus proves his divinity against the Arians.]

For he himself says: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” (John 6:41, 51). But this is too little. Look higher. Let him himself say: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16:28).

“He who is of the earth is of the earth and speaks of the earth. He who comes from heaven is above all, and testifies to what he has seen and heard.” It is not, he says, because we are from the earth, because we are of this world, and because we have been made from the earth, that, when we speak of earthly things—things we speak from what we have seen and heard—we generally speak falsely; rather, what we say is generally true. But if we speak of heavenly things, unless we establish our speech by divine [Col. 0473D] and heavenly authority, who will believe our words [Col. 0474A]? For a witness is not accepted unless he was present and testifies that he saw and heard.

Since, therefore, our Savior is above all, since he came from heaven, since he was present, and since he testifies to what he saw and heard, whatever he testifies is certainly true. “And yet no one receives his testimony.” “But he who receives his testimony has set his seal that God is true.”

Who, then, receives his testimony, if no one receives it? For it appears impossible that no one should receive it and someone should receive it. But this refers back to what he said above: “A man cannot receive anything unless it has been given him from heaven” (John 3:27). Let it therefore be said: No one receives his testimony unless this has been given him from heaven. But he who, enlightened from heaven, receives his testimony has indeed sealed, marked, understood, and known with utter certainty that God is true.

But why is it surprising that he is true, since “we speak the words of God”? For this is what he says: “For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God.” Falsehood cannot be present in God’s words. It follows: “For God does not give the Spirit by measure. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand.”

Therefore, he says, he is true because he both speaks the words of God and is full of the Spirit of truth. For he did not receive the Holy Spirit from the Father by measure, as other human beings do. He is the one “in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2:9). He is [Col. 0474C] “the flower from the root of Jesse” (Isa. 11:1), in whom all the graces of the Holy Spirit rest. He is he of whom the Father says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17:5). And the Father gave all things into his hands: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Matt. 11:27). Since he is less than the Father according to his humanity, he is said to have received all things from the Father according to his humanity.

“He who believes in the Son has eternal life. But he who is unbelieving toward the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.” Since, he says, the Father gave all things into his hands, it is in his power to give eternal life to whom he wills, and eternal punishment to whom he wills. And rightly will he not see life who refused to believe in him who is true life, as he himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” [Col. 0474D] (John 14:6).

X. [CHAP. IV.] Therefore, when Jesus knew that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making more disciples than John and baptizing—although Jesus himself was not baptizing, but his disciples—he left Judaea and went again into Galilee.

[Col. 0475A] Jesus knew that the Pharisees had not been edified by his baptism but had been angered by it; and therefore, lest scandal arise at the beginning of his preaching, he left Judaea for a time.

[Note: [Col. 0475C] St Augustine, Tractate 15 on John: “Because he knew their knowledge, he knew at the same time their envy; for they had not learned this in order to follow him, but in order to persecute him. Therefore he departed from there.”]

He did so until, when his fame had been made manifest through miracles, his baptism and teaching should receive greater authority (John 1:33). But the statement that Jesus himself was not baptizing, but his disciples, concerns the outward washing.

[Note: [Col. 0475C] St Augustine, Letter 265, no. 5: “Both are written concerning the Lord: that he baptized more than John, and that he himself did not baptize but his disciples; so that we might understand that he did indeed baptize by the presence of his majesty, though he did not baptize with his own hands. For the sacrament of baptism belonged to him; the ministry of baptizing belonged to the disciples.”

Likewise, Tractate 15 on John: “He baptized because he commanded; he did not baptize because he did not himself immerse. The disciples supplied the ministry of the body; he supplied the help of majesty. For when does he cease baptizing? When does he cease cleansing?” Bede copies Augustine on this passage.]

For if Jesus did not baptize, what is meant by the statement made to John: “He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, this is he who baptizes”? Jesus baptizes, because he purifies the whole person inwardly and outwardly. Yet he does not baptize personally, because he washes bodies not by himself but through his disciples.

Now he had to pass through Samaria.

XI. He therefore came to a city of Samaria called Sychar, near the estate which Jacob gave to his son Joseph. Jacob’s spring was there. This is indeed the estate of which Jacob, blessing his son Joseph, said: “I give you one portion more than your brothers, which I took from the hand of the Amorite with my sword and my bow” (Gen. 48:22). Jacob’s spring was there. Now if that spring belonged to Jacob, it had good water, since it is written: “In the assemblies bless God, the Lord, from the springs of Israel” (Ps. 67:27 [Vulgate]). This spring seems to be the profound faith and teaching of the patriarchs. Hence it is called not only a spring but also a well.

> **Note:** [Col. 0475D] Augustine explains here which is called a spring and which a well. Cyril, p. 177, presents an elegant allegory of this spring, which was called Jacob’s and was near Samaria, to which Jesus Christ came after leaving Judaea: “Typologically and enigmatically indicating to us that, although evangelical preaching would depart from Jerusalem and the divine word would henceforth go forth to the nations, nevertheless love for the fathers would not perish together with Israel.”  
>   
> Bede explains otherwise: [Col. 0476C] “The well signifies, by its shadowy depth, the earthly toil and error of this world”; this he received from Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 64, and *Tractates on John*, 15: “In the well I see a dark depth. I am therefore admonished to understand the lowest parts of this world, that is, earthly things, to which the Lord Jesus came at the sixth hour, that is, in the sixth age of the human race.”

It is called a spring because of its living water, but a well because of its depth. For the knowledge of the Law and the Prophets is exceedingly profound. Jesus therefore, wearied by the journey, sat thus upon the well. It was about the sixth hour. Jesus is wearied, but according to the flesh.

> **Note:** [Col. 0476D] Augustine, in the same place: “That he came wearied to the well signifies the weakness of the flesh; that he sat, humility; because he both assumed the weakness of the flesh for our sake and deigned to appear among human beings as a man in such humility.”

For unless he were wearied, unless he hungered [Col. 0476A] and thirsted, he would not be believed to be a man. Thus—that is, wearied—he sat upon the well. Therefore, those who are weary and desire rest should come to the well; they should come to the Scriptures of the prophets. There they will find Jesus; there they will hear him saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:18). For this reason Jesus rested, wearied, upon the well: that he might show us where to seek rest.

It was about the sixth hour because it was the sixth age of the world. The first age was from Adam to Noah; the second to Abraham; the third to David; the fourth to the Babylonian deportation; the fifth to Christ; the sixth to the end of the age.

A woman came from Samaria to draw water. This woman seems to me to be the entire [Col. 0476B] Israelite people, who daily comes to Jacob’s well, to the springs of Israel, to the Scriptures of the patriarchs; yet because she has no husband, she cannot be satisfied by drinking.

> **Note:** [Col. 0476D] Augustine explains otherwise, in the cited passage: “It may be asked why he requested a drink from the Samaritan woman. … But undoubtedly the Lord sought the faith of that woman, who, because she was a Samaritan—and Samaria commonly bears the image of idolatry (for they, separated from the people of the Jews, had devoted the glory of their souls to images of mute animals, that is, golden calves)—while our Lord Jesus Christ came in order to bring the multitude of nations, who served idols, to the safeguard of Christian faith and undefiled religion.” Bede has the same words.

This will, however, be explained in what follows. Jesus says to her: “Give me a drink.” Jesus thirsts; the fountain of life thirsts, of whom it is written: “For with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. 35:10 [Vulgate]). But if he is a living fountain, how can he thirst? Jesus thirsts not for water but for our faith. Hence in what follows he says: “My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven.” Now the Father’s will was that he should save the people and convert them to faith. This, therefore, was what Jesus thirsted for.

> **Note:** [Col. 0476D] Augustine, in the same place: “He thirsts for the faith of those for whom he shed his blood.”

But his disciples had gone [Col. 0476C] into the city to buy food. The Samaritan woman therefore says to him: “How is it that you, being a Jew, ask a drink from me, who am a Samaritan woman? For Jews do not associate with Samaritans.” Although the Samaritans were Israelites, nevertheless, having followed Jeroboam, who taught them to worship idols, they had become so estranged from the Law that the Jews regarded them as Gentiles.

Jesus answered and said to her: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ then perhaps [Col. 0477A] you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.” “If,” he says, “you recognized me and were enlightened by the Holy Spirit—for the Holy Spirit is the gift of God—you perhaps would have asked of me, just as I now ask of you; and I would have given you living water: unfailing water, water sufficient for eternal life.”

And the woman says: “Sir, you have nothing with which to draw, and the well is deep. From where then do you have living water? Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well, and himself drank from it, with his children and his livestock?” “You promise me living water,” she says. “But this water is living; yet you have neither a drawing-vessel nor a container, and I see that you have no rope. Moreover, the well is deep, and you cannot reach its depth with your hands. Whence then do you have living water? Or, if you promise another water here, in comparison with which you understand this water to be not living but dead, why did our father Jacob not give it to us? Are you greater than he?”

The woman said this because she did not yet understand Christ’s words. Jesus answered and said to her: “Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again. But whoever drinks from the water which I shall give him will never thirst; rather, the water which I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.” Little by little the Lord draws her away from her own understanding, in order to bring her to a better understanding.

This water is that of which he says elsewhere:

> **Note:** [Col. 0477D] John 7:38. Augustine, in the cited passage, and Bede likewise: “Thus he showed her that he had not asked for the kind of water which she understood, but, because he thirsted for her faith, desired to give the Holy Spirit to her who thirsted. For we rightly understand this living water to be the gift of God, as he himself says: ‘If you knew the gift of God’; and as the evangelist John himself testifies elsewhere, saying: ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink.’”  
>   
> St Jerome, on Amos 4: “That we may know that waters and drinks signify teaching, the Lord says to the Samaritan woman: ‘Everyone who drinks from this water,’” etc. Jerome says the same on Isaiah 5 and Zechariah 14.

“Whoever thirsts, let him come and drink, and rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” What this meant the Evangelist immediately explained, saying: “But this [Col. 0477C] he said concerning the Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive.”

The woman says to him: “Sir, give me this water, that I may not thirst, nor come here to draw.” Now somewhat removed from her former understanding, the woman does not mean the water of that well; she asks for another water, by which, being always supplied, she need no longer come there. But because this understanding also is carnal, the Lord invites her to another understanding, saying: “Go, call your husband, and come here.” “Call your husband,” he says: “bring forth your understanding, and come here; be present; no longer be tossed about among different things.” For the husband of the soul is the understanding, by which it is ruled and governed.

The woman answered and said: “I have no husband.” Jesus says to her: “You have rightly said, ‘I have no husband’; for you have had five husbands, [Col. 0477D] and the one whom you have is not your husband. This you have said truly.” Although these things signify something else, it must nevertheless be believed that this woman had had five husbands; but that she had now consented to someone in fornication? [Col. 0478A] This, certainly, was not hidden from the Lord.

Spiritually, however, the five husbands are the five books of Moses.

> **Note:** [Col. 0478D] Augustine, in the cited passage: “These things are not to be taken carnally, lest we appear to be still like that Samaritan woman herself; but if we have already tasted something of that gift of God, let us treat them spiritually. Some understand the five husbands as the five books which were delivered through Moses.”  
>   
> He himself, however, does not approve this explanation and suggests another concerning the five bodily senses; he does the same in *Tractates on John*, 15, after saying: “Many have understood—not absurdly, nor altogether improbably—the five husbands of this woman as the five books of Moses.” As usual, Bede follows Augustine.

By these books that Israelite people, signified by this woman, had for a time been instructed, as a wife is ruled and governed by her husbands. It had been separated from them for as long as it had forgotten its God and been disobedient to them. For it often followed other lovers and committed fornication with idols; fleeing these lawful husbands, it consented to error. This, then, is the one of whom it is said here: “And the one whom you have is not your husband.” It is error, not a husband; a deceiver, not a lover.

The woman says to him: “Sir, I see that you are a prophet.” For she would not have said this unless she had called her husband. Error has now fled; the fornicator has now departed. It follows: “Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, [Col. 0478B] and you say that Jerusalem is the place where one ought to worship.” “I see,” she says, “that you are a prophet. Answer me, then, what I ask and desire to learn. What is this which you Jews say, that Jerusalem is the place where one ought to worship, when it is certain that our fathers worshiped on this mountain?”

Jesus says to her: “Woman, believe me: the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, because salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming—and now is—when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth.” “The hour is coming,” he says, “and now is, when true and spiritual worshipers will worship God not on a mountain or in a city, but in spirit and truth.

“Although they must pray somewhere, God nevertheless looks not to a mountain or a city, but rather to the heart. He regards neither the higher mountain nor the more illustrious city; but God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart. Enter, therefore, into your chamber, and with the door shut pray to your Father. Pray not with the lips alone, but in spirit and truth. Only Jews, only confessors, only observers of the Law worship what they know; all others worship what they do not know. Why? Because salvation is from the Jews. From which Jews? Hear the Apostle: ‘For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is outward circumcision in the flesh circumcision; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is that of the heart, in spirit, not in the letter’ (Rom. 2:28).

“We therefore are those [Col. 0478D] Jews: we Christians; we members of Christ, for all of whom our head now says: ‘You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know.’”

It follows: “For the Father also seeks such persons to worship [Col. 0479A] him”—that is understood as “in spirit and truth.” But why is this so? Because God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth. For if he were bodily and localized, he would have to be sought on a mountain or in a city; but because he is Spirit, he must be worshiped in spirit.

> **Note:** [Col. 0479C] Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book 2, §31: “Therefore, because God is invisible, incomprehensible, and immeasurable, the Lord says that the time has come when God is not to be worshiped on a mountain or [Col. 0479D] in a temple; because God is Spirit. And Spirit is neither confined nor contained, because by the power of his nature he is everywhere and absent nowhere, overflowing with all things in all things. Therefore those are true worshipers who will worship in spirit and truth.”

The woman says to him: “I know that Messiah is coming, who is called Christ. When he comes, he will declare everything to us.” It is as if she said: “You speak obscurely, and I do not understand what you say. Yet I know that Messiah, who is called Christ, will come. When he comes, he will declare everything to us. He will reveal to us the obscure mysteries both of your words and of the other prophets.”

Jesus says to her: “I am he who speaks with you.” And immediately his disciples came, and they wondered that he was speaking with a woman. Why did they wonder? Because perhaps this was not his custom. Yet no one said, “What are you seeking?” or “Why are you speaking with her?” They entertained no suspicion concerning her in his regard. But when they came, the woman fell silent, though perhaps, had they not come, she would have continued speaking much longer.

She therefore left her water jar. She left her perverse understanding, with which she had been accustomed to drink carnally and not spiritually from the springs of Israel.

> **Note:** [Col. 0479D] Augustine explains otherwise, in the cited passage: “Nor ought this, that she departed leaving behind her water jar, to be carelessly passed over. The water jar perhaps signifies love of this world—that is, desire—by which human beings draw pleasure for themselves from the shadowy depth, of which the well bears the image, that is, from earthly conduct. … But one who believed in Christ had to renounce the world.”

And she went into the city. She went to the Church of the Gentiles. She went into the whole world to preach the Gospel to every creature. And she says to the people: “Come and see a man who told me everything I have done. Is he not the Christ?” Therefore they went out of the city and came to him, signifying those who, having abandoned Gentile life, are converted [Col. 0479C] to him even to this day.

Meanwhile the disciples urged him, saying: “Rabbi, eat.” But he said to them: “I have food to eat which you do not know.” Therefore the disciples said to one another: “Has someone brought him something to eat?” Behold, the disciples do not understand what food the Lord was speaking of, just as the woman above did not understand the water of which the Lord spoke to her.

> **Note:** [Col. 0479D] Augustine, *Tractates on John*, 15, and Bede following him: “What wonder if that woman did not understand the water? Behold, the disciples do not understand the food.”  
>   
> Ambrose, *On Elijah and Fasting*, chapter 3, admirably says: “Not every nourishment is material, nor every food bodily; there is food of the mind, on which the soul feasts, concerning which the Lord says: ‘My food is to do the will,’ etc. This is the food of angels: to serve the divine command. They have no concern for tables, no use for banquets, no stored-up feasts; no drinking of wine or strong drink, no distension of the body, no affliction of the stomach.” [Col. 0480C–D]

Jesus says to them: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, to complete his work.” I delight in this food; by this I am refreshed—something which, because you are still carnal, you do not yet fully understand. “Do you not say that there are still four months, [Col. 0480A] and then the harvest comes? Behold, I say to you: Lift up your eyes and see the fields, because they are already white for harvest.”

For Jesus, seeing that whole city streaming to him and already ripe and prepared for belief, speaks of it under the image of harvesting. He invites his disciples to hear and commands them to lift up their eyes, so that, taking hold of the sickle of God’s word, they might begin to reap, since he saw the harvests already white and fit for gathering. And lest the labor itself seem burdensome and harsh, he promises them the reward of their work, saying: “He who reaps receives wages and gathers fruit unto eternal life, so that he who sows may rejoice together with him who reaps.”

For the prophets were the sowers, who first sowed in that people the seeds of faith and teaching. The apostles were the reapers, who gathered into the threshing floor of the Church peoples already almost instructed [Col. 0480B] and ready to believe. For this they will certainly receive the fruit, eternal life, so that sowers and reapers may rejoice together and together enjoy eternal blessedness. For in this the saying is true: “One is he who sows, and another he who reaps. I sent you to reap that for which you have not labored. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labors.”

For unless the prophets had sown and foretold Christ’s coming and the other things written concerning him, the apostles would not have gathered so great a harvest of believers in that people. And in this the saying is true: one is he who sows and another he who reaps. For the Gospel saying is demonstrated to be true and indubitable in this: that what the apostles affirm, the prophets foretold. What these say has happened, those said would happen.

Many Samaritans believed in him because of the testimony of the woman, who declared: “He told me everything I have done.” Therefore, when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to remain there; and he remained there two days. Let us therefore ask him also to remain with us for two days, so that he may teach us both to love and to hold the two commandments of charity [love] and the faith of the two Testaments.

> **Note:** [Col. 0480D] Augustine, in the cited passage: “What then? He sent reapers, not sowers. To what place did he send reapers? Where others had already labored. … Where, then, were reapers to be sent? Where the prophets had already preached; for they were the sowers.” Bede wrote the same. See St Cyril, on this passage, p. 199.  
>   
> Augustine, in the same place: “The woman first announced it, and through the woman’s testimony the Samaritans believed; and they asked him to remain with them, and he remained there two days. … First they believed through report, afterward through presence. Thus today, when those who are outside … come to Christ, they believe through this report; he remains with them two days: that is, he gives them the two commandments of charity.” And in *Tractates*, 16: “There, after two days had passed, the number two days is mystically commended: the number of the two commandments [Col. 0481C] on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend.”

For these suffice for our illumination and for the fullness of life, because charity [love] never [Col. 0481A] fails; charity has no end. Great, then, are these days, which have no end.

It follows: “And many more believed because of his word than because of the woman’s word.” The woman persisted and preached, while the Word through whom all things were made assisted through a word, as he was able. They therefore said to her, now disdaining to listen to her: “We no longer believe because of your speech; we do not need your preaching. For we ourselves have heard and know that this is truly the Savior of the world.” For the Lord Jesus knew what sort they were when he called them ripe harvests, saying: “See the fields, because they are already white for harvest.” He would not have given them this testimony unless he had foreseen that they were willing to hear and believe.

XII. After the two days he departed from there and went into Galilee, [Col. 0481B] and then indeed came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. When the people of that place, who had known both his mother and himself from infancy, saw him, they began to disparage him, saying:

> **Note:** [Col. 0481C] Matthew 13:55: “Is not this the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary? And are not his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas, and are not all [Col. 0481D] his sisters with us? From where, then, has this man all these things?” And they were offended at him. But Jesus said to them: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country and in his own house.” See Mark 6:2; Luke 4:22; John 6:42.

“Is not this the son of Joseph and Mary? Are not his brothers also with us? From where has he these things?” And they were offended at him. But he said to them: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country.” Hence it is also said here: “For Jesus himself testified that a prophet has no honor in his own country.” What this means we have explained in the other Gospels. Thus far the digression.

When, therefore, he came into Galilee, the Galileans received him, having seen all that he had done in Jerusalem on the feast day. For they too had come [Col. 0481C] to the feast. These words signify that, while others disparaged him, as we have just said, those who had come to Jerusalem and seen his mighty works and miracles on the feast day received him with honor and joy.

And then he came again to Cana of Galilee, where he made water wine. There a centurion, who lived at Capernaum, met him; Jesus healed his son, as is related below.
