XIII. And there was a certain royal official whose son was ill at Capernaum. These matters have been expounded in Matthew. For although he (Matt. 8:6) speaks of a servant and this one of a son, the exposition in each case is nevertheless the same.

XIV. [CH. V.] “And there was a feast-day of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem” (John 5:1). The Lord went up to the Jewish feast-days in order to proclaim the teaching of faith to the peoples gathering from every side, to disclose the mysteries of salvation, and to display the light of truth. Now there is at Jerusalem a sheep-pool, which is called in Hebrew Bethsaida, having five porticoes. This pool signified the waters of baptism.

> [Note: Col. 0481D] Tertullian, *On Baptism*, ch. 5: “That figure of bodily healing proclaimed spiritual healing, according to the principle that carnal things always precede spiritual things in a figure. Therefore, as God’s grace advanced among human beings, more accrued to the waters and the angel: those which healed bodily ailments now heal the spirit; those which brought about temporal salvation now restore eternal salvation; those which once a year set one person free now preserve peoples daily, death having been destroyed through the washing away of sins.” Ambrose appears to have had this passage before his eyes in *On Those Who Are Initiated into the Mysteries*, ch. 4. See also Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, bk. I, ch. 8; John Chrysostom, Homily 35 on John, etc.

It was therefore not without reason called *probatica*, that is, “sheep-pool.”

> [Note: Col. 0481D] Correctly so; for it derives from πρόβατον, “sheep,” or rather from προβατικός, “belonging to sheep or cattle,” from πρόβατον, “sheep” or “cattle.” Thus it was a livestock pool—or, as it is called elsewhere, a bathing-pool (in Greek κολυμβήθρα, from κολυμβάω, “to swim”)—either because sheep intended first for slaughter were customarily washed in it, or because it lay near the gate adjoining the Temple through which the flocks to be sacrificed were brought in; concerning this gate see 2 Esdras 3:1, 32. Perhaps our author drew this from Bede, who writes: “And rightly is the same pool called *probatica*; for πρόβατα means ‘sheep.’ Commonly, however, the sheep-pool—that is, the livestock pool—is said to have been so called because the priests customarily washed the sacrificial victims in it.”

For those who are washed in baptism become God’s sheep. Of them it is said to the Church in the Song of Songs:

> “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing” (Song 4:2).

This pool has five porticoes because there are five books of Moses.

> [Note: Col. 0482D] Augustine, tractate cited: “That water, then, was enclosed, as it were, by five porticoes—the five books of Moses.”

In them the sacrament of baptism is most fully contained, defended by their authority, and explained by their teaching. In these lay a multitude of sick persons—blind, lame, withered—waiting for the movement of the water. By these sick persons lying in the aforesaid porticoes are understood the Jews, who were under the Law and were restrained by the Law’s bridle and regulation; yet they were not justified by the Law’s remedy.

> [Note: Col. 0482D] Augustine, in the same place: “But those books exposed the sick; they did not heal them. For the Law convicted sinners; it did not set them free.”

Therefore the Apostle says: “For if a law had been given which could justify, then righteousness would truly have come from the Law. But Scripture has shut up all things under sin” (Gal. 3:21–22). Thus the Law and Scripture are those porticoes which hold the sick, because they enclose all things under sin. No one was healed in the porticoes, because no law had been given that could justify.

> [Note: Col. 0482D] Augustine: “For this is what the Apostle says: ‘For if a law had been given,’ etc. Why, then, was the Law given?” He continues: “But Scripture has shut up all things under sin, so that the promise from faith in Jesus Christ might be given to believers.”

Yet from there the sick saw the pool, went down into it, and were healed, “so that the promise through faith in Christ might be given to believers through baptism” (ibid.). For the Angel of the Lord came down into the pool at a set time, the water was moved, and whoever first went down into the pool after the movement of the water was made well from whatever infirmity held him.

The Angel of the Lord came down into the pool at a set time when, at the appointed time, our Savior came to baptism. For he is that Angel of Great Counsel, of whom it is written: “And immediately the Lord whom you seek, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire, shall come to his holy temple” (Mal. 3:1). He himself stirred the water. He sanctified the waters of baptism and by his touch removed from them every hidden assault of the enemy. After his stirring, the water received such power within itself that it heals all the infirmities of all who go down into it, drives out diseases, and remits sins.

But it should be noted that only he is healed who is first to go down into the pool after the water’s movement. By him is understood the whole Christian people: alone and unique, first and last, one and indivisible, it is both washed and healed in the waters of baptism. But who is he who goes down after it, except one who does not adhere to this ecclesiastical body? For if he belonged to this body, he would be said to go down not after it but in it. Heretics indeed go down after it, and in going down they gain nothing for themselves.

> [Note: Cols. 0483C–D] Augustine, Tractate 17 on John: “After the water had been stirred, one person who was able threw himself in and alone was healed; whoever threw himself in after him did so in vain. … To go down into the stirred water, therefore, is humbly to believe in the Lord’s Passion. There one person was healed, signifying unity. Afterwards, whoever came was not healed, because whoever is apart from unity cannot be healed.” See Sermon 125.  
> 
> More fully, Bede—whom, I think, our author follows—expounds the entire Gospel passage from Augustine’s Sermons 124 and 125: “The sheep-pool, surrounded by five porticoes, is the Jewish people, fortified on every side by the Law’s guard so that it should not sin. Rightly, indeed, the Law written in the five books of Moses is figured by the number five. … The multitude of sick persons lying in the mentioned porticoes and awaiting the movement of the water signifies those companies of people who, hearing the words of the Law, grieved that they could not fulfill it by their own strength. … Such persons lay in the five porticoes; yet they were healed only when the angel came into the pool, because through the Law comes knowledge of sin, but the grace of remission came only through Jesus Christ. The angel signifies him: descending invisibly into the pool and imparting healing power, he moved the water. For the Angel of Great Counsel came down clothed in flesh. … The movement of the water indicates the Lord’s Passion, brought about amid the agitation and turmoil of the Jewish people. … It is also rightly said that whoever first went down after the water’s movement was made well from whatever sickness held him: for there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God; and whoever is imbued, in Catholic unity, with Christ’s mysteries is made well from whatever sickness of sins holds him. But whoever departs from unity cannot attain the salvation which comes from the One.”

Now there was a certain man there who had been in his infirmity for thirty-eight years. When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had already been there a long time, he said to him, “Do you wish to be made well?” The sick man answered him: “Lord, I have no man to put me into the pool when the water has been stirred. For while I am coming, another goes down before me.”

This man signifies those who commit grave sins after baptism.

> [Note: Col. 0484D] This too seems to be from Bede: “This man, held by infirmity for many years, signifies any sinner worn out by the enormity or multitude of his crimes,” etc.

For them a severe and prolonged penance is imposed, through which the body is indeed afflicted but the soul healed. That you may understand that this man had fallen ill on account of his iniquities, the Lord himself shows it when he says: “Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you.” But such persons, because they do not repent properly, though they may seem to suffer and repent for a long time and to mortify the flesh, are nevertheless healed with great difficulty. For if they had repented properly, they would have had not thirty-eight years but a complete forty in such infirmity.

> [Note: Col. 0484D] Augustine states it somewhat differently; nevertheless, recognizing mysteries in this number, he concludes in Tractate 17: “If, therefore, the number forty has the perfection of the Law, and the Law is not fulfilled except in the twofold commandment of love, why are you surprised that he was sick who lacked two of forty?” See Sermon 125.

For every repentance is imperfect which falls short in any respect of this number. Why perfect repentance is designated by this number, consider. This number consists of four and ten: four times ten, or ten times four, makes forty. In four the New Testament is figured, and in ten the Old: the former consists in the four Gospels, the latter in the ten commandments. No repentance avails for salvation unless it is undertaken under the authority of both the New and Old Testaments. The Lord himself signified this when he fasted forty days and forty nights; Moses likewise, and Elijah likewise.

Therefore whoever wishes his repentance to be fruitful should practice repentance according to this number—that is, should repent according to the teaching and discipline of both Testaments. Let a person then turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it. This is true repentance.

But observe that the merciful Lord deigns to visit, heal, and enlighten even those who repent improperly and merely legally, provided that they have a good will and await the remedies of salvation. Therefore he says even to this sick man, “Do you wish to be made well?” As if he said: You do indeed wish to be healed; for this reason you lie here, are ill, mortify your flesh, and perform this sort of repentance. Yet you are not healed because you do not perform worthy repentance.

The sick man answered him: “Lord, I have no man to put me into the pool when the water has been stirred.” For what else does he signify by these words than a certain impossibility of being baptized and descending into that pool? For it is impossible for those once baptized to be renewed again through baptism and cleansed from the contagion of sins. Thus, although this man is healed, he is not immersed in the pool, because he signifies those who are healed after baptism by repentance alone.

But when he says, “While I am coming, another goes down before me,” he seems to speak of himself while still a Gentile and catechumen. For when he was still a Gentile and catechumen, he went down into the pool. But now, because he is a Christian, he cannot go down into it. Thus the same person is both “another” and the one who goes down before himself.

Jesus said to him: “Rise, take up your bed, and walk.” Do not, he says, seek any longer for a person to put you into the pool. Only rise. Raise your mind. Contemplate heaven. Seek the things above, not those upon the earth. For by this way those who have been baptized recover health if they happen to fall ill.

“Take up your bed”: carry, restrain, and reduce your flesh to servitude. For the body is the bed of the soul; if it is corrupt, the whole soul lies sick and infirm in it. Hence it is written: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15). “And walk.” Do not be idle, for idleness is the enemy of the soul: it nourishes vices and kills virtues.

> [Note: Col. 0485D] Augustine and Bede explain this not very differently: as shaking off the torpor of vices, practicing virtues, and bearing one’s brethren.

“And immediately the man was made well. And he took up his bed and walked.” It is therefore easy for God both to heal a person and to remit sins.

Now it was the Sabbath on that day. Therefore the Jews said to the man who had been healed: “It is the Sabbath; it is not lawful for you to take up your bed.” He answered them: “He who made me well said to me, ‘Take up your bed and walk.’” He who made me well, he says, has greater authority than you.

> [Note: Col. 0485D] Augustine: “He set the author of his healing against his detractors. Would I not accept a command from him from whom I had received healing?”

Therefore I must obey him, not you. They then asked him: “Who is the man who said to you, ‘Take up your bed and walk’?” But the man who had been made well did not know who he was. It is no wonder that he did not know who he was, for it is not easy to know Jesus. Hence the Lord himself says: “No one knows the Son except the Father; and no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27).

Jesus withdrew from the crowd gathered in the place. Afterwards Jesus found him in the Temple. Jesus is everywhere, but he is not known everywhere. He is not known in the crowd.

> [Note: Col. 0485D] Augustine, in the work cited: “It is difficult to see Christ in a crowd; a certain solitude is necessary for our mind. … A crowd has noise; this vision seeks secrecy.” Bede says almost the same.

But he is known in the Temple. Let us therefore flee the crowd, and with Jesus withdraw from the crowd. Let us go into the Temple. May he find us there, and may he there be found by us. For this reason he himself departed from the crowd of people: to teach us also to depart from the crowd of vices.

And Jesus said to him: “Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you.” This happened to you, he says, because you sinned. Therefore sin no more; let there not be in you a will to sin. For not sinning is very difficult and almost impossible. Many sin who do not wish to sin. Hence the Apostle says: “For I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I do not wish, that I do” (Rom. 7:19). Therefore the will to sin is a great sin. “For,” as the Apostle says, “if we sin willfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins” (Heb. 10:26). This is understood, however, of those who willingly persevere in sins to their very end.

That man went away and reported to the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him well.

XV. Therefore the Jews persecuted Jesus because he did these things on the Sabbath. [Col. 0486B] For the Jews understood the Sabbath wrongly, thinking that to heal a person on the Sabbath and to exercise piety and mercy was a sin. But Jesus answered them: “My Father is working until now, and I am working.”

“I,” he says, “ought not to be reproved concerning the Sabbath, because on the Sabbath I do not do what the Law forbids to be done on the Sabbath. But, as my Father, so I also work until now—that is, until the Sabbath; on the Sabbath, however, I rest from work. For God made the first man on the sixth day, and Christ redeemed the whole human race on the sixth day. He rested on the seventh day, and Christ rested in the tomb on the day of the Sabbath.” [Note: [Col. 0485D] See St Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book IV, ch. 2, and Tractate 17 on John.] That rest, therefore, signified this rest. Thus each works until the Sabbath, and each rests on the Sabbath. Yet both Father and Son work in another manner even until today; for, although on the Sabbath, after the seeds or principles of all things had been made, he rested, nevertheless on no day does he rest from justice, mercy, and other things of this kind. [Note: [Col. 0485D] Cyril, p. 213, and Augustine himself in several places explain “working until now” also as the preservation of natural things. Thus Augustine, writing in book IV of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, ch. 12, understands “God to have rested from creating kinds of creatures, because thereafter he created no new kinds. But afterwards, he says, he works until now and beyond in administering those same kinds which were then established.” See also Gaudentius of Brescia, Sermon 10. The same Augustine explains this passage in terms of both kinds of operation, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book V, ch. 20: “The Father abiding in me,” he says, “does his works; and as the Father raises the dead and gives life, so the Son gives life to whom he wills. Then, because he works not only the great and principal things, but also these earthly and outward things themselves.”]

For no good is done anywhere except by him and through him. God, therefore, did not rest on the Sabbath day in such a way that he is to be understood as having done nothing after the Sabbath. Let him therefore say: “My Father is working until now, and I am working.”

It follows: “For this reason, therefore, the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only was breaking the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God.” He was not making himself equal to God, since according to his divinity he was in every respect equal to God; rather, “making himself equal” means showing himself to be equal. Hence the Apostle says: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something seized” (Phil. [Col. 0487A] 2:6).

Jesus therefore answered and said to them: “Amen, amen, I say to you: the Son cannot do anything from himself, except what he sees the Father doing. For whatever he does, these things the Son likewise does.” For according to divinity, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one and the same operation. The Son does nothing without the Father and the Holy Spirit. Likewise, the Father does nothing without the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit also does nothing without the Father and the Son. [Note: [Col. 0487D] Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book VII: “This is the understanding of the true birth, and the most complete mystery of our faith: that from the unity of the divine nature it confesses in the Father and the Son the truth of one and undifferentiated divinity; so that, in doing the same things, the Son does likewise, and in doing likewise the things that he does are themselves the same, because, under this single expression, both works done alike bear witness to birth and identical works to nature,” etc. See Basil, *Against Eunomius*, book IV; Ambrose, *On Faith*, book IV, ch. 3, etc. Hence Bede, on this passage: “He shows the signification of one nature and one operation; for the operation of Father and Son is common, whose nature is one and whose operation likewise is one.”]

Whoever, therefore, speaks against the Son—whether concerning the things he does on the Sabbath or any other operation of this kind—certainly also speaks against the Father and against the Holy Spirit. Let anyone who fears offending God the Father therefore cease to speak thus and such things against the Son. [Col. 0487B]

“For the Father loves the Son and shows him all things that he himself does; and he will show him greater works than these, so that you may marvel.” As regards divinity, the Father shows the Son nothing, for, just as the Father, so the Son is ignorant of nothing. [Note: [Col. 0487D] Hilary, ibid.: “His power is made equal through the unity of an undissimilar nature; and the showing of works is not instruction for ignorance, but for our faith. It introduces into us not knowledge for the Son of things unknown, but confession of his birth, confirming [Col. 0488D] it by the fact that all things which he could do were shown to him.” Bede copied these words here.] But as regards humanity, the Father shows him all things. And he will show him greater works than those which, it is understood, the Son is recorded above as having done. Why? So that, seeing them, you may marvel more and more, and, marveling, may be converted.

That these words concerning the Son are to be understood according to his humanity is made clear by what follows. [Note: [Col. 0488D] Augustine, Tractate 19—whom Bede follows here—Cyril, and many other Fathers explain these and the preceding words as referring to the divine nature, as Petavius noted, *On the Trinity*, book II, ch. 4, no. 5; ch. 12, no. 15, etc.; Natalis Alexander, on this passage. These follow another line of reasoning in explaining the following words concerning the power of judgment given to the Son. Although, in Jansen’s *Concordia*, ch. 36, some hold that these words also do not prevent their being applied to the Son’s divine nature—among whom Chrysostom seems to be included, *Homily 39 on John*, no. 1, saying: “Just as this means the same as that he begot him life, so he gave judgment,” that is, “he begot him as judge”—nevertheless Augustine, Tractate 20, writes: “Because the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, having become man from the Virgin Mary, he is the Son of man; therefore, because [Col. 0489C] he is the Son of man, what did he receive? Power to execute judgment,” etc., and explains this of the human nature. Cyril does the same on p. 224, together with our author, who also explains “he shows him all things,” etc., of the human nature. Elias of Crete, in his fourth theological oration of Nazianzen; Severus of Antioch; Caesarius; and others do the same. See Calmet, Maldonatus, and other interpreters.]

For he says: “For as the Father raises the dead and gives life, so also the Son of man gives life to whom he wills.” Note that he says, “the Son of man.” These works are indeed greater than either healing the paralytic [Col. 0487C] or changing water into wine. But if the Son of man gives life to whom he wills, why does he not give life to all, unless it is because he does not will it? For the Son of man wills to give life to no human being except those believing in him and doing his will. And he himself, because he is judge, has power to put to death and to give life.

Hence it is added: “For neither does the Father judge anyone, but he has given all judgment to the Son.” Why is this? “That all may honor the Son as they honor the Father.” For when the Son of man comes upon the seat of his majesty to judge the world, then all will equally honor both the Son and the Father. Hence the Lord himself says: “Therefore the Lord truly says, ‘To me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall confess’” [Col. 0488A] (Isa. 44:24; Rom. 14:11). Hence also the Apostle: “For this reason God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings may bend, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:9–10).

It is therefore clear that all will honor the Son as they honor the Father. But now, because not all honor the Son, neither do they honor the Father. This is what he says: “Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.” But because the Father gave all judgment to the Son, and the Son himself gives life to those whom he wills to give life, he added the following, so that we may understand who those are to whom he gives life and what that giving life itself is: [Col. 0488B] “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and shall not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life.”

Therefore, the Lord gives life to such persons, and gives life in this way: namely, by giving eternal life. What he says, “whoever hears my word,” is as though he said, whoever hears and keeps my teaching. For that person hears well who obeys when he hears. “For it is not hearers of the Law who are righteous before God, but doers” (Rom. 2:13). Hence the Lord says: “Let the one who has ears to hear, hear” (Matt. 13:43). Those are said not to come into judgment who will not be condemned in judgment. Therefore, what else is it to come into judgment but to be judged and condemned? The good, however, will not come into this judgment.

It follows: “Amen, amen, I say to you: the hour is coming, [Col. 0488C] and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God. And those who hear shall live.” He seems to say this against the Sadducees and others who denied the resurrection of the dead and eternal life. It is as though he said: Do not doubt that those who hear my words and believe him who sent me possess eternal life, since you see the dead rise at my voice. For many have undoubtedly already risen at his voice, dead both in body and soul. Although we read that the Lord raised three persons bodily from death, we do not read how many he raised in soul. But what wonder is it if the dead rise at the voice of the Son of God, since he possesses the same power together with the Father?

And this is what he says: [Col. 0489A] “For as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself, and gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of man.” For, just as the Father, so the Son has life in himself—that is, in his own power and authority—so that he may bestow it upon whomever he wills. All our life is in his power, and we cannot live beyond his will. At his command, therefore, all die; and at his command all shall rise.

The Father gave the Son authority to execute judgment, not according to divinity, by which he is equal to him, but according to humanity, by which he is less. [Note: [Col. 0489C] What we said above concerning the authority to judge applies here; this is why Augustine, who explains the preceding words of Christ’s divine nature, connects this passage with them: “What is meant by ‘the Father has life in himself’? He does not have life elsewhere, but in himself; for his life is in him, and is not from another source. It is not alien; he does not, as it were, borrow life, nor, as it were, become a participant in life—of that life which is not what he himself is—but he has [Col. 0489D] life in himself, so that he himself is that life to himself. … As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son to have life in himself. The only difference between Father and Son is that the Father has life in himself, which no one gave him, while the Son has life in himself, which the Father gave. … How then did the Father give life to the Son? Not as though the Son had formerly been without life and received life from the Father in order to live. For if that were so, he would not have life in himself. … Therefore it is not as the soul is something else before it is enlightened, and is made better when it is enlightened by participation in something better; so the Word of God, the Son of God, was not something else before he received life, so that by participation he might have life. Rather, he has life in himself, and therefore he himself is life. What he says, therefore, ‘He gave the Son to have life in himself,’ I shall put briefly: he begot the Son. For he was not without life and received life; rather, by being born he is life. The Father is life, not by being born. The Son is life by being born. The Father is from no Father; the Son is from God the Father. What the Father is, he is from no one; but that he is Father is on account of the Son. The Son, however, both is Son on account of the Father, and what he is is from the Father. Thus he said, ‘He gave life to the Son,’ so that he might have it in himself.” See Chrysostom’s words cited above. Bede reproduces Augustine’s words.]

And this is what he says: because he is the Son of man. But while they still wondered and did not believe in the resurrection, he added: “Do not [Col. 0489B] marvel at this”—that is, at what you have heard concerning the resurrection—“for the hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs shall hear his voice, and shall come forth: those who have done good, unto the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, unto the resurrection of judgment.”

“Now,” he says, “at my command a few rise bodily. But it will come to pass that, when I call, all will rise: some indeed will rise in order to live eternally with God; others, however, in order to perish with the devil after they have been judged.”

“I can do nothing from myself. As I hear, I judge; and my judgment is just, because I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me.” Because, he says, I am the Son of man, the Father has given me authority to execute judgment according to this aspect, since according to this aspect I cannot do anything from myself. But according to divinity I can do all things, which I always hear speaking within myself; and as I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just. Why is this? Because I do not seek my own will: I do not seek the will of man; I do not seek the will of flesh and blood, but the will of him who sent me. For I have human nature, but I do not have the defect of human nature. For my humanity is so joined to divinity that it cannot sin and can have nothing but good in its will. [Col. 0489C–0490A]

It follows: “If, therefore, I bear witness concerning myself, my witness is not true. There is another who bears witness concerning me, and I know that the testimony which he bears concerning me is true.” It is as though he said: If I, as a man, bear witness concerning myself as man—according to the fact that I am man, according to what you see in me, according to what you believe me to be—and say that I am the Son of God and equal to him, [Col. 0490B] my testimony is not true. [Note: [Col. 0490C] A difficult passage, even in Chrysostom’s judgment, *Homily 40*, no. 1; for he often bore witness to himself—to the Samaritan woman, the blind man, and so forth. Chrysostom therefore holds that he now said this from the standpoint of the Jews; Augustine likewise thinks so, Sermon 128, no. 1: “This was therefore said according to their own view.” Cyril too, p. 242: “Although he was truthful, yet foreseeing what the foolish Pharisees would deny … he anticipated them and said: ‘You will surely say … You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony [Col. 0490D] is not true.’” Jansen, *Concordia*, ch. 36; Estius; and Natalis Alexander follow this explanation. Our author, as is almost his custom, follows Bede, who says that Christ declares his testimony not true according to the frailty of the flesh—namely, as others explain, if I, as a man alone, bore witness concerning myself, I would allow my testimony not to be regarded as true. Maldonatus’s explanation is not far different: it is a proverbial way of speaking that the testimony of a person bearing witness about himself is not true; therefore Christ speaks both by concession and hypothesis, and in a proverbial sense. Cyprian, Letter 69 to Pupianus, seems to offer the same explanation: “When the Lord himself teaches and says that testimony is not true if anyone considers himself a witness concerning himself, since everyone favors himself”; and, having cited this passage from John, he adds: “Since the Lord himself, who will judge all things afterwards, did not wish belief to be given to his own testimony,” etc.]

“But there is another within me, whom you do not see, who, speaking in myself through me, bears witness concerning me; and I know that his testimony is true.” He says this concerning divinity, according to which he says later: “And if I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is true” (John 8:14). For when our Savior, according to divinity, says that he is the Son of God and equal to God, his testimony is true. If he had said this according to humanity, it would not be true. Therefore some things must be understood according to divinity and others according to humanity.

It follows: “You sent to John, and he bore witness to the truth.” For John himself said above: [Col. 0490C] “I have seen, and have borne witness that this is the Son of God” (John 1:34). “But I do not receive testimony from a man; rather, I say these things so that you may be saved.” What does “I do not receive testimony from a man” mean except that I do not need human testimony? [Note: [Col. 0491D] Chrysostom, *Homily 40*, no. 2: “That is: I had no need of this man’s human testimony, since I am God.”] For truth is always truth and needs no one’s testimony to confirm itself. John “came as a witness, to bear witness to the light,” not because the light needed his testimony, but “that all might believe through him” (John 1:8). But I say these things not to glorify myself; for if I glorify myself, my glory is nothing; rather, I say them so that you may be saved. For you cannot otherwise be saved unless you believe that I am God and the Son of God.

It follows: “He was a burning and shining lamp.” John, he says, to whom you sent, who bore witness to the truth, [Col. 0491B] whose testimony not I but you need, was a lamp: he had light not from himself but from elsewhere; he burned with the fire of love for me and shone with my light. “But you were willing to rejoice for an hour in his light.” Well does he say “for an hour,” because they were capricious and that light was temporal. For they rejoiced in his teaching, thinking that he himself was the Christ.

“But I have testimony greater than John’s.” What is it? Do you wish to hear what it is? “The works which the Father gave me to complete—those very works which I do—bear witness concerning me that the Father sent me.” This is what he says elsewhere: “If I had not done among them works which no one else did, they would not have sin. And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness concerning me” (John 15:24). He bore witness when he said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” [Col. 0491C] (Matt. 17:5).

And as though they said: “But we have not heard his testimony,” he added: “You have neither ever heard his voice nor ever seen his form.” This is what John said above: “No one has ever seen God. The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him” (John 1:18). For although God could at times be heard and seen through a created thing placed beneath him, he could never be seen or heard in his own essence.

It follows: “And you do not have his word abiding in you,” by which truth is understood. Why? “Because you do not believe him whom he sent.” For each person has the word of God abiding in himself—that is, firm and stable—only so long as he does not depart from truth. How, then, could the Jews have the word of God abiding in themselves when they did not believe Truth itself? For Truth is Christ, who says of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life. Search [Col. 0492A] the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life. And they are those which bear witness concerning me; and you are unwilling to come to me that you may have life” (ibid. 14:6).

“If,” he says, “you believe neither me, nor my works, nor John the Baptist, nor the testimony of the Father, at least believe the Scriptures; at least believe the sayings of the Law and the prophets. For they are those which bear witness concerning me. Yet you are unwilling to come to me so that you may have the life which you hope to have in the Scriptures.” For what is it to come to him except to believe in him? [Note: [Col. 0491D] Bede: “‘You are unwilling to come’: that is, you are unwilling to believe, because without faith it is impossible to please God. Our coming to Christ means believing that he is the true Son of God and that through him we have true salvation.”] In this manner one comes to Jesus. One comes to Christ not with one’s feet but by faith. Foolish Jews, who do not believe even the Scriptures in which they vainly hope to possess eternal life.

While they heard these things and thought that the Lord spoke in this way for his own [Col. 0492B] praise and display, the Savior answered their perverse thoughts, saying: “I do not receive glory from human beings. But I have known you: you do not have the love of God in yourselves.” “I,” he says, “do not seek glory and praise from human beings; I do not pursue human renown and favor. Rather, I say these things to stir you toward the love of God, which I certainly know you do not possess. For if you loved the Father, you would love the Son also. But you neither love nor receive the Son.”

This is what he says: “I came in the name of my Father, and you do not receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him.” For Antichrist will come, exalting himself in his own name, because he will come to preach as one sent not by God but by his own pride. The Jews will receive him and for a time will venerate him as God. Those who now refuse to believe Truth—that is, Christ—will believe his deceits. But what wonder if they do not believe Truth, when they seek not eternal but temporal glory? This is what he says: “How can you believe, you who receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory which is from God alone?” [Col. 0492C] These words plainly show that those who seek temporal glory alone, and not eternal glory, do not believe rightly. [Note: [Col. 0491D] “It must be considered more carefully,” says Bede, “how great an evil is the ambition for display and human praise, on account of which Truth itself says that certain persons cannot believe because they were desirous of worldly glory.” [Col. 0492D]]

“Do not think that I shall accuse you before the Father. Moses, in whom you hope, is the one who accuses you.” But how does Moses accuse them, except because they do not believe the one whose words they promised to believe and obey in every respect? [Note: [Col. 0492D] Bede: “I do not accuse because I came not to condemn but to save. Moses, however, accuses because you are unbelieving toward his voice. He wrote concerning me when he said: ‘The Lord will raise up for you a prophet,’ etc.”] For Moses commands the Jews to obey Christ, saying to them: [Col. 0492D; Note: Deut. 18:15: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your nation and from your brethren, like me; you shall hear him.” See St Bruno’s Commentary on this passage, Roman edition, p. 199, col. 2.] “The Lord will raise up for you a prophet from your brethren: you shall hear him as myself.” He did not say “prophets,” but “a prophet,” because he was speaking of this one alone, the greatest of all prophets. [Col. 0493A] “You shall hear him,” he says. Yet they refuse to hear him, because they do not believe Moses.

Hence it is added: “For if you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me also; for he wrote concerning me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?” What he says, “perhaps,” he said in reproving their hardness, so that we too may understand how difficult it is for that nation to be converted to good.

XVI. [CHAP. VI.] After these things Jesus went away across the Sea of Galilee, that is, of Tiberias; and a great multitude followed him, because they saw the signs which he performed upon those who were sick. Jesus therefore went up the mountain, and there sat with his disciples. Now the Passover, the feast-day of the Jews, was near.

The Lord, being about to work great miracles and to give the people the delights of a new and marvelous bread [Col. 0493B], went up the mountain [Note: [Col. 0493C] Augustine, *Tractate* 24: “The Lord is on the mountain: the Word is on high. Therefore what was done on the mountain does not lie, as it were, lowly before us, nor is it to be passed by casually, but received.”], so that we too, whenever we desire to be satisfied with spiritual and new feasts, may ascend—not the height of a mountain, but the elevation of mind and the loftiness of understanding. And because those refreshed by such delights are worthy to celebrate the feast and to receive Christ’s flesh and blood, it is fittingly said here that the Passover, the Jews’ feast-day, was near; for those who have been filled with such food come securely to this feast.

Therefore, when Jesus lifted up his eyes and saw that a very great multitude was coming to him, he said to Philip: “Where shall we buy bread, that these may eat?” But he said this to test him; for he himself knew what he was about to do. The Lord indeed knew what he would do; but, by testing Philip, he wished to hear what Philip thought concerning his omnipotence [Col. 0493C]. At the same time he heightened that new miracle by the disciple’s answer, when he fed from five loaves so many persons for whom, according to Philip’s testimony, bread worth two hundred denarii [Col. 0494A] would not suffice even for each to receive a little.

For Philip answered thus: “Bread worth two hundred denarii is not enough for them, that each may receive a little.” One of his disciples, the brother of Simon Peter, said to him: “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish; but what are these among so many?” This boy is the Jewish people [Note: [Col. 0493C] Augustine, *Tractate* 24 on John: “If we ask who this boy was, perhaps he was the people of Israel.”], still possessing an immature understanding. The five loaves signify the five books of Moses. That people carries these loaves everywhere with it, yet does not eat them, because it merely reads the Scriptures and does not understand them.

But since we explained these matters in Matthew [Note: [Col. 0493C] On chap. XIV, no. 61. See there the exposition of St. Hilary, Augustine, and Bede.], it seems not so much necessary as superfluous and burdensome to explain them again. Likewise, the things that follow [Col. 0494B], down to the place where the crowd that had just eaten bread above on the mountain, seeking him and finding him at Capernaum, said: “Rabbi, when did you come here?”—have been dealt with in Matthew.

Jesus answered them: “Amen, amen, I say to you: you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled.” “You seek me,” he says, “not because of the signs you saw, not because of my discourse which you heard, nor because you wish to believe in me or in the signs I perform, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled” [Note: [Col. 0493C] St. Gregory, *Morals*, book XXIII, chs. 25–26: “In Holy Scripture bread is sometimes understood as the Lord himself; sometimes as spiritual grace; sometimes as instruction in divine Scripture; sometimes as the preaching of heretics; sometimes as aid for the present life; sometimes [Col. 0493D] as the pleasure of human delight. The Lord is signified in bread, as he himself says in the Gospel: ‘I am the living bread,’ etc. Again, through bread the grace of a spiritual gift is understood, as it is said through the prophet: ‘He who stops his ears,’ etc., ‘bread is given to him’ . . . Again, through bread the instruction of divine teaching is signified, as it is said through the prophet: ‘You who dwell in the land of the south, meet the fugitive with bread.’ Again, through bread the preaching of heretics is signified . . . ‘Gladly eat hidden breads’ . . . Again, through bread the support of this present life is understood . . . As in the Gospel: ‘You seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of my loaves.’ To follow the Lord when filled with loaves is to have received temporal sustenance from Holy Church, and to seek the Lord not for signs but for bread,” etc.].

Consider now how sweet those loaves must have been, though they were barley loaves, since, captivated by their sweetness, this whole crowd was still following the Lord. It follows: “Work for the food, not that which perishes, [Col. 0494C] but that which endures unto eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you. For God the Father has signified him” [Note: [Col. 0493D] This is plainly how the passage is read in our manuscript, p. 185. Nor does it appear to be a copyist’s error from the interpretation which Bruno subsequently adds: “For God the Father signified [Col. 0494C] this food when he rained manna in the wilderness,” etc. Yet all the old Latin manuscripts in Sabatier read *signavit* (“sealed/marked”), and the Greek reads ἐσφράγισεν, “sealed.” The Fathers’ interpretation nevertheless varies. Chrysostom, Homily 44, no. 1, gives two explanations: (1) “Therefore he sent the one who would bring you this food”; (2) “He showed [him] openly.” He seems to prefer the latter when he adds: “For ‘the Father signified’ means nothing other than ‘he showed’ or ‘revealed by his testimony.’” Some modern writers follow this, such as Jansenius, *Concordia*, chap. 59, p. 300: “He called himself ‘sealed’ either in the sense of ‘anointed’—for one who is anointed is marked—or because he showed himself naturally conformed to the Father. It is therefore as if he said: ‘It will not be difficult for me to give you enduring food. For although I appear as one of you, yet I am anointed and marked by God the Father into complete likeness with him.’” Hilary’s explanation in *On the Trinity*, VIII, seems the same. Cyril therefore has two expositions: (1) Christ sealed in his humanity through union with divinity; (2) sealed through the very generation of the Word. Toletus adopts the latter; Natalis Alexander and Calmet, Augustine, and St. Cyril adopt Cyril’s former exposition together with Chrysostom’s latter one. See Augustine, *Tractate* 25, and Bede, who copies his words: “This Son of Man, set apart by a certain grace of the Spirit, and Son of Man according to the flesh, was excepted from the number of men. What is it to seal, except to assign something proper? For this is sealing: to impose something that is not to be confused with the rest . . . Therefore, when the Father sealed him . . . he gave him something proper, that he might not be compared with other men. Therefore it was said of him: ‘God anointed you,’ etc. What, then, is sealing? To hold him as exceptional—that is, above your companions.” Maldonatus sets forth this interpretation, explained in his own manner and reasoning.].

For this food which endures unto eternal life is the word of God, by which the soul [Col. 0495A] is fed and nourished [Note: [Col. 0495D] Chrysostom, Homily 43, understands it as almsgiving and food given to the poor. Augustine, *Tractate* 25, suitably to the context, understands it as the Lord Jesus himself, in whom they ought to believe; so also Bede. Cyril says that it indicates “the mystical and spiritual food by which, sanctified in body and soul, we live in him.”]. Hence he fittingly says: “which the Son of Man will give you.” For the Son of Man, Jesus Christ, has set before us and ministered to us all the food of this Gospel, all these feasts of such kind and greatness.

But how can we work for this food? Hear the Apostle: “Not the hearers of the law,” he says, “are righteous before God, but the doers” (Rom. II, 13). Let us therefore do what the law commands. Let us do what the Gospels enjoin, if we desire to work for such food. For God the Father signified this food when he rained manna in the wilderness, by which he fed the people for forty years. Of it it is written: “He gave them bread from heaven, containing every delight and every sweetness of taste” (Wisdom XVI, 20). That food, therefore, signified this food.

They said to him [Col. 0495B]: “What shall we do, that we may work the works of God?” Jesus answered and said to them: “This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he has sent.” For those who do not believe in Christ will be unable either to work the works of God, to understand the law, or to receive spiritual and eternal food. The work of God, therefore, the word of God, and this whole spiritual food consist in faith [Note: [Col. 0495D] Thus it is added to Augustine’s interpretation set out above.].

They said to him: “What sign, then, do you perform, that we may see and believe you? What work do you do? Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness, as it is written: ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’” As though they said: “Show us some sign through which we ought to believe in you and your works. You have indeed given us loaves, and we have been filled. The things we have seen are very wonderful. Yet this sign [Col. 0495C] does not suffice for us. We have heard that Moses did something similar. For he too gave bread from heaven to our fathers, which our fathers ate in the wilderness. Yet he did not, as you do, command them to believe in himself.”

Jesus therefore said to them: “Amen, amen, I say to you: Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is that which comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.” “You do not rightly understand,” he says, “what is signified by the words, ‘He gave them bread from heaven.’ In these words another bread, very unlike it and of greater dignity, is signified. Moses gave you bread that signified something, not the true bread descending from heaven. But now my Father gives you the true bread from heaven [Col. 0496A], which that bread nevertheless signified. For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven, who came forth from the bosom of the Father, and gives life to the world.”

They said to him: “Lord, always give us this bread.” They were making an excellent request, if only they had understood of what bread the Lord spoke. But Jesus said to them: “I am the bread of life. I am the bread that came down from heaven. I am that bread which gives life to the world. Whoever comes to me shall not hunger; whoever believes in me shall never thirst. But I told you that you have seen me, and do not believe.”

We have already said above that to come to Christ [Note: [Col. 0495D] Augustine, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chap. 3: “What is ‘will come to me’ except ‘will believe in me’?”] is to believe in him. The more faithful each person is, the nearer that person is to him. Such a person will neither hunger nor thirst for ever, because, after departing from this world, he will enjoy eternal delights for ever [Col. 0496B].

“But I said these things to you,” not, as you suppose, glorifying myself, but because you have seen me—you have recognized me and my power in signs and miracles—and yet do not believe in me. Nevertheless, I know that at some time you will believe, all of you who are predestined to life. This is what he says: “Everything which the Father gives me will come to me,” that is, will believe in me; “and the one who comes to me I will not cast out.” Why? “Because I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.”

Therefore, he says, I shall cast out no one who comes to me, no one who believes in me. Therefore I shall spare even my enemies and persecutors, because I came down from heaven not to do my own will—that is, the will of man, the will of that nature which I took [Col. 0496C] from man—but the will of him who sent me. For it is man’s will to repel enemies and avenge one’s own injuries [Note: [Col. 0495D] Augustine, *Against an Arian Sermon*, chap. 7: “Even the words of Jesus, ‘I came down from heaven,’ etc., are to be referred to this: the first man Adam . . . by doing his own will and not the will of him by whom he was made, made the entire human race, through a corrupted propagation, liable to guilt and punishment. Therefore, by contrast, he through whom we were to be delivered did not do his own will, but the will of him by whom he was sent. Thus in this passage ‘his own will’ is said in such a way that it is understood as a private will opposed to the will of God. For when we obey God and are said by that obedience to do his will, we do not do so unwillingly but willingly. And if we do it willingly, how do we not do our own will? Except that Scripture speaks of ‘our own will’ when it means a private will opposed to God’s will. Adam had this will, so that we might die in him. Christ did not have it, so that we might live in him. This can rightly be said of human nature, in which through disobedience there exists a self-will opposed to God’s will. But as regards the will of the Son, the will of Father and Son is one and the same. It can in no way be different where the whole nature of the immutable Trinity is present. Yet, in order that Christ Jesus, the man who is the Mediator of God and men, might not perform a will opposed to God, he was not merely man but God and man; through that marvelous and unique grace human nature in him could be without any sin.” Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXV, chap. 12: “For what if he had done his own will? He would have rejected those who come to him. But who does not know that the will of the Son does not differ from the will of the Father? Yet because the first man wished to do his own will,” etc. See the explanation suggested by Augustine.].

Let us hear what God’s will is: “This,” he says, “is the will of him [p. 236] who sent me: that of all that he has given me I should lose none, but raise it up on the last day.” Therefore Jesus will save and raise up all those who are predestined to life, even if they were at some time his enemies and opponents. For these are those whom the Father has given me. He gave them, however, according to Christ’s humanity. Confirmation: “For this is the will of my Father who sent me: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last [Col. 0497A] day.”

For not only those who saw and believed, but also those who did not see and believed, will have eternal life, as the Lord said to the apostle Thomas: “Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John XX, 29). Yet “to see” may be understood as “to know.” For what is it to believe in him except to make one’s way toward him and cling to him with, as it were, the feet of faith, hope, and love, so that thereafter not even death can separate a person from him? Thus the Apostle had come to him and believed in him when he said: “For I am certain that neither death nor life can separate me from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. VIII, 38).

Whoever comes to him otherwise, whoever believes in him otherwise, will gain nothing from either coming [Col. 0497B] or believing. That coming to him and believing in him signify the same thing is evident from the fact that he himself sometimes says, “Whoever comes to me,” and sometimes, “Whoever believes in me,” using one expression in place of the other.

XVII. Therefore the Jews murmured concerning him, because he had said: “I am the bread that came down from heaven.” And they said: “Is this not the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then does he say, ‘I came down from heaven’?” For it seemed impossible to them that he had descended from heaven, since they believed him to be merely a man, born of human beings. And indeed, if he were nothing else, he could not have descended from heaven.

Jesus answered and said to them: “Do not murmur among yourselves. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him; and I will raise him up on the last day.” “Do not murmur,” he says; “do not harden your hearts. For I know that you cannot come to me because the Father does not draw you. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.” He draws, however, not by force but by love. In this sense it is said: “Each person is drawn by his own delight” [Note: [Col. 0497D] Augustine’s well-known words on this passage, *Tractate* 26 on John: “Nor should we fear lest . . . perhaps we be reproved and told: ‘How do I believe by my will, if I am drawn?’ I say: Will is too little; you are drawn even by delight . . . There is a certain delight of the heart, to which that heavenly bread is sweet. Moreover, if a poet was permitted to say: ‘Each person is drawn by his own delight’—not by necessity, but by delight; not by compulsion, but by pleasure—how much more strongly should we say that a person is drawn to Christ when delighted by truth, delighted by blessedness, delighted by righteousness, delighted by eternal life, all of which Christ is, etc.?” Bede likewise: “How does the Father draw? By teaching he delights; he does not compel by necessity, because no one believes by necessity but by will.” Augustine treats this evangelical passage often: *On the Predestination of the Saints*, book I, chap. 8; *On the Grace of Christ*, book I, chs. 12 and 14; *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book I, chap. 3; Sermon 131, chap. 1, where likewise: “He did not say, ‘will lead,’ but ‘will draw.’ This force is applied to the heart, not the flesh. Why then are you astonished? Believe, and you come; love, and you are drawn . . . Is not a sheep drawn when grass is shown to it while it is hungry?” etc. See also [Prosper] *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, book II, chap. 9, “Prosper,” etc.].

But God draws no one unless that person is willing to come and desires salvation. Hence it is written: “If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling, the sword shall devour you” (Isa. I, 19). This, then, was why those to whom the Lord spoke these things could neither come to him nor understand him [Col. 0498A].

And because the resurrection of the wicked will bring death rather than life, the Lord here says of the righteous person: “And I will raise him up on the last day.” For that person truly will be raised who will thereafter suffer none of the things belonging to death.

It follows: “It is written in the prophets” [Note: [Col. 0498D] Whoever wishes to see how excellently this passage has been elucidated by the most learned theologian Augustine Anthony Georgi may do so in the recent translation and commentary on a most ancient fragment, written in Coptic-Theban letters, relating to John chapter VI. After the very learned author had conclusively demonstrated the truth of Christ’s body and blood in the Eucharist, he now demonstrates most fully, especially from St. Augustine’s teaching, the gratuitous gift of God’s call to faith and the aid of his grace for salvation. See p. 129 ff. The work was published at Rome in 1790.]: “And they shall all be taught by God.” One is teachable who can be taught. Such are the children of the Church. To them the Lord himself says: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven; but to them it has not been given, so that seeing they may not see and hearing they may not understand. For the heart of this people has grown gross, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and they have [p. 237] closed their eyes, lest at any time they should see with their eyes, hear with their ears, be converted, and I should heal them” (Matt. XIII, [Col. 0498B] 11–14).

Therefore the Father draws those, and they come to the Son, who are teachable—who can be taught and instructed in his faith and doctrine. Hence it is added: “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me.” For that person is teachable who has heard and learned. Hearing alone is not enough. For all these heard the Father, because the Father spoke in the Son and through the Son. Yet they did not come to the Son because they were unwilling to understand and learn what was said.

It follows: “Not that anyone has seen the Father, except he who is from God; he has seen the Father.” He did not say, he explains, “Everyone who has heard from the Father,” as though anyone could either hear or see the Father in his own substance, except the one alone who is from God, who came forth from God, who is God from God, light from light [Col. 0498C]. He alone sees the Father. Hence elsewhere he says: “No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him. Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever believes in me has eternal life” (Matt. IX, 27 [citation as printed; apparently uncertain]).

“I have told you, and I tell you again: whoever believes in me has eternal life. See, I have told you: if you believe, you will be blessed; if you do not believe, no excuse remains. I am the bread of life. Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness and died. This is the bread descending from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it, he may not die.”

“You murmur,” he says, “because I told you, ‘I am the living bread that came down from heaven.’ See, I tell you again that I am bread, and the bread of life, and that I descended from heaven. For angels and men alike are nourished by this [Col. 0499A] bread. Why it is called the bread of life he himself explains when he says: ‘so that if anyone eats of it, he may not die.’

“And he indeed came down from heaven according to his divinity [Note: [Col. 0499D] Cyril, *On the Right Faith to the Queens*: “He says that he came down from heaven and was sent by God and the Father, although he fills all things; thereby, I think, demonstrating and making manifest to all that the Word, being God, descended in the divine economy to humanity for our sake—not leaving behind what he was, God by nature, but rather taking up what he was not . . . Therefore it belongs properly to God the Word, who descended from heaven, through whom he became the firstborn from the dead,” [Col. 0500D] etc. Fulgentius, book II, *To Trasimund*, chap. 3: “From this some, when they hear that he descended, strive to affirm a local descent, because they do not know how to consider God’s power as they ought, nor can they recognize that God became man for humanity in such a way that, having assumed human form, the divine substance remained immutable; nor do they understand his temporal birth so as still to maintain that he has always existed eternally. These are those who even disdain to consider how he descended while remaining immeasurable,” etc.]: ‘Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness and died.’ This bread is therefore better than manna, since those who ate manna died, whereas whoever eats of this bread shall not die.

It is fitting, therefore, that blessed John is described in Ezekiel and the Apocalypse as having the appearance of an eagle, because he flies higher and beholds Christ our Lord, the Sun of Righteousness, more subtly than the other Evangelists. Do you not see how he is now raised from the earth and, flying among the clouds, seems already to penetrate heaven itself?

For Moses and Aaron and the other saints who ate manna died [Col. 0499B]. But did not the apostles too die, though they ate the bread of life? Insofar as the flesh is concerned, both these and those died. Yet both these and those live insofar as the soul is concerned. Therefore there is no difference between these and those. Moses and Aaron, then, are not the fathers of those to whom the Lord spoke these words. For if they were their children, they would have done their works. Rather, their fathers were those whom Scripture recalls as having murmured so often, worshipped idols, and provoked God to anger. Of these, therefore, the Lord says: “Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness and died”—your fathers, certainly, whose imitators and counterparts you are.

It follows:

XVIII. “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.” [Col. 0499C] “If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live for ever; and the bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world.” Now, with the Lord himself explaining it, we understand what this bread is. For this bread is Christ’s flesh, which was offered upon the altar of the cross for the life of the world. The Church eats this flesh and therefore does not die, but lives for ever.

For the bread and wine placed upon the altar are sanctified by heavenly blessing at the priest’s utterance, and are essentially changed into Christ’s flesh and blood, so that the flesh born of the Virgin and that made from bread are one and the same essence. This great and marvelous sacrament [Col. 0500A] began at the time when our Savior, blessing bread and wine, said to his disciples: “Take and eat: this is my body”; and, “This is the cup of the new testament in my blood” (Matt. XXVI, 26, 27).

Before this sacrifice no one ever ate Christ’s flesh bodily. No one could ever eat it bodily unless this sacrifice took place. In this sacrifice, therefore, it is eaten, and, when eaten, is not diminished; and it would never be eaten unless this bread were substantially changed into it by Christ’s blessing. For this change is the work of the right hand of the Most High. But who should wonder that Christ’s flesh, when eaten, is not diminished, when it is certain that five thousand persons were satisfied from five loaves [p. 238], and that the loaves themselves were not diminished but rather multiplied [Note: [Col. 0500D] Cyril argues in nearly the same way against an unbelieving Jew in his work on John, writing upon the following words, “How can this man,” etc.: “How did you come out of Egypt? How, I ask, was Moses’ rod changed into a serpent? How was the hand infected with leprosy and restored again to its former state?” etc.]?

[Col. 0500B] For if the fragments of the loaves were not diminished but rather multiplied as they ate, what did the five thousand persons eat? From what were they so satisfied that, when they came to him, the Lord said: “You seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled”?

Perhaps you say: “These things are wonderful.” God has done nothing that is not wonderful. But since we cannot follow this eagle of Christ in flight, let us at least follow it in faith. For if the Jews had done this, they would not have perished. Concerning them it is added.

XIX. The Jews therefore disputed among themselves, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” For, as the Apostle says: “The natural man does not receive the things that are of God” (1 Cor. 2:14). For the Jews thought [Col. 0500C] that Jesus meant that they should kill him, cut him into pieces, and thus eat his flesh, either cooked or raw, and drink his blood. Jesus therefore said to them: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves.”

[Note: From these words some have claimed that there follows a clear precept to administer the most holy Eucharist to newly baptized infants. The same most distinguished Georgius refutes them conclusively in the Commentary cited above, p. 151 ff. [Col. 0500D; 0501D].]

“He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.” What does this mean? For many eat Christ’s flesh and drink his blood who do not have eternal life. Thus the Apostle says: “For he who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself” (1 Cor. 11:29). Many also do not bodily eat Christ’s flesh [Col. 0501A] or drink his blood in this sacrament of the altar, yet they will have eternal life. Therefore he truly eats and drinks Christ’s flesh and blood who so shares in the sacraments of the altar that he is joined and united to the Son of God, and together with him is made one thing, so that he can thereafter never be separated from him.

For, to take an example from ourselves: this temporal and perishable food which we use is, after digestion, in some part of itself changed into our flesh and blood, so that it is substantially one and the same with them and can no longer be separated from them. For what is eating except adhering inseparably?

[Note: St Cyril speaks excellently to this point on these very words, p. 363: “He therefore who eats the holy flesh has eternal life; for the flesh has within itself the Word, who is life by nature. And therefore he adds that he said, ‘I will raise [him],’ not, ‘My body will raise [him]’; plainly, because he does not exist as something other than his flesh, nor is he altogether other in nature. … For just as, if someone joins wax to wax, he will certainly see the one in the other, so also, I think, he who receives the flesh of our Savior and drinks his precious blood, as he himself says, is found to be one thing with him: in some manner mingled and blended with him through that participation, so that he is found in Christ, [Col. 0502D] and Christ in turn in him.” And, after adding another comparison from the leaven of the woman in the Gospel, he again writes: “Thus the smallest blessing (*eulogia*) mingles our whole body with itself and fills it with its own power; and thus Christ exists in us, and we in turn in him.” [Col. 0501D].]

It follows: “For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.” For we take food and drink [Col. 0501B] in order to live and not perish from hunger and thirst. Therefore that food and drink is truly food and drink which removes every hunger and provides eternal life. “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.” The Lord himself explains how we ought to understand his words. He who, he says, eats my flesh and drinks my blood—as it is fitting to eat and drink such food and drink—is thus joined to me, thus united to me, thus wholly transferred into me, that he abides inseparably in me and has me abiding in himself. He therefore who does not persevere in Christ’s love is unworthy to receive Christ’s flesh.

“As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so he who eats me shall also live because of me.” Although, he says, [Col. 0501C] my flesh is eaten and my blood drunk, I am nevertheless immortal, always live, and cannot die. For as the Father who sent me always lives and never dies, so I too always live, not because of my mother but because of the Father—that is, because of the divinity which I have from the Father. And he who eats me, because I am the way, the truth, and the life, shall likewise not die but shall always live because of me. For how can he die in whom life always abides?

[Note: Exactly so Cyril, p. 363: “For it is altogether impossible that he who is life by nature should not overcome corruption and conquer death.” And again: “For it is incredible—indeed impossible—that life should not make alive those in whom it is.” [Col. 0502D].]

“This is,” that is, such is, “the bread which came down from heaven. Not as your fathers ate manna and died, so do those who eat this bread die. He who eats this bread shall live for ever.” Your fathers, he says—whose wickedness you imitate and to whom you are similar [Col. 0502A]—ate manna and died. But he who worthily eats this bread shall live for ever.

These things he said while teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum. Therefore many of his disciples, hearing this, said: “This saying is hard, and who can hear it?” For the Lord had foreseen this when he said: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.” For these men, as is read below, went back and followed him no longer.

But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples murmured about this, said to them: “Does this scandalize you?” Let not this, he says, scandalize you, because it is not as you understand it. First understand, and then judge. “What then if you should see the Son of Man ascending where he was before? It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing. [Col. 0502B] The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life.” These words, he says, are spiritual; understood carnally, they produce death, but understood spiritually, they provide eternal life. For those understood them carnally who thought that Christ’s flesh was to be cut into pieces and then eaten. But those understand them spiritually who believe that they eat and drink bread and wine divinely changed into Christ’s flesh and blood.

For if flesh and blood visibly appeared to the eyes in their own proper form, and were perceived by taste, horror alone would result. Who could see them; who, seeing them, would not shrink from receiving them? He therefore says: “If you should see the Son of Man ascending where he was before,” then, it is understood, you will recognize that these words which I have spoken [Col. 0502C] to you are spirit and life. For it is the Spirit—that is, spiritual understanding—which gives life; but the flesh—that is, carnal understanding—profits nothing in words of this kind.

For the sequence is thus: “If you see,” he says, “the Son of Man living and whole ascending where he was previously according to his divinity, then you will know that these words are spiritual.” For he would not have ascended there whole if, according to their understanding, he had been cut into pieces and entirely devoured.

[Note: Augustine says exactly this in Sermon 131: “To those thinking these things, though not uttering them aloud, he replied, so that they might know that they had been heard and cease thinking such things. What does this mean? ‘Does this scandalize you?’ Do you suppose that I shall make portions of this body which you see, cut up my members, and give them to you? What then if you should see the Son of Man ascending where he was before? Surely he who could ascend whole could not be consumed.” [Col. 0502D; 0503C].]

It follows: “But there are some among you who do not believe.” For Jesus knew from the beginning who they were who did not believe, and who would betray him. And he said: “For this reason I said to you that no one can come to me unless it has been given him by my Father.” Why “for this reason”? Because you see me, hear me, and yet do not [Col. 0503A] believe in me. For you would believe if it had been given you by my Father.

Jesus stood in their midst: he saw all, knew all, and knew who had been predestined to life and who to death. He called many, but chose few. From this point many of his disciples went back and no longer walked with him. Jesus therefore said to the Twelve: “Do you also wish to go away?” Simon Peter answered him: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life. And we have believed and known that you are Christ, the Son of the living God.” To whom, he says, shall we go if we leave you? For you alone are he, and there is no other through whom the world can be saved. You have words of eternal life, and whoever does not believe them shall perish eternally. But we have believed and known that you are Christ [Col. 0503B], the Son of God.

Jesus answered them: “Did I not choose you twelve? Yet one of you is a devil.” Now he spoke of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot; for he was to betray him, though he was one of the Twelve. For the Lord had chosen Judas not for blessedness but for the apostleship.

[Note: Augustine raises a question in *Questions on Genesis*, question 117, over the word “I chose”: “For,” he says, “the name of the elect is not easily found in an evil sense. But if we suppose that Judas too was chosen, so that the Lord’s Passion might be accomplished through his betrayal—that is, that his wickedness was chosen for some purpose, since God makes good use even of evils—let us attend to the place where he says: ‘I do not speak of all of you; I know whom I have chosen,’ where he declares that only the good belong to election. Thus the statement, ‘I chose you twelve,’ was made by synecdoche, so that under the name of the greater and better part there might also be included that which does not belong to that name.”

He raises the same question in Tractate 27 and offers two answers. The first, which he rejected in the cited passage, concerns election for some purpose in which God might make good use of Judas: “Would he say, ‘I chose eleven’? Is the devil also chosen, and is there a devil among the elect? The elect are customarily named in praise. Was this man chosen, from whom, without his willing or knowing it, some great good would come about?”

His second answer is: “What he said, ‘I chose twelve,’ may also be understood in this way: because the number is sacred. For because one of them perished, the honor of that number was not diminished; another was substituted in place of the one who perished, and the consecrated number, the number twelve, remained.”

Augustine was, however, freed from this difficulty when he wrote in *On Rebuke and Grace*, ch. 7: “When we hear, ‘Did I not choose you twelve?’ and so forth, we should understand that those men were chosen through mercy, but that man through judgment. Thus he chose them to obtain his kingdom, but him to shed his blood.” A. most aptly calls Judas’s election an election to the apostleship. Indeed Jansenius, *Harmony*, ch. 59, Maldonatus, and others think that the matter here concerns the election to apostleship of all twelve; thus they resolve Augustine’s objection from the words, “I do not speak of all of you,” and so forth: there the discourse concerns election simply, by which some are called absolutely elect and others reprobate. [Col. 0503C–0504C].]

And he indeed was a devil, not by nature but by imitation. For the devil himself is a devil not by nature but by vice.

[Note: Epiphanius, *Heresies* 38: “He is a devil not by nature, but in mind.” [Col. 0504C].]

For *diabolus* means “falling away.”

[Note: *Diabolus*, the Greek word διάβολος, is explained as “slanderer” or “accuser,” from διαβάλλω, “I cast across,” that is, “I cast blame upon another.” A., or the author whom he follows, seems to have taken διαβάλλω in the sense of ἀποβάλλω, “to cast away.” [Col. 0504C–D].]

This name suitably belongs to Judas the betrayer, who, falling away from so great an eminence into so great an abyss, fell headlong.

240 XX. [CHAPTER VII.] After these things Jesus walked in Galilee, for he did not wish to walk in Judea because the Jews were seeking to kill him. Jesus did this not because he feared death or the Jews, but in order to provide [Col. 0503C] an example for his faithful. Hence elsewhere he says: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. 10:23).

Now the Jewish feast of Tabernacles was near [Col. 0504A]. For the feast of *Scenopegia* was the festival of booths.

[Note: Augustine, Tractate 28 on this passage: “Those who have read the Scriptures know what Scenopegia is,” etc.; and Jerome on Hosea, ch. 12. See also Leviticus, ch. 23. [Col. 0504D].]

The children of Israel lived in shelters for seven days. But, as the Apostle says: “All these things happened to them in a figure” (1 Cor. 10:11). For that festival signified this festival of ours.

[Note: Theophylact on this passage: “The feast of Scenopegia, which they celebrated in thanksgiving for the gathered crops in the month of September—for then they gave thanks to the Lord when all the crops had been gathered, and therefore booths were made and, as it were, they rejoiced while living in the open air—… signifies the resurrection, when all the fruits of our works are brought to completion, and our tabernacles, destroyed through death, are rebuilt.” [Col. 0504D].]

In it holy men, from Christ’s resurrection until the consummation of the age, rest from servile and wicked work and persevere in good work. It was fittingly observed for seven days, through which all the days from that time onward are signified; for there are only seven days. But why did they live in shelters, except because shelters quickly fail, having no foundation, and are inhabited only for a short time? Hence the Apostle says: “For we do not have here an abiding city, but seek the one to come” (Heb. 13:14) [Col. 0504B]. And the Psalmist: “For I am a sojourner with you upon the earth, and a stranger, as all my fathers were” (Ps. 38:13).

But his brothers said to him: “Leave here and go into Judea, so that your disciples may see the works which you do.
