For no one does anything in secret while himself seeking to be publicly known.” We have often already said who these brothers are: they were his kinsmen according to the flesh, namely blood-relatives of the Virgin Mary.

[Note: Bede on this passage: “The Lord’s brothers were called blood-relatives of St Mary ever-Virgin, in the most customary manner of Holy Scripture.” From Augustine on this passage. [Col. 0504D].]

For it is the custom of the holy Scriptures to call even very close relatives brothers. Thus fleshly brothers gave fleshly counsel, by which our Savior might acquire the world’s glory and spread his name more widely. They therefore urged Christ the Lord to work miracles not secretly but openly and before a great gathering [Col. 0504C].

Moreover, by saying, “that your disciples may see the works which you do,” they show that he had many disciples in Judea, such as Nicodemus and many others [Col. 0505A] who desired to see his works. “If you do these things, show yourself to the world.” This is as if they said: Either cease from miracles, or, if you perform them, do so in such a way that you become known to the world through miracles.

For not even his brothers believed in him. Although they believed him to be a prophet, they did not yet believe him to be the Son of God.

[Note: Cyril on this passage, p. 397: “Since those who were believed to be the Savior’s brothers did not yet acknowledge that God the Word dwelt in the holy flesh … they still thought narrowly of him … since they saw nothing beyond what others saw and, misled by common opinion about him, supposed that he had in fact been born from Joseph as father.” [Col. 0505D].]

Jesus therefore said to them: “My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready.” You tell me, he says, to manifest myself to the world. You tell me to seek praise and glory. But the time of my glory has not yet come. It will come at the judgment, when “every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess” (Isa. 45:24). But your time [Col. 0505B] is always ready, in which you are deceived by the world’s praise, human favor, and vain glory.

[Note: Augustine likewise explains this passage in Tractate 28 on John. Chrysostom, Homily 48, no. 2, explains it otherwise: “‘My time has not yet come,’ that is, the time of the cross and death. Why do you hasten to kill me before the time? ‘But your time is always ready’; that is: you Jews, even if you are always among them, they will never kill you, because you think as they do; but they will immediately attempt to kill me. Thus you may always be with them without danger, but my time will be when I must be crucified and die. For that this is his meaning is clear from what follows: ‘The world cannot hate you,’” etc. [Col. 0505D].]

“The world cannot hate you; but it hates me, because I bear witness concerning it that its works are evil.” What then does he mean by saying, “The world cannot hate you,” when we see that lovers of the world, whom they signify, engage among themselves in so many wars, disputes, and quarrels through hatred? Therefore, “The world cannot hate you” is as though he said: The world cannot hate your habits, your works, and your wickedness. For if it hated them, it would not do them, and consequently it would not be of this world from the world.

“But it hates me because I bear witness concerning it that its works are evil.” This is the greatest and chief reason [Col. 0505C] why all wicked people hate both Christ himself and Christ’s members. Hence tyrants, sacrilegious persons, adulterers, perjurers, and all criminals rise up against the Church.

“Go up yourselves to this feast. For I do not go up to this feast, because my time has not yet been fulfilled.” You, he says, who seek human praise, desire popular favor, and long for the world’s glory—you go up to this feast 241, where mercy, God’s grace, and forgiveness of sins are not sought, but praise alone and empty glory. But I, who do not delight in such things and do not seek glory of this kind, do not go up [Col. 0506A] to this feast. Why? Because my time has not yet been fulfilled. For first the fullness of the Gentiles shall enter, first all Israel shall be saved, first I shall come to judgment, before the time of so great a glory arrives.

Having said these things, he remained in Galilee. But when his brothers had gone up, then he too went up to the feast. He indeed went up to the feast, but not to that feast to which his brothers had gone up. Otherwise what he himself said, “I do not go up to this feast,” would not be true.

[Note: Chrysostom thought otherwise and explained this entire passage differently in Homily 48 on John, no. 2: “Why then did he go up, after saying, ‘I will not go up’? He did not say simply, ‘I will not go up,’ but adds, ‘now,’ that is, with you, because my time has not yet been fulfilled.” Closer to A. is Augustine, Tractate 28: “The brothers went up first, and he did not then go up when they thought and wished, so that this too might be fulfilled which he said: ‘not to this,’ that is, not when you want—on the first or second day. But later he went up, as the Gospel relates, in the middle of the feast: that is, when as many days of the feast had already passed as remained. For, so far as can be understood, they celebrated the festival itself over several days.” Bede follows Augustine in his customary way. See again the most learned Georgius, p. 170 ff., who adduces various readings of this passage and defends John Chrysostom and other Fathers against heterodox critics. [Col. 0506D].]

The Lord’s feast is observed not outwardly but inwardly; not in the face but in the mind. Of it the Psalmist says: “For the thought of man shall confess to you, and the remnant of thoughts shall keep a feast-day to you” (Ps. 75:11). Therefore keep the feast in this way if you wish to come to your own festival [Col. 0506B]. Do not do this openly, nor in order to be seen by people. For those who do so have received their reward. Do you not hear that the Lord himself came to the feast not openly but, as it were, secretly?

For the Lord came secretly to the feast because, although the whole festival was being observed in his honor and glory, he was nevertheless understood there by few or by none. He was therefore at the feast, but hidden. Wretched Jews, in whose festivals Christ always remains hidden. For this was signified by Isaac, who blessed his son Jacob and did not recognize him. The Jews therefore sought him at the feast and said: “Where is that man?” For to this day Jews read and seek Jesus on every Sabbath and at every one of their festivals. Yet they do not find him [Col. 0506C], because they do not seek rightly. For they seek with envy and murmuring. Hence it follows: “And there was much murmuring about him among the crowd. Some said, ‘He is good’; but others said, ‘No, he deceives the crowds.’”

What wonder, then, if wicked people sometimes speak ill of holy and devout men, when they said such things of the very Son of God? Yet no one spoke openly of him for fear of the Jews. Thus those very people who said that he was good did not dare to say it publicly, because they feared men more than God.

XXI. Now when the feast was already half over, Jesus went up into the temple and taught. And the Jews wondered, saying: “How does this man know letters, [Col. 0507A] having never learned?” We have said above that this festival was celebrated over seven days.

[Note: See the Commentary on Leviticus, ch. 23, p. 166, vol. I of the Roman edition of St Bruno; and Commentary on Luke, no. 17, p. 170. [Col. 0507D].]

Thus, when it says, “the feast already being half over,” it is as though it said: While half the days of the entire festival still remained, Jesus went up into the temple and taught. The Jews, hearing him, wondered because they heard him disputing with remarkable eloquence in a learned manner concerning the law and the prophets, though they knew that he had never learned letters in the schools. For because they saw only a man, they believed him to be nothing but a man. But the divinity, the instructor and teacher of all this doctrine, was hidden.

Therefore the Lord himself added: “My doctrine is not mine, but his who sent me.” But if it was his, how was it not his [Col. 0507B]? And if it was not his, how was it his? For he himself says both: that it is his and that it is not his. But it was his because it belonged to his divinity; and it was not his because it did not belong to his humanity. Thus it was both his and not his.

[Note: Augustine almost puts and resolves the question thus in Tractate 29 on John and *On the Trinity*, book I, ch. 3, no. 12: “What shall we say there where he says, ‘My doctrine is not mine’? How is it mine, and how not mine? For he did not say, ‘This doctrine is not mine,’ but, ‘My doctrine is not mine.’ What he called his, the same he called not his. How is this true, unless he called it his in one respect and not his in another? According to the form of God, his; according to the form of a servant, not his.” See also book II, ch. 2; Ambrose, *On the Faith*, book II, ch. 4. [Col. 0507D].]

Likewise must be understood what he said above: “I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38). The Father and the Son are indeed one; for he himself says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:29). Therefore the will of both is one. If, then, he does the Father’s will, he also does his own will; therefore he does his own will and does not do his own will. For he does his own will according to his divinity, but does not do his own will according to the [Col. 0507C] nature of his humanity.

Thus the Lord said to the Jews who wondered at his teaching: “My doctrine is not mine”: my doctrine is not that of a man; my doctrine is not human wisdom. Nor did I learn it from a man. Do not 242 wonder. It belongs to divinity. Within is the teacher who taught me such things. Concerning this teacher he says through Isaiah: “Morning by morning he raises my ear, that I may hear as a teacher” (Isa. 50:4). Thus he himself is both teacher and disciple: teacher according to divinity, disciple according to humanity.

It is therefore plain what he says: “My doctrine is not mine, but his who sent me.” He says something similar to his disciples: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks [Col. 0508A] in you. If anyone wills to do his will, he shall know concerning the doctrine whether it is from God, or whether I speak from myself” (Matt. 10:20). Therefore only those who do the Father’s will can understand and know this doctrine. Now the Father’s will is that we should believe in him whom he sent. For unless we believe, we shall not understand. Hence Isaiah says: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. 7:9). Therefore faith is necessary to us if we are to be able to attain this doctrine.

[Note: Augustine, Tractate 29 on John: “Who does not know that to do God’s will is to work his work—that is, what pleases him? But the Lord himself openly says elsewhere: ‘This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he sent.’ Let this be in you, and you will understand concerning God’s doctrine.” Chrysostom, Homily 49, no. 1, explains it admirably and most fully in accordance with the literal sense: “Cast out wickedness, anger, envy, and also the hatred which you have conceived against me without cause, and nothing will prevent you from knowing that my words are truly God’s. Now these things cover you with darkness and pervert sound judgment in you; if you remove them, you will not suffer that. But he did not speak thus, lest he rebuke them too sharply.” [Col. 0507D; 0508D].]

But what does he mean by saying, “whether it is from God, or whether I speak from myself,” except: whether I speak according to divinity or according to humanity? For the Lord speaks from himself, but according to one part of himself. He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory. But he [Col. 0508B] who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and there is no injustice in him.

Jesus says this not generally about all people but specifically about himself and Antichrist.

[Note: Bede likewise explains it of Antichrist. [Col. 0508D].]

For Antichrist will not speak from the Holy Spirit but from himself. He will seek not God’s glory but his own, who “shall exalt himself above everything called God or worshipped, so that he sits in God’s temple, displaying himself as though he were God” (2 Thess. 2:4). By contrast, Christ Jesus, who is true—indeed, who is truth itself—and in whom there is no injustice, everywhere seeks the glory of the Father who sent him, not his own. Hence he says: “Zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproached you fell upon me” (Ps. 68:10).

“Did not Moses give you the law, and yet none of you [Col. 0508C] keeps the law?” Why he said this he shows by adding: “Why do you seek to kill me?” For if they had kept the law and observed its commandments, they would never have sought to kill one who was innocent and just.

[Note: Chrysostom, Homily 49, no. 2, explains at length how these words answer and are connected with what goes before. Bede, like our A., apparently says: “For you seek to kill [me] because none of you keeps the law. For if you had kept the law, you would recognize Christ in the very writings and would not kill him when present.” I judge Chrysostom’s former explanation to have place here: if you kept the law, you would be free from hatred and envy, which prevent you from recognizing Christ. [Col. 0508D].]

The crowd answered and said: “You have a demon. Who seeks to kill you?” The crowd answered thus because it was foul and disturbed, turbulent and clouded. Jesus answered and said to them: “I did one work, and you all marvel.” He is not moved by their answer, nor does he return abuse for abuse. “I did one work,” he says, “and you all marvel.” You marvel, indeed, not because I did something great—for such wonder would be good—but because I did it on the Sabbath. Why then are you not also indignant with yourselves, who circumcise a man on the Sabbath?

“If a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath so that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you indignant with me because I made the whole man sound on the Sabbath?” Moses gave you circumcision for this reason: namely, that you might be healed from infirmity. Circumcision is not from Moses but from the Fathers. For before Moses said anything about circumcision, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and many others were circumcised. Therefore on every day it is permissible to do whatever pertains to salvation, and for that reason you circumcise a person on the Sabbath. It is unjust, then, for you to be indignant with me because I made the whole man sound on the Sabbath. For if it is not permissible for me, it is not permissible for you. But it is permissible. For if it were not permissible, Moses would not have commanded it. He commanded that an infant be circumcised on the eighth day, whether the Sabbath itself [Col. 0509A] or any other day should occur.

“Do not judge according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment.” Either condemn Moses along with me, or justify me along with Moses. For we both do the same thing. We both work salvation on the Sabbath. But you do not condemn him because you fear him. For this is what it means to judge according to appearance.

[Note: Chrysostom says almost the same: “What is ‘according to appearance’? Do not cast your vote on the basis of rank, because Moses is held in greater esteem among you, but on the nature of the things themselves. For that is to judge justly.” Nor does Augustine say otherwise; here and in *On Christian Combat* he reads, “Do not judge personally.” Lucifer of Cagliari, book II, *For Athanasius*: “Do not judge according to the person.” The Greek is κατ’ ὄψιν, “according to appearance.” He further adds what Bede copied: “This vice, brothers, which the Lord noted in this place, is very laborious to escape in this age: not to judge personally, but to judge righteous judgment.” See St Bernard, Sermon 5 for Lent, and Letter 247. [Col. 0509D].]

Some from Jerusalem therefore said: “Is this not the man whom they seek to kill? Behold, he speaks openly, and they say nothing to him. Have the rulers truly recognized 243 that this is the Christ? But we know where this man is from; and when Christ comes, no one knows where he is from.” This is as though they said: Our rulers have been deceived if they think this man is Christ, since we know both the place of his birth and his parents. They seem to have drawn this assertion, “When Christ comes, no one knows where he is from,” from the passage: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8).

Yet the Jews knew that Christ the Lord was to be born in Bethlehem of Judah, according to the words: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come a leader who shall rule my people Israel” (Matt. 2:6).

Jesus therefore cried out while teaching in the temple, saying: “You both know me and know where I am from; and I have not come from myself, but he who sent me is true, whom you do not know.” What else is signified by these words except that you both know me and do not know me? For since the Father and the Son are one, whoever does not know the Father does not know the Son. They knew [Col. 0509D] him, therefore, because they believed him to be a man [Col. 0510A]; and they did not know him because they were ignorant that he was God.

[Note: A. seems to have borrowed this from Augustine and Bede. Augustine, Tractate 31: “Whence arose among the Jews this opinion that, when Christ comes, no one knows where he is from? For it did not arise without cause. If we consider the Scriptures, brothers, we find how the holy Scriptures said of Christ that he should be called a Nazarene. Therefore they foretold where he was from. Again, if we inquire into the place of his birth, as though he were from where he was born, this also was not hidden from the Jews because of the Scriptures which foretold it, etc. Whence arose among the Jews the opinion which we have just heard … unless because the Scriptures had foretold and predicted both? According to his humanity the Scriptures foretold where he would be from; according to his divinity he was hidden from the impious and sought by the devout … because the saying through Isaiah had generated this opinion in them: ‘But who shall declare his generation?’” Cyril, p. 446, says much the same. [Col. 0509D; 0510D].]

They also knew that he was from Nazareth, but did not know that he was from the Father. Let him therefore say: “You both know me and know where I am from, and I have not come from myself”—not as that other one of whom he said above: “Another will come in his own name, and you will receive him.” “But he who sent me is true” (John 5:43): the Father is true, and therefore I too am true. “I and the Father are one” (John 10:29). “Whom you do not know.” I know him; and if I said that I did not know him, I would be a liar like you. For I know him because I am from him, and he sent me.

He is from him because he is God from God, light from light, of the same substance as the Father. For the Father is from no one; the Son is from the Father; the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. But what does he mean when he says, “who sent me,” except: he who willed that I should become man and take flesh? Yet this operation belongs to the whole Trinity, not to the Father alone. We must therefore note how everywhere he honors and glorifies the Father.

They therefore sought to seize him, but no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come: namely, that hour when he was to be betrayed, apprehended, and crucified. But that hour could not come unless he willed it. For he had power, as he himself says, to lay down his life and to take it up again (John 10:18). But many of the crowd believed in him. This is what he says elsewhere: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11:25). And they said: “When [Col. 0510C] Christ comes, will he do more signs than this man does?” This is an excellent argument, and very well suited to this assertion. For the Lord himself says: “The works which I do in the name of my Father, they bear witness concerning me” (John 5:36).

XXII. The Pharisees heard the crowd murmuring about him, and the rulers and Pharisees sent officers to arrest him. Jesus therefore said to them: “Yet a little while I am with you, and I go to him who sent me.” “In vain,” he says, “do both you and your rulers labour. You were sent for this purpose, and for this you came, that you might arrest me. But this lies not in your power, but in mine.” [Note: [Col. 0510D] Augustine, Tractate 31, and Bede on this passage: “His hour had not yet come”; that is, because he did not will it. So also Cyril, p. 451.]

“Yet a little while I am with you.” Wait until the time comes [Col. 0510D], so that all things may be fulfilled in their proper order. [Col. 0511A] Soon I shall leave you; I shall not remain with you longer. It is near that I should return to him who sent me. “You will seek me, and will not find me; and where I am, you cannot come.”

For the Jews sought Jesus, but sought him wrongly; and because they sought wrongly, they did not find him. They still seek and do not find. They read the Scriptures and do not understand. There they seek Jesus; but because they seek carnally, they do not find him. Do you wish to find Jesus? Go to the temple; go to the Church: there he sits in the midst of the teachers, in the assembly of bishops and presbyters. But what does he mean when he says, “Where I am, you cannot come”? For where then was Jesus? Was he not among them? How could they not come where he himself was? For Jesus was in heaven according to his divinity [Note: [Col. 0511D] Augustine, ibid.: “Christ was on earth according to his visible flesh, but in heaven and on earth according to his invisible majesty. Therefore he says, ‘Where I am, you cannot come’; and he did not say, ‘You will not be able.’”], whither indeed [Col. 0511B] none can come who refuse to believe in him.

The Jews therefore said among themselves: “Where is this man going, that we shall not find him? Is he going into the Dispersion among the Gentiles, and will he teach the Gentiles? What is this saying which he spoke: ‘You will seek me and will not find me, and where I am, you cannot come’?” The Jews cannot understand Christ’s words, because “the natural man does not receive the things that are of God” (1 Cor. 2:14). They suppose that he wishes bodily to go to the Gentile people, as though they could not have followed him there had the Lord wished to go there.

But on the last, great day of the festival Jesus stood and cried out, saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as the Scripture says, from his belly shall flow rivers of living water.” The Lord invites them [Col. 0511C] to drink, because he is the fountain. Of him the psalmist says to the Lord: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35:10). He invites, certainly, those who thirst and desire both to drink and to believe.

But when he says, “From his belly shall flow rivers of living water,” the Evangelist explained it, saying: “This he said concerning the Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive.” Living water, then, is the Holy Spirit. By this water we are both washed and made alive. The Spirit and water are closely joined. Hence also, “the Spirit of God was moving over the waters” (Gen. 1:2). This also is what is said: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom” (John 3:5). Rightly, therefore, is the Holy Spirit called water, and not [Col. 0512A] merely any sort of water, but living water. [Note: [Col. 0511D] Jerome, having interpreted the water in Zechariah, chapter 14, as doctrine, reports the opinion of those who explain this of baptism. Augustine rejects this interpretation in *Against Cresconius*, book II, ch. 13, because “both good and evil persons may possess such water, although without it the good cannot be saved; and though it belongs to the Church, it nevertheless flows out even beyond it.” Therefore in ch. 14 he gives the interpretation followed by our Author: “Thus he was commending not this water, but under the name of water the invisible gift of God, the Holy Spirit, saying: ‘If anyone thirst, let him come and drink,’ as the Evangelist clearly testifies when he adds: ‘But this he said concerning the Spirit,’” etc. Chrysostom, Homily 51, no. 1: “He calls it living because it is always active. For when the grace of the Spirit has entered and been established in the soul, it gushes forth more than any fountain, and neither ceases, nor is exhausted, nor comes to an end.” Cyril, p. 468, also asks and explains why Christ uses the name of water in this place.]

He who believes in Christ is full of this water. The apostles abounded in it. Its rivers flowed from their belly. See now how great a river flows from the breast of this man who here speaks: the river “whose rush makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45:5). Therefore all rivers, all volumes of the holy Scriptures, flow from this water.

But why did he say, “whom those believing in him were to receive,” and not, “whom those believing in him had received”? Do you wish to hear why? Because the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified. For after Christ’s glorification and ascension, the Holy Spirit was visibly given to the apostles in tongues of fire. This had never happened before. Hence our Saviour said to these same disciples [Col. 0512B]: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send him to you” [Note: [Col. 0512D] Augustine had resolved this question thus in Tractate 52 on John: “For the prophets did not foretell things to come without the Holy Spirit,” etc. “But the Spirit had not yet been given,” that is, that abundance of spiritual grace by which, gathered together, they spoke in the languages of all; as though in the languages of all nations the Church yet to come were being foretold. He discusses the same point more fully in *On the Trinity*, book IV, ch. 20, and Question 62 in book LXXXIII of the *Questions*.] (John 7:7). Jesus therefore had first to be glorified, so that the Holy Spirit might be given to believers.

From that crowd, then, when they had heard these sayings of his, some said: “This truly is the Prophet.” Others said: “This is the Christ.” Both said well. But those who said that he was the Christ said better; and better because they believed him to be more than a prophet. But some said: “Does the Christ come from Galilee? Does not Scripture say that Christ comes from the seed of David and from the town of Bethlehem, where David was?” You see, therefore, how necessary it was that Christ should be born at Bethlehem. For I think that these men did not know that our Saviour had been born at Bethlehem [Col. 0512C]. [Note: [Col. 0512D] Cyril, p. 477: “The Jews’ leaderless opinion erred because of Nazareth alone, situated in Galilee, where Christ was said to have been brought up . . . They were entirely unaware that he had been born in Bethlehem of Judaea from the Holy Virgin, who was of David’s seed.”]

A division therefore arose in the crowd because of him. For this is what the Lord says: “Do not think that I came to bring peace upon earth. I came not to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10:34). Some of them wished to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him. They wished to arrest him, but he did not wish it; and because he did not wish it, no one laid hands on him. “He was offered, therefore, because he himself willed it” (Isa. 53:7). Hence he also says: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down and take it up again” (John 10:46).

The officers therefore came to the chief priests and Pharisees, and they said to them: “Why have you not brought him?” The officers answered: “Never did a man speak as this man [Col. 0513A] speaks.” As though they said: “Would that you too had been present! Would that you too had heard his words! Perhaps you would never again do anything against him.” For never did a man speak as this man speaks, who seems to be more than a man. For he is God and man.

The Pharisees therefore answered them: “Have you also been deceived?” Deceived indeed, but beneficially. For those are beneficially led astray who are led from evil to good. But they said: “Has any one of the rulers believed in him, or of the Pharisees? But this crowd, which does not know the law, is accursed.” For these men are not accursed; rather, you are accursed, who [245] refused to believe in him, through whom you ought to have been freed from the curse of the law. [Note: [Col. 0513C] “How are they accursed?” asks Chrysostom, Homily 52, no. 1. “You who do not keep the law are accursed.” And Cyril excellently, p. 481: “It is characteristic of those unable to answer inquiries to drive away questioners angrily. They judge believers to be accursed, though they might much more rightly have said this of themselves.”]

The wise, therefore, are blinded; the foolish are enlightened [Col. 0513B], as the Lord himself says (John 9:39): “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.” Nicodemus said to them—he who had come to him by night, one of their number—“Does our law judge a man unless it first hears from him and knows what he does?” For no one is condemned according to the law unless he has confessed of himself or has been convicted by others. [Note: [Col. 0513D] See Chrysostom and Cyril in the places cited.]

They answered and said to him: “Are you also a Galilean? Search and see that no prophet arises from Galilee.” They understand this, therefore, of Christ, whom the prophets had foretold would be born in Bethlehem and nowhere else. And each returned to his own house, very sorrowful because they had not been able to accomplish their will.

XXIII. But Jesus went to the Mount of Olives; and early in the morning he came again into the temple, and all the people came to him, and, sitting down, he taught them. [Col. 0513C] Now the fact that Jesus was accustomed to go to the Mount of Olives, to pray, and to spend the night, signified that he loved and would always dwell in the holy Church planted with olive trees. For he was one of those olive trees who said: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God; I shall hope in the mercy of my God for ever and unto ages of ages” (Ps. 51:10). Such olive trees are all who love peace and mercy. [Note: [Col. 0513D] “For the Mount of Olives,” says Bede here, “signifies the loftiness of the Lord’s pity and mercy, because in Greek both ἔλεος means ‘mercy’ and ἔλεον means ‘oil’; and the very anointing with oil is accustomed to bring relief to weary and suffering limbs.”]

But when Jesus again came into the temple and, sitting, taught the people, behold, his enemies [Col. 0514A]—the scribes and Pharisees, who were always laying snares for him and persecuting him with unjust hatred—[Note: [Col. 0513D] Calvin first, and afterwards Wetstein, well-known heretics, dared to note this history, transmitted by John the Evangelist, as an interpolation. The most distinguished Georgius aptly meets them, sets forth their cavils and frivolities, and refutes them with victorious hand in his elucidation of the aforesaid fragment of John, chapter 8, p. 184 and following.] brought a certain woman caught in adultery; and, placing her in the midst, they said to him: “Teacher, this woman has just been caught in adultery. Now Moses commanded in the law that such persons should be stoned. What, then, do you say?”

For they knew that he was merciful and compassionate. Hence they hoped that he would attend rather to mercy and compassion than to the words of the law. If he did so, they wished immediately to accuse him of transgressing the law. [Note: [Col. 0513D] Augustine, Tractate 33: “They said among themselves: [Col. 0514C] ‘He is thought truthful; he seems gentle. We must seek a slander against him from justice. Let us bring before him [Col. 0514D] a woman caught in adultery; let us state what has been commanded in the law concerning her. If he orders her stoned, he will not possess gentleness; if he judges that she should be dismissed, he will not maintain justice. But, they say, lest he lose the gentleness through which he has already become beloved by the people, without doubt he will say that she ought to be dismissed. From this we have found an opportunity to accuse him.’” See Ambrose, Class I, Letters 25 and 26.]

Therefore it follows: “But they said this, testing him, that they might be able to accuse him.” But Jesus, bending down, wrote with his finger on the ground. When they persisted in questioning him, he raised himself and said to them: “He who is without sin among you, let him be the first to cast a stone at her.”

That Jesus wrote on the ground with his finger was as though he said: “You bring me testimonies of the law, or recount the law’s words to me, though you do not understand the law itself. This is the finger which wrote it. With this finger those tablets were inscribed, of which it is said: ‘Moses came down from the mountain bearing in his hands two stone tablets, both written with the finger of God’ (Exod. 32:15). I, therefore, composed the law, and you strive to entangle me by instances from the law? You are foolish if you hope to catch and overcome me by my own arguments. For the law commands that such a woman be stoned, but not as you understand it, nor by such persons as you are.” [Note: [Col. 0514D] Augustine, ibid.: “O answer of wisdom! How he brought them into themselves! For they were slandering him outwardly, but were not examining themselves inwardly. . . . You have heard, Jews; you have heard, Pharisees; you have heard, teachers of the law, the keeper of the law; but you have not yet understood the Lawgiver. What else does he signify to you when he writes on the ground with his finger? For the law was written by the finger of God . . . Let the law be fulfilled; let the adulteress be stoned. But must the law in punishing her be fulfilled by those who themselves are to be punished?” etc. See Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, book III, ch. 2.]

“For I am the end of the law. In me the letter of the law has been fulfilled. Behold, I make all things new. [Col. 0514C] Let those things which hitherto have been understood according to the letter be understood spiritually. Therefore, he who is without sin, let him be the first to cast a stone at her.” For who is without sin? “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (John 1:8). A person may indeed be without a crime; but who shall be without sin? [Note: [Col. 0514D] Augustine also distinguishes these matters in Tractate 4 [Col. 0515D] on John, no. [lacuna], on the words, “If therefore the Son shall make you free, you shall be truly free,” writing: “The first freedom is to be free from crimes . . . Examine any man, however just, in this life: although he is now worthy of the name of just, he is nevertheless not without sin. Hear Saint John himself: ‘If we say,’ etc. . . . Yet certainly many just persons are without reproach; this does not mean without crime. For in human affairs no just complaint is made against those who have no crime. A crime, however, is a grave sin, most deserving of accusation and condemnation.”]

Thus in this place sin is used for crime. Otherwise Jesus would be commanding impossibilities. And the Apostle indeed commands that persons of this sort, who are without crime, be chosen for the episcopate. These, therefore, are those who ought first to cast a stone at such a woman.

It must therefore be said what the adulterous woman and these stones signify. Every soul corrupted by heretical depravity is an adulterous woman. She is then stoned when, brought before a council of bishops and priests and convicted of her iniquity, she is excommunicated by the whole council. But he first casts a stone at her who is without sin; by him we understand the bishop whom the Apostle commands to be without crime. Then, all who confirm the excommunication cast a stone at her. Moses, therefore, signified this when he commanded that the adulterous woman be stoned. The Lord also expounded it when he commanded him who was without sin to cast the first stone at her. But the Jews did not understand this and had nothing [Col. 0515B] to reply.

For Jesus so tempered his saying that he neither contradicted the law nor lost compassion. [Note: [Col. 0515D] Augustine, Letter 154, ch. 4, no. 9: “Thus he neither rejected the law, which commanded such a guilty woman to be put to death, nor, by holding them fast, failed to recall to mercy those by whose judgment she could be put to death.”] But when they heard this, they went out one by one, beginning with the elders; and Jesus alone remained [Col. 0516A], with the woman standing in the midst. Why did they go out? Because they all knew themselves to be sinners. But he alone remained because he alone was without sin. [Note: [Col. 0516D] Augustine, Tractate 33: “Two remained: misery and mercy. . . . They, therefore, looking to themselves and confessing concerning themselves by their very departure, had left the woman with her great sin to him who was without sin.”]

The woman was still afraid; she still stood in the midst. From one side she awaited mercy, and from the other judgment. For what is “in the midst” except between mercy and judgment? Therefore the psalmist rightly says: “I will sing to you, Lord, of mercy and judgment” (Ps. 100:1). Jesus, rising up, said to her: “Woman, where are those who accused you? Has no one condemned you?” She said: “No one, Lord.”

Therefore Jesus did not condemn her when he said, “He who is without sin, let him be the first to cast a stone at her.” For had he condemned her, he would by no means have said to her: “Has no one condemned you?” But Jesus said to her: “Neither will I condemn you. Do not be afraid. Be [Col. 0516B] secure. Only believe my counsels. I do not cast away sinners; I receive those who repent. Go, and sin no more.” Thus the wretched woman was set free at mercy’s command.

PART TWO.

[Col. 0515]

247 XXIV. [CHAPTER VIII.] Therefore Jesus spoke again, saying: “I am the light of the world. He who follows me does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.” [Col. 0515C] “I am the light of the world. I am that light which enlightens every person coming into this world. I am that light which grants brightness to the sun, sight to the eyes, and understanding to the mind. Through me the sun shines, eyes see, and the soul understands. I, therefore, am the true light, through whom all things are enlightened and without whom all things grow dark. By this light the blind are enlightened, the dead rise again, and the eyes of the mind are opened to see God. Rightly, therefore, when this light departed, ‘darkness came over the whole earth’” (Luke 23:44).

“He who follows me does not walk in darkness.” In what darkness? For there is the darkness of night; there is also the darkness of ignorance [Col. 0515D] and error. [Note: [Col. 0516D] Augustine, Tractate 35, no. 1: “The darkness to be feared is that of conduct, not of the eyes; and, if of eyes, not external but internal eyes, by which one discerns not white and black, but just and unjust.” See on Psalm 34, no. 9; Chrysostom, Homily 52, no. 2: “He means spiritual darkness; that is, he does not remain in error.”] For if we understand it of night’s darkness, no one follows the light by night. But whoever does not follow this light is not a Christian. Are we then not Christians at night, because at night we walk in darkness, and no one who follows Christ walks in darkness? This, therefore, must not be understood [Col. 0516C] of the darkness of night but rather of the darkness of ignorance. For Christ is both wisdom and truth. But where wisdom and truth are, error and ignorance cannot be. Therefore he who follows Christ does not walk in the darkness of ignorance and error.

The whole world sat in this darkness when Christ, the light of the world, appeared. Hence it is written: “The people that sat in darkness saw a great light” (Matt. 4:16). Let our Saviour therefore say: “He who follows me does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.” To follow, moreover, is to imitate. But the light of life is that which prepares eternal life, by which we understand the doctrine of faith and knowledge of truth.

The Pharisees therefore said: “You bear witness concerning yourself; your witness [Col. 0516D] is not true.” Wretched Pharisees, who say that the witness of Truth is not true! For truth cannot lie. But perhaps they said this because it is written [Note: [Col. 0516D] Proverbs 27:2. See the remarks on John chapter 5, and Cyril here, p. 488, and Augustine, Tractate 36.]: “Let another mouth praise you, and not your own.” For the Lord did not say such things in praise of himself or for empty glory, but in order to teach them [Col. 0517A] what they ought to believe. Hence he himself says: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing.”

It follows: “Even if I bear witness concerning myself, my witness is true.” Why is this? “Because I know whence I come and whither I go.” A wonderful argument. Is your witness therefore true, Lord, because you know whence you come and whither you go? Tell us then whence you come and whither you go. “I came forth,” he says, “from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John 16:28). For if you came forth from the Father and go to the Father, you are the Son of God. If you are the Son of God, you cannot lie. Your witness, therefore, is true because you know whence you come and whither you go—that is, because you are the Son of God. [Note: [Col. 0517C] Cyril, p. 489: “A most certain proof of this is that I know where I shall go; for I shall ascend into heaven to him from whom I am, the Father. No one has ever said that this belongs to any one of us human beings, but it belongs by nature to God, even though he has become man. Thus the phrase ‘whence I am’ indicates that he is Son from the Father by nature.”]

“But you do not know whence I come and whither I go.” Why do you not know? Because you do not believe that I am the Son [Col. 0517B] of God. For those alone know this who believe that I am God’s Son. We therefore know that he came forth from the Father and goes to the Father. Yet we do not know how he came forth from the Father or how he went to the Father. For how does he go or come who is everywhere? Whoever goes, goes where he is not. Or how does he come forth from the Father and go to the Father, when he is always in the Father and the Father is always in him? For he himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 10:38).

“You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one.” What, then, is meant by what he says elsewhere: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (ibid. 5:22), if the Son also judges no one? The Son therefore judges, but not as the Pharisees do: not according to the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0517D] Augustine, Tractate 36: “‘I judge no one,’ either because he had not come to judge the world but to save the world; . . . or because he had said, ‘You judge according to the flesh,’ . . . that we may understand that Christ does not judge according to the flesh, as he was judged by men.” Cyril also explains it in two other ways, p. 490: “I shall for the present refrain from judging you and defer it to the last time.” II. “You despise me on account of the flesh, because in your view I appear as a man. But I shall not condemn you because you are human beings . . . I do not accuse nature; I do not condemn my works.”]

Hence [Col. 0517C] he adds: “And if I judge, my judgment is true.” Why is this? “Because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.” By the same argument he proves his judgment true by which he proved his witness true: namely, because he is the Son of God. Therefore, he says, my judgment is true because I am not alone; because I am not man only—for every man is a liar—but I am God and man, and together with the Father I am one and the same, although in person I am distinct.

“And in your law it is written that the testimony of two men is true.” This does not always occur, that the testimony of two men [Col. 0518A] is true. Otherwise those two elders whom Daniel commanded to be put to death were unjustly condemned. What then? Does the law lie when it says that the testimony of two men is true? Far from it! If the witnesses are such as the laws and canons require, the testimony of two men is true. [Note: [Col. 0517D] Augustine calls this a great question, [Col. 0518C] Tractate 36: for, he says, chaste Susanna was pressed by two false witnesses . . . and the whole people lied against Christ. He explains it by saying “that the matter is established in a mystery . . . because in this way the Trinity, in which there is the perpetual stability of truth, is commended through a mystery.” The literal solution is found in Jansenius, *Harmony*, ch. 77; Maldonatus here and on chapter 5; Estius; Natalis Alexander; Calmet; etc.: the testimony of two is true, that is, it is to be regarded as true and lawful according to the institution of human law.]

If understood spiritually, the two men signify the Catholic men of the two Testaments, whose testimony indeed is true. But if the testimony of two men is true, who would dare contradict what the Father and the Son testify? This is what he says: “I am he who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (Matt. 17:5). The Father bears witness concerning the Son when he says: “This is my beloved Son [Col. 0518B], in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 11:27).

They therefore said to him: “Where is your Father?” Jesus answered: “You know neither me nor my Father. You ask me,” he says, “about the Father, as though you already possessed knowledge of me. First acknowledge me, whom you see; and then afterwards, if you can, arrive at knowledge of the Father. For no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him. If you knew me, perhaps you would also know my Father.” When he says “perhaps,” he says it not in doubt but in rebuke. [Note: [Col. 0518D] Augustine, Tractate 37: “He who knows all things, when he says ‘perhaps,’ does not doubt but rebukes. . . . It is a word of doubt when uttered by a human being who doubts because he does not know. But when a word of doubt is uttered by God, from whom surely nothing is hidden, unbelief is reproved by that doubt; divinity does not form an opinion.” We have elsewhere spoken of the Greek particle ἄν, which is here also in the Greek.]

For an evil servant does not know his master unless he sees him angry. Therefore what is said is true: “The Lord shall be known when he executes judgments” (Ps. 9:17). Thus a teacher is accustomed to say to a stubborn pupil: “If you knew what is being prepared for you, perhaps you would read.” [Col. 0518C] Jesus spoke these words in the treasury, teaching in the temple. Let us therefore place these words in the treasury of our breast. Let us keep this treasure in the chamber of our heart, so that with the Apostle we may be able to say: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7). For these words were spoken in the treasury because they are greatly to be guarded, preserved, and committed to memory.

And no one arrested him, because his hour had not yet come. Why had it not come? Because he himself did not will it. Therefore it was not he who awaited the hour, but the hour that awaited him. For all things are placed in his power. His hour, therefore, was also [Col. 0519A] in his power, so that it should come then, and not earlier, than he himself commanded.

XXV. Jesus therefore said again: “I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sin.” “I am going away,” he says. “I am returning to the Father. But you will seek me, not in order to believe in me, but in order to kill me. And therefore you will die in your sin. Where I am going, you cannot come.” Why? Because you do not believe. Because you seek to kill me. Because you are not predestined to life. For no one comes to the Father except through me.

The Jews therefore said: “Will he kill himself, because he says, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come’?” He will not kill himself; rather, you, because you will kill him, will also kill yourselves, and therefore you will not come to him.

And he said to them [Col. 0519B]: “You are from below; I am from above.” “You are from below,” he says; “you are from the earth, you love the earth, and you savour earthly things. But I am from above, from heaven, from the Father, who is higher than all that is high. You are of this world. I am not of this world.” For so far as his humanity is concerned, Christ, like other human beings, is of the world. But so far as his divinity is concerned, he is not of the world; rather, the world is from him, because he did not begin from the world, but the world from him. “For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). Hence it is also said above: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (ibid., 1:10).

[Note: Col. 0519C–D. A. N. includes two interpretations of the words, “You are from below; I am from above,” which belong to the ancient Fathers. Chrysostom, Homily 53, no. 1: “You are from below; that is, it is no wonder that you, carnal human beings, think such things, since you conceive nothing spiritual. But I shall do nothing of the sort, for I am from above . . . ‘I am not of this world’ does not mean that he did not assume flesh, but that he is far removed from their wickedness. For he says that the disciples are not of the world, yet they had flesh.” But Cyril, p. 502: “I am from above; that is, God from God; for that which is above all things is God. But this description suits you rather: for you are from the lowest realm, namely from a nature subject to death, corruption, and fear . . . That ‘from above’ signifies the generation of the Son from God and the Father is plain to those whose judgment is sound.” Augustine, Tractate 38, has both explanations, writing: “For how was he of the world through whom the world was made? All are from the world after the world, because the world was first; and thus man is from the world. But Christ was first, then the world, since Christ was before the world; before Christ there was nothing, because ‘in the beginning was the Word, and all things were made through him.’ Thus he was from above . . . For this reason he said, ‘You are of this world,’ because they were sinners . . . for all of us are born with sin,” etc.]

“I have therefore told you that you will die in your sins.”

[p. 249] Now hear the reason why you will die in your sins [Col. 0519C]: “For unless you believe that I am, you will die in your sin.” What is this, “I am”? Did the Jews not believe that he existed, whom they both saw and heard? Or is he alone, and are there no other things, because he says, “Unless you believe that I am”? He alone is the one who always is: who is unchangeable; who is the very same; who never began to be; who never ceases to be; who gives being to all things; who does not pass from his own being into being or non-being. Of him it is said through Moses to the children of Israel: “He who is has sent me to you.”

[Note: Col. 0520D. Exodus 3:14. St Bruno has the same words in his exposition of this passage; see the Roman edition, p. 49, col. 2. Augustine, ibid.: “It is a great thing that he says, ‘I am,’ because the Lord had thus said to Moses: ‘I am who I am.’” Bede has nearly the same words as Augustine.]

Whoever, then, does not believe in him as thus possessing being will die in his sin.

They therefore said to him: “Who are you?” Jesus said to them: “The Beginning, even he who speaks to you.” “I,” he says, “am the Beginning; for your sake, according to my humanity, I have both been made and created, appear to you, and speak to you.”

But certain manuscripts read [Note: Col. 0520D–0522C. “The Beginning, even he who speaks to you” is found in the Vulgate and was read by Augustine, Tractate 39 on John and Book V, chapter 13, *On the Trinity*, and by nearly all Latin books, as Francis Lucas testifies. Ambrose, Book IV, chapter 4, *On the Faith*, reads: “The Beginning, which I also speak to you.” Fulgentius, Book II, chapter 5, *To Trasamund*, reads the same. The old Italian version from the Colbert manuscript, in Sabatier, reads: “The Beginning, which I speak to you.” The Greek in Chrysostom, Homily 53, no. 1, Cyril, p. 511, and elsewhere is: τὴν ἀρχὴν ὅτι καὶ λαλῶ ὑμῖν, “the beginning, that which I also speak to you.” The Vercelli codex in Blanchini, *Evang.* I, p. 300, reads: “The beginning which I speak to you”; the Verona manuscript: “In the first place, because I speak to you.” Other readings occur in Francis Lucas and John de la Haye, including this author’s *quia* (“because”). Haye and others think that ὅτι means *quia*, “because,” and has the force of *quod*, so that the sense is “for the reason that.” Mill writes ὅτι; but, according to Francis Lucas, nearly all manuscripts have ὅτι written together. Jansenius, *Harmony*, chapter 77; Toletus, Annotation 14; Maldonatus; Calmet; and others discuss this very obscure passage at length. The accusative τὴν ἀρχήν seems to stand against the first sense proposed by A. The other explanation, that of Augustine and Bede—“Believe that I am the Beginning”—they judge harsh. Thus most modern translators from the Greek, as Francis Lucas says, together with Greek-trained commentators and interpreters of better note, according to Calmet, understand “Beginning” as though it were an adverb. Toletus: “From the beginning I am he who tells you this very thing.” Jansenius: “It is altogether as I tell you.” Maldonatus, Calmet, and others, with the Old Latin and Nonnus: “I speak thus now, as I said from the beginning.” Nevertheless Natalis Alexander defends Augustine’s first interpretation, and a Lapide expounds it.]

“Because I speak to you.” And it is as if he said: “I am the Beginning. Believe that I am the Beginning; because, in order that you may believe me to be the Beginning, I became human, speak to you, and by speaking show you the way of truth and salvation.

“I have much to say and to judge concerning you; but he who sent me is true.” “For the present,” he says, “I do not judge you, though you deserve judgment.” Why? Because the Son of Man did not now come “to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him” (John [Col. 0520B] 3:17). Yet at some time he will judge, and he will judge with true judgment, because the true Son is the Son of the true Father. This is what he means when he says, “He who sent me is true.” “And what I have heard from him, these things I speak in the world.” Therefore, if the Father is true, and the Son speaks what he has heard from the Father, he certainly speaks truth. The Father is true, therefore the Son also is true.

But when he says, “What I have heard from him,” this must not be understood as though one spoke to the other; rather, “I have heard” means “I have known.” The Son has knowledge from him from whom he also has being. For as he is called the Word and Wisdom of God, so he is also called the Knowledge of God.

And they did not understand that he called God his Father. Jesus therefore said to them: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am, and that I do nothing of myself; but as the Father has taught me [Col. 0520C], these things I speak.” Jesus says this not to all who were there, but to some. For he saw there certain people who would believe after his Passion. Many of those who crucified him were afterwards pierced in heart, converted to faith, believed in him, and, truly recognizing him as the Son of God, reverenced and worshipped him.

Moreover, when he says, “As the Father taught me, so I speak,” he shows that he himself is the Father’s teaching. For what is the Father’s teaching but the Father’s Wisdom? Let him therefore say: “And I do nothing of myself.” I am not speaking according to my humanity. This teaching is not that of a human being; it is the teaching of divinity [Col. 0521A]. “As the Father taught me, these things I speak”; that is, I speak according to the knowledge and teaching of divinity. For begetting him was teaching him.

“And he who sent me is with me, and has not left me alone, because I always do the things that please him.” Although the Son was sent by the Father, although he was incarnate and became human—for the sending is the incarnation—nevertheless the Father is always in the Son and the Son always in the Father. For this is that beloved Son in whom he himself was well pleased.

While he was speaking these things, many believed in him. Jesus therefore said to those Jews who had believed in him: “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples; and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” “If you remain in my word,” he says, “if you hold fast my teaching, if you keep what you have learned from me, if you believe the faith which I preach, you will truly be my disciples.” For [p. 250] even your disciple, O man, is your disciple only so long as he does not depart from your teaching and discipline. Whoever does not keep your discipline is not your disciple. Rightly, therefore, does the Lord say: “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples.”

But with what result? “And you will know the truth.” And what will truth do for you? “And the truth will set you free.”

[Note: Col. 0522D. Augustine, Sermon 134: “For a disciple it is not enough to draw near; he must remain. Therefore he did not say, ‘If you hear my word,’ or ‘If you praise my word’; but see what he said: ‘If you remain,’ etc. What shall we say, brothers? Is remaining in the word of God labour, or is it not? If it is labour, consider the great reward; if it is not labour, receive the reward freely . . . What, then, is it to remain in the word of God, except not to yield to any temptations? What is the reward? ‘You will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.’” See also the same author, Book IV, chapter 18, *On the Trinity*; Ambrose, Sermon 10 on Psalm 118; Cyril, p. 533: “He requires of believers a steadfast and firm disposition in preserving the good which they have once embraced . . . ‘You will know the truth,’ he says, ‘if you persevere in my words; and when you know the truth, you will discover its benefit, namely liberation from the legal shadows and the type of future things.’”]

Therefore no one will be set free except one who knows the truth—that is, except one who believes in him, because he is truth and life. But one who is not Christ’s disciple does not know this truth. This teaching is not learned in other schools. And one who does not remain in Christ’s word is not Christ’s disciple.

When the Jews heard this [Col. 0521C], they were indignant and answered him: “We are Abraham’s offspring, and we have never been slaves to anyone. How do you say, ‘You will become free’?” For no one becomes free except one who has been a slave. What freedom, then, do you promise us, who have never been anyone’s slaves?

Jesus answered and said to them: “Amen, amen, I say to you: everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.” Such a slave, unless the truth of which he has just spoken sets him free, does not remain in the house forever. In what house? In the house of the Lord, in the heavenly Jerusalem. Therefore he will not enter it forever, since whoever enters it remains in it forever [Col. 0522A]. “But the Son remains forever. Therefore, if the Son sets you free, you will truly be free.”

The first human being sinned and became a slave of sin. Thus, driven from Paradise and from the Lord’s house, he did not remain there forever. Together with all his posterity, he could not be freed from original sin except through God’s Son. Therefore those who are freed through the Son are truly free.

“I know that you are Abraham’s children; but you seek to kill me, because my word finds no room in you. You say to me, ‘We are Abraham’s offspring.’ I know that you are Abraham’s children, and in this respect you are indeed free. But you have another father, according to whom you are not free. For if you did not have another father, you would not seek to kill me. But you seek to kill me because my word [Col. 0522B] finds no room in you, since your father, the devil, who dwells in you, drives it away from you.

“I speak what I have seen with the Father; and you do what you have seen with your father.” You have a father within; within you have a teacher and counsellor, who teaches you to do such things.

They answered and said to him: “Abraham is our father.” Jesus said to them: “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham.” This does not follow if it is understood of children according to the flesh. He is therefore speaking of those children who are called children by imitation. Hence the Apostle says: “For it is not the children of the flesh who are children, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring” (Romans 9:8).

“But now you seek to kill me, a man who have spoken to you the truth which I heard from God. Abraham did not do this” [Col. 0522C]. Therefore you are not Abraham’s children, since you do not do Abraham’s works. “You do the works of your father,” because he too “was a murderer from the beginning,” and at his persuasion you now seek to kill me.

They therefore said to him: “We were not born of fornication. We have one Father, God.” It is as though they said: “Why do you reproach us so often with a father? We were not born from fornication, so that you should cast a father in our teeth.”

[Note: Col. 0522D–0523C. Augustine, Tractate 42: “They changed their answer, I suppose, saying to themselves: ‘Whenever we name Abraham, he will say to us: Why do you not imitate him, whose lineage you boast of? We cannot imitate so holy, righteous, and innocent a man. Let us say that God is our Father; let us see what he will say to us.’ Falsehood indeed found something to say; but would truth fail to find an answer?”]

“Or perhaps, if you malign Abraham, whom we said was our father, know that we have one Father, God, against whom you dare say nothing. He also speaks of us, saying: ‘Israel is my firstborn son’” [Col. 0523A] (Exodus 4:22).

Jesus therefore said to them: “If God were your Father, you would surely love me. For I proceeded from God and have come. Nor have I come from myself, but he sent me.” “If God were your Father,” he says, “you would surely love me, who am his Son. He begot me; I proceeded from him and came. ‘I, Wisdom, came forth from the mouth of the Most High’ (Ecclesiasticus 24:5), ‘reaching from end to end’ (Wisdom 8:1). ‘Nor have I come from myself,’ that is, I do not exist from myself, but he sent me. What does ‘he sent me’ mean?” He ineffably begot me from himself before the ages. And now, that I might become human and assume flesh, he willed it.

[Note: Col. 0523C–D. Augustine, Tractate 42: “Christ’s sending, therefore, is his Incarnation. But the Word’s proceeding from God is an eternal procession: he through whom time was made has no time . . . Thus he proceeded from him as God, as equal, as the only Son, as the Word of the Father; and he came to us because the Word was made flesh, that he might dwell among us.” See the book *Against the Sermon of the Arians*, chapters 3 and 4. Cyril, p. 553: “When therefore he says, ‘I proceeded from God,’ he signifies his ineffable birth from the Father, which is without beginning. But when he adds, ‘I came,’ he denotes his advent into this world in the flesh.”]

[p. 251] “Why do you not understand my speech? Do you wish to hear why? Because you cannot hear my word.” Thus, he says, your father the devil has blinded you, has stirred you up against me to hatred [Col. 0523B], and has inflamed you with such desire for my death that you cannot hear my word and refuse to understand what I say. Therefore you do not understand my speech and do not heed the words of truth.

“For you are from your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father; because, as he does, so you seek to kill me. This is his desire, and it is also yours. He was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him.” The devil was a murderer from the beginning because, at the very beginning of the world, he tempted the first human beings, slew them by tempting them, and deprived them of immortality.

[Note: Col. 0523D. Augustine, Book II, chapter 13, *Against the Letter of Petilian*: “We ask how the devil was a murderer from the beginning; and we find that he killed the first human being, not by drawing a sword or inflicting some bodily violence, but by persuading him to sin and casting him down from the happiness of Paradise.”]

“But he did not stand in the truth,” because, as soon as he was created, lifted up in pride, he said: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I will exalt my throne; I will sit upon the mount of the Testament, on the sides of the North, and I will be like the Most High” [Col. 0523C–0524A] (Isaiah 14:13).

[Note: Col. 0523D–0524C. Augustine, Book XI, chapter 33, *The City of God*: “What the Lord says of the devil in the Gospel—‘He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth’—must be understood so that he was not merely a murderer from the beginning, that is, at the beginning of the human race, from which time a human being existed whom he could kill by deceiving; but also that from the beginning of his own creation he did not stand in the truth . . . refusing to be subject to his Creator and, exalted by pride as though through a private power, thereby becoming false and deceitful.” See St Leo, Sermon 6 on the Lord’s Passion, chapter 5.]

For even if he sometimes speaks the truth, truth is not in him, because he speaks either unknowingly or under compulsion.

[Note: Col. 0524C. A careful exposition of this Gospel passage may be found in Jansenius, *Harmony*, chapter 77.]

Before him there was no falsehood; from him and through him it came to pass that every human being is a liar. “Whoever speaks falsehood speaks from his own resources, because he is a liar and its father.” The devil therefore left this quality, this wicked inheritance, to his children: that they should lie and follow their father by lying.

It may also be understood thus: that the devil speaks falsehood from his own resources because he himself is a liar and the father of falsehood.

[Note: Col. 0524C–D. Our author offers two explanations: (1) concerning all liars; (2) concerning the devil. The first is also found in Eucherius, or in the author of *Questions on the Old and New Testament*, vol. VI of the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, p. 850. In “when he speaks falsehood,” one must supply “each one of you”; Maldonatus, for some reason, calls this remarkable, though it agrees with the old reading “he who,” rather than “when,” speaks, etc., which Augustine also has, *On John*, I.5, no. 1. Yet here he follows the common reading and admirably comments: “The devil was a murderer from the beginning. We recognize it: he killed Adam. And he did not stand in the truth. We recognize it, because he fell away from the truth. Because truth is not in him. It is true: by departing from truth, he does not have truth. When he speaks falsehood, he speaks from his own resources. He does not obtain from elsewhere what he speaks. When he speaks falsehood, he speaks from his own resources, because he is a liar and its father. He is both a liar and the father of falsehood. For perhaps you are a liar because you speak falsehood, but you are not its father. If you received what you say from the devil and believed the devil, you are a liar; you are not the father of falsehood. But he, because he did not receive from elsewhere the falsehood by which, like a serpent with poison, he killed the human being, is the father of falsehood, just as God is the Father of truth.”]

“But I, because I speak the truth, you do not believe me.” You believe, he says, the devil when he lies; but you do not believe me when I speak truth, show the way of salvation, and lead you back to your homeland.

XXVI. “Which of you will convict me of sin? If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me?” [Col. 0524B] “Which of you,” he says, “will convict me of sin? What have you seen in me that you ought rightly to rebuke? If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me, except because you are not from God? Whoever is from God hears God’s words; and for this reason you do not hear, because you are not from God.”

If all things are from God, how are these people not from God? All things are from God because they were created by him. Hence it is also said above of our Saviour: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). Therefore they are from God according to nature, but they are not from God according to wickedness. They are from God according to creation, but they are not from God according to corruption. For whatever is from God is good; and whatever is not good is not from God [Col. 0524C].

[Note: Col. 0524D–0525D. Cyril, p. 567: “By these words, ‘to be from God,’ one must not think that this is signified . . . according to Paul’s saying, ‘All things are from God.’ Since he is the maker and parent of all things, who gives being to all, the divine Paul says that all things are from God. But it must not be understood in that way here: for all, whether good or evil, are from God insofar as he is the author and craftsman of all. He calls that person ‘from God’ who has been joined to God through virtue and excellence of life, and has been deemed worthy of a certain kinship with him, just as he judges such people also to be counted among his children.”]

Thus the wicked both are from God and are not from God [Col. 0525A].

The Jews therefore answered and said to him: “Do we not rightly say that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” Wretched Jews, you yourselves prove true what the Lord just said: that you are not from God. For if you were from God, you would not say these things to the Son of God. You say them because you are from your father the devil.

Jesus answered: “I do not have a demon, but I honour my Father, and you dishonour me.” Certainly the Lord invites us to an example of patience and gentleness. Having received an insult, he is not angered and does not return abuse for abuse. He answers that he has no demon, yet does not deny that he is a Samaritan. For if he had denied that he was a Samaritan, [p. 252] he would have contradicted his own words, since elsewhere he calls himself a Samaritan [Col. 0525B]. Recall that Gospel in which the Samaritan heals the man wounded by robbers while he was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho (Luke 10:33). And because *Samaritan* is interpreted “guardian,” the Lord is rightly called a Samaritan, of whom it is written: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” (Isaiah 21:11). And the Psalmist says: “Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it watch in vain” (Psalm 126:1).

[Note: Col. 0525D–0526D. St Gregory, Homily 18 on the Gospels: “Consider, dearest brothers, the gentleness of God . . . Let us hear what the Lord answers when he receives so great an insult: ‘I do not have a demon,’ etc. Because *Samaritan* means ‘guardian,’ and he is truly a guardian—the one of whom the Psalmist says, ‘Unless the Lord guards the city,’ and to whom it is said through Isaiah, ‘Watchman, what of the night?’—the Lord did not wish to answer, ‘I am not a Samaritan,’ but, ‘I do not have a demon.’ Two things were laid against him: one he denied, the other he assented to by silence. For he had come as guardian of the human race; and if he had said that he was not a Samaritan, he would have denied that he was a guardian. But he kept silence about what he acknowledged, and patiently rejected what he heard falsely said, declaring, ‘I do not have a demon.’ In these words, what else is confounded but our pride [Col. 0526C–D], which, if it is ever even lightly provoked, returns more grievous injuries than it has received; does the evils it can do, and threatens those which it cannot do? Behold, the Lord receives an insult without anger, without answering abusive words . . . when he received an injury, Truth did not even wish to say what was true, lest he appear not to have spoken truth but to have returned insult when provoked.” This, I think, Gregory took from Augustine; see Tractate 43.]

“I do not seek my own glory. There is one who seeks it and judges.” For the Lord did not seek his own glory when, humbling himself from such exaltation, he became “the reproach of men and the despised of the people.” But there is the Father who seeks and judges. For the Father sought the glory of the Son and judged him glorious above all things [Col. 0525C], when he said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matthew 17:5). This glory is above every glory.

It follows: “Amen, amen, I say to you: if anyone keeps my word, he shall never taste death.” Why, then, do you not believe me? Why do you not keep my word? “Amen, amen, I say to you: if anyone believes me and keeps my word, he shall never taste death.” What does “shall not taste death” mean? He will not feel the pains and bitterness of death—not temporal death, certainly, but eternal death. For his addition “forever” means the same as saying that he shall not taste eternal death.

[Note: Col. 0526D. Cyril, p. 573: “Not as though he entirely removes death according to the flesh, or considers death not to be death . . . Rather, he calls ‘death’ the eternal punishments and the penalty prepared for the ungodly.”]

The Jews therefore said [Col. 0526A]: “Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham died, and the prophets; yet you say, ‘If anyone keeps my word, he shall never taste death’? Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? And the prophets died. Whom do you make yourself?”

It is as though they said: “No such man as you has ever existed, if what you say is true—if those who keep your word do not die. Are you greater than Abraham and greater than all the prophets? For they died; but you are not merely immortal, you also make immortal those who believe and obey you. You exalt yourself too much; you glorify yourself too much.”

Jesus answered: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me [Col. 0526B], whom you say is our God, and you have not known him. But I know him. And if I said that I did not know him, I would be a liar like you. But I know him, and I keep his word.”

But someone may say: How does he not glorify himself, if the Father glorifies him, when the Father and he are one and the same? For he says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). If they are one, then the one whom the Father glorifies and the one whom the Son glorifies are one; therefore the Son also glorifies himself. What then does he mean when he says, “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing”?

Because our Saviour is both God and human, if he glorifies himself according to divinity, his glory is great. For it is great glory to heal paralytics, give sight to the blind, cleanse lepers, command the winds, walk dry-footed upon the sea [Col. 0526C], and raise the dead. But all this glory belongs to divinity. If, however, he glorifies himself according to humanity, his glory is nothing.

[Note: Col. 0526D. Augustine, Tractate 44: “He says this because of what they had said: ‘Whom do you make yourself?’ For he refers his glory to the Father, from whom he has that he is God.” Interpreters commonly explain this passage in the same way as the earlier saying, “If I bear witness about myself, my witness is not true.”]

For human beings are glorified not because they are human, but because they are endowed with wisdom, courage, and other virtues. Wherever these things are found, they belong not to the human being but to God. Hence the Apostle says: “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14). And again: “This is our boast: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1:12).

It follows: “Your father Abraham rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” [Col. 0527A]. For all the patriarchs and prophets awaited with great longing the day of Christ’s birth, through whom they knew that they would come to the glory of heavenly blessedness.

Yet by this day one may understand the day of that time when Abraham, standing by the oak of Mamre, saw three men; in them, through the Holy Spirit, recognizing Christ, he worshipped one.

[Note: Col. 0527D. Genesis 18:2–3. St Gregory, Homily 8, no. 3: “Abraham then saw the Lord’s day when, in the figure of the supreme Trinity, he received three angels as guests.”]

[p. 253] But what wonder is it if Abraham saw Christ before Christ became human, when Nebuchadnezzar also testifies that he saw him in the fiery furnace?

[Note: Col. 0527D. Daniel 3:92: “Then Nebuchadnezzar . . . said to his nobles: ‘Did we not cast three bound men into the midst of the fire? . . . Behold, I see four men unbound and walking in the midst of the fire, and there is no injury in them; and the appearance of the fourth is like a Son of God.’” See Irenaeus, Book IV, chapter 20, and Book V, chapter 5; Tertullian, Book IV, chapters 20 and 21, *Against Marcion*; Jerome on this passage in Daniel: “The appearance of the fourth, whom he calls like the Son of God, must be understood either as an angel, as the Septuagint translated, or, as most suppose, as the Lord and Saviour.”]

The Jews therefore said to him: “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” Jesus said to them: “Amen, I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am.” He speaks according to divinity; but they do not understand this [Col. 0527B], because they see not God but a human being—indeed, a man of little age and far removed from Abraham’s time. Though they ought to have asked him the meaning of words which they knew were neither vain nor idle, so that, since they could not understand him by themselves, he might explain his own words to them, they run for stones and desire to kill him.

Hence it is added: “They therefore took up stones to throw at him. But Jesus hid himself and went out of the Temple.” Jesus hid himself and went out of the Temple, not according to that which he is before Abraham, but according to that which he is Abraham’s son. Thus it is easy to recognize two natures in Christ: one according to which every creature obeys him; the other against which the impious crowd of the wicked rages.

XXVII [CHAP. IX.] And as Jesus passed by, he saw a man blind from birth.
