[Col. 0527C] And his disciples asked him: “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” Our Savior himself most plainly shows that his miracles signify something, when, in performing them, he does something which may seem devoid of rational purpose. For unless it signified something, what need was there, in giving sight to this blind man, to make mud with which to smear his eyes, when it would have been enough merely to speak? For “he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. CXLVIII, 5)—all things.

Let us therefore seek the meaning and see what this blind man signifies. This blind man, blind from birth, appears to be the human race. But why from birth [Col. 0528A], unless from the first man? For when the devil urged the first man to eat from the forbidden tree, saying [Note: [Col. 0527D] Gen. III, 5: “On whatever day you eat, your eyes shall be opened.”]: “Eat, and your eyes shall be opened,” did he not thereby show him to be blind? Yet he was not blind as yet; but by eating he became blind. Thus from this one blind man all human beings are born blind. This blindness, however, is not of the body but of the soul. It is this blindness that makes people fail to know their Creator [Note: [Col. 0527D] Augustine, Tractate 44: “Therefore, if we consider what this event signifies [Col. 0528D], this blind man is the human race: for this blindness befell the first man through sin, from whom we derive our origin—not only of death, but also of iniquity.”].

But let us hear what the Lord answered when the disciples questioned him: “Neither this man,” he said, “nor his parents sinned, so that he should be born blind.” Why, then, was he born blind? “That the works of God might be manifested in him.” For both he and his parents had sinned; yet he was not born blind because of his own sins or theirs, but rather so that [Col. 0528B] the works of God might be manifested in him [Note: [Col. 0528D] Chrysostom, Homily 56 on John, no. 1, also observes this: “He does not say this in order to declare them entirely free from sins. For he did not simply say: ‘Neither this man sinned, nor his parents,’ but added, ‘so that he should be born blind,’ etc. For this man and his parents did sin; but the blindness did not arise from that.”].

It follows: “I must work the works of him who sent me while it is day. Night comes, when no one can work. As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” Therefore the Lord is still at work, because it is still day. He worked in person; he also worked through his disciples. He works even now. He will work through his faithful people until the consummation of the age. Afterwards night will follow, in which no one will be able to work. Therefore, “while we have time, let us do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith” (Gal. VI, 10). And lest you think that this day will end quickly, hear what the Lord himself says: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20).

But as long as he is in the world [Col. 0528C], he is the light of the world [Note: [Col. 0528D] Bede, on this passage: “It is clear that the Lord expressly and definitely called himself here the day, that is, the light of the world. ‘As long as,’ he says, ‘I am in this world, I am the light of the world.’ Therefore he himself works. But how long is he in the world? Do we suppose, brothers, that he was here then but is not here now? . . . What is it that he said to his disciples when ascending into heaven: ‘Behold, I am with you’?” etc.]. Thus he is even now the light of the world, because he is now in the world. For if he is with us, he is in the world, since we too are in the world.

When he had said these things, he spat on the ground, made mud, smeared the mud upon the man’s eyes, and said to him: “Go and wash in the pool of Siloam.” The Evangelist then added the interpretation of Siloam, saying that it means “Sent.” We have already said what this blind man signifies. Now let us see how, and by what medicine, the blind are enlightened.

The spittle, which naturally descends from the head, is Christ’s divinity, whose [Page 254] “head,” as the Apostle says, “is God” (I Cor. XI). This descended upon the earth, came into the Virgin, and became mud, because “the Word was made flesh [Col. 0529A] and dwelt among us” (John I, 14). This, then, is that medicine—the Incarnation of the Son of God—by which the blind are enlightened [Note: [Col. 0529D] Augustine, Tractate 44: “The Lord came; what did he do? He commended a great mystery: he spat upon the ground, etc., because the Word was made flesh . . . He sent him to the pool called Siloam. It belonged to the Evangelist to commend to us the name of this pool, and he said that it means ‘Sent.’ You now recognize who was sent: for unless he had been sent, none of us would have been released from iniquity. Therefore he washed his eyes in the pool whose name means ‘Sent’: he was baptized in Christ,” etc. Bede has the same words. See the notes on Mark, chap. VII, no. 4, p. 17.].

For those eyes are blind which this mud does not touch. Those are touched by this mud who believe that Christ is both God and man. It is not enough to touch earth; it is not enough to touch spittle. But it is sufficient to touch and believe in the mud made from both. Yet if one who has touched the mud believes Christ to be both God and man, he must go to the pool of Siloam, hasten to baptism, and there be washed and regenerated. For “unless anyone has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of God” (John III, 5). Both believing and being baptized are necessary; neither is effective without the other.

Nor is it without mystery that Siloam means “Sent.” For baptism began in the Jordan, and through the apostles was sent throughout all nations for the regeneration of human beings [Note: [Col. 0529D] Ambrose, Class 2, Epistle 80, no. 4: “‘Go and wash in Siloam,’ etc. What is the reason for this? A great one, I think: for the man whom Jesus touches sees more. Observe at once both his divinity and his sanctifying power. As light, he touched and poured in light; as priest, through the figure of baptism, he fulfilled the mysteries of spiritual grace. He spat, so that you might observe that Christ’s inner parts [Col. 0530D] are light. And he truly sees whose inner self is cleansed by Christ. His saliva washes; his word washes . . . But what does it signify that he made mud and anointed the blind man’s eyes, except that you might understand that he restored to health, by applying mud, the man whom he had formed from mud, and that this flesh of our clay receives the light of eternal life through the sacrament of baptism? You too, come to Siloam—that is, to him who was sent by the Father . . . come to baptism,” etc. See also Irenaeus, book V, chap. 15; Tertullian; Ambrose himself, book III, *On the Sacraments*, chap. 2; Gregory of Nyssa, *On Baptism*; Augustine; Cyril; and other Fathers, who recognize here the sacrament of baptism.].

“So he went away, washed, and came seeing.” Therefore the neighbors, and those who had seen him before because he was a beggar, said: “Is this not the man who sat and begged?” Some said, “It is he.” Others, “Certainly not, but he resembles him.” But he said, “I am he.” They therefore said to him: “How were your eyes opened?” He answered: “The man called Jesus made mud and smeared my eyes.” For what does “he made mud” mean except “the Word was made flesh”? He touched the eyes of our mind, that we might see him and understand the truth. “And he said to me: ‘Go to the pool of Siloam and wash.’ So I went, washed, and saw.”

Consider now [Col. 0529C] how full of joy these words are, how they overflow with exultation. They said to him: “Where is he?” He replied: “I do not know.” They asked about the man; he answered about the man. Thus it is not unsuitable that he said, “I do not know,” because, although he was already a Christian, he was not yet a prophet.

They brought to the Pharisees the man who had been blind. Now it was the Sabbath when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes. Therefore those who wish to be enlightened should keep Sabbath from sin and rest from servile work. For the Church keeps such a Sabbath from the time when it came to know and see the Lord.

The Pharisees again asked him how he had gained sight. He said to them: “He put mud upon my eyes [Col. 0530A], and I washed, and I see.” Some of the Pharisees therefore said: “This man is not from God, since he does not keep the Sabbath.” For they were not yet enlightened, since they understood Sabbath observance in this manner. They had not yet touched the mud; they had not yet come to the washing. Others said: “How can a sinful man do such signs?” These were already, in some measure, approaching the light and beginning to see. And there was a division among them.

They said again to the blind man: “What do you say about him who opened your eyes?” He replied: “He is a prophet.” He spoke well indeed; but he could have spoken better, had he not been afraid. For the Lord himself also showed himself to be a prophet, saying: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country” (Matt. XIII, 57).

Therefore the Jews did not believe concerning [Col. 0530B] him that he had been blind and had received sight, until they summoned his parents and questioned them, saying: “Is this your son, whom you say was born blind? How then does he now see?” His parents answered and said: “We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind. But how he now sees, we do not know; and who opened his eyes, we do not know. Ask him: he is of age; let him speak for himself.”

The Evangelist explains why they said this: “His parents said these things because they feared the Jews. For the Jews had already conspired that, if anyone confessed him to be the Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue.” Therefore his parents said: “He is of age; ask him.”

They therefore called again the man who had been blind [Col. 0530C] and said to him: “Give glory to God.” What does “Give glory to God” mean? Deny that this man is Christ [Note: [Col. 0530D] Gregory, book II on the Books of Kings, chap. II: “What does it mean to say, ‘Give glory to God,’ except that you should not attribute the praise for your healing to this man, because he is not God? And since he is declared to be a sinner, not only is he denied to be God, but also to be a righteous man.” Chrysostom, Homily 58: “Give glory to God, that is, confess that he has done nothing.”]; deny that you are a Christian. [Page 255] But this is not giving glory to God; it is taking it away. “We know that this man is a sinner.”

The man therefore said: “Whether he is a sinner, I do not know. One thing I know: whereas I was blind, now I see.” “I,” he says, “do not know his sins; I do not accuse him of sins. I know one thing; that I say and proclaim: I was blind, and now, at his command, I see.”

They said to him: “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?” But he, indignant because they compelled him so often to repeat the same words, said: “I told you already, and you heard. Why [Col. 0531A] do you want to hear it again? What good is it to repeat the same thing so many times? Do you also wish to become his disciples?” If I knew that you too wished to become his disciples, as I am, I would not refuse to say the same things again and again, and many more times.

They cursed him and said: “You may be that man’s disciple; but we are disciples of Moses.” Blessed are those upon whom such a curse falls. Would that this curse might come upon us also [Note: [Col. 0531C] Ambrose, cited work: “Their curse is a blessing. ‘You,’ they say, ‘be his disciple.’ Then they benefit others when they think they are doing harm.”].

It follows: “We know that God spoke to Moses; but we do not know where this man is from.” The man answered and said to them: “This is indeed marvelous: you do not know where he is from, and yet he opened my eyes. Where then is your wisdom? Where is the teaching you proclaim? Why do you read the law if you do not understand it? You say that this man is a sinner. It is unheard of [Col. 0531B] and unprecedented for sinners to perform such deeds. For we know that God does not hear sinners; but if anyone worships God and does his will, God hears him.”

Being still untaught and newly enlightened, he says something ignorantly contrary to the Church’s doctrine [Note: [Col. 0531D] Augustine, book II, *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, chap. 8, no. 17: “What is written in the Gospel, ‘God does not hear sinners,’ etc., was not said by the Lord, but by the man whose bodily eyes had indeed already been restored, though the eyes of his heart had not yet been opened; hence he still thought the Lord a prophet . . . Yet the Lord himself, when the Pharisee and the tax collector prayed in one temple, declares the tax collector, confessing his sins, more justified than the Pharisee, who boasted of his merits.” And Tractate 44 on John, no. 13: “He still speaks as one anointed. For God does hear sinners. For if God did not hear sinners, that tax collector would pray in vain,” etc. See Sermon 135, no. 6, and Sermon 136, no. 2. Toletus, note 9, says that there is a serious difficulty in understanding the statement, “God does not hear sinners.” On this subject see Jansen, *Concordia*, chap. 78, and the commentators. See St. Thomas, II–II, q. 83, art. 16; Suarez, vol. II, *On Religion*, book I, chap. 25; and other theologians [Col. 0532C].].

For it is not true that God does not hear sinners. “From the beginning of time it has not been heard that anyone opened the eyes of one born blind. Unless this man were from God, he could do nothing.” They answered and said to him: “You were born wholly in sins, and do you teach us?” Because he had been born blind, they thought him more sinful than others. It may be understood that Christ’s disciples themselves also held this opinion, since in questioning the Lord they said: “Who sinned, this man or his parents, that he should be born blind?” [Col. 0531C]

“And they cast him out.” It greatly benefited him that they cast him out; for cast out, he deserved to see and know Jesus. For Jews cannot see Jesus unless they first leave the synagogue.

Jesus heard that they had cast him out; and when he found him, he said: “Do you believe in the Son of God?” He answered and said: “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?” He does not doubt the essence; he asks about the person. For he did not yet know personally the one whom he nevertheless believed to be the Son of God. Jesus said to him: “You have both seen him, and he is the one speaking with you.” Then he said: “I believe, Lord”; and falling down, he worshiped [Col. 0532A] him.

Jesus said to him: “For judgment I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.” By these words he showed what the enlightenment of that blind man signified. “For judgment,” he said, “I have come into this world.” For what judgment? For justification and condemnation. The unlearned are justified; the wise are condemned. These are enlightened; those are blinded. These follow the light, while those are plunged into darkness [Note: [Col. 0532C] Chrysostom, Homily 59, no. 1: “‘For judgment’ means for greater punishment, showing that those who condemned him were condemned, and that those who pronounced him a sinner were themselves liable to sin.” Jerome, on Isaiah, chap. VI: “It is not God’s cruelty but mercy that one nation should perish so that all might be saved; that a part of the Jews should not see so that the whole world might receive light. Hence the Lord himself in the Gospel turns the mystery of the man blind from birth, who received sight, toward a tropological meaning, and says: ‘For judgment I came into the world,’” etc. Augustine, Tractate 44: “What does ‘that those who do not see may see’ mean? Those who confess that they do not see and seek the physician, so that they may see. What does ‘that those who see may become blind’ mean? Those who think they see and do not seek the physician, that they may remain in their blindness. Therefore he called this distinction judgment.”].

Some Pharisees who were with him heard this, and said to him: “Are we also blind?” They mean: If those who see become blind, do you say that we too, because we see, are blind? Jesus said to them: “If you were blind, you would not have sin. But now you say, ‘We see’; your sin remains.” Therefore, he says, [Col. 0532B] your sin remains, because while you think that you see, you do not seek to see. For if you considered yourselves blind—that is, if you understood yourselves to be blind—you would not have sin, because you would seek the light.

XXVIII. [CHAP. X.] “Amen, amen, I say to you: he who does not enter by the door into the sheepfold, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber.” What this door is, he himself [Page 256] explains later, saying: “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he shall be saved.” Therefore he is the door, he is the doorkeeper, and he is also the shepherd of the sheep. He is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6). Through him we enter, because he is the way and the door. He brings us in, because he is truth. He feeds us, because he is life.

Therefore, if entering through the door means entering through Christ, and Christ is righteousness and truth [Col. 0532C], one who does not enter through righteousness and truth does not enter through Christ. Thus one who does not enter through righteousness and truth does not enter through the door. But one does not enter through righteousness and truth if one is not elected and ordained according to the canons and decrees of the pontiffs. Therefore all Simonists [Note: [Col. 0532D] He attacks Simonists, as he had done above on Luke, p. 196, p. 265, and on Matthew, no. 86, p. 99, etc. See the Preface.] and intruders are not shepherds, but thieves and robbers. Why? Because they do not enter through the door; because they do not enter through Christ; because they do not enter through righteousness and truth; because they do not enter through the Word of God and according to the ordinances of the canons.

What then do they accomplish in the Church? Let the Lord himself say: “The thief,” he says, “comes only [Col. 0533A] to steal, kill, and destroy.” Therefore whatever they do in the Church is vain and useless [Note: [Col. 0533C] These words, together with others that follow, seem to indicate that our Author held the opinion that the ordinations of Simonists and intruders were invalid. We can understand that this opinion prevailed in that century, namely the eleventh, from Peter Damian, who, in order to persuade others of the contrary, wrote a treatise (in the recension of the Constitutions of Clement VI) entitled *Gratissimus*. In its preface he says: “I do not think that Your Holiness can be unaware how much, during the past three years, the question concerning those gratuitously consecrated by Simonists has been debated in three Roman councils; nor how perplexing and confused uncertainty is daily agitated on both sides—especially since, as the ambiguity of the controversy increased, matters proceeded so far that some bishops ordained by them are known to have ordained clergy anew.”

He further indicates that the matter was extremely uncertain: “When it came back to my mind that the venerable holy Pope Leo IX, in his last synod, earnestly entreated all bishops by divine adjuration to implore God’s mercy together, that he might reveal to those who wavered what ought to be decided in this scrupulous matter.” John Morin argues at length, in Exercise 5 of *On the Sacrament of Orders* and in the preface to the book *Auxiliaries*, that the question was not altogether settled even in the following century, when the distinguished doctors of the scholastics—Peter Lombard, Peter of Poitiers, Hugh of Saint Victor, Robert Pullus, and others—lived.

Witasse, *On the Sacrament of Orders*, part 1, question 4, specifically section 3, *On Simonists*, and section 4, *On Intruders and Usurpers*, shows that sound and orthodox teaching concerning the validity of these ordinations always persisted in the Church. So also Tournely, *On Orders*, question 5, article 1 (both of whom Chardon cites, *On Orders*, chap. 6); Drouet, *On Sacramental Matters*, book VIII, chap. 4; Chardon himself; and theologians generally. Yet Chardon himself admits that this true Catholic doctrine [Col. 0534C] became somewhat obscured from the eighth century onward, and the testimony of some authors of later ages appears to confirm this. Add the Orders published by Martene from manuscripts nine hundred years old, in which the same point is indicated, vol. II, old edition, pp. 345, 360, etc.

As to why our Author distinguishes the case of Simonists and intruders from that of others who had been in the Catholic Church but separated themselves from it through quarrels, disputes, and schisms, he seems to have had no other reason than this: the latter had received a true ordination in the Catholic Church, without any impediment; the former had not. Rather, they—especially the Simonists—had received the curse which Simon Magus received from Simon Peter. Hence also his statement about Simonists and intruders: “They cannot give because they do not possess.” This seems to have been taken [Col. 0534D] from the saying under the name of St. Leo, cited by Gratian, Part II, Cause 1, Question 1, chapter 1: “Grace, if it is not given or received freely, is not grace. But Simonists do not receive freely; therefore they do not receive grace, which works especially in ecclesiastical orders. But if they do not receive it, they do not possess it; and if they do not possess it, they can give it to no one, whether freely or not freely.”].

But what shall we say of those who indeed enter through the door, but afterwards leave the Church through heresies, quarrels, disputes, and schisms? Whether they are in the Church or outside the Church, they can still administer the Church’s sacraments—though to their own peril. But the others, because they do not possess them, cannot give them. For what do they possess except the curse which Simon Magus received from Simon Peter? If such persons return to the Church, they are either entirely suspended from their offices, or, if they remain in them, nothing is repeated in them. For no sacrament should be subjected to injury.

Some of the saints nevertheless say that those baptized by heretics ought to be confirmed by Catholics, because heretics cannot give the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0534D] It is established that certain heretics were reconciled by almost the same rites by which the sacrament of confirmation was conferred; of this St. Gregory speaks, book II, indiction 4, letters 6 and 7. The well-known words of St. Leo to Nicetas are: “Those who have received baptism from heretics, if they had not previously been baptized, are to be confirmed solely by the invocation of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands, because they received only the form of baptism without the power of sanctification.” Earlier still are the words of Siricius to Himerius, where he forbids Arians to be baptized: “These,” he says, “together with Novatians and other heretics, as has been established in synod, we admit into communion with Catholics through the invocation alone of the sevenfold Spirit, by the laying on of the bishop’s hand [Col. 0535C]; and this both East and West observe [Col. 0535D].”

From this arose a theological question concerning the nature of this anointing or laying on of hands. Peter de Marca, on the Council of Clermont, and Sirmond, *Antirrheticus* 2, seem to regard it as confirmation. Those previously cited deny this, especially Chardon, who nevertheless maintains in *On Confirmation*, chap. 5, that the sacrament of Confirmation was absent solely through a defect of intention. Many argue, from their Euchologion—although Goar tries to explain the matter differently—and from other monuments of those times, that in later ages heretics in the East were reconciled by the sacrament of Confirmation. See the theologians and Holstenius, Dissertation 2, *On the Form of the Sacrament of Confirmation among the Greeks*.].

But whoever enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep. It has been said what the door is and what it is to enter through the door. To this shepherd the doorkeeper opens, and the sheep hear his voice. For Christ is both door and doorkeeper: door for the good; doorkeeper for bad and good alike. For only the good enter through this door. But because this doorkeeper both repels the wicked and receives the good, he is doorkeeper for bad and good alike.

But let subjects hear what is said: “And the sheep hear his voice.” Therefore those who do not hear the voice of the shepherd entering by the door are not sheep. And this shepherd, who enters by the door, calls his own sheep by name [Page 257] and leads them out. By these words he most plainly shows that every bishop ought to have compassion and humanity [Col. 0533C] toward those subject to him.

“And when he has sent forth his own sheep [Col. 0534A], he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, because they know his voice.” The shepherd sends out his own sheep when he teaches them to hasten toward the pastures of life by the way of God’s commandments. He goes before them if he does what he preaches. And the sheep follow him, according to the Apostle’s words: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (II Cor. IV, 16). They follow because they know his voice: because they recognize his words and know that his teaching is true and Catholic.

But they do not follow a stranger; rather, they flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers. For every heretic, and whoever is not in the Church, is a stranger. Therefore those who follow such people and delight in their voice and teaching are not among the sheep of the Church. Hence the Apostle says [Col. 0534B]: “Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings” (Heb. XIII, 9). Jesus spoke this proverb to them, but they did not understand what he was saying to them.

XXIX. Therefore Jesus said to them again: “Amen, amen, I say to you: I am the door of the sheep.” This has been explained above. “All, as many as came, are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not hear them.” Observe that he says, “came.” He did not say, “were sent.” But concerning himself he said above: “I have not come of myself, but my Father sent me” (John VIII, 42). The prophet Isaiah also (Isa. VI, 8), when the Lord said, “Whom shall I send, and who will go?” answered: “Behold, here I am; send me.”

Therefore those who came of themselves and were not sent by God were thieves and robbers. Hence the Lord says [Col. 0534C]: “I have come in the name of my Father, and you have not received [Col. 0535A] me. Another will come in his own name, and him you will receive” (John V, 43). For the one who comes in his own name is not sent [Note: [Col. 0535D] See St. Augustine, Tractate 45, explaining this concerning heretics, and concluding: “Hold fast to this: Christ’s sheepfold is the Catholic Church. Whoever wishes to enter the sheepfold must enter through the door. Let him preach the true Christ [Col. 0536C]. Let him not only preach the true Christ, but seek Christ’s glory, not his own,” etc. Gregory says much the same in book IX, indiction 2, letter 49, and book XI, letter 46, indiction 4. See also Jerome on Hosea, chap. VII.].

And the sheep do not hear such persons. For if they hear them, they are no longer sheep. “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he shall be saved; and he shall enter and go out and find pasture.” He who enters through me, he says, shall be saved—but only if through me he both enters and goes out. For one who is lawfully ordained enters the Church through him. And if that person perseveres in goodness, through him also he departs from this life. Such a person shall find pasture both entering and leaving: temporal pasture when entering, eternal life when leaving. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord guides me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture he has set me” (Ps. XXII, 1).

For many enter through him who do not go out through him, because they die in sin and not in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0536D] St. Gregory, Homily 14 on the Gospels, and Bede on this passage: “He enters into faith; he goes out from faith into hope, from belief into contemplation; and he finds pasture in eternal refreshment,” etc. Augustine, Tractate 48: “They are sheep by believing; they are sheep by following the shepherd . . . they are sheep by entering through the door; they are sheep by going out and finding pasture; they are sheep by enjoying eternal life.”].

It follows: “The thief comes only to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and have it more abundantly.” How can they have it more abundantly, unless, beyond this temporal life which they share in common with others, they also possess eternal life in greater abundance than all others?

XXX. I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep. [Note: [Col. 0536D] This was excerpted from the commentary and is a homily circulated under the name of Emisenus; it is assigned to the Second Sunday after Easter.]

“I,” he says, “am the good shepherd.” Hear this, shepherds, and learn from me, the one shepherd, to be good shepherds. For the good shepherd is he who lays down his life for his sheep. This is the definition of a good shepherd. Therefore he did this. Do the same yourselves, if need arises. “For no one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13).

But the hireling, and he who is not a shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees. The hireling is that bishop who, in feeding and governing the sheep, seeks only temporal and passing things: who feeds the Lord’s sheep not out of love for the heavenly homeland, but for gain and for the wage of temporal things. Such a man is indeed no shepherd in God’s sight, though men call him a shepherd. Nor does he have sheep of his own, but sheep hired for wages. For if they were his own, he would love them as his own, and would not hesitate to expose himself to dangers for them.

But he sees the wolf coming; he sees the devil and his followers threatening. For the devil’s followers are heretics and schismatics, and all deceivers. [Note: [Col. 0536D] On both kinds of these wolves, see St Gregory, Homily 14 on the Gospels, no. 2.] And he leaves the sheep and flees. He leaves them, of course, by giving no help, preaching no truth, urging no steadfastness and patience, and resisting no heresy. Hence the Lord says through Ezekiel: “You have not gone up into the breach, nor set up a wall for the house of Israel, that it might stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (Ezek. 1:15). For all these words are a kind of wall by which the sheep of the Church are defended against heretics. By these [258] the wolf is driven away, overcome, and put to flight.

But the hireling flees because he is a hireling, and the sheep are no concern of his. For he would not flee [Col. 0536B] if he were not a hireling. He would not flee if he served out of love and charity rather than for pay. “For perfect charity casts out fear” (John 4:18). And thus he flees, because the sheep are no concern of his.

“I am the good shepherd, and I know my sheep, and my own know me.” For the Lord knows who are his. [Note: [Col. 0536D] 2 Tim. 2:19: “The Lord has known,” etc.] But God’s knowing is loving. [Note: [Col. 0536D] Gregory, in the passage cited: “And I know my sheep,” that is, “I love them.”] Hence he will say to some at the judgment: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12), that is, “I do not love you.” Otherwise, how could he who knows all things be ignorant of anything?

Therefore, when he says, “I know my sheep, and my own know me,” it is as though he said: “I love my own, and I am loved by my own.” But how do I know them? Do you wish to hear how? “As the Father knows me, and I know the Father.” Thus, he says, I know—that is, I love—my own, and am loved by my own, just as I am loved by the Father and love the Father. Hence in what follows he says: “As the Father has loved me, I also love you” (John 15:9). And again: “I pray not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they too may be one in us” (John 17:20–21).

“And I lay down my life for my sheep.” By this, he says, it is proved that I love them: because I lay down my life for my sheep. For unless he had loved them, he would not have laid down his life for them. [Note: [Col. 0536D] See Gregory, in the passage cited.]

“And I have other sheep, which are not of this fold. Them also I must bring; [Col. 0537A] and they shall hear my voice, and there shall be one fold and one shepherd.” This is what the Apostle says: “He himself is our peace, who has made both one” (Eph. 2:14). For he joined two walls, one coming from circumcision and the other from uncircumcision. The Lord was speaking to the Jews, to whom he promised that he would join the Gentiles, so that from two peoples [Note: [Col. 0537D] Augustine, Tractate 47: “From these two flocks, as from two walls, he became the cornerstone.”] one house might be built and one Church constructed. Peace was therefore made between Jews and Gentiles. There is one fold and one shepherd; they hold one law, worship one God, and follow the voice of one shepherd.

“Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, that I may take it again.” What is this? Did the Father not love Jesus before he received his life, or laid it down? Certainly he loved him. But these words must be referred to Christ as man, who is deservedly loved by God because “he became obedient to him unto death” (Phil. 2:8).

Yet it may also be understood otherwise, thus: The greatness of the Father’s love toward me can be understood especially from this: that I myself, as I will, lay down my life and take it again. For this power has been granted to no one else. “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again. This commandment I received from my Father.”

For Jesus had in his power both to live as long as he wished and to die when he wished. He lived as long as he wished; he died when he wished. The Jews often wished to seize him, yet could not. And this was because he did not wish it. Therefore the Jews had only as much power over him [Col. 0537C] as he granted them. [Note: [Col. 0537D] Augustine, Tractate 47: “What does ‘I lay it down’ mean? I lay it down myself. Let not the Jews boast: they could rage, but they could not possess power. Let them rage as much as they can. If I do not will it, what will they accomplish by raging?” Likewise Chrysostom, Homily 72 on John, no. 2: “‘I have power,’ etc. So long as he wished to retain it, no one could prevail against him; but when he permitted it, then it was easy.” See also Homily 60, no. 2, where he discusses the precept or command given to Christ; Cyril discusses this at length, p. 661, interpreting it as concord with the Father. Some Latin Fathers understand it otherwise; see Petavius, *On the Incarnation*, book IX, chapter 8, and the Fathers passim. The author does not sufficiently explain which view he accepts.]

But when he says, “This commandment I received from my Father,” he says it in honor of the Father. For this gift and commandment, given to the Lord according to his humanity, belong to the whole Trinity.

A division again arose among the Jews because of these words. Many of them said: “He has a demon and is mad. Why do you listen to him?” These, indeed, were not of his sheep. Others said: “These are not the words of one who has a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?” But these were now drawing near to the fold and beginning to become his sheep.

XXXI. The feast of the Dedication took place at Jerusalem, and it was winter. And Jesus walked in the temple, in Solomon’s Portico. [Note: [Col. 0537D] Augustine, Tractate 48: “Encaenia was the feast of the dedication of the temple. For in Greek *kainon* means ‘new,’” etc.]

[Col. 0538A] The Jews called *encaenia* the feast that they celebrated for the building, or renewal, of the temple. During this feast Jesus walked in the temple, in Solomon’s Portico, showing himself to be that Wisdom praised in the books of Solomon’s Wisdom. But because it was winter, and because the Jews were frozen by the frost of envy and had no fire of charity, they desired to kill their king and lord. [Note: [Col. 0538D] Augustine, ibid.: “It was winter, and they were cold. For they were slow to approach that divine fire—if to approach is to believe . . . They had grown cold in the charity of loving and burned with the desire to do harm.” Gregory, *Morals*, book II, ch. 2: “It is pleasing to observe how sacred writings, at the beginnings of narratives, express the circumstances and boundaries of their causes. Sometimes they indicate from the setting of a place, sometimes from the position of a body, sometimes from the quality of the air, sometimes from the quality of the season, what they are about to relate concerning the coming action. . . . The event that follows is shown by the quality of the weather: thus the Evangelist, when he was about to say that none of the Jews would then believe while the Lord preached, first stated: ‘And it was winter.’ For it is written: ‘Because iniquity will abound, the charity of many will grow cold.’ Therefore he took care to state the winter season, in order to show that the cold of malice was present in his hearers’ hearts.”]

For cold and death are near one another. Therefore the Jews surrounded him [259], not in order to believe in him, but to destroy him. And they said to him: “How long do you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.” Him whom we call “king,” the Jews call “Christ.” They therefore spoke deceitfully, so that, if the Lord answered that he was Christ, they might immediately hand him over to the Roman officials to be killed, as one who had opposed Caesar. For this is why they say to Pilate: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. For everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar [Note: [Col. 0538D] Here the author has almost copied Bede’s words.]” (John 19:12).

Jesus answered them: “I speak to you, and you do not believe. The works which I do in the name of my Father bear witness to me.” Why, he says, do you question me? I speak to you, and you do not believe. But since you do not believe my words, at least believe the works. Works do not lie. Yet you believe neither my words nor my works, because you are not of my sheep. It is therefore clear that whoever refuses to believe the words of the Gospel is not among Christ’s sheep.

“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, [Col. 0538C] and no one shall snatch them from my hand.” We have already said enough above about these matters. But he proves that no one snatches them from his hand when he says: “What my Father gave me is greater than all, and no one can snatch it from my Father’s hand.” Yet lest anyone should say that it does not follow from this that they cannot be snatched from his own hand, he added: “I and the Father are one.” For if he and the Father are one, then, since no one can snatch them from the Father’s hand, no one can snatch them from the Son’s hand.

But how is either the one proved to be Father, or the other Son? Certainly from what he says: “What my Father gave me is greater than all.” For the Father’s giving was his begetting. [Note: [Col. 0538D] Jerome, on Ezekiel, ch. 18: “And he himself [Col. 0539D] says: ‘What the Father gave me is greater than all, and no one can snatch it from my Father’s hand’; from which the one power, strength, and substance of Father and Son are evident. For if no one can snatch from the Son’s hand what the Father gave, and these same things are in the Father’s hand and cannot be snatched from it, it is plainly proved that all things are common to Father and Son.” Augustine, Tractate 47: “The Father did not add something to the Son as though he had been born imperfect; rather, in begetting him perfect, he gave him all things by begetting.” See also Tractate 48, Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, book III, ch. 18; Chrysostom, Homily 61 on John; Basil, *Against Eunomius*, book I; etc.]

For he who gave was not prior to him to whom he gave, because he who begot was not prior to him whom he begot. Nor was the Father ever without the Son, because he could never be without the Word, without power and wisdom, without life and truth. All this is the Son of God. For he is “truth and life” (John 14:6). He is the Word, power, and wisdom of the Father: the Wisdom, certainly, which the Father begot, not a wisdom that made him wise. Therefore the Father is wise because he begot Wisdom. He is also true because he begot Truth. But because he was never unwise or untrue, he was never before Wisdom and Truth. For one who is wise can never be without wisdom.

Therefore they took up stones to stone him. Jesus answered them: “I have shown you many good works from my Father. For [Col. 0539B] which of those works do you stone me? Is it because I call you back to the way of truth? Or because I rescue you from the dangers of eternal death? Or perhaps because I healed your sick, gave sight to your blind, cleansed your lepers, cured your paralytics, and raised your dead?” These works deserve not stoning, but honor.

The Jews answered him: “We do not stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy; because you, being a man, make yourself God.” Foolish Jews question him as to who he is and ask him to answer plainly; then, because he answers them with the truth, they wish to kill him.

Jesus answered them: “Is it not written in your law, ‘I said: You are gods’?” Here he calls the Psalms “law,” [Note: [Col. 0539D] Augustine, Tractate 48: “The Lord called all those Scriptures ‘law’ in a general sense, although elsewhere he uses ‘law’ in a special sense, distinguishing it from the prophets, as in: ‘The law and the prophets were until John’; and ‘On these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets.’ But sometimes he divides these same Scriptures into three, when he says: ‘Everything written about me in the law, the prophets, and the psalms had to be fulfilled.’”] because they too judge, both condemning the guilty and justifying the good.

“If he called them gods, to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be broken—do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” If, he says, adopted sons are called gods, why should the natural Son not be called God? If those to whom the word of God came are called gods—and are so called because they keep God’s word—why should not the Word of God himself much more be called God? For Scripture cannot be broken, because “not one iota or one stroke shall pass from it” (Matt. 5:18) until all is fulfilled.

And when he says, “him whom the Father sanctified,” it is as though he said, “him whom the Father begot holy.” For to sanctify and to beget were the same thing. [Note: [Col. 0540D] Augustine, Tractate 48: “He sanctified him as he begot him. For by begetting, he gave him holiness, because he begot him holy.” See the same author, *On the Trinity*, book II, ch. 5; Cyril; and other Fathers in Petavius, *On the Incarnation*, book XI, ch. 6. Elias of Crete, on Nazianzen’s Fourth Oration, discusses the word “sanctify” and its various Scriptural uses.]

“If I do not do [260] the works of my Father, do not believe me.” The Father’s works are wonderful; the Son’s works also are wonderful. [Col. 0539D] The Father does what he wills; the Son likewise does whatever he wills. [Col. 0540A] It follows: “But if I do them, even if you are unwilling to believe me, believe the works, that you may know and believe that the Father is in me and I in the Father.” For the Father and Son are one, and the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son. [Note: [Col. 0540D] From this passage of John theologians derive what they call the “circumincession” of the divine persons; see Petavius, *On the Trinity*, book IV, ch. 16.]

Therefore they sought to seize him, but he went out of their hands. Let us also seek him, but not as they did. Let us seek him with faith and piety, and he will not escape from our hands. For Jesus is apprehended and held by such hands.

And he went again beyond the Jordan, to the place where John had first been baptizing, and he remained there. Many came to him and said: “John indeed performed no sign, but everything that John said about this man was true.” And many believed in him. Perhaps the Lord had gone there for this purpose: that these people might [Col. 0540B] come to him, see him, and believe in him.

XXXII. [CHAPTER XI.] There was a certain sick man, Lazarus of Bethany, from the village of Mary and Martha her sister. Mary was the one who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair; her brother Lazarus was ill. [Note: [Col. 0540D] This is the homily of Emisenus, Friday after the Fourth Sunday of Lent, p. 90; it will be judged as the others are.]

The Evangelist wrote these things in great praise of Mary, who was worthy to anoint the Lord and touch his feet. Blessed are those souls which, in the likeness of this Mary, approach the Lord with spices, ointment, and a good fragrance. This is she who speaks in the Song of Songs, saying: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song 5:11).

We read that the Lord raised three dead persons: namely, the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue in the house; the daughter of a widowed woman outside the city gate; and this Lazarus, four days dead in the tomb. Through these three dead persons, three kinds of death are signified. [Note: [Col. 0540D] These points are taken from Augustine, Tractate 40 on John, no. 3, which he had also brought forward in his discussion of Luke, ch. 7, no. 17. See p. 136.]

A person dies by thinking evil and unlawful thoughts; he dies by acting wickedly; he dies by persisting in sins. Do you contemplate doing something unlawful? Your soul is dead, but it still lies in the house and in concealment, because the sin is hidden and has not yet been made public. But if you bring the thought into effect, it is not only dead, but has already been carried outside the city gate; through sin it is separated from the Church and is near to the tomb and destruction. But one who has committed some grave sin and persevered in it for a long time is not merely dead and buried, but already stinks, because all around recoil from hearing his most shameful reputation.

Yet Jesus raises all these, if they cease from sin, repent in heart, and parents, sisters, and a widowed mother entreat for them. Hence it is written: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved. For the persistent prayer of a righteous person is very powerful” (Jas. 5:16). [Note: [Col. 0541D] The author seems to have understood James’s words so that the first part also—on confession of sins, since he cited it—concerns private, non-sacramental confession, by which a person professes himself a sinner even to lay people and implores their prayers to God. Estius, in his commentary on this passage of James, maintains that this explanation is quite probable.]

But what do the four days during which Lazarus lay dead in the tomb signify, except the four ages? For through four ages, as through four days, he lies dead and stinking in the tomb of sin who persists in the evil he began in childhood and adolescence, youth and old age. [Note: [Col. 0541D] Bede here understands four kinds, as it were, of human death: (1) from Adam’s sin; (2) from transgression [Col. 0542D] of the natural law; (3) from transgression of the written law; (4) from violation of evangelical teaching.] Infancy, because it is full of ignorance, is not counted among these ages.

Consider, therefore, how great is the kindness of our Savior, who does not disdain to raise one putrid and stinking after such persistence in evil. [Col. 0541B] Therefore his sisters sent to him, saying: “Lord, behold, he whom you love is sick.” You hear, therefore, that the Lord loves sinners who have already repented. Lazarus signifies such sinners. Of such persons the Lord himself says: “I rejoice over one sinner doing penance more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance.” [Note: [Col. 0542D] Luke 15:7: “There will be joy,” etc.]

When Jesus heard it, he said to them: “This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God may be glorified through it.” Lazarus does not die, he says, in order to remain in death, but in order to rise from the dead for the glory of God.

Jesus loved Martha and her sister Mary and Lazarus. For the Lord loves the active life and the contemplative life, [Col. 0541C] and sinners converted to repentance. [Note: [Col. 0542D] Elsewhere—that is, on Luke 10, book II, section 22, p. 162—the author had said, with many interpreters, that the active and contemplative lives are prefigured in Martha and Mary. Roughly the same Fathers recognize sinners as signified in Lazarus; besides the Augustine cited above, see Gregory, *Morals*, book XXII, ch. 12, and Homily 26 on the Gospels.] These matters will be discussed elsewhere.

Therefore, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he nevertheless remained two days in the same place. Then after this he said [261] to his disciples: “Let us go into Judea again.” The disciples said to him: “Rabbi, the Jews were just seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?” Jesus answered: “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks by day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if he walks at night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.”

What is this, he says, that you are saying? Follow me; come after me. “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). I am the day; you are the hours. “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” I chose you twelve because there are twelve hours in the day. Therefore, because you are hours, [Col. 0541D] follow the day. [Note: [Col. 0542D] See the remarks on Mark 3, no. 2, pp. 8–9.] For this is the proper function of hours. But if anyone follows this day, if anyone walks in him, if anyone believes in me, he will not stumble. Why? Because he sees the light of this world. I am the light of the world. But if he walks at night, if he follows error and the prince of darkness—for this is to walk at night—he will stumble and fall. Why? Because the light is not in him, because the darkness of error has blinded his eyes.

After saying these things, he said to them: “Our friend Lazarus sleeps, but I am going to awaken him from sleep.” Therefore his disciples said: “Lord, if he sleeps, he will be well.” Sleep is usually a sign of recovery for the sick. But, the Evangelist says, Jesus had spoken of his death, whereas they thought he spoke of the sleep of slumber. It was as though he said: Lazarus sleeps to me, but is dead to others. I can raise him from death more easily than any person can awaken him from sleep. Therefore I am going to awaken him from sleep.

Then Jesus said to them plainly: “Lazarus [Col. 0542B] is dead, and I rejoice for your sakes, that you may believe, because I was not there. But let us go to him.” I rejoice, he says, because I was not there. For if Jesus had been there, Lazarus would not have died. Where life is, death cannot be. “I,” says the Lord, “am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25). Therefore I rejoice—but for your sakes. Why for your sakes? That you may believe; that your faith may be strengthened by his resurrection, whose death I announce to you while absent.

Then Thomas, who is called Didymus, said to his fellow disciples: “Let us also go and die with him.” Thomas said this because he knew that the Jews were so inflamed with hatred against Jesus and his disciples that he expected nothing but death and punishment from them.

Jesus therefore came and found that Lazarus had already been [Col. 0542C] four days in the tomb. What the four days signify we have already said above. Bethany was near Jerusalem, about twelve stadia away. Therefore it was not very difficult for Jews to come from there to Bethany to console Martha and Mary. Of them it is added: “Many had come to Martha and Mary, to console them over their brother.”

When Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went to meet him. But Mary remained sitting in the house. Why Martha is everywhere anxious and Mary quiet is understood by those who see in them the glorification of the active and contemplative life. Martha therefore said to Jesus: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.” For how could he die if Life had been present to him? For the Lord says of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). “But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you.” Jesus said to her: “Your brother will rise again.” But she said: “I know that he will rise in the resurrection on the last day. I am certain about that resurrection. I do not doubt that you can accomplish this; but I am not certain whether you will.”

Jesus said to her: “I am the resurrection and the life. Through me all who live and rise again live and rise again. Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, shall live.” Whoever, therefore, does not believe will not live. Yet he will live in punishments; but such life ought rather to be called death than life. For true life does not have the bitterness of death.

Likewise, the one who lives and believes in him—for believing is living, because faith is the life of the soul [Note: [Col. 0543C] Augustine, Tractate 49, no. 15, copied by Bede: “Whence is death in the soul? Because faith is not there. Whence is death in the body? Because the soul is not there. Therefore faith is the life of your soul. ‘He who believes in me,’ he says, ‘even if he has died in the flesh, shall live in the soul, until the flesh too rises again, never afterward to die. That is: he who believes in me, though he die, shall live. And everyone who lives in the flesh and believes in me, though he die for a time because of bodily death, shall not die eternally, because of the life of the spirit and the immortality of the resurrection.’” Likewise Tractate 22, no. 6.]—even though he dies. “Do you believe this?” She said to him: “Certainly, Lord. I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who came into this world.”

After saying this, she went and privately called her sister Mary, [Col. 0543B] saying: “The Master is here and calls you.” When she heard it, she rose quickly and came to him. For Jesus had not yet entered the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him. Therefore the Jews who were with her in the house and comforting her, when they saw Mary rise quickly and go out, followed her, saying that she was going to the tomb to weep there.

When Mary came to where Jesus was, seeing him, she fell at his feet and said to him: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.” Both sisters say the same thing, understand the same thing, and believe Christ to be true life, with whom present and willing [262] no one dies.

Jesus therefore, seeing her weeping and the Jews who came with her weeping, groaned in spirit and troubled himself. He was not troubled, therefore, by anything else, [Col. 0543C] but troubled himself, and by this very act signified something great to us. [Note: [Col. 0543D] Augustine, in the passage cited: “I do not know what he suggested to us by groaning in spirit and troubling himself. For who could trouble him except he himself? . . . Christ’s soul and flesh are one person with the Word of God—one Christ. Therefore, where the supreme power is, weakness is governed at the nod of the will: hence, ‘he troubled himself.’ I have spoken of power; attend to the signification. Great is the offender whom the fourth day of death and that burial signify. What, then, does Christ’s troubling himself mean, except to signify how you too ought to be troubled when you are burdened and oppressed by so great a weight of sin?” These same [Col. 0544D] words are employed here by Bede.]

For this groaning and this disturbance teach us what we too ought to do in such a matter, when we pray to God either for ourselves or for others who are shamefully living and stinking in sins. “For we,” says the Apostle, “do not know what we should pray for; but the Holy Spirit prays for us with unutterable groanings” (Rom. 8:26). Hence also the Psalmist says: “A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. 50:19).

And Jesus said: “Where have you laid him?” Thus God said also to the first man: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3:9). This was as though he said: Consider now from how great a glory into how great a misery you have fallen. And those whom Lazarus signifies are laid in such a way. But by whom are they laid, except by women? For it was through women’s counsel that every human being came to die and to be laid in a tomb.

And Jesus wept. Therefore let us also weep for all whom we perceive lying in the stench of vices, in case the Lord may deign to raise them through our tears. The Jews therefore said: “See how he loved him.” But some of them said: “Could not this man, who opened the eyes of the blind, also have made it so that this man should not die?”

Jesus therefore, again groaning within himself, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone [Col. 0544B] lay upon it. Jesus said: “Take away the stone.” For those who are pressed down and shut in by a stone cannot rise. This stone is the letter of the law, because the law was written and given on stone. “For the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). Let the stone therefore be taken away; let the letter that kills be removed, and let the spirit that gives life draw near. [Note: [Col. 0544D] This too, it seems, is taken by the author from Augustine in the passage cited, or from Bede: “The dead man under the stone is the guilty person under the law; for you know that the law given to the Jews was written on stone. Yet all guilty people are under the law; those who live rightly are with the law. The law is not laid down for the righteous person. What, therefore, does ‘Take away the stone’ mean? Preach grace. For the Apostle Paul calls himself a minister of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the spirit. ‘For the letter,’ he says, ‘kills, but the spirit gives life.’ The killing letter is like a crushing stone. ‘Take away,’ he says, ‘the stone; remove the burden of the law; preach grace.”]

Martha, the sister of him who was dead, said to him: “Lord, by now he stinks, for it is the fourth day.” What the stench and the four days signify, we have said above. Jesus said to her: “Did I not tell you that, if you believe, you will see the glory of God?” Therefore they took away the stone.

Then Jesus, lifting his eyes upward, said: “Father, I thank you because you have heard me. But I knew that you always hear me.” For Jesus, according to that aspect [Col. 0544C] in which he is man, groans, is troubled, weeps, prays, is heard, and gives thanks. [Note: [Col. 0544D] Chrysostom, Homily 63, no. 1: “He displays human nature, for he weeps and is troubled. Human feeling commonly arouses grief; then, correcting that feeling—for this is signified by ‘he groaned in spirit’—he restrained the disturbance.” See Cyril, pp. 685–686.]

Why he said these things, prayed, and gave thanks, he immediately gave as the reason, saying: “I said it because of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me.” Hence he says elsewhere: “I have not come of myself, but my Father sent me” (John 8:42).

When he had said this, he cried out with a loud voice: “Lazarus, come forth!” One oppressed by a deep sleep must be called with a loud voice. For one is weighed down by a deep sleep who, buried in sin, is not awakened in childhood, adolescence, youth, or old age. [Col. 0545A] For those four days signify this: Lazarus, already stinking, lay in the tomb.

And immediately he who had been dead came forth, bound feet and hands with strips of cloth, and his face was bound with a cloth. No occasion for despair is given when Lazarus, already stinking and four days dead, rises from the dead. And it is indeed very wonderful not only that the dead man rose, but also that, bound hand and foot, he came forth. Perhaps the meaning is this: that we may understand that “the sinner, at whatever hour he turns and groans, shall live and shall not die.” [Note: [Col. 0545C] Ezek. 18:21: “But if the wicked man repents of all his sins that he has committed, keeps all my commandments, and performs [Col. 0545D] judgment and righteousness, he shall surely live and shall not die.”]

Yet he still appears bound until he is loosed by bishops and reconciled through the sacraments of the Church. [Note: [Col. 0545D] Augustine, Tractate 49: “What does ‘Loose him and let him go’ mean? ‘Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.’” Bede copies these words of Augustine and adds: “For he who raised the dead man could have loosed the bands; but because of the unity of God’s holy Church and indivisible charity, it is said to the ministers, that is, Christ’s disciples: ‘Loose him,’ because sins are not loosed apart from the unity of the Catholic Church’s faith and the charity of ecclesiastical holiness.”]

For such a person, though he appears outside, is nevertheless not bound within, because, released from the bonds of sins, he is now bound to God through repentance. Hence Lazarus, as though he were not bound at all, [263] came freely out of the tomb. Yet the Lord ordered him to be loosed, so that we too might show those to be loosed who, having heard the voice of the Gospel, have deserved to be raised in soul through repentance.

Therefore many of the Jews who had come to Mary and Martha and had seen what Jesus did believed in him. But some of them went away to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done. Whether they said this in proclaiming his glory or in accusing him may be doubted. [Note: [Col. 0545D] Augustine also doubted this, writing in Tractate 49: “But some of them, whether of the Jews who had assembled or of those who had believed, went away to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done—either announcing it so that they too might believe, or rather betraying him so that they might rage.”]

XXXIII. Therefore the chief priests and Pharisees assembled a council and said, “What are we doing? For this man performs many signs.” [Note: [Col. 0545D] This is in the homily attributed to Eusebius of Emesa for the Friday after the Sunday of Easter. More correctly, it should be called Saint Bruno’s.]

The chief priests and Pharisees had heard [Col. 0545C] that our Savior had raised Lazarus after four days. Alarmed by the greatness of this miracle, they consulted together and said, “What are we doing? Let us kill Jesus.” Why? “Because he performs many signs.” “If we let him go on in this way, all will believe in him,” seeing the signs and mighty works done through him. “And if they do so, the Romans will come and take away our place and nation.”

For they feared that the people might appoint him king and thus stir up against themselves the army of the Romans, to whose rule the Jews, like the other nations, were subject. But, as [Col. 0546A] the Psalmist says, “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Ps. 13:5). For if they had believed in Christ, if they had not killed Jesus, they would have lost neither their place nor their nation. [Note: [Col. 0546C] Augustine, Tractate 50: “They feared to lose temporal things and did not consider eternal life; and so they lost both.” The same, more fully, is found in [Col. 0546D] Saint Augustine on Psalm 52 and Psalm 13, and likewise in John Chrysostom, Homily 65, no. 1.] But because they did not fear to kill Christ, they lost both their place and their nation.

But one of them, Caiaphas, being high priest that year, said to them, “You know nothing at all, nor do you consider that it is expedient for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish.” But this, says the Evangelist, he did not say of himself; rather, because he was high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus was to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but that he might gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad.

“You,” he says, “know nothing, nor do you consider what is necessary. But I know and have recognized [Col. 0546B] that one man must die for the people, and the whole nation must not perish.” Yet he did not say this from himself, but from the Holy Spirit, who directed his words within him to a meaning other than that which he himself understood. Caiaphas thought that he was saying something else and interpreted his own words differently. For his entire intention was that the Jews should kill Christ, lest they themselves be killed by the Romans. Yet he prophesied [Note: [Col. 0546D] Chrysostom, in the passage cited: “Do you see how great is the power of the high-priesthood? Because the office of high priest was powerful, although he was unworthy, he prophesied, not knowing what he was saying. Many others likewise foretold things to come, though unworthy,” etc. Augustine, Tractate 50: “Here we are taught that even wicked persons may foretell the future by the spirit of prophecy; yet the Evangelist attributes this to a divine mystery because he was high priest, that is, chief priest.” See the same author, *Questions on the Book of Judges*, question 49; Book II, chapter 70 of *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*; Book II to Simplicianus, question 1; *On the Trinity*, chapter 7; etc.; Jerome on Jonah chapter 1; Ambrose, sermons 14 and 15 on Psalm 118, Epistle 50, no. 5; Gregory, Homily 10 on Ezekiel; etc.] that Jesus was to die for the nation of the Jews, and not merely for that nation, but in order to gather into one faith and Church the children of God scattered among all nations, so that there might be one flock and one shepherd.

From that day, therefore, they plotted to kill him. As though they had received useful advice, from the time Caiaphas had spoken these words the entire multitude of Pharisees considered how they might kill Christ. [Col. 0546C] Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went away into the country near the wilderness, to a city called Ephraim, and remained there with his disciples.

Jesus did not do this from fear: he was secure everywhere; he held even his enemies in his power; and he could neither be seen, seized, nor killed unless he willed it. Why, then? To teach us, to make us prudent, so that we too may yield to the fury and anger of wicked people if we see that by our presence and conversation they are perhaps not corrected, but made worse. [Note: [Col. 0546D] Augustine, Tractate 49: “Not because his power had failed him—for surely, had he willed to associate openly with the Jews, they could have done nothing to him—but he was setting before his disciples, in the weakness of human life, an example [Col. 0547D] showing that it is not sinful if his faithful ones, who are his members, withdraw themselves from the eyes of their persecutors and avoid the rage of the wicked by hiding rather than inflame it further by offering themselves.”]

Now [Col. 0547A] the Passover of the Jews was near, and many went up from the countryside to Jerusalem before the Passover in order to purify themselves. This Passover the wretched Jews made bloody. At it they killed their King and Lord. At it many gathered in Jerusalem from every quarter. And those who had come to purify themselves, after killing Christ the Lord, returned to their homes far worse than they had been.

They were therefore seeking Jesus and, standing in the Temple, said among themselves, “What do you think? Surely he will not come to the feast?” They were seeking Jesus, he says, and they sought him in order to kill him. They stood in the Temple, not praying, but discussing among themselves the Savior’s death. They wondered that he had not come to the feast, since he was accustomed to teach them on feast days. And they feared that they had lost him—264 him whom they sought to kill. [Note: [Col. 0547D] The same, Tractate 30: “They were therefore seeking Jesus, but wrongly. Blessed are those who seek Jesus rightly. They sought Jesus so that neither they nor we might have him; but we received him as he departed from them. Those who seek are reproved; those who seek are praised: for the intention of the seeker finds either praise or condemnation.”]

[Col. 0547B] The chief priests and Pharisees had given an order that, if anyone learned where he was, he should report it, so that they might seize him. Those who seek Jesus in this way cannot know where he is, nor do they find him. If you wish to know and find Jesus, Jews, come to the Church; come to us, and we shall point him out to you—not by betraying him, but by believing; not that you may kill him, but that you may believe in him with us.

XXXIV. [CHAPTER XII.] Therefore Jesus came to Bethany six days before the Passover, where Lazarus had been dead, whom Jesus raised. They made him a supper there, and Martha served.

It would be strange if the Evangelist had wished to say all this so carefully without some significance; for Bethany is interpreted “house of obedience.” [Note: [Col. 0547D] Jerome on Matthew chapter 21: “He left the unbelievers and, departing from the city of those who contradicted him, went to Bethany, which is interpreted ‘house of obedience.’”] Be Bethany, therefore: be obedient to God, [Col. 0547C] so that, when the Lord comes to you, he may deign to lodge in the house of your heart. Prepare him a supper. Believe in him. Keep his commandments. The Lord delights in such a supper. Thus he himself says: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone opens to me, I shall enter and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. 3:20).

Do not seek these things outside yourself. For you yourself can be Bethany, Martha, Lazarus, and Mary. If you serve well, give alms, clothe the naked, visit the sick, and do other similar things, you will be Martha. For all these belong to the active life, signified by Martha.

Do you wish to be Lazarus? Flee death; come to life; repent; and you shall be raised and numbered among Christ’s guests. For this reason it is said here that Lazarus was one of those reclining with him. “For the sinner, in whatever hour he is converted and groans, shall live life and shall not die” (Ezek. 18:21).

[Col. 0548A] But if this perhaps does not suffice you, and, wishing to ascend higher, you desire to be Mary, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor; despising all worldly things, strive to devote yourself solely to reading, prayer, and divine contemplation. “For Mary has chosen that part which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42).

It follows: “Mary therefore took a pound of precious ointment of genuine nard, anointed Jesus’ feet, and wiped his feet with her hair; and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.” This ointment signifies faith. [Note: [Col. 0548D] See the remarks on Matthew chapter 26, no. 104. Bede here: “This ointment of genuine nard—that is, faithful nard … For without faith it is impossible to please God.”] Hence it is rightly called *pisticum* (“genuine”), because *pistis* means “faith.” Jesus delights in no ointment more than this. Without this ointment one may neither approach nor touch him. “For without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6).

[Col. 0548B] The house is filled with this ointment. The whole Church is fragrant with it. Therefore unbelievers stink before the Lord, because they do not bear this ointment. But because she anoints his feet and wipes them with her hair, she understands him to be beginning and end, God and man. For she joins the head, as it were, to the feet—she who believes that he is God and man. Hence this woman is said to have anointed not only the feet but also the head of our Savior. [Note: [Col. 0548D] See Bernard, Sermon 90 on various subjects: “The head of Christ is God: therefore the divinity in Christ is touched whenever we recall his benefits in praise of him; just as it is necessary to consider not so much the divinity as the humanity … For in assuming flesh he is known to have received those two feet for this purpose, namely mercy and judgment, so that the sinner, who had no access to the head—that is, to the divinity—might approach the feet, that is, the humanity.”]

Then one of his disciples, Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, who was about to betray him, said, “Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?” But lest it be thought that he said this from an affection of piety and a zeal for mercy, the Evangelist added: “He said this not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief and, having the money-box, carried what was put into it.”

Therefore let no one reproach us if we tolerate wicked people and do not hastily separate them from communion with the Church, since our Savior himself endured Judas, whom he knew to be not only a traitor but also a thief and a sacrilegious man.

Jesus therefore said, “Leave her, that she may keep it for the day of my burial.” This is as if he said: What is taking place is a mystery, in which my death and burial are signified as soon to occur. Thus another Evangelist says, “She has anticipated anointing my body for burial. For you will always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me” (Mark 14:7–8).

What, then, is meant by his statement elsewhere: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the end of the age” (Matt. 28:20)? For if he is with them every day, how will they not always have him? The solution is easy if we remember the two natures in Christ. For when he says, “You will not always have me,” [Col. 0548D] we must understand it of the presence of his flesh, [Col. 0549A] which ascended to heaven on the fortieth day after the resurrection. [Note: [Col. 0549D] See Chrysostom, Homily 50 on Matthew, no. 4.]

A great crowd of Jews learned—265 that he was there, and they came, not only because of Jesus, but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead. They were led not by love but by curiosity; and, as human desire is, they wanted to see and hear something new. But the chief priests plotted to kill Lazarus also, because many Jews were leaving on account of him and believing in Jesus. Foolish Jews: they wished to kill one whom the Lord had recently raised, as though he could not raise him again.

XXXV. On the next day, when the great crowd that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him. [Col. 0549B] Palm branches signified the victory which the Lord, triumphing over the enemy, was about to win in those days. For in Scripture the palm is very often used for victory. [Note: [Col. 0549D] Bede on this passage: “The branches of palms are praises signifying victory, because the Lord was about to overcome death by dying and, by the trophy of the cross, triumph over the devil, the prince of death.”]

And they cried, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.” *Hosanna* is an interjection and means nothing other than an expression of the people’s rejoicing and praise of God. [Note: [Col. 0549D] See the remarks on Matthew chapter 21, no. 85, p. 99. See also Bede on Mark chapter 11.]

Now the Lord came in the name of the Lord, as he himself says: “I came in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and you will receive him” (John 5:42). Jesus found a young donkey and sat upon it, as it is written: “Do not fear, daughter of Zion. Behold, your King comes, sitting upon a colt of a donkey.” We have explained this in Matthew. [Note: [Col. 0549D] See the indicated passage.]

For concerning this donkey [Col. 0549C] and colt the patriarch Jacob speaks, saying: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hand shall be upon the necks of your enemies. Judah is a lion’s cub. You have gone up to the prey, my son. You lay down as a lion, and like a lioness. Who shall rouse him?” (Gen. 49:8). And shortly afterward: “Binding his colt to the vine, and my donkey to the vine-stock, O my son” (ibid., 2).

For this donkey is the Synagogue, which is elsewhere called the vine; but the colt is the untamed and wanton people of the Gentiles. [Note: [Col. 0549D] See Matthew, p. 98.] The vine is Christ, who says, “I am the true vine” (John 15:1). He therefore bound his colt to the vine because he joined the Gentile people to the Synagogue, so that there might be one flock and one shepherd. But because he had first joined the Synagogue to himself in some respect, he bound the donkey also [Col. 0549D] to the vine. For he preached to the Synagogue in person, and preached to us through the Synagogue; and by preaching he bound us to the Synagogue and to himself.

It follows: “At first his disciples did not understand these things; but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written concerning him and that they had done these things to him.” What these things signified, [Col. 0550A] he says, his disciples did not understand at first; but when he was glorified—that is, after he ascended into heaven, after he opened their understanding that they might understand the Scriptures—they then remembered that these things had been written of him and had been done to him, in no other manner than that in which they had previously been foretold concerning him by the prophet.

Therefore the crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus from the tomb and raised him from the dead bore witness. For this reason the crowd also came out to meet him, because they had heard that he had done this sign. Thus those whom words did not move were drawn by miracles.

The Pharisees therefore said among and to themselves, “You see that we gain nothing. Behold, the whole world is going after him.” “We fail,” they say, “and make no progress. The whole world is going after him, whose [Col. 0550B] name we had intended to erase. What are these voices resounding in his glory? What is ‘Hosanna to the son of David’? What does the people mean by saying, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’? It is near at hand that he will be made king by all the people, and that, when the Romans come, this place will be utterly destroyed.”

Now there were certain Gentiles among those who had gone up to worship at the feast. Of such a kind was the centurion of whom the Lord himself said, “Amen, I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel” (Matt. 8:10). These approached Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee, and asked him, saying, “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.” Both Jews and Gentiles seek Jesus: the Jews to destroy him; the Gentiles to believe. Philip came and told Andrew; Andrew in turn and Philip told Jesus.
