[Col. 0550C] But Jesus answered them, saying, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” “Now,” he says, “the Son of Man will be killed; now he will be reckoned among the wicked; now the Sun of righteousness will be darkened. But after these things the hour has come for him to be glorified and to be worshipped not only by these people, but by all nations.” This took place after Christ’s resurrection, when the apostles preached everywhere and made Christ’s name known through signs and miracles.

XXXVI. “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” This is that grain of wheat which the virgin and untilled earth brought forth. Of it the Psalmist says: “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven. For the Lord shall give goodness, and [Col. 0550D] our earth shall yield its fruit” (Ps. 84:12–13). By the immeasurable multiplication of this grain, all the granaries of the Church have been filled—266. From this grain of wheat that bread is made of which the Lord himself says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51). [Note: [Col. 0550D] Ambrose on Psalm 36: “He himself was the grain, broken in body and dead for us, that he might bear much fruit in us.” Jerome on Zechariah chapter 9: “We understand by the wheat of the elect … the Lord Savior, who says in the Gospel: ‘Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth,’ etc., ‘and dies, it remains alone,’ etc. From this wheat is made that bread which descends from heaven.”]

It is also literally true [Col. 0551A] that a grain of wheat, if kept in a chest, does not grow; but if it is sown, dissolved in the earth, and dies, it bears much fruit.

“He who loves his soul will lose it, and he who hates his soul in this world keeps it unto eternal life.” The Lord would not have said this unless we could both love our souls well or badly, and likewise hate them well or badly. He himself explains what it is to love wrongly, and he himself explains what it is to hate rightly.

For he loves his soul wrongly who loves it in this world, for this world, and for this present life. [Note: [Col. 0551D] Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, Book III, chapter 16: “When the Lord says, ‘He who loves his soul shall lose it,’ he must not be thought to forbid the care by which each person ought to preserve his soul; but he speaks figuratively: ‘shall lose his soul,’ that is, shall destroy it and lose the use which it now has—the perverse and disordered use by which it bends toward temporal things and does not seek eternal things.” See the same Saint Augustine, Tractate [Col. 0552D] 51 on John.] Such a person loses it because, by loving it thus, he hands it over to eternal death and destruction.

He loves his soul rightly who loves it so that it may live eternally, not so that [Col. 0551B] it may live in pleasures for a short time. Hence he keeps it unto eternal life who thus hates his soul in this world. He seems to hate his soul and life who does not fear to die, who afflicts it by fasts and vigils, poverty and nakedness, and other like things. Finally, one who loves his soul in such a way that he is unwilling, if necessary, to lay it down for faith in Christ will lose it. But one who hates it in such a way that he does not refuse to lay it down in such necessity keeps it unto eternal life.

“If anyone serves me, let him follow me,” so that, as I die for him, so he also, if necessary, may die for me. For to follow is to imitate. Not only bishops and priests and others of that order serve the Lord; rather, whoever gives alms, [Col. 0551C] clothes the naked, visits the sick, and performs other works of mercy and compassion like these serves the Lord. Hence the Lord himself says: “What you did to one of my least ones, you did to me” (Matt. 25:40), showing that those who serve his members serve him.

But what profit will it be to them that they have served him? It follows: “And where I am, there also shall my servant be.” Perhaps you say that this does not suffice you. Hear what follows: “If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him.” Great is the honor, great the grace, behold immeasurable riches. Blessed is the one whom God will honor. For he will be enriched with those goods “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9).

Finally, one who will be where he himself is—what better thing can such a person ever have? Desiring this, the Psalmist says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord. They shall praise you for ever and ever” (Ps. 83:5). And again: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26:4). And the Apostle says: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23).

[Col. 0552A] It follows: “Now my soul is troubled. And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour. But for this reason I came to this hour. Father, glorify your name.” Above he said: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified” (ibid.). But now he says that his soul is troubled. But why troubled, except because from his very glorification he saw that many people throughout the world would not only be troubled but also scourged and killed and afflicted with every kind of torment?

For who would have believed in him had he not been glorified? Unless he had risen from the dead, ascended to heaven, and his faithful ones had worked such great miracles in his name, no one would have believed in him. Let him therefore say, “Now my soul is troubled,” not from fear of my death but from compassion for my faithful ones. For I am a man and am moved by human feelings. And what shall I say when I see my faithful ones so afflicted and tortured for my name? “Father, save me”: save my members; save and preserve my faithful ones from this hour, from this time of my passion and their tribulation. [Note: [Col. 0552D] Chrysostom, Homily 67, Augustine, Bede, and almost all other interpreters think that Jesus Christ said this of himself, in the same manner as, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.”]

For Christ’s passion and the persecution of the Church began together: while he was seized, the apostles fled, Peter denied him, and all were scandalized. But for this reason I came to this hour: that from this hour my faithful ones may be saved and cleansed by my blood. But you, Father, glorify your name, so that, when I rise on the third day, it may be clear and manifest that you are called Father and I Son. [Note: [Col. 0552D] Augustine, Tractate 52: “What does ‘Glorify your name’ mean, except in his passion and resurrection?”] For if they know your name, they will know mine also, [Col. 0552C] because the Father cannot be without the Son.

Then a voice came from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.” I have glorified it through miracles, and I will glorify it again through the resurrection and ascension. I have glorified it to a few; I will glorify it to many; and finally I will glorify it to all. For few were those who heard him saying, “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 17:5). But many believe that he is the Son of God. Yet this will be revealed more fully in the judgment, when “every tongue shall confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:2).

The crowd that stood there and heard it said that there had been thunder. Others said, “An angel has spoken to him.” Thus both groups heard the voice, but neither group understood it. Jesus answered and said: [Col. 0552D] “This voice came not for my sake, but for yours.” For he who knew the Father’s will in all things had no need of such a conversation. For, as the Apostle says, “tongues are for a sign, not to believers but to unbelievers” (1 Cor. 14:22).

“Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out.” For this is done in judgment: the good is distinguished from the evil and the just from the unjust. [Col. 0553A] [Note: [Col. 0553D] Augustine, Tractate 52: “The judgment expected at the end will be the judgment of those to be judged, living and dead; it will be the judgment of eternal rewards and punishments. What sort of judgment, then, is this now? … I have reminded your charity that ‘judgment’ is also said, not of condemnation, but of discernment.” See the remainder in the same Saint Augustine and in Saint John Chrysostom, Homily 67, no. 2.]

From that time, therefore, the world began to be judged and to judge, when it received Christ’s teaching, because then for the first time it knew how to distinguish truth from falsehood. And then the prince of this world—that is, the devil, king and lord of the wicked—was cast out. Certainly not cast out of the world, but cast out from the people cleansed by baptism, whom Christ washed with his blood and purified with the water of baptism.

“And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself.” “He,” he says, “will be cast out and lose his dominion; but I, lifted up, will draw all things to myself”—that is, all things which are to be drawn. [Note: [Col. 0553D] Augustine, Tractate 52: “What are these ‘all things,’ except those from which he is cast out?”] But this, says the Evangelist, he said to signify by what death he was to die.

The crowd answered him: “We have heard from the Law that Christ remains forever. How then do you [Col. 0553B] say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?” The Jews seem here to have understood what the Lord signified by this lifting up, since they understood that, being so lifted up, he could not remain forever.

Jesus therefore said to them: “Yet a little while the light is among you. Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you. He who walks in darkness does not know where he is going. While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may be children of light.”

“There is yet,” he says, “a little light of understanding in you, while you do not know who this Son of Man is.” For only those are enlightened who know him and believe him to be the Son of God and the Son of Man. Walk, hasten, run to the light while you can, while [Col. 0553C] it is near, while you see it and have it before your eyes, lest the darkness of error and death overtake you. For one who walks in the darkness of ignorance and error does not know where he is going. “I am the light of the world. He who follows me does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” (John 8:12). Therefore, while you have the light, believe in the light, that you may be children of light.

Jesus spoke these things, departed, and hid himself from them. This too is a sign. For the Lord hid himself from them then because even to this day he is not found by them. Every day he speaks to them in the Law and the Prophets, and yet is not found by them. This was what he signified when he hid himself from them.

Though he had performed so many signs before them, they did not believe in him, so that the word of Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled, which he spoke: “Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” Christ is the arm of the Lord, which has not yet been revealed to the Jews: “For blindness has happened in part to Israel” (Rom. 11:25). By this arm all things were made, and without him nothing was made (John 1:3).

Moreover, [Col. 0554A] they could not believe because Isaiah again said: “He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, understand with their heart, be converted, and I heal them.” Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory and spoke of him. Of whom? Of Christ. For he says: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne, and the things beneath him filled the Temple” (Isa. 6:1). And shortly afterward: “Go and say to this people: Hear indeed, but do not understand; see indeed, but do not know. Blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, be converted, and be healed” (ibid., 9).

But since, as is said here, this people could not believe [Col. 0554B] because Isaiah had foretold this concerning them, was Isaiah the cause of their unbelief? Far from it! Their own wickedness and impenitent heart were the cause that they could not believe. [Note: [Col. 0553D] Augustine raises and resolves the same question in Tractate 53: “Why, then, could they not? If I am asked, I answer at once: because they would not. For God foresaw their evil will and foretold it through the prophet—he from whom future things cannot be hidden.”]

The prophet indeed foresaw and foretold this; and, as he foretold it, it could not fail to occur. For the prophet would never have foreseen it unless it were going to happen. Even if the prophet had not foretold it, nevertheless it would have happened. It follows: “Nevertheless, many even of the rulers believed in him. But because of the Pharisees they did not confess it, lest they should be cast out of the synagogue. For they loved human glory more than the glory of God.”

XXXVII. But Jesus cried out and said: “He who believes in me does not believe in me, but in him who sent me.” [Col. 0554C] For how does one who believes in you not believe in you? Or how does one who believes in you not believe in him who sent you? For you said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Whoever believes in the Father, therefore, also believes in the Son, and conversely. Something must therefore be understood implicitly, so that the statement is: “He who believes in me believes not only in me but also in him who sent me.” [Note: [Col. 0554D] Augustine, Tractate 54: “‘He who believes in me,’ he says, ‘does not believe in me’—that is, in what he sees—‘but in him who sent me,’ that is, in the Father. But whoever believes in the Father must believe him to be Father; and whoever believes him to be Father must believe that he has a Son. Therefore, whoever believes in the Father must believe in the Son.”]

“And he who sees me sees him who sent me.” Thus the Lord also said to Philip: “Philip, he who sees me sees the Father” (John 14:9). What this means he immediately explained when he said, “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” Likewise: “I and the Father are one.”

“I came as light into the world, that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness.” [Col. 0554D] What does “I came as light into the world” mean except “I came to enlighten the world”? Why? “That everyone who believes may not remain in darkness.” Therefore to believe in Christ is itself to be enlightened. Whoever does not believe in Christ remains in darkness—the darkness, that is, of blindness and error. For such a person does not know the truth, because truth [Col. 0555A] is Christ.

“And if anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him.” Why? “Because I came not to judge the world, but to save the world.” What is said is plain if “now,” or “at the present time,” is understood. [Note: [Col. 0555D] This also from Augustine in the same place: “Hear how the Son says, ‘I do not judge him,’ although elsewhere he says, ‘The Father judges no one,’ etc., unless it must be understood: ‘I do not judge him now.’”] For the Lord will judge, but not now. Otherwise how could this be true which he says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22)?

“He who despises me and does not receive my words has one who judges him: the word which I have spoken, that shall judge him on the last day.” Who, then, but Christ will judge if Christ’s word will judge? For all these Gospel words are Christ’s word. These words will judge—that is, condemn—and rightly so. Why is this? Hear Jesus: “Because I have not spoken from myself, [Col. 0555B] but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment, what I should say and what I should speak. As the Father has spoken to me, so I speak.”

Since he is truth, since he is the Son of God, since he was sent by the Father, and since he did not speak from himself, those who despised his words and refused to receive them will rightly be judged and condemned. Yet all these things must be referred to the manhood. Although Christ, the wisdom of God, spoke in the man, nevertheless according to his humanity he did not speak from himself. But according to divinity he spoke from himself, because according to divinity the Father and he are one. Therefore he spoke from himself and did not speak from himself. Those who do not forget [Col. 0555C] the two natures in Christ can readily understand these and similar matters.

### XXXVIII. [CHAP. XIII.]

Before the feast-day of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come for him to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end. Jesus, it says, knew that his hour had come. For he knew when it would come, since before the foundation of the world he had appointed the time, the year, and the day when it would come. But what hour? That he should pass from this world to the Father. For Passover (*Pascha*) is interpreted from this passing-over, *transitus*.

> [Note: Col. 0555D. See Augustine, Tractate 55: “Behold the Passover, behold the passing-over,” etc.; Bede copies his words.]

Having always loved his own who were in this world, he loved them to the end—that is, he showed to the full how great was the love with which he had loved them. “For no one has greater love than this: that one lay down his life for his friends.”

> [Note: Col. 0555D. John 15:13. And Augustine on this passage: “Because he loved them so greatly that he died for them; for he bore witness to this when he said: No one has greater charity than this,” etc.]

He himself said this. And he both signified this great love in speaking and displayed it in suffering.

And supper having been prepared, when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, that he should betray him—Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come forth from God and was going to God—rises from supper and lays aside his garments.

“And supper having been prepared” means prepared and set before them, but not yet ended.

> [Note: Col. 0555D. Bede on this place: “Thus ‘supper having been prepared’ was said because it had already been made ready and brought to the table and use of those dining.”]

Judas had already been overcome and deceived by diabolical persuasion so as to betray the Lord. Jesus knew that the Father had given all things into his hands; he knew that he was King of kings and Lord of lords; nor had he forgotten that he was the Son of God, and that he had come from God and was going to God. Yet, though he was such, though he knew himself to be such, he nevertheless rises from supper and humbles himself as far as washing the disciples’ feet. He lays aside his garments, takes a linen cloth, girds himself, pours water into a basin, and, so lovingly, so modestly, and so ready to serve, comes to wash and dry the disciples’ feet.

And, so that he might do everything with reason and order, and instruct us by doing it, he came first to Simon Peter. For Peter was greater than the others.

> [Note: Cols. 0555D, 0556D. Bede on this place: “He came therefore to Simon Peter, as though he had already washed some others and had come to the first after them. For who does not know that most blessed Peter was first among the apostles? Yet this must not be understood as though he came to him after some others, but as meaning that he began with him. Therefore, when he began to wash the disciples’ feet, he came to him with whom he began—that is, to Peter.”]

And Peter says to him: “Lord, do you wash my feet?” It is not fitting; it is not proper. You are Lord; I am a servant. You are God; I am a human being. You are Creator; I am a creature. And do you wash my feet?

Jesus answered and said to him: “What I am doing, you do not know now; but afterwards you shall know.” This my humiliation signifies a great mystery, which, when I teach and explain it, you will afterwards know.

But Peter, terrified by so great a condescension of the Son of God, still persisting in the same resolve, replied: “You shall never wash my feet.” I shall never permit this, never endure it, never receive such a service from the hands of my Lord.

Jesus answered him: “Unless I wash you, you shall have no part with me.” Therefore those will have a share with Christ in his kingdom whom he himself loved and washed from their sins in his blood.

Simon Peter says to him: “Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head.” If it pleases you, he says, if your mind is set upon it, if it cannot be otherwise, I am your servant; I submit my whole self to your will, and offer you not my feet alone, but also my hands and head.

Jesus says to him: “He who has been washed has no need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean.” For one who has once been washed does not need to be washed again, except in the feet, which, because they always tread the ground, are often stained by dust.

> [Note: Cols. 0556D, 0557C. Jerome, Epistle 18 to Damasus, no. 12: “What is this, that … he replied: Lord, not my feet only, etc.? Therefore, as the Lord was about to ascend into heaven, because the apostles, as human beings standing upon the earth, still had feet defiled by the filth of sinners, he wished to set them entirely free from offences.” Augustine, *On the Church*, Tractate 56, no. 5: “In those who remain here, even if they are clean because they live righteously, there is nevertheless need to wash the feet, since they are certainly not without sin.”]

“But he is wholly clean”—with the feet understood as excepted. And by these feet, indeed, I think the bodily senses and the affections of the soul are signified. For they carry us outside ourselves, and they are often stained within us.

> [Note: Col. 0557D. Bede on this place: “What do you think, my brothers? Is it not that a person is wholly washed in holy baptism—not excepting the feet, but wholly and entirely? Yet afterwards, while one lives amid human affairs, one certainly treads the earth. These human affections, therefore, without which one cannot live in this mortal state, are as it were feet, through which we are affected by human things; and so affected that, if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us.” These are Augustine’s words in Tractate 56.]

Sight carries you to gaze upon a woman’s appearance: there it is stained and needs washing. Hearing carries you to listen to slander and vain counsel: there it is stained and needs washing. Taste carries you to gluttony and drunkenness: there it is stained and needs washing. So too with the other senses. These, therefore, are those feet which must often be washed even in persons already washed and baptized.

But what shall I say of the affections of the soul, when pride and vainglory often mingle even with good deeds themselves? Here too washing is necessary.

It follows: “And you are clean, but not all.” Since the Evangelist himself explained this, we are not permitted to explain it otherwise. For the Evangelist says that he knew who it was that would betray him; therefore he said: “You are not all clean.”

Therefore, after he had washed their feet and taken his garments, when he had reclined again, he said to them: “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you say well; for so I am.” You say rightly, he says, in calling me Teacher and Lord. As you say, so it is. But because I am Teacher, receive my teaching; and because I am Lord, keep my commandment.

What commandment? Do you wish to hear which? “If I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so you also should do.”

Although to keep this literally is full of charity and humility, it nevertheless appears to signify something greater, as do the other things which our Saviour similarly performed. And this is perhaps what the Apostle says. This is perhaps that law which he commanded us to fulfil when he said: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2), that is, Christ’s commandment. Hence also the apostle James says: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (Jas. 5:16). For while the saints pray for one another, one washes another’s feet.

> [Note: Cols. 0557D, 0558C–D. Augustine, Tractate 68, and Bede: “Indeed, let us recognize that we too are admonished by the profundity of this work of the Lord, that, confessing our offences to one another, we should pray for one another, as Christ intercedes for us. Let us hear the apostle James, who commands this very thing most clearly, saying: ‘Confess,’ etc. For what does the Lord appear to signify in the profundity of this mystery when he says, ‘For I have given you an example,’ etc., except what the Apostle says most plainly: ‘Forgiving yourselves,’ etc.? Therefore let us forgive one another our offences, pray for one another concerning our offences, and thus in some manner wash one another’s feet.”]

“Amen, amen, I say to you: a servant is not greater than his master, nor an apostle greater than he who sent him. If you know these things, blessed shall you be if you do them.” If you know and understand what I have done to you, he says, and, following this example, do the like to others as I have done to you, you shall be blessed.

But why do you not do for your equals what you see me doing for you, my servants and disciples? “I do not speak of all of you. I know whom I have chosen.” I told you, he says, that you shall be blessed; but I did not say it to all. I said it to those who will do these things; to those whom I chose not only to the apostolate but also to blessedness.

> [Note: Col. 0558D. See what has been said above concerning this.]

For Judas too was chosen to the apostolate. Thus the Lord had earlier said: “Have not I chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6:71).

“But that the Scripture may be fulfilled: He who eats my bread shall lift up his heel against me.” For thus it is written: “The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my breads, has magnified treachery against me” (Ps. 40:10).

“From now on I tell you before it happens, that when it has happened you may believe that I am.” That is, he of whom that Scripture says these things.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever receives one whom I send receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.” For although the Father is in the Son in one way and the Son in the apostles in another, nevertheless, because Christ is in them, whoever receives the apostles receives Christ also.

When Jesus had said these things, he was troubled in spirit, and testified and said: “Amen, amen, I say to you, that one of you will betray me.” For he is troubled in spirit because he is troubled spiritually. Spiritual disturbance belongs to piety and mercy; carnal disturbance excites anger and fury.

Jesus is therefore troubled in spirit, either because his disciple betrays him and perishes through betraying him, or in order to teach us what we ought to do when we see someone rushing into a great crime and wickedness.

> [Note: Cols. 0558D, 0559D. Athanasius, *On the Incarnation*: “Thus the Lord displayed the feeling of his own soul for the compassion of our soul, so that we might both understand his suffering and nevertheless confess him incapable of suffering.” Augustine, Tractate 60: “Was Jesus troubled—not in flesh, but in spirit—because he was about to say: ‘One of you will betray me’? … Or rather, is our weakness troubled in him? Let servants therefore believe nothing unworthy of their Lord, but recognize themselves as members in their Head. … Accordingly, when the great, strong, steadfast, unconquered one is troubled, let us not fear for him as though he were failing. He does not perish, but seeks us. Us, I say—he seeks us altogether. Let us see ourselves in his disturbance, so that, when we are troubled, we may not perish through despair. When he is troubled who would not be troubled unless he willed it, he consoles one who is troubled unwillingly. … Let the Christian soul indeed be troubled, not by misery but by mercy; let it fear lest people perish to Christ; let it grieve when someone perishes to Christ; let it desire to gain people for Christ; let it rejoice when people are gained for Christ; let it fear for itself also, lest it perish to Christ,” etc. Bede has the same words. See Cyril, p. 734.]

Now Judas was one of them because he associated with them bodily, though in mind and faith he had already withdrawn from them. He had been chosen among them for the apostolate, but had not been predestined with them to eternal life.

The disciples therefore looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke. Each feared for himself what he did not have in his conscience, because they knew that he could not lie.

Now one of the disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining in Jesus’ bosom. Who is this disciple but the very same blessed John who writes these things? In accordance with the custom of the Holy Scriptures, he speaks of himself as though of another. Thus Moses frequently says: “The Lord spoke to Moses” (Exod. 6:2, 10, 13; Deut. 32:48, etc.); and the other prophets likewise.

This disciple reclined in Jesus’ bosom—that is, upon his breast—and upon that fountain of wisdom and knowledge from which he deserved to draw all these things that he pours forth for us so abundantly throughout this Gospel.

> [Note: Col. 0559D. St Gregory, *Morals*, book 27, ch. 6: “What was dearer than John? Through love he rested upon the very breast of our Author; and he who had come to the refreshment of a bodily supper received spiritual food from the bosom of the Redeemer.”]

Simon Peter therefore motioned to him and said: “Who is it of whom he speaks?” “He motioned,” it says, meaning that he secretly prompted him to ask of whom he spoke.

Therefore, when he had reclined upon Jesus’ breast, he says to him: “Lord, who is it?” Jesus answered: “It is he to whom I shall give the dipped morsel.” And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas, son of Simon Iscariot.

Perhaps in giving him dipped bread, he signified that Judas had already been dipped and infected with diabolical blackness. And after the morsel Satan then entered into him. Satan had already entered him before, to tempt and deceive him; but then he first entered into him in order to possess him. Perhaps he still hesitated and feared that Judas might come to his senses and desist from destruction. But after he saw him marked out by the morsel, he invaded him as his own and subjected him to his service.

Jesus says to him: “What you are doing, do quickly.” He said this not as commanding it, but as foretelling it.

> [Note: Col. 0559D. Augustine, Tractate 62: “He did not command the crime, but foretold it.” St Leo, Sermon 58, *On the Lord’s Passion*, 7, ch. 4: “This voice is not that of one commanding, but permitting; not of one trembling, but prepared. Possessing power over all times, he showed both that he did not delay the betrayer and that he was carrying out the Father’s will for the redemption of the world in such a manner as neither to impel nor to fear the crime prepared by his persecutors.”]

For he saw that Judas’ mind, through excessive desire to hasten what he had begun, could not rest. But none of those reclining knew for what purpose he had said this to him. Some supposed, because Judas had the purse, that Jesus had said to him: “Buy what we need for the feast-day,” or that he should give something to the poor.

Therefore, having received the morsel, he went out immediately. And it was night. Aptly, because it was night: for he was going into night, death, and darkness.

> [Note: Col. 0560D. Augustine on this place: “And he himself who went out was night.”]

Therefore, when he had gone out, Jesus says: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him. If God has been glorified in him, God also has glorified him in himself, and has glorified him immediately.”

“Now,” he says, “because the son of night and darkness has withdrawn from my disciples, now the Son of Man has been glorified in them. Now he senses in them no mist or darkness.”

> [Note: Col. 0560D. Augustine, Tractate 63: “Judas went out, and the Son of Man was glorified. For he had gone out on whose account it had been said to them: ‘And you are clean, but not all.’ Therefore, when the unclean one went out, all the rest remained clean and remained with their cleanser.”]

“And God has been glorified in him,” because divinity never sensed any darkness in him. For he is that “light which shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5). Though he is glorified in others, he is in himself most glorious. For he is glorified in others when those who are his members are glorified.

Likewise, God has been glorified in him because he made him glorious. And this is what he says: “If God has been glorified in him, God also has glorified him.” In whom? In himself. When? Immediately. What does “immediately” mean? As soon as he was begotten. For other human beings are first conceived and born; then, through repentance, baptism, and the ministry of priests, they are regenerated and glorified. But the Son of Man was not first begotten and then glorified. For divinity, united to humanity, sanctified and glorified that assumed human being in the very act of union, and cleansed him from every corruption of the first transgression.

> [Note: Col. 0560D. Augustine, Tractate 63, explains this of glory after the Passion. He interprets “immediately” as follows: “His resurrection was to take place immediately, not at the end of the age, as ours will.” See St Cyril, p. 745.]

Let it therefore be said: Now the Son of Man has been glorified in his disciples. In this Son of Man God was glorified immediately, as he united himself to humanity, which he himself glorified and sanctified in himself.

“Little children, I am with you yet a little while.” This he said concerning the presence of his flesh, which ascended into heaven not many days later. “You will seek me; and, as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come,’ so I say to you now.”

For the disciples sought to see Jesus, and sought him with longing because they desired always to be with him. Thus the Apostle says: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23). But they could not then come where he was going, though afterwards they were to go there. Thus he added: “So I say to you now.”

To the Jews, he says, I said absolutely: “Where I am going, you cannot come.”

> [Note: Col. 0560D. Augustine, Tractate 64: “That is, you cannot come now. But when he said this to the Jews, he did not add ‘now.’”]

But to you I say that you cannot now come where I am going. For first you must go and preach the Gospel to every creature.

“A new commandment I give you: that you love one another as I have loved you.” For loving is not a new commandment; but loving as he himself loved is a new commandment.

> [Note: Cols. 0560D, 0561D. Augustine, Tractate 65: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another: not as those who corrupt one another love, nor as people love one another merely because they are human beings, but as brothers, children of his only Son, loving one another with that love by which he loved them.”]

For the Law commanded people to love their neighbours, but did not command them to die for them. “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

Simon Peter says to him: “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus answered him: “Where I am going, you cannot follow me now; but you shall follow afterwards.” Peter says to him: “Why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.” Jesus answered: “Will you lay down your life for me? Amen, amen, I say to you: the cock will not crow until you deny me three times.”

Mark alone says, “The cock will not crow.” Therefore, in order that the Gospels may agree, it should be said thus: “It will not crow”—that is, it will not complete its crowing—until you deny me three times. This would be like saying: “Jesus did not dine before he washed the disciples’ feet,” that is, he did not complete the supper before washing the disciples’ feet, although he began to dine earlier.

> [Note: Cols. 0561D, 0562D. Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, book 3, ch. 2, states and resolves this question: “A question arises from the somewhat differing words of the Evangelists. Matthew: ‘Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times’; Mark: ‘Before the cock gives its voice twice, you will deny me three times’; Luke and John, in nearly the same words: ‘The cock will not crow today until you deny knowing me three times.’ ‘The cock will not crow until you deny me three times.’” Augustine resolves it in nearly the same manner as the author, though at greater length.]

### XXXIX. [CHAP. XIV.]

And he said to his disciples: “Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid. You believe in God; believe also in me.”

I am going, he says, and where I am going you cannot come now; but you will come afterwards. Yet let not your heart be troubled or afraid on this account. For although I am going, I do not leave you: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

“You believe in God; believe also in me.” For it is not sufficient for you to believe in the Father unless you also believe in the Son: “For I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

“In my Father’s house are many dwellings.” Of these I have purposed to prepare and give you those that are nobler and more glorious. “For you are those who have continued with me in my temptations. And I appoint to you, as my Father appointed to me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit upon thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Luke 22:29–30).

“If I had told you less than fully that I am going to prepare a place for you, you nevertheless ought not to have been troubled but rather to have rejoiced.” If, he says, I had spoken to you inadequately or not sufficiently enough in saying that I go to prepare a place for you, you should nevertheless have greatly desired that I should go there as quickly as possible and introduce you into the glory of so great a blessedness. But now, since I have so often told and promised you this, why are you alarmed?

Therefore be certain and do not doubt that, if I go and prepare a place for you, I shall come again and receive you to myself. Why? “That where I am, you also may be.” Thus I also said above: “Where I am, there also shall my servant be” (John 12:26).

The Lord receives the souls of the saints daily to himself through the ministry of angels and his own ineffable power. But he will do this more fully and abundantly then, when, coming for judgment and joining bodies with souls, he will say to his faithful: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

It was necessary, moreover, that he should go first, open the gates of heaven, and by his own entrance prepare fitting places for each person. For there are many dwellings there, because, as the Apostle says, “Star differs from star in glory.”

> [Note: Col. 0562D. 1 Corinthians 15:41. See St Gregory, *Morals*, book 3, ch. 42; book 35, ch. 24; and Homily 16 on Ezekiel.]

It follows: “And you know where I am going, and you know the way.” For where was he going except to the Father? The apostles knew both the Father and himself, though not by sight but by faith. For they knew by believing, not by seeing. Those, therefore, who knew both the Father and himself surely knew where he was going, because they knew the Father; and they knew the way itself, because they knew himself. But because they did not yet understand these words, they did not know that they knew what they did know.

Thomas therefore replied: “Lord, we do not know where you are going; and how can we know the way?” For some of them thought that he spoke about death, like Peter, who had just said above: “Lord, where are you going?” (John 13:36). To him the Lord replied: “Where I am going, you cannot follow me now; but you shall follow afterwards.” But Peter said: “Why can I not follow you now? I lay down my life for you.” You see, therefore, that he understood it as referring to death, since he said that he would lay down his life with him.

This is why Thomas said: “We do not know where you are going,” because he still did not know what journey he meant—whether one of death or of heaven. And the Lord immediately explained by his answer how they ought to understand these words. For he said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.”

If you know me, he says, you know the way also, because I am the way. And if you know me, you know the Father also, because I and the Father are one.

> [Note: Cols. 0562D, 0563D. John 10:30. Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book 1, ch. 34: “I am the way, the truth, and the life: that is, through me one comes; to me one arrives; in me one remains. For when one arrives at him, one arrives also at the Father himself, because through the equal one, he who is equal is recognized.” Augustine discusses these Gospel words extensively in Sermons 141 and 142. See also Cyril, p. 768.]

If, however, you know the Father, you know also where I am going, because I am going to the Father. “I am the way.” But why the way? Because no one comes to the Father except through me. “I am the truth.” Why is this? Because no one knows the Father except through me: “For no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27). For nothing is known except through truth. “I am the life,” because no one lives except through me.

“If you had known me, you would surely have known my Father also. And from now on you will know him, and you have seen him.” Do you wish, he says, to come to the Father? Do you wish to know him? First know me, whom you see, and thus afterwards you will know him whom you do not yet see. For you have already seen him, though not in himself. You have seen him, however, in me. You have indeed seen him, but with mind and faith. For he speaks in me, because I do not speak from myself. When you hear him, you see him. For one who hears with the mind certainly sees what one hears, because sight and hearing are the same in the mind—and not only these, but taste, smell, and touch as well. Hence the saying: “Taste and see” (Ps. 33:9), that is, see by tasting. Thus you have seen him when you heard him speaking in me. “And from now on you will know him, because he will remain with you and be in you.”

Philip says to him: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.” For Philip desired to see him not only with mind and faith but also with the eyes of flesh, like Moses, who said: “If I have found grace in your sight, show me your face, that I may know you” (Exod. 33:13). To him the Lord said: “No human being shall see me and live” (ibid., v. 20).

Jesus says to him: “Have I been with you so long, and have you not known me? Philip, he who sees me sees the Father also.” Philip spoke of outward sight; Christ, however, directed them to inward sight—that is, to understanding and the eyes of the mind. “Have I been with you so long, have I associated among you for so long, and revealed my divinity and power to you in teaching, signs, and miracles, and have you not known me? Philip, he who sees me—not, as you understand it, with the eyes of flesh, but, as I say, with the eyes of the mind—sees the Father also.

“Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” If you believe this, you see both me and the Father. If you do not believe it, you see neither me nor the Father.

“The words that I speak to you, I do not speak from myself.” From whom, then? From the Father. Where is he? Hear where he is: “But the Father abiding in me, he does the works.” What does “he does the works” mean? He speaks in me. For God works by speaking: “For he spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 32:9). Jesus heals the sick by words and not by herbs.

But this should be carefully noted: although he and the Father are one, he nevertheless everywhere glorifies the Father. For had he said: “According to my humanity I do not speak from myself, but the divinity abiding in me does the works,” he would indeed have spoken correctly. Yet he did not say this, in order that he might refer all glory to the Father.

“Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? Otherwise, believe because of the works themselves.” If you do not believe the words, he says, believe the works. For the works that I do plainly show that I am in the Father and the Father is in me.

But hear a still greater argument, one which no one can contradict: “Amen, amen, I say to you: he who believes in me will also do the works that I do; and he will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father.”

In this, he says, it appears that I am the Son of God: not only do I perform these works, marvellous to all, but those who believe in me will perform similar and greater works.

> [Note: Col. 0563D. See Augustine, Tractate 72; Cyril, p. 804; and especially Chrysostom, Homily 62 on John.]

And this rightly, because I am going to the Father—that is, because I am the Son of God, and he to whom I go is my Father. It is very fitting that those who believe in the Son of God should do such things.

It follows: “And whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son.” For the Father is greatly glorified in the Son when such things are done in the Son’s name.

XL. If you love me, keep my commandments. For by this the powers of this world also test and recognize their friends and faithful adherents: if they obey them and keep their commands. The proof of love, then, is the performance of the deed. [Note: [Col. 0563D] These well-known words of Saint Gregory occur in Homily 30 on the Gospels, no. 1, on John 14:23, where he adds: “For we truly love God if we restrain ourselves from our pleasures in obedience to his commands. For one who still pours himself out in unlawful desires certainly does not love God, because he opposes him in his own will . . . Therefore return inwardly to yourselves, dearest brethren; inquire whether you truly love God. Yet let no one believe whatever his mind answers him without the testimony of works. Concerning love of the Creator, let tongue, mind, and life be examined. The love of God is never idle.” Chrysostom also has splendid words at the beginning of Homily 75 on John: “We always need works, not a display of words; for it is easy for anyone to speak and promise, but not likewise to act.”] Whoever despises the commandment denies love. But what fruit do we gain by loving God? What reward is there for keeping his commandments? Do you wish to hear it? “And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you forever.”

For the Son asks the Father, not according to the divinity in which he is in every respect equal to the Father, but according to the humanity in which he is less than the Father. [Note: [Col. 0564D] See Cyril, p. 809.] By “another Paraclete” he means the Holy Spirit. For the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. But the Father is not one thing, the Son another thing, and the Holy Spirit another thing. For all are one, yet they are not one person. “One” concerns essence; “one person” refers to person and number.

Therefore God gives the apostles another Paraclete—that is, another comforter; for *Paraclete* is interpreted “comforter.” [Note: [Col. 0564D] Augustine, Tractate 74, no. 4: “When he says, ‘I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete,’ he shows that he himself is also a Paraclete. For *Paraclete* is called in Latin *Advocatus* [Advocate], and it is said of Christ: ‘We have an Advocate,’” etc.; the same author, Tractate 94: “That one, therefore, is Comforter or Advocate. For both are the interpretation of the Greek *Paraclete*.” See on this name Estius, Maldonatus, and the other interpreters, and Ciampini’s dissertation on this word.] By this we understand the Holy Spirit, since he who had been accustomed to comfort them would no longer dwell bodily among them. Yet although, according to his humanity, he was not among them, according to his divinity he did not depart from them. Hence he himself says: “I will not abandon you or forsake you.” For where the Holy Spirit is, there are the Father and the Son. It should be known, moreover, that as the Father gives the Holy Spirit, so also does the Son, because he proceeds from the Father and the Son.

It follows: “The Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. But you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you.” He is called the Spirit of truth [Note: [Col. 0564D] Cyril, p. 810: “For he is his Spirit; hence he called him the Spirit of truth.” Chrysostom, [Col. 0565D] Homily 75: “He calls him the Spirit of truth, indicating the figures of the old Law.”], [Col. 0564D] because he teaches nothing except truth. Therefore the sayings of the prophets are true, as are all things composed by the Holy Spirit.

But the world cannot receive him, because the lovers of this world cannot possess and retain him. Hence this same apostle John says: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For everything that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not from the Father but from the world” (1 John 2:15–16). If, then, love is not in those who love the world, and God is love, how can the Holy Spirit be in those who love the world? Those, therefore, who possess love, who place their hope not in uncertain riches but in God, and who devote themselves to virtue, are not lovers of the world, even if they are rich in [Col. 0565B] this world.

But why can the world not receive the Holy Spirit? What is it to receive? Surely, to retain and possess. For the Holy Spirit often comes even upon some wicked person, such as Balaam and Caiaphas, and such as those who will say to the Lord at the judgment: “Did we not prophesy in your name?” (Matt. 7:22). He comes indeed, but he does not remain in them, [Note: [Col. 0565D] Saint Gregory, in the work cited above, explaining the words of John, “We will come and make our dwelling with him”: “For he comes into the hearts of certain persons but does not make his dwelling there, because through compunction they do indeed receive an awareness of God’s regard; but at the time of temptation they forget the very thing for which they had been moved to compunction, and so return to committing sins as though they had mourned only trivial matters.”] as he remains in those to whom the Lord now says, “that he may remain with you forever.” For that which remains in them forever is never separated from them.

Let us now hear why the world cannot receive the Holy Spirit. Let the Lord himself say: “Because it neither sees him nor knows him.” What does “it neither sees him nor knows him” mean, except that it neither recognizes nor understands [Col. 0565C] his sweetness, his goodness, his gifts, his mercy and loving-kindness, and the other things that belong to him? Thus the Apostle says: “The natural person does not receive the things of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:14).

“But you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you.” Those know him who remain with him and do his will. “I will not leave you orphans. I will come to you.” Orphans are those who do not have a father. Christians are not orphans, because Christ has risen. “Yet a little while, and the world sees me no more.” For we read that after his resurrection our Savior appeared not to wicked people and lovers of this world, but only to the apostles and other faithful persons. Of them it follows: “But you [Col. 0565D] will see me, because I live, and you will live.” For it was not fitting that Christ, risen from the dead and now made eternal and immortal, should reveal himself to wicked people, dead to God and separated from the life that is Christ. But he revealed himself to his disciples, so that he who lives might be seen by the living.

“In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you.” On what day? On that day on which I shall send you the Spirit of truth, that he may remain with you forever. For he taught them; he revealed to them the mysteries of faith. Hence the Lord himself says: “But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 16:13). The Son is in the Father because he is one and the same with the Father. We too are in Christ because we are his members. He is in us because he is our life. Therefore that soul is dead, and cannot see God, which does not possess this life.

“He who has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me.” With what fruit? “And he who loves me will be loved by my Father.” What follows from this? “And I will love him.” With what benefit? “And I will reveal myself to him.” If, then, it is not enough for you to be loved by the Father, if it is not enough for the Son to love you, let this be enough for you: that he who is wisdom, truth, and righteousness will reveal himself to you. For in these consists all the blessedness of the soul. Moses desired this alone when he said to the Lord: “If I have found favor in your eyes, show me your face, that I may see you” (Exod. 33:13). Blessed, therefore, is the one to whom he shall reveal himself; once he is revealed, nothing will be lacking for blessedness. “For we know that, when he appears and is revealed to us, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (John 3:2). But for whom is it not enough to be like the Son of God? The one who sees him as he is, is like him. Let this, therefore, suffice us: that he will reveal himself to us.

Judas—not Judas Iscariot—said to him: “Lord, what has happened that you are going to reveal yourself to us and not to the world?” Jesus answered and said to him:

XLI. “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.” [Col. 0566C] “He who does not love me does not keep my word.” For this was the Lord’s answer to a disciple asking why he would reveal himself only to his own disciples and faithful followers, and not to the whole world. A great question, and a most noble solution to a great question. “For this reason,” he says, “I do not reveal myself to the world—that is, to lovers of the world—because they do not love me.” This is proved most plainly from the fact that they do not keep my word.

But my disciples and faithful followers, because they love me and keep my commandments, are worthy for me to reveal myself to them, so that, knowing wisdom, they may be wise; knowing righteousness, they may be righteous; knowing truth, they may be truthful; [Col. 0566D] and, knowing life, may live forever. For Christ is all these things. All these things are revealed in Christ. “And not only this,” he says, “will the one who loves me possess; my Father too will love him.” With what great love! Do you wish to hear how great? “We will come to him,” and not merely come, but “we will also make our dwelling with him.” For the Lord makes his dwelling in those in whom, having come, he remains, and from whom, after coming, he does not depart. The Lord comes into those who believe for a time, but does not make his dwelling [Col. 0567A] in them, and they fall away in the time of temptation.

It follows: “And the word that you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me.” In this he plainly shows that all these words which he spoke in the hearing of his disciples belong not to his humanity but to his divinity. Thus this word was his according to his divinity, and was not his according to his humanity. [Note: [Col. 0567D] Saint John Chrysostom, Homily 75, no. 3: “How is the word yours and not yours? That is: I speak nothing apart from the Father, nor anything of my own, beyond his good pleasure.”]

It can also be understood more deeply, so that it is said thus: “And the word which you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me”; that is, I am not from myself, but from the Father who sent me, whose Word, speech, and wisdom I am. [Note: [Col. 0567D] Saint Augustine, Tractate 76: “When he said that the word—that is, the Word—was not his own but the Father’s, he intended himself to be understood. For in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The Word, therefore, is not his own but the Father’s; just as his image is not his own but the Father’s, nor is he himself his own Son but the Father’s. He rightly attributes to the source whatever the equal one does, from whom he has even this: that he is without distinction equal.” Bede has the same words.]

When I speak, then, what do you hear except the Word of the Father, who in the beginning was the Word, and the speech and wisdom of the Father? But Word, speech, and wisdom are not from themselves but from another. Therefore, “the word which you have heard is not mine,” because I am not from myself. “I have spoken these things to you while remaining with you.” “I, the Word,” he says, “have spoken all these words.” Therefore these words are mine; but I am not my own Word. Whose, then? His of whom it is said: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 32:6).

“But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance everything that I have said to you.” “You are grieved,” he says, “because I do not always remain bodily with you, and because I withdraw from you these words and the presence of my flesh; but do not be sorrowful, because in my place and in my name a great comforter and [Col. 0567C] most wise teacher will be given to you. He will comfort you. He will teach you. He will bring everything to your remembrance and supply all that I have said to you.”

“Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. But I do not give to you as the world gives.” For the world gives peace only to those from whom it receives peace. But what does the Apostle say? “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Rom. 12:18); and the Psalmist: “I was peaceable with those who hate peace; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause” (Ps. 119:7). Jesus gave such peace to his disciples when he said to them: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5:44). We ought to have this peace with the wicked, not in order to agree with them in wickedness, but in order to draw them from injustice to the path of righteousness. Hence the Lord says: “Do not think that I came to bring peace upon the earth; I came not to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10:34).

“Do not let your heart be troubled, nor let it be afraid. You heard that I [Col. 0568A] said to you: I go, and I come to you.” “Do not let your heart be troubled,” he says, “at my death, nor be afraid at my absence. Always remember that I said to you: I go, and I come to you. I did not say only, ‘I go,’ but ‘I go, and I come.’ Therefore, just as you are troubled because I said, ‘I go,’ so be strengthened because I said, ‘I come.’ I go to the Father, but I do not leave you. Greater is the divinity which remains with you than the humanity which will ascend to heaven. For you have already known both the weakness of the latter and the power of the former.”

Christ therefore goes to the Father according to his humanity, he who is everywhere according to his divinity. [Note: [Col. 0568D] Augustine, Tractate 78: “By that in which the Son is not equal to the Father, he was to go to the Father, from whom he will also come to judge the living and the dead; but in that in which the Only-Begotten is equal to the one begetting him, he never departs from the Father, but is wholly with him everywhere in equal divinity, which no place can contain.”] How then does he come? For he says both: “I go” and “I come.” He comes, indeed, and he comes invisibly, by providing aid, giving comfort, strengthening faith, and confirming [Col. 0568B] love. Thus the Lord had come to the Apostle who says: “Do you seek proof of Christ, who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3). In this manner not only the Son but also the Father goes and comes. Hence he said shortly before: “We will come to him and make our dwelling with him.”

“If you loved me, you would indeed rejoice because I go to the Father, because the Father is greater than I.” The apostles loved him, but not yet with spiritual and perfect love, while they grieved only that they were losing the presence of his flesh. John the Baptist did not do this, nor did he bodily associate with one whom he always possessed with him according to divinity and always beheld with the eyes of his mind. “If you loved me,” he says, “as you ought to love me, and [Col. 0568C] as you will love me after the coming of the Holy Spirit, you would surely rejoice in that very thing over which you now grieve. Do you grieve, then, because I go to the Father, because I open the gates of paradise, throw open the doors of heaven, show you the path of life, and send you the Paraclete Spirit? ‘For unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you’” (John 16:7).

“I go, then, to the Father, because the Father is greater than I”; that is, I go to the Father according to that in which the Father is greater. For according to divinity he is equal to the Father, but according to humanity he is less. “And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it has happened you may believe.” Believe what? Whatever I have told you and commanded you to believe.

“I will no longer speak much with you.” [Col. 0568D] Why? Do you wish to hear why? Because I am now approaching my passion. The prince of this world is already coming with his attendants to seize his prey. And this is what he says: “For the prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me.” He comes against me, rages and [Col. 0569A] roars against me, but has nothing in me. “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself” (John 10:18). Consider now what he does at the death of others, he who presumed to come against the very Savior and Lord of the world.

But why is the devil called prince of the world? Why “of this” world? For “of this” was not said without reason. Something is delimited when “of this” is said. He would not be called prince of this world if he were prince of the whole world. He is therefore prince of this world: this wicked, present world which desires to kill Christ. [Note: [Col. 0569D] Augustine, in the work cited: “Paul the Apostle made clearer how the devil is to be understood as prince of the world. After saying, ‘Our struggle is not against flesh and blood,’ that is, against human beings, he added: ‘but against rulers and powers and the world-rulers of this darkness,’ lest anyone understand by ‘world’ the whole creation . . . ‘Of this darkness,’ he says—that is, of lovers of this world.” Chrysostom, Homily 75, no. 4: “He calls the devil the prince of the world, and calls wicked people the world. For he does not rule heaven and earth; otherwise he would have overturned and cast down everything. But he rules those who have surrendered themselves to him; therefore he calls him prince of the darkness of this age. Here he calls evil deeds ‘darkness.’”]

Finally, he is prince of this world; that is, of all those who care for nothing except [Col. 0569B] this present age. And as though someone were to say: “If the prince of this world has nothing [Col. 0570A] in you, and has no power against you, why do you not defend yourself? Why do you permit yourself to be killed?” He says: “But that the world may know that I love the Father, and that as the Father gave me commandment, so I do.” Henceforth, he says, it is not from powerlessness or deficiency, but from obedience. I could have defended myself if I had wished. But so that the world may know that I love the Father and, knowing it, imitate me, I became “obedient” to the Father “unto death” (Phil. 2:8). “And as the Father gave me commandment, so I do”; that is, as the Father willed, so I do. For his willing was his commanding, since the will in both is one and the same.

“Rise; let us go from here.” This is not the place of our dwelling. Look to heaven, because you have your origin from there.

PART THREE

[Col. 0569]

277 XLII. [CHAPTER 15.] “I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he will take away; and every one that bears fruit he will cleanse, that it may bear more fruit.”

Behold, Christ is called a vine, and the true vine. But why a vine, and why true? He is called a vine because he made wine. For all these words of the Gospels are wine—and not merely any wine, but the best wine, harvested and pressed from no vine other than this one. Hence, at the beginning of his preaching, the Lord changed water into wine, so that the new vine might pour forth new wine, with which he might make drunk that wedding feast and the master of the banquet.

He is called the true vine, perhaps in distinction from that vine which, instead of grapes, produced wild grapes, and instead of wine gave vinegar. [Note: [Col. 0570D] Augustine, Tractate 80, and Bede: “But when he says of himself, ‘I am the true vine,’ he certainly distinguishes himself from that vine to which it is said: ‘How have you turned into bitterness, alien vine?’ For how can that be the true vine which was expected to produce grapes but produced thorns?” (Isa. 5).] The wine of this vine is sweet and always pleasant. Its words are always true and uncorrupted by any admixture of falsehood.

Therefore he says: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.” But what does this husbandman do? Do you wish to hear? “Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he will take away; and every one that bears fruit he will cleanse, that it may bear more fruit.” As many Christians as there are, so many branches of this vine there are. Some are good, others evil; the good are fruitful, the evil unfruitful. The unfruitful are removed and burned; the fruitful are cleansed and cut back with the sword of the Spirit, so that they may bear more fruit.

The sword of the Spirit is the word of God, and this discourse of the holy [Col. 0570B] Gospel. Of this it follows: “You are already clean because of the word that I have spoken to you.” You hear, therefore, that the word of God is the sword and the instrument by which these persons have been cleansed and purified of every harmful excess. The first branches of this vine were the apostles. The Lord now says to them: “Remain in me, and I in you.” And he gives the reason why they should remain: “As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me. I am the vine, and you are the branches.”

The Lord himself explains how we ought to understand his words. For the branch withers if it is separated from the vine, because it has its sap and its entire life in the vine. So too the Christian, if separated from Christ, dies, because [Col. 0570C] he is separated from life. “He who remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit.” He, he says, bears much fruit who remains in me, clings to me as though he were my member, and in whom I remain—I who am wisdom, truth, and life. For this reason the apostles brought the Lord so great a harvest from the seed of their preaching: because they could in no way be separated from faith in and love for him. Moreover, the Lord himself was in them, giving growth to their seed. For as the Apostle says: “Neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7).

Hence it follows: “Because without me you can do nothing. And if anyone does not remain in me, he will be cast out like a branch and will wither; and they will gather [Col. 0571A] him and cast him into the fire, and he burns.” Whoever does not remain in faith in Christ is expelled from the Church and the company of the saints, withers and dies, is snatched away by evil spirits, cast into eternal and unquenchable fire, and there is tormented and burns without end.

“If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, whatever you wish, you will ask, and it will be done for you.” A great promise, a great and incomparable gift! Let those who remain in Christ, and in whom Christ’s words remain, ask whatever they will, and it shall be done for them. For if they will evil and ask wrongly, neither do they themselves remain in Christ nor do Christ’s words remain in them. [Note: [Col. 0571D] Augustine, Tractate 81: “Therefore, remaining in him, when his words remain in us, we ask whatever we will, and it will be done for us. For if we ask and it is not done, we are not asking for what belongs to dwelling [Col. 0572D] in him, nor for what belongs to his words remaining in us, but for what belongs to the weakness and desire of the flesh, which is not in him and in which his words do not remain.”]

Let them therefore remember Christ’s words—or rather, let them not merely remember them, but hold them firmly and always keep them in mind—and thus ask as Christ’s words teach them to ask. Let them seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all things will be added to them (Matt. 6:33). Let them ask in faith, without doubting; let them ask for those things which pertain to salvation and are not contrary to God’s ordering and the words of the Gospel.

But these words are said particularly to the apostles, whose holy petitions the Lord always and everywhere heard. The Apostle prayed to the Lord, and prayed three times; and he understood that he had been well heard by the Lord after he recognized that he had prayed against himself. For a person is heard when what he wills is done. But what the Apostle willed was done, because after he recognized that his petition was against himself, he no longer wished to be heard. Hence he says: “Therefore I will gladly boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of [Col. 0571C] Christ may dwell in me” (2 Cor. 12:19).

For it is not simply said here, “Whatever you ask,” but “Whatever you wish, and ask, will be done for you.” “In this my Father has been glorified: that you bear very much fruit and become my disciples.” “In this,” he says, “and for this reason, with me revealing and teaching, my Father has been manifested and glorified in you: that you too, preaching and glorifying him everywhere, may bear much fruit, convert many nations to him, and become my disciples by imitating me not only in life and teaching, but also in the working of miracles.”

“As the Father loved me, I also have loved you. Remain in my love.” For one who is greatly loved ought to love greatly. “If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love, just as [Col. 0571D] I also have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love. I have spoken these things to you, so that my joy may be in you and your joy may be fulfilled.” Christ’s joy is in those who have such joy as Christ has; or, likewise, in those whose holy conduct causes Christ to rejoice.

XLIII. “This is my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you.” Many are the Lord’s commandments, but all are comprehended in this one commandment. Hence the Apostle says that “love is the fulfillment of the Law” [Col. 0572A] (Rom. 13:10): namely, the love by which we love both God and neighbor. “For on these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:40). But these are one because whoever loves God also loves his neighbor, according to this: “For he who does not love his brother, whom he sees, how can he love God, whom he does not see? And we have this commandment from God: that he who loves God should also love his brother” (1 John 4:20–21).

Likewise, whoever loves his neighbor also loves God, provided that he loves that neighbor with true love. For love which considers temporal advantages and does not tend toward the glory of eternal blessedness is not true love. If you love your brother for such benefits, you love him as you love your horse and your donkey. For in these cases love fails together with the benefits themselves. But charity never fails. Hence it is written: “Many waters could not extinguish charity, nor can rivers overwhelm it. For love is strong as death, jealousy hard as hell” (Song 8:7, 6). Of this jealousy the Apostle says: “For I am jealous of you with God’s jealousy” (2 Cor. 11:2).

Therefore the one who loves his neighbor with true love does not love him from carnal affection or earthly advantage, but for God and God’s commandments. The Lord showed that he possessed such love when he said: “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers? Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my mother and sister and brother” (Matt. 12:48–50). “I love,” he says, [Col. 0572C] “my mother and my brothers, not because she is my mother and they are my brothers, but because they do the will of my Father.”

It is clear, then, that whoever loves his neighbor loves God, since he loves his neighbor for God’s sake. Likewise, whoever loves God loves his neighbor, because whoever loves God keeps his commandment. And this is his commandment: that we love one another as he himself loved us. How did he love us? With complete and perfect love. “For no one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends.” Jesus had this love toward us. Let us therefore have it too.

“You are my friends,” but only if you do what I command you. [Col. 0572D] Therefore those who do not keep his commandments are not his friends. “I shall no longer call you servants.” Why? “Because the servant does not know what his master is doing.” What then? “But I have called you friends.” Why this? “Because I have made known to you everything that I heard from my Father.”

He rightly changes the names of those whose functions he changes—not because they have ceased to be servants, but because they have begun to be more intimate. They are no longer sent merely to labor as servants, but are summoned to secret counsels as friends. For he made known to them whatever he had heard from his Father, insofar as it was then to be made known and [Col. 0573A] necessary to them. Hence in what follows he says: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 16:12).

Thus many statements which appear universal must be limited. Such is: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32); likewise: “Preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 15:16); and the Apostle’s words concerning love: “It believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (1 Cor. 13:7); and many similar passages. For the statement just cited, “He will teach you all truth,” must similarly be limited; otherwise what the Apostle says would not be true: “Now I know in part; but then I shall know as I am known” (ibid., 12). [Col. 0573B] For no one in this life knows all truth.

Therefore let Jesus say to his disciples: “Everything that I heard from my Father I have made known to you”—that is, as is understood, what was necessary and to be revealed to you at this time. For not everything is now to be told you, because “it is not yours to know the times or seasons which the Father has placed in his own power.” [Note: [Col. 0573D] Augustine also raised this question in Tractate 86 and resolved it by saying that in the future blessed life all things will be known to God’s friends. Chrysostom differs, Homily 77, no. 1: “When he says, ‘Everything that I heard,’ he wishes to signify nothing else than that he speaks nothing foreign, but what he heard from the Father.”]

“You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain.” What, then, does the Church mean when it says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands” (Song 5:16), if they did not choose him? What also does the Psalmist mean when he says: “And with the chosen one you will be chosen” (Ps. 17:27)? The Lord therefore chose his disciples, and the disciples also chose the Lord. But he chose them first, and they chose him afterward. Certainly they would not have done so unless he had first chosen them. He chose them so that they might be his disciples; they chose him so that he might be their Lord.

“I chose you.” For what purpose? That you should go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature, and bear fruit. This fruit means the multitude of all believers. Hence it fittingly follows: “And that your fruit should remain.” This is what he says elsewhere: “He who believes in me shall not die forever” (John 11:26). And: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John 16:23).

What the Lord promised would happen, we see fulfilled. For we know that the apostles, in the name of Jesus Christ, gave sight to the blind, healed paralytics, cleansed lepers, raised the dead, [Col. 0573D] and received all other things for which they asked the Father in the name of the Son. Yet the Apostle says: “Lest I should be exalted by the greatness of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me. On account of this I asked the Lord three times that it might depart from me; and he said to me: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:7–9). [Col. 0574A] It is as though he said: “You ask against yourself; you seek things contrary to your good; you ask to be stripped of the breastplate of strength.”

Then the Apostle, once he understood the reason, greatly rejoiced that he had not been heard, saying: “Therefore I will gladly boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (ibid.). He was therefore well heard who rejoices precisely because he was not heard. [Note: [Col. 0574D] Thus far the names.]

XLIV. This I command you: that you love one another. Great is the power of charity, which is so often commended to the disciples by the Lord. Whoever keeps this one commandment fulfils the Law and the Prophets. For concerning it the prophet says that “God will make a word shortened upon the earth” (Isa. 10:22). “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you.” Do not, he says, wonder if the world hates you [Col. 0574B]. Do not wonder if lovers of the world persecute you and seek to destroy you.
