Rather, know and remember that they not only hated me before you—me who am greater than all and Lord—but even killed me. “If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own.” For how are those not of the world who were born from human beings and made from the earth?

[Note: Col. 0574D. St Gregory, Book XI, Epistle 2: “By ‘the world,’ namely, he denotes carnal hearts, which love the world.” St Augustine, Tractate 87: “They too were from that source, from which they were chosen so that they might no longer be of it.”]

They certainly had been of the world; but by that time they were no longer of the world, because they had no love for the glory and pleasures of the world. Hence it follows: “But because you are not of the world, and I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.” For he did not say, “because you were not of the world,” but rather, “because you are not of the world”; since, although at that time they were no longer among the lovers of this world, they had nevertheless been taken and chosen out of the world [Col. 0574C]. Therefore the world—that is, lovers of the world—did not love them, because they saw them to be opposed both to themselves and to their works. Thus they also said of our Saviour: “Come, let us kill the righteous man, because he is contrary to our works” (Wis. 2:12).

“Remember my word which I spoke to you: A servant is not greater than his master.” Let us hear for what purpose he said this. “If they persecuted me,” he says, “they will persecute you also. If they kept my word, they will keep yours also.” Do not doubt that what you see happening to me will happen in you as well. But they will do all these things to you, not because of you, but because of my name, which will be preached by you. And this is because they do not know him who sent me. For if they knew the Father, they would know also the Son, whose Father he is [Col. 0574D]. But why do they not know him? Because they are unwilling to know. Now to know is to believe. He came to them, spoke to them, opened the Scriptures, revealed the truth, and performed many signs and unheard-of miracles. Yet they were unwilling to believe him. They therefore have no excuse. And this is what he says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin.”

What does this mean: “If he had not come, they would not have sin”? Were the Jews, then, without sin before he came who came to take away sins? They certainly had sins; but they would not have had this sin if Christ had not come. This must not be understood of every sin, but of the sin [p. 280] of unbelief, by which they refused to believe Christ, hated him, and killed him [Col. 0575A]. Hence it follows: “He who hates me hates my Father also.” Let them not regard it as small or slight that they hate me, since in hating me they hate the Father also. For “I and the Father are one.” “If I had not done among them works which no one else did, they would not have sin.” This alone ought to have sufficed for the Jews: that he said he was the Son of God and performed such great miracles. He certainly could not have done these if he were lying. “But now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father.” Yet all this happened in order that the saying written in their Law might be fulfilled (Ps. 24:19): “They hated me without cause.”

But someone may say: What then was it to them, if the Jews did this in order that the saying of the Law might be fulfilled? Very much indeed. Their own wickedness was the cause why the Prophet foretold this concerning them. Even if he had not foretold it, it would nevertheless have happened. Thus, although what he foretold could not fail to occur, it was not the prophetic saying, but their wickedness, that was the cause of so great an evil.

[Note: Cols. 0575D–0576D. St Augustine, Tractate 89: “What then is meant by: ‘If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin’? Were the Jews without sin before Christ came to them in the flesh? Who, even the most foolish, would say this? But he wishes a certain great sin—not every sin, as though under a general name—to be understood. … This is because they did not believe in Christ, who came precisely in order that he might be believed in. This sin, if he had not come, they certainly would not have had.” So also Bede.]

XLV. “But when the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father—he will bear witness concerning me. And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.” [Col. 0575C]

Our Saviour always mingles joyful things with sorrowful ones, in order to console the grieving hearts of his disciples. “When the Paraclete comes,” he says—*Paraclete* meaning “Comforter”—“he will bear witness concerning me.” He will make both you and many others understand most perfectly who and what I am. For he himself speaks in you and through you. Therefore, “when you stand before kings and governors, do not be anxious how or what you are to speak. For in that hour what you are to speak will be given you. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:19–20). He himself, then, will bear witness concerning me, and by his power and inspiration an innumerable multitude of people will be converted to me. Nor will he alone do so: you too will bear witness to me, because you have been with me from the beginning [Col. 0575D].

That is, you already know many things which you heard from me from the beginning, since you have been with me ever since then; and concerning these things you will bear witness to me. For they had no need to learn again what they had learned from Wisdom itself and had already committed to memory. For the doctrine of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one and the same. Although each may appear to act personally in certain matters, the operation of all three is one [Col. 0576A]. Those therefore whom the Son teaches are also taught by the Father and the Holy Spirit; and likewise in other matters. For they are one, everywhere together and inseparable.

In a few words in this passage it is shown both that the Holy Spirit comes from himself and that he proceeds from the Father and the Son. For in the words, “when he comes,” he is shown to come from himself. But when the Lord says, “whom I shall send to you from the Father,” he is shown to proceed from both.

[Note: Col. 0576D. Council of Florence, session 23; and the interrogation of Toledo, no. 25 and following.]

For what does “whom I shall send to you from the Father” mean except, “whom the Father and I shall send to you”? He is sent by both because he proceeds from both. But because the Father is from no one, the Son from the Father, and the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, the Lord says, “who proceeds from the Father.” It is as though he said: The Holy Spirit proceeds from him from whom I too came forth and came into the world [Col. 0576B]. For, as is evident in this book, the Son has many things in common with the Father, which nevertheless he refers not to himself but to the honour of the Father.

Luke the Evangelist relates most fully in the Acts of the Apostles how and when the Holy Spirit came upon Christ’s disciples. For he says: “When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, all the disciples were together in the same place. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a violent rushing wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And divided tongues, as of fire, appeared to them, and the Holy Spirit rested upon each one of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in diverse tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:1–3).

The Holy Spirit rightly came on the fiftieth day, because he is the remission of all sins. For the fiftieth year, which signified this day, is called the Jubilee: that is, the year of remission, in which slaves were granted freedom and every inheritance returned to its proper owners. This was fulfilled when the leaders of the Church were baptized in the Holy Spirit and freed from every slavery of vices [Col. 0576C].

[Note: Col. 0576D. He treats this at length; and Nazianzen also observed it, Oration 44, On Holy Pentecost, p. 706, Paris edition, 1630.]

Thus the Lord himself says: “John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days hence” (Acts 1:5). “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of God” (John 3:3). On this day, then, both inheritance [p. 281] and freedom were restored to us, because he without whom inheritance and freedom cannot be possessed was given to us [Col. 0576D]. Our inheritance is the kingdom of God, into which one does not enter except through water and the Holy Spirit. On this day, therefore, the human race came to the Jubilee; on this day, to the year of freedom and remission. In this year the apostles began to sound the trumpet, to speak, and to preach in all languages [Col. 0577A]. For those trumpets signified the trumpets by which, at the beginning of the Jubilee, that whole land was then prepared for the festival.

The Holy Spirit appeared in fire so that we might understand most clearly that by his presence the eyes of the mind are enlightened, sins are burned away, and the hearts of believers are kindled with the fire of charity. But because this fire had the appearance of tongues, he showed himself to be the one who speaks in the saints; and, in a manner of speaking, he touched tongues with tongues and thus instructed the apostles to speak.

It follows, [CHAPTER XVI]: “I have spoken these things to you so that you may not be scandalized.” From what? Do you wish to hear from what? “They will put you out of the synagogues”; they will reject you as wicked persons and as transgressors of the Law, and drive you away from the synagogues. But you, remembering my words, do not be scandalized [Col. 0577B], but endure all things patiently and confidently. “I have told you that they will put you out of the synagogues.” Behold, I say something more: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is rendering service to God.”

The whole world will conspire against you. The entire army of Satan will be armed against you. On one side the Jews, on the other the Gentiles: the former because of observance of the Law, the latter because of the worship of their gods. All will abominate you to such an extent that whoever kills you will think he renders a great service to God. “And they will do these things to you because they have not known the Father or me.” For if they had known the Father and the Son, they would certainly have understood that they were mistaken; thus they would have abandoned their error and come to faith.

“But I have spoken these things to you so that, when their hour comes, you may remember that I told you” [Col. 0577C]. Why should you remember? So that amid those very tribulations and distresses you may fight more constantly and firmly, when you recognize that I foreknew and foretold everything. “But I did not tell you these things from the beginning, because I was with you.” For if he were always bodily present with them, there would be no need to fortify them beforehand with such consolation. Hence it follows:

XLVI. “But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’” Blessed Peter had said above: “Lord, where are you going?” (John 13:36). But now, taught and instructed by all his words, none asks where he is going, because they know with complete certainty that he is going to the Father. Why should they ask what they knew and concerning which they had no doubt? “But because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart.” For he saw them grieving at his departure, which they had just heard and understood from his discourse [Col. 0578A]. Who would not grieve to be separated from so great, good, sweet, and delightful a Lord?

“But I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go.” For what can Truth do except speak the truth? He says this, therefore, not so much to confirm his own statement as to console their hearts. “For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I shall send him to you.” Although the Paraclete Spirit was there and everywhere—indeed, “the Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world” (Wis. 1:7)—nevertheless he was to come in another manner. For it had been predestined before the ages that the Son of God should first be born of the Virgin, die, rise again, ascend into heaven, and then at last send the Holy Spirit to console the disciples [Col. 0578B]. Thus it had been ordered and predetermined, and it could not happen otherwise.

[Note: Col. 0577D. Augustine, Tractate 94, gives the reason and explanation: “What then is this: ‘If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you,’ except that you cannot receive the Spirit so long as you persist in knowing Christ according to the flesh?” Likewise St Gregory, *Morals*, Book VIII, chapter 17: “‘If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come,’ as though he openly said: If I do not withdraw my body from the eyes of your attention, I shall not lead you by the consoling Spirit to the understanding of the invisible.” And St Bernard, Sermon 4 on the Ascension of the Lord: “What then is ‘Unless I go away,’ and so forth, except: unless the presence of the flesh is withdrawn from your sight, a mind occupied [with it] does not admit the fullness of spiritual grace; the soul does not receive it; the affection does not grasp it?”]

“And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgement.” He explains this: “Concerning sin, because they do not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father and you will see me no longer; concerning judgement, because the ruler of this world has already been judged.” Behold the three matters in which the Holy Spirit reproves the world—matters concerning which the Son of God had first reproved it. It is therefore as though he said: I indeed go to the Father, but I send you the Paraclete Spirit to teach, strengthen, and fortify you in my place; through you and in you he will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgement [Col. 0578C].

Concerning the sin of unbelief—

[Note: Cols. 0577D–0578D. Augustine, Book III, Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians, chapter 3: “Unbelief makes people children of the devil; this is called the proper sin, as though it alone were sin, when it is not specified what sort of sin is meant. Hence, when the Lord says of the Holy Spirit, ‘He will convict the world concerning sin,’ he intended unbelief to be understood.” And Tractate 95: “He set this sin forward, as though it alone existed, above the others, because while it remains the others are retained, and when it departs the others are forgiven.” But Chrysostom, Homily 78, no. 2: “‘He will convict concerning sin’: that is, he will take away from them every excuse and show that their crimes are without pardon.”]

—because they do not believe [p. 282] in me. And because they do not believe in me, they do not practise righteousness. Therefore the Holy Spirit will also convict them concerning righteousness [Col. 0578D].

[Note: Cols. 0578D–0579D. Chrysostom, in the passage cited: “Concerning righteousness, because I have led an irreproachable life; and the proof of this is that I go to the Father.” Augustine, *Questions on the Old and New Testament*, question 89: “To convict the world is to show it that those things are true which it refused to believe. For it refused to believe that the Saviour came from God; but the Saviour, having maintained righteousness, did not shrink from returning to him who sent him, and by returning proved that he had come from there: because, he says, no one ascends to God except one who descended from God. When the powers saw him ascending, they were confounded, seeing that true what they had hoped was false. Thus this righteousness convicts them, because he was proved righteous by returning to the place from which he had come.” Augustine otherwise, Tractate 95: “How, then, is the world to be convicted concerning righteousness, except concerning the righteousness of believers? … It is convicted concerning the righteousness of those who believe, for the very comparison with believers is the condemnation of unbelievers. … Therefore the world is convicted concerning its own sin, but concerning another’s righteousness; just as darkness is convicted by light. … For how great is the evil of those who do not believe may appear not only in itself, but also from the good of those who believe.”]

But why does he do this in my place and not I myself? Because I go to the Father and you will see me no longer. For he could not make this reproof unless he were ascending bodily into heaven and no longer remaining bodily in this world. And the Holy Spirit will convict the world not only concerning sin and righteousness, but also concerning judgement. What judgement? That concerning which he said above [Col. 0579A]: “Now is the judgement of the world; now the ruler of this world will be cast out” (John 12:31). Hence it is rightly said here: “Concerning judgement, because the ruler of this world has already been judged”—that is, has been cast out.

[Note: Cols. 0579D–0580D. St Augustine, in the passage cited: “Therefore the world is convicted by the Holy Spirit concerning that judgement by which the ruler of the world—the devil—has been judged, because it is judged with its ruler, whom they imitate in pride and impiety. … Let people therefore believe in Christ, lest they be convicted concerning the sin of their unbelief, by which all sins are retained. Let them pass into the number of believers, lest they be convicted concerning the righteousness of those whom, though justified, they do not imitate. Let them beware of the coming judgement, lest they be judged with the ruler of the world whom, though judged, they imitate.” Bede quotes these words of Augustine on this passage.]

For the Psalmist speaks of such a judgement: “Judge my judgement, O Lord, and my cause.” Again: “Judge my judgement and redeem me” (Ps. 118:154). What, then, is the judgement of the world except the redemption of the world? What is the judgement of the world except the judgement in which the ruler of the world is judged, condemned, and cast out of the hearts of believers? Therefore the world is convicted concerning this judgement, because, ungrateful for so great a benefit, it still follows the ruler of the world. Thus the world is convicted concerning sin, because it refused to believe in Christ; it is convicted also concerning righteousness, which it heard him teach but refused to keep [Col. 0579B]; and it is convicted concerning the judgement by which the ruler of the world has been condemned and the world itself liberated. Yet, ungrateful for so great a benefit, it does not yet follow Christ, the author of its salvation, but rather the devil, its deceiver.

“I have many things still to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when he comes, the Spirit of truth, he will teach you all truth.” “I have already told you many things,” he says. “I still have many things to say to you, which you cannot now bear because I do not yet wish to pour into you that great fullness of my Spirit.” Why? So that all things may happen in their proper time: that I may first ascend into heaven and then finally “pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and they shall prophesy” (Acts 2:18).

“But when he comes, the Spirit of truth,” who teaches nothing but truth, whatever things he teaches you, without any admixture of falsehood, he will teach you all truth whole and perfect [Col. 0579C]. “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come.” Thus the Lord also says of himself: “I do not speak from myself” (John 14:10). And again: “The word which you have heard is not mine” (John 5:24). As we explained above, this is as though he said: “I am not from myself” (John 12:49). For the Father is from no one; the Son proceeds from the Father; and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. He does not, therefore, speak from himself because he is not from himself [Col. 0580A]. Yet he speaks also from himself, because “the Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3:8); but not from himself alone, because the Father and Son are one with him. Therefore three speak in one, because the three are one. Let him say, then: “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak.”

[Note: Col. 0580D. Augustine, Tractate 99: “Thus we must understand what was said concerning the Holy Spirit: ‘For he will not speak from himself,’ and so forth, so as to understand that he is not from himself. … Therefore he will not speak from himself because he is not from himself; but whatever he hears he will speak. He will hear from him from whom he proceeds. From whom he has being, from him he has knowledge; from him, therefore, he has hearing, which is nothing other than knowledge.”]

What is “hears”? For it must not be understood as though in that invisible and inseparable Trinity some vocal and clamorous conversation takes place. They hear one another in that they know and will the same thing. The Holy Spirit therefore speaks whatever he hears; that is, whatever he recognizes that the Father and Son will. For as the will is common, so too is the hearing.

“He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and declare it to you.” And he explains this: “All things whatsoever the Father has are mine. Therefore I said that he will receive from what is mine and declare it to you” [Col. 0580B]. “He will glorify me,” he says—that is, he will reveal my glory to you and, through you, make known to many others that I am the Son of God. And this is because he will receive from me. For if the Holy Spirit receives from the things that are the Father’s, he certainly receives also from the things that are the Son’s, because all things whatsoever the Father has are the Son’s. The Holy Spirit [p. 283] is therefore the Spirit of the Son, since he is the Spirit of the Father.

[Note: Col. 0580D. Augustine, Tractate 99: “The Holy Spirit is not the Spirit of one of them but of both. … There are many testimonies by which it is clearly shown that he is the Spirit both of the Father and of the Son.”]

For the Father is related to the Son, and the Son to the Father; but the Holy Spirit is related to the Father and the Son, while nothing is related to the Holy Spirit. For the Father is the Father of the Son, and the Son is the Son of the Father; but the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and the Son. Yet the Father is not the Father of the Spirit, nor is the Son the Son of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0580C]. Nothing, therefore, is related to the Holy Spirit.

Since the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of both Father and Son, from whom he has being, from them he also has being wise and true. For for him, to be is to be wise and true, and similarly in other respects. He is the Spirit of wisdom and understanding; he is also the Spirit of all truth. But he has and receives this from the Father and the Son. This is what the Lord means when he says: “He will receive from what is mine and declare it to you.” But because these things are common to all three and common substantially, the Lord could, had he wished, have said: “He will receive from what is mine and from what is his, and declare it to you.” For when the Son preached, he too received both from what was his and from the things of the Father and Holy Spirit [Col. 0581A], because the wisdom and truth of all three are one. Hence he himself said: “My doctrine is not mine” (John 7:16).

[Note: Col. 0581D. Thus far the homily.]

XLVII. “A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me, because I go to the Father.” For the Lord lay in the tomb for a short time, during which the disciples could not see him. And after the resurrection they saw him again after a short time; for, as Luke says, “For forty days he appeared to them, speaking of the kingdom of God” (Acts 1:3). This is what he says: “A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me.” But why “a little while”? Because I go to the Father. For if he had not gone to the Father, they would have seen him not for a little while, but for a long time.

The disciples, not understanding this [Col. 0581B], said: “What is this that he says to us: ‘A little while, and you will not see me; and again a little while, and you will see me’; and, ‘because I go to the Father’? What is this that he says: ‘A little while’? We do not know what he is saying.” The disciples knew that the Lord was going to the Father, because he had already announced this to them many times. Thus he said above: “I go to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’” Therefore none asks me now where I am going, because you know with complete certainty that I go to the Father. This alone, then, was what the apostles could not understand and wished to learn: what that “little while” meant, in which they would both see him and not see him.

[Note: Col. 0581D. Augustine, Tractate 101: “For this was what troubled them: because he said ‘a little while,’ and so forth. For in the preceding passages, because he had not said ‘a little while’ but had said, ‘I go to the Father,’ and so forth, he appeared to them to have spoken plainly.”]

But Jesus knew that they wished to ask him, and said to them: “Are you asking one another about this, because I said: ‘A little while, and you will not see me; and again a little while, and you will see me’?” [Col. 0581C] “Amen, amen, I say to you: you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy.”

This, then, is the explanation, though obscure. It is as though he said: You do not now understand what “a little while, and you will not see me” signifies. But after a little while, when I have died and been buried and been removed from your sight, when you weep and lament over my death, while lovers of the world—the scribes and Pharisees, namely—rejoice at my death, then you will indeed understand what “a little while, and you will not see me” means. You will also understand what the following means: “And again a little while, and you will see me” [Col. 0581D], when, as I rise on the third day, your sorrow will be turned into joy.

[Note: Cols. 0581D–0582D. Augustine, in the passage cited: “What was then obscure to them and soon made manifest is, of course, now manifest to us: for after a little while he suffered and they did not see him; again, after a little while he rose and they saw him.”]

“For the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord” (John 20:20). Hence the Psalmist says: “Weeping will lodge at evening, but joy in the morning” (Ps. 29:6). “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow because her hour has come; but when she has borne the child, she no longer remembers the anguish, because a human being has been born into the world.” “And you also, therefore, will indeed have sorrow then” [Col. 0582A]. Thus, he says, it will be with you as it is with a pregnant woman in labour. When she gives birth, she has sorrow, because she fears that the hour of death has come. But such great joy follows childbirth that she does not remember all that sorrow, because of the child’s birth.

So too the apostles, when they gave birth and baptized, when through faith they begot children of adoption, had sorrow, because they gave birth by dying. They gave birth, indeed, as the Apostle says: “My little children, with whom I am again in labour until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19). Again: “Though you may have many pedagogues, you do not have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus through the Gospel I begot you” (1 Cor. 4:15). Rachel, who died in childbirth, signified this. Hence, as she was dying, she called her son Benoni, that is, “son of my sorrow” (Gen. 35:18) [Col. 0582B]. The apostles therefore gave birth in pain, because for this kind of birth [p. 284] they were killed, tortured, and suffered many pains and many distresses. Blessed is this birth, by which so great an offspring of such noble children sprang up among all nations.

It follows: “But I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.” For when does he not see those whom he always sees, everywhere, and sees in all things? He therefore speaks of that vision which is eternal and has no end, which is always in joy, and whose gladness and blessedness cannot be taken away. Hence he says: “And no one will take your joy from you.” “And on that day you will ask me nothing.” On what day?

[Note: Col. 0582D. Augustine raises this question and resolves it in the same manner in Tractate 101.]

Certainly on that day on which this your great and such joy will be fulfilled [Col. 0582C]. It is clear, therefore, that after the judgement, once blessedness has been received, no prayers will be necessary. At present the intercessions of the saints are necessary both for those who are in this age and for those who are in purgatorial states. This is that day of which it is written: “For one day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83:11). On this day prayers will cease, because there will be no one to whom mercy and pardon can be granted: some having been eternally condemned, others called to eternal blessedness.

XLVIII. “Amen, amen, I say to you: whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you.” If we consider to whom these words are spoken specially and properly, the solution is easy. For the Lord was speaking to the Apostles, whom we read to have enlightened the blind, healed paralytics, raised the dead, and performed many other miracles in the name of Christ Jesus. Nor do we hear that they asked anything of the Father in the name of the Son which they did not receive. Hence the Apostle James, rebuking certain persons who asked wrongly, says: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (Jas. 4:3). And likewise: “If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach; and it shall be given him. But let him ask in faith, without doubting” (Jas. 1:5).

It is therefore evident from these words that the Apostle also was not heard because he had not asked in Jesus’ name, nor asked rightly. [Note: [Col. 0583C] These are Augustine’s very well-known words, which he repeats on this passage in Tractate 102: “It has already been set forth above . . . [Col. 0583D] that whatever is asked contrary to the purpose of salvation is not asked in the Savior’s name”; Gregory the Great has similar words in Homily 27 on the Gospels.] Yet, if we call him unheard who, as one heard in a better way, rejoices that he did not receive what he asked, he did not wish to be heard after he learned that he had asked wrongly. And he is better heard precisely in this: that he was not heard concerning the things for which he asked. For he is heard, not regarding the things he asked for, but regarding the things he wished for. No one is so heard as the person who usefully receives what he desires.

It follows: “Until now you have asked nothing in my name.” What does this mean? For we read that Christ’s disciples, even before the Lord said these things to them, healed many sick people and cast out demons in the name of Jesus Christ. Thus, as Luke says, when they returned to him with joy, they said: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name” (Luke 10:17). We also read that they rebuked a certain man who did not follow them because he had cast out demons in Jesus’ name. What then does he mean by saying: “Until now you have asked nothing in my name,” when it is clear that they had asked for so many things in Jesus’ name?

Perhaps he says that they had not asked in Jesus’ name—that is, that they had not asked for things pertaining to salvation. Thus some wish to understand this passage. [Note: [Col. 0583D] Thus Gregory the Great, Homily 27 on the Gospels: “For if that which is not beneficial is asked, it is not asked of the Father in Jesus’ name. Hence the Lord says even to these same Apostles, while they were still weak: ‘Until now you have asked nothing in my name,’ as if he were plainly saying: You have not asked in the Savior’s name, because you do not know how to seek eternal salvation.”] But this is not true.

What then shall we say? The disciples say: “Even the demons are subject to us in your name” (Matt. 7:22). The Master says: “Until now you have asked [Col. 0583C] nothing in my name.” Therefore take what he said above: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you.” Then join to it what follows: “Until now you have asked nothing”—understand, “of the Father”—“in my name.” For because they saw not the Father but the Son, they looked to the Son alone. But after the Son ascended into heaven, better instructed and taught by the Spirit of truth, they began to ask both the Father and the Son.

Therefore the Son wills that what is asked in his name should be asked of the Father, and that the Father should always be honored in the Son. [Note: [Col. 0583D] Augustine, Tractate 102, gives two explanations: “Either because you have not asked in my name, which name you have not known as it ought to be known; or, you have not asked anything, because, in comparison with the thing you ought to have asked for, what you have asked must be regarded as nothing.” The first of these approaches A.’s explanation.]

He continues concerning the same petition: “Ask, and you shall receive, that your joy may be full.” He said that they should ask, that they should ask the Father, and that they should ask in his name. Now he teaches them what they ought to ask for. “Ask,” he says. What? “That your joy may be full.” For that joy is full which is perfect and complete, which never ends and is eternal. [Note: [Col. 0583D] Augustine, at the place cited: “The full joy of which he speaks is surely not carnal but spiritual joy; and when it is so great that nothing can any longer [Col. 0584C–D] be added to it, then undoubtedly it will be full.”]

This, therefore, ought to be sought: that one may attain such joy. But the things which separate a person from that joy ought not to be sought. Let us therefore seek temporal things in such a way that the mind and desire are not separated from eternal joy. Let us pass through temporal goods in such a way that we do not lose eternal ones. Let us always hear what is said here: “Ask, that your joy may be full. And you shall receive.” You shall indeed receive—but not now, not in this life. For this joy is not received except after this life. [Col. 0584B] “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. 6:33).

“I have spoken these things to you in proverbs. The hour is coming when I shall no longer speak to you in proverbs, but shall openly announce the Father to you.” This is what another Evangelist says: “Jesus spoke in parables, and without parables he did not speak to them” (Matt. 13:34). For in proverbs one thing is heard and another is understood. But by that hour in which he says he will speak to them no longer in proverbs but openly concerning the Father, the entire time after his resurrection is signified—whether he speaks to them visibly in person, or invisibly through the Holy Spirit. [Note: [Col. 0584D] Thus Chrysostom, Homily 79, no. 2: “This is the time of the resurrection . . . for forty days he remained with them, spoke with them, ate with them, and expounded the things pertaining to the kingdom of God.” Augustine, *On the Trinity*, I, ch. 10, and Gregory, *Morals*, XXX, ch. 22, explain this of the future blessed life. Augustine, however, in Tractate 102 rejects this latter explanation because of the following words: “In that day you shall ask in my name.” For when we have come in the age to come to the kingdom . . . what shall we ask, when our desire is satisfied with good things? . . . For asking belongs to some need; and there will be no need where that satisfaction exists. He therefore explains it “so that Jesus may be understood to have promised that he would make his disciples spiritual from being carnal or merely animal . . . such as he was who said: ‘We speak wisdom among the perfect’; and, ‘I could not speak to you as to spiritual persons,’” etc.]

For when the Holy Spirit came, what they had previously been ignorant of concerning the Father was then openly and clearly announced and revealed to them. Nor was it necessary [Col. 0584C] for them thereafter to say: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14:8), since they saw the Son in the Father, the Father in the Son, and the Holy Spirit in both.

“In that day you shall ask in my name.” In that day, he says, you shall ask in my name, so that in the works of power performed through you my name may be glorified, and also the Father glorified, whom you will ask in my name. For he did not say, “You shall ask my name,” but, “You shall ask in my name,” to show us from whom and in whom we ought to ask.

Above he had said: “In that day you shall ask me nothing.” Now he says: “In that day you shall ask in my name.” This would surely be contrary [Col. 0585A] if it were understood of the same day. This day, then, is the day of this age; the other is the day of the other age. This is before judgment; that is after judgment.

“And I do not say to you that I shall ask the Father for you. For the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came forth from God.” After I have ascended into heaven, he says, I do not say that I shall ask the Father for you. Rather, you yourselves ask him in my name, and whatever you wish, he will give you. For he loves you because you have loved me and believed that I came forth from God.

“I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father.” He came forth from the Father because he was begotten of the Father. [Note: [Col. 0585D] Augustine, Tractate 102: “He came forth from the Father because he is from the Father; and he came into the world because he showed to the world his body, which he assumed from the Virgin. He left the world by bodily departure; he went to the Father by the ascension of his humanity; yet he did not abandon the world in the governance of his providence.”] He came into the world because, by assuming humanity, he made himself visible to the world. How he came forth is unknown, because how he was begotten is unknown. But he leaves the world [Col. 0585B] and goes to the Father, not according to divinity, by which he is everywhere, but according to humanity, by which he is localized.

His disciples say to him: “Behold, now you speak openly and say no proverb. Now we know that you know all things, and that you have no need for anyone to question you.” We wished, they say, to question you because we understood very little of the things you were saying; but without any questioning from us, you yourself have explained to us those things about which we wished to question you. Therefore we know for certain that you know all things and have no need for anyone to question you. And in this way we believe that you came forth from God.

Jesus answered them: “Do you now believe? Behold, the hour is coming—and has now come—when you shall be scattered, each one to his own place, and shall leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me.” When you flee, he says, [Col. 0585C] and each seeks his own hiding place, you will leave me alone as regards your consolation, but not alone as regards the Father’s aid; for the Father is with me and does not leave me alone.

“These things I have spoken to you, that you may have peace in me.” I have commended peace to you; I leave peace to you. I desire that in me and because of me you may have peace with all people—but in such a way that you do not abandon me. “In the world you shall have tribulation; but take courage: behold, I have conquered the world.” As he was about to announce wars, he first sent peace before them, so that they might fight not in hatred but in love, and might not regard as enemies those by whom they are afflicted, but might pray for them, that they may be converted. Let them be confident and not fear the world, because it has been conquered together with the prince of the world. That army is not to be feared which has already been overcome with its own prince. [Note: [Col. 0585D] Leo the Great, Sermon 72, 2, *On the Resurrection*, ch. 4: “Because the earth is full of the Lord’s mercy, Christ’s victory is indeed present with us, so that what he said may be fulfilled: ‘Do not fear, because I have conquered the world.’ Whether, therefore, we fight against worldly ambition, against the desires of the flesh, or against the darts of heretics, let us always be armed with the Lord’s cross.”]

XLIX. [CHAPTER XVII.] Jesus said these things and, lifting up his eyes to heaven, said: “Father, the hour has come: glorify your Son, that your Son also may glorify you.” [Col. 0585D–0586A] He says this not of the hour of the Passion, which was already at hand, but of the hour of the resurrection, which was not far off. [Note: [Col. 0585D] Augustine, Tractate 104: “Some understand the Son to have been glorified by the Father in this: that he did not spare him, but delivered him up for us all. But if he is said to have been glorified by the Passion, how much more by the resurrection? For in the Passion his humiliation rather than his glory is commended.” The former interpretation, concerning Christ glorified in the Passion, is that of Chrysostom, Homily 80, no. 1. Hilary explains this passage at length in *On the Trinity*, III.]

For it was not in the Passion but in the resurrection that both Father and Son were glorified. Had he not risen, no one would have believed in the Son or in the Father through the Son. Jesus prays, not for himself, but for us. For why should he pray to the Father by speaking, he who is always in the Father and in whom the Father always is? Therefore he prays to teach us to pray, and always to place our hope not in our own powers but in God’s aid.

“As you have given him power over all flesh, that he may give eternal life to all that you have given him.” Thus, he says, glorify your Son, as you have given him power over all flesh. For he has this power over all flesh: to give eternal life to all that has been given him, to all that has been predestined to life, and to save it through himself and not through another. But all this must be referred to his humanity. [Note: [Col. 0586D] See Epiphanius, *Heresies*, 69.] For it is that humanity to which power over all flesh has been given.

“And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.” For knowing and believing in this way is called eternal life because one who does not know and believe in this way shall not have eternal life. Here the cause is put for the effect.

“I have glorified you upon the earth. I have completed the work which you gave me to do.” The Son glorified the Father by praising and proclaiming him and by performing many signs and miracles in his name. Thus he himself said: “The works which I do in the name of my Father, these bear witness concerning me” (John 5:36). This [Col. 0586C] is his work, which he had already completed. Only death remained, by which he would restore life to the world.

“And now glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world existed.” Grant me, Father, he says, that glory which I had with you before the world existed. For this is the sense of the sequence. What does “with yourself” mean, except by calling me to yourself? [Note: [Col. 0586D] Augustine, Tractate 105: “For he glorified the Father upon earth by preaching to the nations; but the Father glorified him with himself by setting him at his own right hand.”] Since he assumed flesh, lived among human beings, died as a man, and was buried, unless he rose again and ascended into heaven he would have been thought not merely a man, but even a magician and deceiver. But because he rose and ascended into heaven, he was so glorified in our minds that we believe him to be such as he was with the Father before the world was made.

“I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world.” For this name is known only to those who believe that he is the Son [Col. 0587A] and that the other is the Father. The Jews did not know this name when they said: “According to the Law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John 19:8).

“They were yours, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word.” They were yours, he says, because they were predestined to life. And you gave them to me to teach, redeem, and sanctify. And they kept your word, which they heard while I taught them.

“Now they have known that all things which you gave me are from you.” How or from what did they know this? “Because the words which you gave me I have given them, and they have received them.” And in them they truly knew that I came forth from you—that is, that you begot me—and they believed that you sent me—that is, that you willed me to assume flesh and become man.

“I pray for them; I do not pray for the world, [Col. 0587B] but for those whom you gave me, because they are yours. And all mine are yours, and yours are mine.” These things are not difficult for those who always remember the two natures in Christ. His praying and his saying that something was given to him belong to his humanity. But his equality with the Father and his common possession of all things with the Father belong to divinity. [Note: [Col. 0587D] See Cyril, p. 966: “He who asks, therefore, as man, also in turn distributes as God.” See Chrysostom, Homily 81, where he teaches at length that Christ speaks as man in accommodation to the disciples’ weakness: “For if he had said, ‘I preserve them,’ they would not have believed,” etc.]

But observe that the Lord says he does not pray for the world—that is, for lovers of the world. What shall we say here except what the Apostle says: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to him who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’ Or does not the potter have power over the clay, to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. 9:20).

But when he says, “And I have been glorified in them,” he appears to commend the disciples’ faith. [Col. 0587C] “And now I am no longer in the world, and these are in the world, and I come to you.” He already counts himself as not being in the world because he is about to leave the world suddenly and shortly. Hence he adds: “And I come to you.” But he says that those are in the world whom, as he departs, he leaves in the world.

Or again, he was not in the world because he did not fear the world’s adversities, seek the world’s glory, or experience the world’s pleasures. “Holy Father, preserve in your name those whom you gave me, that they may be one, as we also are.” Preserve them, holy Father, he says, in your name, so that your name may never fail in them, but you may always be their Father and they your children. For the Father’s name perishes in those who, by sinning, cease to be children.

“That they may be one as [Col. 0587D] we also are”: that they may never depart from the truth of faith, and may always remain steadfast and of one mind in charity. [Note: [Col. 0587D] Cyril, p. 972: “He wills that the disciples be preserved in unity of good will and purposes, their minds and spirits in some sense mingled with one another, and that they advance to that unity, so that this union of wills may be an image of the natural unity in the Father and Son.” Thus Ambrose, *On Faith*, IV, ch. 7; John Chrysostom, Homily 82, no. 2; and Innocent III, at the Fourth Lateran General Council: “When, therefore, Truth prays to the Father for his faithful: ‘I will that they may be one in us, as we are one,’ the term ‘one’ is understood of the faithful as the union of charity in grace.”]

[Col. 0588A] “While I was with them, I preserved them in your name.” Although he was still bodily with them, he nevertheless speaks as though he were no longer with them. But what does “I preserved them in your name” mean except: I so formed them that they would always retain and glorify your name? Hence he himself says: “I came in the name of my Father,” that is, to glorify not myself but my Father’s name.

“Those whom you gave me I have kept, and none of them has perished except the son of perdition, that the Scripture may be fulfilled.” This is said of Judas, who alone perished from among the twelve Apostles.

“But now I come to you, and I say these things in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves.” When he says, “Now I come to you,” it is as though he said: “After a few days I come to you.” But how does he say these things [Col. 0588B] in the world if, as he said above, he is not in the world? This teaches us that in one respect he was in the world, and in another he was not. How he was in the world is clear; how he was also not in the world has already been stated. For he was not in the world because he was not in the world’s pleasures. [Note: [Col. 0588D] Cyril, p. 980: “For Christian conduct and life, which we follow to the utmost of our ability, are wholly remote from earthly thinking and worldly ways; thus among worldly people we shall by no means be reckoned as worldly . . . just as the divine Paul himself writes concerning himself and Christ: ‘Through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.’”]

“I have given them your word, and the world has hated them.” I have given them, he says, your word—your words and your teaching. And the world has hated them. Why? Because they are not of the world; they are not among those who love the world. If they were of the world, the world would love what was its own. But how are they not of the world? “As I also am not of the world.” According to creation, then, they are of the world; [Col. 0588C] but according to holy conduct they are not of the world. For the Lord himself was, according to the flesh, of the world, since flesh is of the earth and the earth is of the world.

“I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you preserve them from evil”—lest they begin to become of the world. “Sanctify them in truth. Your word is truth. And for them I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth.”

What does “Sanctify them in truth” mean except, “Sanctify them in myself”? For I am truth, because I am your Word and your utterance. But your utterance is truth. And that they may be sanctified in me, for them I shall sanctify, offer, and sacrifice myself, [Note: [Col. 0588D] Cyril, p. 990: “Sanctify them, therefore, Father, he says, in your truth—that is, in me. For your Word is truth—that is, I. For I have sanctified myself for them—that is, I have consecrated and offered myself, dying one for all, so that I might reform them into newness of life and they might be sanctified in truth—that is, in me.”] that they too may be sanctified in truth. Hence it is written of him [Col. 0588D]: “Because he loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood.”

“As you sent me into the world, [Col. 0589A] I also have sent them into the world.” Therefore he sent them for this purpose: that they might preach to, save, and cleanse the world from sins. It was therefore necessary that those sent to sanctify others should themselves be sanctified.

“But I do not pray for these alone, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you; that they also may be one in us, and that the world may believe that you sent me.” What else do these words declare but the unity of the Church and the perfection of charity? [Note: [Col. 0589D] See the remarks above, and Chrysostom, Homily 78 on John, no. 4. Cyril, p. 996: “He seeks the bond of charity, concord, and peace, by which believers may be brought to spiritual unity, so that they imitate the characteristics of the natural and substantial unity understood to exist in Father and Son: namely, agreement of wills in all things and the convergence of minds into unity.”]

“And I have given them the glory which you gave me, that they may be one, as we are one: I in them and you in me, that they may be perfected into one, and that the world may know that you sent me and loved them as you loved me.” I, he says, have given them the glory which you gave [Col. 0589B] me, so that, just as I did, they too might raise the dead, give sight to the blind, cleanse lepers, and drive away demons, [Note: [Col. 0589D] Nearly thus John Chrysostom, Homily 82, no. 2: “And I have given them the glory which you gave me”—through signs, through teaching, and that they may be harmonious.] and by this means appear illustrious and renowned among all nations. By doing these and similar things, may they be one in us, as we are one.

For they are one with God because they too are gods, and because they have one power with God—though they have it not from themselves but from God. Hence the Lord said above: “Remain in me, and I in you, because without me you can do nothing” (John 15:4–5). “I am in them, and you are in me. Therefore you too are in them.” Hence they are made complete and perfect in one. They are my members; I am their head. You are the Father and I the Son. Behold how we are one.

Let the world therefore know [Col. 0589C] through the works of power performed by them and the miracles which they work in my name that you sent me and loved them as you loved me. For you loved them so greatly that you delivered me to death for them.

“Father, I will that those whom you gave me may also be with me where I am.” Why? “That they may see my glory which you gave me.” But what is seeing this glory except being blessed? [Note: [Col. 0589D] Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, IV, ch. 14, no. 1, explains this passage thus.] Hence this same John says: “We know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

“Righteous Father, the world has not known you. But I have known you; and these have known that you sent me. And I have made your name known to them, and I will make it known, that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.”

[Col. 0589D] L. [CHAPTERS XVIII–XIX.] When he had said these things, he went out with his disciples across the brook Cedron. These matters [Col. 0590A] are explained in the other Gospels. Nor is there any contradiction in the fact that here Jesus is written to have been crucified at the sixth hour, while in Mark at the third hour. For the Lord was crucified by the Jews at the third hour, and by the Gentiles and Roman soldiers at the sixth hour—not that he was crucified twice, but because at the third hour he was condemned by the former, and at the sixth hour raised upon the cross by the latter. For the Jews killed Jesus in no other way than by accusing and condemning him and crying, “Crucify, crucify!” [Note: [Col. 0589D] Thus Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm 63*, no. 5: “One Evangelist says that the Lord was crucified at the sixth [Col. 0590D] hour, and another at the third . . . And indeed, when the Lord was raised upon the wood, it was the sixth hour . . . But when we consider the whole context of the reading . . . we find that it could have been the third hour when they cried, ‘Crucify, crucify!’ Therefore they killed him more truly when they cried out.”] Hence they themselves said: “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.”

LI. [CHAPTER XX.] On the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came early, while it was still dark, to the tomb, and saw that the stone had been removed from the tomb. In the literal sense, great love compelled [Col. 0590B] this woman to seek the Lord at the tomb before daylight. But in the spiritual sense, she was still enveloped in darkness, because she had not yet been inwardly enlightened. She believed in Christ’s resurrection. [Note: [Col. 0590D] The mystical or spiritual interpretation is presented first by Peter Chrysologus in Sermons 74 and 75, explaining the phrase, “At the evening that shines forth.”] Thus the Lord also says to her: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father.”

But what wonder if the woman was ignorant of the resurrection when this same disciple beloved of the Lord says of himself that he did not yet know the Scripture, that Christ had to rise from the dead? Therefore she ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, and said to them: “They have taken the Lord from the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him.” Because the Lord was not in the tomb, [Col. 0590C] she believed not that he had risen but that he had been taken away. This was because she was still in darkness and did not yet have the eyes of her mind opened. [Note: [Col. 0590D] Gregory the Great, Homily 22 on the Gospels: “Mary sought in the tomb the author of all things whom she had seen dead in the flesh; and because she did not find him, she believed that he had been stolen. Therefore it was still dark when she came to the tomb.”]

Yet she grieved for Jesus’ body, because she no longer knew where to seek it. Peter therefore went out, and the other disciple, and they came to the tomb. But how did they come? Running, certainly; and this is what he says: “The two were running together, and the other disciple ran ahead more quickly than Peter and came first to the tomb. And when he had bent down, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but did not go in. Then Simon Peter came, following him, and entered the tomb; and he saw the linen cloths lying there, and the cloth which had been upon his head, not lying with the linen cloths, but folded separately in one place. Then [Col. 0590D] the other disciple also entered, who had come first to the tomb, and he saw and believed.”

These two disciples signify two peoples [Col. 0591A] running to Christ and coming to faith: namely, Jews and Gentiles. [Note: [Col. 0591D] Gregory the Great: “What, then, is designated by John but the Synagogue, and what by Peter but the Church? Nor should it seem strange that the Synagogue is said to be signified by the younger man and the Church by the older; for although the Synagogue preceded the Church of the Gentiles in the worship of God, the multitude of the Gentiles preceded the Synagogue in the course of the world.”] The whole Church consists of these. John indeed signifies the Jews, while Peter designates the Gentiles, because the Jewish people began to come to knowledge of the faith before the Gentile people.

John came to the tomb but did not enter at once, because, hearing of Christ’s resurrection, he did not believe. [Note: [Col. 0591D] Gregory the Great: “John saw the linen cloths lying there, yet did not enter, because the Synagogue indeed recognized the mysteries of Holy Scripture, but delayed entering by faith into the Lord’s Passion.”] For if he had entered at once, he would have touched the linen cloths; and when he perceived that Christ was not there, he would have believed that he had risen.

But what do we understand by Christ’s linen cloths, the garments of the Word of God, except the letter with which the Word is clothed and does not appear? That Word, indeed, which “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1), [Col. 0591B] cannot be seen or known unless it has been stripped of the veil of the letter.

John came to the tomb, bent down, saw the linen cloths, but did not touch them, because even to this day the Jews bend down to read, see the letters, but do not understand. For to touch is to understand. Let us now see what Peter also did, who came to the tomb after John. “Simon Peter came,” he says, “following him.” And what did he do? “He entered the tomb.” Had he not entered, he would not have known. He entered, therefore, saw, and carefully observed that only the linen cloths were lying there. And he knew that the one who had formerly lain hidden, wrapped in those linen cloths, had risen.

Thus also, when we approach the book—that is, Christ’s tomb, in which [Col. 0591C] we remember and are reminded of his death and resurrection—by entering through understanding, we unfold the veils of the letter; immediately we know that Christ the Lord has risen. For when we read, “I lay down and slept; I rose again, because the Lord sustained me,” [Note: [Col. 0591D] Psalm 3:6: “I lay down and slept,” etc.] if we enter this tomb with Peter—indeed, we enter if we understand and unfold the veils of the letter—we know that Christ the Lord has risen.

But the Jews do not know this because, even if they see the tomb and the linen cloths—that is, the book and its letters—they do not enter there through understanding. This is the customary manner of speaking by which we say that we cannot enter into a meaning which we are unable to understand.

Let us also consider [Col. 0591D] what that cloth signifies which had been placed over his [Col. 0592A] head. For if, as the Apostle says, “God is the head of Christ” (1 Cor. 11:3), what does the cloth that covers the head signify except that Scripture which speaks of his divinity? [Note: [Col. 0591D] Gregory the Great, at the place cited: “What, brothers, do we suppose it means that the cloth from the Lord’s head was not found in the tomb with the linen cloths, except that, as Paul testifies, God is the head of Christ, and the incomprehensible mysteries [Col. 0592D] of his divinity are set apart from the knowledge of our weakness; and his power transcends the nature of created things?”]

Do you wish to see the cloth which covers Christ’s head? Read the beginning of this Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). Thus it is rightly said of this cloth that it was not placed with the other linen cloths but was folded separately in one place, because there is a great difference between those Scriptures which speak of Christ’s divinity and those which speak of his humanity. Hence, of certain separate sacrifices, no one eats except Aaron and his male sons.

It follows: “Then the other disciple also entered, [Col. 0592B] who had come first to the tomb, and he saw and believed.” This is what the Apostle says: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 11:25). It is therefore first necessary that Peter enter with the whole fullness of the Gentiles, whom he signifies; then afterward John will enter with the Jewish people, whom he designates.

But when he says, “He saw and believed,” this should be understood not strictly of the resurrection, but of what the woman had said: namely, that the Lord had been removed from the tomb. Hence it is added: “For he did not yet know the Scriptures, that he had to rise from the dead.” For he did not yet know the Scriptures because he still saw the linen cloths from afar. We have said that the Scriptures are signified by the linen cloths. [Col. 0592C] The disciples therefore went away again to their own homes.

LII. But Mary stood outside the tomb, weeping. While she was weeping, therefore, she bent down and looked into the tomb. And she saw two angels sitting in white, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain. The disciples depart; the woman remains and weeps. Jesus, the consoler of the sorrowful, is present and beholds the devout woman’s tears. He waits to see what the woman will do and does not immediately reveal himself. She bends down, and it does not suffice that she has seen once.

> [Note: Col. 0592D. Gregory, Homily 25 on the Gospels: “Certainly she had already seen the tomb empty; she had already announced that the Lord had been taken away. Why is it that she bends down again and desires to see again? But for one who loves, it is not enough to have looked once, because the power of love multiplies the eagerness of the search.”]

Nothing is enough for one who loves. She looks into the tomb and sees two angels, who signified nothing better than the two Testaments.

> [Note: Col. 0592D. The same, ibid.: “We may also understand the two Testaments through the two angels, the one earlier and the other following. These angels are joined to one another by the place of the Lord’s body, because, indeed, while both Testaments with one and the same sense proclaim the Lord incarnate, dead, and risen again, the earlier Testament sits, as it were, at the head, and the later Testament at the feet.”]

As they proclaim Christ’s birth, passion, and resurrection, and everything concerning him, we are most fully instructed and taught. Since they had come especially to announce joy and the resurrection, they appear, not without reason but very fittingly, in white. One of the two Testaments, which are prefigured by the angels, stands at the head of the Lord’s tomb, and one at the feet.

> [Note: Col. 0593D. Thus Gregory in the passage cited. Augustine, Tractate 121, and Bede explain it otherwise: “Why was one sitting at the head and the other at the feet? Was it because … they signified that Christ’s Gospel was to be proclaimed, as it were, from head to foot, from beginning to end?”]

For they now speak to us of divinity, now of humanity. By the head we understand Christ’s divinity; by the feet, his humanity. This is what Moses signifies when, speaking of that Paschal lamb and its symbolic meaning, he says: “You shall eat the flesh of the lamb that night with unleavened bread and wild lettuce; you shall devour its head and feet with its entrails” (Exod. 12:9).

But let us hear what the angels say to the weeping woman: “Woman,” they say, “why are you weeping?” This is no time for weeping but for rejoicing: it is a day of gladness, not of grief.

> [Note: Col. 0593D. Augustine, passage cited: “The angels forbade tears: what else did they thereby announce, in a manner, than coming joy? For they said, ‘Why are you weeping?’ as though they were saying, ‘Do not weep.’”]

“We have come to bring you glad news. Rather, look to him whom you so greatly desire to see.” She says to them: “Because they have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.” “Great sorrow,” she says, “compels me to weep; great grief constricts my heart, because they have taken away my Lord from me, and I do not know where they have laid him.”

When she had said this, she turned back and saw Jesus standing there, but did not know that it was Jesus. Jesus says to her: “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom do you seek?” For the Lord knew what she sought; he questioned her not from ignorance but in order to console her. He therefore repeated the question so that, on hearing his voice, she might recognize him.

> [Note: Col. 0593D. Chrysostom, Homily 86, no. 1: “For when he called her ‘Mary,’ then she recognized him. Thus recognition was made perfect not by sight but by the voice.”]

Thinking that he was the gardener, she says to him: “Sir, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.” She speaks as though of one known; and she supposed that everyone knew the one whom she loved.

> [Note: Col. 0593D. Gregory, Homily 25 on the Gospels: “The force of love is accustomed to work this in the mind: that the one whom it itself continually thinks of, it believes no one else to be ignorant of. Rightly this woman does not name the one whom she seeks; yet she says, ‘If you have taken him away,’ because she does not suppose that another can be ignorant of the one for whom she herself mourns with such unceasing longing.”]

Jesus says to her: “Mary.” But when she heard herself called by her own name, she immediately recognized him; and turning from the tomb—from which, because of excessive love, she had been unable to turn her eyes—she said to him: “Rabboni.” The Evangelist explains the meaning of *Rabboni*: it means “Teacher.” As soon as she recognized him, she fell at his feet.

The Lord says to her: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father.” As if he said: “Do not touch with your hands one whom you have not yet touched by faith. Believe that I have risen and that, having despoiled hell, I have already ascended in soul to heaven; do not seek me in the tomb, for I am everywhere and cannot be confined to a place. You do not yet believe that I have ascended to the Father; you do not yet believe that I am equal to the Father.”

> [Note: Col. 0594D. Jerome, in the Letter to Paula, *On the Death of Blaesilla*: “That is, you do not deserve to touch him risen again whom you suppose dead in the tomb.” And in the Letter to Hedibia, Question 5: “The meaning is: You seek one who is dead; you do not deserve to touch him living. If you think that I have not yet ascended to the Father, but that I was carried off by human deceit, you are unworthy of touching me.” The same, in the Letter to Marcella: “Do not touch me; and the meaning is: You do not deserve to cling to my footsteps, nor to adore as Lord, nor to hold the feet of one whom you do not think has risen. For to you I have not yet ascended to my Father. But the other women, who touch his feet, confess the Lord and deserve to cling to his footsteps, because they trust that he has ascended to the Father.” Saint Ambrose, Book X on Luke, Book III *On Virgins*, and on Psalm 45, agree with the same interpretation, as does Saint Gregory, Homily 25.]

For what is it to ascend to the Father except to be equal to the Father? The Father is not extended higher than the Son: wherever the Father is, there is the Son. Therefore no one who does not believe him to be such and so great should touch him or presume to approach him.

Nevertheless, she held his feet, as did the other women of whom the other Evangelists write: “Go to my brothers and say to them: ‘I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God’” (Matt. 28:9). He entrusts to them words very well known, which he himself had often foretold to them, so that, when they heard them, they might more readily believe the woman’s report to be true. Mary Magdalene came announcing to the disciples: “I have seen the Lord, and he said these things to me.”

LIII. When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were shut where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews, Jesus came, stood in the midst, and said: “Peace be with you.” Whoever understands what is written, “Death enters through our windows” (Jer. 11:21), also understands what the apostles signified when they sat indoors with the doors shut because of fear of the Jews. For under the one name “Jews” are signified all enemies of the Church. Vices, evil spirits, heretics, tyrants, and all persecutors of the Church are understood under this single name.

Let us therefore close our windows; let us close the doors of our body, not so much for fear of the Jews as for fear of demons, the false persuasions of heretics, and the countless corruptions of vices. For this reason the Apostle says: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:33). The Psalmist likewise says: “Turn away my eyes, lest they see vanity” (Ps. 118:37). Many have perished through seeing, many through hearing, many through speaking and eating. These, therefore, are those windows; these are those doors through which death enters into a human being.

Let our first parents be an example to us. Had they not heard the serpent’s voice and believed its evil counsel, had they not seen the forbidden tree and eaten the fruit of desire, they would not have fallen into so great an abyss. This, therefore, is what the apostles signified when they sat in the house with the doors shut.

No one should wonder that Jesus, whose body had now been glorified by the resurrection, entered his disciples though the doors were shut, since while his body was still mortal and corruptible he came forth from his mother’s womb while the Virgin Mother remained always closed and incorrupt.

> [Note: Col. 0595D. Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 84, held the same view.]

For after the resurrection our flesh will be of the same nature, yet of another glory. He commends peace to them, because without peace it is impossible to please God, and where there is no peace, discord reigns. Hence the Psalmist says: “His place has been made in peace” (Ps. 75:3).

> [Note: Col. 0595D. Saint Leo, Sermon 1 *On the Ascension*, ch. 3: “He brings before the eyes of those who doubt the marks of the cross remaining in his hands and feet, and invites them to examine them more carefully, because the traces of the nails and the lance were preserved for the healing of the wounds of unbelievers, so that it might be held with not doubtful faith but the most steadfast knowledge that the very nature which had lain in the tomb would sit upon the throne of God the Father.”]

Coming, he brought peace; departing from here, he left peace. And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and side. Therefore the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord. But why his hands and side? So that, seeing the scars of the wounds, they might recognize him more manifestly and clearly, and no longer doubt his resurrection.

But what the Lord then did to heal the wounds of the mind becomes an occasion through which heretics are wounded in mind: they argue wrongly from this that our bodies cannot be healed from their deformities and defects, not even by the resurrection itself. But if this were true—which God forbid—many saints would have to rise without eyes, hands, feet, and other limbs. The one who promised his disciples that “not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke 21:18) destroys this error.

Therefore he said to them again: “Peace be with you.” He frequently commends peace to them, because the whole perfection of Christian faith and religion consists in peace and love. Thus he himself says to his disciples: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another. As the Father sent me, I also send you” (John 13:35). “I appoint you as my representatives; I commission you in my place; I entrust my office to you. I send you to teach, preach, baptize, save, and glorify my name and that of the Father.”

When he had said this, he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit,” by whose aid and inspiration you may be able to bear so great a burden. And perhaps he breathed upon them in order that by this we may understand and firmly believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him as from the Father. But someone may say: “Did the Lord then give the Holy Spirit to his disciples?” Yes, but not with the fullness with which he was later to give him.

> [Note: Col. 0595D. See Saint Ambrose, Book II *On Jacob*, ch. 2.]

“Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain are retained.” “Whose sins,” he says, “you forgive, whether through baptism or through repentance and holy confession, are forgiven them; and whose you retain, whether through their unbelief, impenitent heart, or disobedience, are retained.” These are the things by which each person is either loosed or bound.

But Thomas, one of the Twelve, who is called Didymus—“the Twin”—was not with them when Jesus came. The other disciples therefore said to him: “We have seen the Lord.” But he said to them: “Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands, put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”

See for what purpose the Lord wished to preserve rather than erase the scars of his wounds: he intended by them to heal his disciple and cure the wounds of his mind. Yet this doubt of the apostle Thomas confirms many others and frees them from doubt. These things would not have been written had Thomas not doubted. They will benefit many readers and hearers until the consummation of the age.

> [Note: Col. 0595D. See Saint Gregory, Homily 26 on the Gospels, no. 3.]

After eight days his disciples were again indoors, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came though the doors were shut and said to them: “Peace be with you.” Then he tells Thomas to put his finger into his side, see his hands, and no longer be unbelieving but believing. Thomas answers and says to him: “My Lord and my God.”

> [Note: Col. 0595D–0596D. Saint Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 84: “Why does Thomas thus seek the traces of faith? Why does he so harshly test one rising again who endured suffering so devoutly? … Brothers, this piety sought, this devotion demanded, that not even impiety itself might hereafter doubt that the Lord had risen. But Thomas was healing not only the uncertainty of his own heart but that of all people.” Saint Gregory’s Homily 26 on this Gospel passage, no. 7, is well known.]

What does “My Lord and my God” mean? “I doubt no longer; I am certain; I affirm the resurrection and proclaim immortality. You are my Lord, my teacher; I am your servant and the son of your handmaid. Finally, you are my God, who created me; who assumed flesh for me; who delivered it over to death in order to redeem me; and who have now risen from the dead in order to raise me with yourself. This is my faith: thus I judge, and thus I believe.”

> [Note: Col. 0596D. Hilary, Book VII *On the Trinity*: “Thomas, therefore, understanding the truth of the evangelical mystery, confessed that he was his Lord and his God. This is not a title of honor but a confession of nature: for he believed him to be God by the deeds themselves and by his powers. And the Lord taught that the religious character of this confession belonged not to honor but to faith, saying: ‘Because you have seen me, you have believed.’”]

Jesus says to him: “Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.” For if he believed because he saw him, it is clear that, had he not seen him, he would not have believed. Therefore those are deservedly blessed who have not seen him with bodily eyes but, hearing these things and others like them, have believed in him.

Jesus indeed performed many other signs in the presence of his disciples which are not written in this book. For it was a sign that he entered the disciples though the doors were shut. But these things are written “that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that, believing, you may have life in his name.” These alone could suffice as evidence for faith, even if the other Evangelists had not written down his other deeds.

LIV.

> [Note: Col. 0597D. John 21:1: “Afterward Jesus manifested himself again to the disciples.”]

**[Chapter 21.] Jesus manifested himself to his disciples by the Sea of Tiberias.** He manifested himself in this manner: Simon Peter, Thomas called Didymus, Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two other disciples were together. Simon Peter says to them: “I am going fishing.” They say to him: “We also will come with you.”

Why is it that the apostle Peter returns again to fishing, as do the sons of Zebedee? For these are the very men to whom the Lord had said: “Come after me; I will make you become fishers of men” (Mark 1:17).
