> [Note: Col. 0597D. See Saint Gregory, Homily 24 on the Gospels, and Saint John Chrysostom, Homily 87.]

This shows that seeking one’s daily livelihood by these and similar occupations is not sinful. Hence the Apostle, laboring with his own hands for his livelihood, urges others also to work, saying: “Let each one labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to those suffering need” (Eph. 4:28).

They went out, embarked upon the boat, and caught nothing that night. They labored to no effect because it was night and Jesus had not yet come to them.

> [Note: Col. 0597D. Saint Gregory, passage cited, no. 3: “Great difficulty in fishing befell the disciples, so that when the Master came there might be a great heightening of wonder.”]

Moreover, they had come to fish of their own accord and had not been sent by another. For they still signified those who come to preach and govern the Church, not by the command of the canons but by their own judgment. Such persons are avoided by God’s fish, which disdain to enter their nets or listen to their preaching.

But when morning had now come, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus. See, they now begin to signify something else: they no longer labor in the night; they come to the day and see the Lord. Jesus therefore says to them: “Children, have you anything to eat?” They answered him: “No.” He says to them: “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find.”

As if he said: “I did not send you on that occasion. You came in the night and labored toward the left; you caught nothing. Now cast the net on the right side of the boat; labor at my command; preach my doctrine. Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing, and you will find.”

> [Note: Col. 0597D. See another allegorical explanation in Peter Chrysologus, Homily 78.]

To fish on the right, therefore, is to preach true and catholic doctrine with sincere devotion and a pure heart.

> [Note: Col. 0597D. Saint Augustine, Tractate 122, offers another allegorical explanation.]

For the apostles are fishers, preachers, and teachers; the nets are the Gospels and every divine utterance. The fish are all the faithful. Such fish swim in the stream of baptism; such fish are caught in the nets of the Gospel and by the love of faith.

They cast the net, and they were no longer able to draw it because of the multitude of fish. A great miracle! Though they had labored throughout the night, they caught nothing; yet, so suddenly at the Lord’s command, such a multitude of fish assembled. By this first and nocturnal fishing we may understand that fishing which the apostles had among the Jews when, because they refused to believe, the Apostle said to them: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be preached to you; but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

For what does “Behold, we turn to the Gentiles” mean except what is said here: “Cast the net on the right side of the boat”? Since the fish of the Jewish stream would not enter the apostles’ nets, the apostles were sent to the streams of the Gentiles. Teachers fish in the night when their hearers, blinded inwardly, do not understand the truth.

They cast the net on the right side of the boat, and were no longer able to draw it because of the multitude of fish. This is what the Psalmist says: “I proclaimed and spoke; they have multiplied beyond number” (Ps. 39:6). Seeing this miracle, that disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter: “It is the Lord.” Simon Peter, when he heard that it was the Lord, girded his tunic about himself—for he was naked—and threw himself into the sea. Everywhere Peter is found to be more fervent in faith and greater in love.

> [Note: Col. 0597D–0598D. Chrysostom, Homily 87 on John, no. 2: “Peter and John display their characteristic dispositions. The former was more fervent, the latter more exalted; the former more impetuous, the latter more discerning. Therefore John first recognized Jesus, but Peter first hastened to him.” Chrysologus, Sermon 78: “He threw himself into the sea so that he who had received primacy in rank might be first in returning.”]

But the other disciples came in the boat, for they were not far from land. What do we understand by this land except the land of the living?

> [Note: Col. 0598D. Saint Augustine, Tractate 122: “The shore is the end of the sea and therefore signifies the end of the age.”]

They were not far from it because, when released from bodily bonds, they would soon be going there. They dragged the net of fish about two hundred cubits.

> [Note: Col. 0598D. Saint Gregory, in the cited passage: “Since, therefore, the preacher of the Church separates us from the waves of this world, it is necessary that Peter draw the net full of fish to land. For he draws the fish to the firmness of the shore who, by the voice of holy preaching, shows the faithful the stability of the eternal homeland … Whenever through him we are converted to the love of eternal rest; whenever we are separated from the tumults of earthly things, what else happens but that, cast into the net of faith, we fish are drawn to the shore?”]

The number one hundred is perfect; it is then doubled when it is fulfilled in word and deed. Teachers therefore draw the net of fish two hundred cubits when, both by word and deed, they lead their hearers after them to eternal life.

> [Note: Col. 0598D. Augustine, Tractate 124: “There the net was torn, to signify schisms; here,” etc.]

When they came down to land, they saw coals laid out, a fish placed upon them, and bread. With this food Christ’s fishers and preachers are always refreshed and gain strength whenever they return exhausted from this work. For whenever they see the coals, the fish placed upon them, and the bread—whenever they recall Christ’s passion and preaching—they forget their labor, weariness, and all their distresses.

For what is a fish roasted on coals except Christ suffering upon the cross? And what is the bread except evangelical preaching, by which the Lord was accustomed to refresh them, saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28). By these things the apostles are refreshed, encouraged, satisfied, and stirred up again for labor.

Jesus says to them: “Bring some of the fish which you have now caught.” For the apostles and teachers always bring fish to the Lord: by example and teaching they always lead the souls of the faithful to him. Therefore it follows: Simon Peter went up and drew the net to land, full of large fish, one hundred and fifty-three; and though there were so many, the net was not torn.

These were good fish, by which the net was not torn. Bad fish are heretics and schismatics, who daily tear the nets of the Gospels.

> [Note: Col. 0599D. Chrysologus, in the cited passage, gives another but elegant explanation: “From Jews and Gentiles he doubles the number one hundred, uniting the life and salvation of the two peoples.”]

But what do the one hundred and fifty-three fish signify except all the baptized and faithful?

> [Note: Col. 0599D. See Saint Augustine’s discussion of this number, Tractate 122; Saint Gregory, Homily 24, no. 4; etc.]

The three signify the same thing as the one hundred and fifty. For if we divide one hundred and fifty into equal parts, there are three fifties and no more. There are three parts of the world, signified by the three fish and the three fifties: namely Asia, Africa, and Europe. Hence the woman hid leaven in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened. Hence the inscription on the cross was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. Therefore the apostles catch three fish and one hundred and fifty, because by their example and teaching all who come to the Church from these three parts of the world are led there.

Jesus says to them: “Come, dine.” And none of those at table dared ask him, “Who are you?” knowing that it was the Lord. Jesus came, took the bread, and gave it to them, and likewise the fish. Every day the Lord invites us to dine. Every day he sets before us both bread and fish. Every day he ministers to us the delights of evangelical food and of his body and blood.

For while we read these Gospels, he refreshes us upon earth with the food of his bread. Here he also gives us roasted fish, because here we find how he suffered.

> [Note: Col. 0599D. Augustine, passage cited: “The roasted fish is Christ who suffered. He is also the living bread who came down from heaven; to share in everlasting blessedness, the Church is incorporated into him.” See also Saint Gregory, Homily 24, no. 5.]

Those who are not continually refreshed by these foods cannot properly draw Christ’s nets. This was now the third time that Jesus manifested himself to his disciples after he had risen from the dead. He speaks here of those manifestations made either to all, or to many gathered together.

LV. When they had dined, Jesus says to Simon Peter: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” He says to him: “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” The Lord asks Peter whether he loves him, though he had always and everywhere seen him display toward himself a greater affection of love. Thus just above, when the others came to him in the boat, Peter could not wait for the boat’s delay; compelled by the immensity of his love, he threw himself into the sea so that he might come to the Lord more quickly.

“Simon, son of John,” he says, “do you love me more than these, since you display toward me an affection of love greater than theirs?” He says: “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you. Yes, Lord, I love you, and you know that I love you. You also know how greatly I love you. But I do not know whether I love you more than the others.” He says to him: “Feed my lambs.”

The Lord does not wish to entrust his lambs to anyone except one who loves those whom he himself loved so greatly that he deigned to die for them. Therefore he first asks the shepherd of the Church whether he loves him, and only afterward entrusts his lambs to him for feeding.

> [Note: Col. 0599D–0600D. Saint Augustine, Tractate 123: “Peter is rightly asked, ‘Do you love me?’ He answers, ‘I love you,’ and is told, ‘Feed my lambs’; and this again, and a third time. Therefore let us love not ourselves but him, and in feeding his sheep let us seek what belongs to him, not what belongs to ourselves … Let those who feed Christ’s sheep not be lovers of themselves, and let them feed them not as their own but as his; nor seek gain from them for themselves, like lovers of money; nor lord it over them, like the proud; nor glory in the honors received from them, like the arrogant,” etc. See Sermons 146 and 147 on these words.]

Again he says to him: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” He says to him: “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He says to him: “Feed my lambs.” A third time he says to him: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” Then Peter, grieved and fearing that he was regarded with suspicion by the Lord because he had said a third time, “Do you love me?”, answered: “Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you.” He says to him: “Feed my sheep.”

He first entrusted lambs, then sheep, to him, because he appointed him not only shepherd but shepherd of shepherds. Peter therefore feeds lambs and also sheep; he feeds children and mothers; he rules both subjects and prelates. Thus he is the shepherd of all, because apart from lambs and sheep there is nothing in the Church—nothing, I say, that the Lord entrusted to his shepherds.

See: Peter, who had denied the Lord three times, answers three times that he loves him, so that love may erase guilt and affection remove offense.

> [Note: Col. 0600D. Ambrose, *Apology of David*, ch. 9: “Some have said that the threefold questioning concerning love was made because there had been a threefold denial, so that the oft-repeated profession of charity might erase the fall of the threefold denial.” Isidore of Pelusium, Book I, Letter 103: “The Lord’s threefold question to Peter concerning charity must by no means be thought to proceed from the Lord’s ignorance, lest they be deceived even in this; rather, the good physician dispelled the threefold denial by a threefold assent.” Augustine’s words in Tractate 123 are also well known: “A threefold confession is returned for the threefold denial, lest the tongue seem to have served fear less than love, and lest impending death appear to have drawn forth more speech than present life.”]

Jesus says to him: “Amen, amen, I say to you: when you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish.” Explaining what this signified, the Evangelist says: “He said this to signify by what death he was to glorify God.” For blessed Peter, placed upon the gibbet of the cross and stretching out his hands there, was girded and bound by others.

And fittingly, after Peter had answered three times that he loved the Lord, the Lord announced to him his death, by which Peter would show most openly how greatly he loved him. Hence it follows:

LVI. And when he had said this, he says to him: “Follow me.” If you love me, he says, follow me; come after me; imitate me, so that, as I die for you, so you too may die for me. On hearing this, blessed Peter began to follow Jesus both in mind and with his feet. But turning around, he saw following him that disciple whom Jesus loved, who also reclined at supper upon his breast and said, “Lord, who is it that will betray you?”

In several places the apostle John, speaking of himself, says: “This is that disciple whom Jesus loved,” as though Christ had loved him alone, or him alone above the rest. Yet if Christ loved anyone more, he surely loved more the one who was better than the others. That he loved all, however, he himself shows when he says: “As the Father loved me, I too have loved you” (John XV, 9). Therefore he loved all perfectly. He did not, then, love John more, since no love is greater than perfect love. But you say: “He is better who is loved more by the Lord.” And I say that he is better who loves the Lord more. It is therefore not readily apparent which is better, Peter or John. For that Peter loves the Lord more, the Lord himself shows when he says: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” But that John is loved more by the Lord, John himself makes clear in saying: “This is the disciple whom Jesus loved.” Therefore, since this does not proceed according to the letter, let us consider its signification. For what is denoted by Peter, if not the active life? What by John, if not the contemplative life?

> [Note: Another explanation is Augustine’s, in his final tractate on John: “Thus the Church which Peter signified, so long as it dwells amid evils, is delivered from evils by loving and following Christ. … But there is another life, immortal, which is not amid evils. There we shall see face to face what is seen here through a mirror and in an enigma, when great progress is made in beholding the truth. The Church therefore knows two lives divinely proclaimed and commended to her: one in faith, the other in sight; one in the time of pilgrimage, the other in the eternity of abiding; one in labor, the other in rest; one on the way, the other in the homeland; one in the work of action, the other in the reward of contemplation,” etc.]

For Peter had both wife and offspring; John always persevered in virginity. The Lord summons the former to labor, the latter to rest. To Peter he says: “Follow me.” Of John he says: “Thus I will have him remain until I come; what is that to you?” For the active life is always weary and passes away; but the contemplative remains and rests. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the harts of the field, that you do not awaken or rouse the beloved until she herself wills it” (Cant. II, 7). Notice now that this life too is called beloved, the life signified by this beloved disciple. John himself also shows in this place that he signifies the contemplative life, when he says that he reclined upon Jesus’ breast.

Those recline upon Jesus’ breast who devote themselves to wisdom and knowledge, and who give themselves to reading and contemplation. Therefore, if Peter signifies the active life and John the contemplative, then the Lord surely loves John more than Peter—that is, he loves the life signified by John more than that signified by Peter—although he loves John and Peter equally.

When Peter saw him, therefore, he says to Jesus: “Lord, what about this man?” “I already know about myself,” he says. “I am certain of my death. You have foretold my passion to me. I also wish to know by what death this brother, fellow-servant, and companion of mine will glorify you.” Jesus says to him: “Thus I will have him remain until I come. What is that to you? Follow me.”

“Follow me,” he says. “You, like me, ascend the cross. You endure the same death as I. But him I will have remain thus. I do not will that he finish his life by the cross, by the persecutor’s sword, or by any violence, but that he end his final day in peace and rest.”

> [Note: Augustine’s explanation in the work cited, no. 6, is well known: “So far as I understand, so far as I grasp it, what is this, except: you follow me by imitating the endurance of temporal evils; let him remain until I come to render everlasting goods.” But Peter Damian, Sermon 64: “Thus I will have him remain,” etc. “For he who willed Peter to triumph with him upon the gibbet of the cross decreed that John should rest in ecclesiastical peace.”]

“I shall come to him, and when it pleases me I shall call him. With no one compelling him, but with his own will consenting and with my call, I shall transfer him from peace to peace, from rest to rest.”

For it is read:

> [Note: Gregory of Tours wrote this, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, book I, ch. 30: “John, the apostle and evangelist of God, after completing the course both of lawful contest and of most salutary preaching, descended alive into a tomb and ordered himself to be covered with earth. His sepulcher even now emits manna in the form of flour, from which blessed relics, carried throughout the whole world, bring healing to diseases. … Of him Christ also said after the resurrection: ‘Thus I will have him remain until I come.’” And in *History of the Franks*, book I, no. 24, speaking of Domitian: “After his death the blessed John, apostle and evangelist, returned from exile. An old man, full of days and of a life perfect toward God, he laid himself down alive in the tomb. It is said that he does not taste death until the Lord comes again to judge, he himself saying thus in the Gospels: ‘Thus I will have him remain until I come.’” See Augustine, Tractate 124.]

that blessed John, worn out by advanced old age, while he governed the Church at Ephesus in peace and rest, summoned the people to himself and, after a lengthy address and the celebration of Mass, descended into a place dug beside the altar; and thus, as though in a light and sweet sleep, passed to God.

What then does “Thus I will have him remain” mean? What is “thus”? “Thus,” he says, “that he be killed by no one, but that, when I call him, he be gently and pleasantly transferred from this life to another.”

Therefore this saying spread among the brethren, that that disciple would not die. Yet Jesus did not say, “He does not die,” but, “Thus I will have him remain until I come. What is that to you?” The disciples, therefore, had not rightly understood what the Lord had said about John: “Thus I will have him remain until I come.” For Jesus’ words do not signify that John does not die. If they did signify this, John would certainly not have said: “Jesus did not say, ‘He does not die,’ but, ‘Thus I will have him remain until I come.’” For what else did Jesus say except what was signified by his words? We do not attend merely to words, but to the meanings of words.

> [Note: Nevertheless, this was an ancient opinion—that John had not died—as may be understood from Tertullian, *On the Soul*, ch. 50, and from Ephrem in Photius, codex 229. Augustine too, Tractate 124, no. 2: “But let whoever wishes still resist and say that what John says is true: that the Lord did not say that that disciple does not die; but let him nevertheless maintain that this was signified by such words as John reports him to have spoken, and assert that the apostle John is alive and sleeps rather than lies dead in his tomb at Ephesus. Let him take as an argument that the earth there is said gradually to ooze and, as it were, bubble; and let him confidently or obstinately affirm that this is caused by John’s breathing. … They relate—something found in certain writings, although apocryphal—that when he ordered a tomb made for himself, he was present there sound and well; when it had been dug and very carefully prepared, he lay down in it as though in a little bed and immediately died. But those who understand the Lord’s words in this way suppose that he did not die, but lay as one dead; and that, when he was thought dead, he was buried asleep, to remain so until Christ comes, indicating his life by the bubbling forth of dust. This dust, they believe, rises from the bottom to the surface of the tomb, driven by the breath of the resting man. I consider it superfluous to contend against this opinion,” etc.]

This is that disciple who bears witness concerning these things. And he wrote these things, and we know that his testimony is true. But there are many other things which Jesus did; if they were written down one by one, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books which would have to be written.

This mode of speech is called by grammarians hyperbole:

> [Note: Augustine, ibid., no. 8: “Teachers not only of Greek but also of Latin literature call this manner of speaking by the Greek name *hyperbole*; and this manner is found not only in this passage but also in certain other divine writings.”]

it is interpreted as exceeding belief. For it exceeds the hearers’ belief, and one does not readily credit what is said in this fashion. Thus David too spoke of Saul and Jonathan as swifter than eagles and stronger than lions. In such statements, however, we must attend not to the words themselves but to the speaker’s intention.

It may also be understood thus: if all that Jesus did were written, the world itself could not fully contain and understand their hidden mysteries and profound meanings. He therefore selected a few out of many, so that they might be understood more easily, sought more diligently, believed by faith, and committed to memory.

**END OF THE BOOK OF THE DILIGENT AND LUCID EXPOSITION.**

## EXPOSITION OF ST. BRUNO OF ASTI, BISHOP OF SEGNI, ON THE APOCALYPSE

## EDITOR’S PREFACE

Not in order to repeat what we have already said concerning this commentary in the general preface do we wish to preface it again, but some additions must be made, so that this interpretation of St. Bruno may be held in greater esteem.

The testimony of the commentator himself contributes not a little to its assessment: he acknowledges that he interpreted the Apocalypse after he had relinquished administration of the Church of Segni; and thus, as a monk in retirement at Monte Cassino and already of mature age, he completed this work. At that time, devoting himself wholly to meditations upon spiritual things and to reading the holy Fathers, he was better able to examine and penetrate this book, so full of the most profound mysteries.

It should also be added that, after spending many years in the episcopate, during which he had discharged various offices and embassies, he had come to know the countenance of the universal Church. Thus, in expounding the Apocalypse, written to the seven bishops of Asia, he discoursed learnedly and appropriately on the office and holiness of the bishop, the conduct of clerics, and the Christian life. Nor did he omit to attack the errors of heretics, especially simony and schism, the two evils which at that time more widely afflicted the Church.

Here it will not be inappropriate to observe how remarkably this commentary of Bruno contributes to confirming the truth and authority of the Apocalypse against heretics who have attempted to weaken and overthrow it. For no one, against the consensus of very many Greek and Latin Fathers, ought to doubt that this revelation depicts, under varied images, the future condition of the Church instituted by Christ the Lord, and warns the faithful thereby not to let themselves be deceived by the devil or fall away from observance of the Gospel law.

Their faith must be tested in many ways, especially at the end of the world through Antichrist and his followers—that is, the heretics—whose cunning, delusions, and false doctrines will attack the unwary and those corrupted by vices so forcefully that, if they believe them, they will perish most miserably.

It was therefore fitting to the infinite mercy of God that he who, so many ages before, had caused the first advent of the Redeemer of humankind into the world to be announced through prophets and figures, so that people might prepare his ways—that is, make themselves ready worthily to receive him—should forewarn them of his second coming to earth, when all things established from eternity shall have been completed and the time shall come in which Christ, the supreme judge, assigns the righteous to joys and the wicked to eternal punishments.

Since everything written in the Old and New Testament is directed to this end, it was necessary to deliver this truth supported by such reasons and arguments that, unless someone should choose to take light for darkness, he would be altogether persuaded of it.

Accordingly, when our author had proposed to himself the treatment and elucidation of these matters, he divided the entire revelation of St. John the Evangelist into seven books. In them he disclosed each secret veiled in figurative signs and showed that it is confirmed by the principal testimonies of the other Scriptures.

Nor shall I pass over in silence the particular praise to be assigned to St. Bruno: he must be numbered among the few Fathers who enriched the entire book of the Apocalypse with commentaries of their own. For although particular passages have been found interpreted by many—among whom I shall name St. Hippolytus and Cassiodorus—few nevertheless undertook to expound it from beginning to end.

I also hope that readers will be very grateful to me because in this edition they will possess St. Bruno’s exposition of the Apocalypse not interpolated, as Marchesius published it, but whole, complete, and entire. By comparison of two manuscripts of excellent quality in the Vatican Library and of the Lyons edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. XX, in which the author’s exposition of the Apocalypse was published, many passages have been restored in a more complete and clearer form.

## AUTHOR’S PREFACE

“John’s Apocalypse has as many mysteries as words. I have said too little; and, in proportion to the work’s merit, every praise falls short. In every individual word manifold meanings lie hidden.”

> [Note: Sixtus of Siena, *Sacred Library*, book IV, uses the same words when he bears witness to the book of the Apocalypse as elucidated by Bruno of Asti’s interpretations; but he mistakenly calls him bishop of Siena, when he should have called him bishop of Segni. St. Dionysius of Alexandria had said the same, whose words Calmet cites in article 1 of the preface to Cassiodorus’s Apocalypse. Cassiodorus’s brief commentary on the Apocalypse, together with his commentary on the Epistles of St. Paul, was published by Marquis Scipione Maffei at Florence, from the press of Giuseppe Manni, in 1721, and dedicated to Gian Gastone, Grand Duke of Tuscany.]

By these few words blessed Jerome—by whose authority and prudence the holy Church is greatly strengthened—plainly demonstrates how great is the dignity of this book. We have therefore taken care to labor in expounding it after many others who have expounded it, because, although they have treated its meanings well, they seem to have said too little about the continuity and division of the visions. Indeed, certain friends of mine asked me to do this very thing for that reason; and I judged it fitting to comply with their request and wish.

Before, indeed, I ascended to the dignity of the episcopate—Christ the Lord calling me, not my merits—I expounded the Psalter, as I was able, for Ingo, bishop of Asti, and the Song of Songs for the canons of Siena, among whom I myself lived as a canon of whatever sort I was. After the episcopate, for the reason mentioned above, I explained this Apocalypse of blessed John; and before it, at the request of the venerable abbot Damian, I set forth rather briefly and clearly Isaiah, the noblest of the prophets.

I have accordingly divided the book now under discussion into seven books, because, although it has more visions, its principal visions are seven; and although their words differ, their meaning appears almost the same. In all of them the persecutions of the Church are narrated, except that in the last the structures of the heavenly Jerusalem are described.

The first book speaks abundantly of the seven Churches and the same number of angels, in whom all are signified until the consummation of the age, and promises its rewards to each victor. The second, beginning from the origin of the nascent Church, includes, in the opening of the seven seals, all its mysteries until the end—blessed John, or rather the Holy Spirit through him.

The third begins with Christ’s preaching and, in the seven angels sounding trumpets, narrates in order all the persecutions of the Church until the coming of Antichrist; after the death and resurrection of Enoch and Elijah, it ends with Christ the Lord coming for judgment.

Likewise the fourth begins from the preaching of our Savior, and from the gate and sufferings of holy mother Church; under the image of a beast deformed with seven heads, it sets forth what the Church has suffered and from whom, until the universal judgment.

But in the fifth it again begins, as in the others, from the beginning; and, with seven angels pouring out seven bowls full of the wrath of God, it signifies the same things and comes to the same conclusion.

The sixth book begins with Christ, who in his time binds and looses the ancient dragon; condemning some by the second death and making others blessed by the second resurrection,

> [Note: Vatican manuscript: “making blessed.”]

it brings the former to a most unhappy and the latter to a most glorious end. In the seventh, however, there remains the sabbath-rest

> [Note: Vatican manuscript: “of the people of God.”]

of God, in which no servile work is done and nothing is narrated; yet the buildings of the heavenly Jerusalem are described—adorned with every kind of stone and decorated through twelve gates with twelve pearls—which receives within itself no inhabitant except one who is fittingly adorned.

# BOOK ONE

# CHAPTER ONE

“Some preface is set before us so that the dignity of the present book may briefly be indicated. For the apostle John says that a vision concerning the end of the age was shown to him by the Lord Christ; and it is shown by whom and why it was shown, so that, when so great a truth had been disclosed, the devout might receive confidence and the conscience of unbelievers might discover fear. He is also praised who chooses to read or keep these things, so that the mind of the devout, invited by such promises, may be more ardently stirred.”

> [Note: Cassiodorus, *On the Apocalypse*, no. 1, Florence edition, 1721.]

“The Apocalypse of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to make known to his servants the things which must shortly come to pass; and he signified it, sending through his angel to his servant John, who bore witness to the Word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ—all that he saw.”

“This,” says blessed John, “is the Apocalypse, that is, the revelation, not indeed mine but of Jesus Christ.”

> [Note: “The Apocalypse is deservedly called the Gospel of Jesus Christ returned to life, since it chiefly teaches what is to occur from the beginning of the Church to its consummation. The earlier Gospels report Christ’s deeds and precepts, by which the new Church was to be instructed, but include little concerning future events.” Sassy, *Commentary*.]

For woe to the prophets who prophesy from their own heart. Hence Jerusalem is told: “Your prophets saw false things for you” (Jer. VI, 31); such as are found in abundance in the books of Kings. Therefore, so that the apostle and prophet might distinguish himself from such persons, after saying “Apocalypse,” he added, “of Christ Jesus.”

But whence, and from whom, did Christ receive it? Do you wish to hear from whom? “Which God gave him.”

> [Note: “But he made known by evident reference who this Lord is—he who is, who was, and who is to come—declaring that he is the Lord Christ himself, who redeemed us by precious blood. He also says what he will be like in his second advent, when people shall see him, his power having been made manifest; for by the voice of his own divinity he confirms that he himself is first, last, and almighty.” Cassiodorus.]

Christ Jesus is both man and God. According to his humanity he is mortal and subject to ignorance; according to his divinity, however, he is immortal and knows all things. Therefore God—that is, the divinity which was, and indeed is, in Christ—gave it to Christ Jesus. This is nothing other than Christ Jesus giving this revelation to himself.

But why he gave it is then asked: “To make known to his servants,” that is, to make it known and reveal it openly to his servants.

> [Note: Vatican manuscript: “to make it openly known.”]

It can also be understood that the Father gave it to the Son. Thus the Son himself says: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Luke X, 22); and again: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me, the Father” (John VII, 16).

It follows: “The things which must shortly come to pass.” Our Savior, he says, made known and revealed to his servants those things which must come to pass quickly and not after a long time. For the sufferings of martyrs are narrated here, and they began to occur while the apostle was still alive. In the sight of supreme providence, moreover, all things are soon, however long they may delay.

“And he signified it, sending through his angel to his servant John.” “He signified it,” he says: he made it known and revealed it.

> [Note: The Vatican manuscript omits “however.”]

He did this by sending through his angel principally to his servant John, who would disclose it to his fellow-servants. But who is this John, who bore witness to the Word of God? What testimony? “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1). Thus he himself says: “This is that disciple who bears witness concerning these things and wrote them, and we know that his testimony is true” (John XXI, 24).

But how did he bear witness to the Word of God? By all the things that he saw. Thus he says in his Epistle: “That which was from the beginning, which we heard concerning the Word of life, and which our hands handled, we announce to you” (I John I, 1).

“Blessed is he who reads and he who hears the words of this prophecy, and keeps the things written in it.” By these words he declares how praiseworthy this prophecy is.

> [Note: Vatican manuscript: “is declared in these words: ‘Blessed is,’ he says, ‘not only,’” etc.]

“Blessed,” he says, “is not only he who reads the words of this prophecy”—which belongs to few—“but also he who hears,” which has been granted to almost everyone, provided that he keeps the things written in it. Great indeed is the promise, but laborious is the observance. Hence the Apostle says: “It is not hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but doers of the law shall be justified” (Rom. II, 13).

“The time is near.” Near, he says, is the time when these things too shall be fulfilled and Christ, coming for judgment, shall repay the merits of those who keep his commandments. Hence at the end of this book he says: “Behold, I come quickly; blessed is he who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book” (Apoc. XXII, 7).

“John, to the seven Churches which are in Asia: grace to you and peace from him who is, and who was, and who is to come.” What these seven Churches are is made clear in what follows. Sending this Apocalypse to them, blessed John says: “Grace to you and peace,” because you have been reconciled to grace and good will, and to the peace of the highest God.

> [Note: Vatican manuscript: “But this.”]

“And from him who is,” whom the Jews suppose not to be, “and who was,” even before he was born of the Virgin, “and who is to come,” namely to judge the world and render to each according to merits.

“Moreover, from the seven spirits which are before his throne.”

> [Note: Commentators differ in their interpretation of this passage. Some think that angels are meant, whose proper office it is to stand before God’s throne; others say that the Holy Spirit is expressly meant, whose gifts or graces are seven. St. Bruno appears to follow the latter opinion.]

Enumerating these seven spirits, or rather the seven graces of the Holy Spirit, the prophet says: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. XI, 2). These are said to be before his throne, by which we understand Christ’s humanity, or holy Church.

Now let us return to what precedes.

> [Note: Vatican manuscript: “Now he returns to what precedes.”]

For since he had said indefinitely, “from him who is, and who was, and who is to come,” he added, so that it might be known of whom he spoke: “And from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and ruler of the kings of the earth.”

The faithful witness is he who says: “Whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess before my Father” (Matt. X, 32). For he daily intercedes with the Father for us. He is also the firstborn of the dead, because before him no one rose from the dead to immortality. For all who rose before him died again.

It may also be understood that he is firstborn not only of those who were alive when these words were spoken, but also of those who had long before died.

> [Note: Vatican manuscript: “Elsewhere he is called ‘before every creature.’”]

Thus elsewhere he is called “firstborn before every creature” (Col. I, 15). He is ruler of the kings of the earth, since he is King of kings and Lord of lords. Grace and peace are therefore rightly said to be granted us from him, because through him we have been reconciled, the Holy Spirit cooperating, in whom we have been regenerated and enlightened.

“He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood.”

> [Note: Vatican manuscript: “For how greatly.”]

How greatly he loved us is most plainly shown when he did not hesitate to die for us all. For, as he himself says: “No one has greater love than this, that one lay down his life for his friends” (John XV, 13). He washed us in his blood, which flowed from his side together with water for this purpose: not only to redeem us, but also to cleanse us from the defilements of sins.

“And he made us a kingdom and priests to God and his Father; to him be glory and dominion for ages of ages. Amen.” He calls the greater part of our kingdom “priests” by privilege, because in the Church of God it is not tyrants and murderers, as among other peoples, but priests and bishops who hold preeminence. For according to the Apostle, our whole kingdom consists in priesthood; commanding all to offer sacrifice, he says: “I beseech you through the mercy of God to present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (Rom. XII, 1).

To him be glory, now that enemies have been routed and conquered, and dominion, because he rules everywhere. This is not for a time, as happened to Roman emperors, but for ages of ages. Confirming this, let us all joyfully say: “Amen.”

> [Note: Vatican manuscript: “that is, let it be so.”]

“Behold, he comes with the clouds, and every eye shall see him, including those who pierced him; and all the tribes of the earth shall mourn over him. Even so: Amen.”

For it is read in the Acts of the Apostles that, when he ascended to heaven, a cloud received him from their eyes; then the angels are remembered to have said: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I, 11). Therefore he will come in a cloud, since he ascended in a cloud.

But by the clouds we may also understand the prophets and apostles, through whose teaching faith germinated in the Church as through rain. He will come with these for judgment, because they too will be judges. “And every eye shall see him,” not only that of the saints but also that of the Jews who crucified and killed him, so that the former may rejoice in faith and the latter grieve over their own unbelief.

> [Note: The prophet Zechariah had foretold the same thing, ch. XII, 10: “They shall look upon me whom they pierced, and they shall mourn for him with a mourning as for an only-begotten son, and grieve over him as men customarily grieve at the death of a firstborn. On that day there shall be great mourning in Jerusalem.”]

“And all the tribes of the earth shall mourn over him”: some indeed for joy, others for fear; some because they served him too little, others because they did not serve him at all.

The words added, “even so, Amen,” one Latin and the other Hebrew, confirm what has been said,

> [Note: Vatican manuscript: “So that, since Latins and Hebrews killed him, Latins and Hebrews may proclaim him king and judge. Nor will they say, ‘We have no judge but Caesar,’ when they see a king even above Caesar.”]

so that all, both Latins and Hebrews, may proclaim him king and judge. Nor will they say: “We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX, 15), when they see a king even above Caesar.

“I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, says the Lord God, who is, and who is to come, the Almighty.” These two letters are so placed in the Greek alphabet that one occupies the first and the other the final position. Therefore Christ is Alpha and Omega, first and last, beginning and end: first before all things, end after all things; from whom all things proceed and to whom all things return.

> [Note: This agrees with the Apostle, who said in Rom. XI, 36: “For from him, and through him, and in him are all things.”]

Within him are all things; outside him is nothing. Whoever has arrived at him has nowhere further to go. He truly is, because he always is. He is who was, because in the beginning he was; and he is also to come, as has been said above.

“I, John, your brother and companion in tribulation and kingdom and patience in Christ Jesus, was on the island called Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus. I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s Day.”

> [Note: So that Christians might not Judaize, the apostles consecrated to God the day after the Sabbath and called it the Lord’s Day, especially in remembrance of Christ’s resurrection and the coming of the Holy Spirit.]

“And I heard behind me a great voice, like a trumpet, saying”:

> [Note: This is the first revelation which St. John received.]

“What you see, write in a book and send to the seven Churches which are in Asia: to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea.”

“I, John,” he says—John interpreted “by God’s grace,” chosen through God’s grace to the apostleship—am “your brother,” whom holy mother Church bore from water and the Holy Spirit, as she bore you; “and companion in tribulation,” lest you fail in tribulations which you see me too, your apostle and teacher, enduring; “companion also in the kingdom,” so that, enduring the same things, we may receive the same glory; and “companion in patience,” so that you too, like me, may prefer suffering to avenging an injury.

You have certainly heard that this patience was in Christ, who, though he could have defended himself, nevertheless endured death and the cross. “I,” he says, “was on the island called Patmos because of the word of God.” Read the histories, and you will find that blessed John, because of his unconquerable constancy in preaching the Gospel and because he bore witness to Jesus, was sent into exile on the island of Patmos.

> [Note: “In this persecution, that of Domitian, John the apostle, likewise the evangelist, who was still alive at that time, is said to have been banished to the island of Patmos on account of the testimony which he bore to the divine Word.” Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, ch. 18.]

He saw this vision on the Lord’s Day so that he might not doubt that it belonged to him whose day it is. He is commanded to write in a book what he sees in the Spirit and send it to the seven Churches, so that in these seven we may understand all the other Churches of the world. The prophet had long before foretold this of them: “Seven women shall take hold of one man” (Isa. IV, 1). They are rightly said to be seven, because they are governed by seven spirits and are enclosed within seven days.

And I turned to see the voice that was speaking with me; and when I turned, I saw seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the seven golden lampstands one like a son of man, clothed in a long robe, and girded at the breast with a golden belt. For Blessed John, turning to spiritual understanding, saw and understood that voice which was speaking with him. Therefore turn also, whoever you are who desire to understand this prophecy [Col. 0611D], so that, thinking nothing carnally, you may be wholly drawn up into spiritual understanding. The seven golden lampstands, as is shown later, are the seven Churches, which he has often mentioned. Churches are rightly compared to lampstands, since bishops are set over them like lamps, that they may provide light to others. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, that it may give light to all who are in the house” (Matt. V, 15). They are said to have been golden because, just as gold is preferred to all metals, so the Church surpasses all nations in the brilliance of wisdom, the soundness of faith, and the incorruptibility of virtues. In the midst is seen one like a son of man, by whom we understand Christ, who is perfect God and perfect man.

> [Note: [Col. 0611D] According to the interpreters, John is to be understood as having seen not Christ himself, but an appearance of Christ set before his imagination [Col. 0612D] and impressed through the ministry of an angel. While the blessed Evangelist was raised in the spirit, all things were enacted symbolically before him, as when he later said that he saw God sitting upon a throne. Cassiodorus wrote excellently on this passage: “Remember, however, that these and other such visions which the Lord deigned to reveal to his servants were formed temporarily according to the nature of the matters represented, while the nature of the Godhead remained in its own excellence. For the divine nature itself, as it is, is shown to no living human being; but after the resurrection it promises to reveal itself, as it is, to pure hearts.”]

He is said to be clothed in a long robe—that is, in virginal and incorruptible flesh, which no stain was ever able to darken [Col. 0612B]. But what is the golden belt about the breasts, except wisdom in the heart? (For the heart lies between the breasts.) Thus, in order to show that all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are stored in Christ’s breast, he said that his breast was girded with a golden belt.

> [Note: [Col. 0612D] Vatican manuscript: “the breasts girded.”]

But if wisdom shines also in your breast—for this is the golden belt about the breasts—gird it lest it flow away; bind it tightly lest you lose it. Say with the Prophet: “I have hidden your words in my heart, that I may not sin against you” (Ps. CXVIII, 11).

His head and hair were white as white wool and as snow; his eyes like a flame of fire; his feet like bronze, as if glowing in a furnace; and his voice like the sound of many waters [Col. 0612C]. His head and hair are compared to wool and snow so that he who recently appeared in Judaea as an adolescent and young man may be understood as ancient, full of days, and older than all patriarchs and prophets. Therefore, though the Jews were angered by it, he himself said to them: “Amen, I say to you, before Abraham came to be, I am” (John VIII, 58). And although he appeared to be of that age at which eyes commonly grow dim, feet become weary, and the voice fails, nevertheless keen eyes, strong feet, a powerful voice, and the other signs of masculine vigor were seen in him.

We may also understand by his eyes the prophets, who by a clear and penetrating gaze foresaw all things even to the consummation of the age; and by his feet like bronze, the apostles, mighty in virtues [Col. 0612D], illustrious in wisdom, and kindled with the fire of charity, of whom it is said: “How beautiful [Col. 0613A] are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things” (Rom. X, 15). His voice, sounding like many waters, is holy preaching and the praise of peoples, which throughout the whole earth magnifies the Lord with the mouths of all the faithful.

And he had in his right hand seven stars, and from his mouth came a two-edged sharp sword; and his face shone like the sun in its strength. That these seven stars are the angels—that is, the bishops—of the aforesaid seven Churches, he himself shows most clearly in what follows.

> [Note: [Col. 0613D] The same bishops who above were called angels, and then the seven golden lampstands, are here called stars, because they ought to shine in the Church with their own enduring radiance. Christ is said to hold those stars in his hand because bishops are under his particular care and providence.]

Christ holds them in his right hand because he orders and governs them by his power. The sharp two-edged sword proceeding from his mouth is the word itself, of which the Apostle says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. [Col. 0613B] VI, 17); and again: “The word of God is living and effective, and more piercing than any two-edged sword” (Heb. IV, 12). This sword is called sharp on both sides because it strikes sinners from every direction. Christ’s face shone like the sun at noon because, though he was old, the pallor and emaciation of old age did not appear in him. When the saints come before this face, they will shine like the sun in the kingdom of God.

And when I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead; and he placed his right hand upon me, saying: Do not fear; I am the first and the last, and I was dead, and behold, I am alive for ever and ever, and I have the keys of death and hell. Therefore write what you have seen, what is, and what must happen after these things. Blessed John fell as though dead because, still mortal [Col. 0613C], he could not endure so great a vision. So Daniel too fell and became sick after that terrible vision. The Lord placed his right hand upon him because the presence of his power strengthened him, and he said: “I am the first and the last.” This has been explained above. “And I was dead,” according to the flesh. “And behold, I am alive for ever and ever.” Hence the Apostle says: “Christ died once; he no longer dies; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI, 9). “And I have the keys of death and hell.”

> [Note: [Col. 0613D] “I have power to punish my enemies and the enemies of the Church with death and Gehenna, and to shut them up in death and hell, as I shall shut up the devil, at the end of the world.” So Andrew and Richard of St Victor.]

For formerly death and the devil wandered everywhere; formerly all the gates of hell stood open, and crowds of peoples rushed there from every side. But now, because the gates of paradise have been opened, the gates of death have been shut; the devil is confined in prison and under lock and key [Col. 0613D]. “Therefore write what you have seen, and what [Col. 0614A] is”—that is, what is now taking place in the Church—“and what must happen after these things.”

> [Note: [Col. 0613D] Here he points to the persecutions under Trajan and other emperors who would persecute the Church.]

This is a great book, in which past, present, and future are contained.

“The mystery of the seven stars which you saw in my right hand, and of the seven golden lampstands: the seven stars are the angels of the seven Churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven Churches.” This is an explanation of what precedes; a mystery is a hidden thing, spoken figuratively or allegorically.

> [Note: [Col. 0613D] The Vatican manuscript lacks the division into chapters; thus what follows continues.]

## CHAPTER II

“And write to the angel of the Church at Ephesus: Thus says he who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks in the midst of the seven [302] golden lampstands: I know your works, your labor, and your patience; and that you cannot endure evil men; and that you have tested those who call themselves [Col. 0614B] apostles and are not, and have found them false; and you have patience, and have endured for my name’s sake, and have not failed.” He calls the bishop of Ephesus an angel because, acting as Christ’s envoy, he proclaimed the Gospel to the people. For *angel* means “messenger.”

> [Note: [Col. 0614D] Leading interpreters maintain that this bishop of Ephesus was St Timothy, to whom St Paul wrote two Epistles. They establish this from chronology: John wrote his Apocalypse in A.D. 97; Timothy died in A.D. 109, the tenth year of Trajan, and had Onesimus as his successor in the Church of Ephesus.]

The seven stars are the seven bishops, of whom this man was one; the definite is used for the indefinite, for through them we understand all others. The Lord is said to hold them in his right hand because they are not under their own authority but his: he rules and governs them; amid the storms and tempests of this world, he upholds them lest they fall. They are called stars because, as the Apostle says: “Thus they shine among sinners as lights in the world” (Phil. II, 15). He walks in the midst [Col. 0614C] of the golden lampstands, which, as he said above, signify the seven Churches.

> [Note: [Col. 0614D] Vatican manuscript: “seven.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0614D] The same manuscript: “He indeed walks.”]

For he walks in the midst of the Churches because, like a good householder visiting both flocks and shepherds, he observes the life and works of each one. He begins to praise the aforesaid bishop for his work, labor, and patience, since evil men persecuted him so severely that he could not endure them. Moreover, he did not wish to associate with false apostles; testing them, he found them false. Therefore he avoided their company; and although he had endured much for Christ’s name, yet, endowed with great patience, he did not fail.

“But I have somewhat against you: you have forsaken your first charity” [Col. 0614D].

> [Note: [Col. 0614D] Warned by John that he had fallen from his first fervor of charity—namely, from zeal in preaching God’s word—Timothy perhaps took up new courage because of his age, after already spending forty years in the episcopate, and because of the resistance of the Ephesians, who were devoted to the worship of Diana. Sharply reproving their impiety, he was martyred by them.]

“Remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the first works [Col. 0615A]. Otherwise I am coming to you, and I shall remove your lampstand from its place unless you repent.” He reproves for having fallen from the height of charity, which he had formerly possessed in great measure, the man whom he had highly praised for labor and patience. He therefore admonishes him to repent; otherwise he will come against him and remove his lampstand from its place. The lampstand is removed from its place when a Church is separated from its own bishop. Such, therefore, is the power of repentance: it reconciles to the Church one who had formerly deserved to be separated from it.

“But this good thing you have: you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate. He who has ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches: To him who conquers I shall give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God.” Though rebuked concerning charity [Col. 0615B], he is nevertheless praised for constancy in faith. The Nicolaitan heretics commanded people to eat things sacrificed to idols, and further wished all women to be held in common.

> [Note: [Col. 0615D] Some—such as Irenaeus, Tertullian, Hilary, and others cited by Baronius, vol. V, A.D. 68—make Nicolas, one of the first seven deacons, the author of this heresy; others exonerate him, namely Augustine, *Heresies* 5, and Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book III, saying that those who understood his words perversely are to be condemned.]

When he says, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches,” he undoubtedly requires not bodily ears but the ears of the heart. Moses teaches us that the tree of life was in paradise, from which the first man was forbidden to eat.

> [Note: [Col. 0615D] Vatican manuscript: “Moses teaches us that it was.”]

Thus what had been denied to one defeated is granted to one who conquers. Conquer first, therefore, and only then approach the tree of life; first cut away vices, drive out hatreds, overcome your enemies, and then eat. “For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (I Cor. II, 29). The paradise of God is the Church, truly a garden of delights; the tree of life is Christ’s flesh [Col. 0615C]; the tree of life is God’s wisdom, of which it is also said: “It is a tree of life to those who lay hold of it, and blessed is he who holds it fast” (Prov. III, 18).

“And write to the angel of the Church at Smyrna.”

> [Note: [Col. 0615D] Commentators consider this bishop of Smyrna to have been St Polycarp, ordained by St John the Evangelist, as St Jerome reports; and he certainly lived in these times. See Cornelius a Lapide.]

“Thus says the first and the last, who was dead and lives: I know your tribulation and your poverty—but you are rich—and that you are reviled by those who call themselves Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan. Do not fear any of the things you are about to suffer.” Because the Jews say that Christ did not exist before he took flesh, he therefore calls himself the first and the last.

> [Note: [Col. 0615D] Vatican manuscript: “Therefore he calls himself the first. But because they think, like other men, that he died, he calls himself the last [Col. 0616D]. Yet he does not deny that he was dead according to the flesh,” etc.]

He does not deny that he was dead according to the flesh; yet he affirms that he rose again—which they do not believe—and lives eternally. He praises the bishop of Smyrna not only for tribulations [Col. 0615D], through which we must enter the kingdom of heaven, but also for poverty.

> [Note: [Col. 0616D] Vatican manuscript: “of the Church.”]

Blessed, therefore, is the bishop who distributes his possessions so that he always lives poor; for such a one is rich, as this man is said to be. Hence the Apostle says: “As having nothing, and yet possessing all things” (II Cor. VI, 10). Many call themselves Jews but are not, and Satan truly dwells in them; for *Jew* means “confessor.” Whoever, therefore, does not confess that Christ is the Son of God is not a Jew. Hear the Apostle: “For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly; but he is a Jew inwardly, and circumcision is not of the flesh but of the spirit” (Rom. II, 28).

“Behold, the devil is about to send some of you into prison, that you may be tested; and you shall have tribulation for ten days. Be faithful unto death, and I shall give you the crown of life. He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says [Col. 0616B] to the Churches: He who conquers shall not be harmed by the second death.” You will suffer much, he says, but fear nothing. For behold, the devil and his members—behold Nero, Diocletian, and Maximian—are about to send many of you into prison, that you may be tested whether you are faithful; that you may be tested, to see whether perhaps they can deceive you. “And you shall have tribulation for ten days.”

> [Note: [Col. 0616D] Some, including Bede, Haymo, Lyra, and Joachim, judge that the ten persecutions of Christians stirred up by Roman emperors, counted from Nero to Diocletian, are signified here.]

No number proceeds beyond ten: everyone who counts, once he has reached ten, begins again from one and returns to ten.

> [Note: [Col. 0616D] Vatican manuscript: “nor does he know how to go farther in counting, unless he begins again to count from one.”]

What then is it to have tribulation for ten days? It is to have tribulation all days. It follows: “Be faithful unto death.” For the holy martyrs proved faithful because [Col. 0616C] even in death itself they did not deny God. But with what result? “And I shall give you,” he says, “the crown of life.” “For no one is crowned unless he has contended lawfully” (II Tim. II, 5). And what is the crown of life except an eternal and immortal triumph? “He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says through my mouth to the Churches. He who conquers the devil’s temptations shall not be harmed by the second death.” No one can ever escape the first death, which occurs in the body; but from the second death, by which souls separated from God are handed over to eternal punishments, only the saints shall not be harmed.

> [Note: [Col. 0616D] “Do not fear,” says Christ (Matt. X, 28), “those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.” The first death, therefore, is that of the body; the second death is Gehenna [Col. 0617D].]

“And write to the angel of the Church at Pergamum: Thus says he who has the sharp two-edged *romphaea* [sword]: I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is; and you hold fast my name, and have not denied my faith.” We said above that a sharp two-edged sword proceeded from his mouth; here he calls it a *romphaea*, by which [Col. 0617A] we understand judicial power. He praises the bishop of Pergamum because he remained good even among evil men, and, although he dwells among those in whom Satan has his throne—

> [Note: [Col. 0617D] Vatican manuscript: “in whom.”]

—that is, in whose hearts the devil sits and reigns—yet he held fast Christ’s name, bore the true name of Christianity, and never denied Christ’s faith.

“And in those days Antipas, my faithful witness, was killed among you, where Satan dwells.” Antipas, it is reported, was a martyr killed at Pergamum by wicked men for Christ’s name. He says, therefore: “In those days Antipas, who was my faithful witness, since he was killed for my name.”

> [Note: [Col. 0617D] During Domitian’s persecution of Christians, Antipas, bishop of Pergamum, publicly preached Christ and compelled demons to confess that they were driven away by the name of Christ when it was invoked against them. For this reason he was seized by the city prefect, dragged to the temple of Diana, and cast into a bronze bull glowing with intense fire. Praising and giving thanks to God for having deemed him worthy of this contest and crown of martyrdom, the martyr flew to heaven about A.D. 93, the tenth year of Domitian.]

“Among you,” that is, in your city, where, because of the wickedness of its inhabitants, Satan himself, their master, is known to dwell [Col. 0617B]. “In those days,” I say, “Antipas”—and your faith, understood—was tested; and it is evident that Satan dwells at Pergamum.

“But I have somewhat against you: you have [Col. 0617B] there those who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling-block before the children of Israel, to eat and to commit fornication; so you too have those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.” The aforesaid bishop is praised for faith and reproved for negligence: namely, because he permitted heretics among his people and did not fight with all his strength against the Nicolaitan heresy.

The story is read that Balaam the prophet came to Balak, king of the Moabites, to curse God’s people. When the king was angered because he would not curse them, the prophet, wishing to please the king, advised him to prepare food for the Israelites when they came and to set women before them who would incite them to fornication. Read the history and you will find into what great ruin this brought the children of Israel (Num. XXIV–XXV) [Col. 0617C]. The Nicolaitan heresy was like this: its adherents taught that it was lawful to eat things sacrificed to idols and to use women indiscriminately.

“Likewise repent; otherwise [304] I shall come to you quickly and fight against them with the sword of my mouth. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.” This bishop too is commanded to repent. If he does not do so, the Lord will quickly come to him—that is, he will judge him suddenly and summon him from this life. Once he has been removed, another will be substituted for him, through whom Christ will fight against the heretics with the sword of his mouth [Col. 0617D]. Let bishops hear this and fight manfully [Col. 0618A], lest they lose the military belt. For this two-edged sword is the New and the Old Testament: those unwilling to believe the new may be convicted by examples from the old.

> [Note: [Col. 0617D] Vatican manuscript: “And let those who do not hear the apostles believe the prophets.”]

I debate with a Jew: he does not fear Paul’s sword; I turn the blade, and he is struck down by Isaiah. Such, therefore, is Christ’s sword.

> [Note: [Col. 0617D] The Vatican manuscript lacks this sign.]

“To him who conquers I shall give hidden manna; and I shall give him a white stone, and on the stone my name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it.”

> [Note: [Col. 0617D] Vatican manuscript: “For who indeed?”]

Who would not fight for such a promise? Who would not run against the enemy for so great a gift?

> [Note: [Col. 0618D] Vatican manuscript: “would not run.”]

I think that this hidden manna is that which Christ once promised to his disciples, saying: “And I appoint for you a kingdom, that you may eat and drink [Col. 0618B] at my table in my kingdom” (Luke XXV, 9). O hidden manna! O unknown delights! Blessed is he who can make his way toward them!

> [Note: [Col. 0618D] Hidden manna is the new name which no one knows except the one who receives it. It is taught not by learning but by anointing, and comprehended not by knowledge but by conscience. St Bernard, *On Conversion to the Clergy*, book I, ch. 21.]

But what is meant by the white stone except an immortal body? A stone, indeed, because perhaps it is impassible; white, because it is new and clean, purified from every stain.

> [Note: [Col. 0618D] Vatican manuscript: “But sinners shall receive not a white stone, but black earth and corruptible flesh.”]

Among sinners, however, there appears not a white stone but black earth and corruptible flesh. What the new name written on the stone will be is not for us to investigate.

> [Note: [Col. 0618D] Vatican manuscript: “For no one knows it except the one who receives it. If I say what something is which no one knows, I lie—certainly because I say what I do not know. For I have not yet received it.”]

Certainly I lie if I say what I do not know, for I have not yet received it. O that I might someday be worthy to receive it! Yet I do not doubt that it is much better and worthier than the name we now use, by which we are called human beings.

“And write to the angel of the Church at Thyatira: Thus says the Son [Col. 0618C] of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire and feet like bronze: I know your works, charity, faith, ministry, and patience; and your last works are more numerous than the first. But I have against you that you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and seduce my servants into fornication and eating things sacrificed to idols.” Why the Son of God has eyes like a flame of fire and feet like bronze has already been explained above. He praises this bishop too, like the preceding one, for work, charity, faith, and ministry, since he always advanced from virtue to virtue and was ever better than himself. Yet he is reproved for not rebuking the woman Jezebel, who, by expounding the prophets perversely [Col. 0618D], compelled God’s servants to sin.

> [Note: [Col. 0618D] Eleazar takes Jezebel to mean the Synagogue, that is, the Jews, who pursued the apostles and Christians with implacable hatred—as Jezebel pursued Elijah and God’s worshippers—and drove them either to death [Col. 0619D] or into their own heresy. They insisted that Christians should at least observe the law of Moses, and thus mingle Judaism with Christianity; by this they deceived many. The bishop, whom some consider St Carpus, is therefore rebuked because he associated with them, falsely and vainly hoping for their conversion.]

For *Jezebel* means “flow of blood.” It signifies the Church of heretics, which rejoices at the death and blood of souls, despises the simple in those times, and taught them to commit fornication after gods and to eat things sacrificed to idols [Col. 0619A].

“And I gave her time to repent, and she does not wish to repent of her fornication. Behold, I shall cast her upon a bed, and those who commit adultery with her shall be in great tribulation unless they repent of their works; and I shall kill their children in death; and all the Churches shall know that I am the Lord who searches hearts and reins, and I shall give to each of you according to your works.” The Lord is most merciful: he does not will the death of the sinner but life, and therefore gives time for repentance lest his creature perish. But because this Jezebel—that is, the impious multitude of heretics—was unwilling to repent, it is said of her: “Behold, I shall cast her upon a bed.” She is cast upon a bed so that, deprived of all Satan’s power, she may languish and lose strength. This indicates that, although she is unwilling to repent, she will not glory much longer in her perfidy; for that heresy was soon destroyed.

Likewise, those who commit adultery with her—that is, who yield to their flatteries and seductions—unless they too repent and cease from such [305] activity, shall be with her in the greatest tribulation and eternal pains.

> [Note: [Col. 0620D] Vatican manuscript: “likewise with her.”]

Hence it follows: “And I shall kill their children in death,” that is, their followers shall die an eternal death. Then at last all the Churches shall know [Col. 0619C] that I am he who searches hearts and reins. For the Lord knows in whose heart perverse knowledge dwells, and whose reins are ruled by lust; and he is called the just judge “who will render to each according to his works” (Matt. XVI, 27), because the saints differ from one another in glory, while the wicked receive punishments according to their deserts.

“But I say to you, the rest who are at Thyatira: whoever have not this teaching, who have not known the teaching of Satan, as they call it, I shall not lay upon you that burden; only hold fast what you have until I come. And to him who conquers and keeps my works to the end, I shall give authority over the nations; and he shall rule them with an iron rod, and break them in pieces like [Col. 0619D] a potter’s vessel, just as I received from my Father; and I shall give him the morning star. He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.” Above he threatened Jezebel and her followers; now he addresses the multitude of faithful persons in the same city. He promises them that he will lay no other burden upon them, nor impose another penance or satisfaction upon them, regarding their association with heretics—provided, however, that [Col. 0620A] they have not received their teaching and have not known the height, pride, and cunning of Satan in order to imitate and love it.

The phrase, “as they call it,” was a proverb among them. Whenever they saw someone puffed up by pride, they said that he knew Satan’s secrets and depth. It follows: “Only hold fast what you have until I come.”

> [Note: [Col. 0620D] Vatican manuscript: “Hold fast constantly and firmly, he says, the right faith and evangelical teaching which you have, until I come. He comes indeed when he calls each person…”]

For he comes when he calls each person by death from the dwelling of this tabernacle. Yet this may be understood of the universal judgment. Whoever conquers Satan’s snares and keeps God’s works to the end will be given authority over the nations—namely, the nations of heretics and Jews. He will rule and restrain them according to his will, so that they have no freedom either to wander or to escape [Col. 0620B]. He will break and crush them with an iron rod—that is, with strong and irresistible authority and teaching—like potter’s vessels, which are fragile.

The words “just as I received from my Father” signify that he gives his servants such power as he himself possesses naturally. Hence he says: “He who believes in me shall also do the works that I do” (John XIV, 12). “And I shall give him the morning star”: a bright and shining star, the star that announces the sun and day, of which it is written: “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel” (Num. XXIV, 17). Nothing greater can be given to one who will always have before his eyes the presence, brightness, and illumination of God’s Son. This was the desire of him who said: “Show your face, and [Col. 0620C] we shall be saved” (Ps. LXXIX, 8).

## CHAPTER III

“And write to the angel of the Church at Sardis: Thus says he who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars: I know your works: you have a name that you live, and you are dead. Be watchful and strengthen the things that remained and were about to die. For I have not found your works complete before my God. Remember, therefore, how you received and heard; keep it, and repent. If, therefore, you do not watch, I shall come like a thief, and you shall not know at what hour I shall come to you.” What the seven spirits and the seven stars signify has already been explained above. This bishop was judged one way by the people and another way by God. Even if he was praised by the people, he was nevertheless already dead and useless before God [Col. 0620D]. He is therefore admonished to keep bodily watch, drive from himself the sleep of dissipation, and strengthen and restore to life the works within himself that were now about to die; for they are not found complete before God. Those works are complete and perfect before God which are done not for popular favor but from a good intention of mind.

He is commanded, therefore, to remember what pure and sincere teaching he had received from the apostles, preserve [Col. 0621A] and observe it, and repent of the matters in which he has sinned; otherwise the Lord will come to him like a thief, at an hour unknown to him, and compel him suddenly to depart from this life.

“But you have a few names at Sardis who have not defiled their garments; and they shall walk with me in white, because they are worthy. He who conquers shall thus be clothed in white garments, and I shall not blot his name from the book of life; and I shall confess his name before my Father and before his angels. He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.” You, he says, have not lived as you ought; nevertheless, among the people entrusted to you, you have a few whose names are already written in the book of life. They have not defiled their garments [306] and bodies by consenting to the foul practices of heretics [Col. 0621B] or enslaving themselves to luxury and idolatry. Rather, they have always walked with me in white, darkened by no stain of vice. “With me,” he says, because they are worthy of such fellowship. Whoever conquers as they conquered shall be clothed in white garments as they are clothed, and I shall not blot his name from the book of life.

> [Note: [Col. 0621D] “And I shall not blot his name from the book of life.” That is, I shall give him the gift of perseverance and shall not allow him to fall into mortal sin, through which he would lose righteousness. So Pererius. St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, I, question 24, article 3, teaches that the saints are written in the book of life in two ways: first, in an initial sense, with respect to present righteousness, as all Christians are written in the book of life at baptism. Hence Paul says to them in Eph. II, 5, 19: “You are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household.” Secondly, completely, with respect to perseverance and glory. Those written in the first way can be blotted out; hence Psalm LXVIII says: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living.” But those written in the second way, because they conquer and persevere in this victory, shall not be blotted out of the book of life. For the book of life is the register of those ordered to eternal life, to which a person is ordered in two ways: by divine predestination, and this ordering never fails; and by grace. For whoever has grace is by that very fact worthy of eternal life; yet this ordering sometimes fails, because some who are ordered by received grace to have eternal life nevertheless fall away from it through mortal sin,” etc. So the Angelic Doctor.]

“And I shall confess his name before my Father and before his angels.” For there no papers or letters are needed, where such a teacher is present to recite the names.

And write to the angel of Philadelphia: These things says the Holy and True One, who has the keys of David, who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens: I know your works, and [Col. 0621C] behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one is able to shut, because you have little strength and have kept my name: behold, I will give some from the synagogue of Satan, who say that they are Jews and are not, but lie: behold, I will cause them to come and worship before your feet, and they shall know that I have loved you, because you have kept the word of my patience.

“These things,” he says, “says the Holy and True One,” namely Christ our Lord, who never lies [Note: [Col. 0622D] Vatican MS: “who [lies] to no one ever.”], deceives no one, and possesses the key and strength of his father David. For David is interpreted “strong of hand”; his vigor and strength were like a key for taking and opening the city of his enemies [Note: [Col. 0622D] Vatican MS: “for taking and opening cities.”]. Christ also possesses this hereditary key: he opens and shuts those two greatest [Col. 0621D] cities, namely hell and paradise, for whom he wills. When he opens, no one shuts; [Col. 0622A] when he shuts, no one opens.
