Therefore the Angel—Christ—took the censer, that is, his flesh, and filled it with the fire of the altar: subjecting it to blows, scourges, nails and a crown of thorns, the cross and vinegar, and every reproach. Our Saviour was consumed for us by such fire. He says “took,” moreover, because his humanity had wholly entrusted itself to the power of divinity. Hence he himself said: “Not my will, Father, but yours be done” (Luke 22:42).

“And [Col. 0646B] cast it upon the earth” can be understood in two ways: either because, after his flesh had been filled and satiated with the fire of tribulation and reproaches, the Lord cast it into the earth, that is, into the tomb, and permitted it to lie there for three days; or because his passion is preached everywhere on earth through his disciples. He cast it when he said: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:16).

“And there were thunders”: doctors loudly praising God everywhere. “And voices”: namely, the people confessing their sins. “And lightnings”: surely the signs of virtues and miracles flashing forth. “And a great earthquake”: some coming to faith, and others raging against the faith.

[Col. 0646C] And the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared themselves to sound the trumpet. With these matters completed, in which Christ’s birth and passion are briefly contained, he returns to what he had undertaken to narrate above. For the seven angels are seven doctors, and the seven trumpets are seven preachings. Since, as we have said above, there are only seven times, angels and trumpets, although almost innumerable, are nevertheless called only seven. Likewise, although there are many Churches, he wrote only to seven [Col. 0647A]; seven angels and seven trumpets are sufficient for the seven Churches.

And the first angel sounded the trumpet, and hail and fire mingled with blood came about and were cast upon the earth; and a third part of the earth was burned, a third part of the trees was burned, and all green grass was burned. For when the first angel sounded the trumpet, that is, when the first doctors began to preach, hail and fire mingled with blood came about: that is, wrath and indignation, not without the ruin and calamity of many. For those who refused to believe the apostles were therefore visited by wrath, indignation, and fury. Hence the Apostle says: “To some we are the fragrance of life unto life; to others the fragrance of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2:16). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “If I had not come and spoken to them [Col. 0647B], they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sins” (John 15:22).

But because he does not say by whom this hail and fire were brought about, it can be understood both of God and of the devil, since the latter does nothing unless permitted, according to the saying: “He sent them into the wrath of his indignation: indignation, wrath, tribulation, and visitations through evil angels” (Ps. 78:49). With such hail and such fire that wicked one crushes and burns up the earth and sinners. Hence it adds: “And it was cast upon the earth.” But what did it do? It follows: “A third part of the earth was burned, and a third part of the trees was burned.”

But what does it mean that only a third part is burned and destroyed, when surely those who are saved are far more numerous?

> **Note: [Col. 0647D]** Vatican manuscript: “who perish, than those who are saved.”

“For many are called, but few chosen” [Col. 0647C] (Matt. 22:14). The two parts that are saved, then, are understood as prelates and subjects, concerning whom the Lord says: “If two of you agree concerning every matter for which you ask, it shall be done for you” (Matt. 18:19). But the third part, numbered neither among the Church’s prelates nor among its subjects, consists of all heretics and unbelievers, who without doubt will be delivered to unquenchable fire. This third part, according to numerical quantity, will be larger than the other two.

Therefore the earth is burned: that is, the bodies of unbelievers are burned, and the trees that bear no fruit: “Every tree which does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. 3:10). “And all green grass was burned”: namely, people devoted to luxury and pleasure, who desire only the world’s flower, verdure, and beauty. “For truly the people are grass” [Col. 0647D] (Isa. 40:7).

And the second angel sounded the trumpet, and something like a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea; and a third part of the sea became blood; and a third part of the creatures having life in the sea died; and a third part of the ships perished.—For the second angel sounded the trumpet because, after the first, the second preaching began; and something like a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea.

That great mountain is he who once said in [Col. 0648A] his heart: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne” (Isa. 14:13). Such is also the mountain of which the Lord says: “Have faith in God. Amen, I say to you: whoever says to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and cast into the sea,’ and does not hesitate in his heart but believes that whatever he says will be done, it will be done for him” (Mark 11:23).

This mountain always burns with the fire of envy, hatred, and perverse desire. Cast into the sea and among the storms of this world, it never ceases to stir up discords and disputes. Hence a third part of the sea became blood: that is, all teaching and knowledge discordant with the two Testaments, whether it belongs to philosophers or heretics, is nothing other than blood and sin. Those who use it therefore die; hence it adds: “And [Col. 0648B] a third part of the creatures having life in the sea died.”

For the living creature that died in the sea—that is, which, made drunk with bitter and erroneous wisdom, departs from truth—consists of those of whom the Apostle says: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; but they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Professing themselves wise, they became fools” (Rom. 1:21). Why the third part dies has been said above. It follows: “And a third part of the ships perished.”

For there are good ships and bad. The good ship is that of blessed Peter, in which Christ sat with the apostles, and the seven Churches mentioned above are seven ships.

> **Note: [Col. 0647D]** Vatican manuscript: “in which Christ, sitting, [Col. 0648D] preached to the people. The good ship is that in which Christ sat with the apostles. And the seven indeed,” etc.

But those in which Jews, heretics, and philosophers sail comprise the third part of the ships [Col. 0648C] that will perish.

And the third angel sounded the trumpet, and a great star burning like a torch fell from heaven, and it fell upon a third part of the rivers and upon the fountains of waters; and the name of the star is called Wormwood; and a third part of the waters became wormwood, and a multitude of people died from the waters, which had become bitter.—The third angel sounded the trumpet when the third preaching began, in which a great star burning like a torch is said to have fallen from heaven upon a third part of the rivers and fountains of waters.

Whenever one of the heretics, separated from the faith of the Church, who seemed to shine with a great light of wisdom, infects with the gall of his bitterness all those who have neglected to hold the pure and sincere faith [Col. 0648D], a star falls from heaven. A star falls from heaven as often as a believer separates from the Church through heresy. But the more cunning and learned he is, the greater flame he seems to bear. And although he falls wholly from heaven, he does not fall there; for he falls where he was.

He falls upon the third part of the rivers. The two rivers are the two Testaments; the fountains are as numerous as the doctors. No one falls in these, because no heresy is in them. The third river, therefore, into which heretics fall is that which they themselves make; for they make it because their heretical doctrine is not found in the aforesaid rivers.

[Col. 0649A] The star is rightly called wormwood, because, like the plant that bears this name, it is full of gall and every bitterness. Its taste is avoided by one who says to the Lord with the Prophet: “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. 119:103). “And a third part of the waters became wormwood”: namely, those which flow from the hearts of heretics and are not derived from the aforesaid rivers. But what follows? “And many people died from the waters because they had become bitter.” Heretics’ teaching, then, is bitter, deadly, and poisonous: “The poison of asps is under their lips” (Ps. 14:3). Therefore flee these waters, Christian; do not drink them. The rivers are known, and the fountains are known—waters springing up into eternal life [Col. 0649B]; if you drink from them, you will thirst no more.

And the fourth angel sounded the trumpet, and a third part of the sun was struck, and a third part of the moon, and a third part of the stars, so that a third part of them was darkened and a third part of the day did not shine, and likewise of the night. The angel preaches; the heretic is stirred up. For perhaps the latter would not speak unless the former had first said something which seemed contrary to this man’s faith.

It should be noted that, just as the persecution of tyrants is described in the second book, so in this third book the persecution of heretics is fully contained.

> **Note: [Col. 0649D]** Other expositors followed Bruno in this interpretation, as may be seen in Cornelius, Calmet, Viegas, and others.

This persecution was so much more grievous than that one because souls are better than bodies, and these men persecuted souls. This heresy of which he now speaks seems properly to be that of the Arians and Sabellians, who disputed wrongly about divinity itself, the former denying unity and the latter the Trinity [Col. 0649C].

> **Note: [Col. 0649D]** Vatican manuscript: “deny.”

Hence it is said here that a third part of the sun was struck. For what ought we to understand by the sun except the Lord himself, by whom all things are enlightened? Arius struck a third part of the sun when, separating the Son from the Father, he said that the Son was less than the Father. Did Sabellius not likewise strike a third part of the sun when he said that the whole Trinity was one person?

This heresy grew to such an extent that it drew almost the whole world to itself.

> **Note: [Col. 0649D]** Something may perhaps be missing here which would connect this passage with the summary in which St Bruno speaks of the Arian heresy. For Sabellianism, with which the following discussion seems connected, did not extend so widely or prove so grievous to the Christian name as Arianism. According to Epiphanius, it prevailed only in Mesopotamia and around Rome. Arianism, however, as is well known, was so deceptive that almost the whole Christian world appeared Arian—not because the bishops at the council subscribed to a formula which they understood as Arian or alien from Catholic doctrine, [Col. 0650D] but because they thought Catholic the formula which the crafty Arians upheld in a perverse sense, a sense not necessarily conveyed by the words of the formula itself, which could be regarded as Catholic.

Hence it adds: “And a third part of the moon was struck.” No one who understands the Holy Scriptures is ignorant that the moon signifies the Church. A third part of the moon was therefore struck [Col. 0649D], because all who perished through this heresy were those unwilling either to believe the doctors or to be numbered among the hearers. [Col. 0650A] Instead, following some third and novel teaching, they alike rejected subjects and prelates. The Church has these two parts; if there is a third, it does not belong to her.

It follows: “And a third part of the stars.” Many were deceived by heretics who, on account of the teaching and knowledge they possessed, seemed to shine like stars in the Church. Because they did not adhere firmly to the heaven and Church of faith, they were struck by heretics. But how were they struck? “So that a third part of them was darkened, and a third part of the day did not shine, and likewise of the night.” What third part is darkened has been sufficiently said. But how can that part shine for day and night—for the perfect and imperfect, the wise and foolish—which follows the king of darkness [Col. 0650B] and, proceeding along the path of error, ends in smoke and gloom?

For heretics so darkened the third part of the sun itself, of which we have already spoken, that even wise persons doubted what they ought to choose.

> **Note: [Col. 0650D]** Vatican manuscript: “were darkened.”

> **Note: [Col. 0650D]** Those experienced in ecclesiastical history, if among the many heresies they keep only Arianism and Pelagianism in mind, will see how long and bitter were the evils they inflicted upon the Church, so that it was necessary to lament not merely simple people but persons eminent in learning and rank who had been deceived. Truly, then, a third part of the stars appeared darkened.

And I saw and heard the voice of one eagle flying through the midst of heaven, saying in a loud voice: “Woe! Woe! Woe to those dwelling upon the earth!” Because the eagle flies higher and, with eyes not dazzled by reflected light, looks more keenly than other animals upon the sun, it denotes those in the Church who are wiser and have deserved to possess greater knowledge of God.

Blessed John therefore saw and heard this eagle: that is, some doctor diligently moving through the midst of the Churches and, perceiving how much danger threatened the people and how great a scandal was arising in [Col. 0650C] the Church, crying out with a loud voice. For the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matt. 18:7). Thus this doctor too, seeing so great a heresy and such great wars rising against the saints, warns each person to take care, saying with a loud voice: “Woe! Woe! Woe to those dwelling upon the earth!”

He now begins to treat, by implication, of the remaining trumpet-voices of the three angels who were about to sound; this is the heading of what follows.

> **Note: [Col. 0650D]** Vatican manuscript: “trumpet.”

## CHAPTER IX

And the fifth angel sounded the trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth, and the key of the pit of the abyss was given to it; and it opened the pit of the abyss, and smoke ascended from the pit like the smoke of a great furnace; and the sun [Col. 0650D] and air were darkened by the smoke of the pit.

For when the fifth angel sounded the trumpet, a star fell from heaven to earth because, [Col. 0651A] when the fifth preaching began, the devil, unable to endure it, fled from the Church and made his dwelling among the wicked and sinners. Since he could not restrain the words of life, he at least stirred up crowds of wicked persons against the saints.

> **Note: [Col. 0651D]** St John continues his prophecy concerning the state of the Church. The devil envied the victories of its earlier centuries: it had triumphed over Jews, idolaters, and the first heretics. He raised up new enemies of this kind—heresy-founders, namely Luther, Calvin, and their followers. The pit of the abyss was in some fashion opened when they published so many errors and blasphemies under the guise of reforming the Church that evangelical truth was darkened in many kingdoms and provinces, and even now remains in the same lamentable [Col. 0652D] darkness.

“And the key of the pit of the abyss was given to it.” The abyss signifies hell; its pit, Antichrist; the key of the pit is the devil’s power. Hence it adds: “And it opened the pit of the abyss.” For before this time the pit of the abyss—that is, the mouth of Antichrist—was closed.

> **Note: [Col. 0652D]** Manuscript: “for before that time.”

What water it contained in the abyss was unknown. The devil, therefore, with the key of his power opened this most wicked man’s mouth to speak, and whatever crime and blasphemy hell possessed he poured forth through that impious mouth for his wretched hearers. It follows: “And smoke ascended from the pit [Col. 0651B] like the smoke of a great furnace.” Antichrist is called so because he works things contrary to Christ. Therefore, because Christ is the true light by which the whole world is enlightened, smoke and darkness rightly ascend from Antichrist’s mouth, by which the sun itself and the air are darkened. Hence it adds: “And the sun and air were darkened by the smoke of the pit.”

For his heresy will be so dark and deceitful, and the cloud of deception so great, that it will almost erase, obscure, and reduce to nothing the very name of Christ, the Sun of righteousness and our God. The air also will not shine, because the gloom of error will thicken everywhere on earth, placed between God and humanity and hiding from their eyes the light of his very brightness.

And from the smoke of the pit locusts came forth upon the earth, and power was given to them, as the scorpions of the earth have power [Col. 0651C]; and they were commanded not to harm the grass of the earth, nor any green thing, nor any tree, but only those people who do not have the sign upon their foreheads. For the locusts which came out from the smoke of the pit onto the earth are the multitude of heretics [Note: [Col. 0652D] This same interpretation is that of Lyra, Aureolus, St Antoninus, and Cardinal Bellarmine, etc., cited by Cornelius. Our writers testify how many monstrous heresies, like a hostile army of locusts, have proceeded from Lutheranism and Calvinism.], who, arising from the error of this wicked man, will fill the whole earth as they devastate it. And heretics are fittingly compared with locusts [Note: [Col. 0652D] Vatican codex: “are compared.”], because, unrestrained and without a yoke, they do not cease everywhere to lay waste the earth and the Church of God with ravenous greed. They are said to possess power like scorpions: with the long arms of their deception they embrace and draw to themselves those whom they can, then finally strike them with their tail and, after many draughts of the pure faith, pour in the poisons of their own heresy. For if they proclaimed their heresy from the beginning, no one would be willing to believe them; therefore they first set forth [Col. 0651D] words of truth [Note: [Col. 0652D] Vatican codex: “propose.”], so that the falsehood which follows may be accepted. They are commanded, moreover, to harm nothing except those people who did not have the sign of God upon their foreheads [Note: [Col. 0652D] The same codex: “do not have.”]. For the person who, fearing nothing, immediately upon the first question confesses himself to be a Christian has the sign of God upon his forehead. But one who conceals Christ’s name out of some fear does not have the sign of God upon his forehead. Such persons, therefore—that is, false Christians, or also those who have never received God’s sign, such as Jews and pagans—can easily be deceived by heretics. But the grass of the earth, every green thing, and every fruitful tree planted in the paradise of God, which is the Church, will not be harmed by their fraudulent cunning; for, with the Holy Spirit giving it life, it is so strong and verdant that it cannot be killed by any poison.

And it was said that they should not kill them, but torment them for five months; and their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it strikes a person. And in those days people will seek death and will not find it, and they will desire [Col. 0652B] to die, and death will flee from them. So great, indeed, is the wickedness of the evil spirits who sit and dwell in those locusts that, if divine providence loosened their reins, they would destroy all people in a single moment. But since they cannot do so, they torment them as much as they can. This lasts for five months: for these limbs of the devil are said to have power to torment for five months. Since this number is imperfect—for it completes neither a year nor half a year—it signifies that Antichrist will reign for a short time. For he will exercise the power of his wickedness for three and a half years: “For unless the Lord had shortened those days, no flesh would be saved” (Matt. XIII, 20).

We may also understand it thus: although he could not deceive people throughout that whole period, yet during those final five months he will devote himself to signs and wonders and every art of deception, so that he may be adored, worshipped, and venerated as though he were God; indeed, he will sit in the temple of God, showing himself as if he were God. For Solomon also says: “Before ruin the heart is exalted” (Prov. XVI, 18). And they are fittingly tormented for five months, since they did not fear to offend their Creator through the five senses of the body. But how are they tormented? It follows: *And their torment is like the torment of a scorpion when it strikes a person.* This shows that he will wound people not so much by open persecution as by hidden persuasion. The words, *And in those days people will seek death and will not find it*, [Col. 0652D] may be understood in two ways. The wicked, seeing by signs now manifest that the last day of dreadful judgment is approaching, would rather die than endure these same terrors. The ungodly will wish to die, but cannot; therefore they will live, so that they may never be free from the peril of death. If this is understood of the good, there will be such tribulation and distress [Col. 0653A], and such fear of being deceived by the wicked, that they will desire to die and to be with Christ: “For then there will be such persecution as has not existed since the beginning of the world, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error” (Matt. XXIV, 21). This is what the good will fear; and therefore they will desire death rather than life. But death will flee from them, so that they may come to that day upon which, by divine dispensation, they were predestined before the ages to depart from this world. It follows:

And the likenesses of the locusts were like horses prepared for battle. And upon their heads were, as it were, crowns like gold, and their faces were like human faces. [Note: [Col. 0653D] Although the above-mentioned heretics, since they poured forth their false teachings, have afflicted the Church with many evils, they have nevertheless very often been defeated and overthrown by the strongest champions of the faith. But in the last times, when Antichrist reigns, they will become stronger and bolder and will threaten the final [Col. 0654D] overthrow of the righteous and those who believe rightly.]

For we have said that heretics are signified by the locusts; they are aptly compared with horses prepared for battle [Col. 0653B], because in the pride of arrogance they always desire wars. Of them the Psalmist says: “Scatter the nations that desire wars” (Ps. LXVII, 31). They wear upon their heads crowns as it were like gold, because, when they dispute against the saints with loquacity and sophistries and refuse to submit to truth, they are thought by foolish and miserable people to be victorious and wise, lest they appear defeated. For a crown signifies victory, and gold wisdom. Thus they have crowns like gold, because they conquer neither truly nor wisely, but only appear to be victors. They display human faces because, producing testimonies from the divine Scriptures, they promise to speak reasonably. But because they are easily overcome in these matters, they strike with the tail like a scorpion and turn to dialectical questions [Col. 0653C]. Though fiercer than wild beasts, they nevertheless pretend to possess human gentleness.

And they had hair like women’s hair, and their teeth were like lions’ teeth. What, indeed, do we understand by the women’s hair which heretics have, except their soft, effeminate life, dissolved into every form of luxury? Understanding this, the Apostle commands a woman to veil her head. They also have teeth like lions, because they slander everyone, are easily angered by slight provocation, and, in avenging themselves, like lions immediately show in their teeth and words what they carry in their minds.

And they had breastplates like iron breastplates, and the sound of their wings was like the sound of chariots of many horses [Col. 0653D] going to battle. Heretics possess iron breastplates because they defend their doctrines by dialectical arguments and chains of syllogisms in such a way that they are not easily refuted even by the very propositions of truth. They also have wings by which, flying swiftly in every direction, they make their heresies known to all. By these wings we can understand nothing better than their disciples. The sound of these wings [Col. 0654A] resounds like the chariots of many horses as they go to war; hence their preaching seems to be carried on with noise, pride, and loquacity rather than with reason and truth.

And they had tails like scorpions, and there were stings in their tails, and their power was to harm people for five months. By the tail, the hindmost part of an animal, is understood the final act of heretical perversity; it is said to be like the tails of scorpions because, just as a scorpion strikes with its tail, so also the heretic, though he first preaches and displays many good things, nevertheless in the end pours in a hidden poison by which he drags human souls to destruction. Hence it follows: *And there were stings in their tails.* For the Apostle also says: “The sting of sin is death” (I Cor. XV, 59). [Col. 0654B] Thus heretics carry death in their tails, because the end of their design will not be without the wound of death. It follows: *And their power was to harm people for five months.* Why they are said to harm for five months has been explained above.

And they had over them as king the angel of the abyss, whose name in Hebrew is Abaddon, but in Greek, ἀπολλύων, “Destroyer,” and in Latin he has the name *exterminans*, “one who exterminates.” One woe has passed; and behold, two woes are coming after these things. Who, then, is this angel of the abyss but Antichrist, who above is also called the pit of the abyss? Thus Christ is the heavenly messenger, Antichrist the infernal one; the former invites his followers to heaven, the latter to Tartarus. And just as Christ is king of all the faithful, so Antichrist is king of all heretics and unbelievers. Blessed [Col. 0654C] John wished to express his name in the three principal languages [Note: [Col. 0654D] The Latin rendering of the Greek word, as Cornelius observes, was added by the translator. For St John wrote the Apocalypse in Greek.] so that all might know him and all might avoid him. For who would not flee the exterminator? For he exterminates and expels from the boundaries of faith and the Church first, and then from the bounds of the heavenly Jerusalem, all who obey him. By the woe said already to have passed, we understand his first preaching and that of his disciples, whom he also called locusts. For he will reign for three years, preach with three proclamations, and afflict people with three woes.

And the sixth angel sounded the trumpet, and I heard one voice from the horns of the golden altar which is before the eyes of God, saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet: Release the four angels [Col. 0654D] who are bound at the great river Euphrates. For the fifth and sixth angels, of whom we have already spoken and shall speak, will be teachers of the Church. When Antichrist comes in their time, he will oppose their preaching with his false words. This altar, adorned with every beauty and wisdom, in which Christ’s passion and his entire sacrifice—how it was accomplished and how it ought to be performed—are most fully contained, we believe to be the New [Col. 0655A] Testament; and we take its four horns to be the four Evangelists. It is rightly said to be before God’s eyes, because, having been composed by his Spirit, it does not depart from his eyes or memory. It is also before God’s eyes because the saints, who are called God’s eyes, are immediately sanctified at all times [Note: [Col. 0655D] Vatican codex: “diligently search that.”] and exercise themselves in it. One of the four horns of the altar therefore speaks—that is, one of the Evangelists; for what one says, all say—and admonishes the sixth angel, who had the trumpet, to release the four angels bound in the great river Euphrates.

[Note: [Col. 0655D] Some commentators understand by these four angels four principal demons, who, as it were, preside over the four regions of the world. They were bound in the Lord’s passion, so that they might not harm people as much as formerly. At the end of the world they will again be released, so as to rage and punish the ungodly. They are bound in the Euphrates, a fitting place for this purpose because the Euphrates nourished Babylon; Babylon, however, is a type of the kingdom of the devil and of the ungodly, etc. So Cornelius.]

For what else do teachers do except teach and preach what the horns of the altar—that is, the four Gospels—teach? The Gospel therefore commands this sixth angel, that is, any one of the teachers, to release the four angels [Col. 0655B] who were bound in the aforesaid river—that is, to show that they have been released. For this river, greater than any other, signifies the world—for many waters are many peoples—and because there are four parts of the world, four angels are likewise mentioned. Now they are said to be bound because they cannot do what they desire; but then they will be released, because with all their strength they will afflict the world. But if you wish to know where one of the horns of the altar commands these things, read Matthew; for he says: “When you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place, then let him who reads understand” (Matt. XXIV, 13). For when the angel and teacher of the Church sees Antichrist sitting in the temple, what else [Col. 0655C] can he say except that the devil has been released and the last day is approaching?

And the four angels were released, who had been prepared for an hour, and a day, and a month, and a year, to kill the third part of humankind; and I heard the number of the army of horsemen, twenty thousand times ten thousand. The angels were released, he says—the ones whom the sixth angel, by the voice of the Gospel, announced to have been released. They had been prepared for an hour, and a day, and a month, and a year: so that those whom they could not overcome in an hour, they would not cease to persecute throughout an entire day; and those who were not conquered in a day [Note: [Col. 0656D] Vatican codex: “and likewise those who in a day.”] would be tempted through the whole month; and those whom they could not defeat even in a month, they would subdue at least by a long siege, as it were, of a year. It is therefore as though he said that they were prepared without interruption and at every time to persecute and kill the third part of humankind: namely, that part which is counted neither among the prelates of the Church nor among its subjects, and which holds the third place in the division and portion [Note: [Col. 0656D] Vatican codex: “prediction.”], concerning which part enough has been said above.

As for the number of the army of horsemen, said to be twenty thousand times ten thousand [Col. 0656A], I think this signifies that, since there are nine orders of angels, we should refer the ten thousand to the tenth order which fell [Note: [Col. 0656D] The same codex: “bring back.”]. By “thousand,” therefore, a multiple number, let us understand them to be infinite and innumerable; but by “twenty,” which contains twice ten, it is shown that the tenth order of evil spirits has been doubled by evil people. Thus “twenty thousand times ten thousand” means nothing other than that the innumerable order of evil spirits has also been doubled by wicked people.

And thus I saw the horses in the vision, and those sitting upon them had breastplates of fire, hyacinth, and sulphur; and the heads of the horses were like lions’ heads, and fire, smoke, and sulphur proceeded from their mouths. What, indeed, do we understand by the horses except heretics? [Col. 0656B] What by their riders except evil spirits? It is therefore no wonder if such horses plunge themselves over the precipices of vices, driven by the never-failing spurs of such savage and mad riders. Evil spirits therefore have breastplates with which to defend themselves and their soldiers. These are rightly said to be fiery, hyacinth-coloured, and sulphurous, so that what they assume for protection may be turned to their harm [Note: [Col. 0656D] Vatican codex: “into torments.”]. Yet with these weapons they rush into battle; with them they saw down and conquer miserable people. To some they show themselves fiery and angry, as once they acted through themselves and their members against the martyrs; to others, shining and hyacinth-coloured, as though coming from heaven, transformed into angels of light—for the hyacinth is similar to the sky in colour. But when they see persons given over to luxury and shamefulness [Col. 0656C], they attack them with sulphurous weapons. For they furnish each person with that in which they perceive that person’s mind takes delight. The heads of the horses, by whom we understand heretics, are said to resemble lions’ heads because, like lions, heretics delight in cruelty and bloodshed. Concerning them the Prophet fittingly says: “Their throat is an open grave” (Ps. V, 10); and likewise: “The Lord will abhor the man of blood and deceit” (ibid., 7). And fire, smoke, and sulphur proceed from their mouths. Fire is that of anger, rage, and hatred; smoke, however, is that of error and blindness, because they make human minds dark, lest they know God. By sulphur, moreover, what else do we understand except their foul and stinking words, by which they do not fear to blaspheme the Lord?

By these three plagues the third part of humankind was killed—by the fire, smoke, and sulphur which proceeded from their mouths. For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails; their tails are like serpents, having heads, and with these they harm. The third part of humankind said to have been killed is that same part of which [Col. 0657A] we have often spoken; for heretics have no power over the two parts of the Church. Some perish indeed by fire, because through fear of affliction, tribulation, and distress they subject themselves to the dominion of heretics. Those whom they blind by the cunning of error and deception are undoubtedly suffocated by smoke. But they die in sulphur who delight in the utterly foul and stinking manner of life of the heretics, and who join their abominable assembly in order to sin more freely. Thus they subdue some by threats, others by cunning, and others by impunity for crimes.

It follows: *For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails.* It is in their mouths for persuasion, in their tails for deception. For those delighted by their sweet song, when struck by the tail of final deception, will perish through an incurable poison. [Col. 0657B] Hence it follows: *For their tails are like serpents, having heads, and with these they harm.* For every deception of the devil began with the serpent, and ends in the serpent. Whatever heretics may say, whatever sweetness and pleasantness they display, the tail must nevertheless be guarded against; the final words of their discourse must be observed. What follows is serpentine: slippery, twisting, and poisonous. Beware lest you be deceived; for the first humans were deceived by a serpent.

And the rest of the people, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands, so as not to worship demons and images of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood, which can neither see nor walk; and they did not repent of their murders, nor of their sorceries [Col. 0657C], nor of their fornication, nor of their thefts. Those, he says, whom the heretics were able to deceive were killed by the three plagues mentioned above. But the rest, who were not killed by these plagues and yet are worthy of death because of their sins—such as Jews and pagans—are to be understood as those who did not repent of the works of their hands, so as not to worship demons and images, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0657D] Two kinds of people are said to be punished by these final plagues: namely, those who did not guard against the deceits and false doctrines of heretics, and those who did not make satisfaction to God through repentance for their wicked deeds or unbelief. As, in Noah’s days, while the ark was being built, many did not believe that the universal flood was imminent, so, when the end of the world approaches, although repeated signs and wonders will announce God’s imminent vengeance upon the ungodly, the same wickedness and unbelief will nevertheless blind very many people. [Col. 0658D]]

For these words declare how much repentance avails.

## CHAPTER X

And I saw another mighty angel descending from heaven, clothed with a cloud, with a rainbow upon his head; his face was like the sun, and his feet like pillars of fire; and he had in his hand an open little book. In this place blessed John—or rather, the Holy Spirit who spoke to him—seems to make a certain digression [Col. 0657D]. For, having undertaken to speak of the seven angels sounding trumpets, and not yet having reached the seventh, he inserted certain other matters which seem very different from this subject. Perhaps he did this because Christ, who is here introduced as speaking [Note: [Col. 0658D] The angel introduced here is, according to many interpreters, Christ himself; for the power which he possesses, the majesty of his countenance and array, and finally the rainbow encircling his head require something greater than an angel (Apoc. XI, 3). God continues: “I will give to my two witnesses, and they shall prophesy clothed in sackcloth.” Thus Calmet.], [Col. 0658A] says, in mentioning the seventh angel, that all things will be completed in the days of his voice. “And I saw,” he says, “another mighty angel descending from heaven.” For this is the angel of great counsel; this is the angel of the Covenant, of whom it is said: “And immediately the Lord whom you seek, and the angel of the Covenant whom you desire, will come to his holy temple” (Mal. III, 1). He is rightly called mighty, since he [Note: [Col. 0658D] Vatican codex: “because.”] overcame the mightiest of enemies. He is seen to descend from heaven so that no one may doubt that he ascended there. He was clothed with a cloud—that is, clothed in human flesh—of whom it is written: “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt” (Isa. XIX, 1). This cloud is the humanity of our [Col. 0658B] Saviour, which watered the whole world with the rain of faith.

The rainbow was upon his head, which he used as a crown, as it were, so that, just as he had once triumphed by water, he might be known to be about to triumph a second time by fire. For the rainbow has two chief colours, green and red: the one signifies water, the other fire. And his face was like the sun, such as he once appeared when transfigured on the mountain before the three disciples. By this brightness the darkness is driven away, the darkness which had arisen from the smoke of the pit and turned all things into gloom. And his feet were like pillars of fire. For the feet are the apostles, of whom it is said: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!” (Rom. X, 15). They are rightly compared with pillars of fire, because they are strong and cannot [Col. 0658C] be bent away from the steadfastness of faith, and because by their brightness they illuminated the whole world. To them the Lord says: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V, 14). And he had in his hand an open book. By the open book we understand the knowledge of both Testaments. “For the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Apoc. V, 5), he who opened the book which had previously been closed and sealed, and disclosed its secret mysteries. And since we have heard the figure of the aforesaid angel, let us now also hear what he did.

And he placed his right foot upon the sea, but his left upon the earth, and cried with a loud voice, as when a lion roars. And when he had cried, the seven thunders uttered their voices; and when the seven thunders had uttered their voices, I was about to write, and I heard a voice from heaven saying to me: Seal [Col. 0658D] the things which the seven thunders have spoken, and do not write them. We have said that the Lord’s feet are the apostles, whom the Lord placed both upon the sea and upon the land, so that we may understand them to have been everywhere. For their sound went out into all the earth. They were upon the sea for baptizing, but upon land for preaching. “I,” says the Apostle, [Col. 0659A] “planted; Apollos watered” (I Cor. III, 6). And because preaching is a greater labour than baptizing, and because preachers suffer more adversities than baptizers, the Lord is said to have placed his left foot upon the land and his right upon the sea. And he cried with a loud voice, as when a lion roars. That which is heard everywhere is uttered with a loud voice. Now Christ’s preaching is proclaimed everywhere; Christ’s Gospel is preached everywhere. It roars like a lion, indeed, because it manifests victory and strength. When he cried, the seven thunders spoke, because when he preached the seven graces of the Holy Spirit resounded in his mouth.

But why does the voice coming from heaven command only that the Apostle seal, while forbidding him to write the things spoken by the seven thunders? What we write, we hand down to the memory of posterity. Hence the Apostle says: “Whatever things have been written were written for our instruction” (Rom. XV, 4). But what we seal, we wish to remain hidden. The voice coming from heaven forbids the writing of what it says in the Gospel: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine” (Matt. VII, 6). The apostles therefore heard what the thunders of the Holy Spirit spoke, but they were forbidden to reveal everything to everyone; for not everything is to be said to everyone. Hence the Apostle says: “I heard secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak” (II Cor. XII, 4). Thus they disclose some things to all, but keep others shut and sealed in their minds, according to the saying: “To you it has been given to know the mystery [Col. 0659C] of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables” (Luke VIII, 10).

And the angel whom I saw standing upon the sea and upon the earth raised his hand to heaven and swore by him who lives for ever and ever, who created heaven and all things in it, and the earth and all things in it, that there would be time no longer. But in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound the trumpet, the mystery of God will be completed, as he proclaimed through his servants the prophets. It is the custom of those who swear to extend their hand toward that by which they swear. The Son of God therefore raises his hand to heaven because the Father, by whom he swears, is in heaven. For every word of his is an oath, since whatever he says is firm and stable. He therefore swears by him who always lives and never shall not be, because the mutability of time will be no more. But when the seventh angel sounds the trumpet, all things that were foretold by the prophets will be completed. And what he swore after the first judgment—that he would no longer bring the waters of a flood upon the earth—is now again sworn: that heaven and earth will pass away. These are the two judgments signified by the rainbow which Christ had upon his head.

[Col. 0660A] And the voice which I heard from heaven spoke with me again [Note: [Col. 0659D] Vatican codex: “And I heard a voice from heaven speaking again.”], saying: Go, take the open book from the hand of the angel standing upon the sea and upon the earth. And I went to the angel, telling him to give me the book, and he said to me: Take it and devour it; and it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey.

[Note: [Col. 0659D] Others, reported by Cornelius, consider this book to be the Apocalypse itself—that is, the revelation of future things—which could have seemed pleasant and sweet in outward appearance, as so many hidden and secret things were being disclosed to him. But when St John began to examine them in serious meditation, and saw the calamities to come upon the world, especially the persecution of Antichrist and the overthrow of many righteous persons, he grieved and groaned exceedingly. [Col. 0660D]]

For he had first heard the voice from heaven telling him not to write what the thunders had spoken; but now that same voice commands him to receive the open book from the hand of the aforesaid angel. “There is,” as Solomon says, “a time to be silent and a time to speak” (Eccl. III, 7). For the open book indicates that it is given to him in order that he may preach. He therefore went to the angel, approached the Lord, and asked him to supply what he should proclaim to his people. For it is not [Col. 0660B] the apostles who speak, but the Holy Spirit in them. And the angel said: Take it and devour it; and it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey. This book, which the saints are commanded to devour, is understood as the knowledge of both Testaments. It is sweet in the mouth but bitter in the belly; sweet in the mouth, bitter in the stomach; sweet to hear, bitter to do. “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII, 103). For when we read and hear them, we still have them in our mouths; but when we strive to do them, we labour, as it were, to digest them gathered in the belly of the stomach. To whom would an exposition of the prophets and Gospels not be sweet for reading and hearing? But is it equally sweet for doing? He gladly heard the Saviour’s words to whom, after everything else, the Lord said: “One thing still lacks for you: go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, follow me, and you will have treasures in heaven” (Matt. XIX, 21). How bitter he found this food is shown when it follows: “And he went away sorrowful, because he had many possessions.” It follows:

And I took the book from the angel’s hand and devoured it; and when I had devoured it, my stomach was made bitter, while in my mouth it was sweet as honey; and he said [Col. 0660C] to me: You must prophesy again to peoples, nations, tongues, and many kings.

[Note: [Col. 0660D] From this passage arose the opinion of some [Col. 0661C] that St John was preserved among the living, so that, together with Enoch and Elijah, he would come when the faith was endangered under Antichrist, in order to bear testimony to the Christian faith, just as they will bear testimony to the law of nature and to the truth of the Mosaic law. But Eusebius, Jerome, Augustine, and Bede teach that St John died at Ephesus in the ninety-third year of his age. By the Gospel which, after being freed from exile on Patmos and restored to the episcopal see of Ephesus, he afterwards wrote—as the same Fathers affirm—he is shown to have prophesied again to peoples, nations, tongues, and many kings. Pico della Mirandola vigorously maintained that St John the Evangelist was preserved alive, as Enoch and Elijah were.]

For the open book was given to him so that he might no longer seal the words as before, but disclose them [Col. 0660D] to all who wished to hear. These things must be understood according to different times; for not every time is suitable for teaching. Just as a farmer does not sow at every season, so a teacher ought not to preach at every season. Therefore God’s ministers sometimes conceal and seal things, while at other times, with the book open, they make them known to all.

## CHAPTER XI

And a reed like a rod was given to me, and he said [Col. 0661A] to me: Rise, and measure the temple of God, and the altar, and those who worship in it; but cast out the court which is outside the temple, and do not measure it, because it has been given to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.

[Note: [Col. 0661D] Other interpreters generally judge that this vision of John, which Bruno expounds spiritually and treats as concerning faith and its works, represents in the temple measured by the reed the Church divided into two parts. In its inner part they say are figured the more perfect and the elect, who will persevere faithfully despite the fury of the persecutors Diocletian and Maximian and finally Antichrist himself, the cruelest of all tyrants. By the outer part, or court of the temple, they understand lukewarm and undisciplined Christians, who will fail in the rage of the enemy and danger to life. The period of this final persecution is said to be fixed at forty-two months, after which the victorious Church will no longer be troubled, but will rise more glorious. See Cornelius and Calmet, etc.]

The reed which was given to him for measuring is understood as the rule of faith and the discipline of life. For this rule is straight; it indicates to what and how far each person ought to extend himself, gives each person what is his own, and apportions to all those things suitable to their respective offices. And he said to me: Rise, measure the temple of God, and the altar, and those who worship in it. Rise, he says; cast off sloth, because you must admonish others to rise. Rise first yourself; and let one who refuses to believe words believe deeds. Measure the temple [Col. 0661B] of God, by which we understand the Church, whose measure extends from the rising of the sun to its setting, from the north to the sea. Measure also the altar—that is, the faith, than which nothing appears to stand higher in the Church. Its measure is that we worship the one true God in unity and Trinity. We must not advance beyond these boundaries. Measure also those who worship in it: teach what prelates and subjects ought to do. Let no one be proud; honour to whom honour is due, fear to whom fear is due. The person has not measured well who, extending himself too far, strives to set himself above his superior.

But cast out the court which is outside the temple, and do not measure it, because it has been given to the nations. By the court, where idle people are accustomed to converse, are understood Jews and heretics, who are certainly [Col. 0661C] cast outside the temple because they will not be in the assembly of the saints. Since they occupy themselves with heresy and empty fables, and have been given to the nations—that is, to vices and evil spirits—the Apostle does not measure them. For why should he measure them? They admit of no measure; they set themselves above all. Among their number is the one who exalts himself above everything called God or worshipped. And they will trample the holy city for forty-two months. For forty-two months make three and a half years. Christ preached for so many years, and Antichrist will reign for so many. And because during those [Col. 0662A] three years persecution in the Church will be greater than at other times, therefore, although the wicked never cease from trampling the Church from the beginning to the end, he says that it will be trampled for only forty-two months.

And I will grant to my two witnesses, and they shall prophesy for one thousand two hundred and sixty days, clothed in sackcloth. These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands standing before the Lord of the earth; and if anyone wishes to harm them, fire shall come forth from their mouth and devour their enemies; and if anyone wishes to injure them, thus must he be killed. These two witnesses are, according to the letter, understood to be Enoch and Elijah; spiritually, however, they are all the teachers of the Church, who, strengthened by the testimonies of the two Testaments, are rightly called witnesses of God. To these the Lord gives [Col. 0662B] the ministry of prophecy, that they may preach for one thousand two hundred and sixty days; for Christ preached for that many days.

> [Note: [Col. 0662D] Since the deception of Antichrist will endure for three years and a half, as we have said, for the same number of days two prophets sent by God will preach against him and perform great wonders, so that they may be two witnesses of the truth. They are commonly believed to be Enoch and Elijah, raised up into heaven for this purpose after the course of their lives.]

Therefore, since the preaching of the servants ought also in the number of its days to correspond to the preaching of their Lord, these likewise shall preach for the same number of days. This may in some manner be understood of all teachers; for they preach nothing other than what Christ preached during three years and a half. They are therefore rightly said to preach for one thousand two hundred and sixty days, which number indeed contains three years and a half. They shall be clothed in sackcloth, by which they will call others to repentance.

> [Note: [Col. 0662D] Vatican manuscript: “such garments.”]

For even to this day we command penitents to wear coarse garments, such as those in which the Ninevites, from the greatest to the least, are reported to have clothed themselves at Jonah’s preaching [Col. 0662C]. These are the two olive trees, because they never lack the oil of mercy; through them we also understand those others of whom it is said: “Your sons are like young olive trees around your table” (Ps. CXVII [118]:3). And again: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God” (Ps. LI [52]:10). They are likewise the two lampstands, by whose light and teaching this world is illumined. They always stand before the Lord of the earth, since they are not deprived of the divine vision.

But the fire which comes forth from their mouth and devours their enemies is that of which the Lord says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire but that it should burn?” (Luke [Col. 0663A] XII:19). This is the fire of charity, concerning which the Apostle says: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he thirsts, give him drink; for in doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head” (Rom. XII:20). Thus, devoured and slain by such fire, they will suddenly become friends from enemies. Yet by this fire we may also understand the vengeance of the divine curse.

These have power to shut heaven, so that it may not rain during the days of their prophecy; and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood, and to strike the earth with every plague, whenever they wish. This is true also according to the letter: Elijah is read to have done this very thing in the time of Jezebel, when, heaven being shut, it did not rain for three years and six months. He also turned waters into blood when [Col. 0663B] he killed four hundred prophets of Baal, and struck the earth during those three years with such a plague that almost all perished by hunger. Spiritually, however, to shut heaven so that it does not rain is to refuse to water the impious and sinners with the rains of God’s word. He turns waters into blood who teaches that the learning of heretics is false and full of blood and sins. He strikes the earth with every plague who, on account of their crimes, anathematizes and rebukes the wicked.

And when they have finished their testimony, the beast which ascends from the abyss shall make war against them, and shall conquer and kill them; and their bodies shall lie in the streets of the great city, which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where also their Lord was crucified. And people from peoples and tribes [Col. 0663C] and tongues and nations shall see their bodies for three days and a half, and shall not permit their bodies to be laid in tombs. When, he says, they have finished their testimony and have preached Christ’s Gospel for three years and a half, the beast that ascends from the abyss shall make war against them.

> [Note: [Col. 0663D] Although Antichrist will rise up with every deceit against Enoch and Elijah, who oppose him, he will nevertheless be unable to destroy them except by God’s permission, after the time of their preaching has been completed. This is because of their marvelous virtue and power, against which none shall prevail; for, as John says [Col. 0664D], consuming fire shall go forth from their mouth. After they have been killed, the bodies of the two prophets shall lie exposed for three days and a half in the streets of Jerusalem. Then, while all are astonished, they shall rise alive and, before the eyes of their adversaries, fly up to heaven.]

The beast is the devil because of the fierceness of the abyss; it is Antichrist because of the most obscure depth of deception. The beast therefore ascends from the abyss, because the devil enters into and goes out from Antichrist, and for a time rises and grows through his deceitful speech. He shall make war against the saints and shall temporarily kill and overcome them. The rest, understood according to the letter, is very plain, although it is not certain to us that it must be taken according to the letter exactly as it sounds [Col. 0663D]. For we know that the Apostle said: “We who are alive, who remain, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep” (1 Thess. IV:15), wishing to show that all must rise together.

Their bodies, therefore, may allegorically be understood as the bodies of all the faithful. “For we all are one body in Christ” (Rom. XII:6). These bodies lie dead for Christ’s name both in Jerusalem and throughout the earth [Col. 0664A]. They are seen for three days and a half—that is, throughout the whole time of Antichrist’s reign, or throughout the whole time of Christ’s preaching. For because Christ preached for three years and a half, his entire preaching is not improperly said to occupy that length of time. But that a day is used for a year, hear what the Lord says to Ezekiel: “You shall bear the iniquity of the house of Judah for forty days: a day for a year; a day, I say, for a year I have given you” (Ezek. IV:6).

Their bodies are not permitted to be laid in tombs because, insofar as it lies in their power, their enemies deprive them of every rest and blessedness; nor do they believe that those whom they see killed by such a harsh death have life after death, according to that saying: “They seemed in the eyes of the foolish to die, and their departure was reckoned an affliction” (Wis. III:2). And again: “We fools considered their life madness, and their end without honor” (ibid. V:4).

And those who dwell upon the earth shall rejoice over them, and make merry, and send gifts, because these two prophets tormented those who dwell upon the earth; and after three days and a half the spirit of life from God entered into them, and they stood upon their feet, and great fear fell upon those who saw them. For the wicked rejoice at the death of the good, and sin with greater license when no one contradicts them in anything. They send gifts to one another because, fearing no one, each encourages the other to commit shameful deeds. How holy men torment sinners who love only earthly and transitory things is sufficiently evident in our own times [Col. 0664C], when we see kings and princes, being simoniacs and schismatics, rise against saints for no other reason than that the saints admonish them to cease from sins and not to perpetrate deeds so unlawful and abominable. Unless they were tormented by this admonition, they would not afterward be so greatly enraged against the saints.

It follows: “And after three days and a half, the spirit of life from God entered into them.” We have said above that three years and a half are signified by three days and a half, since a day is used for a year. The spirit of life—that is, the soul of each individual—sent by God, shall enter into them after three years and a half, because, when Christ the Lord comes for judgment and all bodies are reunited with their own souls [Col. 0664D], all shall rise and, standing upon their feet, shall go to meet him as he comes. Then indeed great fear shall come upon those who see them and cannot be with them, because they shall behold him angry with them—one whom they shall be unable either to resist by strength or to appease by prayers.

And I heard a great voice from heaven saying to them, “Come up here.” And they went up into heaven in a cloud, and their enemies saw them. And in that hour there occurred [Col. 0665A] a great earthquake, and a tenth part of the city fell; and in the earthquake were slain the names of seven thousand persons, and the rest were struck with fear and gave glory to the God of heaven. That great voice which he heard from heaven inviting them to ascend there is the very voice which speaks in the Gospel, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV:34). Their enemies saw them ascending in the cloud, so that from their glory a greater punishment might grow for the enemies.

And in that hour there occurred a great earthquake: namely, that earthquake in which all sinners—who are rightly called earth—are moved so as to fall and shaken so as to perish. And a tenth part of the city fell: this is that tenth part of the world which followed the tenth rank of the fallen angels. And in the earthquake were slain the names of seven thousand persons: the finite is put for the infinite. For whoever sinned within the seven days in which all worldly matters are contained, and did not repent, is counted among those seven thousand. This earthquake shall occur when it is said: “Depart, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid., 41).

“The rest were struck with fear and gave glory to the God of heaven.” The saints indeed were struck with fear, not because any punishment threatened them, but because they saw those who were suffering punishments; or rather, they feared God all the more as they understood his power over sinners. And they shall give glory to the God of heaven, who predestined them to life before the ages and delivered them from sin [Col. 0665C], lest they should suffer the same things together with sinners. The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe will come quickly. I think that this woe is that by which the wicked shall be tormented without end.

And the seventh angel sounded the trumpet, and there were great voices [Col. 0666A] in heaven saying: “The kingdom of this world has become the kingdom of our God and of his Christ for ages of ages.” And the twenty-four elders, who sit before God upon their thrones, fell upon their faces and worshipped God, saying: For when the seventh angel sounds the trumpet, there is no longer any preaching in the Church, but only acts of thanksgiving. God is praised and magnified, who, after all other enemies have been overcome, has received the kingdom which he shall rule without end. Therefore the twenty-four elders, of whom enough has been said above, fell upon their faces and worshipped God, saying:

“We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who are and who were, because you have received your great power and have reigned. And the nations were angry, and your wrath came, [Col. 0666B] and the time of the dead to be judged, and to render reward to your servants the prophets and the saints, and to those who fear your name, small and great, and to destroy those who corrupted the earth.” For when the malignant spirits have been stripped of all power and cast down into darkness, the Lord shall receive his great power, and no one shall any longer contradict him; he shall reign, all others having been expelled and overcome from royal thrones. “And the nations were angry,” according to the saying: “The Lord reigns; let the peoples be angry” (Ps. XCVIII [99]:1). They are angry, indeed, with none but themselves, their deceivers, and their own iniquities.

For the wrath of God and the time of the dead have come, so that some may be tormented and perish eternally, while others, justly judged, receive the reward of good works; but the wicked, having been destroyed, lose even the hope of being saved and returning to their homeland [Col. 0666C].

> [Note: [Col. 0665D] Vatican manuscript: “having despaired.”]

For they corrupted the earth and their own bodies, and subjected themselves and others to every shamefulness, to other vices, and to the pleasures of the flesh.

## Book Four

[Col. 0665]

[Col. 0665C] 332 And the temple of the Lord was opened in heaven, and the ark of his covenant was seen in his temple; and there were lightnings and voices and an earthquake and great hail. For the temple, as we have often said already, is the Church. But the temple of the Lord in heaven is Christ in the Church; for in him all the fullness of divinity rests bodily. Hence he himself said: “The Father abiding in me, he does the works” (John XIV:10). He also showed himself to be the temple when he said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” But, says the Evangelist, “he spoke of the temple of his body” (John II:19).

Beginning therefore with the Head, blessed John, as in the preceding books, runs again to the end and reveals what he saw in the Church; and although he does not use the same words, he seems nevertheless to narrate the same things as above. Here too he narrates the persecutions of the Church. He says therefore: “And the temple of the Lord was opened in heaven.” The temple of the Lord in heaven was opened when, after thirty years, Christ opened his mouth to preach the Gospel; when it had been opened, the ark of his covenant was seen in his temple. The ark of his covenant, filled with the treasures of every kind of riches, signifies his own wisdom. This wisdom had formerly been hidden and was not seen; but when he spoke, all who heard saw and understood how great a treasure of wisdom and knowledge had been laid up in the secret chamber of his breast.

This ark enriched many; many were made wealthy by the riches of this ark. Poor and wretched is the person who has nothing from the riches of this ark.

> [Note: [Col. 0665D] Vatican manuscript: “who has nothing of the treasures of this ark.”]

And there were lightnings and voices and an earthquake and great hail. For when Christ preached [Col. 0667A], at once there were lightnings by which the devil, together with the entire host of vices, was driven from human hearts; so powerful were his words that malignant spirits could not resist him. There were also the voices of many everywhere—

> [Note: [Col. 0667D] Vatican manuscript: “praising the Lord and bearing witness to Christ,” etc.]

—praising and bearing witness to Christ; and an earthquake, as earthly persons and sinners ran with the utmost haste to faith; and great hail. For, as it is written, his preaching was not like that of the Pharisees, but with power. He spoke flatteringly to no one, but steadfastly proclaimed to all what hail, distresses, and tribulations awaited sinners.

## Chapter XII

And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed [Col. 0667B] with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet; on her head a crown of twelve stars; and she was with child and travailed to give birth. This woman is the Church, clothed around with the beauty and splendor of the sun; by the light of her brightness she has drawn many lovers to herself and after herself. For she is clothed with the sun, that she may please the Sun of righteousness.

> [Note: [Col. 0667D] “By the woman clothed with the sun he most clearly signified the Church, clothed with the Father’s Word, which shines more brightly than the gleaming sun. When he says that the moon is beneath her feet, he shows that she is adorned with heavenly brightness in the manner of the moon. But when he says that on her head is a crown of twelve stars, he denotes the twelve apostles through whom the Church was founded.” St Hippolytus.]

The Apostle says: “Put on the new man, who has been created according to God” (Eph. IV:24). “And the moon beneath her feet.” The moon, because of its waning and its changeability, signifies this world; hence, because Jericho is interpreted as “moon,” the man who was going down from Jerusalem into Jericho is said by the Lord to have descended. The Church therefore has the moon beneath her feet, because, despising all earthly, transitory, and changeable things and accounting them as nothing [Col. 0667C], she desires heavenly things alone. She wears on her head a crown adorned with twelve stars, as if with twelve pearls; this crown signifies the number twelve of the apostles. They conquered; they crowned the Church; they, the first soldiers placed at its head, shine like stars in the Church.

“And she was with child and travailed to give birth.” The Church has many in her womb and daily bears many children, though not without a certain anguish and pain. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow, because her hour has come” (John XVI:21); and the Apostle: “My little children, with whom I am again in travail until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. IV:19). Yet while giving birth during the time of persecution, the Church suffered greater pains. For this reason the saints were killed: because, desiring to give birth, they invited others to baptism. There the Church gives birth; there she begets legitimate children for the Lord [Col. 0667D].

And another sign was seen in heaven: behold, a great red dragon, having seven heads and ten horns [Col. 0668A], and seven diadems upon its heads; and its tail drew a third part of the stars of heaven and cast them to earth.

> [Note: [Col. 0667D] Those who attempt to transfer the figurative sense of the text to history recognize in the dragon the Roman Empire devoted to idolatry, and in its seven heads seven emperors hostile to Christians: namely, Diocletian, Maximian Herculius, Galerius, Maximinus, Severus, Maxentius, and Licinius. The ten horns, according to them, are barbarian kings: Alaric, Genseric, Attila, Totila, and others who overthrew the city of Rome and at times usurped its dominion.]

The great red dragon is the devil, who deceived the first human being in the form of a serpent and now appears red because of the blood of martyrs which he does not cease to shed. He is said to have seven heads: namely, the seven capital vices which arose from their mother, pride, and from which, as from principles, all other vices arise. These are vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony, and lust. But the ten horns are all the other vices which derive from these heads; because they are many, he wished to use the number within which all numbers are contained. For number does not go beyond ten, but, returning upon itself [Col. 0668B], completes all other numbers. What, then, are ten horns but many horns? He also has seven diadems upon his heads, because for each vice he wears its own crown; as often as he conquers someone through envy, so often is he crowned by envy.

> [Note: [Col. 0668D] Vatican manuscript: “thus also the evil one.”]

The seven heads may also be understood as seven heresiarchs, and the ten horns as ten kings, who in the time of Antichrist will afflict the holy Church not only by false preaching but also by tyrannical power. Of these things it will be said later: “And his tail drew a third part of the stars of heaven.”

> [Note: [Col. 0668D] Corrected from the Vatican manuscript.]

“And cast them to earth.” What should you understand by the tail except deception? His tail, therefore—that is, his own cunning and the deception of heretical perversity—drew a third part of the stars [Col. 0668C] of heaven: namely, many who seemed to shine in the Church. And it cast them to earth, so that they might no longer love and seek after heavenly things, but earthly and transitory things alone. Of this third part we have already spoken very often. We said that it signifies heretics and false Christians, who are included neither among the prelates nor among the subjects.

And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth; and when she had given birth, he devoured her son. And she bore a male child, who was to rule all nations with a rod of iron; and her child was caught up to God and to his throne. And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, that there they may feed her for one thousand two hundred and sixty days. For the devil often lies in wait for the sons of the Church. He does not greatly concern himself [Col. 0668D] with others, for the elect are his food; and, according to that prophetic saying, he is confident that Jordan will flow into his mouth. For he persecutes no one as he persecutes the sons of the Church, regenerated by the water of baptism. This is what it says: “And when she had given birth, he devoured her son.”

But when it says, “And she bore a male child,” it uses the singular for the plural. The Church bears no child except a male; even if she has many daughters, only those are hers who strive to attain not feminine softness but manly, masculine strength. Nor indeed are they called her sons on account of sex, but on account of steadfastness and courage. Such persons rule nations with a rod of iron; such persons overcome vices and malignant spirits; such persons teach God’s people, by a strong and irresistible authority, to walk in the right way. “And her child was caught up to God and to his throne.” Daily the sons of the Church are caught up to God; daily they are carried by angels to his throne; and, snatched as prey from the very jaws that wish to devour them [Col. 0669B], they ascend to heaven rejoicing and triumphing.

But the woman flees into the wilderness whenever the holy Church, avoiding the company of evildoers, withdraws herself into the secret chamber of the mind and to the contemplation of God. Hence it is written: “Behold, I fled far away and remained in the wilderness” (Ps. LIV [55]:8); and there she has a place prepared by God. But in what sense prepared? Do you wish to hear in what sense? “That there they may feed her for one thousand two hundred and sixty days.” And who are those who feed her but the sacred volumes of the Scriptures? Read Isaiah, and he himself will feed you; read the other prophets also, and there you will find pastures beyond comparison with any delights. Of these it is said: “The Lord guides me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture he has placed me” (ibid. XXII [23]:1).

By the one thousand two hundred and sixty days we understand the whole time from Christ’s preaching until the last day [Col. 0669C], for Christ preached for that many days. And because the preaching does not change, although the days are many more, they are nevertheless said to be as many as those days in which that entire preaching occurred. For we still take no other food than that which Christ prepared for us in those one thousand two hundred and sixty days. It is therefore as though he said that there they may feed her with that most pleasant and sweetest food which the Lord prepared during the one thousand two hundred and sixty days.

And a great battle took place in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon; and the dragon fought, and his angels; and they did not prevail, nor was a place found for them any longer in heaven. And that great dragon was cast [Col. 0669D] to earth—the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, who deceives the whole world—he was cast to earth, and his angels were cast to earth with him. For after the woman gave birth, after the holy Church bore children, a great battle at once took place in heaven; at once persecutions of the wicked arose [Col. 0670A] in the Church. Hence it continues: “Michael and his angels fought with the dragon, and the dragon fought, and his angels.”

> [Note: [Col. 0669D] It had long before been foretold by Daniel, chapter XII:1, that a time would come in which St Michael, the great prince of angels, would fight with Lucifer and his followers for the sons of God’s people. The same prophecy is renewed here by John, predicting Michael’s battle with Antichrist, the minister of diabolical deception, lest the elect succumb to his temptations. Although malignant spirits will always persecute the good throughout the whole time of the flourishing Church, their persecution will become more violent and terrible as its end approaches [Col. 0670D]; consequently, the elect will require greater angelic protection and support. Cassiodorus thinks that John here speaks of the battle which the archangel Michael had from the beginning of the world with Lucifer, who was hurled down from heaven to earth and lost the place of his blessedness, as did the angels who followed him.]

That angels have been given us by God for protection, the Lord himself says: “Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII:10). And the Apostle says: “Are they not all ministering spirits sent for service on behalf of those who shall inherit salvation?” (Heb. I:14). It is a great battle in which Michael, prince of angels, fights against the dragon, prince of demons: a great battle indeed, in which Michael fights against the devil, angels against angels, and saints against the wicked without ceasing. But because Michael is interpreted “Who is like God?”, the interpretation of his name strengthens us to fight manfully [Col. 0670B], so that we may not fear in so great a battle. The Apostle says: “Be strong in battle, and fight—

> [Note: [Col. 0670D] Vatican manuscript: “with the ancient dragon.”]

—with the ancient serpent” (1 Pet. V:9). For who is like God, who helps you? Who fights as does the prince of your army?

> [Note: [Col. 0670D] Vatican manuscript: “Therefore do not fail.”]

Do not fail in tribulations; do not give place to persecutors; oppose the shield of faith, and do not let the devil enter into your army. This is what follows: “And they did not prevail, nor was a place found for them any longer in heaven.” They did not prevail to resist, as battle pressed on them from every side; for they are driven away by baptism, driven away by acts of repentance, driven away by prayers, driven away by the weapons of charity and mercy. They have no place in heaven because the throne of God is there.

What then? “And that great dragon, the ancient serpent, was cast to earth.” Since he has no place in the saints, he persecutes the earth and sinners. For this had been permitted him by the Lord: “You shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Gen. III:14). He eats earth because he destroys and devours sinners. This is that great dragon, this is that ancient serpent, ever twisting and tortuous, never proceeding by a straight way, who deceived the first parents of the human race. He is called *diabolus* (“devil”) because he fell downward from the heights.
