And the seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a great voice came forth from the temple, from the throne, saying: “It is done.” And there were lightnings, voices, thunders, and a great earthquake such as had never occurred since human beings were upon the earth—so great an earthquake. And the great city was divided into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell.

The seventh angel will be the final preaching, which shall take its beginning from Enoch and Elijah. He is rightly said to have poured out his bowl into the air, because, speaking openly and plainly, he will announce that Antichrist has come. It follows: “And a voice came forth from the temple and the throne, saying: ‘It is done.’” The great voice that comes forth from the temple is the voice of the saints, who, upon hearing so dreadful an announcement, will encourage one another to act courageously, saying: “It is done. The last day has come; the Scriptures of the prophets are fulfilled. Let us all therefore die for Christ’s name.”

But immediately, on the opposite side of the wicked, there were lightnings: that is, many signs and miracles by which Antichrist and his disciples became conspicuous; and voices, the voices of the aforesaid frogs; and thunders, the lofty preaching of heretics proclaiming everywhere. “And there was a great earthquake, such as had never been”: that is, all worldly people and sinners will rise with great force against the Church. Of this earthquake the Lord himself speaks: “Then there shall be tribulation such as has not been from the beginning of the world, nor shall be” (Matt. 24:21). Then that great city of the wicked will be divided into three parts, so that no one may be found slain in it, all fighting against the saints according to their measure. The first part is Antichrist and his intimates; the second, the multitude of heretics, working signs and wonders everywhere; the third, the army of tyrants, afflicting the saints everywhere. When he says, “And the cities of the nations fell,” he signifies those who will be deceived by their signs and teaching.

And great Babylon came into remembrance before the Lord, to give her the cup of the indignation of his wrath. And every island fled, and the mountains were not found; and great hail came down from heaven upon human beings, and human beings blasphemed God because of the plague of hail, for it became exceedingly severe.  
[Note: Codex Vaticanus: “so that all alike blasphemed God himself.”]

For just as Jerusalem signifies the Church of the saints, so Babylon signifies the assembly of all the wicked. In a certain sense God appears to have forgotten her, because he permits the wicked to increase and prosper in their iniquities. But then she will be brought to his remembrance, when he gives her to drink of the cup of his indignation. Nearly all the Scriptures testify that the cup signifies suffering and death. But what does it mean that the islands flee and the mountains are not found? It means that many Churches of this world, and many bishops and teachers, already wearied and unable to endure the stormy tempests of the sea, will yield their place to persecutors and hide themselves everywhere lest they be found. We read that this often occurred in the primitive Church, when not merely ordinary persons but apostolic men themselves are said to have hidden in crypts and caverns of the earth.

Why this persecution is so great he adds, saying: “And great hail, like a talent, came down from heaven upon human beings.” This hail signifies the preaching of the seventh angel, which moved and enraged Antichrist with all his army to such anger and indignation that they together blasphemed God himself.  
[Note: Some suppose that the dissolution of the earthly world is here foretold. For, once the final judgement has been completed, when the entire cup of the indignation of God’s wrath has been poured out upon the impious condemned to Tartarus, this whole mass will be dissolved; and, as Christ the Lord says, “Heaven and earth shall pass away,” and all things shall be made new.]

This hail is well compared to a talent, since a talent is seventy-two pounds, the same number as the disciples of Christ are said to have been; the seventh angel has imitated their preaching. This passage must be connected with the preceding words, namely the place where it says: “And a great voice came forth from the temple, from the throne, saying: ‘It is done.’” From there to this point is a punctuation-mark which the Greeks call a *parenthesis*. It follows: “And human beings blasphemed God because of the plague of hail, because it became exceedingly severe.” For just as we regard the words of heretics as arrows and hail, so heretics, wounded by the preaching of the saints, fear it as hail and flee the onset of the storm.

## CHAPTER XVII

And one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and spoke with me, saying: “Come, and I will show you the condemnation of the great harlot who sits upon many waters, with whom the kings of the earth committed fornication; and the inhabitants of the earth were made drunk with the wine of her fornication.”

What is said to blessed John is said universally to the whole Church. Since the angel had begun to speak of Babylon, describing fully what she is like, he admonishes the Church to see and contemplate her.

[Note: If in the preceding chapter St John spoke somewhat obscurely and enigmatically of the city of Rome, here, under the name Babylon, he depicts her in vivid and proper colours, so that she ought not to be understood otherwise. Because of her universal corruption of morals he calls her the great harlot; and because, having desperately plunged herself into idolatry and compelled all peoples to commit fornication with her—that is, to worship false gods—he calls her intoxicated with the wine, or heat, of fornication.]

“Come,” he says, “I will show you the condemnation of the great harlot”—that is, by a change of construction, the great harlot who is to be condemned. “Who sat upon many waters,” because she holds dominion over many peoples. “With whom the kings of the earth committed fornication”: they committed fornication, certainly, because they used her wrongly and unlawfully. For although we cannot conquer without this present life, nevertheless we are said to commit fornication with it if we use it, contrary to the law, too loosely and luxuriously. “And the inhabitants of the earth were made drunk with the wine of her fornication.” What is the wine of her fornication but her unlawful cup? The inhabitants of the earth are intoxicated by it because they are so deceived by the allurements of this life that, like madmen, forgetful of themselves and of their own good, they do not know by what path they ought to proceed.

And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness, and I saw a woman seated upon a scarlet beast, full of names of blasphemy, having seven heads and ten horns. And the woman was clothed in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, precious stone, and pearls, having in her hand a golden cup full of the abomination and uncleanness of her fornication.

A wilderness is ordinarily the habitation only of wild beasts and irrational animals. He is therefore rightly brought into a wilderness who is to see so great and such a monster. “And I saw,” he says, “a woman seated upon a scarlet beast.” This beast consists of many peoples and nations; its head I had not without reason called Rome. Since this beast shed the blood of many saints, it appears wholly scarlet and red.  
[Note: Codex Vaticanus: “whose head I would not without reason call Rome; and this was also Babylon at one time. This beast …”]

Since she served many monstrous idols, she is said to be full of names of blasphemy.  
[Note: St Leo the Great describes what Rome was before the preaching of Peter and Paul in Sermon 80, on the feast of those apostles, when he says: “Here the opinions of philosophers had to be trampled down; here the vanities of earthly wisdom had to be washed away; here the impiety of every sacrilege had to be destroyed, where, through most diligent superstition, whatever had anywhere been established by vain errors was gathered together.”]

For what blasphemy is greater than to call gold, stones, and speech gods? She had seven heads and ten horns, of which we have already spoken above and shall say more below. Such, then, was the beast. But what was the woman seated upon the beast like? It follows: “And the woman was clothed in scarlet and adorned with gold, precious stone, and pearls.” With these ornaments she draws her lovers to her fornication; through them we also understand the other things by which miserable human beings are drawn back from the love of God to the prosperity of this life. She also had in her hand a cup full of abomination and the uncleanness of her fornication. By this we understand a certain persuasion and delight in transitory goods; this persuasion and delight, full, as it were, of some sweet draught of pride, avarice, luxury, and other vices, intoxicates many and makes them depart from the straight path.

And upon her forehead was written a name, Mystery: Great Babylon, mother of fornications and abominations of the earth. And I saw the woman drunk with the blood of the saints and with the blood of Jesus’ martyrs; and when I saw her, I wondered with great astonishment.

There was, he says, written upon her forehead a name containing a meaning other than that which it appeared to sound—a mystery, that is, of many secrets. For she is called Great Babylon. In ancient times no city was so noble, so powerful, or so full of every kind of wealth, luxury, and superstition as Babylon. She took the people of God captive; she destroyed Jerusalem, the city of God, to its foundations; moreover, her king Nebuchadnezzar was the proudest of all human beings. Thus, because she loved present goods alone, invites people to the present life, to the assembly of all evils, and to other things which God abominates and hates, she is rightly called the mother of fornications and abominations. Since she shed the blood of many saints and martyrs of Jesus, she is described as drunk with it, as though already filled and satiated. Blessed John marvelled with no slight amazement at her impiety and cruelty.

And the angel said to me: “Why do you marvel? I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast which carries her, which has seven heads and ten horns. The beast which you saw was, and is not, and is about to ascend from the abyss and go to destruction; and the inhabitants of the earth—whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world—will marvel when they see the beast which was and is not.”

“I,” he says, “will tell you the mystery of the woman and the beast. Hear and understand what each signifies. For the beast that you saw was and is not. This beast indeed was for a time: the powerful people of this age once flourished, were exalted by honours and dignities, and were feared by human beings as though eternal. Yet now it is not, because it continually passes from this life and remains in it for so brief a time that in one and the same hour it seems both to be and not to be. And it is about to ascend from the abyss and go to destruction.”

[Note: Expositors offer different interpretations of this passage. Some refer it to the brief persecution of Licinius, who, though he had formerly favoured Christians as Constantine did, afterwards, when hostilities arose between himself and Constantine, again raged against them and attempted to restore the worship of the gods. But this persecution was brief, for Constantine defeated and killed him in two battles. Others assert that these words foretell Valens, the most vehement patron of the Arians; others, Julian the Apostate, who were permitted to afflict the Church for a short time.]

For it will ascend from the abyss because the souls of the wicked will return to bodies that are to rise again; cast down once more into Tartarus, both souls and bodies will endure eternal torments. Then sinners, whose names are not written in the book of life and who are not judged worthy of God’s remembrance, will marvel and be stunned at this beast, seeing condemned those who had been accustomed to judge others with great power. It follows:

“And here is the meaning which has wisdom. The seven heads are seven mountains upon which the woman sits. And they are seven kings: five have fallen, one is, and another has not yet come; and when he comes, he must remain a short time.”

This is the exposition of the foregoing likeness. “Here,” he says, “is the meaning and understanding of what has been said; and he who has wisdom understands it well. And the seven heads are seven mountains.” For the seven mountains upon which the woman sits, and likewise the seven kings, signify, as will be made clear below, seven periods: namely, six ages and the seventh, final and brief portion of the sixth age. Therefore he adds: “Five have fallen, one is, and another has not yet come.”

[Note: These are Diocletian, Maximian, Galerius, Maximinus, Maxentius, Severus, and Licinius. Five have fallen: namely, Diocletian, Maximian, Galerius, Maxentius, and Severus. One is: namely, Maximinus, who waged a most savage war against the Eastern Church. But when he too was removed, like the others, Licinius came; as we have said, he persecuted the Church for a short time and was overcome by Constantine.]

For five ages and five kingdoms, with their kings, had already passed when blessed John spoke these things; but the sixth age and sixth kingdom, with its kings, was then beginning. It is still unfolding and will continue until the times of Antichrist. The other who has not yet come is Antichrist himself. Since he will come at the end of this sixth age, he is counted as the seventh; and when he comes, he must remain a short time, for he will reign only three and a half years.

“And the beast which was and is not is itself an eighth, and is of the seven, and goes to destruction.” For every whole consists of its parts; and although the whole is nothing other than the conjunction of its parts, it nevertheless differs from each individual part. Thus this beast—the church of the malignant, constituted from the seven periods already mentioned—is in itself the eighth, but in the constitution of its parts is of the seven. Dialecticians readily understand this. And it assuredly goes to destruction with all its parts.

[Note: Those who attempt to fit history to John’s prophecies identify Julian the Apostate as the eighth beast. That most bitter enemy of the Christian name attempted to restore the superstition of idols, but was quickly destroyed by a thunderbolt sent from heaven, after one year and seven or eight months.]

“And the ten horns which you saw are ten kings, who have not yet received a kingdom, but will receive authority as kings for one hour after the beast. These have one purpose and will give their strength and authority to the beast. They will fight with the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings; and those with him are called, chosen, and faithful.”

[Note: Although there is here a clear prophecy of the coming of Antichrist, who will be the last of the persecutors, wicked kings will precede him—destroyers of Roman power and pride. Since that city, even after Christian worship had been established in it, did not cease to adhere to the superstition of the gods, the Almighty sent against it from remote regions most powerful barbarians: Alaric, Genseric, Astolphus, Attila, Odoacer, Totila, and other tyrants. They admitted that they had been sent against it by God, and therefore spared nothing, but utterly demolished and ravaged it.]

Keep in mind that we have said this beast is constituted from all the wicked, and have explained that its parts are the wicked and utterly evil people of every age. Antichrist is therefore a great part of it, since he will be more wicked and detestable than all others; hence he not undeservedly appropriates to himself the name of the whole beast. Ten kings of the same wickedness will adhere to him; by their strength and tyranny he will work many evils against the saints. He will fight with the Lamb, but will be conquered; for, as it is written, “Our Lord Jesus Christ will slay him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming” (2 Thess. 2:8). We pass over these matters briefly, because they are understood literally.

And he said to me: “The waters which you saw, where the harlot sits, are peoples, nations, and tongues; and the ten horns which you saw, and the beast, will hate the harlot and make her desolate and naked; they will eat her flesh and burn her with fire. For God gave it into their hearts to do what pleased him, to give their kingdom to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled. And the woman whom you saw is the city which has dominion over the kings of the earth.”

Since blessed John himself explains these things, there is no great labour required in expounding them.

## CHAPTER XVIII

After these things I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority; and the earth was illuminated by his glory. And he cried out powerfully, saying: “Fallen, fallen is great Babylon, and she has become a habitation of demons, a prison of every unclean spirit, and a prison of every unclean and hateful bird; for all nations have drunk of the wine of her fornication, and the kings of the earth committed fornication with her; and the merchants of the earth became rich through the power of her luxuries.”

This angel may be understood as some great teacher of the Church, and with him and through him the others also, who, now recognizing in manifest signs that the day of judgement is drawing near, will steadfastly and loudly proclaim the peril that threatens this world and its lovers. Hence the earth is said to have been illuminated by his glory, because they will reveal what was previously hidden. He is rightly said to descend from heaven, because he will receive by divine inspiration all that he announces to Christ’s other faithful people.

It follows: “Fallen, fallen is great Babylon.” This is a very common mode of speaking: we say that things which we know will most certainly happen have happened even before they occur. Thus we say that those have already conquered whom we think will be victors, and announce as already dead those whom we see approaching death. Thus in this place, because the angel does not doubt that Babylon will suddenly perish, he speaks as though of past events, as if she had already fallen: “Fallen, fallen is great Babylon.” As though he were saying: Put no further hope in her; place no love in her; for soon you will see her fall miserably. Let her not mislead or deceive you, for all her beauty will suddenly vanish.

“And she has become a habitation of demons.”  
[Note: This description of the overthrown city Babylon is taken from Isaiah, chapter 24: “But beasts shall rest there, and their houses shall be filled with dragons; and ostriches shall dwell there, and shaggy beings shall dance there,” etc. What St Jerome here rendered *pilosi* (“hairy beings”), the Septuagint translated “demons”; for people then believed that demons and apparitions frequented deserted places and solitudes. So Calmet.]

After Babylon—that is, the assembly of the wicked—has fallen into darkness, whom can we believe dwell in her except malignant spirits?  
[Note: Codex Vaticanus adds and completes the printed edition.]  
Who but unclean spirits and unclean birds will guard her? They will guard her because they will always be filled with her punishments. Then she will become hateful to all, when even those whom she served will not cease to afflict her. But to what end is this said? It follows:

“Because all nations shall drink of the wine of her fornication, and all kings of the earth who committed fornication with her.” Her fornication, therefore, is the reason why all nations and all kings of the earth incur and suffer wrath, indignation, and many miseries of this world.

“And the merchants of the earth became rich through the power of her luxuries.” As the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2:4). The merchants of the earth are those who desire to be enriched not by eternal goods but by Babylon’s luxuries.

And I heard another voice from heaven saying: “Come out of her, my people, and do not share in her sins, lest you receive of her plagues; for her sins have reached unto heaven, and the Lord has remembered her iniquities. Repay her as she repaid you, and render her double according to her works.”

In all the Scriptures the Lord admonishes his people, saying: “Come out of her, my people.” Leave the manner of life of the wicked, not so much in body as in heart; and do not share in her sins, lest perhaps you too later receive her plagues and punishments with her.  
[Note: From St Jerome and Orosius we know that many Romans, fearing the savagery of the barbarians, fled to Egypt, Africa, and Syria and lived holy lives in desert places.]

For those who are partners in sins will also be partners in torments. “For her sins have reached unto heaven,” since they have increased so greatly that, because of their magnitude, they are recited before God with a kind of accusation. Therefore he adds: “And the Lord has remembered her iniquities.” Because he allowed them to remain unpunished, he seemed to have forgotten them.

“Repay her as she herself repaid you, and render her double according to her works.” Since the torments of the wicked will take place according to the sentence and will of the saints whom they afflicted, they are therefore said to be inflicted on them by the saints themselves. They are rightly commanded to be doubled because the wicked received power only over bodies, whereas the saints will have power over souls and bodies. Therefore he adds: “In the cup in which she mixed for you, mix double for her; and as much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, give her so much torment and mourning.”

This is what is said to the rich man through Abraham in the Gospel: “Son, remember that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted here, while you are tormented” (Luke 16:25). Thus the number of torments increases in proportion to the quality of the luxuries. “For she said in her heart: ‘I sit as queen, I am not a widow, and I shall not see mourning’; therefore her plagues shall come in one day—death, mourning, and famine—and she shall be burned with fire, because God who judges her is strong.”

For when the multitude of the wicked sees the happiness and prosperity of this life abound for it, it does not consider the evils that will come upon it, but prides and glories itself in present goods alone, which it uses badly. Although it can suddenly be deprived of royal dignity and honour, bereft of vital strength, and filled with every grief and misery, yet, foolish and ignorant, it says in its heart: “I sit as queen; all revere me as their mistress. I am not a widow, nor am I deprived of counsel and aid; and I shall not see the mourning which some falsely promise me.” Therefore in one day—indeed, in one hour, when it is said, “Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire”—her plagues will come: namely, eternal death, unceasing mourning, and insatiable hunger. “And she shall be burned with fire,” namely with that unquenchable fire of which we have just spoken; “because God who judges her is strong,” and no strength can resist his judgement and will.

And the kings of the earth who committed fornication with her and lived in luxury will lament and weep over her, when they see the smoke of her burning. Standing afar off because of fear of her torments, they will say: “Woe, woe to that great city Babylon, that mighty city! For in one hour your judgement has come.”

All kings and powerful persons of the earth, he says, will weep and mourn—not so much for her as for themselves because of her, because they loved her unhappily.

[Note: Augustine, *The City of God*, book I, chapter 33, charged the Romans with this great perversity and disgrace: while eastern peoples and very great cities in the most distant lands mourned the city’s ruin, the Romans themselves, devoted to theatrical entertainments and every pleasure, did and were doing things far more insane than before.]

They loved her unhappily, certainly, because they committed fornication with her: loving this life more for luxury, delicacies, and pleasures of the flesh than in order to serve God, labour in his vineyard, and finally, when their labour was ended, carry away with them the reward of their work. They will weep, he says, when they see the smoke of her burning, “standing afar off”: that is, desiring to stand far off because they fear her torments. They will stand far off in desire, but in fact they will be in her; in her and with her they will burn. They will indeed mourn and say: “Woe, woe! You are that great city Babylon, that mighty city, whom we see thus perish, whom we foolish and unhappy people thought eternal, now delivered over to flames. And behold, in one hour your judgement has come; in one hour your pride has fallen.”

And the merchants of the earth will weep and mourn over her, because no one will buy their merchandise any more: merchandise of gold and silver, precious stone and pearl, fine linen and purple, silk and scarlet; every kind of thyine wood, every article of ivory, every article of precious stone, bronze, iron, and marble; cinnamon, spices, ointment, [Col. 0704A] incense, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, beasts of burden, sheep, horses, carriages, slaves, and human souls.

“They will weep,” he says, “and mourn over the destruction of the aforesaid city.” Although these things may be understood literally, those merchants are the persons who customarily deceive the people of this world through trade in various wares. These, however, are evil spirits, who after the destruction of the people of this world will weep and mourn because they will find no one to whom they can sell the stock of their wicked craft.

Gold and silver, precious stones and pearls, fine linen and purple, silk and scarlet—things belonging to adornment and beauty—signify wisdom, virtues, and moral uprightness. Thyine wood, however, [Col. 0704B] and every article of ivory, and every article of precious stone, bronze, iron, and marble, though the rich do not wear them upon themselves for adornment, nevertheless display their glory and power; they denote the honors and dignities by which the pride of the rich is exalted and glories.

Cinnamon, amomum, spices, incense, and ointments, which especially pertain to the nostrils and sense of smell, and by which sickly and weakened limbs are strengthened and healed, signify the grace of the Holy Spirit. Wine, oil, fine flour, and wheat, by which human life is sustained, signify the study of letters and instruction. All these things evil spirits either sell, or pretend that they sell.

They also sell beasts of burden—those, namely, of whom it is said: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel 1:17). They sell also the sheep of whom the Lord says: “Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves” (Matt. 5:16). For what is it to sell these except to hand them over to death? But what wonder if they sell these, when they did not fear to sell that greatest and chief sheep?

> [Note: Cod. Vat.: “for thirty pieces of silver.”]

Likewise they sell horses, carriages, and slaves, by whom we understand either heretics, in whom and through whom the wicked fight against the good; or also teachers, by whose service people are brought back to their homeland. They also sell human souls; had they not sold them, hell would not today possess so many captives. It follows:

“And the fruits desired by your soul have departed from you, and [Col. 0704D] all rich and splendid things have passed away from you, and you will find them no more.” The merchants of these things, who became rich from her, will stand far away for fear of her torments, weeping and mourning and saying: “Woe, woe to that great city, which was clothed in purple, fine linen, and scarlet, and gilded with gold, precious stone, and pearls, because in one hour such great riches have been laid waste.”

“The fruits,” he says, “sweet and pleasant fruits which your will and soul desired to devour, have departed [Col. 0705A] from you; and all rich things—the richness of virtues—and splendid things—splendid in uprightness of life and morals—have passed away from you, and you will find them no more.”

> [When you found these things, you cruelly persecuted and destroyed them. Therefore, because you killed the saints, you will by no means find them as helpers for yourself.]
>
> [Note: We have supplied this from Cod. Vat.]

The merchants of the things enumerated above will stand far away from her—that is, they will desire to stand far away—for fear of her torments, weeping and mourning, and saying: “Woe, woe to that great city, which was clothed in purple, fine linen, and scarlet, and gilded with gold, precious stone, and pearls.” All these things indicate royal dignity; with them the powerful and noble persons of this age are adorned. By them he displays the power and loftiness of this most noble city. But these things [Col. 0705B] will perish in one hour, because at the sound of a single command heaven and earth will pass away.

“And every helmsman, and everyone who sails upon the lake, and sailors who work upon the sea, stood far away, and cried out when they saw the place of her burning, saying: ‘What city is like this great city?’ And they cast dust upon their heads, and cried out, weeping and mourning, and saying: ‘Woe, woe to that great city, by whose wealth all who had ships at sea became rich, because in one hour she has been made desolate.’”

“Every helmsman,” he says, signifies kings, philosophers, heretics, and the rest to whom the governments of the world have been entrusted. “Everyone who sails upon the lake” means one who lies in wait for heedless fish and baptized persons. And “sailors who work upon the sea” [Col. 0705C] are the rich and powerful of this age, who through this great and broad sea lead their armies and their wicked ships, full of pirates, murderers, and robbers, against the saints and the Church, and who never cease daily to commit slaughter, arson, robbery, and the other works of wickedness.

All these stood far away, as we said above, and cried out when they saw the place of her burning; for this place is hell. They said: “What city is like this great city?” They say this from astonishment and amazement. “And they cast dust upon their heads,” because, even if they repented, yet by making even that repentance fruitless through their iniquities, they will recognize that they are earth and dust. They cry out, weep, [Col. 0705D] and mourn; they are astounded and amazed at the so sudden destruction of this world, which had enriched so many kings and kingdoms, so many peoples and nations, with its honors and wealth. For then all things will appear cheap and without honor which now seem dear and precious.

“Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you apostles and prophets, because God has pronounced your judgment upon her.” Having set forth everything that concerned the confusion and disgrace of the wicked, the angel who was speaking exhorts the faithful to joy and exultation, saying: “Rejoice over her, O heaven,” that is, the whole multitude of the Church, and especially you holy apostles and prophets, because God has pronounced your judgment [Col. 0706A] upon her. “For the righteous will rejoice, as it is written, when he sees vengeance” (Ps. 57:11). For just as the saints continually entreat God on behalf of those who can be saved, so they exult and rejoice in the punishment of those who are irrecoverably condemned, because they know that it pleases God.

> [Note: Cod. Vat.: “and rejoices.”]

“And a mighty angel lifted up a great stone, like a millstone, and threw it into the sea, saying: ‘With such force will Babylon, that great city, be thrown down, and shall be found no more.’”

While he was in an ecstasy of mind, one angel appeared to blessed John, who is called mighty because he performs mighty deeds. He lifted up—that is, he appeared to lift up—a single great millstone and cast it into the sea. In accordance with the weight of its nature, it always seeks the depths [Col. 0706B] and lowest places; and because it is round and rolling, once it inclines toward its fall, even if it wished to be held, it cannot stand. Babylon may aptly be compared to it: once condemned and having received the sentence of its condemnation, it will have no power, effort, or prayers by which to avoid being submerged in the depth of the lake and the lower regions of hell. Therefore he says: “With such force will Babylon, that great city, be thrown down.” And it will be no more.

“And the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute-players and trumpeters, shall be heard in you no more; and no craftsman of any craft shall be found in you any more; and the sound of a mill shall be heard in you no more; and the light of a lamp shall shine in you no more; and the voice of bridegroom and bride shall be heard in you no longer.”

Taken literally, these things signify the utter [Col. 0706C] destruction of that city. Allegorically, however, by harpists and musicians, by players of flute and trumpet, we may understand philosophers and sages, who soothed her with the sweet modulation of their words and persuaded her to love the pleasures of this world—such as Orpheus and Alcaeus, Cicero and Horace, and many others are remembered to have been.

> [Note: Cod. Vat. reads *tibia tubaque canentes* (“flute- and trumpet-players”) in place of *per tibiam tubamque canentes* (“by flute- and trumpet-players”).]

They may also be called craftsmen, since they both taught and practiced the arts themselves. “And the sound of a mill shall be heard in you no more”: where a mill is not heard, there is neither food nor human habitation. “And the light of a lamp shall shine for you no more”: cast down into darkness, she will lack not only the common light of sun and moon, but even the private [Col. 0706D] light of her own lamp; indeed, not even her own eyes will be of use to her. “And the voice of bridegroom and bride shall not be heard in you”: where bridegroom and bride are not heard, the propagation of the human race is removed. Henceforth, therefore, she will be barren, though she gloried in the multitude of so many children. Why these things happen is then added:

“Because your merchants were the princes of the earth, and because in your sorceries all nations went astray. And in her was found the blood of prophets and saints, and of all who have been slain on earth.”

This city was so rich and so noble that the merchants whom it possessed were princes of other nations. Yet this may be understood as adding to the sum of her wickedness: she was so impious and greedy that she made princes of persons who had been merchants. For such men easily deceive through their calculations those over whom they rule; and they not only exact tribute, but through their cunning do not strip them of all that they possess. It follows:

“Because in your sorceries all nations went astray,” etc. For where there are sorceries, there are drugs; there heresies were fabricated, by which all nations went astray; there the blood of saints and prophets was both shed and found—and not only of saints, but even of all who have been slain anywhere on earth. For who except the assembly of the wicked knows how to shed human blood? From her, therefore, [Col. 0707B] will be required all blood shed upon the earth, whoever it may belong to, even if it is the blood of unbelievers.

> [Note: From the beginning of this chapter to its end, St. John has delineated in his own characters and figures the overthrow and ruin of the city and empire of Rome, particularly noting those things which will lead it from the greatest prosperity to the utmost calamity. Yet Bede, Arethas, and others maintain that Babylon should be understood not as Rome, but as the entire heaven—or realm—of the ungodly, who will be exterminated by Christ the Lord at the judgment; nor will any dignity or power remain that can resist his sentence. The blood of prophets and martyrs is said to be found in her because it will be testimony to that impiety, or to the persecutors.]
>
> [Col. 0707D; 0708D]

## CHAPTER XIX

“After these things I heard as it were a great voice of many crowds in heaven, saying: ‘Alleluia: praise, glory, and power belong to our God, because his judgments are true and just; because he has judged the great harlot, who corrupted the earth by her prostitution, and he has avenged the blood of his servants at her hands.’ And they said again: ‘Alleluia.’ And her smoke rose up for ages of ages. And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshipped God seated upon the throne, saying: ‘Alleluia. Amen.’”

This great voice of many crowds is the voice of saints rejoicing, giving thanks to God, and praising him with joy and a voice [Col. 0707C] of exultation. For what else is *alleluia* but “Praise God”? Hence there follows: “Praise, glory, and power belong to our God.” Why is this so? Because his judgments are true and just. How do you prove it? Because he judged the great harlot, since she corrupted the whole earth by her prostitution and fornication. And he avenged the blood of his servants, which was shed at her hands.

> [Note: Cod. Vat.: “For she is truly a harlot, who [the whole earth …],” etc.]

On hearing these things, they again joyfully said “Alleluia,” praising and magnifying God for judgments and deliverances so great and such as these. “And her smoke rose up for ages of ages,” so that, as God’s praises increase, the torments of the wicked likewise increase. After this the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures—by whom we understand all the patriarchs [Col. 0707D] and prophets of the New and Old Testaments, apostles and teachers—fell upon their faces and worshipped God seated upon the throne of his majesty, saying: “Amen, alleluia.” Thus they confirmed the things which they had heard from the voice of the many preceding crowds, and at the same time praised God, in whose praise such great and wonderful things were said.

[Col. 0708A] “And a voice came forth from the throne, saying: ‘Give praise to our God, all his saints, and you who fear God, small and great.’” First the whole Church, then the patriarchs and teachers of both Testaments, and afterward the angels themselves praise God and invite all others, small and great alike, to praise him. This throne is understood to be that one which is numbered among the nine orders of angels. Let us hear what follows at their exhortation:

“And I heard as it were the sound of a great trumpet, and like the sound of many waters, and like the sound of great thunders, saying: ‘Alleluia, for the Lord our God Almighty reigns.’” The sound of the great trumpet signifies teachers; the sounds of waters, the multitude of all believers; and the sounds of great thunders, [Col. 0708B] the entire host of angels. All these, praising God, sang *alleluia*, saying: “Let us rejoice and exult, and give him glory, because the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his wife has prepared herself; and it has been granted her to clothe herself in shining, white fine linen.” Fine linen, however, is the justifications—righteous deeds—of the saints.

“And he said to me: ‘Write: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage-supper of the Lamb.’” All the saints rejoice and are glad and give glory to God, because the marriage of the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world has come, when, with bodies joined to souls, he brings his bride, Holy Church, into the heavenly bridal chambers. For this is what is meant by: “And his wife has prepared herself.” The preparation of the wife is the resurrection of the flesh. And it has been given her, and granted by God, [Col. 0708C] to clothe herself in shining and white fine linen.

Since he himself explains what this signifies, it is not permitted to us to explain it. “Fine linen,” he says, “is the justification of the saints.” For just as fine linen—that is, flax—springs from the earth and, with much labor, is made into cloth and clothing, so the justifications and virtues of the saints arise and grow through many tribulations in mortal flesh. The command to write that those invited to the marriage-supper of the Lamb are blessed demonstrates that God’s judgment concerning their blessedness is firm and immovable. Hence it is added: “And he said to me: ‘These are the true words of God.’” This is what is said in the prophets: “For the mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isa. 40:5).

“And I fell before his feet, to worship him. And [Col. 0708D] he said to me: ‘See that you do not do it. I am your fellow servant, and the fellow servant of your brothers who have the testimony of Jesus. Worship God. The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.’”

Having heard so great a promise concerning the blessedness of the good, blessed John wished to worship the angel who was speaking. The angel forbade him, since he too, like the others who have and bear the testimony of Jesus, is his [Col. 0709A] servant; he commands that God alone be worshipped. But what is it to have the testimony of Jesus? The following answers: “For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.” Whoever, therefore, testifies and believes concerning Jesus what the prophets foretold undoubtedly has the testimony of Jesus.

## BOOK SIX

[Col. 0709]

[Col. 0709A] 357 “And I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse; and he who sat upon it was called Faithful and True, and he judges and fights in righteousness. His eyes were like a flame of fire, and upon his head were many diadems; he had a written name which no one knows except himself. And he was clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood, and his name is called the Word of God.”

Again blessed John, as in the other books, beginning from the beginning of the Church’s birth, describes it until the end. He then saw heaven opened when he first beheld teachers going out everywhere from the Church to preach and introducing believers into it from every side. Therefore, he says: “I saw heaven opened,” that is, mysteries revealed through people entering the Church; and there follows: “And behold, a white horse.” The white horse, made white by baptism and whitened beyond snow, without spot or wrinkle, signifies the apostles and teachers.

“He was called Faithful and True,” because Christ our Lord sat upon it, concerning whom it is said: “You mounted your horses, and your chariots are salvation” (Hab. 3:8). He judges in righteousness and always fights for righteousness. His eyes are like a flame of fire—that is, the apostles and prophets—who shine forth in the head of the Church and, with clear and penetrating vision, see and consider all the Church’s mysteries until the consummation of the age.

“And upon his head were many diadems.” As often as the saints conquer, so often Christ is crowned, because all their victory is referred to Christ, who is wonderful in his saints. Hence they themselves say: “In God we shall do valiantly” (Ps. 59:14). “He had a written name which no one knows except himself.” He himself knows this name because he is the head together with the other members of the Church, who are parts of the same body.

“And he was clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood,” that is, in virginal and incorruptible flesh pierced by the soldier’s lance. Hence the prophet: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?” (Isa. 63:1). “And his name is called the Word [Col. 0709D] of God.” Neither Jew, heretic, nor pagan has known this name. For no one knows this name except himself, that is, his Church together with him.

Listen to what he says through blessed John, who is now speaking, also in the Gospel, concerning the fact that he and the Church are one: “I pray not for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they too may be one in us” (John 16:20). Therefore what the Church knows, no one knows, since the Church and he are one.

“And the armies which are in heaven followed him upon [Col. 0710A] white horses, clothed in clean, white fine linen; and from his mouth proceeds a sword sharp on both sides, that with it he may strike the nations; and he shall rule them with a rod of iron; and he treads the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty. And he has written upon his garment and upon his thigh: ‘King of kings and Lord of lords.’”

“The armies which are in heaven,” he says, are the congregations of saints, among whom are martyrs, confessors, and virgins. They followed him on [Col. 0710B] white horses, by which their bodies made white in baptism are understood, clothed in clean white fine linen—which he himself above explained as the justifications of the saints. They follow him because, walking in the same way, they imitate him insofar as they can.

The sword sharp on both sides which proceeds from his mouth is that of which the Apostle says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6:17); and again: “The word of God is living and effective, and more penetrating than any two-edged sword” (Heb. 4:12). With this sword he strikes the nations, because, sparing no one, he rebukes the iniquities and vices of all. “And he shall rule them with a rod of iron,” that is, by straight and strong authority, by invincible and inflexible rule.

The winepress of the wine of fury and wrath which he treads is that of which it is elsewhere said: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and there was no man with me from among the nations” (Isa. 63:5). As often as he destroys and condemns this wicked world for its crimes, so often he treads the winepress in wrath and fury. Thus once he trod the Jews and filled all the ditches around Jerusalem with their blood.

“And he has written upon his garment and upon his thigh, ‘King of kings and Lord of lords.’” What is meant by garment and thigh except humanity, with which divinity was clothed and through which the propagation of the human race is extended? Therefore he must be believed to be King of kings and Lord of lords not only according to divinity, but also according to humanity, in which he triumphed over enemies.

[Col. 0710D] “And I saw one angel standing in the sun, 358 and he cried with a loud voice, saying to all the birds that flew through the midst of heaven: ‘Come, assemble for the great supper of God, that you may eat the flesh of kings, the flesh of tribunes, the flesh of mighty men, the flesh of horses and of those seated upon them, and the flesh of all, free and slave, small and great.’”

This angel, who appears to stand in the sun, is Christ, concerning whom it is said: “He has placed his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. 18:6). To stand in the sun is to appear openly and manifestly to all. The birds which fly through the midst of heaven may be understood either as teachers of the Church going everywhere [Col. 0711A] or as the evil spirits who rule in this age; for both the former and the latter are assembled for God’s supper, and both eat food prepared for them by God, but in different ways.

The saints eat the flesh of kings, tribunes, and the rest, according to what was shown to blessed Peter: a sheet full of unclean animals, with the command to kill and eat. Understanding its meaning, he said to those with him: “You know how abominable it is for a Jewish man to associate with or approach a foreigner; but God has shown me that I should call no one common or unclean” (Acts 10:28). Unclean spirits, however, eat the flesh of kings and tribunes when they deceive and kill sinners and rejoice and are satisfied in their punishments, according to the sense in which it is said: “They have devoured Jacob and laid waste his dwelling-place” (Ps. 78:7). But what are horses and those seated upon them except bodies and the souls that preside over them?

“And I saw the beast, and the kings of the earth, and their armies assembled to make war against him who sat upon the horse and against his army. And the beast was seized, and with it the false prophets, and him who performed signs before it, by which he deceived those who received the mark of the beast and worshipped its image. These two were thrown alive into the lake of burning fire and sulphur; and the rest were slain by the sword of him who sat upon the horse, which proceeds from his mouth; and all the birds were filled with their flesh.”

In this passage blessed John seems to relate the battle which Christ our Lord will wage against Antichrist at the consummation of the age. “I saw the beast,” he says, that is, Antichrist, of whom we have often spoken already; and the kings of the earth who will follow him. With him will be the false prophets and their armies, that is, the multitude of all the wicked, assembled to make war against him who sat upon the horse and against his army—that is, against Christ and his elect.

“And the beast was seized,” that is, Antichrist, and with it the false prophets, namely many heresiarchs and his disciples. Moreover, he himself who performed signs before it, by which he deceived those who received the mark and image of the beast. More has been said about this in the fourth book. For this is the beast [Col. 0711D] which came up from the earth, having two horns like those of a lamb and speaking like a dragon; exercising before the first beast all its authority, it compelled the whole earth and its inhabitants to worship the first beast. For this one, as though deceived by a king, by Antichrist, will be full of all wickedness and every artifice of deception.

“These two were thrown alive,” that is, Antichrist and his disciples, “into the lake of burning fire and sulphur.” They are alive because they too, like the rest, will rise again and afterward, according to Scripture, will descend alive into hell. For one who does not live does not feel torment; they therefore live in order to feel torments.

“And the rest were slain by the sword of him who sat upon the horse, which proceeds from his mouth.” This may be understood in two ways: either that, according to their former way of life, they are understood to be slain by the word of God, as the Lord says: “I came not to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10:34); or that they will be struck by that terrible and dreadful judgment at the last judgment, saying: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41).

“And all the birds were filled with their flesh.” In a twofold sense, there are good birds and evil birds. The good birds are filled, joining daily with the chief of the apostles in killing and eating. The evil birds are filled because they delight and rejoice in the punishments and torments of these persons as though satisfied by some most delicious food. For it is a sufficiently customary expression among all people to say that we are satisfied by those things in which we see ourselves abound.

## CHAPTER XX

“And I saw an angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand; and he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and cast him into the abyss, and shut and sealed it over him, so that he might deceive the nations no more, until the thousand years should be completed. After these things he must be loosed for a short time.”

For it is characteristic of the prophets neither to attend to time nor order, but now to speak of future things and now to return to past things; and blessed John seems to do this here. “I saw,” he says, “an angel descending.”

> [Note: Bruno followed St. Augustine, who in *The City of God*, book XX, chapter 7, recognized Christ in the angel descending from heaven, to whom the Father gave all authority, so that he might restrain the demon and keep him bound and subject to his command as long as he pleased. Therefore John says that, when he descended from heaven—that is, when he came to earth to assume human flesh—he had the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand, by which he seized and bound the dragon, the ancient serpent. Yet there are others, mentioned by Cornelius, who hold that an angel is to be understood here in the proper sense, the same angel of whom chapter 9 also says that the key of the pit of the abyss was given to him.]
>
> [Col. 0711D; 0712D]

He is not another, but the very one whom above he reported that he had seen standing in the sun, having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand. For the key is his and the chain is his; he shuts and opens, he binds and looses; at his command the gates of the abyss and of heaven alike are shut and opened. He seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, namely the one who deceived and destroyed the first parents of the human race with the poison of his deceit. Hence it is added: “Who is the devil and Satan; and he bound him for a thousand years.”

This number, as we have already said, because it contains the other numbers within itself and has no greater number above it, is sometimes used for all and sometimes for many. Thus it is said here: “And he bound him for a thousand years.” This is as though he said, “for many years.” He bound him so that he might not wander everywhere and freely run about, nor loosen the reins of wickedness according to his own will.

> [Note: “The binding of the devil is that he is not permitted to exercise the whole temptation which he can exercise, whether by force in coercing people violently to his side, or by deceit in fraudulently misleading them.” St. Augustine, same book and chapter.]
>
> [Col. 0712D; 0713D]

He cast him into the abyss, so that there he may now suffer grievous torments and dwell only in those who, covered in the darkness of blindness [Col. 0713A] and ignorance, neither see nor know the Sun of righteousness. He shut over him and sealed it, so that he might not go out as he wishes or when he wishes, and, recognizing Christ’s seal and image, might not dare to tempt or deceive anyone unless permitted. “And after these things he must be loosed for a short time”: when the thousand years are finished, he says, that is, after some length of time, Satan will be loosed for a short time.

> [Note: We prefer to illuminate Bruno’s somewhat obscure exposition with Augustine’s light: “Then Satan will be loosed,” he says, “when there will also be a short time. For we read that for three years and six months he will rage with all his own strength and that of his followers; and those against whom battle must be waged will be such that they cannot be overcome by his great attack and snares. But if he were not loosed, his malignant power would appear less clearly, and the most faithful patience of the holy city would be tested less clearly.” In the same place.]
>
> [Col. 0713D; 0714D]

For the three and a half years during which Antichrist will reign, he will afflict the world with such an onset of fury that he will be thought always to have been bound and never to have been loosed. In comparison with that time, therefore, Satan is said to be bound and shut, just as in Ezekiel, in comparison with Jerusalem, even Sodom is called righteous—though Moses himself testifies how sinful she was.

“And I saw thrones, and they sat upon them, and judgment was given to them; and the souls of those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God; and those who did not worship the beast or its image, nor receive its mark upon their foreheads or hands; and they lived and reigned with Christ for a thousand years. The rest of the dead did not live until the thousand years were completed. This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is the one who has a part in the first resurrection; over these the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and will reign with him for a thousand years.”

“And I saw thrones,” he says, “and they sat upon them,” because throughout the earth the apostles and teachers, distributed each in his own see, province, [Col. 0713C] and city, received the care and authority of rule—authority which we see bishops possess even today. “And judgment was given to them”: these are the judges of the earth and possess judicial dignity; to their judgment the whole multitude of the faithful has resorted.

“And I saw the souls of those beheaded,” namely those who were beheaded by the wicked because of the testimony of Jesus which they bore and because of the word of God which they preached. “And I saw those who did not worship the beast,” that is, Antichrist, “nor its image, nor received its mark,” that is, its faith and teaching, “upon their foreheads or hands.” One has its faith upon one’s forehead who openly and publicly preaches it; one has it upon one’s hands who does what it commands. Hence it is evident [Col. 0713D] that even now many bear its mark upon their hands.

There follows: “And they lived and reigned with him for a thousand years.” Those, he says, who worshipped neither the beast nor its image lived and reigned with Christ for a thousand years. Unless we understand by a thousand years all the years before and after the judgment, what is said is very limited; for a thousand years have already passed since the souls of the martyrs began to reign with him. Therefore let us understand “all” by “a thousand,” since all numbers are contained in a thousand.

“But the rest of the dead did not live until the thousand years were completed.” As regards the body, neither good nor evil live after death before the judgment; but as regards the soul, the good dead also live, because they are where life reigns and where death cannot exist. “I,” says the Lord, “am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

> [Note: “The first resurrection is that of those who rise from sin either through baptism or through repentance, live in righteousness, and are said to reign with Christ for a thousand years—that is, forever. The second resurrection will be that of all, both good and evil, when the final judgment is to take place.” Thus St. Augustine in the passage cited.]
>
> [Col. 0714D]

But the wicked do not live, because they continually pass from torment to torment, as though from death to death. Of them it is said: “For in death there is no one who remembers you” (Ps. 6:6). This is the first resurrection, of which the Apostle says: [Col. 0714B] “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things which are above” (Col. 3:1). For as bodies rise from tombs, so souls renewed through baptism rise again.

Blessed and holy is one who has a part in the first resurrection: that is, one who so rises in baptism that thereafter death and sin do not reign in him. Over these the second death has no power, because they will rise together with their bodies to immortal life, and they will be priests of God and Christ, continually offering themselves to God as a living and spotless sacrifice. Hence the Apostle says: “I beseech you to present your bodies as a living, holy sacrifice, pleasing to God—your rational service” (Rom. 12:1). “And they will reign with him for a thousand years,” that is, forever and unto age of age.

[Col. 0714C] “And when the thousand years have been completed, Satan will be released from his prison, and he will go out and deceive the nations that are at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, and gather them for battle; their number is like the sand of the sea. And they went up over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city; and fire came down from God out of heaven and devoured them. And the devil, who deceived them, was cast into the lake of fire and sulphur, where the beast and the false prophets will be tormented day and night for ages upon ages.”

“When the thousand years have been completed,” he says—that is, after many years, a definite number being used for an indefinite one—Satan is released from his prison, because he will receive such power and licence to harm that, up to that time, he may be said to have been bound and imprisoned [Col. 0714D]; then he will go forth upon the broad and spacious way. “And he will deceive the nations that are at the four corners of the earth,” namely Gog and Magog, “and gather them for battle.” From this we are given to understand that his renown will be spread throughout every land.

By Gog and Magog some have wished to understand the Goths, others the Getae and Massagetae [Col. 0715A]; others say that they are the nations whom Alexander the Great shut in among the mountains, where they have now multiplied into an innumerable multitude. This is what those writers have said. But we shall explain these things, without prejudice to the faith, according to the interpretation of the names.

[Note: [Col. 0715D] “Here is foretold the great deception of Antichrist, which at the end will break out into open war. For all those deceived, gathered from the whole world and having Antichrist himself as their leader, will pursue the righteous everywhere to put them to death. Their slaughter will be very great; but the Church, or beloved city, will not be conquered, but will triumph after the tyrant and his followers have been defeated and overthrown.” Thus St Hippolytus, *On Antichrist*.]

For Gog is interpreted “roof,” while Magog means “from the roof.” But what is the roof except sinners, in whom vices and evil spirits are covered over and dwell? And what is “from the roof” except those same vices and unclean spirits? At present they are in some measure hidden; but then, as though the gates had been opened, rushing everywhere from the roof in battle-array, they will leap forth together with the roof itself into war. Hence it continues: “Their number is like the sand of the sea, and they went up over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city.” For it is the manner of the prophets, as we have already said [Col. 0715B], to use the past tense for future events. “And fire came down from heaven and devoured them.”

[Fire and sulphur, namely hail and lightning, will rain upon the army of Antichrist, as formerly upon the hosts of Gog and Magog, and will destroy it. God will overthrow this savage and destructive enemy by the breath of his mouth.]

[Note: [Col. 0715D] We have supplied this from the Vatican manuscript.]

For once the resurrection has occurred and Christ comes for judgment, fire will immediately follow: it will burn up the world and devour sinners. Passing thus from fire into fire, they will thereafter never be free from torments. And the devil who deceived them will be cast with them into the lake of burning fire and sulphur. For this fire, as the Lord says, “is prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV.41), in which the beast—that is, Antichrist—and the false prophets [Col. 0715C] who follow him will be tormented day and night for ages upon ages.

“And I saw before the throne a white Lamb, and one sitting upon it, from whose sight earth and heaven fled, and no place was found for them. And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne; and books were opened. And another book was opened, which is the book of life; and the dead were judged from the things written in the books, according to their works.”

This white Lamb, stained by no blemish of vices, is he who takes away the sins of the world. He sits before the throne and upon it because he is greater than all the ranks of angels and sits higher than all. It is as though he meant to say: by “the Lamb sitting upon the throne” he signified God in humanity. Earth and heaven flee from his sight, because [Col. 0715D], when he comes for judgment, heaven and earth too will pass away, as he himself says. Their former, customary place will not be found, since all things will be changed [Col. 0716A] for the better.

“And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne,” because, as the Apostle says, “We shall all, whether good or evil, stand before the judgment-seat of God” (Rom. IV.10). “And books were opened,” in which the deeds of all persons, and everything done by all, will be read. These books are the conscience of each individual, accusing or even defending one another, according to the Apostle. “And another book was opened, which is the book of life.” In it are written only those predestined for life; in it only the saints will read and recognize their names. “And the dead were judged from the things written in the books”: for, as we have said, the deeds and words of all were written in them, and every person is judged according to his or her works.

“And the sea gave up its dead that were in it; and [Col. 0716B] death and hell gave up their dead that were in them; and each person was judged according to his works. And hell and death were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death. And whoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire.”

It is certain that the bodies of all persons, wherever they may be, whether on earth or in the sea, will rise at the judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0715D] “And death and hell,” he says, “gave up the dead whom they held within themselves. The sea presented them, because they were present as they had been found; but death and hell [Col. 0716D] gave them back, because they recalled them to the life from which they had departed. Nor is it perhaps without reason that it was not enough to say ‘death’ or ‘hell’: both were named—death on account of the good, because they could suffer death only, not hell; hell on account of the wicked, who also pay penalties among the dead.” St Augustine, *The City of God*, book XX, chapter 15.]

Thus this great and wide sea—the entire extent of the world—will give up the dead in it. Death too will give up its dead: that is, the devil, cause and origin of death; and with him hell, in which the souls of sinners are held shut up. Thus, with souls coming from there and bodies from here, the whole and complete human being may be presented before the Judge, who will judge each person according to [Col. 0716C] his or her works.

Then hell and death will be cast into the lake of fire, because neither death nor the devil, prince of death, will thereafter reign except in hell. “For death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Rom. V.14). This is the second death, in which, without any hope of resurrection, the whole human being, body and soul together, is cast down into darkness. By this death all who are not written in the book of life die and are plunged into the lake of fire; but those found written in the book of life will reign with Christ without end in joy and exultation.

## Chapter XXI

“And I saw a new heaven and a new earth.”

[Note: [Col. 0716D] No one is unaware how great an occasion for controversy these words have afforded the schoolmen. Some have said that the new heavens and the new earth will consist of a purer and more refined material, and have assigned them new inhabitants; so the author of *On the Renewal of Heaven and Earth*, Florence, 1780. Others, however, giving a spiritual sense to the Apostle’s words, have preferred to understand here the upper dwelling of God as paradise under the designation “new heaven,” [Col. 0717C] and the whole multitude of the righteous received into it as “new earth.” Leaving aside this question, which has no place here, we shall report only Augustine’s view: “Once judgment has been completed,” he says in the cited book, chapter 14, “this heaven and this earth will then cease to be when the new heaven and new earth begin. For this world will pass away by a transformation of things, not by utter destruction; whence the Apostle says in I Corinthians VII: ‘The form of this world passes away.’ Therefore its form passes away, not its nature.” He repeats the same point in chapter 16.]

Because, when every worldly corruption has been burned away by the conflagration of the universal fire, every creature will return to its original beauty—except, of course, the devil with [Col. 0717A] his members, who will then receive the final misery and deformity of all. For the first heaven and the first earth have passed away: namely, all things that were corrupt and deformed from their former beauty. “And the sea is no more,” because all bitterness has been expelled; the world will then be such as it was when first created. Nor will the saints of God thereafter endure the bitterness of this sea or the stormy tempests of this world; rather, they will reign with Christ without end in joy and exultation.

“And I, John, saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from heaven, prepared by God, like a bride adorned for her husband.”

“I, John,” he says, “saw the holy city, Jerusalem, new, coming down from heaven.” Not that city which was first destroyed to its foundations by the Chaldeans [Col. 0717B], and afterwards by the Romans, as the Lord says: “There shall not remain in it one stone upon another” (Luke XIX.44); but that new city of which the Apostle says: “But that Jerusalem which is above is free, and she is our mother” (Gal. IV.26). For she is new because, following the new human being, she has striven to walk in newness of life. According to her greater and more excellent part, she is in heaven; for there are the angels and the souls of the saints, and therefore she is said to descend.

Thus blessed John saw this city descending.

[Note: [Col. 0717D] Vatican manuscript: “Thus, then, blessed John saw this city descend from heaven in the Spirit,” etc.]

She will descend at the judgment such as she has been prepared by God, together with him. Therefore he adds: “Prepared by God, like a bride adorned for her husband.” For she is that most noble bride of that most noble bridegroom, whose praises resound so elegantly and sweetly in the Song [Col. 0717C] of Songs. Of her blessed John the Evangelist also says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John III.29). And the Apostle: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (II Cor. XI.2). And the Psalmist: “The queen stood at your right hand in clothing of gold, surrounded by variety” (Ps. XLIV.11).

What adornments, then, do we think she will have, being the bride of so great a husband?

[Note: [Col. 0717D] Vatican manuscript: “She must come forth to meet the one to whom she is to be married, so great a husband.”]

What attendants, what retainers will she bring with her, who is to be presented to so great and such a king? O weddings beyond utterance! O wealth beyond estimation! O delights beyond number!

[Note: [Col. 0717D] The same manuscript: “O ineffable weddings! O wealth beyond estimation! O delights beyond utterance!”]

When, in [Col. 0718A] the heavenly bridal chamber, Christ our Lord will be joined in the chaste embraces of love and affection to his bride—our most fruitful mother, yet ever virgin and incorrupt, namely the holy Church—O truly and eternally blessed are those called to the supper of the Lamb’s wedding! There God himself, and the very contemplation of eternal light, are drink and food and the highest refreshment. It follows:

“And I heard a great voice from the throne saying: Behold, the dwelling of God is with human beings, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them as their God.”

For it is fitting, and very appropriate, that at such a banquet and such great wedding there should be singers, male and female, who soothe souls and refresh the weary, comfort them concerning the past, and make their hearers joyful concerning the future. They sing in lofty tones and send forth great [Col. 0718B] voices, such as are accustomed to come forth from the throne of God.

[Note: [Col. 0718C] What our commentator has expressed under these allegorical figures must be understood of the overflowing joy and exultation of the saints when they see themselves raised to heavenly glory, that is, to the dwelling of God. Having previously fought bravely in the Church, their passage to the triumphant Church will secure for them the perpetual vision of God: “they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them as their God.” Therefore they will be filled with inexpressible joy and, throughout eternity, will offer God thanks and praise for their blessedness.]

For it is not they themselves who speak, but the Holy Spirit, who speaks and sings in them. But let us now hear what, or how, God’s singers—or, so to speak, his minstrels—sing. “Behold,” they say, “the dwelling of God is with human beings, and he will dwell with them.” God’s house, God’s tabernacle, God’s inner chamber, the dwelling of almighty God, which was formerly with angels, is now with human beings. Henceforth God will dwell with them; henceforth he will reign among them and with them. They shall be his people: they will serve and be subject to him. They will pay tribute to no one, give taxes to no one, but will be the people of God alone; and God himself, dwelling with them and in them—he himself, I say, and no other—will be their God. It follows.

[Col. 0718C] “And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes; and death shall be no more; neither mourning nor crying shall be any more, because the former things have passed away.”

“And God,” say those who sing, “will wipe away every tear from their eyes,” so that no trace of sadness may appear in them.

[Note: [Col. 0718D] John proceeds to describe the perfect blessedness of those who have attained their end. From it, he says, death, mourning, and every memory of former evils will be forever absent, so that they may be established, like the heavenly spirits, in immortality, impassibility, and untroubled tranquillity.]

“And death shall be no more,” because, submerged with its prince the devil in darkness, it will neither be able nor dare to approach those in whom nothing will exist that can decay or die. “Neither mourning”: for what could those mourn who, ever abounding in every good thing,

[Note: [Col. 0718D] Vatican manuscript: “overflowing in abundance.”]

having become immortal and impassible,

[Note: [Col. 0718D] The same manuscript: “having been made.”]

will enjoy eternal blessedness with the angels [Col. 0719A]? “Neither crying,” that is, disturbance, assault, and invasion by enemies. “Neither shall there be pain any more.” Where pain is, there is corruption; therefore those who will be incorruptible will not suffer pain. Why is this so? Because the former things have passed away: those things, namely, which were full of tribulation and distress, sickness and sadness, cries and plunder, pain and infirmity, misery and tears. Thus far the singers.

“And he who sat upon the throne said: Behold, I make all things new. And he said to me: Write, for these words are most trustworthy and true. And he said to me: It is done. I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end. To the thirsty I shall give freely from the fountain of living water.”

When the preceding speech has ended, it is no longer the throne of God, but God himself, who speaks directly, saying: “Behold, I make all things new.” Therefore great faith must be given to the words of the saints; there must be no doubt whatever concerning what they say. They say that the former things have passed away; Christ says: “Behold, I make all things new.” You see, therefore, that Christ confirms what they say. Moreover, he commands that it be written down and attests that all those words are true and full of faith, so that they may be believed all the more firmly because his promises are confirmed not only by speech but also by writing and parchment. It follows: “And he said to me: It is done.” What is it that he says has been done? Perhaps it is that which he commands to be written. For “the Spirit searches all things” (I Cor. II.10); thus he knows our understanding far better than we ourselves do.

We may also understand “It is done” to mean that all things foretold by the prophets [Col. 0719C] have now reached their end and been fulfilled.

[Note: [Col. 0719D] Here may be understood the completion of the work of religion, the restoration of God’s kingdom, the rendering back of the Father’s glory, and the bringing of all sacraments of prophecy and all mysteries to their true signification [Col. 0720D] and clarity. Nothing further is to be expected. Whatever it pleased God’s wisdom to do, it has done.]

Hence he adds: “I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end. From me all things have gone forth, and to me all return. I divided them when I wished; now I gather them because I wish. And those things which I allowed to run their course until now, I now command to stand still and to finish their course. But let those hear this who have loved me, who have hated the world, who have come to me thirsty and said with the Prophet: ‘My soul thirsted for the living God: when shall I come [Col. 0720A] and appear before the face of God?’” (Ps. XLI.3). “I shall give freely to the thirsty from the fountain of the water of life.” This is what I wished them to hear.

But what is this fountain of living water? It is surely that of which the Psalmist says: “They shall be intoxicated by the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. XXXV.9). For he himself is the fountain of life. Whoever drinks from it will not thirst again; and, what is greater, will not die for ever. By this we understand the contemplation of God, which anyone able to draw from it will enjoy with every sweetness and delight. This water is given freely; it is obtained by God’s goodness alone, because there is no price by which it can be bought.

“He who conquers shall possess these things, and I shall be his God, and he shall be my son. But the fearful and unbelieving, the accursed, murderers, fornicators, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars—their portion shall be in the lake burning with fire and sulphur, which is the second death.”

He who, he says, conquers the devil’s goads, temptations of the flesh, persecutions of tyrants, the world’s enticements, and the false persuasions of heretics, shall possess the things stated above. “And I shall be his God, and he shall be my son.” For whose inheritance and possessions ought these to be, if not the children’s? But the fearful—those who deny God out of fear and who lack love, since “perfect love casts out fear” (John IV.18)—and the unbelieving, who refuse to believe the words of the saints; the accursed, who have not received the sacraments of the Church; murderers, fornicators, and all liars [Col. 0720C], who deliberately lie and constantly labour to deceive others—to all these, if they persist in evil and do not repent, their portion will be in the lake where fire and sulphur burn. This indeed is the second death; because it occurs in the soul and in flesh already raised again, it will never have an end.

We are compelled, however, to make the books unequal, because we do not wish to mingle the visions and fear to interrupt the continuity.

## Book VII

[Col. 0719]
