[Col. 0719D] “And one of the seven angels came, who had bowls full of the seven last plagues, and spoke with me, saying: Come, I shall show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb. And he carried me away in the Spirit to a great and high mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down from heaven, from God, having the glory of God; and its light was like a precious stone, like a jasper stone, clear as crystal.”

We have spoken much above concerning these seven angels. They are the seven teachers of the Church, through whom the mysteries of all the Scriptures are unfolded; and they may truly be understood as angels, since the Scriptures themselves were composed through the ministry of angels, as is said of the Mosaic law [Col. 0720D], that it was “ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator” (Gal. III.19).

It should be known, moreover, that blessed John represents the entire Church; therefore he says that what is revealed to the Church was shown to him. “Come,” he says, “follow me. I shall raise you in the Spirit and show you what cannot be seen by fleshly eyes: namely, the bride, the wife of the Lamb.” We ordinarily call her bride before the wedding and wife after the wedding; here he uses both terms, wife and bride, as though the day upon which the wedding is to be celebrated had already come.

“And he carried me away in the Spirit to a great and high mountain,” by which we understand ecstasy and the mind’s departure beyond itself—a height which we can ascend with no feet but spiritual ones [Col. 0721A]. “And he showed me the holy city Jerusalem”:

[Note: [Col. 0721D] As we said in the preface to this commentary, the Apostle concludes the book of his Apocalypse by presenting the holy and glorious heavenly Jerusalem. Whatever he says concerning it must be understood mystically: of the majesty of God which fills it; of its inhabitants, the angels and saints standing before God and receiving all their delight from his vision; and [Col. 0722D] of the order and stability of its walls. By this is promised the eternal and immutable possession of that blessedness, so that the righteous who await it may be kindled all the more in the love of God and in the sanctification of their souls.]

That is, the Church of all the saints and the multitude of all believers. It descends from heaven, from God, because it appears to descend from that place where it always is through the contemplation of the mind. It has the glory of God: “For the righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of God” (Matt. XIII.43). Hence blessed John says elsewhere: “We know that, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (John III.2). Its light—

[Note: [Col. 0722D] Vatican manuscript: “that is, the brightness of that city.”]

—is like a precious stone, like jasper, namely clear as crystal. Jasper is serene and green; crystal is of such transparency that nothing can lie hidden or be concealed within it. That which is serene and green is alive; [Col. 0721B] conversely, that which is dry lacks life. Rightly, therefore, is that most blessed city like jasper: it lives eternally and is immortal. It is aptly compared with crystal because, possessing no hypocrisy or dissimulation, it is inwardly what it appears outwardly to be.

“And it had a great and high wall, having twelve gates; and at the gates twelve angels; and names written, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel.”

What do we understand by the great and high wall but the Catholic faith and the protection of angels? Fortified by these, the city of God destroys all the devices of its enemies. The twelve gates are the twelve apostles, to whom the Lord gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the power of binding and loosing [Col. 0721C]. Through them the multitude of all believers enters the heavenly palace, because their teaching shows the entry, the access, and the way.

Each gate has twelve angels because they are joined and united to one another by the bond of charity and love, so that all are what one is and one is what all are. If one is shut, none is open. The teaching of each is confirmed, as by twelve angels, by the testimony of the twelve apostles. The fact that the names of the twelve tribes of Israel’s children are said to be written upon the gates appears to signify that the teaching of the two Testaments is the same. For where the names of Jacob’s twelve sons and Christ’s twelve disciples are read as written together, what else is shown but that the faith and teaching of the two Testaments are one [Col. 0721D]?

“On the east, three gates; on the north, three gates; on the south, three gates; on the west, three gates. And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and upon them the twelve names of the apostles and of the Lamb.”

The gates are divided in sets of three, so that those coming from any direction may immediately recognize in that number what they must profess and by what faith they can be saved. The gates face the four regions of the world because God is not the God of the Jews alone; rather, as the Lord himself says, he will not cast out anyone who comes to him.

Yet those may be understood as coming from the east who, in the very first age, were converted to the faith and serve the Lord in Christ’s Church. Those converted from adolescence enter through the northern gates, for at this age above all the devil deceives the human being, since this age is more subject than the rest to vanity. Of it he himself speaks, saying: “I shall set my throne in the north” (Isa. XIV.14). Hence Solomon, wisest of men, says that it is difficult for him to know a person’s way in youth. For it is unknown whether one who seems so to pursue and devote oneself to every vanity will ever be converted to good.

But those enter by the southern gates who are converted in youth and are set ablaze by zeal for the faith and by love of charity. For this is a stronger age, in which our king triumphed over the enemy. The western gates, however, stand open to those who begin in old age to repent and serve Christ; indeed, even philosophers define old age as the westering of life.

Those came from the East who believed from the first age of the world down to the Babylonian period. From the time of Nebuchadnezzar to Christ, all the faithful entered God’s city through the northern gates. Read the histories, and you will be able to discover how great were the calamities endured by holy men during this span of time. From Christ’s time, of whom it is said, “God shall come from the south” (Hab. III.3), until Antichrist, the southern gates [Col. 0722C] are open. From that point until the end, the western gates will be opened, through which by no small multitude will enter God’s city.

We may also say from this that the eastern and southern gates are opened in prosperity, but the northern and western ones in adversity. What the twelve foundations of the wall of this city signify, he immediately explains when he adds: “And upon them the twelve names of the apostles and of the Lamb.” Thus the Apostle says that it is founded “upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone” (Eph. II.20).

“And he who spoke with me had a golden reed as a measure, in order to measure the city and its gates and wall. And the city was laid out as a square, and its length [Col. 0722D] is as great as its width.”

What do we understand by the measure but the words and preaching of teachers? The Apostle used this measure when he asked the Lord, saying: “That you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the length, breadth, height, and depth” (Eph. III.18). Because a reed is easily moved, it is said to be made of reed, for words are always in motion. [Col. 0723A] But because the words of saints shine with the great light of wisdom and knowledge, it is said to be golden.

By this measure teachers measure God’s city, its gates, and its wall. But what do we think its measure is, except from the rising of the sun to its setting, from the north to the sea? For the Lord himself marked it out when he said: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Matt. XVI.15). Thus the Psalmist says: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII.4). This is the measure of the city.

Let us measure its gates too, if we can; and by one, let us see how great the others are. Blessed Paul is a great gate. He had already preached from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, when he said that he still wished to go [Col. 0723B] into Spain. The lower part of this gate touches the earth when he says: “Husbands, love your wives” (Eph. II.25); and again: “Let the husband render the due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband” (I Cor. VII.3). Yet he himself shows how far upward it extends when he says: “I know a man in Christ who, fourteen years ago—whether in the body or outside the body I do not know; God knows—was caught up as far as the third heaven” (II Cor. XXII.2). Therefore so many thousands have entered and continually enter through this gate because, as he himself says, in condescending to the infirmities of all, he became all things to all people.

But since the wall signifies the faith by which we are defended and fortified, the greatness of the wall is understood to correspond to the greatness of faith. [Col. 0723C]

[For each person, with God’s help, is defended by his or her faith, and where faith is not, there is no defence. Hence the Lord himself says: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will be able to move mountains” (Matt. XIV.31); whence blessed Peter is told: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?”]

[Note: [Col. 0723D] We have supplied this from the Vatican manuscript.]

It follows:

“And the city was laid out as a square.” [For a square, however it is turned, is firm and stable. Moreover, because there are four Gospels, from and upon which, as upon a firm rock, the Church cannot fall anywhere, it is rightly said to be laid out as a square. Such indeed is the Church’s squareness that each corner has three apostles and one evangelist. Therefore [Col. 0723D] it is so wisely measured and apportioned that its length is as great as its width. Finally, it hopes as much as it loves, and conversely loves as much as it hopes; thus by length we understand hope and by width charity. For hope is the long expectation of future things; but of charity it is said: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad.”]

[Note: [Col. 0724D] The same manuscript supplies the edition.]

“And he measured the city with the golden reed: twelve thousand stadia. Its length, breadth, and height are equal. And he measured its wall: one hundred and forty-four cubits, the measure of a human being, which is that of an angel.”

Since there are twelve apostles, the city too is said to be twelve thousand stadia [Col. 0724A], from which it is evident that each side contains a thousand stadia. A finite number is used for an infinite one. For, as we have often said, the number one thousand sometimes signifies all things and sometimes many things; here it signifies many. So too in the statement that Satan will be released after a thousand years. But when it is said of the saints that they will reign with Christ for a thousand years, “all things” is meant: that is, all years. Therefore, by the twelve thousand stadia, all the world’s stadia are understood.

That he says its length, breadth, and height are equal appears, in the literal sense, to indicate the circumference of heaven, which, like all other things, was undoubtedly made in weight and number. We have spoken above allegorically of its length and breadth, in which we signified hope and charity. It remains, therefore, to speak of height, by which we understand faith. Rising as far as the throne of God, faith sees, believes, and venerates him in the Trinity.

The Church’s length, breadth, and height are equal because we love and believe as much as we hope; we believe and hope as much as we love; and we hope and love as much as we believe. For whoever has one of these virtues has all of them, and whoever lacks one has none.

It follows: “And he measured the city’s wall, one hundred and forty-four thousand cubits, the measure of a human being, which is that of an angel.” The number one hundred, which is perfect and whole and consists of perfect works, is composed of ten decades; it signifies the order of virgins and the perfect. The number forty signifies penitents; four, the multitude of all believers who received teaching through the four evangelists. Therefore, because this number includes no one besides these, it is rightly said to be of this measure.

But the addition, “the measure of a human being, which is that of an angel,” must be understood to mean that human beings and angels have one and the same measure: namely, that as many human beings will be gathered within the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem as good angels remained when the wicked fell. But he immediately set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God; and the singular is used for the plural.

And its wall was built of jasper; but the city itself was of pure gold, like clear glass; the foundations of the city wall were adorned with every precious stone. For jasper, because, as we have often said, it is green and is said by a certain natural power to drive away forgetfulness, signifies faith, which is ever green and unfading, and which, as the Lord says in the Gospel, removes and drives away mountains and demons. Thus the building and composition of the city’s wall are of jasper, because all its defence and strength is faith, which continually causes it both to live and to conquer: namely, as it is written, “the righteous shall live by faith” (Rom. 1:17). But the city itself is of pure gold, like clear glass, because the houses, towers, and palaces of that city are composed of that metal which is more precious and worthy than all others: by it we understand wisdom, of which it is said, “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Prov. 9:1). But what house, if not this most noble city? Therefore nowhere in it are there darknesses, nowhere the murk of blindness and ignorance; everywhere gold shines, everywhere all things gleam with the light of wisdom; and as all contemplate one another in turn, there is nothing in anyone’s conscience which is not seen by all. Hence this gold is said to be like clear glass: for gold, although it shines, does not reveal what it contains within; but in glass, if it is clear, there is nothing within which does not appear without. Rightly, therefore, the gold of that city is said to be like clear glass, since all things there will be plain and manifest, nothing dark or shadowy, nothing that can offend the eyes of the foolish.

The foundations of the city wall are adorned with every precious stone. The foundations, as we have said, are the apostles, upon whose faith the whole fabric of the entire city is constructed. But what are the precious stones with which the foundations are adorned? For if the foundations are adorned with precious stones, the foundations themselves seem to be one thing and the precious stones another. Let us therefore say that the apostles are the foundations, while the stones with which they are adorned are virtues and honourable habits. Why, however, these stones themselves are also called foundations will be made clear in what follows.

The first foundation: jasper; the second: sapphire; the third: chalcedony; the fourth: emerald; the fifth: sardonyx; the sixth: sard; the seventh: chrysolite; the eighth: beryl; the ninth: topaz; the tenth: chrysoprase; the eleventh: hyacinth; the twelfth: amethyst. When he says that the first foundation is jasper, this is to be understood as though he said: “The first ornament of the foundation is jasper.” This ornament is rightly placed first, since, as was said above, it signifies faith, without which it is impossible to please God: “For the saints through faith conquered kingdoms” (Heb. 11:33). It is the first thing encountered by those who come to the Church; through it one enters the aforesaid city, of which we are still speaking. Whoever has not brought it cannot enter; and no stone more than this adorns the foundations of God’s city.

The second ornament of the foundation is sapphire, whose colour resembles the clear sky. Adorned and decorated by this precious stone, the apostles despise the earth and desire heavenly things; they long to be dissolved and to be with Christ. And because the dwelling-place of the saints is in the heavenly realms, they look not to earthly gains but to the sapphires with which they are adorned; with all their strength they pant to ascend to that realm whose colour they behold in sapphire.

The third ornament of the foundation is chalcedony. Having a somewhat pale appearance of fire, it sends forth flames of brightness in cloudy and dark conditions, but openly and beneath the open sky it seems to give little fiery light. Adorned with this stone, the holy apostles and doctors—the foundations of the Church—though they are of great merit and shine brightly before God, nevertheless show themselves among people as lowly, insignificant, humble, and despised. Our Saviour himself was adorned with this stone when, shining in glory more brightly than the sun in secret, with only three disciples as witnesses, and unwilling that this should shine openly, he commanded: “Tell no one the vision, until the Son of Man has risen from the dead” (Matt. 17:9).

The fourth ornament of the foundation is emerald, which is greener than jasper and seems in its greenness to surpass even the verdure of grasses. It signifies the life of the saints, which after the resurrection of the flesh will be ever green, because there will be nothing in them able to wither or die. Therefore, although the saints adorned with jasper have attained greenness and immortality through the merit of faith, they are nevertheless also decorated with emeralds according to the increase of their virtues, so that the greener they appear, the more worthy they may be judged of unfading and immortal life. Jasper is therefore rightly joined by emerald, greenness by greenness: for after this blessed life of souls follows also the blessed bodily life of those raised again, so that, rejoicing in a double greenness, the saints of God may live without end both in soul and body.

The fifth ornament placed among the foundations is sardonyx, whose colour is fiery and red, shining brightly like the seed of pomegranates. By it charity is understood: kindled by the fire of love, it affords a pleasing brightness to all who behold it. For who does not delight in it, without which the other virtues, and even martyrdom itself, are nothing? Its flame is so great that it can extinguish the flames of hell itself. Hence Solomon says: “Love is strong as death; jealousy is hard as hell; its lamps are lamps of fire and flames” (Song 8:6). Of this fire the Lord says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I will, except that it burn?” (Luke 12:49). The Lord himself was adorned with this precious stone when he said: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). All the Scriptures are full of its praises.

The sixth ornament of the foundation is sard, which, because it has the colour of blood, most plainly signifies martyrdom. The garments of our Saviour were adorned with this stone when, as he ascended into heaven, the angels, marvelling at the colour of this stone, said: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?” (Isa. 63:1). In the colour of this stone the whole choir of martyrs rejoices and glories.

> [Note: Col. 0725D, Vatican manuscript: Latin *In hujus nimirum lapidis colore* (“In the colour of this stone”).]

The seventh place among the ornaments of the foundation is occupied by chrysolite. Since it has a golden colour, it has received its name from gold. But because in the divine page gold is very often used for wisdom, according to the saying, “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. 14:33), we understand wisdom by this stone. Unless one is adorned with it, I do not know on what grounds one can either be or be called a foundation of the Church. Christ adorned his disciples with this stone when he said: “For I will give you a mouth and wisdom which none of your adversaries will be able to resist” (Luke 21:15).

The eighth is beryl, whose colour resembles that of water reflecting the sun. By it we understand a sincere understanding and sound teaching of the Scriptures. Unless it is illuminated by the Sun of righteousness, it is easily darkened by the disfigurement of error. Thus, when the sun shines back from the waters, beryl’s colour comes about; because when Christ our Lord illuminates the waters of Scripture, a sound and sincere understanding is formed. If heretics beheld the brightness of this sun upon these waters, they would not offer others teaching so foul in both colour and flavour. Therefore, because the foundation does not possess this stone’s colour, one must be extremely careful about building upon it.

The ninth stone follows, adorning the foundation: topaz. It is so rare that even very few kings could with difficulty possess it, and for this reason it is said to be more precious than the rest. The Psalmist also shows this when he says: “Therefore I have loved your commandments above gold and topaz” (Ps. 118:127). It is reported to contain within itself the colours of all stones, though it chiefly possesses two, those of gold and sky. By it we think those are figured who seem to shine not only in wisdom and chastity but also in every other virtue: such as, I should readily believe, were both Johns, the Baptist and the Evangelist. Whether such topazes can be found in the present time may be doubted.

The tenth is chrysoprase, which imitates at once the colour of gold and of flame, and especially in darkness diffuses the radiance of its own light. It adorns and decorates none more than those who shine with wisdom and burn with charity, and who among the sinners of this world—like light in darkness—spread abroad the light of teaching and a good reputation alike, speaking words not for popular favour but for the edification of salvation and faith.

The eleventh among the beauties of the foundation is hyacinth. It has the colour of the clearest sky, which is said also to change according to the seasons. It signifies the discernment of holy men, who, although in mind and contemplation they have their eyes fixed upon heaven and the throne of God, nevertheless adapt themselves to circumstances and, bending the strictness of justice, consent to lesser evils lest greater and more grievous ones arise from them. Adorned with this stone, the Apostle Paul, though he strove to abolish circumcision, nevertheless commanded Timothy to be circumcised for the time being.

The twelfth is amethyst, which imitates the colour of violets. It therefore signifies the choirs of Christ’s virgins, boys and girls. Adorned with this stone, the apostles both give forth a sweet fragrance and draw lovers of virginity after them. For in the slight bright flush which it seems to possess, it also displays the modest shamefastness of those same virgins. Thus, with these and the other stones the foundations of God’s city are adorned, and with the other virtues decorated. What need is there to say how clearly and sweetly they shine? “For the saints shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of God” (Matt. 13:43). Hence also the Apostle: “When Christ, your life, appears, then we too shall appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:4). And blessed John: “For we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Let what has been said concerning the stones suffice.

And the twelve gates are twelve pearls, each one severally; and each gate was made of a single pearl. For if the gates are the apostles, and the gates are made of pearls, then surely the apostles themselves are pearls. But why are the apostles pearls? Is it not because, bright and white, whitened beyond snow, they follow the Lamb in white wherever he goes? In the gates themselves, therefore, one may readily recognize what those too must be like who enter through the gates. For, as is said below: “No defiled and unclean person shall enter through these” (Rev. 27:27 [i.e. 21:27]). Therefore, whoever desires to enter through these gates must bear the gates’ colour.

And the streets of the city are pure gold, like transparent glass. For gold, as we have often said, belongs to the wise. Thus gold is everywhere in the streets, because there no one occupies himself with tales, no one utters idle and empty words; but, as it is written, “Wisdom cries aloud in the streets” (Prov. 1:20). This wisdom will not be merely some ordinary wisdom; rather, it will be perfect and complete. Hence it is compared with exceedingly clear glass. Of this wisdom the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face. Now I know in part; but then I shall know, even as I am known” (1 Cor. 13:12). Therefore, when all know all things and God is all in all, then all the streets of that city will shine with more than gold and wisdom.

And I saw no temple in it; for the Lord Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb. And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine in it, for the glory of God has illuminated it, and its lamp is the Lamb. No man-made temple is seen there, where there is no need for people to gather within the narrow confines of a temple to hear the word. For the king and teacher of that city is such and so great that he cannot be enclosed and comprehended within any temple. For the Lord God Almighty—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is its temple, and the Lamb slain for humankind, who takes away the sins of the world. To this temple the peoples hasten; upon it all look; they admire its beauty and are refreshed by its fragrance. That city has no need either of this sun by which we are now illuminated or of this moon which we now see waxing and waning. For the glory of God illuminates it, and its lamp is the Lamb—he, indeed, who says, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). It has need of nothing, since it is illuminated by such a great and such a light.

> [Note: Col. 0727D, Vatican manuscript: *concludi* (“be enclosed”) for *includi* (“be enclosed”).]

And the nations shall walk by its light, and the kings of the earth shall bring their glory and honour into it. And its gates shall not be shut by day, for there shall be no night there. And they shall bring the glory and honour of the nations into it. And no defiled person shall enter it, nor one who performs abomination and falsehood, except those written in the book of life and of the Lamb. For all nations have been enlightened by the teaching of the apostles and led from the darkness of error to the way of truth; they do not fail to know by what way they ought to walk. The kings of the earth—that is, bishops and teachers—will bring their glory and honour into it, because, bringing with them those whom they converted by teaching and example and freed from the danger of death, they will receive glory and honour on their account. And its gates are not shut by day, “because one day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83:10). If they are not shut by day, they will assuredly never be shut, for night and darkness will not be there. If gates are shut only through fear, why should gates be shut there, where no fear and no snares can exist? Hence the Lord says: “Store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where thieves do not dig through or steal” (Matt. 6:20). They will bring there all the glory and honour of the nations, because whatever throughout all nations is found worthy of glory and honour will be carried into that city by angels. This was signified in the despoiling of Egypt. And no defiled person shall enter it, because whoever enters must first be cleansed of every stain, whether by baptism, martyrdom, penance, or purgatorial fire. One who performs abomination—that is, sins which God abominates—and falsehood, because “a lying mouth kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11). Every corruption may indeed be called falsehood, since it does not belong to the truth of the nature which it corrupts. Thus we call coins counterfeit, although they do not lie, because they have been corrupted by another metal. Only those, therefore, will enter this city who from the origin of the world have been written in the book of life and of the Lamb; for one and the same is called both Life and Lamb, who speaks of himself, saying: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

> [Note: Col. 0729D: “Thus we have restored the text from the manuscript.”]

## Chapter XXII

And he showed me a river of the water of life, shining like crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb. By the river of the water of life is understood the knowledge of both Testaments. This water gives life and, like the best antidote, drives out the venom of the ancient serpent. Shining like crystal, it is not darkened by the blackness or corruption of any heresy. This water proceeds from faith in God and the Lamb, because it is brought forth by the mouth of Christ and by the evangelical teaching of his disciples.

> [For not only the apostles and doctors, but Christ himself also, according to his humanity, is a throne of God. Our Saviour poured out this water when, as Scripture records, on the great day of the feast he cried out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink, and rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7:38). He also promised it to the Samaritan woman when he said: “If you knew the gift of God and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ perhaps you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water” (John 4:10); concerning which the Apostle also says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Cor. 2:6).]

And the Psalmist says: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45:4), and many other things which are rightly perceived not only here in the Church but also in the heavenly Jerusalem: “For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1:17).

> [Note: Col. 0729D, Vatican manuscript: “by the depravity of heresy.”]

> [Note: Col. 0729D: “We have supplied this from the same manuscript.”]

In the middle of its street, and on either side of the river, was the tree of life, bearing twelve fruits, yielding its fruit each month, and the leaves of the tree for the healing of the nations. This is that tree which was planted beside streams of water and yields its fruit in its season. Solomon speaks of it under the figure of wisdom, saying: “It is a tree of life to those who lay hold of it, and whoever holds it fast is blessed” (Prov. 3:18). Hence the Lord himself says: “If they do these things in the green tree, what will be done in the dry?” (Luke 23:31). Whoever eats of this tree shall not taste death for ever. This tree is in the middle of the street, where the people gather, where the wise engage in philosophical discourse, where all assemble to hear some new thing. And it is planted on both sides of the river and bears twelve fruits; for since it contains both Testaments within itself, it seems to stand on both sides of the rivers. For all the rivers of paradise flow out from this tree; from here proceeds every fount of wisdom and knowledge. “For all wisdom is from God, and has been with him always, and is before all ages” (Ecclus. 1). This tree bore twelve most noble fruits, by which the whole world was satisfied.

> [Note: Col. 0730D: “The sense is incomplete, and what is missing is absent from the edition.”]

“For heaven and earth shall pass away,” as he himself says, “but my words shall not pass away” (Luke 1:33). These leaves also give healing to the nations, because, as is written in the Gospel: “If anyone keeps his word, he shall not see death for ever” (John 8:51).

And there shall be no curse any more; and the throne of God and of the Lamb shall be in it, and his servants shall serve him, and they shall see his face, and his name shall be upon their foreheads; and there shall be no more night, and they shall not need the light of a lamp or the light of the sun, because the Lord God shall illuminate them, and they shall reign for ages of ages. Not only persecutions, he says, but curses also will cease. Not only will there be no one to kill, but nowhere will anyone appear who curses. Moreover, the accursed will no longer be above, because they will always be in the fire; and it would indeed have been better for them not to exist than to exist so unhappily. But the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, of whom the Apostle says: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16). Although certain angels are specially called thrones, every glorified creature can nevertheless be called a throne of God. Then his servants will serve him, when there is nothing that can hinder them; that service will be acceptable which admits of no interruption. And they shall see his face, concerning which the Psalmist, full of longing, said: “Show us your face, O Lord, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79:8); and elsewhere: “Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face always” (Ps. 102:4). And his name shall be on their foreheads: for what is borne on the forehead is not hidden. They are rightly said, therefore, to have his name on their forehead, since they never feared to confess him because of punishments and injuries. Hence the Lord himself says: “Whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 10:22). Therefore, for the glory and manifestation of their triumph and victory, they will always have on their foreheads that name because of which they endured many evils. And night and darkness, tribulation and persecution, shall no longer be; nor will they need the light of a lamp or the light of the sun. Why is this? Because the Lord God will illuminate them: he himself will be their sun, their light, their brightness, their radiance, with whom and through whom they will reign for ages of ages.

And he said to me: These words are most faithful and true; and the Lord God of the spirits of the prophets has sent his angel to show his servants what must shortly come to pass. Behold, I come quickly. Blessed is he who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book. Having set forth everything which seemed to concern the city, lest anyone perhaps, through unbelief, doubt that the things they had marvelled at were true, the same angel who was showing these things added, saying: “These words are most faithful and true.” Therefore let no one wish to doubt them; but let whatever has been said concerning the aforesaid city, its structures, and its blessedness be believed without doubt and faithfully. For he could not lie by whose inspiration all these things were revealed and written. Hence it is added: “And the Lord God of the spirits of the prophets has sent his angel to show his servants what must shortly come to pass.”

> [“The Lord God,” he says, “that is, the Spirit of the prophets. For the Holy Spirit, who speaks through the prophets and in the prophets, is both Lord and God. He sent his angel. For what purpose? Namely, to show his servants those things which must shortly come to pass.”]

It is therefore plain that this entire vision was written down through angelic ministry. When he says, “what must shortly come to pass,” he refers to the infinite length of eternity, compared with which all earthly things, however long their duration, seem to flee and pass away with the greatest swiftness. And lest anyone doubt that these things will come to pass shortly, let him also hear what the Lord himself says: “Behold, I come quickly.” Therefore it is true that what must shortly come to pass is said to do so, since the Lord God will come quickly; when he comes, everything of which this book speaks will be fulfilled. Then blessed indeed will be whoever faithfully keeps and believes the words of the prophecy of this book.

> [Note: Col. 0731D: “We have supplied this from manuscript V.”]

And I, John, who heard and saw these things—after I had heard and seen them, I fell down to worship before the feet of the angel who showed them to me. And he said to me: “See that you do not do this. I am your fellow servant, and of your brethren the prophets, and of those who keep the words of this book. Worship God.” “I,” he says, “am John, who heard and saw these things, who bear witness to them and affirm that they are true. Lest anyone think that they are empty dreams and the ravings of fools, let him know in truth that I am John, who heard and saw these things. And after I had heard and seen such great goods and such signs of blessedness, I immediately, filled with joy, fell down to worship before the feet of the angel who showed them to me.” For it was an ancient custom, continuing until that time, that people should worship angels; and the patriarch Abraham too is read to have done this. But after the King and Lord of angels took flesh, it appeared exceedingly dreadful and terrible to angels that they should be worshipped by those whose nature they had seen seated above themselves. Hence the angel says to blessed John, who wished to worship him: “See that you do not do this.” What can human and empty pride say here, which so often demands from people such great honour and undue submission, when it hears that angels forbid such undue honour to be rendered to themselves? “I am your fellow servant,” says the angel: “you and I have one Lord, whom both you and I must worship. I am the fellow servant of all your other brethren, the prophets, and also of all who keep the words of this book. Worship God,” because it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matt. 4:10).

> [Note: Col. 0731D: “The glorified human nature of Christ, placed at the right hand of the Father, holds primacy over all the choirs of angels; accordingly, the angels themselves are said to refuse the adoration and worship due to it.”]

> [Note: Col. 0732D, Vatican manuscript: “Who are filled with the same Spirit as you. And not only of the prophets, but of all …”]

And he said to me: “Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near. Let him who does harm do harm still; and let him who is in filth become filthy still; and let the righteous do righteousness still; and let the holy be sanctified still.” Blessed John—or rather, the Church of the imperfect represented in the person of blessed John—having heard the Lord say, “Behold, I come quickly,” thought that this present life should soon end and Christ come for judgment. Therefore, when he was already wishing to close and seal the book, he was told: “Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book. Let them be open and unsealed, that they may be read and heard by all who wish to hear. For the time is near”—that is, as I have said, what will occur after a thousand years. For the Psalmist also speaks to the Lord, saying: “For a thousand years in your sight are like yesterday, which has passed away” (Ps. 89:4). And as though John himself said: “You see, Lord, that if you delay, the wicked will grow proud and do harm, while the saints will be afflicted and slain.” To this he replies: “Let him who does harm do harm still”: that is, let one who desires to harm and does not wish to repent of his inclination to harm, do harm still, so that by harming he may perish. And let one who is in filth, who delights in sins and despises to obey the admonitions of the saints so as to repent, become filthy still. Nothing worse can happen to sinners than when they are granted power to fulfil their own will. Why this happens, I think no one can fully investigate; for the judgments of God are hidden, according to the saying: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. 35:7). “And let the righteous do righteousness still, and let the holy be sanctified still.” For if there were no wicked people, in what could the righteousness of the saints or of God be exercised?

“Behold, I come quickly, and my reward is with me, to render to each according to his works. I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.” Do not, he says, grieve or consider it burdensome or harsh that I have forbidden you to close and seal the book, because I shall not delay, but shall truly come quickly. And even if I do not come to judgment quite so soon, I shall nevertheless not long delay in calling each individual soul. When I come, let the good rejoice and the evil fear, because my reward is with me. But what reward? Do you wish to hear what it is? “To render to each according to his works.” But lest anyone suppose this to be the angel who above forbade worship of himself, because at the beginning of this chapter the speaker is not identified, the Lord himself, whose words these are, replies: “I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.” These things have already been explained above.

Blessed are those who wash their robes in the blood of the Lamb, that they may have authority over the tree of life and may enter the city through the gates. Outside are dogs, sorcerers, the unchaste, murderers, idolaters, and everyone who loves and practises falsehood. Blessed, he says, will be only those who wash their robes in the blood of the Lamb—that is, those redeemed by Christ’s blood and cleansed by the water of baptism—who preserve their garments and bodies not as they formerly were, but as they deserved to receive them cleansed and purified by God. Hence it is written: “Let your garments be white at all times” (Eccles. 8:9). They have authority over the tree of life, that they may take from it and live. Because the first man had been forbidden it, the entire human race succumbed to death until Christ came. When he came and said, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6:53), permission and authority were given to humankind now to approach the tree of life in security—provided, however, that they have clean and white garments. Otherwise, “whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11:29). Those who have authority over the tree of life enter the city through the twelve gates, because, placing confidence neither in the wisdom of heretics nor in their own wisdom, they hold and believe the teaching of the apostles, through which they do not doubt that they will be saved and enter the gate of the heavenly city.

Outside are dogs—that is, Jews barking without cause—

> [and sorcerers, that is, heretics who devise poisonous doctrines by which they kill souls; and the unchaste, that is, all fornicators and adulterers; murderers, namely of soul or body; idolaters, among whom the greedy are included; and everyone who loves and practises falsehood.]

For many imitate him who did not stand in the truth and from whom all falsehood proceeds.

> [Note: Col. 0733D: “We have supplied this from the Vatican manuscript.”]

“I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you of these things in the Churches. I am the offspring and root of David, the bright morning star; and the bridegroom and the bride say, ‘Come’; and let him who hears say, ‘Come’; and let him who thirsts come; let whoever wishes receive the water of life freely.” When he says, “I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify,” the plural “to you” and “in the Churches,” rather than the singular “to you,” shows that these things were said not only to blessed John but to all. We may also understand blessed John himself as the angel sent by the Lord to testify to these things in the Churches. Who, then, would not believe what Jesus himself enjoins and declares to all the Churches through so great a messenger? It follows: “I am the offspring and root of David”: his offspring, because I derive my origin from him according to the flesh; his root, because both Christ from David and David from Christ sprang forth, as a tree from its root. Christ is from David according to the flesh, but David is from Christ according to divinity. “For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). And he is the bright morning star. Of this star it is written: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a man shall rise from Israel” (Num. 24:17). It is so bright that it gives light even to the sun itself, which, compared to it, admits that it has light. It is also morning, herald of that day which will have no end. The words which follow, “And the bridegroom and bride say, ‘Come,’” are as though he said: “There is henceforth no excuse: all have heard. The bridegroom and bride—Christ and the Church—say daily, ‘Come.’” For these are the bridegroom’s words: “Come to me, all who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:8). But of the bride it is said: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:4). “And let him who hears say, ‘Come.’” For preaching is permitted in every place. If all hear, and whoever hears says, “Come,” there is no one who does not preach. The Apostle also teaches women to preach when he says: “For the unbelieving husband is saved through the faithful wife” (1 Cor. 7:14). Even if not everyone is permitted to preach in the Church, each person nevertheless preaches when reproving evil and inviting someone to do good. Whoever does not do this should not doubt that he sins against brotherly charity. And let one who desires to hear the teaching of faith and words of life come.

> [Note: Col. 0735C, Vatican manuscript: “And let him who thirsts come.”]

Let him not be ashamed, having so many imitators; nor let him fear the price if perhaps he is poor. Rather, let him come confidently and without hesitation, and receive the water of life freely. These matters having thus been arranged, because this book is very difficult and can be understood and expounded in many diverse ways, lest anyone because of its obscurity—as those of lesser capacity are wont to do—call it empty dreams, or, wishing to bend it to his own understanding, attempt to expound it perversely and contrary to the faith, blessed John bears witness and solemnly adjures all not to presume to do this against the salvation of their souls. And this is what is said:

I bear witness to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this [Col. 0735C] book: if anyone adds to these things, God will add to him the plagues written in this book; and if anyone takes away from the words of this prophecy, God will take away his share from the book of life, from the holy city, and from the things [Col. 0736A] written in this book.

I, John, bear witness and testify to everyone who hears the words of this prophecy: if anyone, with meddlesome zeal and evil ingenuity—as heretics are accustomed to do—adds to these things a perverse and erroneous interpretation, God likewise will add to him the plagues written in this book. Conversely, if anyone takes away from the words of the prophecy of this book, and, by asserting that what the Holy Spirit has spoken is empty and false, attempts to diminish and erase them, let him most firmly believe and in no way doubt that God also—whom he does not fear to oppose so shamelessly—will take away his share which he was to have in the fellowship of the saints, from the book of life and from the holy city Jerusalem, whose praises have been expounded above, and from those things written in this book, in which are contained all the glory, honour, and blessedness of the saints [Col. 0736B].

He who bears witness to these things says: “Yes, yes, amen: I am coming quickly.” Although he who bears witness to these things may be understood as blessed John, who also says in the Gospel, “This is the disciple who bears witness concerning these things and wrote them” (John 21:24), Christ is more fittingly understood, whom blessed John affirms to be the witness of the matters here spoken. In order also to reveal what is true and false, to illuminate the hidden things of darkness, and to render to each according to his works, he adds: “I am coming quickly.” To this promise blessed John also responds joyfully, saying: “Come, Lord Jesus; we await your coming. Receive us in peace, and join us to the company of angels” [Col. 0736C]. May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ—by which, without any preceding merits, we have been saved freely—be with us all. Amen.

**END OF THE EXPOSITION OF THE APOCALYPSE.**

[HOMILIES AND SERMONS.]

[Col. 0735]

**INDEX OF THE HOMILIES AND SERMONS OF SAINT BRUNO, BISHOP**

According to the edition of Marchesi, with which the codex of Segni agrees, except for what is missing at the beginning and end of the codex.

[Col. 0735D] 373 **HOMILY I.—First Sunday of Advent.** Begins: “For this is what the Psalmist says: God will come openly, our God,” etc. Ends: “But the words of truth cannot be changed from their settled state.”

**HOMILY II.—The same Sunday.** “Certain persons questioning the Lord and our Saviour,” etc. “And that which they deny could happen, would have happened.”

**HOMILY III.—Second Sunday of Advent.** “John the Baptist, placed in chains and in prison,” etc. “Understanding this literally, that John was Elijah.”

[Col. 0736D] **HOMILY IV.—Third Sunday of Advent.** “For all thought that John was the Christ.” “These things took place in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.”

**HOMILY V.—Wednesday of the Ember Days.** “Gabriel the angel was sent, he says, whose name is interpreted ‘the strength of God.’” “Be it done to me according to your word; and the angel departed from her.”

**HOMILY VI.—Friday of the Ember Days.** “The Virgin, full of God, ascends into the hill country,” etc. [Col. 0737A] “Who exulted with such great joy at his coming.”

Begins: **HOMILY VII.—Fourth Sunday of Advent.** Ends: “For, as the Lord says, every kingdom divided against itself,” etc. “I shall await your salvation, O Lord.”

**HOMILY VIII.—On the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord.** “First, however, it must be asked why blessed Mary,” etc. “Therefore it is clear that Jesus is interpreted ‘Saviour.’”

**HOMILY IX.—On the Nativity of the Lord.** “For the whole world is enrolled.” “And on earth peace to people of good will.”

**HOMILY X.—On the same feast, at the second Mass.** “The shepherds, he says, spoke to one another,” etc. “Proclaiming faith in him, and praising and glorifying him everywhere.”

[Col. 0737B] **HOMILY XI.—On the same feast, at the third Mass.** “Other evangelists relate [that] the Lord and our Saviour…” “And your right hand shall lead you wonderfully into righteousness.”

**HOMILY XII.—On the feast of Saint Stephen.** “Above, in this Gospel, the Lord [said] to the scribes and Pharisees…” “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God.”

**HOMILY XIII.—On the feast of Saint John, apostle and evangelist.** “Above in this Gospel it is read that [he spoke to] his disciples,” etc. “When at supper he reclined upon the breast of that same Jesus Christ.”

**HOMILY XIV.—On the Nativity of the Holy Innocents.** “In those days the Magi had come to the Lord,” etc. “They would receive from those things perfect consolation through grace,” etc.

[Col. 0737C] **HOMILY XV.—On the Circumcision of the Lord.** “The Lord is circumcised for us, not for himself, just as he was born for us.” “He delivered all Egypt from famine and saved it by his wisdom.”

**HOMILY XVI.—On the day of the Epiphany of the Lord.** “For it is not without mystery that the blessed Virgin Mary,” etc. “This way leads back to the homeland.”

**HOMILY XVII.—First Sunday after Epiphany.** “Each year the devout parents went to Jerusalem.” “But according to the humanity by which he was made like us.”

**HOMILY XVIII.—Second Sunday after Epiphany.** “The evangelist relates that these wedding festivities took place on the third day.” “Christ’s glory is made manifest and the faith of believers is increased.”

[Col. 0737D] **HOMILY XIX.—Third Sunday after Epiphany.** “When Jesus, he says, had come down from the mountain,” etc. “Where eternal delights are prepared for all the faithful.”

**HOMILY XX.—Fourth Sunday after Epiphany.** “For what is the little boat but the Church, and what the sea but the world?” etc. “May the long-awaited prosperity come, and may there be a great calm.”

**HOMILY XXI.—On the Purification of Saint Mary the Virgin.** “For it is written in the law of Moses that a woman who, having conceived, bears a male,” etc. “It is a great glory for them that so great a light arose from their people.”

**HOMILY XXII.—Sunday in Septuagesima.** “The Creator of the human race, our Lord Jesus Christ.” [Col. 0738A] “For many are called to the vineyard and to faith who are not predestined to life.”

**HOMILY XXXIII.—Sunday in Sexagesima.** “A great crowd followed Jesus; many came together from every direction,” etc. “One brought forth thirtyfold fruit, another sixtyfold,” etc.

**HOMILY XXIV.—Sunday in Quinquagesima.** “Many things had already been fulfilled which [were said] concerning the Son of Man,” etc. “That all may praise him who alone performs great wonders.”

**HOMILY XXV.—Ash Wednesday.** “Hypocrites are called sad because, as religious persons,” etc. “And may it always strive toward that with all its strength and desire.”

Thursday after Ash Wednesday: The Gospel and homily are the same as [Col. 0738B] on the Fourth Sunday after Epiphany.

**HOMILY XXVI.—Friday after Ash Wednesday.** “Through the teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ, we have learned.” “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise.”

**HOMILY XXVII.—Saturday after Ash Wednesday.** “But the evangelist Matthew says this concerning it,” etc. “Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved.”

**HOMILY XXVIII.—First Sunday of Lent.** “Jesus, having been baptized, immediately came up from the water,” etc. “He might show fasting of the heart by the number of days.”

**HOMILY XXIX.—Monday after the First Sunday of Lent.** [Col. 0738C] “For the Lord, who first came humble and in the form of a servant,” etc. “And these shall go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”

**HOMILY XXX.—Tuesday after the First Sunday of Lent.** “For, being about to wage wars nearby and to triumph over enemies,” etc. “They learned by experience itself what the Lord had promised.”

**HOMILY XXXI.—Wednesday after the First Sunday of Lent.** “How great is the pride of the scribes and Pharisees,” etc. “Therefore he is nearer to Christ because he is better.”

**HOMILY XXXII.—Thursday after the Sunday of Lent.** “This, therefore, is why God does not hear the woman who cries out,” [Col. 0738D] etc. “He shall live and shall not die.”

**HOMILY XXXIII.—Friday after the First Sunday of Lent.** “The Lord went up to the Jewish feast days,” etc. “And he announced to the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him well.”

**HOMILY XXXIV.—Saturday after the First Sunday of Lent.** “The Lord and our Saviour, as is read a little above,” etc. “When, stripped of the mortality of the flesh, he would be clothed with the glory and splendour of the new resurrection.”

Second Sunday of Lent: The Gospel and homily are the same as on the preceding day.

[Col. 0739A] **HOMILY XXXV.—Monday after the Second Sunday of Lent.** Begins: “I go, he says. I return to the Father,” etc. Ends: “While he was saying these things, many believed in him.”

**HOMILY XXXVI.—Tuesday after the Second Sunday of Lent.** “What does it mean to sit upon Moses’ seat?” etc. “He has cast down the mighty from their seat and exalted the humble.”

**HOMILY XXXVII.—Thursday after the Second Sunday of Lent.** “These words are very necessary both for the rich and for the poor,” etc. “They fear and pray lest they too be deceived.”

**HOMILY XXXVIII.—Friday after the Second Sunday of Lent.** [Col. 0739B] “In the figure of this householder, God the Father is signified.” “This, then, was the reason why those wishing to seize him could not seize him.”

**HOMILY XXXIX.—Saturday after the Second Sunday of Lent.** “This man is understood in this place to be God himself,” etc. “And we possess them in such a manner that we do not wish to possess them otherwise.”

**HOMILY XL.—Third Sunday of Lent.** “Blessed Matthew the evangelist [calls] this man,” etc. “For unless she had done this, she could have been neither happy nor my mother.”

375 **HOMILY XLI.—Monday after the Third Sunday of Lent.** “Above in this Gospel it is read that, when the Lord had come into his own country,” [Col. 0739C] “He despises the dogs barking on every side.”

**HOMILY XLII.—Tuesday after the Third Sunday of Lent.** “But these [words apply] to the apostles and their successors, the bishops,” etc. “Seven is no less than seventy times seven.”

**HOMILY XLIII.—Wednesday after the Third Sunday of Lent.** “For the traditions of the elders, not the sayings of the prophets,” etc. “To eat with unwashed hands is rusticity, not sin.”

**HOMILY XLIV.—Thursday after the Third Sunday of Lent.** “For we must know who Peter’s wife is if we are to know who his mother-in-law is,” etc. “Therefore the Lord forbids burying such a father, and burying him in this way.”

[Col. 0739D] **HOMILY XLV.—Friday after the Third Sunday of Lent.** “This is that field of which Jacob, blessing his son Joseph, said,” etc. “Unless he had foreseen them willing to hear and believe.”

**HOMILY XLVI.—Saturday after the Third Sunday of Lent.** “For Jesus’ going to the Mount of Olives and praying,” etc. “Thus the wretched woman was delivered, at mercy’s command.”

**HOMILY XLVII.—Fourth Sunday of Lent.** “The Lord, about to perform great miracles, [provides] a new and wonderful bread.” “And he adds fish to them, with which they could more easily be eaten.”

[Col. 0740A] **HOMILY XLVIII.—Monday after the Fourth Sunday of Lent.** “These matters have indeed been expounded in Matthew,” etc. “He knew what fraud and iniquity were in each person.”

**HOMILY XLIX.—Tuesday after the Fourth Sunday of Lent.** “We have said above that this feast is celebrated for seven days.” “They themselves bear witness concerning me.”

**HOMILY L.—Wednesday after the Fourth Sunday of Lent.** “Jesus himself, our Saviour, shows most clearly,” etc. “You would not have sin, because you would seek the light.”

**HOMILY LI.—Thursday after the Fourth Sunday of Lent.** “But this widow, whom a great crowd follows,” [Col. 0740B] etc. “He is said to have come forth bound hand and foot.”

**HOMILY LII.—Friday after the Fourth Sunday of Lent.** “The evangelist wrote these things in great praise of Mary.” “There can be no doubt that they said it by way of accusation.”

**HOMILY LIII.—Saturday after the Fourth Sunday of Lent.** “I, he says, am the light of the world; I am that light which enlightens every human being,” etc. “Therefore his hour too was in his power, so that it should come then, and not before he himself commanded.”

**HOMILY LIV.—Passion Sunday.** “The Lord had commanded the priests of the Jews through Moses.” [Col. 0740C] “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”

**HOMILY LV.—Monday after Passion Sunday.** “In vain, he says, do you and your rulers labour.” “And they returned, because they could not carry out their will.”

**HOMILY LVI.—Tuesday after Passion Sunday.** “For Jesus did this not because he feared death or the Jews.” “They did not dare, because they feared human beings more than God.”

**HOMILY LVII.—Wednesday after Passion Sunday.** “The Jews called that feast the Dedication.” “That these might come to him, see him, and believe in him.”

**HOMILY LVIII.—Thursday after [Col. 0740D] Passion Sunday.** “In this Gospel the pride of the Pharisees is checked,” etc. “Who so readily has mercy upon those converted from the heart.”

**HOMILY LIX.—Friday after Passion Sunday.** “The chief priests and Pharisees had heard our Saviour.” “Not that you may kill him, but that you may believe in him with us.”

**HOMILY LX.—Saturday after Passion Sunday.** “Foolish Jews wished to kill him whom the Lord had recently raised [from the dead].” “This was what he signified when he hid himself from them.”

**HOMILY LXI.—Palm Sunday.** “The Lord sends two of his disciples ahead of him,” [Col. 0741A] etc. Begins: “Which resounded in the mouth of the entire people to Christ’s praise and glory.” Ends:

**HOMILY LXII.—Palm Sunday. The Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ.** “The Lord announces the Passover after two days, and announces his passion also,” etc. “That the Lord had risen, and that, placed thus, he could by no means have been stolen.”

376 **HOMILY LXIII.—Monday of Holy Week.** “It would be strange if the evangelist [recorded] all these things without some significance.” “As human greed is disposed, they desired to see and hear new things.”

**HOMILY LXIV.—Tuesday of Holy Week.** “If, he says, you know and understand what I have done to you,” etc. [Col. 0741B] “He did not finish supper earlier, although he had begun to dine earlier.”

**HOMILY LXV.—Wednesday of Holy Week.** “But the day of unleavened bread came, on which the Passover had to be sacrificed,” etc. “The remaining matters that follow have been expounded in Matthew.”

**HOMILY LXVI.—Thursday, at the Supper of the Lord.** “The evangelist relates above that, before the feast day of Passover, our Saviour came to Bethany,” etc. “The saints pray to God through one another; each washes the other’s feet.”

**HOMILY LXVII.—Holy Saturday.** “For the evening star, also called *hesper*, is the star which by another name is called Lucifer.” “Behold, you kill him again, while you deny that he rose and lives.”

**HOMILY LXVIII.—On the Sunday of the Holy Resurrection of Our Lord Jesus Christ.** [Col. 0741C] “For on the Sabbath it was permitted neither to sell nor to buy anything.” “There I sit with you, live, and reign for ages of ages.”

**HOMILY LXIX.—Monday after Easter Sunday.** “One of those who writes these things is thought to have been blessed Luke.” “Jesus Christ our Lord expounded the Scriptures to us and opened their meaning.”

**HOMILY LXX.—Tuesday after Easter Sunday.** “The disciples spoke of Jesus and of the things they had seen,” etc. “Therefore they order that those baptized by them be sealed by Catholics.”

**HOMILY LXXI.—Wednesday after Easter Sunday.** [Col. 0741D] “For what does it mean that the apostle Peter is called by the Lord from fishing?” etc. “He speaks of those manifestations made either to all, or to several gathered together in one place.”

**HOMILY LXXII.—Thursday after Easter Sunday.** “The disciples depart; Mary remains and weeps,” etc. “Because I have seen the Lord, and he said these things to me.”

**HOMILY LXXIII.—Friday after Easter Sunday.** “When this vision took place, I do not know.” “In God we shall do valiantly, and he will bring our enemies to nothing.”

**HOMILY LXXIV.—Saturday in Albis.** “As regards the letter, great love compelled this woman,” etc. [Col. 0742A] “We have said that Scripture is signified by the linen cloths.”

**HOMILY LXXV.—Sunday in Albis, the Octave of Easter.** “Whoever understands that which is written,” etc. “Even if the other evangelists had not written his remaining deeds.”

**HOMILY LXXVI.—First Sunday after Easter.** “I, he says, am the good shepherd. Hear this, shepherds.” “What these things signify, however, we have expounded in Exodus.”

**HOMILY LXXVII.—Second Sunday after Easter.** “For the Lord lay in the tomb for a short time.” “And no one shall take your joy from you.”

**HOMILY LXXVIII.—Third Sunday after Easter.** [Col. 0742B] “Above, blessed Peter had said: ‘Lord, where are you going?’” “For he will not speak on his own authority, but will speak whatever he hears.”

**HOMILY LXXIX.—Fourth Sunday after Easter.** “If we consider to whom these words especially [apply],” etc. “Who has now been overcome together with his prince.”

**HOMILY LXXX.—At the Greater Litany.** “For by these words we are admonished [to ask] for the spirit of wisdom.” “But evil persons, requesting evil gifts from an evil father, receive evil gifts.”

**HOMILY LXXXI.—On the Nativity of the Apostles Philip and James.** [Col. 0742C] “I, he says, am going, and where I am going you cannot come.” “For the Father is greatly glorified in the Son when such things occur in the name of the Son.”

**HOMILY LXXXII.—On the Finding of the Holy Cross.** “This good man Nicodemus, now believing,” etc. “That everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

**HOMILY LXXXIII.—On the Apparition of Saint Michael the Archangel.** “The disciples came to Jesus indeed not by speaking, but by thinking,” etc. “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death.”

**HOMILY LXXXIV.—On the Ascension of the Lord.** “The Lord Jesus came to his disciples and found them reclining,” etc. [Col. 0742D] “Their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

377 **HOMILY LXXXV.—Sunday after the Ascension.** “Our Saviour always mingles joyful things with sorrowful.” “It would not have been necessary to fortify them beforehand with such consolation.”

**HOMILY LXXXVI.—On the Day of Pentecost.** “A little above, the Lord our Saviour speaks to his disciples,” etc. “Look to heaven, because you have your origin from there.”

**HOMILY LXXXVII.—Eighth Sunday of Pentecost.** “Be merciful, he says; but how? As your Father too is merciful.” “And he will reveal the counsels of hearts. And then praise will be given to each one by God.”

**HOMILY LXXXVIII.—Second Sunday after Pentecost.** [Col. 0743A] Begins: “The lake of Gennesaret is the same as the Sea of Galilee.” Ends: “And concerning these matters, indeed, we have said enough in Leviticus.”

**HOMILY LXXXIX.—Third Sunday after Pentecost.** “For the apostle, writing to the Corinthians, says: ‘If anyone is called a brother,’” etc. “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”

**HOMILY XC.—Fourth Sunday after Pentecost.** “For this man himself, who speaks these things, is Jesus Christ our Lord,” etc. “No one will be joined with the saints, nor enter into the banquet feast.”

**HOMILY XCI.—On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist.** “Today John the Baptist is born, greater than the prophets, lesser than the angels.” [Col. 0743B] “And remaining upon him: this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.”

**HOMILY XCII.—On the Vigil of Saint Peter.** “The Lord asks Peter whether he loves him, whom [Peter had loved] always and everywhere,” etc. “By which he showed most openly how greatly he loved him.”

**HOMILY XCIII.—On the Feast of Saint Peter.** “The Lord asks his disciples what opinion people have concerning him.” “If the prelate refuses to receive it, then let them know that they are released.”

**HOMILY XCIV.—Fifth Sunday after Pentecost.** “The righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees consisted in preaching well.” “To the last farthing: a payment that is always being made and never ended.”

**HOMILY XCV.—Seventh Sunday after Pentecost.** [Col. 0743C] “Take heed, he says, and beware of false prophets,” etc. “May Jesus Christ our Lord deign to deliver us from that shipwreck.”

**HOMILY XCVI.—Eighth Sunday after Pentecost.** “And his master called him and said to him: ‘What is this that I hear concerning you?’” “And these things have been predestined for us, if the strength of this fidelity is found in us.”

**HOMILY XCVII.—Ninth Sunday after Pentecost.** “A doctor of the law arose, he says, wishing to reproach the lawgiver,” etc. “Great is the mercy through which eternal life is possessed.”

**HOMILY XCVIII.—Tenth Sunday after Pentecost.** [Col. 0743D] “Arrogance has never pleased God; pride has never been justified,” etc. “Pride is the root of all evils; humility the guardian of virtues.”

**HOMILY XCIX.—Eleventh Sunday after Pentecost.** “The evangelist describes by what way the Lord returned into Galilee,” etc. “For the mouth of those speaking wickedly is stopped.”

**HOMILY C.—Twelfth Sunday after Pentecost.** “We are all on the way; we all hasten toward our homeland.” “Faith justifies, and faith heals the inward person as well.”

**HOMILY CI.—Thirteenth Sunday after Pentecost.** “For just above our Saviour spoke concerning treasure,” etc. [Col. 0744A] “If all people wished to be such, there would not be lacking the means to feed them.”

Fourteenth Sunday after Pentecost: The Gospel and homily are the same as on Thursday of the week after the Fourth Sunday of Lent.

**HOMILY CII.—Fifteenth Sunday after Pentecost.** “In that he went to the house of a leader of the Pharisees to eat bread,” etc. “Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted.”

**HOMILY CIII.—Sixteenth Sunday after Pentecost.** “In this parable, then, [we see] how great is God’s patience.” “For they recognized power and glory in Christ’s words and miracles.”

**HOMILY CIV.—Seventeenth Sunday after Pentecost.** [Col. 0744B] “The Pharisees, hearing that he had imposed silence upon the Sadducees.” “And from that day no one dared ask him any more questions.”

378 **HOMILY CV.—Eighteenth Sunday after Pentecost.** “On that day, he says, on which the Pharisees departed defeated,” etc. “Thus, therefore, what was formerly observed according to the letter in the Synagogue is now observed spiritually in the Church.”

**HOMILY CVI.—Nineteenth Sunday after Pentecost.** “For in this place his own city is not Nazareth,” etc. “And they glorified God, who gave such authority to human beings.”

[Col. 0744C] **HOMILY CVII.—Twentieth Sunday after Pentecost.** “For this king himself who speaks is God and man, Jesus Christ our Lord.” “For it is not enough to forgive with the lips unless mouths and hearts agree.”

**HOMILY CVIII.—Twenty-first Sunday after Pentecost.** “Foolish Pharisees, who think they can catch the Word of God in speech.” “They seek to catch Christ in speech, but discover that they themselves have been caught in their own words.”

**HOMILY CIX.—Twenty-second Sunday after Pentecost.** “For what is meant by this ruler, if not Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,” etc. “In your will you have led me, and with glory you have received me.”

**HOMILY CX.—Twenty-third Sunday after Pentecost.** [Col. 0744D] “Then, having dismissed the crowds, he came into the house, and his disciples came to him.” “A parable is a comparison in which one thing is said and another is understood reasonably.”

**HOMILY CXI.—Twenty-fourth Sunday after Pentecost.** “For after Lazarus had been raised, Jesus came to Jerusalem,” etc. “By what means we may do this without harm to the Church.”

**HOMILY CXII.—Twenty-fifth Sunday after Pentecost.** “Let us now see what the prophet Daniel says concerning this abomination,” etc. “But the words of truth cannot be changed from their settled state.”

**HOMILY CXIII.—Twenty-sixth Sunday after Pentecost.** [Col. 0745A] Begins: “But another evangelist added: ‘Neither the Son,’” etc. Ends: “For the present it torments the soul; afterwards, however, both body and soul.”

**HOMILY CXIV.—Twenty-seventh Sunday after Pentecost.** “For then the Lord Father, who is king and lord of all, made a marriage for his Son Jesus Christ,” etc. “But few are brought into the king’s bridal chamber and glory.”

**HOMILY CXV.—Twenty-eighth Sunday after Pentecost.** “Kings are worthy to be heard. None are so intimate with God as good kings.” “That we may live and die no further, but may be led, sound and immortal, into the heavenly kingdoms.”

[Col. 0745B] **HOMILY CXVI.—On the Feast of Saint Lawrence the Martyr.** “This is that grain of wheat which a virgin and untilled earth produced,” etc. “And the Apostle: ‘I desire,’ he says, ‘to be dissolved and to be with Christ.’”

**HOMILY CXVII.—On the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary.** “All the works of our Saviour are full of mysteries.” “She herself chose the better part, which shall not be taken away from her.”

**HOMILY CXVIII.—On the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist.** “What opinion people held concerning blessed John the Baptist.” “They took his body and buried it; and, coming, they announced it to Jesus.”

**HOMILY CXIX.—On the Nativity of Mary, Mother of God.** [Col. 0745C] “Why blessed Matthew the evangelist begins with Christ’s genealogy,” etc. “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, shall by no means be least among the rulers of Judah.”

**HOMILY CXX.—On the Feast of Saint Matthew the Apostle.** “For blessed Matthew speaks of himself as though of another.” “Because Christ’s sacrifice was mercy.”

**HOMILY CXXI.—On the Vigil of Saint Andrew the Apostle.** “At the beginning of this Gospel a great question arises for us.” “When Christ the Lord shall appear in his majesty.”

**HOMILY CXXII.—On the Feast of Saint Andrew the Apostle.** “Above, the evangelist relates that the Lord and Saviour,” etc. [Col. 0745D] “He sees the fish themselves too, namely those who are baptized and believe.”

**HOMILY CXXIII.—On the Feast of Apostles I.** “There are indeed ten commandments of the law, of which the first is that wherein it is said: ‘You shall have no other god besides me.’” “Therefore he who rejoices that his prayer has not been heard is well heard.”

**HOMILY CXXIV.—On the Feast of Apostles II.** “Great is the power of charity, which the Lord so often commends to his disciples.” “But what shall I say? These are those heavens that declare the glory of God.”

379 **HOMILY CXXV.—On the Feast of Apostles III.** “Above in this Gospel the Lord and our Saviour had said to his disciples: ‘Go, preach,’ etc.” [Col. 0746A] “For those who are always found in good are never judged except in good.”

**HOMILY CXXVI.—On the Feast of Apostles IV.** “Above, the evangelist relates that a certain young man came to Jesus,” etc. “For those whom we love greatly we customarily call by these names.”

**HOMILY CXXVII.—On the Feast of Apostles V.** “Blessed Luke the evangelist says thus: ‘For the Lord appointed,’ etc.” “May they be subjected to a more severe punishment than those to whom truth was not announced.”

**HOMILY CXXVIII.—On the Feast of Apostles VI.** “But the Lord and our Saviour seems to say this for this reason,” etc. “The former, indeed, both bad and good persons can possess together; but the latter only good persons will possess.”

[Col. 0746B] **HOMILY CXXXI.—On the Feast of Several Martyrs I.** “Such are the battles of Christ, such the wars of the New Testament.” “Those who suffer persecution for Christ’s name.”

**HOMILY CXXX.—On the Feast of Several Martyrs II.** “What, then, does the Psalmist mean when he says: ‘In his days righteousness shall arise, and abundance of peace’?” “If, therefore, they have lacked reward here, they will not on that account have reward there.”

**HOMILY CXXI.—On the Feast of Several Martyrs III.** “A great crowd followed Jesus, and not only followed but even pressed upon [him],” etc. “May their example teach you, if their blessedness delights you.”

**HOMILY CXXXII.—On the Feast of One Martyr I.** [Col. 0746C] “A little earlier the Lord Jesus had said to his disciples,” etc. “Such as he will appear after this life in his kingdom to all his faithful.”

**HOMILY CXXXIII.—On the Feast of One Martyr II.** “For elsewhere the Lord says: ‘You shall love your neighbour.’” “For, if necessary, they did not fear to lose these things together with life itself.”

**HOMILY CXXXIV.—On the Feast of One Martyr III.** “Behold, Christ is called the vine, and the true vine,” etc. “Great is the power of patience: without it [the soul] is lost, and through it the soul is possessed.”

**HOMILY CXXXV.—On the Feast of Confessors I.** “This man is the Lord and our Saviour,” etc. “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

**HOMILY CXXXVI.—On the Feast of Confessors II.** [Col. 0746D] “This nobleman himself, who speaks, is our Saviour,” etc. “Which has been prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

**HOMILY CXXXVII.—On the Feast of Confessors III.** “For the reason that the Lord commands us to gird our loins.” “It is not fitting, therefore, that each person should be set over all things there.”

**HOMILY CXXXVIII.—On the Feast of Confessors IV.** “But these words and many others [the Lord spoke] then to his disciples,” etc. “Whoever does and teaches shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.”

**HOMILY CXXXIX.—On the Feast of Confessors V.** “Therefore, if the light which is in you is darkness,” etc. “The entire body of virtues and the whole mass of deeds shall be bright.”

[Col. 0747A] **HOMILY CXL.—On the Feast of Confessors VI.** Begins: “Where there are no eyes, there is no need of light.” Ends: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”

**HOMILY CXLI.—On the Feast of Virgins I.** “The kingdom of heaven in this place [means] the heavenly homeland,” etc. “Who brings forth from his treasure new things and old.”

**HOMILY CXLII.—On the Feast of Virgins II.** [Col. 0748A] “Just above, the Lord and our Saviour had said: ‘But concerning that day,’ etc.” “Watch therefore, because you know neither the day nor the hour.”

380 **HOMILY CXLIII.—On the Dedication of a Church.** “From the time when the first human being went down from Jerusalem.” “Those who are healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are ill.”

*Unpublished Sermons of Saint Bruno, Bishop.*

[Col. 0747]

[Col. 0747A] **SERMON I.—On the Epiphany of the Lord.**

Begins: “The final little verse of the Gospel reading, dearest brothers, pertains to the edification of the faithful,” etc. Ends: “We shall enjoy in heaven, with the angels, the joys of the homeland of everlasting life,” etc.

**SERMON II.—On the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary.**

“The Lord, Creator and Redeemer of the human race,” etc. “Circumcise your hearts, and not your bodies.”

**SERMON III.—On the Feast of One Martyr.**

[Col. 0748B] “Moreover, the Lord himself was in them, who gave increase to their seed.” “For in such joy sorrow and sadness cannot exist.”

[Col. 0747]

**HOMILIES OF SAINT BRUNO, BISHOP OF ASTI AND SEGNI.**

381 **FIRST HOMILY. FIRST SUNDAY OF ADVENT.**

[Col. 0747C]

[EDITORIAL NOTICE.]

**EDITORIAL NOTICE.** We said in the prolegomena that the homilies of Saint Bruno were published by Marchesi in the same order in which we found them transcribed in the manuscript codex of the Medicean Laurentian Library; for they begin with the first Sunday of Advent, which is the beginning of the ecclesiastical year. Neither the Vallicellian codex nor the edition of homilies published at Paris in 1575 under the name of Eusebius of Emesa agrees with these. We did not shrink from comparing the editions with the manuscript codices and consulting the same Saint Bruno’s Commentary on the Gospels. We have therefore established and ascertained what has been extracted from that commentary and what has been added, as is clear from this first homily, in which we have enclosed the addition in brackets; this will likewise be done in those following. Saint Maximus of Turin also has a homily on the same subject, which is the second in our edition, p. 6.

**READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (24:27).**

[Col. 0747D]

Jesus said to his disciples: “For as lightning comes forth from the east and appears as far as the west, so shall the coming of the Son of Man be.” And the rest. Homily on the same reading. (See edition, p. 115, col. 1.)
