For this is what the Psalmist says: “God will come openly, our God, and will not keep silence” (Ps. XLIX [50]:3). He will not come hidden, as before, but shining forth like the sun in his majesty; he will appear everywhere, shine everywhere, and be revealed to all, even unwillingly: “Wherever the body may be, there the eagles also will be gathered” (Matt. XXIV:28). For the eagles are the souls of the saints, which both fly higher and see more clearly. When they then come to their own bodies, wherever and however those bodies may have been scattered, they will put them on again, so that the whole, complete, and immortal human being may rise again. This may also be understood thus: wherever Christ’s body may be, there too souls prepared to obey his commands will assemble.

“But immediately after the tribulation of those days, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light; the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven will be shaken; and then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven; and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty.” Since Christ, our God, the Sun of righteousness, more splendid than every light, will descend from heaven, this sun which we see will be darkened, and this moon will not give its light, being obscured by the immeasurable brilliance of the greater light. For just as the moon and stars grow pale before the brightness of this sun, so, before that unfailing radiance, the sun itself will be turned into darkness. When he says that the stars will fall, he signifies either that the souls of the saints will descend to their bodies, or that the stars themselves, literally falling and passing away, will lose their customary light. [Col. 0748C–D]

[Moreover, the stars will fall because the saints, signified by the stars, will be killed by the wicked. The moon will not give its light because the holy Church will no longer display its customary brightness in signs and miracles; and the sun will be darkened because the heretics then existing will not fear to condemn and rebuke Christ the Lord, the Sun of righteousness, and his faith.]

“The powers of heaven will be shaken,” because that whole host of angels will follow Christ our Lord to judgment. “And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven,” by which we may understand either his cross or some other sign of victory. “And then all the tribes of the earth will mourn for him.” Hence it is written in the prophet Zechariah: “They shall mourn for him with mourning as for an only-begotten son, and they shall grieve over him as men are accustomed to grieve at the death of a firstborn. On that day there shall be great mourning in Jerusalem, like the mourning at Remmon in the plain of Megiddo; and the families of the land shall mourn, each family separately” (Zech. XII:10). For how will they not mourn for him when they see in such glory him whom they crucified with such disgrace?

It follows: “And he will send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice, and they will gather his elect from the highest points of the heavens to their farthest bounds.” By the ministry of angels, the saints of God will be gathered and raised from every part of the world, their souls descending from the highest heavens and coming to their limits. But since the heavens are called saints, we may understand by the highest heavens the patriarchs and apostles, and by their limits all other believers. Thus the principal elect of God will be gathered from the highest heavens to their limits, because the greater and the lesser, the first and the last, will all come together into one. What he says, “with a trumpet,” he himself explained in saying, “and with a loud voice.” For the voice will be great: it will raise the dead and fill the whole world. [Col. 0749A–B]

“Learn the parable from the fig tree: when its branch has already become tender and the leaves have sprung forth, you know that summer is near; so also, when you see all these things, know that it is near, at the doors.” For just as the fig tree, when new branches and leaves arise, announces the approaching summer, so all these things, so great and so unprecedented, will most plainly announce Christ’s coming. “Amen, I say to you: this generation will not pass away until all these things take place.” This is understood of the generation of the scribes and Pharisees, upon whom he had previously said that all righteous blood would come. Therefore that generation will not pass away first, nor fail first, nor wholly cease from its wickedness, before all these things are fulfilled. “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.” What Truth says is unchangeable and cannot pass away; otherwise it would not be truth. Heaven and earth, therefore, will pass away because, as regards what they now are, they will be changed for the better; but the words of truth cannot be altered from their condition. [Col. 0749C–D]

(In Marchesius, certain matters foreign to this homily are added, and the ending leaves the sense incomplete.)

## HOMILY II. THE SAME SUNDAY

### [NOTICE]

**NOTICE.**—Since the exposition of this Gospel passage in the Commentary, no. 47, begins with the same words and continues with the same words as far as: “And what sorrow there will be for the wicked,” we shall not repeat matters that may be read in our edition, but shall here present the addition. This homily was wrongly attributed to Eusebius of Emesa in the Paris edition, and was thereafter reprinted in the Lyon *Library of the Fathers*, vol. VI, published by the Anisson press, p. 1677, under the name of Eusebius Gallicanus.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (XXI:25)

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “There will be signs in the sun and moon and stars, and upon the earth distress of nations.” And the rest. [Col. 0750A]

When certain persons questioned our Lord and Savior, etc. Hence Daniel says (Dan. VII): “I looked in a vision of the night, and behold, the Son of Man was coming in the clouds of heaven, and he came even to the Ancient of Days.” For he had said that he had seen four great beasts, unlike one another, of which “the first was like a lioness and had wings like an eagle. As I watched, her wings were plucked off, and she was lifted from the earth; she stood upon her feet like a human being, and a human heart was given to her. And behold another beast, like a bear, stood on one side; and there were three rows in its mouth and in its teeth; and thus they said to it: Arise, devour much flesh. After this I looked, and behold another, like a leopard, and it had four wings upon it like those of a bird, and the beast had four heads, and power was given to it. After this I looked in the vision of the night; and behold, a fourth beast, terrible, wonderful, and exceedingly strong; it had great iron teeth, devouring and crushing, and trampling the remainder beneath its feet.” [Col. 0750A–B]

It had ten horns; and as Daniel looked at them, “another horn arose among them, before whose face three of the former horns were plucked out. The horn had eyes like human eyes and a mouth speaking great things. It made war against the saints and prevailed; and it thought that it could change times and laws, and the kingdom of the saints was delivered into its hand for a time, and times, and half a time, until the Ancient of Days sat down and thrones were set.” [Col. 0750B–C]

Daniel had seen these things; and, unable to understand them, he asked one of those standing by to explain what they meant. He was told: “The four beasts are four kingdoms which shall arise from the earth. But the saints of the Most High God shall receive the kingdom and possess it unto an age, and unto the age of ages.” What concerns the fourth beast will be said more fully below. But concerning the three, since the angel explained nothing further, we shall now speak, God granting it.

The first beast, then, is the kingdom of the Greeks, whose beginning was Alexander the Great. Like a roaring lion, in so brief a time he seized lands on every side that he seems rather to have flown than fought. Hence he is not undeservedly described as having the appearance of a lion and the wings of an eagle. But because he reigned only a short time, its wings are said to have been plucked off. It stood upon its feet like a human being because at last he understood himself to be mortal; and he received his own heart, so that he thought more of death than of honors. How greatly this kingdom afflicted the people of God is shown by the Book of Maccabees. [Col. 0750C–D]

The second beast is understood as the kingdom of the Romans. It did not begin with such strength as the Greek kingdom, but it reached greater power, for a lion is stronger than a bear. The three rows in its mouth and teeth signify the senate, the people, and the emperors or consuls themselves. By these three ranks the Roman kingdom devoured all nations and subjected them to its dominion. Hence it is here told: “Arise, devour much flesh.” And it did not cease to afflict the people of God until the time of Constantine. [Col. 0750D–0751A]

By the third beast we understand the kingdom of the heretics, namely from the time of Arius and Constantius, that heretical and most cruel emperor. For then the people of God suffered a greater persecution than those kingdoms mentioned above had inflicted upon them. For suffering persecution in body and soul is worse than suffering it in the body alone. This beast is described as like a leopard and as having four wings, because the preaching of the heretics swiftly filled the whole world in a short time, as though flying. The world has four regions, signified by the four wings and four heads. This beast had four heads because the heretics had their preachers in the four regions of the world. How great a power was given to the Arians is made clear by the Council of Rimini. [Col. 0751A–B]

Now let us hear what the angel answered Daniel about the fourth beast: “The beast,” he says, “will be a fourth kingdom upon the earth, greater than all kingdoms; it will devour the whole earth, trample it down, and crush it. The ten horns of that kingdom will be ten kings, and another will rise after them; he will be more powerful than those before him, and will humble three kings; he will speak words against the Most High and crush the saints of the Most High; and he will think that he can change times and laws, and they will be delivered into his hand for a time, and times, and half a time.” [Col. 0751B–C]

We await this fourth kingdom, of which we have now heard the angel’s explanation, near the end of the age. For then, as we have already said, there will be a tribulation such as has not existed from the beginning of the world and never will exist. Hence the fourth beast is described as unlike the others, more terrible and stronger. By the ten horns we may understand all the kings of this world; for in Holy Scripture all are frequently signified by ten. That horn, at whose rising three horns were plucked out, which had eyes and a mouth speaking great things, is Antichrist, stronger and more powerful than other kings. After overcoming those three kings and subjugating their kingdoms, he will be raised to such pride that he will not fear to speak against the Most High and impiously declare himself God. [Col. 0751C–D]

Filled with the spirit of Satan, he will perform many powers and miracles through diabolical art, and will bring some to his will by signs and others by swords. He will wage war against the saints, because Enoch and Elijah will then come; since he will be unable to overcome them by argument, he will have them killed by the sword. He will think that he can change times and laws because he will attempt to transform the New Testament according to the practice of the old Law. He will reign for a time, and times, and half a time, by which we understand three and a half years: “whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the manifestation of his coming” (II Thess. II:8). And then, indeed, as we heard in the Gospel today, they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and majesty. He will come even to the Ancient of Days, because he will show himself equal to the Father and of the same eternity. “But when these things begin to happen,” etc. [Col. 0751D–0752A]

(The addition to this homily extends only to this point. The few things that remain may be seen in the Commentary.)

## HOMILY III. SECOND SUNDAY OF ADVENT

### [NOTICE]

**NOTICE.**—Let readers consult the Commentary on Matthew, no. 41, chapter 2; they will see that the things presented by Marchesius under the title of a homily, vol. II, p. 3, were taken from it. Nor does Eusebius, to whom this homily has been falsely attributed, offer anything new; rather, he seems to agree in every respect. It exists in the Laurentian manuscript, but placed on the Third Sunday of Advent, while the preceding homily is assigned to the Second Sunday.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (XI:2)

At that time, John, having heard in prison of the works of Christ, sent two of his disciples and said to him: “Are you he who is to come, or do we await another?” And the rest.

**Beginning:** “John the Baptist, placed in chains and in prison, when he had heard of the miracles,” etc.

**Ending:** “Understanding this literally, he judges John to be Elijah.”

## HOMILY IV. THIRD SUNDAY OF ADVENT

### [NOTICE]

**NOTICE.**—The exposition of the Gospel according to John, no. 3, chapter 2, is the same as the homily published by Marchesius, vol. II, p. 3, and appropriated by the author of the Emesan collection, who placed it on the Fourth Sunday of Advent. [Col. 0752C]

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN (I:19)

At that time the Jews sent priests and Levites to John to ask him: “Who are you?” And he confessed and did not deny it, and confessed: “I am not the Christ.” And the rest.

**Beginning:** “For everyone thought John to be the Christ,” etc.

**Ending:** “These things were done at Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.”

## HOMILY V. WEDNESDAY OF THE ADVENT EMBER DAYS

### [NOTICE]

**NOTICE.**—No one need expend much effort to obtain this homily, which Marchesius published in vol. II, p. 4. Let him read the Commentary on Luke, no. 3, and he will find the same work with not a word changed. It was falsely attributed to Eusebius, like the others. We found it placed under the same day in the Laurentian manuscript and compared it with Marchesius’s edition. [Col. 0752D]

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (I:36)

At that time the angel Gabriel was sent by God into a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man named Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary. And the rest.

**Beginning:** “Gabriel the angel,” he says, “was sent, whose name is interpreted ‘the strength of God.’”

**Ending:** “Let it be done to me according to your word. And the angel departed from her.” [Col. 0753A]

## HOMILY VI. FRIDAY OF THE ADVENT EMBER DAYS

### [NOTICE]

**NOTICE.**—Before the Commentary of St. Bruno on the Gospels was published, doubt existed as to which author this homily should be ascribed: Eusebius of Emesa, Peter Damian, or Bishop Bruno. But that edition provided certain proof that Bruno was its author. Let Marchesius, vol. II, p. 6, and Eusebius of Emesa be compared with our edition of the same Commentary on Luke, no. 4; anyone will see that it was drawn from that source. The most distinguished prelate Stephen Borgia transcribed it from a Cassinese manuscript under the title “on the Octave of the Visitation,” and, with his great kindness, communicated it to us along with other writings of the same St. Bruno.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (I:39)

At that time Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country, to a city of Judah; and she entered the house of Zachariah and greeted Elizabeth. And the rest. Homily on the same reading. [Col. 0753B]

**Beginning:** “The virgin full of God ascends to the hills, seeks the higher regions,” etc.

**Ending:** “At her departure he grieved not a little who had exulted with such great joy at her coming.”

## HOMILY VII. FOURTH SUNDAY OF ADVENT

### [NOTICE]

**NOTICE.**—Since the author seemed to have spoken sufficiently of John the Baptist’s preaching in the desert in his exposition of chapter III of the Gospel according to St. Matthew—as he himself testifies in no. 13 of the Commentary on Luke—he passes over in silence everything reported by the same Evangelist at the beginning of chapter III. Yet there exists a homily of his, published by Marchesius for the Fourth Sunday of Advent, and circulated under the name of Eusebius Gallicanus in vol. VI of the *Library of the Fathers*, Lyon edition of 1677, p. 1718; we have taken care to transcribe it with the Lyon edition before us. [Col. 0753C]

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (III:1)

In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate governing Judaea; Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and Philip his brother tetrarch of Ituraea and the region of Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene; under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came upon John, son of Zachariah, in the desert. And the rest.

Since, as the Lord says, “every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste” (Luke XI:17), the Evangelist was already showing that the desolation and destruction of the Jewish kingdom were near when he said that it was divided into so many parts. He shows most carefully, by naming the rulers of the land, at what time John began to preach. John preached a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins, teaching and proclaiming that forgiveness of sins cannot be effected except through baptism and repentance. He preached, indeed, but did not confer it; he taught the remedy, but did not heal. For the form of baptism had not yet been given; the Lord had not yet said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Mark XVI:15). This is the form of baptism. Otherwise baptism has no validity. The Lord had reserved this form for himself; he had come to give it in person, because it was most fitting that the universal remedy should be given by the universal physician. [Col. 0753D–0754A]

John therefore came into all the region about the Jordan, preaching but not administering a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins, as is written in the book of the sayings of Isaiah the prophet: “A voice crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.” Thus John did as Isaiah had foretold concerning him. He cried out, preached the way of the Lord, and taught baptism and repentance. For these are the ways by which one comes to the Lord and by which the Lord comes to us.

When John was asked who he was, he answered: “I am the voice crying in the wilderness.” John was the voice, for Christ is the Word. Just as a voice precedes a word, so John preceded Christ. For as soon as some sound proceeds from the speaker’s mouth, it is a voice, but it is not yet a word, because every word signifies something. John is rightly called the voice; Christ is rightly called the Word. This voice cried in the wilderness because it called the impious and cruel to faith—people who imitated, not human beings in piety, but wild beasts and animals in cruelty. For the wilderness is not a dwelling place of human beings but of wild beasts. Such was this world; such were its inhabitants. Hence the Psalmist says: “In a desert land, pathless and waterless, so I appeared before you in the sanctuary, that I might behold your power and your glory” (Ps. LXII [63]:2). [Col. 0754A–B]

John therefore preached in the wilderness. But what did he say? “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.” We prepare the Lord’s way and make his paths straight if what we do, we do not for empty glory but with sincere devotion and chaste love. Of those who do all their works in order to be seen by people, the Lord said: “Amen, I say to you: they have received their reward” (Matt. VI:2). This is because they traveled by a crooked way and twisting paths.

“Every valley will be filled, and every mountain and hill will be brought low.” What do we understand by valleys but the humble, and by hills but the proud? The valley, therefore, will be filled and raised up, because the humble person, filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, will be exalted to heavenly things. But the mountain and hill will be brought low, because the proud person will be cast down and hurled into darkness. Hence it follows: “The crooked places will become straight, and the rough places level ways.” For then crooked places will be straightened and rough places made level, because no pride, power, strength, or height will remain that can resist the saints. [Col. 0754C–D]

“And all flesh will see the salvation of God.” Not all flesh will see Christ the Lord at his first coming; but at his second coming every eye will see him, as he himself says: “‘As I live,’ says the Lord, ‘every knee will bend to me, and every tongue will confess’” (Isa. XLV:23). Concerning this salvation, the patriarch Jacob, filled with the Spirit of God, said while blessing his sons: “Let Dan become a serpent in the way, a horned serpent in the path, biting the hoofs of the horse, so that its rider falls backward; I will await your salvation, O Lord” (Gen. XLIX:17). This is as though he said: I know, Lord, that my sons—my offspring, deceived by their own perversity—will await Antichrist. But I will await your salvation, Jesus Christ your Son, O Lord. For Antichrist will arise from the tribe of Dan; the Jews await him and call him Messiah. He will be a serpent in the way and a horned serpent in the path, because he will lie in wait for all who run in the way of God’s commandments and hasten to their homeland, so that he may obstruct their journey. [Col. 0754D–0755A]

For we are all on the way; we all return to our homeland, because “we do not have here an abiding city, but seek one to come.” The way is as long as life itself. Therefore on this way we must take great care lest that serpent encounter us and infect us with his venom. Of him it is written: “The dragon will draw his tail and will separate a third part of the stars of heaven” (Apoc. XII:4). *Cerastes* means “horned.” This beast and this dragon are described as having ten horns, by which we understand all the wicked kings and rulers of this world. All who imitate or will imitate his deeds will be counted in his army. Hence blessed Job says: “He will draw after himself every human being, and before himself those without number” (Job XXI:33). These words plainly show that many who never saw him bodily will be reckoned in his army; for he will draw both those who were before him and those who will be after him. [Col. 0755A–B]

It follows: “Biting the hoof of the horse, so that its rider falls backward” (Gen. XLIX:17). What do we understand by the horse but this world? And what by its rider but all kings and powerful persons who preside over it, govern it with the reins of their authority, and turn it to their own will? The horse’s hoof signifies the final part of the world, because the hoof is the final part of the body. This horse, therefore, already fleeing and nearly finishing its course—dragging its foot, so to speak, and displaying only its hoof, that is, its final part—the *cerastes*, that is, Antichrist, will bite; and he will infect it with the corruption of his poison so that the horse itself perishes and its riders, falling backward, perish as well. His deception will be so great, his persuasion so fraudulent and venomous, that, if possible, even the elect will be led into error. The Jews await this beast; the scribes and Pharisees await this plague. They heed neither the patriarch Jacob prophesying nor understand him blessing and saying: “I will await your salvation, O Lord” (ibid.). [Col. 0755C–D]

## HOMILY VIII. ON THE VIGIL OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

### [NOTICE]

**NOTICE.**—St. Bruno must beyond all doubt be judged the author of this homily, since his Commentary on Matthew, no. 2, chapter 1, presents it in precisely the same words from beginning to end. We need no other proof to convict the editors of Eusebius of Emesa and Eusebius Gallicanus of appropriation. Marchesius published it in vol. II, p. 8.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (I:18)

When Mary, his mother, had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit. And the rest. [Col. 0756A]

**Beginning:** “The first question, however, must be why blessed Mary was betrothed.”

**Ending:** “It is clear, therefore, that Jesus is interpreted ‘our Savior.’”

## HOMILY IX. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

### [NOTICE]

**NOTICE.**—Those who have read the often-praised Commentary will immediately recognize the author of the homily. It is indeed read entire in no. 6 on Luke. Nor will those who have called Eusebius of Emesa, or another author invented by themselves, its author hesitate to condemn the false attribution. It appears in Marchesius, vol. II, p. 9, as does the following homily, which is read at the second Mass of the same feast.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (II:1)

A decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled. This first enrollment was made by Quirinius, governor of Syria. And the rest. [Col. 0756B]

**Beginning:** “For the fact that the whole world is enrolled and reduced to tribute under one authority,” etc.

**Ending:** “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

## HOMILY X. ON THE SAME SOLEMNITY, AT MASS II

### [NOTICE]

**NOTICE.**—We said above that, in Marchesius, this homily immediately follows the preceding one. The same is true in the Commentary, where the exposition of one Gospel passage follows the other, and the author composed it as no. 7, p. 158. Here too the false attribution to other writers is demolished.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (II:15)

The shepherds said to one another: “Let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this word which has happened, which the Lord has shown us.” And the rest. [Col. 0756C]

**Beginning:** “The shepherds,” he says, “spoke to one another concerning those things which they had heard and seen,” etc.

**Ending:** “Proclaiming his faith, and praising and glorifying him everywhere.”

## HOMILY XI. ON THE SAME SOLEMNITY, AT MASS III

### [NOTICE]

**NOTICE.**—Had the editors of Eusebius of Emesa observed the teaching concerning the divinity of the Word, whose complete equality and consubstantiality with the Father are most fully affirmed by the author of this homily, they would have regarded Eusebius as an opponent, not an advocate, of the Arians, as very many have thought. For the Arians, who asserted that the Word, the Son of God, was less than the Father, denied his eternal generation, his substance of the same nature, and the other attributes of divinity. Catholic doctrine, however, holds that the Son of God, Jesus Christ, is true God and true man: less than the Father according to the flesh, but equal and like to the Father in every respect as regards divinity. In his humanity he bore the form of a servant; in the divine person, in which Christ united both natures, he was able to do and did all things as God. St. Bruno prefaces his commentary on the Evangelist John with certain matters reproduced here, and then attaches the interpretation of the Gospel text from the first number of the Commentary through the second. [Col. 0756D]

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN (I:1)

In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. And the rest.

The other Evangelists recount that our Lord and Savior was announced by an angel, born of a virgin, revealed to shepherds, made known by a star, worshiped by the Magi, brought to the Temple, and presented to Simeon. They further recount how he fled Judaea with his parents, how he returned from Egypt into Judaea, and how he grew and advanced in strength and wisdom. But when the Evangelists wrote these things and similar matters, they affirmed that he was a true human being and had assumed true flesh. [Col. 0757A]

But John the Evangelist, ascending higher and extending himself even to divinity, “mounted upon the cherubim and flew, flew upon the wings of the winds”; he penetrated the heavens, transcended the archangels, and came even to the throne of God. There he saw the Word of God; there he saw the Lord Jesus Christ in the bosom of the Father; and then he understood what was written: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. XLIV [45]:1). He understood, indeed, and said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Jesus Christ our Lord, etc. (The remainder, as we have said, is contained in the Commentary.) [Col. 0757A–B]

**Ending:** “Your right hand will guide you wonderfully.”

## HOMILY XII. ON THE FEAST OF ST. STEPHEN THE PROTOMARTYR

### [NOTICE]

**NOTICE.**—Since the following homily, except for a few passages taken here and there from the Commentary on this passage of Matthew, no. 98, gives a different exposition, we again bring it to light as it was published by Marchesius, vol. II, p. 11.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (XXIII:34)

At that time Jesus said to the crowds of Jews and to the chief priests: “Behold, I send to you prophets, wise men, and scribes; and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues.” And the rest. [Col. 0757C]

Above in this Gospel our Lord and Savior speaks to the Scribes and Pharisees, saying: “Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who build the tombs of the prophets and adorn the monuments of the righteous, and say: If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have been their partners in the blood of the prophets. Thus you bear witness against yourselves that you are the sons of those who killed the prophets.” Woe, he says, to you—not because you build and adorn the monuments of the prophets, for this is a work of piety, but because you are the sons of those who killed the prophets: sons not so much by nature as by imitation and wickedness. For just as the good are called sons of Abraham because they imitate Abraham, so all wicked people are called sons of the wicked because they imitate the wicked. Hence the Lord says to such men: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would surely do the works of Abraham” (John 8:39). Woe, therefore, to those who are not sons of Abraham, nor of the prophets, nor of the righteous, because they do not imitate them; indeed, they are sons of those who killed the prophets, imitating them in every malice and wickedness. They further say that, had they lived in the days of their fathers, they would not have shared in the blood of the prophets; whereas they were far worse than those fathers, killing not only the prophets but even the Lord of the prophets himself. Therefore it is added: “And you, then, fill up the measure of your fathers”; run, hasten, until you attain the full and perfect measure of their wickedness. For it is disgraceful that you should be found inferior to your fathers and lesser than they in wickedness. He says this because he saw that they were already exceedingly inflamed by envy toward the killing of himself and his disciples. This mode of speech is called irony by grammarians.

“Serpents, brood of vipers, how will you escape the judgment of Gehenna?” They are serpents because they are cunning and venomous; they are a brood of vipers because they are more wicked than all the wicked, since neither wife spares husband nor children their parents. They will certainly be unable to escape the judgment of Gehenna otherwise than by killing their mother, just as she too kills their father. For vipers are said to have this nature: when the female conceives, she kills the male; but when she gives birth, she is likewise killed by her young. For they do not wait to emerge in the customary order of nature, but, tearing open their mother’s womb, burst violently forth. The Synagogue, therefore, is the viper; her husband is Christ. Christ came to the Synagogue and poured into her the whole seed of evangelical preaching. But she, like a viper—venomous and impious—rose up against him and killed him. Her children, bursting forth from her impious womb, kill her, because Jews who come to the faith excommunicate and condemn her. Hence the Apostle says: “But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace” (Gal. 1:15), etc. For all who return from heresies to the Church condemn heresies. Therefore: “Behold, I send to you prophets, wise men, and Scribes”; therefore, he says, so that you too may fill up the measure of your fathers: “I send to you prophets, wise men, and Scribes; and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues.”

Such was blessed Stephen, concerning whom we have just heard while the reading was being read: he was full of grace and power and performed great wonders and signs among the people. Certain men of the Synagogue arose and disputed with him, but they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke. Hence the Lord says: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict” (Luke 21:15). Thus the saints fought; thus the Lord taught them to fight: they did not fight with weapons, but with speech. Gideon had fought in this manner before them, and his battle signified all these battles of the saints. For Gideon, about to fight against the Midianites, ordered those who were with him to prepare trumpets and lamps (Judg. 7:16). He commanded them to conceal the lamps within jars, and so he went forth to battle. But by night, entering the enemy camp, they broke the jars; holding trumpets in their right hands and lamps in their left, they filled everything around them with the trumpet blast and the brightness of the lamps. Their enemies, terrified, began to flee and, as if mad, for the most part killed one another with their own swords. Gideon therefore conquered with such weapons, and with such weapons the holy martyrs also conquered.

For what do we understand by the trumpets except the voices of preachers? And what is figured by the lamps except the radiance of miracles? The jars are earthen vessels formed from the earth, of which the Apostle says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7); for the Lord had previously said: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28). Not fearing either the breaking of the jars or the suffering of the body, the holy martyrs were ready for every kind of torment. See, then, how fittingly the battle of Stephen the protomartyr and the battle of Gideon correspond to one another. For if the trumpets signify the voices of preachers, then blessed Stephen surely sounded the trumpet when he rebuked the unbelieving Jews. But when he performed great wonders and signs, then indeed he held lamps in his hand. For the brightness of miracles is greater than the brightness of fire, and the fame of miracles shines much farther than the flame of lamps. Then the raging Jews, running for stones, broke the jar of the protomartyr because they stoned him and killed him with stones. Blessed Stephen nevertheless conquered, since he ascended crowned into heaven. But the Jews were conquered, since after a few years, their city having been destroyed, they were led into captivity.

It follows: “And you will persecute from city to city, so that upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth.” For the apostles, martyrs, teachers, prophets, wise men, and Scribes were those whom the Lord sent to the Jews and to all the nations of the world to preach. But the Jews killed, crucified, scourged, and persecuted them from city to city. For no Christian was ever killed anywhere who was not killed either by their hands or by their will. Hence they are said to be guilty of all, and the Lord himself testifies that the blood of all the righteous shall come upon them. He explains from whom and as far as whom, saying: “From the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the Temple and the altar.”

Since elsewhere it is written: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, but each one shall die in his own sin” (Ezek. 18:20), what does it mean that here it is said that all righteous blood shall come upon this generation? By these words our Savior seems to say that this impious generation shall suffer as great a punishment for its crime as it would suffer if it had shed all the blood of our people shed from Abel down to Zechariah. And rightly so. For it was a greater thing to kill Christ and to persecute with wicked hatred his body, which is the Church, than if they had shed the blood of all the preceding righteous. Yet Zechariah son of Barachiah is nowhere read to have been killed; rather, Zechariah son of Jehoiada is read to have been killed in the court of the Temple—namely, between the Temple and the altar, which stood in the open air, where the blood of victims was poured out.

But why did he say “as far as Zechariah,” rather than “as far as himself,” or “as far as the consummation of the age”? For the Jews shed much righteous blood not only as far as Zechariah, but also after Zechariah. Since these things do not fit the historical account, a spiritual understanding must be sought. I think that our Lord calls himself Zechariah and uses the past tense for the future. For *Zechariah* is interpreted “memory of the Lord.” Just as Christ Jesus is called the Word of the Lord, the Speech of the Lord, the Power and Wisdom of the Lord, so he is also called the Memory of the Lord. And he is the son of Barachiah, which is interpreted “blessed of the Lord.” Hence, when the ruler asked him whether he was Christ, the Son of the Blessed, he answered: “I am.” The Jews killed him between the Temple and the altar because there they took counsel among themselves concerning Christ’s death. For the Jews killed Christ the Lord only by taking counsel, accusing, and condemning him. Thus they themselves said: “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death” (John 18:31). That counsel concerning his death was taken in the court of the Temple, he himself shows through the Psalmist, saying: “Those who sat in the gate practiced themselves against me, and those who drank wine sang of me” (Ps. 78:13). Thus Zechariah son of Barachiah was killed between the Temple and the altar.

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you, how often I wished to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling!” “I,” he says, “wished many times to gather your children and recall them from wickedness, just as a hen gathers her chicks and hides them beneath her wings, lest troublesome birds snatch them away; but you were unwilling. Therefore I wished—but on the condition that you too should wish. Since you were unwilling to be gathered and saved, I too now no longer wish to gather and save you.” Hence I say: “Scatter them in your power and destroy them, O Lord, my protector” (Ps. 58:12).

For the Lord, who can do whatever he wills, wishes to save no one other than the person who wishes to be saved by him. Hence he also says through the prophet: “If you are willing and hear me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling, the sword shall devour you” (Isa. 1:20). Thus it is manifest that the Lord does not will the death of the sinner, but that he should be converted and live (Ezek. 33:11); and it is likewise manifest that “he wills no one to perish, but wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of truth” (1 Tim. 2:4)—yet only if they believe and are baptized, repent of their sins, and do his will. It is equally manifest that God does not wish to save those who wish neither to believe, nor to be baptized, nor to repent; who despair of God’s goodness and do not care for the glory promised to the saints; and who persevere in this perverse will to the end. For who would dare say that he wishes to save those who cannot be saved? Since they are unwilling to believe, they cannot attain that blessedness. For without faith it is impossible either to be saved or to please God. Therefore the Lord said to the Jews: “Where I go, you cannot come” (John 8:21), because they had no faith in him.

Moreover, the Jews could not believe because Isaiah had thus foretold concerning them: “Blind the heart of this people, lest perhaps they be converted and healed” (Isa. 6:10). But why could they not believe, except because they were unwilling to believe? Faith, therefore, lies in the will. For if they had wished to believe and had been unable, they would not have had sin. We have spoken briefly of these matters in the commentary from which they have been taken; whoever does not understand them should read it in order to understand.

It follows: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate.” Likewise in the Psalms: “Behold, I fled far away and remained in solitude” (Ps. 54:8). For, having left the Jews, the Lord dwells among the Gentiles. “For I tell you: you shall not see me from now on until you say: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Luke 13:35). “After,” he says, “I leave you here in the bodily presence in which I have lived among you for a time, you shall not see me from now on until you recognize more fully that I am coming again for judgment, and all together, with one harmonious voice, say: ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’” This is what he says elsewhere: “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bend to me, and every tongue shall confess” (Isa. 45:23). “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God.” He who with God the Father, etc.

390. HOMILY XIII. ON THE FEAST OF ST. JOHN, APOSTLE AND EVANGELIST.

[EDITORIAL NOTICE.]

[Col. 0761C] EDITORIAL NOTICE.—The Cassinese, Medicean-Laurentian, and Vallicellian manuscripts agree in attributing this homily to St. Bruno, which Marchesius published in vol. II, p. 13. It is also contained in the commentary on this passage of John, nos. 55 and 56; but because certain additions seem to have been made in the earlier part of Marchesius’s lection, we have decided to reproduce it here as far as the point at which it can be compared with the commentary.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN (21:19).

At that time Jesus said to Peter: “Follow me.” And the rest.

It is read above in this Gospel that the Lord had invited his disciples to breakfast. And fittingly to breakfast, because these were Paschal days, days of which he himself had said: “The sons of the bridegroom cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them” (Matt. 9:[15]). On such days Christ’s faithful ought to have taken part in Christ’s banquets, not once only, but throughout the whole day if possible, and to have been refreshed by spiritual food. But when they had breakfasted, the Lord questioned Peter, and questioned him three times whether he loved him. To the question he likewise answered three times: “Lord, you know that I love you.” He said: “Feed my lambs; feed my sheep.” First he entrusted lambs to him, then sheep, because he established him not only as a shepherd but as shepherd of shepherds. Therefore Peter feeds the lambs and feeds the sheep; he feeds sons and mothers; he governs both subjects and prelates. Therefore he is shepherd of all, because besides lambs and sheep there is nothing in the Church—nothing, I say—that Christ has entrusted to his shepherds.

Behold Peter, who had denied the Lord three times, answered three times that he loved him, so that love might erase guilt and affection remove offence. And Jesus says to him: “Amen, amen, I say to you: when you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you shall stretch out your hands, and another shall gird you and lead you where you do not wish.” Explaining what this signified, the Evangelist says: “He said this to signify by what death he was to glorify God.” For blessed Peter, placed upon the gibbet of the cross and stretching out his hands there, when he had indeed grown old and come to the end of life, was girded and bound by others. Rightly, after he had answered three times that he loved the Lord, the Lord announced to him his death, in which he most openly showed how greatly he loved him. And when he had said this, he says to him: “Follow me.”

What is said to Peter is said to all. Since Peter was greater than the others, the whole Church was fittingly signified in Peter. Therefore let all the faithful understand that what was said to Peter alone was said to themselves: “Follow me. If,” he says, “you love me, follow me; come after me,” etc.

(The remainder of this homily may be read in the commentary on this passage of John.)

HOMILY XIV. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE INNOCENTS.

[EDITORIAL NOTICE.]

EDITORIAL NOTICE.—The interpolation of many additions, by which, as we have it in Marchesius, vol. II, p. 14, the exposition of this Gospel passage under no. 4, p. 11, has been enlarged, has compelled us to give it entire to readers. Anyone who compares the homily and commentary can ascertain whether this is so.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (2:13).

At that time an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying: “Arise, take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and remain there until I tell you.” And the rest.

In those days the Magi had come to the Lord and, as the Evangelist relates, offered him gifts; and, warned by an angel in a dream not to return to Herod, they went back to their own region by another route. After they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying: “Arise, take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt.” One may indeed question how Christ could have been presented in the Temple at Jerusalem after the days of purification had been completed, if he went off in flight to Egypt immediately after the Magi departed; or perhaps the Magi remained in Egypt so long that Joseph, together with the child and his mother, returned from Jerusalem after the purification. But it seems better to me that the words should be understood thus: “After they had departed,” after some interval of time had passed and all things required by the Law had been fulfilled, “behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying: Arise, take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt.”

For all was still quiet; Herod, still awaiting the Magi, had not yet revealed the malice of his heart. Hence they went safely to Jerusalem to fulfil the commandments of the Law. But from there they were commanded to flee into Egypt, where Abraham, Jacob, and the sons of Israel had lived as sojourners. For the prophet foretold this, saying: “Behold, the Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud and shall enter Egypt, and all its idols shall fall” (Isa. 29:1). The light cloud, not weighed down by the burden of any corruption, is the Virgin Mary, who carried Christ into Egypt, so that light might shine in darkness and the people sitting in darkness might see the light. There are also those who wish to understand this literally: that when Christ the Lord entered Egypt, all the idols immediately fell.

Moses had prefigured this persecution of Christ in himself. For there are many respects in which Moses signifies Christ. Just as Moses suffered persecution from Pharaoh, so Christ suffered it from Herod; and just as infants were killed in Judaea because of Christ, so in Egypt infants were killed in the river because of Moses. Josephus relates that a certain Egyptian priest and magician prophesied that a man would be born from the Hebrew people who would destroy that whole land; therefore he advised Pharaoh that all Hebrew infants should be killed. Pharaoh accordingly ordered the male Hebrews to be killed and the females spared. He did this so that the one who was sought might thus be killed among the others. Herod had the same intention: since he could not find Christ, he ordered so many thousands of boys to be killed.

In those days Moses was born. A long history is written concerning how he was hidden by his parents, cast into the river, taken from the water by Pharaoh’s daughter, and adopted as her son; and how that very girl rescued him from the hands of the impious priest who had tried to kill him when, as the aforementioned historian relates, while playing in infancy he knocked the crown from Pharaoh’s head. Perhaps Moses omitted these things so as not to appear to write his own praise. Yet afterward he saw fulfilled in Pharaoh and his army that which he signified when he acted thus as an infant, unknowingly.

It follows: “He arose, took the child and his mother by night, withdrew into Egypt, and remained there until the death of Herod.” Behold, Christ flees—and flees by night—so that the flight, difficult in itself, may become more difficult through the darkness of night. If, then, Christ fled Herod, how much more ought we to flee the devil and his members! Let us not be frightened by any difficulty of the journey, because it is better to be wearied by hard labor than killed by enemies: “For narrow and confined is the way that leads to life” (Matt. 7:14). Yet one ought neither always to flee nor always to resist; according to the circumstances of the time, both must be done. For the saints sometimes fled and sometimes voluntarily confronted their enemies. Our Savior himself, who commanded us to flee from city to city and could himself have fled if he wished, voluntarily confronted his enemies at the time of his Passion. Therefore we must flee visible and invisible enemies, not from fear of death—if we consider death just and beneficial—but from fear of sinning.

Why Christ fled into Egypt, the Evangelist then explains: “That what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Out of Egypt I called my son.’” For if he had not gone into Egypt, he could not have been called out of Egypt. Thus both the prophecy and the purpose of the prophecy were fulfilled. Then Herod, seeing that he had been mocked by the Magi, was greatly enraged; and he sent and killed all the boys in Bethlehem and throughout all its borders, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had inquired of the Magi. Since Herod had heard from the oracle of the prophets that Christ was to be born in Bethlehem, he killed all the boys in Bethlehem and throughout all its borders, so that, because he could not find the one, he might kill that one together with the rest. But why “from two years old and under”? Because, from the answer of the Magi, he knew Christ to be of this age. For, being occupied by other affairs, when nearly two years had passed and the Magi had not returned to him, he understood that he had been deceived and, greatly enraged, ordered all these boys to be killed.

> [Note: [Col. 0763D] St. Bruno seems to have followed the opinion of certain ancient Fathers—namely Origen, Eusebius of Caesarea, and Epiphanius—that Herod ordered the massacre of the children only after two years from Christ’s birth. But far more writers teach that, according to the more probable meaning of Matthew’s Gospel, that edict was promulgated by the most savage king shortly after the Lord’s Nativity. See Natalis Alexander, vol. III, *Historia ecclesiastica*, dissertation 2. [Col. 0764D]]

Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, saying: “A voice was heard in Ramah, much weeping and wailing: Rachel weeping for her children, and she would not be comforted, because they are not.” *Ramah* is interpreted “the heights.” Therefore that voice is heard in Ramah which, greatly raised because of its magnitude, spreads far and wide. For much weeping and much wailing were there, where so many mothers, so many parents, so many persons of both sexes, seeing such great cruelty, could not restrain their voices even if they wished to do so.

But why is Rachel said to weep for her children, when, literally speaking, all these were not Rachel’s children but children of her sister Leah? For Judah was the son not of Rachel but of Leah, and in his tribe this immense slaughter took place. But because *Rachel* means “sheep” and signifies the holy Church, which imitates the simplicity of the sheep, those are rightly called Rachel’s children who, like innocent lambs, are slaughtered without a sound. For whose children are lambs? Are they not the children of a sheep? They are therefore Rachel’s children: she is the sheep, and they are the lambs.

Rachel—that is, the holy Church—also weeps for her children to this day. Although she understands that they go to rest, she nevertheless grieves because they are physically separated from her. Thus those also grieved to whom the Lord said: “You indeed now have sorrow; but I shall see you again, and your heart shall rejoice” (John 16:22). And although they are far better off than they were—for now they are with God—she nevertheless does not receive consolation for a time, because they are not in this life. Scripture passages must be supplemented where something is lacking for understanding. For who could understand, “She would not be comforted, because they are not,” unless something were added? You will find something similar where it is said of the Lord that, “seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: ‘Because if you also had known’” (Luke 19:41). Who can understand what “you also” means unless something is added?

The saying may also be understood thus: “Rachel, weeping for her children, would not be comforted, because they are not.” For although the holy mother Church grieves greatly over the death and harsh sufferings of her children, she does not receive consolation because, in such an event, consolations ought neither to be offered nor accepted. Where joy overcomes tears and glory overcomes suffering, consolation is not necessary. Rather, we ought to rejoice over the life which the saints have deserved than grieve over this life which they have lost. What is this life in comparison with that life? And the Lord says: “He who loves his life shall lose it, and he who loses his life for my sake shall find it” (Matt. 10:38). Finally, why should one who is full of consolations seek consolations from elsewhere? Consolation is necessary for those who mourn people concerning whom they cannot have good hope. But, having good hope concerning Christ’s martyrs, we trust that through the grace of the same Jesus Christ we shall receive perfect consolation from them—he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

HOMILY XV. ON THE CIRCUMCISION OF THE LORD.

[EDITORIAL NOTICE.]

EDITORIAL NOTICE.—There is no discrepancy between Marchesius, the editor of this homily, and the Laurentian and Signine manuscripts; for it begins and ends in the same manner. We do not transcribe the whole homily here from Marchesius, vol. II, p. 15, since the greater part may be read in the commentary on the Gospel of Luke, no. 8; but we give readers the addition which begins after the words “they should thereafter uselessly wound themselves.”

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (11:21).

At that time, when eight days had been completed for the circumcision of the child, his name was called Jesus, which had been called by the angel before he was conceived in the womb. And the rest.

This, then, is the holy circumcision concerning which the Lord says to Joshua: “Make for yourself stone knives, and circumcise the children of Israel a second time” (Josh. 5:2). And shortly afterward: This, therefore, is the reason for the second circumcision: the people who had been born during forty years in the wilderness had not been circumcised. Why, then, is it called a second circumcision, or why are those circumcised a second time who had not previously been circumcised? For “second” refers to “first,” and without a first there can be no second. Let the first circumcision, then, be bodily and the second spiritual; the first that of the Jews, the second that of Christians; the first that of those who crossed the Jordan, the second that of those who did not cross the Jordan.

For this people born in the wilderness, concerning whom it is now said that they should be circumcised a second time, was first circumcised only after it crossed the Jordan. This is because it did not signify the circumcision performed before baptism, but that performed after baptism. For the Jordan signifies baptism, in which the Lord was baptized, giving the beginning and pattern of true baptism. Thus both the circumcision before baptism and that after baptism signify repentance. For the saints used to impose repentance on those who were to be baptized; and that was the first circumcision. For what is circumcision but the cutting away of vices and sins? But after they have been baptized—that is, after they have crossed the Jordan, for to be baptized is to cross—then the second circumcision follows. But why is it second? A person is circumcised as many times as, after sinning, he returns to repentance. Whoever never sinned would never need either circumcision or repentance after baptism.

Since sins are removed only through Christ—for he is the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world—circumcision is therefore commanded to be performed with stone knives, because, as the Apostle says, “the Rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 15:4): “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash his little ones against the rock” (Ps. 136:9). But why was the Lord circumcised after eight days had been completed? Why was circumcision also performed on the eighth day? For the eighth day is itself the first day; it is the day called the Lord’s Day. On that day the world began; on that day Christ rose from the dead; on that day he gave the Holy Spirit to the apostles; and on that day the final and universal resurrection will occur. Then every person will be circumcised perfectly, because then, all vices cut away, the world, clean and pure from sin—as it was created in the beginning—will be led into eternal life.

It follows: “And his name was called Jesus, which had been called by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.” For *Jesus* is interpreted “Savior.” Of this salvation the patriarch Jacob said: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord” (Gen. 49:18). Therefore Joseph, who signified Christ, was called Savior of Egypt by Pharaoh. For there are many respects in which Joseph signified Christ. He too was a shepherd of sheep; then, sold through the counsel of his brothers, he was adored; he spoke wisdom among princes; he delivered all Egypt from famine and saved it by his wisdom, etc.

When Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the east, etc. And the rest.
