HOMILY XX. FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY.

[EDITORIAL NOTICE.]

EDITORIAL NOTICE.—Here we transcribe only the addition supplied by Marchesius, vol. II, p. 21, at the end of the homily, since the preceding part is entirely found in the commentary on Matthew, no. 27, chapter 2. The addition therefore begins after the words: “Whose voice it heard and feared.”

Beginning: “For what is the little boat except the Church? What is the sea except the world?”

**Addition:** But why do you say, people, “What sort of man is this?” You seek one like him who has no like. Yet do you wish to know what he is like? I know that you do; hear, then: as is the Father, so is the Son, so is the Holy Spirit. Behold, such is he; no other is such. But what wonder is it if the winds obey him who made them, who [Col. 0768B] created them, “who brings forth winds from his storehouses” (Ps. 134:7)? How this happens, I think, has been fully revealed to no human being.

There are four regions of the world, and the winds which come from them, over which God exercises no small power on sea, land, and air. For they bring rain and storms; they drive away clouds and grant fair weather. Therefore they not undeservedly signify all the powers of this age. Thus Daniel says that he saw the four winds of heaven warring upon the great sea. And through Solomon the Lord says: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow” (Song 4:16). This garden and this little boat signify the same thing; and the winds here and there likewise signify the same thing.

Indeed, in this garden are many [Col. 0768C] kinds of trees, many species of flowers and spices. Here, among the roses, the martyrs rest; among the lilies, the confessors and virgins. This is the enclosed garden and sealed fountain; this garden is most secure, most holy among holy things. It lacks neither lilies nor roses, nor are its trees deprived of their fruits; there is a fountain of sweetest taste. Now the blasts of the winds—the troops of tyrants—trouble and toss it about in fury; the martyrs seek heaven in honour; the Lord delights in their fragrance.

And concerning the north it is written: “From the north evils shall be opened upon all the inhabitants of the earth” (Jer. 1:14). But concerning the south: “God shall come from the south” (Hab. 3:6). By the former, therefore, adversities are represented; by the latter, prosperities. [Col. 0768D] Therefore the Lord says: Arise, north wind—depart, yield place, be still; do not disturb my garden. Let the south wind come; let peace and security come; let long-awaited blessings come, and let a great calm take place.

## HOMILY XXI. ON THE PURIFICATION OF ST MARY THE VIRGIN

### [EDITORIAL NOTICE.]

**EDITORIAL NOTICE.**—Since the greater part of this homily is contained in the Commentary on Luke, no. 9, we have taken care to reproduce here what remains of it. The Signine, Laurentian, and Cassinese manuscripts, in which it is Homily 23, bear witness to it; consequently the edition attributed to Eusebius of Emesa, in which it is falsely assigned to him, is of no account.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (2:22)

“After the days of her purification were fulfilled according to the law of Moses, they took him to Jerusalem, that they might present him to the Lord, [Col. 0769A] as it is written in the law of the Lord.” And the rest.

For it is written in the law of Moses that a woman who, having received seed, bears a male child shall be unclean for seven days, and on the eighth day the infant shall be circumcised; but she herself shall remain thirty-three days in the blood of her purification. She shall touch no holy thing, nor enter the sanctuary, until the days of her purification are fulfilled.

Now the blessed Virgin Mary was not bound by this law: having received no seed, she conceived as a virgin and gave birth as a virgin; closed before childbirth, closed in childbirth, and remaining closed after childbirth. To distinguish her case, Moses did not simply say, “A woman who bears a male child,” but added, “who, having received seed, bears a male child, [Col. 0769B] shall be unclean for seven days.”

*(Here the writer of the homily begins the continuation of the Gospel commentary by this additional section, which follows.)*

Spiritually, however, this woman seems to be the Synagogue. Having received the seed of the divine law, she gave birth to a male child as often as she performed some good action. For a male child is a good work. Yet, although she had borne a male child and produced many children of good works, she was nevertheless unclean for seven days. For those seven days signify the entire span of time from Moses to Christ’s incarnation. In that week the Lamb was born who takes away the sins of the world, concerning whom it is written: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his [Col. 0769C] blood” (Rev. 1:5).

Yet although the week had ended and Christ had been born, the Synagogue was not yet entirely cleansed, because Christ’s blood had not yet been shed. She therefore remained still thirty days in the blood of her purification. She awaited the day—or rather, the thirty-third year. For in that year Christ was sacrificed, without whose blood the world could not be cleansed and washed. That a day may stand for a year you will find in Ezekiel, where he says: “A day for a year, a day for a year, son of man, I have given you” (Ezek. 4:6).

Why an infant is circumcised is very well known; but why on the eighth day must be explained. For the eighth day is also the first: on it the world began, Christ rose, and on it the universal resurrection [Col. 0769D] will take place. Then, not merely circumcised, but with all their sins cut away, the clean and spotless will receive for ever the name and inheritance of saints.

This, then, has been said concerning the male child. But if she had borne a female child, she was unclean for two weeks and remained sixty-six days in the blood of her purification. For the Synagogue gives birth to a female child as often as she commits iniquity. For this daughter she is unclean for two weeks: one, namely, before Christ’s incarnation; the other after Christ’s incarnation. By these two weeks both this time and that time are signified. [Col. 0770A] Unless, therefore, she ceases to bear this daughter and converts herself wholly to faith in Christ, the Synagogue will never be cleansed.

But sixty-six days are granted her for purification, by which we may understand all the days until the consummation of the age. For this number consists wholly of sixes; and even the Jews are permitted to work on six days, since the Sabbath is not included among the six days. Thus there will be no excuse if they have not been purified during these sixty-six days. Although the days of purification did not apply to the blessed Virgin Mary, she too waited, etc.

*(Here ends the addition; what follows through the conclusion of the homily is found borrowed from the commentary.)*

## HOMILY XXII. SUNDAY IN SEPTUAGESIMA

[Col. 0770B]

### [EDITORIAL NOTICE.]

**EDITORIAL NOTICE.**—The zeal with which the holy bishop of Segni was fired to feed his flock with heavenly instruction led him to compose a fuller exposition than he had made in the Commentary on Matthew, no. 82. In order that what Marchesius added on p. 23 may conveniently be available to readers, we have transcribed it, omitting the final portion, which is to be read in the same commentary. We have the agreement of the Cassinese, Laurentian, and Signine manuscripts, by which we entirely refute the attribution to Eusebius of Emesa, etc.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (20:1)

“At that time Jesus said to his disciples: The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire labourers for his vineyard.” And the rest.

[Col. 0770C] The Creator of the human race, our Lord Jesus Christ, has just above set forth the saying: “Many who are last shall be first, and the first last.” [Note: [Col. 0769D] Here begins St Bruno’s exposition of this Gospel passage from St Matthew, p. 95, col. I.] What this saying means the following matters will show. For the entire parable which follows concerns this point; hence it is said also in the conclusion: “So the last shall be first, and the first last.”

If this is understood of the ages of the world, I do not see in what manner the first are last, or the last first. For the patriarchs and prophets, and the other persons predestined to life under the former testament, were first; but we are the last, of whom John says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18). And the Apostle says: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11). And just as these were [Col. 0770D] first in time, so they received the denarius first. For immediately after his Passion, Christ the Lord rescued them from punishments and brought them into glory.

The Apostle likewise says: “We who live, who remain, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep; for the Lord himself shall descend from heaven at the command, at the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ shall rise first; then we who live, who remain, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord” (1 Thess. 4:15). How then are the last first?

But now let us hear the parable itself: “The kingdom [Col. 0771A] of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire labourers for his vineyard.” This is as though he said: Thus it happens in the kingdom of heaven, as the householder did in the vineyard, into which he himself went out early in the morning and hired labourers.

The kingdom of heaven is the Church. The householder is Christ our Lord; angels and human beings belong to his household. It is indeed a great household, because its householder is great. This householder came to hire labourers for his vineyard, for “the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel.” The vineyard of God is the Church. Outside it, whoever labours receives no reward; within it, whoever labours receives the denarius. For this denarius is the reward of eternal blessedness; therefore one denarius is given to all: one to the first and one to the last.

[Col. 0771B] Some begin working early in the morning; others about the third hour; others about the sixth and ninth hour; and still others about the eleventh hour. For this is what he says: “Having agreed with the labourers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard. And going out about the third hour, he saw others standing idle in the marketplace, and said to them: Go also into my vineyard, and I shall give you what is just. And they went. Again he went out about the sixth and ninth hour, and did likewise. But about the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing, and said to them: Why do you stand here all day idle? They say to him: Because no one has hired us. He says to them: Go also into my vineyard.”

Those come to labour in God’s vineyard early in the morning who begin to serve in adolescence. Those also come about [Col. 0771C] the sixth and ninth hour who turn to repentance either in youth or in old age. But the eleventh hour is that which, at whatever age, approaches the end and is near to death. Not only young and old persons, but children too have this hour. Therefore, in this hour, both one who turns to God from the whole heart in decrepit old age and one who does so in severe sickness begin to labour. “For the sinner, in whatever hour he is converted and groans, shall live and not die” (Ezek. 33:16).

Let him therefore turn, even at the eleventh hour, even at the last limit of life, who was previously idle in good and diligent in evil. For if he wishes and is converted, or begins to labour over a book [perhaps: “at the book”], he too shall receive the reward along with the others [Col. 0771D] and the denarius. [Note: [Col. 0771D] Up to this point St Bruno used the Commentary on Matthew; after this he adds what follows.]

These distinctions of hours, or ages, also seem to be signified by the gates of that temple concerning which John the Apostle says in the Apocalypse: “Three gates from the east, three gates from the north, three gates from the south, 397 three gates from the west” (Rev. 21:13). The temple and the vineyard therefore signify the same thing. For the holy Church is both the vineyard in which we labour and the temple in which we pray.

Into this vineyard and this temple boys and infants enter both early in the morning and through the eastern gates. Adolescents, however, enter at the third hour through the narrower [Col. 0772A] and more difficult gates of the north. Young and old persons who began to labour in the Lord’s vineyard at the sixth and ninth hour enter through the southern gates. We have called the northern gates narrow and difficult because many obstacles confront those who must enter through them. But what wonder is it, since the devil has placed his seat in the north and evils are opened from the north upon all the inhabitants of the earth?

Wretched adolescents, stiffened by the blasts of the north; wretched those whom the devil blows upon and tosses! Blessed are those who have been able to pass through this age without shipwreck. Hence Solomon says: “Rejoice, young man, in your adolescence” (Ecclus. 11:9). But this is said to those young men who have lived in adolescence in such a way that they are not ashamed of their youth. The same Solomon also says that it is difficult for him to know the way of a man in his adolescence.

Hence through the prophet Isaiah (21:15) the Lord commanded those who dwell in the land of the south to meet with bread and water those coming from the land of the north and fleeing Babylonian captivity. For they fled from the face of the threatening sword, from the face of the drawn bow, and from the face of grievous danger. Therefore we ought to meet with spiritual food and drink those whom we see fleeing the pursuing devil and returning to the Church through repentance.

But what shall we say of those hindrances which adolescents suffer at the very entrance of the gates, even when they think they have already escaped? For the prophet Ezekiel says: “I turned to the gate which faces north, and behold, women [Col. 0772C] were sitting there, weeping for Adonis” (Ezek. 8:14). See then that at the northern gate sit the harlots of Venus, lamenting the loves of luxury and composing love songs. These are indeed the things, and others like them, by which adolescents are hindered from being able to labour in God’s vineyard, enter the temple, and pray. Therefore the sacred canons rightly forbid their becoming bishops and priests until this age has passed.

*(The remainder of the homily may be read in the same words in the commentary on this passage of Matthew.)*

## HOMILY XXIII. SUNDAY IN SEXAGESIMA

### [EDITORIAL NOTICE.]

**EDITORIAL NOTICE.**—Although St Bruno had expounded this parable at length in the Commentary on Matthew, chapter 13, no. 52, when it recurred in Luke, chapter 8, he offered another interpretation. Lest readers lack it, we have extracted it from Marchesius, vol. II, p. 24, and present it here. It survives in the Laurentian, Cassinese, and Signine manuscripts and, after collation with them, agrees perfectly.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (8:5)

“At that time, when a very great crowd gathered together and people were hastening to Jesus from the cities, he spoke in a parable: A sower went out to sow his seed.” And the rest.

A great crowd followed Jesus; many gathered from every direction; many hastened to him from the cities, [Col. 0773A] desiring to hear his words and to see him and the miracles which he performed. When they had all flocked to him, he spoke in a parable. For the Lord spoke in parables, and without parables he did not speak to them. Thus he said through the Prophet: “I shall open my mouth in parables; I shall utter things set forth from the beginning” (Ps. 77:2).

Now let us hear the parable, or comparison, itself. “A sower,” he says, “went out to sow his seed; and as he sowed, some fell beside the way, was trampled down, and the birds of heaven ate it. Some fell upon rock; and when it sprang up it withered, because it had no moisture. Some fell among thorns; and the thorns sprang up with it and choked it. Some fell into good ground and, springing up, bore fruit a hundredfold.” Saying these things, he cried: [Col. 0773B] “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

Jesus did not cry without cause. Whoever cries desires to be heard. The Lord rightly cries out, therefore, because few among them were hearing him. They heard the voice and the comparison, certainly, but they did not hear what was signified by that voice and comparison. Thus he required ears for hearing, because it is not the ears of the body but rather the ears of the heart that hear and understand this cry.

His disciples asked him what this parable might be. And they had not yet applied to his word the ears for hearing, although he said to them: “To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables.” But to the rest it is in parables, “that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.” This is as though he said: that, seeing the shadow, they may not see the truth; and, hearing with bodily ears, they may not understand with the ears of the heart. Their hardness and unbelief cause them not to deserve to understand God’s words.

This is the parable: the seed is the word of God. Those beside the way are those who hear; then the devil comes and takes the word from their hearts lest they should believe and be saved. Those upon the rock are those who, when they hear, receive the word with joy; but they have no roots, because they believe for a time and fall away in the time of temptation. Those among the thorns are those who hear, but, going their way, are choked by anxieties, riches, and pleasures of life, and bear no fruit. Those in the good ground are those who, hearing the word in a good and excellent heart, [Col. 0773D] keep it and bear fruit in patience.

Behold, with the Lord himself explaining, we have learned what the seed is; what the field is; what ground lying beside the way, rocky ground, thorny ground, and good ground signify. The seed is the word of God. The seed is abundant because the field is great. With this seed we have two great granaries full: namely, the New and the Old Testament. From them we take whatever is sown anywhere.

See, therefore, what kind of ground you offer to this seed. Take care that you are not the ground beside the way, whose seed those evil travellers trample underfoot, who say to the soul that obeys evil: “Bend down, that we may pass over.” The devil takes away this seed, because through his persuasion and deception it very quickly slips from memory.

Take care that you are not rocky ground, in which the seed of God’s word cannot put down roots; nor ground in which it is pressed down and choked by vices, riches, and pleasures of the flesh, which are signified by thorns. [Col. 0774A] These things are fittingly signified by thorns because, although they are soft and pleasant to the flesh, they wound and afflict the soul.

But those are good ground who, hearing the word in a good and excellent heart, keep it; and who not only hear and keep it, but also put it into practice and bear the fruits of patience. “For not the hearers of the law are righteous before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified” (Rom. 2:13). Hence it is written: “Good understanding belongs to all who do it” (Ps. 110:10). And blessed John says in the Apocalypse: “Blessed is he who reads and those who hear the words of this prophecy and keep the things written in it” (Rev. 1:3).

But note that he says, “in a good and excellent heart.” For one ground is good, another better, and another excellent. Thus Matthew the Evangelist says: “The seed fell into good ground and bore fruit: some thirtyfold, some sixtyfold, some a hundredfold.” Good is that which bears thirtyfold; better, that which bears sixtyfold; excellent, that which bears a hundredfold.

If you gladly hear the word of God, rightly and catholicly understand what you hear, and practise what you understand, you are good ground. What is it to understand rightly and catholicly? It is to understand in two ways: first according to the letter, then according to spiritual understanding. There are ten words of the law, on which the whole law and the prophets depend. [Col. 0774C] If we understand them in two ways, we ascend as far as Christ. If, moreover, we put into practice each of the things we have thus understood, both literally and spiritually, they become thirty.

Good ground, then, understands the ten commandments of the law first literally and then spiritually, and practises what it understands. Thus married persons yield thirtyfold if they believe and understand the law not simply, as Jews do, but doubly, as Christians do, and perform and observe what they understand.

Let us now come to the sixtyfold return, which is rendered by the continent, who are as much better than married persons as this number exceeds the other, since the whole former number is found doubled in the latter. They preserve chastity very strictly—more strictly than those who observe continence of the soul alone. The number sixty consists of six and ten, since six times ten, or ten times six, makes sixty. In ten we understand the whole knowledge of the law, because, as we have said, the whole law and the prophets depend upon the ten commandments. In six, however, complete action is represented, because God appointed all our labour and activity within six days only; for the Sabbath day was appointed not for labour but for rest.

It remains for us to speak of those who render a hundredfold fruit to the Lord. The number one hundred is perfect both in itself and in its parts, because it may indeed be multiplied but cannot be increased: ten times ten makes a hundred. And ten, [Col. 0775A] one hundred, and one thousand are called perfect numbers because there is no place for them to increase. Therefore those who are perfect in the Church are quite suitably understood to render a hundredfold fruit. Of such the Lord says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and follow me” (Matt. 19:21). Again: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow, and do not be concerned for your life, what you shall eat, nor for your body, what you shall put on” (Matt. 6:25). Such also were those who said: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. 19:25).

Thus only the perfect render a hundredfold fruit. Even virgins themselves should not be counted among them unless, on account of virginity, they too possess this perfection. Thus the seed that fell [Col. 0775B] into good ground bore fruit: some thirtyfold, some sixtyfold, and some a hundredfold.

## HOMILY XXIV. SUNDAY IN QUINQUAGESIMA

### [EDITORIAL NOTICE.]

**EDITORIAL NOTICE.**—For the same reason that we supplied the preceding homily from Marchesius, vol. II, p. 25, we have likewise received this one from him, since it is lacking in the commentary. The same manuscripts cited under the name of St Bruno the bishop transmit it.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (18:31)

“At that time Jesus took his twelve disciples and said to them: Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and all things written through the prophets concerning the Son of Man shall be fulfilled,” etc. And the rest.

Many things that the prophets had foretold concerning the Son of Man had already been fulfilled; many things that they had prophesied concerning his humanity had already been accomplished; only a few things remained to be fulfilled in those days. The Lord wished to foretell these to his disciples so that, when we understand that he suffered voluntarily, no one may ever dare to doubt that he knew and foresaw the things that were to come upon him.

It follows: “For he shall be delivered to the Gentiles, mocked, scourged, and spat upon; and after they have scourged him, they shall kill him, and on the third day he shall rise again.” Yet they understood none of these things. For this saying was hidden from them, and they did not understand what was being said.

All these things had been foretold by the prophets; all had to happen, because he himself willed them to happen. Thus elsewhere he said to certain persons: “O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken. Was it not necessary for Christ so to suffer and thus to enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:25–26). Again: “How then shall the Scriptures be fulfilled, that thus it must happen?” For whatever the Lord has determined shall happen must happen.

Then, as Matthew says, the mother of the sons of Zebedee came to him with her sons, worshipping him and asking something from him. Then, he says, when the Lord was going up to Jerusalem to suffer for all, the mother of the sons of Zebedee—that is, James and John—came to Jesus at the prompting of her sons, to request the chief seats for them. In this it is clearly apparent that, as the Evangelist says, the disciples had not understood the words which the Lord had just spoken to them concerning [Col. 0776A] his Passion. For if they had understood, they would sooner have been turned to weeping and tears than have spoken of honours: “Therefore the mother of the sons of Zebedee came to him, worshipping and asking something from him” (Matt. 20:20). This woman was devout and intimate with Christ, etc.

*(What follows may be seen in the Commentary on Matthew, chapter 20, verse 17, as far as the words: “He did not disdain to wash the feet of his disciples.” We add the remaining part of the homily as it stands in Marchesius’s edition, p. 25, and is lacking from the commentary.)*

The Lord spoke these things on the road, instructing his disciples by these and similar matters after his own example, nor did he wish to be idle even during the journey. It happened, however, as he drew near to Jericho, which is interpreted “new moon,” whose changeability is so great that it never remains in the same state. It signifies this world, whose changes are infinite. To say nothing of other things, who could describe the changes of human beings alone?

History relates in what way, with what weapons, and in how many days Joshua captured this city. If this is properly understood, this world is subdued by Jesus Christ our Lord in the same manner, with the same weapons, and in the same number of days. The Lord drew near to Jericho when he became human and took upon himself the mutability of our flesh.

Then this blind man was enlightened, in whom many blind persons are understood. Thus Matthew says not that there was one blind man, but two, by whom we understand the two peoples, Jews and Gentiles. For when the sun of righteousness rose, “the people that sat in darkness saw a great light” (Isa. 9:2). He is the one “who enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9). For all were blind, and when this light appeared, few—or none—had been enlightened.

But are people not blind even now? Many are indeed blind even now. For how are those not blind who follow the devil and are continually hurled headlong along the path of vices? Truly those whom the devil drags are blind. You have seen blind people drawn sometimes by children and sometimes even by dogs; and these are drawn better than those who are led by the devil. For these fall and rise again; but those whom the devil drags, once they have been cast into the pit, are never raised again.

Every proud person, every greedy person, every adulterer and fornicator is blind. In short, all are blind who do not follow that light which says: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” (John 8:12). Whoever you are, therefore, who understand yourself to be blind, 400 return to life. For the more wicked anyone is, the farther he is from the way. But to what way? To that along which Jesus passes and walks: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:11).

Return, therefore, to these ways; learn to walk by them; cry out and beg. Cry not with the mouth, but with the heart. The heart’s cry is heard more deeply; it penetrates heaven and resounds in God’s ears. Cry out, then; say: “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David.” Beg with the Prophet: “Incline, O Lord, your ear to me and hear me, for I am needy and poor” (Ps. 108:22). O how rich was this man who begged in this manner and called himself needy and poor!

Do not dare to heed the crowd that rebukes you and forbids you to cry out—a wicked crowd, which drives a person away from such a cry. This crowd is understood as the host of evil human beings and malign spirits, who always try to hinder us when we cry to God and seek mercy. For if the blind man had kept silent and believed the rebuking crowd, he would still not have been enlightened.

But Jesus, standing still, commanded him to be brought to him; and when he drew near, he asked him, saying: “What do you wish me to do for you?” He said: “Lord, that I may see.” Behold how much prayer can do; behold the force of the cry of the mind: it conquers the crowd and makes Christ stop. He is held by a cry who could not be held by force. Jesus stops, calls, and waits for him; he asks what he wants. He asks for nothing but light; he speaks with the light and seeks light from the light. He could ask for nothing better: “For blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

Jesus said to him: “See; your faith has saved you.” And immediately he saw and followed him, glorifying God. Between God’s saying and doing there is no interval. He said to him, “See,” and immediately he saw. This faith accomplishes, without which it is impossible to please God. And he followed him, glorifying God. The blind do not follow Jesus; those follow him who have been enlightened. Those are enlightened who believe in him, understand truth, and drive the darkness of error away from themselves. Such persons glorify and praise him, because praise in the mouth of a sinner is not precious. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God. For it is fitting that all should praise him who alone does great wonders.

## HOMILY XXV. ASH WEDNESDAY

### [EDITORIAL NOTICE.]

**EDITORIAL NOTICE.**—In the Laurentian manuscript this homily, numbered 28, begins with these words: “For hypocrites are called sad because, that they may appear devout, they display a certain sadness and severity in their countenance”; it is then wholly in agreement with the editions of Eusebius of Emesa and Marchesius, in which the beginning of the homily is: “For hypocrites are called sad because, that they may appear devout,” with which the Vallicellian and Signine manuscripts agree. The exposition of this Gospel, no. 16, chapter 1, begins in the same manner and has the same ending. Since certain intervening passages are absent from the commentary, we transcribe them as Marchesius published them, lest readers be deprived of them. Those wishing for fuller teaching against hypocrisy should consult the homily of St Maximus for Ash Day, p. 103.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (6:16)

“At that time Jesus said to his disciples: When you fast, do not become sad like the hypocrites.” And the rest.

For hypocrites are called sad because, so that they may appear devout, they display a certain sadness and severity in their countenance, as though worn out by much fasting. Thus it follows: “For they disfigure their faces, that they may appear to people to be fasting.” They disfigure their faces because they allow them, beyond the bounds of their own beauty and nature, to become frightful through neglect and ugliness. For if deformity pleased God, he would not have formed the human being with so beautiful a face.

But why do they do this? “That they may appear to people to be fasting.” For it is written: “A human being sees the face, but God looks upon the heart” (1 Sam. 16:7). Since, therefore, they wish to please not God but people, they disfigure what is seen by people. And because they seek praise from people, they receive no reward from God. This is what the Lord says: [Col. 0778B] “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6:2).

*(Thus far the commentary; what follows has been added.)*

Intention alone, therefore, makes our fasts and all our works pleasing to God. Hence in what follows he says: “The lamp of your body is your eye. If your eye is single, your whole body shall be full of light; but if your eye is evil, your whole body shall be dark.” For the eye of the soul is intention; if it is good, all its activity will be full of light. Hence a certain wise man says: One should consider not so much what a person does, as with what intention he does it.

Those who fast and disfigure their faces in order to appear to people to be fasting do this with foolish and vain intention. Such persons, as the Lord says, have received their reward. Likewise, those who do all their works in order to be seen by people shall receive no other reward. But to those who do this with good intention the Lord commanded that they should perform their works before people: “So let your light shine before people, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

Intention alone, therefore, makes our works appear good or evil to the Lord: “For a human being sees the face, but God looks upon the heart.” Therefore he himself says: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged” (Matt. 7:1). You judge what you do not know; you often condemn what you do not understand. It appears one way to you and another way to me. First ascertain the intention, and then judge. For it can happen that one and the same work is done with different intentions. Giving alms openly can be done with either a good or a bad intention. If you give in order to offer another a good example, and that God may thereby be glorified, the intention is good.

Thus, in all things, intention alone must be sought. If it is good, the entire body of virtues and the whole mass of actions shall be full of light. But you say: How, then, shall I fast?

*(Readers may draw the remainder of the homily from the commentary.)*

## HOMILY XXV. THURSDAY AFTER ASH WEDNESDAY

[Col. 0779A]

### [EDITORIAL NOTICE.]

**EDITORIAL NOTICE.**—This homily supplies a new argument for recognizing that sermons taken from Bruno’s commentary and published under the name of Eusebius of Emesa are spurious. Besides the uniformity of style which we have observed under Matthew no. 25, there is the testimony of three manuscripts—namely, the Signine, Laurentian, and Cassinese—which name Bishop Bruno as author. It is not listed in the sequence of homilies because it already occurs on the Fourth Sunday after Epiphany.

### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Matthew (5:5)

At that time, when Jesus had entered Capernaum, a centurion came to him, beseeching him and saying: “Lord, my servant lies at home paralyzed and grievously tormented.” And the rest.

[Col. 0779B] Begins: “How the centurion approached Jesus, the Evangelist Luke shows,” etc.

Ends: “Amen I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel.”

## Homily XXVI. Friday after Ash Wednesday

### Notice

In the edition of the supposed Eusebius of Emesa, published at Paris in 1575, this is Homily 30, entitled “Friday after Ash Wednesday.” It lacks the prologue found in Marchesius and begins at once with different words: “For the remaining things said above are not contrary to the Law.” The Laurentian and Signine manuscripts, however, agree exactly with Marchesius. The reading of the Laurentian manuscript is much more complete.

### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Matthew (5:44)

Jesus said to his disciples: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’” And the rest.

Begins: “Through the teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ we have learned that the greatest and first commandment is: ‘You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart’; and the second, like it, is: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself,’” etc. But the words here, “and you shall hate your enemy,” I think refer to what the Lord commanded the children of Israel: that they should kill the Ammonites and Moabites and never make peace with them. Likewise, he commanded concerning the Jebusites, Hittites, Canaanites, and the other inhabitants of that land that they should not spare them, but should destroy them all by the sword: “But I say to you: Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you,” etc.

[Col. 0779D] (After this prefatory introduction, the homily proceeds in the same words as the exposition of the Gospel found under no. 14. Nothing further need be desired by readers, since the Gospel words are learnedly and copiously explained. The exposition begins on p. 26, col. 1, and ends on p. 28, col. 2: “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise.”)

## 402. Homily XXVII. Saturday before the First Sunday of Lent

### Notice

Since nothing is found in the exposition of this Gospel passage in St. Mark, almost the whole homily has been taken from the Commentary on Matthew 14:22, no. 62, where the same event is narrated. But because certain preliminary matters are added and other things altered, we have transferred into our collection the homily as Marchesius published it in vol. II, p. [Col. 0780A] 28, and as the Paris printers published it as no. 31 under the name of Eusebius of Emesa.

### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Mark (6:47)

At that time, when evening had come, the boat was in the middle of the sea, while he was alone on the land. And the rest.

But the Evangelist Matthew says of this as follows: after the Lord had fed five thousand people with five loaves, “he ordered his disciples to get into the boat and go before him across the water, until he had dismissed the crowds. And when evening came, he was there alone; but the little boat in the middle of the sea was being tossed by great waves, for the wind was contrary” (Matt. 8:24).

From the time when Christ, the sun of righteousness, departed from this world, evening came upon the Jewish people. For at his birth light arose for them; but at his death darkness came upon them. The boat’s being tossed by waves in the midst of the sea signified that, after Christ’s Passion and Ascension, the holy Church would suffer many adversities in this world. Thus it is fittingly said that the wind was contrary to it. For what is a contrary wind but the raging persecution of tyrants?

In the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking upon the sea. The fourth watch has been in progress from the time when our Savior came into the world. The first watch was from Adam to Moses; the second from Moses to David; the third from David to Christ. The first watch, oppressed by excessive sleep, was without law; the second had the Law; the third, the prophets; the fourth, the Gospel. In the fourth watch he came to them, because in this watch, more than in all the others, the Lord deigns to visit his servants.

He walks upon the sea because the whole world is subject to him. Seeing him walking upon the sea, they were troubled and said, “It is a phantom,” and they cried out in fear. Their confused and disorderly cry shows that they were greatly disturbed by fear. Immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying: “Take courage; it is I; do not be afraid.” Thus the Lord also said to Moses: “I am who I am. Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 4:14). Or perhaps he said, “It is I,” so that, on hearing the voice they knew, they might recognize who he was. For when we hear someone’s voice from afar, we immediately recognize who it is, even though we do not see the person.

Peter answered and said: “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you over the waters.” And he said: “Come.” Blessed Peter is everywhere shown to have been of most ardent faith. He would not have entrusted himself to the deepest sea unless he had possessed the surest faith in the Lord. For he knew that our Savior could do all things, and he believed that his power was no less great on the sea than on land.

Yet Peter’s walking upon the sea shows that this world is subject not only to the Master but also to the disciples. This also had to happen because of the heretics who later said that Christ the Lord, because he walked upon the sea, possessed not a real but a phantom body. They are refuted when they hear that blessed Peter also walked upon the sea, though they surely do not doubt that he had a real body.

Peter descended from the boat and walked on the water to come to Jesus. But seeing the strong wind, he was afraid; and when he began to sink, he cried out: “Lord, save me.” At once Jesus stretched out his hand, caught hold of him, and said: “Man of little faith, why did you doubt?”

By this event blessed Peter was already foreshadowing what would later happen to himself. In the name of Christ he walked confidently, as it were, upon the waters, when he said: “Even if all are scandalized, I shall never be scandalized” (Matt. 26:33). But he saw the strong wind and was afraid when the Lord was seized by the Jews, and he himself fled with the other disciples. He sank when he denied him; then he cried, “Lord, save me,” when he went outside and wept bitterly. His weeping itself was his rising again.

But Jesus immediately stretched out his hand and caught him when, by the angelic message consoling him and in a sense drawing him back to himself, the women were told: “Go, tell my disciples—and Peter—that he goes before you into Galilee” (Mark 16:7). By calling him by his own name, the Lord raised him to the hope of grace as though he had grasped by the hand one who trembled and feared that he was perishing.

In these things the prosperity and adversity of the Church may also be signified. At one time she seems to sink, and at another to rise. “And when he had entered the boat, the wind ceased.” This must not be understood as though Jesus had then entered the boat. For he first came to Capernaum, where he said many things in the synagogue which John records but Matthew and Mark omit. John says that the disciples wished to take him into the boat, but immediately the ship reached the land toward which they were going, namely Capernaum. Thus it is clear that he did not then enter the boat.

For, as stated above, the Lord had commanded his disciples to go ahead of him. Having arrived at Capernaum and not found him there, they turned back and returned toward him. Then the Lord appeared to them, walking on the sea. After all that is now said in this Gospel had been fulfilled, and after he had spoken the things narrated by John down to the place where it says: “Jesus said these things in the synagogue while teaching at Capernaum” (John 6:59), they returned to the boat. When he entered the boat, the wind ceased. For the wind had not yet ceased, nor had the sea rested from its turbulence; both by night and by day they were still being tossed by the same waves. But as soon as Jesus entered the boat, the wind stopped.

Those who were in the boat, astonished at so great a miracle, came and worshipped him, saying: “Truly you are the Son of God.” Mark, however, rebukes them, calling them forgetful and blind because they were astonished at this miracle, though the preceding day they had known that the Lord had done so great a miracle with the five loaves. Hence he says: “For they had not understood concerning the loaves.” If they had remembered the miracle of the loaves, they would no longer have had cause to marvel at the miracle of the calmed sea.

When they had crossed over, they came into the land of Gennesaret and made land. And when they had gone out of the boat, they immediately recognized him. Matthew says this more clearly. Mark seems to say that the disciples did not recognize him until they left the boat; but this is not so. It is not said of the disciples, but of the people of that region, who, as soon as they recognized him, brought to him from every side their sick to be healed. This is what Matthew says: “When the men of that place recognized him, they sent throughout that whole region and brought to him all who were ill. And they begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment; and all who touched it were made well.”

Let us also pray to the Lord that he may deign to enter the little boat of our breast and make the gusts of pride and the storms of rising vices be still. Let him also enter his own little boat, that is, the holy Church, and reveal himself there—he who seems in a sense not to be there while he allows her to be tossed by so great a storm of persecutions. Let him command the winds and the sea, and there will be a great calm.

When it says, “When the men of that place recognized him, they sent throughout that whole region and brought to him all who were ill, that he might heal them,” what else does this signify but that holy men, who have deserved to know God, ought to pray for the sins of others and commend and offer others to God?

But what is it to touch the fringe of Christ’s garment? It is one thing to touch Christ, another to touch Christ’s garments. Thomas, touching Christ, said: “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28). Philip touched the garments, and not Christ, when he said: “Lord, show us the Father, and that is enough for us” (John 14:9). Thomas, then, touched Christ more closely than Philip. Thus Thomas was told: “Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed” (John 20:29); but Philip: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? He who sees me sees the Father.” The former is therefore said already to have seen and believed; the latter not yet to have seen or believed rightly.

Those touch Christ who, believing in him perfectly, know the truth of the Catholic faith. Those touch Christ’s garments who, although unable to understand, nevertheless believe what is preached to them by true Catholics. Thus each person touches Christ at a greater distance to the degree that he understands and knows Christ less. Yet all who touch even the fringe of his garment are healed: “For everyone who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Matt. 16:16).

## Homily XXVIII. First Sunday of Lent

### Notice

St. Bruno composed this homily from his Commentary on Matthew, as we have established by comparison with the Vallicellan and Laurentian manuscripts, adding only a few things that need not be repeated. He takes his beginning from the preceding text, found at the end of Matthew chapter 3, no. 6, col. 2, and attaches the whole to no. 6. His interpretation is outstanding.

## 404. Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Matthew (4:1)

At that time: Jesus was led into the wilderness by the Spirit, to be tempted by the devil. And the rest.

When Jesus had been baptized, he immediately came up from the water; and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him. And behold, a voice from heaven said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

Why are the heavens opened when the Lord is baptized? This is a great mystery, and it foreshadows great joy for those who are baptized. Heaven had previously been closed; before baptism no one entered there. But now it has been opened—opened, however, to those who are baptized. Thus the Lord says: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5).

Then Jesus was led into the wilderness by the Spirit to be tempted by the devil; and after he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he afterward became hungry. The foremost holy doctors of the Church explain that the Lord Jesus was led into the wilderness by his own Spirit.

Here the explanation of the Gospel begins and continues to the end, which is as follows: “So that in the fast from foods he might signify to us the fast of the body, and in the number of days might show the fast of the heart.”

## Homily XXIX. Monday after the First Sunday of Lent

### Notice

Both the editions and the manuscripts cited above agree in the text of this homily, which is almost wholly contained in the Commentary on Matthew under no. 103. So that the point to which the addition pertains may immediately be seen, we copy it faithfully.

### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Matthew (25:31)

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him.” And the rest.

For the Lord, who first came humble and in the form of a servant, will come again exalted and sublime, in his majesty and the glory of his Father. All the angels will also come with him, so that his might and all his power may be made manifest by the very multitude of his host. Then he will sit on the throne of his majesty, because then he will be revealed as equal and like to the Father, coeternal with him. Nowhere is royal dignity better displayed than on a royal throne.

“All nations shall be gathered before him,” according to the saying: “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me and every tongue shall confess” (Isa. 45:23). It will not be difficult for him to gather all nations, for whom it was not difficult to create and raise them. And he, the good Shepherd who knows his sheep well, will separate the good from the evil; and he will place the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left.

The good are called sheep because of simplicity and innocence; the evil are called goats because of vanity and wantonness. In that very placement at the right hand, either party will already be able to know for whom reward and for whom punishment is impending. Then the King will say to those at his right: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” Why is this so? Do you wish to hear why? “For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you took me in; naked, and you clothed me; I was in prison, and you came to me.”

If the kingdom was prepared for them before the foundation of the world, it is evident that before they came into being they were predestined for life. But those predestined for life can in no way perish. Yet God’s predestination is conditional, and nothing is predestined without some condition. It was predestined that the world should be saved, but through the water of baptism and the death of the Son of God. All good persons are predestined for glory, but on the condition that they have held faith, charity, humility, patience, mercy, piety, and the like.

For God foresaw that those whom he predestined to life would be such persons. In predestining them, he might be said to tell them: “I indeed predestine you for life, if you are such and such; if you keep my commandments; if you have faith and mercy; and if at last you are found in goodness.” Therefore, one who does not wish to be such, who does not strive to keep God’s commandments, does not attain predestination because he does not keep the condition.

[Note: [Col. 0783D] Here everyone can see that the holy bishop speaks of consequent predestination, which includes good works, without which eternal salvation cannot be obtained; for it is a reward, and is earned by keeping God’s commandments. [Col. 0784D]]

Therefore do not attend to God’s predestination, which you do not know; attend to what you hear and understand. For just as God is truthful in his predestination and cannot change, so also his words are true and cannot change. Hence in the Gospel the Lord says: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Luke 21:33).

But let us hear what these words are: “‘The sinner,’ he says, ‘in whatever hour he is converted and groans in repentance, shall live and shall not die’” (Ezek. 33:12). Likewise: “If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the earth; but if you are unwilling, the sword shall devour you” (Isa. 1:20). And in the Gospel: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark 16:16). Again: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will forgive you your sins; but if you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6:14).

Do not seek another predestination; for in these words consists every predestination both of life and of death. If you do these things, be secure and believe without doubt that you are appointed for eternal life. But if, with hardened heart, you refuse to do them and persist in this wickedness, know certainly that you are predestined to death. For although no human being is predestined to sin, every human being is nevertheless predestined either to glory or to punishment.

It follows: “Then the righteous will answer him, saying,” etc.

(The remainder of the homily will be supplied by the commentary.)

## Homily XXX. Tuesday after the First Sunday of Lent

### Notice

Even if no manuscript testimony existed—which in fact is abundant: the Vallicellan, Laurentian, and Cassinese manuscripts—this homily ought to be attributed to our Bruno alone. For its subject, namely the condemnation of simony, which was very prevalent in the Church in his time, sufficiently establishes its genuine author and exposes the false attribution made by the editor of Eusebius of Emesa, who published it among Eusebius’s homilies. It is also found entire in the Commentary on Matthew, no. 86, col. 2. It was previously published by Marchesius, vol. [Col. 0785B] II, p. 31, but the reading of the commentary is far superior. Because of the importance of the matter, of which there will very often be occasion to speak, we present it here again.

### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Matthew (21:10)

At that time, when Jesus entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred and said: “Who is this?” But the people said: “This is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth of Galilee.” And the rest.

The Lord came, about to wage war and triumph over his enemies, to the impious city and the place of contest, with triumph and glory. Certain of victory before the battle—which does not usually happen—he received a triumph. Entering the city in so great glory, the whole city was stirred, saying: “Who is this?” All rush to meet him; all desire to see him and long to know by sight the one whom they had already known by the glory of his miracles. For in those days the Lord had raised Lazarus, and all were astonished at the greatness of that miracle.

Jesus entered the temple of God and cast out all those selling and buying in the temple, and overturned the tables of the money-changers and the chairs of those selling doves. Hear this, Simoniacs; hear this, accursed traffickers. Either cease from your commerce or leave the temple. For the Lord of the temple cast out of the temple not merely one or two, but indiscriminately all sellers and buyers. He overturned both the tables of the money-changers and the chairs of those selling doves.

You are money-changers; you sell doves; you do nothing without money and price. Those sell doves who bestow for a price either churches or the graces of the Holy Spirit. The Lord overturns their chairs, so that by this we may understand that they are not bishops.

[Note: [Col. 0785D] For they are validly ordained, but illicitly; and, according to the canons, because of the crime of simony they are suspended from the exercise of their order. Consult the preface of Lazarus in the [Col. 0786D] Commentary on the Gospels, and what we shall say in the treatise on the mysteries and sacraments of the Church.]

And he says to them: “It is written: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer’; but you have made it a den of thieves.” For you are thieves: “He who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold is a thief and a robber” (John 10:1). Christ is the door. Since you did not enter through him, he overturns your chairs; for those enter through this door who are appointed according to the institutions of the canons. Therefore leave the house of prayer, which has become a den of thieves because you dwell in it.

The blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them. Whoever is blind and does not understand the truth, whoever is lame and does not walk on the right path, should hasten to the temple. There he will find Jesus; there he will be enlightened and healed.

When the chief priests and scribes saw the wonders he had done and the children crying out in the temple and saying, “Hosanna to the Son of David,” they were indignant and said to him: “Do you hear what these are saying?” But Jesus said to them: “Certainly. Have you never read: ‘Out of the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise’?” The indignation of the chief priests and scribes is envy; the praise of God by the children is the fulfillment of prophecy. For David himself had prophesied that the Lord would be proclaimed and praised out of the mouths of infants and nursing children.

Leaving them, he went outside the city to Bethany, and remained there. The Lord remains even now in Bethany, whose name means “house of obedience,” because, having abandoned the synagogue, he dwells in the Church, which is obedient to his will.

In the morning, returning to the city, he was hungry. Seeing a fig tree beside the road, he came to it and found nothing on it but leaves alone. And he said to it: “May fruit never be born from you forever.” When the Lord, who never does anything without reason, seems to do something without reason, it signifies some great matter. For to whom would it seem reasonable that he should seek fruit on a tree at the season when trees are without fruit? Does the Creator of fruits, trees, and seasons fail to know the season for fruit?

The Lord therefore hungers not for figs, but for faith; he seeks not the fruit of a tree, but the fruit of a work. This fig tree is the synagogue, planted beside the road and offering no refreshment to passersby. The Lord came to it and found nothing but leaves. The leaves are words; the leaves are the letter. The synagogue has these: it speaks well but does not do what it says.

Yet all these things must be understood of that part of the synagogue which persists in its unbelief and, shaded by the leaves of verbosity, yields no fruit of spiritual understanding. The Lord cursed this part. But for the other part of the synagogue he prayed, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Those who are cursed and who never yield fruit are therefore the scribes and Pharisees, who burned with excessive envy in the death of our Savior. “And immediately the fig tree withered.” Seeing this, the disciples were astonished and said: “How did it wither immediately?” “But on the next day, as Mark says, when they were passing that way in the morning, Peter said to Jesus: ‘Rabbi, behold, the fig tree which you cursed has withered’” (Mark 11:12).

Every day the Lord curses fruitless trees and wicked people; and every day those whom he curses wither and are delivered to fire. He curses both in person and through his servants. Hence it follows: Jesus answered and said to them: “Amen I say to you, if you have faith and do not waver, not only shall you do this to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and cast into the sea,’ it shall happen.” Christ’s disciples later possessed this faith, because by enlightening the blind, cleansing lepers, raising the dead, and performing other miracles, they learned by experience itself that what the Lord promised was true.

## Homily XXXI. Wednesday after the First Sunday of Lent

### Notice

Since the following homily published by Marchesius for the Wednesday after the First Sunday of Lent has been pieced together from four passages in the Commentary on Matthew, nos. 48, 49, 50, and 51, and entirely different matters are treated in them, I can scarcely agree with those writers [Col. 0787B] who assert that St. Bruno was its author. It seems more probably to have been stitched together by some copyist, whose purpose was to compose any homily whatever and fill a place in the series of homilies. Yet because Marchesius adds some material to the first part, which is under no. 48, col. 1, I shall provide readers with it.

### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Matthew (12:38)

At that time, scribes and Pharisees came to Jesus, saying: “Master, we wish to see a sign from you.” And the rest.

How great is the pride of the scribes and Pharisees! How great their folly and unbelief! They do not ask; they do not make a humble request. Rather, with puffed-up breast and erect neck, they say: “We wish to see a sign from you.” They wish to see signs, but do not wish to believe. But why do they seek signs when they have already seen so many? Are not these signs: that the dead rise, the blind receive sight, lepers are cleansed, paralytics are cured, and demons cast out? All these are signs. Hence, when the Lord was about to heal the centurion’s servant, he said: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.”

He answered them: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign; and no sign shall be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah.” Since the Pharisees wish to see signs, they deservedly hear what they do not wish to hear: “An evil and adulterous generation,” which has so often committed fornication with idols and followed the gods of the Gentiles, seeks a sign. “For Jews ask for signs, and Greeks seek wisdom.” “And no sign shall be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah.”

For great is the sign of the prophet Jonah, in which are signified Christ’s death, burial, and resurrection, the destruction of the Jews, and the salvation of the Gentiles. “For as Jonah was in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights, so the Son of Man shall be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights.”

But what is “in the heart of the earth” except in the affection and desire of the Jews? It is as if he said: “Let this be a great and wondrous sign to you: that for three days and three nights I shall so subject myself to your power that you may do to me whatever you desire.” The Jews are called earth because, forgetful of heavenly things, they seek only earthly and transitory things. This is that stony and thorny ground in which the seed of God’s word cannot grow and bear fruit.

The Jews often wished to seize and hold Jesus, but could not. But what is surprising in this? They could never have had power over him if he had not willed it. Therefore he said to Pilate: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above.” Likewise: “This is your hour and the power of darkness.”

The Lord was therefore in the heart of the earth—that is, in the will and power of the Jews—for three days and three nights. He was in their power both on the night when he was seized and through the whole night of the Sabbath day; likewise through the whole day on which he suffered, through the whole Sabbath day, and at the beginning of the Lord’s day. For they crucified him alive, buried him dead, and kept him buried under guard.

It is very customary, not only in Scripture but also in ordinary speech, to put a part for the whole. Thus, when looking from a distance, we customarily say, “I see a man,” though we see not the whole person but only some part of him. Likewise we say, “That man sees well, hears well, speaks well,” though eyes alone see, ears alone hear, and the tongue alone speaks. We also say, “That man has been wounded,” though only his foot or hand has been wounded.

Thus the Lord was in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights, although not for three complete days and nights. This interpretation seems to me plainer and clearer than all the others. It follows: “The men of Nineveh shall arise,” etc.

(The following material belongs to nos. 48 and 49 and may be read in the edition from p. 66 to p. 68.)

## Homily XXXII. Thursday after the First Sunday of Lent

[Col. 0788C]

### Notice

Readers should consult the Commentary on Matthew under no. 64, col. 2; they will find the entire homily appointed for this day without even one word changed. They will be made all the more certain of the appropriation from St. Bruno by the editors of Eusebius of Emesa when they see that it has been torn entire from that same commentary: its beginning and end are identical. In the Paris edition it is on p. 59; in Marchesius’s edition, on p. 33. St. Maximus of Turin also composed an elegant homily on the Canaanite woman, p. 674.

### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Matthew (15:1)

At that time, Jesus went away into the region of Tyre and Sidon. And behold, a Canaanite woman came out from those borders and cried, saying: “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David. My daughter is grievously tormented by a demon.” But he did not answer her a word. His disciples came and begged him, saying: “Dismiss her, for she cries after us.” And the rest.

Begins: “This, then, is the reason why God does not hear the woman when she cries out,” etc.

Ends: “He shall live and shall not die.”

II, p. 33, we found nothing new.

At that time, it was a feast day of the Jews, and the Lord went up to Jerusalem. And the rest.

## 408. Homily XXXIV. Saturday after the First Sunday of Lent

### Notice

Because some portions of this homily are absent from the commentary, we reproduce it as Marchesius gave it in vol. II, p. 34 and following, so that the connection of its parts may be evident to readers. We note that it differs in no respect, either at its beginning or end, from the version circulated among the Eusebian homilies on p. 62. The editors of the Lyons *Bibliotheca Patrum* published it, as we have said, under the name of Eusebius Gallicanus along with the rest. In the Commentary on Matthew it is found under no. 70, p. 84, col. 2, at the end.

### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Matthew (17:1)

At that time, Jesus took Peter, James, and John his brother, led them apart up a high mountain, and was transfigured before them. And the rest.

Our Lord and Savior, as is read a little earlier, had promised his disciples, saying: “Truly I tell you, there are some standing here who shall not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.” For if we understand this of that kingdom and that glory in which he has now promised that he will come with his angels to judge, the statement cannot stand. For no one was there when the Lord said these things who has not by now tasted death; yet he himself has not yet come for judgment. The words that follow, however, show how these things ought to be understood. For the Evangelist says: “And after six days Jesus took Peter, and James, and John his brother, and led them apart up a high mountain; and he was transfigured before them.” These, then, are those of whom he had just said: that they would not taste death until they saw the Son of Man coming in his kingdom—that is, appearing in the power and glory of his kingdom.

[Note: Col. 0789D. Saint Bruno continues from the Commentary on the Gospel, no. 70, chapter 1.]

For when the Lord was transfigured, he appeared on the mountain to these three disciples as he will appear after this life, in his kingdom, to all his faithful. But why did our Savior will to transfigure himself into that form of his brightness, unless it was to make us more certain of the glory which he proclaimed? Therefore he willed that his three disciples should be present—those elsewhere called pillars of the Church—that they might be witnesses of so great a vision. These three suffice for this testimony, because, as it is written, “By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Matt. 18:16). For who would not believe Peter, James, and John as witnesses? It was fitting, moreover, that these things should take place upon a high mountain, since they are hereafter to take place in heaven. They take place after six days because, as the Apostle says, when the labor of this life, which is performed in six days, has ended, “there remains a Sabbath-rest and repose for the people of God” (Heb. 6:9).

We should therefore greatly desire that these six days may pass, so that we may behold our King in his beauty and in the glory of his majesty. “For we know,” says John, “that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. And his face shone like the sun, while his garments became white as snow” (1 John 1:3). The Evangelist could find nothing brighter than the sun to which to compare Christ’s face and garments. Yet we do not doubt that he is brighter than the sun; for no creature can be wholly like the Creator.

“And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, speaking with him.” But why Moses and Elijah? In Moses we see the Law, and in Elijah the Prophets. Thus the apostles see Moses and Elijah speaking with Christ: they see the Law and the Prophets bearing witness to him. Hence the prophet Habakkuk says: “You shall be known in the midst of two living creatures” (Hab. 3:2 [Vulgate 3:3]). For even to this day Christ is known and seen in the midst of two living creatures—in the midst of Moses and Elijah, that is, in the Law and the Prophets. Read the books of Moses; read the books of the Prophets: there you will find Christ; there you will know and see him. For there he is transfigured; there the glory of his majesty is revealed to his faithful.

These two men, as Luke says, were speaking with Jesus about his death, which he was soon to suffer in Jerusalem; and perhaps they rejoiced because they saw the day of their redemption and of the redemption of the whole human race drawing near. Peter answered and said to Jesus: “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you wish, let us make three tabernacles here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” Peter thus recognized Moses and Elijah, whom he had never before seen; although, as the other Evangelists say, he did not know what he was saying.

[Note: Col. 0790D. Thus far the commentary.]

He did not know, indeed, because he was not speaking from himself; for another was speaking in him. There is no need to make three tabernacles: three are sufficient. Writing of three tabernacles, the Apostle says: “The first tabernacle was made, in which were the lampstand, the table, and the presentation of loaves; it is called the Holy Place” (Heb. 9:2). Of the second he says: “But after the second veil was the tabernacle called the Holy of Holies, having a golden censer and the ark of the covenant covered round about with gold; in it was a golden vessel containing manna, and Aaron’s rod which had budded, and the tables of the covenant” (ibid., 3–4). Of the third he says: “Christ, appearing as High Priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle not made with hands, that is, not of this creation, entered once into the Holy Place—not through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood—having obtained eternal redemption” (ibid., 11–12).

The first tabernacle, therefore, is the Synagogue; the second, the Church; the third, heaven. The first belonged to Moses, who was leader of that people. “Elijah indeed shall come and restore all things” (Matt. 17:11). The third belongs to Christ, concerning whom the Apostle says: “For Jesus did not enter into holy places made with hands, but into heaven itself, that he may appear before the face of God for us.”

[Note: Col. 0791D. The Vulgate reading at Hebrews 9:24 is: “For Jesus did not enter into holy places made with hands, copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself, that he may now appear before the face of God for us.”]

The first was in shadow and figure; the second is in figure and truth; the third is in the hall of truth. In the first, life is shown; in the second, it is given; in the third, it is possessed. For the sacraments of the Church do not merely teach and display the remedy, as do the sacraments of the Synagogue; rather, they themselves are the remedy and the remission of sins.

The first tabernacle had a lampstand—that is, it had the patriarchs and prophets—and a table, namely, the Law according to the letter. On that table were loaves, that is, spiritual foods contained in that letter. But what profit was it to them to have the lampstand, the table, and the loaves? For the Apostle says: “Blindness has happened in part to Israel” (Rom. 11:5). And the prophet says: “Who is blind but my people?” (Isa. 42:19). Again: “Blind the heart of this people” (Isa. 6:10). And the Psalmist says: “Let their table before them become a snare, a recompense, and a stumbling-block” (Ps. 68:22 [Vulgate]). And elsewhere: “The little children asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them” (Lam. 4:4). Thus the Jews possessed, yet did not possess; they held the Law, yet did not understand it.

The second tabernacle had a golden censer, namely the apostles themselves, who, making manifest in every place the fragrance of the knowledge of God, were to some a fragrance of life unto life, and to others a fragrance of death unto death. The ark and the Church signify the same thing. It is rightly said to be covered with gold, because inwardly it shines through knowledge and holiness, and outwardly through preaching and works. Within it is the golden vessel containing manna, namely Christ our Lord, so that by the vessel we understand his humanity and by the manna his divinity. Within it also is Aaron’s rod that budded, by which we understand the Blessed Virgin Mary, who flowered against nature, conceived against nature, and gave birth against nature. So too that rod, though dry, brought forth against nature flowers, leaves, and nuts. The tables of the covenant that were there signify that holy Church both has and possesses the knowledge of both Testaments.

But of the third tabernacle nothing of this sort is said. No lampstand, table, ark, or vessel is placed there; nothing there is in figure, but all things are in truth. Hence the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face. Now I know in part; but then I shall know even as I am known” (1 Cor. 13:12). These are the three tabernacles which blessed Peter, placed in ecstasy, is said to have wished to make.

[Note: Col. 0792D. Here the addition ends; what follows is borrowed from the commentary.]

It continues: “While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. And behold, a voice from the cloud saying: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him.” For God appeared in the cloud because in his majesty he cannot be seen by human beings, as he himself says: “No man shall see me and live” (Exod. 33:20). By this cloud, however, we may understand Holy Scripture, which appears bright to those who understand it, being full of the water of wisdom, but dark to those who do not understand it. In this cloud almighty God can indeed be heard, but he cannot be seen and understood as he is. For everywhere we have heard him speaking, but nowhere do we see him except through a mirror and in an enigma; for he himself speaks in the prophets, he himself in the apostles. Hence the Lord himself says: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of my Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20). We can therefore see the cloud, but we cannot see him who speaks in the cloud. For just now, too, we heard him speaking in this cloud of the holy Gospel; nevertheless, we do not see him.

For whose voice is it, if not his, that these letters sound forth: “This is my Son, in whom I am well pleased”? For he was well pleased in his Son, whereas in the creation of man he was displeased with himself. Hence he says: “It repents me that I made man” (Gen. 6:7). He admonishes us to hear him, to believe him, and to obey him. For in whom should we believe, if not in wisdom, truth, and justice? For he is the power of God and the wisdom of God; he is the way, the truth, and the life.

“And when the disciples heard this, they fell upon their faces and were greatly afraid.” What if they had seen his form, when they could not endure even his voice? “And Jesus came and touched them, and said to them: Arise, and do not be afraid.” Blessed are those whom Jesus touches; blessed are those whom salvation and life touch. For they rise without fear and are secure. Let us therefore ask him to touch us also, to awaken us from the sleep of dullness and foolishness, and to open our eyes for the sight of himself. “But lifting up their eyes, they saw no one but Jesus alone.” It is enough to see Jesus; it is enough to see that light: “he who follows it does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” (John 8:12). “And as they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, saying: Tell the vision to no one until the Son of Man has risen from the dead.” For it was fitting that this great glory of his should first be proclaimed when, having put off the mortality of the flesh, he should be clothed with the glory and beauty of the new resurrection.
