## Homily XXXIX. Saturday after the Second Sunday in Lent

[Editorial Notice.]

Editorial Notice. The publication of Saint Bruno’s Commentary on the Gospels was timely, so that by reading it the many errors that crept into Marchesius’s edition of the Homilies might be corrected. Had the same commentary become known shortly after the middle of the sixteenth century, no one would have dared to fabricate an Eusebius—whether Emisenus or Gallicanus—and ascribe to them works which are most certainly shown to be the works of Saint Bruno of Asti. This homily was excerpted in its entirety from the same Commentary on Luke, no. 36, but was nevertheless attributed to the same Emisenus.

### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Luke (15:11)

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “A certain man had two sons.” And the rest.

[Col. 0794A] Beginning: “This man is understood in this place to be God himself.”

End: “And thus we possess these things, so that we do not wish to possess them otherwise.”

## Homily XL. Third Sunday in Lent

[Editorial Notice.]

Editorial Notice. The Commentary on the Gospel according to Luke lacks an exposition of chapter 2 of the passage read on this Sunday. In its place may be supplied the homily published both by Marchesius and under the familiar name of Eusebius Emisenus, which we too again print under Luke. Readers should be warned, however, that an exposition from Matthew chapter 12:25, where the demon Beelzebub is discussed, has been stitched onto the first part, from no. 47, chapter 1, down to the words: “For I hold them bound and fettered.” What follows after Luke 11:23, “He who does not gather with me scatters,” may be read in the same Commentary on Matthew under nos. 49 and 50.

### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Luke (11:14)

At that time Jesus was casting out a demon. And the rest.

Blessed Matthew the Evangelist relates that this man was not only mute but also blind (Matt. 12:22). For everyone is blind who does not follow that light which says: “I am the light of the world; he who follows me does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” (John 8:12). He is mute, moreover, who does not know how to confess his sin and to open his lips in the praises of God. And he has a demon who perseveres in some great sin; therefore the Apostle admonishes us, saying: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. 6:12). For as long as sin reigns in a person, so long is that person conquered, captured, and possessed by the devil.

If, then, this blind and mute man is brought to the Lord, if he is converted to repentance, Jesus will immediately heal him, so that, once the demon has been cast out, he speaks and sees. Let him speak, however, not vain and useless things as before, but holy and religious things, such as it is fitting for a Christian to speak. And let him see, not vanities with the eyes of the heart, but the light of life and truth with the eyes of the mind.

But some of them said: “By Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons.” Of these Matthew the Evangelist says: “But when the Pharisees heard this, they said: This man casts out demons only by Beelzebub, prince of demons.” The more the Pharisees appeared better and wiser than the rest, the more often they were stirred by a far greater envy against the Lord. But Pharisees, who taught you these things? Unless you were disciples of Beelzebub, you would not utter such things in his praise. You see Jesus raising the dead, giving sight to the blind, cleansing lepers, curing every disease and every infirmity, and you say that he casts out demons by Beelzebub? Could Beelzebub, the god of flies, ever have done these things?

“But others, tempting him, sought from him a sign from heaven” (Luke 11:16). Another Evangelist explains what the Lord answered them, saying: “This wicked and perverse generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given it except the sign of Jonah the prophet. For as Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so shall the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights.”

[Note: Col. 0795D. In the Vulgate, Matthew 16:4 reads: “A wicked and adulterous generation seeks a sign,” etc.]

Let this sign suffice you; no other sign shall be given you, either from earth or from heaven. For it is a great and marvelous sign that he who has all things in his power allowed himself to be in the power of men for three days and three nights. And what is “in the heart of the earth,” except in the affection, power, and desire of sinners? Hence the Lord himself said to Pilate: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11). And as heaven signifies the righteous, so earth signifies sinners. These matters have already been explained above.

It continues: “But he, seeing their thoughts, said: Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste, and house shall fall upon house. And if Satan is divided against himself, how shall his kingdom stand, since you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebub?” By an evident syllogism he refutes those who say that he casts out demons by Beelzebub.

[Note: Col. 0796D. From this point begins Saint Bruno’s exposition of Matthew chapter 12, no. 47.]

For if it were as they say, Beelzebub would already have entirely lost the strength of his dominion and kingdom. If demons made war against one another, they would have little or no strength against human beings. But what is worse: scarcely any people are found who have as much concord in good as evil spirits have in evil. For although they are infinite and innumerable, they all agree in desiring to do nothing but evil. If, therefore, they had not possessed this concord in iniquity and had wished—and been able—to turn to repentance, Beelzebub’s kingdom would already have been laid waste. We see this happen in other kingdoms. It is not therefore as they say; Satan does not cast out Satan, but rather all of them help one another in all things.

Hence also, through blessed Job, the Lord says to the devil: “His body is like cast shields, compacted with scales pressing one upon another; one is joined to another, and not even a breath passes between them. One clung to another, and those holding together could in no way be separated” (Job 41:6). By these words he indicates that evil spirits have such concord among themselves that they can by no means be separated from one another. For the devil’s body is understood to be that entire army of evil spirits. Evil spirits are called cast shields because of their strength; they are also called scales pressing one another, holding one another, and clinging to one another because of the exceeding concord and unity which they have in every wickedness and in the desire to do harm. Would that, if it could happen, this great peace and concord of theirs might be broken and that kingdom of iniquity dissolved.

It continues: “And if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out?” “If,” he says, “you think such things about me, what do you say also about my disciples? For I know that you do not think well of the disciples who think such abominable things about their master.” This is what he had said above: “If they called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more his household?” The apostles are called sons of the Pharisees because they, and all others who believed in the resurrection preached by the Pharisees, had the Pharisees as fathers and teachers, as it were. Hence they may also be understood to have belonged to that sect; for this sect was better than the others, though it too was not good in many respects. Therefore in the Acts of the Apostles the Apostle Paul is also read to have cried out: “I am a Pharisee; I am judged concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead” (Acts 23:6). This, then, is why Christ’s disciples are called sons of the Pharisees.

It continues: “Therefore they shall be your judges.” For they shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. “But if I cast out demons by the finger of God, then truly the kingdom of God has come upon you.” Another Evangelist shows what this means, saying: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Luke 11:20). This is certainly true and must not be doubted; therefore the kingdom of God has come upon you. For where the Spirit of God is, there is the kingdom of God. The Holy Spirit is called the finger of God because of the manifold distribution of graces. In no part of the body is there so great a division as in the fingers. It is as though he said: “I cast out demons by the Spirit of God and the power of divinity, because they are subject to me, because they are in my power, because they cannot resist me, because I hold them bound and fettered.”

Thus far from the cited Commentary on Saint Matthew. And this is what he says: “When the strong man, armed, guards his court, the things which he possesses are in peace. But if one stronger than he comes upon him and defeats him, he shall take away all his armor in which he trusted and distribute his spoils.” The devil was strong; but I am stronger. I entered his house; I came into this world, which he possessed as his own house. But it is near that the prince of this world shall be cast out. I bound him, plundered his vessels, and freed from his slavery the wretched people whom he had seized. Therefore he is not with me, nor does he gather with me, nor does he cast out demons with me. He does not heal people as I do; he does not gather sheep or lead them to the pastures of life as I do. What, then, does he do? Do you wish to hear what? He scatters, disperses, kills, and drags with himself to death and eternal condemnation all whom he can. For this is what he says: “He who is not with me is against me; and he who does not gather with me scatters.”

## Homily XLIII. Wednesday after the Third Sunday in Lent

[Editorial Notice.]

Editorial Notice. I can never sufficiently praise the edition of Saint Bruno’s commentaries on the Gospels, published through the care and industry of the distinguished Lazzari, because in it the bishop’s wisdom and elegance of expression shine forth in the highest degree. On the other hand, the numerous errors of Marchesius’s edition frequently obscure the sense and cloud the light of sound interpretation. Let this homily serve as an example: it is read in a far more correct form in the Commentary on Matthew, no. 63, chapter 2. Eusebius Emisenus also has it as no. 45.

### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Matthew (20:1)

At that time scribes and Pharisees came to Jesus from Jerusalem, saying: “Why do your disciples transgress the tradition of the elders?” And the rest.

Beginning: “For the traditions of the elders, not the sayings of the prophets,” etc.

End: “To eat with unwashed hands is rusticity, not sin.”

## Homily XLIV. Thursday after the Third Sunday in Lent

[Editorial Notice.]

Editorial Notice. The manuscript codices agree with the editions of Marchesius and of the spurious Eusebius in assigning this day to this homily; likewise, they agree in its beginning and end. But it is lacking in the commentary. We have therefore copied it from Marchesius and compared it with the Paris edition of Eusebius.

### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Luke (4:38)

At that time Jesus, rising from the synagogue, entered Simon’s house; and Simon’s mother-in-law was afflicted with a great fever. And the rest.

We must know who Peter’s wife is in order that we may know who his mother-in-law is. Peter’s wife is the Church, because it was entrusted to him in a special way by the Lord, who said: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John 21:17). Its mother-in-law, then, is the Synagogue, because the Synagogue is the mother of the Church. Hence in the Song of Songs the Lord says to it: “Under the apple tree I raised you up; there your mother was corrupted, there your mother that bore you was violated” (Song 8:5). This woman lies in Peter’s house and is feverish because, even to this day, the infirm Synagogue remains and dwells among Christians. For wherever the Church is, there is Peter’s house. Near the end of the world the Lord will touch her hand; then, with the fever driven away, she will rise and minister to the Lord. For he touches her hand when he approves her works.

“When evening had come, they offered him many who had demons, and he cast out the spirits by a word and healed all who were ill, that what was said through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘He took our iniquities and bore our sicknesses’” (Isa. 53:4). He cast out the spirits by the Word of whom it is written: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). By a word, indeed, because by his own power.

But why when evening had come, unless because he had come in this last age, this final hour, to heal, cure, and drive out demons? For that people should not have been healed until evening had come, since it does not return to the physician until evening. Hence the Psalmist says: “They shall return at evening, suffer hunger like dogs, and go around the city” (Ps. 58:15 [Vulgate]). Then they shall come, then return; then the Jews shall bring to the Lord their sick, their souls worn away by much weakness, and he shall heal them and cast demons out from them. “For when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 11:25). “And if the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall return to the Lord” (Hos. 1:10).

But Jesus, seeing many crowds around him, commanded them to cross the sea. I think that Jesus commanded them to cross the sea because, unless we crossed through the waters of baptism, we could not escape the crowds of vices and the armies of evil spirits. And one scribe came to him and said: “Master, I will follow you wherever you go.” Jesus said to him: “Foxes have dens, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8:19–20). Nothing is hidden from God; no pretence is concealed from his eyes. He sees all things and answers the thought. The scribe says: “Master, I will follow you wherever you go.” Jesus says: “It is not so. You do not wish to follow me; you do not wish to keep my commands. I see in you no place where I may lay my head.” The head of Christ is God. But God dwells in one who is humble, quiet, and fears his words.

As though he said of you: “Foxes have dens”; you speak these things with cunning and pretence. For foxes are called evil spirits because of their craftiness. They are also called birds of the air because they hold dominion in this air. These indeed make nests and dens in sinful and wicked people; in their hearts they beget evil thoughts and the seeds of iniquities.

But another of his disciples said to him: “Master, I will follow you.” He said to him: “Follow me.” But he said: “Lord, permit me first to go and bury my dead.” Jesus said to him: “Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead.” This man spoke in another spirit. Hence he is rightly called not a scribe but a disciple, nor is he forbidden to follow the Lord; rather, he is commanded to follow and imitate him. Yet he wished first to go and bury his father. He wished to perform a work of piety; but that piety did not please the Lord. Why was this? Because it signified something else and, by this deed, gave us an example. It was as if he said: “You have come to life; do you wish to return to death? I am life; I am your creator and father. Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead.”

For the dead bury the dead when sinners—dead indeed, because the life of which we have spoken is not in them—hide and conceal within themselves mortal works and criminal sins. And not only these: they also bury in the tomb of their breast their father the devil, concerning whom the Lord said to the Jews: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44), and preserve and hide him as though he were some good thing. The Lord therefore forbids the burial of such a father, and forbids it in such a manner.

## Homily XLVII. Fourth Sunday in Lent

[Editorial Notice.]

Editorial Notice. We have found that this homily was composed from two commentaries, on John and on Matthew: its first part is in the Commentary on John, no. 16, and its second part in Matthew, no. 16. Among the other homilies published under the name of Eusebius Emisenus and assigned to this same day, it agrees with Marchesius in its opening words, but its ending differs there. So that readers may readily obtain the earlier part, we set it down here.

### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to John (6:1)

At that time Jesus went across the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias; and a great multitude followed him, because they saw the signs which he performed upon those who were sick. And the rest.

[Col. 0800B] Beginning: The Lord, about to perform great miracles and to give the people the delights of a new and wondrous bread, went up the mountain, so that we too, whenever we desire to be filled with spiritual and new banquets, may ascend not the height of a mountain but the elevation of mind and sublimity of understanding. Since those refreshed by such delights are worthy to celebrate the feast and to receive Christ’s flesh and blood, it is rightly said here that the Passover, the festival day of the Jews, was near. For they come confidently to this feast because they have been filled with such food. Therefore, when Jesus lifted up his eyes and saw that a very great multitude was coming to him, he said to Philip: “Where shall we buy bread for these people to eat?” But he said this to test him; for he himself knew what [Col. 0800C] he was going to do.

For the Lord knew what he was going to do; but by testing Philip he wished to hear what Philip thought of his omnipotence, and at the same time he magnified that new miracle by the disciple’s answer. For he was about to feed so many people from five loaves, though, according to Philip’s testimony, bread worth two hundred denarii would not suffice for them, even if each received only a little. Thus Philip answered, saying: “Bread worth two hundred denarii is not enough for them, for each to receive a little.” One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him: “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are these among so many?”

This boy is the Jewish people, still childish in understanding and intelligence. The five loaves signify the five [Col. 0800D] books of Moses. That people carries these loaves everywhere with it, yet does not eat them, because it merely reads the Scriptures and does not understand them. But concerning these things the blessed evangelist Matthew speaks as follows.

(The continuation through the end is contained in the Commentary, no. 61.)

[Col. 0802B]

## HOMILY LIV. PASSION SUNDAY

[NOTICE.]

NOTICE. The prologue of the homily, beginning, “God had commanded through Moses,” down to the words, “Why do you not believe me?” has been added; nevertheless, what follows agrees perfectly with the Commentary throughout no. 26. The Paris printers rendered good service in publishing this sermon under the name of Eusebius of Emesa, and placed it among his spurious [Col. 0802C] homilies as no. 54. Marchesius also published it for the same Passion Sunday, vol. II, p. 53.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN (8:46)

At that time Jesus said to the Jewish crowds and the chief priests: “Which of you will convict me of sin? If I tell you the truth, why do you not believe me?” And the rest.

The Lord had commanded through Moses that the Jewish priests should approach absolutely no dead person, except a father or mother, brothers, or an unmarried sister. He further commanded concerning the high priest that he should approach neither father nor mother nor any dead person whatsoever. But what is signified by a dead person except sin? For sin was the cause of death, since, had the first [Col. 0802D] man not sinned, no human being would ever have died. To approach a dead person, therefore, is to approach sin; here the effect is put for the cause. The Lord therefore commands that priests should not approach a dead person—that is, that they should not commit mortal sins. Although no one can be without sin, nevertheless a priest ought to be without grave crime.

But because no one can be without original sin, priests are not forbidden to approach the death of parents and close relatives. For original sin is common to all; therefore there is no doubt that all approach it. But what should we understand by an unmarried sister except those souls who are separated from their father’s house and from the Church? Let Jews and heretics serve us [Col. 0803A] as an example: following their own pleasures, they perish outside the Church. These indeed are those dead sisters whom one may not approach. Let our priests hear this, and keep themselves free from every dead work and from every contagion of sin. For all these things happened to them as a figure; but they were written for our correction.

Now let us consider the high priest, by whom we understand our Lord and Savior, the greatest of all priests. He approached no dead person, because he neither derived original sin from his parents nor committed any sin of his own. He is the one of whom it is written: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.” He alone, therefore, did not approach the death and sin of father and mother. Let him then say—and say confidently—“Which of you will convict me of sin?” For this is what that red heifer signifies, which we heard read just now in the Apostle’s words and which is described as without blemish. Thus the Lord said to Moses: [Col. 0803B] “Command the people to bring you a red heifer without blemish, of full age, and one which has never borne a yoke” (Num. 19:2), and what follows.

But what is the red heifer except the flesh of our Savior, taken from the herd of patriarchs and prophets? Why red, except because it was bloodied with his own blood? Why of full age, except because the Lord suffered in youth? It bore no yoke because it committed no sin. “Do not,” says the Apostle, “bear the yoke with unbelievers” [more literally, “Do not be yoked together with unbelievers”] [Col. 0803C] (2 Cor. 6:14). Hence it is called spotless; and hence the Lord now says: “Which of you will convict me of sin?”

(What follows should be consulted in the Commentary under no. 26.)

## HOMILY LV. MONDAY AFTER PASSION SUNDAY

[NOTICE.]

NOTICE. Those who compare the Commentary on this passage of John’s Gospel will not merely be more certain that the homily published by Marchesius in vol. II, p. 54, was drawn from it; they will also be able to obtain a much improved text. No confidence remains in the Paris printers, who falsely ascribed it to Eusebius of Emesa.

[Col. 0803D] At that time: The chief priests and Pharisees sent officers to seize him. Jesus therefore said to them: “I am with you yet a little while, and then I go to him who sent me.” And the rest.

Beginning: “In vain,” he says, “do you and your rulers labor,” etc.

End: “And they returned, because they could not accomplish their own will.”

## HOMILY LVI. TUESDAY AFTER PASSION SUNDAY

[NOTICE.]

NOTICE. Without playing with words, it will be enough to say that the same Commentary supplies this homily in its entirety, from no. 20 in the Commentary on John through no. 21, and plainly reveals the false attribution to Eusebius, since a wholly similar homily is found there as no. [Col. 0804A] 56. For it begins with the same words and ends with the same words. In Marchesius it is found on p. 54, etc.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN (7:1)

At that time Jesus walked in Galilee, for he did not wish to walk in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him. And the rest.

Beginning: “Jesus did this not because he feared death,” etc.

End: “They did not dare, because they feared human beings more than God.”

[NOTICE.]

[the author’s name is uncertain as printed] did not confine his exposition within narrow limits. [NOTICE.]

NOTICE. I, p. 58. Readers can readily satisfy themselves from both, since we consider it useless to reproduce what has already been published. ### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (24:13)

[Col. 0807D] At that time two of the disciples were going on that very day to a village. And the rest.

Beginning: “One of these men, it is thought, was the blessed Luke who wrote these things.”

End: “And that they in turn might announce their joys to one another.” (The following occurs in the homily.) Yet Jesus is never so well known as in the breaking of bread. This bread is spiritual, not carnal; this bread is the food of the soul. By this bread the soul is nourished, and understanding grows rich. Of this bread it is written: “A human being does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 15:11 [the citation is printed thus]). Of this bread the prophet says: “The little children asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lam. 4:4). [Col. 0808A] Wretched Jews, who indeed possess bread, but do not possess one to break the bread for them. But for us he broke the bread. Jesus Christ our Lord expounded the Scriptures to us and opened their meaning—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXIII. FRIDAY AFTER EASTER SUNDAY

[NOTICE.]

NOTICE. St Bruno is the author of the homily. Since the matters he had introduced in the Commentary for elucidating this Gospel appeared too few, he took only its opening words and added what we copy here; the remainder is found in the Commentary on Matthew, no. 106. In Eusebius it is Homily 92, and in Marchesius, p. 73.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (28:16)

At that time the eleven disciples went away into Galilee, etc.

When this vision took place, I cannot say with certainty, since Thomas, who was one of these men, is related to have seen the Lord before [Col. 0809A] the eighth day. But it is not without mystery that the Lord commanded his disciples to leave Judea for Galilee and wished to manifest himself to them there. For the evangelists relate that women came to the Lord’s tomb and heard the angel say to them: “Do not be afraid, for I know that you seek Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. But go quickly and tell his disciples and Peter that he will go before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he told you” (Matt. 28:5).

What the women signify, why the Lord wished to manifest himself first to them after his resurrection, and why Peter too is called by name, we have already explained above. We must therefore say what is signified by Galilee and by the mountain to which he appointed them to come. Galilee, whose name is interpreted “migration,” signifies the Church. Great indeed is the migration of sinners to it; great also is the migration of the righteous from it. But what good does it do to come to the Church unless we also ascend the mountain on which the Lord appointed that he would be seen? This mountain, it seems to me, is the Gospel in which Christ’s passion and resurrection are proclaimed, and in which he manifests himself to his disciples. But do you wish to hear Jesus speaking to his disciples upon this mountain? Hear and understand: “O foolish and slow of heart to believe all the things spoken by the prophets! Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer thus, to rise from the dead, and so to enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:25). “Therefore touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” [Col. 0809C] (ibid., 39). There are also many other things by which the Lord manifests himself to his disciples on this mountain.

Do you also wish to see Jesus manifesting himself upon the mountain of David—that is, in the Psalter—and speaking to his disciples? “I,” he says, “slept and began to sleep, and I rose again, because the Lord sustained me” (Ps. 3:6). And again: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones. But they looked and gazed upon me; they divided my garments among themselves and cast lots for my clothing” (Ps. 21:17). But why do we speak thus? There are as many mountains as there are prophets; as many mountains as there are volumes of books. For of these mountains it is written: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence help will come to me” (Ps. 121:1). And elsewhere: “Why do you look with envy upon the curdled mountains? The mountain in which God was pleased to dwell” [Col. 0809D] (Ps. 67:17). “Come, therefore, let us ascend the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths” (Ps. 2:3).

For this reason the apostles went away into Galilee, and to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them; and seeing him, they worshipped him, though some doubted. I indeed think that those who doubted signified heretics, who went out from us but were not of us. It follows: “And Jesus approached and spoke to them, saying: All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth,” etc.

(The remainder of this homily is found in the Commentary.)

## HOMILY LXXVI. FIRST SUNDAY AFTER EASTER

[Col. 0810C]

[NOTICE.]

NOTICE. Since the homily for the present day consists partly of the exposition of John’s Gospel, no. 30, p. 465, and partly of additions made both at its beginning and near its end, we present it to readers as published by Marchesius, vol. II, p. 75, and by the editors of Eusebius of Emesa as no. 94, but corrected in many places.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN (10:11)

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “I am the good shepherd.” And the rest.

“I,” he says, “am the good shepherd.” Hear this, shepherds, and learn from me, the one shepherd, to be good shepherds. For the good shepherd is he who lays down his life for his sheep. This is the definition of a good shepherd: this I have done, and you too must do it, if need be. “For no one has greater love than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends. But the hireling, and he who is not a shepherd, whose sheep are not his own, sees the wolf coming, and abandons the sheep and flees” (John 15:13).

Jacob was a good shepherd; Moses too was a good shepherd; and David was likewise a good shepherd, who, to protect the sheep, did not fear to confront bears and lions, though he was still a boy. For he himself killed both lion and bear, as he testifies when speaking to Saul. Those bears and lions signified vices, evil spirits, heretics, and schismatics, against whom the shepherds of the Church now fight and contend. He was not a hireling, one who would abandon the sheep and flee, fearing the assaults of wolves. Therefore that good shepherd signified this best shepherd, [Col. 0811A] who now speaks in this Gospel, saying: “I am the good shepherd,” etc.

But would you also see that David himself fulfilled the definition of the good shepherd described here, and wished to lay down his life for his sheep? For when the angel came down upon the people and, with sword drawn, had slain many, David offered himself to death and cried out: “It is I, Lord, who have sinned; it is I who have acted wickedly. But these, who are sheep—what have they done? Turn, I beseech you, your hand against me and against my father’s house” (2 Kings [= 2 Samuel] 24:17). Let therefore our David say—David’s son, indeed, but stronger than that David—“I am the good shepherd.”

That the Lord calls himself a shepherd is condescension, not presumption; abasement, not any exaltation of rank. Yet he does not disdain [Col. 0811B] to call himself a shepherd, he who did not disdain to perform the office, suffer the indignities, and undergo the labours of a shepherd. He is the one of whom the prophet says: “Like a shepherd he feeds his flock; he will gather the lambs in his arm, lift them in his bosom, and himself carry those that are with young” (Isaiah 40:11).

To whom would it not seem degrading to gather lambs, foul and dirty sheep into his bosom and carry them upon his shoulders? Yet such were Christ’s sheep; such formerly were all human beings. He washed them in his own blood, cleansed them in the waters of baptism, and carried them back to pasture on his own shoulders.

But let the same prophet say what he is according to divinity, he who according to humanity chose to humble himself so greatly. “Who,” he says, “has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, or weighed the heavens with his palm? Who has held the mass [Col. 0811C] of the earth in three fingers, weighed the mountains in scales, and the hills in a balance?” (ibid., 12). He, I say, who bore the indignities of the shepherd, is he who made heaven and earth. He is the one who measures the earth in the hollow of his hand, who knows the drops of rain and the number of the stars. He is the one who, by the operation of the almighty Trinity, as though by three fingers, weighed the mountains and balanced the hills. He established the earth in the midst of the firmament: though poised by its own weights and having no foundation, it can nevertheless fall nowhere.

Indeed, he is the one of whom it is written that he made all things in weight, number, and measure. For he set a fixed weight, a fixed number, and a fixed measure for all things, beyond which no creature can extend itself. [Col. 0811D] Therefore there shall be as many human beings as he has ordained; each shall possess the amount and measure of that gravity and strength, that power, wisdom, honour, and dignity, which he disposed before the ages that each should have.

For this reason it is written also that he gave weight to the winds: because he bestowed upon angelic powers and upon the souls of the righteous such gravity and strength that they could not be moved from their proper station by the weight of pride. But he did not possess this gravity and weight who, raised up by the lightness of pride, said: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I will exalt my throne” (Psalm 14:13 [citation as printed]).—“Therefore, Lord, all things are set in your will, and there is none who can resist your will” (Esther 13:9).

It follows: “But the hireling, and he who is not a shepherd, whose sheep are not his own, sees the wolf coming and abandons the sheep and flees.” [Col. 0812A] The hireling is that bishop who, in feeding and governing the sheep, seeks only temporal and passing things; who feeds the Lord’s sheep not out of love for the heavenly homeland, but for profit and the reward of temporal goods. Such a man is not a shepherd in God’s sight, even if human beings call him a shepherd; nor does he possess sheep of his own, but sheep hired for wages. If they were his own, he would love them as his own and would not hesitate to expose himself to dangers for their sake.

But he sees the wolf coming: he sees the devil and his attendants threatening—for the devil’s attendants are heretics and schismatics, and all deceivers—and he abandons the sheep and flees. He abandons them, certainly, by not helping them, not preaching the truth, not urging steadfastness and [Col. 0812B] patience, and not resisting heresy. Hence the Lord says through Ezekiel: “You have not gone up into the breach, nor set up a wall for the house of Israel, that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (Ezekiel 13:5). For all these words are, as it were, walls by which the sheep of the Church are defended from heretics; by them the wolf is driven back, conquered, and put to flight.

But the hireling flees because he is a hireling, and the sheep are no concern of his. For he would not flee if he were not a hireling; he would not flee if he served out of love and charity rather than for wages. “Perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). And indeed he flees because the sheep are no concern of his.

“I am the good shepherd, and I know my sheep, and my sheep know me.” For the Lord knows [Col. 0812C] who are his. To know God, moreover, is to love him. Hence he will say to some at the judgment: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matthew 25:12), that is, “I do not love you.” Otherwise, how could he who knows all things be ignorant of anything? Therefore, when he says, “I know mine, and mine know me,” it is as though he said: “I love mine, and am loved by mine.”

But how do I know them? Would you hear how? “As the Father knows me, and I know the Father.” Thus, he says, I know—that is, I love—my sheep and am loved by them, just as I am loved by the Father and love the Father. Hence he also says later: “As the Father loved me, I have loved you” (John 15:9). And again: “I pray not for these alone, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that all [Col. 0812D] may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, so that they too may be one in us. And I lay down my life for my sheep” (John 17:20 [with John 10:15 joined, as printed]).

By this, he says, it is proved that I love them: because I lay down my life for my sheep. Had he not loved them, he would not have laid down his life for them. “And I have other sheep that are not of this fold; them also I must bring to myself, and they shall hear my voice, and there shall be one fold and one shepherd.” This is what the Apostle says: “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2:14). For he joined two walls, one coming from circumcision and the other from uncircumcision. The Lord was speaking to the Jews, to whom he promised that the Gentiles would be joined, so that one house might be built from two peoples and one Church constructed.

Thus peace was made [Col. 0813A] between Jews and Gentiles: there is one fold and one shepherd. They hold one law, worship one God, and follow the voice of one shepherd.

[Moses likewise signified these two flocks of sheep, these two walls of the Church, when, at the Lord’s command, he ordered the tabernacle to be made from ten curtains. There were five curtains in one wall, joined to one another at the corners with loops of blue. There were also another five in the other wall, woven together in the same manner. The five and the five—that is, the two walls—were mutually joined by golden clasps, from which two walls one tabernacle was constructed. All the curtains, moreover, were woven with embroidered work and marked out in beautiful variety. What these signify we have explained in Exodus.]

## HOMILY LXXVII. SECOND SUNDAY AFTER EASTER

[Col. 0813B]

[EDITORIAL NOTICE.]

EDITORIAL NOTICE. We indicate that this homily is composed of two parts. The first, namely from the beginning to the words, “So great an offspring of such noble children has sprung up among all the nations,” may be seen under no. 47 of the Commentary on John; the other is in the exposition of Revelation, chapter 12. Readers will find the text much improved in our edition over that in Marchesius, pp. 76–77. It is the same homily as no. 97 among the writings attributed to Eusebius of Emesa.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN (16:16).

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me.” And the rest.

Beginning: “For the Lord lay in the tomb only for a short time.”

[Col. 0813C] Ending: “And no one will take your joy from you.”

## HOMILY LXXVIII. THIRD SUNDAY AFTER EASTER

[EDITORIAL NOTICE.]

EDITORIAL NOTICE. In composing this homily, the author made use of his Gospel commentaries, as he very frequently did in other cases. Since the Gospel of the current Sunday is the first part of John chapter 16, the first part of the homily is found in the exposition of the text, as is the conclusion. But in the middle the holy bishop added a number of things. Lest readers be deprived of these, we have taken care to transcribe them along with the first part from Marchesius, p. 77, first comparing it with the other editions and removing many errors; the remainder may be compared with the Commentary on John, no. 46. In Eusebius it is Homily 98.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN (16:5).

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “I am going to [Col. 0813D] him who sent me.” And the rest.

Above, blessed Peter had said: “Lord, where are you going?” (John 13:36). But now, taught and instructed by his words, none asks him where he is going, because each knew with complete certainty that he was going to the Father. Why should they ask what they knew and about which they had no doubt? “But because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart.”

For he saw them troubled at his departure, which they had just heard and learned from his discourse. Who would not grieve at being separated from such a good, sweet, and gracious Lord? “But I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go.” For what can Truth do except speak the truth? He says this not so much to confirm his discourse as to console their hearts. “For if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you.”

Although the Paraclete was always there and everywhere—for the Spirit of the Lord filled the whole world—he was nevertheless to come in another manner. For it had been predestined before the ages that the Son of God should first be born of a virgin, die, rise again, ascend into heaven, and only then that the Holy Spirit should be sent to console the disciples. Thus it was ordered, thus determined; and he could not come otherwise.

“And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment.” He himself explains this: concerning sin, because they do not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father and you will see me no longer; concerning judgment, [Col. 0814B] because the ruler of this world has already been judged.

See: he sets forth three matters in which the Holy Spirit reproves the world, matters for which the Son of God had himself previously reproved it. It is as though he said: “I indeed am going to the Father, but I send you the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, to teach, strengthen, and fortify you in my place; he will speak in you and for you, and through you he will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment.”

Concerning the sin of unbelief, because they do not believe in me; and because they do not believe in me, they do not practise righteousness, and therefore the Holy Spirit will convict them also concerning righteousness. But why does he do this in my place, and not I myself? Because I am going to the Father and you will see me no longer. For he could not carry out this reproof except because, according to the flesh, he was ascending to heaven and was no longer remaining bodily in this world.

And the Holy Spirit will convict the world not only concerning sin and righteousness, but also concerning judgment. What judgment? Certainly that of which he said above: “Now is the judgment of the world; now the ruler of this world will be cast out.” Hence it is well said here: “Concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world has already been judged,” that is, has been cast out. The Psalmist speaks of such judgment when he says: “Judge, O Lord, my judgment and my cause” (Psalm 73:22); and again: “Judge my judgment and redeem me” (Psalm 118:154).

What, then, is the judgment of the world except the redemption of the world? What is the judgment of the world except the judgment in which the ruler [Col. 0814D] of the world is judged, condemned, and cast out from the hearts of the faithful? The world is therefore convicted concerning this judgment because, ungrateful for so great a benefit, it still follows the ruler of the world. Thus the world is convicted concerning sin because it refused to believe in Christ; concerning righteousness, which it heard him teach but refused to observe; and concerning judgment, because the ruler of the world has been condemned and the world itself set free, yet it remains ungrateful for so great a benefit and does not yet follow Christ, the author of its salvation, but rather the devil, its deceiver.

The saying, “He will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment,” may also be understood thus, as though he said: “He will convict the world concerning its sin, my righteousness, and the judgment of its wicked choice.” Concerning sin, indeed, because they did not believe in me. “For if I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin.” [Col. 0815A]

He will convict the world concerning my righteousness, which I possessed when I said that I was the Son of God. They, however, cried out unjustly in opposition: “According to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.” But this righteousness of mine will now be revealed because, behold, I now go to the Father and you will see me no longer. For I could not have gone to him as to a Father unless I had been his Son. All others went to him as to Lord, but the Son alone went to him as to Father.

Moreover, the Holy Spirit will convict the world concerning the judgment of its wicked choice, by which judgment it chose to serve the ruler of the world, who has already been condemned and judged, and condemned and rejected me, the author of its salvation.

It follows: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth.” “I have already said many things to you,” he says; “I still have many things to say to you, which you cannot bear now because I do not yet wish to pour into you that great fullness of my Spirit.” Why? So that everything may take place in its proper time: that I may first ascend to heaven and then pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and they shall prophesy.

But when that Spirit of truth comes—who teaches nothing but truth—whatever things he teaches you, he will teach you all truth whole and perfect, without any admixture of falsehood. And because the Holy Spirit teaches all truth, [Col. 0815C] our Lord and Saviour seems to say of the Holy Spirit that every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven human beings, but blasphemy against the Spirit shall not be forgiven. Indeed, whoever sins against the Father shall be forgiven, and whoever sins against the Son shall be forgiven; but whoever sins against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come.

There is, therefore, one sin—and apart from it there is no other—which is not forgiven to human beings: refusal to believe the truth. For this reason Jews and pagans perish: because they are unwilling to believe the truth. Whoever, then, wishes his sins to be forgiven, let him believe the truth; and if he is not a Christian, let him turn to the faith and be baptized. For Truth says: “Whoever has not believed shall be condemned.”

But if he is a Christian, let him believe the truth, depart from sin, repent, and his sin shall be forgiven. The Prophet says of the Holy Spirit: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Psalm 94:8). The Apostle also says through the Holy Spirit: “According to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God” (Romans 2:5).

This, then, is true: whoever refuses with a hardened heart to believe the truth shall not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come. But just as it is proper to the Son to have assumed flesh and, by his blood, to have delivered the world from everlasting death, so it seems properly to belong to the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son, [Col. 0816A] to teach and preach all truth through the apostles and the doctors of the Church. Hence the Lord says: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20).

Although whoever sins against one of the three persons sins against the whole Trinity, nevertheless whoever does not believe the truth and contradicts the Holy Spirit’s teaching and instruction seems to sin against the Holy Spirit. It follows: “For he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak,” etc.

## HOMILY LXXXIV. ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

[EDITORIAL NOTICE.]

EDITORIAL NOTICE. Although only very few things are added at the beginning of this homily to the Gospel exposition, as is found in the edition and likewise in Homily 82 of Eusebius of Emesa, nevertheless, because from them Saint Bruno’s authorship is recognized ever more clearly, we judged that they should not be omitted. For he attacks the Simoniacs, as he constantly does whenever the opportunity occurs. It is in Marchesius, p. 83.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK (16:14).

At that time, as the eleven disciples were reclining at table, Jesus appeared to them and reproached their unbelief, etc. And the rest.

Beginning: The Lord Jesus came to his disciples; he found them reclining, found them eating and drinking, reclined with them, ate and drank with them, to show that he had assumed not a phantom but a true body, and to strengthen them by his presence. He rebuked them for their unbelief and strengthened them by his conversation. And, as it is written, “While eating with them, he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father” (Acts 1:4). Whoever you are, therefore, who await the promise of the Holy Spirit, do not depart from Jerusalem; do not leave the Church; do not abandon the fellowship of the saints. Wait there; remain there, because the Holy Spirit is given to no one outside the Church, and even those who possess him he abandons if they separate themselves from her.

He rebuked them for their hardness; he reproved them for the unbelief of their hearts. Although Simon Peter, as Mary Magdalene, etc.—the exposition of the Gospel begins with these words and the homily continues in the same way to its conclusion: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

## HOMILY LXXXVII. EIGHTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

[EDITORIAL NOTICE.]

EDITORIAL NOTICE. We have transcribed from Marchesius, p. 86, this homily, of which there is no trace in the Commentary on the Gospel of Luke. We nevertheless acknowledge that some passages have been drawn from chapter 6 of Book I of the *Sentences*, entitled “On Mercy.” This homily is not found in the collection of the homilies of Eusebius of Emesa.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (6:36).

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Be merciful.” And the rest.

“Be merciful,” he says; but how? “As your heavenly Father also is merciful.” For he is the one who makes his sun rise upon good and evil and rains upon the just and unjust. He is not only merciful, but mercy itself; he wills no one to perish, but wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of Truth.

Thus be merciful yourselves; hold to this rule of mercy. Mercy is a great virtue, superior to every other virtue. Hence it is said to the people: “The Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Psalm 144:9). Therefore among the Greeks it is fittingly called *eleos* (ἔλεος, “mercy”), [Col. 0818D] which is akin in sound to *elaion* (ἔλαιον, “oil”). For as oil is superior among liquids, so mercy is superior among good works. Whatever liquid you pour into oil, the oil always floats on top. Baptism is sanctified with oil; the Church is consecrated with oil. We too have therefore been anointed with oil so often, that we may always be mindful of mercy and never forget piety and compassion.

Hence the Lord also says: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Matthew 9:13). There are many other things that can be said concerning mercy, since “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Psalm 32:5). But “who is wise and will keep these things, and understand the mercies of the Lord?” (Psalm 106:43).

Therefore be merciful, and so merciful as your Father is merciful. Love all people; hate no one; pray for those who persecute and slander you, “that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:45).—“Do not condemn, and you shall not be condemned.” Why, then, have judges been appointed? Why have laws been established? Let murderers then rejoice, adulterers celebrate, sacrilegious persons exult: they have nothing further to fear, if judgment and condemnation are now forbidden.

Why, then, is it written: “Cursed is everyone who withholds his sword from blood” (Jeremiah 48:10)? Why are the sons of Levi praised, who through zeal for justice did not spare even their own parents? Why does God’s wisdom say: “Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Psalm 2:10 [citation as printed])? Why does the Psalmist also say: “Judge for the needy and the fatherless; vindicate the humble and poor” (Psalm 81:3)? Why is it commanded so often in the Law: “If anyone does this or that, let him surely die”?

It must be understood otherwise. The authority to judge is not removed, justice is not forbidden; rashness is taken away, ambition prohibited, and cruelty forbidden. It is therefore as though he said: Do not judge without mercy where mercy can be shown and preserved. Do not condemn; do not be hasty in giving sentence. Wait until anger passes; endure until the mind rests from its fury. Let our judgment be not according to will, but according to justice. Do not judge according to your will; but after long deliberation, finally condemn the guilty and ungodly.

For thus does your Father in heaven act; thus does he act who is full of mercy, who even in condemning the ungodly never departs from mercy. He does this—he who “does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live” (Ezekiel 18:33 [citation as printed]). Why, then, does he kill them? Why does he condemn and judge them? He does not wish them to die, provided that they are converted, cease acting perversely, and return to repentance.

If you do this and judge in this way, you shall neither be judged nor condemned. Judge the unjust; condemn the proud and ungodly—namely, those ungodly and proud persons who neither return to repentance nor cease from their impiety. But in matters not proper to you, and in matters in which you have not been appointed judges, forgive all; grant pardon to all, so that your brothers may not be able to sin against you more than you are able to forgive their sins.

“For if you forgive all their sins, your Father will forgive you your sins” (Matthew 6:12); but conversely: “Unless you forgive all their sins, neither will your Father forgive you your sins” (ibid.).—“A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing, they will give into your bosom.” [Col. 0820A] By these words, what else is signified than that you shall abound in every good, all joy, every dignity, and every blessedness, if you too forgive those who sin and do not depart from piety and mercy?

Hence it is added: “With the same measure with which you measure, it shall be measured back to you.” He also spoke this parable to them: “Can the blind lead the blind? Will not both fall into a pit?” It is as though he said: It does not belong to everyone to judge; it does not belong to everyone to condemn; not everyone has the office of pronouncing sentence on sins. This belongs only to judges; this belongs only to prelates.

Therefore all who presume to do what is not their office and has been forbidden them are blind and have lost the eyes of the mind. And while such persons rashly condemn and judge others, although those others may indeed be wicked, they fall with them into the pit—the pit, that is, of eternal condemnation. The latter fall because of their sins; the former because of their rash and unjust judgments.

“The disciple is not above the master; but everyone will be perfect if he is like his master” (Matthew 10:24). This refers to what precedes, and is as though he said: I told you, “Be merciful, and be as merciful as your Lord and master is merciful.” Follow him; imitate him; retain his form and example. Live according to his form and example.

“For why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not see the beam that is in your own eye? And how can you say to your brother, ‘Allow me to remove the speck from your eye,’ while you yourself do not see the beam in [Col. 0820C] your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3). “Do not judge,” he says, “and you shall not be judged.” Judge yourself first, whoever you are; condemn and correct your own sins first. “First cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye” (Luke 6:42; Matthew 7:5).

For the difference between a speck and a beam is the difference between a sin and a crime. The Apostle says: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? Before his own master he stands or falls” (Romans 14:4). But he shall stand: the Lord is able to make him stand. “Therefore do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts. And then each shall have praise from God” (1 Corinthians 4:5). He lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.
