## HOMILY XCI. ON THE NATIVITY OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

[EDITORIAL NOTICE.]

ADMONITION. Readers should allow this homily [Col. 0821C] to be compiled from two passages of the Commentary on Luke. The first is no. 5 and begins, “John the Baptist is born today, greater than the prophets,” and continues as far as these words: “And you will be unable to speak until the day when these things take place.” The other, with a few intervening additions, appears in no. 2 and begins, “How shall I know this? For I am an old man,” and continues as far as: “For the Old Testament speaks, but now no longer in its own sense, but in a proper sense.” Then, from no. 5, the author again joins the remainder, beginning with these words: “But while Zechariah was speaking, fear arose,” to the end. We have the homily, composed from these different passages, published in Marchesius, p. 89, and in Eusebius of Emesa, no. 114.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (1:57).

At that time, the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. And the rest.

“John the Baptist is born today, greater than the prophets, [Col. 0821D] lesser than the angels—indeed, lesser than him who was made a little lower than the angels,” etc.

(The remaining material may be read in the Commentary as far as these words: “You will be silent and unable to speak until the day when these things take place.” We append what is added.)

For, as is read above, he entered the temple of the Lord, while the whole multitude of the people was praying outside at the hour of incense. Then an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right side of the altar of incense; and because he was unwilling to believe, he lost his speech. This solemn observance was performed on the tenth day of the seventh month, when the high priest alone, once a year and not without blood, entered [Col. 0822A] the Holy of Holies; no one else was permitted to be in the temple. What this signifies is explained by the Apostle in the Epistle to the Hebrews; and we too have spoken sufficiently of this observance in Leviticus [Note: [Col. 0821] Chapter 16, Roman edition of St Bruno, vol. I, p. 157, ch. 2.]. Then an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right side of the altar of incense. The angel stood—and stood at the right—because he announced mighty things. And Zechariah was troubled at the sight, and fear came upon him. But the angel said to him: “Do not fear, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard.” For this is the custom of angels, by which they are also distinguished from those who transform themselves into an angel of light: at the beginning of their speech, they comfort those to whom they speak and urge them not to fear.

Yet when he says, “your prayer has been heard,” let no one suppose that Zechariah [Col. 0822B] was beseeching God for a son, especially since he doubted on account of his own age and that of his wife, and did not believe the angel who promised it. What, then, was he praying for, except what the Law commanded him to pray? For it says: “This shall be an everlasting ordinance for you, that you pray for the children of Israel and for all their sins once a year” (Lev. 16:34). Thus, it was this prayer that Zechariah was offering which the angel said had been heard.

Zechariah said to the angel: “How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in her days.” Perhaps Zechariah did not remember that Abraham and Sarah begot a son in old age. For nothing is impossible to God; and all things are possible to one who believes. The angel promises, and the priest asks for a sign, as though he ought to have believed the sign more than [Col. 0822C] the angel. And the angel answered and said to him: “I am Gabriel, who stand before God, and I have been sent to speak to you and bring you this good news. Why then do you doubt? Why do you not believe? Neither he who sent me nor I can lie to you. You seek a sign”—the Jews seek signs. You say, then, “How shall I know?” You will be given a sign which, after receiving it, you may perhaps regret having received. This, therefore, will be the sign: “Behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day when these things take place, because you did not believe my words, which shall be fulfilled in their proper time.”

(Here ends the addition of St Bruno; the homily continues from the Commentary on the Gospel.)

Because, he says, you were unwilling to believe the words, believe at least the sign. Behold, you will be silent until a voice born from you arises. And because you are to beget a voice, do not regret having been silent for a while. For from you will arise the one who says: “I am the voice crying in the wilderness.”

And the people were waiting for Zechariah and wondered that he remained in the temple. But when he came out, he was unable to speak to them; and they realized that he had seen a vision in the temple. And he made signs to them, and remained mute.

By the aged Zechariah we may understand the Old Testament, and by the child John the New. For at the time when the New began to arise from the Old, the Old Testament lost its voice; because after the apostles and teachers began to preach and expound the new Law, the former understanding of the Law ceased. But it finally recovered the voice which it had lost when, after the New Testament had been born and spread everywhere, it learned from it what it ought to say. For the Old Testament speaks, but now no longer in its own sense, but in a proper sense. “But while Zechariah was speaking,” etc.

(The material that follows to the end appears in the Commentary, as far as the words: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending,” etc.)

HOMILY XCII. ON THE VIGIL OF ST PETER.

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. What St Bruno said in no. 55 of his exposition of this Gospel has been repeated in the homily without any alteration; and it contains a distinguished testimony concerning the primacy of Peter [Col. 0823B] and the jurisdiction of his successors throughout the universal Church. Marchesius published it on p. 90, as did Eusebius of Emesa.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN (21:15).

At that time Jesus said to Simon Peter: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” He said to him: “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” And the rest.

Beginning: “The Lord asks Peter whether he loves him, whom he always,” etc.

Ending: “For he showed most plainly how greatly he loved.”

HOMILY XCIII. ON THE FEAST OF ST PETER THE APOSTLE.

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. No less in elegance than in abundance of expression does the commentary of the holy bishop shine forth on [Col. 0823C] this Gospel passage, chapter 16. In it he treats of Peter’s appointment as prince of the apostles, and of Christ the Lord’s making him the chief foundation of the Church and entrusting to him all the power of binding and loosing on earth. Nothing is read in the homily which is not wholly contained in the exposition of the Gospel reading under no. 68. Marchesius reports it on p. 99.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (16:18).

At that time Jesus came into the district of Caesarea Philippi and asked his disciples, saying: “Who do men say that the Son of Man is?” And the rest.

Beginning: “The Lord asks his disciples what opinion they hold concerning him.”

Ending: “And if a prelate refuses to receive it, then let them know that they are loosed.”

HOMILY XCIV. FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[Col. 0823D]

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. In Marchesius, p. 91, these three homilies on saints are followed by the homily designated above. It appears to have been copied in its entirety from the Commentary, beginning at the end of no. 12 on Matthew and continuing to the end of the following no. 13. The manuscripts of Segni, Florence, and Monte Cassino agree with Marchesius.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (23:2).

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.” And the rest.

Beginning: “The unrighteousness of the scribes and Pharisees consisted in preaching well,” etc.

[Col. 0824A] Ending: “Its final farthing is never reached, since it is always being paid and is never brought to an end.”

HOMILY XCV. SIXTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. The homily set forth below is wholly from Marchesius, p. 92, since the Commentary on Mark contains no exposition of this Gospel passage. It is nevertheless found in Eusebius of Emesa for the seventh Sunday after Pentecost, and in the Laurentian manuscript under the name of Blessed Bishop Bruno.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK (8:1).

At that time, when a great crowd was with Jesus and had nothing to eat. And the rest.

We read above that, when Jesus had come beside the Sea of Galilee, he went up a mountain and sat there. And great crowds came to him, bringing with them the mute, [Col. 0824B] the blind, the lame, the infirm, and many others; and they laid them at his feet, and he healed them. Thus the crowds marvelled, seeing the mute speaking, the lame walking, and the blind seeing; and they glorified the God of Israel.

Jesus rightly ascended the mountain when he was about to perform such great and extraordinary miracles, so that in the mountain which he ascended the loftiness of his power, and in the miracles that he performed the magnificence of his divinity, might appear. Therefore, let all who desire to be enlightened and healed follow him upon the mountain of spices. Of these mountains the Church says: “Arise, my beloved; be like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of spices” (Song 8:14).

But Jesus, calling his disciples, said: “I have compassion on the crowd, because they have now remained with me for three days and have nothing to eat.” [Col. 0824C] For the three days are the three ages of the world: namely, before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. Thus the crowds remain with the Lord for three days, because throughout all these three periods holy men, filled with the Spirit of God, believe in God, await Christ, and earnestly desire to be refreshed by his bread and teaching. And they had nothing to eat, because the living bread which came down from heaven had not yet been set before them; the lion of the tribe of Judah had not yet opened the book, nor broken its seven seals.

Therefore, on the third day—that is, in this third age of his incarnation—he refreshes the crowds and no longer allows them to perish from hunger. Hence he says: “I do not wish to send them away fasting, lest they fail on the way.” For we are all upon the way; we are all making for our homeland. Of this way the Psalmist says: “I have run in the way of your commandments” (Ps. 118:32); and likewise: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (ibid., v. 1). [Col. 0824D] Yet those who are fasting fail upon this way; those who have not been refreshed by Christ’s bread cannot run on this way—especially if they have come from afar: “Salvation is far from sinners” (ibid., v. 55). For just as this way is short and easy for the good, so it is long and difficult for the wicked.

And the disciples say to him: “From where can anyone here satisfy them with bread in the wilderness?” Perhaps Christ’s disciples had forgotten that he had already fed five thousand persons from five loaves. And Jesus said to them: “How many loaves have you?” They said: “Seven, and a few little fishes.”

The seven loaves are the seven books of the Old Testament, which we call the Heptateuch; or they are also the seven gifts of the grace of the Holy Spirit. The few little fishes are the few books of the New Testament in comparison with the Old Testament. Yet, if these few are joined to those seven loaves, they suffice to refresh the souls of all human beings. Without those loaves they can neither be eaten, nor give fullness or strength to those who eat them.

For the seven loaves are wisdom and understanding, counsel and fortitude, knowledge and piety, and fear [Col. 0825A] of the Lord. For who is wise without wisdom? Who is understanding without understanding? Who is provident without counsel? Who is strong without fortitude? Finally, who is knowing without knowledge, pious without piety, or fearful without fear of God? Therefore these fishes cannot be eaten without those loaves. And these books are rightly called fishes, because they swim in one fountain, of which it is written: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. 33:10).

And he commanded the crowd to recline upon the ground. For all recline upon the ground who acknowledge that they are dust and earth. Hence it is said: “Why are you proud, dust and ashes?” (Ecclus. 10:9.) And Jesus, taking the seven loaves, gave thanks, broke them, and gave them to his disciples.

The Lord breaks both the loaves and the fishes because, as he wills, the Holy Spirit both grants grace to each person and opens the deep mysteries of the holy Scriptures. But to whom does he give them except his disciples? To whom does he grant the task of preaching these things except bishops and priests? These are those whom [Col. 0825B] the Lord set over his household, to give them food in due season. These feed a hundred; these refresh the entire multitude of the Church with the bread of the divine word.

“And they all ate and were filled.” Therefore let us too eat and be filled; let us read in order that we may understand. The more one eats this food, the more one desires to eat it. This food delights the mind and does not burden the stomach; the more it is eaten, the more it grows.

Hence it is added: “And they took up seven full baskets of the fragments that remained.” The fragments are more numerous, as it were, than the loaves, because more people now receive the fragments than those who then ate those loaves and fishes. Do you not see how many volumes of books have multiplied from these four Gospels? But what do the seven baskets signify except the seven Churches, by which all Churches are understood? Hence John the Evangelist writes to seven Churches; and hence Isaiah says: “In that day seven women shall take hold of one man, saying: ‘We shall eat our own bread’” (Isa. 4:1)—the bread now given to us, the bread by which we have been filled and refreshed. And they seem to say: We are those seven baskets which the apostles long ago lifted up in the wilderness, full of fragments. Therefore, because we have bread, let us eat our own bread.

Now those who ate were four thousand men, besides little children and women. Why, then, are little children and women not counted? Because those who imitate either little children in foolishness and folly, or women in softness and weakness, are not worthy to be reckoned among the people of God. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not become children in understanding; but be little children in malice” (1 Cor. 14:20).

HOMILY XCV*. SEVENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. To learn the homily assigned to this Sunday by Marchesius, p. 92, one must again consult the Commentary. For it was drawn from it, with a few additions inserted. See the exposition on Matthew, no. 22, chapter 2. Eusebius of Emesa also has it for the eighth Sunday after Pentecost, as does the Laurentian manuscript.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (7:5).

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Beware of false prophets.” And the rest.

Beginning: “Beware, he says, and guard against false prophets,” [Col. 0826B] etc.

Ending: “May Jesus Christ our Lord deign to deliver us from that shipwreck.”

HOMILY XCVI. EIGHTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. The edition of his Commentary on Luke, no. 37, spares us the labour of copying this homily, which Marchesius included among the others of St Bruno on p. 94; anyone may consult it. It is absent from Eusebius of Emesa, as from the Laurentian manuscript, but not from the manuscript of Segni, where it is assigned to this Sunday.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (16:1).

There was a certain rich man who had a steward, and this man was accused to him. And the rest.

Beginning: “And his lord called him and said to him: ‘What is this that I hear about you?’”

[Col. 0826C] Ending: “May the virtue of this faithfulness be found in us.”

HOMILY XCVII. NINTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. Of the entire homily now to be noted, apart from a few additions made for the sake of its opening, Marchesius, p. 95, offers nothing which is not contained in fullest form in the Commentary on Luke, no. 21. It is very similar to the one placed under the thirteenth Sunday in the edition of Eusebius of Emesa.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (10:25).

At that time a certain lawyer stood up, testing Jesus and saying. And the rest.

Beginning: “The lawyer, he says, rose up, wishing to rebuke the giver of the Law,” etc.

Ending: “Great is the mercy through which eternal life is possessed.”

HOMILY XCVIII. TENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[Col. 0826D]

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. Eusebius of Emesa, under the eleventh Sunday after Pentecost, and Marchesius, p. 96, who publish the same homily, agree perfectly with the exposition of the Gospel both at the beginning and at the end, and have neither one word more nor one less.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (18:9).

At that time Jesus spoke this parable to some who trusted in themselves as righteous and despised others. And the rest.

Beginning: “Arrogance has never pleased God; pride has never been justified.”

Ending: “Pride is the root of all evils; humility is the guardian of virtues.”

HOMILY XCIX. ELEVENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[Col. 0827A]

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. The homily is the same in the Commentary and in the frequently cited editions. In Eusebius of Emesa it is read for the twelfth Sunday after Pentecost, and in Marchesius on p. 96. Against heterodox persons who disparage the ceremonies, or rite, of administering baptism in the Catholic Church, all that is done is shown to be holy.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK (7:31).

At that time Jesus, departing from the territory of Tyre, came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee. And the rest.

Beginning: “The Evangelist describes the route by which the Lord returned to Galilee.”

Ending: “Because the mouth of those speaking iniquity has been stopped.”

HOMILY C. TWELFTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. St Bruno wrote his commentaries on the Gospels not merely to expound what had been handed down by the divine word concerning heavenly things, but also to instruct his flock by salutary admonitions. He does this admirably at the beginning of this homily. That readers who possess the complete exposition of the Gospel in no. 51 may not be deprived of it, we communicate it to them from Marchesius, p. 97, and from Eusebius of Emesa, on the fourteenth Sunday after Pentecost.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (17:11).

At that time, while Jesus was going to Jerusalem, he passed through the midst of Samaria and Galilee. And as he entered a certain village, ten leprous men met him. And the rest.

438 Beginning: “We are all upon the way; we are all hastening to our homeland—some indeed to the heavenly Jerusalem, others to the land of misery and darkness. [Col. 0827C] There is no delay on the journey: every day we draw nearer to the place for which we are bound. Our Lord and Saviour did not disdain to travel this way. Thus he himself says elsewhere: ‘I went forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father’ (John 16:28).

“While the Lord was taking this way, leaving the world and going to the Father, he passed through the midst of Samaria and Galilee. But what are we to understand by Galilee but the Jews? And what by Samaria but the Gentiles? Hence it is said: ‘The Jews do not associate with Samaritans’ (John 4:9). Jesus passed through their midst because he called both these and those, preached to both these and those, healed both these and those, and converted them to faith.

“While doing this, it happened that he entered [Col. 0827D] a certain village, by which we understand the holy Church. For he first entered it when he began to build it by preaching and teaching. Hence he says: ‘Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone opens to me, I shall enter in to him and dine with him, and he with me’ (Rev. 3:20). Many reasons may be given why the Church is called a village. But what are the ten leprous men?” etc. (Here begins the exposition of the Gospel.)

HOMILY CI. THIRTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. As we have said elsewhere, our author customarily adds to his expositions of the Gospels, which he generally uses, something at the beginning, middle, or end of his homilies. In this homily an addition was made [Col. 0828A] after the words, “He has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.” It contains the prophecy of Zechariah, chapter 5, verse 6, or the allegory of the woman enclosed in a jar, who figures avarice, and continues as far as these words: “Therefore I say to you, do not be anxious about your life.” All that follows appears in the Commentary, no. 18, chapter 1. In Marchesius the homily is on p. 98, and in Eusebius of Emesa it occurs as the fifteenth homily after Pentecost.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (6:24).

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “No one can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will endure the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and mammon.” And the rest.

Beginning: “For our Saviour has just spoken above concerning treasure.”

[Col. 0828B] Ending: “If all people wished to be such, God would not lack the means to feed them.”

FOURTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

The Gospel and homily are the same as on Thursday in the week after the Fourth Sunday of Lent.

HOMILY CII. FIFTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. The exposition of this Gospel, being instruction in morals, was rightly taken for a homily, since the commentator teaches much both for the correction of vices and for the advancement of Christian virtues. Nothing was added to it either in Eusebius of Emesa, where it occupies the place of the seventeenth Sunday after Pentecost, or in Marchesius, p. 99. The same appears in the manuscript of Segni.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (14:1).

At that time, when Jesus had entered the house of one of the [Col. 0828C] chief Pharisees to eat bread on the Sabbath, they were watching him. And the rest.

Beginning: “In the Evangelist’s writing that Jesus entered the house of a chief Pharisee in order to eat bread,” etc.

Ending: “He who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted.”

HOMILY CIII. SIXTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. This homily displays the same style of expression as the preceding one. Let the reader consult the Commentary on Luke, no. 30, and draw from it excellent moral teaching. We have it in Marchesius, p. 100; but it is absent from Eusebius of Emesa.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (13:6).

[Col. 0828D] At that time Jesus spoke this parable to the crowds: “A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none,” etc. And the rest.

Beginning: “How great, then, is the patience of God in this parable.”

Ending: “In Christ’s words and miracles they recognized power and glory.”

HOMILY CIV. SEVENTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. This entire homily discusses the commandment of love toward God and one’s neighbour. It was taken for the sermon of this day from the Commentary on Matthew, no. 92. It breathes the author’s singular wisdom throughout and kindles one to attain the perfection of the twofold love [Col. 0829A]. In Marchesius it is found on p. 101, and in Eusebius of Emesa under the eighteenth Sunday after Pentecost; both have the same beginning and the same end.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (22:34).

At that time the Pharisees came to Jesus, and one doctor of the Law asked him, testing him: “Master, which is the great commandment in the Law?” And the rest.

Beginning: “But the Pharisees, hearing that he had imposed silence upon the Sadducees, gathered together. When the Pharisees had withdrawn,” etc.

Ending: “And from that day no one dared to question him any further.”

HOMILY CV. EIGHTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[Col. 0829B]

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. This homily needs no proof to be assigned to our St Bruno, since, besides lying entire in the Commentary, no. 91, the greater part of it is also found in the exposition of Deuteronomy, chapter 25, in our edition, vol. I, p. 220. It is absent from Eusebius of Emesa, but Marchesius published it on p. 101; the manuscript of Segni agrees with him.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (22:22).

At that time the Sadducees, who say that there is no resurrection, came to Jesus. And the rest.

Beginning: “On that day, he says, on which the defeated Pharisees withdrew, the Sadducees came in order to be defeated,” etc.

Ending: “Which was formerly observed according to the letter in the Synagogue.”

HOMILY CVI. NINETEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[Col. 0829C]

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. Briefly, I shall say that Eusebius of Emesa and Marchesius, p. 102, published this homily with the same beginning and ending as it appears in the Commentary, no. 29. All the intervening material likewise agrees perfectly.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (9:1).

At that time Jesus, entering a boat, crossed over and came to his own city. And the rest.

Beginning: “For in this passage we should understand his own city not as Nazareth but as Capernaum.”

Ending: “And they glorified God, who had given such power to human beings.”

HOMILY CVII. TWENTIETH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[Col. 0829D]

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. The homily assigned to this Sunday is entirely similar to the preceding one, namely because it is the same exposition of the Gospel passage. Such it plainly appears in Eusebius of Emesa, where it is for the twenty-second Sunday after Pentecost, and in Marchesius, p. 103; in their editions no difference from the Commentary occurs. See no. 77.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (18:23).

At that time Jesus spoke this parable to his disciples: “The kingdom of heaven is likened to a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants. And when he began to settle accounts, one who owed him ten thousand talents was brought before him.” And the rest.

[Col. 0830A] Beginning: “For this king is himself God who speaks, and the man Jesus Christ our Lord.”

Ending: “For it is not enough to forgive with the lips, unless mouths and hearts agree.”

HOMILY CVIII. TWENTY-FIRST SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. St Bruno admirably illuminates and magnifies, in his Commentary on this Gospel passage, no. 90, the most celebrated and most wise reply given by Christ the Lord to the Pharisees when they asked him about paying tribute to Caesar; from this the homily for this Sunday was taken. It is also read in Eusebius of Emesa for the twenty-third Sunday after Pentecost and in Marchesius, p. 104, where the following is added.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (22:15).

At that time the Pharisees went away and took counsel [Col. 0830B] how to trap Jesus in speech. And the rest.

Beginning: “Foolish Pharisees, who think that they can catch the Word of God in speech.”

ADDITION.—“Let us make man in our image and likeness.” It is a great honour, a great nobility, that man was made in God’s image and likeness. We lost this image in the first man; we recovered it in the second. For the Apostle says: “The first man is earthly, of the earth; the second man is heavenly, from heaven. As we have borne the image of the earthly, let us bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Cor. 15:49).

Let us render his image to the Lord; let us render our souls to God. We have nothing dearer; therefore we ought to pay this tribute. Let us hear Solomon; let us hear Wisdom itself [Col. 0830C] saying: “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the time of your affliction comes, and the days of which you shall say, ‘They do not please me’” (Eccl. 12:1). And a little afterward: “Before the silver cord is broken, and the golden band returns, before the pitcher is broken over the fountain, and the wheel is shattered over the cistern, and the dust returns to its earth, whence it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it [Note: [Col. 0829D] Ibid., v. 6: “Before the silver cord is broken, and the golden band returns, and the pitcher is shattered over the fountain, and the wheel is broken over the cistern, and the dust returns to its earth,” etc.].”

“Remember,” he says, “your Creator, in whose image and likeness you were made; imitate him, lest you lose his likeness. For a human being has the image and likeness of whomever he imitates—before the time of his affliction comes,” by which we understand the hour of death, “and the days of which you shall say: ‘They do not please me.’” The impious, condemned to eternal death, have such days, because after they leave this life, they see, hear, and feel nothing that pleases them.

But let a person do this in the days of youth, and in the days of gladness and prosperity, of which the Apostle says: “While we have time, let us do good to all” (Gal. 6:10). It follows: “Before the silver cord is broken and the golden band returns.” For the difference between body and soul is that between silver and gold: by silver we understand the body, and by gold the soul itself, bright and wise. This golden band returns when the soul, released from bodily bonds, seeks heavenly things. The body is also called a cord because, by certain laws of nature, it binds and constrains the soul to itself. This cord is broken when the [Col. 0831A] soul is separated from the body—“before the pitcher is broken over the fountain and the wheel is shattered over the cistern.”

A person is called a pitcher because he was made from earth. The pitcher is broken over the fountain when a person, burdened by extreme weakness and already near death, is unable even to receive death itself: scarcely lifted from the bed by the hands of others in order to take the water for which he has long thirsted, he is unable to swallow it when brought to his mouth, because his breath is faint and his throat now closed. Then indeed the wheel is shattered over the cistern, because it is written: “On that day all their thoughts shall perish” (Ps. 145:4). For the wheel of our thoughts, which is above the cistern of our heart—for “thoughts proceed from the heart” (Matt. 15:19)—always turns and returns; then it will first rest, because there is no longer either ability or desire to think vain and useless things. For “he knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain” (Ps. 93:11).

Then the dust returns to its earth, whence it was. For as the Lord said to the first man: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3:19); but the spirit returns to God who gave it and, by his judgment and sentence, will either be drawn to punishment if it does not possess God’s image and likeness, [Col. 0831C] or led to glory if it has preserved God’s image and likeness.

(Here the homily concludes in the same words by which the exposition of this Gospel is completed in the Commentary.)

HOMILY CIX. TWENTY-SECOND SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION.—Readers will find a more perfect text of this homily in the Commentary on this Gospel passage than in Marchesius’s edition. This is not the place to list the errors; but let this be said for those who, possessing St Bruno as published by Marchesius, have thought this new edition of his works of little use to them. It appears in the said Commentary, no. 32, chapter 2, with the same beginning and end as in Marchesius, p. 104, and in Eusebius of Emesa, whose editors placed it on the twenty-fourth Sunday after Pentecost.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (9:18).

[Col. 0831D] At that time, while Jesus was speaking to the crowds, behold, one ruler came and worshipped him, saying: “Lord, my daughter has just died; but come, lay your hand upon her, and she shall live.” And the rest.

Beginning: “For by this ruler what are we to understand but Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, and Aaron,” etc.

Ending: “And by your will you led me, and received me with glory.”

HOMILY CX. TWENTY-THIRD SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION.—Whatever is presented in Marchesius’s edition, p. 105, as a homily is given in the same words in the Commentary under nos. 53, 54, and 55, which include in the same order three expounded parables. Eusebius of Emesa seems to agree, placing this homily on the twenty-fifth Sunday after Pentecost.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (13:24).

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field. But while people were asleep, his enemy came and sowed tares in the midst of the wheat, and went away. When the blade had grown and produced fruit, then the tares also appeared,” etc. And the rest.

Beginning: “Then, having dismissed the crowds, he came into the house,” etc.

Ending: “In which one thing is said and another is rationally understood.”

HOMILY CXI. TWENTY-FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[Col. 0832B]

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION.—Those who compare Marchesius’s edition with the Commentary will discover not only that many passages of this homily have been corrected, but will enjoy much learning by which the most learned commentator illuminated it in his Commentary on Luke, no. 46. The editors of Eusebius of Emesa printed it for the tenth Sunday after Pentecost.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (19:41).

At that time, as Jesus drew near to Jerusalem, seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: “For if you also had known.” And the rest.

Beginning: “For after raising Lazarus, the Lord came to Jerusalem,” etc.

Ending: “That we may be able to do this without harm.”

HOMILY CXII. TWENTY-FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[Col. 0832C]

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION.—Our author first sets forth an exposition of Daniel’s prophecy, which the Evangelist mentions, and then continues with the interpretation of the Gospel. Since this first part of the homily is absent from the Commentary, we present it as Marchesius published it on p. 107. All manuscripts seem to agree in their text of this homily, since the manuscript from which the edition of homilies under the name of Eusebius of Emesa was made gives the same interpretation of Daniel at the beginning and places it on the twenty-seventh Sunday after Pentecost. We do not think it ought to be omitted; readers have the remaining part of the homily in the Commentary, no. 100.

READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (24:15).

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “When you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by [Col. 0832D] Daniel the prophet, standing in this place—let him who reads understand.” And the rest.

Let us now see what the prophet Daniel saw, heard, and said concerning this abomination of desolation: “Know,” says the angel who was speaking to him, “and take heed: From the issuing of the word that Jerusalem is to be rebuilt until Christ the leader, there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks; and the street and the walls shall again be built in the straitness of the times. And after sixty-two weeks Christ shall be killed, and his people—the people who are to deny him—shall not be his. And the city and the sanctuary shall be destroyed by the people with the leader who is to come; and its end shall be desolation, and after the end of war desolation is decreed. But he shall confirm [Col. 0833A] the covenant with many for one week, and in the middle of the week sacrifice and offering shall cease. And in the temple there shall be the abomination of desolation; and desolation shall endure until the consummation and the end” (Dan. 9:25–27).

Let us therefore see what these things signify, and let us ask the almighty Lord to deign to reveal to us these his mysteries, so hidden. In the time of King Artaxerxes [Note: [Col. 0833D] This was Artaxerxes Longimanus, in the twentieth year of his reign, as the better chronologists—Petavius, Calmet, Berti, and others—hold.] Nehemiah was his cupbearer, as he himself testifies. When he was serving him at table, the king said to him: “Why does your face seem sadder than usual?” [Note: [Col. 0834D] In the Vulgate, 2 Esdras 2:2 reads: “Why is your countenance sad, when I do not see you to be ill?”] But he said: “May the king live for ever, for the city of our fathers has been destroyed.” To him the king said: “Go, and rebuild it” (2 Esdr. 2:2).

And this is what is said: “Know, Daniel, and take heed: From the issuing [Col. 0833B] of that word which the king speaks to Nehemiah, that Jerusalem is to be rebuilt, until Christ the leader, there shall be sixty-two weeks.” For if anyone carefully wishes to calculate the years, months, and days of the kings who lived from that time onward, he will find that sixty-two weeks were completed from the day on which this word was spoken to Nehemiah until Christ’s Passion. Yet five years beyond this number seem to occur in the chronicle; this, I think, happened through the ignorance of copyists. For they could err in their reckoning, but Daniel could not err.

But what he says, “seven weeks,” must be understood as though he said: From the issuing of the word commanding that Jerusalem be rebuilt, there shall be seven weeks until the walls are fully restored. [Col. 0833C] These seven weeks, that is, extend to the fiftieth day. Hence Nehemiah himself says: “For the wall was completed on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty-two days” (2 Esdr. 6:25). Those, indeed, are weeks of days; but the sixty-two weeks extending from Nehemiah to Christ’s Passion are called weeks of years. For just as seven days make one week, so also seven years make one week. Thus sixty-two weeks are completed in four hundred and eighty-three years, and that number is indeed calculated from Nehemiah to Christ.

Thus, then, the order stands. “Know,” he says, “Daniel, and take heed that from the beginning of the word spoken to Nehemiah, that Jerusalem should be rebuilt, there shall be [Col. 0833D] seven weeks of days until the completion of the walls. Likewise, from the beginning of that same word until Christ the leader there shall be sixty-two weeks of years.” And because the walls of the city were built in a few days, he accordingly adds: “And the street and the walls shall again be built in the straitness of the times.”

It follows: “And after sixty-two weeks Christ shall be killed, and his people—the people who are to deny him—shall not be his.” Wretched Jews, who do not understand these things: because they denied Christ [Col. 0834A] and said, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15), they became the people not of the Lord but of the devil.

Let us see what follows: “And the city and the sanctuary shall be destroyed with the leader who is to come, and its end shall be desolation, and after the end of war, desolation.” For after forty-two years the city and temple were destroyed. The leader who is to come is understood to be Antichrist. Although he comes much later in time, Scripture speaks as if of the present because they always worship and venerate him. But the end of the city will be devastation, and after that end everlasting desolation.

That wicked leader, however, will confirm the covenant for one week, promising that he will live and reign forever. For what is one week except seven days? And what are seven days except all days? For there are no days except seven. Therefore, if he were with them for one week, he would certainly be with them for all days. But it is not so. Whence is this? “For in the middle of the week sacrifice and offering shall cease.” [Col. 0834B] Half a week, if it is understood as a week of years, makes three and a half years. Then, when he perishes, sacrifice and offering will cease—the sacrifice, of course, of the Jews—which he himself will judge, since he will attempt to restore everything to the ceremonies and customs of the old Law.

Hence it is added: “And in the temple there shall be the abomination of desolation.” It will indeed be in the temple, because he will sit in the temple as though king and priest. Of him the Apostle says: “For he shall be exalted above everything that is worshipped, so that he sits in the temple [Col. 0834C] of God, showing himself as though he were the Lord” (2 Thess. 2:4). It is rightly called an abomination because he is to be abhorred by all; through him so great an abomination shall be brought about throughout all nations. This desolation will endure until his consummation, and until his utterly shameful and fully deserved end.

“But when you see this abomination of desolation,” etc. (The continuation may be read in the commentary.)

## HOMILY CXV. TWENTY-EIGHTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

### [ADMONITION.]

[Col. 0835B] **ADMONITION.**—This is one of the few homilies not found among the Expositions of the Gospels. We copied it from Marchesius, p. 110; the editors of Emisenus likewise published it under the Twenty-First Sunday after Pentecost. It begins in the same words, but the homily concludes differently. To this is added the testimony of the Laurentian manuscript, which, under the heading bearing the name of Bishop Bruno V, has it, as Marchesius reports, as no. 145.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN (4:46)

At that time there was a certain royal official whose son was ill at Capernaum. And the rest.

Kings are worthy to be heard. None are so intimate with God as good kings. Kings have a very good significance in divine Scripture. For every person who honourably and wisely orders and governs himself and the army of virtues [Col. 0835C] which is within him may, by a true definition, be called a king. Therefore, if you wish to govern and order yourself and your household well, guard the senses of your body, and do not permit them to wander through unlawful things. For they are leaders and hold authority throughout the whole house.

“Turn away your eyes, that they may not see vanity” (Ps. 118:37). Say also with the righteous man: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I should not think upon a virgin” (Job 31:1). Hear also what the Psalmist says: “My eyes are ever toward the Lord, for he himself will draw my feet out of the snare” (Ps. 24:15). For one who always has his eyes fixed upon the Lord does not desire to see vain things; thus sight is governed.

But what shall I say of hearing? It too must be governed. Therefore close your ears, lest they be open to slanders, lest they gladly hear empty and useless words. Open them to the Gospel; open them to the Word of God. For this reason the Psalmist says: “Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear” (Ps. 44:11); and for this reason the Lord says: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Mark 4:9); and Isaiah says: “Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken” (Isa. 1:1).

The tongue also needs governance; whoever does not govern it should not be called a king. For whoever guards his tongue guards his soul: “Death and life are in the hand of the tongue” (Prov. 18:21). “He who does not stumble in speech is a perfect man. If anyone thinks himself religious, while not restraining his tongue but deceiving his heart, that person’s religion [Col. 0836A] is vain” (Jas. 3:2). Hence the Psalmist says: “I said: I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue” (Ps. 38:2).

Unless the mouth too is guarded, it sins in many ways. It sins in gluttony and drunkenness. If our first parents had guarded it well, they would not have eaten of the forbidden tree. But the Lord taught us to govern this, when he answered the devil’s evil counsel: “A human being does not live by bread alone, but by every word which proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4:4). The Apostle too governed it well, saying: “Nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth” (Acts 10:11).

Let us govern our hands too, so that they may be opened to the poor and not stretched out to theft and plunder. The prophet marked such hands when he said: “Your hands are full of blood” (Isa. [Col. 0836B] 2:15). Let us govern our feet as well, lest they run to shed blood; rather, let them always be ready to proclaim good tidings, and able to tread upon serpents and scorpions. Concerning feet the Church also says: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song 5:3).

Thus the senses of the body are governed. But what shall I say of the inner household? It too needs governance. Hence the Psalmist says: “Examine me, O Lord, and test me; burn my reins and my heart” (Ps. 25:2). And again: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within my inmost parts” (Ps. 50:12). “For from the heart,” says the Lord, “come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, thefts, fornications, blasphemies. These are the things which defile a person” (Matt. 15:19). For this reason the rational breastpiece is placed over the heart and breast of the bishop: that the heart may be well governed and guarded.

Therefore let no one say that he is not a king, when he has so great a household to govern. Such kings, then, were signified by this royal official, who came to Christ to ask on behalf of his son. And perhaps he is called not a king but a *regulus*, a lesser king or royal official, because he did not yet believe perfectly. Hence the Lord says: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.” For if he had believed perfectly, his son would not have been ill. What, indeed, should we understand by his son except his spirit and his soul?

But the son of the *regulus*, that is, the soul of the *regulus*, was ill at Capernaum, which is interpreted “village of consolation.” An evil village, an evil consolation. This village is the flesh, in which the sick soul [Col. 0836D] lies and is made still weaker because it is not well consoled. “For,” says the Apostle, “the spirit desires against the flesh, and the flesh against the spirit” (Gal. 5:17). The soul wishes to turn and return to repentance; the flesh says—and speaks as though offering consolation—“Not yet; let us wait until tomorrow; let us act with deliberation. We are young; much time remains for us. It is better not to make vows than not to fulfil vows.” Thus Capernaum speaks; thus the flesh speaks; thus the village of consolation speaks. It seems to speak well, but it does not speak well.

Hence Solomon says: “Do not delay,” he says, “to turn to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day” (Ecclus. 5:8). He who gave the present day has not promised an uncertain tomorrow. Therefore imitate this royal official, whoever you are, O human being [Col. 0837A] whose soul is ill: hasten to Jesus; go to the physician. Ask him to come down; ask him to heal your soul and free it from its death. Beware lest it lie in Capernaum; do not console it badly and subject it to everlasting death. Do not seek signs and wonders; only believe, and you shall be saved. Persist with the royal official; persist, and say: “Lord, come down before my son dies.” For if you do this, you too will hear from the most merciful Lord what that royal official then deserved to hear: “Go; your son lives.”

It is therefore true, and without doubt true, that “at whatever hour a sinner turns and groans, he shall live with life and shall not die” (Ezek. 33:12). For he did not say, “He shall live,” but “He lives,” because repentance is born and life is given in one and the same hour.

The man believed the word which Jesus spoke to him and went away. This man should now be called not a *regulus* but a king; he was a *regulus* when he came, but he departs a king, full of faith. “For Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. 4:3). “All things are possible to one who believes” (Matt. 9:23).

As he was now going down, his servants met him and announced to him that his son was alive. He asked them at what hour he had begun to improve, and they said to him: “Yesterday, at the seventh hour, the fever left him.” These servants seem to be the bishops and priests of the world, who announce life to the sinner converted to repentance and promise healing. For they are servants of all, since by obligation they serve all. Hence the bishop of Rome [Note: [Col. 0837D] How ancient is the inscription used by the Roman pontiffs in their letters.]—the greatest [Col. 0837C] of all bishops—writes in his letters that he is “servant of the servants of God.”

Nor is it without mystery that the fever is said to have left the boy at the seventh hour. For the seventh hour, and the seventh day, is the final age of humankind, of which the Apostle says: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11). At this seventh hour the Lord came to heal and give life. Before this hour no one was healed. Whoever, therefore, is healed is healed in this hour and in no other.

The father therefore knew that it was the hour at which Jesus said: “Your son lives”; and he himself believed, and his entire household. Let us therefore also know and firmly believe that in this hour, in this appointed time, in this time predestined beforehand, Jesus came and, having suffered for us, commanded [Col. 0837D] that we should live and die no more, but be brought healed and unharmed into the heavenly kingdoms. He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CXVI. ON THE FEAST OF ST LAWRENCE, MARTYR

### [ADMONITION.]

**ADMONITION.**—Since we have proposed to follow the order of the homilies according to Marchesius, so that readers may more easily compare whatever they wish, after the homilies assigned to movable feasts and Sundays we conform our collection to that editor by producing the remaining homilies on the saints. The homiliary of Emisenus likewise contains this homily under the same title. But because no small part of it [Col. 0838A] is found in the commentary on this Gospel passage, we shall set down here only what is lacking.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN (12:24)

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” And the rest.

This is that grain of wheat which the virgin and untilled earth brought forth, of which the Psalmist says: “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. 13:3). “For the Lord will give goodness, and our land will give its fruit” (Ps. 84:13). By the immeasurable multiplication of this grain all the granaries of the Church have been filled. From this grain of wheat that bread is made, concerning which the Lord himself [Col. 0838B] says: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” (John 6:51).

It is plain, moreover, and literally true, that if a grain of wheat is kept in a chest, it does not grow; but if it is sown, dissolved into the earth, and dies, it bears much fruit.

*(Thus far the commentary on John, no. 36.)* God loves nothing unfruitful; he wishes nothing in his garden, vineyard, or field to be unfruitful. Hence he himself says elsewhere: “Every tree which does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. 7:19). And in another place: “I,” he says, “am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman: every branch that does not bear fruit he will remove; and every one that bears fruit he will cleanse, that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:1).

For this is that true [Col. 0838C] vine from which all this wine has flowed, which is offered to us in this Gospel. This is the ever-fruitful vine, all of whose branches are fruitful, whoever faithfully cleave to it. For this reason the unfruitful are removed from it: although by the sacrament of baptism they are in it, by the merit of their life they are not in it.

Such an unfruitful tree was that of which the Lord said to the vine-dresser: “Behold, for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree and have found none. Cut it down, therefore; why should it also occupy the ground?” (Luke 13:7). It would indeed immediately have been cut down, had not the good cultivator of that vineyard interceded for it, saying: “Lord, leave it also this year, until I dig around it and put in manure; and if indeed it bears fruit—but if not, you shall cut it down hereafter” (ibid.).

Such also was that fig tree on which, because he found no fruit, the Lord pronounced a curse, and it withered. Such are many other unfruitful trees, which will finally be cut down and cast into the fire. I for my part would not believe that any unfruitful tree was planted in paradise, especially since the Lord says to the first human being: “Eat of every tree of paradise; but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat; for on whatever day you eat of it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2:17). For in saying that he may eat of all, he shows that all those trees were fruitful.

[Col. 0839A] Since paradise signifies the Church, the trees of the Church too ought to be fruitful. For there are many trees in the Church. There is the tree of life, from which whoever eats, provided he eats worthily, shall not die. Of this tree it is written: “And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which shall give its fruit in its season” (Ps. 1:3). And elsewhere: “To the victor I will give to eat from the tree of life which is in the paradise of my God” (Rev. 2:7).

There is also that tree which says: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord; I have hoped in the mercy of my God for ever and unto age upon age” (Ps. 51:10). But what shall I say of those most noble trees to which the Lord says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain?” (John 15:16). The Church, therefore, possesses such trees as were signified by the trees of paradise.

But I think that the tree from which God forbade the first human being to eat signifies heretics. Their fruits are deadly, their apples poisonous; whoever receives their teaching will incur everlasting death.

It follows: “He who loves his soul shall lose it” (John 12:25), etc.

*(The remaining part of the homily is to be taken from the commentary.)*

## HOMILY CXVII. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF ST MARY THE VIRGIN

### [ADMONITION.]

**ADMONITION.**—Readers will find almost the whole of this homily in the commentary on Luke, no. 22; we transcribe here the remaining [Col. 0839C] part, taken from Marchesius, p. 111. As has already been said, it was also attributed to Emisenus. It is found in the Laurentian manuscript, where it is no. 118 and ascribed to St Bruno, as also in the Signino manuscript.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (10:38)

At that time Jesus entered a certain village, and a woman named Martha received him into her house. She had a sister named Mary, who, sitting also at the Lord’s feet, listened to his word. And the rest.

Beginning: “All the works of our Saviour are full of mysteries. Whatever he does anywhere is a signification.”

Ending in the commentary: “And she began to bear children.” *(After this the homily follows.)*

These two most prudent women are the leaders and forerunners of the whole ecclesiastical host. The rest of the multitude follows them. Some go after Martha, others after Mary. For none enter that heavenly homeland unless they follow one or the other. Therefore the holy Fathers rightly established that this Gospel should be read on the solemnity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, who is signified by these two women. For, among all creatures, the most blessed Virgin preserved, more than all others, the privileges of both kinds of life—namely, the active and the contemplative.

Like Martha—or rather, better than Martha—she received Christ not only into her house, but even within the enclosure of her womb. She conceived him, bore him, brought him forth, carried him, and ministered to him more than [Col. 0840A] Martha and more often. Finally, like Mary, she not only heard his word, but pondered it in her heart and preserved it for us to read and hear. Thus it is written: “But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2:19). She deserved not only to contemplate but also devoutly to know him according to his humanity and according to his divinity. Therefore she chose the better part, which shall not be taken from her.
