## HOMILY CXXI. ON THE VIGIL OF ST ANDREW THE APOSTLE

[Col. 0841A]

### [ADMONITION.]

**ADMONITION.**—We give readers the first part of this homily, which is absent from the commentary, copied from Marchesius, p. 114; the remainder agrees perfectly when compared with the same commentary. Concerning this work, as concerning the preceding ones, the editors said that Emisenus had rendered excellent service. It is among the homilies on the saints, no. 8, Paris edition, 1575.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN (1:35)

At that time John was standing with two of his disciples; and looking upon Jesus as he walked, he said: “Behold the Lamb of God.” And the rest.

At the beginning of this Gospel a great question arises for us. For the evangelist says that on another day John was again standing [Col. 0841B] with two of his disciples and, looking upon Jesus walking, said: “Behold the Lamb of God.” But on the next day he wished to go out into Galilee; and he found Philip and said to him: “Follow me.” Then on the third day a wedding took place at Cana of Galilee.

This wedding day, which is said to be the third from the day of which we have just spoken, appears to be the fourth from the day on which the Lord was baptized. Read a little higher and attend carefully to what is said. For the evangelist says that the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to John to ask him whether he was the Christ, whether he was Elijah, whether he was the prophet; and blessed John replied that he was not. But on the next day after this reply [Col. 0841C] John saw Jesus coming and said: “Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” And then indeed he baptized him.

But again on another day—the day of which it is now said at the beginning of this Gospel, “John was standing with two of his disciples”—he saw Jesus coming and likewise said: “Behold the Lamb of God.” On the following day he found Philip and said to him: “Follow me.” But on the third day a wedding took place at Cana of Galilee.

But how can the wedding day be the fourth from the day of baptism, when the other evangelists say that immediately after he was baptized he was led by the Spirit into the desert? For if from the day of baptism the Lord fasted forty days and forty nights in the desert, it cannot possibly be that on the fourth day he ate at the wedding with his disciples. How too can it be true that, when they saw the miracle of the wine, his disciples believed in him, when the apostles were not there? For as yet the Lord had called no one but Philip alone, to whom he has just said: “Follow me.” Finally, how can that be true [Col. 0841D] which the whole Church believes to be true: that these three miracles occurred on one and the same day when the Lord came to the wedding? This, then, is the question, to whose solution I wish you to attend closely.

On the same day on which the Magi came to the Lord—that is, the thirteenth day after his birth—on that same day, when he had entered upon his thirtieth year, he came to the Jordan and was baptized. Hence the evangelist says: “Jesus was beginning to be about thirty years of age, being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph” (Luke 3:23). But from the day [Col. 0842A] on which he was baptized, when almost the whole year had passed and only three days remained, John came again to where Jesus was. This is that other day of which we have now heard at the beginning of this Gospel: that “on another day John was standing with two of his disciples, and he saw Jesus walking and said: ‘Behold the Lamb of God.’”

But *another* here is not referred to yesterday; it is used in the sense of “a different [day].” Properly, *altera* is said of two things. Then, on the third day from this other day, a wedding took place at Cana of Galilee. This wedding day was, indeed, the anniversary of the day on which, in the preceding year, the Lord had been baptized and on which the Magi came to him with gifts.

Thus these three miracles occurred on one and the same day, because on the very day [Col. 0842B] on which the Magi came to Jesus, he was baptized, having entered upon his thirtieth year; and when that thirtieth year had been completed, on that very day he came to the wedding. The wedding day, therefore, was not the fourth but rather the anniversary of the day of baptism.

It is clear, therefore, that from the year in which he was baptized our Lord and Saviour neither preached publicly nor performed miracles; when that year was completed, he came to the wedding and there performed his first miracle. Thereafter the fame of his name suddenly filled the whole earth. But when it says, “And his disciples believed in him” (John 2:11), this must be understood not of the apostles, whom he did not yet have, but of those disciples who were then with him. For he had some disciples, like John, who followed and listened to him.

[Col. 0842C] But now let us return to the words of the Gospel. “On another day,” he says, “John was again standing with two of his disciples. And looking upon Jesus walking, he said: ‘Behold the Lamb of God.’ And the two disciples heard him speaking and followed Jesus.”

*(Thus far the addition, or first part of this homily; the commentary on John, chapter 1, no. 4, will supply the reader with the remainder.)*

## HOMILY CXXII. ON THE FEAST OF ST ANDREW THE APOSTLE

### [ADMONITION.]

**ADMONITION.**—I shall deal briefly with the publication of this homily. It will be enough to advise the reader that it is composed from the two expositions on the Gospel of Matthew, nos. 8 and 9; it appears in Marchesius, p. 115, and in Emisenus, homily 9 on the saints, where a concise narration of the Gospel precedes it and the first exposition follows. [Col. 0842D] The remaining material, as it stands in the commentary, is supplied by the homily.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (4:1)

At that time, as Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea. And the rest.

Beginning: “The evangelist relates above that when our Lord and Saviour had heard, etc.”

Ending: “You see also the fish themselves: that is, those who are baptized and believe.”

## HOMILY CXXIII. ON THE FEAST OF THE APOSTLES I

### [ADMONITION.]

**ADMONITION.**—No long discussion is required to vindicate for St Bruno this homily attributed to Emisenus, [Col. 0843A] since, besides Marchesius, who published it on p. 116, the Vallicellan, Laurentian, and Signino manuscripts explicitly ascribe it to him. A few passages have been added at the beginning of the homily, in which the ten commandments of Christ the Lord are distinctly enumerated; the rest comprises the interpretation of the Gospel of St John from the commentary, no. 43.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN (15:12)

Jesus said to his disciples: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.” And the rest.

Beginning: “There are indeed ten commandments of the Law, the first of which is that which says: ‘You shall have no foreign god besides me,’ etc.”

Ending: “He was therefore rightly heard, who rejoices that he was not heard.”

## HOMILY CXXIV. ON THE FEAST OF THE APOSTLES II

[Col. 0843B]

### [ADMONITION.]

**ADMONITION.**—It will suffice to note that nearly the entire exposition of this Gospel passage, no. 43, has been used as a homily. What is lacking is presented to readers from Marchesius, where the homily occurs on p. 117. Upon comparison with Emisenus, where it is homily 11 on the saints, it is found to agree perfectly.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN (15:17)

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “These things I command you, that you love one another.” And the rest.

Beginning: “Great is the power of charity, which the Lord so often commends to his disciples.”

ADDITION. — Consider now, my brethren, with what devotion we ought to honor the holy apostles, whom the Lord himself now calls not servants but friends; of whom he himself says that, having been chosen out of this world, they overcame the world together with the prince of the world; to whom he himself bears witness, saying: “You are the salt of the earth. You are the light of the world” (Matt. V, 13)—“To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables” (Luke VIII, 10). These are the twelve fountains by whose abundance the whole earth is satisfied. Moses says: “The people came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water” (Exod. XV, 27). O what a great spring is this man who wrote these things, the blessed John the Evangelist! These are the twelve hours of the day and the twelve gates of the heavenly Jerusalem. Of them it is said: “On the east, three gates; on the west, three gates; on the south, three gates; and on the north, three gates” (Apoc. XXII, 13). Of them the Prophet says: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion [Col. 0843D] above all the dwellings of Jacob” (Ps. LXXXVI, 2). And indeed the Lord loves the gates of the Church alone more than all the buildings of the Synagogue.

These are the living stones that roll upon the earth; placed in the rational breastpiece of the high priest, they teach and preach even without a voice. For they preach not by shouting, but by signifying. We ought always to have them in our breast, that our hearts may be instructed and fortified by them. Let all the people look to these and diligently inquire what they signify. These are the foundation, the towers, and the pillars of the Church; these are the mountains that leaped like rams; these are the cedars of Lebanon; these are the stags that do not fear poison and kill serpents. These are the cocks crowing in the night, and the raging lions, girded about the loins and strongest among beasts, who will fear no encounter with anyone [Col. 0844A]. But what shall I say? These are those heavens that declare the glory of God.

## HOMILY CXXV. ON THE FEAST OF THE APOSTLES, III

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. — Apart from a few things at the beginning and certain intervening passages which are omitted, the whole homily may be found in the Commentary on Matthew, no. 38. It is read in Marchesius, p. 118, and in the Pseudo-Eusebius, Homily on the Saints 12.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (X, 16)

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves.” And the rest.

Beginning: Earlier in this Gospel the Lord and our Savior had said to his disciples: “Go and preach,” etc.

End: For those who are always found in goodness are never judged except in goodness [Col. 0844B].

## HOMILY CXXVI. AGAIN ON THE APOSTLES, IV

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. — Excerpts from the Commentary on Matthew, nos. 80 and 81, follow. When joined together they compose the entire homily published by Marchesius on p. 118, and likewise attributed to Eusebius, where it is Homily 13 for the feast of the apostles; it begins in the same words and concludes in the same words.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (XIX, 27)

At that time Peter answered and said to him: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you.” And the rest.

Beginning: Above, the Evangelist relates that a certain young man came to Jesus, etc.

[Col. 0844C] End: For we are accustomed to call those whom we love greatly by these names.

## HOMILY CXXVII. AGAIN ON THE APOSTLES, V

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. — As in the preceding cases, we take from Marchesius, p. 119, the earlier portion of this homily, which is not found in the exposition of the Gospel according to Matthew, and communicate it to readers. The remainder appended to it has been transcribed from the aforesaid Commentary, nos. 36 and 37; no difference occurs between the two editions. In the Pseudo-Eusebius we likewise have it published under this title: *Homily 4 on the Feast of the Apostles*; it gives the same opening words and the same concluding words.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (IX, 37)

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few.” And the rest.

The blessed Evangelist Luke says thus: “For the Lord also appointed seventy-two other disciples and sent them two by two before his face into every city and place where he himself was about to come; and he said to them: ‘The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few’” (Luke X, 1). Jacob had twelve sons; but Moses, at the Lord’s command, chose seventy-two men from the elders of Israel, by whose counsel and assistance he might more easily bear the burden of so great a people. Thus our Lord and Savior, who was signified through these two patriarchs, both chose twelve apostles and appointed seventy-two disciples. The bishops now hold the place of the apostles, while presbyters perform the office of the other disciples.

The Lord sent them [Col. 0845A] two by two to preach because there are two commandments of charity. Moreover, it is written: “Woe to one alone, because when he falls there is no one to lift him up” (Eccles. IV, 10). There are also two Testaments, which always proceed together, teach together, and preach together. If they enter the city of our breast, they prepare a dwelling and lodging for the Lord who is coming, just as those disciples did then. Miserable Jews, to whose cities not two disciples—that is, not two Testaments—but only one came; and therefore they do not understand what it says.

For this was signified by the two cherubim placed above the ark of the covenant, looking toward one another with their faces turned toward the mercy-seat. *Cherubim* is interpreted “fullness of knowledge.” But where, I ask, is knowledge so great as in both Testaments? That the two cherubim look at one another signifies the friendship and harmony of the two Testaments. For both bear witness to the same thing; both say and preach the same thing. Their faces were turned toward the mercy-seat, by which the ark is covered, so that they might be seen and recognized by all, and so that there might be no one in the ark—that is, in the Church and congregation of saints—who regarded their countenance as foreign and unknown.

Let those hear this who neglect to meditate upon the sacred Scriptures. For, not to mention others, even bishops themselves sometimes do not know these cherubim. Although their faces are turned toward them so that they may be known, they nevertheless disdain to look upon them. Therefore let those who love one another so greatly not proceed without each other: let them go together, preach together, [Col. 0845C] and together announce Christ’s coming to towns and cities. It follows: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few,” etc.

(The continuation of this homily is found in the Commentary under the numbers indicated above, as we have said.)

## HOMILY CXXVIII. ON THE FEAST OF THE APOSTLES, VI

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. — So that readers may not be wearied by having to assemble the parts of this homily—some of which occur in the Commentary, no. 20, on this Gospel passage, while very many others are read in Marchesius, p. 121—we have transcribed it in full. It was likewise attributed to Eusebius among Homilies on the Saints 15, under the title: *On the Feast of Very Many Martyrs*. The homily enjoys the testimony of the Signinus manuscript, with which it agrees exactly.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (X, 16)

[Col. 0845D]

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me. But he who despises me despises him who sent me.” And the rest.

The Lord and our Savior seems to have said this because the Samaritans would receive neither him nor his disciples. For the Evangelist says above: “And it came to pass, when the days of his assumption were being fulfilled, that he himself set his face to go to Jerusalem; and he sent messengers before his presence, and they went and entered into a city of the Samaritans; and they did not receive him, because his face was that of one going to Jerusalem” (Luke IX, 51).

“It came to pass,” he says, [Col. 0846A] “when the days of his assumption were now being fulfilled,” and when the time of his passion, resurrection, and ascension or assumption was drawing near, that the Lord set himself to go to Jerusalem, as was plainly evident in his countenance and face. For the will is easily discerned in the face; whence *will* is said to derive its name from *face*. “And he sent messengers before his presence; and they went and entered into a city of the Samaritans, and they did not receive him.” Why? “Because his face was set to go to Jerusalem.” For, as is said elsewhere, the Jews do not associate with the Samaritans (John IV, 9). Therefore the Samaritans were unwilling to receive Jesus because he showed that he wished to go to Jerusalem, already reckoning him almost as an enemy, just as one who loved their enemies.

For even to this day all wicked people do not receive Jesus, his messengers, or his Gospel because they recognize that he and they tend and hasten toward Jerusalem—toward peace, mercy, and loving-kindness. Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace.” When the disciples, James and John, saw this, they said: “Lord, do you wish us to say that fire should come down from heaven and consume them, as Elijah did?” (Luke IX, 54). And turning, he rebuked them, saying: “You do not know of what spirit you are. The Son of Man did not come to destroy souls, but to save them” (ibid.). And they went into another town.

For the apostles did not know of what spirit they were, since they desired so earnestly to avenge themselves. Had they known themselves to be servants and disciples of the spirit of compassion, patience, and meekness, they would never, in any stirring of their own spirit, have wished angrily to kill so many people. This was proved afterward, when they prayed for their enemies and persecutors.

And Jesus said to them: “He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me; but he who despises me despises him who sent me.” This is as though he said: The Samaritans despised not you alone, but me.

[The Lord spoke these words to his disciples and their successors, namely bishops and priests. Therefore, whoever you are who scorn to hear bishops and priests and disdain to comply with their words and exhortations, at least do not make light of God himself, and do not disdain to hear him. You despise hearing the priest; but it is no wonder, because he is poor, weak, and humble; because he is lowly and contemptible; because he was born of poor parents [Col. 0846D]. Yet hear the Lord speaking in him, admonishing you through him, and leading you back to eternal life. For the Apostle says: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (I Cor. XIII, 3). Thus Christ speaks in bishops and priests, and in them is honored by some and rejected by others. At present he endures and does not readily avenge his injuries. But hear him say: “I have kept silence; shall I always keep silence?” (Isa. XLII, 14). Let the Psalmist say: “O God, who is like you? Do not keep silence, nor be restrained, O God; for your enemies have made a noise, and those who hate you have lifted up their head” (Ps. LXXXII, 3).

Do not therefore despise Christ’s disciples and messengers; indeed, do not despise God himself in his disciples. For unless he himself were despised in his disciples, he would never have said: “He who despises you despises me; but he who despises me despises him who sent me.” Let the Jews hear this; hearing, let them fear; fearing, let them repent—if only they can appease him whom they did not fear to offend. For they not only despised Christ the Lord, but even crucified him.

But the seventy-two returned with joy, saying: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name.” For, as was said above, the Lord had sent them two by two before his face into every city and place where he himself was about to come.] What these signify, why the Lord sent them before himself, and why he also commanded them to go two by two, we have already explained elsewhere. But now, returning, they reported with joy to the Lord, who knows all things, those things which not they themselves but he had wrought in them [Col. 0847B]. For they rejoiced in the name of Christ, whose power they had experienced. They rejoiced in the immense grace bestowed upon them by the Lord: not only did they heal illnesses and infirmities, but they also commanded demons and saw subject to themselves those whom they knew to be kings and princes of this world, and all wicked people.

They said therefore: Lord, not only diseases and infirmities, not only wicked persons, but the demons themselves are subject to us in your name—those to whom all things are subject that are far from communion with you. And he said to them: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven; behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions.” By heaven are understood either the Church or the souls of the saints. The Lord therefore saw Satan falling from heaven. [Col. 0847C] He saw the devil fleeing from the Church and the dwellings of the saints, and affirmed that he had already foreseen and known what the disciples told him. Hence elsewhere he says: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out” (John XII, 31). Unless he had foreseen this, why would he have come into the world? And why would he have assumed flesh? For this purpose the Lord came into the world: to drive away the devil and free human souls from his impious power. What was now beginning to happen, then, he foresaw before it happened and ordained to happen in its own time.

We too see Satan to this day falling like lightning from heaven and abandoning the holy Church with great fury and indignation. For as often as some wicked person returns to repentance, so often does Satan fall from heaven. Many adulterers, perjurers, and murderers are in the Church, which is called the kingdom of heaven; as soon as they are converted, they are abandoned by the devil. And lightning does not fall from heaven more swiftly than the devil falls from their minds.

[Satan also falls from heaven when some heretic is separated from the Church, having previously appeared in it to shine with great splendor through his teaching. Such was Simon Magus, whom the blessed apostle Peter first expelled from the Church because of his wickedness, and afterward cast down from the air when he attempted to fly. Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “An angel sounded the trumpet, and a great star, burning like a torch, fell from heaven; and it fell upon a third part of the rivers and upon [Col. 0848A] the springs of waters; and the name of the star is called Wormwood” (Apoc. VIII, 10). For, as we have just said, a star falls from heaven as often as someone is separated from the Church through heresy. But the wiser and craftier he is, the greater a flame he seems to bear. And although he falls wholly from heaven, he does not fall everywhere. For where he errs, there he falls.

But he falls into a third river. The two rivers are the two Testaments. The springs are as numerous as the books of the teachers. No one falls in these, because no heresy is in them. But the third river, into which heretics fall, is that which they themselves make. For they make it because their erroneous teaching is not found in the aforesaid rivers. Indeed, heretics have made many rivers and many volumes of books. And this star is rightly called Wormwood, because, like the plant designated by this name, it is full of gall and every bitterness; yet whoever tastes it will not die. Therefore flee these waters, Christian; do not drink them. The rivers are known, and the springs of water leaping up to eternal life are known; if you drink from them, you will thirst no more.]

It follows: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy; and nothing shall hurt you.” By serpents and scorpions may be understood not only evil spirits, but also tyrants [Col. 0848B] and all persecutors of the Church, because they are poisonous and never walk by a straight path. What, moreover, can better be understood by “the power of the enemy” than Nero and Simon Magus, Diocletian and Maximian, and Antichrist himself, the son of perdition? The power of the enemy is also pride, avarice, and every kind of lust; many are overcome by these and made subject to the devil. Hence Job, speaking of him, says: “His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly” (Job XL, 11).

These things, however, will not harm Christ’s disciples, since the Lord protects and everywhere defends them. They certainly will not harm them if they resist them and do not consent to them. It follows: “Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that spirits are subject to you; but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” For there are many to whom demons are subject, but whom not joy, but lamentation and sorrow await. To some who say at the judgment, “Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons, and perform many mighty works?” the Lord will say: “Depart, workers of iniquity; amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. VII, 22). Therefore Christ’s disciples ought not to rejoice because demons are subject to them. Rather, let them rejoice because their names are written in heaven. For that joy is vain and temporal, but this is profitable and eternal. That looks toward vain glory; this looks toward everlasting glory. The former may be possessed by both good and evil people; the latter shall be possessed only by the good.

## HOMILY CXXIX. ON THE FEAST OF VERY MANY MARTYRS, I

[Col. 0849A]

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. — The author prefaces his exposition of the Gospel with certain remarks about Christian flight. Lest readers lack them, we transcribe them here from Marchesius, p. 122. This homily is not found among the Eusebian homilies.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (X, 23)

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “When they persecute you in this city, flee into another.” And the rest.

Such are Christ’s battles; such are the wars of the New Testament; thus Christ’s faithful know how to fight. The Lord had said to them above: “Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves” (Matt. X, 16). He had commanded them to be prudent as serpents; [Col. 0849B] now he tells them to flee and not to resist persecutors who pursue them. The Israelites fled the Egyptians and conquered. David too fled and was made king by the Lord.

This flight was signified by the patriarch Jacob, who, after great and prolonged servitude, is said to have fled from his father-in-law Laban together with his wives, children, and all his possessions. Laban himself pursued him for seven days and at last found him on Mount Gilead. Now Laban, which is interpreted “white,” signifies this world. For these two names, *white* and *world* [*mundus*: “clean,” “pure”], are very closely related and seem in some manner to signify the same thing. For one who is white seems also to be clean. I think that almighty God wished to call his creation by such a name because “he saw all things that he had made, and behold, they were very good” (Gen. I, 31). For if all things were good, there was nothing in them except what was clean.

But from the time when the earth is said to have been corrupted with blood, the world has been unclean. Therefore, Jacob’s flight with his wives, children, and all his possessions seems to signify that we too ought to flee this world, and rescue from its servitude our friends, relatives, and all whom we can. Laban follows Jacob for seven days because, as long as we live, this world does not cease to persecute us. For there are only seven days. Thus, what persecutes us for seven days never rests from persecution at any time.

Where then shall we flee? Let us flee to the mountains of Gilead and pitch our tents there. For *Gilead* is interpreted “heap of testimony,” by which we understand the book of both Testaments, in which are set forth all the examples and testimonies of the Law, the prophets, the apostles, and the teachers. In it the apostle John cries: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (I John II, 15). There the Lord says to his disciples: “If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of the world, and I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you” (John XV, 19). Such things and others like them are heard on Mount Gilead.

Let us therefore flee there and hear the Lord saying: “When they have persecuted you in this city, flee into another. Amen, I say to you, you shall not finish the cities of Israel until the Son of Man comes” [Col. 0850A]. Everywhere the Lord teaches patience and innocence, etc.

(The addition ends here; the remainder occurs in the Commentary, no. 39.)

## HOMILY CXXX. ON THE FEAST OF VERY MANY MARTYRS, II

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. — Apart from a few additions to the words, “He who does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me,” this entire homily has been taken from the Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew, no. 40. Marchesius published it in vol. II, p. 123. It is likewise read under that title in the Pseudo-Eusebius and agrees with it. The manuscripts cited above support our Bruno.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (X, 34)

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Do not suppose that I have come to send peace upon the earth; I have not come to send peace, but a sword.” And the rest.

[Col. 0850B] Beginning: What then is it that the Psalmist says: “In his days righteousness shall arise, and an abundance of peace”? etc.

End: If they have lacked reward here, they will have no reward there on that account.

## HOMILY CXXXI. ON THE FEAST OF VERY MANY MARTYRS, III

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. — We omit the very brief introduction to this homily, which is read in Marchesius, vol. II, p. 125, since the Commentary on the Gospel, p. 70 ff., supplies all the rest. In it, the celebrated beatitudes commended by Christ the Lord are learnedly explained. You will likewise find it in the Pseudo-Eusebius among Homilies on the Saints 19, p. 217 of the Paris edition.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (V, 1)

At that time, seeing the crowds, Jesus went up [Col. 0850C] onto the mountain; and when he had sat down, his disciples came to him. And the rest.

Beginning: A great crowd followed Jesus, and not merely followed him, etc.

End: If their blessedness delights you.

## HOMILY CXXXII. ON THE FEAST OF ONE MARTYR, I

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. — Here follows another homily not unlike the preceding, since it consists of two passages from the Commentary on Matthew, namely no. 64 and the beginning of no. 70. The introduction to the homily, which the Commentary lacks, is given thus by Marchesius, vol. II, p. 124; the Pseudo-Eusebius repeats it and otherwise agrees perfectly.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (XVI, 24)

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “If anyone wishes [Col. 0850D] to come after me, let him deny himself.” And the rest.

A little before, the Lord Jesus had said to his disciples: “He must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things from the elders, scribes, and chief priests, be killed, and rise again on the third day.” Taking him aside, Peter said to him: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you.” And turning to Peter, he said: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me, because you do not savor the things of God, but the things of men.”

Then, wishing to show how he must go first and how we must follow him, he added: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself.” For in predicting future things and showing that he would suffer willingly, the Lord also confirms their faith, as he himself says elsewhere: “And now I tell you before it happens, that when it has happened you may believe” [Col. 0851A] (John XIV, 29).

But what he said to blessed Peter, “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me,” is as though he said: Get behind me, so that, as I die for you, so you too may die for me. Do not oppose me; do not resist my will; do not stand in the way of the divine counsels. For this must happen, because it was thus predestined before the ages and foretold by the prophets. This is what he says elsewhere: “O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that Christ should suffer thus, rise from the dead, and enter into his glory?” (Luke XXIV, 25).

Peter therefore savored the things of men because he offered human counsel; he did not savor the things of God because he did not know these secrets of the divine counsel by which [Col. 0851B] humanity was to be redeemed. Then Jesus said to his disciples: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself.” For every person ought to deny himself.

(The remainder should be consulted in the Commentary.)

End: Such as he will appear after this life in his kingdom to all his faithful.

## HOMILY CXXXIII. ON THE FEAST OF ONE MARTYR, II

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. — Since a few things have been added to this homily which are absent from the Commentary, we pass them over. It is found in Marchesius, p. 124, and at no. 34 in the Commentary on Luke. It does not appear to have been inserted among the homilies of the Pseudo-Eusebius.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (XIV, 26)

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “If anyone comes [Col. 0851C] to me and does not hate his father and mother…” And the rest.

Beginning: For elsewhere the Lord says: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” etc.

End: They did not fear to lose it together with life itself.

## HOMILY CXXXIV. ON THE FEAST OF ONE MARTYR, III

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. — Since the entire homily published by Marchesius on p. 127 consists of parts not connected with one another, someone may suppose that it was not delivered to the people by St. Bruno, but composed by an unskilled author. The first part begins from the Commentary on John, no. 42: “Behold, Christ is called a vine, and the true vine.” The second comes from the Commentary on Matthew, no. 99: “Amen, I say to you, there shall not be left here one stone upon another,” down to: “For they shall deliver you up in councils and in their synagogues.” The third part, finally, I would call a rhapsody. The same occurs in the Pseudo-Eusebius, Homily 20 among the Homilies on the Saints, p. 218.

Beginning: Behold, Christ is called a vine, and the true vine, etc.

End: Great is the power of patience, without which the soul is lost, and through which it is possessed.

## HOMILY CXXXV. ON THE FEAST OF CONFESSORS, I

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. — Only certain words at the beginning seem to have been altered; everything that follows has been taken from the Commentary on Matthew, no. 102. The Pseudo-Eusebius gives the same reading in Homily 22 among the saints.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (XXV, 14)

At that time Jesus said this parable to his disciples: “A certain man, going abroad, called his servants and entrusted his goods to them.” And the rest.

[Col. 0852A] Beginning: This man is understood to be our Lord and Savior, who, returning from this world to the Father, etc.

End: And then the unprofitable servant shall be cast into the outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

## HOMILY CXXXVI. ON THE FEAST OF CONFESSORS, II

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. — Those who compare the homily published by Marchesius on p. 129 with the Commentary on Luke, no. 45, will observe complete agreement in every word.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (XIX, 12)

At that time Jesus said this parable to his disciples: “A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive a kingdom for himself and return. Having called [Col. 0852B] his ten servants, he gave them ten minas.” And the rest.

Beginning: This nobleman is he himself who speaks, our Savior, etc.

End: Which has been prepared for you from the foundation of the world.

## HOMILY CXL. ON THE FEAST OF CONFESSORS, VI

[ADMONITION.]

ADMONITION. — Marchesius also published this same homily in Book VI of the *Sentences*. But since his text is most imperfect, as we learned by comparison with Vatican Reginensis manuscript 100, we publish it as it stands in that manuscript and have assigned it a place among the homilies on confessors.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (XI, 33)

“No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house [Col. 0853B].” And the rest.

Where there are no eyes, light is unnecessary; where there are no ears, voices resound to no purpose; where there is no one to eat, there is no need to set out table and food. Rightly, therefore, the holy canons do not permit bishops to be ordained in lowly and insignificant places, but in cities and populous localities. For this is to set a lamp upon a lampstand: to ordain a bishop in an elevated place. Why? “That it may give light to all who are in the house.” Therefore let it not be placed under a bushel, where no one is present, but rather where there are many eyes. What we ought to understand by the lamp, however, the Lord himself added when he said: “The lamp of your body is your eye. If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light; but if it is evil, your whole body will be dark.” [Col. 0853C]

This world has its own eyes, namely the sun and moon, by which all things are bodily illuminated. Of these it is written in Genesis: “And God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night” (Gen. 1:16). Likewise, the Church has her own eyes, by which, as we have just said, bishops are signified. Our body also has its own eyes. In the same way the soul is adorned with its own eyes.

Consider now where the Lord placed the eyes of the world: surely in heaven, in the higher place, so that they may be seen by all and, like a lamp set upon a lampstand, may give light to all who are in the house. And where are our own eyes placed? Are they not in the head, like a lamp set upon a lampstand? So too our bishops ought to be established like lamps upon a lampstand, in a great and populous place. Almighty God did not will that his Church should be blind: he gave it eyes to illuminate it, to show it the way of truth, not to allow it to go astray, and to lead it by the straight path to the heavenly kingdoms. See, people, how greatly you ought to love your bishops and prelates. They are your lights, your eyes, and your lamps. Thus you ought to love them as your own eyes. There is nothing that human beings love more than their own eyes. Therefore they ought to love nothing more than their prelates.

But bishops must take care not to shut their eyes, not to hide the lamp, not to bury in the ground the money entrusted to them. Both the table and the lampstand were placed not within but outside the veil, where food might be shared by all and the light seen by all. “He who hides grain is cursed among the people.” Let the bishop interpret his own title, so that, placed on the watchtower, he may look down upon everyone and everything. For this purpose the first man was placed in paradise: that he might work and guard it.

But now let us consider the eyes of our mind, by which we understand wisdom, reason, understanding, and a holy and single intention. For of this eye our Savior seems to speak when he says: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light; but if it is evil, the whole will be dark.” For although bad bishops do very great harm, and the eyes of the weak waste away through their wickedness, nevertheless it is chiefly the eyes of the mind, if they are evil, that make the whole person dark. [Col. 0854B] For what light or brightness can be in one in whom wisdom itself, reason itself, understanding itself, and the whole intention are evil? Hence they are called wise persons of this age, because they have such eyes and do all their works in order to be seen by men—of whom the Lord himself says: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Luke 6:2).

That eye, therefore—that reason, that wisdom—is single which flees sins, despises transitory goods, desires eternal things, and leads by the straight path to God. Rightly, therefore, the Lord says: “The lamp of your body is your eye.” This is as though he said: Just as the lamp of the world is the sun and moon, the lamp of the Church bishops and teachers, and the lamp of your body your eye, so the lamp of your soul is wisdom, reason, and good intention. This is the single eye, which does not allow people to go astray. For, as someone has said, no one can be mad while possessing reason. And just as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Everyone who does evil hates the light” (John 3:20), that is, departs from reason and wisdom. When someone departs from wisdom, without doubt he loses the eye of singleness and truth. Reason and wisdom, therefore, never deceive. Even an intention that seems good often deceives.

For with a good intention the Apostle persecuted the Church of God, because he did this from zeal for the Law. Yet he was mistaken, because he was guided not by wisdom but by error. Likewise Elijah, with a good intention as it seemed to him, wished to avenge the blood of the prophets and his own persecutions; yet neither that will of his nor that great zeal pleased God. For the word of the Lord came to Elijah, saying: “What are you doing here, Elijah?” And he answered: “I have been very zealous for the Lord God of hosts. For the children of Israel have forsaken the covenant of the Lord; they have destroyed your altars and killed your prophets with the sword; and they seek my life, to take it away.” And he said to him: “Go out and stand upon the mountain before the Lord.” He went out and stood upon the mountain. And behold, the Lord passed by; and a great and strong wind, overthrowing mountains and shattering rocks before the Lord. The Lord was not in the wind; and after the wind, an earthquake. [Col. 0855A] The Lord was not in the earthquake; and after the earthquake, a fire. The Lord was not in the fire; and after the fire, the whisper of a gentle breeze” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 19:10).

Behold, we have now heard of three zealings—that is, three agitations and disturbances of the mind—which did not please the Lord. For if they had pleased him, it would by no means have been said: “The Lord was not in the wind,” “the Lord was not in the earthquake,” and “the Lord was not in the fire.” Religious persons are sometimes stirred up and disturbed, both against others and against themselves, more than is necessary. This disturbance sometimes passes quickly; at other times it rises into so great a flame that it can scarcely be extinguished and calmed.

For the holy man Elijah was so stirred by zeal against the prophets of Baal and the faithless people that, if authority had been granted to him by the Lord, he would have killed them all without mercy. Thus on another occasion, with the same zeal, he is read to have killed with his own hands four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal beside the torrent Kishon. Sacred history likewise relates that, by fire sent down from heaven, he consumed two captains of fifty, and twice fifty men who were with them.

Therefore the Lord commanded him to go out and stand upon the mountain: namely, upon the mountain of mercy, the mountain of charity and peace. For those who stand upon these mountains love all people from their heart, seek the death of no one, and do not desire the sinner’s death, but rather that he may be converted and live. Elijah, therefore, was led to these mountains so that the great agitation of his mind might be softened. And behold, the Lord passed by; but before the Lord passed, a great and strong wind, overthrowing mountains and shattering rocks, passed before the Lord. [Col. 0855C]

This great and strong wind, then, which overthrew mountains and shattered rocks, signified Elijah’s spirit and zeal. So far as lay in his power, he wished not only to overthrow, shatter, destroy, and ruin the people, but even powerful men, who are called mountains because of their height and rocks because of their strength. But “the Lord was not in the wind.” Since the Lord was not in that wind, and did not will to pass by together with it, Elijah could clearly understand that such zeal and such a spirit did not please God.

We also read that the apostles possessed a similar spirit when the Samaritans refused to receive the Lord, and they said: “Do you wish that we command fire to come down from heaven and consume them, as Elijah did?” Rebuking them, the Lord said: “You do not know of what spirit you are. The Son of Man did not come to destroy souls, but to save them” (Luke 9:54). Notice what he says: “of what spirit you are.” This is as though he said: The Spirit who is in you and in whom you have been reborn is not a spirit of zeal and vengeance, but of mercy and compassion.

“After the wind, an earthquake: the Lord was not in the earthquake.” The earthquake too is shown to be not good, since the Lord does not appear to be in it. In such an agitation Elijah himself was stirred against himself and said: “I beseech you, Lord, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 19:4). He seems to have said this not so much from desire for the other life as from hatred of Jezebel, whose persecutions he could no longer endure. Yet in the Gospel the Lord calls blessed not those who flee persecutions, but rather those who suffer persecutions for righteousness’ sake.

Finally, when blessed Job was oppressed by such great afflictions, he could not be provoked to impatience, although his wife, by diabolical persuasion, urged him to blaspheme, saying: “Bless God, and die” (Job 7:9). He answered her most patiently and without any agitation: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women” (ibid.). What blessed Paul says, “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23), he surely did not say when stirred or darkened by weariness of persecutions, but rather from desire for that blessedness.

That agitation, then, is evil which excludes the good of patience, whether through the persecution of tyrants or through any other bodily suffering. Hence the Lord says to his disciples: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21:19). We have heard many people, stirred by such agitation, pray for death for themselves. But this agitation was not like that by which certain saints placed amid persecutions prayed that the Lord might receive their spirit, although they most willingly endured the suffering of martyrdom; they feared only the frailty of the flesh.

It follows: “After the earthquake, however, a fire: the Lord was not in the fire.” This fire is that of which we spoke above, which is sometimes kindled by so great an agitation that it cannot be extinguished; it signifies, that is, inveterate anger and hatred. [Col. 0856C] We see that even those considered religious very often suffer from this vice. Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, was divided from the Church by this fire when he refused to receive Arians. Others often wish to conduct very necessary disputations in the holy Church, but others, inflamed by this fire, do not endure them. Inflamed by this fire, the wretched Donatists preferred to perish in their own faithlessness rather than return to the peace of the Catholic Church. Rightly, therefore, it is said that the Lord is not in the fire, because God is not in such anger and wrathfulness.

“But after the fire, the whisper of a gentle breeze: there is the Lord.” “If your eye is single”—of this the Lord now speaks in the Gospel: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light.” That noble poet teaches us how pleasing the whisper of a gentle breeze is to people wearied by intense heat and great labor. For Virgil says, at the end of *Eclogue* 5:

> For neither does the whisper of the coming south wind delight me so much,  
> nor shores struck by the wave . . .  
> as do your songs, etc.

What, then, should we understand by this whisper of the coming breeze except the breath of the Holy Spirit? Whomever he deigns to touch, he so cools and restrains from every burning of anger, indignation, and agitation that he compels the saints to pray even for their enemies. This is what the Lord says: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you, that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:34).

Filled with the sweetness of this gentle and delightful breeze, the Lord and our Savior himself, while suffering amid his very torments, prayed for those who crucified him, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:59). Blessed Stephen also, strengthened by this whisper of the breeze, cried out amid the very stones for those stoning him: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:5). And so that you may understand what the Lord said there, hear him saying: “Behold, I see the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God” (ibid.).

When Elijah saw that the Lord had passed in this final agitation, he could clearly understand what he ought to reject and what he ought to hold fast, and that mercy pleased God more than vengeance. This is the final agitation; this is the intention of compassion. This is the single eye of which the Lord now says: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light.” With such eyes the Lord will be seen. Such eyes belong to those of whom it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

## HOMILY CXLI. ON THE FEAST OF VIRGINS I

[ADMONITION.]

**ADMONITION.**—We have taken the homily presented here from Marchesius, p. 132. The greater part is composed from the commentary on Matthew, nos. 56, 57, and 58, in which the expositions of three parables are concluded. But since the author added some intervening material and much else after them, we publish the entire sermon, also collated with the Laurentian manuscript.

## READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (13:44)

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field, which a man who finds it hides; and in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.” And the rest.

“The kingdom of heaven” in this place means the heavenly homeland, which is rightly compared to a treasure hidden in a field, because its riches do not yet appear manifest to all. Yet they are found, if not fully, since the teaching and preaching of the saints disclose in large measure what it is and how great it is. The holy apostles found this treasure when Christ the Lord preached, and in their joy sold all things and bought it. “If you wish,” says the Lord, “to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and follow me, and you shall have treasure in heaven” (Matt. 19:21). Thus this field with its treasure is bought most perfectly.

The person who hides this treasure is one who, once he has learned what it is like, holds it in his heart, loves it in his mind, and in no way forgets it. For we hide what we hold dear and fear to lose.

Again: “The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls. When he found one precious pearl, he went away, sold all that he had, and bought it.” This comparison and what was said above signify nearly the same thing, except that here the kingdom of heaven is understood not as the heavenly homeland, as there, but as the holy Church. What is called a treasure there is called a pearl here. Therefore the kingdom of heaven—that is, the holy Church—is like a merchant, because just as he sells everything out of desire for one pearl and buys it, so she, for love of the heavenly homeland and eternal blessedness, has not only sold what she possessed, but has subjected herself to servitude in order to be able to buy and possess it. [Col. 0858A]

For the shrewd merchant buys, from things which he cannot possess for long, something which he need never fear losing, and in which he may possess all things. We may also understand by this merchant our Lord and Savior, who, having found one precious pearl—by which we understand the holy Church without spot or wrinkle—sold all that he had; that is, he allowed himself to be sold and killed, and bought her. Thus the Apostle also says: “For you have been bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:20).

Again: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind. When it was filled, they drew it out, sat down by the shore, chose the good fish into vessels, and cast the bad outside.” Rightly is the kingdom of heaven—that is, the holy Church—said to be like a net, because it was entrusted to fishermen and every day encloses and catches countless fish in the waters of baptism. Of these the Lord himself says to his disciples: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matt. 4:19).

The Lord cast this net into the sea when he commanded the same disciples, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. [Col. 0858C] 28:20). This world is called the sea, of which the Psalmist says: “This sea is great and broad; there are creeping things without number” (Ps. 103:25). This net has gathered fish of every kind, because the holy Church has called to faith and gathered into her bosom persons of every kind. For there are Jews and Greeks, Latins and barbarians, rich and poor, wise and foolish, wheat and tares, grain and chaff, righteous persons and sinners together.

But it has not yet been filled: fish still enter; people are still baptized. It will be filled when the fullness of the Gentiles enters into it and when Israel is saved. Then those who draw it out and sit beside the shore will select the good fish and cast out the bad. The shore of the sea is the end of the age. Explaining this, the Lord himself says: “So shall it be at the consummation of the age: the angels shall go forth, separate the wicked from among the righteous, and cast them into the furnace of fire; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” This furnace is hell, in which neither the worm dies nor the fire is extinguished; the weeping and gnashing of teeth signify the extremity of pain and the intolerability of punishments.

“Have you understood all these things?” They say to him: “Yes.” He says to them: “Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old.” This is as though he said: I spoke to them in parables, and they did not understand; but to you I have explained the parables themselves, and you have understood. To them, indeed, because they are still old, I brought forth old things; but to you, because you are new, both new and old things. To them I spoke in the customary manner of the prophets; to you, in the manner of a teacher and master.

Therefore speak and teach in this way; keep this rule of speaking. For one must speak differently in the kingdom of heaven, differently in the assembly of the scribes and Pharisees, differently in the Church, and differently in the Synagogue. Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven—every teacher and preacher of the Church—if he is wise and learned, is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure, from the riches of his breast and the knowledge of his heart, things new and old. The scribes of the Synagogue, because they are not instructed, bring forth old things; but the scribes of the Church, because they are instructed, bring forth both new and old things. The former follow the letter alone; the latter follow both letter and spirit. To the latter, indeed, it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but it has not been given to the former, so that seeing they may not see and hearing they may not understand. [Col. 0859B]

“For this people’s heart has grown fat, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and they have shut their eyes lest they see and be converted and I heal them.” These are old things, taken from the book of the prophet Isaiah; but the rest are new things, spoken by the Lord in parables after the place where he said these things. Thus teachers of the Church also ought, in accordance with their Master’s practice, to bring forth new and old things from their treasure.

For this reason the Lord sent his disciples two by two before him. For this reason the two Cherubim looked toward one another. For this reason deep calls to deep. For this reason the New Testament calls to the Old, and the Old to the New. For each Testament is called a deep because of the profound depth of wisdom and knowledge.

Hence too the Psalmist speaks to the teachers of the Church, saying: “If you sleep between the two portions, you shall be the silvered wings of a dove.” The two portions are the two Testaments. The dove is the Church, which is called silvered because it is adorned with every virtue, and especially with truth. The teachers and masters of the Church sleep between these two portions if they delight, as in sleep and rest, in the knowledge and teaching of both Testaments, now confirming new things by old, now old things by new.

In doing this, they become the wings of the dove, because by such wise and rational preaching they enable the holy Church to fly and carry it with them to heavenly things. For this reason it is said of the saints that “they shall take up wings like eagles, they shall fly and not fail” (Isa. 40:31). For this reason too the tabernacle was made in large part with featherwork, so that we may all take up wings and learn to fly.

It follows: “And the hinder parts of her back” (Ps. 67:14). They will follow you in the appearance of gold. For the first part of the Church was the apostles and all who believed in their time. But we are the later part, together with all who are to believe until the consummation of the age. The later therefore follow the first; shining with the splendor of heavenly wisdom, they will fly after them by the same way and with the same wings of virtues to heavenly things. [Col. 0860A] This will happen because the wise teachers of the Church, sleeping between the two portions, bring forth new and old things from their treasure. For the Lord himself did this, taught his disciples to do it, and therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven ought to be like a householder—that is, like our Lord Jesus Christ—who brings forth new and old things from his treasure.

## HOMILY CXLII. ON THE FEAST OF VIRGINS II

[ADMONITION.]

**ADMONITION.**—Because the greater part of this homily has been taken from commentary on Matthew, no. 102, with only a few things added in the middle concerning Dinah, the foolish virgin, and Iphigenia, the wise virgin, we refer readers to the commentary itself, lest matters already expounded be presented again. The homily has also been attributed to Emesenus.

## READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW (25:1)

At that time Jesus spoke this parable to his disciples: “The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom and bride.” And the rest.

**Beginning:** “The Lord and Savior had just said above: ‘But concerning that day,’ etc.”

**End:** “For not to know God is to reject him. Watch therefore, because you know neither the day nor the hour.”

## HOMILY CXLIII. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

[ADMONITION.]

**ADMONITION.**—Marchesius presents this composition in two places, but in markedly different forms. First it is read at the end of the homilies, and he calls it a homily. Secondly, it occurs in Book I of the *Sentences*, after chapter 8, entitled “On the Gospels,” and he calls it a sermon. We select the latter, because it conforms more closely to the exposition of Luke’s Gospel, no. 44. The former, although it takes much from the same commentary, heaps together materials so disparate and foreign to the subject that it can in no way be regarded as a genuine work of St Bruno.

## READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE (19:1)

Jesus entered and was passing through Jericho. And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus; he was a chief tax collector and was rich. And the rest.

From the time when the first man descended from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers, all of us who inhabit this world walk through Jericho. For Jericho is interpreted “moon,” whose changeability is so great that it never remains in the same state. Hence it fittingly signifies this world, whose mutability is perpetual and which cannot remain without changes. To say nothing of heaven, of time, of days, months, and the year—which are always turning and circling back upon themselves—neither air, land, sea, nor human beings themselves permanently retain their form. Who could ever recount all their changes? Rightly, therefore, is this world signified by the moon, since, in its likeness, it is continually varied by so many changes.

The Lord and Savior deigned, according to his humanity, to assume this mutability, in order to heal the man wounded by robbers and free the world from everlasting death. Hence he is rightly said to have walked through Jericho, because, though immutable according to divinity, he assumed our changes in his flesh. For he hungered and thirsted, and sat wearied beside the well.

“And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus,” which is suitably interpreted “one to be justified,” because he was called and justified by God. He was not merely a tax collector, but even chief of the tax collectors. Moreover, he was rich, and it is difficult for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven—difficult indeed, and impossible with human beings; but what is impossible with human beings is possible with God.

Although he was such a man, he nevertheless sought to see Jesus. He sought him, but could not see him. Why could he not? Because of the crowd and because he was small in stature. These two things greatly hinder a person from being able to see Jesus: the evil crowd, which drives a person away from so great and such a good; and smallness of stature, which belongs to one who has not yet reached the maturity and perfection of knowledge. Thus the Apostle warns us: “Do not become children in understanding, but be little children in malice” (1 Cor. 14:20). And again: “As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food. For you could not yet bear it; indeed, even now you cannot, for you are still carnal” (1 Cor. 3:1).

Whoever wishes to see God must leave the crowd: flee vices and sins, avoid the company of evil persons, rise and stretch himself out, grow in faith and knowledge, and advance in every goodness. Zacchaeus signified this when he ran ahead and climbed the sycamore tree. He climbed the tree so that from it he might see him whom he could not see by himself. This tree is faith. Many who come to it, although small in stature and not much advanced in knowledge, nevertheless deserve from it to see and know God.

Hence it is said here that Jesus was to pass that way. For this is the way, and Jesus passes beside this tree of faith. From it he is seen and sees; from it he is known and knows. The Lord deigns to look upon and call to himself those who climb this tree. Its fruit is blood-red, signifying the martyrs, who, cleaving to the tree of faith, were bloodied for the constancy of their faith. Such fruits, then, does the sycamore bear; such fruits does the tree of faith bear: those who cling to it so firmly that they can sooner be killed and bloodied by their own blood than separated from their tree—that is, from faith in Christ.

The Lord, passing by, therefore looked up, saw Zacchaeus, and said to him: “Zacchaeus, come down quickly, for today I must remain in your house.” Today, he says, you have begun to seek me, have come to faith, have climbed the tree; today I must remain in your house. True indeed is what is said through the prophet: “In whatever hour the sinner is converted and groans, he shall live and not die” (Ezek. 33:12). What happened then in Zacchaeus undoubtedly happens daily in other sinners too, if only they are converted from the heart, seek Christ, and hold fast to faith.

It follows: “And he came down quickly and received him joyfully.” He was already burning inwardly with the fire of faith; he had already grown greatly in faith, though he was small in stature. “When all saw it, they murmured, saying that he had turned aside to a sinful man.” All knew Zacchaeus to be a sinner, as chief of the tax collectors. But this sinner was better than those who murmured and called themselves righteous. The following words make this clear: “But Zacchaeus, standing, said to Jesus: ‘Behold, I give half of my goods to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone, I restore fourfold.’” By this single statement they all immediately ceased from murmuring, astonished at the tax collector’s so sudden repentance and conversion. Perhaps no one there would have wished to make such a great profession even under compulsion.

For he was very rich, as the evangelist himself testifies; yet he promises to give half of all his goods to the poor and to restore fourfold if he has defrauded anyone. See, then, from what great perfection he began, though he had then for the first time seen Christ the Lord and heard him preaching. It is indeed true that human beings see the face, but God looks upon hearts. What kind of man and how righteous the Lord saw that he would shortly become, though people judged him a sinner!

Jesus said to him: “Today salvation has come to this house,” and every infirmity, every disease, every contagion of vices has been driven out and healed; the whole house, outwardly and inwardly, has been sanctified, because he who is the inhabitant of this house is no longer a tax collector but a son of Abraham. For sons of Abraham are all who imitate Abraham and do Abraham’s works. Abraham received angels as guests; Zacchaeus received the Lord of angels as a guest.

“For the Son of Man came to seek and save what was lost.” He did not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance. For this reason he came; for this reason he descended from heaven: that he might save and free sinners and call them to repentance. Of such persons the house of God is built; of such persons the holy Church is fashioned.

This too is commanded to the children of Israel: that they build an altar to the Lord of unpolished stones, stones untouched by iron. Unpolished stones are sinners not yet shaped by the tool of the Holy Spirit according to the standard of beauty. The altar of God is the Church, daily built from such stones. The temple of God was constructed from foreign timber and stones brought from elsewhere. Hence blessed Peter is commanded to eat unclean animals (Acts 10:13). Hence not only clean animals but unclean animals too are preserved in the ark (Gen. 7:2). Hence Moses took an Ethiopian woman as his wife. Hence peacocks and apes were brought to Solomon. Finally, what are hair-cloths doing with the tabernacle? Why in the desert were thorns and elms planted among cedars and firs?

If you wish to understand these and similar things, learn what this means: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Matt. 9:13). If God had not called sinners, he would not have had Paul and Matthew, two great and lofty lights. Read in the *Song of Songs*, and hear from where and from what nation the Lord commands his bride to come to himself: “Come,” he says, “my sister, my bride; come from Lebanon, come from the summit of Amana, from the height of Sanir and Hermon; come from the dens of lions and from the mountains of leopards” (Song 4:8), so that you may not be ashamed. Only forget your people and your father’s house, and you shall be crowned.

The Psalmist too, marveling at this fullness of mercy, said: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God.” And what glorious things? “I shall remember Rahab and Babylon, those who know me. Behold foreigners, and Tyre, and the people of Ethiopia: these were in her” (Ps. 86:4). This, then, is the cause; let this reason suffice you—I speak to you who are indignant that the Lord turned aside to a sinful man, and that our teacher and Lord eats and drinks with sinners—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages.

## HOMILY CXLIII. ON THE FEAST OF THE TWELVE HOLY MARTYRS

[Col. 0864A]

[ADMONITION.]

**ADMONITION.**—This discourse, by which Marchesius closes the homilies of St Bruno, is no more fortunate than the preceding one. For the passages excerpted from the commentary on Matthew, no. 81, are connected by no bond with the praises of the holy martyrs. There is indeed something complete, said for another purpose. But what follows concerning those saints offers nothing distinctive about their glorious contest and does not savor of St Bruno’s style. It lacks the Gospel text, etc.

**Beginning:** “Not only had the blessed apostle Peter left behind, etc.”

**End:** “They glory with him in heaven, ever crowned with laurel.”

[Col. 0863]

# THREE UNPUBLISHED SERMONS OF ST BRUNO, BISHOP OF ASTI AND SIGNI

[Col. 0863]

## SERMON ONE. ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

[Col. 0863B]

[ADMONITION.]

**ADMONITION.**—We have extracted this sermon from a thirteenth-century quarto parchment manuscript in the Library of San Marco, Florence, since it has not yet been printed in any edition of the works of St Bruno. Its similarity of style and the designation “holy bishop,” under which it is inscribed, provide sufficient grounds for the conjecture that it should be attributed to the same author.

For the edification of the faithful, dearest brethren, the final verse of the Gospel reading which has just sounded in your ears is pertinent: namely, that the Magi, guided by the star, came from the east to Bethlehem, entered the house in which the blessed Mother and Virgin remained with the Child, and, opening their treasures, offered the Lord three gifts—gold, frankincense, and myrrh—thereby confessing him to be true Lord, true man, and king. [Col. 0863C] Holy Church, indeed, never ceases daily to offer these gifts to her Lord and Savior. She offers frankincense when she confesses and believes that he is the true Lord, the creator of all things; myrrh when she maintains that he assumed the substance of our flesh, in which he willed to suffer and die for our salvation; gold when she does not doubt that he reigns eternally with the Father and the Holy Spirit, according to the prophet’s saying: “His dominion shall be multiplied, and of his kingdom there shall be no end.”

The offering of these gifts may also be understood otherwise, mystically. By gold is signified heavenly wisdom, according to Solomon’s words: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. XXI, 20); and elsewhere: “The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom” (Ps. XXXVI, 20). By frankincense, pure prayer; whence the Psalmist says: [Col. 0863D] “Let my prayer be directed, O Lord, as incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL, 2). For our pure prayer gives forth to the Lord a sweeter fragrance [Col. 0864B] than the smoke of incense; and as that smoke rises on high, so our prayer is directed to the Lord. By myrrh, the mortification of our flesh; whence, in the Song of Songs, Holy Church says concerning her faithful who contend for Christ even unto death: “My hands have distilled myrrh” (Cant. V, 5).

Therefore, we offer gold to the Lord when we shine in his sight with the light of heavenly wisdom. Of this the Psalmist says: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. I, 16). To fear the Lord, indeed, is to omit none of the good things that must be done; hence he says elsewhere: “Those who fear God lack nothing.” We offer frankincense when we direct pure prayer before him; myrrh when, through abstinence, mortifying our flesh together with its vices and desires, we bear the cross [Col. 0864C] after Jesus. Thus the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Luke IX, 13). Therefore, to bear the cross for Christ Jesus is to mortify our flesh by afflicting it for love of him.

Nor is it without mystery that the Magi returned to their own country by another way. Our country is the heavenly Jerusalem, the holy city, from which, through the fault of the first man—that is, by pride, disobedience, and eating the forbidden food—we have gone far away, to the farthest ends of the earth, according to the Psalmist’s saying: “My soul has long been a sojourner” (Ps. CXIX, 6) in a foreign land. Nothing is found more excellent than this country: nothing safer than its glory, nothing happier than its blessedness, [Col. 0864D] nothing sweeter than its love, nothing more fruitful than its labor; for it knows how to yield fruit a hundredfold. What exile has ever not longed to return to his country?

[Col. 0865A]

Who does not strive with all his might to have a lost inheritance restored to him? Who can ever forget a lost homeland? If, therefore, we wish to return to our heavenly country in order to receive an inheritance, we must return by another way—that is, by humbling ourselves to the Lord with all our strength. For God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart. Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God, obeying the divine commandments in all things and trampling visible and carnal desires underfoot. Thus, having returned by this way to our country, we shall enjoy in heaven, with the angels, the joys of eternal life, through the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

465. SERMON II. ON THE PURIFICATION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY.

[Col. 0865B]

[EDITORIAL NOTICE.]

EDITORIAL NOTICE.—From the same manuscript we likewise publish this second sermon, also previously unpublished. In it elegance shines forth no less than learning, and it seems wholly worthy of its author.

The Lord, creator and redeemer of the human race, who came down from heaven to earth for the salvation of all the people and did not wish to abolish the Law but rather to fulfil it, was today presented in the temple by his parents, clothed in the substance of our flesh, according to the ordinance of the Law. And although his undefiled mother, the Blessed Virgin Mary, who had not conceived from received seed, was bound by none of the legal ordinances, nevertheless, in order to show that she had borne God as man, observing the precept [Col. 0865C] of humility, “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things,” she came today with the Child to the threshold of the temple, bringing the prescribed offerings according to the rite of the Law. Because she was poor and could not use large and costly offerings, she offered what she could for her Son: turtledoves and doves.

Nor did the Lord without reason will that such animals should be offered for him: they lacked the bitterness of gall and, content with their own mates, observed a natural disposition toward chastity. Let us therefore consider most carefully what is mystically signified for us by the offering of these animals. But first let us consider the temple.

Those stones from which Solomon’s temple was built, hewn elsewhere, some polished, and carried thence by the builders, were found suitable for the building, so that in so great a work no sound of hammer or axe was heard. They signify the souls of the saints, [Col. 0865D] of whom Isaiah says: “Living stones roll over the earth.” And the Apostle says: “You, like living stones, are built up into spiritual houses.” They are hewn elsewhere and thus set suitably in the building, because holy souls are prepared in the present life through repentance, compunction of heart, and compassion for their neighbors; and thus, polished and clean, they are fittingly placed in the structure of the temple.

That wondrous temple built by Solomon therefore signifies the holy city Jerusalem, which the true Solomon—Christ, that is, the peaceful King—does not cease daily to build from living stones, that is, from the souls of the faithful. Hence the Psalmist’s words: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city” (Ps. CXXI, 3).

By the doves, moreover, which bear no bitterness of gall, [Col. 0866A] are signified the simple hearts of the blessed, who, always free from the savage goads of anger, always meditate upon heavenly things. Anger, infected by the contagion of poisons and obscuring reason so that it cannot discern the truth, disturbs the inward eye. Of it the Psalmist says: “My eye is troubled because of anger” (Ps. XXX, 10); hence the Apostle says: “Anger does not work the righteousness of God” (James I, 20).

By the turtledoves, however, which, content with their own mates, do not seek an alien lover, is signified the chastity of the outer and inner human being. Thus Augustine says in *The City of God*: “Virginity of the flesh is an untouched body; virginity of the soul is an incorrupt mind.” Concerning outward chastity the Lord also says: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke XII, 35); and through [Col. 0866B] Moses he commands the children of Israel: “You shall gird your loins” (Ezek. XII, 11). To gird the loins or reins is, having uprooted every defilement of lust and every carnal desire, to bind them with the firm bonds of chastity, according to the Apostle’s words: “Mortify your bodies, which are according to wrath” (Col. III, 5).

Far be it from us to seek an alien lover—that is, the devil! For once we have come to Christ, we must by no means return to him. Let us therefore say with the Apostle: “I chastise my body and reduce it to slavery” (I Cor. IX, 27). I chastise it by trampling unlawful motions of the body; I reduce it to slavery by using lawful things sparingly. For to serve the Lord is secure freedom; and to die for his name is the beginning of new and eternal life. [Col. 0866C] Hence the same Apostle says: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I, 23); and David: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. CXV, 5); and elsewhere: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Rev. XIV, 13).

The chastity of the inner human being is to preserve the mind undefiled by every stain of sins. Hence through the outstanding preacher each faithful soul is told: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (II Cor. XI, 12); and through the Prophet: “Circumcise your hearts, and not your bodies” (Jer. IV, 4). May our Lord himself deign to grant this to you, etc.

466. SERMON III. ON THE FEAST OF ONE MARTYR.

[EDITORIAL NOTICE.]

[Col. 0866D] EDITORIAL NOTICE.—If we adorn our edition of Saint Bruno with this third previously unpublished sermon, we confess that we owe it to the utmost diligence and labor of the most reverend present abbot-bishop of Monte Cassino, Father and Lord Thomas Capomatius. He extracted it from manuscript 194 of the Cassinese archive, from which, as we have said, he generously communicated many other items. Something is lacking at the beginning, but the remainder appears complete and finished.

Moreover, the Lord himself was in them, giving increase to their seed.
