For, as the Apostle says: “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the increase” (I Cor. III, 7). Hence it is also added: “Because without me you can do nothing. And if anyone does not remain in me, he shall be cast forth like a branch, and shall wither; and they shall gather him, cast him into the fire, and he burns” (John XV, 6). For whoever does not remain in the faith of Christ [Col. 0867A] is cast out from the Church and the fellowship of the saints; he withers and dies, is seized by malignant spirits, is cast into eternal, unquenchable fire, and there he shall be tormented and burn without end.

“If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, whatever you will, you shall ask, and it shall be done for you” (I Cor. III, 7). Those remain in Christ who can be separated from his love, from his faith, and from his embraces by no consideration—neither by love nor fear, neither by disasters nor flatteries. In this manner the Apostle remained in Christ, when writing of himself he said: “For I am certain that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor strength, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature shall be able to separate us from the love of God [Col. 0867B] which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. VIII, 38).

Christ’s words remain in those who keep his commandments in their minds, believe them in their hearts, and never forget them. For the Lord’s commandment is: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Luke XII, 5). The Lord’s commandment is: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke IX, 13). The Lord’s commandment is: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate father and mother, brothers and sisters, etc., he cannot be my disciple” (Matt. XIV, 26).

These, then, and similar sayings are those words of which the Lord has just said: “If you remain in me, and my words [Col. 0867C] remain in you, whatever you will, you shall ask, and it shall be done for you” (John XV, 7). A great promise, a great and incomprehensible gift. Let those who remain in Christ, and in whom Christ’s words remain, ask whatever they wish, and it shall be done for them. For if they wish evil and ask evil, then they themselves no longer remain in Christ, nor do Christ’s words remain in them.

Let them therefore remember Christ’s words—or rather, not merely remember but hold them firmly; let them keep them in memory, and so ask as Christ’s words teach them to ask: “Seek first, therefore, the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things [Col. 0868A] shall be added to you” (Luke XI, 25). Let them ask in faith, without doubting, and ask for those things which pertain to salvation and are not contrary to the divine dispensation and the Gospel’s words.

But these things are said especially to the apostles, whose holy petitions the Lord always heard everywhere. For the Apostle asked the Lord, and asked three times; and he understood that he had been rightly heard by the Lord after he recognized that he had been asking against himself. A person is heard when what he wishes comes to pass. Now what the Apostle wished came to pass, because, after he understood that his petition was against himself, he did not wish to be heard. Hence he says: “I will gladly glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (II Cor. XII, 9).

For the text does not simply say here: “Whatever you ask,” but “Whatever you will [Col. 0868B] and ask shall be done for you. In this my Father has been glorified: that you bear much fruit and become my disciples.” In this, and for this purpose, with me revealing and teaching, my Father has been made manifest and glorified to you: so that you also, preaching and glorifying him everywhere, may bear much fruit, convert many nations to him, and become my disciples by imitating me—not only in life and teaching, but also in the working of miracles. For those are truly disciples who imitate their master in all things. Hence the Lord says elsewhere: “Those who believe in me shall themselves do the works that I do, and shall do works greater than these.” For such is the order and meaning.

It follows: “As the Father loved me, [Col. 0868C] I also have loved you; remain in my love” (John XV, 9). “If you keep my commandments, you shall remain in my love, as I too have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love. I have spoken these things to you that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be fulfilled.” Christ’s joy is in those who have such joy as Christ has, or in those whose holy manner of life gives Christ joy. Therefore they possess full joy, since in such joy grief and sorrow cannot exist.

[SENTENCES.]

[Col. 0867]

467. THE EDITOR TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS BISHOP LORD DOMINIC COPPOLA, SECRETARY OF THE SACRED CONGREGATION OF RITES.

[Col. 0867]

I earnestly desired, most illustrious bishop, to produce some testimony, consecrated to perpetual memory, of your merits toward me. You yourself provided me with such an opportunity by making available an anonymous letter published at Naples in 1788 and dedicated to the most learned advocate Lord Xavier Matthei. In it, the author, who identifies himself as a Carthusian, claims for his founder, Saint Bruno, the six books commonly called the *Sentences*, against the opinion of those who rightly maintain that they were written by Saint Bruno of Asti, bishop of Segni.

Your learning is well aware that this controversy did not arise recently, but was disputed long ago and for a long time between Benedictine and Carthusian writers, both sides contending for their respective opinions. Since the Benedictine position must be maintained for truth and for the merit of the cause, I undertake it. Having begun a new edition of the works of Saint Bruno of Asti, I must establish each work, show it to be his own, and reclaim whatever has been wrongly appropriated from him. Even before the Neapolitan letter reached my hands, I had brought this question to examination, weighed the arguments of the opposing writers, and carefully read the other writings of the same holy bishop of Segni. From these I became certain that the Carthusian writers had built their structure upon sand. For it is clearer than noonday light that a plagiarism was committed against Saint Bruno of Asti by those who asserted that Saint Bruno the Carthusian was the author of those books and published them among his works.

The first printing of these books was arranged by Guillaume Bibaucius, general superior of the Carthusians, in 1521, at the Paris press of Josse Badius Ascensius. Since that edition did not suffice for those demanding it, another was issued at Paris in 1524; a third appeared also at Cologne through the labor and diligence of the most learned Theodore Petraeus, a member of the Cologne Charterhouse, who dedicated it in 1611 to the most illustrious Lord Laurence Alamand, bishop of Grenoble. The first two editions of the works of Saint Bruno the Carthusian were divided into two volumes; the third into three, and in them the editors placed the six books of the *Sentences*. From that time until the year 1649, therefore, the opinion prevailed on the authority of Carthusian editors that Saint Bruno, founder of the Carthusian family, had been the author of the six books of the *Sentences*.

But when Dom Maurus Marchesius, a monk of Monte Cassino, first turned his attention to collecting the works of Saint Bruno, abbot of the same monastery and bishop of Segni, he was granted access to the very rich archive of manuscripts. He published a dissertation in which he openly demonstrated that those books had been falsely attributed to Saint Bruno the Carthusian, and by very strong documents showed that they should not be denied to Saint Bruno of Segni. Marchesius’s study appeared again in 1651, when the works of Saint Bruno of Asti were published at Venice by the Brentan presses.

Having completed these preliminaries for the controversy, most excellent bishop, I must add something concerning the life and writings of both Brunos. I shall say, therefore, that these most holy men were contemporaries, but that Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, died first, departing to heaven in 1101. Bruno, bishop of Segni, lived twenty-two years longer and, released from the bond of human flesh, was received among the blessed in 1123. As regards their writings, much has already been noted in the prolegomena and in the testimonies of ecclesiastical writers. From these it is clear that commentaries on the Pentateuch, the Book of Job, the Psalms, the Song of Songs, the Gospels, and the Apocalypse are conceded to Bruno of Asti without anyone dissenting. The works attributed to Bruno the Carthusian, on the other hand, are only an exposition of the Psalms and a commentary on the Epistles of Saint Paul.

The whole controversy concerns sermons on the praises, figures, and prerogatives of the Church, divided into six books and commonly called the books of the *Sentences*. We must therefore determine to which of the two Brunos they should be assigned. Who would refuse to accept as author the person who gives testimony in the disputed books concerning his own writings, who uses those writings very often, who includes much material word for word, and who treats subjects proper to himself? Since this person is our Saint Bruno, we shall have sufficiently ascertained and established that he composed the six books of the *Sentences*.

I proceed to demonstrate all this. In Book I, chapter 6, where Saint Bruno treats of the holy city Jerusalem and expounds its description mystically, after some remarks he says: “We have explained all these matters more fully in the Apocalypse, and this is not now the time for discussing each of them individually.” Likewise, in Book I, chapter 2, he who very often attacks Simoniacs and heretics in his commentaries says: “No animal enters the ark except through the door. But Simoniacs and heretics strive to enter the Church by another way. They do this because they are thieves and robbers,” etc. In the same chapter he describes the ecclesiastical hierarchy, from which it is evident that not a monk but a bishop wrote it.

A little later, citing Psalm LXXXV, “I shall remember Rahab and Babylon who know me,” he explains it in the same words with which he had illustrated it in his commentary on that Psalm. See p. 488, vol. I. Moreover, in Book II, chapter 4, entitled “On the Four Cardinal Virtues,” after setting forth what is to be understood in the construction and ornamentation of the ancient tabernacle, he concludes the exposition in these words: “Those four colors, which were everywhere placed together and never separately, signified these four virtues: namely, hyacinth, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted fine linen. We have spoken sufficiently of these in Exodus.”

Furthermore, in chapter 5 of the same book, treating “On the Virtue of Humility,” where he cites the divine command in Leviticus XXIII concerning the feast of Tabernacles, he gives the same mystical meaning which he had offered in his commentary on that passage of Leviticus. Likewise, in Book II, chapter 7, entitled “On Peace,” he illustrates the words of the Song of Songs, chapter VIII, “There was a vineyard for the peaceful one,” in a manner not unlike that in his commentary. Book III follows; and in chapter 8, entitled “On the New Sea and New Fishers,” when he uses the passage in Job XL, “Behemoth, which I made with you,” he does not depart from the interpretation given in that book, but faithfully repeats it.

Again, in Book IV, chapter 2, sermon 2, “On the Trinity,” he expresses the essence of the divine nature in the same words as he had employed in his commentary on Exodus III: “I am who I am. Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: He Who Is has sent me to you.” Likewise, in chapter 7 of Book IV, “On the Octave of Epiphany,” he recalls the Lord’s command to Moses to place two goats at the entrance of the tabernacle for sacrifice, and gives the same interpretation which he had given in his commentary on this passage of Exodus. Similarly, in sermon 2, “On Palm Branches,” under chapter 8 of the same book, where he cites Matthew chapter 21, he brings forward nothing but the same exposition of the Gospel. He does the same in sermon 2, chapter 10, Book IV, entitled “On the Preparation Day, or on the Resurrection of the Lord”; there he draws the whole explanation from the storehouse of his commentaries.

The following books also provide many passages from which it is plainly proved that Saint Bruno, when writing them, used his previously prepared interpretations of both Testaments. Thus, in Book V, chapter 2, citing Job XL; and likewise in Book VI, sermon 3, “On the Nativity of Many Martyrs,” the explanation of the passage of the Apocalypse is not dissimilar from that found in his commentary. But if these things were not yet sufficient, sermons 4 and 5 of Book VI, which are entitled concerning the same martyrs, settle the controversy with complete certainty, since they most plainly reproduce the exposition of Psalms CXXXI and CL. To avoid excessive length, I omit mention of sermon 6 of Book VI, since its exposition of Exodus chapter 28 seems entirely copied from the commentary. Since these arguments for assigning the six books of the *Sentences* to Bruno of Segni are so numerous and so clear, no fair judge will refuse to grant me that the case is complete and won.

But the pious and praiseworthy opposing writers should be heard, lest we seem to dismiss them contemptuously—especially the most learned Dom Benedict Trombius, member of the Neapolitan Charterhouse of Saint Martin. In 1775 he published at Naples a large volume, *Critical, Chronological, and Diplomatic History of Saint Bruno the Patriarch and of His Order*; in Book X, chapter 232, pp. 241–250, he treats at length the question of the author of the six books of the *Sentences*, which he judges should be assigned to his founder. There are chiefly four grounds on which the Carthusians support their case. The first is drawn from the antiquity and number of manuscript codices; the second, from the long possession of the opinion; the third, from the authority of the Sacred [Col. 0871] Congregation of Rites; the fourth, from the agreement of certain writers who ascribe the work to Saint Bruno the Carthusian.

First, they mention an outstanding manuscript of the Charterhouse of Saint Stephen of the Desert in Calabria. It had long been possessed by Cistercian monks, formerly inhabitants of that same monastery; when they departed, toward the end of the twelfth century, they left it to the new Carthusian residents. This manuscript bore the name of the holy patriarch. When it was brought to the Great Charterhouse near Grenoble, and other similar and uniform manuscripts were found in the same monastery, they moved the highly esteemed Dom Guillaume Bibaucius, general superior, a man whom they call holy and learned, to arrange for the printing at Paris, as we have said, of the books of the *Sentences* together with the remaining works of the holy founder.

This sort of argument, which formerly might have carried some weight, is now considered very weak, since the Benedictines of the Congregation of Saint-Maur removed from their editions of Saints Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, and other Fathers many writings that ancient but unskilled copyists had falsely attributed to them. Let me, however, oppose to these the testimony of other manuscripts equally ancient, in which the name of Bruno, bishop of Segni, is likewise found inscribed. First I shall mention two Vatican manuscripts, nos. 994 and 1264, in quarto. They bear not so much at the beginning but at the start of each book of the *Sentences* the heading: “Of Lord Bruno, bishop of Segni.” One is of the twelfth century, the other of the thirteenth.

Moreover, I shall cite manuscript 36 of the Vallicellian Library, parchment folio, and a manuscript of the Florentine Library of Saint Mark, Order of Preachers, in quarto, likewise parchment, very neatly written in the twelfth century. I compared them with Marchesius’s edition. Of the same age is Cassinese manuscript 196 [otherwise 317], carefully collated, as I said in the preface, by the very learned bishop Stephen Borgia, now deservedly a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. Slightly later is the Turin manuscript of the Royal Athenaeum Library, no. 787, c. 11, 23, which bears the name of our Saint Bruno [469] and contains the aforesaid books of the *Sentences*.

But three other manuscripts provide still fuller proof. The most illustrious Philip Amedeus Millo, canon of the metropolitan church of Turin—whom I have frequently commended—in a letter of 28 June 1786 informed me of them. He says that he found the first in Savoy: a parchment manuscript of excellent quality, dating from the twelfth century, containing the six books of the *Sentences*, whose titles and numbering he reports:

1. On the Figures of the Church.  
2. On the Ornaments of the Church.  
3. On the New World.  
4. On Festivals.  
5. On the Festivals of the Blessed Virgin Mary and of the Saints.  
6. The book concerning the festivals of martyrs, confessors, and virgins is contained in Book V.

He observed written at its beginning: “The books of Master Bruno, bishop of Segni”; but the words “bishop of Segni” had been erased and replaced by: “founder of the Carthusians.” The prefect of the library of the Great Charterhouse of Grenoble supplied the remaining two in writing. They plainly bear the name of Bruno, bishop of Segni; he affirms that they are very well written in Roman script and judges that they should be dated to the twelfth century. Since far more manuscripts, distinguished by antiquity and authority, name Saint Bruno of Asti as author of the six books of the *Sentences*, the Carthusian opposition completely collapses and vanishes on this ground.

Nor is the second argument, concerning long and peaceful possession of the opinion assigning the books to Bruno the Carthusian, maintained any better. Before Marchesius no one had thought of publishing the writings of Bruno of Segni, and no one had consulted the Cassinese manuscripts for this purpose; consequently no controversy arose. But scarcely had Marchesius recognized that writings belonging to Saint Bruno had been usurped and attributed to the Carthusian patriarch than he at once exposed the plagiarism and proved that Bruno of Segni, formerly superior of that same Cassinese monastery, must be held their genuine author. Who would say that the ignorance of obscure times proves anything, when we possess so many and such excellent manuscript testimonies, all of which agree most fully in favor of our Bruno? Later ages render this service to the republic of letters: through the study and diligence of posterity, uncertain knowledge of matters becomes more certain, and, if any error has crept in, it is expelled by the light of more rigorous criticism.

The Carthusians—and especially the anonymous Neapolitan writer—derive their third argument from the authority of the Sacred Congregation of Rites. It permitted the Carthusians to recite certain lessons in the breviary peculiar to their order, lessons drawn from the disputed sermons. From this they argue that the Sacred Congregation approved those lessons published under the name of Saint Bruno the Carthusian, not under that of the bishop of Segni. This is easily refuted, because it is known to all that the Sacred Congregation of Rites abstains from judgment in controversies of this sort when nothing contrary to the faith is involved, and permits certain rites, such as particular lessons, to individual churches or bodies of religious, although it forbids them in the universal Church. The agreement of writers, the fourth point, ought to be discussed; but the testimonies amassed in the prolegomena are more than sufficient.

Passing over other arguments of the slightest weight, we must linger briefly over the objection that appears to have some force. I note beforehand that the anonymous Neapolitan author, on p. 24 of his letter, assumes that in the list of sermons, etc., there are two bearing this title: “On basilicas dedicated by bishops.” First, I say there is only one. It is placed seventh in the first book of the *Sentences* by the two Vatican manuscripts, and likewise bears this title in other manuscript codices and in Marchesius’s edition. Second, I say that Saint Bruno, bishop of Segni, performed two dedications of churches, as his *Life*, chapters 7 and 9, records; hence it is likely that he delivered this sermon on the occasion of one or the other dedication.

Third, I add that throughout this sermon “On Basilicas” nothing appears that can properly be referred to religious men; indeed, it seems to be a discourse addressed to the people. The words “dearest brethren” are entirely absent from the manuscripts and editions mentioned; yet even if they were present, they could have been used in addressing the people. Nor does the document published by the anonymous Carthusian in the cited letter, p. 25, prove anything. It reports that in 1094 Archerius, archbishop of Palermo, consecrated a church of the Carthusians in Calabria, dedicated in honor of God and the Blessed Virgin Mary. Yet the charter merely records that “Master Bruno, Lanuinus, and the other hermit brethren” were present at that dedication, together with other good men. The assertion that Bruno the patriarch preached on that occasion is gratuitous and supported by no firm argument.

On the contrary, I shall demonstrate most conclusively that our Saint Bruno was the author of the sermon “On Basilicas Ordained by Bishops.” In the sermon “On the Tabernacle of the Covenant,” which is the third in Book I of the *Sentences*, he had said that at that time he did not wish to explain individually everything signified by its parts and figures, but reserved all this for another occasion. Our Bruno fulfilled this in two ways: first, in the discourse “On Basilicas,” or, as others title it, “On the Dedication of a Church”; second, in a separate treatise written most fully and learnedly, which we shall publish in this volume. Let the Carthusians therefore show that this work was composed by their founder, and produce one writer who has assigned it to him. But if in all editions the name of Saint Bruno of Asti, bishop of Segni, is found prefixed to that treatise, it will be entirely certain that our Bruno, not Bruno the Carthusian, must be declared to have rendered excellent service through such ecclesiastical learning and doctrine.

The same opponents further say: If the defenders of Saint Bruno of Asti insist on assigning the books of the *Sentences* to him, [Col. 0873] what sermons will they leave to Saint Bruno the patriarch, when not a few affirm that, besides expositions on the Psalms and the Epistles of Saint Paul, he wrote several moral discourses? I do not wish to support those writers—namely Le Long, Cave, and Mabillon—who allow only those commentaries to Bruno the Carthusian. But I shall say rather that the discourses of that most holy man either still lie hidden or are confused with other works of uncertain authorship. Indeed, whoever carefully examines the books of the *Sentences* will find not sermons or treatises addressed to monk-brethren or to an uneducated rustic people, but highly polished compositions of a bishop instructing clergy and cultivated hearers, and explaining more elevated doctrines.

One passage may stand for all: in Book VI, chapter 1, “On Paradise.” After giving an exposition of the place of paradise in which the first man Adam was set, he adds: “But what should we understand by Adam except the guardians of the Church—that is, bishops and priests? Let these men hear what Scripture says about Adam, who was sent into paradise in order to work and guard it. Let them not be idle, because they are workers; let them keep watch, because they are guardians.”

At what time our Saint Bruno wrote the Books of Sentences, although he mentions some of his other works, he is altogether silent about these. Nevertheless, it may be inferred that he composed them when, having relinquished the government of the monastery of Cassino, he returned to his church at Segni. For by then he had already completed his commentaries on both Testaments, and he made use of them in writing these books. Since, as we have established in his Life, he lived twelve years after returning to his episcopal office, it is probable that he produced this work of Sentences during that period.

I must answer the second objection of the Carthusians. I am indeed astonished how they could think they saw agreement of meaning and similarity of expression between the Books of Sentences and the commentaries on the Psalms and on the Epistles of St Paul, when our Bruno is entirely unlike and discordant with them. Lest I be endless, I shall collect a few instances here as representative of all; the rest may be inferred from these.

For, in chapter 13 on the words of Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians, “Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels,” after explaining the literal meaning concerning the properties of charity, St Bruno the Carthusian treats of the abolition of knowledge—namely, that in the vision of God human knowledge will be wholly destroyed, and so forth. Yet our Bruno has not a word on this subject, but wonderfully expounds and commends the excellence of charity. Nor does anything occur in chapter 14 of the same commentary that agrees with the teaching of Bruno of Asti, who discusses the same virtue. The Carthusian, rather, is wholly occupied with explaining the words, “Though I speak with the tongues of men,” etc., while treating of the different kinds of tongues and of prophecy.

Likewise, no one will discover any similarity or relation between the aforesaid commentaries of St Bruno the Carthusian on chapter 11 of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians and the sermon of the bishop of Segni, “On the Virtue of Patience.” The Carthusian expounds St Paul’s meaning: that the Corinthians ought to bear with his inadequacy, by which nevertheless he teaches them the truth, lest they believe false teachers and false prophets who preach false and perverse things in order to deceive souls. Bruno of Asti, on the other hand, delivers a discourse on patience as a Christian virtue most necessary and most richly meritorious.

Bruno the Carthusian treats of the chastity of marriage in his commentary on chapter 7 of First Corinthians. First he speaks of the guilt of fornication, then of continence—when and for whom it is necessary. He asks whether St Paul took a wife or remained a virgin. Finally, he asks whether there is a command concerning virginity. But our Saint Bruno, taking another path in chapter 3 of Book II, sets himself to commend the excellence of the virtue of chastity. He teaches that abstinence from every work of the flesh is necessary for those who have either vowed chastity or chosen it as a virtue for themselves without a religious vow.

The fourth chapter of the same book is entitled by our Bruno, “On the Cardinal Virtues.” Yet, having compared it with what Bruno the Carthusian commented upon Psalm 35, which begins, “The unjust man said, that he might sin within himself,” I found not even a trace showing that our author had taken anything from the teaching of that commentary. I do not hesitate to say the same concerning “Peace,” the title of chapter 7 of the same book. For throughout that Psalm—namely Psalm 82—in which the Prophet sings of the scattered enemies of the people of Israel and of peace secured for that people, Bruno the Carthusian attempts nothing but the exposition of the words and names contained in the psalm. Our author passes over all this, but shows the usefulness of peace and God’s exceptional benefit toward humankind.

Since these matters are sufficiently clear and proved, I think no one will take offence if I assert that the Carthusians, defenders of their patriarch, have not sufficiently examined either his commentaries or the Books of Sentences of Bruno of Asti. Had they devoted themselves to reading and comparing them, they would have refrained from defending this cause.

Nor should they think to press me by saying that the sermons “On Obedience” and “On Abstinence,” which are numbers 10 and 11 of Book II, give no obscure indication that they were composed not by a bishop but by a man devoted to sacred contemplation, such as St Bruno the Carthusian was. For in the first, on obedience, the anonymous Neapolitan reports on page 28 these words: “What, then, shall disobedient monks say, who do their own wills and thereby do not please God, when the entire monastic religious life consists in obedience, and without obedience there is nothing?” In the other, on abstinence, likewise commending it to monks, he says: “It is the saying of the elders: Let the monk eat in such a way that he is always hungry; and let the bishop drink in such a way that he does not know whether he has drunk.”

Whoever reads these treatises or sermons will admit that these things were said in passing by Bruno of Asti, formerly a monk. For he did not treat expressly of the perfection of abstinence and obedience, to which monks are bound to devote themselves; rather, he gathered and set forth common teachings, suitable also for men living in the world, drawn from the sacred writings and already treated in his commentaries. From this very repetition of passages and Sentences from both Testaments—contained in almost the same words in these and other sermons, as also in other writings certainly composed by our Bruno—there arises so powerful an argument for confirming my opinion that no room for doubt remains.

A few matters remain to be refuted which the same anonymous Neapolitan author brings forward from Jodocus Badius Ascensius. First, in the sermon “On Basilicas Consecrated by Bishops,” also called “On the Dedication of a Church,” the preacher plainly says that he is not a bishop. Second, it is not irrationally argued that the Books of Sentences ought to be assigned to Bruno of Asti, because they mention commentaries on Exodus and the Apocalypse, which may be said either to have been lost or not yet brought out of obscurity. Third, nothing better follows from the fact that the same author frequently calls himself a son of St Benedict and calls Benedict his patriarch and parent; for the Carthusians too can acknowledge themselves bound to St Benedict under the same titles, since St Benedict was the patriarch of all monks in the West, and Bruno drew many things from his laws for establishing his own community.

To the first objection I reply that the author of that sermon would call himself neither monk nor bishop; but from what he has argued he shows himself rather to be representing the person of a bishop than that of a monk. The second objection rests upon a pitiful evasion. Even if the loss of the commentaries on Exodus and the Apocalypse, which are ascribed to Bruno the Carthusian, is granted, must the same be supposed concerning the remaining interpretations of Holy Scripture, from which the author everywhere draws authorities and examples and illustrates his own lucubrations? Shall we affirm that they suffered the same misfortune? But it is ridiculous to invent dreams of this sort and to withhold credit from writers of the highest authority.

[Col. 0875]

By way of conclusion, I shall say that St Bruno the Carthusian nowhere calls St Benedict his parent or his patriarch; whereas Bruno of Segni adorns him not only with these titles but with clear praises as well. I shall offer one or two testimonies out of many. In chapter 4 of Book II of the *Sentences* he says:

> “Blessed Benedict also, whose authority is greatest—since the Holy Spirit spoke in him—likewise commands that there be nothing excessive.”

And in sermon 4, entitled “On the Same Martyrs,” mystically expounding that passage of Genesis, chapter 26, in which it is narrated that the servants of Isaac dug a well, etc., he says of St Benedict:

> “But what shall I say of blessed Benedict, who made so excellent a well, whose most healthful and most sweet water benefits all who thirst and wish to drink, both for refreshment and for salvation? After the Apostles and Evangelists no well has been made which has satisfied so many people and delivered them from the danger of death and from every affliction,” etc.

I pass over chapter 16 of his Life, where it is said how great was our Bruno’s love for the Benedictine order and how great his commendation of regular observance—things that could not have been expressed with such zeal by another unless he had professed the institution of that same holy patriarch.

To summarize the entire dissertation briefly, it will be useful to remember that far more manuscript codices ascribe the Books of Sentences to St Bruno of Asti, and that in them he transferred very many things from his commentaries, in their very sense and their very wording. We have also said that the similarity of style and the complete agreement in the interpretation of the divine Scriptures are manifest in these books and in the other works of the holy bishop of Segni. We have likewise plainly shown that our Bruno transferred nothing from the commentaries of the Carthusian into the Books of Sentences. We consider equally overthrown and wholly destroyed the objections produced by Carthusian writers in defence of their cause; nor have we passed over anything to which the fullest answer has not been given.

Finally, Natalis Alexander settles the entire controversy. In volume VII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, centuries XI and XII, article 9, he says of Bruno of Asti:

> “He likewise composed many sermons, among which Peter the Deacon enumerates those in chapter 34 of his book *On Illustrious Men of Cassino*, which Theodore Petraeus, a pupil of the Carthusian house of Cologne, published under the name of St Bruno the patriarch in volume III of his works. Yet they are certainly not his, as both the authority of Peter the Deacon and other monuments demonstrate.”

Therefore, most learned prelate, I ask you to receive favourably and graciously this work of vindication for St Bruno, bishop of Segni, and to admonish the anonymous Neapolitan that I have intended nothing other than to defend the truth of my opinion, supported by so many and such great arguments, and to establish it more firmly among learned persons after every doubt has been removed. Farewell.

[Col. 0875]

# THE SENTENCES OF ST BRUNO OF ASTI, BISHOP OF SEGNI

[Col. 0875]

# BOOK I. ON THE FIGURES OF THE CHURCH

## 472 PROLOGUE

[Col. 0875A]

Since there are many, indeed almost innumerable, things in the divine books that signify the bride of Christ, the holy Church, yet there are certain things in which her praises and greater mysteries seem to be contained more clearly and fully. Such, for example, are Paradise with its trees and rivers, and the ark which Noah built at God’s command. Likewise, the tabernacle which Moses constructed; likewise, too, the temple which Solomon built. The Church is also figured by a woman, as the Song of Songs plainly shows. The holy city Jerusalem likewise, and the basilicas now everywhere dedicated by bishops, openly signify the Church of God. Concerning these, therefore, in the order in which they have been set forth, we shall explain—not indeed everything, but such matters as may suit the time and subject—with the Lord’s help in what follows.

## CHAPTER I. On Paradise

Moses wrote in the book of Genesis [Note: [Col. 0875A] A comparison of Marchesius’s text with the Paris edition of St Bruno the Carthusian by Jodocus Badius Ascensius, 1534, folio, and with the manuscript codices noted below.] that “the Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning, and in it he placed the man whom he had formed, that he might cultivate and guard it” (Gen. 2:8). There he relates that every tree beautiful to behold and pleasant for food had been planted; there also the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. From one fountain, he says, four rivers proceed, by which all that land is watered.

We must therefore say what Paradise signifies; what Adam, the guardian of Paradise, signifies; what those kinds of trees, so many and so noble, signify; and what those rivers signify. Paradise is interpreted “a garden of delights,” and concerning this garden the Lord speaks to the Church in the Song of Songs, saying: “Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits of apple trees” (Song 4:3). This is as though he said: Great are your gifts; pleasing are your presents. Others send a portion and give to others what is of little value; but you give the whole garden, and with a generous hand entrust and bestow every better thing upon your children [Note: [Col. 0877D] Codex of St Mark, Florence: “and upon your friends”; likewise both Vatican codices.] and your friends.

Of this garden [Note: [Col. 0877D] The same codex of St Mark, Florence: “Concerning which garden.”] he says in the same place: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, and a fountain sealed” (Song 4:12). Let thieves therefore be shut out [Note: [Col. 0877D] Ascensian edition of St Bruno the Carthusian: “Let them withdraw”; likewise the Vatican codices.]; let the devil too withdraw, prince of thieves, who always goes about seeking whom he may devour. The garden is enclosed, the fountain sealed: he can steal neither fruit nor water. For the Lord himself bears witness to this, saying: “My sheep hear my voice, and I, the Lord, give them eternal life; nor shall anyone snatch them from my hand” (John 10:27). But concerning those who are deceived and snatched away by the devil, the apostle John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19).

Again, in the same book: “I went down into my garden to see the fruits of the valleys, to see whether the vines had blossomed and the pomegranates had budded” (Song 6:10). In the Gospel too it is said of the Lord: “For he went out across the brook Cedron, where there was a garden, into which he himself and his disciples entered” (John 18:1). From these and similar passages it is evident that by the garden—that is, by Paradise—the Church is signified.

But what are we to understand by Adam, except the guardians of the Church, namely bishops and priests? Let these, then, hear what Scripture says of Adam, who was placed in Paradise for this purpose: to cultivate and guard it. Let them not be idle, for they are labourers; let them keep watch, for they are guardians. This is what the Apostle also did, who [Note: [Col. 0878D] The same edition: “Who continually devoted himself to preaching”; likewise a Vatican codex.] devoted himself to preaching and worked with his own hands to provide his livelihood. Hence the Psalmist says: “You shall eat the labours of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. 127:2).

But it must especially be noted what the Lord said concerning Adam after he had sinned [Note: [Col. 0878D] Vatican Codex 994: “See lest perhaps,” etc.]: “Lest perhaps he take also from the tree of life and live for ever,” etc. (Gen. 3:22). After his sin the tree of life is forbidden him, though it had not previously been forbidden. The tree of life is Christ, of whom the Psalmist says: “And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of waters, which shall give its fruit in its season” (Ps. 1:3). And elsewhere: “She is a tree of life to those who grasp her, and blessed is he who holds her fast” (Prov. 3:18). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “If they do these things in the green wood, what shall be done in the dry?” (Luke 23:31).

Let those, therefore, to whom Christ’s body and blood are forbidden on account of their sins beware lest they presume to approach the tree of life. Let them hear the Apostle saying: “For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:29). Therefore the tree of life is the flesh of Christ, of which the Lord himself says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6:55).

But the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is understood as the sin of disobedience. For as often as we sin, so often do we eat from this tree, because we are disobedient to God, who forbade sin. Great is the sin of disobedience, by which the whole world perished; great is the virtue of obedience, by which the whole world was saved. The first man, made disobedient, destroyed himself and us; the second man became obedient unto death, in order to save us.

This tree is called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil because then the first human beings understood their good and their evil—that is, their blessedness and their misery—after they had eaten from this tree. For just as health is understood through illness, sweetness through bitterness, and light through darkness, so blessedness is known through misery. Nor does one who has never been ill perfectly know how great a good health is.

But what shall we say of the other trees with which that place of delights was planted? We read in the writings of the ancients—and Solinus [Col. 0878C] also testifies to this—that in certain regions there are trees whose fragrant sweetness so satisfies people that they require no other food. How great, then, do we think the delight, sweetness, fragrance, and fruitfulness of the trees of Paradise must be, if even those outside it are such? By these trees, however, we understand the children of the Church.

A good tree was blessed Paul, who laboured more than them all. Good also was he who said: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God” (Ps. 51:10). Such also are those of whom it is said: “Your sons are like young olive shoots around your table” (Ps. 127:3). Such likewise are those to whom the Lord says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you to go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John 15:16). Behold, such are the trees of the Church; nor are they inferior to those, but rather so much the better [Note: [Col. 0878D] Codex of St Mark, Florence, and the edition: “because reality is better than a figure.” Likewise both Vatican codices and the Ascensian edition.] as reality is better than a figure. Greater sweetness of fragrance, greater abundance of fruit, and the sweetness of a greater delight are found in them.

Let Christians, who are signified by the trees of Paradise, beware lest they be fruitless; for no tree is recorded to have been fruitless. But what are the four rivers flowing from the fountain, except the four Evangelists receiving the teaching of faith from the one breast of Christ [Note: [Col. 0879D] The cited edition: “shall we understand?”]? By these rivers the whole world is watered; by the abundance of their teaching the whole Church is made fruitful and healed. Hence the Psalmist says: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45:5). And elsewhere: “The rivers have lifted up, O Lord, the rivers have lifted up their voice” (Ps. 92:4).

It is reported that the rivers named above possess such sweetness of taste that they surpass the pleasantness of every drink; and that they do not lose this sweetness until it is spoiled by rivers rushing into them. This too seems well suited to our rivers, that is, the holy Gospels: their sweetness is very often corrupted by the waters of heretics; but unless they have been corrupted by these, nothing can equal them.

Wretched is the man who lost such blessedness through his disobedience; wretched, who lost such delights and, cast out of Paradise, after infinite miseries rushed into death. For it is written that the Lord cast Adam out of Paradise: “And he placed before the paradise of delight cherubim and a flaming, turning sword, to guard the way to the tree of life” (Gen. 3:23). We see this also in the Church of God: sinners unwilling to obey are daily seen driven from her by the sword of God’s word. For if God did not spare the first man, how shall he spare others who imitate him?

Let us therefore keep obedience; let us imitate the master of obedience, “who, though he was in the form of God, humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. 2:6). To him, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER II. On Noah’s Ark

It is right that so great a multitude of peoples should gather from every direction for the dedication of churches. For the holy Church is signified by that ark into which so innumerable a multitude of every kind of animal entered. Thus you have it written in the book of Genesis (Gen. 6:14) that the Lord commanded Noah to make for himself an ark of smoothed timbers, to make chambers in it, and to coat it within and without with pitch. He also commanded him to make in it a door and a window, and to finish its top in one cubit. “And Noah entered it, with his sons, his wife, and the wives of his sons with him. And animals, both clean and unclean, entered into it” (Gen. 7:7).

Let us therefore see what this ark signifies; what the smoothed timbers signify; what the chambers and pitch signify; what the door and window signify; and what the clean and unclean animals signify. For it is written of this ark: “Arise, O God, into your rest, you and the ark of your sanctification” (Ps. 131:8). This ark, therefore, is the holy Church, outside which no one is saved, and whoever is found in her on the day of vengeance shall not perish. Many seem to be in her who will then be found outside her, like those to whom the Lord says [Note: [Col. 0879D] Cited edition: “Amen, I say to you.”]: “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). Those, therefore, will be in her of whom the Saviour says: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24). Hence he says elsewhere: “If anyone does not remain in me, he shall be cast out like a branch and shall wither; and they shall gather him and cast him into the fire, and he burns” (John 15:6). For as the first punishment was by water, so the second vengeance will be by fire.

Thus this ark is the Church. What are the smoothed timbers except human beings? Christian human beings, indeed: timbers hewn by the tool of faith, smoothed by the sword of the Holy Spirit, and anointed and joined by the pitch of charity. Such timbers were those of whom it is said: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and no one said that anything was his own, but all things were common to them” (Acts 2:32).

[Note: [Col. 0879D] Vatican Codex: “Let canons rejoice in so great a privilege,” etc. Vatican Codex 1254 reads: “Let monks rejoice.” [Col. 0880D] Likewise the Ascensian edition.]

Let monks rejoice in so great a privilege, for they have one spirit and nothing is private property. For pitch is said to have such a nature that it joins timbers coated with it indissolubly and preserves them uncorrupted. Charity is therefore fittingly designated by pitch, since it is greater than all virtues and without it no virtue is anything. It also joins enemies together, and makes those whom it joins eternal and incorruptible. Therefore let it anoint and join us inwardly by love and outwardly by action. Let it suffer with others in the heart and work through the hands. For this is what “You shall coat it within and without” means (Gen. 6:14).

The many chambers in one ark are the many peoples in one Church. The chambers are different, and the orders and ways of life are different; for the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14:2). “For one star differs from another in glory” (1 Cor. 15:41).

Clean and unclean animals remain in their chambers; they rest and have peace. No one harms another; no one wrongs another. Yet, what is greatly to be lamented, human beings are often more cruel than beasts. [Note: [Col. 0880D] Likewise the codex and Ascensian edition: “Their own chambers suffice for them, but their own possessions do not suffice for these.” Likewise Vatican Codex 954 and Codex 1254.] Their possessions suffice for them. Therefore, if there was no discord or persecution within the ark, then without doubt, whoever hates brothers and breaks the bond of charity is not of the Church, though he may seem to be in the Church.

But what do we understand by the door and the window? Let the Lord himself speak: “I,” he says, “am the door; if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” (John 10:7). Therefore those who do not enter through the door are not saved. No animal enters the ark except through the door. But simoniacs and heretics strive to enter the Church by another way. They do this because they are thieves and robbers.

The windows are those who supply the Church with light; hence the Lord says to his disciples: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14). Blessed Paul was a great window, who was blinded by the Lord so that he might enlighten many. Nor is it without mystery that he says: “And you shall finish its top in one cubit” (Gen. 6:16). One cubit is the one God, in whom all our completion and perfection lie. “The Lord is exalted above all nations, and his glory above the heavens” (Ps. 112:4). He is our head; we are his members [Note: [Col. 0881D] Codex of St Mark: “In him we are made one and joined together, and we are one.” Likewise both Vatican codices.].

For this reason the ark was broad below, but narrow above, and finished in one cubit: because the holy Church is broad and great in those subject to it, but is brought to completion in one father and teacher. Hence the Lord says: “For one is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. 23:9). Finally, the wicked are far more numerous than the good; more seek earthly than heavenly things. Narrow is the way that leads to life; broad is that which leads to destruction.

If anyone wishes also to consider the orders of the Church—how clerics rank above the laity, priests above clerics, bishops above priests, archbishops above bishops, patriarchs above them in order, and finally the Roman pontiff seated above all—he may understand in this way too how the ark of God, broad in its lower parts, gradually narrows and is completed in one cubit.

The clean and unclean animals appear to signify the righteous and sinners alike. For good and evil, righteous and sinners, grain and chaff, tares and wheat live together in the Church of God. They live from one bread and drink from one cup; and to show themselves to be brothers, all say with one harmonious voice: “Our Father who art in heaven” (Matt. 6:9). [Note: [Col. 0881D] The same Codex of St Mark: “And do not be called masters, for one is your master, Christ.”]

Nor is it without mystery that human beings and birds occupied the upper place in the ark, while beasts of burden, cattle, and similar creatures lived below. Those who imitate the nature of birds ought to be set above others in the holy Church. Therefore, whoever desires to be above others should devote himself to wisdom and religion, fly higher in mind, and be raised in spirit to heavenly things. But those are rightly lower and unworthy of every honour and dignity who, given over to the desires of the flesh and to pleasures alone, follow the nature of beasts of burden—a nature that their very downward inclination and obedience to the belly have fashioned.

It remains now to speak of the raven, which went out from the ark and neglected thereafter to return to it. By it are figured those who, separated from the Church for their offences, disdain to return to her thereafter. Such were Arius and Sabellius, and such were the Donatists, who, divided from the Church because of their iniquities [Note: [Col. 0881D] The same Codex of St Mark: “unworthy of honour and dignity.” [Col. 0882D]], refused to return to her and be reconciled to her. Hence not undeservedly every kind of raven is called unclean.

[Note: [Col. 0882D] Vatican Codex: “But what indeed”; likewise the Ascensian edition.]

But by the dove, which returned to the ark with a branch of green olive [Note: [Col. 0882D] The same codex: “with green leaves.”], who are signified except those who are gentle, wise, and humble? Because they love peace and concord, whenever they understand that the Church of God and the congregation of their brothers has been stirred up against them in any way, they immediately humble themselves, return to it prepared to make every satisfaction, offer peace, and humbly seek mercy.

Therefore, whoever fears to perish and desires to be saved must not depart from the unity of the Church. Let him hear the Lord saying: “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49). He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER III. On the Tabernacle of the Covenant
“How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs for and fails away [Note: Vatican codex 1254: “My soul has longed for and failed away.”] in the courts of the Lord!” (Ps. 83:1). Although he had used the plural, “tabernacles,” he immediately added not concerning many tabernacles but concerning one house, saying: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (ibid., v. 5). Hence elsewhere he says: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26:5).

The Apostle writes of three tabernacles: the first exists in shadow and figure; the second in figure and truth; while the third consists in truth alone. For he says: “The first tabernacle was made, in which were the lampstands, the table, and the setting forth of the loaves, which is called the Holy Place. But after the second veil was the tabernacle called the Holy of Holies, having a golden censer and the ark of the covenant covered all around with gold. In it was a golden vessel containing manna, and Aaron’s rod which had put forth leaves, and the tablets of the Covenant” (Heb. 9:2 ff.). Concerning the third he says thus: “Christ, appearing as High Priest of the good things to come, entered through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made by hands—that is, not of this creation—nor through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood, once for all into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption” (ibid., v. 11).

The first tabernacle, therefore, is understood as the Synagogue; the second as the Church; the third as heaven itself. “We have a high priest who has passed through heaven,” as the Apostle says, “Jesus Christ our Lord, and there indeed he now appears before the face of God for us” (Heb. 4:14).

The first tabernacle, therefore—that is, the Synagogue—has its lampstands, by which we undoubtedly understand the patriarchs and prophets, through whose teaching and knowledge that people was illuminated when the other nations sat in darkness and in the gloom of the shadow of death. Moses, however, set down not “lampstands” but a “lampstand,” signifying Christ, the true light, from whom, as from one stem, all the other lampstands proceed. This lampstand, therefore, is both one and many: one in its stem, but many in the branches proceeding from that one stem.

But what is signified by the table except the books of the Law and the Prophets? The setting forth of the loaves is their very understanding. Concerning this table it is written: “Let their table before them become a snare, a recompense, and a stumbling block” (Ps. 68:22). “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6).

And the fact that the lampstand stood before the table, so as to illuminate the table and shed its light upon the loaves placed upon it—what else, we think, does this signify except what blessed John writes in his Apocalypse: “I saw a book sealed with seven seals, and no one was found worthy, neither in heaven nor on earth nor beneath the earth, to open the book and loose its seven seals; and I wept greatly. And it was said to me: Do not weep; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered, to open the book and loose its seven seals” (Rev. 5:4–5). For if the table is signified by the book, what is it to loose the book except to illuminate the table? He himself, therefore, is both lion and lampstand; for the opening of the book is nothing other than the illumination of the table.

Now a veil was placed between the two tabernacles, lest perhaps those who were in the first tabernacle should be able to see what was done in the second. [Note: The same codex of St Mark: “To this day, when Moses is read, a veil,” as the Apostle says, “is placed,” etc.] For to this day, when Moses is read, “a veil,” as the Apostle says, “is placed before the face of the Jews” (2 Cor. 3:15). [Note: The Vulgate reads: “over their heart.”] This veil, however, was removed when the veil of the Temple was torn. From that time onward the Holy of Holies has been revealed to all who believe in Christ; but the rest remained in their blindness, “so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand” (Rom. 9:8).

Let us now consider the second tabernacle. “After the veils,” he says, “is the second tabernacle, which is called the Holy of Holies.” How much more perfect [Note: Vatican codex: “more excellent,” or rather.] the second tabernacle is than the first is openly demonstrated by its very name. But what is signified by the golden censer except the apostles and teachers, who by the sweetness of their fragrance filled both heaven and earth? Blessed Paul carries such a censer, speaking of himself and others: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place, among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing. To some we are an odor of life unto life; to others, an odor of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2:15).

The Lord himself also carries a censer; sensing its fragrance, the Church says: “Draw me after you, and we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:4). Hence it is also written that the angel received a censer and filled it with fire from the altar: “And the smoke of the aromatic offerings rose before the Lord from the hand of the angel” (Rev. 8:4). The angels are teachers, whose breasts are censers; their words and prayers, like the smoke of aromatic offerings, are pleasing to the Lord.

And because [Note: Vatican codex: “But that.”] the ark of the Covenant was covered everywhere, within and without, with the purest gold, what else does this signify except that the holy Church shines entirely in word and deed, wisdom and devotion? Those, therefore, are not her members who willingly defile themselves with the contagion of vices. For of her it is written: “One is my dove, my perfect one, my spotless one” (Song 6:8).

The golden vessel containing manna is Christ’s humanity, full of divinity: by the gold, which is from the earth, we understand his humanity; by the manna, which came down from heaven, his divinity. But what is signified by Aaron’s rod that had put forth leaves except the blessed Virgin Mary, who both, though dry, bore a flower and, though incorrupt, bore the Savior? [Note: The same codex of St Mark: “And, being incorrupt, gave birth to the Savior.” Likewise the Vatican codex.]

In the tablets of the Covenant let the fullness of all knowledge be understood, because the ten words were in them, through which all the commandments of both Testaments are prefigured. For since all numbers are contained in ten, not without reason are all things sometimes understood through ten. Such were the instruments in the ark; such are the relics in the Church. There, the censer; here, the apostles. There, the golden vessel; here, Christ, God and man. There, the tablets of the Covenant; here, the fullness of all knowledge. There, Aaron’s rod; here, the rod from the root of Jesse.

It remains for us now to pass to the third tabernacle, by which, we said, heaven is signified. For it profits nothing to have remained in these unless at some point we pass to that one. For this is why we labor in these things: that we may one day arrive at that place. There is no figure there: whatever occurs there is truth. For not only in the Synagogue but even in the Church we see many things done in figure and signification. For walls are sprinkled with water—and not ordinary water, but salt water; pavements are inscribed; stones and altars are anointed with oil; twelve candles are lit in twelve places: these are figure and signification. But we reserve their exposition for another time. [Note: All these matters were explained by St Bruno of Asti in his treatise *On Mysteries and Sacraments*.]

Let us therefore hasten to enter that house, where we may see all things not through a mirror and in an enigma, but face to face. Let us say again with the Psalmist, and repeat the same words: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83:5); and: “One thing I have asked; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26:4). This is not the kind of request that we ought to consign to forgetfulness.

How great are the good things prepared in that house for the saints, the Apostle briefly enumerates: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9). May he deign to grant these things to us, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER IV. On Solomon’s Temple

[Col. 0885A]

David wished to build a temple for the Lord, and it was said to him: “You shall not build me a house, because you have shed much blood; but your son, who shall come forth from your loins, he shall build me a house, and I shall be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me” (2 Sam. 7; 1 Chron. 17:22).

Solomon therefore built a temple for the Lord out of great squared stones. Its length was sixty cubits, its breadth twenty cubits, and its height one hundred and twenty cubits (1 Kings 6). While the house was being built, neither hammer nor axe nor the sound of any iron tool was heard in it. He also made two columns before the doors of the Temple, one of which he called Jachin, that is, “firmness,” and the other Boaz, that is, “in whom is strength.”

The walls of the Temple were covered with cedar boards, [Note: The same codex of St Mark: “he covered [them] with cedar boards.” Both Vatican codices.] which he overlaid with sheets of the purest gold. He carved cherubim, palms, and other very prominent sculptures. Solomon also made two cherubim from olive wood, and, like all the other things, covered them with the purest gold. They were two cubits high; standing with straight feet before the oracle and facing into the Temple, they touched one another with two wings, while with two wings they extended to the walls. It is thus evident that the outspread wings of the cherubim occupied the entire breadth of the Temple.

He also made a bronze sea before the Temple, which twelve oxen appeared to bear: three faced east, three north, three south, and three west. This is not the time to expound everything made in that most noble Temple. The Temple of the Lord, however, was built in seven years.

This temple is the Church; this temple is ourselves. Of us the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3:17).—“The Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord has his seat in heaven” (Ps. 10:4).

But what do those two columns mean, which, placed before the doors of the Temple, appear to stand idle because they support nothing? Yet it is not idle that one is called firmness and the other strength. We must speak first of these, because they first meet those entering the Temple.

By one of them I understand the patriarchs and prophets and the other leaders and princes of the Old Testament. Such columns were Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; such were Moses, Joshua, David, and Daniel; and such were many others who through faith conquered kingdoms. Because they were firm and strong, they could not be torn away from justice and truth by any violence of storm or assault of winds.

In the other I see the apostles and martyrs, confessors and bishops; their deeds plainly show how strong and steadfast they were. Look to Peter, James, and John, who were called pillars of the Church (Gal. 2:9). Look to Stephen and Lawrence; behold also Martin the bishop and confessor, and our father Benedict, [Note: St Benedict is called “Father” by the author.] and you will at once be able to understand what those columns signify. For it is not fitting that anyone should enter the Temple unless he has first come to know these. Therefore it is written: “I considered the days of old, and kept eternal years in my mind” (Ps. 76:6). We must always keep in mind their life and teaching, their faith and manner of life, their steadfastness and morals. Let us believe thus, live thus, serve the Lord thus, walk thus, and persevere thus in good; that is sufficient for us.

Concerning the nets and pomegranates which were above the capitals of the columns, let it suffice to say briefly that our fathers always had nets by which they caught not fish and birds, but drew hearers and the obedient to the Lord. They also had pomegranates by which they might satisfy souls and heal them from the heat of desire.

Since we have considered the columns and heard what they signify, let us now enter the Temple and inquire what that immense arrangement of gold accomplishes there. Nothing is seen there except gold: gold in the beams, gold on the walls; the very floors shine with the purest gold. This is not without cause: it is mystery, it is signification, intended not to feed an empty gaze but spiritually to refresh the understanding. All this pertains to the Church, which is wholly golden, free from every corruption of vices, and made whiter than snow.

This gold is the virtues with which all the members of the Church have been gilded. If we hold faith, hope, and charity, we are golden. Without these, not even the angels themselves are beautiful; this is easily proved in those who, having lost humility, fell and became more ugly than every other creature. Some are gilded and adorned by humility, others by patience, others by obedience. Whatever virtue you possess is an ornament to you; without virtues there is no beauty in the soul.

We have seen the gold, and it is pleasing to have seen it; it remains now for us to consider the carvings. [Note: Vatican codex: “let us look upon.”] “There were,” he says, “cherubim and palms and other very prominent carvings on the walls.” The cherubim summon us to knowledge; the palms to victory. In the former we are taught to fly; in the latter, to fight. Nothing in the Temple is idle: whatever is written or carved has been written for our instruction. The very walls teach us and, in a manner, speak to us.

But since we have begun to speak of the cherubim, let us look toward those which stand before the oracle and look toward us. They have hands, feet, and a human face: all this is familiar and customary to us. Their wings alarm me, because I do not see wings in the image of a human being. This might appear to be an image of a man if the wings alone were absent. Since, therefore, no such creature exists in nature, it is only figure and signification. They are not to be worshipped as gods; [Note: Ascensian edition: “as though they were gods, but let them perform that for which they were made,” etc.] rather, they should perform that for which they were made.

To God, these two cherubim are the two Testaments; what the two books signify, the two cherubim signify. For *cherubim* is interpreted “fullness of knowledge.” We understand this fullness of knowledge more readily in books than in those images. Yet everything contained in the divine Scriptures is signified by many images.

You too, if you wish, can become a cherub. Cherubim are better made from human beings than from tongues; [Note: From the Vatican codex, editions reading “human beings” are corrected.] indeed, many human beings have already become cherubim. Do you wish to see a cherub? Look to Paul, full of all knowledge, teacher of the Gentiles and master of the Churches. Since he is debtor both to the wise and to the foolish, he supplies milk to little children; but among the perfect he speaks wisdom.

If you wish to see him flying, hear him say: “I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago—whether in the body or outside the body I do not know, God knows—was caught up as such a one even to the third heaven” (2 Cor. 12:2). He who flies thus has wings; and he who speaks thus is not only wise but may truly be called the fullness of knowledge.

But why were these cherubim made from olive wood, if not to summon us to mercy? Great is the power of mercy, without which even cherubim themselves cannot exist. For what in Greek is *eleon* [ἐλεον], whence *oleum*, “oil,” we call mercy. Nothing in the cherubim deserves more attention than the material of which they were made: namely, the olive, or mercy. Hence the Lord himself says: “Be merciful, as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36). Much could be said concerning mercy; indeed, “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. 118:64).

The ark of the Covenant is rightly said to stand beneath the wings of the cherubim, because nothing so defends and fortifies God’s Church as the divine word and knowledge of the Scriptures. Enough has been said about the ark of the Covenant in the preceding discourse.

And it was fitting that, when the house of the Lord was built, neither hammer, axe, nor sound of iron tool was heard, because the Church of God, signified by it, was to be built not with iron but with the tongue. No inarticulate sound, but the power of the Holy Spirit constructed it. Arius is an evil tool, Sabellius an evil hammer, Nestorius an evil axe: they attempted not to build but to destroy. May the sound of such tools never be heard in the Church. Rather, may the voice of the turtledove be heard in our land. Let Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John sing to us. For I also delight always to hear Paul’s voice. Let Augustine, Ambrose, and many other sons of the Church sing sufficiently, melodiously, and sweetly.

It remains to speak of the bronze sea, concerning which much should be said; but because this discourse must now be concluded, I shall say briefly: the bronze sea is baptism, and the twelve oxen are the twelve apostles. God placed the bronze sea upon them when he commanded them, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). That some face east, some north, some south, and some west means what follows: “They went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark 16:20).

And because the Temple of the Lord was built in seven years and dedicated for seven days, what else, we think, does this signify except that, during the time when holy Church is in this life, which proceeds in seven days, she is always being built and dedicated? For some are daily converted to faith, others are baptized, and others are consecrated to the Lord through penitence and holy conduct and cleansed from the contagion of sins.

When this sevenfold period has ended, the eighth day follows: namely, the day of resurrection, when, all things having been perfected and completed, we shall be transferred to eternal life. May he deign to grant this to us, he who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER V. On the Woman by Whom the Church Is Prefigured

Blessed John the Evangelist relates (Rev. 12:1) that he saw holy Church in the appearance of a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon beneath her feet, a crown of twelve stars upon her head, and suffering in labor so that she might give birth.

Great is the praise of God’s Church, which is reported to be clothed with the sun. She is clothed with the sun because she is adorned with every brilliance and beauty. [Note: Likewise the codex of St Mark: “Because [she is adorned] with every splendor and every brightness.” Likewise the Vatican codex.] Those too are clothed with the sun to whom the Apostle speaks, saying: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 13:14). For he is the sun of righteousness, of whom he says elsewhere: “All of you who were baptized into Christ Jesus have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27).

The Church has the moon beneath her feet because she despises the world and considers it nothing. The world is rightly called the moon because, like the moon, it is always in motion, always changing and varying. What is there in the world that is not mutable? Heaven and earth change; the sea too is always changeable; and the air is now clear, now cloudy. But why speak of human beings? They themselves experience their changes: now joyful, now angry, now sad, now healthy, now sick, and countless others besides.

This woman despises all these things because she strives toward what is immutable, where there is eternal joy, eternal health, eternal life; and because all things there are eternal, nothing there is mutable. She has upon her head a crown of twelve stars, by which we understand the twelve apostles. They crowned her; they made her both queen and mistress; they brought her into the bridal chamber of the eternal king.

“And she suffered in labor so that she might give birth”: this is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow because her hour has come; but when she has borne the child, she no longer remembers the distress because of her joy that a human being has been born into the world” (John 16:21). So great is the desire to give birth, so great the love of begetting children: she thinks little of torments, does not fear sufferings, and desires to die so that she may bear children of adoption to the Lord. Thus Rachel gave birth while dying, so that the Synagogue might have Benjamin and we might have Paul the Apostle.

Solomon also says of this woman: “Who shall find a strong woman? Her value is far off and from the furthest bounds” (Prov. 31:10). He could not find such a woman in his own times; he knew that the Church of the Gentiles would be born and come from afar, after many ages. Because her honor, glory, and every blessedness will be revealed at the end of the world, he said that her value was “from the furthest bounds.”

“She put forth her hand to strong things, and her fingers grasped the distaff” (ibid.). In this the wisdom of the Church is displayed: she orders all things so well. She sends her hand—that is, those who are stronger and wiser—to greater tasks, and appoints such persons rulers and bishops. Her fingers grasp the distaff because she entrusts lesser tasks to those who are more imperfect and less skilled.

“She opened her mouth to wisdom, and the law of gentleness is beneath her tongue” (ibid.). She speaks no vain or useless things; her speech is seasoned with salt and heals and refreshes her hearers. The law of gentleness is that by which we are commanded both to love even our enemies and to forgive all persons from the heart.

“Her husband is noble in the gates, when he sits with the senators of the land.” This is the Church’s one praise, greater than her other praises: that her husband is so noble. Yet this nobility has not yet appeared. He came humble and in the form of a servant. He came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many; he was judged as though guilty and numbered among the wicked.

Then, therefore, he will be noble; then his nobility will appear, when he sits with the senators of the land, when God comes openly—our God, and he will not be silent. For he says: “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bend and every tongue shall confess” (Isa. 45:23). The senators of the land are the apostles, to whom the Lord said: “You who have followed me shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28). Then the gates will open: for the good, the gates of life; for the wicked, the gates of death.

This woman, [Note: Likewise the codex of St Mark, Florence: “That latter bride of Christ.”] that most noble bride of Christ, is she to whom the Lord says in the Song of Songs: “Come from Lebanon; come, you shall be crowned, from the summit of Amana, from the peak of Sanir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards” (Song 4:8).

Behold, we have heard whence the Church came, where she was born, and among whom she lived. These mountains, these dry and desert places, signify wild and barbarous peoples, from whom holy Church was gathered into the one faith of Christ. The lions and leopards are evil spirits that dwelt in them and had houses and dens among them. We should therefore not care what she was or whence she came, but what she now is and where she has come.

The order of the words, however, is as follows: “Come from Lebanon, my sister, my bride; come from Lebanon, come; come from the summit of Amana, from the peak of Sanir and Hermon; come from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards”; then one must add, “you shall be crowned.” “No one,” says the Apostle, “shall be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5). Coming itself, therefore, is competing. For it was not easy for her to leave country and parents, abandon former customs, her old manner of life, and the gods she had worshipped. She fought because she came; she conquered because she could not be held back. Therefore she shall be crowned, and she shall be crowned with that crown of which it was said above: “Upon her head a crown of twelve stars” (Rev. 12:2).

Yet by the one who comes from Lebanon we may understand those who believed from among the Jews. To hear that Jerusalem is called Lebanon, listen to the prophet: “Open your gates, Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars” (Zech. 11:1). Since, therefore, by noble trees we understand most illustrious men—kings, priests, and prophets—this is that woman, or rather that queen (for she is crowned, which belongs properly to queens), of whom the Psalmist speaks: “The queen stood at your right hand in golden raiment, surrounded by variety. Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, because the king has desired your beauty” (Ps. 44:10). [Note: Vatican codex: “Forget the mountains of leopards and the dens of lions.”]

Let us also hear what the Lord and our Savior said concerning her. “The queen of the south,” he says, “came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon” (Matt. 12:42). As the Books of Kings testify (3 Kings 10), she came with cavalry and much equipment. She offered gifts to Solomon: true gold and aromatic spices such as had not previously been brought to Jerusalem. At last, having been instructed in everything that she desired to hear and enriched by the king with great gifts, she returned joyfully and exultantly to her own country.

This is not the time to expound everything that appears to be signified by these words. Let us imitate this queen, for she is our mother.
