Let us always devote ourselves to wisdom and always desire to hear the wisdom of Solomon—namely, of that Solomon who says: “And behold, one greater than Solomon is here” (Matt. 12:25). She came from the ends of the earth; let every earthly desire also be brought to an end in us. Let us say with the Psalmist: “From the ends of the earth I cried to you” (Ps. 60:3).

We offer gold to God if we are pure in mind and body. But what are spices except virtues? There is no other gift more worthy to be offered to God; indeed, God receives none of our gifts without them. We can offer God nothing except what we have received from him. “For what do you have,” says the Apostle, “that you have not received? And if you have received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7). Let us return to God what is his; he does not receive what is ours. [Note: Both Vatican codices: “For nothing is ours except sin.”] For nothing is ours except sin; whoever does not possess this is rich. Therefore we should be rich if we possessed nothing of our own.

There are also other women who signify holy Church: Sarah, first called Sarai, whose name is interpreted “my princess.” Yet it was not fitting that she who was the princess and mother of all should be called “my princess.” [Note: Vatican codex: “And she was mistress.”] Let her therefore be called not “my princess” but “our princess,” because in the son whom she bore all nations are blessed.

Likewise Rebecca, whose name is interpreted “much patience,” Leah, who is called “laborious,” though bleary-eyed yet fruitful in her womb, Rachel, beautiful in face, and Zipporah, whose name is interpreted “beautiful,” bear the figure of the Church. This one is called beautiful; that one lovely. Yet both names signify the same thing. A beautiful mother makes beautiful children; a lovely mother bears lovely children. [Note: Vatican codex: “makes [them].”] If, therefore, the parents are beautiful, why are their children ugly? Those children who were ugly and did not have her image and likeness will one day deny that these are their parents. [Note: Vatican codex: “Those who will be ugly and will not have her image and likeness.”]

May he who is beautiful in form beyond the children of men deign to refashion and renew us into that image and likeness: he who, God, lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Holy City Jerusalem
Raised in the Spirit upon a great and high mountain, blessed John, as he himself testifies (Rev. XXVIII, 2), [Col. 0891C] saw there the holy city Jerusalem being built by a new work and wondrous craftsmanship. Its walls were constructed of precious stone, and the very streets of the city of the purest gold, like the clearest glass. It had twelve gates, 481 each made from a single pearl; three faced east, three north, three south, and three west. This is that Jerusalem which, as it is written, “was built as a city whose sharing is in unity itself” (Ps. CXXI, 3). For theirs is a sharing in unity itself whose heart is one and whose soul is one. Among them there is no discord, and their concord is most firm.

Let us therefore also be raised together with blessed John onto the great and high mountain, so that, lifted up in an ecstasy of mind, we may understand these things not literally but spiritually. [Col. 0891D] This holy city is the Church; these walls and these precious stones are human beings: namely, noble and illustrious people endowed with virtues and wisdom, such as the apostles and martyrs, and all others who have pleased the Lord through faith and holy conduct. Thus divine discourse speaks and uses such figurative expressions, calling men most illustrious and worthy of praise not men but angels; now stars of heaven, now sun [Col. 0892A] and moon, now clouds and thunder, now mountains and hills, and things like these. Thus we see the same done in this passage, where the holy Church is said to be built not of human beings but of gold and stones.

The first stones of this building are the apostles, who, set in the foundation, are said to bear the whole city. Hence the Apostle says: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone, in whom the whole building, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord” (Eph. II, 20). Rightly, then, they are identified and set forth by that very number: there are twelve of them; and although the other stones too are precious, none are compared with these. No stone in the wall of this building is other than precious; yet some are more precious [Col. 0892B] than others. For star differs from star in glory, and not all members are the same members; it is enough for all that they are precious.

But what are we to understand by the purest gold and the clearest glass [Note: [Col. 0891D] The Ascensis edition wrongly reads *nitrum*.] with which the streets are paved, if not wisdom? That wisdom, namely, which cries aloud in the streets and gives forth its voice among the saints. Blessed are those streets in which the assembly of the faithful is occupied not with idle tales but with wisdom, and drinks water not from the springs of Egypt, which are turned into blood, but from the springs of Israel, springing up into eternal life.

It should be observed that these same apostles are called both foundations and gates. They are foundations because in the whole building they are first and bear the others. They are gates because no one is joined to the fellowship of [Col. 0892C] the Church, or enters the palace of heaven, except through them—that is, through their faith and teaching. To them were given the keys of the kingdom of heaven; they are both gates and gatekeepers. We have explained all this more fully in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0891D] He affirms in the Apocalypse that he has expounded all this more extensively [Col. 0892D]]. Nor is this now the time for discussing each point individually.

And who but the Holy Spirit could ever have dictated these things and raised the praises of the Church by such great proclamations? But let us see what the Psalmist also says of this most noble city [Note: [Col. 0892D] Codex Ascensis adds]: “Her foundations,” he says, “are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tabernacles of Jacob” (Ps. LXXXVI, 1). The foundations have already been discussed above: “No one,” says the Apostle, “can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus [Col. 0892D]” (I Cor. III, 11). Of him the Lord also says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI, 18). Therefore Christ is the foundation of foundations, since the apostles and prophets too are foundations. Hence of the city founded upon such mountains it is rightly said: “Her foundations are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves her gates above all the tabernacles of Jacob” [Note: [Col. 0892D] Saint Bruno gave the explanation of this passage in these same words in his commentary on Psalm 86, where it is printed in full, whereas it appears mutilated in Marchesi’s edition.].

If he so greatly loves Zion’s gates alone, tell me, I ask you, how greatly does he love the whole city? [Col. 0893A] By the tabernacles of Jacob are meant those Jews who, departing from the Lord, were scattered among all the nations. “Glorious things have been said of you, city of God” (Ps. LXXXVI, 3). But what glorious things? Perhaps that it is said to be built wholly of gold, pearls, and precious stones? These things are indeed glorious; but the other things—that is, those said of it—are still more glorious. Do you wish to hear what they are? “I shall remember Rahab and Babylon, who know me” (ibid., 4). And truly these things are glorious, more than glorious. Consider now what righteous persons may hope for and confidently expect from God’s mercy, if the Lord will remember even Rahab and Babylon. One was a prostitute; the other held God’s people captive. The former hid the spies so that they might not be killed. The latter, however, for some time held in servitude, by God’s command, a people that had transgressed. [Col. 0893B] The Lord, therefore, will remember such figures because he remembers all who know him. For he would not remember them unless they had merited to know him and, though after many crimes, nevertheless to believe in him.

It is especially to be noted that he says, “who know me.” Whatever a person may formerly have been—whether a prostitute or a persecutor of saints—if at last that person is converted and comes to know the Lord, that person shall be saved. Thus the Lord himself says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII, 3).

Let us now hear the other glorious things said of the city of God: “Behold,” he says, “foreigners, and Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians—those who were in her” (Ps. [Col. 0893C] LXXXVI, 4). This is what [Note: [Col. 0893D] Codex of San Marco, Florence] the Apostle says: “Is God the God of the Jews only? Is he not also of the Gentiles?” (Rom. III, 29). Likewise the apostle Peter: “Truly,” he says, “I have discovered that God shows no partiality. But in every nation, whoever fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts X, 34).

Whoever, therefore, fears God and works righteousness, wherever that person comes from, is received by this most merciful city, and is regarded not as a foreigner but as a citizen and native-born inhabitant. Thus Cornelius the centurion was received; he became the Church’s first son from among the Gentiles. This also was signified by that vessel full of unclean animals, when it was said to the apostle: “Kill and eat” (ibid., 13); and likewise by the apes [Col. 0893D] that were brought to Solomon along with peacocks. What is uglier than an ape? What is more beautiful than a peacock? In the Lord’s tabernacle there were both hair-cloths and goats’ hair. Nor did the Lord reject a goat for a burnt offering, although lambs too were offered to him. The gold, stones, wood, and other materials from which the Lord’s temple was built were not produced there but brought from elsewhere. Thus the Church too, built from all nations, receives all people and rejects none who come to her.

“And Tyre and the people of the Ethiopians, those who were in her.” These things [Col. 0894A] are glorious, able to give both righteous people and sinners great hope and to bring them boundless joy. Do you wish to be received in the Church? Imitate the Tyrians, by whose work and aid the temple was built. Imitate also the centurion who built a synagogue for the Jews. Moses, as we read, took an Ethiopian woman as his wife. Because his sister Miriam murmured against her, she was struck with leprosy by the Lord and driven outside the camp. The children of this Ethiopian woman are those Ethiopians of whom it is now said: “And the people of the Ethiopians, those who were in her.” This is that Ethiopian woman who speaks in the Song of Songs, saying: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem” (Song I, 5). Because she hates the Synagogue, however, Miriam was struck with leprosy and shall not be received within the Church’s camp until the consummation of the age.

These, then, are glorious—indeed most glorious—things said of the city of God, in which slaves become free and the low-born become glorious. And there, and nowhere else, is that water which can change the colour of Ethiopians. This city has such great care and concern for human beings, and it is not without reason called the mother of all; hence it follows: “A man shall call Zion ‘Mother’ [Note: [Col. 0893] Psalm LXXXVI, 5; the Vulgate reads: ‘Will Zion say?’]” (Ps. LXXXVI, 5). It is as if he said: This is a mother—and truly a mother—who opens the bosom of her affection to all, closes her maternal heart to none, receives all, and cherishes and nourishes all in love.

It continues: “And a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (ibid.). Many glorious things have been said above of this city; but what is now said is more glorious than every glory. No glory [Col. 0894C] can be compared with this glory: the Most High himself, who founded and made her, became man and was born in her. And how do the prophets establish this? Do you wish to hear how? “The Lord has recorded in the writings of the peoples and of their rulers, who were in her” (ibid., 6). “Ask your fathers and they will tell you; your elders and they will declare it to you” (Deut. XXXII, 7). Read the Scriptures of all peoples—that is, of the prophets and apostles—which are common to all and were written for our instruction and the instruction of all; they will teach you. Read Moses, Isaiah, and Jeremiah, and you will find it. Read the Gospels, which are of no lesser authority than those writings. Read Paul, the apostle of Jesus Christ, who “was called an apostle and set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in [Col. 0894D] the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him of David’s seed according to the flesh” (Rom. I, 1). It has therefore been proved that he became man, and that the Most High himself founded her.

One glorious thing remains that has been said of this city; let us hear it too: “As the dwelling-place of all of us who rejoice is in you” (Ps. LXXXVI, 7). For this too is very glorious: the inhabitants of this city will possess everlasting joy and feel no misery. Where there is no misery, every joy is found. This joy, however, is spiritual; it is not the joy [Col. 0895A] of temporal things but of eternal blessedness. Of it the Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18).—“Therefore rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous; glory, all you upright in heart” (Ps. XXXI, 11).—“Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. IV, 4). May he himself now deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

483 CHAPTER VII. On basilicas dedicated by bishops. [Note: [Col. 0895D] The title in the Vatican codex is: “At the dedication of a church.”]

You know, my brothers [Note: [Col. 0895D] Codex of San Marco, Florence: “You know, dearest brothers.”], who have gathered for the dedication of this basilica, that this building is called a church because it signifies the holy Church. For this building, whether great or small, [Col. 0895B] signifies the holy Church no less than that most noble temple of Solomon, the holy city Jerusalem, or the tabernacle of testimony. *Ecclesia* is a Greek name; it means an assembly [Note: [Col. 0896D] Vatican codex: “collection.”] of people—namely, people who fear the Lord and serve the Lord. For just as one house is made from many stones arranged with order and skill, so one Church is established from many people joined in fellowship by the love of charity and brotherhood.

Just as this building has a foundation, stones, and walls; gates and windows, and similar things; so too the holy Church is known, as the Apostle says, by a certain analogy to possess all these things. But let him speak; let him teach us; let him show its foundations and the building laid upon the foundations. “Now,” he says, “you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone, in whom every structure, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord” (Eph. II, 19).

The Church, therefore, has a foundation: namely, the apostles and prophets, and Jesus our Lord and Saviour, the foundation of all foundations. Of him the Apostle says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (I Cor. III, 11). These are called the foundation because the whole Church has been built upon their faith and teaching. They are also called gates because others [Col. 0895D] enter through them. These are the gates of which it is said: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tabernacles of Jacob” (Ps. LXXXVI, 1).

Hell too has its gates, of which the Lord says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI, 19). And in the Psalms: “You who raise me from the gates of death, that I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. IX, 19). The Church, therefore, has such gates, signified by the gates [Col. 0896A] which you see here.

It also has pillars, such as Peter, James, and John, who are called pillars of the Church by the Apostle himself. These pillars were signified by the two pillars which stood before the temple doors, one of which was called Jachin and the other Boaz (III Kings VII, 21). These pillars too are signified by those which you see supporting these walls. The stones from which the walls are constructed signify the whole multitude of this people. And just as those stones easily collapse and cannot stand unless they are joined by mortar or iron, so these people, unless they are joined and united by harmony in charity and by the bond of peace, cause the whole ecclesiastical building suddenly to collapse and prevent it from standing long. Hence, among all people, those are deservedly cursed and hated by God who sow discord among brothers. For as peace and concord alone bind these stones, so discord alone separates them.

Let these walls, therefore, teach us; let these stones instruct us how we ought to love one another and preserve peace and concord. By the windows, moreover, we may understand bishops, teachers, and all others by whose teaching and example this house of the Lord is illuminated. Windows are made for this purpose; this is their office and usefulness: to provide the brightness of light and drive away the darkness of gloom. Such a window was Gregory; such were Jerome and Augustine; such were Ambrose and Hilary; and such were many others who illuminated the world with the splendour of their teaching.

If anyone wishes to run through the details, no part of the entire [Col. 0896C] building can be found that cannot have its own symbolic meaning. Let what we have said about the construction of a house suffice; now let us consider its dedication [Note: [Col. 0896D] Saint Bruno gives this same exposition of the rite of church consecration in a separate treatise entitled *On Mysteries and Ecclesiastical Rites*.].

You have seen today what the bishop did when he came to consecrate this sanctuary. First of all, he made litanies and invoked to his aid almighty God himself, the most blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, all the choirs of angels, and the hosts of all the saints. We ought not to doubt that they are present, and that this dedication is performed through their blessings. Then he consecrated water by adding salt, so that this church might be baptized outwardly with that water and its walls sprinkled. I say “outwardly,” because another water is prepared inside. Salt, however, signifies wisdom and is therefore fittingly mixed with this water, which is rightly called the water of wisdom. Indeed, this is the water of wisdom, which alone makes people wise and without which no one can become wise. The baptized alone are wise, because they alone are free from the vanities of the world and the wiles of the devil.

The walls are sprinkled with water three times as the bishop goes around them, because it is impossible for the whole building to be immersed in water. This sprinkling appears to be done with a bundle of hyssop, so that what is written may be fulfilled: [Col. 0897A] “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall become whiter than snow” (Ps. L, 9). This herb is lowly and grows naturally. “The rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 4), says the Apostle. It signifies the priestly order, to whom the Lord says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI, 29). They may indeed be killed, but they cannot be torn away from this rock. Such persons are therefore worthy to baptize and sprinkle the Church of God.

The bishop also strikes the church doors with the pastoral staff, showing himself to be the vicar of him of whom it is written: “He shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the spirit of his lips he shall slay the wicked” (Thess. II, 8). By this stroke the devil is driven away, so that he may no longer have a place in the shelters [Col. 0897B] of the Lord’s house. Bound by the words of the Holy Spirit, he flees when it is said: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. XXIII, 7).

Then the bishop enters the temple and consecrates another water, through which the Holy Spirit is signified; to it are mixed not only salt but also wine and ashes. That the Holy Spirit is signified by water, hear the Lord himself saying: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John VII, 38). The Evangelist immediately explains this: “He said this concerning the Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive” (ibid.). Wine and ashes are fittingly mixed with this water, by which the Holy Spirit is signified, because those whom the Holy Spirit washes and touches are beyond doubt both made drunk with the wine of knowledge and sprinkled with the dust of repentance.

It is indeed very necessary that those newly baptized should be made drunk with such wine and sprinkled with such dust. Made drunk with this wine, the apostles spoke in every language. Inviting us to the drunkenness of this wine, the Lord says: “Eat, my friends; drink and be made drunk, my beloved” (Song V, 1). Of this the Psalmist also says: “They shall be made drunk with the abundance of your house, and you shall make them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. XXXV, 9). Those sprinkled with dust are those who know themselves to be sinners. We read that the ancient fathers often did this in their afflictions. Sprinkled with such dust, Abraham said: “I shall speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. XVIII, 27). [Col. 0897D] Sprinkled likewise, the Ninevites (Jonah III, 5) deserved to receive pardon. Hence the custom has grown up in the churches of sprinkling heads with dust at the beginning of Lent.

See how orderly and reasonable all things are done. Outwardly with water and inwardly with the Spirit, the house of God is washed and baptized, so that the Lord’s saying may be fulfilled: “Unless someone has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III, 6). Since [Note: [Col. 0897D] Vatican codex: “But since.”] the whole alphabet is written twice on the pavement, what else does this signify except that one who has been baptized ought to commit to memory the knowledge of both Testaments? [Col. 0898A] The letters are few, yet the fullness of all knowledge is contained in them. Let these letters, therefore, be written on the pavement of our heart, through which we may be able to know and do God’s will.

The twelve candles are the twelve apostles, by whose knowledge, faith, and teaching the whole Church is enlightened. Now let us approach the altar and see what the bishop does there. The altar in the Church is what our heart is in our body. For we too are God’s temple and ought indeed to have an altar within us. Your altar, therefore, O Christian, is your heart. Let it be anointed; let it be offered in sacrifice; let the relics of the saints be placed here; here let there be a sweet fragrance; here let the sacrifice of praise be offered.

Oil is mercy. Whoever has not been anointed with it is wholly dry and weak. Let our hearts, therefore, always swim in this oil, so that we may never forget mercy. Let our high priest, then, approach the altar of our heart: that great high priest Jesus Christ, of whom it is written, “You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX, 4). Let him approach, I say, pour oil upon it, and say: “Be merciful, as your Father is merciful” (Luke VI, 36). He himself abounded in this oil when he prayed for those crucifying him, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34).

Not only the altar of the heart, then, but all our members ought to be anointed with this oil. A dry hand does not open to the needy; and because it is not anointed, it does not know how to show mercy. Much can be said about this [Col. 0898C] anointing, much about the oil of mercy, since “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. XXX, 5). But what are the relics of the saints that are placed in these altars? I understand the saints’ relics to be their teaching and words. Therefore we can possess on the altar of our heart the relics not only of the saints, but even of our Saviour himself. For he too says: “Whoever has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me” (John XIV, 21). He who said, 485 “I have hidden your sayings in my heart, that I may not sin against you” (Ps. CXVIII, 11), had placed these relics upon the altar of his heart. Blessed are those altars on which such relics have been placed; blessed are those hearts that have merited to receive such relics. Great are these relics, exceedingly many and wondrous, which can be enclosed in so small a vessel. But now we commend these altars of ours to God: may he possess and guard our hearts, and deign to dwell in the temple of our breast—he who lives and reigns, etc.

CHAPTER VIII. On the Gospels.

“It is not a good tree that bears bad fruit, nor a bad tree bearing good fruit” (Matt. VII, 17). Our Lord and Saviour teaches us how we ought to recognize good and bad trees. Good [Col. 0899A] trees are good people. Trees are known by their fruit; people are known by their works. The good trees of Paradise were both beautiful to behold and pleasant for food. Such trees the Church produces; we delight to read and hear of their beauty and devotion, and our minds are nourished and refreshed by their words and teaching.

Such a tree was blessed Paul, who was so beautiful to behold that he was conscious of no fault in himself, and so pleasant for food that he nourishes both little ones with milk and the wise with solid food. Such trees also are the other apostles, whose fruits are commended by the Lord himself when he says to them: “You did not choose me, but I chose you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John XV, 16). These are those [Col. 0899B] fruits; these are those apples of which the Church says to the Bridegroom: “All manner of fruit, new and old, my beloved, I have kept for you” (Song VII, 13). The old fruit is the teaching of the prophets and patriarchs; the new, that of the apostles and teachers of the Church. These are those of whom it is said: “They bring forth from their treasures things new and old.”

Such trees are not difficult to recognize by their fruits, because all their teaching and action are holy, true, devout, without deceit or rivalry. Hypocrites sometimes also seem to be good trees; but because they seek only earthly and passing things, and because they lack the humility and patience of the saints, they are readily detected and exposed in their very cunning. The Lord commanded the children of Israel, when they had entered the land of promise, to circumcise the trees of that region and abstain from their use until the fourth year (Lev. XIX, 23). Unless human beings were signified by trees, it would seem absurd to command those trees to be circumcised. But foreign trees are unbelieving people who come to us and whom we ought to circumcise—that is, cleanse from their sins through baptism and repentance.

What then is signified by the four years but the four Gospels? Whoever has not yet passed through them and has not yet heard their teaching is still unclean; that person’s fruit must not yet be received, nor should one yet trust that person’s words and teaching. Let us hear what John, the Lord’s forerunner, said of bad trees: [Col. 0899D] “Already,” he says, “the axe has been laid to the root of the tree. Every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. III, 9). Such was the fig tree which the Lord cursed and which withered. Such also were the branches of which he says: “Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he shall take away” (John XV, 2). And what follows? Do you wish to hear? “But if anyone does not remain in me, he shall be cast out like a branch and wither; they shall gather it, cast it into the fire, and it burns” (ibid.).

Many are cursed daily by the Lord and removed from his body, which is the Church; they are cast out and thrown into the fire. A man had planted a fig tree in his vineyard, and when for three years he had sought fruit on it and found none, he commanded the keeper [Col. 0900A] of the vineyard to cut it down (Luke XIII, 6). It would then have been cut down had not the keeper of the vineyard interceded for it. Consider, therefore, and carefully attend to how greatly you are indebted to your keepers, namely bishops and priests, who intercede daily for you lest perhaps you be cut down and cast into the fire.

He has waited for you three years; he will wait for you a little longer, or not at all. He waited for you in adolescence, he waited in youth, he waited in old age. In short, he waited for you while you thought evil, while you did evil, and while you persisted in evil for a long time. What more do you seek? The years are finished; it is the last hour. Yet if you are converted today, pardon is promised you, though unworthy: “For the sinner, on whatever day he is converted and groans, shall live and shall not die” (Ezek. XXXIII, 12). Likewise, on whatever day a righteous person turns away from righteousness and turns to iniquity, that person shall die in the iniquity he has committed. “You shall know them by their fruits” (Matt. VII, 16).

Let us look to the fruits; let us examine the works; let us ask not what someone was, but what someone is. If today one has begun to bring forth good fruit, that person is a good tree; if today one has begun to produce bad fruit, that person is a bad tree. Why? Because Truth says: “You shall know them by their fruits.” Therefore good fruit and bad fruit are a great and true proof for recognizing trees. A tree is good for as long as good fruit is in it. For they do not gather figs from thorns, nor harvest grapes from a bramble. But if this should ever [Col. 0900C] happen, I too would call a thorn a fig and a bramble a grape. Why? Because every tree is known by its fruit. “A good person brings forth good from the treasure of the heart” (Luke VI, 45), and an evil person brings forth evil from his treasure. “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (ibid.). You cannot see what is in the heart; the secrets of the heart are closed to you. Look to the mouth, attend to its words, and what is in the heart will be disclosed by the mouth: “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” Good waters flow from a good spring; poisonous waters issue from a poisonous spring. Nor can it happen that the fruit does not reveal its own tree: “Nothing is covered that shall not be revealed, and hidden that shall not be known” (Matt. X, 26).

“Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke VI, 46). If you were good trees, you would do what I say; you would keep my commandments, and render me not leaves but fruit. Words are leaves; works are fruit. It is better to do than to speak. You call me Lord: acknowledge that you are servants. Good servants are those who keep their Lord’s commands. “Whoever hears my words and does them—I will tell you whom that person resembles. That person resembles a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation upon solid rock. When a flood came, the stream dashed against that house, and it did not fall, for it was founded upon solid rock” (ibid., 49).

See how great is the power of keeping God’s commandments. [Col. 0901A] Whoever keeps Christ’s commandments builds for himself a great tower and constructs a most strongly fortified citadel. Such a person is secure and fears the assault of no storm; because he has laid a firm foundation, he fears neither floods nor rain nor wind. If you wish your building to rise higher and be erected more loftily, you must seek a foundation deep below. Let one who desires to be greatly exalted humble oneself greatly.

The temple of the Lord was raised to a height of one hundred and twenty cubits because it had a firm and deep foundation. Let us, therefore, stretch ourselves toward this measure. We have a good foundation: our foundation is Jesus Christ. “For,” says the Apostle, “no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (I Cor. III, 11). Let us not suppose it happened by chance [Col. 0901B] that the Lord’s temple had this measure of height. There is also some beautiful [Col. 0902A] significance in this number. For ten times twelve, or twelve times ten, make one hundred and twenty. Whoever can extend oneself from ten to twelve, or from twelve to ten, is sufficiently high and great and should not seek to rise higher. Let this measure suffice.

There are ten words of the Law, while there are twelve apostles. Therefore one ascends from ten to twelve who, through keeping the ten commandments, has merited to attain the life and fellowship of the apostles. Likewise, one who has learned through the teaching of the twelve apostles to keep the ten commandments of the Law arrives, indeed, through twelve at ten. May he himself deign to stretch us toward this measure and raise us to the height of this measure—Jesus Christ our Lord, who willed that we should be his temple; who lives [Col. 0902B] and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages.

SECOND BOOK OF SENTENCES ON THE ORNAMENTS OF THE CHURCH

[Col. 0901]

487 CHAPTER ONE. On Faith.

[Col. 0901B]

The first ornament of the Church is faith, which is first in the whole army of virtues. All the other virtues follow it, and without it they do not enter the palace of the heavenly kingdom. Should humility come, patience, chastity, even charity itself, which the Apostle calls greater: unless faith is present, all are turned away and not permitted to enter. How many pagans and philosophers have shone in these virtues, yet, lacking the ornament of faith, did not please the Lord? “Without faith,” says the Apostle, “it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6).

For, to say nothing of the other virtues, we read that many were endowed with such great charity [Col. 0901C] that they did not hesitate to give themselves over to death for their country, their fellow citizens, and their friends. Yet the Lord says that no one has greater charity, or love, than that someone should lay down his life for his friends (John 15:13). All these, however, although they shone with many virtues, nevertheless perished because they did not possess faith.

Rightly, therefore, does the holy Church receive no one who comes to her unless he has first been clothed with the ornament of faith. Behold: someone comes to the Church and wishes to be baptized; he asks to be received. He is asked whether he believes, whether he holds the catholic faith. If he answers that he believes and holds the catholic faith, he is received, baptized, and joined to the children of the Church. But if he says otherwise, he is by no means received, but is set aside as profane [Col. 0901D]. Those to whom the gates of the Church are closed never have those of heaven opened to them. For thus the Lord says to blessed Peter: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound [Col. 0902B] also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19).

Great, therefore, is the power of faith, concerning which the Lord himself says: “All things are possible to one who believes” (Mark 9:23). He ascribes the might of his own power not to himself but to faith, and affirms that faith does what he himself does. We read that he healed many men and women and delivered them from grievous illnesses; to them he was accustomed to say only this: “Your faith has made you well; go in peace” (Matt. 9:12). At one time, the Gospel says, he came into his own country; and because the people there doubted his omnipotence and had no faith, he could not perform many mighty works there—except that, to use the Gospel’s words, he healed the sick by laying hands upon them [Col. 0902C]—and he marvelled at their unbelief.

Does faith, then, have such power that he who can do all things is hindered from the strength of his power by its absence? Likewise, when he was once going to Jerusalem, he approached a fig tree planted beside the road; and because he found no fruit on it, he cursed it and it withered. On the next day, when the disciples passed that way and saw the fig tree drying up, they said to him: “Master, behold, the fig tree which you cursed has withered.” To them he said: “If you have faith, you will not only do this to the fig tree, but you will also be able to move mountains” (Matt. 21:21).

Every day the Lord curses many fruitless fig trees; every day he condemns many wicked people, and they wither. Moreover, he moved mountains when he sent evil spirits into the swine [Col. 0902D] and commanded them to go into the abyss. We are taught by countless testimonies of the holy Scriptures that faith has also done this many times through the saints. Rightly, therefore, when the disciples asked for faith, saying, “Increase our faith” (Luke 17:5), they knew that through faith one can do all things, and without faith can do nothing.

For blessed Peter, when by the power of faith he began to come to the Lord upon the waters, as soon as he doubted and the faith by which he was borne withdrew from him, was submerged amid the waves. The Lord took him by the hand and raised him up, immediately teaching him the cause of his sinking: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14:31). It is as though he said: If you had not doubted, and faith had not departed from you, you could safely have run upon the waters. Behold: if Peter sinks while the Lord is present but faith absent, who could ever be secure without faith, even though all virtues stood around him?

If without faith it is impossible to please God, what other virtue can there be [Col. 0903B] that brings a human being to the Lord? “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. 4:3). “The saints through faith conquered kingdoms” (Heb. 11:33). “This is the victory which conquers the world: our faith” (John 5:4). “Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16:16). “If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach; and it shall be given him. But let him ask in faith, doubting nothing” (James 1:5). For whatever is not from faith is sin. “But the righteous 488 shall live by faith” (Gal. 3:11).

But what faith is, the Apostle teaches: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. 11:1). This is as though he said: Faith is a certain virtue by which we most certainly believe those things that are spoken to us, although they do not yet appear, and do not doubt that they will come to pass. Let us hear the Lord himself on what the measure of faith is: “If,” he says, “you have faith like a grain of mustard seed” (Luke 17:6), “you shall say to this mountain, ‘Remove yourself and cast yourself into the sea,’ and it shall be done” (Matt. 21:21).

Faith seems very small if it is reduced to the size of a mustard seed. And why is it said to the Canaanite woman, “O woman, great is your faith” (Matt. 15:28), if faith is compared to so tiny a grain? Something more, therefore, is signified by these words than their letter appears to express. There are three things in a mustard seed which indeed seem worthy of our notice. For although the mustard seed, as the Lord says, is the smallest [Col. 0903D] of all seeds, it nevertheless grows and becomes a tree, so that the birds of heaven come and dwell in its branches (Mark 4:31). Its fruit, moreover, I would not say that it ordinarily yields thirtyfold, sixtyfold, or a hundredfold, but often more than a thousandfold. The seed itself, if it is not injured or crushed, seems to have no power. But if it is crushed, its virtue and power are immediately revealed in their greatness.

Therefore, whoever possesses such faith—faith which always grows in this way, always multiplies the fruit of good works in this way, and in the time of persecution and crushing manifests the power and strength of its virtue—that person [Col. 0904A] is undoubtedly worthy both to move mountains, to cast out evil spirits, and to have all things become possible for him. Nothing, therefore, could more fittingly have been compared with a mustard seed.

But now let us see also in the examples of the saints how much faith has always accomplished. Abraham was old, and his wife according to nature could not bear children; yet because he believed, he deserved to receive a son contrary to nature itself. This certainly could not have happened unless faith had been present. Likewise Moses afflicted Egypt with ten remarkable and astonishing plagues, opened the sea, brought water from the rock, and performed many other works possible to God alone; he certainly would not have done these unless faith had been present.

Thus Joshua dried up the channel of the Jordan, overthrew the walls of Jericho from their foundations by the sound of trumpets [Col. 0904B], and compelled the sun itself to stand still; this certainly could not have happened unless faith had been present. What shall I say of Gideon, who likewise struck down, routed, and overcame the Midianites by the blast of trumpets and the brightness of lamps? This certainly could not have happened unless faith had been present.

> [Note: [Col. 0903D] Codex of St Mark, Florence, and Vatican codex: “The three youths also walked unharmed in the furnace of fire. They sang and rejoiced, uttered a hymn, and did not feel the fire” [Col. 0904D]; this certainly could not have happened unless faith had been present.]

But these things are small if one considers what Christian faith has accomplished through apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins. Read the Gospels; read the Acts of the Apostles, the passions and lives of the saints; and then you will see what faith can do. Yet what is remarkable, when the Lord himself promised them, saying: “He who believes in me shall also do the works that I do” (John 10:12)?

O wretched and utterly unhappy people who do not possess the catholic and apostolic faith: it shall be taken away from them. Let us therefore hold fast the faith [Col. 0904C] and hear Christ saying: “I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me shall not die for ever” (John 11:25). And so forth.

## CHAPTER II. On Hope

Hope is a great ornament of the Church of God; whoever does not have it is stripped of every good and more unhappy than every creature. Evil spirits do not possess it, and therefore strive with all their might to bring to despair whomever they can deceive. But whoever has suffered this evil is not partly, but wholly possessed by the devil. This is the sin which is not forgiven to human beings, neither in this age nor in the age to come (Matt. 12:32).

For there is no sin which is not forgiven through repentance, and without repentance no sin will be forgiven. Thus the Psalmist, after saying, “Have mercy on me, O Lord, according to your great mercy” (Ps. 50:1), knowing that he could not obtain this without repentance, immediately added: “For I know my iniquity” (ibid., v. 4). For the person who repents and is ashamed of his sin knows his own iniquity. Therefore, if sins are not forgiven without repentance, it is evident that the sin of despair is never forgiven, since it excludes all repentance and does not permit the wretched person [Col. 0905A] to depart from his iniquity.

Accordingly, our Lord and Saviour, having demonstrated by a most certain argument that he did and said all things not through Beelzebub but through the Holy Spirit, immediately added: “Every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven to human beings, but the blasphemy of the Spirit shall not be forgiven” (Matt. 12:31). This was as though he said: Wretched Pharisees—for he was speaking to them—offspring of vipers, evil trees bearing evil fruit: the devil has so blinded you 489 and hardened you in wickedness that you will never believe the Holy Spirit or depart from wickedness; and this sin indeed shall never be forgiven you.

But since this sin of despair alone is said to be committed against the Holy Spirit, although it is evident that whoever sins against the Holy Spirit also sins against the Father and the Son—for Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one, and consequently whoever offends one person certainly offends them all [Col. 0905B]—this is a difficult question. But may the Holy Spirit, of whom we speak, himself teach us how we ought to understand it.

This much, I think, is now plain: apart from the sin of despair, there is no other sin that cannot be blotted out by repentance. But this sin is not blotted out by repentance because it admits no repentance. For if it admitted repentance, it too, like the others, could be blotted out by repentance. It should be known, moreover, that just as it belonged to the Son alone to assume flesh in order to redeem us, so it belonged to the Holy Spirit alone [Col. 0905C] to appear in fiery tongues in order to teach and enlighten us. Hence he is said to have appeared not only in fire but also at the same time in tongues and fire, so that teaching may be understood in the tongue and illumination in fire, since teaching is given through the tongue and illumination through fire.

That the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son, came to teach and enlighten the world, the Lord himself showed while speaking to the disciples: “When that Spirit of truth comes,” he said, “he will teach you all truth” (John 16:13). The Lord could himself have done this if he had wished; but it so pleased the supreme and undivided Trinity that the Son should redeem us and the Holy Spirit should teach us.

Therefore, whoever does not receive the Holy Spirit’s teaching [Col. 0905D] and does not obey such and so great a master sins against the Holy Spirit. His counsels are whatever is written in the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospels. Whatever the apostles and teachers preach, and all others who proclaim the truth from the heart and with sincere understanding, are counsels not of a human being but of the Holy Spirit. Thus the Lord himself says: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:29). “Today, therefore, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Ps. 94:8).

Hear the Apostle—or rather, the Holy Spirit speaking through the Apostle: “According to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s judgment” [Col. 0906A] (Rom. 2:5). Therefore, since, as has just been shown, every sin and every disobedience seems especially and pre-eminently to be committed against the Holy Spirit—because he, who is the teacher through all the teachers of the Church, forbids this daily—yet only those who persist in evil and despair of God’s mercy never turn to repentance. And this is because of the enormity of the crime, compared with which other sins seem in some sense not even to be sins.

For there is a great difference between those who sin and immediately, or at some time, turn back, and those who sin in such a way that they never turn back. Far better is the servant who returns after fleeing than one who never returns after fleeing. The former is worthy of pardon; the latter of every punishment [Col. 0906B].

How much hope and joy these words produce! Behold, every sin and every blasphemy shall be forgiven to human beings. The Lord says this: Do not doubt; there is only one sin which is not forgiven (Matt. 10). What is it? To persist in wickedness and therefore despair of God’s mercy. For one who does not depart from sin and does not seek repentance cannot hope for any good, especially when the Lord says: “Unless you are converted and become like little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:3). You have sinned: stop. Turn away from evil and do good, and be secure.

But let us now see what hope is. Hope is the expectation of future goods. Those possess this expectation [Col. 0906C] who most certainly hope that they will one day receive whatever God has promised them. Sins alone obstruct this expectation. Remove sins, and hope is most certain. You will remove them if you return to repentance. “For at whatever hour the sinner is converted and groans, he shall live and shall not die” (Ezek. 33:12). Behold, we have been converted; the obstacle has been removed; the way is clear. Now, secure, let us say with the Psalmist: “Let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us, as we have hoped in you” (Ps. 30:22).—“In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me not be confounded for ever” (Ps. 71:1).—“O Lord my God, I have hoped in you; save me” (Ps. 7:2).—“Preserve me, O Lord, for I have hoped in you” (Ps. 15:1).

Let us hear the same man himself saying: “Hope in the Lord, and do goodness” (Ps. 36:3).—“And hope in him, all the assembly of the people” (Ps. 61:9).—“For it is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes. Cursed is the man who places his hope in a human being, and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord” (Ps. 117:9).—“For,” says the Apostle, “we were saved in hope. But hope which is seen is not hope. For what a person sees, why does he hope for it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it through patience” (Rom. 8:25).

Our Lord and Saviour himself also speaks to the Father through the Psalmist, saying: “Our fathers hoped in you; they hoped, and you delivered them. [Col. 0907A] They cried to you and were saved; they hoped in you, 490 and were not confounded” (Ps. 21:5). Therefore let us also hope, that we may not be confounded. Let us imitate our fathers, that we too may be saved and delivered from dangers.

Noah hoped in the Lord and was safe in the flood. Abraham hoped in the Lord, and the Lord delivered him from Ur of the Chaldeans.

> [Note: [Col. 0907D] We have elsewhere refuted this story, drawn from Hebrew traditions.]

The Hebrews relate that Abraham, because he refused to worship the fire which the Chaldeans worshipped, was thrown by them into the fire and delivered by the Lord without any injury. For *Ur* is interpreted as “fire.” The children of Israel hoped in the Lord, and he delivered them from the harshest slavery of the Egyptians. David hoped in the Lord, and, as he himself testifies, God rescued him from the hand of his enemies and from the hand of Saul. Hezekiah hoped in the Lord [Col. 0907B] and was delivered from the hands of the king of the Assyrians; and in one night the angel of the Lord struck down one hundred and eighty-five thousand from the camp of Sennacherib.

What shall I say of Job and Tobias? What of Judith? What of Esther? What of the three youths? What shall I say of Daniel and the Maccabees? All of them, hoping in the Lord, were divinely delivered from the greatest dangers. But concerning apostles and martyrs, confessors and virgins, it is better to be silent than to say little. Having placed all their hope in the Lord, they deserved to receive power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and upon all the enemy’s power, and nothing could harm them. If you wish to know how great their hope was, read their lives and passions, and you will see how “God is wonderful [Col. 0907C] in his saints, the God of Israel; he himself gave power and strength to his people. Blessed be God” (Ps. 67:36).

## CHAPTER III. On Charity

Blessed Paul the Apostle shows how great the power of charity is and how necessary it is to all people, saying: “If I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and have all faith, so as to move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor [Col. 0907D], and if I hand over my body so that I burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:1 ff.).

By these words the blessed Apostle most plainly shows [Col. 0908A] that whatever eloquence or fluency, whatever wisdom or knowledge, whatever fullness of faith or of all virtues a person may have, if he does not possess charity alone, he is nothing, it benefits him nothing, and he is accounted as nothing. Yet it is very remarkable if anyone can attain such great, as it is thought, perfection without charity. For it seems impossible—or, even if perhaps it is not impossible—to move mountains through faith, to give all one’s possessions to the poor, to hand over one’s body to the flames, to possess the spirit of prophecy, and to understand the hidden mysteries of God without charity.

> [Note: [Col. 0907D] St Bruno seems to doubt whether it is possible to move mountains through faith without charity. Yet the Gospel—Matthew 17:19 and Luke 17:6—states this absolutely possible, and attributes the cause of impossibility to the disciples’ unbelief, or their small faith. On the following page, after the middle, he says that casting out demons is moving mountains. Perhaps he interpreted it allegorically, because in Matthew the discussion concerned casting out a demon, which Christ’s disciples could not do; and he answered them that, if they had faith, they could also move a mountain. [Col. 0908D] But in Luke the statement is absolute, attached to no circumstance; Christ says absolutely to the apostles that through faith they could uproot a mulberry tree and plant it in the sea. Bruno seems likewise to doubt whether anyone may possess the spirit of prophecy through faith alone, without charity; yet around the middle of p. 491 he says that Balaam, Caiaphas, and many others possessed the spirit of prophecy without charity. Shortly afterward he adds that the Acts of the Apostles shows that certain non-Christians cast out demons through faith. Therefore they can also move mountains through faith without charity.]

But what shall we say about the tongues of human beings and angels? This grace was once very necessary, especially in the primitive Church, when they were sent to preach God’s word to all nations [Col. 0908B]. For how could they have taught them if they did not know their language? “The apostles therefore spoke in diverse tongues the mighty works of God” (Acts 2:11). Hence the Apostle also says: “I give thanks to my God that I speak in the tongues of all people” (1 Cor. 14:18).

But now few or none are found who possess knowledge of all languages. Each person’s own language is enough, because it is now enough for each person to preach in his own country. But how anyone speaks in the tongues of angels, or indeed in what tongues angels speak, may be doubted. We read that many spoke with angels; we have not heard them speaking and do not know how they speak. Those who spoke with them know how fluently, sweetly, pleasantly, readily, and elegantly [Col. 0908C] they speak. Nor do I much doubt that they spoke more pleasantly, sweetly, and readily than any human language can be spoken through mastery of an art.

Thus Moses, when he heard an angel speaking to him, said that he was of impeded and slow speech (Exod. 4:10), after he had heard the angel’s eloquence. Not because his own speech had become slower or more impeded through the angelic speech, but because, compared with that angel’s fluency and sweetness, he seemed to himself altogether mute and without speech.

We may understand by “human beings” philosophers and the other wise people of this world. By “angels,” however, we may designate patriarchs, prophets, and all others who announce God’s word and are worthy of the angelic name. Let the Apostle therefore say, and let each of us say: “If I speak with the tongues of human beings and angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” (1 Cor. 13:1), because I can benefit others, but cannot benefit myself. Sounding bronze and a clanging cymbal can indeed benefit others by calling, gathering, [Col. 0909A] delighting, and inviting them to battle; but because they are insensible, they cannot benefit themselves.

Likewise teachers of the Church, who ought to be better than all others, even if they speak all languages and imitate not only philosophers and orators but the angels themselves in eloquence and sweetness of speech, can benefit others but cannot benefit themselves if they lack charity alone. Therefore, when they speak with the intention that God may be glorified and the brethren edified, it is beyond doubt that their speech benefits them and that charity is present [Col. 0909B]. But if they expect a human reward from their preaching, let them hear the Lord saying: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6:4).

“And if I have prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have all faith, so as to move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13:2). For we read that Balaam, the Sibyl, Caiaphas, and many others possessed the spirit of prophecy; because they lacked charity, it profited them nothing. Many even to this day are endowed with great knowledge and expound deeply the mysteries of the holy Scriptures; because they lack charity, it profits them nothing.

We read in the Acts of the Apostles [Col. 0909C] concerning the sons of Sceva (Acts 19:14) that, although they were not Christians, they nevertheless cast out demons through faith [*per fidem*; evidently misread in the supplied text as *per finem*], adjuring them in the name of him whom Paul preached. They too will say at the judgment: “Lord, did we not prophesy in your name and cast out demons?” To them the Lord will say: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 7:12). They certainly would not have heard this had they possessed charity. Those who cast out demons are understood to move mountains.

“And if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3). When he says, “I am nothing” and “it profits me nothing,” this should be understood to mean that these and similar things without charity [Col. 0909D] contribute nothing toward receiving blessedness, although they help much to lessen punishments.

It should be noted, however, that in distributing possessions and giving alms the Lord seeks a sincere disposition more than a generous hand. We have heard concerning the Donatists how they frequently gave themselves over to flames, precipices, and other kinds of death, in order to become martyrs not of God, as they foolishly supposed, but rather of the devil. But, as has been sufficiently shown, no virtues and no good things can benefit anyone when charity is absent.

Behold, we have learned how great a good it is to possess charity; now let us hear what charity itself is like. Tell us, then, blessed Paul, what charity is like. “Charity is patient.” And from where do you prove this? Because [Col. 0910A] “it does not envy, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious; it does not seek its own. It is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice in iniquity, but rejoices together with truth” (ibid. 4–6).

Behold, it has been proved—and proved excellently—that it is patient and kind; this alone could have been sufficient. “It is patient” because it is angry with no one and is stirred by no injuries, but intercedes even for its enemies themselves. For if it were angry or stirred, it would not be patient. And because “it is kind,” it performs kindness and mercy for all whom it can. Therefore, since through patience it forgives all things and through kindness has mercy, what more can it do?

Because it is kind, “it does not envy”: it is not jealous. “It does not act perversely,” that is, it does nothing rashly and unjustly [Col. 0910B]. “It is not puffed up” into pride. “It is not ambitious,” because it does not seek worldly honours. “It does not seek its own,” but what belongs to all, so that they may be saved. It puts aside its own interests and attends to those of others. “It is not provoked,” otherwise it would not be patient. “It does not think evil,” which is contrary to kindness. “It does not rejoice in iniquity, but rejoices together with truth,” both of which pertain to kindness. “It believes all things” which ought to be believed.

What, then, are those things that must be believed, endured, and hoped for? Do you wish to hear what they are? All those things which both Testaments command us to believe, hope for, and endure. “Charity never fails” (ibid. 8). This is the respect in which charity is greater than the two virtues mentioned above, namely faith and hope; hence it continues: “But [Note: [Col. 0909D] The Vulgate reads ‘of these.’] charity is greater than these” (ibid. 13). It is greater because “it never fails,” because it is eternal, because it always exists and has no end. The other virtues will not be necessary after this life, because they concern only things which are awaited and do not yet appear. For hope is the expectation of future things. “But faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. 11:1). Where, then, will these virtues be after we hope for nothing and all things appear? For God will be all in all, and what they see and possess will suffice for all.

But let us hear also what the bridegroom says to the bride concerning charity in the Song of Songs: “Set me,” he says, “as a seal [Col. 0910D] upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm; for love is strong as death, jealousy hard as hell. Its lamps are lamps of fire and flame. Many waters could not quench charity, nor shall rivers overwhelm it” (Song 8:6 ff.). The Lord and our Saviour commands us always to have him as a seal upon our heart and never forget him; this pertains to great love, and this is what he says elsewhere: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart” (Matt. 22:37).

Therefore, let this always be upon our heart; let it always be upon our arm, so that charity may not be idle and the love that is in the heart may be manifested in the hands. [Col. 0911A] Let us go forth to meet our enemies when provoked by them, and let us not fear death, because “love is strong as death”—indeed, stronger. For stronger is the one who overcomes than the one who is overcome. “Jealousy is hard as hell.” What are we to understand by hell except every kind of punishment? Hence we are accustomed to say that those whom we see in the greatest torments are in hell. Therefore, because love cannot be overcome by torments, its steadfastness is rightly compared to hell and its punishments.

“Its lamps are lamps of fire and flame.” Let blessed Lawrence and those most famous youths be examples for us: kindled by the fire of charity, they did not fear the flames of the conflagration. The lamp of charity had so inflamed them within that they did not feel the fire of that lamp without. Hence the martyr of Christ [Col. 0911B] said: “Learn, wretch, that I do not feel your torments.” “Many waters could not quench charity, nor shall rivers overwhelm it.” Many waters are many peoples: not one or two, but a whole city rose against the martyr; yet so great was the fire of charity burning in the martyr’s heart that the entire flood of the raging people could not quench that flame. I do not put an end to this discourse, because charity has no end.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Four Cardinal Virtues
Four virtues govern the whole world, so joined to one another that they cannot exist apart from each other. Whoever possesses one possesses them all; whoever lacks any one of them possesses none. The first is called prudence, the second justice, the third fortitude, and the fourth temperance. [Note: Codex of St Mark, Florence: “of the heavens” (*coelorum*).]

Prudence, also called wisdom, is the knowledge of divine and human things. I do not mean the wisdom of this world, which is foolishness before God, concerning which the Apostle says: “God has made foolish the wisdom of this world” (1 Cor. 1:20); rather, I mean that wisdom which pertains to moral rectitude and to the salvation of souls. Not that which philosophers and rhetoricians teach, but that which the apostles and doctors preach. [Note: The same Codex of St Mark alone reads: “These alone possess knowledge of divine things.”] These indeed possess knowledge of divine things, as the Lord himself says: “He who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him” (John 14:21). This is the true knowledge of divinity: to know him who is true Wisdom, without whom there is no wisdom. [Note: Vatican Codex 1254: “This, therefore, is the true …”] “For all wisdom is from the Lord God, and has always been with him, and is before all time” (Ecclus. 1:1).

Wisdom among the other virtues is as gold among all metals. Thus, not without reason, wisdom is commonly signified by gold in the sacred page. Consider the tabernacle of testimony; consider Solomon’s temple. When you see that almost everything was fashioned from the purest gold, understand at last that wisdom is the greatest adornment and the supreme beauty of the saints. Where it is absent, everything is blind, dark, and obscure. Who, then, can rule or govern without it his kingdom, province, land, household, or even himself? Understand, you mighty ones of the age, and devote yourselves to wisdom.

How necessary justice is is sufficiently shown by the imperial laws, canons, and decrees of the saints that were made for its preservation. Take away justice and the world perishes. Where justice is absent, wrongdoing rules: there are frauds and robberies, thefts and murders, fear and distress, and no security. Justice is the fear of the wicked and the security of the good. What, then, is justice itself? “Justice is the constant and perpetual will to render to each person his due.” [Note: Codex Vaticanus: “rendering to each person.”] Whoever always has this will—to render each person his due and to permit no one to usurp what belongs by right to another—is certainly just.

But the devil has no right over human nature. God, not the devil, made man. Therefore man belongs by right to God: he must reign in us; he must possess our members. Thus the Apostle says: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires” (Rom. 6:12). [Note: Codex of St Mark, Florence, and the cited Vatican codex: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body.”] He is a thief, a plunderer; what he possesses is not his by right. Drive him from yourself; restore to God his possession, and you will be just. For that person is just who renders to each one his due.

For this reason the name is common to all saints, and all saints are called righteous: because they work this justice within themselves, and, having expelled vices, render to the Lord what is his. [p. 493] Otherwise, how would those be called righteous to whose judgments no one comes? [Note: The cited Vatican codex reads: “to whose judgment.”] Hence the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. 11:31).

Above all, emperors, kings, and other authorities were established from the beginning for the sake of justice: that they might render each person his due, prohibit injuries, restrain the wicked, protect the good, and order everything equitably. If they do this, they will be blessed. For it is written concerning them: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and perform justice at all times” (Ps. 115:3). And again: “Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wis. 1:1).

But what shall I say of fortitude, without which both wisdom and justice seem useless? Fortitude is not bodily strength, but steadfastness of mind, by which we overcome injuries, endure every adversity, and are not puffed up by prosperity. Whoever is overcome by pride, anger, greed, lust, drunkenness, and similar things does not possess this fortitude. Nor are they strong who, when placed amid adversity, strive to escape it at the expense of the soul’s salvation. Hence the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28). Likewise, those who exalt themselves in prosperity and dissolve into excessive joy cannot be called strong. How are those strong who cannot conceal and restrain the impulse of their heart? Fortitude is not conquered; if it is conquered, it is not fortitude. The saints possessed this fortitude: they could be overcome neither by vices, nor torments, nor flatteries.

It remains to speak of temperance, which does not exceed due measure in its actions, since it seeks nothing superfluous. [Note: Codex of St Mark reads instead: “Let this, then, be present in all undertakings”; the Vatican codex reads as in the edition.] Let this, then, be its definition. It is so necessary that the world itself could not endure without it. Since man is composed of contrary elements, unless there were some nature that tempered things opposed and hostile to one another, he could not remain long amid such discord and immense conflict. But this is a philosophical question and cannot be settled in one discourse.

Temperance is useful in every undertaking. Hear what blessed Paul says concerning wisdom itself, and how he shows that it needs temperance: “Do not be wise beyond what it is fitting to be wise, but be wise unto sobriety” (Rom. 12:3). [Note: The same Vatican codex: concerning justice it is written in Ecclesiastes 7, “Do not be excessively righteous.”] Blessed Benedict also, whose authority is very great—for the Holy Spirit spoke in him—gave a similar command: “Let there be nothing excessive.” Concerning fortitude, moreover, he says: “He who presses the breasts hard to draw out milk brings forth butter; and he who squeezes violently brings forth blood.” Temperance is therefore necessary here as well. He presses the breasts violently who, after they have been exhausted of milk, still does not cease to press them and to demand from them what they do not possess. Whoever, then, strives to press and afflict himself or others with fasts, vigils, and other mortifications beyond what his own or their nature can bear, truly presses the breasts violently; and from that whence he hopes for the fruit of life, he often draws the fruit of sin and death.

Hence the Apostle says: “I beseech you, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God—your rational service” (Rom. 12:1). That service is rational by which not nature itself but vices are destroyed.

Enough has now been said briefly concerning the four principal virtues: what they are, and how necessary they are to all, especially to the powerful, to whom the governance of the world has been entrusted. Let us now see how they follow one another and cannot exist apart from one another. Whoever thinks it impossible to possess them all should strive as far as possible to possess even one; if he has that one, the others will undoubtedly follow it.

Therefore, O ruler, whoever you may be, see to it that you possess and retain justice. It seems more necessary to you; and through this one virtue you will immediately appear wise, strong, and well-governed in all things. Yet take care that, while you administer justice to others, you do not forget yourself; and while you exercise justice among the people, exercise it also within yourself.

Abraham was just, for it is written of him: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as justice” (Rom. 4:3). What justice is greater than to believe and obey one’s Creator? Because he possessed this one virtue, there can be no doubt that he possessed the others also.

Joseph was strong, for he overcame the woman who provoked him to lust; and in this fortitude he appears wise, just, and temperate. The three youths were just, for they refused to worship the idol contrary to the laws of their homeland; by this deed it was shown how wise and temperate they were. Daniel was wise, since God had revealed his secrets to him. [Note: From the Vatican codex the edition is supplied: “to whose wisdom the prophets themselves bear witness.”] How just he was, the two elders proved; how strong, the lions proved, who did not dare attack him when he was placed in the den. Since he had already overcome vices, the lions feared him. What temperance he possessed is attested by the vegetables on which he fed and by his long fasts. [p. 494]

But do you wish to hear of those who lost the other virtues because they lacked one of these? David lost fortitude when bodily pleasure, at the sight of Bathsheba, overcame him; [Note: The edition is corrected from the Vatican codex.] the other virtues immediately fled from him in terror. Who can doubt that he was then foolish, unjust, and without temperance, when, overcome by lust, he committed such grave sins at once? Yet happy was he, because, led by repentance, he deserved to hear: “Your sin is forgiven you” (2 Kings 12:13).

Solomon likewise, having lost the wisdom in which he surpassed others, sacrificed to idols; justice, fortitude, and temperance immediately departed from him. Examine each case in this way and you will discover that the four virtues cannot exist apart from one another.

But if you wish to see them well joined and associated, consider the apostles and martyrs; consider the confessors and doctors of the Church. These virtues surrounded and embraced them in such a way that they could indeed be killed, but could never be separated or torn away from them.

This was signified in Exodus 25 by the four golden rings on the ark of the covenant, through which two poles were passed and never removed from them. Those poles were covered with the purest gold. That the ark of the covenant signifies the holy Church is well known. The four rings are the four virtues mentioned above—golden, certainly, and more splendid than every beauty; whoever is not adorned by them is neither splendid nor beautiful. By the two poles I understand Peter and Paul, and the other saints, without whom the Church of God can neither be raised, carried, nor governed. They are golden because they shine with the light of blameless life and wisdom. The poles are never withdrawn from the rings because holy men are never separated from the aforesaid virtues.

By these, therefore, the ark is carried: for by their faith, teaching, and examples the holy Church is governed; and by the steps of the virtues, through the ministry of bishops and priests, it is lifted up to heavenly things. But bishops and priests must always fear greatly lest they attempt to carry the ark of God without poles. Heretics carry the ark of God without poles: preaching their own foolish inventions, they flee apostolic authorities and depart from Catholic faith and teaching.

Let them always remember what happened to the sons of Eli, namely Hophni and Phinehas, who caused the ark of God to be captured, and themselves perished in battle. They were exceedingly blameworthy and arrogant in life and conduct. Hence Hophni is not inappropriately interpreted as “unshod,” and Phinehas as “mute mouth.” It is not fitting for one who is mute, and who does not yet have feet shod with the preparation of the Gospel of peace, to undertake the governance of God’s Church. Such men capture the Church of God and hand it over into the slavery of evil spirits; but they too die in battle, though they ought to have freed others from death.

The four colours with which the veils and curtains of the tabernacle were woven—always placed together and never separately—signified these four virtues: namely hyacinth-blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted fine linen. [Note: The text bears witness that the author expounded Exodus.] We have spoken sufficiently about them in our exposition of Exodus; now we merely provide material for discourse. By those colours the tabernacle, and by these virtues the Church, is adorned and beautified; for without wisdom, justice, fortitude, and temperance, no soul can be adorned or beautified. These are the ornaments of which it is said: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment embroidered with gold, clothed round about with varieties” (Ps. 44:10).

## CHAPTER V. On Humility

[Col. 0915C]

The most blessed Virgin Mary, mother and daughter of humility, teaches us how great a virtue humility is. “My soul magnifies the Lord,” she says, “and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior, because he has looked upon the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:46). She did not say, “because he has looked upon my patience, my piety, my mercy, my innocence, my virginity,” and the other virtues in which the most blessed Virgin abounded, with which she was clothed as with royal ornaments. Rather, she wished to say this alone: “because he has looked upon the humility of his handmaid.” “For upon whom does God look, except upon the humble and quiet person, and upon one trembling at his words?” (Isa. 66:2). [Note: Codex Vallicellianus and Vatican codex 994: “trembling at his words.”]

Our Virgin was clothed in many ornaments; more fittingly I could have called her our Lady, our Queen. Yet this one quality shone more brightly than the rest: humility, upon which, she says, God and Lord looked. Perhaps this is what the Lord says especially to her in the Song of Songs: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart with one lock of your neck and with one of your eyes” (Song 4:9). For humility can nowhere be detected more readily than in the neck and eyes. It is characteristic of humble persons to walk with bowed neck and eyes lowered to the earth; whereas the proud always walk with raised neck and uplifted brows.

Hence Moses commands, concerning the turtledove and pigeon when it is sacrificed, that its head be bent back toward its neck. [p. 495] God does not accept the sacrifices of the proud: “He is exalted, and looks upon humble things; and he knows lofty things from afar” (Ps. 137:6). What are lofty things but those that are raised up and proud? He deigns not to look upon these. Thus the one lock, which does not stand erect but lies low in humility, is humility itself, by which the Virgin’s neck is adorned.

He said “one of your eyes” because he was speaking not of several virtues but of one. Yet the sister and bride of Christ has two eyes: with one she looks upon earth, with the other upon heaven. By these are signified humility and contemplation. Often the eye of humility, which looks upon the earth, pleases God more than the eyes of contemplation, which sometimes search out things that it is not permitted to know. Hence elsewhere he says: “Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me flee away” (Song 8:22). For if it were lawful to know everything, the Apostle would not say that there are things “which it is not lawful for a man to utter” (2 Cor. 12:4).
