What it is not lawful to utter, it is not lawful to know.

It was excellently done that the Lord chose a humble mother: the humble Son ought to have a humble mother. A lamb is born not from a lioness but from a sheep; nothing among animals is humbler than the sheep and the lamb. Strike, slaughter, cut its throat, kill it: they neither complain with their voice, threaten with horn, nor defend themselves with tooth or hoof. Hence it is elegantly said of the Lord himself through the prophet: “Like a lamb he was led to slaughter, and he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 57:7).

The devil, through pride, so far as lay in him, ascended above all the heavens; Christ, through humility, descended to earth. “He humbled himself,” as the Apostle says, “becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. 2:8). By his humility those were saved who had perished through the other’s pride. The devil wished to become like the Most High; Christ assumed the form and likeness of a servant. Eve displeased God through pride; Mary pleased the Redeemer through humility. Eve, in pride, refused obedience and approached the forbidden tree too boldly and rashly. Mary, however, modest and humble, professes obedience, saying: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38).

God therefore looked upon such great humility, and for this reason she alone, out of all women who are, have been, or will be, was chosen by the Lord to become the Mother of God and to be called Queen of heaven and earth. Therefore let the most blessed Virgin say: “My soul magnifies the Lord, because he has looked upon the humility of his handmaid” (ibid., v. 47). Let her say what glory, honour, and blessedness she received because the Lord so wished to look upon her: “For behold,” she says, “from this time all generations shall call me blessed.”

See, then, how great is the power of humility: it makes God descend to earth and man ascend to heaven. It is that which brings down the mighty from their seat and exalts the humble. “For everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14:11). How well these two testimonies of mother and Son agree: what the mother said, the Son confirms.

Our Savior relates that two men went up to the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a publican; one proud and the other humble (Luke 18:13). One looked upon everyone else; the other did not dare even to raise his eyes to heaven. He stood bowed down, which, as we said above, is a sign of great humility. The proud man gained nothing; the humble man returned to his house justified.

Whoever does not understand how great a good humility is should strive to understand how great an evil pride is. For each thing can easily be understood through its opposite. Humility and pride are opposites. Concerning pride the Psalmist says: “Let not the foot of pride come upon me, nor let the hand of the sinner move me. There all who work iniquity have fallen; they have been cast out and could not stand” (Ps. 35:12).

An evil foot, an evil hand: all fall through the one, and all are cast out through the other. Our first parents had good feet before they sinned through pride. They sinned, they fell, and with those weak, gout-afflicted feet they could not stand. As many as are the vices, so many are the feet of pride; and these may likewise be called the hands of the sinner. This sinner is the devil, whose envy moves many hands, drives many people onward, tears many away from honour and justice, and compels them to go headlong toward death.

He used “foot” and “hand” in the singular because Scripture commonly uses the singular for the plural, as in: “He sent among them the dog-fly,” that is, the biting fly, “and it devoured them; and the frog, and it destroyed them” (Ps. 77:45). [Note: From the Vatican codex: “Saint Bruno says the same elsewhere.”] “There all who work iniquity have fallen”: there the miser has fallen, there the robber, there the lustful person, there the sacrilegious person, there the murderer, there the perjurer, there the adulterer and fornicator. They were cast out and moved by the devil’s hand because, their feet already weak, they could not stand.

Nor is it unsuitable if someone wishes to understand it thus: “Let not the foot of pride come upon me,” that is, let pride not be my foot; let it not carry me, for in it all evil spirits fell, who everywhere work iniquity. They were expelled from the heavenly seats and could not stand.

If someone carefully considers why the Lord wished to call himself not a cedar or fir, which are exceedingly tall, but rather a vine, which is humblest among trees and needs another’s help, [p. 496] he will be able to recognize from this also how greatly the Lord always loved humility. “I am the vine,” he says, “and you are the branches” (John 15:5). He was speaking to the disciples, whom he was inviting to the glory of humility. It was as if he said: From a small tree come small branches; from a slender tree come slender branches—yet branches able to occupy wide stretches of ground around them.

This is the vine of which it is written: “He extended his branches even to the sea, and his shoots to the river” (Ps. 79:12). For “their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5). No tree provides human beings so much benefit by its fruit as the vine, though it is small and humble.

Grain too grows not on trees but upon a lowly herb. Concerning it the Lord likewise says: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24), clearly signifying that he himself is the grain of wheat. Nothing is more useful to human life on earth than these two kinds, through which our Savior wished to signify himself because they are very humble.

It should also be observed that nearly all humble trees are found to be more fertile and fruitful. As I consider these things, that most noble tree which sacred Scripture itself calls most beautiful suddenly comes to mind; and because it too is very humble, I must not pass over it in silence. [Note: Vatican codex: read in Leviticus, chapter 23.] Read Leviticus, and you will find where the Lord speaks through Moses to the children of Israel concerning the feast of tabernacles. This feast was celebrated for seven days, and the Lord commanded the children of Israel to take the fruits of the most beautiful tree, branches of palms, boughs of trees with dense foliage, and willows from the torrent, and to rejoice before the Lord. [Note: Compare what Bruno said concerning this passage of Leviticus.]

We, who are commanded to celebrate this feast for seven days, ought to celebrate it all our days. What is it to celebrate a feast except to refrain from iniquity and persevere in good work? Those remain in tabernacles who, unwilling to remain in this world, hasten toward another homeland, saying with the Apostle: “We do not have here an abiding city, but seek the one to come” (Heb. 13:14).

We cannot worthily celebrate this feast of ours unless we have the fruit of the most beautiful tree. By the most beautiful tree the Hebrews understand the citron tree, which is indeed so noble in fragrance, taste, leaf, flower, and in the size and beauty of its fruit that it is difficult to find anything worthy of comparison with it. By this most beautiful and humble tree we understand the blessed Virgin Mary, concerning whom it is written: “And our land shall yield its fruit” (Ps. 49:9); and again: “Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne” (Ps. 131:11). Whoever understands the tree does not doubt concerning the fruit. For the fruit is Christ, whose whole feast may be celebrated.

Let us therefore receive this fruit in our feasts; let us be refreshed and satisfied by it; let us be fattened and made drunk by his flesh and blood. Nor should we ever forget this most beautiful tree. Let us always look toward it and seek from it the fruit of life and salvation. O truly most beautiful wood, worthy to bear such fruit! We call her a tree, but Scripture calls her wood. Because the Virgin gave birth, she is called not a tree but wood. She was signified by Aaron’s rod, which, though dry, produced flowers, leaves, and almond nuts.

By the palm-branches, required at this feast, are signified the instruments of victory. *Spatula* is a diminutive of *spatha*, while the palm signifies victory. The instruments of victory are virtues and good works, by which vices and evil spirits are overcome. These little palm-branches are therefore very necessary at feasts, because then people are especially attacked by the snares of enemies.

By the branches of trees with dense foliage are understood the books, discourses, words, and examples of the saints. Blessed Paul is such a tree: his foliage is very dense, his words most abundant; his leaves do not fall, and all his words must be fulfilled. He is so necessary to you in our feasts that without him we can scarcely deliver a single discourse. If you wish to know how humble a tree he also is, hear him say: “For I am the least of the apostles, and am not worthy to be called an apostle” (1 Cor. 15:9).

Some wish to understand the tree with dense foliage literally as the myrtle, which is indeed a rather small and humble tree. Perhaps because of this humility he said not full palm-branches but little palm-branches; for although the palm is a tall tree, *spatula* is a diminutive, in which humility is most plainly declared.

There remain the willows from the torrent, by which memory is signified: because whatever is done and said in feasts is bound together in memory as though in a single bundle, so that it may not slip away from the heart and may always be remembered. The willow is a most tenacious tree, and beyond this it seems to possess nothing by which it could, even if it wished, become proud. [p. 497] Willows are rightly taken from the torrent, because the memory most necessary in our needs is that drawn from the rivers of Holy Scripture. For we ought to recount not our own words but those of the saints, and not things drawn from our own heart but those drawn from the springs of Israel.

We see that small trees please God; we see that every height of pride displeases God (1 Pet. 3:6). Let us therefore humble ourselves under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt us in the time of tribulation—he who lives and reigns for ages of ages.

## CHAPTER VI. On Mercy
“The mercies of the Lord I will sing for ever” (Ps. 88:1). What King and Prophet David thought concerning mercy is sufficiently declared by these words, as he promises that he will sing the praises of mercy for ever. Elsewhere also he says: “Mercy and judgment I will sing to thee, O Lord” (Ps. 100:1). Thus the Lord is merciful, so that he does not abandon justice [Col. 0920A]. [Note: Cod. Vat.: “abandons.”] Thus he is just, so that he does not forget mercy. He shows mercy, but to the penitent and to those who show mercy. Therefore show mercy, if you wish him to have mercy on you; forgive, and you shall be forgiven; give, and it shall be given to you. He himself says: “If you forgive men their sins, your heavenly Father also will forgive you your sins; but if you do not forgive men their sins, neither will your Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6:14). “Be therefore merciful, as your heavenly Father is merciful: who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust” (Luke 6:36).

Our Saviour calls us to mercy; he shows the way of salvation; he teaches us by what road we may return to our homeland. There is no [Col. 0920B] other way by which we can return. But see how easy the way is: forgive, and you shall be forgiven. Are you unwilling to forgive a hundred denarii, so that a thousand talents may be forgiven you? Know that torturers await you, to thrust you into prison; nor will they permit you to depart from there until you have paid the entire debt. Alas! How many are there now in that place who, because they were unwilling to forgive in this world, now grieve, now accuse themselves, now repent; but such repentance is late, useless, and fruitless. If it were now said to them, “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke 6:37), with what joy they would now forgive and spare their debtors! Yet these will not be able to sing the mercies of the Lord for ever, because his mercy is only in this world; in hell, however, there is no redemption.

[Col. 0920C] But the good shall sing the mercies of the Lord for ever, because without end they shall give thanks to God. They shall praise him who prepared for them so great a blessedness, not from their merits, but from his own mercy. “The Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and greatly merciful” (Ps. 85:15). When he suffered for us on the cross, overflowing with exceeding mercy, he prayed even for those who crucified him, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). Hence it is fittingly added: “The Lord is gracious to all” (Ps. 145:9)—to all indeed, since he is gracious even to his enemies—“and his compassions are over all his works” (ibid.). God made heaven, earth, sea, angels, and human beings; but his compassions are over all his works.

[Col. 0920D] Considering these compassions, the prophet was awestruck, saying: “O Lord, I heard thy report and was afraid; I considered thy works and was terrified. Thou shalt be known in the midst of two living creatures” (Hab. 3:1). And indeed these works of his, these acts of his working, are above all his works; and it is greatly to be feared that the King of kings and Lord of lords, who made all things out of nothing, for the sake of most wicked servants was reckoned among the wicked and condemned to a most shameful death. The Greeks aptly call mercy *oleon* [ἔλαιον, “oil”], because, just as oil is uppermost among liquids, so mercy is supreme among all God’s works, as he said above: “His compassions are over all his works.”

[Col. 0921A] Whatever liquid you pour oil over, the oil always floats on top. Oil, therefore, signifies mercy. For this reason we have been anointed so often: that we may never forget mercy. All of us have been anointed alike on the crown of the head, on the forehead, and on the breast. Kings and priests, however, receive other anointings besides these, because, being appointed judges among God’s people, they ought to show mercies more numerous and greater than others.

We are anointed on the crown of the head so that, all pride being cast out from there, mercy may have its seat there, and all our senses may always obey it. For the five senses of the body are in the head, and all ought to serve mercy. They do so if the eyes look upon the needy and poor, [Col. 0921B] if the ears hear the cry of the poor, and if the tongue orders its words in judgment. “For pleasant is the man who has compassion and lends; he orders his words in judgment, because he shall not be moved for ever” (Ps. 111:5).

The anointing upon the forehead ought to make a person’s whole countenance cheerful and ready for mercy, so that the good will that is in the heart may be recognized in the face itself. “For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7). We are anointed on the breast, moreover, so that the good of mercy may never depart from our heart and memory. [498] The hands that have been anointed are not closed to the poor; they do not know how to seize or strike; they always labour at what is good, so that they may have something to give to those suffering need.

Whoever, therefore, [Col. 0921C] after so many anointings does not stretch himself out toward mercy, but still lies hard, contracted, weak, and paralysed, because he is far from mercy—what forgiveness can he hope for? Whoever cannot do otherwise, let him at least stretch himself out by affection or desire. Even walls, mountains, and trees invite us to mercy. Altars, stones, and walls are anointed for this reason: that the people signified by them may understand their own anointings through these things, and, understanding them, preserve them.

Our Saviour often used to ascend the Mount of Olives and pray. From there he also ascended into heaven; there he left the disciples, whom nevertheless he never abandoned. Thus he called us to mercy not only by words and examples, but by the very act itself. The Mount [Col. 0921D] of Olives is the mountain of peace and mercy. Peace and mercy are very closely joined; hence both are fittingly signified by the olive.

As many as are the virtues, so many are the mountains to which we may ascend and upon which we may pray. Upon the mountain of humility the humble stand and pray; upon the mountain of patience the patient stand and pray; upon the mountain of obedience the obedient stand and pray. Thus, standing upon the mountain of mercy, the peaceable and merciful also pray. Let us therefore remain upon this mountain. Here the Lord left his disciples; from here is the way by which one goes to heaven. Nor is it without reason that Cherubim made from olive wood are said to have stood in the Temple with wings spread, teaching the people.

[Col. 0922A] Do you wish to fly? Take up the wings of mercy; they will bear you to the Father of mercies and to the God of all consolation. When the Lord comes to judgment, as the words of the holy Gospel seem to teach, he speaks only of mercy: praising some for mercy, rebuking and condemning others because they did not have mercy. “I was hungry,” he says, “and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you received me; naked, and you clothed me; sick, and you visited me. Come therefore, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:36). When they ask him when they saw him thus or ministered to him thus, he says: “What you did to one of my least [Col. 0922B] ones, you did to me” (ibid.). But for the others, who were unwilling to do this, there is only the sentence of condemnation.

See how his compassions are over all his works. Whatever we have done out of compassion, generosity, liberality, or piety—provided we have done it for God’s sake—all pertains to mercy. All the divine Scriptures, all the books of the apostles and prophets, are full of the praises of mercy; but especially the book of Psalms, which overflows so much with praises of mercy as though there were no other subject of which it could speak.

“Let them confess to the Lord his mercies, and his wonders to the children of men. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures for ever. Let Aaron now say that he is good, for his mercy endures for ever. Let all who fear the Lord now say that he is good, for his mercy endures [Col. 0922C] for ever.” But “who is wise, and will keep these things, and will understand the mercies of the Lord?” (Ps. 106:1 and following). He lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER VII. On Peace

[Note: Col. 0921D: Cod. Vat. adds: “On peace at the Nativity of the Lord.”]

“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:13). This is not the voice of a human being; it is the voice of angels. The multitude of angels sang this when Christ was born, as the words of the Gospel testify. And indeed, then glory was restored to heaven and peace to earth, when our Saviour, the Prince [Col. 0922D] of Peace, was born of the Virgin; when the people who sat in darkness were illuminated by the true light. Having abandoned the worship of idols, they began to praise, magnify, and glorify the Creator, rendering to him alone that glory which they had formerly been accustomed to render to demons.

Then people began to possess peace: loving God and neighbour, casting anger, hatred, and discord away from themselves, coming together in the concord of one faith, agreeing with one another, fleeing the vain doctrine of philosophers and heretics, all speaking with the Apostle to him himself and doing injury to no one.

[Note: Col. 0922D, Cod. Vat. 994: “That is indeed our peace, that stable, firm, and everlasting security.”]

Such is peace in the Church of God; such is peace for people [Col. 0923A] of good will. Beasts cannot possess peace, since they delight in blood and are nourished by cruelty. This peace is not given to people of evil will, because “there is no peace for the wicked,” says the Lord (Isa. 68:22). That is the peace of the saints; this is the concord of those of whom it is said: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32).—“Behold how good and [499] how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132:1).

Jerusalem possessed this peace; its name is interpreted “vision of peace.” That is, the Jerusalem in which the peaceable King dwells, “whose face the whole earth desires” (3 Kings 10:24). “And his place was made in peace, and his dwelling in Sion; there he broke the powers, the bow, shield, sword, and [Col. 0923B] war” (Ps. 75:4). Do you not hear that every instrument of discord, every instrument of strife and contention, has been broken in Sion? Peace and concord alone reign in Jerusalem.

[Note: Col. 0923D, Ascensian edition adds: “For this reason such great peace, such riches, such wisdom and eloquence were given to Solomon, who dwelt for a short time in Sion and Jerusalem: because he signified this our Solomon, truly peaceable, truly wise, eloquent, and abounding in all riches, of whom we have just said: ‘And his place was made in peace, and his dwelling in Sion.’ He promised his disciples, saying: ‘Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age.’ Thus [Col. 0924D] his dwelling in Sion and his place in Jerusalem were made not temporarily, but for eternity. ‘He who does not love peace,’” etc.]

He who does not love peace drives the Prince of Peace away from himself. Christ dwells nowhere but in Jerusalem, nowhere but in a place of peace and rest; nor was it fitting that the peaceable King should dwell elsewhere than in a place of peace. Concerning this peaceable King it is written in the Song of Songs: “A vineyard belonged to the peaceable one; in that which has peoples he gave it to keepers. A man brings for its fruit a thousand pieces of silver. My vineyard is before me. A thousand are yours, peaceable one, and two hundred for those who guard its fruits” (Song 8:11–12).

The sense and order of the words, briefly, are as follows: “A vineyard belonged to the peaceable one,” among [Col. 0923C] that nation which has many peoples. Who this peaceable one is, is plain; and “he gave it to keepers,” namely, the apostles and teachers.

[Note: Both Vatican codices: “A man brings for its fruit a thousand pieces of silver,” speaking of his vineyard.]

“My vineyard is before me,” says therefore he who speaks to the Church, to whom he speaks. Those thousand pieces of silver of your peaceable one, and another two hundred, are given to the keepers who guard its fruits. This is my judgment; this seems good to me. But now let us discuss each point.

The Church had said: “I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower; since I became before him as one finding peace” (ibid., 10). Then follows: “A vineyard belonged to the peaceable one in that which has peoples.” The Church says: Before I possessed peace, before I knew the peaceable King, I was weak and feeble [Col. 0923D] and unable to defend myself against enemies. But now I am strong and have become like an impregnable wall; and my breasts—

[Note: Both Vatican codices: “my teaching.”]

—my teachings, by whose milk I nourish my children, have become like most strong towers against all the wisdom of this world and against the arguments of philosophers and heretics [Col. 0924A].

To this someone may quite fittingly reply: “Strong indeed you are, but all this your strength is in the keepers.” Concerning them it follows: “A vineyard belonged to the peaceable one; in that which has peoples he gave it to keepers.” This peaceable one is our Saviour, who reconciled the world to God the Father: “For he is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2:14). His vineyard is the Church, within whose boundaries Hebrews, Greeks, Latins, and barbarians—all races, peoples, and nations—are contained. He gave it to keepers, namely, apostles and teachers, that they might guard, cultivate, nourish it, prune away what is superfluous, and plant other vines in place of others.

A man also brings for its fruit a thousand pieces of silver to these keepers, so that they may be able to pay all that is necessary [Col. 0924B] for proper expenses and debts. The number one thousand is perfect, for it consists of denarii alone: ten times one hundred, or one hundred times ten, makes a thousand. Therefore those to whom a thousand pieces of silver were given deserved to receive all knowledge of both Testaments and the fullness of every grace.

[Note: The exposition in the same Bruno’s commentary on the Song of Songs is shorter, but conveys the same spirit and teaching.]

The man is Christ, of whom it is written elsewhere: “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the wicked” (Ps. 1:1). In order that he might not lose all the fruit of his vineyard, he bestowed this fullness of graces upon its keepers. The whole praise of this vineyard lies in its fruit alone; therefore it is praised, therefore loved, therefore handed over and entrusted to keepers, because it yields much and good fruit. Just as, [Note: Cod. Vat. 1254: “on the contrary.”] conversely, [Col. 0924C] that other vineyard was condemned and rejected because, having turned to bitterness, it gave wild grapes instead of grapes and vinegar instead of wine (Isa. 5:4). Good fruit consists in virtues and good works, with which both angels and human beings were created.

What it says, “My vineyard is before me,” means as if he said: “I gave it to keepers, but I have not ceased to guard it. It is always before me; I do not cease to guard it myself. For unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it watch in vain” (Ps. 126:1). Let us now see what Solomon—or rather the Holy Spirit through Solomon—says to the Church concerning the keepers: “A thousand are yours, peaceable one, and two hundred for those who guard its [Col. 0924D] fruits.” As if he said: “Let the thousand pieces of silver of your man, your king, and your peaceable one, of which mention was made above, and another two hundred beyond those thousand, be given to those keepers who guard its fruits.” They are worthy to receive both the former and the latter. By the thousand pieces of silver, we have said, is signified the fullness of every grace [500] and of all knowledge [Col. 0925A].

Yet we read that many possessed this fullness who did not attain the glory of eternal blessedness. Such are those who will say at the judgment: “Lord, did we not prophesy in thy name, cast out demons, and perform many mighty works?” (Matt. 7:22). To them the Lord will say: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you.” A thousand pieces of silver, therefore, do not suffice to receive blessedness, although they seem sufficient for governing the Church. Let another two hundred be given to the saints; by these we understand the perfection and sufficiency of all souls and bodies, so that nothing may be lacking to blessedness for those who possess double portions in the land. For one hundred is a perfect number, because it consists of denarii alone, in which all numbers are contained; its [Col. 0925B] doubling seems to pertain to the perfection of both aspects of the human person.

But if we wish to say what, of what kind, and how great peace is, the Apostle confronts us, saying: “And may the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your thoughts” (Phil. 4:7). For who can say what, of what kind, or how great is that which surpasses every sense and transcends every understanding? And indeed, since so great a price was paid in order that the peace lost in the first human being might be restored to humankind in the second human being, Jesus Christ, the mystery of God’s will can neither be spoken nor conceived.

Therefore, if it is possible and insofar as it lies within us, let us have peace with all people. For even if another flees peace, yet if you offer it and desire to possess it, then, insofar as it lies within you, you are not deprived of the benefit [Col. 0925C] of peace. Hence the Psalmist says: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceable” (Ps. 119:6). “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matt. 5:9).

Rightly, while the ark still floated in the flood and nothing but waters appeared everywhere, the dove returned with an olive branch, through which restored peace and tranquillity were signified. In that ark was the whole human race: all races, peoples, and nations were there. Then, in that dove, the Holy Spirit was in some manner speaking to them and seemed to say: “Have peace, keep peace, love peace, without which no one shall see God, and the God of peace and love shall be with you. You are few indeed, but small things grow through concord, while great things fall apart through discord.”

[Col. 0925D] All animals were gathered there, and a few chosen from all, so that they might possess and keep peace and not harm one another. I think that this peace remained among them for some time even after they had gone out from the ark. For lions and griffins, tigers and leopards, wolves and bears, and other beasts accustomed to live by prey, would have wholly consumed sheep and goats, oxen and asses, and other gentle animals—especially since they could not so quickly have separated and gone away from one another. The same may also be understood of birds. But their children later violated this peace, ignorant of their parents’ covenants.

If, therefore, holy peace existed among beasts in the ark, how great should peace and concord be among Christians in the Church? Let us then hear the Lord speaking, and commit to memory what he says: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you. I do not give to you as the world gives” (John 14:27). The world’s peace is temporary and quickly passes away; Christ’s peace is eternal and never ends.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Patience

Our Lord and Saviour, inviting the apostles to constancy and strength in patience, speaks to them in the Gospel, saying: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is [Col. 0926B] the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:10). Not all who suffer persecution are therefore blessed.

[Note: The same Codex of St Mark at Florence, and both Vatican codices: “But those alone are blessed who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake.”]

For lovers of this world, perjurers, adulterers, and robbers both inflict and suffer many persecutions. Yet they are not blessed but miserable, because they often suffer such things not for righteousness’ sake, but for their own desires and pleasures, for worldly honours and dignities, and for the many iniquities which they commit. Who could enumerate their miseries, torments, and the carefully devised kinds of every torture by which these children of iniquity torment and afflict one another, so that one may possess another’s goods? Here are the dark shadows of prison, hunger and thirst, cold and heat, severing of limbs, [Col. 0926C] tearing out of eyes, intolerable stench, and the other things which the children of the devil, at his urging and instigation, can inflict upon his martyrs.

For Satan too has his martyrs: the greater the torments they endure in his service in this world, the stronger those that await them in the next. This is his peculiar and singular practice: those who serve him more suffer from him greater and harsher torments. Judas Iscariot and the most impious Nero were his martyrs, who strangled and killed themselves by a deserved hanging and death. [501] His martyrs also are those who, even to this day, fight against one another not for righteousness but for their own greed and wickedness, attack one another in turn, and, pursuing one another with unjust hatred, slaughter themselves cruelly like beasts. Such people, therefore, are not blessed but miserable who suffer persecutions of this kind and in this manner, because they shall never enter [Col. 0926D] the kingdom of heaven.

Only those, then, are blessed in their persecutions who suffer them for righteousness’ sake. How is this proved? Because theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Hence the Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18). Blessed therefore are the apostles and martyrs, blessed the confessors and virgins, who suffered such harsh torments and such great persecutions not for transitory things, fleeting riches, vain honours and dignities, or their own offences and iniquities, but solely for the righteousness which they preached.

Ask Paul about his persecutors, and he will answer you: “From the Jews five times I received forty lashes less one; three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned; three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I spent in the depth of the sea; often in journeys, in dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own people, dangers from the nations, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers on the sea, dangers among false brethren; in labour and hardship, in many watchings” (2 Cor. [Col. 0927A] 11:24–27). Elsewhere: “I do not wish you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning our tribulation that befell us in Asia: we were burdened beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we even despaired of life” (2 Cor. 1:8).

[Note: The same Vallicellian codex and both Vatican codices: “Ask him for what cause and for what crimes he suffered all these things.”]

Ask him why he suffered all these dangers, and you will hear: for no other cause than the righteousness and truth that he preached, and because he said that Christ is the Son of God. Read in the Acts of the Apostles, where the Jews command the apostles no longer to speak in Jesus’ name, and you will hear Peter answer: “It is necessary to obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). Therefore, having been thrust into prison and scourged, “they went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been judged worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus” (ibid.).

But let us be silent about the apostles for the present. Let us come to the martyrs. Look upon Lawrence—

[Note: Both Vatican codices and the Vallicellian: “lying upon [Col. 0928D] the gridiron.”]

—stretched upon a gridiron, suffering voluntarily, and saying to Caesar: “Unhappy man, I have always desired these feasts.” Ask what he did, what sin he committed, to deserve to be roasted [Col. 0927C] in this way. What else can he answer but that he preached righteousness and declared the idols to be vain and false, unable to help either themselves or others? The same we say of all the rest. Ask any one of them, and he will give you no other answer. Blessed, therefore, are these, and blessed also all others who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake.

He did not say, “Those upon whom persecutions are inflicted for righteousness’ sake,”

[Note: Both Vatican codices and the Vallicellian: “Because it is not the infliction but endurance that makes one blessed.”]

because it is not the infliction that makes one blessed. The blessed person is not the one who flees persecutions, but the one who endures them—although flight is sometimes lawful as well. Yet one cause of blessedness belongs to the person fleeing, another to the one enduring. It is one thing to escape an enemy by fighting and another by fleeing, although both pertain to salvation. Better to fight than to flee; better [Col. 0927D] to flee than to deny. But “each has his own gift from God” (1 Cor. 7:7).

The Lord commands both: fleeing and fighting. “If,” he says, “they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. 10:23). But conversely: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both body and soul in Gehenna” (ibid., 28). A good physician answers the sick in one way and the healthy in another. A good commander arranges cavalry one way and infantry another.

“Blessed shall you be when people hate [Col. 0928A] you and persecute you and say every evil thing against you falsely for my sake. Rejoice on that day and exult, for behold, your reward is great in heaven” (Luke 6:23). Thus they persecuted the prophets who were before you. “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21:19). Hence the Apostle says: “Whatever was written was written for our instruction, that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we may have hope” (Rom. 15:4). When we hear that the patriarchs and prophets suffered many persecutions; when we read that the holy Fathers, through the great patience they possessed, pleased God and were often delivered from the greatest dangers: such reading ought to instruct and teach us, call us to patience, [Col. 0928B] and give us great hope and consolation in tribulations.

[Note: Ascensian edition: “give.”]

Such were Job and Tobit; such were Isaiah and Jeremiah; such were Haggai and Zechariah; such were the three youths and Daniel; such was the prophet Ezekiel; such were Nehemiah and Zerubbabel. Search the books of the Maccabees, and you will see Eleazar, a devout old man whose praises are difficult to set forth, suffering such harsh torments because he refused to eat pork. But why do I say that he refused to eat it, when he could not even be compelled to pretend? Likewise, seven brothers together with their mother, because they refused to eat unlawful foods prohibited by the law, were killed by horrible tortures. [502] Of such people the Lord says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs [Col. 0928C] is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:10).

For others, the precious dwellings they shall have there may suffice, concerning which the Lord says: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling-places” (John 14:2). But what shall we unhappy people do, who cannot endure not only such torments but even flies and fleas? At a slight injury, sometimes at a single careless word, and often even at a brother’s laughter and a light mockery, we become so angry that we can scarcely ever be appeased.

In food and drink likewise we are usually so impatient that we observe neither hour nor measure; and unless we have them every day not according to necessity but according to desire and excess, we reproach our masters [Col. 0928D] and superiors, who ought to have provided them for us. “Nature,” says someone [Seneca], “is content with few things—indeed, with the smallest things—whereas for pleasure nothing is enough.” In clothing likewise we have no patience, because we often seek more garments and more precious ones than are necessary; nor is envy absent if perhaps we see a brother possess them. But if sickness comes, there is no patience at all, although it is then more necessary, when death is feared to be near.

We cannot enumerate all the ways in which, through impatience, we sin against the good of patience. Let us not be among those people—which is greatly to be feared and lamented for us—but would that we might someday deserve to be among those of whom the Lord says: “In your patience you shall possess your souls.” What possession, I ask, will the person have who neither has nor possesses himself or his soul? Patience is therefore greatly necessary for a human being, without which one loses that very thing which one is.

[Col. 0929A] The Apostle praises certain people who received the plundering of their goods with joy. And the Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other also; and to the one who takes your tunic, offer your cloak also. And if anyone compels you to go a thousand paces, go with him another two” (Matt. 5:39). These words seem indeed to be spoken literally; nevertheless, not generally to everyone, but especially to those who are so dead to the world that in all humility and patience they desire to please God alone.

## CHAPTER IX. On Chastity
Blessed Paul the Apostle, teacher and master of the Gentiles, who learned wisdom not on earth but in the schools of heaven, speaks thus when he treats of chastity: “Let those who have wives be as though they had none, and let him who is free from a wife not take a wife” (1 Cor. 7:30). If, therefore, those who do not have wives ought not to take them, and those who have them ought to have them as though they had none, what else follows but that all should devote themselves to continence and chastity?

What, then, is the meaning of what he said a little earlier in the same place: “Let the husband render the due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband” (ibid. [Col. 0929C], 3)? [Note: [Col. 0929D] Vatican MS 1254 omits “there.”] And again: “For if they cannot contain themselves, let them marry, but only in the Lord” (ibid., 9). [Note: [Col. 0929D] The same Vatican MS 1254: “And that: ‘Let him who cannot contain himself marry, but only in the Lord.’”] These statements seem contrary to one another: let the husband render the due to his wife, yet let him have her as though he had her not. Likewise, let him who is free from a wife not take a wife, yet let him who cannot contain himself marry. They seem contrary.

But the Apostle has used one word in which this whole question appears to be resolved: namely, when he says, “those who cannot contain themselves.” For one who contains himself and can preserve chastity—provided that the same continence is also present in his wife—ought certainly to have a wife as though he had none; that is, he ought to have her as a sister, not as a wife: not for pleasure of the flesh, but for the necessity of marriage. Likewise, one who has no wife, if this grace has been given him by God [Col. 0929D], so that he can preserve continence, ought not to take a wife. The reason why he ought not to take one is this: one who is free from a wife thinks—that is, is able to think—upon the things of God, how he may please God. But those who are unable to contain themselves are not forbidden either to take a wife or to render the marital due.

The Lord himself also seems to say this. For when he had said that, except for the cause of fornication, a man should not dismiss his wife, and when the disciples replied, “If such is the case of a man with a wife, it is not expedient to marry,” he added: “Not all receive this saying, but those to whom it is given. For there are eunuchs who were so born; others who were made so by men; and others who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19:11).

This is as if he said: You say that it is not expedient to marry; you speak truly, if there is someone to whom this power has been given by God, so that he can contain himself and preserve chastity. But not all receive this saying; not all obey this judgment, but only those to whom this grace has been given by God. For there are eunuchs who were so born: that is, there are some persons naturally chaste, who do not feel the assaults of desire. There are others made such by men, like those who, by force, are so kept under discipline in monasteries and other religious places [Col. 0930B] that, even if unwilling, they must remain chaste and continent. But such chastity, because it is not voluntary, has no great reward. There are, however, eunuchs—and these are better—who, compelled by no one, but of their own accord, have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven. Let such persons, as though stationed in battle against the pleasure of the flesh and the assaults of luxury, fight courageously and preserve continence and chastity.

There is a difference between chastity and virginity, [Note: [Col. 0929D] Vatican MS 1234: “Nor are all chaste women virgins, nor are all virgins chaste.”] because not all chaste persons are virgins, nor are all virgins chaste. Hence the Apostle says: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2). For if “virgin” and “chaste” signified the same thing, it would not have been necessary to say both together. A virgin, indeed, is one who keeps himself from the defilement of the flesh, according to the saying: “These are they who were not defiled with women, for they are virgins” (Rev. 14:4). Virginity without chastity is not sufficient for blessedness; but chastity without virginity is often sufficient. Chastity, therefore, is greater than virginity. Virginity is considered in one member; chastity in all the members.

For it is written: “The words of the Lord are chaste words” (Ps. 11:7). And again: “Who can boast that he has a chaste heart?” Thus, as the tongue is called chaste and the heart chaste, so the eyes, ears, hands, feet, and other members are called chaste. Chastity and circumcision seem almost to be the same, so that wherever circumcision is found, chastity also has a place. [Col. 0930D] [Note: [Col. 0930D] This is drawn not in words but in sense from Romans, chapter 2.] “Circumcise,” he says, “the foreskin of your hearts.” Moses says that he is uncircumcised in lips, and blessed Stephen rebukes the Jews as uncircumcised in ears and heart. Moses also commands trees to be circumcised. Such circumcision is chastity.

The word *castus* [“chaste”] seems to be derived from one who lacks foolishness; while a fool is one who has been *tultus*, that is, lifted away from his proper state. Therefore a tongue which speaks vanity cannot be called chaste, because it does not lack foolishness. Likewise the eye, the ear, and the heart itself, when it thinks vain things [Col. 0931A], are not chaste, because they do not lack foolishness. And they do not lack it because they have been lifted away from their proper state and do not remain in their natural goodness.

Thus a virgin who is wandering in heart and deed, in hands and feet, tongue and eyes, though she is a virgin, is nevertheless not chaste. [Note: [Col. 0931D] Vatican MS 1254: “On the contrary, whoever honourably and wisely preserves the virtues of continence and guards his members is chaste, even if he renders the marital due to his wife; but he is not a virgin.” The same also in the cited edition.] When the blessed Virgin Mary said, “My soul magnifies the Lord,” she immediately added, saying, “because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:47). She did not say, “because he has regarded virginity,” but rather humility; for although each virtue is great, humility is the greater. There were many virgins then, but God regarded this one alone, because she was humbler than the rest. I do not know whether a virgin, precisely insofar as she is a virgin, can be called more or less chaste. If, therefore, God had regarded virginity alone [Col. 0931B], there were many virgins who might have become mothers of Christ. Virgins, then, should not be proud of virginity, but should attend to chastity and humility.

Let them hear him who says: “Who is my mother, and who are my brethren? Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother” (Matt. 12:48). Although all Christians ought to possess continence and chastity, it is especially necessary that clerics maintain and observe this virtue. Therefore the Lord commanded Moses to make linen breeches for the priest Aaron and his sons, without which they should never approach the altar, lest perhaps they die (Exod. 3:28; Lev. 16). The breeches signify chastity, because they restrain and keep chaste those members in which luxury especially rules. Those priests and clerics do not have breeches who do not restrain these members, but allow them to wander in unlawful ways. Yet one must greatly fear what is said: “lest perhaps they die.” If you do not wish to die, either preserve chastity or do not approach the altar.

For this reason Solomon’s servants are read to have brought him ivory among the other things they brought. We are Solomon’s servants, and we ought to vow and offer to Christ the Lord the beauty and whiteness of ivory, by which chastity is signified. Elephants are most chaste animals and are said to mate only once. But of us it has been said: “Let my priests marry once.” We read of Solomon that he made himself an ivory throne, whose excellence no other could equal. [Col. 0931D] There were two lions there, one at the right and the other at the left, between whom he himself sat in the middle. It had six steps, upon which were placed twelve little lions, six on this side and six on that.

Tell me: what beast would ever dare approach there, where so many lions were gathered, especially since it is written: “The lion, strongest of beasts, will fear no assaults” (Prov. 30:30)? As many as the vices are, so many are the beasts that lie in wait for Solomon’s throne. I understand the two lions as the two Testaments [Col. 0932A], which by their strength slay all beasts; by their teaching and counsel we overcome all Jews, Gentiles, and heretics. The twelve little lions are the twelve apostles, who guard Solomon’s throne—that is, the holy Church—day and night. No one can ascend to this throne, and to him who sits upon it, except by ivory steps, that is, through continence and chastity. Whoever wishes to sit upon such a throne should preserve chastity. Your flesh is your throne and the seat of your soul; if it is chaste, it is ivory.

In the Song of Songs (chap. 5), Christ’s belly is called ivory. The belly is in the middle of the body, and being in the middle pertains to dignity. Let us hear what the Psalmist says concerning ivory steps: “Myrrh and drop and cassia from your garments, from ivory houses; from which the daughters of kings have delighted you” (Ps. 44:10). [Col. 0932B] These daughters of kings, who delighted the king through ivory steps—that is, through the degrees of continence and chastity—were ascending to God. [Note: [Col. 0932D] The same Vallicellan MS and Vatican MSS: “Consider, therefore, how great is the power of chastity; and if you cannot understand it otherwise, consider at least how great an evil luxury is.”]

It is said of the diamond that it can be neither broken nor subdued by fire or by any force, yet it is dissolved by the warm blood of a goat. The goat is a most foul and lustful animal. Its blood, therefore, is luxury. By the diamond, however, strong men are understood, who, although very strong in other respects, are nevertheless often overcome by luxury. David was strong; yet, on seeing Bathsheba, he was dissolved by luxury. Solomon, strong and wise, sat upon an ivory throne and among lions; yet at one time, separated from his throne and found among women, he was so softened by luxury [Col. 0932C] that he miserably bent his neck before idols.

Therefore whoever wishes to be secure should not depart from the ivory seat and the guard of lions; that is, he should not abandon continence and chastity and the books of the saints. I rejoice in the strength of Joseph and Judith: the one could not be held by luxury itself when it tempted him, but escaped her impious hands naked; [Note: [Col. 0932D] Both Vatican MSS: “could not be held.”] the other courageously beheaded covetousness itself. David, whom the wife of Uriah the Hittite had thrown down from the ivory seat, afterwards rested with Abishag the Shunammite in an ivory bed; and he who had lived incontinentally with Bathsheba afterwards maintained continence with Abishag. Let this example be for imitation to all, and for consolation to all who happen to fall from the ivory seat.

Abishag is well interpreted “my father is superfluous”; and “Shunammite,” “despised,” because chastity, which is signified by Abishag, had indeed been despised by David, since he superfluously pursued other men’s wives, though he had so many wives and concubines. But Abishag was not David’s wife but his daughter, because he slept with her not as with a wife, but as with a daughter. Therefore let Abishag say, “My father is superfluous”—for this is how her name is interpreted—“he despised chastity and continence in Bathsheba, but in me he loved and embraced it.”

## Chapter X. On Obedience

[Col. 0933A]

Our Lord and Saviour himself taught us how great is the good of obedience. Of him it is written: “He became obedient to the Father unto death” (Phil. 2). Through the disobedience of the first man the world had perished; through the obedience of the second man, Jesus Christ, the world was saved. The former, disobedient, approached the forbidden tree; the latter, obedient, ascended the tree of the cross. The former, by approaching it, seized what he ought not; the latter, by ascending it, then paid what he had not seized.

The prophet Jeremiah relates (Jer. 25) concerning the sons of Jonadab, son of Rechab, [Note: [Col. 0933D] St Bruno of Asti treats the obedience of the Rechabites in his commentary on Psalm 70, p. 447 of the Roman edition.] that, when Nebuchadnezzar came with his army to besiege Jerusalem, the sons of Jonadab, son of Rechab, fled from the fields in which they lived into the city. Jeremiah approached them by the Lord’s command, led them into a chamber of the Temple [Col. 0933B], set before them cups of wine, which they did not drink, and commanded them to drink. But they answered: “We shall not drink, because Jonadab commanded us not to drink wine, not to build houses, not to cultivate fields, not to plant vineyards, but only to live in tents.” And the Lord said: “The word of Jonadab has prevailed over my words. Day and night, through my servants the prophets, I do not cease to admonish this people, yet they do not hear my voice; while the sons of Jonadab, son of Rechab, keep their father’s commands so diligently and fear to transgress them.”

And Jeremiah said to the sons of Jonadab: “Because you have obeyed your father’s commands, thus says the Lord: There shall not fail from your seed a man to stand before the Lord all days.” [Col. 0933C] [Note: [Col. 0934D] Drawn from Jeremiah, chapter 35, not in words but in sense.] But to the people he said: “Because you have not heard the commandments of the Lord and have not kept his precepts, all the afflictions which the Lord has spoken shall come upon you and upon this city; and you shall be a reproach to all nations.”

Although these words are a great example and contribute greatly to the keeping and observance of obedience, they nevertheless seem to signify something else. This Rechab, whose name is interpreted “Ascending,” seems to me to signify him of whom it is written: “Christ, ascending on high, led captivity captive and gave gifts to men” (Ps. 67:19). Jonadab, however, is said to be interpreted “gift of the Lord,” or “he gave a dove.” What could better signify the Holy Spirit, who is often called both the gift of God and a dove in the holy books? His sons are all those reborn of water and the Holy Spirit. Therefore blessed Peter is told: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona” (Matt. 16:17), that is, Simon, son of the dove, because *Bar-Jona* is interpreted “son of the dove.” Jonadab, therefore, is rightly interpreted “he gave a dove,” because we have nothing good except what this dove has given us.

These sons of Jonadab, that is, Christians and believers [Col. 0934A], because they have obeyed the Holy Spirit, shall stand before the Lord in the heavenly Jerusalem for ever. Nor are these called only sons of Jonadab, but also sons of Rechab: of him, namely, of whom it is said, “who ascends above the heaven of heaven toward the east” (Ps. 67:34). As the good of obedience was proved in the sons of Jonadab, so the evil of disobedience may be proved in Saul and his sons.

The Lord commanded Saul to fight Amalek and to kill all with the edge of the sword, sparing neither man nor beast nor any animal. But after conquering Amalek, he spared Agag their king and reserved whatever was best of their flocks. Therefore his seed was rejected by the Lord, so that it should not reign over Israel. Samuel said that God desires obedience more than sacrifice, because not to obey is like the sin of divination, and refusing to submit is like the crime of idolatry. [Col. 0934B] This is the Agag of whom Balaam prophesied, saying: “His king shall be raised up because of Agag, and his kingdom shall be taken away” (Num. 24:7). This was fulfilled in Saul, who was the first king of Israel; but because he spared Agag, king of Amalek, his kingdom was destroyed, so that his sons should not reign after him.

Let the disobedient hear these things and understand that not even sacrifices please without obedience. By Amalek, whose name is interpreted “brutish people,” we may understand the army of vices; it must certainly not be spared, but ought to be entirely destroyed unto extermination. Its king is called Agag, which is interpreted “upright”; by him we understand the devil, whom such an army serves and in whom it is gathered together, as it were beneath one roof and in one house. From there it is spread abroad into the breadth of this world and troubles all people everywhere. An evil house has evil inhabitants.

But what shall I say of Noah’s obedience? Of him it is written: “Noah was a just and perfect man in his generations; he walked with God and did all that God had commanded him” (Gen. 6:9). [Col. 0934C] See how obedient this man was: he completed everything commanded him by the Lord. For who would not grow weary at labouring over one structure for a hundred years? Yet long obedience earned a long and enduring reward: when the whole world perished, he alone with his household was saved in the flood.

The greatness of Abraham’s obedience cannot be set forth in a few words. He is the one to whom the Lord said: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and go into the land which I shall show you” (Gen. 12:1). Abraham therefore did what had been commanded him; and, as the apostles did later, leaving everything, he began to go where he did not know. Let us also leave our land, leave the desires of our flesh, and go into the land which the Lord shows, of which the Psalmist says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord [Col. 0935A] in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13).

When this most blessed man was already old, and his wife, who was also barren, had advanced in years, they deserved to receive a son from God. When he had become a youth, God called Abraham and said to him: “Take your son Isaac, whom you love, and offer him to me as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I shall tell you” (Gen. 22:2). “Your very son,” he says, “whom I know you rightly love—not Ishmael, but Isaac—take him and offer him to me as a burnt offering. Thus I will, thus I command, thus it pleases me.”

And what did Abraham then do? Consider the man’s obedience: he did not wait until morning, but rose by night and came to the mountain of vision, that is, Mount Zion, interpreted “watching-place,” where the Lord was afterwards crucified. [Col. 0935B] He prepared himself to sacrifice his son. Isaac said to him: “Behold fire and wood; where is the victim for the burnt offering?” (ibid., 7). As Joseph relates, he was already of an age at which, had he wished, he could have defended himself against his aged father. [Note: [Col. 0935D] St Bruno has the same in his commentary on Genesis, chapter 22, p. 18.] Nevertheless, after he knew the will of God and his parent, he did not resist, but willingly allowed himself to be bound, rejoicing that he was worthy to become God’s victim.

[Note: [Col. 0935D] Vatican MS 125: “Which of these two seems to you to have shown the greater obedience, when Abraham obeyed God and his son obeyed both his parent and God? Great indeed was the obedience in each, and worthy of such a father and such a son.”]

Which of these two seems to you to have shown the greater obedience, when Abraham obeyed God and his son at once obeyed his parent and God? Great indeed was the obedience in each, and worthy of such a father and such a son. This history is not to be understood simply, but seems to signify some other great thing. For what do we understand by Abraham except God the Father, [Col. 0935C] “who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us” (Rom. 8:32)? And what by Isaac except the Son of God, our Saviour, who gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savour?

It was excellently done that not Isaac but a ram was sacrificed in his place, because it was not the Son of God according to divinity, [Note: [Col. 0936D] Both Vatican and Vallicellan MSS: “but rather the Son of Man according to humanity.”] but the Son of Man according to humanity, who “was led as a lamb to the slaughter, and did not open his mouth” (Isa. 52:7). Let us therefore hear the Apostle Peter saying: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:21). What does “that you should follow his footsteps” mean except that you should learn and keep [Col. 0935D] his obedience?

It would take too long, and exceed the length of one discourse, if we wished to set forth all who pleased God through obedience. What, then, will disobedient monks say, who do their own wills and by this do not please God, when the whole religion of monks is obedience and without obedience a monk is nothing? What will they say when they see not only rational creatures such as angels and men, but even things lacking sense and reason, obeying the will of the commanding Lord? Hence “the heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:1); hence “the winds and the sea obey him” (Matt. 8:27); hence our earth has given its fruit; hence every tree gives fruit in its season. In short, the rod is changed into a serpent and water into blood; the sea is opened; the rock pours forth waters; manna rains down; the ass speaks; the Jordan turns backward; at a man’s command the sun does not move: all this obedience accomplishes.

There are innumerable other things of this kind which can be found and gathered from the divine books. Above all, whoever has read the sacred pages will there learn how much obedience can accomplish; there he will see demons flee at a human command, the dead rise, elements change [Col. 0936B], lepers cleansed, the blind enlightened, and paralytics healed. But why say more? There he will see that the nature of things can do nothing against the will of him who created nature.

But, O misery ever to be lamented, to be expressed more by tears than by words! Every creature is obedient to God except that creature made in God’s image. The devil alone and man are found disobedient, whereas no other creature is found disobedient.

## Chapter XI. On Abstinence

The Lord himself admonishes us concerning the virtue of abstinence in the Gospel: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke 21:34). Our Lord and Saviour does not at all forbid us to eat and drink, [Col. 0936C] because he himself [Note: [Col. 0936D] St Mark’s MS: “knows our frame.”] “knows our frame” (Ps. 102:14). To eat and drink is not sin, for he himself ate and drank. Of him it is written: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22).

But gluttony and drunkenness are sin, because they are superfluous, exceed measure, weigh down the heart, corrupt the body, provoke lust, overthrow the mind, and render both the outward [Note: [Col. 0936D] The same MS; and “inward” in the MSS of St Mark, Florence, and both Vatican MSS.] and inward person weak. The Lord grants what is necessary and forbids what is superfluous. Each person knows the measure of his own body. If someone becomes glutted by eating little and drunk by drinking little, let him reduce even that small amount until he receives everything according to measure and obeys necessity rather than pleasure. [Col. 0936D] For it cannot be that one who follows pleasure in eating and drinking will not eventually come to gluttony and drunkenness. [Note: [Col. 0936D] The same MS and the Vatican MSS: “the will of the flesh.”]

It is an opinion of the elders: let a monk eat so that he is always hungry, and let a bishop drink so that he does not know whether he has drunk. In such cases, I think, gluttony and drunkenness have no place. Hence blessed Peter the Apostle says (ibid., 11): “I beseech you, as strangers and pilgrims, to abstain from fleshly desires [Col. 0937A] which wage war against the soul,” which stir up wars against the spirit. “I do not command you as subjects to me, but I entreat you as outsiders to abstain from fleshly desires which wage war against the soul, make war upon the spirit, assault the mind, and attack the soul’s defences. For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do whatever you wish.”

In such a conflict, some assist the flesh, others the spirit. [Note: [Col. 0937D] Likewise both Vatican MSS: “In such a conflict, some assist the flesh, others the spirit. Those who flee fleshly desires aid the spirit. Conversely, those who are subjected to the service of the flesh and follow fleshly desires oppress the spirit.”] Conversely, those who follow fleshly desire oppress the spirit. There are two kinds of abstinence: [Note: [Col. 0938D] Vatican MS: “one carnal.”] one animal (bodily), the other spiritual. Both are great, but the latter is greater, because it is greater to abstain from vices than from foods. [Col. 0937B]

Yet abstinence from foods is also great, so much so that it is confirmed not only by the prophets but by the Lord himself. [Note: [Col. 0938D] Vatican MS: “First, indeed.”] For first Moses, then Elijah, and afterwards our Lord Jesus Christ himself are read to have fasted forty days and forty nights. What degree of abstinence, moreover, do we think blessed John the Baptist displayed? He drank neither wine nor strong drink; his food, we are told, was locusts and wild honey. Our first parents died because they lacked abstinence. The Ninevites had already received the sentence of death, when the prophet said: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah 3:4); but they were delivered by a three-day fast.

David also says of his abstinence: “I have become like a pelican in the wilderness” (Ps. 101 [Col. 0937C]:7). The pelican is said to be a bird as large as a vulture, always solitary and dwelling in the wilderness; it is so abstinent that, as other birds delight in fullness, it delights in fasting. [Note: [Col. 0938D] Vatican MS: “delights.”] Such a bird was Antony; such were Paul and Hilarion; such was blessed Benedict, whose delight was fasting and whose life was abstinence.

Of such persons the Lord also speaks to Job, saying: “Who has sent forth the wild ass free? And who has loosed his bonds? To whom I gave a home in solitude and dwellings in a land of salt. He despises the multitude of the city; he does not hear the cry of the taskmaster; he surveys the mountains of his pasture, and seeks out every green thing” (Job 39:5). Those whom David signifies by the pelican, the Lord signifies by the wild ass. The wild ass is a wild donkey, never departing from the wilderness; using its own freedom, it may indeed be killed, but it cannot be tamed by human bonds.

By the donkey, therefore, which is a foolish animal, are understood those of whom the Apostle says: “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the strong, and things which are not to destroy things which are” (1 Cor. 1:17). The people of this world regarded these most renowned and God-beloved men as donkeys and foolish animals, [Col. 0938A] because, having abandoned the pleasures of this age and dwelling in solitude, they seemed to live not like human beings but like cattle and brute beasts. Naked and without shelter, they endured cold and heat by day and night. Free from every worldly care and released from all the bonds of vices and desires, they wandered through the wilderness, singing and rejoicing and attending only to contemplation.

This is what the Lord says: “To whom I gave a home in solitude and dwellings in a land of salt” (Job 39:6). Such persons despise the multitude of the city because, dead to the world, they desire to please God alone; and already living in mind among the angels, they do not seek human society, saying with the Apostle: “But our conversation [Col. 0938B] is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). They do not hear the cry of the taskmaster because they serve not the belly but the spirit. This taskmaster is our belly, to which, unless we pay its daily provision, it does not cease, like an impious tax-collector, to torment and torture us. It is so importunate that our whole substance can scarcely suffice for it. Yet they do not obey it; refreshed by another food, they endure its cries and torments as though they did not feel them. For “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4:4).

They therefore survey the mountains of its pasture and seek every green thing. These are the mountains of which it is said: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence help shall come to me” (Ps. 120:1). The two great mountains are the two Testaments; the rest are as many as there are books of prophets. In them are found pastures ever green and never failing, to which no preparations of food and no luxuries can be compared. Refreshed by these, God’s wild asses do not hear the cry of the taskmaster. Let those, therefore, who seek to know the good of abstinence look to these.

The Apostle also says of it: “The night has passed, and the day has drawn near. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armour of light; let us walk honourably as in the day, not in revelries and drunkenness, not in beds and indecencies, not in contention and envy; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 1:12). [Col. 0938C] Do you not hear that the Apostle too forbids not necessities, but superfluities? For revelries, drunkenness, and provision for the flesh are superfluous, not in necessities, but in desires and pleasures. Whoever is clothed with wisdom, righteousness, truth, chastity, humility, and the honourableness of every virtue puts on the Lord Jesus Christ. Where there is no abstinence, there can be neither chastity nor honourableness.

Noah planted a vineyard, became drunk, and unknowingly uncovered his shameful parts (Gen. 9). Behold: the parts that should always be covered are revealed by drunkenness. Therefore the Apostle says: “Do not be drunk with wine, in which is luxury” (Eph. 5:18). If so great a patriarch, when drunk, could not cover his shameful parts, how shall a drunkard preserve the honourableness and chastity of his members? [Col. 0939A] Lot also, made drunk with wine, violated the modesty of his daughters. Scripture records him as so overcome—or rather, buried—by wine that, drunk, he did not know the evil he had committed.

Therefore Solomon says not without reason: “The vision of Samuel, by which his mother instructed him: Do not, Samuel, do not give wine to kings, for there is no secret where drunkenness reigns, lest they drink and forget judgments and alter the cause of the children of the poor” (Prov. 31:1). Samuel is interpreted “God is in him,” [Col. 0939B] and by him we understand the apostles, who are called friends of God, of whom the Lord himself says: “You are my friends” (John 15:14), and, “As the Father has loved me, I also have loved you” (ibid., 9). Instructed by their mother—for their mother is the Church—these men forbid wine to kings.

These kings are bishops and priests, who rule and correct others and must keep themselves from every state of drunkenness and wine-bibbing. Thus blessed Paul, full of God, commanded that bishops and priests of this kind be chosen: not given to wine but moderate; not drunkards but sober. Yet he tells Timothy the bishop to use a little wine for the stomach and his frequent infirmities. He commands deacons also not to be addicted to much wine. Thus Samuel both does not give wine to kings and gives wine to kings: he does not give it for drunkenness and excess, but gives it for moderation, sobriety, and the body’s need.

For our Saviour himself was reproached by the Jews as though he were a wine-drinker and friend of publicans. Necessities, therefore, are not forbidden, but superfluities are. Both the drunkenness of wine and the drunkenness of desire are evil, because there is no secret where either kind of drunkenness rules. Such drunkards cannot say: “I have hidden your words in my heart, that I may not sin against you” (Ps. 118:11). Often, having lost sense and understanding, they call good evil and evil good, “putting light for darkness and darkness for light” (Isa. 5:20), calling sweet bitter and bitter sweet; and, drunk with both wines, [Col. 0939D] they pervert the cause of the children of the poor—namely, of that poor one who, though rich in all things, became poor for us.

Since abstinence from food and drink is so useful, how necessary must we judge abstinence from vices and pleasures to be? “For this,” says the Apostle, “is the will of God: that you abstain from fornication; that each one of you know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour, not in the passion of desire, as also the Gentiles who do not know God” (1 Thess. 6:3). In one phrase he comprehends every vice. But in saying, “not in the passion of desire, as also the Gentiles who do not know God” (ibid.), he includes every spiritual and carnal abstinence. For sin seldom seems to occur without a desire of mind or flesh. Yet it sometimes happens when some compel others—even unwilling persons—to sin, either by force or by enticements. [Col. 0940A]

## Chapter XII. Where, That Is, in What Things, the Church Is Adorned
We have spoken above of the Church and of her ornaments. It remains now for us to see her clothed in her ornaments and to delight in her form and beauty, concerning whom the Psalmist says to the Lord: “The queen stood at thy right hand in a gilded garment, surrounded by variety” (Ps. 44:11). This queen of whom we speak is the Church of God herself, rightly said to stand at the right hand because joyful and prosperous things are prepared for her. At the judgment, as the Lord says, the lambs shall stand on the right, but the goats on the left. Many are her garments, many her ornaments; and therefore she is said to be wrapped about with variety. Yet she has no ornament which is not either golden or gilded. She has no ornament without gold. We have often said already that by gold either wisdom or integrity and purity of life are signified, without which no ornament is beautiful, and whatever is not adorned by these is cheap and abominable. [Note: Col. 0939D. The Vatican manuscript omits “ornaments.”] With such ornaments Rebecca is said to have been adorned, to whom Abraham’s servant is related to have brought golden earrings, golden bracelets, and golden garments (Gen. 24). Enter Solomon’s Temple (3 Kings 10) and look carefully round: there you will be able to see nothing but gold, and that of the purest kind [Col. 0940C]. Why is this? Because nothing foolish or stupid, nothing shameful or unclean, ought to appear in the house of God. The Queen of Sheba, by whom the Church is prefigured, when she came to Solomon brought him one hundred and twenty talents of the purest gold. Thus the Church is described as beautiful in a garment of gold, so that she may be understood as wholly wise, wholly pure, and incorruptible; concerning her the Lord says through Solomon: “My dove is one, my perfect one, my spotless one” (Song 6:9); and the Apostle says of her: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5:27).

Therefore none of her ornaments, however precious and beautiful it may seem, is such unless it is gold. For heretics, pagans, philosophers, and Jews seem to possess the same ornaments [Col. 0940D] which the bride of Christ uses; but they differ in this, that theirs are not golden, though they may appear golden. For no wisdom is golden except that which is confirmed by evangelical and apostolic doctrine. Whatever faith, whatever charity, whatever humility, mercy, peace, patience, justice, or obedience there may be, if it does not shine with the gold of apostolic doctrine, it is false, corrupt, unclean, and to be fled from as death and poison. Rightly, therefore, is the Church portrayed in a garment of gold, since all her ornaments are interwoven with gold of such surpassing purity.

The holy Church is always clothed with all her ornaments, although not all are visible at the same time. At one time she is seen clothed with the ornament of faith, at another with that of hope, at another with that of charity, while the rest are in some manner hidden beneath a single one and do not appear. [Note: Both Vatican manuscripts: “But when the ornament of faith appears, then—marvellous to say—you see demons flee, the dead rise,” etc.] But when the increase of faith appears, then you see marvellous things: demons flee, the dead rise, the blind receive sight, paralytics are healed, lepers cleansed, and other miracles occur which are believed impossible by those not clothed in this same ornament of faith. For a long time after Christ’s Passion the children of the Church employed this ornament of faith, because the gentiles and unbelievers especially delighted to see these things and were thereby drawn to the love of Christ, so that they might plainly understand that all things are possible to one who believes.

But when the ornament of hope is made manifest, then she is wholly raised into contemplation [Col. 0941B] and lifted from earthly to heavenly things, so that, although she is bodily in the world, she may confidently dare to say: “Our commonwealth is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). “For by hope we were saved” (Rom. 8:24). And then she promises things so great that she seems in some sense to speak outside herself, and sets her hearers aflame with the desire to obey; so that a hearer may say with the Apostle: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23); and with the Psalmist: “As a servant longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for thee, O God. My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain: when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41:1). Yet what wonder is it, since she promises as things to be hoped for without doubt those things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him?” (1 Cor. 2:9).

This contemplation of hope causes the Bridegroom sometimes to say of her: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the harts of the fields, that you do not awaken or rouse my beloved until she herself wills” (Song 3:5). That woman of whom the Lord himself said, “Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken from her” (Luke 10:41), was held fast by this longing of hope.

But if the Church reveals herself in the ornament of charity, then you see all greeting one another in the kiss of peace; then you understand “how good” and “how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132:1), and how “the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul; and all things were common to them, and no one said that anything was his own” (Acts 4:32).
