When this ornament appears, all will and do not will the same things. “For to will the same thing and not to will the same thing,” says one author, “is firm friendship” (Cicero). “But no one,” says the Lord, “has greater charity than this: that one lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). Whenever the children of the Church are clothed in the garments of charity, hatred, anger, envy, indignation, rage, detraction, quarrels, rivalries, and dissensions are driven away and destroyed. For charity and concord, peace and mercy, come together and assist one another; before them such monstrous things cannot stand.

There are certain other ornaments of the Church not artificially joined to one another, such that she cannot put on one without all the others. There are four: the first is called prudence, the second justice, the third fortitude, and the fourth temperance; we have spoken sufficiently above concerning these. The children of the Church are especially accustomed to be clothed with these in Lent, at the great solemnities, and whenever councils are held. Then it is very sweet and delightful to see and hear wisdom preaching, justice judging, fortitude separating, and temperance usefully interceding for certain persons.

But when the children of the Church are clothed in the ornament of humility, all pride is confounded and arrogance dispersed, in accordance with the saying of the Blessed Virgin Mary: “He has put down the mighty from their seat and exalted the humble” (Luke 1:52). Her Son, our Savior, confirming the same saying, declares: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke 18:14). Then you may behold choirs of virgins and armies of monks clothed in wool and skins, garments in which humility especially glories; among them too our father Benedict, seated upon an ivory chair [Col. 0942C], distributes the whole ornament of humility into twelve parts.

But when the Church makes herself manifest in the garments of mercy, then guests are received, the naked clothed, prisons opened, the sick visited, and the hungry fed. She herself, a humble and most merciful mother, following the example of her Lord, does not disdain to minister to the poor and to wash feet. There is no garment in which all who are oppressed by poverty, illness, or any calamity more desire to see her adorned. Clothed in this garment, the Lord himself and our Savior said: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:8 [as printed; cf. Matt. 11:28]); and: “Allow the little children to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Mark 10:14). There are also other ornaments by which the beauty and glory of this most noble queen are made manifest; but for the present let it suffice that we have spoken of these few.

## THIRD BOOK OF SENTENCES

[Note: Col. 0943D. Manuscript 1254: “Here begins the book of Lord Bruno, bishop, *On the New World*.”]

[Col. 0943]

## CHAPTER I. ON THE NEW WORLD

[Col. 0943A]

A new man came into the world, who created both the new and the old world. For he went forth from the Father and came into the world in order to make clean out of what was unclean—he “who enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9). But how did he come who is everywhere, who was in the world, and through whom the world was made? How also did he go forth from the Father, when he never departed from the Father? For God’s coming is his appearing; when he shows himself, he is seen to go forth and to come. Of him it is also written: “This is our God, and no other shall be accounted beside him, who found out all the way of knowledge. After these things he was seen upon earth and conversed with men” (Baruch 3:37). For through his humanity he was seen [Col. 0943B], though according to his divinity he cannot be seen, because “no one has ever seen God” (John 1:18).

In coming, moreover, he made all things new, according to what he himself says: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. 21:5). “Therefore, as the Apostle says, we ought to walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6:4), and imitate not the old but the new man. When the Lord was being held by the Jews, showing himself to be king of another world, he said: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 28:36 [as printed; cf. John 18:36]). For in saying that it is not of this world, he shows that his kingdom is of another world.

There is therefore another world above this world, of a nature and dignity far more excellent than this world, which lies in evil. Of it the Lord himself says: “If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of the world, and I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you” (John 15:4 [as printed]). By these words he also shows a third world, by which we understand the Church: it has indeed been chosen from the world, but even now is not of the world. For it too is a world, that world, namely, of which it is written: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life. For he did not come to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him” (ibid. 2:17). This world that is saved through him can be understood as none other than the Church.

This, therefore, is that world of which the Lord says: “Behold, I make all things new” (Isa. 43:19 [as cited]). [Note: Vatican manuscript: “But if they are new,” etc.] For if all things have been made new in this world, then the Church has a new heaven, a new earth, a new sun, a new moon [Col. 0944A], new stars, clouds and rains, lightning and thunder, mountains and forests, new human beings, and everything else—things nevertheless signified by the old ones, and having a certain likeness to them.

For the heavens are new of which it is said: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Ps. 18:1). The new earth is that of which it is said: “And our land shall give its fruit” (ibid. 84:13). Would you see a new sun? “For you who fear God the sun of righteousness shall arise” (Mal. 6:2 [as cited]); and “the righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of God” (Matt. 13:43). Would you also see a new moon? “Who is this that comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army drawn up in battle array?” (Song 6:9). Blessed John also says that he saw a woman “clothed with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet” (Rev. 12:1). A new and unheard-of moon, which the woman has beneath her feet.

The Virgin Mary is a new star, whose name is interpreted “star of the sea”; and likewise she is the one of whom it is said: “A star shall arise from Jacob; a man shall rise from Israel” (Num. 24:17). It is something new for stars to arise from human beings. See also new clouds and new doves: “Who are these, who fly like clouds and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. 60:8). Behold, we have found the new world, which alone is called a world by a true definition, because out of water and the Holy Spirit, from uncleanliness, it has been made clean (*mundus*). Let this, therefore, be the subject of our discourse and of our composition of sermons in praise of God, with the help of him who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER II. ON THE NEW HEAVENS

“The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Ps. 18:1). The holy apostles are called heavens, and we must say why they are called heavens. For just as, in that world which was made from the beginning, which consists of heaven and earth, of which Moses says, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1), heaven is its greatest [Note: Vatican manuscript: “And noblest.”] and noblest part; so in this new world, of which the Lord says, “The Son of Man did not come to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him” (John 3:17), the apostles are greater and more illustrious than the rest. Of them it is written [Col. 0944D]: “The princes of the peoples are gathered together with the God of Abraham” (Ps. 46:10). [Note: Vatican manuscript 1254: “They are gathered together with the God of Abraham.”] These are those senators of whom the Lord says: “Her husband is noble in the gates [Col. 0945A], when he sits with the senators of the land” (Prov. 31:23). To them the Lord himself says: “You who have followed me shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28); and for them he asks the Father, saying: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:21).

The whole world is enclosed by heaven; the whole Catholic Church is contained within the bounds of apostolic faith and doctrine. Whoever is outside these bounds is profane and unbelieving. Hence the Lord says through Solomon: “Do not overstep the boundaries which your fathers have set” (Prov. 22:28). Rightly, then, are the apostles called heavens, since they possess so great a likeness to heaven as well as its name.

Now, as some hold, *caelum* (“heaven”) is called so because it is *caelatum*, that is, ornamented, or engraved, with various carvings or sculptures, and diversified. For there are placed the sun and moon, and stars both greater and lesser; by their brightness and beauty it is so adorned that nothing among creatures can be found comparable to its beauty. Indeed, in Solomon’s Temple palm trees carved in relief, and other carvings projecting prominently, are reported to have been present; and all these things seem applicable to the apostles as well. For it is not difficult to find in them both sun, moon, and stars. They are those to whom the Lord says: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14). Thus the whole Church is illuminated by their faith and doctrine, just as the whole earth is illuminated by the brightness of this sun and moon; [Note: Vatican manuscript: “is made bright.”] and in them the beauty of every virtue shines like particular stars.

But if heavens are so called from concealing (*celando*), because they conceal and hide heavenly mysteries, I hear the Apostle too speaking of his mysteries: that, caught up into paradise, he heard secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to utter. The Lord also commands them to conceal his secrets, saying: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor scatter pearls before swine” (Matt. 7:6). It is of these, then, that it was said: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Ps. 18:1).

Yet those other heavens also, in their own way, declare and proclaim God’s glory. I said “other,” because they too are many, in accordance with: “Praise the Lord from the heavens” (Ps. 148:1), and “heavens of heavens, praise the Lord” (ibid., 4). The Apostle likewise posits three heavens; Moses, two. For he says: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1): behold one. On the second day, “God made the firmament in the midst of the waters, and divided the waters above the firmament from those below the firmament, and called the firmament heaven” (ibid., 7): behold another. This latter is the heaven revealed to our eyes through the sun, moon, and stars that shine in it.

For it is impossible to see the first heaven of this world, since what we see lies between us and it. But what excellence and beauty must we suppose it to possess, when we see such greatness in this lower heaven? The first heaven, moreover, was made and illuminated immediately on that same day, the Lord saying: “Let there be light, and there was light” (Gen. 1:3). But this lower heaven is related to have received the sun, moon, and stars on the third day after it was made. It therefore remained without light until that day, especially since, while the waters still covered everything, dry land had not yet appeared. For on the third day it was said: “Let the waters that are under heaven be gathered into one place, and let dry land appear” (ibid., 9). Thus dry land had not yet appeared because the firmament did not yet have light. But the first heaven already shone with its own light; and that light was called day by the Lord, Scripture saying: “And the Lord called the light day, and the darkness night” [Col. 0946B] (ibid., 5). But day could not exist without light.

By what means the light of that heaven and that day was produced, when neither sun nor moon nor any instruments of light had yet been made, may be questioned. Yet we read that that world did not need the light of the sun, and that night was not there; for where angels are, darkness cannot exist. For it is said of the saints that “they shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of God” (Matt. 13:43). The devil himself, now black and dark, was formerly called Lucifer because of his exceeding brightness. Therefore, where there are so many suns, this sun is not necessary.

Now, since this world was illuminated on the third day—for the first world, as we have just said, never lacked light from the time it was made—this seems to signify to us that in the third age, so to speak [Col. 0946C], the Sun of Righteousness, our Savior, born of a Virgin, illuminated the world. The first day was from the beginning to Moses; the second from Moses to Christ; but the third from Christ, God our Lord, to the end of the age. Then indeed “the people of the gentiles, who sat in darkness, saw a great light; and light arose for those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death” (Isa. 9:2). [Note: Vatican manuscript 1254: “because Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, was born for them. But the rest,” etc.] But the days which preceded Christ were without light.

Therefore the first heaven, which was made together with light—for heaven and light were not made separately, with light later; both were made on the same day—belongs not to this world but to that world whose inhabitants are angels and of which holy men will be inhabitants after this life. By light and darkness, or by day and night, we may understand good and evil angels; because they were divided on the same day, they seem to signify the sudden fall of the evil spirits. Hence the Lord says of their prince, in the Gospel of the blessed apostle and evangelist John, that “he was a liar from the beginning and did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44). For he says to the Pharisees [Note: These words are omitted in Vatican manuscript 1254]: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to accomplish the desires of your father” (ibid.). [Note: The cited edition adds: “He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own resources, because he is a liar and its father.”] “For he speaks because he is a liar, and truth is not in him.”

Our heavens also, in likeness of the firmament, were by no means both called and illuminated at once; rather, in the third year after they were called, they deserved to receive the illumination of the Holy Spirit. For, as blessed Luke says, they did not yet understand the Scriptures: that Christ had to rise from the dead (Luke 24:46). They were therefore without light, still oppressed by such great darkness. As the firmament was illuminated on the third day, so the apostles were illuminated in the third year.

Moreover, in the division of the waters above the firmament from the waters beneath it, the apostles seem to possess the likeness of the firmament. Placed in a sense between them, they divide waters from waters, because they separate the New Testament from the Old. The Apostle divides waters from waters when he prohibits the teaching and observance of the Old Testament. The Apostle says: “I, Paul, say to you: if you are circumcised, Christ profits you nothing. For the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (Gal. 5:2; cf. 2 Cor. 3:6). This firmament, these heavens, taught us how greatly the waters of the Law and the waters of the Gospel differ from each other.

These, then, are the heavens that declare the glory of God. But at whose teaching and instruction do they do so? Let the Psalmist say: “Day utters a word to day, and night declares knowledge to night” (Ps. 18:2). The day, then, is he who teaches; the days are those who are taught. He who teaches is one; those who are taught are many days. Yet “one day in the courts of the Lord is better than thousands” (Ps. 83:10). Therefore Christ is day, and his apostles are days, because he is light and there is no darkness at all in him; and he likewise says to his disciples: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14). If they are light, then they are day; for it was written above that “he called the light day, and the darkness night.”

Therefore day utters the word of the Lord to day, because the Lord, our Savior, the “true light which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9), teaches his disciples the doctrine of faith and the word of preaching, and instructs the Church. This Church is rightly called, in the singular, “day” because of the unity of faith, although it contains within itself many and almost innumerable days; for there are as many days as there are saints. Of them it is said: “Days shall be formed, and no one among them” (Ps. 138:16). For among them there is no one but day; among them no one but one who is bright and shining. For they shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of God.

But O stupidity! O impiety! O madness! Although day utters the word to day, although Truth itself is revealed through the Son of God and through Wisdom itself—for Wisdom preaches in the streets—yet night is not ashamed to declare its knowledge, or rather its folly, to night. For scribes and Pharisees still preach, because they are blind and guides of the blind, plunging themselves and others with them into the darkness of night’s ignorance. These blind men are night without light, and possess nothing but darkness; therefore they teach and preach nothing but error.

It has now been said who the heavens are, what they proclaim, and from whom they received what they declare and proclaim. It remains for us to hear in what languages and by what words they announce these things. “There are no speeches,” he says, “nor words, whose voices are not heard” (Ps. 18:3). This is what is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “The apostles spoke in various languages the mighty works of God” (Acts 2:12). They spoke in all languages—that is, they taught every kind of knowledge. But where? Would you hear? “Their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:4).

And what did they say? “He placed his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself as a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber. He rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18:6 [as printed]). “In the sun,” he says—that is, in the light, in what is clear and manifest—he placed his tabernacle, that is, his flesh and humanity, in which, as in a tabernacle, divinity lay hidden and concealed, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God” (Isa. 52:10). He was above the sun and could not be seen; he humbled himself and descended, that he might be seen in the sun and made manifest through the flesh which he assumed.

“And he himself as a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Ps. 18:5): he rejoiced to run his course, made as a giant—that is, strong and unconquerable, and, not according to human opinion but according to the truth of the matter, of a twofold nature, both God and man. For giants, according to human opinion, are thought to be both gods and men—“mighty men from ancient times, men of renown,” as it is written (Gen. 6:4). Therefore he came forth as a bridegroom from his chamber, because he came forth from the Virgin’s womb not alone but wedded. In that womb, namely, the Son of God celebrated his nuptials, took a wife, and before he was born joined our humanity to himself.

He rejoiced to run his course because, in order to redeem and save humankind, he endured the Passion itself with joy. He could truly say: “I ran the way of thy commandments, when thou didst enlarge my heart” (Ps. 118:30). For he is that “blessed man who did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stand in the way of sinners, nor sit in the chair of pestilence” (Ps. 1:1), “who did no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22). On this way he ran, on this way he rejoiced, and on this way he taught us also to run.

“His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his course reaches to its height” (Ps. 18:6). This is what he himself says: “I went forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John 16:28). Finally, his course is from the highest point to the highest point, because according to his divinity he is equal to the Father in every respect. Daniel also says of him: “I looked in the vision of the night, and behold, the Son of Man came in the clouds of heaven; and kingdom, honour, and power were given to him, and he came even to the Ancient of Days” (Dan. 7:13). For the Lord will come even to the Ancient of Days when he appears like the Father and equal to him in all respects. For if there were anything in which he differed from him according to divinity, he would surely not reach even to him. He therefore reaches even to him [Col. 0949A], because in nothing does he differ from him. Blessed are those heavens which thus declare the glory of God.

## CHAPTER III. ON THE NEW CLOUDS
“**The Lord made darkness his hiding-place; round about him his tent was dark water in the clouds of the air**” (Ps. 17:12).—“**Before the brightness in his presence the clouds passed by: hail and coals of fire**” (ibid., 13).

The new world has new darknesses. [Note: Col. 949D, Vatican MS: “It has new clouds.”] The old things have passed away, and all things have been made new. This world is the Church, in which there are new heavens, a new earth, new human beings, and all things are new and clean. What, then, should we understand by the clouds, if not the apostles? Of them it is written: “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. 60:8). And the holy apostles are called heavens, clouds, mountains, fountains, and by many other names, because of certain significations appropriate to them.

But where do they fly? Let the Psalmist say: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:4). Whence do they come? “He brings forth clouds from the end of the earth; he made lightnings into rain” (Ps. 134:7). These clouds rain upon good and evil alike, and by the showers of teaching make the barren and fruitless earth fruitful. Wretched is the land not watered by their rains. Wretched Judaea and the Synagogue, of which it is written: “I will command my clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isa. 5:6). Hence the Apostle also says: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be preached to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

Therefore the apostles fly like clouds, [Note: Col. 949D, Vatican MS: “raining everywhere.”] showering rain everywhere, making the whole earth fruitful, calling it to faith, flashing with miracles, and making lightnings into rain. For lightnings become rain when miracles accompany teaching. Thus the Gospel says of the apostles that “they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark 16:25). Thus by clouds let us understand the apostles; by rain, teaching; by thunders, voices; and by lightnings, miracles. Hence James and John are called Boanerges, that is, “sons of thunder”: through their high-sounding voices, as through certain great thunders, the world was terrified and converted from unbelief to faith.

[Note: Both manuscripts and the cited edition read: “Likewise Bartholomew is interpreted ‘son of one suspending waters.’ For in a wondrous and ineffable manner he suspends waters in the clouds. How clouds raise these waters, hold them, and pour them out is far beyond human knowledge. But if, as Bartholomew, son, etc.”]

Likewise Bartholomew, “son of one suspending waters,” draws new and fruitful clouds; from the fountain of life, from the fountains of Israel, he draws waters springing up into eternal life, and knows how both to retain and to pour them out at their proper time. By these waters all our land is irrigated, and our body and soul are washed. But the south wind and the north wind scatter these clouds, concerning which it is written: [Note: Col. 950D, Vatican MS: “The north wind comes and scatters the clouds.”] “The north wind disperses rain” (Prov. 25:23).—“From the north evils shall be opened upon all the inhabitants of the land” (Jer. 1:14).—“The devil says, ‘I shall place my throne in the north and shall be like the Most High’” (Isa. 14:14).

He, therefore, is the one who drives away the clouds, persecutes the saints, expels the apostles from cities of unbelievers, and compels them to flee to other cities. For the Lord himself commands them: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. 20:23). But if the Lord, rising from sleep, commands the winds and the sea, there will immediately be a great calm (Matt. 8:26). And it will be said to the north wind, “Rise, north wind”—rather, flee—“and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and its spices shall flow” (Cant. 4:16).

There are good winds and bad winds; good clouds and bad clouds. Bad clouds are heretics and schismatics, who bring not rain but [Note: Col. 950D, Vatican MS: “hail.”] hail. From them proceed arrows and lightnings which kill not vices but souls. Good winds are brought forth from the Lord’s treasuries, of which it is said: “He brings forth winds from his treasuries” (Ps. 134:7). Such a wind is charity, devotion, mercy, and the other virtues that are brought forth from the heavenly treasuries. By these the clouds are borne; by these the apostles are guided. These compel them to fly, traverse the world, and preach the Gospel. Hence the apostles say: “We cannot but speak the things which we have heard and know.” “For the charity of God presses us” (2 Cor. 5:14).

It is wholly fitting that such clouds should be carried about by such winds, of which it is written: “The waters saw you, O God; the waters saw you and feared; and the depths were troubled. The multitude of the sound of the waters—the clouds gave their voice” (Ps. 76:17). But how could waters see the Lord, or with what eyes could they see? [Note: Col. 950D, Vatican MS: “Why did they also fear? What are these sensible things that can see and fear?”] Why indeed did they fear? What are these waters? For insensible things cannot see or fear. “Many waters,” Scripture says, “are many peoples” (Rev. 17). Peoples are rightly called waters, since they always run downward and hasten toward death.

Yet of the Jordan it is said: “And you, Jordan, why have you turned back?” (Ps. 113:5). You were running downward; now I see you ascending to higher things. For what is signified by the Jordan except the baptized people? There the sacrament of baptism began; there the Lord was baptized. This river alone, therefore—this Christian people alone—ascends upward and climbs toward heavenly things; but the other waters, that is, the other peoples, are submerged in the sea and cast headlong into hell.

Those waters, however, of which it is said, “The waters saw you, O God, and feared,” seem to be good waters, since they deserved to know and fear the Lord. Hence the depths were troubled, because a multitude of the sound of waters arose. This, he says, was why the depths were troubled—why hell and the evil spirits feared and were confounded—because those waters of which we have just spoken saw the Lord and feared. Moreover, there arose a multitude of the sound of waters praising and confessing God, and converting to the end. All this happened because the clouds gave their voice: because the thunders of the apostles were heard; because the arrows of the word of God [Note: Col. 951D, cited edition: “were pressed out.”] were shot forth; and because the flashes of miracles were seen. For this is what he says: “For your arrows passed through; the voice of your thunder was in the wheel. Your lightnings shone upon the world; the earth was moved and trembled” (Ps. 76:19).

What is meant by “the earth was moved and trembled,” except what he had just said: “The waters saw you, O God; the waters saw you and feared”? Thus the earth was rightly moved and trembled. For to be moved and to tremble in this manner pertains to the salvation of souls. “The voice of your thunder was in the wheel,” because the preaching of the apostles—for they are the thunders of God—was heard throughout the whole circuit of this world.

These, therefore, are they who fly like clouds. These clouds are clear and brilliant. These are the cherubim upon whom the Lord ascended and flew upon the wings of the winds. And he who formerly made darkness his hiding-place—for the water in the clouds of the air was obscure and dark—has now been revealed to all nations through bright and radiant clouds. He whom his own tabernacle could not formerly behold is now known by the Gentiles with unveiled face. *Cherubim* is interpreted “fullness of knowledge.” Therefore, just as the apostles are called clouds because they abound in the waters of faith and teaching, so they are also called cherubim because they are full of wisdom and knowledge. The Lord, ascending upon them, flew, because through them he revealed the glory of his name to all nations.

He flew upon the wings of the winds because, leaving aside at first the rulers and wise persons of this age, he revealed himself to the poor and foolish. Hence the Apostle says: “See your calling, brethren: not many noble, not many wise; but God chose the foolish things of the world to destroy the wise, and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong, in order that he might destroy the things that are” (1 Cor. 1:26). The powerful and wise of this age are very aptly called winds, because they are the ones who everywhere agitate and disturb this great and broad sea, that is, the world.

The hiding-place of God means the books of the Law and the Prophets. They are called a hiding-place because the Jews were unable to grasp there the power and wisdom of God, Jesus Christ our Savior, hidden within them, although they read them day and night and meditated upon them. And this is what he says: “Round about him was his tabernacle” (Ps. 17:12). The Synagogue was the tabernacle of God; sitting round about this hiding-place even to the present day, it spends the whole course of its life in fruitless labor. Hence the Lord said to them: “You err, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God” (Matt. 22:29).

For the water in the clouds of the air is dark; that is, the knowledge in the books of the prophets is exceedingly obscure and cannot be understood except through the Holy Spirit. But our clouds are clear and bright: their rain is sweet, their teaching flows with honey, and their preaching is suited alike to the wise and the unwise. And this is what he says: “Before the brightness in his presence the clouds passed by” (Ps. 17:23). But where they passed has already been said above: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:3). Thus the clouds of God fly and thus they pass by. As they pass, hail and coals of fire were everywhere, understood to have been scattered.

These are the clouds of which it is said: “Do you know the paths of the clouds, the great and perfect knowledges?” (Job 37:6). For the paths of the clouds are those great and perfect knowledges by which the apostles teach us to seek heavenly things and despise all earthly things. The Lord and Savior himself also taught us these lofty and great paths and more-than-perfect knowledges, saying: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me; and you shall have treasure in heaven” (Matt. 19:31). For he himself is also a cloud, as it is written of him: “Behold, the Lord ascends upon a light cloud and enters Egypt, and all its idols shall fall” (Isa. 19:1).

## Chapter IV. Concerning New Mountains

“**I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence help shall come to me**” (Ps. 120:1). These mountains too are new and belong to the new world. We ought to lift our eyes to them and expect help from them. By these mountains are understood the patriarchs and prophets, the apostles and teachers, who, raised above all earthly things and made nearer to heaven, despise all worldly things. Of them the Lord says: “Let those who are in Judaea flee to the mountains; and let them say to the mountains, ‘Fall upon us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us’” (Luke 23:30).

These are the mountains that “leaped like rams, and the hills like lambs of sheep.” But why did they leap? Because “the earth was moved at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob” (Ps. 113:7). They did not leap like wolves and lions and other beasts that delight in blood and live by cruelty. Such is the leaping of tyrants and heretics. Rather, they leaped like sheep, like lambs, like creatures gentle and without blemish. They are mountains indeed, but not proud; they are hills, but gentle. This is signified by the rams and lambs.

Let them rejoice that the earth was moved, because sinners hasten from unbelief to faith and to the pastures of life. For just as the saints are called heaven, so sinners are called earth. These are the eternal mountains of which it is said: “The foolish in heart were troubled by the eternal mountains” (Ps. 75:6). Other mountains are not eternal: “For the fashion of this world passes away” (1 Cor. 7:31).—“Heaven and earth shall pass away” (Luke 21:33).—“But the righteous shall live for ever, and their reward is with the Lord” (Wis. 5:16).

All the foolish in heart—namely Jews and Gentiles, foolish in speech and foolish in heart, speaking philosophically and understanding nothing—were troubled by these mountains. Why were they troubled? Because of the signs they saw and because they could not resist them. For it was not they themselves who spoke, but the Holy Spirit in them, to whom the Lord had given a mouth and wisdom which none of their adversaries could resist or gainsay. Therefore they were troubled: some beneficially, others harmfully; some believing, others raging.

And “therefore we shall not fear when the earth is troubled and the mountains are carried into the heart of the sea” (Ps. 45:3), because “God is our refuge and strength, a helper in the tribulations which have found us exceedingly” (ibid., 1). What is the heart of the sea except kings, princes, and the other powerful persons of this age? For they are in this world as our heart is in our body. All believe their counsel; all obey their will. For they are the heart of the sea, that sea, namely, of which it is said: “This sea is great and broad; there are creeping things there without number” (Ps. 123:25).

When, then, our mountains—the eternal mountains, namely the holy apostles—are carried into the heart of the sea, into the deep whirlpool of this ocean, when they are drawn before kings and rulers, and when the earth is troubled and the Church trembles in terror, then indeed we need not fear, because the Lord is our refuge. Its waters did indeed roar and were troubled, so that the mountains themselves were troubled for a moment in its strength. Yet we need not fear even then, because the Lord is our helper in the tribulations which have found us exceedingly. The greater the tribulation, the more abundant the consolation.

The waters of the sea roared: not one or two persons, but the whole city raged against the martyrs. But what did the mountains do? What did the martyrs do amid so great a tempest? “The mountains,” he says, “were troubled in its strength” (Ps. 45:4). This is what the Apostle says concerning the tribulation that came upon him in Asia: that he was burdened beyond measure, beyond his strength, so that he was weary even of life (2 Cor. 1:8). And what did this strongest mountain of the earth do when so many and such great storms rose against him? Hear him say: “Neither death nor life nor any power shall be able to separate me from the charity of the Lord which is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8:39).

The Church, therefore, is fittingly founded upon such mountains, as Scripture says: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. 45:1). Hence the Lord himself says: “I have been established king by God upon Sion, his holy mountain, preaching the commandment of the Lord” (Ps. 2:6).—“Come, therefore, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob” (Isa. 2:3). For the Lord himself is called a mountain: “Mount Selmon, mountain of the Lord; rich mountain; why do you look with suspicion upon the curdled mountains?” (Ps. 67:17). This mountain is like Sinai, “in which it pleased God to dwell; indeed the Lord shall dwell unto the end” (ibid.).

This mountain indeed is the Lord, whereas the others are not the Lord but the Lord’s chariots. The prophet speaks to those who thought Elijah, Jeremiah, and John the prophet to be Christ. Let us examine the preceding words so that we may understand this more plainly: “When,” he says, “the heavenly one distinguishes kings over her, they shall be made white as snow in Selmon” (ibid., 15). [Note: Col. 953D, Vatican MS: “Who is this heavenly one, if not the Lord Jesus, etc.”] Who is this heavenly one? Our Lord Jesus, king and lord of the heavenly, earthly, and infernal realms, who, when he distinguishes, arranges, and orders kings and teachers over his Church, spoke the things contained above in this psalm. Read the psalm from its beginning and you will understand.

These kings shall be whitened as snow; that is, they shall receive the whiteness and beauty of snow. The saints receive this whiteness and beauty when they are baptized, when they are made whiter than snow and cleansed from every stain of vices. This purification takes place in Selmon, that is, in Christ. For he is the one who washes us from our sins in his blood. No one is baptized and no one cleansed from the contagion of sins except in him and through him. “For as many of us as were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized in his death” (Rom. 6:3).

*Selmon* is interpreted “an image of strength” or “the shadow of an obstacle.” For the Apostle says of Christ: “Who, being the brightness of glory and the figure of his substance” (Heb. 1:3). He is also the stone of stumbling and the rock of offence (1 Pet. 2:7), upon which those who are not enlightened but blind stumble: those who behold not himself but his shadow, that is, who know not his divinity but only his humanity. For a shadow belongs not to spirit but to body.

Therefore this is “Mount Selmon, the mountain of the Lord; a rich mountain, a curdled mountain, a rich mountain.” The very repetition of the words most plainly shows how abundantly this mountain possesses wisdom and knowledge, every fertility of virtue, and richness of graces. For, as the Apostle says, “in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Col. 2:9). He is the flower from the root of Jesse, upon whom “rests the Spirit of the Lord: the spirit of wisdom and understanding; the spirit of counsel and strength; the spirit of knowledge and devotion; the spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. 11:2).

Foolish, therefore, are those who admit other mountains, even though these are curdled, rich, and fertile; even though milk and honey flow in them; even though they nourish many trees and sheep, cattle, and many animals feed upon them; even though fountains of wisdom and knowledge flow from them. Foolish, I say, are those who suppose that that mountain is these mountains in which it pleased the Lord to dwell—not as something different in something different, but as the same in the same. Hence the Lord himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:11); and: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

But those others are not the Lord; they are the Lord’s chariots, the Lord’s soldiers, the Lord’s riders and horses, of whom it is said: “You mount upon your horses, and your four-horsed chariots are salvation” (Hab. 3:8).

There are also other mountains by which we understand virtues. We must climb them if we wish to see Christ fighting, conquering, and choosing disciples; if we wish to see him feeding many thousands from a few loaves; and if we wish with the apostles to see him ascending above the heavens. Finally, when he was transfigured upon a mountain, the evangelist testifies that he ascended it: “For he took Peter, James, and John and led them apart up a high mountain; and he was transfigured before them” (Matt. 17:1).

Abraham dwelt safely in the mountains. Lot was taken captive by enemies in the plain, but was delivered by those who dwelt in the mountains. David also, fleeing Saul, stayed in the safest places, accessible only to wild goats. So too Jacob, when about to offer sacrifice to the Lord, is read to have gone up Mount Bethel. By these and similar examples we are taught that, if we wish to be safe, to please the Lord, and to see his glory, we must flee to the mountain.

There are many mountains and many virtues: whichever you ascend, you will be safe. Abraham was saved on the mountain of faith; Moses on the mountain of gentleness; David on the mountain of meekness; Job on the mountain of patience; and Tobias on the mountain of mercy. The blessed Virgin Mary too was found by the angel on the mountain of humility, as she herself says: “My soul magnifies the Lord, because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:47).

Let us hear the prophet saying: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who proclaim good news to Sion” (Isa. 40:9). I understand the high mountain to be charity, concerning which the Apostle says: “I show you a still more excellent way: pursue charity.” Those who proclaim good news to Sion preach upon this mountain. [Note: Col. 955D, cited edition: “let them ascend.”] Let the preachers and teachers of the Church ascend this mountain. Blessed Peter had ascended this mountain when the Lord entrusted his sheep to him. For he was first questioned three times by the Lord concerning charity, and first professed charity three times; then he received the care of feeding the sheep.

The Lord was accustomed frequently to ascend the Mount of Olives and take his disciples with him, so that we too may delight in ascending and remaining on the mountain [Note: Col. 955D, Vatican MS: “on the Mount of Olives.”] of oil, the mountain of peace and mercy; and so, when the Lord ascends, may observe the way by which we may climb after him.

But there are other mountains [Note: Col. 956D, Vatican MS: “and these too are evil.”] which it is dangerous to ascend or approach. Of these the prophet says: “I trust in the Lord; how do you say to my soul, ‘Migrate to the mountain like a sparrow’?” (Ps. 10:1). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will be able also to move mountains” (Matt. 17:19).

Evil mountains are those upon which Lot, drunken, violated his own daughters. Evil are the mountains of Gilboa, which David cursed when he said: “Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain fall upon you, where the mighty men of Israel, Saul and Jonathan, fell” (2 Kings 1:23). *Gelboe* is interpreted “slippery.” The Psalmist says: “Let their ways become darkness and slipperiness” (Ps. 34:6). Thus the mountains of Gilboa are heretics: shifting, slippery, unstable mountains in which there is no truth. All who climb them, believe them, and take refuge in them easily fall. There the mighty of Israel fell, and there they fall to this day, as the Lord himself says: “Pseudo-Christs and pseudo-prophets shall arise and shall give many signs and wonders, so that, if it were possible, even the elect may be led into error” (Matt. 24:24).

Such a mountain was Arius; such was Sabellius; such was Simon Magus; and many others were such, among whom innumerable bishops themselves fell. Such mountains are accursed; if the dew of heavenly glory or the rain of true and spiritual teaching had fallen upon them, they would by no means have been accursed. Therefore let us flee these mountains and return to the catholic mountains, the rich and fertile mountains; and let us see the Lamb standing on Mount Sion, and with him one hundred and forty thousand (John 14:1). “I,” he says, “have been established king by him upon Sion, his holy mountain, preaching the commandment of the Lord” (Ps. 2:6).

## Chapter V. Concerning New Trees

After speaking of mountains, it was fitting that we should speak of trees. But because, as it seems to us, we have said enough above about trees—in that place, namely, where the Lord speaks of good and bad trees, by which good and bad people are signified—it does not seem necessary to repeat the same matters here. It is easier to turn back the pages than to write those same things again.

## Chapter VI. Concerning New Animals
“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the hinds of the fields, that you do not rouse or awaken the beloved until she herself wishes” (Song of Songs 3:5).” Solomon, most wise, would never have adjured the daughters of Jerusalem in this way [Col. 0956D], unless he had intended something else to be understood through these hinds and roes. For who, when adjured by these creatures in such an exorcism, would be turned back from the pursuit of his own will? What reverence, indeed, ought to be shown to hinds and roes, that so solemn an adjuration should be made through them? Therefore, by these new stags and new roes we are to understand the apostles and teachers, whom we ought to honor as fathers and to show every reverence as to those who have begotten us for the Lord. Hence the Apostle says: “My little children, for whom I am again in travail until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4:19). And again: “Even if you have many instructors, yet not many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (1 Cor. 4:15). Therefore, after the Lord, he could find nothing greater to which the daughters of Jerusalem ought to be obedient.

Now the daughters of Jerusalem are the souls of the saints, who love peace and concord. For Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace,” and they repel from themselves every discord, quarrel, and contention. The beloved, however, may be understood as every soul that has been betrothed and joined to God through the sacrament of faith. This beloved is said to sleep when, having forgotten all earthly things, she rests as though lulled by the sweetest sleep in contemplation of the Lord alone. Therefore, to awaken her from such sleep, to separate her from so great a repose, and to wish to call her back to the cares of the world is a perfect thing—unless perhaps she herself wishes it, moved by another zeal, and inclined not by any force but [Col. 0957B] by the prayers of the brethren, so that she may at times undertake ecclesiastical government for the salvation of many.

This is more openly signified in the Gospel, where Martha said to Jesus: “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to minister alone? Tell her, therefore, to help me” (Matt. 10:40). He neither compelled her to rise nor forbade her to rise, leaving it to her own will [Note: [Col. 0957D] Vatican Codex: “Which of these.”] which of the two she preferred. By this example, therefore, such persons may indeed be asked, but they cannot be compelled.

Let the prophet therefore say: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, daughters of concord, daughters of peace, by the roes and hinds of the fields,” through whose faith and teaching you have attained so great a grace that, from evil servants, you are called brides and daughters, “that you do not rouse or awaken [Col. 0957C] the beloved until she herself wishes.” Offer her no force, but place everything in her own decision and power. [Note: [Col. 0957D] Cited edition: “place.”]

But when the apostles are called stags, or roes, or unicorns, or camels, or wild asses, horses, oxen, sheep, rams, or anything of this kind, one must inquire in those animals whether perhaps something is found in their nature that accords with virtue and is not contrary to apostolic dignity. For all these things can bear both a good and an evil meaning. Plato, it is said, used to call light-minded and unstable people roes and stags; cruel and savage people lions; lazy and foolish people asses; and lustful people swine and goats. Hence some fools, understanding his words in an evil sense, came to such madness [Col. 0957D] that they believed that, after some ages, human beings are changed into beasts and beasts into human beings. Let them say this.

But as for us: why are the apostles and other saints called stags or roes? Because they are clean and harmless animals, which, though they suffer much persecution from others, inflict no persecution on others—except that stags kill serpents. This especially seems fitting to the apostles, because, while pursuing vices and malignant spirits, they know no other hostility, since they love even their enemies.

Stags are swift in running, but not as swift as the apostles, who in a short time traversed not [Col. 0958A] merely one province but the whole world. Roes likewise, which the Greeks call *doreades*, are said to possess keen sight; but those have sight keener still who contemplate God himself and all invisible things with the eyes of the mind. Thus the apostles are not stags, but are called stags on account of these and similar qualities.

“For as the Psalmist says, ‘As the stag longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God’” (Ps. 41:2). Behold another likeness on account of which the soul of the righteous is called a stag. The apostles are also called lions, not because they delight in blood or are cruel, but because they are the strongest of beasts and fear the fall of none. This is written concerning the lion. No lions were so strong as the apostles; none slew such great beasts; [Col. 0958B] none gave forth such mighty roars in the wilderness. The evangelist Mark also belongs among these lions. They are those who, by their strength, defend Solomon’s throne, the Church of the Lord.

The apostles are also called unicorns because with the single horn of faith they scatter all powers. For this animal is said to have one horn in its forehead above its nose; hence it is also called in Greek *rhinoceros*. At four feet in height, its horn is so strong and sharp that no strength of any animal can ever withstand it, since it pierces and casts down even elephants by its charge. Yet greater strength resides in the horn and faith of the apostles, to whom the Lord gave power, as the Gospel says, to tread upon serpents and scorpions and upon every power of the enemy. No [Col. 0958C] power is excepted; rather, every power of the enemy is cast down by this one horn. [Note: [Col. 0957D] Vatican Codex: “every power of the enemy is cast down by this one horn of their faith.” [Col. 0958D]] For by faith the saints conquered kingdoms. “And everything born of God conquers the world; and this is the victory that conquers the world—our faith” (John 5:4).

This, then, is why the apostles are called unicorns; and not only the apostles, but even the Son of God himself does not disdain to be called a unicorn. Hence: “And he built his sacrifice like that of unicorns” (Ps. 77:69). [Note: [Col. 0958D] Vatican Codex and cited edition: “Like the sacrifice of a unicorn,” etc.] And fittingly, like a unicorn, because “the Lord himself is strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. 23:8). Such power and strength were necessary for so great an edifice to be founded.

Elsewhere likewise it is written concerning him: “The voice of the Lord breaks the cedars, and the Lord shall break the cedars of Lebanon; [Col. 0958D] and he shall crush them like a calf of Lebanon, and the Beloved like a son of unicorns” (Ps. 28:5–6). Behold, consider how great is the strength of this unicorn, who can break cedars so great and of such a kind by his voice alone. For what are we to understand by these cedars except the powers and authorities of this world? Some of them indeed have been broken well, others badly, when the Gospel’s voice thundered over them. Those were broken well from which the temple is built; but those are evil which are cut down and cast into the fire.

The calf of Lebanon seems to me to be that calf which, on feast days, was offered at the temple, divided [Col. 0959A] into pieces and broken up, and offered to the Lord. In likeness of this, therefore, these trees are broken up, whether they offer themselves to the Lord or are cast into the fire at the Lord’s command. Lebanon, moreover, is called Jerusalem, as the prophet says: “Open your gates, Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars” (Zech. 11:1). For when the powerful men of Jerusalem, signified by the cedars, were slaughtered in that city by enemies, then the cedars of Lebanon too were broken up, as if a calf to be sacrificed.

But what follows—“and the Beloved, a son, like a son of unicorns”—means as though he had said: The beloved Son of God shall come thus, shall fight thus, shall cast down and overcome all things by his strength, like a unicorn and the son of a unicorn. For David and the other kings and judges of Israel, from whom our Savior [Col. 0959B] drew his origin according to the flesh, like a unicorn conquered and cast down by their strength all the nations around them.

It is said concerning the unicorn that it cannot be caught or held by any device; but if a beautiful virgin is placed before it, it approaches her with all gentleness and, while humbling itself in her lap, is caught or held by hunters. Similarly, our Savior could never have been held unless he had come into a Virgin and received flesh from her.

The apostles are also called wild asses, that is, wild donkeys. Of them the Lord himself speaks to blessed Job, saying: “Who has let the wild ass go free, and who has loosed its bonds? To it I gave a home in the wilderness and dwellings in the land of salt. It despises the multitude of the city; it does not hear the cry of the taskmaster. It surveys [Col. 0959C] the mountains, its pasture, and seeks out every green thing” (Job 39:8). We explained this above in that sermon published on abstinence. These words seem sufficiently to show why holy men are called wild asses.

Furthermore, the apostles are called horses and oxen, because through them the Lord has both waged his wars and cultivated his field. No animal is found so fit for war as horses, nor any so fit for agriculture as oxen. These are those horses of whom it is said: “You ride upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation.” They are signified by the white horse in the Apocalypse, upon which the Lord is described as sitting with a bow; a crown is given to him because he went forth in order to conquer. These are those of whom it is written: “I did not know. My soul was troubled [Col. 0959D] because of the chariots of Aminadab” (Song of Songs 6:11).

Aminadab is interpreted “the willing one of his people.” He is our Savior, who endured voluntary death in order to free his people from everlasting death. But the Synagogue did not recognize him, because, as she herself says, she saw him proceeding with humble equipment and a rustic following.

These are the twelve oxen by which the bronze sea is borne, signifying baptism. They are those of whom the Apostle says: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing” (1 Cor. 9:9). The apostles are also called dogs because they guard the Lord’s sheep against wolves and robbers. Of them it is said: “The tongue of your dogs from the enemies, by him” (Ps. 67:24).

They are also called [Col. 0960A] rams, concerning whom it is written: “All the flock of Kedar shall be gathered to you; the rams of Nebaioth shall minister to you” (Isa. 60:7). And Solomon says: “A ram, girded about the loins, is a king whom none can resist” (Prov. 30:31). What kind of rams are these, who both minister to the Lord and do not fear to fight against kings? Such rams are Peter and Paul, who, girded with the sword of the Spirit, overcame Nero himself, the most wicked and cruel king of all, and cast Simon Magus down from the air.

Nebaioth is interpreted “prophet of the beginning,” namely, of that Beginning who says: “I am the Beginning, who also speak to you” (John 16:25). Whoever has drunk of his prophecy is altogether worthy to minister to the Lord. If we wished to write down all the animals by which the apostles [Col. 0960B] are figured, we would have to produce not a discourse but a large volume. Let each person, therefore, add to these whatever pleases him; for us, it is enough to have said these few things.

## CHAPTER VII. On the new powers

“Behold, we have left all things and followed you; what then shall we have? The Lord says: You who have left all things and followed me shall receive a hundredfold in this life, and after this life you shall possess eternal life. And because you have followed me, you shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:27).

The new world has a new emperor, new kings, new leaders, new princes, and [Col. 0960C] judges. The new kings, leaders, princes, and judges are the apostles. They are new in the Lord because they are wiser, more powerful, stronger, more just, and richer than all the powers of this world, whatever they have been or shall be.

They are wiser because they were taught all truth, as the Lord himself says: “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 16:13). They are likewise wiser because they received from the Lord a mouth and wisdom which all their adversaries cannot resist or contradict. Hence the Apostle says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Cor. 2:6).

They are also more powerful because they possess authority not only on earth but also in heaven. Thus the Lord himself says: “Whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 18:18). Earth does not suffice for them: heaven itself is contained within their rule and dominion. They have power to close and to open; they receive whom they wish and exclude whom they wish.

What shall I say about their strength, whom even malignant spirits fear? At their coming these spirits flee and cannot stand before their presence. And what need is there to speak about their riches, when they are so rich that they desire to possess nothing further? For, as the Apostle says, they are “as needy, yet enriching many; as having nothing, and possessing all things” (2 Cor. 6:10). [Col. 0961A] He is richest whose own possessions suffice him. Diogenes possessed only necessities and was richer than all emperors, because he did not wish to possess anything more.

The poor man is he who begs; and emperors beg—not indeed with their voices, though sometimes even with their voices, but by desire—because, for one house which they have, people of this kind desire a hundred. But the Lord says on the other hand: “You who have left all things shall receive a hundredfold in this life,” because they had enough and desired nothing more. This sufficiency itself is reckoned as more than a hundredfold. [Note: [Col. 0961D] Vatican Codex: “But emperors beg—not indeed with the voice, though sometimes even with the voice—and they beg by desire. Therefore the Lord rightly says: ‘You who have left all things,’ etc., ‘shall receive a hundredfold in this life,’ because when they had all things, they were poor. Whoever had one house desired a hundred. Now he has none, and it is enough for him. This sufficiency is reckoned as a hundredfold.”]

The saints therefore received not only a hundredfold but even more than a hundredfold, because when they cling to Christ, every desire which avarice could arouse in them has come to an end. Sufficiency is greater than all riches. He [Col. 0961B] therefore who has sufficiency has all riches, and more than all riches. Thus they possess not only a hundredfold but more than a hundredfold.

It follows: “You who have followed me shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28). Only those are worthy to judge who follow Jesus, who walk after him on the same path, who love truth and justice, and do not regard the person of a man. Such are our judges; such are the holy apostles, who sit upon twelve seats and judge the twelve tribes of Israel.

But why upon twelve seats? Because there are as many divisions of the world, according to the words: “When the Most High divided the nations, when he separated the sons of Adam, he established the boundaries of peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel” (Deut. [Col. 0961C] 32:8). The Lord made this division when he commanded the disciples to go and preach, saying: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 19:20). He left no part of the world aside when he commanded that the Gospel be preached to the entire world.

Thus the Lord divided the nations and separated the sons of Adam, so that some might be converted to faith through Peter, others through John, and others through other apostles. This also seems to be signified by what is read of Christ in the Psalms: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth” (Ps. 44:17). For sons were born to our Savior in place of fathers, because the number of sons corresponded to the number of fathers. There were twelve sons of Jacob, from [Col. 0961D] whom the entire Synagogue sprang; and there are twelve sons of Christ, from whom the multitude of churches has grown.

Our Savior does not disdain to call fathers those from whom he derived his origin according to the flesh. Hear him himself saying: “Our fathers trusted in you; they trusted, and you delivered them” (Ps. 21:5). Therefore the apostles are called kings and princes; they are called leaders and judges; and they are called by other names that can fittingly belong to men.

O judges above all [Col. 0962A] judges, who shall judge not only human beings but even the angels themselves! For the Apostle also says: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6:3)—in that fearful judgment before which every rational creature shall stand; when angels and all human beings shall come together into one place; when the noble Bridegroom and Lord shall sit at the gates of the Church with these senators, the judges of the earth. That proud one also, with all his army, must stand there—the one who threatened to ascend above the heavens and set his throne there. By their judgment he shall be condemned, he who does not cease to accuse them.

These alone, therefore, are to be called kings and princes; these alone leaders and judges. These are they of whom it is said: “The princes of Judah, their leaders; the princes of Zebulun; the princes of Naphtali” [Col. 0962B] (Ps. 67:28). These are those kings of whom it is said: “From your temple in Jerusalem kings shall offer gifts to you” (ibid., 30).

The apostles are also shepherds—not shepherds who feed sheep with grass, but who refresh souls with spiritual words. If they are shepherds, they also have sheep. We are their sheep, if indeed we are sheep. But if we are not sheep, we do not belong to their flocks, because these shepherds guard only sheep. Hence the Lord says to Peter: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John 21:17). And the Lord says of himself: “I am the good shepherd, and I know my sheep” (John 11:14).

Do you wish to be a sheep? Be humble and innocent; be patient and gentle; cast off pride and rapacity; harm no one and wrong no one. Let Christ’s poor live on your milk and be warmed by your wool. Such shepherds love such sheep.

They are also merchants, able to exchange earthly things for heavenly, and transitory things for eternal. These are those merchants who, having found one precious pearl, sold everything and bought it. These are they to whom the Lord, departing into a far country, entrusted his goods, saying: “Trade until I come” (Luke 29:13); and when he returns, they restore to him all the money increased. Hence, rejoicing with each one of them, he says: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:21).

It is written of the Church that “she became like a merchant ship, or a trader’s vessel, bringing her bread from afar” (Prov. 31: [Col. 0962D] 14). These merchants deceive no one, and they sell incomparable and great riches for a cheap price.

The holy apostles are also architects, not inferior to Bezalel and Oholiab, whom the Lord filled with all wisdom for constructing the tabernacle of testimony. Their construction and work have now been consumed and dissolved by excessive age; but the building of these apostles remains forever. Those clothed priests with gold and gems; these clothe priests with virtues, of whom it is said: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness, and [Col. 0963A] let your saints rejoice” (Ps. 131:6). But those men prefigured these, whose work, if understood spiritually, belongs not to them but to the righteous.

What an architect was blessed Paul, who speaks of himself, saying: “According to the grace given to me, as a wise architect I laid a foundation. But no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus. But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble, each person’s work shall be made manifest. For the day of the Lord will declare it, because it shall be revealed in fire, and the fire shall test what sort each person’s work is. If anyone’s work that he has built upon it remains, he shall receive a reward. If anyone’s work burns, he shall suffer loss; but he himself [Col. 0963B] shall be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. 3:10).

These lengthy words need exposition, and many have already labored upon them. Nevertheless, I shall briefly state what I understand. Christ is the foundation upon which the entire Church, both good and evil persons, is founded. Hence the Lord himself says: “Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he shall take away” (John 15:2), showing that even evil branches are founded in him through the sacrament of baptism. And although they are at some time to be taken away, they are nevertheless still in Christ, because they are in the Church.

Gold, silver, and precious stones are good works; wood, hay, and stubble signify sins. We therefore do great wrong to this most noble foundation when we compel it to bear [Col. 0963C] and endure our sins in us. Yet it is written of him that he bore our sins and suffers pain for us (Isa. 13:11). For he endures and willingly waits, provided only that we turn back, do penance, and cast off the useless burden. If we do so, we shall be saved, yet as through fire.

Whoever has been worthily converted and has done penance shall be freed not only from lesser sins, as some have refused to understand, but also from greater sins, and shall be saved. For every sin, the Lord says, and every blasphemy shall be forgiven to human beings; but blasphemy of the spirit, by which persistence in evil is understood, shall not be forgiven (Matt. 12). Behold, the Lord says that every sin is forgiven; only one is excepted, which those commit who refuse to repent.

Every sin is indeed forgiven through penance, but the punishment of sin is not altogether remitted. In baptism, however, both are remitted. From martyrs likewise no punishment is exacted after martyrdom. Therefore the Lord has power both to shorten the punishment of sin as much as he wishes and to remit it altogether to whom he wishes. “Blessed, therefore, is he to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Ps. 41:2).

Let penitents therefore rejoice, because their sins have been forgiven; yet let them fear, because they do not know whether the punishment of sin has also been forgiven them. For on whatever day they are converted, if only they are worthily converted, they shall be saved. And this is indeed through fire. Thus they are saved, but the fire remains; sin has been forgiven, but not the punishment of sin.

[Col. 0964A] We read that some people shone by miracles after death and yet were assigned to purgatory. Concerning such persons there can be no doubt that their sins had been forgiven, but that the punishment of sin had not been forgiven. Of such, therefore, it was said: “If anyone’s work burns, he shall suffer loss; but he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. 3:10).

But other human beings whose sins shall burn will certainly not be saved through fire; rather, they shall be cast into eternal fire—other human beings, I say, apart from those who have done penance for their sins. By doing penance I mean not departing this life without the remedy of penance; for those who die without penance shall be tormented without end. This is that one sin which is not forgiven to human beings, neither in this age nor in the age to come. “Watch [Col. 0964B] therefore,” says the Lord, “because you know neither the day nor the hour” (Matt. 25).

There are also other names highly fitting for the apostles, which one who wishes to make the discourse longer may add to those already mentioned.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the new sea and the new fishers.

> “This great and wide sea: there are creeping things without number; little and great living creatures; there ships shall pass through” (Ps. 103:25).
>
> The Evangelist Matthew relates that the Lord and our Savior, passing along the Sea of Galilee, saw Peter, Andrew, and John, and called them, saying: “Come after me; I will make you become fishers of men” (Mark 1). When I hear human beings called fish [Col. 0964C], and Christ’s disciples made fishers of men—which cannot, of course, be understood literally—I am compelled to understand a new sea, new nets, new fishers, and new fish.
>
> Therefore this world is the new sea, of which we spoke above: “This great and wide sea: there are creeping things without number.” The nets are the Gospels; the fish are human beings; and the fishers are the apostles. This sea is as vast as the world, in which there are great creatures and, as Genesis records, great sea-monsters: by these are understood kings, princes, and other greater and more powerful persons. But the little creatures and creeping things without number may be understood as the remaining infinite multitude of humankind: people of either sex, of every age, rank, condition, language, and nation [Col. 0964D].
>
> Just as among the fish of the sea some are gentle and live simply, while others are predatory, pursuing and devouring the rest, so we see this among human beings in the world: the simple multitude is daily devoured by robbers and wicked people, and we see it devoured in many ways.
>
> There is also in this sea that great dragon, the ancient serpent who is the devil and Satan, whom the Lord formed for sport with him. The Lord himself speaks of him to blessed Job, saying: “Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you; he eats grass like an ox. He is the beginning of the ways of God; he who made him shall bend his sword” (Job 40:10). “The mountains bring him herbs; all the beasts of the field shall play there” [Col. 0965A].
>
> The devil is God’s creature: God formed him and made him, but did not make him as he now is. For the words, “This dragon whom you formed for sport with him” (Ps. 103:26), are not to be understood of his first creation. Rather, because, lifted up through pride, he did not stand in the truth, he was fashioned thus after he fell. He was reduced to such a form and such a measure of weakness that human beings can now make sport of him. For unless he were thus held bound by the Lord, who could have resisted his pride and cunning? Hence it is said: “He who made him shall bend his sword” (Job 40:14). If his sword had not been bent, who could have endured the wounds of so sharp an edge? The bending of his sword, therefore, shows the weakness of his power.
>
> [Note: [Col. 0965D] The same exposition occurs in the commentary on this passage, vol. I, p. 293, col. 1: “For the devil is the beginning of God’s ways, that is, of his operations, because he was made first among all creatures. But the Lord bent his sword, because [Col. 0966D], unless it had been bent so that he might not always strike with a straight point, very few could escape the sword of his deception.”]
>
> All who flee from him and return to repentance make sport of him [Col. 0965B]. Blessed Paul rightly made sport of him: while he was persecuting the Church, he was in the dragon’s mouth and already being gripped between his teeth; but, immediately converted to the faith, he left him sorrowful. So too Mary Magdalene deceived him, when, converted to the Lord, she “chose the best part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42). By a single utterance he is mocked, and by a single word prey already devoured is thrown back out from his very belly. It is enough for the sinful woman to confess her fault, and he can no longer hold her. Thus he is greatly mocked, and his sword has been much bent.
>
> He is called *Behemoth*, which means “beast,” because he is cruel and acts with a beastly mind. Deprived of angelic dignity, he imitates in every respect the most savage beasts [Col. 0965C]. “Behold,” he says, “Behemoth, whom I made with you, whom I made like you”—for there is one creator of both—“he eats grass like an ox.” Let the prophet say: “Truly the people are grass; the grass has withered, and the flower has fallen” (Isa. 40:8). Behemoth, then, does not eat men who are wise, but the foolish and undisciplined people.
>
> He is the beginning of the Lord’s ways. He is believed to have been made before the other creatures. Yet this can also be understood as though it said: he is the cause and beginning by which the Lord’s one way was divided into two ways, so that not all might now ascend to heaven by one way, but some might descend by another way into hell—while to some it is said, “Go,” and to others, “Come.”
>
> “And the mountains bring him herbs.” Evil mountains nourish the devil and supply food to the dragon [Col. 0965D]. The devil’s food and refreshment are sin. Whoever sins more prepares greater banquets for him. No one serves him in this way so much as evil kings and princes, and all the avaricious and rich, who are signified by mountains. For they not only sin themselves, but compel others to sin with them. Consider now how many murders, how many robberies, how much disturbance is everywhere caused through them. Thus it is fittingly said: “All the beasts of the field play there” (Job 40:15 [Col. 0966A]). The beasts of the field are vices and evil spirits.
>
> These beasts, therefore, play there—that is, in the mountains mentioned above, namely, in the hearts of the wicked. There they delight themselves; there they rest pleasantly; there they establish theaters and build palaces. There they introduce their companions, in order to make their latter state worse than their former. Wretched are those sheep, wretched those souls that have become the dwelling-place of such cruel beasts.
>
> Such fish dwell in this sea, where there are creeping things without number, little and great creatures, and this dragon whom the Lord formed for sport with him—of all of whom we have spoken until now. The apostolic fishers are sent into the great and deep sea, coming to fish in this sea. It is difficult fishing, where one must both fight and fish [Col. 0966B]. On one side they cast nets to catch fish; on the other they extend swords to repel enemies.
>
> What shall I say of those fish who are caught of their own accord and enter the nets, yet afterward strive to tear and scatter those same nets? Such fish were Arius, Sabellius, the Manichees, and many others who attempted to nullify apostolic preaching and the catholic faith. By them the holy Church and the apostolic ships were wearied and shaken more than even by the tyrants themselves who persecuted her with bloody swords.
>
> The Prophet foresaw this immense disturbance when he said: “Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing work in great waters, they have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep. He spoke, and a stormy wind stood forth, and its waves were lifted up. They ascend to the heavens and descend to the depths; their soul melted away in evils. They were troubled and shaken like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up. And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their distresses. He made its storm a gentle breeze, and its waves were silent; and they rejoiced because they were still, and he led them to the harbor of their desire” (Ps. 106:23 ff.) [Col. 0966C].
>
> In a few words the Psalmist comprehends the apostles’ preaching, the efficacy of miracles, the cruelty of tyrants, and consolation given from heaven. For when the holy apostles and other teachers descended into the deepest sea of this world to preach, “doing work in great waters”—that is, among many peoples—in individual cities, raising the dead, giving sight to the blind, cleansing lepers, healing paralytics, and performing other wonders, then they saw the works of the Lord and his marvels which the Lord wrought through them in this deep.
>
> “He spoke, and a stormy wind stood forth, and its waves were lifted up” [Col. 0966D] (ibid.).
>
> [Note: [Col. 0966D] This exposition agrees perfectly with St Bruno’s commentary on this Psalm.]
>
> Thus, at his command, the sea was then troubled and its waves were raised: some in a good sense, others [Col. 0967A] in an evil sense.
>
> [Note: [Col. 0967D] Vatican manuscript and edition: “For at his command the spirit of the storm stood forth; that is, it did not pass away but persisted. For he is the one of whom it is written: ‘I am the Lord who troubles the sea, and its waves swell.’ [Col. 0968D] Thus, etc.”]
>
> Some were on their side; others against them. Some said, “Let them go, because they are good”; others said, “Let them be killed, because they are evil.” Some, seeing the signs they performed, called them gods and exalted them with praises up to heaven; others, indignant and attacking them, attempted to submerge them in the abyss. This is what he means by: “They ascend to heaven and descend into the abyss” (ibid.).
>
> Hence their soul melted away in evils, sometimes unable to endure such great torments. Thus the Apostle says: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning the persecution that happened to us in Asia: we were burdened beyond measure, so that we were weary even of life” (2 Cor. 1:8). They were therefore troubled and shaken like a drunken man—not drunk with a cup of wine, but with the cup [Col. 0967B] of suffering and affliction. And all their wisdom was swallowed up, as blessed Job says of himself: “My thoughts are scattered, tormenting my heart” (Job 17:11). The good thoughts in which the holy man was accustomed to devote himself to contemplation of God had been scattered by the affliction of such great distresses; and the force of suffering and abundance of pain were so great that he could think of nothing else. Thus in this passage too all their wisdom was at times swallowed up by the immensity of their pains.
>
