> Since they could not bear it, they cried to God, were heard, and he led them to the harbor of their desire. At times they did not even feel the very torments inflicted on them by their persecutors. This is fittingly signified in the Gospel when the disciples cried out: “Lord, save us; we are perishing.” Rising, he commanded the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm (Matt. 8:26) [Col. 0967C].
>
> This immense disturbance of the sea continually troubled the holy Church from the times of the apostles to those of the Emperor Constantine, and scarcely ever rested. Thereafter peace and calm came about; Christ’s fishers began to fish in quiet and security and to draw the dragnet to land. Of this the Gospel says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a dragnet cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind. When it was filled, they drew it out; and, sitting by the shore, they selected the good into their vessels but cast the bad away” (Matt. 13:47).
>
> But [Col. 0967D] the dragnet is not yet full: fish are still entering. “But when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 11:25). Then, when the bad fish have been rejected, the good will be led into eternal life.

## CHAPTER IX. On New Birds

We read in Genesis that the Lord commanded the waters to bring forth fish according to their kinds and birds according to their species. And it was so. “And God blessed them and said: Increase and multiply, [Col. 0968A] and fill the waters of the sea; and let birds multiply upon the earth” (Gen. 1:23).

Fish and birds have one origin, and both were created from the waters. The former seek the depths; the latter are raised toward heavenly things. Both are good, because among all other creatures they deserved to receive the first blessing. By them, therefore, holy men are signified, who have been regenerated from waters. For “unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5). They thoroughly search out the depths of the Scriptures, signified by waters, and rise to heavenly things on the wings of virtues.

But we have spoken enough above concerning fish. It is fitting that we now speak of birds. Unless other birds—of a far better and worthier nature—were signified by these birds which we see flying before us [Col. 0968B], the Church would never be called a dove, as the Lord says: “My dove is one” (Song 6:8); John the Evangelist would never be called an eagle; and King David would never be called pelican, night-owl, and sparrow, as Scripture calls him: “I have become like a pelican in the wilderness, and like a night-owl in its dwelling. I kept watch and became like a solitary sparrow on the roof” (Ps. 101:7).

Moreover, not only human beings, but even the angels themselves appear to assume the form and nature of birds. Everywhere we see them as winged and feathered. They are described as flying rather than walking, which is properly characteristic of birds. The curtains of the tabernacle are also read to have been made in feather-work (Exod. 26) [Col. 0968C]. And the four living creatures in Ezekiel and the Apocalypse are said to be full of eyes before and behind and to have six wings: “The first living creature is like a man; the second, like a lion; the third, like a calf; and the fourth, like a flying eagle” (Ezek. 1:8; Rev. 4:6). Likewise Isaiah says: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high throne, and the whole earth was full of his majesty, and the things beneath him filled the temple. Seraphim stood above it: six wings to one and six wings to the other” (Isa. 6:1).

Birds, then, are in the sea; birds on the earth; birds in heaven; and birds above heaven. All the elements teach us to fly; all summon us toward what is higher and heavenly. “Who will give me [Col. 0968D] wings like a dove, that I may fly and rest?” (Ps. 54:7). We have already become birds, because we have been regenerated in the waters. We lack wings alone.

[Note: [Col. 0968D] Vatican manuscript and edition: “Let us seek them, since we cannot fly without wings and feathers.”]

The feather of the ostrich is unlike the feather of the hawk and the heron, which are among the swiftest of birds; but the ostrich, because of the weakness of its wings, cannot raise itself from the ground. It therefore has wings, but weak ones; it has feathers, but feeble ones. Such are hypocrites and heretics, who appear to be hawks and herons but are ostriches: they do not have wings by which they can fly or rise to heavenly things.

Wings, therefore, are virtues; wings signify good works [Col. 0969A], without which we cannot fly. Let these carry us; let these raise us to heaven. Do you possess humility? It is a wing for you. Do you possess mercy? It is a wing for you. Do you possess patience? It is a wing for you. As many virtues as you have, so many wings you have. If you possess charity, so that you love God and your neighbor, you possess two wings, which can suffice for flight.

Yet two wings are not enough for the Seraphim and the four living creatures: they have six, because with some they fly, and with others they cover their heads and feet. By head and feet we understand beginning and end. The living creatures cover their heads, lest we should perhaps wish to inquire of them into the things that happened before the beginning of the world. They likewise cover their feet, because they do not wish to disclose to us the things that will happen in this world after its end [Col. 0969B]. Thus Isaiah, mocking the gods of the nations, says: “Tell me what things came first, and what last things shall be, and I shall say that you are gods” (Isa. 41:23). But you cannot, and therefore you are nothing.

It therefore seems superfluous either to inquire into what existed before the world’s beginning or into what will happen after its end. Even if you inquire, there is no one who can tell you. If you could remove the wings from the heads and feet of these living creatures, then perhaps you could know first and last things. For people customarily ask these questions and, though unnecessarily, labor over such matters, wishing to know whether, after the world’s end, the heaven will revolve; whether the sun, moon, and stars will be carried in their customary course; whether rivers will run and springs burst forth; whether trees and plants will exist; and many other matters [Col. 0969C] that commonly stir human curiosity. To those who ask such questions the most fitting answer is that the feet of the Seraphim and the four living creatures are covered with wings and cannot be seen; nevertheless, one must wait until the wings are removed.

But they fly with the two wings that are in the middle, because they speak most fully concerning everything that happens in this world from beginning to end. They are full of eyes before and behind, because they see the future and do not fail to know the past. Everything in them is light and brightness. In them there are as many eyes as words. Whoever does not believe them is blind and without light. Hence the Lord says to some: “You err, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God” (Matt. 22:29) [Col. 0969D].

The eyes in the Scriptures, therefore, are spiritual understandings, by which holy men, enlightened, cannot err. Since the Pharisees lacked these eyes, they are called blind by the Lord, and guides of the blind. We have said what is signified by the creatures’ wings and by their eyes. May we too have wings for flight, and eyes before and behind, so that we may come to God by a straight path and, mindful of our sins, say with the Psalmist: “For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 50:4).

We have eyes before us if we walk on the royal road, flee evils [Col. 0970A], and hold fast to good things. Hence Solomon says: “The eyes of the wise man are in his head; the fool walks in darkness” (Eccl. 2:14). Those have eyes behind who, mindful of the fathers of old, strive to imitate their life and holy conduct—like him who said: “I considered the days of old, and I held the eternal years in mind” (Ps. 76:6). He had eyes behind when he considered the days of old, but eyes before when he held the eternal years in mind. If we keep this verse alone, we are full of eyes before and behind.

Nor is it without mystery that the first living creature is described as having a human face, by which Matthew the apostle and his Gospel are understood. Beginning from Christ’s birth, he shows him to be a perfect man, born from human beings [Col. 0970B], setting out his entire genealogy from Abraham down to Christ himself. Mark, however, appears to have the face of a lion, since at the beginning of his Gospel a voice is described as crying in the wilderness. Blessed Luke has the face of a calf, because he begins to write from the priesthood, which was instituted especially for sacrifices; and among sacrificial offerings the ox is the greater victim. Why John has the face of an eagle is shown most plainly by the beginning of his Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). He who speaks thus flies far more loftily than an eagle.

Yet these four different faces of the living creatures seem to offer us something: for the human being summons us to reason, the lion to courage [Col. 0970C], the ox to labor, and the eagle to contemplation.

[Note: [Col. 0969D] Cited edition: “to contemplation.”]

Thus the human being teaches us to preach, the lion to fight, the ox to labor, and the eagle to fly. Let us therefore imitate these kinds of living creatures.

[Note: [Col. 0970D] Same edition: “Let us therefore imitate these birds,” etc.]

Let them be examples for us. Let us not look to the ostrich, whose wings are weak; let us not attend to hypocrites, who pretend to be what they are not, whose wings will fail when they are most needed. Rather, let us take up the wings of the hawk and heron—not in order to seize anything, but in order to perform with the greatest speed the obedience imposed upon us.

For among such birds, and among all birds that live by rapine, wings and feathers can indeed bear a good signification; but claws, beaks, and their action bear an impious sense and signification [Col. 0970D]. By such birds evil spirits are signified, whose every operation is theft and plunder. These are the birds driven away by Abraham. These are they who snatch the good word of God from human hearts, lest those who believe may be saved. The whole air is full of such birds; and because they are swift and invisible, they everywhere inflict great persecution on all people.

## CHAPTER X. On New Rivers

> “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God; the Most High has sanctified his tabernacle” (Ps. 45:5).

We read in Genesis that a river went forth from Paradise and was afterward divided into four heads. The first is named Phison; the second Gyon; the third Tigris; the fourth Euphrates. By these the whole land is watered and made fertile [Col. 0971A].

[Note: [Col. 0971D] Vatican manuscript: *Geron*.]

[Note: [Col. 0972D] Vatican manuscript omits “likewise.”]

Likewise we read in the Apocalypse that from that most noble city—whose walls are built of precious stones, whose individual gates are made from individual pearls, and whose streets are paved with the purest gold—a river flowed, whose water is most clear, like crystal. Along the riverbanks there are also most noble trees, which bear twelve fruits, one in each month, and whose leaves themselves are for the healing of the nations.

Nature itself forbids us to understand these things literally; they seem to signify something much more exalted than what the letter sounds like [Col. 0971B], especially since it is written elsewhere: “The rivers shall clap their hands together” (Ps. 97:8). How can rivers, which have no hands, clap with their hands? These are new rivers and belong to a new world. This new world is the city of God, which the rush of the river makes glad.

This river is Christ, whose most abundant wisdom and knowledge gladden the holy Church. Hence it is also said elsewhere: “Wisdom preaches, cries aloud outside, and utters her voice in the streets” (Prov. 8:1). She also cries in the temple, saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink, and from his belly shall flow living waters” (John 7:38). This is [Col. 0971C] that fountain of which it is said: “For with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. 35:10). He also speaks to the Samaritan woman, saying: “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:14).

This river, then, by which Paradise is cleansed and the Church made glad, is divided into four heads, by which the four Gospels are signified. The first is called Phison, which means “change of speech.” For evangelical preaching changed people’s mouths and tongues, so that those who formerly praised and proclaimed false gods now praise and proclaim the one true God and his wonders. What, indeed, changed blessed Paul’s mouth except the Gospel? He who had previously preached circumcision afterward spoke with a changed mouth, saying: “Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing” (1 Cor. 7:19) [Col. 0971D].

Read the histories of the saints, and you will see one who a little earlier praised Jupiter as almighty God immediately affirm, with altered speech, that Jupiter himself is not a god but a demon. You will also see one who used to sing, in play and madness, the empty fables of poets, now joyfully singing hymns and psalms. Phison produces this change of mouths and tongues, because evangelical speech both loosens the mouths of the mute and makes the tongues of infants eloquent. How great a change of speech occurred when the apostles, who, as poor and rustic men, scarcely knew how to speak one language, immediately, divinely kindled, began to speak in every language [Col. 0972A]!

Gyon means “breast.” Look now at the breast of the high priest and see there the breastplate. Ask too why high priests receive the breast from the sacrifices as their portion. Perhaps it is because this river Gyon, which is called “breast,” ought to flow from the high priest’s breast. Indeed, the Christian people and the city of the Lord should always be gladdened and satisfied from the breast. For the heart is in the breast, and in it is the seat and source of all wisdom and knowledge. Blessed John drank from this river when, reclining at supper upon the breast, he saw what he later wrote: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). Whenever we wish to drink from the river Gyon, let us look to the breasts of high priests [Col. 0972B]. They are adorned in this way so that we may understand that a great treasure of wisdom is stored there.

Tigris means “arrow,” because this river is swift as an arrow. But what has such speed as evangelical preaching, which, running everywhere, filled the whole world in a very brief time? That noble archer, blessed Paul, had already preached the Gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum when he said that he wished to go on to Spain, so that there too he might shoot the arrows of the Gospel. For the Lord “sent his arrows and scattered them” (Ps. 17:15). Of them it is also said elsewhere: “Indeed, his arrows passed through” (Ps. 76:18). What else are the words of the Gospels but arrows, by which evil spirits are put to flight and the whole army of vices is destroyed and scattered [Col. 0972C]?

Hence it is written: “Unless you are converted, he will brandish his sword; he has bent his bow and prepared it; and on it he has prepared instruments of death; he has made his arrows fiery” (Ps. 7:13). These are “the sharp arrows of the mighty, with desolating coals” (Ps. 119:4). “For as arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the children of those cast out. Blessed is the man who has filled his desire from them; he shall not be confounded when he speaks with his enemies at the gate” (Ps. 126:4–5).

God’s words are made into arrows, against which no fortifications of enemies can stand. Thus the Lord says to the disciples: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom which all your adversaries shall not be able to resist or contradict” (Luke 21:15).

There remains Euphrates, which means “fertility” [Col. 0972D]. How fitting this meaning is for the Gospels is evident to all. Look upon the whole world converted from error to faith by evangelical preaching, and you will then understand how fertile Euphrates has been and how greatly it has benefited us by its fertility. Marveling at this fertility, the Psalmist says: “But your friends have been exceedingly honored to me, O God; their dominion has been exceedingly strengthened. I will number them, and they shall be multiplied beyond the sand” (Ps. 138:18 ff.). Elsewhere he says: “I have declared and spoken; they have been multiplied beyond number” (Ps. 39:6). Hence the Lord says to his disciples: “You did not choose me, but I chose you, that you should go and bear [Col. 0973A] fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John 15:16).

Hence too it is said through Solomon concerning the Church: “Your belly is a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies” (Song 7:2). Since the holy Church—the field of God, the vineyard of God, the garden of God—is so fruitful, this is brought about by Euphrates, by whose stream it is bathed and watered.

These are the four rivers of Paradise, proceeding from one fountain and flowing from Christ’s one breast, by which the whole world is watered. From them many other rivers have arisen. For there are as many rivers as there are volumes of books. The Old Testament too has its rivers; unless these are mingled with, and come together with, those rivers, they are deadly and unpleasant to drink. “For the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” [Col. 0973B] (2 Cor. 3:5); the words are those of the Apostle. But if they come together, they surpass every drink.

There are also other rivers, themselves deadly, whose waters kill people because they are bitter. In the Apocalypse the Apostle John says that he saw a great star, burning like a torch, fall upon a third part of the rivers (Rev. 8:10). The name of the star is called Wormwood. Many people died from the waters because they were made bitter. By these rivers is understood the erroneous writing of all heretics, philosophers, and poets [Col. 0974A]. Since it does not accord with the two rivers of the New and Old Testaments, it is not without reason called a third part of the rivers.

Flee these waters, Christian: they are bitter and deadly. The rivers are known; the volumes of Holy Scripture are known; known are the waters springing up into eternal life, from which whoever drinks shall not thirst again [Col. 0974B].

# FOURTH BOOK OF SENTENCES

[Col. 0973]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the Holy Trinity

[Col. 0973B]

“Audi, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God. [Col. 0973C] You shall have no foreign god besides me” (Deut. VI; Exod. XX). Likewise it is written in the Psalms: “Israel, if you will listen to me, there shall be no new god in you, nor shall you worship a foreign god; for I am the Lord your God” (Ps. LXXX, 9). Reading these words without understanding them, the Jews mock Christians, as though they worship not one God but three gods. To them the Lord fittingly says in the Gospel: “You err, knowing neither the Scriptures nor the power of God” (Matt. XXII, 29).

For we worship not three gods, but one God in three persons; and we adore the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. God is indeed one, but the persons are three. For the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; yet they are not three gods, but one God. For these three persons are one essence [Col. 0973D], one Godhead, one power, one majesty, one wisdom, one strength, one omnipotence, one light, one beginning, one brightness; and whatever else, apart from personal property, is said of one person is likewise said equally of all. For as the Father is God, so also are the Son and the Holy Spirit God; they are omnipotent, strong, great, wise, and whatever else may similarly be said. Yet they are not three gods or three omnipotent beings, but one God, one omnipotent being, one strong, great, and wise being.

Personal property, however, consists in this: that the Father is believed and understood to be begetter, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit neither begetter nor begotten, but proceeding from both. This faith of ours has not been set forth by arguments, syllogisms, or human reason [Col. 0974B], but is established solely by the authorities of the holy Scriptures—not invented by man, but divinely inspired. Hence the Lord says to the unbelieving Jews, who contradict themselves: “If you believed Moses, you would certainly believe me, for he wrote concerning me” (John V, 46).

If anyone asks where Moses wrote concerning Christ himself, let him hear Christ saying: “At the beginning of the book it is written concerning me” (Ps. XXXIX, 9). Moses began with him; he placed him at the beginning, so that the Jew might quickly and easily find the one whom he does not wish to find, and might not toil in seeking, since he cannot reach, by reading, the other things written there except through him: “In the beginning,” he says, “God made heaven and earth, and the Spirit of God moved over the waters” (Gen. I, 1–2).

Perhaps it would have been fitting for the Father’s name to be placed first, since he is everywhere most highly honoured by the Son himself. But Moses—or rather the Holy Spirit, who spoke through Moses—did not wish this. He placed first the name [Col. 0974D] of the Son, lest the Jew go astray in seeking. But perhaps you will ask: What is “the beginning”? Let him himself answer you; let him himself tell you. He said it once, but you did not understand; let him say it again, if perhaps you may understand: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John VIII, 25).

Believe Moses, therefore; believe the authority of the Scriptures; or let that authority itself compel you, and let the Holy Spirit constrain you, to confess one God in three persons. Behold: immediately at the beginning of this book, which is first among the others, one God and three persons are set forth: namely, God the Father, who made heaven and earth; and the Spirit of God, through whom the Father and the Son disposed and ordered all things made in heaven and on earth. For this appears to be signified by the words: “The Spirit of God moved over the waters” (Gen. I, 2).

For the Holy Spirit [Col. 0975A], proceeding from the Father and the Son, disposes, by the counsel and will of both, whatever the Father works through the Son. Since the Son is called Wisdom, so that so beautiful a work may be understood to have been made by wisdom, it is rightly declared to have been made through the Son, who is called Wisdom—although it is not to be doubted that it was made by the whole holy and indivisible Trinity. The Father and the Son are rightly said to dispose, in the Holy Spirit, who is common to them both, whatever they please to dispose, so that the disposition may be common to those whose operation is common.

God, therefore, made heaven and earth, by which God the Father is understood. For “God” is a common name and belongs to the Son and the Holy Spirit just as it belongs to the Father. But because he had previously said, “In the beginning he made,” the Father is necessarily [Col. 0975B] understood, because he worked through the beginning—that is, through the Son. [Note: [Col. 0975D] The cited edition reads: “worked.”] Thus the first person is the Father; the second, the Beginning—that is, the Son; and the third, the Spirit of God, who moved over the waters, by whom the Holy Spirit is most clearly indicated.

If Moses had written nothing further, this alone—what is written at the beginning of this book—could suffice for the affirmation of our faith: that we ought to worship one God in three persons. Therefore the Lord fittingly says through the Psalmist: “You did not require burnt offering and sacrifice for sin; then I said: Behold, I come, to do your will” (Ps. XXXIX, 8). And as though someone had asked him who he was, he says: “At the beginning of the book it is written concerning me” (ibid., 9). This is as though he said: I am that Beginning which is written at the beginning [Col. 0975C] of the book, in which the Father created heaven and earth. For this reason I now come to do the Father’s will: because the world could not be saved through sacrifices and burnt offerings.

Moses possessed this faith. Let us see what faith David also possessed: “By the word of the Lord,” he says, “the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. XXXI, 6). There is no difference between them: what one says, both say. Their faith is one; each worships and venerates one God in three persons. For the Lord, the Word of the Lord, and the Spirit of the Lord are three persons and one God, by whom heaven and earth were created.

See how one Spirit speaks in both. See how the Lord’s saying, “At the beginning of the book it is written concerning me,” agrees with both. [Col. 0975D] For “at the beginning of the book it is written concerning me: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Therefore the Son of God is understood in what is written at the beginning of the book, so that we may find Christ at the beginning of our book, and the Jews may find the same one at the beginning of their book and ours. For the one whom David and John called “the Word,” Moses called “the beginning.” Therefore the same thing is signified by “Word” and “beginning.”

But he ought to be called the Word for us, who are teachable and prepared to hear and learn his word and teaching. For them, however, he ought certainly to be called the Beginning, since they did not believe him to be the Beginning [Col. 0976A], but said that he had only recently begun, had not existed before his mother, and was not yet forty years old. Behold, O Jews: your own books, authors, and fathers—whom you will not dare contradict—compel you to worship one God in three persons. But perhaps you still err, knowing neither the Scriptures nor the power of God; and therefore you believe neither Moses nor David, each of whom, as has been shown above, confesses one God and three persons.

“For the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, that of the Holy Spirit another.” Why is this so? Because one is the person who speaks, another the one to whom he speaks, and another the one concerning whom he speaks. The Father speaks concerning the Son where he says: “He shall call upon me: You are my Father” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 27). The Son too speaks concerning the Father where he says: “The Lord [Col. 0976B] said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. II, 7). The Father speaks concerning the Son where he says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matt. XVII, 5). The Son also speaks concerning the Father where he says: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John V, 17). He speaks to the Father himself where he says: “Righteous Father, the world has not known you; but I have known you, and these have known that you sent me” (John XVII, 25). And again: “Father, I will that where I am, there also my minister may be” (ibid., 24). The Son speaks concerning the Holy Spirit where he says: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father—he shall bear witness concerning me” (John XV, 26).

It would take too long [Col. 0976C] to gather every testimony in which the Son speaks in the Gospel concerning the Father, to the Father, and concerning the Holy Spirit. But let these few statements suffice for believing and understanding that the person of the Father is one, the person of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another; since one person speaks, another is addressed, and another is spoken of.

But the Jews do not accept the authority of the Son of God; we, however, possess this single authority above all authorities. Let him therefore tell us what we ought to believe; let us hear it from him; let him teach us our faith. We see what he said when he sent his disciples to preach: “Go,” he says, “teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19). Why in the name [Col. 0976D] of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit? Because we necessarily had to be restored and sanctified by him by whom we were created. He did not say that they should baptize in the name of the Father alone, because the Father did not create us alone; he added the Son, because he too is creator; and he added the Holy Spirit, because he likewise is no less creator. He added nothing further, because all other things are creatures. All things were created by these three persons; and these three persons are not three gods but one God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The Lord would never have placed these three persons in this equality unless they were equal in all things—unless they were alike in Godhead, majesty, [Col. 0977A] omnipotence, and in every other respect. “For such as the Father is, such is the Son, and such is the Holy Spirit. The Father is immeasurable, the Son immeasurable, the Holy Spirit immeasurable. The Father eternal, the Son eternal, the Holy Spirit eternal. Yet not three eternals nor three immeasurables, but one eternal and one immeasurable.”

Foolish and utterly insane are those who attempt to dispute concerning the supreme and omnipotent Trinity by Platonic syllogisms and Aristotelian arguments. For the substance of God is one thing, and the substance of all creatures another. The former alone is eternal; the others are temporal. The former alone is immutable; the others mutable. The former alone admits no contraries; the others are capable of contraries. For Aristotle defined substance thus: “Substance is that which, while one and the same in number, is capable of contraries according to a change in itself.” [Col. 0977B] But God’s substance is not included in this definition, because, though one and the same in number, it admits neither contraries nor change. Since we cannot adequately treat this question in the present discourse, we shall defer it to another treatise.

## CHAPTER II. On the Same Subject

There are certain Sabbaths called “Sabbaths of Sabbaths,” just as certain holy things are called “Holy of Holies,” because they are greater; certain songs are called “Song of Songs,” because they are greater; and the blessed Virgin Mary is called “Virgin of virgins,” because she is greater than all virgins. In the same way, certain feasts may be called “feasts of feasts,” because they are greater than all other feasts. Such are all those feasts which we observe and celebrate for the special praise of almighty God, such as today’s feast, celebrated in honour of the Holy Trinity.

This unity is invisibly divided [Note: [Col. 0977D] Vatican manuscript, and likewise the edition, reads “indivisibly.”], because although the persons are three, God is nevertheless one: not divided into parts, but wholly present in each. Since the one substance of God exists in each of the persons, it seems in a manner to be divided; but because it is wholly in each, it is proved to be undivided. The whole essence of the Godhead is in the Father, wholly in the Holy Spirit, since the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, and these [Col. 0977D] three are one God. Since there is no God except one, another God cannot be predicated of the Father, another of the Son, and another of the Holy Spirit; rather, the same God, one in number, is predicated of all and of each.

We must indeed wholly believe that this is so; but we ought by no means to ask how it is, or how it can be, since we cannot at all understand the profundity of this mystery except by divine inspiration. Perhaps this is so because nothing of the kind can be found in any other substance. For what is not confirmed by any likeness or example is believed with difficulty. There is no other substance [Col. 0978A], whatever it may be, which can be one and the same in number in several things: for example, this man, this eye, this foot, this hand, this head. Since each of these is one in number, none of them can be in several things.

But if the article—which signifies a determinate number—is removed, so that we do not say “this man,” “this eye,” “this foot,” “this hand,” or “this head,” but simply say, without articles, “man,” “eye,” “foot,” “hand,” “head,” nothing prevents any one of these from being predicated of several things. Thus expressed, they are no longer one in number but one in essence. Hence the philosopher says: “By participation in the species, several men are one man.” For Peter, James, and John, although several in number, are one in the species “man,” since Peter is a man, James is a man, and John [Col. 0978B] is a man. But if an article or a proper name is added, and one says, “Peter, James, and John are this man,” it will not be true. Likewise, it is not true to say: “These three men are Peter,” or “These three are James,” or “These three are John.”

It is therefore manifest that no substance is indicated as one and the same in number either by an article or by a proper name. What I said universally—“no substance”—should be understood as though I had said: no temporal substance, no mutable substance capable of contraries. For philosophers speak only of this kind of substance, and Aristotle defined only this kind. No such substance, while one and the same in number, is predicated of several things.

The divine substance, however—eternal, immutable [Col. 0978C], incapable of any contrariety, always simple and one, and the same in number—is nevertheless always in several persons. For God is always one, and he who can never be without number is one: namely, this God of ours, to use the article, who made heaven and earth. He is always Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; wholly Father, wholly Son, wholly Holy Spirit. Yet the Father is never the Son; the Son is never the Father; and the Holy Spirit is never either Father or Son.

This is far beyond human understanding, because nothing of the kind can be found in temporal and mutable substance. For if this man, whom I point out to you with my finger, is Simon and Peter, and is always Simon and Peter, and wholly [Col. 0978D] Simon and Peter, it necessarily follows that Peter is Simon and Simon Peter. For such a syllogism can be made by this inference: If Simon-Peter is this man, and this man is Peter, then Simon is Peter.

But in divine and eternal substance it is otherwise. It is always true to say: This God of ours, whom I point out to you not with my finger but by faith, is both Father and Son; and he is always Father and always Son, wholly Father and wholly Son. Yet it is not true to say: therefore the Father is the Son and the Son the Father. Such a syllogism can indeed be made from these premises, but it does not prove its conclusion: If the Son of God is this God, and God is Father [Col. 0979A], then the Son is Father and the Father is Son. To say and believe this is impious and false.

If Arius had understood this, and had distinguished these two substances, eternal and mutable, so different from one another, neither would he have erred himself nor caused so many others to err. For, wishing to confine eternal and immutable substance within the limits of temporal and mutable substance, he imagined that everything occurs in the former which he knew to occur in the latter. Thus he said that the Son was less than the Father and that the Father was older than the Son, because among human beings this is unquestionably so. No son is born who is not less than his father in age and person. Foolish man: he did not consider that simple and eternal substance can admit neither greater nor lesser.

For God is always one, eternal, immutable; and what is proper to him always is what it is. Hence, when Moses asked and wished to know who he was, he said: “I am who I am. Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: He Who Is has sent me to you” (Exod. III, 14). For he alone is said to be in the true definition who always is, who is immutable, who never began to be and never ceases to be, whose whole essence is always one and the same. For God is always and wholly wisdom, always and wholly power, truth, light, beginning, and the like. His being and his being omnipotent are not different things; all these are one in him. The Father is all these things, the Son all these things, and the Holy Spirit all these things.

How then can the Father be greater or older than the Son, when the Son [Col. 0979C] is eternal? Could anything exist before the eternal? Could the Father have existed before the Son? But nothing can exist before the eternal; therefore the Father is not before the Son—especially since the Son of God is the Word of God, the Power of God, and the Wisdom of God. For the Father could not have existed before the Word, before Power, or before Wisdom. What would he have been if he were not strong and wise? One cannot be strong without power, nor wise without wisdom.

Wisdom in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, and apart from it there is none. It is that Wisdom of which it is said: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CIII, 24). It is also the Word of God, through whom, as it is written, “All things were made, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 3). Therefore, if this is the only wisdom in God and no other, either the Father was at some time without wisdom—which is wicked even to say or think—or he was never before this Wisdom. It is therefore impossible that the Father existed before the Son.

But Arius says: The one who begets is prior to the one begotten, because the begetter must exist; for one who does not exist cannot beget. But the one begotten does not yet exist, because, according to the philosophers’ opinion, what is coming to be is not. Wretched and unhappy man, who supposes the generation of the Word of God to occur as do all other generations! The prophet marvels at the generation of the Son [Col. 0980A] of God and says: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. LIII, 8). Yet unhappy Arius does not think that this one singular and wonderful generation differs from other generations.

But even among creatures we can find cases in which the begetter is not prior to that which is begotten. From fire come heat and brightness simultaneously with the fire. Hence [Note: [Col. 0979] The Vatican manuscript reads: “From fire both heat and brightness are begotten. Hence,” etc.] the Son of God is not without reason called the brightness of the Father, as the Apostle says: “Who, being the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance” (Heb. I, 3).

But it is better to seek the image of the Trinity in ourselves, who have been made in the image and likeness of God. For nowhere should God’s likeness be found more readily than in the creature made in God’s image and likeness. Only angels and human beings are said to possess God’s likeness. There can be no doubt concerning the good angels, since even of the evil ones it is written: “You are the seal of likeness, full of wisdom, perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God” (Ezek. XXVIII, 12). But what of humankind? “Let us make,” God says, “man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26).

Angels and human beings therefore possess this likeness to God because they are naturally full of wisdom, and because no other creature can attain this wisdom. This wisdom is the understanding of divine and human things. No creature besides angel and human being can possess this understanding. To pass over angels: what other creature [Col. 0980C] can possess knowledge of letters [Note: [Col. 0979] The Ascensian edition reads: “To pass over other things, what other creature, or who except a human being, can possess knowledge of letters?”] or knowledge of numbers?

Accordingly, we have been made in the image and likeness of God in this respect, in which we also possess a certain likeness of the Trinity itself. Our trinity is this: “understanding, memory, and use.” These three are in a sense one and cannot exist without one another; nor is one of them prior or subsequent to the others. Understanding, as has already been said, is knowledge of divine and human things. Memory is that by which we retain what we have understood. By “use” I mean a certain natural capacity by which we can teach others what we have understood and committed to memory.

Thus, as the Son is, as it were, begotten from the Father, so memory is begotten from [Col. 0980D] understanding. For it is impossible to possess memory except of something understood. “Use,” however, appears to bear the likeness of the Holy Spirit, because it proceeds from understanding and memory. For no one can teach what he has not understood or committed to memory.

Yet understanding is not prior to memory, although memory comes from understanding, because no understanding of anything, however small, can be possessed without memory. For example, a name of two syllables is indeed very small, yet it cannot be known or understood without memory. For unless memory is present, how will the second [Col. 0981A] syllable be joined to the first, or how will the first itself be known without memory? As soon as it is spoken, it will be forgotten—or rather, it will not be forgotten, because it will never be understood without memory. Therefore understanding is not prior to memory.

Nor is use—that is, the capacity for teaching—subsequent to these two, because we do not first understand something or commit it to memory before we also possess the capacity to teach it. Therefore, since no other creature can possess this trinity and unity, angels and human beings are rightly seen to have the likeness of God according to this unity and trinity. Thus, even among creatures, there is something which, although begotten from something else, is nevertheless not subsequent to that from which it is begotten.

## CHAPTER III. On the Same Subject

[Col. 0981B]

When we speak of the unity and trinity which is God, we desire, with dimmed eyes and feeble lights, to see the invisible and eternal substance of our God. We must greatly fear lest perhaps those words from the Song of Songs be addressed to us: “Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me fly away” (Cant. VIII, 22). Hence the Apostle says: “Do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think soberly” (Rom. XII, 3). And in the Psalms: “Man shall approach unto a deep heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. LXIII, 7). And Solomon says: “I said: I shall become wise; and wisdom itself fled far from me” (Eccl. VII, 24). Elsewhere he says: “As one who eats much honey, it is not good for him; so he who searches out majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. XXV, 27).

Moses spoke with the Lord face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend. Yet he said: “If I have found favour in your eyes, show me your face, that I may know you” (Exod. XXXIII, 13). But the Lord says: “No man shall see me and live” (ibid., 20).—“No one has ever seen God” (John I, 18). Moses could hear the voice, but he could not see any form or image. The apostles too heard his voice when he spoke from the cloud, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. II, 18). They heard him indeed, but did not see his form. We too often hear him speaking in the holy volumes [Col. 0981D], but do not see his form. For no human being shall see him and live. He will not be seen in this life, because he cannot be seen with these eyes. But after this life he shall be seen, as John the Apostle says: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III, 2). And the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face. Now I know in part; but then I shall know even as I am known” (I Cor. XV, 12).

If Moses and the apostles, who were filled with the Spirit of God, and in whom and through whom the Lord spoke, were unable to see, hear, and understand him as he is, it seems exceedingly rash for us to judge concerning his essence [Col. 0982A]. [Note: [Col. 0981D] The Vatican manuscript reads: “to investigate his essence.”] This is especially so when he himself says: “No human being shall see me and live.”

God is invisible; for he is seen not with bodily but with mental eyes—mental eyes renewed, illumined by the glory of the resurrection, and freed from every bodily corruption. Such then will be human nature: able to contemplate Christ’s humanity with bodily eyes and his divinity with the eyes of the mind. Consider how great the joy of those seeing God may then be: with bodily eyes they see Christ’s humanity abiding in one place, and with the eyes of the mind contemplate his divinity containing all things. Neither sight will be idle; each will behold that good in which it can greatly delight and which it cannot exhaust by beholding.

But meanwhile [Col. 0982B], let him who is of the earth speak of the earth; let no one wish to stretch himself above himself. Let us say with the Psalmist: “Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up. Nor have I walked in great matters or in wonders above me” (Ps. CXXX, 1). Wretched Arius did not understand these words. He exalted his heart excessively and lifted up his eyes excessively; and, because with an unclean heart and impure eyes he could neither see nor understand God’s majesty, he began to blaspheme and tried to divide the Son from the Father. The unhappy man did not fear to walk in great matters and wonders above him, matters exceeding his understanding and surpassing his ability.

For what can be said or thought concerning God that is not great and wonderful? It is exceedingly great and wonderful that he is Father and is not prior [Col. 0982C] to the Son. Because Arius could not understand this, he would not believe the authorities of the saints or consent to humility, but exalted his soul. He despised the counsels of bishops and, raised in pride, condemned the judgment of Catholics. Therefore, just as a weaned child is upon his mother, so recompense was made in his soul. And as a weaned child, torn from milk, is accustomed importunately to throw himself upon his mother in order utterly to drain breasts now dried up, so evil spirits, with the whole host of vices, never cease without end to tear, torment, and destroy that unhappy soul.

Let the faith of the saints therefore suffice us. We are not better than our fathers; nor should we seek beyond what has been divinely revealed to them. Since we cannot understand ourselves and the things in us, let us not labour to stretch ourselves toward things above us. Let us hear the Prophet saying: “Your knowledge has become wonderful from me; it has been strengthened, and I shall not be able to attain it” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 6). The Prophet says: I began to consider myself and wished to investigate what human nature was and of what kind; and I found in myself a knowledge so miserable that I cannot at all stretch myself toward it. For it has been strengthened; it has become stronger and higher than every human capacity, and I shall not be able to attain it. Behold, the Prophet does not know himself, and do you wish in this life to see and understand the nature of divinity itself [Col. 0983A]?

Tell me, if you know: whence comes sight to the eyes and hearing to the ears? How do the nostrils perceive odour, and the throat and palate taste? If you understand these things, climb higher. Ask where so vast a structure is fixed, what place surrounds it, and of what sort and size it is. It could not be turned except by being fixed in some place empty and free from obstruction. I myself seem to see such vastness of place and space around this heaven that this whole world appears to me a small thing. Hence this very sight of mine seems a great marvel to me: how it can ascend so far in a single instant and comprehend such immense spaces about it. I perceive nothing else in myself which more compels me to say, with the Psalmist, to God the creator of all: “Your knowledge has become wonderful from me.”

Consider also the earth, balanced by its own weights and established in the middle of heaven in such a way that, although it has no foundation, it cannot incline in any direction. Hence the Prophet rightly says: “Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and weighed the heavens with his palm? Who has suspended the mass of the earth upon three fingers, and weighed the mountains in scales and the hills in a balance?” (Isa. XL, 12). Consider, if you can, how great is that hand which cannot be filled by such waters; how great is the strength of him who weighed the heavens with his palm; and what those three fingers are by which so vast a mass of the whole earth is suspended. Those three fingers are the three persons of the omnipotent Trinity, through whose operation one strong and mighty God made all things.

Of these three fingers it is written: “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. XXXI, 61). Indeed, Christ’s three fingers are invited to make humankind, where the one supreme God says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26). For God, the Word of God, and the Spirit of God are three persons and one God. This is he who suspended the mass of the earth upon three fingers; this is he who weighed the mountains and the hills in the balance.

And although, on one side of the world, so vast a mass and weight of mountains rises up, while on the other only a plain remains, the whole is nevertheless so balanced that the weights on one side cannot move the other [Col. 0983D]. The nature of the heavens, however, is thought to be such that it repels all heavy things from itself. Hence we suppose that the sun, moon, and globes of the stars are without weight. For just as it repels all heavy things, so it draws all light things to itself. This is why fire, clouds, and mist always rise upward.

It is reported that a gilded iron image of wondrous size was placed in the air in a certain temple. Since it was held by no chains or instrument, it produced a marvel for all who saw it and did not know how it stood thus. But there were there two stones of a balanced quality, called magnets: one was fixed in the pavement and the other high in the vault. The property of this stone [Col. 0984A] is naturally to draw iron to itself. Therefore, while the statue stood in the middle and was drawn by both stones with equal force and carefully adjusted weight, it could neither rise upward, because the lower stone held it, nor fall downward, because the upper stone drew it. It stood fixed in the middle and was held by the force of the stones so that it could incline in neither direction.

Thus perhaps we may also suppose something similar concerning the earth: because it is situated in the middle, it cannot incline in any direction through a natural heavenly force; or, because both sides seek the centre by reason of their weight, one supports the other. Yet I think rather that it stands firm and immovable by the power of God than by the power of heaven; and if heaven has any power, it is not heaven’s power but God’s.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Nativity of the Lord

[Col. 0984B]

The greatest of the prophets, Isaiah, speaks of the incarnation of the Son of God, saying: “And the Lord said to me: Take for yourself a large book, and write in it with a human pen: Swiftly take away the spoils; quickly plunder. And I took to myself faithful witnesses, Uriah the priest, and Zechariah son of Berechiah; and I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son. And he said to me: Call his name, Hasten to take away the spoils, hurry to plunder. For before the child knows how to call father and mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of the Assyrians” (Isa. 8:1–4).

Now let us see what these things signify. “Take,” he says, “for yourself a large book, and write in it with a human pen.” This great book is understood to be this whole world; as many are the people, so many are the sheets of this book. [Col. 0984C] These words were to be written not on tablets of stone but on the tablets of our hearts. “Take,” he says, “for yourself a large book, and write in it with a human pen.”

[Note: [Col. 0983D] Vatican manuscript and the Ascensian edition.]

What is “with a human pen”? Certainly, with plain and easy speech—the sort in which people are accustomed to speak with one another, and which all who hear it can understand. Perhaps for this reason this prophet is easier than all the rest. The other prophets do not write with a human pen, because their Scripture is far removed from the manner of speech of other human beings. “Write,” he says, “with a human pen”: and this is what I want you to write: “Swiftly take away the spoils; quickly plunder.”

How great is the book, and how few the words! Yet these suffice, if there is someone able to understand and keep them. Let us prepare our hearts to receive this Scripture. Would that our heart were ready to receive these words into itself, and that they might be written there with such ink that they could never be erased from it. Behold, we have heard and received the command that we should be despoilers and plunderers. For this is signified by the words: “Hasten to take away the spoils; hurry to plunder.” Until now thieves and robbers have held this office; this, I say, is what people have been accustomed to do. Yet no laws forbid force to be repelled by force; nor is it sinful to pursue robbers. Would that those who have been unjustly despoiled and plundered might at some time be able to avenge themselves!

Remember that Gospel in which the man descending from Jerusalem [Col. 0985A] to Jericho fell among robbers, who also stripped him (Luke 10:30). In this one man all human beings were stripped and plundered. Let us therefore pursue these robbers and seize our spoils, in which they glory. Let us say with the Psalmist: “I shall pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I shall not turn back until they fail; I shall crush them, and they shall not be able to stand; they shall fall beneath my feet” (Ps. 17:38). If we cannot take any other plunder or spoils from them, let us at least reclaim what is our own; let us free ourselves from their impious servitude. Let us believe the Apostle when he says: “As you presented your members to serve impurity and iniquity unto iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification” (Rom. 6:19).

[Col. 0985B] We have made good plunder and have given up great spoils if we have freed our members from their servitude. We have had no closer friends for whom we ought to fight. Abraham pursued his enemies and freed his nephew Lot from their hands (Gen. 14). Behold, thanks be to God, we have fought and stripped our enemies. Therefore let us rejoice, “as victors rejoice when they have captured prey, when they divide the spoils” (Isa. 9:3). Henceforth let our members serve not vices but God, by whose help we have been freed.

“And I took,” he says, “faithful witnesses.” For the Jews could not have believed without witnesses; and people already defeated could not have hoped for so sudden a victory over their enemies—that they should now, with matters reversed, overcome and despoil those whom they had been unable to resist. Isaiah therefore acted well [Col. 0985C] in taking faithful witnesses for himself, who would affirm that they had heard these words from the Lord together with him. And this is what we too must now do when we promise forgiveness to converted sinners and victory over enemies through repentance: if they refuse to believe our words, let us bring forward faithful witnesses whose testimony they cannot doubt.

But what witnesses? “Uriah the priest, and Zechariah son of Berechiah.” These two witnesses are the two Testaments, by whose authority we ought to confirm whatever we say. If a sinner does not believe me when I promise forgiveness, and despairs of being able to be saved after so many crimes, I shall bring forward the Gospel as a faithful witness: “He who believes,” it says, “and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16:16). I shall also bring forward another witness: “At whatever [Col. 0985D] hour the sinner is converted and groans in repentance, he shall live and shall not die” (Ezek. 33:12).

Thus Uriah is well interpreted as “fire,” by whom we understand the Law, concerning which it is written: “At his right hand was a fiery law” (Deut. 33:2). Zechariah, however, is called “help,” by whom the Gospel is signified; by its great and ineffable help we have indeed been freed. His father is called Berechiah, which is interpreted “the blessed Lord.” The Father of the Gospel is Christ, who is God and Lord, blessed above all.

“And I approached the prophetess, who conceived and bore a son.” After the prophet had received this promise of such great remembrance and blessedness, he aptly says that he approached the prophetess, so that he might at last [Col. 0986A] see him born of the Virgin Mother, in whom and through whom so great a promise would be fulfilled. This prophetess is the blessed Virgin Mary, who, full of the Holy Spirit, uttered for us that most beautiful prophecy: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior,” etc. (Luke 1:47). The prophet approached the prophetess when, led by the Holy Spirit, he was granted to see in the Spirit the mystery of Christ’s birth. For so the prophets approached everything they saw.

“And he said to me: Call his name, Hasten to take away the spoils, hurry to plunder; for before the child knows how to call his father or his mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of the Assyrians.” Behold our child, whose birth we celebrate today: before he took flesh and was born of the Virgin, and before, according to the flesh, he completed infancy and reached manhood, he took away the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria, and conquered the king of the Assyrians. For they fought against Jerusalem and most violently afflicted the children of Israel in the days in which Isaiah prophesied.

[Col. 0986B] Wretched Jews, who did not receive him when he came—the one and no other whom they had always had as helper and defender! But by what name ought our mighty and powerful king to be called, if not despoiler and plunderer? For he is the one of whom it is written: “You have gone up for the prey, my son” (Gen. 49:9). He is the one who first despoiled Egypt and afterward hell. For that first despoiling signified this second one to come.

[Col. 0986C] He is the one who, through his angel, killed one hundred and eighty-five thousand from the camp of the Assyrians and made the children of Israel rich with their spoils. Isaiah, who wrote these things, saw them with his own eyes and related that this victory had been accomplished by this child of ours. This child is old, the Ancient of Days; and before Abraham came to be, he is. He now appears a little child, having now been born according to the flesh; but his birth according to divinity has no measure of time. For he is the one of whom it is written:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing that was made was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of human beings. And the light shines in darkness, [Col. 0986D] and the darkness did not comprehend him. There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. He came as a witness, to bear witness concerning the light, that all might believe through him” (John 1:1–7).

Read the whole Gospel; stretch yourself out, and together with blessed John, whose words these are, take the wings of the eagle and ascend above the Cherubim, so that you may be able to fly above the wings of the winds. Approaching even to the throne of glory, there see this child who is born today, who has now come to plunder and despoil, reigning and glorified in the bosom and heart of the eternal and supreme Father, so that you may hear him saying: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. 44:1)—“With you is dominion in the day of your power, amid the splendors of the saints; [Col. 0987A] from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109:3).

## CHAPTER V. On the Circumcision of the Lord

“After eight days were completed for the child to be circumcised, his name was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb” (Luke 2:21).

Abraham was the first of all human beings to be circumcised at the Lord’s command. Of him the Apostle says: “And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith” (Rom. 4:11). Circumcision, then, is a sign by which the Jewish people, who were to be scattered among all nations and led into captivity, might be distinguished from other nations. It is also a seal—that is, a certain signification—of the righteousness of faith, because the righteousness of Christians, [Col. 0987B] which is possessed not through circumcision but through faith, was signified in that circumcision.

[Note: [Col. 0987D] The same manuscript of St. Mark, Florence: “Because Christian righteousness, which was signified through circumcision, is accomplished not in one member alone but in all.”]

For no one can truly be called righteous unless he has circumcised not merely one member, as the Jews did, but all his members. Of this circumcision it is written: “Cut your hearts, and not your garments.”

[Note: [Col. 0987D] Vatican manuscript: “Circumcise your hearts, and not your bodies.”]

(Joel 2:13). Hence Moses says that he is uncircumcised in lips (Exod. 6); he thereby indicated that circumcision of the tongue also is necessary. Thus blessed Stephen, reproving the Jews as though they had not been properly circumcised, says: “Uncircumcised in ears and heart, you always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so do you” (Acts 7:51).

Thus all the members ought to be circumcised, and all that is superfluous and harmful ought to be cut away and cleansed from all the members. The superfluous and harmful things are sins and vices alone. Let these be removed from every member, and the whole person is rightly circumcised. If the eyes do not look upon vanity, if the ears do not hear detractions, if the tongue does not speak idle words and falsehood, it is circumcised. This is true circumcision: that all the members should be circumcised. The circumcision of our father Abraham signified this circumcision, and for the sake of this circumcision that former circumcision was given, as likewise were all the other things which happened to them figuratively.

[Col. 0987C] This sign and seal are no longer necessary, because the two peoples are one, the wall of enmity has been removed from the midst, and from two flocks there has come to be one fold and one shepherd. Everything formerly performed in signification is now understood by all and observed in truth.

The reason why our Savior received this circumcision in his flesh is entirely fitting: he did not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it. “For Christ,” says the Apostle, “is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4). In him the Law was fulfilled; those who are circumcised after him gain nothing. Hence the Apostle says: [Col. 0988A] “I, Paul, tell you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2). “For if a law had been given which could make alive, righteousness would truly be from the Law; but Scripture,” he says, “has shut up all things under sin, that the promise from faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe” (Gal. 3:21). “The Law brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7:19). It is evident, moreover, that no flesh shall be justified before the Lord from works of the Law (Rom. 3).

Circumcision therefore had this effect: whoever in that people was not circumcised perished from the people of God, nor was he freed and redeemed together with the others by Christ’s blood. But all the rest, down to Christ’s Passion, were freed by Christ’s blood not only from original sin but also from all other sins, provided that they received that circumcision [Col. 0988B] and kept the Law. For if original sin could have been removed through circumcision, Christ’s Passion would not have been necessary. But it was impossible for original sin to be dissolved without the shedding of that blood.

[Note: [Col. 0987D] These statements must be understood according to the mind of St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, III, question 1, article 2, response to objection 2, as explained by Cardinal Gotti, vol. XII, question 3, *On the Fittingness and Necessity of the Incarnation*, doubt III, §1. There he teaches that, if God required strict satisfaction in justice for original sin and other sins committed by humankind, it could not have been rendered except through the shedding of Christ’s blood.]

Thus the apostle John says: “Who is it that conquers the world, except the one who believes that Christ is the Son of God? This is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ: not in water only, but in water and blood” (1 John 5:5). Do you not hear that our Savior came to save and redeem the world not through circumcision but through water and blood? And not in water only, because it was impossible for a human being to be freed by baptism alone without the shedding of Christ’s blood, but in water and blood, so that the blood might avail as the price and the water for washing.

[Col. 0988C] “For there are three that bear witness on earth: the Spirit, the water, and the blood; and these three are one. And there are three that bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one” (ibid., 7–8). Both heaven and earth testify to us that the Son of Man came into this world to redeem and save us. Hence the Apostle says: “The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first” (1 Tim. 1:15).

“There are three,” he says, “on earth who bear testimony to us and make us certain of our salvation: namely, the Spirit and water, from which we have been regenerated in baptism, and the blood of the Son of God, by which we have been redeemed.” And concerning baptism it is written: [Col. 0988D] “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16:16). Concerning the blood: “He who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1:5). And again: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6:52). “And these three are one.” These three, namely Spirit, water, and blood, are one, because the Spirit washes, the water washes, and the blood washes. For all three are one in that in which they do not differ from one another in turn. Therefore these three are one because they accomplish one thing.

And there are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and [Col. 0989A] the Holy Spirit; and these three are not only one, but substantially one. Read all the Scriptures of both Testaments, composed under the inspiration of these three—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—and then you will understand what and how great are the testimonies we possess in heaven concerning our salvation. But if there is no leisure to read more, let this one saying suffice us for the present: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved.” For what the Son says, the Father says also, and the Holy Spirit.

But the clause inserted there, which says, “And it is the Spirit that bears witness, because Christ is truth” (1 John [Col. 0989B] 5:6), looks back to what he said above: “Because Jesus is the Son of God” (1 John 4:15). As though someone were to say: “How do you prove that this Jesus of yours, whom you preach, is the Son of God?” he added: The Spirit who is in him, through whom he accomplishes such great things and others besides, most clearly shows that he is the Son of God, that he is truth, that there is no falsehood in him, and that whatever he says concerning himself or others is wholly true.

[Note: [Col. 0989D] The Ascensian edition reads *unity* (*unitas*), but the Vatican manuscript has *truth* (*veritas*); so too the manuscript of St. Mark in the same place.]

[Note: [Col. 0989D] These words are lacking in the Ascensian edition; but the Florentine manuscript of St. Mark contains them, and with them concludes the sermon, as in the edition of Marchesius and in the Vatican manuscript.]

## CHAPTER VI. On the Epiphany of the Lord

We have just heard, as the Gospel was being read, that three Magi came from the East.

[Note: [Col. 0989D] Some Fathers held that these Magi were three in number, as St. Maximus of Turin, Homily X, *On the Epiphany*, Roman edition, 1785, p. 78, where he says: “And fittingly, dearest beloved, the three Magi came together by one journey to adore him, because in the one Christ, who is the way of all believers, the Trinity to be adored was inseparable from them.” In the Gospel, however, the number of the Magi is not stated.]

A new star led them to Jesus, and immediately, “having opened [Col. 0989C] their treasures, they offered him gifts—gold, frankincense, and myrrh; and having received an answer in a dream not to return to Herod, they returned by another way into their own country” (Matt. 2:12). We must therefore say what these three Magi signify, what the star, what the three gifts, and what the change of route signify. For it is not devoid of mystery that our Savior wished to reveal the glory of his birth to only three men of an alien nation.

There were three sons of Noah, saved in the ark at the time of the Flood, from whom the whole human race was scattered everywhere. The whole world was divided into three parts: Asia, Africa, and Europe. Three women came to anoint Jesus: Mary Magdalene, Mary of James, and Salome (Mark 16). The woman in the Gospel likewise hid leaven [Col. 0989D] in three measures of flour, until the whole was leavened (Matt. 13). There are many other things which have the same signification.

These three men, then, coming to Jesus, signified the holy Church to be gathered into one faith from all parts of the world. For all were descended from three men, and [Col. 0990A] all must worship one Lord in three persons; and all dwelt in the three parts of the world, because all were created by one.

[Note: [Col. 0990D] Vatican manuscript: “And all dwell in the three parts of the world, and all must worship one God in three persons, because all were created by one.”]

By the heavens which gave this new star we understand the apostles, concerning whom it is said: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:1). The new star is their faith and doctrine. The heavens preach to us, the heavens call us, the heavens invite us to the Lord. There are many heavens but one star, because there are many apostles and teachers but one faith and doctrine. For all say one thing. All preach one faith. One Lord, one faith, one baptism are preached by all. Let us follow this star; let us hold this faith and doctrine. It will lead us to Jesus; by this light we shall come to our own [Col. 0990B] Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0990D] Vatican manuscript: “we shall come to Jesus.”]

Nor will it permit us to go astray on the journey, provided only that we do not abandon it, always look to it, and travel the royal road. Let us not turn aside to Herod, let us not listen to his counsel, nor seek the answers of the scribes and Pharisees. For if the Magi had done this—if they had not come to Herod, if they had continued by the straight road and had not sought Christ in the impious house—they would never have lost the star. This may be proved from the fact that, after the Magi had withdrawn from Herod and left his company, immediately, as the Evangelist says: “The star which they had seen in the East went before them, until it came and stood over where the child was. And when they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy” (Matt. 2:9).

[Col. 0990C] Therefore let their error be our correction; and let us, enlightened by the new star and the true light, by catholic faith and apostolic doctrine, flee the house of Herod—the teaching of heretics and Jews, which is the synagogue of Satan. They are stationed on the road and prepare snares for those hastening to Christ. But see how great is Herod’s wickedness, how great the devil’s cunning. He pretends to wish to worship him whom he plans to kill. He sends the Magi to Jesus and asks them to return from him to himself. “For he is confident,” as it is written, “that the Jordan may flow into his mouth” (Job 40:18). For his food is choice; nor does he greatly care to devour others, [Col. 0990D] except those who have already come to Jesus through faith and baptism and have been enrolled in Christ’s service, having merited to receive his seal.

“And entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother, and falling down they worshiped him” (Matt. 2:11). The Valentinians did not find the child with his mother Mary, because they did not believe that Christ had a mother.

[Note: [Col. 0990D] This passage is corrupt in the Ascensian edition. It was not the Nestorians who denied that Christ had a mother, but the Valentinians, who blasphemously asserted that Christ’s body had been formed in heaven and descended into the womb of the Virgin Mary. The Nestorians, however, denied that Mary should be called Mother of God, since they said that she had conceived a mere human being, Christ. Therefore the text must be restored as it is read here.]

The Nestorians, however, denying the divine maternity, said that Mary was the mother of Christ as [Col. 0991A] man, not as God; consequently, in detestation of this error, the blessed Virgin Mary was called *Theotokos* (θεοτόκος).

[Note: [Col. 0992D] The same manuscript of St. Mark, Florence: “That is, mother of God and of man.” So also the Vatican manuscript.]

That is, mother of God, who is also man. “And having opened their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh” (ibid.). These men were Gentiles; they did not know the Law and the prophets, yet they fulfilled the sayings of the Law and prophets. For it is written: “You shall not appear empty before the presence of your God” (Deut. 16:16). These are they of whom it is written: “All shall come from Sheba, bringing gold and frankincense and proclaiming the praise of the Lord” (Isa. 60:6). And in the Psalms: “The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of the Arabs and of Sheba shall bring offerings. And all kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Ps. 71:10).

[Col. 0991B] These men, who were the firstfruits of the Gentiles and through whom the whole human race was signified, teach us how we ought to seek Christ and come to Jesus.

[Note: [Col. 0992D] The same manuscript of St. Mark, Florence: “O happy peoples of the Gentiles, with whom and among whom the whole human race was signified!”]

We must not come without gifts; we must not approach him without spices. Thus the queen of Sheba—who also signified the Church of the Gentiles—came to Solomon, offering him much gold and many spices, such as had never before been brought to Jerusalem (3 Kings 10). So too the women, of whom we have already spoken above, bought spices so that they might come and anoint Jesus. Read the Song of Songs, and you will see that the whole book is fragrant with the finest ointments and spices. There the bride, anointed with sweet ointments and delighted by the fragrances of the bridegroom, says: “Draw me after you; we shall run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:4).

[Col. 0991C] And the bridegroom, no less delighted by fragrances, says: “Your lips, bride, drip honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense” (Song 4:11). Concerning Wisdom it is also said that “in the streets, like cinnamon and aromatic balsam, I gave forth fragrance; and like choice myrrh I gave sweetness of scent” (Ecclus. 24:20).

From these and similar passages it is evident how much God delights in good fragrance and holy spices. Good fragrance and holy spices are virtues, without which one may not approach Christ’s cradle and the mother of all virginity. Faith, hope, charity, humility and patience, mercy and obedience are spices, whose fragrance is most sweet and in which both Christ and Christ’s mother greatly delight.

[Col. 0991D] These men were very wise in offering such gifts to the Lord. Let us then imitate them and offer gold and spices to the Lord. Of all metals, gold is the most precious; it is diminished neither by fire nor corrupted by age. All the vessels of the tabernacle were golden: the table, altar, lampstand, censer, tablets, bowls, cups; and the Cherubim themselves were made of purest gold. Nothing but gold [Col. 0992A] was to be seen in the whole temple.

These things concern us, brothers: we are the vessels of the tabernacle, God’s riches, God’s mysteries, God’s wisdom. If these are stored in your heart, you are the ark of God; if you feed others with spiritual food, you are a table; if from your holy way of life you spread good fragrance in every direction, you are a censer; if you prepare in your heart a dwelling for the Holy Spirit, you are God’s temple. For the Apostle says: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16).

Therefore we must be golden, since we are vessels of the tabernacle. But let each person see what sort of gold he offers to the Lord. For he cannot be deceived: he is a craftsman and the son of a craftsman—not Joseph, as the Jews said, but of him who made heaven and earth, as we say. He is the one of whom it is written: [Col. 0992B] “He shall sit, refining and cleansing silver; and he shall purify the sons of Levi and strain them like gold and silver” (Mal. 3:3). “If anyone’s work remains, he shall receive a reward; if anyone’s work is burned up, he shall suffer loss, though he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. 3:14–15). These are the Apostle’s words.

What shall we wretches do, who have not gold but lead? Yet the Lord is able to turn our lead into gold, he who was able to turn solid earth into so many and such diverse animals. Behold, we have heard what we ought to offer the Lord. Let us also hear by what way we may return to our homeland. Let the Evangelist speak: “And the Magi,” he says, “having been warned in a dream not to return to Herod, returned by another way into their own country” (Matt. 2:12).

[Col. 0992C] One road is forbidden; the others are good. To return to Herod is evil; let us flee this road. This road does not lead to our homeland. This Herod is the devil; this Herod is sin. Every road which leads to him is evil. Let us therefore take other roads, which will bring us without error into our homeland. “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10). These two suffice for us; yet the two are one. The Lord says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6).
