All ways meet in this one; none brings us to the Father and to our homeland except through this one.

Let us therefore keep this way, so that at last we may be able joyfully and safely to return to our ancient homeland, [Col. 0992D] with the help of him who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Octave of the Epiphany
“After Herod’s death, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying: ‘Rise, take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel; for those who sought the child’s life are dead’” [Col. 0993A] (Matt. 2:13). As John the Evangelist says, our Lord and Savior “came unto his own,” and his children “received him not” (John 1:11). Therefore, leaving the Synagogue, he passed over to the nations and went into Egypt, where the patriarchs and prophets had lived as sojourners, so that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and will enter Egypt, and all its idols will fall together” (Isa. 19:1). Hence the Lord himself says: “Behold, your house shall be left desolate to you” (Luke 15:38 [OCR error for Matt. 23:38]). And in the Psalms: “Behold, I fled far away and remained in solitude” (Ps. 34:8 [citation as printed]). In the Temple also, as Josephus relates, voices of angels were heard saying: “Let us leave these seats.” Hence the Apostle says: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be preached to you; but since you have rejected it and made yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations” [Col. 0993B] (Acts 13:46).

This, then, was signified by the Lord’s flight. He came into Egypt so that the people who sat in darkness might see the light. Concerning this people he had previously foretold through the Prophet: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me. Foreign sons lied to me; foreign sons grew old and limped from their paths” (Ps. 12:46 [citation as printed]). And elsewhere: “I will call ‘my people’ that which was not my people, and ‘having obtained mercy’ that which had not obtained mercy” (Rom. 9:25). And those to whom it had formerly been said, “You are not my people,” are themselves called children of the living God. “Praise the Lord, therefore, all nations; praise him, all peoples, [Col. 0993C] for his mercy has been made strong over us, and the truth of the Lord remains forever” (Ps. 116:1).

O happy peoples of the nations [Note: Codex Vaticanus: “O happy peoples of the nations.”], among whom and in whom the Lord dwells! Wretched Jews, who refused to receive him and cried: “We have no king but Caesar!” (John 19:16.) Moreover, they sent an embassy after him, saying: “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke 19:14). Herod has not yet died for them; the devil still reigns over the Synagogue. Nor have all those who seek Christ’s life yet died—those who try to kill his name and faith in the hearts of believers. But let the Jews know that, unless all these first die and the devil ceases to reign in their hearts, Jesus will not come to the land of Israel [Note: Codex Vaticanus adds: “and to the Synagogue.”]. [Col. 0993D] For the Lord disdains to dwell with such people, and flees all over whom Herod and the devil reign. When these have died, he will return to them; Jeremiah the prophet testifies that this will occur at the end of the age [Note: Codex Vaticanus corrects the editions of Marchesini and Ascensius, in which “the second” is read.] For he says: “In those days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell securely, [Col. 0994A] and this is the name by which they shall call him: The Lord our righteousness” (Jer. 33:16).—“For though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved” (Rom. 9:27).

Hence it is also read in the Psalms: “They shall return at evening, suffer hunger like dogs, and go around the city” (Ps. 58:15). Then indeed the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue will be raised. Then he who led the he-goat, or scapegoat, wandering through the desert for so long [Note: Codex Vaticanus: “leads through the desert”], will return to the camp after washing his garments in clean water.

These matters are obscure unless explained more clearly. Moses relates (Lev. 16:7) that the Lord commanded two goats to be placed before the entrance of the Tabernacle: one of them was to be sacrificed to the Lord, but the other was to be sent into the desert by a man appointed for this [Col. 0994B] office [Note: Codex Vaticanus corrects the editions cited above, which read “instead of a man appointed for this office”]. That man remained unclean until evening and at last, after washing with water, returned to the camp. How trivial these things would seem, unless they signified something great.

The two goats signify Christ and Antichrist. Under the Law, a goat was offered for sin: it is indeed a clean animal, but foul-smelling and lustful. For clean animals are those that divide the hoof and chew the cud. We abhor Antichrist as a goat. Likewise, the Jews call our Savior a deceiver and a sinner. Isaiah the prophet speaks in their person, saying: “And we accounted him as though he were leprous, stricken by God, and humiliated. But he was wounded for our iniquities and crushed [Col. 0994C] 539 for our crimes” (Isa. 51:4 [citation as printed]). This goat, therefore, was brought to the entrance of the Tabernacle and before the gates of the Temple, condemned, and sacrificed to the Lord for our sins.

Let us now consider the other goat, upon whose head the sons of Aaron laid their hands and invoked every curse. We are the sons of Aaron, who daily condemn and curse Antichrist. Cursing him, the Apostle says: “Then that lawless son of perdition shall be revealed, who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshipped” (2 Thess. 2:8). Likewise, blessed John in the Apocalypse curses him with many curses. The man who leads him into the desert is the Jewish people: led into captivity throughout the whole world and scattered as though through some vast desert, it carries with it Antichrist, whom they call the Messiah; it preaches him, proclaims him, and says that he will come for their deliverance.

[Note: In his commentary on Leviticus 16, St. Bruno gives the same exposition: “The first goat,” he says, “is Christ; the second is Antichrist. The first was allotted to the Lord and, spotless, was offered for sin; the second, after receiving many prayers—indeed, many curses—is sent into the wilderness. For the Jews, scattered throughout all lands, carry their goat into captivity and into the wilderness. This is the Messiah whom they themselves preach and await.”]

Thus, until evening—until the end of this day and age—that people will wander together with its goat through the vastness of this [Col. 0995A] wilderness. At last, washed with water, sanctified by baptism, and cleansed, it will be joined to the camp of the Church. And, as we said above, “In those days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell securely.” Then at last the Lord will return to the land of Israel and dwell in the city of Nazareth, whose name is interpreted “purity.” This single city suffices [Note: Codex Vaticanus: “will suffice.”] for the two peoples, so that, when all have been gathered together into one, there may be only one flock and one shepherd.

And you, whoever you are, if you wish to receive Christ into your house and into the temple of your breast, be Nazareth: be a house of beauty and purity. Say with the Psalmist: “Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Ps. 50:12). Hear the Lord saying in [Col. 0995B] the Gospel: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). Fittingly, then, Nazareth signifies the whole Church gathered from the two peoples, because she is wholly clean, wholly pure.

[Note: The Ascensian editions have a different reading: “She is wholly beautiful, wholly whitened beyond snow; of her the Lord himself says: ‘Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you.’ Hence our Savior, as the Evangelist says, was called a Nazarene from this Nazareth [Col. 0996D], because, as we have said, Nazareth is interpreted ‘purity’ and Nazarene ‘clean’; and *clean* is derived from *purities*, etc.”]

It was fittingly, moreover, that he was called Nazarene from Nazareth, because, as we have said, Nazareth is interpreted “purity,” and Nazarene “clean”; and *clean* is indeed derived from *purities*. Moses says many things about Nazirites: like men very devoted to religion, they vowed and consecrated themselves to the Lord, guarded themselves from everything from which the Law commands abstinence, and drank neither wine nor strong drink nor anything that could intoxicate [Col. 0995C] them. They did not shave the hair of their heads and did not approach a dead person. At last, when the period owed by their vow had been completed, they offered to the Lord the sacrifice of their entire profession [Note: Codex Vaticanus: “of their entire perfection”]. But if, during the time of their consecration, they happened for any reason to approach a dead person, all the preceding days became void; immediately on that same day, and likewise on the seventh day, they shaved their heads [Note: Codex Vaticanus corrects the printed editions]. On the eighth day, however, they offered a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.

Nazirites are made in one way in the Synagogue, in another in the Church. Few are made in the Synagogue, but many in the Church. For all who are baptized are Nazirites, since they are washed and sanctified from every sin. Although all Christians become Nazirites in baptism, these matters nevertheless seem to concern bishops and the other [Col. 0995D] clergy, and especially the monastic order, who, being united to the Lord by a stricter vow, ought to guard themselves from every impurity more carefully than others. Such persons must therefore abstain from wine, strong drink, and everything else that can intoxicate, lest, intoxicated, they lose their understanding and forget their profession. This must be understood not so much of bodily as of spiritual drunkenness. [Col. 0996A] Both are evil, but that of the soul is worse. Those intoxicated by the cup of vices are easily cast down by the devil. All proud persons, all avaricious persons, all lustful persons, all robbers, and all whom rage and anger rule are drunk with such a cup. Their very irrational impulse shows that they are drunk. Therefore, one who does not restrain himself from such drunkenness is not a Nazirite.

Jesus drank wine [Note: Codex Vaticanus: “Jesus used to drink wine.”] and was a Nazirite. This most clearly proves that wine and strong drink signify something else. Nazirites are also forbidden to approach a dead person—that is, to commit criminal and deadly sins. Although no one can be without sin, a Nazirite must nevertheless be without crime; for if he commits a crime, he is no longer [Col. 0996B] 540 a Nazirite. Therefore Nazirites are commanded that, if for any reason they approach a dead person during the entire period of consecration, they must shave immediately on that day, and likewise on the seventh. The days which they had observed under their vow up to that day were also rendered void. Before the appointed term, Nazirites were never permitted to shave their heads, unless perhaps they had first approached a dead person. Those, therefore, who shaved their heads before the appointed term did not wish to appear outwardly to possess what they knew they had lost inwardly.

We too must imitate them: whenever we commit some grave sin, we must hasten to repentance on that very day and not put it off until another day, as it is written: “Do not delay to turn to the Lord, and do not defer it from day to day” (Ecclus. 5:11). Let us shave our heads, so that the conscience may appear wholly clean and the grief that is in [Col. 0996C] the heart may be made visible in the face. As good hair must be allowed to grow, so bad hair must be shaved. Good hair is good thoughts, of which it is said: “For the thought of man shall confess to you, and the remnant of thought shall keep a festival for you” (Ps. 75:11); blessed Job lamented that he had lost these, saying: “My thoughts are scattered, tormenting my heart” (Job 17:11). With these the head of the inward person is adorned; when they are lost, the soul is weakened. Thus Samson lost his strength because he had been shorn of such hair.

Bad hair, however, is that of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “From the heart proceed evil thoughts, thefts, adulteries, perjuries, and the like” (Matt. 15:19). This must be shaved, because it is this that [Col. 0996D] defiles a person and makes Nazirites unclean. Let it be removed from the heart; let the soul’s head be shaved of it, and the whole person will be clean. But one who has sinned must shave his head on both the first and the seventh day, because “he who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 24:13). For the seventh day is the last; on the eighth day, however, let him offer a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons. By this we understand that, when he comes to the resurrection—which will indeed occur [Col. 0997A] on the eighth day—wholly clean in body and soul, he will be offered to the Lord as a worthy and acceptable sacrifice. Many things may be said about Nazirites, but let it suffice that we have said a few.

## CHAPTER VIII. SERMON I ON PALM BRANCHES

[Note: The title in Codex Vaticanus is: “Palm Sunday.”]

“When Jesus had come to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives” (Matt. 21:1), and what follows. Dearest brothers, our Lord and Savior, coming to his Passion for the redemption of the human race, first approached the Mount of Olives. From there he sent two of his disciples ahead to Jerusalem and said to them: “Go into the village opposite you, and there you will find an ass tied, and a colt. Untie them and bring them to me” (ibid., 2). When they [Col. 0997B] had brought them, Christ sat upon them and came to Jerusalem. At his coming the whole city was moved and came out to meet him. It displayed such devotion that some spread their garments in the road, while others cut palm and olive branches to be spread there; and all alike, those going before and those following, together with the children cried out with one voice in his praise: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; hosanna in the highest” (ibid., 9).

All these things happened literally, yet they signified something spiritually. The Mount of Olives, which our Redeemer first approached, signifies what else but our Savior himself? For just as a mountain, although it is of the earth, rises above the earth, so our Savior was a human being like us, mortal; but because he was without sin, because he is God and man, he has been raised and exalted above all. Of him the Prophet says: “The mountain in which God is pleased to dwell; indeed, the Lord shall dwell there unto the end” (Ps. 67:17). He is the Mount of Olives because, as the Apostle says: “He is the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation” (2 Cor. 1:3). For *oleon*, or *eleon*, is the Greek word for “mercy.”

The two animals, the ass and the colt, signify the two peoples, the Jews and the nations. For just as the ass was tamed by the yoke and accustomed to receive a rider, but the colt was not, so the Jewish people had received the yoke of the Law and the prophets and the worship of the one God; whereas the people of the nations had received neither the yoke of the Law nor that [Col. 0997D] of the prophets, and worshipped not God but demons. Yet both peoples were beneath the yoke of sin, as the Apostle says: “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3:23). So that they might be untied from this yoke, Christ sent two disciples—that is, two orders of disciples, one into Judea and the other among the Gentiles. Hence blessed Paul says: “He who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked through me among the nations” (Gal. 2:8). In converting them from sins, the apostles untied them and made them the temple and seat of God; hence Holy Scripture says: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.”

After the apostles came the holy martyrs, who spread their garments in the road because they handed over their bodies for the covenant of God. Then the holy confessors cut branches from the trees when they take for us examples of good living from the books of the New and Old Testaments. All cry: “Hosanna to the Son of David,” because all [Col. 0998A] 541 the saints praise God with one voice and one spirit, him who by his mercy freed us from the power of the devil. Together with them, brothers, let us mortify our flesh with its vices and desires, and let us possess, against the devil, the palm of victory through true repentance and through works of mercy, which the olive signifies, so that, with our Redeemer as guide, we may one day reach the heavenly Jerusalem and rejoice there for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON II. AGAIN ON PALM BRANCHES

[Col. 0998B] Blessed John the Evangelist relates that a great crowd, assembled for the feast day, hearing that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, took palm branches, went out to meet him, and cried: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (John 12:13). Good was the crowd that assembled for the feast day; good was the crowd that went out to meet our Savior. Even the scribes and Pharisees feared it; though they desired to kill Christ, they did not dare lay hands on him. Hence they said: “Not on the feast day, lest there be an uproar among the people” (Matt. 26:5).

To come to a feast day, to go to meet the Son of God, and not merely to go out but to go out to meet him with palms belongs to religion and virtue. The Jews kept this great solemnity for seven days, during which it was not permitted to eat leaven or perform servile work. But, as the Apostle says: “All these things happened to them as figures, but they were written for our sake” (1 Cor. 10:11). This is our feast. The Jews killed Christ, but Christ was killed for us and on our behalf; the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world was sacrificed for us and on our behalf. Therefore we must celebrate this feast “not with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5:8): that is, not in the oldness of the letter, which kills, but in the newness of the Spirit, because the Spirit gives life.

We ought to celebrate it for seven days, that is, every day and for as long as we are in this life. Since there are only seven days, the seven days signify all time and every day. Servile works are not those that slaves perform, but rather those that make even free people slaves. For it is not servile work to kindle a fire on the Sabbath, wash a dish, heal the sick, or cure paralytics, as the Jews, reviling our Savior, said: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John 9:16). [Col. 0998D] Likewise the ruler of the synagogue, indignant, said: “There are six days on which work may be done; come therefore on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day” (Luke 13:14), considering it servile work to heal and free miserable persons themselves from demons.

But if you wish to know what servile [Col. 0999A] works are, hear the Evangelist saying: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Luke 18:20; Exod. 20:13 ff.; Deut. 5:17 ff.). These are servile works. These make people slaves; these hand miserable people over to the devil’s slavery. Let us therefore flee these and things like them; let us keep ourselves from them, and we shall perform no servile work in our feasts. Those who celebrate feasts in this way are worthy to make a procession for the Lord and go to meet him with palms. For one may not go to meet Christ without palms, because victory is signified by palms. Thus the Law commands judges not to regard persons in judgment; but whoever has a just cause, to him they shall give [Col. 0999B] the palm.

Let those go to meet Jesus, then, who are victors and have conquered their enemies. If you have conquered pride, you have one palm; if you have conquered lust, you have another; and however many vices you have overcome, so many palms you possess. But if you have conquered none, you have none. Therefore do not go to meet Christ: he will not receive you, because you are unworthy to be received in such a triumph.

Let us now see what the ass also signifies, upon which this humble and gentle king deigned to sit. The ass is a stupid animal, of little price and without distinction, subject to every injury and every kind of servitude. But the Apostle says of the saints: “Consider your calling, brothers: not many among you are wise, not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the strong, and things that are not to destroy things that are” (1 Cor. 1:26). And elsewhere: “If anyone seems wise in this age, let him become foolish, that he may be wise” (1 Cor. 3:18). Isaiah likewise says of such persons: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger” (Isa. 1:3). Hence Deborah—whose name means “bee”—says: “You who ride upon shining asses, bless the Lord” (Judg. 5:10).

The shining asses are those adorned with the garments of the apostles, such as the one upon which the Lord now sits. Of it the Evangelist says that the apostles “put their garments upon it and made him sit above” (Matt. 21). The garments and ornaments of the apostles are virtues and honorable conduct: faith, hope, charity, courage, temperance, [Col. 0999D] humility, mercy, peace, patience, and the like. These are the ornaments with which the holy apostles were adorned and with which they adorn others, so that they may be fit and beautiful persons upon whom God may deign to sit and in whom he may dwell. Those, then, who are adorned with such ornaments and adorn others are said to have their souls seated upon shining asses. These, therefore, are God’s seats; from ignoble and most lowly animals they have become the throne of God.

There are nine orders of angels, but no order is above the thrones. How much better it is to become Christ’s asses with the simple and gentle than, with the proud and arrogant, to become the horses and chariots [Col. 1000A] of Pharaoh! For it is written of the latter: “He cast Pharaoh’s chariots and his army into the sea” (Exod. 15:4); but of the former: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). Finally, upon what other animal ought Jesus to have ridden when he was going to the cross, except upon that which is naturally seen to bear the sign of the cross upon itself? For this animal naturally bears the sign of the cross marked upon it.

Let us also hear what those signify who, cutting branches from trees, prepared the way for the Lord. Of such people the Forerunner of the Lord says: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God” (Luke 3:4). This office is not for everyone, nor have all been given the tools by which branches of this kind are cut from trees. It belongs to bishops [Col. 1000B] and priests: they ought to cut such branches from trees and prepare the way for the Lord, by which we too may be able to go to him and he may deign to come to us.

The trees signify the patriarchs and prophets, apostles and evangelists. We cut branches from them when we set forth to others their faith and teaching, their lives and holy conduct, and offer these for imitation. Such trees were Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Daniel; such were Peter, Paul, and John. Such also was the one who says: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God; I have hoped in the mercy of my God forever and ever” (Ps. 53:10). From this tree branches are cut, by which that way is prepared of [Col. 1000C] which it is said: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 118:1).

The children of Israel are commanded, at the Feast of Tabernacles, to take the fruit of the most beautiful tree, palm fronds, branches of thick-leaved trees, and willows from the brook, and to rejoice with them before the Lord (Lev. 23). Those who understand these things do not fail to know what the trees and their branches signify, by which the Lord’s way to us and our way to the Lord is prepared.

Let us hear also what the two crowds signify, of which it is said here: “The crowds that went before and those that followed cried out, saying: ‘Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’” (Matt. 21:9). The crowd that went before is the host of patriarchs and prophets, and of all who pleased the Lord from the first human being until Christ. The crowd that followed signifies the whole Church of the faithful, from the Savior’s coming until the end of the age. Read the books of the prophets and you will see how the preceding crowd praises and blesses the Lord. Read the volumes of the Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles, and then you will understand how greatly the following crowd resounds daily with Christ’s praises.

It was therefore excellently done that our Savior was placed in the midst, namely between the two Testaments: the Synagogue goes before, and the Church follows. He himself stands in the midst, and each people praises and blesses him with one harmonious voice [Note: The same author’s mystical interpretation is evident both in this sermon and in his commentary on Matthew.], [Col. 1001A] he who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER IX. ON THE LORD’S SUPPER
On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when it was necessary to eat the Passover, our Lord and Savior sent Peter and John ahead of him into the city, to prepare lodging and supper for him. This supper is the end of the Old and the beginning of the New Testament. Thus our Savior chose to divide one supper into two suppers, so that by the first we may understand the Old Testament, and by the second the New.

Concerning this supper the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron in Egypt, saying: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first of the months of the year. Speak [Col. 1001B] to the whole assembly of the children of Israel, and say to them: On the tenth day of this month let every man take a lamb for his families and houses” (Exod. 12:2).

[Note: [Col. 1001D] This interpretation has been taken, in the same words throughout, from the same Bruno’s commentary on this passage of Exodus, in the edition, vol. I, p. 58.]

“This month,” he says, “is the beginning of the other months; among us it is called March. Let it be our first—that is, the greatest and principal—month of the year, because greater sacraments occur in this month than in the others. ‘Speak to the assembly of the children of Israel, and say to them: On the tenth day of this month let every man take a lamb for his families and houses; but if the number is too small to be sufficient for eating the lamb, he shall take his neighbor who is joined to his house, according to the number of souls sufficient for eating the lamb. And [Col. 1001C] the lamb shall be without blemish, a male of one year. According to this rite you shall also take a kid, and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month. And the whole multitude of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it at evening’” (ibid., v. 3 ff.).

For on the tenth day the lamb and the kid are taken and kept until the fourteenth day of the same month, and then they are sacrificed. For since the tables of the covenant had ten sayings—that is, ten chief commandments—written upon them, in which the whole Law was in a manner contained, the whole Old Testament is therefore frequently understood through the number ten. And because there are four Gospels, in which the New Testament is enclosed, the New Testament is designated through the number four. The tenth day, therefore, signifies the Old Testament; the fourth day [Col. 1001D] after the tenth signifies the New.

The lamb is taken on the tenth day but kept for sacrifice until the fourteenth, because Christ’s Passion, prefigured in the Old Testament [Note: [Col. 1001D] Codex V: “signified through figures and enigmas.”] and signified enigmatically, was at last truly fulfilled in the New. There Christ is shown; here he is sacrificed. There he is signified; here he is offered in sacrifice. There, finally, the sacrifice of the lamb is narrated; here Christ’s Passion is proclaimed.

The Old Testament came to its end when Christ our Lord [Col. 1002A] said to his disciples: “Amen, I say to you, I shall not drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of God” (Matt. 26:29). Thus the old wine is rejected and the new [Note: [Col. 1001D] The Ascensian edition must be corrected, where it reads “is permitted.”] is promised. Not because the old Law is wholly destroyed, but because it is to be understood in a new and spiritual sense; and this is in the kingdom of God, which is the Church.

Christ is both lamb because of innocence, and is called a kid because of the likeness of sinful flesh. Of him it is said: “Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). Likewise, of him it is said: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk” (Exod. 23:19). We ought, therefore, to invite our neighbors and those near to us to eat him, so that the love by which we desire the salvation of all may become known.

[Col. 1002B] For every Christian is our neighbor, and everyone who is not far from the Church. This lamb is without blemish, because, as it is written: “He committed no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22). He is male, one year old, because he has nothing soft, nothing [Note: [Col. 1002D] In the Vatican codex, *non* (“not”) is absent.] feminine, nothing subject to corruption, nothing that feels the stirring of the flesh.

The lamb, indeed, is eaten household by household; but the kid is sacrificed by the whole multitude. By this is most plainly signified both the sacrifice now continually received in the Church and that which was offered by the Jews in their madness upon the altar of the cross. Although this and that are one, they are nevertheless so in different ways [Note: [Col. 1002D] Vatican codex: “takes place.”]. Thus they kill the kid, reckoning the Savior of the world among the wicked and sinners, [Col. 1002C] as it is written: “And he was numbered among the wicked” (Luke 21:37). And again: “If he were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you” (John 18:30).

But we, because we believe him to be the innocent, holy, and righteous Son of God, without every contagion of sin, both offer and receive the lamb without blemish. Therefore, although lamb and kid are sacrificed, the lamb alone is eaten by the people. That sacrifice is received in this one, because this is changed into that [Note: [Col. 1002D] Vatican codex: “For that would never be eaten unless this were changed into that. And this is, moreover, etc.”]. “For this is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 76:11).

Now the whole multitude of the children of Israel sacrificed the kid. But when? At evening: because Judas the traitor spoke with the Jews at about this hour, sold Christ, and received the money; and on the following day, at about the evening hour—that is, after the ninth hour—our Savior gave up his spirit. Hence the Psalmist says: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140:2).

[Note: [Col. 1002D] Thus far the reading of the commentary.]

“And they shall take of the blood of the lamb and put it upon both doorposts and upon the lintels of the houses in which they shall eat it.” They put the lamb’s blood upon both doorposts who receive him both with the mouth and with the heart. But those who receive unworthily, [Col. 1003A] or who, while receiving, do not believe it to be Christ’s blood, put Christ’s blood upon only one doorpost. Of them the Apostle says: “He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11:29).

Therefore, receiving with the mouth and believing with the heart that it is Christ’s blood, let us put it upon both doorposts; let us receive it both in body and in mind. And when we make upon our foreheads the sign of the cross, which was made bloody by Christ’s blood, then we put Christ’s blood upon the lintels of the houses.

It follows: “And they shall eat the flesh that night, roasted with fire, and unleavened bread with wild lettuces” (Exod. 12:8). In this place we understand the same thing by the flesh and by the unleavened bread; and he fittingly set down both, because [Col. 1003B] this flesh is made from bread. They eat this with wild lettuces who receive it with a contrite and humbled heart, and who, in compassion with Christ, as it were taste on the palate of the heart the bitterness of the cross.

“You shall not eat any of it raw, nor boiled in water, but only roasted with fire” (ibid., v. 9). For the flesh of the lamb, whether eaten raw or boiled in water, readily tends to upset the stomach. But if roasted, it both strengthens and is eaten more eagerly [Note: [Col. 1003D] Vatican codex: “is received.”]. Therefore, one who does not distinguish it from other flesh, who does not understand it to be sweeter and more health-giving than every food, and who, as though disdaining it, does not believe that it gives salvation and life to those who receive it worthily, eats this flesh either raw or boiled in water.

But one eats it roasted with fire [Col. 1003C] who, believing that life is in it, receives it most eagerly and, in receiving it, shares in Christ’s Passion. For the Lord himself says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6:54). Moreover, this flesh is not to be eaten raw, because Christ suffered; nor boiled in water, because he was crucified not secretly but openly, before the eyes of all. Flesh gives off its fragrance when it is roasted; Christ’s Passion too gives off its fragrance.

“You shall devour its head with its feet and entrails, and none of it shall remain until morning.” “For the head of Christ,” as the Apostle says, “is God” (1 Cor. 11:3). The feet, which touch the earth, signify his flesh, which was taken from the earth. And what are his entrails except wholly hidden things—every profound mystery?

[Col. 1003D] Thus those devour his head with his feet and entrails who believe him to be both God and man, and worthily and faithfully receive everything written concerning him. For it is not enough for us to believe that he is both God and man, unless, receiving his entrails also, we believe without hesitation that he was born of the Virgin, circumcised, truly suffered, rose on the third day, and all else written concerning him.

Therefore it is added: “None of it shall remain until morning” (Exod. 12:10). Let all be received; let all be believed. Let nothing concerning this lamb remain which is not enclosed [Col. 1004A] in the breast of faith. Morning signifies the end of this life, when Christ, the Sun of righteousness, shall appear; darkness having been driven away, night shall be no more. Then there will be no time for conversion or for eating the lamb’s flesh, because those who then begin to believe will hear with the foolish virgins: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12).

—“If anything remains, you shall burn it with fire” (Exod. 12:10). The remains are those things that cannot be eaten, such as the skin and bones. The lamb’s skin is Christ’s flesh: precisely how it is united to God—that is, how the Word became flesh—cannot be either spoken or understood. But who can eat, or, so to say, gnaw the bones: who can, if it be granted, understand through the most prolonged and unceasing inquiry how he was begotten of the Father before all ages?

There are many other things which, because they cannot be eaten and understood, should be burned with the fire of charity and the ardor of faith. It is enough to believe, if understanding is not granted. For many eat this flesh more by believing than by understanding. Therefore let those eat who can; but those who cannot, let them believe and burn it with the fire of charity.

It follows: “Thus shall you eat it: you shall gird your loins, have sandals upon your feet, hold staffs in your hands, and eat in haste. For it is *phase*, that is, the Lord’s passing-over” (Exod. 12:11–12). To gird the loins is to restrain luxury with the girdle of chastity and continence. Hence the Lord himself says: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35).

[Col. 1004C] Those have sandals on their feet who, as though prepared to go elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1003D] Vatican codex: “otherwise.”], know themselves to be pilgrims in this world. Running the way of [Note: [Col. 1003D] The same codex: “God’s.”] commandments, they safely and fearlessly, being well shod, tread upon serpents and scorpions.

Let them hold staffs in their hands, so that they may be able to defend themselves from adversaries rushing upon them. Do you possess humility? It is a staff for you: by it you overcome pride. Do you possess chastity? This too is a staff by which luxury is conquered. But why say more? As many virtues as you have, so many staffs you possess. Thus let one who comes to eat this flesh be prepared, thus fortified, thus inflamed.

You shall eat it swiftly and in haste, so that when the Lord comes you may already be full and satisfied, and may not then begin to believe when you ought to be delivered through faith. In receiving faith there must be no delay. “Watch therefore, because you know neither the day nor the hour” (Matt. 25:13).

After our Savior had eaten [Note: [Col. 1003D] Vatican codex: “the first supper.”] that supper and that figurative lamb with the apostles, he passes to the true sacrament of Passover, in order to do again in truth what he had first done in figure. He first acted according to the order [Note: [Col. 1004D] Vatican codex: “according to the order of Aaron, but afterward according to the order of Melchizedek.” The Ascensian edition likewise; in place of “afterward,” it has “subsequently.”] of Melchizedek, in order to show himself the author of both Testaments. By fulfilling one priesthood, therefore, he brought it to an end; the other he ordained to be performed and to remain forever. Of this it is written [Col. 1005A]: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4).

Rising from supper and taking a linen cloth, he girded himself; then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet. He washed their feet because one who has bathed has no need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean. He did this so that they might be pure and clean when approaching so great a sacrament, giving us too an example: we who are about to approach his flesh and blood should first wash ourselves. For, as the Apostle says, “He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 15:29). Therefore let a person first prove himself, wash his feet and his conscience, and so approach.

After he had washed their feet, when [Col. 1005B] he had reclined again, before he began to perform the second supper, he said: “Do you know what I have done to you? You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for I am. If therefore I, Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you too ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13:13).

[Note: [Col. 1005D] Vatican codex: “with a few words inserted.”]

And after a few words had intervened, taking the cup, he drank and said: “I shall not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine until I drink it new with you in the kingdom of God” (John 13:13).

[Note: [Col. 1005D] The same codex: “This was as though he were saying.” [Col. 1006D] Likewise, the cited edition.]

This was as though he were saying: “The old things have passed away; behold, I make all things new.” For this is why Luke the Evangelist sets down two cups, saying: “Take and divide it among yourselves. For this is the cup of my blood, of the new covenant, which shall be poured out for you and for many for the remission of sins” [Col. 1005C] (Luke 21:17, 20).

It is as though he were saying: “I once told you: ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves’” (John 6:54); “but you did not understand. Now I explain what I said; and what you now see me doing is the explanation of those words.”

Some of the disciples, hearing these words at that time and not understanding, were scandalized; they turned back and departed, and followed him no longer. For they thought that they ought to eat his flesh cut limb from limb, either raw or cooked. These men were still far too fleshly and understood in a far too fleshly manner.

Behold, Jesus now sits with his disciples; he eats and drinks with them; and although he suffers nothing in [Col. 1005D] his members, his flesh is nevertheless eaten and his blood drunk by his disciples. This is effected by the power of divinity—that power of which it is written: “Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses” (Ps. 134:6).

—“For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 32:9).

Thus, when he said: “This is my body, and this is my blood” (Luke 22:19), such was the power in his word that immediately the bread was changed into flesh and the wine was changed into blood. Do you marvel at this? I know that you marvel [Note: [Col. 1006D] Vatican codex and edition: “I know that you marvel.”]. For it is marvelous; indeed, God has done nothing that is not marvelous.

Likewise, [Col. 1006A] I marvel at you: how your food and drink are changed into your flesh and blood. Your food does not make the flesh which has already been made, but nourishes and is changed into it—namely, into your flesh, which you possess and received from your mother. Thus this bread and wine, consecrated upon the altar, are changed at the command and by the power of the heavenly blessing into Christ’s blood—not into another flesh of Christ, for he has no other flesh than that born of Christ’s mother.

Could your digestion, then, change your food into your flesh, and could the heavenly blessing not change bread and wine into Christ’s flesh and blood? How then is this true: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created”?

You must therefore grant [Col. 1006B] that, just as through digestion food is changed into your flesh, which you received from your mother, so this bread is changed by heavenly blessing into Christ’s flesh—not into another flesh, indeed, because he has no other than that which he received from his Virgin Mother.

Hear something more wonderful still. Though so great a quantity of bread, which throughout the whole world is daily changed by heavenly blessing into Christ’s flesh and eaten by Christ’s faithful, Christ’s body itself is neither increased when the bread is changed into it nor diminished when it is eaten.

Let the five loaves with which our Savior satisfied five thousand persons, apart from little children and women, who are not counted in that number, be an example for us (John 6). If each [Col. 1006C] one of those loaves had been divided into a thousand pieces, I do not think one piece could have filled one person’s mouth. Yet that tiny amount which each received was multiplied so greatly in every person’s mouth that, until complete satisfaction, neither was there too little for teeth to chew nor for the stomach to fill.

Those very small crumbs which fell from the loaves as they were broken, and were not needed by those who had eaten, were multiplied so greatly that twelve baskets could have been filled from them. Certainly, if it had pleased him, the Lord could have fed from these remnants alone all the people of this world for as long as this world should endure. So great is the Lord’s power, and so powerful is Christ’s blessing.

Behold, we have found a very fitting example of something eaten by many without being diminished. So Christ’s body, although daily eaten by all, suffers no diminution; because, as the Apostle says, “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall have no further dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9).

I have seen some persons—and it is not difficult to find many such—who became larger and stouter with no abundance of food, although not much food was changed into their flesh. I say this, although perhaps it does not seem an apt example, so that you may understand that something may not be increased although [Col. 1007A] something is added to it daily. If this can occur in mortal flesh, how much more in the Savior’s flesh, already glorified through the resurrection? For whatever can in any respect be increased or diminished is not yet consummated and perfect.

But why do we labor over such matters? His own words suffice us. He himself said: “This is my body”; afterward he says: “This is my blood.” He himself says: “My flesh is truly food and my blood is truly drink” (John 6:56). He himself says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6:55). If we do not believe Christ, whom shall we believe? Where such authority exists, arguments are unnecessary.

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 1007B]

## SERMON I FOR PARASCEVE

To be delivered to the brethren on this day, or on any other, concerning the imitation of Christ in poverty, mercy, charity, and the other virtues.

“Be imitators of God as dearly beloved children, and walk in love, as Christ also loved us and gave himself for us, an offering and sacrifice to God as a sweet-smelling odor” (Eph. 5:1).

In all that our Lord Jesus Christ did and said, dearest brethren, he left us a pattern of humility and instruction in good conduct; for as he wished to teach us by words, so also by examples. Hence it is written: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1). And concerning humility the Lord himself says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble [Col. 1007C] in heart” (Matt. 11:29).

Though he himself is almighty and Lord, he chose for our sake to be poor, rejected honors, willingly endured sufferings, and even prayed for his persecutors. He did all this so that we might not neglect to follow him in all things, according to the capacity of our weakness; otherwise we are not true Christians. For one who says that he loves Christ ought himself to walk as Christ walked.

Therefore, in choosing to be poor, he taught clearly enough that we too should neither esteem riches greatly nor desire them too immoderately. For such persons are proved to be covetous, concerning whom the Apostle says: “The covetous, fornicators, and unclean shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:11). And elsewhere: “Those who wish to become rich in this world fall into temptations and snares of the devil” (1 Tim. 6:9).

Observe that he said, “those who wish to become rich,” not “those who are rich.” He condemns blameworthy desire, not riches. People may be rich and good; but they are those concerning whom it is said: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61:11). Such, we read, were Abraham, Jacob, and David, whom we know both to have possessed riches and to have shared them with those who did not possess them.

And we have it written in the Apostle: “Command the rich of this age not to think proudly, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God. Let them be rich in good works and give readily” (1 Tim. 6:11). These, behold, are good rich persons: those who do not think proudly and do not hope in the uncertainty of riches—that is, do not place their trust in riches, which are uncertain, possessed today and readily lost tomorrow.

[Col. 1008A] “Let them give readily,” so that they may endeavor, from the abundance they possess, to relieve a brother’s need; and so that it may be said of each of them: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7). This is why, though the Lord was rich in heaven, he chose to be poor on earth.

And because he willingly endured Passion and cross, by his very death he delivered us from the devil’s power; and, hanging upon the cross, he prayed for sinners. There he gave us an example that human beings should endure, with great patience, evils inflicted by their neighbors, since he, Lord of all, so kindly bore such great things from servants, the righteous one from sinners.

And we, brethren, when set amid tribulations, ought especially to persist in prayer. These tribulations are twofold. There is tribulation when we suffer losses of temporal things; and there is tribulation, far greater, when we are inclined toward any sins whatever. Nevertheless, one must pray in such a way that one’s prayer is not turned into sin.

We must likewise give alms, and give them perfectly. Perfect almsgiving consists in two things: giving and forgiving. Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel: “Give, and it shall be given to you; forgive, and it shall be forgiven you” (Luke 6:37). Again: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7).

Otherwise, as Scripture testifies, he who asks in vain to be delivered from sins stretches out his hands to the Lord while, as far as he is able, he does not stretch them out to the poor. And if anyone offends you, forgive from the heart, so that God may forgive [Col. 1008C] you your offenses; because “unless you forgive, neither will the Father in heaven forgive you” (ibid. 6:14); “for he who hates his brother is a murderer; and we know that no murderer has eternal life or a share in the kingdom of Christ and God” (John 3:15).

These are the means by which one must attain the kingdom of heaven. May Christ our Lord lead us to it, he who lives and reigns unto ages of ages.

## SERMON II FOR PARASCEVE, OR FOR THE LORD’S RESURRECTION

“This is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptance: that our Lord Jesus Christ came into this world to save sinners” (1 Tim. 4:9).

Blessed Paul the Apostle, teacher and master of the Gentiles, says that his words are true and faithful, worthy of all acceptance, and such as no one ought ever to contradict: that our Lord Jesus Christ came into this world in order to save sinners. [Col. 1008D] For he did not come to call the righteous but sinners, because those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick do.

The whole purpose of our Savior—that the Word became flesh, that he was born of the Virgin, that he lived among human beings, that he suffered and rose again—his whole purpose, I say, was to redeem and save sinners. Today, therefore, this purpose, so devout; this will, so holy; this mercy, so boundless, has been fulfilled.

He himself also showed this in the words by which he said: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and all things that have been written through the prophets concerning the Son of Man shall be fulfilled. For he shall be delivered to the Gentiles, mocked, scourged, crucified, and on the third day shall rise again” [Col. 1009A] (Matt. 20:18). Do you not hear that in the resurrection are fulfilled those things which the Law and the Prophets foretold concerning him?

There was no other way by which humankind could return to its homeland, no other medicine by which it could be healed. O most merciful physician, who made medicine from his own blood, lest those whom he came to heal should perish! For he is the one of whom it is written: “Who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1:5).

Thus Christ’s blood is the price by which we were redeemed, the washing by which we were washed, and the antidote by which we were healed. “For if a law had been given which could give life, righteousness would truly be from the law; but the law brought nothing to perfection” (Gal. 3:21). For it is manifest that “by works of the law no flesh is justified before God” (ibid. 2:16). These are the Apostle’s words.

“This,” therefore, says blessed John, “is he who came through water and blood, to redeem, to wash, and to save” (John 5:6). Not by water alone, because this great salvation, redemption, and deliverance could not be accomplished by baptism alone, but by water and blood, so that blood might avail for the price and water for the washing. Hence water flowed together with blood from his side.

Our Savior had already died, and still, in the very shedding of his blood, he taught and proclaimed where we ought to seek and believe that the help of our redemption lies. Once he had revealed to the disciples the mystery of his Passion, [Col. 1009C] and blessed Peter had understood it, he was displeased by it and said: “Far be this from you, Lord; let this not happen.” Jesus answered him: “Get behind me, Satan, because you do not savor the things of God, but those of man” (Matt. 10:22).

For blessed Peter did not yet know [Note: [Col. 1009D] Vatican codex: “not yet.”] that great and ineffable sacrament of the divine counsel; he had not understood that original sin could not be loosed except by Christ’s blood. He did not yet know that “Christ had to suffer, rise from the dead, and so enter into his glory” (Luke 24:12). Had he understood this, he would never have stood opposed to Christ’s will as Satan—that is, as an adversary.

Yet he himself went after Christ, because he followed him not only in death but also in a similar death. In the days when John the Baptist was beheaded, some came to Jesus saying: “Go out and depart from here, for Herod seeks to kill you” (ibid. 13:31). They spoke as human beings and gave human counsel. The Lord replied to them: “Go, tell that fox: Behold, I cast out demons and perform healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am consummated. Nevertheless, I must walk today, tomorrow, and the following day” (ibid. 32:33).

What is it that Herod seeks to kill me? Go and tell that fox; tell that cunning plotter: “Behold, I cast out demons, which are stronger and more powerful than he; and if I will, I cast him out too, and can cast him out both from his kingdom and from the tabernacle of his body.”

[Note: [Col. 1009D] He said the same thing in his exposition of the Gospel of Luke.]

I do this today and tomorrow, and for as long as it pleases me. For “tomorrow” is frequently put for future time in the divine page. In this sense Jacob speaks to Laban: “My righteousness shall answer for me tomorrow” (Gen. 30:33).

But what would it profit Herod if he killed me, when immediately on the third day I shall be consummated—that is, shall rise from the dead? For whoever kills me shall have power over me only for that span, and no longer, between my Passion and resurrection. Yet, although Herod seeks to do this, although he has this foolish and impious desire, I must nevertheless walk, preach, and do the Father’s will today, tomorrow, and for whatever following time after tomorrow it pleases me.

Why? Because “a prophet cannot perish outside Jerusalem” (Luke 13:33). “Cannot,” he says: prophetic speech and the divine disposition do not admit, receive, or permit a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem.

[Note: [Col. 1009D] “But this: God’s providence, God’s disposition, and the word [Col. 1010D] of the prophets do not admit, receive, or consent that he should perish and die outside Jerusalem,” etc. The same St. Bruno, Commentary on Luke, ch. 13, v. 31.]

I shall suffer there and nowhere else, because the place, time, and day—where, when, and by whom this must occur—have been ordained and established, and it cannot happen otherwise. Foolish, therefore, is Herod, who claims another’s office and sin for himself and strives to change the place, time, and the other unchangeable matters.

The Jews often wished to seize and kill Jesus, [Col. 1010C] but could not. Accordingly, when those same people sought a sign and spoke proudly, he said: “A wicked and perverse generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For as Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so shall the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth, [548] three days and three nights” (Luke 11:29–30).

You have heard it; what more do you seek? For the Son of Man shall be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights, and no longer.

[Note: [Col. 1010D] The same exposition is found in St. Bruno of Asti’s treatise *On the Incarnation*.]

What is “in the heart of the earth”? In the inclination and desire of sinners. For three days and three nights the Jews were given power from above to do to him what they desired. For just as the righteous are called heaven, so sinners are called earth. Hence it was said to the first man: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:29).

Therefore the Son of Man was in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights, although not for three whole days and three whole nights. For on the night when he was seized by the Jews in their madness, rushing upon him—when he himself said: “If you seek me, let these go” (John 18:8)—our Savior was in their power. Likewise, during the other two nights which follow that night [Col. 1011A] until the Lord’s Day, his body was guarded so that he should not rise; only his body was in their power.

The three days are likewise counted as Friday, the Sabbath, and the beginning of the third day, upon which the Creator and Lord of the world rose from the dead very early. It is most customary throughout all Scripture sometimes to put the whole for a part and a part for the whole. Hence the Prophet used “fly” and “frog” in the singular when he should have said “flies” and “frogs” in the plural: “He sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them; and the frog, and it destroyed them” (Ps. 77:45).

Let this sign suffice you, O Jews, and seek no other sign further. For it is a great and marvelous sign that, to your evil and our good, to your destruction and the salvation of all nations, you were able to seize, bind, and kill him who at once created all things from nothing. Of him it is written: “He who remains forever created all things together” (Sir. 18:1). All things are set within his power and will, and there is none who can resist his will, because he himself is Lord and Creator of all.

Thus Jesus was in the heart of the earth for as long as he willed. Neither before nor after did he surrender himself to anyone’s power—he who, rising from the dead on the third day, “dies no more, and death shall have no further dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9); who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit unto ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER XI. ON THE HOLY DAY OF EASTER
> “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it” (Ps. 117:24).

Among all the solemnities, most beloved, which Holy Church observes and venerates in honour of our Redeemer, she celebrates and contemplates the solemnity of this present day as chief and outstanding, surpassing all others. Just as of old the Holy of Holies was so called by way of pre-eminence, and the high priest dared to enter it only once a year, so this feast may by way of pre-eminence be called the Feast of Feasts. For through it hell was despoiled of the righteous held there, and the gate of paradise—guarded against the whole human race by a cherub with a fiery sword—was opened. For what benefit would the Word’s being born have brought humankind, unless by death he had triumphed over hell, [Col. 1011D] and by his resurrection had given us hope of rising again?

There were, indeed, two lives. One, subject to many miseries, all of us knew by experience. The other, unknowable and immortal, we did not know. Christ therefore took up this mortal life by being born; he received the other, immortal life by rising again. Hence Paul says: “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9).

So too there is a twofold death: one is the death of the body, by which it is separated from the soul; it is common to all people, righteous and unrighteous alike. Of it David says: “What human being shall live and not see death?” (Ps. 88:49). This death is the punishment [Col. 1012A] of sin, imposed upon the whole human race on account of the sin of the first human being, to whom God said: “From every tree of paradise you may eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat. For on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die the death” (Gen. 2:16); that is, you shall become possessed of a mortal body. For on the day when Adam ate this, he did not die bodily, but began to possess a mortal body; had he not sinned, he would have possessed an immortal body.

The other death is that of the soul, namely, by which the soul is separated from God through sinning. Thus Ezekiel the prophet says: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18:20). For just as the body lives from the soul, so the soul lives from God; and just as the body dies when the soul departs, so, when God departs because of sin, [Col. 1012B] the soul dies.

Therefore, although we were held by a twofold death, namely that of body and soul, Christ did not take both upon himself; for then he would have freed us from neither. Yet he took one death, that is, the death of the flesh, and through it freed us from both deaths. For this reason he lay in the tomb for only one day and two nights: so that by the one day our twofold death, brought upon us by that sin, might be signified. Therefore, through the one death of Christ we have been delivered from our own twofold death, because through him we can rise in soul and body.

Rightly, then, the Psalmist exhorts us because of the glory of the resurrection, saying: “This 549 day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it.” Although God made all days in creating them, he is especially said [Col. 1012C] to have made this day because on it he recreated humanity unto better things by his blood, and recalled humanity to the immortal life both of body and soul through the resurrection of each. Therefore we ought to exult on it, because the death of the body has been swallowed up in victory through Christ’s resurrection; and we ought to rejoice, because through the triumph of Christ’s resurrection we have been delivered from the death of the soul. To the Lord and God who has risen and gives us hope of rising again be praise and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER XII

## SERMON I: ON THE LORD’S ASCENSION

> “After the Lord Jesus had spoken to the disciples, he was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God” (Mark 16:19).

Since our Redeemer, most beloved, ascends today into [Col. 1012D] heaven in the form of his body, it is fitting that we rejoice and exult. For we, who through the sin of the first human being had been cast down from heaven’s glory, are now brought and borne with our head to the heavenly palace, to the fellowship of angels, and to the ineffable vision of God.

Today, indeed, was fulfilled that prophecy of David: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings” (Ps. 67:19). For we, brothers, were that captivity, because through sin we had been taken captive by the devil. But when Christ ascended into heaven, he led this captivity—that is, us—captive: he received us with himself into his own power, after the likeness of a triumphant prince liberating his own people, [Col. 1013A] as Abraham did.

This captivity of Christ, brothers, by which we are taken captive and carried back to heaven, is good; but the captivity of the devil, by which we are irreparably suffocated, is evil. Let us therefore, most beloved, avoid this captivity of the devil, namely sins, and love Christ’s captivity, which raises us from earth to heaven and carries us from darkness to the inaccessible light of God.

But none of us can ascend to this light unless we take upon ourselves the image of our Redeemer, so that, just as he walked, we too may walk. Thus Ezekiel the prophet, while he was in captivity in Babylon, saw a vision of God. In it, among other things, he saw the appearance of electrum, and in it the likeness of four living creatures: one had the likeness of a human being; the second, [Col. 1013B] the likeness of a calf; the third, that of a lion; and the fourth bore the likeness of an eagle.

What, brothers, does the appearance of electrum signify except the nature of our Redeemer? For when two different metals, namely gold and silver, are joined in electrum, the gold is moderated and diminished in its brilliance, while the silver is illuminated with greater brightness. Thus our Redeemer was electrum, joined from the gold of divinity and the silver of humanity: that is, from two natures, divine and human, in one person. In this Christ, the gold—that is, divinity—was as though diminished from its splendour, as is read in the Psalm: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:7). But the silver, that is, human nature, [Col. 1013C] grew into greater splendour, because, as is read in the same place: “You crowned him with glory and honour, O Lord, and set him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things beneath his feet: all sheep and oxen, and also the beasts of the field; the birds of heaven and the fish of the sea” (ibid., 7–9), and so forth. And blessed Paul says: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2:9).

In the appearance of this electrum Ezekiel saw the likeness of four living creatures. This fourfold likeness likewise signifies our Redeemer. He had the likeness of a human being because he was a true human being, was made in the likeness of human beings, and was found in appearance [Col. 1013D] as a human being. He had the likeness of a calf because he was a priestly victim, dying on the cross as a sacrificial calf. He had the likeness of a lion by rising from the tomb on the third day and enlivening his body as a lion gives life to its cubs by its roar. He had the likeness of an eagle by ascending into heaven on the fortieth day after the resurrection.

Therefore we, brothers, according to Paul’s saying, “As we have borne the image of the earthly human being, let us bear the image of the heavenly human being” (1 Cor. 15:49)—that is, of Christ—so that in virtues we may be born as human beings; in vices we may die as calves; resisting vices courageously, we may rise to better things; and, on the wings of virtues, like eagles, we may be raised through contemplation. May Christ himself help us, he who reigns in heaven and everywhere for ever, etc.

> [Note: The two preceding sermons are absent from the Vatican manuscript.]

## SERMON II

On this day, as it is written (Luke 24), Christ’s disciples assembled on the Mount of Olives, reclined there, and Jesus appeared to them and reclined with them. After reproving them for their unbelief, 550 and commanding them to go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature, “while they watched, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes” (Acts 1:9).

All the works of our Saviour are full of mysteries; whatever he does is figure and signification. For this most blessed and joyful banquet, [Col. 1014B] at which the King of kings and Lord of lords deigned to recline together with the princes of the whole earth, is not devoid of mystery. Indeed, the place itself and the name of that place seem to signify something great. It is called the Mount of Olives, by which the exalted power of mercy is signified; for in Greek *eleon*, and in Latin *misericordia*, means “mercy.”

Jesus often used to ascend this mountain and stay there with his disciples, as it is written in the Gospel: during the day he preached in the temple, but at night he remained on the mountain called Olivet.

> [Note: Vatican manuscript: “And elsewhere it is said that he went up, according to his custom, to the Mount of Olives.”]

Notice that it says, “according to his custom.” The disciples themselves therefore observed this custom of their Master, [Col. 1014C] and frequently assembled on this mountain of oil and mercy. Perhaps this is why the Lord himself is called the son of oil, as the prophet says: “My beloved had a vineyard on a horn, the son of oil” (Isa. 5:1). What is “the son of oil” except the son of peace and mercy? Consider now how abundantly he possesses the oil of mercy: in order to release a servant—

> [Note: Vatican manuscript: “in order to redeem a servant”]

—he did not spare his Son. Therefore the Lord invites us to the mountain of mercies—

> [Note: Vatican manuscript: “to the mountain of mercy.”]

—and commands us to ascend the mountain of peace and mercy. Hence the prophet says: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who proclaim good news to Zion” (Isa. 40:9). No one is permitted to proclaim the Gospel before ascending this high mountain.

> [Note: Same manuscript: “ascends.”]

For although the mountain is not [Col. 1014D] high in itself, the virtue signified by it is most exalted. Rightly therefore the apostles ascended this mountain when they were about to receive the office of preaching the Gospel. For today it was said to them: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:16).

Let bishops hear this; let all who undertake the office—

> [Note: Same manuscript: “the task of evangelizing.”]

—hear it, and let them not presume to preach the Gospel before they have ascended the mountain of peace and mercy. Nor should anyone presume that what was not permitted to the apostles was permitted to himself.

> [Note: Same manuscript: “Nor should anyone think anything permitted to himself which was forbidden to the apostles.” Also in the Ascensian edition.]

“Be therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful” (Luke 6:36). — “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. 30:5). — “I will sing to you of mercy and judgment, O Lord” (Ps. 100:1). — “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures for ever” (Ps. 103:1).

Great is this mountain from which Christ ascended to heaven and from which the way to heaven is raised. Let all, therefore, who desire to share in the banquets of Christ and the apostles ascend it. If you wish Christ to come to your banquets, recline upon the Mount of Olives; recline upon the mountain of mercy. Prepare banquets there with the apostles: “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy and homeless into your house” (Isa. 58:7). Jesus will immediately be present and say [Col. 1015B] to you: “What you did to one of my least ones, you did to me” (Matt. 25:6).

Wherever peace and mercy are, there also is this Mount of Olives. As oil is supreme among other liquids, so mercy is supreme among the other virtues. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 99:5). This is why we have so many anointings among us; this is why we see so many anointings performed at the consecration of churches. Therefore let our banquets always take place on this mountain; let our hearts always float in the oil of mercy.

There are other mountains too which we ought to ascend and upon which we ought likewise to dwell. Of these the Prophet says: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help shall come to me” (Ps. 120:1). Jacob the patriarch likewise invited his children to these mountains when he was about to offer sacrifice to the Lord, saying: “Come, let us go up to Bethel, that we may sacrifice to the Lord” (Gen. 35:3).

Good is the mountain on which the Lord was transfigured; good also is that upon which he chose the twelve apostles and preached the eight beatitudes. Evil are the mountains of Gilboa—

> [Note: Vatican manuscript: “Good also are the mountains on which, from [Col. 1016D] a few loaves, he satisfied so many thousands of people.”]

—to which David, uttering a curse, said: “May neither dew nor rain come upon you, where the mighty men of Israel fell” (2 Sam. 1:21). Evil also are those mountains in which Lot, made drunk, made his daughters pregnant. These mountains are heretics, who destroy all who come to them and in whom even strong men themselves are often corrupted. “For evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:33). — “How then do you say to my soul: ‘Migrate to [Col. 1015D] the mountains like a sparrow’?” (Ps. 10:1).

I trust in the Lord, because we shall migrate not to these, but to the eternal mountains. The eternal mountains are the prophets and apostles, upon whom the Church is founded, according to the saying: “Its foundations are upon the holy mountains” (Ps. 8:1). There are as many of these mountains as there are books of the two Testaments, because in these mountains you can find whatever belongs to delight, joy, health, and blessedness. Faith, hope, and charity, along with the other virtues, are mountains whose height the Lord beholds. Those who take refuge in them [Col. 1016A] will be safe.

Noah was saved on the mountain of obedience; 551 Abraham on the mountain of faith; Joseph on the mountain of chastity; Moses and David on the mountain of meekness; and others—

> [Note: Vatican manuscript: “and others on others.”]

—were saved on other mountains. Yet today Christians ought especially to ascend the Mount of Olives, the mountain of peace and mercy, so that, as they receive the poor for Christ’s sake, they may deserve also to receive Christ himself.

We have said what the Mount of Olives and the banquets held upon it signify. Now let us return to the words of the Gospel and hear what the Lord commanded his disciples. “Go,” he says, “into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:16). Another Evangelist explains this more plainly: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. [Col. 1016B] 28:19), intending by “every creature” to signify all nations. Hence the Apostle says: “All creation groans and travails until now” (Rom. 8:22), although he was speaking not of all creation but of humanity alone.

“Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved; but whoever does not believe shall be condemned” (Matt. 16:17). What does believing here mean except preserving faith together with works? For “faith without works is dead” (Jas. 20:26). — “And indeed the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken, was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God” (Mark 16:19). Hence it is written: “Ascending on high, the Lord led captivity captive” (Ps. 67:19).

For ascending on high, the Lord made our captivity captive by his own captivity; and we, previously held beneath the harsh captivity of the devil, were taken captive by him unto better things and set free. Consider now with how great glory, how great joy, what triumph, and what array, all that host of the heavenly army came to meet its Creator, our Saviour; with what praises, hymns, and rejoicings it escorted him to the throne of glory.

I seem to see the entire way by which our Saviour ascended, from earth to heaven, lined everywhere by the soldiers of all the orders above. I seem to see the evil spirits terrified by that army, so great and so terrible; all turned to flight and casting themselves into darkness, leaving empty and free this whole air which they had been accustomed to possess. [Col. 1016D] “Therefore our God ascended amid rejoicing, and the Lord at the sound of a trumpet” (Ps. 46:6). He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER XIII

## SERMON I ON THE COMING OF THE HOLY SPIRIT

> [Note: Title in the Vatican manuscript: “On the holy day of Pentecost.”]

On today’s solemnity, most beloved, we are urged to consider how great is the love with which our Redeemer is bound to us. First, by the appearance of the flesh he assumed, while conversing with us, he strengthened us for heavenly things; [Col. 1017A] afterwards, by sending his Spirit from heaven, he assured us of his promise.

Today, indeed, while Christ’s disciples were praying together, the Holy Spirit came in the appearance of fire. Those who had earlier faltered at Christ’s passion he now made inwardly burn and strengthened in such a way that they no longer feared merely the voice of one maidservant, nor, when scourged, dreaded the sight of the Jewish council, nor even shuddered at the threats of Rome herself, mistress of the world.

For this reason the Holy Spirit came in the appearance of fire: that he might consume and cleanse every rust of sins; kindle and make them strong against every earthly dominion; and illuminate them in every spiritual knowledge. For just as fire has a threefold nature—namely, to consume, warm, [Col. 1017B] and illuminate—so also the Holy Spirit, who is a consuming fire, consumed and purged in the apostles every old stain of sins; warmed and kindled them to so great a love of God that, having been scourged, they rejoiced because they had been deemed worthy to suffer disgrace for Jesus’ name. He also illumined them with such knowledge that they spoke the mighty works of God in every language, so that the languages of the nations, once confused through pride at the building of the tower of Babylon, might now be united through the apostles’ humility.

Since the whole world was to return to the knowledge of the one true God, one language was to resound through apostolic mouths and spread Christ’s praise throughout all the earth. Moreover, because the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples on the fiftieth day after Christ’s resurrection, it signifies the figure of the Old Testament. For [Col. 1017C] we read that from the crossing of the Red Sea by the Hebrew people to the day on which the Law was given through Moses on two tablets of stone there were fifty days. Hence that day too is called Pentecost, because it is the fiftieth day from Christ’s resurrection. And all these things agree fittingly.

For just as, after crossing the Red Sea, God’s people were delivered and the Egyptian enemies drowned, so at the death and resurrection of our Redeemer they were delivered from hell, and the demons were submerged and perished through his power. Hence the Lord says through the prophet Hosea: “O death, I shall be your death; and I shall be your bite, O hell” (Hos. 13:14). For Christ’s death was the destruction of death, in that he utterly destroyed it in his elect. [Col. 1017D] He bit hell, in that, as one who bites bread, he left one part behind, namely the evil, and drew out another part, namely the good.

And just as that Law was given on the mountain on the fiftieth day, with sound and fire, so our law of grace, namely the Holy Spirit, was given in the upper room, in the appearance of fire and with a sudden sound. Hence it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “Suddenly a sound came from heaven like that of a violent wind” (Acts 2:1). But that Law was given on tablets of stone, signifying the hard hearts of the Jews; ours, however, was given on the tablets of the heart, not in a spirit of fear, as Paul says (Rom. 8:15), but in the Spirit of adoption as children of God, in whom we cry, “Abba, [Col. 1018A] Father.”

Therefore, brothers, if we wish to have this Holy Spirit in ourselves, let us remain in the upper room, seeking the things above, not those upon earth, and becoming one spirit with the Lord, cleaving to him through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON II ON PENTECOST
