> [Note: This title is prefixed to this sermon in the Vatican manuscript.]

> “When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, all the disciples were together in the same place. Suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a violent wind arriving, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And divided tongues, as of fire, appeared to them; and the Holy Spirit rested upon each of them” (Acts 2:1–3).

There are certain feasts among the Hebrews, themselves indeed the greatest and chief, such as all those celebrated according to the number seven. Today’s feast also belongs among them: after seven times seven days have been completed, that is, after seven weeks have passed, it is observed and venerated both by us and by them.

Their first feast is celebrated every seventh day, concerning which they are commanded in the Law to observe the days of Sabbaths. The second is called Passover and is observed in the first month, when two weeks have been completed. The third is Pentecost, observed when seven weeks have been completed. The fourth is observed in the seventh month and is called the Feast of Tabernacles. In the seventh year there is a fifth feast, that whole year being regarded as entirely festive. The sixth feast is the Jubilee itself, most solemnly observed in the fiftieth year, after the cycles of seven times seven years have run their course. [Col. 1018C] Then the seventh and eternal feast is expected in heaven, signified through all these others over so many and such great ages.

It is therefore clear not only among us but also among the wise of this age that the number seven is most sacred and most perfect, since all times and all numbers are contained in it. For it consists of an even number, namely four, and the first odd number, namely three. But every number is either even or odd. Therefore every number is constructed from the parts of seven, and thus all other numbers are contained in this number.

This is why the Jews eat unleavened bread for seven days; why they celebrate feasts for seven days; why the hands of priests, when they are ordained, are anointed and consecrated for seven days; [Col. 1018D] why the high priest, dipping his finger in blood, sprinkles seven times toward the propitiatory and the doors of the tabernacle; why the leper is shut up for seven days; why Miriam, Moses’ sister, remained outside the camp for seven days; why the walls of Jericho are encircled seven times and fall; why we speak praise to the Lord seven times a day; why we are commanded to forgive our debtors not only seven times, but up to seventy-seven times; and why Solomon’s temple was built in seven years and dedicated in seven days.

These things appear to signify the seven churches, the seven lampstands, the seven lamps, the seven seals, the seven [Col. 1019A] angels sounding trumpets, the seven loaves feeding the great multitude in the wilderness, and the seven graces of the Holy Spirit. There are also many other things capable of having the same meaning, which the diligent reader may find in the sacred books.

Those feasts, therefore, are arranged according to the number seven which have a complete and perfect celebration. For this number is so perfect that it includes all numbers and all days within itself. Now let us return to Pentecost and the Jubilee and see with what sort and what degree of care they ought to be celebrated. These two feasts are adjacent: one is observed on the fiftieth day, the other in the fiftieth year. We cannot now speak of all the feasts, because each one is so great in itself that it demands not a general but its own particular sermon.

It has been said, and must still be said, that almighty God willed to arrange all these feasts according to the number seven; therefore he also appointed the seventh and final day as festive and solemn. What the seventh day signifies, the seventh week, the seventh month, and the seventh year signify as well. Therefore the fact that feasts are celebrated on the seventh day seems to signify that, when this life conducted in seven days is ended, there shall remain, as the Apostle says, a sabbath-rest and repose for the people of God; so that as he himself rested on the seventh day from his works, we too may then rest from our labours and weariness.

Through the number seven, according to which these [Col. 1019C] feasts are arranged and in which all days and numbers are also contained, what else must be signified except that our feast ought to be continual and perfect? Thus, for as long as we are in this world, we should never perform servile works, but should strive to devote ourselves to God’s praises and good works. For the person who abstains from good works keeps the Sabbath badly.

Moreover, the Jubilee, interpreted as “the year of remission,” cannot be observed otherwise than through continual celebration. In this year liberty is restored to slaves and inheritance to masters; all things growing in fields, vineyards, and trees become common to all. This whole year is festive, joyful, and solemn. No one is permitted to perform servile work, so that by its very image it may show that a person belongs not so much to this life as to the other.

Although in this life, in the times of the apostles, the feast of Jubilee was continually observed in the holy Church—

> [Note: Vatican manuscript: “is continually observed.”]

—especially among those who are of one heart and one soul, for whom not merely the fruits of trees, as for the Jews, but all things entirely are common to Christians, because, having already been granted liberty and inheritance, [Col. 1020A] they perform not servile but free works. Servile work, however, is not what a slave does, but that which draws even free persons into the devil’s slavery. “If sin does not reign in our mortal flesh, we are free and do free works” (Rom. 6:12).

As soon as the Jubilee began, priests sounded trumpets throughout the land, by which the whole people was prepared for the festival of the entire year. This too happened in our Jubilee, when our priests—the holy apostles—first began to sound trumpets and call the nations to faith and baptism. As it is written: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:4). And elsewhere: “Sound the trumpet at the beginning of the month—

> [Note: The Vulgate reads: “Blow the trumpet at the new moon,” etc.]

—on the notable [Col. 1020B] day of your solemnity, for it is a commandment in Israel” (Ps. 80:4).

But if we look to that feast and raise the eyes of our mind to that Jubilee which will be in heaven after this life, once all the weeks have been completed, this whole celebration of ours will seem to be a kind of shadow and image. “The Son of Man will send his angels with a trumpet and a great voice, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from the highest parts of heaven to their limits” (Matt. 24:31). These, indeed, will announce that eternal Jubilee. “For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise incorruptible” (1 Cor. 15:52). Then that feast will begin which shall be eternal and never have an end. Of this feast it is better to be silent than to say little, since no tongue is sufficient to proclaim its glory.

Now let us see what that fire and those tongues which appeared over Christ’s disciples signify, when all, as the Evangelist says, had gathered in one place. “Our God is a consuming fire” (Heb. 12:29). Rightly, therefore, did the Holy Spirit appear in fire: to consume sins, illumine the eyes of the mind, and set the whole human being ablaze with love of God. This is the baptism which John promised when he said: “I baptize you in water, but another comes after me who will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. 3:11).

The Holy Spirit also had to appear in tongues because he is the one who speaks in the apostles.

> [Note: Ascensian edition: “Because he is the one who speaks in us. The Holy Spirit, therefore, is the tongue; for he is the one who speaks in the apostles.”]

For who speaks without a tongue? This office belongs to no other member. Those who speak with this tongue do not need to consider how or what they should speak. Therefore, having received this tongue, [Col. 1020D] “the apostles spoke in diverse tongues the mighty works of God” (Acts 1:12). He lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

# THE FIFTH BOOK OF SENTENCES: ON THE PRAISES OF THE MOST BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

[Col. 1021]

## 554 CHAPTER ONE: On the Praise of Blessed Mary as the City of God

[Col. 1021A]

The Holy Spirit invites us, most beloved, through the mouth of David, the father of that Virgin, to praise the Mother of the Lord, saying: “Glorious things have been said of you, city of God” (Ps. 86:2).

A city is commonly called any great gathering of people, fortified on every side by walls and towers, so that by its fortifications they repel enemies and defend themselves through them. Therefore the Virgin Mary is not inappropriately called the city of God: virginity of mind and body so enclosed her on every side, as though with a wall, that no access of lust could ever be present, and every enemy was kept away from corrupting her virginity.

Thus Solomon applauds her praise, saying: “You are beautiful and fair, daughter of Jerusalem, terrible as an army drawn up in battle order” (Song 6:9). The Virgin Mary is rightly called daughter of Jerusalem, because she was daughter of the vision of peace: that is, daughter and mother of him who made peace for those far from God, namely the idolatrous Gentiles, and those near, namely the Jews, who were near to God through knowledge of the Law. Thus at his birth the angels sing: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

This daughter of Jerusalem is beautiful through the loveliness of inward virtues and fair through the example of virginity which she offered to the whole world. She is also terrible as an army drawn up in battle order, for no enemy dares approach one so surrounded by every virtue, since she is protected by the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit.

Thus glorious and mighty things are rightly said concerning this [Col. 1021C] city, not only by those of the present day but also by the ancient Fathers and angels. Is not what David, her own father, says of her in this same Psalm very glorious? “A human being was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86:5). In the case of other human beings, it is impossible for someone to be the founder of the city in which he is born, since before being born he cannot found a city. But Christ, who is the Most High, insofar as he is God founded this city before all ages—that is, he created his mother—and yet, insofar as he is human, he was born in her at the end of times, taking flesh from her. Thus it is marvellous and glorious in this city that he who founded it was born in it.

It was glorious and wonderful that, as a figure of this city, Aaron’s rod suddenly blossomed [Col. 1022A] in the temple and produced almond nuts without any moisture (Num. 17). For it signified that this glorious rod, which according to Isaiah (ch. 16) was the rod from the root of Jesse, bore the flower—that is, Christ—who is the flower of the field, that is, of the world, and the lily of the valleys, according to Solomon; and that she conceived him not from the heat of the mind, but from the Holy Spirit’s coming upon her.

Thus Solomon sings of the glory of this Virgin in the Song of Songs, saying: “A garden enclosed is my sister, bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain. Your outflowings are a paradise” (Song 4:12). The Virgin Mary was a garden in which were diverse flowers of virtues, and enclosed because it was fortified on every side by virginity. She is also a fountain sealed with the seal of the most holy Trinity. And her outflowings—that is, her fruits—[Col. 1022B] are paradise, that is, delights in which God takes pleasure. Isaac long beforehand smelled its fragrance, saying: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 27:27).

And Isaiah says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. 7:14). And Jeremiah: “The Lord will perform a miracle upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31:22); that is, the Virgin Mary shall carry in her womb Christ, whom the whole world cannot contain. And Ezekiel (ch. 46): “I saw a closed gate in the house of the Lord, through which the Lord entered and departed, and left it closed,” because she was a virgin before and after childbirth.

> [Note: This gives not the prophet’s words but the sense of the words.]

Thus the angel says to her: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you. Behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son; but the Holy Spirit shall come upon you, [Col. 1022C] and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1:28, 31, 35).

Rightly, therefore, did David say: “Glorious things have been said of you, city of God” (Ps. 86:3). Let us also, brothers, proclaim and praise the Mother 555 of the Lord as glorious with patriarchs, prophets, and angels, so that we may perceive her praying for us before her Son, and recognize that the Son assents to her on our behalf, for ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER II: On the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary
“**The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham. Abraham begot Isaac; Isaac begot Jacob; Jacob begot Judah and his brothers**” (Matt. 1:1). And so forth.

We have just heard in the Gospel reading [Col. 1022D] from what people, tribe, and [Col. 1023A] lineage the most blessed Virgin Mary drew her origin—the one from whom the Lord and our Savior himself was made according to the flesh. It was indeed very pertinent that the Evangelists should arrange and set in order this very long line of Christ’s generation, so that we may know not only from which fathers he was born, but also whence we have death and whence we have life.

The first head of this line is Adam; the second is Christ. This line begins with Eve and ends in Mary. At its beginning stands death; at its end, life. Death came through Eve; life was restored through Mary. The former was conquered by the devil; the latter bound and conquered the devil. For, since the line extends from Eve down to Mary herself, in her at last that hook was bound and incarnate, by which that Leviathan—the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan—was caught: so that he who entered into the kingdom through a woman might be driven out of the kingdom through a woman; and he who deceived the woman and bound her in his own bonds might himself be deceived and bound by this one woman.

For this is what the Lord says to blessed Job: “**Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook, and bind his tongue with a cord? Can you make sport of him as of a bird, and bind him for your maidservants?**” (Job 40:20). It is as though he said: You will not bind for your maidservants one whom even strong men could not bind. Yet I shall bind him through one maidservant of mine and deprive him of his strength.

This is that noble maidservant of whom we are now speaking: the most blessed Virgin Mary, who also speaks of herself, saying: “**My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced [Col. 1023C] in God my Savior, because he has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid. For behold, from this time all generations shall call me blessed**” (Luke 1:46–47). Observe her humility: she calls herself a handmaid, though God established her as queen of heaven and earth. For she had read: “**The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you shall find grace before God**” (Ecclus. 3:20).

But consider the power of God, who subdued such great pride through the humility of one virgin. He did not choose to send heavenly powers to overcome it; he sent one of his handmaidens, by whose humility and wisdom he was bound and overcome. Of his power and strength the Lord himself speaks to the same Job, saying: “**Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you: he eats grass like an ox. [Col. 1023D] Yet he trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth. There is no power under heaven that can be compared with him. He sees everything lofty, and he himself is king over all the children of pride**” (Job 40:10).

These are words of consolation, by which the Lord comforts blessed Job in his great afflictions, with which this most proud and wicked enemy afflicted him. For it is some consolation to him, when he hears against how great an enemy he waged war and, under the Lord’s protection, was not overcome. For behold, he who devours and destroys all peoples and nations as an ox devours grass was nevertheless unable, with all his strength, to conquer this one man—to provoke him, as he supposed, to blasphemy or to some other sin [Col. 1024A]. Hence it is also written: “**In all these things Job did not sin with his lips, nor did he speak anything foolish against God**” (Job 1:22).

That grass signifies peoples is attested by the prophet, who says: “**Truly the people are grass**” (Isa. 7:8). And why grass? Because it quickly loses its flower and beauty, withers, and perishes. But this Behemoth swallows all rivers and does not marvel; indeed, he even trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth. Scripture teaches us what we should understand by rivers where it says: “**The many waters are many peoples**” (Rev. 17:15). Yet Behemoth neither marvels nor considers it a great thing that he swallows other rivers, unless the Jordan itself should also flow into his mouth—the Jordan in which the Lord was baptized and through [Col. 1024B] which the people of the baptized are signified.

[Note: [Col. 1023] Saint Bruno interprets this passage no differently in his commentary on chapter 40 of the Book of Job.]

For, as it is written, his food is choice. He did not fear to sift even Christ’s disciples, and he incited Judas to betrayal (Luke 22). He does not concern himself with thieves and adulterers; he does not concern himself with the ignoble crowd. He persecutes monks and priests, and seeks to devour even bishops. “There is no power under heaven that can be compared with him.” Therefore he fears only those powers which are above the heavens, and he has already experienced both these and those. He conquered the former, but was overcome by the latter, according to the words: “**Michael and his angels fought with the dragon; and the dragon fought, and his angels, and they did not prevail, nor was their place found any longer in heaven**” (Rev. 12:7).

Therefore he fights against those who are [Col. 1024C] under heaven and who are still subject to vanities. Yet he sees everything lofty: his heart is exalted, his eyes are raised high; he still walks amid great things and wonders beyond him, and does not know how to think humbly. But if you wish to know how lofty are the things he sees, ask him himself, and he will answer you: “**I shall ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I shall exalt my throne. I shall ascend above the height of the clouds; I shall be like the Most High**” (Isa. 14:13). For this pride he was cast down, but he has not yet been humbled; he still persists in the same disposition. Thus it is not without reason that he is called king over all the children of pride. For all the proud, and the children of pride, serve him, obey him, follow him, and are ruled by him.

Yet this being, so proud and arrogant, so powerful and strong, was caught, mocked, and bound by one handmaid. O handmaid most blessed among women, Mother of God and most noble daughter of the heavenly King: by whose hook Leviathan was caught; by whose humility he was mocked as a bird; by whose wisdom he was bound as a thief and worthless slave. For in the flesh born from her, the incarnate Word was hidden as a hook in bait, because “**the Word was made flesh**” (John 1:14). What, then, is the Word in the flesh except a hook in bait?

Leviathan saw this bait and desired it. He did not think that anything lay hidden within; he believed it to be a mere man. He stretched out his tongue, and that tongue was bound and suspended by the cord of its own destruction [Col. 1025A]. Judas was the devil’s tongue, because through him he spoke to the chief priests, saying: “**What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?**” (Matt. 26:15). But this tongue was bound with a cord, because the unhappy traitor immediately went away and hanged himself with a noose.

All those through whom he speaks and reveals his plans are the devil’s tongue. But the Lord binds these tongues when he destroys their counsels and compels them, defeated by Catholic men, to be silent. Thus Arius was bound as a tongue with the cord of truth when his impious heresy was condemned by a council. But when he says, “**Can you make sport of him as of a bird?**” (Job 40:21), the sense is the same. For a bird, while it pays attention to bait, is often deceived and, suspended by a snare, is suffocated.

Hence it is said in the Psalms [Col. 1025B]: “**This dragon, which you formed to make sport of him**” (Ps. 103:26). He who made him also folded back his sword and reduced him to such a condition that not only men but women too can make sport of him. How many thieves, how many prostitutes, how many adulterers and murderers mock him daily! While he rejoices that he has already devoured them and holds them in his belly, they suddenly turn to repentance, burst forth from his impious womb, and leave him empty and void. “**The sinner,**” says the prophet, “**at whatever hour he is converted, shall live and shall not die**” (Ezek. 33:12).

In this passage the devil is called by three names. He is called Behemoth—that is, “beast”—because of his cruelty, for “**like a roaring lion he goes about seeking whom he may devour**” (1 Pet. 5:8). For he is the one [Col. 1025C] who says: “**I have gone around the earth and walked through it**” (Job 2:2). He is also called dragon because he is cunning and venomous and never proceeds by a straight path; for “**from the beginning he was a liar and did not stand in the truth**” (John 8:44). He is called a bird on account of pride, because although he has lost the wings of angelic dignity, he nevertheless still attempts to raise himself and, insofar as lies in him, is lifted above the heavens by proud intent.

Consider, then, how great the thanks are which we owe to the most blessed Mother of God; consider with what praises we ought to exalt and proclaim her—if only we are worthy that she should deign to receive, among all creatures, our praises—she by whose humility and wisdom this great enemy was caught, bound, and driven from the kingdom which he had unjustly possessed for so long. As her Son himself, our Savior and Redeemer, says: “**Now is the judgment of the world; now the prince of this world shall be cast out**” (John 12:31). Therefore let us praise her, let us proclaim her, and together with the archangel Gabriel say: “**Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb**” (Luke 1:48). He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER III. On the Purification of Saint Mary the Virgin

“**After the days of her purification according to the law of Moses had been fulfilled, they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law [Col. 1026A] of the Lord: Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord; and to offer a sacrifice, as it is written in the law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons**” (Luke 22:24).

There are two matters of which we shall speak in this sermon: the woman who gives birth, and the offering which she ought to make. For Moses says (Lev. 12:1) that a woman who, having received seed, gives birth to a male shall be unclean for seven days, and on the eighth day the child shall be circumcised. She herself, however, shall remain thirty-three days in the blood of her purification. But if she bears a daughter, she shall be unclean for two weeks; she herself, however, shall remain sixty-six days in the blood of her purification.

These two women, one of whom bears a male and the other a female, are the two parts of the Synagogue [Col. 1026B], one of which is good and the other evil. The evil part is that of which John the Apostle says to the bishop of the church at Smyrna: “**You are blasphemed by those who call themselves Jews and are not, but are the Synagogue of Satan**” (Rev. 2:9). Thus the Synagogue is divided into two parts: into the Synagogue of God and the Synagogue of Satan, into the people of God and the people of the devil.

The women, then, signify the parts of the Synagogue. That part of the people was good which, having received the seed of God’s word, bore a male; whereas the part which bore a female—that is, which was held by no observance of the law or any kind of righteousness—was evil and not good. Male children signify good works; female children are understood as evil works. The holy prophets are read to have had many sons and few daughters.

But let us first speak of the woman who was good, who bore males, who was unclean not for two weeks but for one only. The two weeks are the two periods: under the law and under grace, one of the Old and the other of the New Testament. The first extends from Moses to Christ; the second from Christ’s birth to the end of the age. That good woman, therefore—that part of the people which bore males, kept the law, and exercised itself in good works—was unclean for seven days because, until Christ’s birth, when that week was completed, it could not be freed from original sin either by circumcision, by the begetting of children, or by any other observance of the law. [Col. 1026D] For, as the Apostle says, “**the law brought nothing to perfection**” (Heb. 7:19). Thus throughout that whole period that woman could not be called clean, stained as she was by so great a blemish. She had original sin, and it was impossible for her to be clean.

[Note: [Col. 1025] Vatican manuscript: “and for her to be clean.” Likewise the Ascensian edition.]

But you say: Therefore this woman was cleansed when Christ was born, since the week ended at his birth? It is not so. Why? Because she still had to remain thirty-three days in the blood of her purification. Original sin was not removed by Christ’s birth but by his Passion and blood. For our Savior suffered in the thirty-third year from his birth, so that by the thirty-three days we understand the same number of years. Then, indeed, all who kept the law and bore males—that is, persevered in good works—were cleansed from original sin [Col. 1027A].

Christ’s blood therefore redeemed both those who were before him and those who were after him. Whoever held the faith and kept the law before Christ’s Passion was cleansed and redeemed by the shedding of his blood. Likewise are those of whom the Apostle says: “**Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. He who believes and is baptized shall be saved**” (Mark 16:7).

Let us now consider the evil woman, she who bears not males but females. Pride is an evil daughter; envy, avarice, [Col. 1027B] lust, discord, and disobedience are evil daughters. Any souls which bear these cannot be clean. Let them therefore cease from such childbearing if they wish to be clean; otherwise they shall be unclean for two weeks. We have already said that the first week extended to Christ, in which no one could be cleansed; the second extends to the end of the age. Therefore every soul that has neither kept the old law nor received the New Testament is unclean for two weeks.

Moreover, because she remains sixty-six days in the blood of her purification, she appears to be far from every purification. The number itself indicates this, showing such souls to be transgressors. There are ten words of the law, and whoever transgresses them is proved to be a transgressor [Col. 1027C]. Six times eleven makes sixty-six; and because in that number the number ten is exceeded and transgressed, transgression of the Decalogue is most clearly demonstrated. For six times ten is contained within the Decalogue; six times eleven exceeds the Decalogue. And what is it to exceed the Decalogue except to transgress the law? Such persons, therefore, are not redeemed or washed by Christ’s blood. Of this John says in the Apocalypse: “**He loved us and washed us from our sins**” (Rev. 1:5), so that they might keep God’s commandments and bring forth males.

Yet the things said of the aforementioned women do not seem to pertain to the blessed Virgin Mary, although she too kept the law—especially since it was not simply said, “a woman who bears a male,” but with the addition and qualification [Col. 1027D], “who, having received seed, bears a male.” This was said particularly in regard to her, because she alone gave birth without receiving any seed; she remained a virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, and a virgin after childbirth.

But the offering of turtledoves and pigeons, which she offered together with the Lord her Son, seems to pertain chiefly to her, who excels in the virtues both of chastity and gentleness. For these are signified in those birds, one of which is commended for chastity and the other for innocence. Therefore today the most blessed Virgin Mary offered to the Lord a most pleasing offering, one indeed prefigured by many other offerings before it, but such an offering as had never before been made [Col. 1028A].

We also, if we wish to offer God a worthy offering, ought to imitate this our queen and lady. Let us therefore offer a pair of turtledoves and two young pigeons, and render to the Lord integrity of soul and body, and innocence. Moses teaches us how we ought to make this offering. He wishes the priest who receives it to bend back the birds’ head toward the neck; after tearing open the wound, to let the blood run down upon the rim of the altar; to cast the crop and the feathers toward the eastern side; and to break the wings, but not cut them off completely.

This offering seems to belong to the perfect, and especially to monks. A man comes with an offering, asks to be received, offers turtledoves and pigeons, promises integrity of body [Col. 1028B] and soul, and—to speak in the example of blessed Benedict, who was most skilled in this matter—promises obedience, stability, and conversion of life. In these few words that most blessed man expounds to us the whole of this sacrifice.

Behold, the man has become a turtledove and a pigeon: let his head be bent back toward his neck, and let him walk with bowed head, which is a sign of humility. Let the crop be removed from him, where he used to store food, so that he may now learn to fast, having formerly devoted himself to gluttony. Let him cause the blood of his defilement to run upon the altar, so that, always mindful of his sins, he may say with the Psalmist: “**For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me**” (Ps. 50:5). For blood signifies sins, according to the words: “**Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, God of my salvation**” (ibid., 16).

He is stripped of feathers because he is commanded to abandon all possessions and to possess nothing of his own any longer. He casts them toward the eastern region so that, having them behind his back, he may no longer remember them. For since we are always tending toward the west and toward our end, we have the eastern region, as it were, behind our back. Let the wings be broken, because freedom to wander is taken away and stability of place and purpose is commanded. But they are not cut off altogether, because, if necessity should arise, he is still permitted to fly again for the good of the place.

Happy are those who become turtledoves and pigeons, who together with the Son of God are offered to the Lord by the Mother of the Lord and are joined to the Lord in one and the same offering. Who, etc.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary

[Col. 1028D]

“**The angel Gabriel was sent from God into a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a Virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the Virgin’s name was Mary. And when the angel entered to her, he said: Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women**” (Luke 1:26, 29).

Let us consider—

[Note: [Col. 1027D] Vatican manuscript: “If we consider.”]

—the person of the sender, the person carrying out the embassy, and the person to whom this embassy was made. If we also consider the embassy itself—of what sort and how great it is, and what counsels, what secrets, what and how great benefits it contains—then surely we shall understand that, from the creation of this world [Col. 1029A], no embassy has ever been made that can compare with this embassy. Never before or afterward were such words, such joyful counsels, such profound mysteries announced to this world.

In this embassy there was treated the incarnation of the Son of God, the renewal of the world, the restoration of the human race, the liberation of the saints, and the recovery of the heavenly homeland. Today the counsel was revealed by which death would be killed, original sin removed, life restored, and humankind—freed from the devil’s bondage and adopted by God as a son—returned to its ancient homeland. If the world understood what great glory this day had brought it, it would hold this day festive and celebrated above all days.

Today the Word was made flesh; today the Son of God was incarnate [Col. 1029B]. Had this not happened, he would never have been born, suffered, risen, despoiled hell, ascended into heaven, or sent the Holy Spirit to the apostles—in whom we have been baptized and in whom and through whom forgiveness of sins takes place. This, then, is the first feast; this is the beginning and cause of all other feasts. Let us all therefore celebrate this feast together, and rejoice with the blessed Virgin Mary at such tidings.

Let us now hear what the archangel Gabriel said: what words, what embassy, and, so to speak, what news he brought our Virgin from heaven. This messenger is faithful; he who sends him is truthful. Whoever does not believe this embassy to be true, let him be anathema maranatha. Speak then, Gabriel; speak to the Virgin, that we may hear. “**Do not fear, Mary, for you have found grace with the Lord. Behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Jesus. He shall be great and shall be called the Son of the Most High; and the Lord God shall give him the throne of David his father, and he shall reign over the house of Jacob forever, and there shall be no end of his kingdom**” (Luke 1:30, 34).

Behold, we have heard the embassy; we have heard the mystery of the eternal counsel; we have heard the words of our liberation. We have also heard that King and Prophet David speaks to this our queen, his daughter, concerning this embassy: “**Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people [Col. 1029D] and your father’s house, because the king has desired your beauty, for he himself is the Lord your God**” (Ps. 44:11–12).

“Hear,” he says, “my daughter, of my race and lineage, the nobility and glory of my family: hear what the angel says, what the heavenly messenger promises you.”

[Note: [Col. 1029D] Saint Bruno has the same passage, in the very same words, in his commentary on this passage of Psalm 44.]

Be cautious, be attentive, listen carefully, for the things announced to you are very great. See, therefore, understand, and receive the Word in your heart and in your womb: as a virgin you shall conceive and as a virgin you shall give birth, because he who shall be born from you will enter into you through the ear. For he is the Word, and the ear is the way of the word. The blessed Virgin Mary conceived in no other manner than by hearing and believing.

[Note: [Col. 1029D] The commentary quotes as far as this point.]

[Col. 1030A] Had she not heard, she would not have believed. She heard and believed, and by believing she conceived. “**Behold,**” she says, “**the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to your word**” (ibid., 28). Such was Christ’s conception; thus was he conceived, and thus the Word was made flesh.

“**And forget your people and your father’s house.**”—“**Rise, take the child, and flee into Egypt**” (Matt. 2:13). Flee to the Gentiles, because your people and your ancestral house will not receive you; rather, together with your Son, they will persecute and hate you. And indeed no creature is hated by the Jews as much as this Mother and Son. For they cannot love the mother who pursue the Son with such wicked hatred. Hence John the Apostle says: “**He came unto his own, and his own did not receive him**” (John 1:11).

[Col. 1030B] But what does the Lord say? “**A people whom I did not know has served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me**” (Ps. 17:44). “**Forget, therefore, your people and your father’s house.**” Leave all things; let your Son suffice for you, because he is your king and Lord your God, because he has loved your beauty and loveliness. Let him suffice for you. Let neither love of country nor affection for relatives be able to hold you back. If you possess him alone, you are rich, and in him you shall possess all things.

“**And the daughters of Tyre shall worship him with gifts**” (Ps. 44:13). All beautiful and noble virgins, whoever they are to whom the pleasure of this world is not pleasing and who know themselves to be in straits and in prison, will desire to unite themselves to him and will hasten to him with great gifts. For Tyre is interpreted “straits.” But those souls which are wandering, to whom pleasure and desire are pleasing, who walk not by the narrow path but along the broad way, desire to marry not Christ but the devil. Therefore the daughters of Tyre shall worship him with gifts, offering themselves and all that is theirs.

“And **all the rich of the people shall entreat your face**” (ibid.). What wonder, indeed, if rich and noble virgins should desire the countenance and beauty of the Mother, when it was said just above, “**because the king has desired your beauty**” (ibid., 12)? For she is exceedingly beautiful, she who could draw God himself into love of her by her beauty. It was indeed most fitting that he who is beautiful in form beyond the sons of men should choose a beautiful mother.

[Note: [Col. 1030D] Vatican manuscript: “should choose for himself a most beautiful mother.”]

Consider now [Col. 1030D] how great was her beauty, whose radiance and loveliness penetrated the heavens. There the angels marveled at her; from there Gabriel came straight to her. For he was sent to her who shone beyond all others, who was beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, and who surpassed every beauty by her own beauty. We cannot now recount all that this psalm contains in praise of her. Let us return to the words of the Gospel.

“**He shall be great and shall be called Son of the Most High**” (Luke 1:32). For he is indeed very great, since he is equal to the Father. “**And the Lord God shall give him the throne [Col. 1031A] of David his father, and he shall reign over the house of Jacob forever**” (ibid.). Concerning this throne it is written in that psalm in which the Lord, speaking of both Davids, says: “**I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him**” (Ps. 88:21). And a little later: “**He shall call upon me: You are my Father, my God, my God and the protector of my salvation. And I shall make him firstborn, exalted above the kings of the earth. I shall preserve my mercy for him forever, and my covenant faithful to him**” (ibid., 27–30).

Therefore the throne shall be eternal, since “**I shall establish his seed for age upon age, and his throne as the days of heaven**” (ibid., 30). The throne, then, shall be eternal, since the days of heaven too shall be eternal. “**If my sons violate my law and do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my ordinances and do not keep my commandments**” (ibid., 31–32), what shall I do to them? Certainly I shall not kill them, nor separate them from my kingdom, nor take my grace away from them. What then? “**I shall visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with stripes**” (ibid., 33). This is what the Apostle says: “**If anyone’s work is burned, he shall suffer loss; but he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire**” (1 Cor. 3:15): as through a rod, as through correction.

“**But I shall not scatter my mercy from him**” (Ps. 88:34). Yet he was certainly speaking of sons. Why, then, did he say “from him,” rather than “from them,” unless because all who are in his body are one in him? Those are not in his body who do not have faith, [Col. 1031C] or who, persisting in wickedness, do not care to return to him through repentance.

“**Nor shall I injure him in my truth, nor profane my covenant, nor make void the words that proceed [Col. 1032A] from my lips. Once have I sworn by my holy one: if I lie to David, his seed shall remain forever, and his throne as the sun before me, and as the perfect moon forever, and as a faithful witness in heaven**” (ibid., 35–39).

It was fitting, indeed, that we should believe what the Lord says even without an oath. Yet it pleased him to confirm his words by oath, in order to make us more certain of our salvation. Behold, he who had none greater by whom he might swear swore by his truth, by his holy one, by his beloved Son, by himself, because the Son and he are one. But what did he swear? That he would not injure the members of his Son, would not profane his covenant, would not make his words void, and that his Son’s seed and throne would remain forever.

What joy overflows in this psalm; what hope is given in it to sinners, whoever remain in the Church and do not depart from her. For she is the body [Col. 1032B] of Christ; she is the seed and throne of Christ, which, as has been sworn, shall remain forever. Otherwise the covenant confirmed by oath would be profaned, if either falsehood were found in it or all that it contains were not fulfilled. This psalm is the Church’s testament. This alone could suffice her, even if she had no other documents. Let her therefore rejoice in her testament; let her rejoice that she has been made God’s throne—the throne which shall shine as the sun in God’s sight, and as the perfect moon forever, and shall itself be the faithful witness in heaven to all these things. For no one who sees the heir there in such great glory can reproach either the testament or the testator.

## CHAPTER V. [Col. 1032C] On the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary

“**Because he has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid**” (Luke 1:48).

The most blessed Virgin Mary, mother and daughter of humility, teaches us how great is the power of humility. Seek this sermon above, in the second book *On the Ornaments of the Church*, chapter 5.

# SIXTH BOOK OF SENTENCES: FOR THE FEASTS OF MARTYRS, CONFESSORS, ETC.

[Col. 1031]

561

## FIRST CHAPTER: ON MARTYRS

[Col. 1031D]

### SERMON I
“Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone” (John 12:24). But if it dies, it bears much fruit. This is that grain of wheat which the virgin and untilled earth brought forth. Of it the Psalmist says: “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. 84:12).—“For the Lord will give goodness, and our earth will yield her fruit” (ibid., 13). By the immeasurable multiplication of this grain all the granaries of the Church have been filled [Col. 1032D]. From this grain of wheat is made that bread of which the Lord himself says: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” (John 6:41). It is also certain, and literally true, that if a grain of wheat is dissolved in the earth and dies, it bears much fruit. For God loves nothing unfruitful. He wills that nothing in his garden, nothing in his field, should be unfruitful. Thus he says elsewhere: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. 3:10). And in another place: “I am,” he says, “the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he will take away; and every one that bears fruit he will cleanse, that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:1).

For this is that true vine from which all this wine has flowed forth, which is offered to us in this Gospel. This is that vine, ever fruitful, whose every branch is fruitful, whoever faithfully clings to it. For the unfruitful are removed from it because, although they are in it through the sacrament of baptism, they are not in it through the merit of their life. Such an unfruitful tree was that of which the Lord said to the keeper of the vineyard: “Behold, for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree and have found none. Cut it down, then; why should it also occupy the ground?” (Luke 13:7). It would indeed at once have been cut down, had not that good keeper of the vineyard interceded for it, saying: “Lord, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it [Col. 1033B] and put in manure; and if indeed it bears fruit—but if not, you shall cut it down hereafter” (ibid., 8).

Such also was that fig tree in which, because he found no fruit, the Lord cursed it, and it withered. Such too are many other unfruitful trees, which are finally cut down and cast into the fire. And I would not believe that any unfruitful tree was planted in paradise, especially since the Lord says to the first human beings: “Eat of every tree of paradise. But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat; for on whatever day you eat of it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2:17). For in saying that they may eat of them all, he shows that all those trees are fruitful.

Therefore, since paradise signifies the Church, all the trees of the Church also ought to be fruitful [Col. 1033C]. For there are many trees in the Church. There is the tree of life, of which whoever eats—provided that he eats worthily—will not die. For of this tree it is written: “And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which shall yield its fruit in its season” (Ps. 1:3). And elsewhere: “To the victor I will give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God” (Rev. 2:7). There too is that tree which says: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord; I have hoped in the mercy of my God for ever and for age upon age” (Ps. 51:10). But what shall I say of those most noble trees, to whom he himself says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain?” (John 15:16).

The Church, then, has such trees as the trees of paradise signified. Thus the wheat of the Church grows, and thus abounds in thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold fruit. Its womb is not undeservedly compared with a heap of wheat. For it is she of whom it is written: “Your womb is like a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies” (Song 7:2). For so great a multitude of saints has been multiplied from this one grain of wheat [Col. 1034A] that it cannot be numbered because of its multitude. Hence the Psalmist says: “I proclaimed and spoke; they have been multiplied beyond number” (Ps. 39:6). “I shall number them, and they shall be multiplied beyond the sand” (Ps. 77:27).—“Your children are like young olive trees around your table” (Ps. 127:3).

This is that seed promised to the prophet Abraham, when the Lord said to him: “And your seed shall be like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the shore of the sea, which cannot be counted because of its multitude” (Gen. 12:17). Hence the Prophet also says: “Look to the hollow from which you were cut, and to Sarah who bore you” (Isa. 71:1). For to whom would it not seem wonderful that so great a multitude of people should come from one womb? “Rejoice, then, barren woman, you who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not give birth, because the children of the desolate woman are many, more than of her who has a husband” (Gal. 4:27).

But this whole heap of wheat, this whole multitude of all the saints, begotten from the one womb of mother Church, is surrounded by lilies [Col. 1034B]. For what do we understand by lilies except the protection of angels, the fragrances of virtues, and the white-clad host of teachers? For these are they who guard this heap of wheat, defend the children of the Church from the snares of malicious spirits, and by such a guard the people of God seem worthy always to imitate their fragrance and beauty.

The whole Church is fruitful; no part of it is unfruitful. For the Lord himself shows this when he speaks to her, saying: “Your teeth are like flocks of sheep that have come up from washing, all bearing twins, and there is none barren among them” (Song 4:2). Hence she herself says: “All fruits, new and old, my beloved, I have kept for you” (ibid. 7:2).—“For every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasury new things and old” (Matt. 13:52). For animals which do not reproduce and are barren are therefore forbidden to be offered to the Lord. Humility is good fruit; mercy is good fruit. Such fruits are gathered from the trees of paradise; God loves such fruit, and such fruit we ought to offer him.

## SERMON II

[Note: Title of the Ascensian edition: “On Christ the vine and his vineyard; applicable to any martyr.”]

### ON THE FEAST DAY OF ONE MARTYR

“I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he will take away; and every branch that bears fruit [Col. 1034D] he will cleanse, that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:1).

Behold, Christ is called a vine, and the true vine. But why a vine, and why true? A vine is so called because it bears wine. For all these words of the Gospels are wine—and not wine of any ordinary kind, but the finest wine, gathered and pressed from no other vine than this. Thus, at the beginning of his preaching, the Lord changed water into wine, so that the new vine might pour forth new wine, with which it might gladden those wedding guests and the steward of the feast.

[Note: Marchesius reads “might intoxicate”; so too the Vatican manuscript. Better is the reading of Cassinese manuscript 194, which has “might gladden.”]

It is also called the true vine, perhaps to distinguish it from that vine which bore wild grapes instead of grapes, and vinegar instead of wine. Its wine is sweet and ever pleasant; its words are ever true and are corrupted by no admixture of falsehood.

[Note: The same manuscript: “By no falsehoods.” The Ascensian edition reads: “by the admixture of no falsehood.”]

[Note: From the same Cassinese manuscript.]

But his Father is the husbandman. What does this husbandman do?

[Note: Vatican manuscript: “Do you wish to hear what? ‘Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he will take away, that it may bear more fruit.’ As many Christians as there are, so many are the branches of this vine,” etc.]

He cuts off barren branches, and prunes fruitful ones also, that they may bear more fruit. As many Christians as there are, so many are the branches of this vine. Some are good, others bad. The good are fruitful, but the bad unfruitful. The unfruitful are removed and burned; the fruitful are cleansed and pruned with the sword of the Spirit, that they may bear more fruit. The sword of the Spirit is the word of God and this Gospel discourse. What branches were those whose feasts we celebrate today! [Col. 1035B] How cleansed, how pruned, how carefully purified from every excess!

[Note: From the same manuscript.]

[Note: Vatican manuscript and the cited edition: “For it befitted such a vine to have such branches, which both abounded in fruit [Col. 1036D] and did not degenerate in flavour: like that vine of which we have already spoken above, which gave wild grapes instead of grapes and vinegar instead of wine. Not every vineyard is good,” etc.]

For such a vine ought to have such branches, which do not degenerate either in abundance of fruit or in sweetness of flavour. Not every vineyard is good, nor is every wine pleasant to drink. The wine of heretics is evil, and the Nazarenes fear to drink it. “Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable poison of asps” (Deut. 32:33).

[Note: The same manuscript and edition: “No vineyard is good except that which has been planted from this vine, which now speaks in this Gospel: ‘I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.’ Of this vine it is written: ‘A vineyard was made for the beloved on a horn, the son of oil,’ etc.”]

No other vineyard is good except one which is of the stock of the vine. Of this it is written: “A vineyard was made for the beloved on a horn, the son of oil” (Isa. 5:1). Solomon also says of it: “A vineyard belonged to the peaceful one in that which has peoples, and he handed it over to keepers. A man brings for it a thousand silver pieces. My vineyard is before me. A thousand are yours, peaceful one, and two hundred for those [Col. 1035C] who keep its fruits” (Song 8:11). These matters have been explained in that sermon entitled “On Peace.” Seek it above in the book *On the Ornaments of the Church*.

Those vineyards also are good of which the Church says: “The sons of my mother fought against me; they made me keeper in the vineyards. My own vineyard I did not keep” (Song 1:6). What charity: that someone should at times neglect his own vineyard and himself for the common benefit of all! This was done by him who says: “No one seeks what is his own, but what belongs to all, that they may be saved; he who became all things to all, that he might gain all” (1 Cor. 9:19).

That vineyard was once good too, of which it is written: “You transferred a vineyard from Egypt; you cast out the nations and planted it. You made a way [Col. 1035D] before it, planted its roots, and it filled the earth. Its shade covered the mountains, and its shrubs the cedars of God. It stretched out its branches to the sea and its shoots as far as the river” (Ps. 79:9). This vineyard was once good [Col. 1036A], but because it was changed into bitterness and degenerated from its first goodness, “the boar from the forest destroyed it, and the solitary wild beast devoured it” (ibid., 24), so that the Lord’s saying might be fulfilled: “Amen I say to you, there shall not be left here one stone upon another that shall not be destroyed” (Matt. 24:2).

For this is that evil vineyard whose wicked husbandmen first killed their master’s servants by diverse torments; then, when the heir came, said: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance shall be ours” (Luke 20:14). Concerning it the Lord himself rightly says: “Do you wish to know what I will do to my vineyard? I shall command my clouds not to rain upon it; I shall remove its hedge, and it shall be trampled down. I shall tear down its wall, and it shall be plundered; and [Col. 1036B] I shall make it desolate. The vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5:5). Its branches are the Jews, who because of their impiety have been scattered throughout the whole world and are a reproach among all nations.

This evil vineyard was signified by that vineyard from which Noah, drunk, lay sleeping and exposed his shame. Because the younger son mocked his nakedness, he was subjected to perpetual servitude with all his posterity. But the others, because they prudently and modestly covered their father, received the due blessing. These things refer to our Saviour, who, intoxicated by the cup of suffering, rested on the cross in the sleep of death. By his shame, of course, they understand death itself, spittle, scourges, and the ignominy of the cross. For these are what the Jews object against us, and they reproach us, as though with a shameful thing [Col. 1036C], because we worship as God a man who died and suffered things so disgraceful and shameful.

But we, covering our Father, say that these are not shameful but worthy of veneration. For Christ “had to suffer and thus rise from the dead. For how would the Scriptures be fulfilled, that thus it had to happen?” (Acts 12:3). For this is what the prophets foretold; it was necessary for us, since otherwise original sin could not be loosed. Yet the Jews do not believe this; persisting in their malice, they do not cease to mock the shame of the cross and Christ’s Passion. But what does Scripture say? “The Lord awoke like one sleeping, like a mighty man drunken with wine. And he struck his enemies upon their backs; he gave them everlasting reproach” [Col. 1036D] (Ps. 77:35). This was said of the Jews, whose entire posterity, because of their impiety, has been handed over as a reproach among all nations.

But what is said of the others? “Praise the Lord, all nations; and praise him together, all peoples. For his mercy has been strengthened over us, and the truth of the Lord remains for ever” (Ps. 116:1). He who lives and reigns, etc.

## SERMON III

[Note: Title of the Vatican manuscript and the edition: “On the Martyrs.”]

### ON THE FEAST OF MANY MARTYRS

“O God, the nations have entered into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have made Jerusalem into a keeper’s hut among fruits. They have given the dead bodies of your servants as food to the birds of heaven, the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth. They have poured out the blood of the saints like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them” (Ps. 78:1).

The inheritance of God, the temple of God, the city of God, and the garden of God are the holy Church, spread throughout the whole world, which suffers many persecutions from tyrants and malicious spirits.

[Note: Marchesius’s text is corrected from the same Cassinese manuscript.]

Therefore, seeing through the Holy Spirit this most noble city [Col. 1037B]

[Note: Vatican manuscript: “being destroyed by impious and wicked men.”]

being laid waste by impious enemies, and sympathizing with so great a calamity, the Prophet says: O God, the nations have violently entered into your inheritance, and tyrants have rushed upon your Church with excessive cruelty. Your inheritance is devastated, your temple defiled, your holy city destroyed, and your saints killed. Only a watch-post remains; exceedingly few remain. Elijah lamented this when he said: “Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have dug down your altars, and I alone remain” (3 Kings 19:10), as a watchman.

[Note: Vatican manuscript and cited edition: “And they seek my life. O cruelty! O impiety! It is not enough for them that they kill the saints by such harsh and refined tortures; but, to complete their iniquity and malice, they do not allow them to be buried. The flesh of the saints is exposed to birds and delivered to the beasts of the earth to be devoured and torn apart. Their precious blood is poured out—for precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints—and is trampled under the feet of the wicked as though it were something worthless. In them is fulfilled what is said in the Gospel: ‘Behold, I send you like lambs among wolves.’ And the Apostle,” etc.]

It is as though he said: It is not enough for them that they have cruelly killed the saints; they do not even permit their bodies to be buried, and the precious blood of your saints [Col. 1037C] is trampled beneath the feet of the wicked. Therefore the Apostle says: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are reckoned as sheep for slaughter” (Rom. 8:13).

Blessed John relates in the Apocalypse, where all the sufferings of the martyrs and all the disturbances of the Church are most fully described, that he saw a white horse, and he who sat upon it had a bow in his hand; and a crown was given him, and he went forth conquering so that he might conquer.

[Note: Vatican manuscript and edition: “This white horse, wholly beautiful and spotless, signifies the host of holy martyrs, in whom our Saviour sat and fought for them, as it is written.”]

That white horse, upon which he who sat had a bow in his hand, signifies our Saviour, who went forth fighting for his martyrs, as it is written: “You ride upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation” (Hab. 3:8).

[Note: The same interpretation occurs in the commentary on the Apocalypse.]

He has a bow in his hand, by which his preaching is signified; the words and sayings of that preaching are arrows by which the army of vices and malicious spirits is put to flight [Col. 1038A]. These are those arrows of which it is said: “The sharp arrows of the mighty, with desolating coals” (Ps. 119:4). What is signified by the crown given to him except victory? For the Apostle says: “No one is crowned unless he has contended lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5). Christ is crowned in each saint, because all their victory is his. And this is what he says: “He went forth conquering, that he might conquer” (Rev. 6:2), since the holy martyrs likewise say elsewhere: “In God we shall do valiantly, and he himself shall bring our enemies to nothing” (Ps. 77:59).

But after this horse another, a red horse, went forth; and it was given to him who sat upon it to take peace [Col. 1038B] from the earth, so that people might kill one another; and a great sword was given him.

[Note: The same manuscript and edition: “This red horse, stained with the blood of the saints and with the spurs of the raging enemy, signifies the host of tyrants. The devil sits upon them and makes them rush without any mercy to kill the saints. In these are those horses of which it is said: ‘He cast Pharaoh’s chariots and his army into the sea.’ In these are those horses and mules in which there is no understanding. This is also that wicked one who takes peace from the earth,” etc.]

The red horse which followed him whose rider was given power to take peace from the earth signifies the army of tyrants, bloodied with the blood of saints. The devil sits upon them and impiously drives them to kill the saints. Of these horses it was said: “He submerged Pharaoh’s chariots and his army in the sea” (Exod. 15:4). This rider is that wicked one who takes away peace from the earth, because, as prince of discord and enemy of peace, he continually disturbs the human race by laying snares and tempting it. He makes people kill one another and wage civil wars among themselves.

[Note: From the same Cassinese manuscript.]

He has a great sword while he strives to slaughter different people in different ways, binding some to one vice and some to another [Col. 1038C].

[Note: Vatican manuscript and edition: “A great sword was given to him, because he deceives wretched people by slaughtering them in many ways: killing and destroying one through pride, another through avarice, another through lust, another through envy, and another in some other way. By his counsel, therefore,” etc.]

Thus by his counsel and leadership blood is shed through the hands of tyrants. Of this the Prophet now says: “They have poured out the blood of the saints like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them” (Ps. 78:3).

Those sufferings of the holy martyrs, that great outpouring of their blood, were signified by those holocausts and sacrifices which the holy Fathers offered daily without number. Consider now how much animal blood was poured out when Solomon’s temple was dedicated. For at the dedication of that temple, one hundred and twenty-two thousand sheep and twenty-two thousand oxen are reported to have been slain, besides the offerings which they were accustomed to make every day, by which Christ’s Passion was signified. Thus, at the dedication of the Church, many thousands of saints were slaughtered for Christ’s name, whom that blood of animals and those offerings signified.

For what does one read there—“The Lord smelled an odour of sweetness” (Gen. 8:21)—except what the Psalmist says: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:5)? God does not delight so much in that smoke and the blood of animals as in the Passion of the holy martyrs, which those sacrifices signified.

After the flood, Noah the patriarch came out of the ark and offered God a great holocaust and sacrifice from every kind of clean animal. At that time no human being was offered, because the fullness of time had not yet come, when our Saviour was to be offered. All those clean animals which were then taken in one sacrifice signified this suffering and offering of the holy martyrs [Col. 1039B].

[Note: Vatican manuscript: “Who were later slaughtered for Christ’s name from every nation, every sex,” etc.]

They were later slaughtered for Christ’s name, of both sexes, every age, and every condition. We read of three sacrifices of holy martyrs: the first in signification, the second in suffering, the third in commemoration. The priests of the Old Testament performed the first; tyrants performed the second; our priests perform the third daily in the Church.

Of the third it is written: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and render your vows to the Most High. And the sacrifice of praise shall honour me; there is the way in which I shall show the salvation of God” (Ps. 49:14 ff.). And the Prophet says: “Remove all iniquity, and receive good; and we shall render the calves of our lips” [Col. 1039C] (Hos. 14:3). And the Apostle: “Through him,” he says, “let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name” (Heb. 14:15).

This sacrifice, therefore, which the Church daily offers in the praise and commemoration of the holy martyrs, was signified in that victim—

[Note: The Vatican manuscript corrects editions which read “is sacrifice.”]

—in which Moses commanded the priests first to make a pile of wood; then, after dividing the victim to be sacrificed piece by piece, first to place its head upon the pile of wood, and afterwards arrange the remaining members over it as far as the tail, which, as it is last in the whole body, is also to be placed last.

We make a pile of wood when we gather the people into one place. But when we recount a martyr’s suffering to the people, then we arrange the victim of rejoicing upon the pile of wood. In this victim the head is first to be placed, because one must first state where he was born, of what parents, and the beginnings of his life. Then one must state how he lived: that he was wise and humble; how from childhood he served God [Col. 1040A]; how he distributed all his possessions to the poor; how many miracles and wonders God worked through him; how steadfast he was in suffering; and how courageously he endured every torment.

[Note: Vatican manuscript and Ascensian edition: “This is the order [Col. 1040D] of the sacrifice: thus the victim of rejoicing is to be offered, and then finally,” etc.]

Such ought to be the arrangement of this victim in sacrifices; and finally, when fire is applied, the devouring flame consumes everything. By this it is understood that whatever is recounted to the praise and glory of a martyr should be faithfully believed and received with love. Read the passions of the martyrs, and you will find them written in this order. Thus in the Gospel blessed John first set forth the very head, saying: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1); then he set forth in order, down to the Passion, his words, miracles, and the rest.

There was once among the saints such love of martyrdom, and they hastened to the glory of martyrdom with such desire, that they voluntarily presented themselves and, though not questioned, declared that they were Christians. Someone was being tortured with harsh torments, and suddenly another person from the crowd cried: “I am a Christian, and I desire to die for Christ.” Each said in his heart that prophetic saying: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I shall take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115:3). He who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV: ON THE SAME SUBJECT

“Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity! For there the Lord commanded blessing and life for ever. It is like ointment upon the head, which descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron; which descends to the edge of his garment, like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion” (Ps. 131:1 ff.).

[Note: Those who have read Bruno’s exposition on this psalm will find it copied here word for word from beginning to end. It differs completely, however, from the commentary of St Bruno the Carthusian on the same psalm.]

Such is the sequence of the text. Let us now consider its meaning. Blessed are these brothers, upon whom God’s blessing and so great an abundance of graces descended. These are those brothers of whom the Lord says: “I shall announce to my brothers” (Matt. 28:10). And elsewhere: “You are all brothers, and do not call anyone on earth your father; for one is your Father who is in heaven” (ibid. 23:8). He is the one to whom we daily say: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (ibid. 6:9).

Rich and poor, noble and lowborn, master and slave, emperor and beggar—all say with one voice, “Our Father, who art in heaven,” in order to show themselves the children of one Father [Col. 1040D]. The more noble is he who is better. Many here are slaves who will be masters in the other life; and conversely, many here are masters who will be oppressed by harsh servitude in the other life.

What brothers were those whose feasts are celebrated today? Good brothers were blessed Sergius and Bacchus, who suffered such great torments for Christ. Good were Cosmas and Damian, good John and Paul, good Maurice and his companions, good also were many others who gave themselves over to death for Christ’s name. “The kingdom of heaven belongs to these, who despised the life of the world, attained the rewards of the kingdom, and washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. 7:14).

Such brothers dwell together in unity; their heart is one and their soul one. No one calls anything his own, but all things are common to them. Evil brothers are together in body, but far from one another through hatred. “It is good,” he says, “and pleasant for brothers to dwell together in unity.” Why is this so? Because there—that is, among such brothers—the Lord commands his blessing [Col. 1041B] and life which has no end. How does he command it? “Like ointment upon the head, which descends from the head upon the beard, and from the beard to the edge of his garment; and like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion” (from the same psalm).

Christ is the head of the Church, of whose body we are all members. Concerning this body the Apostle says: “For as in one body we have many members, and all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another” (Rom. 12:4).

[Note: From the same Cassinese manuscript.]

[Note: Vatican manuscript and edition: “Christ therefore has a beard in his body; he has hands and feet and the other members. Christ’s beard is the apostles,” etc.]

Christ’s beard is the apostles, who are first in the whole body, being joined to the head itself.

[Note: The same manuscript and edition: “The beard signifies that, having nothing soft or womanish in themselves, they are manly, strong, and masculine. Thus they are rightly called not bearded men, but rather the beard itself. The Lord commands priests not to shave the beard or let their hair grow. To grow the hair and have no beard belongs to women. Priests ought to have not womanish but manly faces. Not only the apostles,” etc.]

They are the beard because they were strong and manly as men, in accordance with the Apostle’s command that they should not shave their beard, since those dedicated to sacred things ought to have a manly face [Col. 1041C]. Not only the apostles, but also the holy martyrs of Christ may be called his beard, because they fought manfully and conquered most powerful enemies.

Thus the ointment descends from the head to the beard because the grace of the Holy Spirit came first from the divinity of our Saviour to the apostles and martyrs. Of this ointment the Lord says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach good news to the poor” (Luke 4:18). And the Psalmist says: “You loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44:8). Feeling this, the Church says: “Draw me after you, and we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” [Col. 1041D] (Song 1:4).

By this ointment the sick are healed; by it Jesus healed every illness and every infirmity. By this chrism the priests of the Church are consecrated; and from this Christ himself and Christians receive their names. Therefore it descends from the head to the beard, from Christ to the apostles. For the apostles had no virtue or grace which they did not receive from him. Hence the Apostle says: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7). “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge; to another prophecy; to another discernment of spirits; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another gifts of healing; to another kinds of tongues; to another interpretation of utterances. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each individually as he wills” (ibid. 22:8).

But from the apostles this great abundance of graces runs through the whole ecclesiastical body to the other members, reaching to the edge of the garment [Col. 1042A]. By the edge of the garment are understood those who will be the very last of all at the end of the age. See, therefore, how great is the abundance of this ointment: it flows down through so long a course, anoints and heals so many nations. Simon Magus wished to buy this ointment from the apostles; therefore he was deservedly condemned together with all his money.

Our Saviour is called Aaron, namely the first and greatest of all priests; his sons are priests, and those who are not his sons cannot be priests. Aaron is interpreted “mountain of strength,” an interpretation which seems especially fitting for him who is called the strong Lord and the Lord mighty in battle.

It follows: “Like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion” (Ps. 132:3). Hermon means *anathema*, that is, “division”; Zion means “watching” or “contemplation.” Hermon signifies the apostles, and Zion the Church. They are rightly called Hermon because they were first of all divided and separated from the Synagogue and followed Christ the Lord. Hence the Apostle says: “But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace” [Col. 1042C] (Gal. 1:13), and the rest.

Not only the apostles, however, but all Christians may be called by this name. For all receive this name in baptism, because there, renouncing the devil and his pomps, they are separated from all sins and vices; passing from the left to the right, they are divided from the goats and joined to the lambs and sheep. Hence it is said in the Psalm: “My soul was troubled within me; therefore I shall remember you from the land of Jordan and Hermon, from the little mountain” (Ps. 41:7). The land of Jordan and Hermon are those who have been separated from vices through baptism, because Jordan signifies baptism and Hermon division and separation.

Thus only the souls of the baptized praise God from the land of Jordan and Hermon. Of these it is said elsewhere: “Tabor and Hermon shall rejoice in your name” (Ps. 88:13). Therefore dew descends from Mount Hermon upon Mount Zion; by it are understood the faith, teaching, and Gospel preaching which came from the apostles into the Church. By this dew and rain the whole holy Church is watered, made fruitful, washed, and cleansed.

The evil mountains are Gilboa, upon which David, pronouncing a curse, said: “Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain come upon you, where the mighty men of Israel, Saul and Jonathan, fell” (2 Kings 1:21). For by these are signified heretics, who are drenched not with apostolic dew but with diabolical whirlwind. Blessed are those brothers who, filled with such dew, such rain, such ointment, and such grace, merited to hear: “Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity! For there [Col. 1043A] the Lord commanded blessing and life for ever” (Ps. 132:1 ff.). May he deign to grant this to us, he who lives, etc.

## SERMON V

[Note: The title of the Ascensian edition reads: “On praising God with musical instruments, by which the sufferings of martyrs and the afflictions and confessions of confessors are signified.”]

[Note: This entire sermon, word for word, except for the inserted verses, is taken from Bruno’s exposition of this Psalm; and the commentary of St Bruno the Carthusian on the same Psalm is wholly different.]

### ON THE SAME SUBJECT
“Praise the Lord in his saints; praise him in the firmament of his power” (Ps. 150:1). The Prophet had invited heaven [Col. 1043B] and earth and all the creatures that are in them to praise God; now he supplies them with the material by which they may praise him, and the instruments with which they may praise him. Let each take what pleases him and what seems suitable and useful to him. “Praise,” he says, “the Lord in his saints.” Take up this matter for praise, because in no other thing is he shown to be more praiseworthy. Say therefore: “God is wonderful in his saints. The God of Israel will give power and strength to his people: blessed be God” (Ps. 67:36). For if anyone wishes to consider the faith, wisdom, constancy, patience, and other virtues of the saints, which they deserved to receive from God, he will readily be able to recognize that God is exceedingly praiseworthy and wonderful in his saints. [Note: Vatican MS: “to be wonderful.”]

[Col. 1043C] Hence elsewhere, speaking in his own person and that of others, he who is speaking here now says: “Your knowledge has become wonderful beyond me; it has grown strong, and I shall not be able to attain it” (Ps. 138:6).

“Praise him in the firmament of his power.”

> Remember to praise the Lord for the firmament,  
> The earth made strong in faith, which the Creator of the world gives you.

For this firmament, which is called heaven and which God made by his ineffable power and might, signifies the apostles and the other saints. They have been endowed with such strength and brilliance that no creature can be compared with them.

“Praise him in his powers.”

> Man, the strength by which you fight is not your own, but Christ  
> [Col. 1043D] bestowed it upon you on the cross, on which, dying, he conquered.  
> Be certain therefore that you fight by his powers.

Whether we understand the powers of heaven, or the powers of miracles which God worked through the saints; or likewise wisdom, justice, fortitude, temperance, and the other virtues with which we read that the saints were adorned, and by which they overcame vices, evil spirits, and all their adversaries: it is altogether fitting that God should be praised and glorified in all these things.

[Col. 1044A] “Praise him according to the multitude of his greatness.”

> Let him be praised forever, whom no end confines.
