Perhaps you do not know how greatly you ought to praise him. Consider how great he is, and multiply your praises according to his magnitude. Therefore never rest from praise, because he whom you praise is immeasurable. “Therefore let my mouth speak the praise of the Lord, and let all flesh bless his holy name” (Ps. 144:21), not merely for a time, but for ever and ever.

“Praise him with the sound of the trumpet.”

> Let the lofty voice of our trumpets never fall silent;  
> The trumpet is the lofty voice; its sound is holy praise.

Having given the matter for praise, he next set forth the instruments [Col. 1044B] with which we ought to praise.

For trumpet, psaltery, and harp, likewise drums and choir, strings, organs, and cymbals, are instruments of the musical art suitable for divine praises. It is not everyone’s part to sound the trumpet; this is the office of bishops and teachers. To them it is said: “Sound the trumpet at the beginning of the month” (Ps. 73:4); and: “Cry aloud; do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58:1). They are the angels sounding trumpets in the Apocalypse. At the sound of trumpets the walls of Jericho fell, and on every side they afforded the people an entrance. By trumpets the Israelites were stirred up to battle, and by trumpets recalled from battle. By trumpets the year of Jubilee was announced, and the people prepared for the solemnity of the whole year. This was done through the ministry of priests, [Col. 1044C] because it signified the voice of bishops and priests, to whom it is said through the Prophet: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I shall require his soul from your hand” (Ezek. 3:21).

“Praise him on the psaltery.”

> The person whom a new life reforms bears the psaltery,  
> So that he may be able to devote himself to the ten words of the Law.  
> Every well-twisted string will give forth a tuneful sound.

To play upon the psaltery belongs to the perfect. God himself established this instrument and showed upon it ten strings with his finger, by which the Ten Words of the Law are signified. God, who is one, is called the first string: “You shall have no other god besides me.” [568] The second: “You shall not make for yourself an image.” The third: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain.” The fourth: [Col. 1044D] “Keep the Sabbath day.” But the fifth: “Honor father and mother.” The five which follow have these names: “You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness. You shall not covet your neighbor’s property.” Such harmony exists among these that whoever offends in one necessarily offends in all. Hence the apostle James says: “Whoever keeps the whole Law, but offends in one point, has become guilty of all” (Jas. 2:10).

David had once sinned against two strings [Col. 1045A], committing both adultery and murder, and had lost the whole psaltery. But after it was said to him, “Your sin has been forgiven” (2 Sam. 12:14), he immediately approached the psaltery and said: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” (Ps. 56:9).

Truly great is the glory of one who can keep these ten words and who touches and plays these strings without offense. Hence the Apostle says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12). For that person does not sin on the psaltery whose conscience does not accuse him.

“Praise him on psaltery and harp.”

> He sings on the harp who calms hearts by gentleness;  
> For the harp soothed the king’s breast from its frenzies.

As we have just said, the psaltery has ten strings. Three strings suffice on the harp, through which the mystery of the Trinity is signified. Hence the four living creatures and the Seraphim themselves, singing day and night, say: “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God of Sabaoth; the whole earth is full of his majesty” (Isa. 6:3). Many sing on the harp who cannot strike the psaltery. The psaltery pertains to action; the harp, to speech. One who preaches well but lives badly has a harp indeed, but does not have a psaltery. The psaltery is pleasant with the harp when speech accords with action and action with speech. Otherwise the harpist profits himself little, although by singing he may profit many others [Col. 1045C].

“Praise him on the drum.”

> Bright drums teach us to put to death  
> The mortal members of the flesh, because skin is that of an animal.

This instrument properly belongs to martyrs, although it also seems to belong to those who crucify their flesh with its vices and desires. For a drum sounds when struck, and unless it is beaten and struck it does not sound. It is dry, stretched skin, which resounds farther under repeated blows. But if you delight to hear the sound of a well-sounding drum praising God, hear the Apostle saying: “From the Jews five times I received forty lashes less one; three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned” (2 Cor. 11:23 [Col. 1045D]). The drum of blessed Stephen likewise, when it was struck and he was stoned by the Jews, gave forth such a great sound that it was heard on high before God’s throne. He said therefore: “Behold, I see the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7:55). Thus those praised God on drums who first afflicted and dried their flesh through fasts, and then gave it over to be scourged by the blows of tyrants.

“Praise him with drum and choir.”

> There will be no choir where the clergy lack a rule;  
> For they sit in order, and therefore ought to live in order.

Thus those praised in choir of whom it is said: “The multitude of believers had one heart and [Col. 1046A] one soul” (Acts 4:32). For those clerics and monks who love one another, honor one another, mutually obey and serve one another, rise for one another, bear one another’s burdens, and live under rule and discipline—these, I say, praise God in choir. For God looks not so much to harmony of voices as to concord of souls and minds.

“Praise him with strings.”

> When the saints are tortured by the hands of a tyrant,  
> The Lord is praised with strings; for “string” is called  
> The torture of flesh, the harsh affliction of the heart.

By these strings we understand no instruments other than the very bodies of holy martyrs, which were often stretched upon the rack, the scaffold, and the cross, like strings upon a psaltery. Those therefore who endured such things undoubtedly praised on strings.

“Praise him with strings and organ.”

> May our organs praise God without end of days.  
> The organs are called the voices of teachers,  
> Which they sound with tongues, conceived from their deep bellows.

Organs and drums have one meaning. Both signify the mortification of the flesh, whether through abstinence or through martyrdom’s passion. For those preachings of bishops are performed on the organ which proceed from a body dried and mortified by abstinence [Col. 1046C]. Hence the Apostle says: “I chastise my body and reduce it to slavery, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become rejected” (1 Cor. 9:27). That preaching, therefore, is rejected which proceeds not from a chastised and mortified body, but from flesh fattened and indulged. For organs are made from the skins of dead animals and dried hides. Thus they fittingly signify those who live in many abstinences.

[569] “Praise him with cymbals of jubilation.”

> The sounding cymbals of God are the two choirs:  
> This one new, that one old; here Paul, and here blessed Peter,  
> Once sang when he called both us and Judah.

For he praises on well-sounding cymbals who confirms his words and discourse by the authority of both Testaments. The two Testaments are two cymbals, which sound sweetly when one strikes the other and they answer each other mutually. Hence deep calls to deep; hence we are commanded to sleep between the two choirs; hence the two Cherubim look mutually upon each other; and hence disciples are sent out by the Lord two by two.

“Let every spirit praise the Lord.”

> Let every spirit bless him now and forever. Let it praise and lovingly worship him, whom mother Rachel adores—  
> Now indeed fruitful, but formerly barren and without seed.  
> May the Father, the Spirit, and the Son hear this. Amen.

## CHAPTER II. ON CONFESSORS

[Note: [Col. 1047D] The title in the Ascensian edition reads thus: “On salt and light from the Lord’s words, and the city set upon a mountain: concerning the apostles and the other teachers and confessors.”]

## SERMON I

[Col. 1047A]

We have just heard, while the Gospel was being read, the Lord saying to his disciples: “You are the salt of the earth; you are the light of the world. A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5:13–14). What beautiful and fitting names the Lord gives to his disciples! How worthy and appropriate it was that such names should be bestowed on such men, who were being sent to season and illuminate the whole breadth of the world! [Note: [Col. 1047D] These same words have been taken from St Bruno’s Commentary on Matthew.] “You,” he says, “are the salt of the earth; you are the seasoning of humankind. Other people ought to be instructed by your example, taught by your wisdom, and shaped by your humility and patience” [Col. 1047B].

For salt signifies wisdom not only in Holy Scripture but also in secular literature. Hence a certain comic poet says [Note: [Col. 1047D] Terence, *Eunuchus*.]: “He who has the salt that is in you,” plainly using “salt” for wisdom. Hence it is said of another man [Note: [Col. 1047D] Horace on Lucilius, *Satires*, Book I.] that “he scrubbed the city with much salt”: that is, he wisely and fittingly reproved all whom he found throughout the city worthy of rebuke. Salt is excellently used for wisdom, because just as foods without salt are insipid and have no taste, so the other virtues without wisdom are useless and make no progress. Hence children coming to the faith are fed with salt immediately at the beginning, because without wisdom [Col. 1047C] they can neither possess faith nor know God himself.

We are not now speaking of the wisdom of the world, which is folly before God, but rather of that wisdom which leads people to eternal life. We are not speaking of the wisdom taught by Plato and Aristotle, but rather of that which Peter and Paul taught through the Holy Spirit. This wisdom is easily learned because it is found by believing. [Note: [Col. 1047D] The Vulgate has: “Unless you believe, you shall not remain.”] “Unless you believe,” says the prophet, “you shall not understand” (Isa. 7:9). Do you wish to be wise? Fear God and keep his commandments, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1:16). Fishermen and peasants who fear God are wiser than very learned bishops and priests who neglect salvation. This, then, is the wisdom of Christians: to turn from evil and do good. The Jews and Gentiles do not possess this wisdom, and therefore they are blind and walk in darkness. Every food without this salt is insipid; every virtue without wisdom is useless. Other peoples have humility, patience, justice, mercy [Col. 1048A], and other virtues; but because they do not possess this wisdom, whatever they possess, they possess uselessly. For this alone leads people to the kingdoms of heaven, concerning which the Lord himself says: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:49). Likewise it is said: “Everyone shall be salted with fire, and every sacrifice shall be salted with salt” (ibid., 48). Hence Moses also says: “You shall not remove the salt of the covenant of the Lord your God from your sacrifice. In every offering of yours you shall offer salt” (Lev. 2:13).

It is clear, therefore, that no sacrifice, no service, none of our gifts is pleasing to God without this salt, without faithful and humble wisdom. The waters of Jericho, as is read, were bitter, barren, and unhealthy; but when Elisha cast salt into them, they were healed. What does it mean [Note: [Col. 1047D] Vatican MS and edition: “But Elisha came, having been asked by the people of that place to heal the barrenness of the waters. Therefore he took salt and cast it into the waters, and immediately they were healed of every harmful affliction. What, then, does it mean,” etc.] that [Col. 1048B] these waters could not be healed without salt? “Many waters,” says Scripture, “are many peoples” (Rev. 17:15). The whole world was sick, barren, and full of bitterness. But when the apostles came—to whom it is now said, “You are the salt of the earth”—and had seasoned the waters with the salt [570] of this wisdom and sprinkled the peoples, [Note: [Col. 1048D] From the same Cassinese MS.] all bitterness was driven away; and those peoples sprinkled by those waters were made, from barren, most fruitful in good works. [Note: [Col. 1048D] Vatican MS and edition: “All sickness was healed; and those who had previously been barren became most fruitful and began to bring forth good fruit. Matt. 7: ‘For every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and thrown into the fire.’ Therefore this was what that salt and those waters signified. Hence also,” etc.]

Hence too all churches cannot be dedicated without salt. For a church cannot be washed and baptized in any water other than that which has been seasoned and sprinkled with salt. This, then, is the water of wisdom, by which we both drink and are washed. It is rightly called the water of wisdom, because it has been seasoned with the salt of wisdom; it alone makes people wise, and no one can be wise without it. “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5). Every wisdom is foolish which tends elsewhere and shows another way [Note: [Col. 1048D] Vatican MS: “not that one.”] than the way which leads to the kingdoms of heaven.

Because Lot’s wife was turned into a pillar of salt, it ought greatly to profit us as an example and warning, so that her punishment may become our salvation and medicine. Let us not look back, nor seek in thought and desire those things which we have already left behind; but, stretching toward the things before us, let us hasten to the blessedness promised to us. Since the apostles are called the salt of the earth and the light of the world, the two expressions seem to signify one and the same thing: divine wisdom is both light and seasoning to us. Whoever does not have it is blind; whoever does not have it is tasteless, unfit, and foolish.

The holy apostles and teachers are also signified by that city set [Col. 1048D] upon a mountain [Col. 1049A]. Of this mountain it is written: “Come, let us ascend the mountain of the Lord and the house of the God of Jacob, and he shall teach us his ways” (Isa. 2:3), etc. And elsewhere: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who proclaim good news to Zion. Raise your voice with strength, you who proclaim good news to Jerusalem” (Isa. 40:9). Our Savior himself also speaks of himself, saying: “I have been established by him as king upon Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming his commandment” (Ps. 2:7).

The mountain, therefore, is the Church; the city is the apostles and teachers, by whose protection and strength the rest are defended, and to whom all flee as to an impregnable refuge. There are therefore as many cities as there are bishops and teachers, because those placed on mountains cannot be hidden or concealed [Col. 1049B]. Hence the saying: “Son of man, I have appointed you a watchman to the house of Israel” (Ezek. 3:17). This man who had been stationed as a watchman sat upon a mountain. Hence bishops are interpreted as “overseers” or “those who attend.”

Not only churches, however, but also each individual virtue may be called a mountain. Great is the mountain of humility; great is the mountain of mercy; likewise peace and patience are mountains. Bishops and priests, therefore, are invited to these mountains when it is said through the prophet: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who proclaim good news to Zion.” Therefore one who wishes to undertake the office of preaching should first ascend the mountain. This is what our Savior signified when he so often led with him into the mountains not only his disciples but also the crowds which followed him. “Seeing the crowds,” says the Evangelist, “Jesus went up the mountain” (Matt. 5:1). And elsewhere: “Jesus took Peter, James, and John and went up the mountain” (Matt. 17:1). Hence the Evangelist says that he went up the Mount of Olives according to his custom. Notice that he says, “according to his custom.” The disciples too retained this custom and frequently assembled on this mountain. Jesus found them reclining there when he ascended into heaven.

The Mount of Olives is interpreted as the mountain of mercy, because in Greek *eleon*, in Latin, means mercy. Blessed is that city, blessed is that bishop, who is situated upon this mountain. This is the high mountain from which the Lord ascended into heaven, [Col. 1049D] from which a straight way to heaven is prepared for us; whoever dwells on this mountain is secure. At judgment, it will be asked upon what mountain each person lived. But the dwellers of no mountain will have such glory at judgment as those who have dwelt on the Mount of Olives: the mountain of mercy and peace, the mountain of charity and loving-kindness. For peace, loving-kindness, mercy, and charity appear to signify almost the same thing.

And see now what the Lord will say at judgment: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25:34). Why? “Because I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was a stranger and you received me; I was sick and you visited me; [Col. 1050A] I was naked and you clothed me; and I was in prison and you came to me” (ibid., 35 ff.). Whose works are these, if not mercy, charity, loving-kindness, peace, and holiness, without which, as the Apostle says, no one shall see God?

Let the Prophet therefore say, and say again: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who proclaim good news to Zion.” Do you wish to preach? Do you wish to evangelize? Do you wish to be believed? Do you wish your speech and preaching to be received? First ascend this high mountain; be merciful and kind; love peace, loving-kindness, and charity; then preach and speak confidently. For all will obey you and gladly receive your words. Many preach well but live badly, concerning whom the Apostle says: “You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege? Why then, you who teach another, do you not teach yourself?” (Rom. 2:21–22) [Col. 1050B]. Such men have not ascended the high mountain. Yet the Prophet commands all preachers to ascend the high mountain.

But the Lord and our Savior draws and leads with him into the mountains not only preachers but all people: “When,” he says, “I have been lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12:12). To him the Church also says: “Flee, my beloved; become like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of spices” (Song 8:14). We see, then, that the Lord loves mountains. “Therefore those who are in Judea should flee to the mountains” (Matt. [Col. 1050C] 24:16). It is not granted to all to ascend every mountain, for they are many. Have you ascended the mountain of faith? Pass on to the mountain of mercy; follow Jesus ascending. [Note: [Col. 1049D] Vatican MS: “into heaven.”] “Whoever follows him does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” (John 8:12). May he himself deign to grant this, he who, etc.

## SERMON II. ON THE SAME SUBJECT

“No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house” (Luke 1:33).

A little earlier in this Gospel, the Lord and Savior says that the queen of Sheba came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom (Matt. 12). Solomon, therefore, was a lamp [Col. 1050D] burning and shining, who, placed upon the lampstand of his whole kingdom, illuminated all the surrounding nations by his splendor and enlightened them by his wisdom. This queen came, as is written in the Books of Kings, with a great retinue and camels carrying abundant riches. She gave Solomon one hundred and twenty talents of the purest gold, many precious stones, and much spice—such as had not formerly been brought to Jerusalem. She came to question the king about many questions which she had in her heart. After receiving a sufficient answer concerning them all, she said: “The report which I heard [Note: [Col. 1050D] Vatican MS 1294: “concerning you.”] in my own country is true, and not even half [Col. 1051A] of your wisdom has been reported to me” (3 Kgs. 10:8). Seeing his houses, households, servants, royal food, and the burnt offerings which were offered, she had no spirit left in her. Solomon gave her whatever she requested of him, besides those things which she had offered as a royal gift.

We must therefore say what the queen of Sheba signifies; what her retinue and camels signify; what the riches, precious stones, and spices she brought with her signify; and likewise what Solomon, the houses, households, servants, and the other things signify. This queen is the holy Church, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “The queen stood at your right hand in clothing embroidered with gold, clothed round with variety” (Ps. 44:11). This woman came from the ends of the earth. She came from the rising and setting of the sun, and from the south [Note: [Col. 1051D] Vatican MS: “from the north and the sea.”], to hear [Col. 1051B] the wisdom of Solomon—namely, that Solomon who says of himself: “Behold, one greater than Solomon is here” (Luke 10:31).

Those camels bringing such great riches seem to be the patriarchs and prophets. These are the camels of whom it is said to the same Church: “A multitude of camels shall cover you, the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah. All shall come from Sheba, bringing gold and frankincense and proclaiming praise to the Lord” (Isa. 60:6). “All,” he says, “shall come from Sheba,” following this queen of Sheba of whom we speak. If you wish to see the riches which these camels bring to us and to our kingdom, open the treasures which they carry, and you will see inestimable riches. We call the books treasures; in them are stored purest gold, precious stones, and much spice. By all these we understand spiritual riches, the fullness of every wisdom and knowledge, and all things able to suffice for the adornment and healing of the soul. Therefore there are as many treasures as there are books of the prophets.

From these treasures the Lord and Savior himself sometimes took what was necessary for him. For when, after his resurrection, he appeared in the form of a traveler to the two disciples of whom the Gospel speaks, in order to strengthen their faith, beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them all the Scriptures concerning himself. In doing this, he plainly put his hand into the treasures of the prophets and drew out those riches from them by which he healed the weak minds of the disciples and strengthened them in [Col. 1051D] faith and love for himself.

The unique and singular office of camels is to carry burdens; no other animal is considered so fit for this service. If anyone wishes to consider these very great burdens of our camels, he will rightly understand that holy patriarchs and prophets are signified by camels. Moses alone, so to speak, brought us five sacks filled with such riches and full of such a weight of gold that scarcely all the people of this world can lift and carry them—yet this single camel carried them. Likewise Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the other prophets brought us great weights of every kind of wealth [Col. 1052A], which the queen of Sheba—that is, the holy Church, our mother—does not cease daily to offer to our Savior, the true Peaceful King signified by that Solomon.

That psalm whose title is “For Solomon” must be understood of this Solomon, because it cannot be understood of the first Solomon. [Note: [Col. 1052D] Vatican MS: “cannot in any way be understood.”] For how could it be understood of him? “All kings of the earth shall adore him; all nations shall serve him. And he shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the world” (Ps. 71:11, 8). Let us therefore offer him our gold; let our wisdom, purity, and religious devotion serve him; whatever honorable conduct we have, let us offer it to him. Let us always come to him with fragrances and spices, as this queen of Sheba did, and as Mary Magdalene, Mary of James, and Salome did, who bought spices in order that, coming, they might anoint him—Jesus, that is.

Let us ask him about our questions; let him teach us, let him answer us; let us seek no other teacher. One taught by Truth cannot err. “All wisdom is from him, and was always with him, and is before the age” (Ecclus. 1:1). We have seen his houses; we have seen his servants and ministers; we have tasted the foods of his table. We have approached his burnt offerings and sacrifices. When the queen of Sheba saw only the figure of all these things, she lost her spirit through excessive wonder and astonishment. Let us likewise lose the spirit of arrogance and pride, that we may deserve to possess his Spirit. “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3) [Col. 1052C]. Blessed is that spirit whose poverty is good. Of it it is also said elsewhere: “Answer me quickly, O Lord; my spirit has failed” (Ps. 142:7).

We ought to be his houses, servants, handmaids, and ministers. The saints are called not only God’s house but also his temple. “Do you not know,” says the Apostle, “that you are the temple of God and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16). The Lord himself speaks of such ministers, saying: “Father, I will that where I am, there my minister may also be” (John 12:26). The apostles, then, are ministers; bishops and priests are ministers; deacons too are interpreted as ministers. For the Lord himself deigned to become a minister, as he says: “I came not to be served but to serve, and to lay down my life as a redemption for many” (Matt. 20:28) [Col. 1052D].

The pages of both Testaments are his table. Of this table it is written: “You have prepared a table before me against those who afflict me” (Ps. 12:5). We have two great tables, the New and Old Testaments, whose foods are most sweet and beneficial both for refreshment and for health. Upon this table hot loaves are commanded to be placed every Sabbath, before the lampstand set there to illuminate those great delicacies. Thanks be to God, we are now accustomed to these foods and know their sweetness and taste [Col. 1053A]. This table shows us the living bread which came down from heaven. It taught and showed us the cup of the New Testament. At this table the apostles minister; Paul, the servant of Jesus Christ, ministers at it; from it he receives the wisdom which he speaks among the perfect.

The queen of Sheba brought so much gold that, if it were divided, ten talents would fall to the share of each apostle. For one hundred and twenty makes twelve times ten. But what more can a person who has ten talents possess? For when the Lord commanded that the hundred minas should be given to him who had ten, the answer was: “Lord, he has ten minas” (Luke 1:31), as if to say: What more can be given to one who has attained the height of all perfection? Similarly, the king of Tyre brought Solomon one hundred and twenty talents of the purest gold, from which the vessels of the temple were made. It was not without mystery that the king of Tyre and the queen of Sheba agreed in this number.

The Lord and Savior, to whom none can be compared except the Father alone and the Holy Spirit, after saying, “The queen of Sheba came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom,” added most excellently: “Behold, one greater than Solomon is here.” For how could he fail to be greater than Solomon, when he was Solomon’s creator and Lord? [Note: [Col. 1053D] From the Cassinese MS, Marchesius is corrected. Both Vatican MSS add: “He said this of himself: ‘Behold, one greater than Jonah is here.’ And I say, and say truly, not concerning himself but concerning his servant—namely, that servant whose feast we celebrate today, the most blessed Benedict—‘Behold, one greater than Jonah is here,’ etc.”]

He indeed wished this to be understood truly of himself; nevertheless, concerning his servant, blessed Benedict, whose feast we celebrate today, I can truly say: “Behold, one greater than Solomon is here.” Perhaps you ask in what respect he is greater. In [Col. 1053C] wisdom, justice, fortitude, temperance, and, beyond all these, richer and more powerful than Solomon. I do not speak of the wisdom of this world, which is folly before God, and to which Benedict never wished to draw near; but of that wisdom which is true and leads a person to eternal life. Nor do I speak of temporal riches, which were carried away from the temple by Egyptians and Chaldeans, but of eternal and ever-abiding riches, which are stored in heaven by angels. [Note: [Col. 1054D] The same Vatican MS adds this.] Blessed Benedict abounded in these riches; he was always exceedingly rich in them, and stored them there “where thieves do not dig through or steal” (Matt. 6:20). Of such riches the Apostle says: “As needy, yet enriching many; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things” (2 Cor. [Col. 1053D] 6:10).

I do not dare call that man wise and just who, abandoning the God of his fathers—besides whom there is no other God—worshipped and adored the gods of the nations, which are nothing but demons. Who would say that he possessed fortitude and temperance, when, emasculated among women, he was so overcome by lust and softened by the blandishments of women that he built temples for his wives in which they might sacrifice to their idols? It is true what our holy Fathers say about this man: that from good beginnings he came to a bad end. Yet there are some—would that it were true!—who affirm that he later chose discipline and performed penance. [Note: [Col. 1054D] The opinion of certain Fathers: that Solomon did penance at the end of his life.] For God is merciful and readily forgives; he receives the repentant and repels no one who comes to him. “For the sinner, in whatever hour he is converted, shall live and shall not die” (Ezek. 43:12).

Oh, if this queen of Sheba had come to blessed Benedict and heard wisdom from his mouth; and if she could even now come and see his houses, his sons and brothers, his tables and food; how all things are ordered and so well arranged; how all have one heart and one soul, and no one calls anything his own, but all things are held in common among them; how all love one another [Col. 1054B]; how all obey one another; what love, what charity, what affection is among them all—if, I say, that queen of Sheba, so prudent, wise, devout, and dedicated to God, could have seen all these things, she would truly have lost all her former spirit, because she would have deserved to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Yet the queen of Sheba comes to us daily—indeed, she does not come, because she is always with us. We are her members; she is our mother, namely the holy Church, signified by that queen. She bears and offers many spices to our Savior Jesus Christ, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III. ON THE SAME SUBJECT
[Col. 1054C] We read in Genesis (Gen. 26:15) that Abraham’s servants dug wells, while the Philistines filled them with earth. Abraham’s servants dug many wells, which he gave various names. One he called *Calumny*, another *Enmities*, another *Breadth*, another *Beersheba*, that is, abundance or satiety; another was called that of the *Living and Seeing One*. These names assigned to the wells show most plainly that something besides the literal sense must be sought here.

Let us say, then, what Abraham, the servants, the Philistines, and these wells signify. Abraham, whose name is interpreted “father of many nations,” is Almighty God, the Father and Lord of all creatures. His servants—those, I mean, who dig the wells—are understood to be the apostles, bishops, [Col. 1054D] and teachers. Among them blessed Paul was exceptionally skilled in such work, and by his natural ability and practice left us great expertise in this art.

These wells may be understood as the books of the prophets and that other depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, to which few have been able to reach by digging. The Philistines, however, are heretics, as also Jews and philosophers, who, not understanding the teaching of the apostles and prophets yet expounding it, always try to stop up [Col. 1055A] these waters. Thus the Philistines are rightly interpreted as “falling through drink,” because, drunk with the vineyard of Sodom and the cup of Babylon, they fall everywhere through error and cannot walk with firm steps in the way of truth.

The wells are both many and one. For although there are many books in the two Testaments, all nevertheless say one thing: all proclaim one faith and one teaching. Similar water and similar knowledge are found in them all. The names are different, but the faith and teaching are one.

Therefore, wherever in Holy Scripture there is something which Jews and heretics misunderstand wickedly and perversely and use to calumniate us, there undoubtedly is the well called *Calumny*. For example, when we speak of the Trinity, the Jews immediately [Col. 1055B] bring a charge against us and object to us that Scripture which says: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord” (Deut. 6:5). Likewise the Arians, when we say that the Father and Son are equal, cite against us the authority of the Son himself, where he says: “The Father is greater than I” (John 10:28). Thus the well of enmities is also set between us and them: we dig it, while they fill it in.

Scripture says that the Philistines disputed concerning the well called *Breadth*. This, therefore, is the well of Breadth of which it is said: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 118:96). For there are few matters in which heretics and Jews contradict us, if we look to the field of the Holy Scriptures and their very great breadth. Even against our Savior himself, while he was still [Col. 1055C] living among them, the Jews customarily made this one charge: that he healed on the Sabbath and said that he was the Son of God.

Thus, in that well called Breadth is understood all that Scripture in which we and they think alike and do not contradict one another. But [574] where there is contention between us and them, there are wells of calumnies [Note: [Col. 1055D] Vatican manuscript: “of calumny.”] and enmities.

But the well of Beersheba, interpreted “satiety” and “abundance,” signifies the whole fullness of both Testaments, by which we are refreshed most abundantly every day. The same is signified by that well which is called of the Living and Seeing One. For all divine Scripture and all wisdom belong to him who always lives and sees all things. Hence it is also written: “All wisdom is from the Lord God, and has always been with him, and is before the age” (Ecclus. 1).

[Col. 1055D] Abraham lived beside this well of Beersheba when Abimelech came to him to make a covenant with him. And he gave him seven ewe-lambs; when Abimelech received them from his hand, Abraham said: “These shall be a testimony for me that I dug this well” (Gen. 26). So too, if heretics, Jews, or Gentiles ever wish to make a pact with us, let us approach the well; let us come to the Gospels; let us all drink together from one spring and hold one faith. Let them receive the seven ewe-lambs from our hands, by which are signified the seven [Col. 1056A] graces of the Holy Spirit—graces which no one but Christians can either give or receive. In no other way may a covenant and concord be made between us and them. Only those receive these ewe-lambs who are reborn from water and the Holy Spirit. They are a testimony to us of the well from which we drink and of the faith we hold.

Abraham’s servant found Rebecca at the well (Gen. 23), through whom Holy Church was signified. She was to dwell among these wells and never depart from them. And when she was now returning and drawing near to the house, behold, Isaac had gone out into the field to meditate; and he was going along that road which leads to the well called that of the Living and Seeing One.

It is not without reason that all men and women make their way to wells and hasten to the [Col. 1056B] waters. By these we are washed and satisfied, and, what is greater, united to the Creator of all. Likewise Jacob, fleeing Esau and coming into Mesopotamia, found Rachel by a well (Gen. 29). She was feeding sheep; and after removing the stone from the mouth of the well, by which the well was closed, he watered the sheep and kissed her, showing her that he was her brother.

It is not devoid of mystery that the holy man is said to have found his sister and wife at a well. For no soul can be the sister or wife of our Savior, who is signified by Jacob, unless it first comes to the waters of baptism and to the wells of the Holy Scriptures, and drinks from the springs of Israel. For he is the one who removed from the mouth of the well of both Testaments the stone; he is the Lion from the tribe of Judah who opened the book; he is the good Shepherd, “who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1:5).

[Col. 1056C] Moses also, fleeing from Egypt (Exod. 2) and coming into the land of Midian, found Zipporah at a well, whom he afterward took as his wife. The priest of Midian had seven daughters, who also fed their father’s sheep. When they wished to water the flocks, shepherds came upon them and drove them away. Then Moses defended the maidens, drove out the shepherds, and gave drink to the sheep.

He signified our Savior, who was to take Holy Church as his bride; Zipporah signifies this Church, since *Zipporah* is interpreted “beautiful.” Of the Church it is written that she has neither spot nor wrinkle [Col. 1056D] (Eph. 5). And in the Song of Songs it is said: “You are altogether beautiful, my beloved, and there is no spot in you” (Song 7). He himself defended her from evil shepherds, by whom heretics are signified. Of them the Lord himself also says: “If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women, go out and feed your kids beside the shepherds’ tents” (Song 1:8).

The history relates (Num. 21) that the people came to the torrent Arnon; and when they had no water to drink, Moses commanded that only the leaders of the people should dig a well with their staffs. When they did so, water came forth in abundance. Therefore they all sang together: “Let the well rise up.” They sang responsively: “The well which the princes dug, and the leaders of the multitude prepared, by the giver of the law and with their staffs” (Num. 21:18–19).

[Col. 1057A] In these leaders of the people are figured the apostles, bishops, and all prelates of the Church. For they are those who bear staffs [Note: [Col. 1057D] Vatican manuscript and the Ascensian edition: “Moses explained to us most clearly that Abraham’s servants who dug wells must be understood as the apostles. For the princes are the apostles and these men, and all prelates of the Church. These are those who bear staffs,” etc.], although some of them do not understand why they bear a staff, nor do they wish to dig wells; and at times they hinder those who wish to dig.

Behold, Moses commands—or rather the Lord, who is signified through Moses—that the princes and those who bear staffs should dig wells and open the Scriptures. Yet bishops hide their staffs and bury in the ground the money entrusted to them [Note: [Col. 1058D] Vatican manuscript: “dig under,” *suffodiunt*.], allowing the people to perish of thirst. What sort of diggers once existed! What wells, and how many, they dug! What waters they drew up [Col. 1057B] from the deep—living waters, indeed, springing up into eternal life!

Such a man was blessed Gregory; such were Jerome and Augustine; and such were Ambrose and Hilary. Such also were many others who refused to be idle. But what shall I say of blessed Benedict, who made for us so excellent a well [575], whose most healthful and sweetest water benefits all who thirst and wish to drink, both for refreshment and for salvation? After the apostles and evangelists no well has been made which has satisfied so many people and delivered them from the danger of death and from every affliction.

Whatever toil has wearied us, brethren, let us hasten to the wells. There we shall find Jesus himself, weary and seated at the well, speaking with the Samaritan woman. [Col. 1057C] For the Evangelist says: “Jesus, wearied from his journey, was sitting at the well. And behold, a woman came from Samaria to draw water” (John 4:6). Great mysteries were revealed at that time, when our Savior deigned to reveal himself to that woman at the well. Let it now suffice us to say only this: if weary Jesus came to the well, how much more ought we, in all our weariness and labors, to seek every consolation at the wells of the Holy Scriptures! And, as the Apostle says, “through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures let us have hope” (Rom. 15:1).

For Jesus is always found there; his consolation is ready there; there all who are weary are restored, comforted, and made glad. We have said enough about wells. [Col. 1057D] We have said nothing about cisterns. They too have good water, as it comes from above and descends from the clouds. “For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1:17).

Solomon speaks of cisterns, saying: “Drink water from your own cistern and streams from your own well. Let your springs flow abroad; distribute waters in the streets. Have them for yourself alone, and let strangers not share in them” (Prov. 5:16). My cistern is the Gospel; from it I delight always to drink. Since it is difficult in certain [Col. 1058A] matters, it is not without reason also called a well. And since we ought not conceal its waters and teaching, but hold them in common with all Christians, it is rightly said: “Let your springs flow abroad, and distribute them in the streets” (ibid.).

But because it is written, “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine” (Matt. 7:6), it is fittingly added: “Have them for yourself alone, lest strangers share in them.” For strangers are all who do not belong to our faith. This water, which flows from that most noble spring, is not to be shared with such persons. Of that spring it is written: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. 33:10). May he deign to grant this to us, he who lives and reigns, etc.

## SERMON IV. ON THE SAME SUBJECTS

[Col. 1058B]

“Let your loins be girded, and burning lamps be in your hands” (Luke 12:35). None can be burning lamps except those who have their loins girded. They may indeed be lamps, but they cannot be burning. Unless the lower fire is extinguished, the higher one cannot shine. The lower fire is lust; the higher—what else is it but the grace of the Holy Spirit? The lamps, moreover, are those who, unless they possess self-restraint and chastity, minister not light and brightness but darkness and blindness. “For if the blind lead the blind, both fall into a pit” (Matt. 15:14): this is the Lord’s sentence.

Of such lamps the Prophet says: “There I shall bring forth a horn for David; I have prepared a lamp for my Christ” (Ps. [Col. 1058C] 131:17). Hence the Gospel also says: “John was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5:35). Of such persons the Lord also says: “No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place or under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house” (Luke 11:33).

Therefore, whoever wishes to be a lamp must gird his loins and keep continence and chastity. Thus those who guard Solomon’s bed must be girded. Solomon’s bed is the Church—of that Solomon, namely, who says: “Behold, more than Solomon is here” (Matt. 12:42). Thus it is said in the Song of Songs: “Behold Solomon’s bed: sixty mighty men surround it, of the mightiest of Israel, all holding swords, most skilled in war, each with his sword upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night” (Song 3:7).

Those are well girded who have their sword upon their thigh: that sword by which most chaste Judith killed Holofernes (Judith 13). The Apostle commands not only bishops and priests, but indeed all Christians, to be holy, chaste, and continent. For he says: “Let those who have wives be as though they had none; and he who is loosed from a wife, let him not take a wife” (1 Cor. 7:27).

## SERMON V. ON THE SAME SUBJECTS

“A certain man, going abroad on a journey, called his servants [Col. 1059A] and entrusted his goods to them. To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one, to each according to his own ability; and [576] immediately he departed” (Matt. 25:14–15).

This man is our Savior, who is true God and true man. He went abroad not according to his divinity, which is everywhere, but according to his humanity: he bore our flesh up to heavenly things and placed it at the Father’s right hand. Happy is that journey abroad, where strangers, immediately made citizens, are enriched with such great riches that they forget all that has gone before.

The five talents, the two, and the one signify the same thing; and the two mean as much as the one. Some wish to understand by the five talents the five senses of the body: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. [Col. 1059B] They are called bodily senses because their instruments are in the body and are members of the body itself; but the senses themselves belong not to the body but to the soul. Take away the soul, and the instruments remain empty; for neither do the eyes see nor [added leaf: the ears] hear, nor are they instruments of sight and hearing themselves; and the same is true of the others.

It is therefore evident that the instruments belong to the body, while the senses themselves belong especially to the soul. The five senses consist in the soul’s intelligence alone. There are no other instruments there by which the senses are differentiated. Intelligence itself alone serves in place of eyes, ears, nostrils, mouth, and hands. The soul sees, hears, smells, tastes, and touches by intellect alone. It does not employ different [Col. 1059C] instruments for different senses, because intellect alone suffices in all.

Therefore the one talent is intellect, in which alone both the five talents and the two are contained, since the five senses, memory, and will consist in intellect alone. Whoever has one talent—that is, intellect—also has two talents, that is, memory and intellect. He also has the five talents: namely, sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. For whoever has that one has all; and whoever does not have all cannot have that one.

For, to say nothing of greater matters, we cannot understand even one word of two syllables without memory. For example, when *homo* is said, unless we commit the first [Col. 1059D] syllable to memory so that we can join it to the following syllable, we shall certainly never understand the whole word, whose parts we do not retain in memory. It is therefore evident that intellect cannot exist without memory.

Whoever has the one talent necessarily has the two; and the two—memory and intellect—cannot exist without the five senses. For what is without sensation can possess neither intellect nor memory. Therefore whoever has the two also has the five. The one talent, then, signifies the same thing as the five and the two. To whom intellect is given, to him memory and intellect are given together; and in addition the five spiritual senses are given to him.

Hence another Evangelist does not mention five or two talents, but only one [Col. 1060A] talent, which he calls not a talent but a mina. For he says: “A certain man going abroad called his servants and gave them ten minas” (Luke 19:13). There were ten talents and ten servants. He did not give ten to each, but one to each. This is understood from the fact that, when the Lord returns, they say: “Lord, one mina has gained ten minas”; and: “Your mina has made five minas” (ibid., 16, 18). In saying “one” in the singular, they show that they received not ten but one.

And it is rightly said that there were ten talents and ten servants, because all numbers are contained in this number, of which we have often already spoken. But when he says that this man, going abroad, called his servants and entrusted his goods to them, it may perhaps seem unsuitable if this is understood [Col. 1060B] of the five senses. For how could our Savior then have given his disciples senses which they had received at birth, and which are possessed not only by Christ’s servants but even by the devil’s servants?

This must therefore be understood not of the senses of the body but of the senses of the soul, through which, as we have said, spiritual understanding is signified. The Lord gave this understanding to his servants when he went abroad; no human being can possess it except from him and through him. The Jew does not possess this understanding; it belongs properly to Christians. Hence the Apostle says: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 6).

Those possess this understanding who seek not earthly things but heavenly, and who always desire to [Col. 1060C] please God in all they do. Behold, the money has been given; let each person consider how he works with it. Soon, and after a little while, the Lord will come to settle accounts with his servants. “But who, do you suppose, is the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord has appointed over his household, to give them food in due season? Blessed is that servant whom, when the Lord comes, he finds doing so” (Matt. 24:46).

Blessed is he whom he finds faithfully dispensing his money, his food, his spiritual provision, and the banquet of the divine word. For he will deserve to hear: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I shall appoint you over many things. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:23). Then [Col. 1060D] some will be appointed over ten cities, others over five cities. This plainly shows that the glory of the saints, though great enough for all, will nevertheless be greater for some and less for others.

“For,” says the Apostle, “star differs from star in brightness; so also is the resurrection of the dead. One is the brightness of the sun, another the brightness of the moon, and another the brightness of the stars” (1 Cor. 15:41). But although brightness in glory will differ, blessedness, however, [577] will not differ; it will be altogether the same, because the glory of each will be the common joy and gladness of all. For as there is now harmony among all the members of our body, so it will be among all the members of that heavenly city.

Let us now see what the Lord will say also to him who hid his [Col. 1061A] talent and buried his lord’s money in the earth. The Evangelist says that the one who had received one talent came and said: “Lord, you entrusted one talent to me, which I kept stored away in a cloth. Behold, you have what is yours. I feared you, because you are a harsh man: you reap where you did not sow and gather where you did not scatter” (Luke 19:14).

I thought to myself, as though he were saying: I should hide your words in my heart, lest, if I spent your money in vain and proclaimed your words to those who would not obey, there should be labor for me alone and a greater punishment for them, because they could no longer have an excuse—since they would know and understand their lord’s will. For when you are to judge and [Col. 1061B] condemn even those upon whom you did not sow and over whom you did not scatter the seeds of your word, what, we think, will you do to those who heard the words daily yet refused to obey them?

Yet how empty and useless such an excuse is, the Lord’s own answer shows: “Wicked and slothful servant, you knew that I am a harsh man, reaping where I did not sow and gathering where I did not scatter. Why then did you not give my money to the bank, so that, when I came, I might at least have demanded it back with interest?” (ibid., 22).

“If you knew,” he says, “that I was such a person, how did you not fear to offend me?” It was not fear but sloth that caused this. For “the sluggard would not plow because of the cold; therefore he will beg in summer, and nothing will be given him” (Prov. 20:4). Therefore, whether those subject [Col. 1061C] to their prelates obey or do not obey, the prelates must not be silent. Hence the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Son of man, I have set you as a watchman over the house of Israel. Unless you announce to the wicked man his wickedness, I shall require his soul from your hand. But if you announce it and he refuses to listen to you, he shall die in his wickedness, but you have delivered your own soul” (Ezek. 3:17).

Let no one, therefore, wish to hide the money entrusted to him or the talent committed to him. “He who hides grain is cursed among the peoples” (Prov. 11:26). Let no one put a lamp under a bushel. The table of the shewbread was also set not within the veil but outside it. It is said of the priest that, when he enters or leaves the sanctuary, unless the bells are heard [Col. 1061D], he shall die (Exod. 28). The bells of priests are their tongues, voices, and words. To these it is said: “You who remember the Lord, do not be silent, and give him no silence” (Isa. 62:6).

All of us have some share in these talents; no one can excuse himself, except perhaps one who has neither sense nor understanding. Whoever lacks these is lower than beasts, since even beasts have sense and understanding. What sensation is in the body, intellect is in the soul. No one can do either any good or any evil without them. Nor is anything imputed to righteousness or sin to those who act without them.

[Col. 1062A] At present anyone may hide his talent; but the Lord will come, and he does not fail to know what he gave: it will be required from each person—whatever he was able to do and refused to do. From evil and slothful servants will then be taken both the talent and its reward, and it will be given to him who has ten talents. But whoever has been faithful and has worked well with the talent entrusted to him [Note: [Col. 1061D] Vatican manuscript: “entrusted.”] will hear from the Lord with joy and exultation: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I shall appoint you over many things. Enter into the joy of your Lord,” etc.—he who lives and reigns, etc.

## SERMON VI.—ON THE SAME SUBJECTS

“Watch, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come. But know this: that if the master of the house knew at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly watch and would not allow his house to be broken into” (Matt. 25:13).

[Col. 1062B]

“God will come manifestly [Note: [Col. 1061D] Ascensian edition: “manifestly.”]; our God, and he will not be silent” (Ps. 39:1). This will occur at the judgment. But even now the Lord comes daily: daily he calls his servants, and those whom he finds watchful and persevering in good works he brings with him to heavenly things; and, as the following words show [Note: [Col. 1061D] Vatican manuscript and the cited edition: “He will appoint them over all his goods” [Col. 1062D]: “Blessed,” he says, “is that servant whom, when the Lord comes, he finds watching. Amen, I say to you, he will appoint him over all his goods,” etc.], “he will appoint him over all his goods” (Matt. 21:48).

[Col. 1062C] If we look to the final coming, he will find both good and evil all awake. Then there will be no time for sleeping, nor for either good or evil persons to do anything, but only for fear and awaiting judgment. “Therefore, while we have time,” as the Apostle says, “let us do good to all” (Gal. 6:10). For this is what it means to watch: to persevere in good works.

That soul sleeps—indeed, lies as though dead—which is negligent and slothful and does no good. People keep watch to guard their [578] houses. Yet riches are greater and thieves fiercer here than there. Those riches are temporal; these are eternal. Those thieves are visible; these cannot be seen. “For our enemy the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5:8).

But anyone can watch, since even thieves watch. Hence someone says:

> To slaughter men, thieves rise by night.  
> *(Horace, Epistles.)*

[Col. 1062D] Will you not awaken to preserve yourself? But such watchings are evil. He, however, watched well who said: “At midnight I rose to give praise to you” (Ps. 118:62). He not only watched, but by watching also praised God. Those watches are good which are not idle and are kept in the praises of God. Of these he says elsewhere: “If I give sleep to my eyes, or slumber to my eyelids, or rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob” (Ps. 131:4).

He watched, then, in order to build in the dwelling-place of his body a house worthy of God, not in order to give himself to idle words and vanities. [Col. 1063A] The Apostle calls for such watchfulness when he says: “It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep, for our salvation is nearer now than when we believed. The night has passed; the day has drawn near. Therefore let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light; let us walk honorably as in the day” (Rom. 13, following).

Truly, that person watches well who flees the works of the devil and of darkness and, clothed in the arms of light and truth, serves God honorably and in good order. Hence he says elsewhere: “Watch, you righteous, and do not sin.” It is better not to watch than to watch and sin. “Watch and pray, stand firm in the faith, act manfully, be strengthened in the Lord, and let all things be done in charity” (1 Cor. 16:13). He watches well who does all these things; one who watches thus is not idle.

[Col. 1063B] Scripture says of the Savior himself that he spent the night in prayer on the Mount of Olives—that is, on the mountain of peace and charity, the mountain of mercy and compassion. Those who watch and pray on this mountain will hear at the judgment: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 15:34). Why? Because you watched and prayed well; because you dwelt with me on the mountain of mercy. “For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you received me” (ibid., 5:25).

Such watchfulness is good; it is not idle; it pleases the Lord, and he commands us to practice it. Judith kept such watches, she who killed Holofernes while he slept, leaving us an example so that, if we too wish to destroy the spirit of fornication, we may [Col. 1063C] devote ourselves to fasts and prayers. By these arms she conquered; by these he was overcome.

It is said of the valiant woman, through whom the Church is understood, that “her lamp shall not be extinguished in the night” (Prov. 31:18). It is also said that “she rose in the night and gave prey to her household and provisions to her maidservants”; in this her watchfulness is most clearly praised.

When our Savior was born, he appeared not to sleepers but to those watching. For the Evangelist says: “There were shepherds in the same region, keeping the watches of the night over their flocks” (Luke 2:8). To them the angel of the Lord appeared and said: “Behold, I announce to you great joy, which shall be for all the people, because today there has been born to you the Savior of the world, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David” (ibid., 10).

[Col. 1063D] Let the shepherds of the Church hear, let bishops and priests hear this: let them watch over their flocks; let them always watch and be concerned for the people entrusted to them. Let them hear the Apostle saying: “Apart from the things which are outside, my daily pressure—the concern for all the churches” (2 Cor. 11:28).

When our Savior came to the disciples and found them asleep, he commanded them to watch, saying: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. 26:81). Watchfulness and prayer, then, have great power against all diabolical temptations. If the disciples were afraid while the Lord slept in the boat, and could not be secure [Col. 1064A] until he awoke, how can the sheep be secure while their shepherd sleeps or does not watch?

Noah, sleeping, exposed his shame, which his son Ham saw and mocked. Let prelates therefore watch, lest they perhaps become the laughter and reproach of those subject to them. Lot also, sleeping, corrupted his daughters. Had he watched, he would have retained awareness of himself and never committed so great a crime.

You likewise, whoever you are, who sleep securely and violate and destroy both daughters—namely, soul and flesh—when you allow them to wander unlawfully and commit fornication. Of the rich it is written: “They slept their sleep, and all the men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 75:6). Therefore, as often as the rich sleep—as often as those wise persons who are rich in heavenly treasures give themselves to idleness and negligence—they lose true and spiritual riches.

[Col. 1064B] Two harlots disputed before Solomon; one of them had killed her son, for while asleep she crushed him. The other was so negligent and drowsy that, without her knowing, her son could be taken from her bosom. Both were evil, both were harlots, since they had been so negligent and drowsy. Yet the one was worse, because after killing her own son she also tried to kill the other woman’s son.

It is also written in the Gospel that “a certain man sowed good seed in his field, and while men slept, an enemy came and oversowed tares among the wheat, and went away” (Matt. 13:24). Let those who are watchful and prudent rejoice, into whose [Col. 1064C] [579] harvest the enemy cannot enter and whose good works he cannot defile with the seed of his falsehood. But let those who sleep and are negligent fear lest the good seed of God’s word, sown in their breasts, be snatched away by this enemy. As is read elsewhere in the Gospel: “The devil comes to take the word from their heart, lest, believing, they should be saved” (Luke 8:12). “For blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it” (ibid. 11:28). May he deign to grant this to us, he who lives, etc.

## SERMON VII. ON THE SAME SUBJECTS
Our Lord and Savior speaks in the Gospel, saying: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). Hence the Psalmist says: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit [Col. 1064D] within me” (Ps. 50:12). That heart is not clean which is full of hatred, wickedness, and evil thoughts. Of it the Lord himself says: “From the heart proceed evil thoughts, fornications, thefts, murders, adulteries, false testimonies, and the like, which defile a person” (Matt. 15:29). Such hearts, therefore, are not clean. “For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Luke 6:45): what overflows from the heart is made manifest.

That heart is clean in which vain and false things are not stored up, but rather the sayings and utterances of God. Such a heart, plainly, was possessed by him who said: “I have hidden your utterances in my heart, that I may not sin against you” (Ps. 118:71). Hence Solomon also says: “With all vigilance guard your heart.” [Col. 1065A] The publican beat his breast, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13), for he understood that by the counsel of his heart he had sinned and offended God. For this reason priests receive from every offering the breast and the right shoulder (Lev. 7): so that, being sound of heart and strong of breast, they may be able to give good and useful counsel, from the good treasure of their heart, to all who come to them. Many hearts are needed by those who must fill other people’s hearts with their counsel and answer all who question them concerning many matters.

This, indeed, is our treasure; here our riches are stored. Therefore let us keep and guard our hearts with all watchfulness and diligence. Among the other priestly ornaments, by God’s command, the breastpiece of judgment was made [Col. 1065B] to adorn and fortify the breast and heart of the high priest, and, as though by a sign placed upon it, to display the treasure stored within.

> [Note: The commentary of St. Bruno gives the same exposition on Exodus, chapter 28.]

The breastpiece of judgment was square and double, a span in measure, made of gold, blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted fine linen, in embroidered work. It had twelve stones set in four rows, upon which were engraved the names of the twelve sons of Israel. Its very name shows that something great is signified in this ornament: namely, that it is called not merely a breastpiece, but a breastpiece of judgment. He whose breast is adorned with such an ornament must consider that the judgments proceeding from it should be reasonable, and should never depart from justice and reason.

Let the bishop always look upon the breastpiece; let him read in the book of his own breast; let him see what it is called. It is great wisdom, and greatly profitable, to know its name. This book alone could suffice, if only there were one who understood what is signified through it and in it. The Jews saw this breastpiece, but did not understand what was signified through it. Those understand it to whom the Lord says: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables” (Luke 8:10).

Whatever is contained in both Testaments is all figured in this ornament. Hence it is rightly placed over the breast and heart of the high priest, so that in that treasury of the divine volume the fullness of all truth and knowledge may be understood to reside. Let all [Col. 1065D] approach here; let all seek wisdom here, at the bishop’s breast and at the ornament placed upon it. Nor should it suffice merely to behold its beauty: let them ask, point by point, what those colors, what the gold, what the stones, and all the other things signify.

For its measure itself is not without significance. It was made to the measure of a span: namely, of him of whom it is written, “Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and weighed the heavens with his span?” (Isa. 40:12). The heavens, therefore, and the breastpiece are of one measure: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Ps. 18:1)—that glory, namely, which is contained in the breastpiece.

[Col. 1066A] If the breastpiece were not square, it would not have the appearance and form of a book. At its four corners are set the four Gospels. Thus you have the New Testament, and you also have the Old, which show you those twelve names of the sons of Israel, from whom the whole Synagogue proceeded. The breastpiece is double, so that you too may seek a twofold understanding in both Testaments. For it does not suffice to understand according to the letter alone, unless a spiritual understanding is also added.

You see gold there: it invites you to purity and beauty, to the adornment and brightness of the whole soul and body. It gives you an example of how pure and free from every corruption you ought to be. If any corruption still remains in you, remove it, until you are wholly brought to the purity [Col. 1066B] and beauty of gold.

The four colors which you see there are the four principal virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. By these four virtues the world is governed; and they are so joined together that one cannot exist without the others. Where wisdom is, justice, fortitude, and temperance must also be. Likewise, where justice is, there are wisdom, fortitude, and temperance. So also with the others.

The blue, because it is the color of the air, calls you to the wisdom which is from above; for “all wisdom is from the Lord God” (Ecclus. 1). Of this Solomon says: “Send her forth from the seat of your greatness, that she may be with me and labor with me” (Wis. 9:10). For wisdom is higher than the other virtues, and the others are illuminated by its radiance. Purple, however, is justice, because both purple and justice belong to kings, who are makers of laws and are especially clothed in purple. To them too it is said: “Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wis. 1).

> [Note: The cited edition has: “Scarlet, which is red and blood-colored,” etc.]

Scarlet, being red and blood-colored, invites us to fortitude. Armed with it, the holy martyrs could indeed be killed, but could not be conquered. Scarlet is twice dyed because there are two kinds of martyrdom: not only are those martyrs whom tyrants kill, but also those who have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires. Through the whiteness of linen, however, temperance is figured: always cheerful and showing nothing harsh, it endeavors to draw all things toward harmony and peace.

It is very useful [Col. 1066D] always to examine these colors and understand what they signify. What the stones signify is shown by the names written upon them. The twelve stones, therefore, are the twelve patriarchs, through whom the twelve apostles are signified. How useful, how necessary it is to look upon them, always to keep them in memory, and to preserve their faith and manner of life, need hardly be said. Yet not only the twelve patriarchs and twelve apostles are signified in those stones, but also the whole multitude of all saints of both Testaments, [Col. 1067A] which takes its origin from these twenty-four elders. Among them all martyrs and confessors are counted. There are Stephen and Lawrence; there are Martin and Benedict. Enclosed in gold, shining with great splendor and great whiteness, they pour abundant light into our minds.

Let us always direct our attention to them; let us turn the eyes of our mind toward them, and say with the Psalmist: “I considered the days of old, and kept the eternal years in mind” (Ps. 76:6). Blessed are those who always bear these stones upon their breast. Blessed are those who always bear their memory in heart and breast. Would that we might always have the name and memory of blessed Benedict in our heart, so that, while we remember him, we may always be able to imitate and preserve his life and holy manner of living.

[Col. 1067B] That the stones were arranged in four rows, three stones in each row, signifies nothing other than that the books of the four Gospels never cease to praise the mystery of the Trinity. Together, harmoniously, with one voice, without interruption day and night, they cry and say: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty; the whole earth is full of his glory” (Isa. 61). He lives and reigns, etc.

## CHAPTER III

## SERMON I. FOR ANY FEMALE SAINT

“The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls; and, having found one precious pearl, he went away, sold all that he had, and bought it” (Matt. 13:45).

[Col. 1067C] In the example and comparison of one merchant, the Lord and our Savior teaches us what kind of merchants of the Church we ought to become. He says that there was a merchant who devoted himself to purchasing pearls; and, when one precious pearl had been greatly praised to him, and he had learned the province in which to seek it and the person from whom to buy it, he went away, sold everything he had, and bought it.

Such a pearl is not found everywhere: it has its own place, where it is not discovered without labor. The road also by which one reaches it is long and difficult. There are many robbers, many dangers, deserted places, beasts of various kinds along the way; [Col. 1067D] and the road itself which brings merchants to it is exceedingly narrow. Yet blessed is the one who can reach it and possess it.

There is no great question concerning the high or low price at which it is bought: for both rich and poor may buy it, and often the poor acquire it better than the rich. It is attained more by affection and disposition than by price. It is worth as much as you possess. The one who sells everything and buys it deserves worthily to purchase and possess it. Do not fear to give all: it alone will suffice for you; nothing will be lacking to you if you possess it. You will possess in it all things that you desire.

It flees hypocrites and rejects the greedy. Those who seek it falsely, or who seek something more than it; those who love something else along with it, cannot possess it. It offers itself willingly to those who seek it in love; and one who loves it greatly [Col. 1068A] can never lose his way while journeying to it. And what is especially praiseworthy in it is this: it itself defends from danger those who come to buy it out of love and desire. It does not greatly care if they are killed in body, because it is easy for it to raise them from the dead. It counts visible enemies, who have power over the body alone, as little. But invisible enemies create a great obstacle for merchants seeking it. Lying in wait along the road, they send after them beasts of various kinds. Avarice delays some, lust others, pride others, envy others, vainglory others, gluttony others, and disobedience others. There are many other beasts besides, which evil spirits set against merchants, lest they be able to reach this desirable pearl.

This is [Col. 1068B] the little stone which the Lord promises to give. For the apostle John says in the Apocalypse: “To the conqueror I will give a white stone, and on the stone is written a new name which no one knows except the one who receives it” (Apoc. 2:27). This pearl, therefore, is given to conquerors, and is not given except to conquerors. Where there is victory, there is struggle: “For no one is crowned unless he has contended lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5). Thus fought this virgin, whose feast is celebrated today, and therefore she deserved to receive the white stone.

This pearl may therefore be understood as eternal life, blessedness, the highest good—what it is like, indeed, no one knows except the one who receives it. Hence the Apostle says: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love him” [Col. 1068C] (1 Cor. 2:9). No one can know that which has not entered into the human heart.

The merchants of God’s Church are such as this merchant whom the Lord set forth as an example: having found one precious pearl, he sold all his goods and bought it. Thus Peter and Andrew, James and John, whom he called from fishing, immediately left their nets and followed him. Thus also the other apostles; thus the martyrs and confessors; thus the monastic order, who not only leave their possessions but subject even themselves to servitude out of desire for this pearl.

This is the treasure hidden in the field, which the man who finds it hides, and, having sold everything, buys it. Of this our Savior also answered one who questioned him: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything that you have and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven” [Col. 1068D] (Matt. 19:12). For what does “you shall have treasure in heaven” mean except: you shall have that precious pearl; you shall have eternal life, blessedness, the highest good, the white stone, upon which is written a name no one knows except the one who receives it?

By these words we are taught most plainly that our Savior himself is the one who showed merchants the pearl, its place, its price, and the path by which they might come to it. For he too is a merchant, and is accustomed to sell such pearls. Hence in the Apocalypse he says to the bishop of Laodicea: “I counsel you to buy from me gold tried in fire, that you may become rich” (Apoc. 3:28).

But this good merchant, full of all loving-kindness and mercy, contrary to the custom of other merchants, sells more cheaply and buys more dearly. He sells his own things at a low price and other people’s things at a high one. Thus the Apostle speaks to us, who were bought by his blood: “For you were bought at a great price: glorify and bear God in your body” [Col. 1069A] (1 Cor. 6:20). If, in this exchange made between his blood and our redemption, you consider what was given and what was received, you will easily understand that he gave the greatest things for the least.

Therefore this noble merchant came, bringing with him the greatest wares, by which the lost world might be redeemed. But what did he buy? Things of the lowest worth: weak and sickly sheep. Not because he needed them, but that he might heal and restore them, [Col. 1069B] and place them in a pasture. For he is that good shepherd who laid down his life for his sheep; who, leaving the ninety-nine in the wilderness, came to seek the one that had perished. Hence his birth was first announced to shepherds. For it was fitting that men of the same occupation should be the first to meet him as he came. Such is the custom of people: when they come into foreign places, they first seek people of their own occupation.

Having paid a great price, then, he bought a few sheep—but good and fruitful ones, from which many flocks of sheep were born. Of such sheep it is said in the Song of Songs: “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing, all bearing twin offspring, and none among them is barren” (Song 4:2). Good sheep are those who have been baptized and made whiter than snow. Good sheep are those who, shorn and stripped, leaving all things for God, wish to possess nothing as their own. Good sheep are those among whom none is barren, each being adorned with twin offspring: teaching, namely, and action.

[Col. 1069C] Such, indeed, ought to be the teeth of the Church; such ought bishops and priests to be, and whoever undertakes in the Church the office of teeth and nourishes others with spiritual food. They ought to be so white, so clean, so fruitful, so stripped of every superfluous and harmful burden. For all are to be formed after the beauty of those sheep which first came up from the washing: by these, plainly, we understand the holy apostles and the others who believed in those times, “all of whom had one heart and one soul, and no one said that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were held in common among them” (Acts 4:32).

> [Note: Vatican manuscript: “Nor did any one of them say, concerning the things which he possessed,” etc.]

Hence the Apostle says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 11:1). We must therefore imitate these sheep, because we have been born from them. “For in Christ Jesus,” says the Apostle, “I begot you through the Gospel” (1 Cor. 4:15). For in the flock of God, in the people of God, there are only sheep. Be patient and innocent; be humble and gentle. Let infants be nourished with your milk, and let the poor be clothed with your wool.
