Blessed Paul was a good sheep, though he had been a wolf, born from the tribe of Benjamin, which is interpreted “ravening wolf.” [Col. 1070A] There are two reasons why our Savior came into the world: one, namely, to buy sheep; the other, to teach the art of trade. Both came to pass, because those sheep were bought and redeemed, and these people were taught and instructed. He is the one who, “going abroad, called his servants and delivered his goods to them, saying” (Matt. 25:14): “Trade until I come” (Luke 19:13).

He taught them what they ought to do and where they might find true riches. He gave the price, showed the road, and taught where the pearl so precious is found: that it must be sought, bought, held, and preferred to all riches and honors, because it alone can make its possessors blessed and eternal. It leads people to the highest good, above which there is no other [Col. 1070B] good, and in which all goods are had and possessed.

This good cannot be found in this world. For no one in this life has ever been so rich, so happy, and so powerful that something was not lacking which he wished to have. But one to whom something is lacking, and to whom what he has does not suffice, has not yet reached the final and highest good. For if he had reached the final good, there would be no good that he could desire. O how many goods do the richest and most powerful people of this world desire most ardently and yet cannot possess! Such persons always have too little either of health, wisdom, or something else which would take long to enumerate. Therefore they are not blessed, nor can those who fall short in such goods and in so great a degree attain the highest and final good.

[Col. 1070C] Our merchants of the kingdom of heaven alone, therefore, are wise: despising the perishable, passing, and fleeting goods, reckoning the honors and dignities of this world as nothing, they strive only toward that good which is highest, above which there is no other good, and in which they trust that they themselves will possess all goods. May he grant this to us, etc.

## SERMON II. ON THE APOSTLES, EVANGELISTS, AND DOCTORS

“The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind; when it was full, they drew it out and, sitting beside the shore, selected the good into their vessels but threw the bad away, etc.” (Matt. 13:47).

Seek this in the book *On the New World*, and in the sermon entitled “On the Sea and the New Fishers,” whose title is: *This Is the Great Sea*.

## SERMON III. ON THE PREACHING OF THE EVANGELICAL LAW

“Every scribe learned in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder, who brings forth from his treasure things new and old” (Matt. 13:52).

The kingdom of heaven, the kingdom of angels, the kingdom of apostles, is the holy Church; for it is fortified by heavens, enclosed by heavens, governed and defended by heavens. Of them it is written: “The heavens declare the glory of God.” Every learned scribe, therefore, every preacher of the Church, who undertakes in the kingdom of heaven—in the kingdom [Col. 1071A] of the holy apostles—the office of preaching and teaching, ought to be like a householder who brings forth new and old things from his treasure, from the secret place of his breast, from the treasury of his heart.

He must consider where he is, and in what kingdom and in what house he delivers his discourse. One must speak differently in the kingdom of heaven and differently in the Synagogue of the Jews; riches must be dispensed differently in imperial palaces and differently in poor huts. Let him consider what teachers, rulers, and stewards were in that kingdom and household before him. Let him imitate them, follow their manners and life, and speak with their tongue and speech. “There are,” he says, “no languages nor speeches whose voices are not heard” (Ps. 18). They therefore brought forth new and old things from their treasures, but spoke in every language and speech. At one time they brought forth the riches of the New Testament, at another those of the Old.

Thus the bride speaks to the bridegroom, saying: “I have kept for you all fruits, new and old” (Song 7:13). If there are new and old fruits, there must also be new and old trees. The old trees are understood as the patriarchs and prophets, while the new are the apostles and teachers. The former have their fruits, and the latter have theirs. Both are good; both these and those must be kept and guarded.

As the trees are different, so fruits of different kinds are found. Some may be eaten raw and together with their skin; others, unless cooked and stripped of their skin, are neither suitable nor pleasant for eating. This is not difficult to find in our trees and in the trees of both Testaments, whose fruits are sayings and judgments. Read in the books of Moses and you will find fruits of various kinds, which cannot be eaten by everyone nor in one manner. Some things there are such that even children receive them without difficulty, such as: “Honor your father and mother; do not kill; do not commit adultery; do not steal; do not bear false witness; do not covet your neighbor’s property” (Luke 18:20). Since these are understood according to the letter, they are difficult for no one to eat. For to understand is itself to eat.

[Col. 1071D] But you will find other things there which even young men can scarcely gnaw, and it belongs to few to cook them and strip away their skin. This is the office of bishops and priests: for example, when we read of a leprous house, of trees to be cut around, of fields not to be sown with different seed, and of many other matters which, if understood according to the letter, seem empty, but if understood spiritually are useful to weak minds.

Moses gives a law in one place (Lev. 25): if anyone sells his house in a walled city, he has the power to redeem it until a full year is completed. But after the year has ended, he could neither redeem it nor recover it at the Jubilee. The Jews observed this literally, but it contains a spiritual meaning. This city is the Church, whose wall is of precious stones. Hence it is also written: “Zion, the city of our strength: the Savior shall be set in it as a wall and a forewall” [Col. 1072A] (Isa. 26:1).

A person sells this house of his when he commits grave sins. The Apostle also says in the person of such a one: “The law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin. For whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (Rom. 7:14). The year in which the power of redemption is granted means the whole present life of each person. Therefore a person can redeem his house, his flesh, his whole self, for as long as he remains in this life. But when this life is ended, he no longer has the power of redemption.

Redemption exists only in repentance; therefore no redemption remains for those who die without repentance, not even at the Jubilee, because, once the final sentence has been received, the saints are transferred to the glory of the eternal feast.

This saying seems similar to what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Walk while you have the light, lest the darkness overtake you” (John 12:35). And the Apostle: “While we have time, let us do good to all” (Gal. 6:10). Elsewhere: “According to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works” [Col. 1072B] (Rom. 2:5).

Behold, these things are new and those are old. But if we wish to see the richest householder bringing forth new and old things from his treasure, let us hear our Savior say from heaven: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not kill; and whoever kills shall be liable to judgment.’ But I say to you that whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment; whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ shall be liable to the council; and whoever says, ‘Fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. 7:21).

Those things said to the ancients are old; those which he himself said are new. The old commandments forbid murder; the new forbid not only murder but anger and every injury as well. Whoever has offended a brother, and understands that he is stirred and angered against him, if he persists in his malice and pride and scorns reconciliation with his brother, because he has broken the bond of love and peace—without which, as the Apostle says, no one shall see God—shall be liable not merely to judgment or council, but even to the fire of Gehenna.

For the Lord himself makes this clear when he says: “If you offer your gift [Col. 1072D] at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go first to be reconciled with your brother; then, when you come, you shall offer your gift” (Matt. 5:23). For God abhors the offerings of those who sin and refuse to repent.

Again, you have heard that “it was said to the ancients, ‘An eye for an eye’; but I say to you not to resist evil. Rather, if anyone strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other also” (ibid., 39). Tell me, then: how can one be permitted to inflict injury if one is not permitted to resist it? “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall love your friend and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you: Love your enemies; bless those who hate you” (ibid., [Col. 1073A] 44).

When our Savior said these and similar things, he brought forth new and old things from that noble treasure of his heart, and he wished scribes learned in the kingdom of heaven to be like himself. Let us therefore also bring forth new and old things, not from our own treasure, but from that given to us by the Lord our God. We have two great treasures, one new and the other old. Let us take from them what is necessary for us and bring forth new and old things from them, so that we may nourish, clothe, govern, and teach God’s household, and may be able to attain eternal blessedness together with it, with his help, etc.

## SERMON IV. ON VIRGINS

“The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins, who, taking their lamps, went forth to meet [Col. 1073B] the bridegroom and bride. Five of them were foolish and five prudent. But the five foolish, having taken their lamps, did not take oil with them; whereas the prudent took oil in their vessels with their lamps, etc.” (Matt. 15:1).

The kingdom of heaven is the Church. All its children, even if they are sinners, are virgins in comparison with other nations, because they alone have been redeemed by Christ’s blood, regenerated from water and the Holy Spirit, and cleansed from that first corruption, since all human nature has lost its virginity.

Yet all these virgins are no more than five, and five are shown to make ten, and no more. For the five bodily senses are signified by these virgins: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. But because these are divided into two parts, that is, into foolish and prudent, they unquestionably rise to the number ten. Every person, therefore, has five virgins, whether foolish or prudent.

The prudent are those who fear to sin and desire to do good. Where prudence is, sin has no place. Hence philosophers said that the wise person will not repent. For who needs repentance if he commits no deed requiring repentance? He was endowed with this wisdom who said: “In all my life my heart has not reproached me” (Job 27:6).

Those are wise of whom it is said: “My eyes are always toward the Lord” (Ps. 24:15); and he of whom it is written: “My eyes have failed for your utterance” [Col. 1073D] (Ps. 68:4); and, “I have lifted up my eyes to you, who dwell in heaven” (Ps. 122:1). Blessed Martin also had wise eyes; of him it is read: “His eyes and hands were always fixed upon heaven.” Such eyes had he who said: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I might not think upon a virgin” (Job 31:1).

Likewise wise ears take no pleasure in idle talk, lies, detractions, or idle words. The Lord sought such ears when he said: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8). Hence all the friends of blessed Job are said to have given him one golden earring and one sheep. Abraham’s servant, too, having found Rebecca, is related to have given her golden earrings and bracelets. Good also are those who, loving the Lord, have pierced ears.

Likewise, wise taste is that which delights not in excess of eating and drunkenness but in fasting and abstinence; which seeks not superfluous and luxurious foods but measured, wholesome, and necessary ones. Wise, too, is that sense of smell which does not draw the soul into sin and takes no delight in unlawful fragrances. I myself think that there is no bodily sense in which a person sins less.

[Col. 1074A] Wise hands are those of which it is said: “She has opened her hands to the needy, and stretched out her palms to the poor” (Prov. 31:20). Of them the Psalmist also says: “You shall eat the labor of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. 127:2). And the Apostle: “Let him who stole steal no more; but rather let him labor with his hands at what is good, that he may have something to give to one suffering need” (Eph. 6:28). Wise hands are not idle but always desire to be occupied with some useful work.

These things have been said concerning the prudent virgins. Whoever knows them cannot fail to know the foolish as well, since those who are not such must be foolish. Each person knows his own virgin; it is difficult to know another’s. For many foolish virgins are thought to be prudent. But this foolishness will be revealed in the judgment, because then it will become known to all which are prudent and which foolish. This will be recognized in the lamps, which will appear either with light or without light.

The virgins who are not corrected in this life, nor transferred from foolishness to prudence, will go from this life as they are and, unchanged for the better, into eternal punishment. For when they say to the prudent: “Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out” [Col. 1074C] (Matt. 25:8), they will receive an answer worthy of their merits. They will receive no fruit of repentance because they were unwilling to repent: “Lest perhaps,” say the prudent, “there be insufficient for us and for you, go rather to the sellers and buy for yourselves” (ibid., 9).

These words seem not compassionate but mocking. Yet the counsel would be good if they could carry it out. They refused to do this when they could; now they wish to do it, but cannot. Yet why should it be surprising that they are mocked by Christ’s members, when, as the Psalmist says, Christ himself mocks and derides them? “He who dwells in heaven,” he says, “will laugh at them, and the Lord will deride them” (Ps. 2:4).

They receive the counsel, but receive it without benefit. They know that it is good, but recognize that for them it is late and useless. They go to the sellers of oil—not with their feet, but with desire. What is it to go with desire except to desire sluggishly? Thus all who are in hell return to us daily, because they are tormented by this one desire alone: that permission to return, that is, a leave of absence, may be granted them.

Oh, if they could have had that permission, with what zeal they would have labored to call back their virginly faculties and senses from that first foolishness to prudence! How they would have turned their eyes from vanities, shut their ears against detractions and [Col. 1075A] evil counsels, restrained taste from gluttony and drunkenness, withdrawn their nostrils from unlawful fragrances, and prepared their hands for works of almsgiving and mercy! No longer would they despise the sellers of oil; no longer would they despise bishops and priests. For these are the ones who sell oil; these are the ones who teach us to perform works of mercy. Whoever lacks such works will indeed have lamps, but will not have oil or sustenance for light at the judgment.

“But while they went to buy, the bridegroom came; and those who were ready went in with him to the wedding, and the door was shut” (Matt. 25:10). This journey will never end for them, because this desire will never leave them. But while they labor in this desire, while miserable people accuse themselves and condemn their deeds, the Lord will suddenly come, who will render to each according to his works. Then the gate of heaven will be opened to the good and closed to the evil. The latter will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life. May he deign to grant this.

## SERMON V. ON SAINT MICHAEL THE ARCHANGEL
“Then a great battle took place in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon; and the dragon fought, together with his angels, but they did not prevail, nor was any place found for them any longer in heaven” (Rev. 12:7–8). And that ancient serpent, who is the Devil and Satan, was cast down to the earth, and all his angels were sent down to the earth. This is a great battle, in which Michael, prince of the angels, fights with the devil, prince of the demons. This battle occurs daily in the Church, for the Church is called heaven. Read the Gospel: wherever the Lord says, “The kingdom of heaven is like this or that,” it is understood especially and properly of the holy Church. Likewise, in the Apocalypse the Church is frequently called heaven.

This, therefore, is to be understood of the Church; although, even if it were understood of another heaven, it would not seem altogether unsuitable. For it is manifest that the dragon was cast out from there on account of his pride. Of him the Prophet also says: “How you have fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, who rose in the morning! You who said in your heart: ‘I shall ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I shall set my throne; I shall sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; and I shall be like the Most High’” (Isa. 14:12–14). [Col. 1075D] Of him the Lord says in John’s Gospel: “Because from the beginning he was a liar, and did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44). And elsewhere in the Gospel the Lord says: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18).

It is therefore established that he fell from there, whether through the strength and power of the angels, or because God’s will alone hurled him down to the lower regions. For God has accomplished many things through the ministry of angels which, had he wished, he could have done by a mere nod. For what is there that he cannot do? All things are subject to his will, and nothing can resist it. How, indeed, could the malignant [Col. 1076A] spirit have fought and resisted the holy angels there, except perhaps through a desire for fighting and a perverse will? This is not easily apparent. But in the Church it is manifest that such battles occur daily.

This world is divided between good and evil angels; and at times good angels, at times evil angels, make no small prey and plunder upon the other. Hence there are endless and irreconcilable disputes, and great daily battles, among them. Thus a certain angel speaks to Daniel, saying: “Do not fear, Daniel, for your words have been heard, and I have come because of your words. The prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me for twenty-one days; and behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came first to help me” (Dan. 10:12–13).

This prince of the kingdom of the Persians is understood to be one of the malignant spirits, who presided over the Persian kingdom and people, inciting them to works of his own will and wickedness, and creating a great obstacle for God’s people, who were held captive there. But by the help of Michael the archangel and Daniel’s prayers—which, he says, were heard—this prince of wickedness is shown to have been overcome. Behold how good and evil angels fight one another. Behold how they strive to defend and assault kingdoms and provinces over which they are set.

For there are certain ranks among the good angels and among the evil [Col. 1076B] ones, to which they are respectively preferred. Hence blessed Dionysius the Areopagite says in his book *On the Hierarchy* that there are three orders of angels. [Note: [Col. 1075D] Book I, chapters 6, 7, 8, 9. See Nicolas de Nourry’s dissertation on the works of St Dionysius the Areopagite, reissued [Col. 1076D] by Dom Placidus Sprengher, *Thesaurus*, vol. I, p. 235, Würzburg edition, 1784.] In the first order are cherubim, seraphim, [Col. 1076C] and thrones. In the second are powers, virtues, and dominions. In the third, which is the last, are angels, archangels, and principalities.

And, as he says, certain secrets of the divine counsel are sometimes revealed to those in the first order which the lower orders do not know. But those things which are revealed to the lower orders cannot be unknown to the higher. In this matter no small difference among them is shown. All, indeed, are called spirits; but the name “angel” denotes an office, not a nature. Hence it is written: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire” (Ps. 103:4). Those who are merely spirits there become angels when they are sent.

Thus those are called angels in the proper sense who have been sent by God for the governance and protection of this world, [Col. 1076D] among whom blessed Michael holds the primacy. He is called not only an angel and archangel, but also prince of angels and archangels. For he has many angels and archangels subject to him, appointed throughout kingdoms, provinces, and cities. Just as we see among the powers of this world, so among these: some hold authority over many, some over few, and some over none. Those who are given by their superiors for individual protection are such as the Lord speaks of in the Gospel: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones; for I tell you that their angels always see [Col. 1077A] the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 18:10). And the Apostle says: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth for service for the sake of those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation?” (Heb. 1:14).

There are, therefore, principalities that preside over archangels; archangels, however, rule over angels alone. See, then, how great thanks we owe to blessed Michael the archangel, from whom we have received angels appointed as ministers for our protection. The same angel who spoke above says also to Daniel: “Now I announce to you what is set forth in the Scripture of truth; and there is none who helps me in all these things except Michael the archangel, your prince” (Dan. 10:21).

Therefore he, together with his angels, does not cease day and night to fight against that dragon, who is the devil [Col. 1077B] and Satan. Since he cannot dwell in heaven—that is, in holy persons—he has been cast down to the earth, by which sinners are signified, so that he may eat, devour, and destroy it all the days of his life. [Note: [Col. 1077D] Vatican manuscript and cited edition: “Behemoth, whom I made with you, shall eat grass like an ox. And can you …?”] Of him the Psalmist says: “This dragon, whom you formed to play with him” (Ps. 103:26). Of him also the Lord himself speaks to blessed Job, saying: “Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook, and bind his tongue with a cord [Note: [Col. 1077D] ‘Will you play with him as with a bird, and bind him for your maidservants?’]?” (Job 40:20).

“Will you play with him as with a bird, or bind him for your maidservants? There is no power upon the earth that can be compared to him; he was made so that he should fear no one. He sees every lofty thing, and he is king over all the children of pride. He will swallow up rivers and not marvel, and he is confident that the Jordan will flow [Col. 1077C] into his mouth.”

Consider now what sort of being this is—how strong and powerful—against whom Michael the archangel fights. But Michael, whose name is interpreted “Who is like God?”, strengthens us by his very name for battle. Since the dragon wished to be like God, [Note: [Col. 1077D] Vatican manuscript and edition: “He strengthens us for battle [Col. 1078D] and exhorts us not to fear him. Since he wished to be like God,” etc.] he was cast down. Yet he still does not rest; and, made such by his pride that he knows no fear, he could not have been resisted by any power on earth unless the powers above the heavens, which come from heavenly beings, resisted his pride and strength.

Let no one glory in his own strength, for neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase. Who could escape the savagery and strength of this dragon unless the Lord fortified us by the protection of his angels? For he will swallow up rivers and not marvel: he makes light of devouring and destroying all the peoples and nations of this world, unless even the Jordan itself [Col. 1077D] should flow into his mouth. For his food is choice food: not the crowd or an undisciplined people, but he persecutes the very best; he often attacks bishops and priests themselves. [Note: [Col. 1078D] Vatican manuscript: “But he persecutes the better sort, bishops themselves,” etc.]

He desires to swallow no river so greatly as that one in which the Lord was baptized, by which the baptized people is signified. Many waters are many peoples; many rivers are many nations. But the single river Jordan is the one Christian people alone. This dragon persecutes it, and for its sake fights with the angels. At some time, as it is written, he will draw his tail and separate a third part of the stars of heaven. The dragon’s tail will be Antichrist: he, the last and greatest son of perdition, will perform many signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led [Col. 1078A] into error. “Whom, as the Apostle says, the Lord [Col. 1078B] Jesus will kill by the breath of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming” (2 Thess. 2:8).

And then, as is written in Daniel: “Michael the archangel, the great prince who stands for the children of your people, shall arise; and there shall come a time such as has not been since men began to exist until that time” (Dan. 12:1). In that time, as Daniel is told, “all your people who are found written in the book of life shall be saved. And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to eternal life and others to reproach, that they may live forever. But those who have understanding shall shine like the brightness of the firmament; and those who instruct many in righteousness, like stars for everlasting eternities” (ibid., 1–3).

[Col. 1078C] Behold, the whole battle has taken place; this great dragon has been overcome and cast down into darkness together with all his host. It remains that there should come upon the good and the evil a time such as has not been since human beings began. “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matt. 18:7); yet for the good it is necessary and very useful that scandals should come. “Nevertheless, woe to that man through whom the scandal comes” (ibid.).

If, therefore, your hand or your foot causes you to stumble—if a father, mother, brother, or anyone else who is as your own limb to you, and whom you love as feet, hands, and eyes, wishes by evil counsel or perverse conduct to separate you from God—separate that person from yourself and flee him as an enemy. It is better for you to live alone than to perish with [Col. 1078D] parents and relatives. “See that you do not despise one of these little ones; for I tell you that their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (ibid., 10). He who lives and reigns, etc.

[Col. 1079]

**THE TREATISES OF ST BRUNO OF ASTI BEGIN.**

[Col. 1079]

**FIRST TREATISE. ON THE INCARNATION OF THE LORD AND HIS BURIAL.**

[Col. 1079A] Just as the Word of God created man in the beginning on the sixth day, so at the end of time, at the sixth hour of the sixth day, in the sixth age also, he redeemed that same man. But in this chief and wondrous redemption, four matters seem to require consideration: why the Son of God, and not another, was incarnate; concerning the repose of burial; on what authorities it is to be believed that he descended into hell; and how long he lay in the tomb.

Man was created by God as it were in the morning, because, retaining God’s likeness, he seemed close to the true light. For he could behold God near at hand, namely, in himself and through himself, with no external thing intervening. But he lost both nearness and likeness alike when he subjected himself to the evil of disobedience. A nearby sun is accustomed to draw moisture together, and, by withdrawing, to loosen it. Thus the true sun—that is, our Lord, “who enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9)—as by his presence he had dried up the frailty, that is, the corruption adhering to man formed from clay, so by withdrawing he loosened it. Hence after his fault Adam deserved to hear from the Lord: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3:9), as one distant in nearness and unlike in likeness. For the sun of righteousness had set, as the night of sin descended.

But almighty and merciful God, lest his works should lapse into impotence or folly—for he is truly powerful and perfectly wise—resolved to redeem, from an unrighteous man, which was difficult, the angelic order that had fallen through wickedness, since he could no longer restore it from a righteous man. Therefore he first determined to rescue man himself [Col. 1079C] from the devil’s power, and thereafter to recover the angelic nature itself. [Note: [Col. 1079C] This conflicts with the teaching of St Thomas, who teaches in *Summa Theologiae*, I, question 64, article 1, that the sin of the angels was unforgivable not because of the gravity of the fault but because of the condition of their nature or state; there he cites the saying of Damascene: “Death is to human beings what the Fall is to angels.” [Col. 1080C] But if by the words, “he determined to recover the angelic nature itself,” St Bruno meant that God intended to save as many human beings as angels had perished by falling into the sin of pride, his teaching accords with that of the other Fathers.] And this was not without sacrifice.

But because in every sacrifice four fitting elements seem to be present—namely, to whom it is offered, by whom, what is offered, and for whom—in this sacrifice also, which had to be made for the salvation of the whole human race, the same fitting conditions were properly present. For if any of these is lacking in any immolation, not only will that sacrifice itself not profit, but it is manifest that it very often harms, as is repeatedly shown in the Old Testament.

When Moses ascended the mountain and conversed with the Lord for forty days in order to receive the law, delighting most sweetly in his vision, the people of Israel offered sacrifices not to God but to a molten calf (Exod. 22:4); and, insulting him, they are recorded as having been struck by the Lord himself and condemned to a violent death, so that they lost twenty-three thousand men through that sin. The Psalmist indicates this, saying: “They made a calf in Horeb and worshipped a graven image” (Ps. 105:19), etc. Then follows: “And he said that he would destroy them” (ibid.). For because of that sin they were scattered by serpents. Therefore it was necessary to examine with the utmost care to whom this victim should be offered.

[Col. 1080B] Whatever exists is either creature or Creator. Let us see whether it was fitting to offer sacrifice to the Creator or to a creature. It appears just and reasonable, and all hold, that offering is due not to a creature but to the Creator. It remained, therefore, that with great providential arrangement a creature should be sacrificed to the Creator. But since there is a great difference among creatures—some are sentient, others insentient—it must be carefully weighed whether this sacrifice should be offered by a sentient or by an insentient creature. For it often happens that, if a sacrifice is offered by one unworthy, we find that the sacrifice itself is not accepted and that the offerer is condemned.

As is read in Numbers (Num. 16:32), Dathan and Abiram rose up against Aaron and his sons contrary to God’s will and offered sacrifice in God’s tabernacle. But because they were unworthy participants in that sacrifice, the earth opened and they were buried; and those who were there are shown to have been devoured by fire, as the Psalm says: “The earth opened and swallowed Dathan, and closed over the congregation of Abiram. Fire blazed in their congregation, and flame consumed the sinners” (Ps. 105:17). For the same fire by which sins were thought to be punished rose from the altar and reached those sacrificing unjustly, [Col. 1081A] and burned them.

Therefore it was unworthy that this sacrifice should be offered by an insentient creature. It remained, then, that the immolation should be made by a sentient one. But because there is a very great difference among sentient creatures, since some are rational and others irrational, we must see whether this sacrifice ought to be offered by an irrational creature. But it is unfitting and wholly absurd that an irrational creature should be sacrificed for a rational one. It is established, therefore, that this immolation must be made by a rational being.

But because there is still a great difference among rational beings, it must be considered whether this immolation ought to be made by an angelic creature. An immolation, however, must be visible, while angels are invisible; and something visible cannot be offered by an invisible being. [Note: [Col. 1081D] St Thomas teaches in *Summa Theologiae*, III, question 4, article 2, that God could, by producing a new angelic nature, unite it to himself in unity of person.] It was thus established that this offering had to be made by a human being.

Two divisions having been completed, we must deal with the remaining matters: namely, what is to be sacrificed and for whom. It is established by authority that the sacrifice must be equal to or greater than that for which it is offered; and this sacrifice, as we have said, existing for the salvation of the human race, had to offer an equal and not a lesser victim. Therefore the insentient and irrational are excluded; but a rational victim for a rational being was fitting.

Among rational beings, however, since there is still too great a difference, it must be observed whether the sacrifice ought to be made from a human being or an angel; for each possesses reason. But no human being was found worthy of so great a victim, because all human beings were not free from original and actual sin, as the Prophet says: “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. 115:11). And as the blessed Evangelist John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). Thus one human being, himself a sinner, would have been an unfit victim for the redemption of the whole human race. Therefore man alone was excluded from this sacrifice.

But an angel could not be admitted in his own nature, because what is invisible can neither be held, nor suffer, nor even be killed. Perhaps he could be sacrificed through an assumed nature; but angelic charity would grow cold if punished for an unrighteous person, and this not without reason. For scarcely does anyone righteous die for a righteous person, much less be condemned for an unrighteous one. Moreover, before Christ’s coming, human beings were hated by angels on account of sin. And perhaps, if man were redeemed by an angel, he would venerate that angel as God. Let this not seem impossible to anyone, since the aforementioned human beings are often found worshipping stones, wood, and bronze as God. For these and many other such reasons the angelic victim was excluded.

Accordingly, the Creator alone remained, who, in his mercy and customary kindness, compassionating the human race, would free the aforementioned man and rescue him, entangled, from the devil’s jaws. And he would do this not in his own nature but through an assumed human being, so that God and man might be sacrificed, who had come to redeem man alone. [Col. 1082A]

But in the Godhead, because the Catholic Church believes that there is a distinction of persons—namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—it must properly be considered to whom this assumption was fitting. If the Father assumed humanity within a virgin’s womb and were born from her, the same one would be Father and Son: Father according to divinity, Son according to humanity. To believe or say this is wicked. Another and greater impiety would follow, since there would be two sons in the Godhead: the Father, son according to humanity, and the Son of God, son according to divinity. Avoiding so great an error, therefore, the aforesaid assumption was not fitting for the Father.

It remains to consider whether the Holy Spirit was suited to be sacrificed. [Col. 1082B] If that Spirit assumed humanity and wished to be sacrificed for it, the aforesaid error would fall upon the Godhead; for truly two sons would be believed and held to exist in it: the Son of God according to divinity, as we said, and the Holy Spirit, son according to humanity. Therefore the aforesaid assumption was fitting to neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit, since neither could be admitted in such an undertaking.

The Son alone, therefore, was suitable for this work. It belonged to him in justice both to save the human being created through himself, to withstand the devil demanding his own authority, to deceive the very one deceiving man, and, after taking away the sovereignty of the whole world, to bind him forever in hell. [Note: [Col. 1081D] See St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, III, question 3, article 8, where he proves on several grounds that it was most fitting for the person of the Son to become incarnate. The mind of the holy doctor is explained more clearly by Cardinal Gotti, vol. XII, question 3, *On the Fittingness and Necessity of the Incarnation*, book I, §2.]

For it is read in the Gospel of blessed John that “all things were made through him” [Col. 1082C] (John 1:3), and thus man also. Moreover, if man, created through him, were redeemed by someone other than him, weakness could truly be ascribed to the Son: that one created through him was not redeemed through him. But if the Father, to whom power is attributed, were incarnate, there would be two sons, which conflicts with the sacred Scriptures that speak of one Son of God. The same applies to the Holy Spirit, who is goodness.

But it was fitting for wisdom alone—that is, the Son of God—that the devil should be deceived wisely. What cause could be more proper or more just than that the man formed by the Word should return to his former state through the Word, that is, through the Son of God in assumed flesh? Thus it was rightly done and confirmed in a just order [Col. 1082D] that man should be redeemed not by the Father or the Holy Spirit, but by the Son of God, who would be called Son in divinity and humanity, and should enter into the original blessedness from which he had fallen by transgression. These matters having been thus fittingly and appropriately set forth, it remains to discuss the repose of burial.

Because the Son of God, the Word of the Father, the splendour of glory, the Creator of human beings, compassionating the world as it rushed toward ruin, descended to us by assuming our humanity, with the Father and Holy Spirit working together with him. “He became man and lived among human beings” [Col. 1083A] (Bar. 3:38): he ate, drank, hungered, wept, and did the other things belonging to human beings, except sin. For it was fitting that he who had come to save man and forgive him sins should be without sin. Therefore it was said of him: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22).

If he was born for humanity and performed in due order the other things recounted above, it was fitting that he should die, because what human being is there who shall not see death? And it was more humanly fitting that he should be buried. Since this was reasonable, after his death Joseph of Arimathea, as the evangelists relate, obtained the Lord’s body by asking for it, with the utmost attentive diligence concerning the burial, and buried it in his own new tomb. David the prophet testifies, saying: “In peace I shall sleep and rest, for you, Lord, have established me uniquely in hope” (Ps. 4:9).

Truly, uniquely: because by dying and resting in the tomb he conquered the devil. Who else could conquer in battle by dying except him who can do all things? Therefore he was uniquely established by the Father in hope. And again the Prophet says: “My flesh shall rest in hope” (Ps. 15:4), until the resurrection on the third day. We have this confirmed by many other authorities concerning how the Lord Jesus rested in the tomb. But among the many, these authorities of our faith—the Evangelists and David—are sufficient: they most truly affirm that he lay in the tomb and rested peacefully in that mausoleum. Whoever sleeps in peace possesses the greatest confidence of the hoped-for rising. Hence he himself said that he was falling asleep.

[Col. 1083C] The repose of burial has been discussed. It now remains to ask by what authorities it is believed that he descended into hell. The Saviour of the world, the wisdom of the Father, nourishing manna, the sweetest rock and one abundantly flowing with water, accepted our death for salvation; he was buried and anointed by Nicodemus with myrrh and aloes, so that Solomon’s words might be fulfilled: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh” (Song 1:13).

The Lord was truly a bundle of myrrh, and not a great burden. Although his Passion seemed bitter to the Blessed Virgin and his disciples, it was nevertheless a bundle because it was momentary. But we must not wander too far through digressions. Rather, we must examine very carefully which authorities are to be believed concerning the Lord’s descent into the lower regions and his drawing out of his faithful by his blessed power.

David the prophet says concerning that descent: “You will not abandon my soul in hell, nor give your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10). And elsewhere, with the prophet Hosea bearing witness, it is said: “O death, I shall be your death; I shall be your bite, O hell” (Hos. 13:13). The Lord was truly death to death, because he left it in perpetual death. [Note: [Col. 1083D] “Let us hold most firmly what faith, established by the most solid authority, holds: that Christ … was among those in the lower regions.” St Augustine, *Letter* 164 [otherwise 99], ch. 5, no. 24.]

The Saviour and Lord Jesus Christ was also the bite of hell, because he drew out not everyone but only his own from there. [Note: [Col. 1084D] St Augustine held the same view: “What is written, ‘the pains of hell having been loosed,’ may be understood not of all but of certain persons whom he judged worthy of that deliverance.” Same letter, chapters 4–5.] For if he had drawn all out, he would not have been a bite but a devourer [Col. 1084A] of human beings. One who bites something takes not the whole but a part. Thus Christ was the bite of hell, because he redeemed one part and left another. Elsewhere David says: “Lord, you have drawn my soul from hell; you have saved me from those descending into the pit” (Ps. 29:4), that is, from those who will be burned in eternal fire.

### How Many Hours He Was in the Descent and the Ascent

Having dealt with the authorities by which it is believed that the Lord descended into hell, it remains to investigate and write how long he lay in the tomb. It is fully, truly, and most plainly evident that from the hour of his death, when Joseph, asking for the Lord’s body, placed it in his own sarcophagus, “in which no one had yet been laid” (Luke 23:[Col. 1084B] 53), the Lord lay from that hour until the morning of the Lord’s Day.

Others object: if the Lord rested in the tomb from that hour until Sunday, then it was not three days, as he himself foretold. This is resolved by the following plausible argument. Truth, who is Christ, never uttered a falsehood when he said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall raise it up” (John 2:19); and: “As Jonah was in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights, so shall the Son of Man be” (Matt. 12:40), who is Christ. Speaking truly, he most truly confirmed that he was in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights and was raised after three days.

In truth, from the hour when the Lord was seized and condemned to death, he lay in the heart of the earth—that is, in the heart of earthly and faithless people—who said: “Where are the words [Col. 1084C] by which he said, ‘Before Abraham was made, I am’” (John 8:58), and many others? He lay also in the heart of the earth—that is, in the hearts of the apostles, who were still earthly and doubted his resurrection, and who fled when they saw him delivered to death, remaining in deepest sorrow. Thus he lay in their hearts, because they retained the Lord in their minds.

Or, alternatively, he lay in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights because, from the evening when he was seized, through that whole night and the day of Preparation, the night of the Sabbath and the Sabbath itself, and the Sunday night until the morning of the Lord’s Day, he truly rested in the tomb. For from the moment he was condemned to death, he lay as though already in burial. They say that even thus three days were not completed. To this we say that there is here the figure of synecdoche—that is, the part for the whole—because the morning of the Lord’s Day is counted for the whole day.

[Col. 1084D] Now, as clearly as our ability allowed, the proposed questions have been resolved. But may he who was pleased to suffer all these things for our salvation hold us, his redeemed adopted children, in peace—that is, in himself and in his holy incarnation—and deliver us from every sin by his death; and may he place us in his most holy kingdom, so that after the passage of this life we may be able with joyful countenance to behold him reigning with the Father and the Holy Spirit through infinite ages of ages. Amen. Thanks be to God, who satisfies us from your gifts—us [perhaps “destitute”].

**SECOND TREATISE. ON THE UNLEAVENED SACRIFICE, TO LEO THE MONK.**

[Col. 1085]

[Col. 1085A] You very often urge—and all the more press—our lowliness, dearest brother Leo and venerable monk, to write something briefly and summarily concerning the observance of the sacrifice for the spiritual lords, the monastic brethren dwelling in the city of Constantinople, who are frequently reproached for their excessive verbosity and immoderate zeal by the Greeks. For it has been reported by you and by many others that they are often deceived, indiscriminately, by the bishop of that see or by his clerics—sometimes with flattering persuasion, sometimes with furious speech—so that you may abandon the rite of our unleavened sacrifice and offer to God leavened sacrifice after the Greek custom. To these persons, let us answer fearlessly—not from our own presumption, but from the authoritative learning of the holy theological Fathers—on the contrary.

[Col. 1085B] Although their religious Fathers and teachers have undertaken to offer sacrifice to almighty God from leavened bread, we never find that they nullified or mocked our offering. What shall we say to this? “Has Christ been divided in his body” (1 Cor. 1:13), so that one Christ is in the Roman sacrifice and another in the Constantinopolitan? What wise person could say this? Only one who knows how to tear the Lord’s garment, such as Arius and the other heretics. But we truly maintain—indeed, firmly believe—that, although the customs of the churches differ, there is one faith, inseparably united to its head, that is, Christ; and he himself remains one and the same in his body, which he willingly offered to God the Father for our salvation.

Let them therefore recover their senses from this notorious *chacheton* [an uncertain or corrupt word], this controversy, and cease disparaging Latin purity. For if, with stopped ears, they refuse to assent to our truth, we demonstrate beyond all doubt that our sacrifice, being prior and purer than theirs, was prefigured not only by evangelical and apostolic authority but also by the legal institution of the Old Testament.

[Col. 1085C] For we read in the book of Exodus (chap. 11:1), where God commanded holy Moses that, on the fourteenth moon of the first month at evening, the children of Israel should sacrifice to the Lord an unblemished lamb and eat its flesh roasted with fire, together with unleavened bread. Meanwhile, should they answer you that this was an old commandment, now ended and passed away, confidently set before them the saying of the blessed Apostle Paul:

> “All these things happened to them in figure; but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 1:11).

[Col. 1085D] Take note, beloved. If it was a figure of the Old Testament, then it foreshadowed our times; and what lay hidden in shadow now shone forth in the light of the New Testament. It was therefore written, and was to be observed even by the faithful themselves.

[Col. 1086A] For just as, in the sacrifice of the lamb, the Passion of our Redeemer was prefigured; in the Red Sea, baptism; in the pillar of cloud, the Holy Spirit; in the heavenly manna, the gift of grace; and in the rock that followed them, Christ—so in unleavened bread the sacrifice of our time was shown forth.

The Creator and Redeemer of humankind, coming into this world clothed in our mortality without losing his divinity, after all that had been foretold concerning him had been fulfilled, and having determined by the Father’s counsel to redeem the world by his death, wished at the appointed time to offer to God the Father for our life that most pure and most sacred body which he had received from the immaculate Virgin.

[Col. 1086B] At that most holy supper, therefore, when he celebrated the Passover with his disciples, he took bread into his holy hands, broke it, and gave it to them, saying:

> “Take and eat: this is my body, which shall be given for you. Do this in remembrance of me” (1 Cor. 11:14).

Let the brethren say, I beg them: what sort of bread was that? Was it unleavened or leavened? If they say leavened, then the Lord’s statement is false when he says: “I came not to abolish the law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5:17). How could he who gave the law bring blessing down to us if he had not observed what belonged to the law?

> [Note: Col. 1085D] “When we read concerning the Lord, when he made his body from bread, that he took bread and blessed it, neither ‘unleavened’ nor ‘leavened’ is added. Yet it is certain that he blessed unleavened bread—perhaps not because the act being performed required this, but because the supper in which it was performed required it.” Anselm of Canterbury, *Treatise on Unleavened and Leavened Bread*, chap. 1.

[Col. 1086C] Had he done otherwise, he would justly have been punished as a transgressor of the law, and would not have died for the redemption of us all. For the Lord Jesus himself says through Moses that from the fourteenth day of the first month—when the Passover was slain—until the twenty-second day of the same month, whoever was found among the people of Israel to have leaven in his house would perish from the assembly of the children of Israel, because he had made void God’s covenant.

592 Let it now suffice us to have brought forward testimony from the legal observance of the command. Let the following discourse proceed to the grace of the Gospel and the light of the New Testament. For at that time he could not otherwise have celebrated that Passover alone and without all the rest, though it had been appointed for all in common, while fulfilling both Testaments in himself.

The holy evangelists likewise spoke thus concerning the celebration of his Passover and the observance of bread.

[Col. 1086D] One says: “The feast-day of unleavened bread, which is called Passover, was approaching” (Luke 22:1). Another repeats the same thing: “It was Passover, and the unleavened bread was two days away” (Mark 14:1).

[Col. 1087A] Again: “On the first day of unleavened bread his disciples came to him, saying, ‘Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?’” (Matt. 26:17). “Jesus knew that his hour had come to pass from this world” (John 13:1).

Therefore, if Passover, which in Hebrew is called *phase*, takes its name from passing over, not from suffering—as many wrongly interpret it—then surely the Lord Jesus, at his passing, that is, in his death, handed over to his disciples no bread other than that which paternal tradition had commanded to be kept.

Nor did he do this only before his Passion. After the resurrection he repeated the same thing (Luke 24:31): with the disciples at Emmaus unable to recognize him except in the breaking of bread, and constrained to remain with them, he broke for them and gave them to eat the same unleavened bread.

[Col. 1087B] Certainly, throughout all Judaea leaven was absent, because they were still celebrating the Passover—unless this is meant to make you recognize more clearly that after the resurrection he gave them the same bread that he had already given before the Passion.

Let it suffice thus far that we have supplied you with the teaching of the Gospel. Now we must turn our attention to the Epistle of the blessed Apostle Paul, where he diligently urges us concerning the sacrifice itself, that it be unleavened and not leavened:

> “Brothers, purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new dough, as you are unleavened; for Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed. Therefore let us feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5:7–8).

[Col. 1087C] But why, dearest brothers, did the holy Apostle preach this? To show that Christ’s bread should not be contaminated with the execrable and abominable corruption of any teaching of heretics or schismatics—that is, with leaven—but should always be preserved in the purity and simplicity of unblemished Catholic faith, lest the soul of anyone who eats it unworthily perish from the assembly of the true children of Israel, that is, of those who are to be saved.

Again the Lord speaks through Amos, saying:

> “Come to Bethel, and act impiously, and sacrifice praise from leaven” (Amos 4:4).

What is expressed by Bethel except an idol, except the corruption of sacrilege? Hence the Lord warns in the Gospel:

> “Beware of the leaven [Col. 1087D] of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy” (Luke 12:1);

that is, beware their carnal doctrine and puffed-up learning, concerning which the Apostle says: “Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up” (1 Cor. 8:1). And again: “A little leaven corrupts the whole mass” (Gal. 5:9).

Let these few testimonies, drawn from many, suffice. Will they still dare, with irreverent brow, to press their argument against us by saying that we eat unleavened bread with the Hebrews according to Jewish custom? To this insane objection we answer with sound understanding:

> [Note: Col. 1087D] Saint Anselm also refutes this same objection in chap. 3: “Therefore, when we sacrifice unleavened bread, we do so not in order to signify by the figure of unleavened bread that the Lord Jesus would be such; but in order, by divine power, to sacrifice that very bread into his body. Thus we do not at all keep the oldness of the law, but celebrate the truth of the Gospel.”

Far be this from the Catholic and Apostolic Roman [Col. 1088A] Church, which is called—and is shown to be—the head, foundation, and mirror of all churches, and which God and our Lord Jesus Christ deigned to build through himself. He promised especially to his beloved disciple, the Apostle Peter, saying:

> “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16:17).

And again:

> “I have prayed to the Father for you, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brethren” (Luke 22:32).

Far be it from the Lord of the whole world that the Roman Church should Judaize with the Hebrews merely because it is said to offer sacrifice to the Lord from unleavened bread. Far be it that the Roman Church should do this for such a reason: rather, she does it in order to show her faithful established throughout the world that the Lamb who took away the sins of the world received pure and holy flesh from the immaculate Virgin, without every corruption, defilement, or contagion of sin.

[Col. 1088B] The angel testifies to this when he announced the incarnation of the Lord himself to that venerable Virgin, saying:

> “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore that holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

That overshadowing, said to overshadow the virginal womb, is to be understood in no other way than that it kept untouched and pure forever—that is, unleavened—that most chaste temple of the Lord in which he deigned to dwell, free from every heat of concupiscence or corruption of any sinful act. As Solomon says: “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Prov. 9:1).

[Col. 1088C] 593 For, to repeat what we have said above: why should we not retain sacrifice from the old commandment? Why should we not see fulfilled spiritually in ourselves what was commanded to them carnally? Do we not retain from them the temple, priesthood, anointing, incense, priestly garments, and Lent? If the Israelite people first possessed all these things and, afterward, through the Lord’s cooperation, they were granted to us, why should unleavened sacrifice also not be offered to the Lord among the other commandments, since, as we have often testified, it signifies purity, simplicity, and cleanness?

And we find that the very first and chief of all the apostles, after the Lord’s Ascension, first offered sacrifice in no other manner than that which he had been commanded by the Lord and his teacher to offer.

[Col. 1088D] After him, blessed Clement, to whom blessed Peter entrusted the high-priestly office, instructs James, who governed the Church of Jerusalem, in his Epistle concerning the observance of the same sacrifice, saying:

> [Note: Col. 1088D] The learned do not recognize this as genuine.

> “When my lord and teacher Peter entrusted to me the dignity of the highest priesthood, among the many exhortations by which I was admonished by him, when he came to the Lord’s sacrifice, he spoke to me concerning it thus: ‘See, Clement, that you do not act otherwise concerning the body [Col. 1089A] of the Lord than I command you. For I do not speak this from myself; but as I heard it from the mouth of the Lord and my teacher Jesus Christ, so I speak it. Likewise, leave this example forever to your successors, who after you shall succeed to this Apostolic See.’”

Thus after him Saint Silvester, who baptized at Rome the illustrious Augustus Constantine, the perfect son of the Church, perfectly fulfilled the same commands and ordered them to be preserved by posterity as well.

Finally, Saint Gregory, the outstanding teacher, who overcame Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople, and his supporters in the presence of Emperor Maurice with admirable reasoning, did not celebrate in another way, nor prescribe that we celebrate, the sacrifice otherwise than as all his most holy predecessor popes—whom it would take too long to enumerate—had been commanded to celebrate it in the most holy Apostolic See.

[Col. 1089B] Therefore, most beloved brothers, stand manfully in firmness [Col. 1090A] and in the secure foundation of the orthodox pillar. Let no one, by persuasive words, separate you from the custom of the holy Catholic and Apostolic faith of the aforesaid See—the Roman mother Church. For, as Augustine, the most eloquent teacher and African bishop, testifies, there is no other see in heaven or earth more worthy or more ancient than that held by the Roman Church.

Hold fast to this; love it with a pure heart; and do not depart from its unity. For it is written: “Do not overstep the boundary which the ancient Fathers established” (Prov. 22:28); and “He who breaks down a hedge shall be bitten by a serpent” (Eccl. 10:8). That serpent is, of course, the one who cast Adam out of Paradise. May the Lord always deliver you from its pestiferous mouth, through the intercession of the apostles and all the saints, by the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages. Amen.

594 ADMONITION TO THE FOLLOWING TREATISE

[Col. 1089]

That this little work was written most wisely and devoutly is demonstrated not merely because it was published at Venice by Mauro Marchesio in 1651 among the other works of Saint Bruno, but because it was reprinted by the editors of the *Bibliotheca Maxima Veterum*, Lyons edition, 1677, vol. 20, p. 1725; again by Dom Luc d’Achery in the *Spicilegium*, vol. 12, Paris edition, 1725; and at Turin in a separate small volume, without a date.

But its reputation is greatly enhanced by the editor of the *Codex Liturgicus*, the distinguished Philip Zazzera, who discovered it among the manuscripts of the Vatican Library, illustrated it with his learned notes, and published it at Rome in 1784, dedicating it to the most holy pontiff, our lord Pius VI.

Since I had proposed to prepare a new edition of this work of Saint Bruno, complete in every respect, I did not hesitate to consult at Florence a thirteenth-century manuscript in the Library of San Marco of the Order of Preachers, and another manuscript of roughly the same age written in the Vatican archives. From these manuscripts and editions I extracted many variant readings. They correct a great many errors, especially in Marchesio and in the Turin edition, and yield a cleaner and more complete text.

Here an especially fitting opportunity opens to me to provide information, where it is lacking, about the excellent work entitled *Explanation of the Rites of the Holy Church and of the Divine Offices*. Its autograph, as I have said, is preserved in the Vatican Library. The distinguished Philip Zazzera, who rendered outstanding service to the study of ecclesiastical institutions, published it adorned with abundant and learned commentaries.

At the beginning it is noted that this explanation was composed by an anonymous writer of the twelfth century and was then first brought forth from Vatican manuscript no. 5046. One point remains to be noted: the anonymous author begins his explanation of rites with this little work of Bruno. From this it may be inferred that the work was already held in high esteem by churchmen at that time, being placed before other writers on sacred rites, as though it were itself the leader of their chorus.

595 THIRD TREATISE. ON THE SACRAMENTS OF THE CHURCH, THE MYSTERIES, AND ECCLESIASTICAL RITES

(From the Turin edition.)

[Col. 1089B]

> [Note: Col. 1089C] We give this inscription according to the most distinguished Carlo Sebastiano Berardi, who in part 2, vol. 2, p. 116, of his amended edition of Gratian mentions this bishop; not according to the erroneous Turin edition [Col. 1090C], which reads: “To his most beloved brother Gualter, bishop of Maguelonne.” This reading is also found in Marchesio and other editors.

To his most beloved brother GALTERIUS, bishop of Maguelonne [Col. 1089C], Bruno, bishop of Segni, greetings.

When we were once together at Rome, on the Island, in the house of the bishop of Porto, and when we were reading in the book of Exodus certain typical things, significant of a great mystery, concerning the tabernacle of testimony and Aaron’s garments, you began to wonder, and I began to wonder with you, that [Col. 1090B] we still see some things like these done in the Church, although the old things have passed away and all things have become new.

[Col. 1090C] For many things take place in the dedications of churches, and many in the other sacraments of the Church, which seem no less than those earlier things to be performed under shadow and figure.

[Col. 1091A] You therefore asked me to attempt to explain these things as I had explained those. I promised that I would do it, but, hindered by other business, I had almost forgotten both your request and my promise, when Helbert, a hermit and venerable priest, came from you to us and demanded, as though a debt, what I had promised. Remembering your affection, therefore, although greatly occupied, I have begun to do what you commanded me to do.

596 On the Consecration of a Church

> [Note: Col. 1091D] The Turin edition lacks this title, which the manuscripts and the Roman edition give. In d’Achery it reads: “Explanation: On the Consecration of a Church.” Dom Philip Zazzera omitted Saint Bruno’s letter to the bishop of Maguelonne.

As we are about to speak concerning the sacraments of the Church, let us first set forth the rites themselves; afterwards, as the Lord grants, let us explain what they signify.

> [Note: Col. 1091D] Luc d’Achery reads: “Afterwards let us explain what they signify.”

For when a church is consecrated, the deacon alone enters it, shuts the doors,

> [Note: Col. 1091D] The same author reads: “shuts the doors,”

and there waits to answer [Col. 1091B] the bishop. Then the bishop blesses water outside, not without salt. Taking a bundle of hyssop and water which he has just sanctified, he sprinkles the church walls while making three circuits. He likewise strikes the doors three times with the pastoral staff, saying:

> “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. 23:8).

The deacon answers from within:

> “Who is this King of glory?” (ibid.)

And the bishop says:

> “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (ibid., v. 9).

After the third striking, he enters the church, taking a few ministers with him while the rest of the multitude waits outside. Then the bishop writes the entire alphabet twice on the pavement in the form of a cross.

[Col. 1091C] Next, as before, he sanctifies other water, to which he adds not only salt but also ashes and wine. With this the altar and church are sprinkled and consecrated. Afterwards, having poured oil and chrism upon the altar, the bishop anoints the stone itself.

> [Note: Col. 1091D] This section is absent from the Venetian, Lyons, and Turin editions.

And then at last he places and arranges relics there. These matters having been completed, let us consider their meanings.

But first one must ask: why is water blessed? Why are stones and walls sprinkled? Why, rather, are the stones and walls themselves not blessed directly? Why are they not sanctified without water? Why is the same blessing given to water not given to the stones? All this has a meaning.

> [Note: Col. 1091D] The Vatican manuscript has another reading: “But first one must ask why the water is blessed with which the stones and walls are sprinkled; why, rather, these stones and walls themselves are not blessed directly; why they are not sanctified without water; why the same blessing which is given to water is not given to the stones. All this is a signification.” D’Achery differs in some particulars: “But first,” he says, “one must ask why the water is blessed with which stones and walls are sprinkled. Why, then, are these stones and walls not blessed by prayer? Why are they not sanctified without water?” In the rest he agrees.

Listen, then, to what the Lord says: “Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5). Water is suitable for washing bodies; it has merited to receive such power that, just as it washes bodies of dirt, so it cleanses souls from sins.

What Water Signifies

[Col. 1092A]

It is thus clear that this water signifies baptism, by whose sprinkling the church is consecrated and, in a manner, baptized.

What the Church Signifies

The church building itself signifies, surely, that Church which is contained in it—that is, the multitude. It is called *ecclesia* because it contains the Church. Grammarians call this figure metonymy: when that which contains is put in place of that which is contained. Such is the Lord’s saying in the Gospel: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets” (Matt. 23:31), although it was not Jerusalem itself but its inhabitants who killed the prophets.

Likewise, we commonly say: “That house is good,” because it has good inhabitants; and “that one is bad,” because bad inhabitants dwell in it.

[Col. 1092B] In this sense, then, this church constructed of wood and stones signifies the Church built of living stones. Its stones are joined and united not by lime but by charity; its foundation is Christ; its gates are the apostles; its pillars are bishops and teachers; and in it each stone shines the more brightly, the more faithful and better it is.

What Salt Signifies

Since, then, it has been said what water and what the house signify, let us also say why this water is mixed with salt. For when our Savior spoke about baptism, [Col. 1092C] he made no mention of salt. He did not say, “Unless one is reborn of salt water,” or “water mixed with salt,” or anything of that sort. But what did he say? “Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5).

The same may be said of oil and chrism, but of them elsewhere. For the present, let us speak of salt.

597 For in divine speech salt is frequently used for wisdom. Thus: “Let your speech be seasoned with salt” (Col. 4:6). And the Lord says to the disciples: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:43). Again: “You are the salt of the earth; but if salt has become foolish, with what shall it be seasoned?” (Matt. 5:13).

Hence also, according to the law (Lev. 2:23), no offering is made without salt, but it is placed in every sacrifice.

[Col. 1092D] It is therefore clear that salt

> [Note: Col. 1092D] The Roman edition adds “salt,” absent from the other editions.

is used for wisdom. For wisdom is the seasoning of all virtues, just as salt is the seasoning of all foods. But what wisdom? Certainly not the wisdom of the world, which “is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3:19), but the wisdom of which the Lord says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Luke 10:11).

[Col. 1093A] But do you wish to hear what this wisdom is—how simple it is, how easy to learn? Let someone now come to this water, let someone now come to baptism; let him hear this wisdom and taste this salt. For no one is baptized before being fed with salt; this is known to everyone, I mean literally.

When infants come to the faith, salt is immediately placed in their mouths:

> [Note: Col. 1093D] See Theodulf, *On the Order of Baptism*, chap. 5, in Menard’s notes to the *Sacramentary of Saint Gregory the Great*, col. 364; and Menard himself on that work, col. 377 and following.

so that what they cannot possess in act, they may possess at least in the signification of the sacrament.

I therefore ask someone about to be baptized: “Do you believe in [Col. 1093B] God the Father almighty, creator of all things visible and invisible?” He says: “I believe.” “Do you also believe in Jesus Christ, his Son, our only Lord, born and having suffered?” He says: “I believe.” “Do you also believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy Catholic Church, the communion of saints, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life?” He says: “I believe.”

This person has been well instructed; he is wise and has been sufficiently fed with salt. This, then, is the salt mixed with water: these are the first rudiments of faith. Without them baptism has no efficacy.

> [Note: Col. 1093D] The distinguished Philip Zazzera aptly noted on this passage: “He does not mean that baptism is invalid where the matter and form prescribed by Christ are administered, but that, if we consider the grace of righteousness and salvation, it is received in vain by an adult who, besides the desire for baptism and faith, does not bring repentance for a life previously ill-lived and a firm resolve to abstain from sins.” See the Roman Catechism, *On the Sacrament of Baptism*, no. 35 and following; and Saint Thomas, *Summa theologiae*, III, q. [Col. 1094D] 68, art. 6 and following.

For if you take away either the water or these words, there is no baptism. In saying this, however, I do no injury to infants and those who do not yet understand, who are baptized and saved by another’s faith, not their own. They are indeed saved if they either die beforehand [Col. 1093C] or, upon reaching maturity, faithfully believe and keep the faith promised on their behalf. Otherwise the water of baptism has no efficacy, because it has not been seasoned.

> [Note: Col. 1094D] That is, even though they have received baptism, they do not attain eternal life because of the lack of works which ought to follow faith.

It has therefore been said what water, salt, and the house to be dedicated signify. It remains now to speak concerning the hyssop with which the aforesaid water is sprinkled upon the church walls.

What Hyssop Signifies

Hyssop naturally grows upon rock. “And the Rock,” says the Apostle, “was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). Hyssop is a good herb: it grows, grows again, and takes root in Christ. Although the whole multitude of the faithful can be understood through it, those are especially represented by hyssop who, rooted and founded in Christ’s faith, cannot be torn away or separated from his love.

[Col. 1093D] What better persons can we understand by this than bishops and priests, who,

> [Note: Col. 1094D] Vatican Archives manuscript: “because.”

the greater dignity they hold in the Church, the more firmly [Col. 1094A] they ought to adhere to Christ’s faith? Through them water is sprinkled; through them and by them the faithful are baptized; to them is given the power to perform the sacraments of baptism.

Nor should this be passed over: the bishop goes around the church three times and sprinkles the walls with water three times.

What Is Signified by Going Around

Here too the figure of baptism is evident. Listen to what the Lord says to his disciples: “Go,” he says, “teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). Hence the sacred canons command that those being baptized be immersed in water three times.

> [Note: Col. 1094D] Saint Thomas treats whether triple immersion is necessary to baptism, *Summa theologiae*, III, q. 66, art. 8; on the authority of Saint Gregory he teaches that it is not necessary, but that a simple washing with water suffices: “For a single immersion signifies the unity of Christ’s death and the unity of the Godhead; triple immersion, however, signifies the three days of Christ’s burial and also the Trinity of persons.”

Since the Church cannot be immersed in water, therefore, it is sprinkled with water three times as the bishop makes his circuit. You see, then, [Col. 1094B] how well all that has been said above agrees with the sacraments of baptism.

Let us now consider also why the bishop strikes the doors of the church three times with the pastoral staff.

598 What the Staff Signifies

What is meant by the pastoral staff except the divine word and evangelical preaching? That speech is called a staff is attested by the prophet concerning the Lord, saying that “he shall strike the earth with the staff of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked” (Isa. 11:4). The staff of the mouth is speech.

To strike the doors with the staff, then, is to strike the ears of hearers with the voice of preaching. For ears are gates through which we bring the words of holy preaching into the hearts of those who hear. Hence the Psalmist says: “You who raise me up from the gates of death, [Col. 1094C] that I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. 9:15). What are the gates of the daughter of Zion except the ears and hearing of the faithful?

Nor is it without mystery that the bishop strikes the doors three times. This number is most well known and most sacred. For in every dedication the bishop must always strike the doors three times, because no sacrament is performed in the Church without the invocation of the Trinity. Let us therefore strike the doors of the church and devote ourselves to preaching, so that we may be able to reach the inner chamber of the heart and bring in faith in Christ.

What the Letters Signify

Having explained all that the bishop does outwardly in the dedication of a church, let us now see what he does within. Entering the church, [Col. 1094D] he writes the whole alphabet twice upon the pavement. By this are represented either both Testaments or the twofold understanding of the holy Scriptures.

[Col. 1095A] In these few letters all knowledge is contained. The alphabet is written once in the synagogue and twice on the pavement of the church. For the Jews receive only one Testament,

> [Note: Col. 1095D] D’Achery reads “the Old [Testament].”

which they interpret not in two ways as we do, but only simply and according to the letter alone. But the children of the Church receive both, and understand both in two ways—that is, literally and spiritually.

The alphabet is therefore written twice upon the pavement of our body if we receive both Testaments and understand each in two ways. Thus those animals are called unclean which neither chew the cud nor divide the hoof. For animals that chew the cud—what I say is very well known—eat the same food twice. Sacred reading is the food of the soul; and we eat it twice, because we expound and understand it once according to the letter and again spiritually.

[Col. 1095B] To divide the hoof is likewise to interpret sacred Scripture in two ways. It is called a hoof because, on the path of good works, it steadies and protects our feet.

Why It Is Written in the Form of a Cross

But why are these letters written not straight, but diagonally and in the form of a cross? It is because one cannot attain the understanding of the sacred Scriptures unless one receives the mystery of the cross and believes that one has been saved by Christ’s Passion. Only Christians possess this understanding, marked as they are with the sign of the cross. For them “the lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered to open the book and to loose its seven seals” (Rev. 5:5).

For in Christ’s [Col. 1095C] Passion,

> [Note: Col. 1095D] Vatican Archives manuscript: “For in Christ’s death.”

the veil of the temple was torn and the Holy of Holies was revealed.

> [Note: Col. 1095D] Vatican manuscript: “the bodies of the saints were revealed.”

Let us consider the remaining matters.

What the Water Blessed Within Signifies

After this the bishop likewise blesses another water, to which he adds not only salt, as to the first water discussed above, but also wine together with ashes.

> [Note: Col. 1095D] Vatican Archives manuscript: “and ashes.”

This water signifies the Holy Spirit, without whose breath nothing is ever sanctified and without whose grace there is no remission of sins.
