That the Holy Spirit is called water is shown by Truth himself, who says: “He who believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7:38). The Evangelist immediately explains what this means: “Now he said this concerning the Spirit, [Col. 1095D] whom those who believed in him were to receive” (ibid., v. 39).

Water, therefore, is the Holy Spirit. Observe also the order of the sacrament: outwardly it is consecrated by water, inwardly by the Holy Spirit. This is what the Lord says: “Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit” (John 3:5). Behold the water; behold the Spirit.

In the sacrament of baptism, therefore, there is neither water without the Spirit nor Spirit without water. The Spirit himself signified this when, in the first creation of the world, he “was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1).

With this water both the altar itself and the entire inner sanctuary are sprinkled. Concerning the salt [Col. 1096A] added to it, however, enough has been said above. We have said that it signifies the first rudiments of faith. These alone could have sufficed for the sacrament of baptism; but our holy Fathers, who established these things by the Spirit of God, wished to satisfy us not only in those things which pertain to the efficacy of the sacrament, but also in those which pertain to signification.

599 Water and the Spirit suffice for the perfection of baptism; the other things added pertain to signification. For the Apostle Philip did not have oil or chrism when he baptized the eunuch. Nevertheless, these things that have been added by the careful exposition of the saints to signify something are not now to be passed over.

> [Note: Col. 1096D] Thus the Council of Trent defined, session 7, canon 13, that the Church’s rites in the administration of the sacraments are to be observed without exception.

What Wine Signifies
[Col. 1096B] Let us therefore say what wine signifies. Wine in this place denotes a deeper and spiritual understanding of the divine law. Thus, when our Saviour was invited to the wedding, he changed the waters into wine, so that he might instruct us by a fuller understanding and satisfy us with the nectar of spiritual and new teaching. For divine Scripture, understood according to the letter, is water without taste or delight; but if it is understood spiritually, it becomes wine—indeed, of wondrous flavour and great sweetness. For the difference between water and wine is the difference between letter and spirit; hence the Apostle says: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (1 Cor. 3:6). Promising this wine long ago, the Psalmist says: “They shall be made drunk with the abundance of thy house, and thou shalt give them to drink from the torrent of thy delight” (Ps. 35:9). And again: “Thy inebriating cup—how splendid it is!” (Ps. 22:5). And again: “He humbles this man and exalts that man, because the cup of the Lord is full of pure wine, mingled” (Ps. 74:8–9). For the Lord humbles the Jew and exalts the Gentile. Why? Because the former follows the letter, which kills; the latter drinks pure wine and spiritual understanding. For the whole ruin of the Jews lies in this: trusting in the letter, they refuse to receive spiritual understanding. Hence the Psalmist says: “Let their table before them become a snare, a recompense, and a stumbling-block; let their eyes be darkened, and bow down their back continually” (Ps. 68:23). This table is divine Scripture: souls are nourished by its delicacies; yet whatever animal eats or drinks of them shall not live unless it chews the cud. This wine, therefore, is good—but good for those who use God well and faithfully.

For drinking this wine the Lord himself invites us in the Song of Songs, saying: “Eat, my friends, and be made drunk, my beloved. I sleep, but my heart keeps watch” (Cant. 5:1–2). The Lord therefore now commands us to be made drunk, although elsewhere he says that drunkenness must be avoided: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with revelry and drunkenness” (Luke 21:34). Thus there is both good and bad drunkenness; [Col. 1097A] for what the Lord commands can only be good, and what he forbids can only be evil. Good drunkenness is drunkenness of the mind.

[Note: [Col. 1097D] The editions lack what the Vatican manuscript has: “Bad drunkenness is drunkenness of the belly.”]

And enough has been said concerning what wine signifies.

### What Ash Signifies

It remains now to speak of ash. But what is ash except penitence? To sit in ashes and be clothed in sackcloth belongs to penitents. Thus it is said of the penitent Ninevites: “The king himself rose from his throne, put on sackcloth, and sat in ashes” (Jonah 3:6). Thus too David says: “I ate ashes as bread, and mingled my drink with weeping” (Ps. 101:10). Thus too Abraham: “I will speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18:27). Thus the sinful human being is told: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Ecclus. 10:9). The Lord also speaks through the prophet to Babylon:

[Note: [Col. 1097D] These words are absent from the Vatican manuscript, though not from the Vatican Archive manuscript.]

“Come down; sit in the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon: there is no throne for you any longer” (Isa. 47:1). Hence the custom has become established in the Church that, every year at the beginning of Lent, we sprinkle our heads with ashes. From these and similar passages it is easily shown that ash denotes penitence.

Since, then, it has been said what water, salt, wine, and ash signify, let us now say why they are mixed together, so that the church may be consecrated by their sprinkling. For I think that without these—if even one of them is absent—the people of the Lord, which is the Church, is neither sanctified [Col. 1097C] nor released from sins. This is evident concerning water: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5). Nor is there doubt concerning salt, because no one can ever be saved without the seasoning of faith signified by salt, even if sprinkled with the water of baptism.

But what shall I say of wine, through which spiritual understanding is signified? Whoever has not been sprinkled with it, whoever has not drunk from it or believed those who offer it to drink, shall not attain the blessedness of eternal life. The sprinkling of ash also, by which penitence is understood, [600] is so necessary that without it there is no remission of sins.

[Note: [Col. 1097D] Saint Bruno must here be understood to speak of adults approaching baptism, for whom penitence is necessary, as Saint Thomas likewise teaches, III, question 68, articles 4 and 5, and the Roman Catechism, On the Sacrament of Baptism, no. 40.]

For by it one comes to baptism; after baptism it is the one unique and singular refuge of sinners [Col. 1097D]. Hence baptism is not without reason so called, since the Gospel says of John: “He came into all the region of Galilee, preaching a baptism of penitence for the remission of sins” (Luke 3:3). For he said: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 3:2).

[Col. 1098A] Thus John’s preaching began; thus Christ’s preaching began. In all this, only little children and others without understanding are excepted. This, therefore, is the reason why all these things—water, salt, wine, and ash—are mixed together: because, as we have said, if even one is lacking for little children, the others are of no use.

[Note: [Col. 1098D] The Vatican manuscript reads “little or nothing”; all editions read “the others are of no use.”]

When these have thus been mixed, the bishop approaches the altar and, taking a bundle of hyssop, sprinkles with this aforesaid water and sanctifies the church and the altar.

### What the Altar Is

But what does the altar in the temple signify? The Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3:17). If, therefore, we are God’s temple, we also have an altar: our altar is our heart. For [Col. 1098B] the heart is in the human being what the altar is in the temple. On this altar the sacrifice of praise and jubilation is made.

[Note: [Col. 1098D] D’Achéry: “the sacrifice of praise and tribulation.”]

Hence the Psalmist says: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God; a broken and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. 50:19). On this altar commemoration is made of Christ’s body and blood. From here prayers ascend to heaven, because God looks upon the heart. This altar, therefore, is sprinkled with water when human hearts are cleansed of sins by Gospel preaching.

### Water Is Preaching

For preaching too is water, according to the saying: “All who thirst, come to the waters” (Isa. 55:2). And again: “The words from a man’s mouth are deep water” (Prov. 18:4). And again:

[Note: [Col. 1098D] The Vatican manuscript and the Vatican Archive manuscript have *exspectetur* (“let it be expected”). Yet the Vulgate, from the Septuagint version, reads: “Let thy speech flow as dew.”]

“Let thy speech be accounted as rain” [Col. 1098C] (Deut. 32:2). By this water, that is, Gospel preaching, and by the sanctification of the Holy Spirit, the altar of the heart and the whole person are cleansed and sanctified. Behold, the altar has been sprinkled; it has been baptized with waters. It remains, then, that it be confirmed and anointed with chrism. For we see this done in human beings themselves: they are first baptized and afterwards confirmed with chrism.

### What Oil Is

Let us therefore say what oil and chrism signify. For those already baptized and cleansed from the filth of sins are not anointed with oil and chrism without cause. Oil signifies mercy; whoever does not have it has lost the very thing for which he was baptized. Hence Truth itself says:

[Note: [Col. 1098D] In the Vatican manuscripts, *ipsa* (“itself”) is not read.]

“If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your Father forgive you your sins” [Col. 1098D] (Matt. 6:15). Hence that servant was condemned who would not remit a hundred denarii to his fellow servant, the Lord saying: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all your debt because you begged me. Should you not therefore also have had mercy [Col. 1099A] on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?” (Matt. 18:32).

Oil fittingly signifies mercy, because, just as oil is above other liquids, so mercy is pre-eminent among good works. Whatever liquid you pour oil into, the oil always floats on top. It is likewise written concerning mercy: “The Lord is gracious to all, and his mercy is over all his works” (Ps. 144:5). “For mercy exalts itself above judgment” (Jas. 2:13). Hence also the Lord says: “I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (Matt. 9:13). There is much that can be said concerning mercy. For “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. 32:5); and “Who is wise and will keep these things, and understand the mercies of the Lord?” (Ps. 106:43).

Let the altar of our heart therefore be anointed and smeared with this oil, so that, always mindful of mercy, we may not lose the sprinkling of water and the regeneration of baptism. For what benefit is it that we have been sprinkled with hyssop and baptized by priests, if our Father in heaven does not forgive us our sins?

[Note: [Col. 1099D] These words, found in both Vatican manuscripts, are absent in D’Achéry.]

Let our hearts always float in the oil of mercy, so that our sins may be forgiven us. This is what is to be said about oil.

[601]

### What Balsam Is

If balsam is added to it, chrism is made, by which kings and priests are anointed. For balsam is joined to oil when a good fragrance is added to mercy. But what is a good fragrance? Spiritual joy and good will. Hence the Apostle says: “He who shows mercy, let him do so with cheerfulness” [Col. 1099C] (Rom. 12:8). “For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7). Let Christians therefore be anointed with such chrism, that they may truly be called Christians; for *Christianus* is named from Christ, and *Christus* from chrism. He is anointed with such chrism who, by the honourableness of his life and the merit of holy conduct, spreads far and wide the fragrance of his good reputation. Hence the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ unto God, who makes known through us in every place the fragrance of his knowledge” (2 Cor. 14:15). Thus the Church is consecrated; thus God’s people are renewed, blessed, and sanctified.

### What the Consecration of Chrism and Oil Signifies

We must now say why, in the consecration of oil and chrism, the bishop breathes upon it three times. For we read in the Gospel that the Lord breathed upon his disciples, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20:22). This breathing signifies that breathing; and it is performed three times because the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, and does not come from himself. Our Saviour could indeed have given the Holy Spirit without any breathing; but he gave it by breathing in order that we might understand that the Spirit proceeds from him also, as from his Father.

[Col. 1100A] Although we do not know how the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son—for this is revealed to no one in this life, in which we see only through a mirror and in an enigma—nevertheless we know most certainly and do not at all doubt that he proceeds from the Father and the Son, that is, from the substance of the Father and the Son. This is proper to him: he proceeds from no other substance, is sent by no other, and is given by no other—the Holy Spirit. He is given through the office of priests, but not by priests. Thus Christ’s power is present through the breathing performed by priests in honour of the signification of the Holy Spirit, through words spoken in his name.

[Note: [Col. 1099D] The Vatican manuscript edited by the distinguished Zazzera reads: “which is performed by priests in honour and in the sanctification of his Holy Spirit, just as through the words spoken in his honour.” [Col. 1100D]]

### What the Candles Are

The twelve candles are the twelve apostles, [Col. 1100B] by whose teaching darkness was driven away and by whose preaching the world was enlightened. The altar-stone signifies not only Christ, but also Christ’s members. Of this stone it is written: “Jacob set up a stone as a memorial, pouring oil upon it” (Gen. 28:18). And of it the Psalmist says: “Thou art fairer in beauty than the children of men; grace is poured forth upon thy lips. Thou hast loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, thy God, has anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy companions” (Ps. 44:3). Therefore not only he himself, but also his companions were anointed through him with the oil of gladness. Hence it is plain that both he and his members are signified in that stone.

Since relics of saints are placed in the altar, the altar of our heart likewise ought not to be without saints’ relics. For we bear the relics of saints in our heart if we keep them in mind; if we retain their sayings and examples and commit their words to memory. Blessed are those altars, blessed are those hearts, that have deserved to receive such relics. How many relics blessed Paul left us, and how many the other saints left! Would that the altar of our heart might be filled and seasoned with them. Enough has been said concerning the consecration of a church.

### On the Rite in Administering Baptism

These matters having thus been set forth, it must be said how one newly coming to faith receives these sacraments. One who comes to the Church is first questioned concerning faith. After he answers that he believes, the priest breathes upon his face, so that the Holy Spirit [Col. 1100D] may enter and the malignant spirit may be expelled by the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 1100D] Vatican manuscript: “That the proud spirit may be driven away, and by the Holy Spirit,” etc.]

For, as we have just said, the Holy Spirit is present not only in words spoken in his name, but also in signs performed in his honour. Then the person is brought into the Church and joined to the people of the faithful; and the priest places salt in his mouth, concerning whose meaning we have spoken above. This salt signifies the first teachings of faith, without whose seasoning every human being is tasteless.

Afterwards he touches the person’s nostrils and ears [Col. 1101A] with saliva. The Lord and Saviour [602] himself explained this to us when, leaving the district of Tyre and coming through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, he healed a deaf and mute man. For he spat, touched the man’s tongue, put his fingers in his ears, and said: “Ephphatha,” which means “Be opened”; and immediately, as the Evangelist says, “his ears were opened, the bond of his tongue was loosed, and he spoke rightly” (Mark 7:35). Christ’s saliva, therefore, is the sweetness of the words flowing from Christ’s mouth, and Christ’s divinity itself heals us. His nostrils are touched so that he may receive divine truth, by which he may distinguish good from evil and separate fragrance and sound teaching from the stench of heretical perversity. Hence it is said to the Church: “Thy nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which [Col. 1101B] looks toward Damascus” (Cant. 7:4). His ears too are touched, so that they may be opened to Gospel words and reject vain and useless tales: “For evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:35).

Then, when he comes to baptism, he is first anointed with oil on the breast and between the shoulders, so that he may understand that without the oil of mercy, even if he is baptized, he still cannot please God. Concerning oil we have spoken above. He is fittingly anointed on the breast, where are the heart, memory, reason, and understanding, so that he may always have mercy in his heart and never forget piety and mercy. But because it is insufficient that mercy be held only in the mind unless it is exercised also in the body, he is anointed between the shoulders as well, so that he may hear the Apostle saying: [Col. 1101C] “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2). Burdens are borne upon shoulders and upper backs. The Lord himself showed this when he said of the Pharisees: “They bind burdens heavy and unbearable and place them upon men’s shoulders” (Matt. 23:4). Thus oil is transferred from the heart to the shoulders when mercy conceived in the mind is brought to completion in action. Enough has been said above concerning baptism.

After a person has been baptized, he receives a white garment, by which the chastity and purity of the inner and outer person are signified; and let him hear Scripture saying: “Let thy garments always be white” (Ecclus. 9:8). He is also anointed with chrism [Col. 1101D] by the priest on the crown of the head, so that he may receive at once Christ’s name and humility. For both Christ and Christian are named from chrism. The sign of the cross and the name of humility are fittingly inscribed on the crown, where pride itself seemed to sit; [Col. 1102A] for pride always seeks the higher places. Thus we see the humble stand with bowed head and the proud with stiff neck. Humility bends the former; pride raises the latter. But what does Scripture say? “Yet God will shatter the heads of his enemies, the hairy crown of those who walk on in their sins” (Ps. 67:22). By this anointing pride is removed and humility commended.

### On Confirmation

There remains now only confirmation, which is ordered to be performed by bishops, and in which the fullness of the mystery of the whole Christian religion is completed. For in baptism remission of sins is given through the Holy Spirit. But here that same Spirit is invited to come and deign to defend and [Col. 1102B] inhabit the house which he has sanctified. The apostles themselves likewise received the Holy Spirit after baptism, though they had indeed already received him in baptism for remission of sins. For it must not be believed that they were unbaptized—

[Note: [Col. 1101D] Saint Augustine, Letter 265, formerly 108, to Seleuciana, *On the Baptism and Penitence of Peter*, no. 4, vol. II, col. 897, Paris edition, says: “It is written when the Apostle Paul was baptized, but it is not written when the other apostles were baptized. Nevertheless, we must understand that they too were baptized, just as it is written when the peoples of the Churches in Jerusalem and Samaria were baptized; but when the other peoples of the Gentiles, to whom the apostles sent letters, were baptized is certainly not written. Yet we do not in the least doubt that they too were baptized, because of that saying: ‘Unless one is born again of water [Col. 1102D] and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.’”]

—who both baptized others and had heard the Lord himself say: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5). They received the Holy Spirit again, however, so that they might bind and loose from sins. For, as the Evangelist says, “The Lord breathed upon them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain are retained’” (John 20:22). They received him yet again on the day of Pentecost, for the perfection of all power and knowledge. In likeness and signification of this, this final confirmation is ordered to be performed. Thus it is clear that this sacrament is not repeated, since it is bestowed for a different purpose.

[Note: [Col. 1102D] Saint Thomas, III, question 72, article 1, distinguishes confirmation from baptism as follows: “Through baptism, which is a spiritual regeneration, a human being receives spiritual life. In confirmation, however, a human being receives, as it were, a certain perfect age of spiritual life.”]

Although chrism is applied first on the crown and afterward on the forehead, the sacrament of chrism is not repeated, because, as we showed above, one and the other act are performed for different purposes; just as we do not say that baptism is repeated when we are sprinkled with water many times. For the sacrament is repeated where the very same thing is given for the very same purpose. For example, if a baptized person were immersed again in baptismal waters [Col. 1102D] [603] so that he might be released from original and other sins. Otherwise, one is not rebaptized, even if someone is immersed many times in baptismal waters.

This final sealing—

[Note: [Col. 1102D] Vatican manuscript: “confirmation.”]

—is performed on the forehead because it belongs to the perfect always to have Christ’s name not in secret but openly and publicly.

[Note: [Col. 1102D] On why, in administering confirmation, the bishop applies the chrismal anointing to the forehead, see Saint Thomas, III, question 72, article 9, in the body of the article.]

Hence the Apostle John says: “I saw the Lamb standing upon Mount Sion, and with him a hundred and forty-[Col. 1103A]four thousand, having his name and the name of his Father written upon their foreheads” (Apoc. 16:1). To stand, to stand on the mountain, and to stand with the Lamb belong to the perfect. For the apostles themselves, before they were anointed, did not yet stand; they were not yet perfect; they still feared and did not yet bear Christ’s name on their foreheads.

[Note: [Col. 1103D] The same Vatican manuscript has a fuller reading: “For the apostles themselves, before they were anointed, before they were confirmed by the Holy Spirit, did not yet stand; they were not yet perfect; they still feared and did not yet bear Christ’s name upon their foreheads. This confirmation must be observed for seven days, on account of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit.”]

### On Episcopal Vestments: What Episcopal Garments Signify

[Note: [Col. 1103D] After Saint Bruno of Segni, many writers have treated of pontifical or priestly vestments; Philip Zazzera lists them on p. 379. The holy bishop therefore furnished others with light, so that they might explain what is mystically contained in the rite of sacred vestments. [Col. 1104D]]

Having explained all that was said above, let us consider priestly vestments and what sandals, amice and ephod, girdle and subgirdle, orarium and tunic, dalmatic and chasuble, pallium and pins, mitre, and maniple signify. We read in the Gospel that Christ’s disciples were sent by the Lord [Col. 1103B] wearing sandals (Mark 6:9): shod, indeed, in preparation for the Gospel of peace. For if they had not been shod, how could they have trodden upon serpents and scorpions? Let bishops therefore look to their sandals, look to the apostolic footwear, consider why they are thus shod, and imitate the examples of those whose footwear they imitate. Let them devote themselves to preaching, so that they too may be shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace. This footwear is not for honour but for labour; those who are shod are shod not for resting but for making a journey. This, therefore, is why bishops use sandals.

### On the Amice and Ephod

The amice, ephod, and the other priestly garments [Col. 1103C] made of linen have almost the same signification. They signify the chastity and purity of both the inward and the outward person, because linen is whiter than other materials and washed more frequently. They have the same significance in the New as they had in the Old Testament. The amice, which binds the neck and covers the breast, denotes the chastity of the inner person: it covers the heart so that it may not think vain things; it binds the neck so that falsehood may not pass from it to the tongue. For by these two things—thoughts and falsehood—the soul is corrupted; by them it loses chastity and begins to commit fornication. Hence the Lord himself says: “The things that come out of the heart are those which defile a person; for from the heart come evil thoughts, adulteries, thefts, perjuries, murders, [Col. 1103D] and the like. These are what defile a person; eating with unwashed hands does not defile a person” (Matt. 15:18–20).

Let the heart feel the linen amice and white garment by which it is pressed, and understand what is signified in it; thus let its love of chastity and purity never be corrupted by lustful and wicked thoughts. Yet if it should at some time be corrupted, let evil thoughts nevertheless not be able to burst outward: the linen amice girds and binds the neck. Let the bishop’s neck therefore always be bound by the linen amice, so that his utterances may be chaste utterances and falsehood may not pass from it.

Likewise bodily chastity is represented by the ephod, which is bound at the loins by a girdle, because lust especially rules there.

[Note: [Col. 1104D] *Ephod* signifies the priestly garment which in Exodus and Leviticus is called the *superhumerale*, “shoulder-garment,” as though it were a garment.]

Hence Truth itself says: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:15). To gird the loins is to restrain the impulses of lust under the rule of chastity. Thus it is said of the devil: “His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly” (Job 4:11). It is therefore necessary that the ephod—that is, the power and strength [Col. 1104B] of chastity—be bound and represented in the places in which lust most strongly rules.

The girdle signifies law and justice, because, as a girdle supports garments so that they do not touch the filth of the earth, so law and justice bind the faithful lest they bend [604] their soul toward the delights of this world. From this belt or girdle hangs a double subgirdle, because there are two things by which chastity is strengthened and without which it is difficult to preserve: prayer and fasting. Let bishops therefore attend to the subgirdle and devote themselves to fasting and prayer; with these weapons let them defend themselves from the assault of lust and the spirit of fornication. “For this kind is not cast out except by prayer and fasting” (Matt. 17:11). These are the Lord’s words.

### On the Orarium

[Col. 1104C]

But what do we understand by the *orarium* except what the Lord says: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls; for my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. 9:28)? The *orarium*, therefore, is both yoke and burden. Hence it is placed around the neck and over the breast of priests in the form of a cross, so that they may always remember the Crucified One; and it is placed over the shoulders of deacons, for as the yoke is borne on the neck, so burdens are borne on the shoulders. Read Leviticus, and you will see that Levites alone were assigned to carry burdens (Lev. 1 and 2). It is called an *orarium* because, although without other priestly garments it is permissible to baptize, seal, and perform many other acts in prayer, without the *orarium* it is not permissible, unless great necessity compels, to perform any of these acts. Its extension down to the feet expresses the virtue of humility and perseverance.

### On the Tunic

In the Old Testament the tunic was only hyacinth-blue and of no other colour; by it angelic life and heavenly conduct are signified. For hyacinths have the colour of the sky.

[Note: [Col. 1105D] Vatican manuscript: “hyacinth-blue.”]

The Apostle, clothed in such a tunic, said: “Our commonwealth is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Let the bishop therefore look to this tunic and transfer himself wholly in mind and desire to heavenly things. If it is white, it signifies that all who minister the nourishment of Scripture to the Church ought to be white and unstained. But if the tunic is of another colour, it should have another signification.

### On the Dalmatic

[Note: [Col. 1105D] The Vatican manuscript begins this explanation thus: “By the dalmatic, which is white and adorned before and behind from top to bottom with two scarlet lines, is signified purity of mind, together with the preaching of both Testaments and love of God and neighbour, with which priest and deacon ought to shine. [Col. 1106D] The fringes,” etc.]

The dalmatic, however, seems to belong more to ornament than to signification, and it is shown to have been introduced after the other priestly garments. Yet the fringes which hang from the left side of dalmatics [Col. 1105B] can signify the hindrances, superfluities, and cares of this life. Since these do not exist in the other life, fringes are rightly not placed on the right side; for right and left commonly signify the two lives. Thus also: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Cant. 2:6). Let one who puts on the dalmatic, therefore, remember both lives and choose the better—that life, namely, which has no hindrances, superfluities, cares, or anxieties.

### On the Chasuble

But what does the chasuble, also called *planeta*, signify except charity?

[Note: [Col. 1106D] The Venetian and Lyons editions, and D’Achéry, have “denotes.”]

Hence it is rightly the outermost garment. For God is charity. This garment encloses and contains all other garments within itself, just as all the commandments of the law and the prophets are contained in charity. The Apostle says: “Charity is the fulfilment of the law” (Rom. 13:10).

[Note: [Col. 1106D] “Therefore love is the fulfilment of the law.” Thus Saint Paul, Rom. 13:10.]

And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and thy neighbour as thyself: on these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets” (Matt. 22:37 ff.). Therefore, because the *planeta* contains all other vestments within itself, it fittingly signifies the virtue which contains within itself all the commandments of the law and prophets.

### What the Pallium Signifies

It remains now to speak of the pallium, by which we understand both the shoulder-piece (*superhumerale*) and the breastpiece (*rationale*).

[Note: [Col. 1106D] Vatican manuscript: “is signified.”]

Because it lies over each shoulder of the pontiff [Col. 1105D], it is called a shoulder-piece. Because it descends from there and is joined upon the pontiff’s breast, it is called a breastpiece. Aaron had a shoulder-piece and breastpiece, joined together by golden chains. The shoulder-piece extended from shoulder [605] to shoulder. The breastpiece was square and double, just as the pallium is double. It measured one palm both in length and breadth, a size sufficient to adorn and cover the pontiff’s breast [Col. 1106A]. Thus the pallium has the same signification as the shoulder-piece and breastpiece, although not the same construction.

Let us briefly state what the shoulder-piece and breastpiece signify, since we have sufficiently discussed them in Exodus. What is the shoulder-piece, by which a bishop’s shoulders are adorned and burdened, except the burden of episcopal rank? Episcopal rank is a great burden. Those shoulders ought to bear the burdens of the whole Church, weak sheep, and the people’s sins. Bishops who refuse to bear others’ burdens do not have the shoulder-piece: such were those of whom the Lord said, “They bind burdens heavy and unbearable and place them on men’s shoulders, but they are unwilling to move them with a finger” (Matt. 23:4).

But our supreme Pontiff was adorned with such a shoulder-piece: leaving the ninety-nine sheep, he came to seek the one that was lost; after finding it, he placed it upon his own shoulders and brought it back to pasture. What the breastpiece signifies may be understood both from its name and from the place upon which it is put. It is placed on the pontiff’s breast to guard the treasure of the heart and the repository of wisdom. This breastpiece is upon the breast of the one who said: “I have hidden thy words in my heart, that I may not sin against thee” (Ps. 118:2). For where the breastpiece is, there are reason, wisdom, and knowledge: this is what the breastpiece signifies. Where these are not in the breast and heart, the breastpiece ought not to be placed; if it is placed there, [Col. 1106C] it is useless, like a seal guarding nothing.

It is called the breastpiece of judgment, so that one who uses it may judge reasonably, wisely, and truly—judging nothing rashly, nothing incautiously, nothing disorderly. These things are said of the breastpiece and shoulder-piece so that by them it may be understood what the pallium signifies. The pallium is double on the left because, so long as we are in this life, signified by the left, we cannot be without doubleness: now we are raised by prosperity, now crushed by adversity; now we seek earthly things, now cling to heavenly things; now we serve the flesh, now the mind. But on the right the pallium is not double, because in the other life there is no doubleness. There is prosperity without adversity, joy without sadness, happiness without misery; that life is therefore free from doubleness, having neither spot nor wrinkle.

The pallium is made of wool, a cheap material, so that it may have value not from itself but from what is signified in it; so that it may be seen not with the eyes but with the mind, and understood to be worn not for adornment but to signify something.

### On the Bands

We think that the bands placed before and behind on the pallium, drawing the breastpiece and shoulder-piece downward, signify the cares and anxieties of this [Col. 1107A] life. By them the pontiff’s heart and shoulders are very often so weighed down and hindered that he is turned from his proper state and compelled to think and carry certain vain and transitory things. Let the bishop therefore look upon these bands and shake off from his heart and shoulders their oppressive weight.

### On the Pin
Needles, however, were devised not for pricking—that is, not on account of the stings of this life, as some suppose—but for joining the chasuble and the pallium. In ancient times certain loops were placed in the chasuble, into which the needles were inserted, fastening the pallium together with the chasuble, lest the pallium be displaced from its proper position. By the needles, moreover, since there are three of them, we may understand faith, hope, and charity [Col. 1107B], without which the pallium cannot be retained by a bishop. Therefore, whoever has the pallium should also have needles, by which he may bind, fasten, and hold the pallium. And let what we have said concerning the pallium suffice.

### On the Mitre

The mitre, since it is of linen [Note: [Col. 1107C] On the linen mitre, see Joseph Catalanus, *Prolegomena on the Roman Pontifical*, ch. 19; on the mitre, vol. I, [Col. 1107D] p. 24. “The use of the mitre,” says the *Ceremonial of Bishops*, book I, ch. 17, §1, “is most ancient, and its kinds are threefold. One is called precious, because it is usually woven with gems and precious stones, or with plates of gold or silver; another is embroidered with gold, without gems or plates of gold or silver, ‘but composed either of some small pearls, or of white silk intermingled with gold, or of plain cloth of gold without plates and pearls.’ The third is called simple, without gold, made of plain damask silk or some other material; or even of linen, made from white cloth with red strips, or fringes and hanging bands.” See more at the cited place, art. 13. This passage was elucidated by the learned Zazzera, p. 396.], signifies the brightness and purity of chastity, as also do the amice and ephod, of which we spoke above. It is fitting that the bishop be covered wholly in linen from head to foot [606], because all his honour and glory consist in chastity and purity. This ornament was especially necessary for the head, because there are the five bodily senses, by whose corruption chastity is easily violated. Hence the Psalmist says: “Turn away my eyes, lest they see vanity” [Col. 1107C] (Ps. 118:37). And blessed Job says: “I have made a covenant with my eyes, that I should not think upon a virgin” (Job 31:1). Therefore, lest the bishop’s senses be violated, his head is rightly adorned and covered with the mitre of chastity.

### On the Maniple

But what are we to understand by the maniple, if not good works? Hence also: “Going they went and wept, casting their seed; but coming they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 125:6). Therefore let the bishop consider what the maniple in his left hand signifies, lest at any time he forget good works [Col. 1108A] in the present life, which is signified by the left. For if it signified nothing, carrying a maniple in one’s hand would seem a certain absurdity. “It is therefore,” as it is written, “a certain sign upon our hand, and as it were something suspended before our eyes” (Exod. 13:16) [Note: [Col. 1107D] “In ancient times it was also called a *sudarium* [sweat-cloth]: for they then carried a *sudarium*, or little linen cloth, in the left hand for wiping away sweat or tears, and especially for polishing vessels.” Thus Zazzera.].

### On the Gloves

Perhaps you ask why the hands too are covered with gloves. I answer briefly: that they may be chaste, clean, free from every defilement, and bright.

### On the Ring

The ring also on the bishop’s finger seems to be a certain sign by which he is understood to be Christ’s vicar, so that he may govern and guard His bride, which is the Church. For John speaks of this bridegroom and bride, saying: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” [Col. 1108B] (John 3:29); but who is the bridegroom’s friend? . . . Therefore the bishop is both friend and vicar of the bridegroom; and if he is vicar, he himself is in a certain sense also a bridegroom.

### On the Supreme Pontiff

For these reasons the supreme pontiff also bears the *regnum*—for so it is called—and uses purple, not for symbolic meaning, I think, but because the Emperor Constantine formerly handed over to blessed Sylvester all the insignia of the Roman Empire [Note: [Col. 1108C] To these words, which the author of the *Explanation of the Divine Offices*, published by Philip Zazzera, excerpted from Bruno, the same author appends this note on p. 396. Dominicus Georgius, *On the Liturgy of the Roman Pontiff*, ch. 27, vol. I, p. 240, has the following: “The common run of writers thinks that the origin of wearing this *regnum* must be derived from Constantine’s fabricated Donation, and consequently that St Sylvester was the first to use it. Daniel Papebrochius strongly contends that this origin should by no means be referred to the spurious Donation of Constantine, although he ascribes the beginnings of wearing the tiara to St Sylvester, who of his own choice took up a cap according to Roman custom—that is, as a symbol of liberty—and adorned it with gold embroidery, or a diadem, which is added to the head to signify the royal priesthood conferred by Christ upon the greatest of all priests. Boniface VIII, however, added another crown to express the prerogative of spiritual and temporal rule; Urban V added the third because of the mystical number.”]. Hence in great processions the pontiff is accorded all that display which was formerly provided for emperors. Let this suffice concerning priestly vestments.

### On the Consecrations of Bishops

We must now say what is signified in bishops’ [Col. 1108C] consecrations by the book of the Gospels placed upon the shoulders, and by the anointing of the head and hands. For these things appear to be done figuratively, and not for consulting lots, as fools suppose. The book of the Gospels is placed on the shoulders of the man being consecrated, so that he may thereby understand to what labour and burden he is subjected [Note: [Col. 1108D] Vatican manuscript: “so that he may thereby understand to what labour and burden he may be subjected.”], and that he may not shrink from carrying everywhere the weight of preaching. Since not only a bishop but also a king is appointed in the Church, according to the custom of the ancients his head is anointed and his crown consecrated with chrism. For it is written concerning this ointment: “Like ointment upon the head, which descended upon [Col. 1109A] the beard, the beard of Aaron” (Ps. 132:2). One must most firmly believe that by this anointing he receives both Christ’s blessing and a greater grace of the Holy Spirit. The hands too are anointed, so that whatever they bless may be blessed, and whatever they sanctify may be sanctified.

Yet this anointing should not be idle in a bishop. He is anointed outwardly: let him also be anointed inwardly. [607] He is anointed on the head: let him also be anointed in mind; for the mind too is a head—the head, certainly, of the better and inward person. Of this head the Lord says: “But when you fast, anoint your head” (Matt. 6:17). Anoint it, He says; but with what oil? Not with olive oil, but with mercy. Therefore let the mind be anointed with the oil of piety and mercy, that by a good life and holy conduct it may spread far and wide among all [Col. 1110A] a sweet and delightful fragrance. For whatever mind has been anointed with such oil will have mercy on all and will be moved with heartfelt compassion for everyone. But because it is not enough to show mercy only in mind and will, the hands too are anointed, so that the mercy conceived in the mind may also be exercised by the hands. Therefore let the bishop’s hands be anointed with the oil of piety and mercy; let them be closed to no one and open to all. Let him hear what is said concerning the Church: “She has opened her hand to the needy, and stretched forth her arm to the poor” (Prov. 31:20). A withered hand, a greedy hand, a hand contracted by grasping cannot be opened. Therefore let it be anointed and healed; anointed and opened, and let it generously give alms to the needy.

[Col. 1109]

## The Life of Pope St Leo IX, by St Bruno

[Col. 1109]

[Col. 1109B] **Bruno, Bishop of Signi, to all the faithful and all Catholics.**

Grace [Note: [Col. 1109C] The Bollandists mention this *Life of Pope St Leo IX*, written by St Bruno, bishop of Signi, under 19 April, and use its testimony in several places. The most learned prelate Stephen Borgia, now most eminent cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, also mentions this *Life* in vol. II of his *History of Benevento*, pp. 293, 311, and 313. It is likewise commended in the distinguished work, printed last year, in defence of the temporal dominion of the Apostolic See in both Sicilies; there it cites many writers agreeing in their praise of Bruno. Wibert, archdeacon of the Church of Toul, likewise published the deeds of St Leo. To him is added an anonymous writer, whose life of the holy pontiff was first brought to light from a Beneventan manuscript by the same most eminent Borgia in the cited *History of Benevento*, vol. II, p. 299 ff. Leo, cardinal bishop of Ostia, likewise frequently commemorates with the highest praise the notable deeds of this same pontiff in the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*. The celebrated Lodovico Antonio Muratori included Bruno’s *Life of St Leo*, among other memorials most worthy of preservation, in part II, vol. III of the *Rerum Italicarum*.] to you, and peace from God our Father and from our God Jesus Christ. The Psalmist speaks, saying: “Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt His name together” (Ps. 33:4). In this he most plainly teaches that we too should invite all whom we can to the praise and magnification of God. For every praise, every power, and glory of the saints is referred to Him who is wonderful in His saints, and who also says to His disciples: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:7). He is crowned in each one and honoured in all; He speaks in them, fights in them, and conquers in them. Thus the faithful themselves, His servants, rightly say: “In [Col. 1109C] God we shall do valiantly, and He Himself shall bring our enemies to nothing” (Ps. 107:14). Let us therefore praise God’s saints and honour God’s friends, since He who gave them so great glory, powers, and splendour is Himself praised and magnified in them. I beseech you, [Col. 1110B] magnify the Lord with me, and in this great solemnity of blessed Leo, supreme pontiff and universal pope, let us exalt His name together.

The whole world [Note: [Col. 1110C] It should not seem surprising if Bruno, filled with zeal for the house of God, employs expressions of this kind, which seem in themselves to show the entire Christian world deformed by many vices, and especially infected with the crime of simony [Col. 1110D]. Yet although that error and corruption was widespread, ecclesiastical history sufficiently establishes that many bishops and other ecclesiastical men shone in that age through integrity of life and proved themselves excellent guardians of sacred and canonical laws. Other Fathers too, in similar circumstances, used a similar manner of speech.] lay in wickedness; holiness had failed, justice had perished, and truth had been buried. Iniquity reigned; avarice held dominion; Simon Magus possessed the Church; bishops and priests were given over to pleasures and fornication. Priests were not ashamed to take wives: they married openly, contracted abominable marriages, [608] and endowed by legal instruments women with whom, according to the laws, they ought not even to have lived in the same house. For the sacred canons permit no women to live with men of this order except those who are wholly beyond suspicion. But, worse than all this [Col. 1110C], scarcely anyone could be found who either was not a simoniac or had not been ordained by simoniacs [Note: [Col. 1110D] Among Leo IX’s first concerns, when he ascended the Roman [Col. 1111B] See, was to hold a council of bishops at Rome, in which their ordinations were examined with the greatest care [Col. 1111C], and many bishops were found free of simony. Some were recalled to penance; others, being obstinate, were forbidden to exercise their order. This concern of St Leo is mentioned in canon I of the Roman council convened by Alexander II in 1063, in which simony was again condemned. This canon is given by the celebrated Carlo Berardi, part II, vol. II, p. 401, as follows: “First, with God as witness, as was first decreed by St Pope Leo and Nicholas of holy memory, we determine that no mercy is to be shown to simoniacs in preserving their rank; but, according to the sanctions and decrees of the holy Fathers, we wholly condemn them and decree by apostolic authority that they shall not preside in the Church.” Canon II is also relevant to our matter; it treats those simoniacs who were ordained without payment by bishops infected with simony, and says that, in view of the circumstances of the times, indulgence must be shown them. It accordingly says: “Those who until now have been ordained without payment by simoniacs [Col. 1111D], we permit to remain in the orders they have received, not so much on grounds of justice as out of mercy, unless perhaps some other fault in their lives should, according to the canons, stand in their way. For their number is so great that we cannot maintain the rigour of the canons against them; it is necessary that for the present we incline our minds, by dispensation, towards the practice of compassionate accommodation,” etc.].

Hence even to this day there are some who, reasoning wrongly, maintain that the priesthood in the Church had already failed from that time. [Col. 1111A] For they say: “If all were such—that is, if all were simoniacs or ordained by simoniacs—then you who now exist, whence did you come here? Through whom did you pass, if not through them? There was no other way. Therefore those who ordained you received their orders from those—and not from others—who either were simoniacs or were ordained by simoniacs.” We shall answer them later, because this question requires no small discussion. For the moment, let us continue what we have begun.

Such was the Church; such were bishops and priests; such had been some of the Roman pontiffs, who ought to enlighten all. All the salt had lost its savour, nor was there anything with which it might be seasoned. And unless the Lord of Hosts had left us a seed, [Col. 1111B] we should have been as Sodom, and should have become like Gomorrah. Amid so great a tempest, therefore, blessed Leo ascended the chair of the apostolic height [Note: [Col. 1111D] He succeeded Damasus II in the Roman pontificate. Damasus had held the Roman See only twenty-three days and had been appointed successor of Benedict IX after Benedict’s withdrawal to perform penance for his sins. Writers of that period report that this pontiff was raised once to the chair of St Peter by the power of the counts of Tusculum, then expelled, and occupied it a third time. Spondanus under the year 1045 and Fleury, book LIX, following Leo of Ostia and many others, say the same. The celebrated Carlo Sebastiano Berardi dissents from them in part II, [Col. 1112B] vol. II of the *Correction of Gratian*, p. 375; he places Leo IX’s election in 1048.], so that this great and such a lamp, set upon the universal lampstand, might give light to all who are in the house.

For there was at that time a bishop of Toul, Bruno by name, noble in birth and handsome in appearance, but more handsome in holiness; learned, mighty in teaching, adorned with moral virtues, and possessing together all things necessary to this office. Such a master was indeed needed—one who should have such disciples in such a time.

[Col. 1112A] Religious men therefore assembled with the Emperor Henry [Note: [Col. 1112C] Henry II, in the third year of his reign.], a man most prudent in every respect, and with the envoys of the Romans who were then there. They earnestly entreated the aforesaid bishop, for love of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, to come to the aid of the Roman Church and not fear to expose himself to dangers for the sake of Christian faith and religion [Note: [Col. 1112C] When Damasus had died, therefore, as has been said, and Benedict was seeking again to claim the See for himself, the Romans sent a necessary embassy into Germany to the Emperor Henry, requesting that he provide them with a pontiff, lest the holy Church be compelled once more to endure such a monster. But this embassy was sent by the cardinals not so that the emperor himself should elect a pope, but so that he might send to Rome the man whom he considered suitable, in order that the pontiff might be elected in the City according to custom, with the counsel of the cardinals. Spondanus, under 1049. St Leo IX, formerly Bruno bishop of Toul, restored its former splendour to the Apostolic See; elected at the assembly of Worms, he repeatedly condemned simoniacs, proscribed the heresy of Berengar, removed Gregory of Vercelli from the honour of priesthood as guilty of adultery and perjury, and conquered enemies more by religion than arms. In the sixth year of his pontifical office, he passed to the heavenly kingdom on 19 April 1054. Berti, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. II, p. 6. He adds in a note: Leo IX’s election occurred in 1048, but upon the condition that it be approved by the Roman clergy and people. Accordingly, on coming to Rome, he ascended the papal throne in the following year, 1049, on the day before the Ides of February, with the consent and applause of all. He was son of the count of Dagsburg, born in 1002. He was made bishop of Toul in 1026 from a monk of the Order of St Benedict. For more on him, see Richer, in the *Chronicle of the Abbey of Senones*, edited by D’Achery in vol. II of the *Spicilegium*.]. For that people feared dwelling in this land of ours, as people passing from very healthy places into unhealthy places.

But that blessed bishop declined to ascend, not on account of the unhealthiness of the place, but because of the exalted rank of so great a Church. Thus Moses too is recorded to have acted. When the Lord wished to set him over the people of Israel, he said: “I beseech You, Lord, send [Col. 1112B] whom You will send” (Exod. 4:13). At last overcome by their entreaties, he promised that he would do what they requested under this condition: “I,” he said, [609] “will go to Rome; and there, if clergy and people of their own accord elect me as their pontiff, I shall do what you ask. Otherwise I shall accept no election” [Note: [Col. 1112D] Wibert, ch. 2 of the cited book, and the anonymous Beneventan writer likewise confirm this; the latter describes the splendour of the City and the celebration on the day when Leo assumed the Roman pontificate by public votes and acclamations.]. Rejoicing, they affirmed his decision and approved the condition.

In those days there was there a certain Roman monk, named Hildebrand, a young man of noble character, brilliant intellect, and holy religious devotion [Note: [Col. 1112D] A Tuscan by nation and native of Sovana, he had been a disciple [Col. 1113D] of Pope Gregory VI, who had brought him into Germany. There he received the cowl of St Benedict in the monastery of Cluny.]. He was there both for the sake of learning and in order to serve in some religious place under the Rule of blessed Benedict [Col. 1113A]. The blessed bishop therefore called him to himself, and as soon as he learned his purpose, disposition, and religious commitment, he asked him to return to Rome with him. “I will not do so,” he replied. The bishop answered: “Why not?” Hildebrand said: “Because you are going to receive the Roman Church not according to canonical institution, but through secular and royal power.” But the bishop, being by nature simple and most gentle, patiently satisfied him, giving an account of everything as Hildebrand wished. In this deed he clearly showed himself an imitator of the blessed apostle Peter, whose successor he was soon to become. For when Peter had baptized Cornelius, a Gentile and a stranger to the Jewish religion, the other apostles rebuked him because he had entered the house of a man possessing uncircumcision [Col. 1113B]; yet he did not disdain to give an account of everything (Acts 10).

The bishop then came to Rome, bringing the aforesaid monk with him. In so doing he rendered a great service to blessed Peter the Apostle, since he brought back with him the man by whose counsel and wisdom the Roman Church was one day to be directed and governed. For this is Pope Gregory VII, whose prudence, steadfastness, and courage, whose struggles and labours, belong to another time and work to recount [Note: [Col. 1113D] Here Bruno’s intention of writing the deeds of St Gregory VII is evident; would that he had completed it! For no one had lived with Gregory longer or more intimately. Yet the few things Bruno handed down about him, along with what other writers have recorded, sufficiently refute the envy and rashness of all heterodox detractors from Gregory’s illustrious name. They also confound the frivolity of those who in our own day abolished the observance of his feast.].

According to Roman custom, Bruno was elected pope with great praises from clergy and people. Then, raised to the chair of the blessed Apostle Peter, he was called Leo, his name being changed, as I think, through the working of divine providence. For the Lion of the tribe of [Col. 1113C] Judah had conquered; and this Leo, deriving his origin from that Lion, feared no attack from any beast by his most valiant deeds. His roar immediately shook the earth, terrified and disturbed the sacrilegious, and wounded the army of married men. [Note: [Col. 1113D] Leo held two synods in the first year of his pontificate, the first at Rome and the second at Pavia. In them many canons were enacted to restore Church discipline, especially against simoniacs and incontinent clerics. The anonymous Beneventan writer likewise relates that Leo convened the Roman synod immediately: “For,” he says, [Col. 1114D] “after first holding a synod, he diligently investigated how the pastors of the churches conducted themselves in their orders. Those whom he found Catholic he increasingly urged in words that each should watch more zealously over his flock. But those whom he found to be simoniacs or associates of simoniacs, he either restored to their former rank after imposing the proper penance, or completely and irrevocably deprived of their order.”] For this blessed pontiff, inflamed with the fire of the Holy Spirit, burned especially against simoniacs; and so that the order of clerics might live chastely and religiously, he confirmed the ancient canons. Where necessity required, he accommodated matters by dispensation, imposed a light penance, forgave past offences by apostolic authority, and warned them not to commit such things thereafter. Yet this should not be adopted as a precedent, for the pontiff acted not voluntarily but from necessity, unless perhaps the cause and circumstances are likewise similar [Col. 1114A]; for Church rulers are often compelled to tolerate things that cannot be corrected. Who can tell how great was his kindness towards all, his humility, his gentleness, his generosity, his affability, and his compassion for everyone? He became all things to all, that he might gain all (1 Cor. 9). His speech was seasoned with salt: it soothed the devout and terrified the ungodly [Note: [Col. 1114D] In this testimony Bruno embraces St Leo’s outstanding virtues, especially his prudence and generosity, by which he wonderfully won the hearts of all. Is not the divine providence which gave such a pontiff to its Church for restoration admirable and highly worthy of praise?].

But let us now come to what the Lord worked through him—not because we wish to write everything we have heard or even found written concerning him [Note: [Col. 1114D] We do not wish to omit Leo’s settlement of the long-disputed controversy concerning the reordination of those ordained by simoniacs, on which Peter Damian had written and had refuted those who asserted that ordination must be repeated. [Col. 1115C] St Leo therefore decreed, as Gregory VII reports in epistle 45, that those upon whom simoniac bishops had laid hands were validly ordained.]. Blessed Pope Gregory, whom we mentioned above, often used to tell us many things concerning this man; and I remember that from him I heard, in large part, the matters I have related so far. Once, while he was speaking of Leo in our hearing, he began to rebuke us—and especially me, it seemed to me, since his eyes were fixed on me [Col. 1114B]—because we allowed blessed Leo’s deeds to perish in silence, and did not write what would bring glory to the Roman Church [610] and furnish many hearers with an example of humility. But because he spoke generally, and none of us was especially commanded to undertake this work, no one wrote what he had enjoined upon all to write. Nor indeed would I now have written these things, had I not in some manner been compelled to write them, as I shall show in what follows. May each pontiff forgive me, for I acknowledge that in this matter I have offended both.

Let us first relate what, we have heard, was done through him in the regions of Gaul by the wonderful providence of God [Col. 1114C]. When blessed Leo was holding councils there and many bishops were accused of the heresy of simony, one man among the rest was accused who was held more suspect than the others. But since the accusation against him could not be established by certain evidence, the pontiff adjured him to speak the truth concerning himself. When he refused to tell the truth and tried in every way to conceal his iniquity, blessed Leo said to him: “If, then, as you assert, you are not a simoniac and have not sinned against the Holy Spirit, tell me, if you can: ‘Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.’” When the man had said, “Glory be to the Father, and to the Son,” although he made great effort, he could in no way say, “and to the Holy Spirit.” Repeating this same attempt frequently, with his mouth open he was wholly unable to name the Holy Spirit. Thus it became manifest to all present [Col. 1115A] that he had sinned against the Holy Spirit, whose name he was unable to pronounce [Note: [Col. 1115C] By a manifest portent he convicted of simony the bishop who had refused to confess his guilt. At the Roman synod convened by Pope Leo IX in [Col. 1115D] 1049, Kilian, bishop of Sutri, who denied upon oath that he had committed the crime of simony, was struck by God to the terror of all. Berti, *Abridgment*, vol. II, p. 11.]. All therefore gave thanks together to God, who had deigned to show them so new a sign and unheard-of miracle. Terrified by this judgment, some came of their own accord to the pontiff, accusing themselves and revealing their consciences to him.

At that time also the abbot of Cluny, a young man of good promise, was asked by blessed Leo whether he had ever entertained ambition for his position at so great a monastery. Being a disciple of truth, he answered what was true: “According to the flesh, indeed, I have had it; according to the spirit, I have not [Col. 1115B].” This answer was so pleasing and praiseworthy to all that, because of their immense joy, it was immediately written in every heart. They asked one another what he had answered, and were able to retain those very words. He himself, not old yet full of days, venerable and beloved by all, still governs that same venerable monastery with the greatest wisdom: a man altogether praiseworthy, difficult to compare with any other, and of singular religious devotion.

I also heard blessed Gregory recount another miracle concerning the same pontiff, which I think should by no means be omitted. Blessed Leo, he said, had had a certain teacher, a wise and very religious man, who gave him a wooden cup after he had assumed the pontificate of the Roman Church. The pontiff held this cup [Col. 1115C] in reverent affection, and out of veneration for blessed Remigius, to whom the cup was said to have belonged, he preferred to drink from it rather than from gold and silver vessels. It happened that, being carelessly placed, it fell to the ground and broke into two pieces. When, according to custom, the blessed pontiff ordered wine to be brought to him, the cupbearer stood before him troubled in countenance and conscious of the damage that had occurred through him. The pontiff said to him: “What is the matter?” He replied: “The cup [Col. 1116A] has been broken.” Blessed Leo said: “Is it truly broken?” The cupbearer replied: “Broken, my lord.” He said to him: “Bring it to me.” When he had brought it, the pontiff took it into his hands and, fitting the pieces together according to the joins by which they had previously appeared to adhere to one another, held it for a little while in his hands. Then he returned it to the servant whole and sound, saying: “Go, and mix.” Blessed Gregory was present at this miracle and told it to us. Afterwards another man, not of equal authority, likewise told me that he had been present and had seen it.

But while blessed Leo was in Rome and governed the apostolic see in peace, many came from the regions of Apulia, with their eyes gouged out, their noses cut off, and their hands and feet mutilated, lamenting pitiably the cruelty of the Normans. Therefore it came about that this most gentle man, full of piety and mercy, sympathizing with so boundless an affliction of the wretched, attempted to humble the pride of that people.

> [Note: Col. 1115D. Leo had returned from Germany in the fifth year of his pontificate, 1053. There, among other matters, at the demand of Emperor Henry II, he exchanged Bamberg—which Henry I had granted to the Holy Roman Church—for Benevento and its county; and he obtained from him an army against the Normans, who had violently occupied Apulia and other lands subject to Roman authority.]

Accordingly, having gathered an army of his own people—small indeed, but of brave soldiers—he went forth to fight against the Normans,

> [Note: Col. 1115D. Leo of Ostia reports concerning Gebehard, then bishop of Eichstätt, who was accompanying Pope Leo on his return to Italy, that, by a treacherous design, after Leo had already completed much of his journey, he induced the greater part of the army to desert. For this guilt, when he was later made pope under the name Victor II, he did penance throughout his life. Thus Spondanus.]

having zeal for God, though perhaps not according to knowledge. Would that he himself had not gone there in person!

> [Note: Col. 1116C. The most eminent Cardinal Stefano Borgia long ago observed, in vol. II of his *History of Benevento*, § VII, p. 25, note, that Bruno of Segni here disapproved of St Leo’s expedition to war against the Normans, and that Peter Damian and Herman the Lame had preceded him in this opinion. Yet that most learned historian, as was his custom, defends St Leo copiously and learnedly against every criticism, showing that it is lawful for Roman pontiffs, just as for secular rulers, to raise armies, marshal battle lines, and employ force of arms in order either to recover ecclesiastical dominions and those of their own see from usurpers or to defend them against enemies. As an example he adduces the most valiant Maccabees, high priests and princes, who undertook long wars against idolaters and King Antiochus in defense of their ancestral laws. He also mentions Moses, who checked and routed by arms the Amorites and other nations harassing the people of Israel. But it is established that before Leo IX, St Leo IV and John X, like several successor pontiffs, used their own and summoned forces against the Saracens in order to repel enemies invading the temporal goods of their Church.]

But why say more? The armies of both sides meet: many are about to fight against few.

> [Note: Col. 1116D. This battle was joined on 18 June. The army of the Church consisted partly of Germans and partly of Italians [Col. 1117D]. The former fought vigorously; but when the Italians turned their backs after the first assaults, the Normans won a complete victory. The pope himself was taken captive. He had not been present at the battle, but had withdrawn to a nearby fortress.]

A vast slaughter takes place; much blood is poured out on both sides. These press on by courage, those by numbers. In their death these men could have said what we read that our Savior said in his Passion: “They would have no power over us unless it had been given them from above.” But what is this: that the good are defeated and the evil conquer? “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33). Those who fight for justice are overcome; those who assail justice prevail. Yet the Apostle consoles us concerning such persons, saying: “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God” [Col. 1117A] (Rom. 8:28). Whether they die or live, whatever happens to them is good for them: all things work together for good. Indeed, death is better than life for those of whom it is said: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:6); for all who die for justice are counted among the martyrs: “May the Lord place them with the princes of his people” (Ps. 112:8).

We pass over much and gather a little from much, because we have been commanded to write not the whole, but a part of the whole. Behold: suddenly the report flies abroad, the land is filled, and everywhere it is told that a battle has taken place, that Christ’s soldiers and the army of the saints have been defeated. Then the pitiable pontiff made for the city of Benevento, certainly faithful and devoted to blessed Peter.

> [Note: Col. 1117D. This testimony of St Bruno concerning the subjection of the city of Benevento to St Peter—that is, to the Roman Apostolic See—and its fidelity toward the pontiffs, is held in very high esteem by writers who maintain and defend by right the temporal dominion and very ancient possession of that province by the Roman pontiffs. See the eminent Borgia, *History of Benevento*, vol. II, p. 33 ff.; likewise, on the temporal dominion of the Holy See over the Two Sicilies, p. 112. Pope St Leo IX himself was the first to grant the city of Benevento [Col. 1118D], with its dependencies and so forth, in fief to Humfred, prince of the Normans, and his successors. See Borgia in the places cited.]

When the arrival of the pontiff was heard of [Col. 1117B], the whole city went out to meet him—men and women, young men and maidens, old men with younger men—not as for a procession, but as if for tears and mourning. They stood stunned, watching those coming from afar; and now the pontiff drew near, bishops and clerics proceeding with sorrowful faces and bowed heads.

> [Note: Col. 1118D. Leo was brought to Benevento by the victorious Normans, but they treated him with the greatest humanity, admiring the holiness of so great a man. The pontiff immediately took care that the bodies of the slain soldiers should receive burial and the prayers of the Church; and he assisted individually those who remained from the conflict either captive or wounded.]

After the venerable pope came among them and, raising his hand, blessed them, a cry and wailing rose to heaven; the whole land resounded with weeping and lamentation. Thus he entered the city in such a procession, and with such psalmody came to the church. Having remained there some time, he returned to Rome, and in each city tears and weeping were renewed.

> [Note: Col. 1118D. From the end of June 1053 until 12 March 1054 Pope Leo remained in the power of the Normans. At last, freed by them, he returned to the City.]

For who could refrain from tears, having seen him go out with such an army, and afterward seeing him return, bereft of that so noble soldiery, with clerics alone?

Therefore, when he came to Rome, he hastened as quickly as possible to the church of the blessed apostle Peter, humbly and most devoutly commending to him the souls of those who, out of love for him and obedient to him unto death, had not feared to shed their own blood in defense of justice. While he remained there, it was shown to him by a revelation in sleep that he would soon depart from this world.

Accordingly, he ordered bishops, cardinals, and other clerics to be summoned to him; and he urged them most graciously to live chastely and to fight manfully against the Simoniac heresy. He said to them:

“My brothers, know that after a few days I shall depart from this age. For this night, wretched and unworthy as I am of the seat of this Church [Col. 1117D], I was, in a vision, in that other life; and I am now weary of dwelling in this one. [Col. 1118A] Yet I rejoice exceedingly because I saw there, among Christ’s martyrs, those brothers and friends of mine who followed me into Apulia and died in defense of justice. They were splendidly adorned, holding palms in their hands, so that those who thought them defeated might understand that they were victors. And indeed, ‘whatever is born of God conquers the world; and this is the victory that conquers the world: our faith’ (John 5:4).

“All of them cried aloud to me, saying: ‘Come, beloved of us, and remain with us, for through you we have attained so great a glory.’ But from the opposite side I heard certain others saying: ‘By no means; rather, on the third day you will come to us.’ If, therefore, I remain in this life after the third day, know that what I saw was not true.”

Let no one [Col. 1118B] wonder if malicious spirits wished to delight him by an earthly vision, to whom such joyful things were announced; for they once dared to approach the Lord and Savior himself. Thus the Lord himself says: “For the prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (John 14:30).

Then he said: “Go, my brothers, each to his own house, but return to me tomorrow.” Throughout that whole night he prayed to the Lord, prostrate upon his knees. When morning came, he ordered a tomb to be prepared for himself. The bishops and priests assembled again, as that most blessed man had commanded them the previous day. They sat in the church, while he sat upon his bed and said:

“Hear me, brothers and fellow bishops, and likewise all who have assembled here. Before all else I command [Col. 1118C] you: do not sell the lands, vineyards, castles, houses, or other possessions of the Church, and let no one wish to claim them for himself by possession. Do not make a practice of swearing. Beware of your relatives. Do no injury to the servants of blessed Peter who come here, nor deceive them in their business affairs. Freely give tithes from all that you possess.”

Then, turning toward the cross, he poured out great prayers to the Lord for all of them, humbly asking and entreating that he might deign to forgive them all their sins. When he had done this, looking again toward heaven, he said:

“Lord Jesus Christ, good Shepherd, who for us assumed the form of a servant, chose twelve apostles for the conversion of the nations, and said to your blessed apostle Peter: ‘Whatever you bind on [Col. 1118D] earth shall be bound in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven’ [Col. 1119A] (Matt. 16:19): I, his unworthy vicar, beseech your boundless mercy that you absolve from all their sins those servants, my brothers, who were slain for love of justice, and bring them into the rest of the blessed.

“For those, Lord, whom I have excommunicated, do you absolve and convert to truth. Destroy the Simoniac heresy and every heretical perversity. Deign to bless and preserve your faithful Beneventans, who received me so honorably in your name and served me so generously, and all your other faithful; for you are God, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.”

After the pontiff had ceased speaking, they remained there a little while, then all returned, each to his own home. Throughout that whole night, as on the preceding one [Col. 1119B], he continued in vigils and prayer. On the next day—the third, namely, which was the last day in this life of blessed Leo, supreme pontiff—all assembled in a much greater crowd.

The blessed pontiff arose and went before the altar; for about the space of an hour he remained in prayer, weeping greatly. Then he returned to his bed and addressed them briefly. When this was finished, he called the bishops to himself; after making confession, he received the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. Then he lay back upon his little bed and shortly afterward fell asleep in the Lord.

One of the bishops arose and touched him, thinking that he was still living and sleeping. When they realized that he had already died, they immediately gathered from every side and made great lamentation over him. The blessed pontiff died [Col. 1119C] on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigns—to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

> [Note: Col. 1119D. Bruno differs from certain other writers who place the death of St Leo on 19 April [Col. 1120D] 1054. See the most learned Borgia, *History of Benevento*, vol. II, p. 39.]

On the day after blessed Leo’s death, a certain woman came from the region of Tuscany. As she ascended the steps, she began to be tormented by a demon and to utter dreadful cries and great howlings. When she had named blessed Leo, those present drew her to his tomb. One of the bishops questioned the demon tormenting her, saying: “I adjure you by him who lives and reigns for ever: tell us whether Pope Leo has power among the saints.” He answered: “Truly, the Leo about whom you ask is among the saints and has great power among [Col. 1119D] them; and that sorcerer today drives me out of this house, which I have held in my possession for nine years and two months.”

Then another unhappy woman who was there began to disparage blessed Leo and to say: “Will Pope Leo drive out demons—he who caused so many men to be killed? At the very hour when he drives out demons, I shall certainly be queen and shall raise up all those whom he destroyed by his crime.” She had scarcely finished those words when she was immediately seized by a demon and began to be tormented in a marvelous manner. At once the other woman—the one we said had come from Tuscany—was freed.

[Col. 1120A] Then all 613 who were present, struck with astonishment and wonder, began to cry out and say: “Saint Leo, spare us; Saint Leo, forgive us; and, because we have sinned greatly, have mercy on us.” At that same hour two crippled persons were also healed, who could not walk by themselves. On that same day, now toward evening, a certain deaf and mute man came to the tomb of the blessed man; and, to crown so great an evil, he was afflicted by a most severe paralysis. But as soon as he approached the tomb, he was made sound and whole and received both speech and hearing.

Christ the Lord worked many other miracles through blessed Leo in those very days, in order to reveal to us, his faithful, through whose merits they were performed. Nor should that miracle be passed over which [Col. 1120B] John, an eminent man and bishop of Porto, told me. He said that about those same days the bishop of the city of Chur, in the regions beyond the Alps, came to Rome, and in his retinue was a little fellow who had been mute from infancy and had never spoken. The bishop’s servants took him with them among the baggage-carriers, because he was very faithful and suitable for guarding baggage.

One day, while the aforesaid bishop was still staying in the City, that mute man of whom we have spoken entered the church of blessed Peter. When he saw crowds of people flowing from every side to the tomb of blessed Leo, he too went there.
