Then those standing around, understanding that he was mute, began—as people are accustomed to do with such persons—to indicate to him by signs [Col. 1120C] that he should humble himself at the blessed man’s tomb and entreat the Savior of all for his healing, making him understand that this was the tomb in which blessed Leo rested. For the report of his power had been openly spread everywhere, and many coming there from all sides were healed of various illnesses.

After lying there for a long time, he fell asleep, overcome by sleep. Soon afterward he awoke and rose, and began to speak as fluently as though he had otherwise suffered no impediment of the tongue. All were amazed; they rejoiced and exulted, nor was it enough to have heard him only once. For they delighted in questioning him and hearing him speak and answer. At length he returned to his companions. When they heard him speaking, they were exceedingly glad and led him before the bishop with great [Col. 1120D] astonishment. The bishop asked him how all this had happened to him. He recounted everything in order and said that he had seen blessed Leo; and that, while he had fallen asleep before his tomb, Leo came, put his fingers in his mouth, and loosed the tongue that had long been bound.

Now the time reminds me to explain what I promised above: namely, that I did not dictate these things without a command. For in the past Lent, while I was in Rome, the greatly venerable man John, bishop of Tusculum, came to me one day when we had assembled at church. I was standing [Col. 1121A] in the presence of Ubald, a most religious man, bishop of Sabina, and certain others. He said to me: “I have been sent to you as a messenger.”

I stood attentively waiting to hear what he wished to say. Then he said: “Pope Leo commands you to give him one hundred thousand solidi.” But I said: “What are you telling me?” And he said: “I tell you the truth: this is his command to you.” Then he began to recount in order what he had seen.

“This night,” he said, “while I was asleep, blessed Leo appeared to me in a dream, arrayed in pontifical vestments, saying: ‘Go and tell the bishop of Segni to give me one hundred thousand solidi.’ And when I thought within myself that you were not so wealthy that you could give him such a sum, he understood my thought and said: ‘Go and tell him to give me either one hundred thousand or fifty [Col. 1121B] thousand.’ This he commands you. See, therefore, what you will answer him.”

Then I began anxiously to consider what such a vision might mean for me. Shortly afterward I asked the bishop whether blessed Leo had commanded me to give, lend, or repay that money. He answered: “No: to give.” Then I was somewhat comforted, for there is a great difference between whether we owe something as a gift or as a repayment. For I feared that perhaps I had offended him in some matter which I was bound to pay and necessarily to render as a debt.

Moreover, I remembered that his feast used formerly to be celebrated in our church; but because I had behaved negligently, that entire celebration there had ceased. May he pardon me, for I know that I have sinned in this no small measure. When I returned home from church and [Col. 1121C] recounted this vision to our clerics, they explained it to me exactly as I myself had already conceived in my mind. They said:

“We think that this money which blessed Leo demands of you is nothing other than that you should write something concerning him worthy of his memory [Col. 1122A]; for this is your money, and he does not seem to need other money.”

It pleased me that the understanding of others agreed with my own. Knowledge, moreover, is signified by money, as is also understood in that place of the Gospel where our Savior distributes talents to his servants. But why does he demand one hundred thousand or fifty thousand? Of these two numbers, one is perfect and the other imperfect. For a hundred times a thousand, or a thousand times a hundred, makes one hundred thousand; and each number, that is, a hundred and a thousand, is perfect because it has no possibility of increase. For every thing is imperfect so long as it can increase in some respect; but the number one hundred or one thousand can indeed be repeated, yet cannot be increased. It is therefore perfect. [Col. 1122B] For everyone who counts, after reaching one hundred or one thousand, finishes there and begins to count again from one. But the number fifty is imperfect, because it stands in the middle of a hundred: it does not make an end and can extend beyond itself.

Therefore, when that most blessed man commanded me to give him fifty thousand solidi, because, as it seemed to him, I could not give one hundred thousand to him who was speaking, what else does this signify except that I should begin to recount perfectly those things which pertain to his praise and glory? I therefore gave him fifty thousand solidi, because I could not give one hundred thousand—that is, because I could not recount everything perfectly.

I pray, most blessed pontiff, that you may receive favorably these little gifts of mine; and by your holy [Col. 1122C] prayers obtain from Jesus Christ our Savior that he forgive me my offenses. He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1121]

## RESPONSE to the Question: Why the Condition of the Church Was Corrupt at That Time

[Col. 1121]

It remains for us now to answer the question which we promised above [Col. 1121D] that we would answer. For we said that, already from the times of blessed Leo, the Church had become so corrupt that scarcely anyone could be found who either was not a Simoniac or had not been ordained by Simoniacs.

> [Note: Col. 1121D. Fleury likewise testifies, bk. LXII, no. 65, that Gregory VII wrote to St Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and lamented with him the most unhappy condition of the Church.]

Hence even to this day there are certain persons who, arguing wrongly and not understanding properly the Church’s dispensation, maintain that from that time onward the priesthood in the Church had failed. For they say: “If all were such—that is, if all either were Simoniacs or had been ordained by Simoniacs—what are you who now exist, or whence have you come? Through whom did you enter, if not through them? There was no other way. Therefore those who ordained you received their orders from them and from no others, who either [Col. 1122C] were Simoniacs or had been ordained by Simoniacs.” This, therefore, is the question we must answer.

But first it is necessary to say what Simoniacs are and whence they are called such; then, indeed, because there is a great difference between Simoniacs and those ordained by Simoniacs—provided that they do not know those men to be Simoniacs. For anyone who does not doubt that a certain bishop is a Simoniac, if he is ordained by him, differs little in his order from the man by whom he is ordained.

> [Note: Col. 1122D. The eminent Pierre de Marca teaches that under the kingdom of the Goths and in the time of King Theodoric, simony was introduced into sacred ordinations, because a fixed sum of gold was demanded from those elected to bishoprics for confirmation of their election [Col. 1123C]. He observes, however, that it had already been condemned under penalty of deposition by Constitution 30 among the Apostolic Canons, and likewise by Canon 2 of the Council of Chalcedon. See *De concordia sacerdotii et imperii*, bk. VIII, ch. 13, col. 1159.]

For he knows that he is a thief and robber, and that in his ordination he has received nothing [Col. 1123A] other than a curse and the power to curse.

> [Note: Col. 1123D. The time when St Bruno wrote this must be taken into account: namely, those days in which the Simoniac pestilence was widely undermining the Church’s sacred ministers. Therefore, in order to deter them, he strove to set forth the force of that perversity so strongly that he called orders conferred simoniacally void, nonexistent, and full only of a curse. The Church’s teaching, however, is that ordinations performed by Simoniac bishops, or received simoniacally, are valid indeed but unlawful; consequently, ordainers and ordained alike are subject to penalties established by councils: suspension, excommunication, deprivation of benefices, and irregularity. See Berardi, *De Simonia*, dissertation, pt. 1, ch. 2, and on Gratian’s canon; Concina, *De Simonia*, diss. 2, ch. 3; Van Espen, titles 2 and 3, *De Simonia*; Lazzari, commentary on Bruno on John, ch. 10, p. 459.]

For all Simoniacs are ordained as Simon himself was ordained, to whom blessed Peter said in that very ordination: “May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money. For you have neither part nor lot in this matter” (Acts 8:20).

Simoniacs, then, are those who attempt to buy the gift of God, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit. For whether they actually buy or do not buy, if only they offer money and promise to give something for this grace, they are Simoniacs. Simon himself did not buy anything—for there was no one to sell it—but because he wished to buy, he was cursed; and he certainly left that curse as an inheritance to all his disciples. From this [Col. 1123B] Simon, all who imitate him in this act are called Simoniacs.

This Simon, baptized by Philip, adhered to him. When he saw that many mighty works and miracles were performed by the apostles through the laying on of hands, he offered them money, saying: “Give me also this power, that anyone upon whom I lay my hand may receive the Holy Spirit” (ibid., v. 19). To him, as we have just said above, blessed Peter replied: “May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money. For you have neither part nor lot in this matter.” This, then, is Simon’s ordination. Thus Simoniacs who offer money are ordained. Why? Because they think that the gift of God can be possessed with money.

But what blessing do they receive? Let blessed Peter say it, whose voice is most efficacious and whose curse penetrates the inward parts: “May,” he says, “your money perish with you.” This blessing is given them; this prayer is invoked upon their wicked heads. Thus they are blessed; thus they are consecrated; thus they are ordained.

> [Note: Col. 1123D. These statements must be understood concerning the absence of sanctifying grace, not the absence of the character of order, which is impressed even upon the sinner, to his greater condemnation if he does not repent.]

For as soon as they offer money, no matter to whom they offer it, the apostle is present as their consecrator. Even if they are consecrated by Catholic bishops—which indeed often happens—the apostle is nevertheless present among them. Let those bishops [Col. 1124A] say whatever they please; let them pour holy chrism upon their heads: Simon Peter does not alter his judgment, because he does not fail to know what they have brought to him. Those men bless; he curses. They are deceived, but he cannot be deceived.

They suppose that these men are Catholics; they suppose that they have been canonically elected, and for this reason they bless them. For if they had known them, they too would have said with the apostle: “May your money perish with you.” Rightly, therefore, their blessing is turned into a curse, because God looks not to the lips but to the heart. Jacob feared this when he was sent by his mother to his father, that the latter might unknowingly bless him. He said: “You know that my brother Esau is a hairy man, while I am smooth. If my father touches me and perceives it, I fear he may think that I wished to mock him, and bring a curse upon me instead of a blessing” (Gen. 27:11).

But Jacob need not have feared, because he was sent by his mother. These men, however, are not sent by their mother; they are not sent by the Church—these who deceive Isaac, deceive bishops, and wish secretly and by robbery to steal their father’s blessing. Hence, and not without reason, a curse is brought upon them instead of a blessing. For only those are sent by their mother, only those are sent by the Church, who are sent to the fathers, sent to the bishops to be blessed and consecrated by them, not through money, not through any promise, not through secular power, but solely through the election of clergy and people,

> [Note: Col. 1124C. That is, their approval as testimony to character, not an election properly so called.]

and that election itself pure and free from perversity.

We have therefore spoken of the consecration of Simoniacs [Col. 1124C]: how they are ordained, how they are consecrated, how the apostle Peter curses them, and how the bishops’ blessing is turned into a curse for them. Thus ordained, thus consecrated, thus cursed, thus tainted by gain, they come to the churches entrusted to them. There, if indeed they are openly such persons, apart from baptism and sound counsels—which they themselves also often give—whatever they do is vain and useless.

> [Note: Col. 1124C. Sacraments performed and conferred by Simoniacs are indeed held to be valid, but entirely lack the effect of grace unless those receiving them approached the Simoniac minister unknowingly and in good faith. Although many theologians uphold this opinion, there are nevertheless others who have rendered excellent service to ecclesiastical learning and who, in accordance with conciliar definitions and papal decrees, teach that Simoniac ordinations are altogether void and nonexistent. They rely especially upon Canon 4 of the Fifth Roman Council under Pope Gregory VII, in 1078. Morin, certainly, in *De sacris ordinationibus*, pt. 3, exercise 5, ch. 9, p. 82, admits this power in the Church: to impose certain conditions for administering sacraments, so that, if these are absent, their matter becomes unsuitable and ineffective for the intended result. Thus the Council of Trent not only prohibited clandestine marriages, but declared them null and void. In the same way, they say, the Church could exclude from orders persons infected by the stain of simony and declare them incapable of ordination, so that they receive from such persons nothing except, as St Bruno says, a divine curse.
>
> “Certain matters,” says Morin, “belong to ecclesiastical institution and may lawfully be changed and observed differently according to variations of times and regions [Col. 1125C]. Yet, so long as they have not been recalled or abrogated by the Church, they are of such importance that their omission renders ordination not merely unbecoming and unlawful, but also void and null [Col. 1125D], devoid of every effect and grace. All such conditions affect and determine the matter of the sacrament in such a way that, if they are absent, the matter is rendered unsuitable for ordination. They may concern either the ordainer or the person ordained. For the Church, in my judgment, can determine under what conditions the ordaining bishop should exercise his authority, and with what gifts and in what manner the person to be ordained should present himself to the ordainer, so that he may receive ordination validly and effectually from him. Thus, if the ordainer or the person ordained neglects this definition and acts contrary to it, the act is null and void and must be repeated for its effects to be produced. The same must be said analogically of this sacrament as of marriage and penance, whose matters we see the Church has often restricted, enlarged, and variously determined at different times, under threat of a void sacrament.”
>
> Berardi agrees with Morin in the correction of Gratian, I, pt. c. 22; so does Dupin in his defense of Bruno of Asti; and, most recently, the learned Bergamasque Giovanni Battista Locatelli Zucchala, in *On the Power of Priests in Administering the Sacrament of Penance*, p. 224, Bergamo edition, 1787, octavo. These things are said not in order that we should depart from the opinion which we adopted a little earlier, but in order to excuse the opinion of St Bruno [Col. 1126D].]

How these things are to be understood, we shall now explain.

[Col. 1125A] Baptism, for whoever gives it, is good, because it rests not on the faith of the giver but on the faith of those who receive it. But where the Catholic faith is not, baptism does not operate. Hence, one baptized outside the Church is not freed from sins. For remission of sins takes place nowhere except in the Church—provided, however, that he returns to her also in body and manner of life, from whom he had not departed in mind. Otherwise, if he is baptized outside the Church and remains outside, and at the time of baptism has no intention of returning, for such a person there is not even for a moment remission of sins.

But what wonder is there in this? Even those who are baptized within—who are certainly cleansed from all sins—if they depart from her and do not return to her before they die, perish [Col. 1125B] eternally. This was signified by that ark: all things placed within it were saved, while all things found outside it perished.

Hear also what the Lord says: “I am the vine, and you are the branches. Whoever remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit. If anyone does not remain in me, he shall be cast out like a branch and wither; and they shall gather him and cast him into the fire, and he burns” (John 15:5). If, therefore, Christ is the vine and Christians are the branches, then just as branches cannot live if they are separated from the vine, so Christians cannot live if they are separated from the body of Christ. The body of Christ is the Church. Whoever, therefore, does not wish to be separated from Christ should remain in Christ’s body, so that he may be a member of Christ. For if he does not remain in Christ’s body, if he does not remain [Col. 1125C] in the unity of the Church, “he shall be cast out like a branch and wither.”

And what more? “And evil spirits shall gather him.” For he who separates himself from the Church is handed over to them. But what will they do? “They shall cast him into the fire.” For what purpose? “That he may burn.” These are Christ’s words; let us seek no other canons.

It is therefore evident that no one separated from the Church will be saved, whether baptized within it or outside it. Whence this? Let the Lord himself speak again: “If anyone does not remain in me, he will be cast out like a branch and wither; and they will gather him and cast him into the fire, and he burns” [Col. 1126A]. If, then, one who was at some time in Christ perishes because he does not remain in him, how shall he not perish who was never in him and never remained in him? Whoever is baptized outside the Church, unless before leaving this life he is joined to the Church, has never been, and will never be, in Christ, because he has never been, and will never be, in the body of Christ. [Note: [Col. 1126D] How this passage of Bruno is to be understood will be explained below. It cannot be understood of children baptized either within or outside the Church, but of adults (of whom St. Bruno declared in the preceding section that he was speaking), who, if they receive baptism without the necessary disposition, are indeed united to the body of Christ through the sacramental character, but do not attain the effect of grace.]

For a member of Christ exists only in the body of Christ. If one is separated from Christ’s body, one is not a member of Christ. But Christ’s body is not outside the Church; otherwise the Church itself would be outside herself (since the Church herself is Christ’s body), which is absurd. Baptism, therefore, may be administered outside the Church, but it cannot be beneficial there. For baptism administered outside the Church possesses the form of the sacrament [Col. 1126B], but not the power of the sacrament. It possesses the form, because it is performed in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But it does not possess the power, because it does not effect the remission of sins. [Note: [Col. 1126D] St. Bruno’s meaning here likewise requires explanation. From what has been said above, it is sufficiently clear that he is speaking of adult baptism. He maintains that in them the sacrament lacks power—that is, that they do not receive sanctifying grace whenever they are separated from the Church and neglect to become its members through faith and repentance.]

Why, then, are those who come from heretics not rebaptized? Do you wish to hear why? Because they possess the form of baptism—that is, because they have already been regenerated from water through the invocation of the Trinity. It remains for them now also to be regenerated by the Holy Spirit, who may work in them the remission of sins which that visible form could not give: “Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5). Both are necessary there: both the form of the sacrament and the power of the sacrament. Both are necessary [Col. 1126C]: water and the Spirit. For neither water without the Spirit nor the Spirit without water frees a human being from sins. The form of the sacrament may be given both within and outside the Church; but the power of the sacrament is given only within the Church. [Note: [Col. 1126D] Baptism rightly conferred outside the Church upon children regenerates them for eternal life. Likewise adults become Christians, though not righteous, unless through faith they are united to the body of the Catholic Church.]

Hence the most holy Roman pontiffs, filled with the Spirit of God, established with admirable providence that those who come from heretics are not to be rebaptized, because they possess the form of baptism; but because they lack the power of this sacrament, they are to be confirmed by the imposition of hands, with most sacred chrism, at the invocation of the Holy Spirit—whom heretics cannot give [Col. 1127A]. [Note: [Col. 1127C] This was once the opinion of Cyprian, who writes as follows in Epistle 70 to Januarius: “For who can give what he himself does not possess, or how can one perform spiritual acts when he himself has lost the Holy Spirit?” Since St. Bruno was wholly engaged in contesting the validity of simoniacal ordination, he drew, as it were, a parallel from confirmation, which some wished to regard as null if conferred by heretics, relying on the principle that no one can give what he does not have. But, as everyone knows, Pope St. Stephen opposed Cyprian, and the whole Church agreed with Stephen. Hence St. Augustine says in *On Baptism*, book III: “If sacraments are the same, they are entire everywhere, even if they are wrongly understood and administered in discord,” etc. Bruno must be said to have recalled these things as suited to his own case, not because he considered confirmation among the repeatable sacraments.]

Perhaps you ask for authority. It shall be given to you; and this is indeed necessary, since not all appear to agree with this opinion: namely, that although those who come from heretics should not be rebaptized, they should nevertheless again be confirmed with sacred chrism. This is especially so since blessed Augustine says, at 617, that “no sacrament is to be wronged”; and in this matter he seems greatly to differ from others. For what is an injury to a sacrament except the repetition of the sacrament? Yet that certain sacraments are repeated is abundantly established both by examples and authorities. I say certain sacraments, because baptism and holy orders may not be repeated. Thus we read also in the African councils: “Rebaptism [Col. 1127B] and the translation of bishops are not permitted.” But at the Council of Nicaea it is ordered that Paulianists coming to the Church be baptized again, because, like Sabellians, they denied the real distinction of the divine Persons. Their clergy also, if worthy, are to be ordained again. This clearly shows that this ought to be done only in their case and not in that of others. For they did not baptize according to the Church’s form. Had they been baptized according to the form just stated, such a law would certainly not have been specially promulgated concerning them, especially when it is said of all other heretics that, upon coming to the Church, they are neither to be rebaptized nor reordained, but reconciled to the Church solely by the imposition of a bishop’s hand.

That these two sacraments—baptism and [Col. 1127C] holy orders—ought not to be repeated is the belief of the whole Church; nor is there any disagreement among the saints. [Note: [Col. 1127D] Here the holy bishop expressed his own mind more clearly, teaching that, except for Paulianists, those coming to the Church from any heretics whatsoever ought neither to be renewed by the sacred washing nor to receive orders again [Col. 1128C]. Yet no one is admitted to orders according to the canons unless first confirmed. Since the imposition of hands takes place both in the sealing with chrism and in reconciliation to penance, Bruno most plainly admits [Col. 1128D] that it is not to be repeated.]

Hence blessed Augustine also says: “The imposition of hands, like baptism, ought not to be repeated”; speaking of that imposition of hands concerning which the Apostle says to Timothy: “Lay hands hastily on no one” (1 Tim. 5:22). For both the sealing with chrism and the reconciliation of penitents are called an imposition of hands. Hence the sacred canons also forbid bishops to lay hands upon clerics among the other penitents.

[Col. 1128A] That certain sacraments may lawfully be repeated [Note: [Col. 1128D] It is quite clear that Bruno uses the word *sacrament* broadly in this treatise, since he applies the name of sacrament to the consecration of churches. Strictly speaking, only those are sacraments which were instituted by Christ and have sanctifying grace attached to them; the others, akin to sacraments, are called sacramentals and are repeated when their use requires it. For the reasons why church consecrations may be repeated, see Berardi, *On the Emendation of Gratian’s Canons*, part I, chapter 7, p. 97 and following.] is most plainly demonstrated both by the Church’s frequent practice and by one example of blessed Gregory. For every day we see consecrations of churches repeated, not only from necessity but even at the will of bishops. Thus the canons prescribe concerning churches that, if an altar has been moved, it must be consecrated anew. Blessed Gregory too, as he himself testifies, consecrated at Rome a certain church in the Subura because it had been held by Arians for a long time. How acceptable to God that consecration, or reconsecration, was is shown by the mighty works and miracles which the Lord performed there in the very days when it had been consecrated.

How then is it true that no sacrament is to be wronged [Col. 1128B]? Likewise, that the sealing with chrism must be repeated in heretics is proved by the following authority of the saints. Pope Eusebius says of this sealing:

> “We decree that all heretics who by God’s grace are converted, and have been baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity, are to be reconciled by the imposition of hands, observing the rule of the Roman Church. The sacrament of the imposition of hands is also to be held in great veneration; it cannot be performed by others except the high priests. Neither in the time of the apostles is it read or known to have been performed by anyone but the apostles themselves; nor, as has already been said, can it be performed or ought it to be performed by anyone other than those who hold their place. For if it is presumptuously attempted otherwise, let it be held void and empty, [Col. 1128C] and never reckoned among ecclesiastical sacraments.”

[Note: [Col. 1128D] That this canon cited by Gratian—found at *De consecratione*, distinction 5, canon 5—is apocryphal and an invention of Pseudo-Isidore is demonstrated by Carlo Sebastiano Berardi, part II, vol. I, p. 171.]

Let us hear also what was decreed at Rome on this matter in a council in the time of blessed Sylvester. [Note: [Col. 1128D] This second canon attributed to Sylvester suffers from the same defect. Berardi’s words are: “It seems to me sufficiently established that this council first appeared in the collection of Pseudo-Isidore, so that at once there arises such [Col. 1129C] a suspicion that it should rather be reckoned among apocryphal documents,” part I, chapter 6, *On Roman Councils under Sylvester*, p. 62.]

> “At the same time,” he says, “on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, when the aforementioned great council was assembled at Nicaea, after the pope had already canonically summoned them to the city of Rome, he too, with the counsel of the Emperor Constantine, assembled two hundred and seventy-seven bishops; and he again condemned Calixtus as well as Arius and Sabellius. He decreed that no one should receive a repentant Arian bishop [Col. 1129A] unless the bishop of that place reconciled him and, by an episcopal imposition of hands with most sacred chrism, confirmed him with the [618] grace of the Holy Spirit, which cannot be given by heretics.”

[Note: [Col. 1129D] The Church rejected the baptism of certain Arians, who baptized “in the name of the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit”; therefore those withdrawing from such heresy had to be examined by bishops, baptized again, and confirmed. The same did not apply to those coming from other heretics who held right views concerning the most Holy Trinity or used the proper baptismal form.]

What could have been said more plainly or more manifestly? Is not this sacrament repeated? Let us give still other examples, so that this opinion, which many dispute, may become clearer and more certain. Let Pope Siricius speak, then:

> “At the beginning of your letter you have indicated that many baptized by impious Arians are hastening to the Catholic faith, and that some of our brethren wish to baptize them again. This is not permitted, since the Apostle forbids it, the canons oppose it, and the general decrees, sent to the provinces by our predecessor Liberius of venerable memory after the annulment of the Council of Rimini, prohibit it. As established in the synod, we associate them, together with Novatians and other heretics, with the Catholic assembly through the invocation alone of the sevenfold Spirit by episcopal imposition of hands; this is also observed throughout East and West.”

[Note: [Col. 1129D] This is chapter 1 of Pope Siricius’s epistle to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, who had written to Damasus, Siricius’s predecessor; it is reported in the code of canons and in the constitutions of the Roman Church. What can be inferred from it except that, on the assumption that Arians, Novatians, and other heretics use the due form in conferring baptism, the sacrament must not be repeated for those coming to the Church, but confirmation must be administered to them, which bishops give by the imposition of hands.]

Let us also see what Leo says, whose constancy and courage strengthened the faith when it was already about to perish, and whose judgment, I think, no one will dare contradict:

> “Those concerning whom you have written do not deny that they were baptized, but profess that they do not know of what faith those were who baptized them. Therefore, since they have in some manner received the form of baptism, they are not to be baptized, but by the imposition of hands they are to be joined to Catholics through the power of the Holy Spirit, which they could not receive from heretics [Col. 1129C].”

[Note: [Col. 1129D] This is chapter 7 of Pope Leo I’s epistle to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, which is number 129 in the collection. The passage quoted above is not found in this letter, nor have I encountered it elsewhere. What, then, did St. Leo establish? [Col. 1130D] First, that those baptized by heretics with the requisite form are not to be rebaptized; second, that they need only the imposition of hands, either because heretics did not confer chrismation, or because Leo himself thought they could not confer the power of the Holy Spirit. Therefore confirmation was not repeated in Leo’s sense; rather, it was then first conferred by Catholic bishops.]

The same authority again says:

> “Those who received baptism from heretics, when they had not been baptized before, are to be confirmed by the invocation alone of the Holy Spirit through the imposition of hands, because they received only the form of baptism without the power of the Holy Spirit. And, as you know, we preach that this rule must be observed in all churches: that the washing once begun is not violated by any repetition, according to the Apostle’s saying, ‘One God, one faith, one baptism’; its washing is not to be rashly repeated. But, as we have said, the sanctification of the Holy Spirit alone is to be invoked, so that what no one receives from heretics may be obtained from Catholic priests.”

Likewise, the Council of Laodicea records:

> “Concerning those converted from heretics—that is, Novatians and Photinians—whether they are baptized or catechumens, they are not to be received before they have anathematized every heresy, especially that by which they were held; then finally those called believers among them are to be instructed in the creed of our faith and, anointed with sacred chrism, thus to communicate in the most sacred mysteries.”

[Note: [Col. 1130D] This is canon 7, from which, however, nothing may be inferred to establish the repetition of confirmation.]

We could still furnish other authorities on these matters, but, I think, these suffice.

Yet one may doubt concerning what blessed Augustine says: “No sacrament is to be wronged.” [Col. 1130B] Again he himself says: “Those who come from heretics are received into the Church through the imposition of bishops’ hands, lest they perhaps think that nothing has been conferred upon them by the Church which they did not have outside the Church.” Defining what the imposition of hands is, he also says: “What is the imposition of hands except prayer over a person? And that very imposition of hands is repeated.” For the imposition of hands is nothing other than prayer over a person. Therefore prayer over a person is not to be repeated in those sacraments which may not be repeated.

It has been said that certain sacraments may be repeated while others may not, and this has been proved by authorities. It has also been said that those coming from heretics ought to be received only through the imposition of hands. [Col. 1130C] It has indeed been said that all sacraments outside the Church have their form but lack their power. We have also said that no one is saved outside the Church. We said likewise of simoniacs, when they are consecrated, that every blessing is turned into a curse for them.

If anyone asks concerning the children of heretics why they perish although they have been baptized, [Note: [Col. 1130D] Bruno here again advances Cyprian’s opinion that baptism conferred by heretics is invalid, though above he had said: “Baptism, from whomsoever it is given, is good, because it consists not in the faith of the giver but in that of the recipients.” In the case of infants, the Church’s faith supplies what is lacking; otherwise their baptism would be invalid and illicit, contrary to the Church’s practice and teaching. By baptism they have been regenerated into Christ, are in the Church, and have become heirs of God’s kingdom.] I answer: because [619] they are not in the Church. But if someone says, “What sin have they committed, that they are not in the Church?” I answer in turn: What sin have the children of pagans and Jews committed, that they have not deserved [Col. 1131A] to be baptized? [Note: [Col. 1131D] The children of pagans and Hebrews who lack baptism perish; but their adverse lot must be referred to God’s free and not unjust election. On the validity of infant baptism, even where the faith and intention of those presenting the child are absent, provided it is correctly administered, see Berardi, Dissertation II, part IV, p. 56.] Yet the Lord himself says: “I know whom I have chosen” (John 3:18). But if the children of excommunicated persons are baptized in the Church, their parents’ excommunication does them no harm: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” [Note: [Col. 1131D] Bruno himself says in the treatise *On the Sacraments*: “In saying this, however, I do no prejudice to infants who are baptized and saved not by their own faith but by that of others.”] (Ezek. 18:20). Nevertheless, once they reach an age at which they can recognize their own sins, they can no longer be delivered from sins. But if they are baptized outside the Church, all who are excommunicated remain outside the Church; unless before leaving this life they are reconciled through bishops, they seem to me to be in great danger.

Having thus disposed of these matters, we must now speak of those who, although not simoniacs, were nevertheless ordained by simoniacs. For it is clear that simoniacs must never in any way be received in their orders. “For they have neither part nor lot in the word of God” [Col. 1131B] (Acts 8:21). It is the Apostle who speaks. But you say: Why then are other heretics received in their ordinations, while simoniacs are not received? Are simoniacs worse than Arians, Novatians, Donatists, Nestorians, and Eutychians? For we read that from all these groups both bishops and presbyters have been received in their orders and not deprived of their proper rank.

I answer: whether simoniacs are worse, I do not know. But I know one thing: it is a great crime to sell or buy the Holy Spirit. For if it was a great sin to sell or buy Christ, it is certainly a great sin to sell or buy the Holy Spirit. For the Father, [Col. 1131C] Son, and Holy Spirit are equal. Judas is he who sells; a Jew is he who buys; but the Lord cast both seller and buyer out of the temple. Many things are indeed done in the Church by dispensation, owing to the necessity of the time and the character of the matter, which certainly would not be done if strict canonical judgment were applied. [Note: [Col. 1131D] Thus the canon of the Roman council under Alexander II, cited above.] When the Lord spoke of wheat and tares, he said: “Let both grow until the harvest” (Matt. 13:30). Yet such dispensation must be exercised with great care.

Other heretics did not err in receiving orders; rather, some other cause and doctrine impeded their faith. But the heresy and sin of simoniacs [Note: [Col. 1131D] See Berardi, part I, dissertation III, chapter 2, *On Simony*, where he says that in the sacred canons simony is commonly called heresy and that one infected by it must be deemed a heretic “who holds not merely that he does it, but that it can be done—the detestable commerce of sacred things or things attached to sacred things” [Col. 1132D]. Thus understood, Innocent III did not hesitate to write, chapter 32, *On Simony*, that the “enormity of simoniacal heresy” is so great “that, in comparison with it, other crimes are reckoned as nothing.”] is their ordination itself. If, therefore, they are reconciled to their ordination—which, as we showed above, is nothing but a curse [Col. 1131D]—to what are they reconciled except to their own [Col. 1132A] heresy and sin, and to the curse which they received? Therefore let them not seek reconciliation, lest they perhaps incur a curse. Let them seek the grace of the Holy Spirit, not for episcopal rank, but for the wiping away of their iniquity.

Simoniacs are rightly not received in their orders, since they sinned in those orders themselves. Arians, however, erred and sinned not in episcopal rank but in faith concerning the Trinity; and other heretics likewise, each in his own heresy. Simoniacs alone sin in buying sacred orders. Therefore they alone are rightly not received, by any ecclesiastical dispensation, in the things in which they sinned. But apart from these, we read in many places of ecclesiastical history that heresiarchs have been received in their orders. For the Council of Nicaea received the Cathari, or Novatians, by imposition of hands and ordered their clergy to remain in their orders [Col. 1132B].

We have said enough above concerning this imposition of hands, without which heretics are not received. Blessed Gregory too, writing to the bishops of Iberia concerning Nestorians, says:

> “Therefore let all who turn from Nestorius’s perverse error confess, before the holy assembly of your brotherhood, this truth concerning Christ’s Nativity; let them anathematize Nestorius himself with all his followers and the remaining heresies; let them promise to receive and venerate the venerable synods which the universal Church receives. Then, without any doubt, let your holiness receive them into your communion, preserving their own orders, so that, while through vigilance you discern the hidden things of their minds, teach them through true knowledge the right doctrines which they ought to hold, and through gentleness cause them no opposition or difficulty concerning their own orders, you may snatch them from the mouth of the wicked enemy.”

There are also many other arguments by which this same point could be proved. But these two examples are sufficient concerning the reception of [620] heretics and their not being deprived of their proper ranks.

We have digressed greatly. Let us now return to our subject and speak of those ordained by simoniacs. Those ordained by simoniacs either know that they are simoniacs or consider them Catholics. If they know them to be simoniacs and allow themselves to be ordained by them, they deserve no pardon such that they should be received while retaining their own [Col. 1132D] orders. [Note: [Col. 1132D] At the fourth Roman council under Gregory VII, said to have been held in 1048, nearly one hundred bishops were present, besides abbots and a great many others among clerics and laity. There certain bishops were first condemned and deposed from their rank because they had been simoniacally ordained and had also ordained others simoniacally. These were Theald of Milan, Guibert of Ravenna, Roland of Tarvis, Cardinal Hugh, and Geoffrey of Narbonne.]

For many ambitious persons are shown to allow themselves to be consecrated by such men for the sake of some dignity, though they do not doubt that they are cursed by those men. Who indeed doubts that simoniacs are heretics? [Note: [Col. 1133D] In the sense explained above. For, as Berardi himself states, “one who certainly knows that sacred things cannot be bought or sold, yet nevertheless acts otherwise and buys or sells sacred things for a price, sins very gravely, indeed, not through an error of understanding but of will; yet he is not a heretic. But we shall call it simoniacal heresy when someone holds not merely that he does it, but that it can be done—the detestable commerce of sacred things or things connected with sacred things” [Col. 1134D].] Who, then, would spare one who permits himself to be ordained by a person whom he does not doubt to be a heretic?

But if he is considered Catholic and lives in the Church together with Catholics, what he does must be valid, because God looks not to him but to the devotion and faith of the one who subjects himself to that man’s hands as though to a Catholic bishop for God’s sake. God also looks to the Church, which offers her children to him with a simple heart. Because he is within the Church, the Holy Spirit is certainly present, and even works holy orders through an evil person. A human being speaks, but it is the Holy Spirit [Col. 1133B] who sanctifies. The faith of the recipient and of the one presenting him accomplishes all this. For we read that the Lord himself said to many that it should be done for them according to their faith. If then those persons were healed through their faith, why are these not consecrated through theirs? Nothing here is done contrary to faith; all that is done is faithful. If they acted rashly or contrary to faith, the Holy Spirit would rightly be absent, since “the Spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (Wisdom 1:5).

We said above concerning a simoniac that, while pretending to be Catholic, he is consecrated by Catholic bishops, and all that blessing is turned into a curse for him, because God looks not to lips but to the heart: their hearts do not intend to bless a simoniac. Conversely, we can likewise say that, while a simoniac pretends to be Catholic and blesses a Catholic, although his blessing is a curse, all his curse is nevertheless turned into a blessing. For the Holy Spirit is present and looks not to the petitions of the heretical speaker and consecrator, but to the mind and devotion of the recipient.

But should such a thing occur outside the Church, this reasoning ought not help one ordained outside the Church by a simoniac, even though he considers him not to be a simoniac; for he is neither offered by mother Church nor is the devotion good of one who is ordained outside the Church by anyone whatsoever [Note: [Col. 1134D] The ordination of schismatic and heretical bishops is held valid, but not lawful, provided that they themselves received it correctly and validly.]. It is therefore evident concerning those who, within the Church, are ordained non-simoniacally by simoniacs whom they nevertheless regard as Catholics, that their ordination must be valid.

[Col. 1133D] Therefore let those be silent who chatter that from the time of blessed Pope Leo [Note: [Col. 1134D] He speaks here of Blessed Leo IX, who flourished shortly before Bruno.] the priesthood has already failed in the Church because all were either simoniacs or ordained by simoniacs. The same must be understood likewise of other heretics: if they are ordained within the Church and are regarded as Catholics, then, as long as they remain there, the sacraments they perform must be valid.

We must now answer those who maintain that, since they did not purchase holy orders themselves, they are not simoniacs, although they purchased churches or parts of churches. But let them answer this: Did they reach holy orders through that purchase and sale? Or did they receive, in the churches which they purchased, through that purchase, the authority to celebrate the sacred mysteries? If this is so, they can scarcely defend themselves against being simoniacs. For a simoniac is one who seeks to attain holy orders for a price. A simoniac is also one who endeavors to buy the authority by which the gifts of the Holy Spirit are procured.

This bishop gave or promised payment, as he pretends, not for holy orders but for lands and vineyards, castles and villages, as though for a canonical election or consecration. But if [Col. 1134B] he intended to become bishop in that manner, he was certainly seeking to attain holy orders for a price. He did not do this merely in order to possess those things as a layman, but rather so that he might at some time possess episcopal dignity on their account. We see that such men, who are canonically elected, after such an invasion press much more urgently to attain [621] holy orders as quickly as possible. In this they show their intention most openly and reveal what that purchase signified. Whenever, therefore, they come to consecration, blessed Peter will be present to say to them in his customary manner: “May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money” (Acts 8:20).

But if they do not come to consecration, but repent beforehand and abandon that very wicked opinion, one may indeed doubt whether they ought ever afterward to be placed over other churches. Yet one should consider what blessed Peter said to Simon: “Repent,” he says, “of this wickedness of yours, and pray to God, if perhaps this thought of your heart may be forgiven you” (ibid., 22). For if he had perhaps repented, he would afterward have had freely what he had previously been unable to have for a price, although the Apostle’s words signify only the forgiveness of sin.

What we have said of a whole bishopric, we understand also of individual churches or their portions. For it is a similar sin to commit fornication with a rich person or a poor one. Whoever purchases one church, or part of one, how much more willingly would he purchase a whole [Col. 1134D] bishopric if he could? Whoever purchases a church purchases, indeed, that authority of which Simon Magus said to the Apostle: “Give me this authority, that whomever I lay my hand upon may receive the Holy Spirit” (ibid., 19). Before purchasing a church, the one who purchases it had no free authority in it to baptize, sacrifice, or celebrate any other mysteries; and all these are gifts and workings of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1135A]. Therefore he purchases that authority: namely, he purchases the authority to baptize or sacrifice, which he did not have in that church before purchasing it. For just as it is impious to think that the Holy Spirit can be possessed with money, so too it is impious to think that his gifts and workings ought to be given and exercised for a price.

But you say: “I possessed this authority—that is, to baptize and perform similar acts—even before I purchased the church.” Why, then, did you purchase it? “Because I was not permitted to perform these acts in it before I purchased it.” Now I recognize your intention and see that it corresponds in the highest degree to Simon’s intention. You did possess the authority, but you did not wish it to remain idle, because it brought you little or nothing unless [Col. 1135B] you exercised it somewhere. You would never have purchased it unless you hoped for profit from it. This, therefore, is Simon’s intention; this is what he was doing. He wished to buy what he hoped to be able to sell for much.

For he did not say, “Give me this authority so that I may possess the Holy Spirit”; but what did he say? “Give me this authority, that whoever receives the laying on of my hand may receive the Holy Spirit.” For he would have retained no hope of profit if he had merely possessed it and could not have given it to others. Likewise, if you merely possess this authority, yet do not exercise it profitably, you regard what you have as nothing. How then are you not a simoniac, if in so great an evil you are like Simon?

These things, however, have been said concerning those who purchase churches after ordination [Col. 1136A]. For if they purchase them before ordination and come to orders through that purchase, they are certainly simoniacs—especially those who, by purchasing a church, seek to attain holy orders. But if they desire to obtain not orders themselves but church benefices through money—for we see many such persons who, after buying churches, wholly disdain to be ordained—they seem to be not so much simoniacs as thieves and robbers. “For whoever does not enter through the door is a thief and a robber” (John 10:1). But one who enters through money does not enter through the door; therefore he is a thief and a robber. Yet whether they are called by this name or by the other, they ought not to hold the Church: for the Lord cast all sellers and buyers out of the temple [Col. 1136B].

The great Council of Chalcedon also decreed: “If anyone ordains any cleric, steward of the Church, or minister for money, let both giver and receiver be deposed; but those who consent are to be struck with anathema.” Observe, therefore, that not only clerics but also stewards are cast out of the Church—all who buy or sell holy orders, churches themselves, or parts of churches. Since the punishment is alike, why should there be contention about the name? Whether they are called simoniacs or not, the punishment is the same.

Let this be enough of our answer to the question which we promised above to answer.

[Col. 1135]

# LIFE OF SAINT PETER, BISHOP OF ANAGNI

From that composed by St. Bruno, bishop of Segni, briefly described by the reverend Lord Gaspare Viviani of Urbino, bishop of the same Church of Anagni.

[Col. 1135]

## ADMONITION

622 All authors agree that the *Life of St. Peter of Anagni* was written by Bishop Bruno of Segni; indeed, this very point is affirmed in the aforementioned privilege or diploma of canonization. Yet it must be exceedingly rare, since Mauro Marchesi, among the works of St. Bruno of Segni which he published at Venice in 1631, was compelled to omit it and to present in its place the compendium of the Most Reverend Gaspare Viviani, bishop of Anagni from 1579 to 1605. Moreover, Mabillon testifies in the *Benedictine Annals* that it has not yet been published in its entirety.

We have what we believe to be the complete acts of St. Peter; nevertheless, we do not yet venture with certainty to ascribe them to St. Bruno of Segni. For, to pass over chronological anachronisms and other arguments for interpolation, they narrate certain things concerning Bruno himself which St. Bruno probably did not write about himself.

Yet although Baronius, in his *Ecclesiastical Annals*, publishes under the name of Bruno of Signi fragments of this Life which agree with our text almost word for word, we nevertheless judge that our Acts have been enlarged and interpolated by some author. It would indeed be desirable for Benedictine writers to discover the work of Saint Bruno of Signi. Meanwhile, we publish the Life of this saint as best we can, since we are not permitted to do so as we would wish. Finally, since the copyist, unskilled in ancient characters and perhaps even in the Latin language, has miserably corrupted those Acts, as we warned above, we prefer to publish them without a definite author’s name rather than rashly attribute them to the learned Bruno of Signi. It now remains only to submit to the press and to the reader’s judgment this very Life of Saint Peter, here and there supplied within brackets and corrected according to our conjecture.

In the Life in question, chapter 3, no. 34, it is stated: “But the aforementioned Bruno, bishop of Signi, while keeping vigil in prayer during the silence of the night in the church of Saint Peter in his own city, saw from his watchtower a light kindled over the city and the church of Anagni, and heard a heavenly chant in the air. Foreseeing Saint Peter’s death, he summoned his household and, after preparing conveyances, hastened to Anagni. After tears of pious compassion, he commended the death of the blessed bishop Peter to the Savior of all with fitting obsequies, and honorably committed him to burial within the church with his own hands and those of the priests. Then he delivered a most eloquent oration in his praise,” etc.

> [Note: [Col. 1135B] We drew this from the Bollandists under 3 August; nor do we omit to inform readers that D. Giovanni Battista Federici, prefect of the Cassinese archive, left nothing undone at our request to procure the Life of Saint [Col. 1136B] Peter, bishop of Anagni, written, as quite a few writers report, by Saint Bruno of Signi; but all efforts expended were in vain.]

## COMPENDIUM OF THE LIFE OF SAINT PETER, BISHOP OF ANAGNI

[Col. 1137]

[Col. 1137A] 623 Peter of Salerno, born of a most illustrious family of princes, was entrusted by his parents to the guardianship and faithful care of his uncle, who was also abbot of the Benedictine monastery at Salerno. Bereft of both parents while still a little boy, he was educated by a certain religious and thoroughly upright man. Then, as a youth endowed with excellent character and learning, he transferred his possessions to that same monastery; embracing the rule of Saint Benedict, he likewise consecrated himself to the Lord.

Thus, bearing Christ’s sweet yoke from youth onward, he was humane and gentle toward all, and an outstanding cultivator of the religious life. He accurately observed the monastic laws of blessed Benedict, which he also committed to memory, and spent all his time in fasting, prayers, and sacred reading. He also added knowledge of law to his knowledge of divine matters, [Col. 1137B] while in this way the Lord was preparing him, without his expectation, for the office of bishop.

Accordingly, when Aldebrandus, cardinal and legate of the Holy Roman Church, once came to Salerno, moved by the holy man’s reputation, he obtained him from his uncle the abbot and brought him to Rome before Pope Alexander II. By him Peter was first placed over ecclesiastical affairs, and then, though unwillingly, was created bishop of the Church of Anagni, to the great joy of clergy and people.

Having therefore undertaken the pastoral office, he began to consider restoring the sacred buildings and recovering the Church’s possessions, as well as seeking out relics of the saints—above all the sacred body of blessed Magnus. The church of Anagni was said to be adorned by its presence, though this did not seem [Col. 1137C] sufficiently certain. But God thus removed every doubt.

For Peter ordered a certain paralytic woman, brought to him at that time by her husband, named Franco, to pour out prayers at the tomb in which Saint Magnus’s body was thought to lie. The woman and her husband Franco spent the night there in prayer with abundant tears; when both returned home sorrowfully, blessed Magnus appeared to the woman on the following day, clothed in episcopal and splendid vestments. He ordered her, restored to health, to tell the bishop that he should no longer doubt the presence of his body resting in the church. She obeyed; and joyfully, with blessed Peter and a very great multitude of people roused by the report of so great a miracle, she gave thanks at Saint Magnus’s tomb to the most gracious God for the benefits received.

Meanwhile Peter, having recovered certain goods of the church, provided with paternal charity both for his clergy and for the needy. One night, as was his custom, while praying in the church, he saw Bishop Magnus, shining with great splendor, coming to him together with the Mother of God. Magnus foretold that Peter would be sent eastward to the emperor, would drive away from him a long-standing illness, and would obtain whatever he wished for restoring the church.

Not long afterward Peter was sent as apostolic legate to Emperor Michael at Constantinople. Having already discharged his office, he also recounted what he had seen at night in the church at Anagni. At first the emperor replied that he knew absolutely nothing of who blessed Magnus was or what church [Col. 1138B] of Anagni might be. But that night, when the emperor was suffering most severely and was thought nearly dead, blessed Magnus appeared, arrayed in episcopal mitres, together with the most holy Mother of God. They warned him that, if he wished to be saved, he should comply with the apostolic legate.

As soon as the emperor recovered the power of speech, he ordered the bishop to be summoned. When the bishop arrived, the chain placed upon him—as was customary in those times—was suddenly broken apart in the imperial hall, as though it were frail material being torn. Therefore the emperor, as a suppliant, began to ask the bishop for the benefit of health through the Mother of God and Saint Magnus, while at the same time recounting the vision.

Then the holy and truly merciful bishop, having invoked the aid of the most holy Trinity, the most blessed Virgin, Saint Magnus, and all the saints whose sacred [Col. 1138C] bones are preserved in the church of Anagni, lightly touched the afflicted limbs and said: “Rise, most illustrious prince, and rejoice in lasting health.” Immediately the emperor rose and, falling at the bishop’s feet, called him father—the man whom the day before he had nearly dismissed as a foreigner.

Finally, having generously granted him workmen, a great quantity of gold, and gilded vessels, he promised that he would provide further expenses to complete the basilica; and this he actually did. Blessed Peter, having governed his Church most excellently for about forty-three years, passed to heaven on the third day before the Nones of August [3 August], under Pope Paschal II, by whom he was also enrolled among the saints.

> [Note: [Col. 1137D] Mabillon, in the *Benedictine Annals* for the year of Christ 1105, noted that the Life of Saint Peter, bishop of Anagni, written by Saint Bruno of Signi, had not been published complete in print. See the Acts among the Bollandists under 3 August. Peter is said to have administered the Church of Anagni for forty-three years.]

## PRIVILEGE OF THE CANONIZATION OF BLESSED PETER, BISHOP OF ANAGNI

[Col. 1137]

[Col. 1137D] 624 Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren at Anagni and others established throughout Campania: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Keeping before our eyes the most high Lord, [Col. 1138D] who is praised and blessed in his friends, and therefore considering the merits of the vigorous and approved life by which the holy man Peter, formerly bishop of Anagni, taken from the monastic rule, served God in the pastoral [Col. 1139A] office with purity, simplicity, watchful diligence, and example; and also admiring the distinguished miracles with which divine grace adorned its saint before and after his death—as Bruno, bishop of Signi, faithfully records—and continues to adorn him down to our own times: by the authority of these presents we will and command that on the third day before the Nones of August you duly celebrate and solemnly commemorate the heavenly birthday of this memorable confessor and bishop, who is to be numbered in the catalogue of saints, so that by his pious intercessions we may deserve grace in the present life and eternal glory in the life to come, with the help of divine mercy.

Given at Signi, on the second day before the Nones of June [4 June], in the eleventh year of our pontificate. In the year of the Lord 1109.

## LETTERS OF SAINT BRUNO

[Col. 1139]

### 625 I. TO PETER, BISHOP OF PORTO

[Col. 1139B]

To the venerable Peter, bishop of Porto, Bruno, sinful bishop and servant of blessed Benedict: greeting.

We have heard that certain of our brethren not only do not condemn the things recently done against the Church, but even rashly attempt to defend them. Yet everyone who defends heresy is a heretic. Nor can anyone say that this is not heresy, because the holy and apostolic Church has called it heresy and excommunicated it in many councils. Those, indeed, are especially called heresies which have been judged and condemned in councils. Hence Guibert was not without reason called a heresiarch, and was condemned and excommunicated together with his followers.

[Col. 1139C] Therefore, whoever, abandoning the Catholic Church, crossed over to Guibert’s party and defend and maintain his impious heresy are without doubt heretics, excommunicated, and bound by apostolic bonds. But those who are excommunicated and bound can bind or loose neither themselves nor others.

> [Note: [Col. 1139D] Saint Bruno added the following to this letter, as reported by Baronius and Marchesius. “I sent these letters to the bishop of Porto, in which I said that no one is a heretic except only those who defend and maintain heresy; and I judged that such persons should be avoided, even if we love them with the affection due to parents, eyes, and hands. For we had been told that those who had been captured through the treachery of the impious king, all but a very few, said with one unanimous voice: ‘What we have preached, we preach; and what we have condemned, we condemn.’ Who can doubt that those who say this are Catholics?”]

### II. TO THE BISHOPS AND CARDINALS OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

To the bishops and cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, Bruno, bishop of Signi: greeting.

Some time ago I sent a letter to the bishop of Porto, my most beloved friend, in which I said that those who defend heresy are heretics. I therefore said that all [Col. 1139D] those are heretics who, abandoning the Catholic Church, crossed over to Guibert’s party and defend and maintain his impious heresy. Yet I do not understand as having crossed to Guibert’s party those who never praised or defended his heresy, even if, compelled by necessity or for some other reason, they may seem to have consented for the moment.

This heresy concerning investiture is said to belong especially to Guibert and Henry because Guibert was ordained pope for this purpose by King Henry—indeed, by the devil himself—[Col. 1140B] so that through him the king might obtain what he claimed had been left to him by his forefathers: namely, investiture and the appointment of churches. This was what he sought; this was what he hoped to obtain through Guibert. In other matters they did not seem to differ much from us. For they too condemned simoniacs and despised other vices, as we did. But they sought servitude, while we sought the liberty of the Church. [626]

Therefore whoever says that Guibert was not a heretic denies that we are Catholics. For Catholics are those who praise and defend the faith and teaching of the Catholic Church; conversely, heretics are those who, with obstinate mind, oppose the faith and teaching of the Catholic Church. How, moreover, they wickedly fought there against the faith and teaching of the Catholic [Col. 1140C] Church, we shall show in what follows.

There was no small dispute between us and them concerning investiture. For concerning the simoniacal heresy, as we have already said above, there was no dispute between us and them, because that heresy was condemned alike by us and by them … [lacuna]

*(The remainder is lacking in the Riccardian manuscript, from which we copied this letter.)*

### III. TO PASCHAL, SUPREME PONTIFF

To Paschal, supreme pontiff, Bruno, sinful bishop and servant of blessed Benedict: that which is due to so great a lord and father.

My enemies tell you that I do not love you and that I speak ill of you; but they lie. For I love you as I ought to love a father and lord, [Col. 1140D] etc. See above under Paschal II, at the year 1118.

### IV. TO B., PROVOST, AND ALL THE BRETHREN OF SAINT GEORGE

*(From the same Riccardian manuscript.)*

627 To the most beloved brother B., provost of Saint George, and all the brethren who are with him: greeting and blessing.

You have informed us by your letter that the holy and venerable bishop of Lucca and Parma, and the ministers of the sacred [Col. 1141A] congregations of Camaldoli and Vallombrosa, wish to know our opinion concerning the heresy called that of investiture, and whether the lord pope has accepted, and will accept, our counsel.

First, however, know this: the lord pope neither loves me nor my counsel. But a good resolve ought not to be changed. And I say what I have said, and remain most firmly in the judgment of Gregory and Urban; and I hope in the mercy of almighty God that I shall persevere in this resolve until the end. I have sent you this little book, and ask you that, just as you have shown our other letters to the aforementioned venerable bishops and to the rest of Christ’s faithful, so you may show them these also, etc.

## ODO OF ASTI, BENEDICTINE MONK

[Col. 1141]

## EXPOSITION OF THE PSALMS, WRITTEN THROUGH CONTEMPLATION, ADDRESSED TO BRUNO, BISHOP OF SIGNI

*(Works of Saint Bruno, Venetian edition of 1651, edited by Dom Mauro Marchesi.)*

[Col. 1141]

[Col. 1141B] To Bruno, bishop, Odo, monk.

Because I left incomplete the work begun at your command and gentle admonition—not indeed through pride, but owing to the changeableness of our age and to leisure—I thought that I would make satisfaction and please you by composing this work with much greater care; especially since I have written concisely according to your wish and have arranged it, according to the poverty of my ability, with a certain forethought. Thus I avoided the confusion of nearly all the verses without anywhere interrupting the continuous course of the meanings.

Finally, in many places I removed what would be harmful even without an obelus, and added what would be useful even without an asterisk. Moreover, I have not forgotten that at times I have put an equivalent expression in place of the original words; nor indeed was this without labor. [Col. 1141C] For I knew that the heavier the labor, the more welcome the deed.

Therefore I have endeavored to commend myself to you not by flattering words—which, as the Lord knows, have no place in me—but truly by obedience to your commands. Hence it happened that I pursued so great a stag, so swift and elusive, which now by the speed of its course wholly eluded my gaze, now of its own accord, like a stag, presented itself to the one seeking it; at last, captured and overcome, it came to rest.

Receive, therefore, David’s prey, the worthiest of all hunts, which, because I lack a messenger, I offer you more slowly than I ought. If anyone objects that my shoulders are not equal to so great a burden, citing Matthew 11, “The Lord’s yoke is sweet, and his burden light,” I shall reply: if he seeks counsel [Col. 1142B] or a protector by mockery—for scarcely can anything, however small, be composed without the wrinkled mockery of someone—then you, venerable bishop, will be an easy answer for me to such a question.

But if anyone should presume with venomous tooth to gnaw at your Psalter, let your most loving pastoral care resist him, and, while you remain unharmed, let it, innocent, never suffer violence. If anything absurd, superfluous, or insufficiently coherent is found in it, let your own and Odo’s modest diligence correct it, erase it, and add what is needed. For I am at the service not only of the builder, but also of one bringing stones together from every quarter into one place.

I have prefixed the titles so that the purport of the Psalms may be grasped more easily and briefly.

## EXPOSITION OF THE TITLES

[Col. 1142C]

### Explanation of the Psalm Titles

**Psalm III.** “O Lord, how they have multiplied. When David fled from the face of his son Absalom.”

David is interpreted as “strong in hand.” He signifies Christ, whose hand was always so strong that he conquered the devil, drove away infirmities by touch alone, gave sight to the blind, and finally touched the bier and raised the dead. Absalom, whose name means “the father’s peace,” signifies Judas. Absalom perished while hanging from the branches of a tree; Judas hanged himself with a noose. When Absalom died, David had peace; when Judas died, Christ has peace. Christ himself indicated this whenever, after his Passion, he commended peace to the disciples, saying in Luke 24: “Peace be with you,” as though saying: “He who made us sorrowful is dead.” Likewise [Col. 1143A] in John 14: “My peace I give to you; my peace I leave to you.” He would not have said this unless he possessed peace.

**Psalm IV.** “When I called. Unto the end, in songs.”

This psalm, he says, must be referred “unto the end,” to Romans 10: “For Christ, as the Apostle says, is the end of the law.” For he completely fulfilled the law, and in him the letter came to its end. Sacrifice ceased when the true Lamb was sacrificed. He is Alpha and Omega, first and last, beginning and end. “In songs,” that is, in praises, because his praises are proclaimed here.

**Psalm V.** “My words. For her who receives the inheritance.”

The Lord indeed promised an inheritance to the synagogue; but because it killed the heir when he came, [Col. 1143B] Matthew 21 says: “The Lord destroys the wicked miserably, and leases his vineyard to other husbandmen.” Therefore the Church receives the inheritance under the leadership of Jesus, as is said in this psalm: “But I, in the multitude of your mercy, shall enter into your house.”

**Psalm VI.** “O Lord, not in your fury. For the eighth.”

When this life has ended and this sevenfold period has passed, the eighth day follows, on which the Lord will come for judgment. Therefore, concerning this eighth day, the Church says: “Have mercy upon me, O God, for I am weak.” For on that day the person to whom he himself shows no mercy will have much to fear.

**Psalm VII.** “O Lord my God, in you I have hoped. Unto the end; a psalm of David, which he sang to the Lord concerning [Col. 1143C] the words of Chusi, son of Jemini.”

“Unto the end” always points to Christ, but sometimes denotes his Passion and sometimes his Resurrection. When a psalm is said to be David’s, it is applied to Christ. Chusi means “silence”; Jemini, “the right hand.” Chusi are all those who set a guard upon their mouths and do not pour out useless and idle words; for he who guards his tongue guards his soul. These are sons of Jemini, sons of the right hand: Psalm 117, “The right hand of the Lord has wrought strength.” Therefore this psalm is sung for and by the perfect, who know not only how not to act wickedly but also how not to speak wickedly; whose counsel is useful and whose faith is most steadfast.

**Psalm VIII.** “O Lord, our Lord. Unto the end, for the winepresses.”

In this word, both [Col. 1143D] *torcularia* and *torculares* may be understood and read both as “winepresses” and as “those who press.” Thus we may call the teachers “pressers,” and the Church “the winepresses.” In this psalm there is discourse concerning the teachers of the Church, who are called infants and sucklings.

**Psalm IX.** “I will confess to you, O Lord. Unto the end, for the hidden things of the Son.”

By the “hidden things of the Son of God” we understand the coming of Antichrist and the day of judgment, which, when questioned by the disciples, he would not disclose. These matters are therefore hidden, since they were not made known even to the apostles. For the Son of God, who disclosed all other things, chose that this day should remain hidden.

**Psalm XI.** “Save me, O Lord. Unto the end, for the eighth.”

It was said above that the eighth [Col. 1144A] day means the day of judgment, on which the wicked will walk round about, to whom the gate of the heavenly city will be shut. The eighth day is also the Lord’s Resurrection.

**Psalm XV.** “Preserve me. In the inscription of the title, for David himself.”

The title’s inscription was, in Luke 23: “This is Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.” Written in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew letters, it signifies the calling of all nations. But because the Jews said, “Do not write ‘King of the Jews,’” this psalm says: “I will not gather their assemblies from blood,” which is understood of those who killed the prophets. Or “from blood,” that is, from those from whose stock he was born according to the flesh. But of the Gentiles it says: “The lines have fallen [Col. 1144B] to me in splendid places.”

**Psalm XVI.** “Hear, O Lord, my justice.”

The prayer of David—that David, namely, of whom we spoke above, who overcame the devil with a most mighty hand.

**Psalm XVII.** “I will love you, O Lord. Unto the end; for David, servant of the Lord, who spoke to the Lord the words of this song, on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of his enemies and from the hand of Saul, and he said.”

These words, he says, are to be referred unto the end, namely to David, the servant of the Lord. He is the one of whom Isaiah 9 says: “A little child is born to us.” “The words of this song, which David himself spoke to the Lord.” But at what time? “On the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of his enemies,” that is, from the power of the Jews, “and [Col. 1144C] from the hand of Saul.” Saul is interpreted as “desire” or “an earthly kingdom”; under his name the devil is understood, whose kingdom is earthly—or rather, earth, flesh, and blood—which shall not possess the kingdom of God. It is pursued by many through desire: they persecuted Christ the Lord with treachery and snares even to the cross.

**Psalm XXI.** “My God, my God, look upon me. Unto the end, for the morning taking-up,” which in Hebrew is called “for the morning stag” (Mark 16).

The morning reception was the Resurrection, which occurred very early on the first day of the week, when Christ took up immortality. He is also called the morning stag because he made certain very great leaps: from heaven into the Virgin, from the Virgin into the manger, from the manger [Col. 1144D] to the cross, from the cross to the tomb, from the tomb into hell, and thence returned to the Father (Pope Gregory, Homily 29).

**Psalm XXIII.** “The earth is the Lord’s. The first day of the Sabbath.”

The first day of the Sabbath is understood as the Lord’s Day, on which, when Christ the Lord rose from the dead, apostles, angels, and human beings sing because of his triumph and victory: “The earth is the Lord’s; the Lord has risen; the enemy has been defeated; the Creator and Savior reigns.”

**Psalm XXVI.** “The Lord is my illumination. A psalm of David, before he was anointed.”

This psalm does not have “unto the end” in its title, because it is understood of the first David, which David himself sang in praise of God, considering [Col. 1145A] what he was before he was anointed. For he was the least of his brothers and a shepherd of sheep. Seeing himself pursued by Saul and other enemies, he says: “Whom shall I dread? Whom shall I fear, when the Lord is my protector and illumination, he who took me from behind the nursing ewes?”

**Psalm XXVIII.** “Bring to the Lord. At the completion of the tabernacle.”

This psalm, he says, must be referred to the completion of the tabernacle. This tabernacle is understood as the holy Church, of which Christ is the foundation. He blessed it in himself when the ark was brought back from Philistine captivity—that is, when the Church itself was brought back from the power of the devil. But because true sacrifice is not made outside the Church, it is said at its completion: “Bring to the Lord.”

[Col. 1145B]

**Psalm XXIX.** “I will exalt you, O Lord. A psalm of a song, at the dedication of David’s house.”

Christ is the Church, or the flesh assumed by him. He dedicated and confirmed it when, his sackcloth being cut away, he was girded with gladness.

**Psalm XXX.** “In you, O Lord, I have hoped. In ecstasy.”

This psalm speaks of the Passion; it is therefore entitled “In ecstasy,” which signifies departure from the mind. Hence it follows: “I said in the excess of my mind.”

**Psalm XXXI.** “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven. The understanding of David.”

David, as we have often said, is Christ, whose understanding is written in this psalm. Therefore whoever understands that he is saved not by his own merits but through faith, mercy, and [Col. 1145C] confession of sins should recognize that his understanding is not human but divine: that of him who says in this psalm, “I will give you understanding and instruct you.”

**Psalm XXXIII.** “I will bless the Lord at every time. A psalm of David, when he changed his face before Abimelech, and he dismissed him and went away.”

Abimelech means “the kingdom of the father.” Judaea and Jerusalem were formerly the kingdom of him who is Father and Lord of all. There Christ changed his face, taking the form of a servant; or because in the Passion he appeared without form or beauty, and dead. “And he dismissed him and went away.” “Again,” says the Lord, “I leave the world and go to the Father” (John 16).

**Psalm XXXV.** “The unjust man said. Unto the end, for David himself, servant of the Lord.”

These things, he says, are understood of that servant of the Lord, David, who was born from a virgin womb and saved both human beings and beasts. Or: “Unto the end, for David himself, servant of the Lord,” because, though he was in the form of God, he took the form of a servant.

[Col. 1145D]
