**Psalm XXXVII.** “O Lord, not in your fury. A psalm of David, for the remembrance of the Sabbath day.”

Sabbath means “rest.” Therefore this psalm is sung by all who remember that rest, peace, and blessedness which we lost in Paradise, and who always ask for God’s mercy, that when this life has ended they may find sabbatical rest.

**Psalm XXXVIII.** “I said: I will guard my ways. [Col. 1146A] Unto the end, a song of David for Idithun.”

This song of David must be referred unto the end—that is, to the Church, in the last age. First Corinthians 10: “For we are those,” says the Apostle, “upon whom the ends of the ages have come.” Idithun means “one who surpasses them.” These are perfect men, who transcend others in virtue and holiness, and who, storing up treasures in heaven, say: “And now what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord? And my substance is with you.”

**Psalm XLI.** “As the stag longs for fountains of water. Unto the end, the understanding for the sons of Core.”

Core means “baldness.” Christ was crucified on Mount Calvary; therefore this understanding is to be attributed to the sons of Core, that is, to the sons of Christ, whom he begot and redeemed in the place of Calvary. Of these, then, it is understood: “For they shall pass [Col. 1146B] into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even unto the house of God, with the voice of rejoicing and confession.”

**Psalm XLIII.** “O God, we have heard with our ears. Unto the end, for the sons of Core, unto understanding.”

Not for you, he says, who follow the letter, but for Christ’s sons this psalm is composed for spiritual understanding. For it is beyond doubt that the works which the Lord performed in ancient days happened to them as a figure, but were written for our correction.

**Psalm XLIV.** “My heart has poured forth a good word. Unto the end, for the other sons of Core, who shall be changed unto understanding; a song for the Beloved.”

This song is sung for and concerning [Col. 1146C] that Beloved of whom it is written in Matthew 3: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” It is thus for the Church, which, having forgotten its people and its father’s house, has been changed to faith and understanding.

**Psalm XLV.** “God is our refuge. Unto the end, for the sons of Core, concerning secret things.”

Truly concerning secret things, because it contains the mystery of Christ’s birth. Hence “the Lord of hosts is with us” is said here, that is, Emmanuel, which means “the Lord with us.” This psalm is given to the sons of Core for preaching.

**Psalm XLVI.** “All nations, clap your hands. For the sons of Core”—that is, the apostles, of whom it is said: [Col. 1146D] “The princes of the peoples are gathered together with the God of Abraham.”

**Psalm XLVII.** “Great is the Lord. A psalm of a song for the sons of Core, on the second day of the Sabbath.”

The Lord rose on the first day of the Sabbath; but on the second day of the Sabbath, the sons of Core—that is, the holy apostles, now strengthened and believing in the Resurrection—said: “Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise.”

**Psalm XLVIII.** “Hear these things, all nations. Unto the end, for the sons of Core.”

Understand: believe and obey.

**Psalm XLIX.** “The God of gods, the Lord. A psalm of Asaph,” which means “assembly” or “synagogue.”

This psalm says: “Gather to him his saints.” You see, therefore, that Asaph fulfills his office.

[Col. 1147A]

**Psalm L.** “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy. Unto the end; a psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, when he went in to Bathsheba.”

Because it says “unto the end,” he intended to teach us his repentance, so that whenever we are rebuked for any sin, either by the Lord or by a priest, his vicar, we may repent in like manner.

**Psalm LI.** “Why do you glory in wickedness? Unto the end; the understanding of David, when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul, saying: David has come to the house of Abimelech.”

Doeg means “motion”; Edomite, “earthly” or “bloody”; Saul, “an earthly kingdom”; Abimelech, “the kingdom of the Father.” This Lord is the one who said in John 11: “Let us go again into Judaea,” that is, [Col. 1147B] into the house of Abimelech, since Judaea was his Father’s kingdom. But Doeg the Edomite—bloody motion, worker of iniquity, betrayer of his master, most wicked merchant—ran to Saul, ran to Pilate, ran to the princes of the earth, and said: “Behold, Christ is here”; Matthew 26: “What will you give me, and I will deliver him to you?” But because David’s understanding is set forth as Christ, who was ignorant of nothing, he says in the same passage of Matthew: “One of you will betray me.” This was the man to whom it is said: “Why do you glory in wickedness?”

**Psalm LII.** “The fool has said in his heart: There is no God. Unto the end, for Maeleth; the understanding of David.”

Maeleth means “one giving birth.” This David, [Col. 1147C] who composed this psalm for Maeleth, sings for those who devise and bring forth iniquity, who said of Christ, the Son of God: “There is no God.”

**Psalm LIII.** “O God, save me in your name. Unto the end, in songs; the understanding of David, when the Ziphites came and said to Saul: Is not David hidden among us?”

The Ziphites, whose name means “flourishing ones,” are the Jews, who flourished in abundance of every sort of wealth, dwelling in a land flowing with milk and honey. When they heard that Christ had come to the house of Simon the leper, they reported it to the priests and rulers of the land. Understanding this, he says: “O God, save me in your name, for strangers have risen up against me.”

**Psalm LIV.** “Hear, O God, my prayer, and do not [Col. 1147D] despise my supplication. Unto the end, in songs; the understanding of David.”

The Jews were taking counsel together; Judas pressed forward with betrayal. But Christ, understanding all things, says: “But you, a man of one mind with me, my guide and my acquaintance, who together with me took sweet food,” are plotting my death.

**Psalm LV.** “Have mercy upon me, O God, for man has trodden me down. Unto the end, for the people who have been made far from the saints; in the inscription of the title, for David, when the Philistines held him in Geth.”

In the title’s inscription the Jewish people was made far from the saints, condemning the title and saying that he whom all the saints rejoice to have as their king ought not to be called King of the Jews. The [Col. 1148A] Philistines, whose name means “without a head,” signify these same Jews, who, despising Christ, the head of all men, live without king and priesthood. At that same time they held Christ in Geth, that is, in the land of his own dwelling. For *Geth* is Greek for “earth” in Latin, or “winepress.”

**Psalm LVI.** “Have mercy upon me, O God, have mercy upon me. Unto the end: do not destroy; for David, in the inscription of the title, when he fled from Saul’s face into the cave.”

“Unto the end,” he says: these things must be referred to Christ, in the inscription of whose title Pilate said: “Do not destroy,” that is, in John 19: “What I have written, I have written.” Then David—that is, our Savior—fled from the face of the Jews, shut within the cave of the tomb.

[Col. 1148B]

**Psalm LVII.** “If indeed you truly speak justice. Unto the end: do not destroy; for David, in the inscription of the title.”

For Pilate could not destroy what the Holy Spirit so often forbids to be destroyed.

**Psalm LVIII.** “Deliver me from my enemies, my God. Unto the end: do not destroy; for David, in the inscription of the title, when Saul sent and guarded his house to kill him.”

Be silent, Jews; you accomplish nothing. The title will not be corrupted. Devise something else; send guards to keep the tomb.

**Psalm LIX.** “O God, you have rejected us. Unto the end; for those who shall be changed; in the inscription of the title, for David himself, for instruction, when he set Mesopotamia of Syria and Sobal on fire, and Joab returned and struck Edom in [Col. 1148C] the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand.”

“Unto the end,” he says: this psalm should be attributed to David himself, composed for those who, “in the inscription of the title”—that is, through Christ’s Passion—will be changed into holy and apostolic instruction. This will happen at the time when the Lord, who in Luke 12 came “to cast fire upon the earth,” kindles Mesopotamia of Syria—that is, the pride, swelling, and evil counsels of the proud. For Mesopotamia means “pride,” and Syria “loftiness.” And Syria of Sobal, that is, the exaltation of vain antiquity, so that those who are raised up into pride, vanity, and the erroneous teaching of ancient philosophers, once kindled by the Holy Spirit, may not be wise above what they ought to be wise. For Sobal means “vain antiquity.” “And Joab shall return,” [Col. 1148D] that is, the army of enemies; for Joab means “enemy.” “And he shall strike Edom,” that is, earthly persons, so that, struck and pierced by divine love, they may obey not earth and flesh but the soul. But where shall they be changed? “In the Valley of Salt,” that is, in the holy Church, into flavorful humility, where the apostles dwell, who are called the salt of the earth. “Twelve thousand” is a definite number used for an indefinite one; hence in Revelation 7 “twelve thousand sealed” are said to be from every tribe.

**Psalm LX.** “Hear, O God, my supplication. Unto the end, in David’s hymns.”

This psalm throughout represents Christ.

**Psalm LXI.** “Shall not my soul be subject to God? Unto the end, for Idithun.”

Where Idithun appears—he [Col. 1149A] who means “surpassing others”—the perfect lovers of God are understood. Therefore this is a psalm of the perfect, who call themselves subject to God, not further moved by him, and not leaning walls.

**Psalm LXII.** “O God, my God, I watch for you from the light. A psalm of David, when he was in the wilderness of Idumaea.”

Idumaea means “bloody” or “earthly.” From the time when Christ was in the wilderness of Idumaea—that is, in this world—the Church keeps watch. Previously it slept, because it was in night; but when the light came, it said: “O God, my God, I watch for you from the light.”

**Psalm LXIV.** “A hymn is fitting for you, O God, in Sion. Unto the end: a song of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, or Haggai, concerning the word of pilgrimage, when they began to depart.”

Jeremiah means “exalted”; Ezekiel, [Col. 1149B] “the strength of the Lord.” Therefore this psalm suits those who are raised up to heaven and, having conquered their enemies by the Lord’s strength, are about to receive a crown. When they begin to depart from the pilgrimage of this world toward the heavenly Jerusalem, they utter this word of their pilgrimage.

**Psalm LXV.** “Make a joyful noise to God, all the earth. Unto the end: a psalm-song of the Resurrection.”

Let the world rejoice; let the Church be glad. “Make a joyful noise to God, all the earth,” because your beloved has risen wondrously.

**Psalm LXVIII.** “Save me, O God, for waters have entered in. Unto the end, for those who shall be changed, for David himself.”

“For those,” he says, “who will be changed from unbelief to faith and to David.” In this psalm [Col. 1149C] our Savior says: “Let not those who wait for you, O Lord, Lord of hosts, be ashamed because of me; let not those who seek you, O God of Israel, be confounded because of me.”

**Psalm LXXI.** “O God, give your judgment to the king. Concerning Solomon; a psalm of David.”

Solomon means “peaceful.” “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2). Of him this psalm says: “He shall descend like rain upon the fleece”; “In his days justice shall arise, and abundance of peace”; and “He shall rule from sea to sea.” And Isaiah 45: “All the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him.” This is false of the first Solomon; but of Christ we know that every knee shall bow to him.

**Psalm LXXII.** “How good God is to Israel. The hymns or praises of David [Col. 1149D] son of Jesse have ended: a psalm of Asaph.”

He did not say “have ended” because David will speak no more, but because the second book ends here. “A psalm of Asaph” is the title of this psalm. Asaph speaks here, whose name means “assembly” or “synagogue.” He signifies teachers who say at the end of this psalm: “That I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Sion.”

**Psalm LXXIII.** “Why, O God, have you rejected us unto the end? The understanding of Asaph.”

For teachers understand this: that God “has wrought salvation in the midst of the earth.”

**Psalm LXXIV.** “We will confess to you, O God. Unto the end: do not corrupt; a psalm-song of Asaph.”

This psalm should be understood of Christ, of whom [Col. 1150A] John 19 says: “You shall not break a bone of him.” “A psalm of Asaph”: the apostles and teachers say this at its beginning: “We will confess to you, O God; we will confess and call upon your name; we will recount your wonders.”

**Psalm LXXVI.** “With my voice. Unto the end, for Idithun; a psalm of Asaph.”

Those who speak in this psalm are perfect.

**Psalm LXXVII.** “Attend, my people, to my law. The understanding of Asaph. Unto the end, for the secret things of Core.”

The history is not narrated simply as it appears, he says; rather, it contains great understanding for those who gather and feed God’s people and are rightly called Asaph.

**Psalm LXXX.** “Rejoice in God our helper. Unto the end, for the winepresses; a psalm for Asaph himself, on the fifth [Col. 1150B] day of the Sabbath.”

The pressers and winepresses are the apostles and churches. The apostles tread grapes in the churches, lest the winepresses burst through lack of wine. Isaiah 63: “I,” says the Lord, “have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me.”

**Psalm LXXXIII.** “How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts. Unto the end, for the winepresses; for the sons of Core.”

The sons of Core—the sons of Calvary, the sons of Christ—are the pressers and the winepresses. Christ, the first presser, made his disciples pressers. They pressed out the clusters of the New and Old Testaments and poured their exposition into our breasts.

**Psalm LXXXIV.** “You have blessed your land, O Lord. Unto the end; a psalm for the sons of Core.”

The sons of Core rejoice because “truth has sprung from the earth, and justice has looked down [Col. 1150C] from heaven.”

**Psalm LXXXVI.** “Its foundations are in the holy mountains. For the sons of Core; a psalm-song.”

Where there is both psalm and song, there are praise and activity.

**Psalm LXXXIX.** “O Lord, you have become a refuge to us. A prayer of Moses, the man of God.”

The narration of this psalm is rightly said to be Moses’, so that he who taught us humanity’s constitution may also teach us its miseries and ruin.

**Psalm XCI.** “It is good to confess to the Lord. A psalm-song for the Sabbath day.”

Sabbath means “rest,” on which performing servile works is forbidden. Therefore whoever sings this psalm should rest from worldly works, perform no servile labor, but serve the Lord as a most valiant soldier.

[Col. 1150D]

**Psalm XCIII.** “The Lord God of vengeance. A psalm for David himself, on the fourth day of the Sabbath.”

On the fourth day of the Sabbath God made the lights of heaven: the sun, moon, and stars. This psalm speaks against those who, oppressing God’s people, say: “The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand.” Let them therefore remember the fourth day of the Sabbath, on which God made such great lights, so that they may understand that he sees all things and may be enlightened in the inner person.

**Psalm XCV.** “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth. A song for David himself, when the house was being built after the captivity.”

We were in Babylon; we were in captivity. But now our houses, which the ancient enemy had destroyed, [Col. 1151A] have been rebuilt by the water of baptism. Therefore let us sing a new song to the Lord; let us lift up and offer him sacrifices of rejoicing.

**Psalm CVII.** “My heart is ready, O God. A psalm-song.”

Praise of works.

**Psalm CVIII.** “O God of my praise. Unto the end; a psalm of David.”

Concerning Christ.

**Psalm CX.** “Confess to the Lord, for he is good. Who shall declare the powers of the Lord? Alleluia, alleluia.”

This means “Praise the Lord.” *Alleluia* is in the New Testament and *alleluia* in the Old Testament. The first *alleluia* belongs to the preceding psalm; the following one to the next.

**Psalm CXIX.** “To the Lord when I was troubled. A song of steps.”

And of ascent to heaven.

[Col. 1152A]

**Psalm CXLI.** “With my voice. The understanding of David, when he was in the cave.”

The Jews and other followers of the letter do not possess the understanding of this psalm; David does, and others who have likewise been imbued and filled with the Holy Spirit. By the cave we understand the Lord’s tomb. Hence it says here: “Bring my soul out of prison.”

**Psalm CXLV.** “Praise the Lord, O my soul. Alleluia; a psalm of Haggai and Zechariah.”

Haggai means “swift”; Zechariah, “the remembrance of the Lord.” Therefore those sing this psalm who, always remembering the Lord, serve him with the greatest haste.

## Odo of Asti’s Exposition on the Psalms

[Col. 1151]

## Exposition of the First Psalm

[Col. 1151B]

“Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly.” What is it to walk in the counsel of the ungodly except to assent to wicked counsels?

“And has not stood in the way of sinners.” To stand in the way of sinners is to persevere in evil deeds.

“And has not sat in the seat of pestilence.” Those sit in the seat of pestilence who teach others to do the evil things which they themselves do. Let the ungodly person state his counsel: “Kill,” he says, “steal, commit sacrilege,” and such things. This counsel is evil, yet a great many assent to it; therefore they will not be blessed. These same things of which we have spoken are the way by which sinners go to destruction. Many enter this way who do not remain in it but, doing penance, turn back. Such persons are not deprived of blessedness; but those who have stood in it, or persevered in it, undoubtedly cannot be blessed.

It must be known, however, that one seat is of pestilence and another of salvation. The seat of Peter, Paul, the apostles, and pastors is one of salvation; that of heretics is nothing but death and pestilence. The latter brings death, the former salvation. Therefore those will be blessed, but these miserable. Yet to whom can what has been said be applied more fittingly than to Christ, of whom it is written in 1 Peter 2: “Who committed no sin?” For if, as is true, he committed no sin, he certainly did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, stand in the way of sinners, or sit in the seat of pestilence.

The contrary statement:

“But his will was in the law of the Lord.” The law of the Lord is immaculate, converting souls: Psalm 18. The law of the Lord is to forgive those who forgive; indeed, to turn from evil and do good. Christ willed this, taught it, and sat in this seat.

“And in his law”—that is, in this law—“he shall meditate day and night.” Christ preached both by day and by night. By day he taught the crowds; by night, the disciples. Hence Matthew 10 says: “What you hear in chambers, preach upon the housetops.” Or “day and night” means at every time. In another sense, by day and night we understand prosperity and adversity. He was in prosperity when he fed five thousand persons from five loaves (Matthew 14), for all obeyed him. He was in adversity when the Jews persecuted him and when he hid himself and went out of the Temple: John 8.

“And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of waters,” which never lacks greenness or moisture. Although Christ may be compared to it, as he himself says in Luke 23, “If they do these things in the green tree, what shall be done in the dry?” there is nevertheless another tree to which he may be compared more aptly. We read in Genesis 2 that in Paradise there is a tree of life, where there is also a flow of four rivers: Gihon, Pishon, Tigris, and Euphrates. Of this tree Genesis 3 says: “See lest perhaps he take from the tree of life and live forever.” Therefore, if those who take from this tree shall live forever, Christ is rightly compared to this tree in John 6: he is the living bread, and whoever clings to him shall live life and shall not die.

“Which shall give its fruit in its season.” This fruit will indeed be the reward and crown given to the righteous on the day of judgment. It also gave the fruit of preaching and power. Moreover, it gives fruits by which human beings and all animals are fed; and there is no doubt that all these things occur at distinct and fitting times.

[Col. 1153A] “And its leaf shall not fall.” What do we understand by leaves except words? “For,” he says, “heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matthew 24). Therefore, if leaves are words and words shall not pass away, neither shall the leaves fall.

“And whatever he does shall prosper.” For whom? Certainly for the saints. For his being born, circumcised, baptized, suffering, preaching, rising again, and ascending into heaven—all prosper for the saints.

“Not so the ungodly, not so.” The ungodly, he says, shall not be blessed; they shall not meditate in the law of God; they shall not prosper. “But they shall be like dust”: wretched, subject to all things, unstable, carried about by every wind of doctrine. The wind and swelling of pride have separated them from the land of the living: [uncertain: *illatio*].

“Therefore the ungodly shall not rise in judgment.” Therefore, because they are such, the ungodly shall not rise in judgment: they have already been judged, and therefore shall not be judged. Nor indeed shall they judge. For how will those rise who die at every moment? “Nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous.” Someone may say: Who, amid so great a multitude of people, will distinguish the righteous from sinners? The Lord, certainly. It follows:

“For the Lord knows the way of the righteous.” “The Lord knows those who are his,” as he himself says (2 Timothy 2). “I am the good shepherd, and I know my sheep” (John 10).

“And the way of the ungodly shall perish.” The ungodly indeed will always exist; they will not perish so as no longer to be. But their way will not exist at all, because they will no longer be able to sin. Better, therefore, is the way of the righteous, which will always exist, than the way of the ungodly, which will be utterly destroyed.

This may also be understood of each righteous person, so that it may be said: Every man shall be blessed who has neither thought, done, nor taught evil; whose will and meditation have been in the law of the Lord. He shall be compared to the tree of life, which is spiritually understood as Christ. He is rightly compared to Christ, since, made in Christ’s image, he did not lose his likeness, but was always holy with the holy and spotless with the spotless.

## Exposition of the Second Psalm

[Col. 1153D]

“Why have the nations raged?” Since he was such as was said above, why, he says, did the nations rage against him, saying, “Crucify him?” “And why have the peoples meditated vain things,” imagining that they could kill one who is immortal? “Why have the kings of the earth stood up?” Namely Herod and Pilate; and the rulers Annas and Caiaphas gathered together in one place and took counsel against the Lord the Father and against Christ his Son, saying: “Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke away from us.” This amounts to saying: “This man, with his disciples, has bound us, put a yoke upon our necks, and thinks to drag us after himself in bonds and bring us into a new law. Lest this happen, let us break their bonds and cast their yoke away from us.”

[Col. 1154A] O wretched men, why did you not understand him himself saying: “For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matthew 11)?

“He who dwells in heaven shall laugh at them, and the Lord shall mock them.” Because they despised Christ’s yoke and took up the devil’s, the Lord will show them on the day of judgment to be worthy of laughter and mockery.

“Then he shall speak to them in his wrath.” Once they have been laughed at and mocked, he shall speak to them in his wrath. For when he says to so many thousands of persons, in Matthew 25, “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire,” although he is not angry, he will nevertheless appear angry.

“And in his fury he shall trouble them.” For those placed in hell, where there is only weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matthew 13), will undoubtedly be troubled.

[Col. 1154B] “But I have been established king by him.” Then at last “God shall come openly, our God, and shall not keep silence,” but shall say: “I whom you crucified, whom you denied to be the Son of God and king, have been established king by him.” Where? “Upon Sion, his holy mountain.” Sion means “watchtower”; it signifies the holy Church, which does not lie in low places or in darkness, but, set upon a mountain and on the high watchtower of the mind, can never be caught unawares, as though unwary, by enemies rushing upon it. In this Church Christ, established as king, preached the Lord’s commandments.

“The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” As though he said: The Lord, who begot me before time, also willed that I should be born in time from the Virgin through the Holy Spirit; for “today” signifies time.

[Col. 1154C] “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.” Because you are my Son, says the Father, ask for an inheritance and I will give you the nations. For the Jews rejected you and your possession—not one or two provinces, but the ends of the earth.

“You shall rule them with a rod of iron,” that is, with a strong, invisible, unconquerable authority which no one will be able to resist.

“Thou shalt break them like a potter’s vessel.” As though he were saying: But if any deny that thou art king, if any attempt to oppose thy rule, thou shalt break them as frail beings [Col. 1154D] and devoid of strength; or thou shalt slay and destroy them in such a manner that they can never again be restored to life. For a potter’s vessel, once broken, cannot be made whole again.

“And now, O kings, understand.” Understand, O kings, and learn from this one King to be kings yourselves, and do not be proud; for you also have a King. But what must you understand? It follows:

“Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling.” Fear is the trembling of the soul, trembling that of the body. Therefore no understanding is so profitable as this: that we should serve the Lord in soul and body.

“Be instructed, you who judge the earth; embrace discipline, lest the Lord at some time grow angry.” Here it appears most plainly that no one ought to approach the governance of the Church [Col. 1155A] unless he has first embraced discipline. Hence, in the appointment of bishops, the Apostle commands that such men be ordained as know well how to provide for their own household (1 Tim. 3). For how shall he govern the Church of God and teach others, who is undisciplined and does not know how to govern himself? The Lord is angry with such persons. Therefore he “will perish from the righteous way”; that is, those who stray from the way of the righteous will without doubt perish eternally. “For when the Lord’s wrath has flared up in a short time,” a wrath which will end “in a moment” and “in the twinkling of an eye” (1 Cor. 15), “blessed are all, and they alone, who trust in him.” Hence we do not doubt that those will be miserable who depart from the way of the righteous and do not trust in the Lord.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM III

[Col. 1155B] “O Lord, why have those who trouble me multiplied? Many rise up against me.” He said “multiplied” because not only Jews and Gentiles, but even his own disciple raised his heel against him.

“Many say to my soul: There is no salvation for him in his God.” Many promise death to me and to my life, and think that there is no one able to snatch it from their hands. But they lie, since “thou, O Lord, art my protector,” because in receiving me thou wilt free me from my enemies; “and my glory,” because thou wilt glorify me; “and the lifter up of my head,” because on the third day thou wilt raise me up (he has put a part for the whole). Hence he declares the whole Passion and Resurrection in order, using the past tense for the future, [Col. 1155C] saying:

“With my voice I cried unto the Lord.” “Placed upon the cross,” he says, “I shall cry to the Lord, that he may not deliver me into the souls of those who trouble me. And he heard me from his holy mountain,” that is, from the secret place of his divinity. Or again, he cried when he said: “Father, glorify me in this hour”; and the Father heard him—indeed, answered him—saying: “I have glorified, and I shall glorify again” (John 12).

“I slept and was put to sleep.” I shall sleep, because I shall die in the flesh which I assumed; I shall rest in the tomb as though asleep; on the third day I shall rise, “because the Lord has sustained me. Therefore I shall not fear thousands of people surrounding and afflicting me.” For thou, O Lord, wilt rise to help me and save me. I know [Col. 1155D] that thou hast smitten and condemned to eternal death “all who oppose me without cause.” Truly without cause, since they acted both vainly and against one to whom they owed no such thing. Hence he himself says in John 18: “If I have spoken evil, bear witness concerning the evil; but if I have spoken well, why dost thou strike me?”—“Thou hast crushed the teeth of sinners.” The Lord crushed the teeth of sinners because the scribes and Pharisees, and many false witnesses, withdrew defeated after fruitlessly uttering the little judgments with which they tried to gnaw away at Christ.

“Salvation belongs to the Lord.” The Jews had said above concerning Christ: “There is no salvation for him in his God.” But he, on the contrary, testified that he had been heard, raised by the Lord, saved, and taken up into heaven. [Col. 1156A] Therefore the Jews lied. Hence, drawing his conclusion, he says: “Therefore salvation belongs to the Lord.” And, having himself been saved, he blesses his own people when he says: “And upon thy people be thy blessing.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM IV. THE VOICE OF CHRIST

“When I called upon him, the God of my righteousness heard me.” The mediator of God and men, our Lord Jesus Christ, in this psalm speaks now to the Father, now to men. He speaks to the Father when he says: O God, conscious of love and ever mindful of righteousness, when I called upon thee, thou didst hear me.

“In tribulation thou hast enlarged me.” That is, thou hast given me a heart enlarged, expanded, and joyful; for enlargement and constriction are, as it were, contraries. Rightly, therefore, does he call himself enlarged who is freed from tribulation and straits. When, I say, I called upon thee, thou didst hear me. But what did I call?

“Have mercy upon me.” For in that respect in which he was a frail man, he was mortal and capable of suffering; therefore he sought mercy, because he needed mercy. “And hear my prayer”: hear, he says, my prayer, which I pour out before thee both for myself and for my own. Thus far he has spoken to the Father; now, turning to men, he speaks.

“Sons of men, how long [will you be] heavy of heart?” As though he said: I indeed pray for you, but you are sons of men and not of God—because you do not do God’s works but men’s—how long will you be heavy of heart? For what is stony is heavy; and stony hearts [Col. 1156C] are those in which God, love, and words of salvation cannot be impressed. They are therefore heavy. “Why do you love vanity?” That is, why do you worship idols that are deaf, mute, and vain? “And seek falsehood,” rather than the word of the Lord.

“Know that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful.” As though he said: Understand what recompense the Lord gives to those who abandon vanity and seek him: he has made them wonderful, makes them wonderful, and adorns them with virtues and holiness. Therefore do not seek falsehood, but the truth of the Lord, that you too may be holy and wonderful—if you are willing to do this. I indeed shall pray for you, and “the Lord will hear me when I cry to him” for you.

[Col. 1156D] “Therefore be angry”—with vices, he says, and with the devil their prince. You have been his friends until now. Lest my prayer be in vain, now be angry with these things, “and do not sin any longer.”

But concerning those things “which you say in your hearts, be pricked in your beds.” For the heart is the bed of thoughts. “For out of the heart thoughts proceed” (Matt. 15), since they lie there; from them the Lord urges us to be pricked and to do penance. But after compunction:

“Offer,” he says, “the sacrifice of righteousness.” Not of goats or bulls, but the sacrifice of praise and rejoicing: a living and spotless victim. Then “hope in the Lord” to receive the reward—namely, eternal [Col. 1157A] goods. “But many” foolish and unbelieving persons without hope say: “Who will show us good things? What certain messenger has come from there?” Thus speak the foolish. But holy and Catholic men say:

“The light of thy countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us.” As though they said: Until now, blindness and the devil’s darkness impressed upon us had darkened our eyes; but now the light, brightness, understanding, image, and beauty of thy countenance have been marked upon us, because we now seek not passing but eternal things. “Thou hast given joy in my heart.” The Catholic congregation says: Because thou hast enlightened me and drawn me out of darkness, thou hast indeed given great joy to my heart.

“They have multiplied from the fruit of their wheat, wine, and oil.” As though he said: I, once enlightened and brought into hope of eternal goods, regard all temporal things as of little account. But those who, as we have said, have no hope and do not believe that eternal goods exist, embracing temporal things alone, have multiplied and become rich from the fruit of wheat, wine, and oil; and because these are perishable, they too will perish with them.

“In peace I shall sleep and rest in the same [thing].” I, he says, running and hastening not toward perishable or changing things, but rather toward “the same,” toward God, who does not change, shall sleep and rest with him in eternal peace; and rightly so.

“For thou, O Lord, hast established me singularly in hope”: that is, I alone and uniquely have hoped, and shall receive the things hoped for; but they, as we have said, [Col. 1157C] did not hope. What, then, will they receive?

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM V

“Give ear to my words, O Lord; understand my cry.” The voice of any righteous person. “Give ear to my words, O Lord” means “understand my cry,” and does not differ from: “Attend to the voice of my prayer.” He adds the reason why God ought to do this. For thou art “my king and my God.” The very one who made this prayer also sets forth why he was not heard and at what time he ought to be heard. For he says: I prayed in the night and was not heard; therefore I shall pray in the morning, that is, after the night has passed.

“For I shall pray to thee, O Lord; in the morning thou wilt hear my voice.” We are in the night while we lie in the darkness of vices; but once we are in the morning, [Col. 1157D] we may pray confidently.

“In the morning I shall stand before thee and see.” I shall leave the night, flee the devil, and come into the morning; and when I am in the morning, I shall not lie down nor be idle, but I shall stand, fight against vices, and persevere in good works. And this “before thee,” that is, for thine honor. And I shall see “that thou art not a God who wills iniquity,” because thou art fair and just and dost not will iniquity.

“For there is no truth in their mouth.” He says this on account of enemies, whose deception is greatly to be feared; for there is no truth in them. And what wonder? For “their heart is vain,” and truth cannot proceed from vanity.

“Their throat is an open sepulchre.” He uses “throat” for words. An open sepulchre signifies hell, because it is never closed to anyone delivered over to death. Therefore, since the words of heretics lead the souls of sinners into hell—which, we have said, is an open sepulchre—what are those words themselves but hell and an open sepulchre? Thus we call the devil death because he leads souls to death. “With their tongues they dealt deceitfully,” that is, they spoke deceitfully. “Judge them, O God,” that is, condemn them to eternal punishment. “Unless they fall away from their counsels, expel them according to the multitude of their impieties”: that is, unless they cease from their perverse thoughts, expel them from the fellowship of the saints into outer darkness because of their many impieties. “For they have provoked thee, O Lord,” that is, provoked thee to anger.

[Col. 1158B] “And let all who hope in thee rejoice.” All, he says, who hope in thee, let them rejoice in thee. “They shall exult forever,” because they shall always be with thee, who art their joy and exultation. “And thou shalt dwell in them”; for the saints are the temple of God. Hence the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 3: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you?”

“And all who love thy name shall glory.” Others glory in chariots and horses, riches, and worldly honors; but those who love thy name shall glory in none but thee. “For thou wilt bless the righteous,” that is, their righteousness.

“O Lord, thou hast crowned us as with the shield of thy good will.” He has put “crown” for victory, because a crown follows victory. And it must be understood thus: O Lord, thou hast crowned us as with the shield of thy good will; that is, thou crownest us with thy protection, because we acquire the crown not by our own merits, but by God’s protection.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM VI. THE VOICE OF THE CHURCH

“O Lord, rebuke me not in thy fury, nor correct me in thy wrath.” As though he said: I indeed desire, O Lord, that thou rebuke and correct me, but not in anger or fury. Rebuke me as a father; correct me as a teacher. For a thief is rebuked when he is hanged; an adulterer is corrected when he is blinded. But do not correct me in this way, O Lord; rather in mercy and kindness. This is what follows:

[Col. 1158D] “Have mercy upon me, O Lord.” For I need thy mercy. “For I am weak; heal me, O Lord, for my bones are troubled.” The body has bones, and the soul also has bones. The bones of the soul are memory, understanding, hope, patience, abstinence, and good will. When these are weakened, the soul cannot stand. It falls, and therefore must be corrected; for one who sins must be corrected. But while the soul’s bones are shaken and troubled by vices, which they ought to have resisted, the soul, now unable to stand, falls, sins, and becomes weak. This is what he says:

“And my soul is greatly troubled.” As though he said: The city has been captured; within it there is the tumult of enemies, [Col. 1159A] and the inhabitants have been driven out. So the soul has been captured: vices reign, virtues are driven away. What then? Shall it be hanged like a thief? Far be it! For he says: “But thou, O Lord, how long?” Understand: how long wilt thou delay the remedy?

“Turn, O Lord, and deliver my soul.” As though he said: Thou hast become distant from me, because “salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. 118). But turn, O Lord, toward me and rescue my soul, which is held by enemies; “save me,” not by my merits but because of thy abundant mercy.

“For in death there is none who remembers thee.” Death is the separation of body and soul. Yet one also dies who separates himself from the world and its desires. One also dies who is separated from the Lord. Hence it is said here that in death there is none who remembers thee. As though he said: I am in vices, joined to the devil, divided from thee, dead to thee and forgetful of thee. Therefore justify me, that I may remember thee. “For the dead shall not praise thee, O Lord, nor all who go down into hell. But in hell who shall confess thee?” For everyone bound by the devil’s chain is in hell; and one who is in vices is bound by diabolical chains. He is therefore in hell, and cannot praise God.

“I have labored in my groaning.” I have sinned, he says, but I do not persist in sins; rather, I do penance and labor in groaning. Therefore have mercy upon me. [Col. 1159C] “Every night I shall wash my bed”: the bed of the soul is the body; and because it has drawn many nights, vices, and darknesses to itself, it must be washed for each one. Repetition: “With my tears I shall drench my couch.”

“My eye is troubled by fury.” “Eye” stands for the mind, which, unless it remains steadfast, is troubled by the fury and assault of vices. “I have grown old among all my enemies.” As though he said: It is no wonder that my eye is troubled, for I have grown old among all my enemies; for a long time I have been besieged and stirred up by enemies.

“Depart from me, all you who work iniquity.” By groaning and tears, he says, I have been joined to the Lord and to righteousness. Therefore depart from me, all you who work iniquity, for henceforth I shall not work it. Like seeks like. “For the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.” I wept for righteousness, to which I desired to join myself; I have been heard, and therefore I shall no longer be moved from it.

“The Lord has heard my supplication; the Lord has received my prayer. Let all my enemies be ashamed and greatly troubled.” Let them be troubled either by eternal condemnation, or in opposition to their vices and become good. Let them turn into hell, or toward good. And let them be ashamed of their sins, very swiftly.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM VII. THE VOICE OF THE PERFECT

“Lord my God, in thee have I hoped.” For I have not hoped [Col. 1160A] in my bow, nor in gold or silver, nor in my own strength; but I have hoped in thee, who art God and my Lord, and therefore “save me.” Thou art Jesus, thou art Savior, thou save, because thou art able to save. For my sword will not save me. “Deliver me from all who persecute me.” Avarice, pride, lust, faithlessness, and discord persecute me: deliver me from all these. Why?

“Lest at any time he seize my soul like a lion.” Our enemy, “the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5); his nets are the aforesaid vices. This most wicked hunter, pursuing souls, finds some entangled in avarice, some in pride, and others in lust. “While there is none to redeem or save”: redeem thou, who art able to redeem, because there is no other able to redeem or save.

“O Lord my God, if I have done this”—that is, “if there is iniquity in my hands.” What do we understand by hands but works? For we work with our hands. “If I have rendered evil to those rendering good to me.” O what perfection in a man who knew not only not to do evil, but not even to return evil to those repaying him with good! In Luke 6, he did not take eye for eye, tooth for tooth, or hand for hand; but, struck on one cheek, he offered the other. If, I say, I have done this or that, “I shall fall”: I shall not ascend upward, I shall not come to thee, but shall fall with sinners into hell. And this deservedly, because I have committed such or such a sin, “empty at the hands of my enemies,” [Col. 1160C] so that I may fall as weak and empty, as devoid of strength, defeated by my enemies.

“Let the enemy pursue my soul.” Already he has spread his nets, already the hunter has found his prey; let him pursue it, let him seize it. “And trample my life to the earth”: let him trample it into carnal desires and kill it with earthly persons and sinners. “And bring down my glory into the dust.” What is meant by glory but resurrection? What by dust but the resurrection of the flesh? Therefore a person’s glory is brought down into dust when he does not rise with the righteous to glory.

“Arise, O Lord.” Because I have not committed the sins mentioned above, arise, O God, to help me; for to help belongs not to sitting but to standing. “In thy anger”: show thyself angry, for if thou show thyself angry on our behalf to our enemies, they will no longer dare to harm us. “Be exalted in the borders of my enemies.” Until now, he says, our enemies have possessed all the ends of the earth. Now, O Lord, arise, take flesh, aid the human race, prepare thyself for battle, show thyself angry, and be exalted throughout all lands. Correct and rule those whom the devil oppressed:

“Arise, O Lord my God, in the commandment which thou hast commanded.” For thou didst command the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall rebuild it” (John 2). And: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3). Therefore let this temple be destroyed, let the Son of Man be lifted up, [Col. 1161A] and let the Lord my God arise and ascend the cross in his commandment. In another sense, thou didst command preaching in the apostles; therefore their preaching was thy commandment. In this commandment thy kingdom, dominion, and power rose, grew, and were exalted. “And the synagogue of the peoples shall surround thee”: that is, all nations shall believe in thee.

“And because of this return on high.” Because of this gathering—for *synagoga* means “gathering”—return on high, ascend into heaven; for when thou hast been raised from the earth, thou wilt draw all things after thee (John 2). Return, therefore, on high, “and draw us after thee, and we shall run in the fragrance of thy ointments” (Song 1).—“The Lord judging peoples.”—“The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). Therefore the Son is the Lord judging peoples. “Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness”: because thou art judge, judge me; and because thou art righteous, judge the righteous man justly. “And according to my innocence upon me”: that is, according to the innocence considered in me.

“The wickedness of sinners shall be consumed.” Since thou art judge, thou wilt judge both righteous persons and sinners. But how [wilt thou judge] sinners? They shall be consumed in their wickedness. What then will be the judgment of the righteous? It follows: “And thou shalt direct the righteous.” Where? Assuredly toward thyself. What, then, is the judgment of the righteous but election? “God searches hearts and reins”; for thoughts are in the heart and the reins. Therefore, since God searches not only deeds but also thoughts [Col. 1161C] (Wis. 6), he is a true judge, because he judges both deeds and thoughts.

“My righteous help is from the Lord.” Because the Lord directs the righteous to himself, the judgment of the righteous is righteous. Shall I call it judgment, or help? Not judgment, but help, since through it both misery is driven away and blessedness acquired.

“Who saves the upright in heart.” For one who is upright in heart can neither do nor think crooked things. For if he thinks them, he is not upright; but if he does them, he is a camel.

“God is a righteous judge.” Truly righteous, because he both saves the righteous and condemns sinners. “Strong and patient.” Strong, because no one can resist him; patient, because he does not punish immediately. “Does he become angry every day?” Truly he is patient, because although we offend him every day—indeed every hour—he nevertheless does not grow angry every day.

“Unless you are converted,” you will perish. It is as though he said: Though he is patient, nevertheless, unless you are converted, you will perish. And deservedly. For he has brandished his sword. What is meant by the sword but Christ? For this sword slew the devil. Therefore, because he brandished the sword and sent his Son into the world, whoever is not converted will perish. Hence he himself says in John 15: “Unless I had come and spoken, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse.”

“He has stretched his bow.” What is his bow? [Col. 1162A] The Old Testament. Before Christ’s incarnation this bow was not stretched. But when Christ came, he stretched it and added the string. For the New Testament is the string: the New Testament softened the severity of the old law. For the law said in Exodus 31: If anyone does this or that, let him die. This saying is excessively harsh and rigid. But how is it softened? Do you wish to hear how? If anyone does this or that, let him repent for so many years, and he shall be saved. This is what the New Testament contains; this is what the canons contain. This is a sweet saying, which causes one not to despair but to hope (2 Cor. 7).

“And he has prepared it.” He prepared it because he made it intelligible; he prepared it because he removed its obscurity and darkness. “And in it he prepared vessels of death.” By “vessels of death” [Col. 1162B] we understand the apostles, who were full of living water. Some drank this water unto salvation; others as though it were a toxin and poison. Hence the Apostle says in 2 Corinthians 2: “To some we are an odor of life unto life; to others, an odor of death unto death.”—“He made his arrows for those who burn.” For what is signified by vessels is likewise signified by arrows. The arrows are the apostles, because they secretly destroy the devil and vices. The Lord made and ordered these arrows for the benefit of those who have been kindled with love of the Spirit and fire.

“Behold, he has brought forth iniquity.” This verse is joined to the one which says: “Lest at any time he seize my soul like a lion,” because I greatly fear him. For he is wicked, deceitful, and unjust. This is what it says: “Behold, he has brought forth iniquity.” This malignant father joins himself with souls and begets children—but what children? Namely, injustice, sorrow, and iniquity.

“He opened a pit.” At the time when he first caused the first man to sin, he opened hell and the pit. He also opens it every day while leading wretches into sins. Yet it is not enough for him merely to open it; he moreover “dug it,” for he prepares a smaller ditch for some and a larger one for others, because whoever sins more falls into greater torments.

“And he fell into the pit which he made.” For eternal fire is prepared for the devil and his angels, and no punishment greater than that due to the prince of punishments is owed to anyone. “His sorrow shall return upon his own head,” for he who was the author of sorrow will not be without sorrow. “And his iniquity shall descend upon his own crown.” For after there is no one who sins or wishes to sin, all iniquity will return upon him; and his evil will, which he will be unable to exercise, will itself be no small punishment to him.

“But I will confess and praise the Lord according to his righteousness, and sing psalms to the name of the Lord Most High.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM VIII

“O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is thy name in all the earth! For thy magnificence has been raised above the heavens.” The voice of the prophet rejoicing over Christ’s ascension. God’s magnificence is Christ, because through him God is magnified. For before Christ’s ascension God was known in Judaea alone: “His name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75). But now, when his Son has been raised above the heavens (Acts 1), his name is most wonderful, not in Judaea alone, but in all the earth.

“Out of the mouth of infants and nursing children thou hast perfected praise.” This can be understood of Hebrew children. We may also understand the apostles by “infants and nursing children.” They were infants because, being rustic and unlearned, they scarcely knew how to speak; they were nursing children because they sucked the New and Old Testament as though from two breasts. From their mouths the Lord perfected his praise, because through their preaching the Church grew. “Because of thy enemies.” The enemies of God are the Jews, who, after crucifying the Son of God, also attempted entirely to erase his name. Because of these [Col. 1163B] enemies, therefore, God caused himself to be praised from the mouths of infants and nursing children. “That he may destroy the enemy and avenger.” The Jews were avengers and defenders of the Scriptures, lest anyone understand them concerning Christ. But the apostles, on the contrary, praised Christ and interpreted the Scriptures with reference to him. Therefore, because the apostles’ interpretation prevailed, the enemies and avengers were destroyed by God, so that not even one now dares to speak against Christ.

“For I shall see thy heavens.” As though the Prophet said: I rejoice, O God, because I know that I shall see “the works of thy fingers,” namely, thy children in whom thou hast “founded” faith—namely the heavens, “the moon and stars.” By the heavens we understand the apostles; by the moon, the Church; and by the stars, teachers.

[Col. 1163C] “What is man, that thou art mindful of him?” Although this can be understood of every righteous person, the Apostle has nevertheless interpreted it of Christ in the Epistle to the Hebrews. “What is man, that thou art mindful of him?” As though he said: Thy magnificence has been raised up: man and the Son of Man have been exalted (Heb. 2). But is he merely man? For if he were a mere man, thou wouldst not have been mindful of him in this manner. “Or the Son of Man, because thou visitest him”: truly Son of Man, because he is the son of a virgin; thou visitest him because thou never forsakest him.

“Thou hast made him a little lower than the angels.” Because he was mortal, he was made lower than the angels. “Thou hast crowned him with glory and honor”: with glory, [Col. 1163D] indeed, because he rose again; with honor, because he conquered, received dominion, and ascended into heaven (Acts 1).

“And thou hast set him over the works of thy hands,” because “at the name of Jesus every knee bends, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2).

“Thou hast subjected all things under his feet.” What things? “All sheep and oxen, moreover the beasts of the field, the birds of heaven, and the fishes of the sea, which pass through the paths of the sea.” By sheep we understand simple people; by oxen, teachers; by beasts of the field, good married persons; by birds of heaven, philosophers and wise men; by fishes of the sea, the rich and those entangled in worldly business. Therefore, because all things are subject to thee: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is thy name in all the earth!”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM IX

[Col. 1164A]

“I will confess to thee, O Lord, with my whole heart.” “I will confess to thee,” says the Church, “O Lord,” not with lips alone—not as those of whom it is said in Matthew 15, “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me”—but with my whole heart I shall worship thee, praise thee, and confess my sins to thee. “I will recount all thy wonders”: I shall indeed recount everything that I find written in the New and Old Testament.

“I will rejoice and exult in thee.” In thee I shall rejoice, in thee I shall exult, as it is written in Psalm 31: “Rejoice in the Lord.” Likewise in 2 Corinthians 10: “Let him who glories, glory in the Lord.”—“And I will sing psalms to thy name, O Most High.” For until now whatever [Col. 1164B] I did, I did in the name of Jupiter, Mercury, Saturn, and the others; but henceforth whatever I do, I shall do in thy name.

“When my enemy is turned backward.” When, I say, I turn my enemy backward, I shall sing psalms in thy name, because I shall praise not my own strength but thee for the triumph. He fittingly says, “when I turn him,” because before Christ’s incarnation the devil, as it were prince and leader of the way, went before us; but now, like a thief and most wicked dog, creeping behind, he lies in wait for our heel.

“They shall be weakened and perish before thy face.” By the enemy whom he mentioned above, he understood not one enemy but the entire company of enemies. Hence it is said here in the plural: “They shall be weakened and perish.” Our enemies have been weakened, having lost their strength, dominion, and power; but they shall perish on the day of judgment, fleeing from the face of the Lord, because they will be condemned with their attendants to eternal punishment.

“For thou hast accomplished my judgment and my cause.” Truly I shall turn the enemy backward, because thou didst die so that I might live; thou didst fight so that I might conquer. Thou hast made thy judgment mine and thy cause mine, because thou wast judged by the Jews for my salvation and benefit. Now thou sittest upon the throne, because angels and archangels, thrones and dominions are subject to thee. “Who judgest righteousness”: thou dost ever judge righteously, because thou ever humblest the proud and exaltest the humble.

[Col. 1164D] “Thou hast rebuked the nations, and the ungodly man has perished.” For the Lord rebuked the nations through apostolic preaching. The apostles said in Luke 13: “Unless you repent, you shall all perish likewise.” Likewise in Matthew 3: “Already the axe is laid to the root of the tree.” By these and similar words the Lord rebuked the nations; whence it came about that the ungodly person perished—that is, ungodliness. “Thou hast blotted out their name forever, and unto age upon age”: for the Lord blotted out the names of the ungodly, because those who had previously been called ungodly, idolaters, and sons of the devil are now called saints, righteous persons, and sons of God.

“The enemies have failed.” How? “By the sword.” What is this sword? Christ Jesus, who slew them. “To the end,” that is, wholly. “And thou hast destroyed their cities.” The malignant spirit had, and has, many cities and congregations, which the Lord does not cease daily to destroy. For every assembly of heretics, robbers, pagans, and proud persons is a city of the devil; and while we join ourselves to the Lord, these are destroyed according to their former condition.

“Their memory has perished with a sound.” Great indeed was the remembrance, praise, and fame of malignant spirits in the aforementioned cities; it was wholly destroyed by the sound of the apostles (Ps. 18). For through the preaching of the apostles idols were broken, temples destroyed, and the religion of the gods made abominable. “And the Lord remains forever”: in the very places where the devil reigned, the Lord himself shall remain king forever. But what Lord? It follows:

[Col. 1165B] “Who prepared his throne in judgment.” The apostles are God’s throne, because he sits and dwells in them. He prepared them for judgment because, when he comes to judge, they will sit upon twelve seats judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matt. 19). “And he shall judge the world in equity; he shall judge peoples in righteousness.” Will he judge alone? Will not the apostles also judge? For it has been said that they themselves will judge (1 Cor. 6). The apostles shall indeed judge, and the Lord shall judge: the Lord as judge, the apostles as law.

“And the Lord has become a refuge for the poor.” The Lord, I say, will judge the world; meanwhile he has become a refuge for the poor. For which poor person? For the one who has nothing and possesses all things (2 Cor. 6), because he has sold what he had and distributed it to the poor, and has become poor in earthly things in order to become rich in heavenly things. “A helper in opportunities, in tribulation”: “in opportunities, in tribulation” means nothing other than “in timely tribulation,” for the tribulation of the saints is timely, by which everlasting life is obtained.

“And let those who know thy name hope in thee.” Because thou hast become their helper—those who know thy name and are called Christians—therefore, whenever they are in tribulations and straits, let them hope in thee; for thou wilt deliver them, “because thou hast not forsaken those who seek thee, O Lord.”

“Sing psalms to the Lord who dwells in Zion.” Since he does not forsake those who seek him, you apostles and teachers who seek him, sing psalms to the Lord. “Declare his devotion among the nations”: among the nations declare the zeal, love, and affection which he had toward you, because “he did not spare his own Son, but delivered him to death for us all” (Rom. 8).

“For he who requires their blood has remembered.” Likewise, apostles, proclaim the Lord and preach the Gospel; do not fear death, because he who requires the blood of those who die for him has remembered—not because he had forgotten, but because he seemed to have forgotten. “He has not forgotten the cry of the poor,” who say: “Have mercy upon me, O Lord; [Col. 1166A] see my humiliation” and affliction endured “from my enemies.”

“Who liftest me up from the gates of death.” The gates of death are vices, heretics, and sinners, because through them, as through certain gates, death and punishment are brought upon human beings. But saints are lifted up from these when they are taught how they may avoid them. He fittingly says “liftest up,” because whoever is separated from these seeks the heavenly kingdoms.

“To proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion.” Zion, which, as we have said, is interpreted “watchtower,” signifies the Church; and by the daughter of Zion are understood all the faithful. The gates are the ears, through which divine words enter our minds. Thus the apostles proclaim the praises of God in the [Col. 1166B] gates of the daughter of Zion when they preach the Gospel to the hearing of the faithful.

“I shall rejoice in your salvation.” I shall rejoice in salvation and in your Son; I shall fear no one, nor shall I be silent because of death, since “the nations have been fixed fast in the destruction which they made.”

“In the snare which they hid, their foot has been caught.” They provide life for me, but punishment and destruction for themselves: while I am delivered from snares, they entangle themselves in inextricable traps.

“The Lord shall be known as one who executes judgments.” For at this time sinners neither know their Lord nor have wished to know him; yet he shall be known by all when he comes to judge. Then at last “the sinner has been caught in the works of his hands” [Col. 1166C]: sinners will indeed be caught in their own works, when they hear this royal sentence thundered over them: “Let sinners be turned back into hell.” And: “Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV). He aptly said, “let them be turned back,” because now they are in hell without their bodies; at the time of the righteous judgment, once they have received the flesh again, they shall be returned to hell—“all the nations that forget the Lord.”

“For the poor man shall not be forgotten unto the end.” As if he said: I know that sinners, who have forgotten their Lord and Creator, will be forgotten by the Lord; but the poor man mentioned above, who sold all his possessions and gave them to the poor, shall not be forgotten for ever.

[Col. 1166D] “The patience of the poor shall not perish unto the end.” Not so that they may suffer anything, but because they shall always rejoice in patience. Thus far the Prophet has spoken in the person of the Church; here, however, in his own person, he announces Antichrist’s coming, dominion, and death.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM IX

“Arise, O Lord; let not man prevail.” As if he said: Who is this man, Lord, who rises with such arrogance, such pomp, and such pride? Who is this son of perdition, who exalts himself above everything worshipped, displaying himself as though he were God? (II Thess. II.) Who is this judge before whose presence all nations are judged? Arise, O Lord; aid your saints, lest the man who prevailed over sinners should also prevail over the righteous; “let the nations be judged in your presence.”

“Set, O Lord, a lawgiver over them.” Aid the righteous, I say, and arise to help the saints; but over those who await him and rejoice at his coming, set this lawgiver. He will indeed be a giver of law, because he himself has also preached his own law.

“That the nations may know that they are men.” For “men” are frequently used in divine speech for fools and sinners. Hence the Apostle says in I Cor. I: “When one says, ‘I am Paul’s,’ another, ‘I am Apollos’s,’ and another, ‘I am Cephas’s,’ are you not men?” Thus they too, when they come to judgment, will know themselves to be fools and sinners, [Col. 1167B] because they worshipped a man and not God.

“Why, O Lord, have you withdrawn far away?” Seeing through the Holy Spirit the exceedingly harsh affliction of the righteous, the Prophet cries out: “Why have you withdrawn far away?” Why have you abandoned your saints? Why do you permit them to be afflicted thus? I know indeed, I know, that “you despise” them and do not care to deliver them in such fitting tribulation.

“While the ungodly man acts proudly, the poor man is set on fire.” Truly fitting is the tribulation which kindles the saints, by the fire of the Spirit, into God’s love. Hence it is written in Rev. XXII: “Let the righteous still be justified, and let him who is in filth become still more filthy.” For when the ungodly person behaves proudly against the righteous, there is no doubt that he becomes [Col. 1167C] still more filthy. But when the poor man is kindled, the righteous man is indeed justified. “They shall be caught in the counsels which they devise”: they devise evil, and in evil they shall be caught.

“For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul.” The sinner always desires to act wickedly; he is also continually praised by sinners for evil deeds. Hence he never comes to his senses. Therefore he shall be caught in evil counsels. “And the unrighteous man is blessed.” By whom? By flatterers and unrighteous people, certainly. For he is unrighteous who blesses an unrighteous person on account of unrighteousness.

“The sinner has provoked the Lord.” He has not ceased, he says, from evil, but has offended the Lord in every way. “According to the multitude of his wrath, he will not seek”: [Col. 1167D] will not the Lord, he says, seek that man’s destruction? He shall certainly seek it according to the multitude of his wrath.

“God is not before his eyes.” For if God had been before his eyes, he would never have provoked him. “His ways are defiled at every time,” because, not knowing God, he has defiled himself with vices at every time.

“Your judgments are removed from before his face.” Apostrophe. Your judgments, O Lord, are all true and just; but true judgments are removed from him.

“He shall rule over all his enemies.” His enemies will be those who can never in any way be friends—namely, vices and malignant spirits. Antichrist will rule over all these, because he will always have such servants with him and will command them as if they were [Col. 1168A] his household servants. By his enemies we may also understand the saints.

“For he said in his heart: ‘I shall not be moved from generation to generation without evil.’” How great his wickedness was, and how perverse his thought will be, is disclosed in these words: never shall he pass without evil from nation to nation, from kingdom to kingdom, from the generation of the living to the generation of the dead.

“Whose mouth is full of cursing.” Because all his words are curses; “and bitterness,” because they are poisoned and deadly; “and deceit,” because they are uttered with deception. “Under his tongue are labour and pain,” because the exhortations of his tongue lead people to labours and pains.

“He sits in ambush.” What does “he sits” mean? That is, he persists. [Col. 1168B] With whom? “With the rich.” Woe to you rich people, who sit with the devil. In what ambushes? “In hidden places.” For what purpose? “That he may kill the innocent,” because he loves the guilty and hates the innocent.

“His eyes watch the poor man; he lies in wait in secret, like a lion in his den.” For just as a lion lies in wait in his den for gentle animals, so this man will lie in wait in the hidden place of his heart for the innocent.

“He lies in wait to seize the poor man.” What is it to seize the poor man? “To seize the poor man” means “while he draws him in”; and he draws him in whenever he deceives him.

“In his snare he shall humble him.” First, he says, he will lie in wait; then he will seize him; and once seized, he will humble him in his snare. For he will afflict many by hunger, sword, prison, and other torments. “He shall bow down and [Col. 1168C] fall when he has ruled over the poor.” The saints, though humbled and afflicted, shall be exalted above the heavens; but he shall bow down and fall into hell, deservedly.

“For he said in his heart: ‘God has forgotten; he has turned away his face so that he may never see.’” Because he said that the Lord had forgotten and did not behold the end and death of the saints, he shall therefore justly fall into hell; and there, receiving the due reward of his wickedness, he may know that the Lord was not forgetful. We may also understand “the end” as the earth.

“Arise, O Lord God.” Antichrist indeed shall fall, but you, O God, arise. “Let your hand be exalted”—that is, your strength, power, and glory. Or “your hand” means the Church. “Do not forget the poor,” [Col. 1168D] as that unrighteous man supposed.

“Why has the ungodly man provoked God?” A reproach. Seeing his fall, he says that this has happened to him deservedly because he provoked the Lord. How did he provoke him? “For he said in his heart: ‘He will not seek.’” What will he not seek? The death of the saints, because he thought that he would receive no punishment from the Lord for the affliction of the saints. In this, he says, he provoked the Lord.

“Do you see?” What do you see? That this man too thought that you did not see—namely, the affliction of the saints. Why? “Because you consider labour and pain,” which they suffer from the wicked for your sake. To what end do you consider them? “That you may deliver them into your hands”—that is, into your power, or into the assembly of the saints; and this deservedly.

[Col. 1169A] “For the poor man is left to you.” By whom? By the devil, certainly, by whom he was previously held. Therefore “you will be a helper to the orphan.” O exceedingly blessed people, who, bereft of such a father, deserve the Lord’s help!

“You shall break the arm of the sinner and the malignant man”—that is, the strength, power, and dominion of the men mentioned above. “His sin shall be sought, and shall not be found.” What is his sin? Pride and exaltation of kingship. If you seek this, you will not find it, because it shall be destroyed with him.

“The Lord has reigned for ever and unto age upon age.” Truly, this man’s sin and kingdom shall quickly perish; but the Lord shall reign for ever. With whom? Certainly with the saints. But what shall become of the wicked? It follows: “You nations shall perish from his land,” because [Col. 1169B] none of them shall enter the land of the living. Then at last “the Lord shall hear the desire of the poor.” Who can be understood here as the poor man more aptly than the Apostle, who says that he desires to depart and be with Christ? (Phil. I.) This desire will then be heard. “Your ear has heard the preparation of their heart”—that is, their hearts prepared and cleansed of vices. When shall these things happen? When the universal Judge comes, “to judge the orphan and the humble.” These things were said “that man may no longer continue to magnify himself upon the earth.” “For everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Matt. XXIII).

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM X

“In the Lord I trust.” The answer of the good against [Col. 1169C] Jews and heretics: Why, O heretics, do you strive to overthrow me? Why do you tell me images of deception, saying, “Flee to the mountain like a sparrow”? For a sparrow situated in the valleys, if it perceives an archer approaching it, flies to the mountain. But you who are human and rational, when you see perverse archers coming upon you, why do you not flee to us, who are lofty in intellect, fortified by wisdom, and to our invincible judgments? For, says the holy man, you tell me this without ceasing; but I, trusting in the Lord, do not fear your fables.

“For behold, sinners have bent the bow.” You even call sinners those who are holy and righteous; you say that those who labour always for universal salvation have bent the bow of deception. “They have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in darkness at the upright in heart.” They do indeed have arrows prepared—splendid and useful ones—in their hearts, but not in order secretly to deceive the upright in heart, as you claim. “For they have destroyed the things which you perfected.” Apostrophe. You see, O Lord, that they have nearly destroyed the true and sound understanding of the Scriptures which you perfected in your saints; and, by preaching error everywhere, they destroy the Church and turn the imperfect to themselves. This, says the Prophet, the righteous will say. But what has the righteous man done?

“The Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord—his throne is in heaven,” with “is established” understood. But what are his thrones? Certainly the saints, in whom he sits and dwells. He shall establish them in his holy temple, in which they shall rejoice with him without end.

“And his eyes look upon the poor.” For God’s looking is showing mercy. “His eyelids question the children of men”: that is, by his gaze alone he knows the righteous and sinners. Or his eyelids are the divine Scriptures, which, like an eyelid, are sometimes closed and sometimes opened. They question the children of men because in them each person can, as it were in a mirror, know himself.

“The Lord questions the righteous and the ungodly.” God’s questioning is knowledge; thus the phrase means: the Lord knows the righteous and the ungodly. But who is the ungodly? “He who loves iniquity” is ungodly and [Col. 1170B] “hates his own soul”; he hates it, indeed, because he kills it.

“He shall rain snares upon sinners.” Once the righteous and sinners have been known, he will establish the saints with himself in the heavenly kingdoms; but upon sinners he shall rain snares. Why did he say “rain”? Because at the judgment he will pour out upon sinners innumerable kinds of torments; once caught by them, they shall never again be able to escape. He also rains in this age, because he permits them to be bound by various vices, which are the devil’s snares. “Fire, sulphur, and a spirit of storms shall be the portion of their cup.” Understand “cup” as death. Hence in the Gospel the Lord says: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (John XXVI [sic]). The unquenchable fire, sulphur, and intolerable stench—the spirit of storms, that is, the onset of many torments—shall be the portion of their death [Col. 1170C]. We may also interpret this according to the nature of each deed: let us say that he who was wrathful and envious dies in fire; he who was lustful and adulterous, in sulphur; and he who sinned indiscriminately in every respect, in the spirit of storms. But if all these, as the Prophet says, are “the portion of their death,” it is clear that other and perhaps worse things await them.

“For the Lord is righteous and loves righteousness.” He loves righteousness because he assigns to each person rewards deserved by his deeds. Repetition: his countenance has seen equity.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XI

“Save me, O Lord, because the holy man has failed.” The voice of the righteous before Christ’s incarnation: [Col. 1170D] Save me, O Lord, lest I be deceived by the vanity of the wicked. For the holy man has failed—that is, holiness has failed in all.

“Because truths have been diminished among the children of men.” Truth has been diminished because falsehood has increased. “Each one has spoken vain things to his neighbour”: because all speak vain things, truths perish; they have deceitful lips, that is, lips filled with deception. “They spoke in heart and heart”—that is, with a double heart, because one thing is said and another understood. Hence a historian says: “One thing he keeps hidden in his breast, another he brings forth on his tongue.”

“May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue”—that is, the tongue that speaks great things about itself. These are those who said: “We will magnify our tongue” [Col. 1171A]. Arius did this, Sabellius did this, Simon Magus did this, magnifying their verbosity above the Church. “Our lips are our own”—that is, we ourselves invent the opinions that we utter. “Who is our Lord?” This person is excessively exalted.

“Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I shall arise, says the Lord.” The Lord heard the voice of the righteous crying above, “Save me, O Lord”; now he promises to arise to help them.

“I shall place [it] in salvation,” that is, I shall place this office of my assistance in my Son. “I shall act confidently in him”—that is, with him as leader I shall wage the battle for your salvation and “shall not fear.”

[Col. 1171B] “The words of the Lord are pure words.” The saints rejoice in the Lord’s promise, because they know that they will truly receive what he promised, since the words and promises of the Lord are pure and uncorrupted by any falsehood, like “silver tried by fire, tested in the earth”—that is, silver tested and approved, not corrupted by any earthly admixture of lead or brass. “Purified sevenfold,” that is, many times: a finite number for an infinite one. Alternatively, “tested in the earth” means tested by earthly people—namely Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the rest—to whom he promised, since in no respect did he lie to them. “Purified sevenfold” means the sevenfold grace of the Spirit. For by the graces of the Holy Spirit which the apostles possessed, they purified from the Old and New Testament the understanding of error; and these are without doubt the words of the Lord. Therefore, because the Lord who promised us his Son’s incarnation is so truthful, there is no doubt that Christ will come.

“You, O Lord, shall save us and guard us from this generation for ever.” As if he said: We desired you, O Christ; we awaited you long. At last you have come: you shall save us, you shall guard us from this present generation for ages upon ages. But what shall happen to the wicked? It follows:

“The wicked walk round about.” Because even now, wandering around the Church, they refuse to enter it; or they walk round about by carrying on earthly business. Or because, labouring around the circumference of the Scriptures, they consider only the surface and external matters, wholly failing to know the marrow and what lies hidden within [Col. 1171D]. Or they walk round about because, like dogs roaming about on every side, they could not enter that eternal city.

“According to your height you have multiplied the children of men.” That the children of men and sinners outnumber the saints and children of God has occurred according to your lofty and ineffable knowledge. Or, “according to your height,” that is, by the exaltation of the cross, you multiplied and caused the Church to grow. Or again, you multiplied the children of men in virtues and holiness.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XII

“How long, O Lord, will you forget me unto the end?” That is, entirely.
