Or: How long will you forget me as I tend [Col. 1172A] toward the end—that is, toward you, who are Alpha and Omega, beginning and end? “How long will you turn your face away from me?” How long, he says, angered by my sins, will you disdain to look upon me?

“How long shall I place counsel in my soul?” That is, you will be angry with me as long as I do my own will and not yours, as long as I follow human rather than divine counsel. “Sorrow in my heart by day”: that is, how long shall I grieve over lost things or approaching misery? Alternatively: “How long shall I place counsel in my soul?” That is, unless I place counsel in the soul rather than the flesh, so that I perform not the desires of the body but of the soul, you will be angry with me continually. “Sorrow in my heart by day”: that is, unless I grieve and lament in penitence [Col. 1172B], because I have lost Christ and the day, and have imitated the devil and night.

“How long shall my enemy be exalted over me?” How long shall I be overcome by my enemy the devil and by vices? “Look upon me and hear me, O Lord my God”: because I cannot withstand the enemy by my own strength, you, O Lord, do not turn your face away from me, but look upon me and hear me.

“Enlighten my eyes,” which the devil had blinded so that I might not know you. “Lest I ever sleep in death”: that is, lest I die in sins; or lest I delight in death, that is, in the devil; or lest my sleep—which is death—become like that of the ungodly, rather than everlasting rest in the image of the good. “Lest at any time my enemy say, ‘I have prevailed against him’” [Col. 1172C]—which he surely would do if, life ended, he found me in sins.

“Those who trouble me shall rejoice if I have died”: that is, my enemies, who thrust me into these miseries and troubles from the joys of paradise, shall rejoice if I am moved away from you and from your faith. “But I shall hope in your mercy.” Defend me, he says, from the enemies mentioned above; I shall hope not in my own strength but in your mercy.

“My heart has rejoiced in your salvation,” that is, in your saving help. I know that I have hoped in you, because you will save me. “I shall sing to the Lord who has bestowed good things on me”: because the Lord has bestowed good things and salvation upon me, I shall sing with the voice of both the inward and outward person. “And I shall make melody to the name of the Most High Lord”: that is, [Col. 1172D] I shall perform good works and without ceasing praise his name, by which I am defended from enemies.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XIII

“The fool has said in his heart: ‘There is no God.’” The foolish people of the Jews, seeing Christ clothed in human flesh, thought that he was not God. Or the Gentiles likewise affirmed that there was no God other than Fortune and the human mind. Hence “they were corrupted and made abominable in their pursuits”: that is, defiled and corrupted by such perverse thoughts, they became abominable to God in the law and ceremonies in which they were especially zealous. “There is none who does good; there is not even one.” They were deservedly made abominable, because none of them does good—indeed, none even as far as “one,” that is, as far as those who worship one God, one faith, one baptism, and whose heart and soul are one.

“The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God.” It is proof from divine authority that no one separated from the Church does good anywhere, because the Lord, looking upon the children of men, saw none who understood or sought God. What, then, did he find? It follows:

“All have turned aside together”: that is, falling in one manner from God’s lofty command, they submitted themselves to the devil’s yoke. Hence “they became useless.” They became useless to God because they do not perform the deeds pleasing to their Father. [Col. 1173B] “There is none who does good; there is not even one.” What divine authority has demonstrated, no one dares refute. Now, confirming this as established, he says: Therefore there is none who does good, there is not even one.

“Their throat is an open tomb.” He seems here to make a certain division, as if saying: some of the wicked are an open tomb, that is, heretics; others are “swift to shed blood,” that is, tyrants; while others are those “who have not known the way of peace,” that is, Jews. Yet none of these is good. It follows that no goodness belongs to anyone separated from the Church. Their throat is an open tomb because their words are outwardly sweet and whitened with deceit. Or, as we said above, an open tomb—that is, hell—is their tongue, because it leads souls into hell, which is closed to no one. “With their tongues they acted deceitfully”: that is, they uttered deceitful words. “The poison of asps is under their lips,” because they pronounce honey and sweetness with their lips; but poison and bitterness lie hidden in their hearts and understanding, and one who has once been imbued with it can scarcely ever be healed.

“Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.” Of cursing, because all their words are cursed by God; of bitterness, because, like poison and venom, they kill souls. “Their feet are swift to shed blood.” This is said of tyrants who thirst for the blood of saints and are ready and swift to shed it. [Col. 1173D] “Destruction and misery are in their ways.” This seems to be said of the Jews, because through the works of their wickedness they shall come to destruction and the utmost misery. “And they have not known the way of peace”: Christ is the way of peace, and the Jews did not know him, “because, if they had known him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II). “There is no fear of God before their eyes”: they certainly did not fear when they crucified his Son, nor do they fear even now, since they do not repent of so great a crime. A rebuke.

“Will not all who work iniquity know?” Here the voice of the Father is introduced, speaking and threatening: “Will not all who work iniquity know?” That is, the heretics. “And those who devour [Col. 1174A] my people like bread to eat,” that is, tyrants. And those who, seeing Christ, “did not call upon the Lord, but there trembled with fear where there was no fear,” because they thought that unless they killed Christ they would lose both their place and their nation (John XI). Or because at one time, worshipping idols, they feared them as gods, though they certainly were not to be feared. Or because, though they still read the Law and the Prophets, they do not dare to apply to them a spiritual understanding.

“You have confounded the counsel of the poor man, because the Lord is his hope.” Thus far God the Father. Now the Church speaks, saying: You Jews have confounded the counsel of the poor man, that is, Christ, who, “though he was rich in all things, became poor for our sake” (II Cor. VIII); that is, you mixed it with other counsels and did not prefer it [Col. 1174B] to your own—indeed, you regarded it as more worthless. “Because the Lord is his hope”: because he hoped in the Lord and, as is true in Matt. XXVII, confessed himself to be the Son of God, you did not believe even his words; but, what is worse, you condemned him to death.

“Who shall give salvation to Israel out of Zion?” Since you have killed Christ, who else shall come from Zion, as your prophets say, and give salvation to Israel? For it is read in the prophets that one shall come from Zion who will remove and turn away captivity from Jacob. This will happen “when the Lord has turned away the captivity of his people.” This has already occurred in part, because the Church, which was held captive by the devil, has been redeemed. In what other [one] shall “Jacob rejoice and Israel be glad”? Alternatively, by Zion understand the Church of souls [Col. 1174C] already established in heaven; by Jacob, his earthly people and the Church which vices still undermine; and by Israel, all the saints and those who see God. Who else, therefore, coming from Zion—that is, from the heavenly assembly of holy souls—will give salvation to Israel on the day of judgment? And when the Lord shall turn captivity away from his people, which will happen at that same time—as Rev. XXI says, because “there shall be neither mourning nor crying, nor shall there be any more pain”—in what other [one], I say, shall “Jacob rejoice,” that is, the Church, and that same Church be glad, now made “Israel” because it will see God? In no other. Therefore the Jews are deceived.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XIV

[Col. 1174D]

“Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle?” God’s tabernacle is the Church, which is a pilgrim in this world. Those dwell in it who persevere in good works. For many are in the Church who do not dwell in it, but make their station in various vices as though in different cities. Or God’s tabernacle is Christ, and he dwells in Christ who delights in him. Or “in your tabernacle” means in the heavenly Jerusalem. Repetition. “Or who shall rest on your holy mountain?” That is, in the lofty dwelling of heaven; or, as it is written concerning Christ, “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord” (Isa. II). Answer: “He who walks without stain.” He used “stain” for a grave sin; for no one can be without any stain, not even an infant of one day old, “and works righteousness.” For it is not enough for anyone to be without stain unless he also works righteousness. He works righteousness who corrupts neither himself nor another unjustly, and who rules himself and another with respect to wrongdoing.

“He who speaks truth in his heart”: one who does not devise deceitful falsehoods, but weighs the truth that builds up. “Who has not practised deceit with his tongue”: he practises deceit with his tongue who deceives others by duplicity of speech.

“Nor has done evil to his neighbour.” Our neighbour is every faithful person. “And has not accepted reproach.” He has not accepted reproach done against his neighbours: he has not conceived it in his mind, nor considered reproach against neighbours acceptable. [Col. 1175B] “The malignant man is reduced to nothing in his sight,” because he is reckoned as nothing by him. Or because he counted as nothing those by whom he himself was killed. Or, on the day of judgment, when they come before his sight, “they shall be reduced to nothing and led back to death.” But the Lord glorifies those who fear him, for he both crowns them and avenges them upon their enemies.

“He who swears to his neighbour and does not deceive.” The promise of a righteous person is an oath. “Who has not given his money at interest”: this may be understood literally. Yet preachers also give their money at interest if they preach the Gospel for some gift or favour. Those too give money at interest who give alms in order to be seen by people, [Col. 1175C] because, as it is written, “they have received their reward” (Matt. VI)—that is, their interest. “And has not accepted gifts against the innocent.” He accepts gifts against the innocent who, for a gift, distorts a right judgment, so as to make “good evil and evil good, white black and black white,” as the prophet says (Isa. V). Or one who, for a gift and earthly gain, despoils and kills the innocent. “He who does these things”—namely, who walks without stain, works righteousness, speaks truth, and practises no deceit—“shall not be moved for ever,” because on the mountain mentioned above he shall remain with the Lord without end.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XV

[Col. 1175D] “Keep me, O Lord.” The voice of the Mediator speaking for the Church. For just as a master speaks for servants, and the tongue for each member, so Christ speaks for the whole Church. “Keep me, O Lord”—that is, keep those whom you have given me, because I have hoped in you. For I hoped in you and made myself lower than the angels (Ps. VIII), in order that you might keep them. Before he became man, he could not hope in anyone greater; therefore, because he took flesh, he hoped in the Lord. Thus “because I have hoped in you” means nothing else than that I took flesh in obedience to you. Or, “I have hoped in you” means that I caused those to hope in you who formerly hoped in man and in princes. “I said to you, ‘O Lord, you are my God’”: because I called you God and Lord, therefore keep them. “Because [Col. 1176A] you have no need of my goods”: keep them, and do not say, “They are unworthy; they have not served me.” For you do not need their service; rather, they need your benefit.

“The saints who are in his land: I have made all my wills wonderful in them.” What were his wills? The incarnation, birth, passion, resurrection, and the like. Not only unbelievers but also saints marvel at these things. Unbelievers marvel and deny; saints marvel and believe. It is therefore as if he said: Keep them, O Lord, for I do not wish to lose them. I love them so greatly that I have suffered so much for them; and they marvel not only at my passion, but even at my willingness to suffer.

“Their infirmities have been multiplied.” As if [Col. 1176B] he said: Keep them, for they altogether need your protection. This is a responsive *antipophora*. They need a physician because they have many infirmities; they need one because they have committed many sins; because they are afflicted by many things; because they have worshipped many idols. For in the Hebrew, “idols” is written in place of *infirmitates* (“infirmities”). Alternatively: Keep them because they know and confess their infirmities.

“Afterward they hastened.” First, he says, they sinned, worshipped idols, and became infirm; afterward they hastened and ran eagerly to me, the true physician. Or afterward the righteous hastened, namely to reward, while the unrighteous hastened to punishment. For before the physician came, both righteous and unrighteous went to hell. Or, they hastened afterward because, mourning their former life, all girded themselves for God’s service.

“I shall not gather their assemblies from blood.” Because, he says, they have done this and that, I shall not hold an assembly or judgment concerning their blood and sins. Or, their assemblies shall be such as are “born not of blood, nor of the will of man, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God” (John I).

“Nor shall I remember their names with my lips.” This should also be observed literally; for he called Simon Peter (John I) and Saul Paul (Acts XIII). Spiritually, however, it is understood thus: I shall not call them sinners, idolaters, or seed [Col. 1176D] of Canaan, but righteous people, saints, and most beloved sons.

“The Lord is the portion of my inheritance.” The Church is God’s inheritance; and the Lord is its portion, because from the two it chose him for its own share. Others chose the devil. For God and the devil are necessarily divided among all people in such a way that no one can exist without one of these two. Therefore, because the saints chose such a portion for themselves, they will deservedly be called sons of God. “And of my cup,” that is, of my people; for the Lord is the portion in the death of saints, because they die partly for him and partly to obtain blessedness. Or, “of my cup,” because he is food, drink, and the highest refreshing of good things. “You are he who will restore my inheritance to me,” because in place of the Jews whom I lost you will subject the Gentiles to me [Col. 1177A]; or you will restore it on the day of judgment, because, when bodies are joined to souls, I shall say to the saints: “Come, you blessed of my Father” (Matt. XXV); or because you will give me back the glory which I had with you before the world existed (John XVII).

“The measuring-lines have fallen to me in splendid places.” He speaks by comparison with those who divide estates: to some, the lines and rods used for division fall in good lands; to others, in stony ground. He rejoices because, after losing the Jews, he has received so splendid an inheritance among the nations. “Indeed, my inheritance is splendid to me”: splendid, indeed, to me, even though it perhaps seems worthless to others. Or it is splendid in them to my heirs—that is, in the land of the living.

“I shall bless the Lord, who has given me understanding.” [Col. 1177B] In this, he says, I bless the Lord: that he gave understanding to my faithful, who were formerly unlearned and foolishly worshipped the works of their hands. “Moreover, even unto night my reins rebuked me.” Moreover, I shall bless the Lord in this also: that my reins—that is, the Jews, from whose loins were my fathers and from whose flesh I was born—by rebuking and blaspheming me compelled me to go even unto death and hell. Or I shall bless the Lord because my reins—that is, the understandings and thoughts of my people—taught them to go even to death in order to preserve the faith.

“**I kept the Lord always before my sight.**” As if he said: Although both I and my people were in the passion of death, nevertheless I always beheld God as helper before my own eyes and those of my people. [Col. 1177C] And “because he is at my right hand, that I may not be moved; therefore my heart rejoiced.” Therefore, he says, my heart rejoices, because the Father and divine mercy stood at my right hand, lest I should be shaken and, through the pain of death, grow angry and thus slay all nations. Or again, I rejoice because the Lord is at the right hand and in aid of the saints, lest they be moved from his faith by any tribulation. “And my tongue exulted,” that is, the apostles in preaching. “Moreover, my flesh shall rest in hope,” namely, in the hope of resurrection.

“**For thou wilt not leave my soul in hell.**” Truly I shall rise again (Matt. xxvii), nor shall I be held in hell and death with sinners (Eph. [Col. 1177D] iv); but rejoicing and triumphing, with the spoil captured, I shall ascend into heaven (Mark xvi). “Nor wilt thou give thy Holy One to see corruption.” For neither was Christ corrupted in soul or body. Nor are the saints’ souls corrupted, although they suffer losses of the body.

“**Thou hast made known to me the ways of life.**” Therefore, he says, I shall not be held back by death, because the way of life is known to me. I shall not wander from the way, but shall go by a straight path to the Father. Or again: thou hast made known to my people the ways of life, that is, the works by which one goes to life.

“**Thou wilt fill me with joy in thy presence.**” Because, he says, I know the way, I shall come to thee without any hindrance. But when I am with thee, I shall rejoice in the countenance and glory received. Exposition. “Delights also for me [Col. 1178A] at thy right hand unto the end” of delights, that is, delights without end. This may also be understood of the saints, because they have known the ways of life, shall rejoice in the countenance and glory of God, and, placed at his right hand, shall receive eternal delights.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XVI

“**Hear, O Lord, my righteousness.**” He repeats this: “Attend to my supplication.” This is the voice of the Lord speaking, as man, for himself and his own. “Give ear to my prayer,” made “not with deceitful lips,” so that we may not say one thing and think another. This is what heretics and flatterers do.

“**Let my judgment come forth from thy countenance.**” Let the judgment by which I was judged before Pilate come forth and be made manifest (Luke xxiii). From thy countenance—that is, let it be understood to have happened according to [Col. 1178B] thy will, lest anyone attribute it to their strength or my weakness, but rather to thy will, which none can resist; for they would have had no power over me unless this had been given them by thee (John xix). Otherwise: “Let my judgment come forth from thy countenance,” that is, judge my people according to thy will, yet so that “thy eyes behold equity.”

“**Thou hast proved my heart and visited it by night.**” Rightly, he says, oughtest thou to hear me and my people, because when thou visitedst both me and them even in the very night of adversity and tribulation, thou hast proved that we are faithful to thee and obedient in all things. “And iniquity has not been found in me.” For it is fitting that a son obey his father and a servant his lord; and therefore Christ, who is the Son, [Col. 1178C] “became obedient unto death” (Phil. ii), and we, who are servants, ought to obey, so that iniquity may not be found in us. Another explanation.

“**That my mouth may not speak the works of men: for the words of thy lips I have kept hard ways.**” The lips of God are the prophets, apostles, and teachers, because he speaks through them. For their words, the Church says, I have kept hard ways, because I have endeavoured to fulfil in deed what they uttered by mouth. “That my mouth may not speak the works of men,” that is, what I say, I do not say in boasting of myself or accusing thee; rather, in order that thou mayest hear my prayer, I recall it as though to remembrance. Otherwise, I have indeed kept hard ways to such an extent that I have been unwilling not only to do, [Col. 1178D] but even to pronounce with my mouth the works of men; no temporal discourse or idle word has proceeded from my mouth. Christ may also say this of himself, since, fulfilling the commands of the Law and the prophets, he endured from the Jews a hard and bitter passion. Supplication:

“**Perfect my steps in thy paths.**” Because, he says, I have now begun, perfect my steps in thy paths, so that I may be able to persevere unto the end. For righteousness, peace, patience, majesty, and concord are paths by which one goes to the Lord. Our feet are perfected in these when they cannot be torn away from them. This is what follows: “That my footsteps be not moved.”

“**I have cried.**” I, he says, the man of the Lord, [Col. 1179A] placed upon the cross, cried to thee, Father (Luke xxiii). But thou “hast heard me, O God; incline thine ear unto me, and hear my words,” that is, the words of my people. For it would not benefit me to have been heard unless thou also hear them for whom I suffered. He aptly said, “Incline”; for everything that is inclined comes nearer to the one who inclines himself. “Make thy mercies wonderful.” Make, he says, thy mercies merciful, by giving servants the same power which the Lord has. Or “make wonderful,” that is, make them dear and acceptable; for what we admire we in some measure exalt. Therefore those admire God’s mercies who love the nativity, passion, and resurrection: “Guard me, as the pupil of the eye, from those who resist thy right hand.” The right hand of God is Christ; those who resist are all unbelievers. [Col. 1179B] Therefore the Son asks the Father to defend him from those resisting him, as one who is the pupil of the eye. Christ is called the pupil of the eye (Zech. ii), because he is brighter than all things and the light by which all human beings are enlightened. Otherwise: Guard, Father, my members from those who resist me, because, like the pupil of the eye, they may quickly be injured. The Church of the perfect may also say this of itself, that God may defend it from heretics as he defends the pupil of the eye—that is, the apostles, in whom the whole body of the Church is enlightened.

“**Protect me under the shadow of thy wings.**” The love of God and of neighbour, and the New and Old Testaments, are wings of God. Likewise, righteousness, charity, and the other virtues are [Col. 1179C] God’s wings, because without these no one can fly to him. Thus Christ here says: Protect me, Lord, placed under the shadow of thy wings. For if vices and desires burn, these are rightly said to provide shade and refreshment. Or: “Under the shadow of thy wings,” that is, under thy protection, protect me from the face of the ungodly who afflicted me—that is, in the presence of the Jews. This may also be understood concerning the Church; for the Church stands beneath those same wings and has likewise been persecuted by enemies.

“**My enemies have surrounded my soul.**” Namely, the Jews in the Passion. “They have shut up their fat,” that is, they have embraced pride and an abundance of vices, though the true physician desired to heal them. Or, “they have shut up their fat,” because, [Col. 1179D] killing Christ and shutting him in the tomb (Luke xxiii), they lost all the riches of that land flowing with milk and honey. “My mouth has spoken pride,” because they said, “He is guilty of death,” and “Crucify, crucify” (Matt. xxvii). “Casting me out, they have now surrounded me.” Formerly, he says, they cast me out of the city; now too they cast me out when they say that they have no king but Caesar (John xix). Yet not as formerly: for formerly, casting me out, they allowed me to depart unharmed; now, casting me out, they also surrounded me. “They fixed their eyes to turn downward to the earth,” certainly not looking at things above, but bending their eyes to earthly things alone; because they thought they would lose their place, their nation (John xi), and earthly riches, they preferred to kill Christ. [Col. 1180A] Or they fixed their eyes upon the earth because they believed Christ to be earth and a mere human being.

“**They received me as a lion prepared for prey.**” Me, he says—whom they ought to have received honourably, as God, and with the highest reverence—they received with bloody jaws, like lions and lions’ cubs prepared for prey. They dwell indeed in hiding-places, because “everyone who does evil flees and hates the light” (John iii).

“**Arise, O Lord,**” etc. Arise to help me. But go before that Jewish people, which is always unwary and fears nothing. “And trip him up,” that is, give to the nations the inheritance which this people promised itself. “Deliver my soul from the ungodly,” namely, from the aforesaid people of the Jews. [Col. 1180B] “And deliver thy sword from the enemies of thy hand.” Deliver me, he says, who am thy sword, who slew the ancient enemy, and who shall divide the righteous from sinners in judgment. “O Lord, divide them from the few of the earth.” For the good are few in comparison with the evil. Hence it is also said: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. xx). As if he said: “Divide, O Lord, these enemies by the hand of thy power” from the saints who dwell in the Church. For great will be the division and separation when the former seek hell, but the latter heavenly kingdoms (Matt. xxv). “In their lifetime their belly was filled from thy hidden things”: while, he says, the saints lived, they desired to be filled with the heavenly bread and the hidden understanding of the Scriptures. But those others—that is, the Jews—“were filled with children,” [Col. 1180C] that is, with vices and sins which they themselves begot. “And they left their remnants to their little ones”; for they did not wish the guilt of the cross to end in themselves, but cried: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. xxvii). They sent it on to their descendants. Otherwise, “they were filled with children,” that is, just as they were filled with riches, so also with abundant fruitfulness. “And they left their remnants to their little ones,” because, despising the living bread and Christ’s body, they left them for the humble people of the nations to eat. “But I,” says the Church, “in righteousness shall appear before thy countenance.” They indeed are filled with children, but I, filled with thy hidden things, shall be manifested before thy countenance, and at last “I shall be satisfied when the glory” of thy Son “has appeared.” Or [Col. 1180D] Christ himself may say this: The Jews, calling me unjust and a sinner, thought that I would be held in hell with the unjust and sinners. But I, ascending into heaven with righteousness, shall appear before thy countenance, Father. When thy glory is revealed to the saints, I shall then be joined with them in eternal blessedness.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XVII

“**I will love thee, O Lord,**” etc. In this psalm the Church sometimes speaks, and Christ sometimes speaks. “My strength,” because through thee I am strong. “The Lord my firm support,” because according to the flesh I am frail. “And my refuge,” because I do not trust in other weapons or fortifications. “And my deliverer,” because thou wilt deliver me from the Jews, O my God, according to that in which I am human. “My helper,” in the time [Col. 1181A] of tribulation. “And I shall hope in him.” In such a one, he says, shall I hope, not in another helper. “My protector,” because he protects and defends me. “And the horn of my salvation,” that is, a strong and lofty defence. “And my supporter,” because on the third day he raised me up.

“**Praising, I shall call upon the Lord.**” For the reasons stated above, in the time of the cross I shall call upon thee in praise, “and I shall be saved from my enemies.” Do you have enemies? What follows is:

“**The pains of death surrounded me.**” He has put the past for the future, as if he said: “Behold, we go up to Jerusalem, and all things written through the prophets concerning the Son of Man shall be fulfilled” (Matt. xx). The pains of death surrounded me, that is, the Jews bringing pains of death; or the pains endured in death. “And torrents of iniquity disturbed me,” because behold, a crowd comes, and he who was called Judas. The torrent came, and the onset of the wicked to disturb the flock of disciples, because, when the shepherd is struck, the sheep of the flock shall be scattered (Mark xiv).

“**The pains of hell surrounded me,**” that is, those for whom infernal pains await. “The snares of death came before me,” because they would come upon me from every side with swords and clubs. They are called snares of death because the deceits of diabolical fraud were in them. “In tribulation I called upon the Lord, and cried unto my God.” Christ, placed upon the cross, cried, saying: “Eloi” (“My God”; Mark xv); and: “My God, into thy hands I commend my spirit” (Luke xxiii). [Col. 1181C] “And from his holy temple he heard my voice.” By his holy temple we understand either the secret of his divinity or the Lord’s body itself. “And my cry, ever present before him, entered into his ears.”

After these things, the Church says: “**The earth was moved and trembled.**” This also happened according to the letter, because at Christ’s Passion the whole earth trembled (Matt. xxvii). Spiritually, however, the earth was moved and trembled because those who were mere earth, caring nothing for the soul, were moved from unbelief to faith and began to serve the Lord with fear and trembling. “The foundations of the mountains were troubled and moved.” As Christ, the apostles, and [Col. 1181D] prophets are the foundation of the Church, so the evil spirit himself, pride, and the other vices are the foundation of the rich and proud, who are understood by the mountains. These foundations were moved and troubled because they were confounded by baptism and repentance. Or they were moved and troubled when Christ plundered Tartarus (Eph. iv), “because he was angry with them,” that is, because he will show himself angry with them. For unless Christ revealed his anger, the evil one and the aforesaid vices would not be disturbed more than usual.

“**Smoke ascended in his wrath.**” Since tears are brought forth by smoke, he put smoke for tears; this is cause for effect, as if he said: When the Lord was angry and the vices were expelled and troubled, people, now cleansed, began to weep in tearful compunction. [Col. 1182A] “And fire flamed forth from his countenance.” For the fire and fervour of the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Lord’s countenance flamed in all, because it both shook off vices and enlightened the saints.

“**Coals were kindled by him.**” The coals had indeed been extinguished, because when the first human being sinned, he took light, fervour, and brightness from the human race and brought upon it blindness, death, and blackness. Therefore human beings were thus extinguished; the grace of the Holy Spirit made them burn.

“**He bowed the heavens and came down.**” First, the Church says, the Lord bowed the heavens—that is, he sent prophets and angels to announce his coming to the world. Isaiah said: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive” [Col. 1182B] (Isa. vii). But Gabriel said to Mary: “Thou shalt bear a son, and shalt call his name Jesus” (Matt. i). Then he came down and assumed flesh. “And darkness was under his feet.” “Heaven,” he says, “is my throne, but earth is the footstool of my feet” (Acts vii). Therefore, because earth is the footstool, it is beneath his feet; and by the earth which we have said is under his feet we understand the Lord’s body. Yet in this body there was such darkness that scarcely a few could recognize the divinity hidden in him. There was also darkness in this body because all the depth of the Scriptures, all fullness of wisdom and knowledge, remained in Christ (John i). Otherwise: just as by the heavens you understand the apostles, so by sinners understand hell. [Col. 1182C] Therefore the Lord bowed the heavens when he sent the apostles among sinners to preach (Mark xvi). For what is more bowed down than one who descends from heaven into hell? And how did he descend? By apostolic preaching. Where did he descend? Into all lands. Hence it is said elsewhere: “He came down like rain upon the fleece” (Ps. lxxi). “And darkness was under his feet”: for those same apostles are his feet, in whom are darkness and the depth of all the Scriptures. Or, because they trampled underfoot the devil, vices, and the threats of rulers, darkness is said to be beneath his feet. Hence the Apostle says: “The God of peace shall swiftly crush Satan beneath your feet” (Rom. xvi). Here darkness is rightly spoken of, since he is “the prince of darkness” [Col. 1182D] (Eph. vi). “And he ascended upon the cherubim”: *cherubim* is interpreted “fullness of knowledge,” and signifies the same apostles, who were made drunk from the fountain of all knowledge. Therefore the Lord bowed the heavens, prepared horses for his journeys, ascended upon the cherubim, and ascended upon his horses. “And he flew.” Where? “Upon the wings of the winds,” that is, over the unstable and proud, because he found no place of dwelling in them. We may also understand souls by winds, and virtues by wings. Therefore he flew upon the wings of the winds because he surpassed all souls in holiness. This verse may also be understood of the Ascension, because he was exalted by angels above the heavens, where winds cannot ascend. “And he made darkness his hiding-place.” By darkness we understand the obscure [Col. 1183A] words of teachers and prophets. These are God’s hiding-place, because in them he is most truly apprehended. “His tabernacle is round about him,” that is, the Church of God. This tabernacle stands around God’s hiding-place when we are occupied with the Psalter, or whenever faithful people devote themselves to the Scriptures. “Dark water in the clouds of the air”: because the Scripture of the prophets, whom the clouds signify, is dark and obscure, it is thereby known that the Lord made darkness his hiding-place. We may also understand by dark water the erroneous wisdom of heretics. Otherwise: “He made darkness his hiding-place,” because, having assumed the garment of flesh, he was not known by all. “His tabernacle round about him,” that is, the apostolic assembly or the flesh [Col. 1183B] itself which he assumed. Objection: Why was he not known, when he had been proclaimed by all the prophets? (Jer. ii.) His answer: “Dark water in the clouds of the air,” that is, because not all understand the sayings of the prophets.

“**Before the brightness in his sight the clouds passed.**” “Before the brightness” is one part of the sentence, so that it may be read thus: “Before the brightness”—that is, the bright and shining clouds always present before the Lord, namely the apostles—passed over to the nations, as it is written: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations” (Acts xiii). “Hail and coals of fire”: as if he said, The clouds passed; but how did they pass? By crying out, threatening, preaching the future judgment, casting fire everywhere, [Col. 1183C] and kindling human hearts with the fire of faith. This is what follows: “And the Lord thundered from heaven,” because he taught the nations by the apostolic voice, as he himself says: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. x). Repetition: “And the Most High gave his voice,” from which, as above, hail and coals of fire proceeded.

“**And he sent forth his arrows and scattered them.**” What are meant by arrows except teachers? Therefore, sending teachers, the Lord “scattered them,” that is, the vices in them. “He multiplied lightnings,” that is, miracles and the brightness of his power. “And he troubled them,” because they did not know what to do—like those who said to Peter: “What shall we do, brethren?” [Col. 1183D] To whom he replied: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized” (Acts ii).

“**And the fountains of waters appeared,**” because from a few preachers many arose and began to preach throughout the whole world. Or because the New and Old Testaments are fountains of many waters, they were then first understood and made manifest. Exposition: “And the foundations of the world were revealed.” The foundations of the earth are the two Testaments, the apostles, and the prophets, because the Church is founded upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Eph. ii). But in what order were they revealed? What follows:

“**At thy rebuke, O Lord, at the breathing of the spirit of thy wrath.**” Thou who saidst: Unless you repent, [Col. 1184A] you shall die. Here, the Church says, the Lord “sent from on high,” because from himself. But what did he send? His mercy, a Saviour and defender who came forth from the Father and came into the world (John xvi). “And he took me, and drew me out of many waters,” because he established me from many peoples; or because he cleansed me from many vices; or because he delivered me from many tribulations. “He delivered me from my very strong enemies,” that is, persecutors or evil spirits. “From those who hated me.” They were indeed very strong and hated me utterly. “For they were strengthened against me”: because, as though victors, they prevailed over me, and are thereby proved very strong. “They came before me in the day of my affliction,” that is, at the time when they afflicted me, they assailed me with snares, flatteries, and reproaches. [Col. 1184B] “And the Lord became my protector”: a friend is tested in necessity.

“**And he brought me forth into breadth.**” Whoever is led into breadth is drawn out of narrowness. “He saved me because he desired me”: because he did not wish to lose me, he saved me. “And the Lord shall repay me according to my righteousness,” because, he says, I was righteous and shall receive the reward of righteousness. Repetition: “According to the purity of my hands,” that is, according to the purity of my works, which are not mixed with vices, “he shall repay me.” And this deservedly, “because I kept the ways of the Lord,” that is, I did not err in his commandments, “nor did I act impiously against my God.” What wonder is this? “For all his judgments were before [Col. 1184C] my sight”: I knew, he says, his judgments, by which he will repay merits according to works. “And I did not cast away his righteousnesses from me”: because I knew the Judge, I observed righteousness. “And I shall be spotless with him,” as if he said: I have done so, shall do so, and shall always be spotless with him who has no stain; “and I shall guard myself from my iniquity.” Nor is this without reason. For I know that “the Lord shall repay me according to my righteousness and according to the purity of my hands,” existing “before the sight of his eyes.” For the works of the good are always before God’s sight, but he does not regard those of the wicked, as it is written: “The Lord looked upon Abel’s offerings, but upon Cain’s offerings he did not look” (Gen. iv). Apostrophe.

[Col. 1184D] “**With the holy thou wilt be holy.**” Thou, he says, wilt be holy with the holy, “and wilt dwell innocent with the innocent.” “For the wicked shall not dwell beside thee” (Ps. v). “And with the chosen thou wilt be chosen”: first thou didst choose the Church, then it chose thee; but thou wilt always be chosen with it, the chosen one. “And with the perverse thou wilt be perverted.”

“**For thou dost light my lamp, O my God; enlighten my darkness.**” Because, he says, thou hast enlightened me in the things I know, enlighten me also in those which I do not know. Or, because thou hast enlightened the apostles and the perfect, enlighten the unlearned and imperfect. Or because thou hast enlightened the righteous, enlighten sinners too. “For in thee I shall be delivered from temptation.” Therefore, he says, I beseech [Col. 1185A] thee and no other, because with thee alone I shall be delivered from the temptation of vices. “And in my God I shall pass over a wall,” that is, the obstacle of sins which the enemy set before me lest I should be able to come to thee. Or, supported by thy help, I shall easily pass through a way which to others seems a steep wall and exceedingly difficult.

“**My God, his way is spotless.**” A commendation of God, as if he said: This my God is not like the others; for his ways are spotless and his words true. “The sayings of the Lord, tried by fire,” that is, his words are tested in tribulations themselves, because he does not abandon those who hope in him. This is what follows: “He is the protector of all who hope in him.” We ought indeed to hope in him. “For who is God besides the Lord, or who is God besides [Col. 1185B] our God?” Hence he himself says: “I am the Lord, and there is no other; apart from me there is no God” (Isa. xlv). And this is that “God who girded me with strength,” that is, with faith, hope, and charity. “And made my way spotless,” that is, my works. “Who made my feet like those of stags,” swift for running, so that they might not quickly fail in the course of good works, and might freely present themselves to the eyes of persecutors. “And setting me upon high places,” that is, in the heavenly kingdoms, where the saints dwell. Therefore the psalms are difficult, because the speaker changes quickly: now he turns to the second person, now to the third, addressing the Lord and recounting his benefits.

“**Who teaches my hands for battle.**” For righteousness, [Col. 1185C] peace, patience, and the other virtues are like hands to us, by which we overcome the devil. Hence the Apostle: “Put on the armour of God” (Eph. vi). “And thou hast made my arms a bow of bronze”: the love of God and of neighbour are two arms to us, by which we embrace God and human beings, and by which, like a strong and unconquerable bow, we overcome vices. “And thou hast given me the protection of thy salvation,” that is, of thy Son. “And thy right hand has supported me,” because it drew to itself the world lying in death.

“**And thy discipline corrected me unto the end,**” that is, completely. “And thy discipline itself shall teach me.” Whoever reads the Holy Scriptures, in which God’s discipline is contained, is both corrected from vices and taught to go from virtue [Col. 1185D] to virtue unto the end.

“**Thou hast enlarged my steps beneath me.**” I, he says, began in straits to pursue vices; but thou hast enlarged and made my feet swift, and hast given them strength, lest they grow weary in such a course. “Therefore I shall pursue my enemies,” that is, vices and evil spirits; “and shall overtake them”: I shall overtake and bind them, lest they grow by fleeing. “And I shall not turn back until they fail,” that is, I shall not cease to afflict the flesh until every desire is slain. “I shall break them, and they could not stand” against me, but “they shall fall beneath my feet,” because they are put to death by good works. How could they stand? For I am girded with strength, but they, already tripped up, flee and perish. This is what he says: “And thou hast girded me with strength for [Col. 1186A] battle, and hast tripped up beneath me those who rose against me, and hast given me the back of my enemies,” because when they have turned in flight we destroy and wound only their rear. Voice of the Head.

“**They cried, and there was none to save them.**” Thus far the Church; now Christ speaks, and he begins from the verse at which he previously ended his speaking, namely: “And from his holy temple he heard my voice.” I indeed cried, he says, and was heard; but they cried, “and the Lord did not hear them.” On the day of judgment, he says, the Jews and sinners will cry to the Lord: “Lord, Lord, open to us” (Matt. xxv); and there shall be none to save them, because they did not receive the Saviour, nor will the Lord hear them.

[Col. 1186B] “**And I shall grind them like dust before the face of the wind.**” I shall not save them, he says, but, broken and ground to pieces, I shall cast them down into hell in a mighty whirlwind. “I shall wipe them away like the mud of the streets,” which, once quickly dried, is no longer seen.

“**Thou wilt deliver me from the contradictions of the people.**” Because some said, “He is good,” while others said, “No, but he deceives the crowds” (John vii). Or: from those contradicting me. Hence it is written: “All day long I stretched out my hands to a people that did not believe but contradicted me” (Rom. x). “Thou wilt set me as head of the nations,” because, the Jews having been lost, I shall rule over the nations. “A people whom I did not know has served me.” For to know God is to love him. Hence he will say to sinners: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” [Col. 1186C] (Matt. xxv). Thus it may be said: The people of the nations, whom I had not loved at all, served me. “At the hearing of the ear it obeyed me,” because, hearing the Gospel through the apostolic voice, it believed.

“**The sons of strangers lied to me.**” The Jews were sons of God, but by killing Christ they became sons of the devil. “They lied,” because they did not remain in truth. “The sons of strangers grew old,” growing old in the sin of the first human being because they would not receive the new human being. “And they limped from their paths,” that is, from the Law and the prophets, or in their own understandings; or in faith, standing on one foot alone—that is, worshipping the Father and not the Son; or following the Old but not the New Testament; or likewise [Col. 1186D] the letter but not the spirit. On these feet the Church walks.

“**The Lord lives.**” He who avenged me upon them. “And blessed be my God, and let the God of my salvation be exalted,” now at last to destroy them. Apostrophe.

“**O God, who givest me vengeance**” upon the wicked Jews, “and subduest beneath me the peoples” of the nations; thou who art “my deliverer from my angry enemies”—thou, I say, who dost this and wilt do it. What follows:

“**And thou wilt exalt me above those who rise against me,**” because, rising again, I shall ascend into heaven. “And thou wilt deliver me from the unrighteous man,” that is, from the aforesaid people. “Therefore I shall praise thee among the nations, O Lord,” that is, through my faithful people throughout the world I shall praise thee, “and shall sing a psalm [Col. 1187A] to thy name,” because they shall do good deeds in thy name. Voice of the Father.

“**Magnifying the salvation of his king.**” Magnifying, he says, I shall magnify the salvation of his king, of the aforesaid people, as if he said: Because the peoples obey their king by hearing alone, I shall magnify the salvation both of king and people. “And showing,” I shall show, “mercy to David his anointed,” because on the third day I shall raise him from the dead; “and to his seed,” that is, to the Church, which shall remain “unto eternity.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XVIII

“**The heavens declare the glory of God,**” that is, the apostles announce to the nations the nativity, resurrection, and ascension in which God is glorified. Confirmation.

[Col. 1187B] “**And the firmament declares the work of his hands.**” For the firmament is the same as the heaven.

“**Day pours forth speech to day,**” that is, God the Father sent his Son to the apostles. “And night shows knowledge to night,” that is, Judas delivered Christ to the Jews. He indicated him when he said: “Whomever I shall kiss, he is the one; seize him” (Matt. xxvi). Otherwise: “Day pours forth speech to day,” that is, teachers announce the Gospel to the Church. “And night shows knowledge to night,” when a heretic imparts error to heretics. Or again, “day pours forth speech to day” when the apostles disclose the incarnation of the Word and the profound understanding of the Scriptures to the wise and perfect. Hence the Apostle says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Cor. i). “And night shows [Col. 1187C] knowledge to night,” when the same apostles, who were an abyss and a deep profundity, announced such moderate knowledge as they could to the imperfect. As it is written: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. iii).

“**There are no languages nor speeches whose voices are not heard.**” For they spoke in every language and preached every kind of knowledge, feeding the weak with a little milk and the strong with bread. “Their sound has gone forth into all the earth.” Above he said who would preach, what they would preach, and how; now he says where: because their preaching went forth into all the earth. Repetition: “And their words unto the ends of the world,” saying:

“**He has set his tabernacle in the sun.**” Because he made the flesh in which he served God the Father visible to all. [Col. 1187D] Or his tabernacle means the Virgin’s womb; for Mary is interpreted “star of the sea.” Therefore he set his tabernacle in the sun because from this star he made the sun. For this pearl is brighter than all things. “And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber,” because Christ, with divinity joined to flesh, came forth from the virginal womb. “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course.” Coming forth from the womb, he says, he rejoiced, having become as a giant, strong and unconquerable. But for what did he rejoice? “To run the course,” that is, to endure every worldly adversity. Hence he himself said: “With desire I have desired this Passover” (Luke xxii). “His going forth is from the summit of heaven,” because he came forth from the Father and came into the world (John xvi). [Col. 1188A] “And his course unto its summit,” because he again left the world and went to the Father (ibid.). His course is from summit to summit because he is equal to the Father in divinity and power. Hence it is said elsewhere: “O Wisdom, who camest forth from the mouth of the Most High, reaching from end to end” (Wis. viii). “And there is none who can hide himself from his heat,” since some are burned with the fire of the Spirit, but others with the fire of Gehenna. Or, as some maintain, no one is without some grace of the Holy Spirit, since all possess understanding and reason.

“**The law of the Lord is spotless.**” Another preaching of the apostles: Keep the law of the Lord, because God’s law will make you righteous, holy, and spotless. “Converting souls.” Whence and whither? From iniquity to righteousness. “The testimony of the Lord is faithful,” and therefore [Col. 1188B] is to be kept. It is faithful because it does not lie. The testimonies of the Lord are: “Give, and it shall be given to you; forgive, and it shall be forgiven you” (Luke vi), and the like. “Giving wisdom to little ones,” that is, to the humble. Hence it is written: “Allow the little children to come unto me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Mark x). And elsewhere: “Because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Luke x). “The righteousnesses of the Lord are right,” because “he will render to each according to his works” (Rom. ii). “Gladdening the hearts” of the good. “The commandment of the Lord,” that is, the luminous New Testament, which is covered by no veil. “Enlightening the eyes,” namely, the eyes of the heart. “The fear of the Lord is holy,” because it makes people holy and therefore is to be feared. “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. cx). “Enduring unto [Col. 1188C] ages of ages,” because it is exercised with love, which shall always remain.

“**The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves**”—not by another. For since God is righteous by nature, his judgments are righteous by nature. “**More desirable than gold and many precious stones**”: that is, God’s judgments are to be preferred to every worldly wealth. “**Sweeter than honey and the honeycomb**,” because they lead the saints to ineffable delight and sweetness. But to whom are they sweet? To the saints, certainly. Whence is this clear? “**For your servant keeps them**,” as though he said: If they were not sweet, your saints would not keep them. “**In keeping them there is great reward.**” “If you keep my commandments,” says the Lord, “you will remain in my love” (John 15), [Col. 1188D] than which no greater reward can exist.

“**Who understands transgressions?**” Who, he says, recognizes that he is a sinner? Who confesses his sins to the Lord, unless he is one who says: “**Cleanse me, O Lord, from my hidden faults**,” that is, from those things which I have done in the secrecy of my heart, or while no one else knew? “And spare your servant from others’ [faults],” that is, from those which are done openly, or which I have not yet done.

“**If they shall not have dominion over me, then I shall be immaculate.**” If, he says, these sins shall not have dominion over me. For sins are ours when we have been ruled and overcome by them; otherwise they would be alien. Then I shall be immaculate, “**and I shall be cleansed from the greatest transgression**,” namely pride, which must be guarded against even in good deeds [Col. 1189A]. “**And the words of my mouth shall be such as please [you].**” If, he says, I have been cleansed from sins, then my words will be such as can please you, because “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Sirach 15). “**And the meditation of my heart**” will thereafter always be before you, O Lord, my helper and my redeemer.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XIX

“**May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation.**” The voice of the Prophet: Come, O Christ; you have come, O Savior; you go to be sacrificed for us. You are human; you need help. Entreat the Father, and the Lord will hear you in the day of tribulation, that is, at the time of the Passion. “**May the name of the God of Jacob protect you.**” Because you came in the name of the Lord. Hence he himself says: “I do not speak from myself” [Col. 1189B] (John 14).

“**May he send you help from the sanctuary**,” that is, from himself. “**And defend you from Zion.**” Zion is interpreted “watchtower.” It signifies both the Church and the heavenly Jerusalem. “May he defend you from Zion,” that is, may he who dwells in the lofty watchtower of heaven defend you.

“**May he remember every**” and universal “**sacrifice of yours**,” because he was offered for the salvation of all.

“**And may your holocaust become rich,**” that is, joyful and acceptable. Or, “may it become rich”: that is, may it redeem and save all who believe in you, whether Jews or Gentiles.

“**May he grant you according to your heart,**” that is, according to your desire and your will. “**And may he establish all your counsel**” [Col. 1189C]. Let someone ask counsel from Christ: “Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?” “You shall love,” he says, “the Lord your God with your whole heart, and your neighbor as yourself” (Luke 10). This is Christ’s counsel, and in many persons it was so fully established that they died for love of God.

“**We shall rejoice in your salvation.**” Therefore, says the Prophet, I pray for salvation for you, because both I and the rest who await your coming shall rejoice in your salvation. This may be understood both transitively and intransitively. “**And in the name of the Lord our God we shall be magnified,**” because “whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Acts 2); or through Christ’s name, because we shall be called Christians.

[Col. 1189D] “**May the Lord fulfill all your petitions.**” Hear the petitions of the Son: “Father, glorify me with yourself.” To him the Father says: “I have glorified [you], and I shall glorify [you] again” (John 12). Likewise: “Father, preserve those whom you have given me” (John 17). These petitions were fulfilled, because he himself was glorified and they were preserved.

“**Now I have known that the Lord has saved his anointed.**” Foreseeing through the Holy Spirit the resurrection and ascension, he uses the past for the future. “**He will hear him from his holy heaven,**” that is, he will send him help from the sanctuary.

“**In the powers is the salvation of his right hand.**” Because through it all nations will believe, “and death shall no longer have dominion over him” [Col. 1190A] (Romans 6). Or, because those whom he himself saves will be mighty.

“**These in chariots, and these on horses.**” Sinners, he says, rejoice in riches and worldly honors, and in fortune, which is depicted on wheels. He has put forward that part which is more worthy than the rest.

“**But we shall call upon the name of the Lord our God,**” through our Lord Jesus Christ, always saying so.

“**They are bound and have fallen.**” They are bound by vices and riches, worldly honors, and the fetter of death. Therefore they fall into punishment and death. “**But we have risen,**” from unbelief, from the mire of the deep. “**And have been raised upright,**” to contemplate heavenly and divine things, looking upon those things which are above.

[Col. 1190B] “**O Lord, save our king, and hear us on the day when we call upon you**” in his name, because he himself says: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, may he give it to you” (John 15).

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XX: THE VOICE OF THE PROPHET

“**O Lord, in your strength the king shall rejoice,**” that is, in the divine strength by which he overcame the devil. “**And he has exulted exceedingly in your salvation,**” that is, in salvation bestowed through himself either upon himself or upon his own. “**You have granted him the desire of his heart,**” because beyond his own desire he rose again, despoiled hell, and redeemed the world. “**And you have not defrauded him of the will of his lips.**” The lips of God are the prophets and apostles. The prophets wished [Col. 1190C] that Christ would assume flesh and rescue them from hell; the apostles, however, desired the resurrection. All these things came to pass.

“**For you have gone before him with blessings of sweetness.**” As though he said: You have fulfilled all his wishes, because you loved him greatly and beyond all others. You loved him indeed, because you went before him with blessings. For before he became man, he was blessed by all the patriarchs and prophets. “**You have placed upon his head a crown of precious stone.**” He conquered the devil, took away his kingdom, and ascended crowned into heaven. He called the Church a crown, because apostles, martyrs, confessors, virgins, and bishops shine in it like precious stones.

“**He asked life of you,**” that is, resurrection. “**And** [Col. 1190D] **you gave him length of days for age upon age,**” because “in that he died, he died to sin once; but in that he lives, he lives to God” (Romans 6). “**Great is his glory in your salvation.**” Great, he says, is his glory in you, because he rose again, ascended into heaven, and sits at your right hand. “**You have placed glory and great splendor upon him.**” You have built glorious and splendid persons upon him, who is the foundation of the Church; for, as the Apostle says, no one can lay another foundation except Christ (1 Corinthians 3). Or, glory because he rose again; honor because he is honored by all.

“**For you will make him a blessing for ages upon ages.**” And this, he says, I know: that he will be honored and venerated by all, because all will bless him forever. For there is no day on which “the Lord God of Israel” and “blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” are not sung in the Church. Or, you will give him to the nations as a blessing, because “in him all nations shall be blessed” [Col. 1191A] (Galatians 3). “**You will make him glad with joy in the presence of your face.**” Christ will rejoice on the day of judgment, when the countenance and glory of God, which he promised to those believing in him, are revealed to the Church. “**For the king hoped in the Lord.**” Rightly, he says, will you make him glad, because according to his humanity he hoped in you.

“**And in the mercy of the Most High he shall not be moved,**” because he is never, and never will be, without mercy.

“**May your hand be found by all your enemies.**” [Col. 1191B] Here he turns to the king himself and speaks thus: May your strength, power, and majesty, O king, be discovered by those who refused to receive you in humility. Or, may they find and acknowledge them, and believe that you are God. Repetition. “**May your right hand find all who hate you,**” either to save or to destroy. “**You will make them like a furnace of fire,**” because they shall burn in eternal fire. When? “**At the time of your countenance,**” that is, on the day of judgment, when they will see him face to face, and then the countenance and glory of the Lord shall be revealed, “and all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3). “**The Lord in his wrath will trouble them,**” saying: “Depart, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matthew 25). But what will the fire do? Do you wish to hear? “**And fire will devour them.**”

“**You will destroy their fruit from the earth.**” Because you will destroy them together with their [Col. 1191C] works. Or, he will separate their imitators from the fellowship of the saints and from the land of the living. Confirmation: “**And their seed from the children of men,**” that is, from the saints. And deservedly. “**For they turned evils upon you.**” Namely, the evils which they saw would befall them; nevertheless, they preferred to kill [him] rather than lose their place and nation. Or, they turned evils upon you because, by crucifying you, they inflicted upon you all their fury and wickedness. Or because they compelled you to suffer and discharge the death and punishment which the first man had deserved. “**They devised counsels which they could not establish.**” For they devised to remove your name from the earth, and to guard the tomb lest perhaps you should rise again. But they could not establish this, because you rose again and your name is proclaimed everywhere. Hence I know that “**you will set them behind,**” [Col. 1191D] that is, put them to flight, so that they neither repent nor are saved. Or, “behind,” so that they may be subject in all things. Or, “behind,” so that they may love only earthly and transitory things.

“**Among your remnants you will prepare their face.**” Because they are prepared and willing for those things which you wholly forsake and do not wish. What you wish, they do not wish. Otherwise: “Among your remnants you will prepare their face.” Because Elijah and Enoch, whom the Lord left alive to appear before Antichrist, will wipe error and stains from their faces and join them to the Church, which has neither spot nor wrinkle. And in order that this may happen:

“**Be exalted, O Lord, in your strength,**” that is, rise again [Col. 1192A] and remain equal with the Father. Or, display your power and majesty, since you first came in humility. But we “**will sing and chant your powers.**”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXI

“**My God, my God, look upon me.**” The voice of the Lord’s man hanging on the cross. Look, he says, O Father, and behold my humility; see what and how great evils I suffer in obedience to you and for the redemption of the world. Look upon your Son hanging on the cross; look upon the nails; look upon the crown; look upon servants insulting their Lord. “**Why have you forsaken me?**” Could the Father forsake the Son? Is not the Son always in the Father, and the Father in the Son? Certainly. How, then, did he forsake him? Let him himself say, who alone is true [Col. 1192B] and must above all be believed. “**Far from my salvation.**” You hear what he says. He complained that he was forsaken; above, he sought salvation—for the words already quoted seem to signify this. But now he says that the prayer made above is far from his salvation. What, then, was he seeking, since he was not seeking salvation for himself? It follows: “**The words of my transgressions.**” As though he said: When I say that I am forsaken and pray for salvation, I do not deserve this; rather, these are the words of my transgressions—that is, on account of the transgressions of my own people.

“**My God, I shall cry by day, and you will not hear.**” As though he said: You truly seem to have forsaken my people, since you do not hear them when they cry. “**O God, I shall cry by day and night,**” that is, my people will cry without interruption at every time. “**And you will not hear.**” Or, they cried [Col. 1192C] by day—that is, for lost prosperity to be restored to them—and you will not hear. “**And by night,**” that is, concerning impending adversity, that they may be delivered from it, “and you will not hear. And it is not unto folly for me.” That they are not heard, he says, will happen to them not unto folly but unto the greatest wisdom: because, while they are not heard when seeking the prosperity of this world, they will know that they cannot please you by worldly, transient things and the seductions of this life. Likewise, when they pray concerning adversity, that they may be freed from it, and you do not hear, they will know that “through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Acts 14), which alone is wisdom.

“**But you dwell in the Holy One, the praise of Israel.**” Since above he said, “Why have you forsaken me?”, who would not err in the ambiguity of this statement? He added: “But you dwell in the Holy One.” You have not forsaken me, he says, as the Jews thought, saying: “God has forsaken him” [Col. 1192D] (Psalm 70). But you were always with me, from whom you differ in no respect in divinity. “**The praise of Israel**”: that is, he whom the Church praises, or through whom it is praised. “**Our fathers hoped in you**”—the patriarchs and prophets—“**they hoped, and you delivered them**” from their enemies and adversaries. “**They cried to you in the time of tribulation and were saved; they hoped in you and were not confounded.**”

“**But I am a worm and not a man,**” that is, vile and contemptible. For what is more vile than a worm? Otherwise: You saved those who were born in sins; but I, who am a worm and not merely a man, became [Col. 1193A] “**the reproach of men and the outcast of the people.**” For just as a worm is born from wood alone, without a father, so Christ was born from the Virgin alone, without male seed. Hence Isaiah says: “Do not fear, worm Jacob” (Isaiah 41). He became the reproach of men on account of the cross and the crown of thorns; and “the outcast of the people,” because they chose Barabbas. All who saw me mocked me, saying: “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God,” and, “If you are the Son of God, come down now from the cross” (Mark 15). “**They spoke with their lips,**” that is, they thought and spoke wickedness, “**and shook their head,**” because those passing by mocked him, shaking their heads. Or, they shook their head because they rejected Christ and made for themselves another head, namely the devil or Caesar. “**He hoped in the Lord; let him deliver him**” from [Col. 1193B] our hands. “**Let him save him, because he wants him,**” as he himself says. The Jews spoke ironically concerning Christ, and yet they spoke the truth.

“**For you are he who drew me from the womb.**” He drew him forth because, contrary to the law of nature, he brought him out from the virgin womb. Or, he drew him forth from the Synagogue, which is a repository of shame and iniquity, and joined him to the Church, in which heavenly treasures are stored. “**My hope from my mother’s breasts,**” that is, from the time when I became man; for before he became man, he could not hope in any greater being than himself. “**I was cast upon you from the womb,**” that is, into your protection, from the time I came forth from the womb; for his humanity was protected by divinity. “**From my mother’s womb, you are my God,**” and therefore “**do not depart from me,**” because you will always be with me. This is necessary, “**because tribulation is near.**” Hence in the Gospel: “Rise, let us go; behold, he who betrays me has drawn near” [Col. 1193C] (Matthew 26). “**And there is none to help,**” neither angel nor man, except you alone.

“**Many calves have surrounded me.**” The Jews, fat, wanton, and stiff-necked; “**fat bulls have besieged me.**” Annas and Caiaphas and the other leaders: bulls indeed because proud; fat because full of malice. “**They opened their mouth against me,**” blaspheming me openly and in a loud voice. Or, “their mouth,” that is, their intention and desire, by which they killed me. “**Like a ravening and roaring lion, I have been poured out like water,**” namely for the cleansing of the whole people, because we have been cleansed by his blood. I have been poured out like water for the ruin and death of many, for poured-out water often causes people to fall as their feet slip. Or, poured out like water because the teaching of the Gospel, proceeding from me as from a single fountain, makes the dry hearts of the nations throughout the world sprout forth. “**And all my bones were scattered.**” Christ’s bones are the apostles, by whom his body, which is the Church, is supported and strengthened. They were scattered because “all fled, abandoning him” [Col. 1193D] (Mark 14). Or, they were scattered also for preaching.

“**My heart became like melting wax.**” This may be understood as the pain of death, because he said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26). Or, Christ’s heart is the apostles, and his belly the Church [Col. 1194A]. The apostles were like melting wax in the midst of the Church, because they enlightened others, afflicted themselves with fasts and prayers, and were troubled by the ungodly. Or, his heart means the whole Church, which he loved above all others, to which he gave his counsel, and which he imbued with divine wisdom: formerly stony and hard, it is now humble, devout, and full of every mercy.

“**My strength has dried up like a potsherd.**” Because before he was mortal and corruptible, but afterwards he became immortal and incorruptible. Or, it dried up because he showed himself dead and without strength, nor did he defend himself, though he was accustomed to aid others. “**And my tongue clung to my jaws.**” Because “like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and he did not open his mouth” [Col. 1194B] (Isaiah 53). “**And you brought me down into the dust of death,**” that is, into the place of burial, or into hell. “**For many dogs have surrounded me,**” that is, the Jews barking without cause, unable to distinguish robbers from strangers; they rejoiced over Barabbas the robber and barked against me, their guardian and friend. “**The counsel of evildoers**”—of the Jews—“**besieged me. They pierced my hands and my feet,**” literally. “**They numbered all my bones,**” that is, they made them countable by stretching me out upon the cross. Or, they numbered all my bones because, while counting the disciples, they said: There are so many; see that all are captured.

“**But they watched and looked upon me.**” These same people, unaltered in their purpose of wickedness [Col. 1194C], considered what I was like and, seeing only the body, thought that I was a mere man. “**They divided my garments among themselves,**” literally. “**And upon my clothing they cast lots.**” Their division of the garments signified their discord, error, and division of the kingdom. Their not dividing the seamless and better garment signified the concord of the Church, which is without spot or wrinkle. “**But you, O Lord, do not remove your help far from me,**” because on the third day I shall rise again. “**Look toward my defense,**” lest my enemies prevail against me.

“**Deliver my soul from the sword, O God.**” Deliver, he says, my soul—or the holy Church—from the sword, from death, from the devil, and from the snares of heretics, for the love it has toward me. “**And my only one from the hand** [Col. 1194D] **of the dog.**” His soul is unique because it alone is without sin; the Church is unique because it alone believes. By “dog” hell is meant, which, after the manner of a dog, greedily devours everything. Or, deliver [it] from the hand of the dog, that is, from the power of the Jewish people barking without cause.

“**Save me from the lion’s mouth.**” By the lion we mean the same people, who surpass all others in wickedness. “**And my humility from the horns of unicorns.**” The Jewish people was a unicorn because it alone lifted itself up with one horn—that is, it was proud of the Law and covenant, by which it scattered and overcame the other nations. If you do this, “**I shall declare your name to my brothers.**” Christ did this after the resurrection, because he opened the understanding of the apostles so that they might understand the Scriptures [Col. 1195A] (Luke 24). “**In the midst of the Church I shall praise you,**” because I shall send the apostles to preach throughout all the earth. Or, I shall praise you in the congregation of the apostles, which is the primitive Church, saying: “You who fear the Lord, praise him.” You apostles, he says, praise the Lord, you who fear him. “**All the seed of Jacob, glorify him.**” Jacob, the supplanter of vices, signifies the Church, which daily supplants the devil through repentance. The whole seed of the Church is the apostles, because, springing from them as though from a few grains, it filled the whole world. They glorified the Lord because they preached him everywhere. “**Fear him, all the seed of Israel.**” The seed of Israel is the same as the seed of Jacob. “**For he has not rejected nor despised the prayer of the poor man,**” [Col. 1195B] of which poor man? Of him of whom it is written: “Though he was rich in all things, for our sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8). “**Nor has he turned his face away from me; and when I cried to him, he heard me.**” Here it appears most plainly that above he did not say of himself, “My God, I shall cry by day and you will not hear”; for being heard and not being heard are contrary. Here he says that he was heard; there, however, “you will not hear.”

“**My praise is from you in the great Church.**” Change of person: that I, he says, am praised in the great and universal Church comes from you. Or, the praise that is in the Church is indeed offered concerning you. Hence the Apostle says: “He who glories, let him glory in the Lord” (2 Corinthians 10). “**I shall pay my vows in the sight of those who fear him.**” Now, he says, I am offered in the sight of the Jews; thereafter [Col. 1195C], in the sight of the saints who fear God, I shall be sacrificed daily in the Church. “**The poor shall eat and be filled,**” of whom it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matthew 5). These poor will eat Christ’s body and be filled with bread, and will suffer hunger no more. “**And those who seek him shall praise the Lord. Their hearts shall live for ever and ever,**” because they will eat the living bread and therefore live eternally; hence it was also said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6). “**All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord.**” Forgetting the devil, he says, they will remember the Lord, whom they had forgotten through the forbidden tree. And, abandoning their vices, they will turn to the Lord: “all the ends of the earth.” “**And all the families** [Col. 1195D] **of the nations shall worship before him,**” because at the name of Jesus every knee shall bend (Philippians 2). “**For the kingdom is the Lord’s,**” because, after conquering the devil, he received the kingdom. “**And he shall rule over all nations.**”

“**All the rich of the earth have eaten and worshiped.**” Of the aforesaid sacrifice, he says, all the saints—who are curdled and rich mountains—shall eat. And they shall worship the Lord.

“**All who go down into the earth shall fall before him.**” For no one is born, no one comes into this world, no one falls to the earth, who does not at some time worship God. Or, all who descend from the exaltation of pride into humility and into the Church fall simply before the Lord. Or, all [Col. 1196A] who descend into the earth, who desire earthly things alone and do not contemplate heavenly things, shall fall into hell before the Lord and in his sight on the day of judgment. “**And my soul shall live for him,**” though the Jews thought it dead. Or, “my soul” means the Church, for which I suffered, since a man will give all that he has for his soul; for Christ had nothing human which he did not give for the Church. It shall live for him because it will seek not its own interests but those of Jesus Christ, which are for the salvation of all. Repetition: “**And my seed shall serve him,**” that is, the children of promise.

“**The generation to come shall be declared to the Lord.**” For although the apostles preached, they did not preach themselves or their own selves, but proclaimed the Lord and the Gospel to the Lord. Or, the generation that is to come to the Lord through faith and baptism shall be proclaimed and taught by the apostles. Confirmation: “**And the heavens,**” that is, the apostles, [Col. 1196B] “**shall declare his righteousness.**” To whom? “**To the people who shall be born**” and regenerated by the font of baptism—whom the Lord made his own and predestined before the ages.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXII

“**The Lord rules me.**” The voice of the Church: Hitherto, she says, while the devil ruled, I was wretched and in need of everything; but now, after his defeat, because the Lord reigns—he who is rich and abundant in all things—“**nothing shall be lacking to me. He has placed me in a place of pasture.**” How, she says, can anything be lacking to me when I have been placed in a place of pasture and amid every abundance? For in the Church are both the New and Old Testament, and God himself, who is the living bread, by which the souls of the saints are refreshed. “**He has led me beside the water of refreshment,**” because the Church is nourished by divine wisdom. Hence it is said: “All you who thirst, come to the water” (Isaiah 55). Or, “beside the water of refreshment,” that is, in baptism, washing away sins. “**He converted my soul.**” He converted my soul to himself, she says, which had been weighed down by the burden of sin.
