“**He led me upon the paths of righteousness.**” He led me upon paths by which the righteous walk toward heavenly things. “**For his name’s sake,**” not because of my merits; and therefore I now fear nothing. “For if God is for us, who is against us?” (Romans 8). “**For even if I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evils.**” Though sufferings [Col. 1196D] of death are inflicted upon me—which are nothing but a shadow of death, since they grant not death but rather life—I shall nevertheless fear nothing. Or, “the shadow of death” means the midst of sinners, over whom death and the devil prevail. “**For you are with me,**” as it is written: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28).

“**Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me.**” By the rod we understand rule and scepter; by the staff, support and assistance. Therefore, because the Lord rules, sustains, and defends the Church, it fears no enemy, comforted by so great a helper. We may also understand by the rod and staff the correction of discipline.

[Col. 1197A] “**You have made my head rich with oil.**” By the head we signify the mind; by oil, the grace of the Holy Spirit or mercy. Thus he says: You have made my head rich with oil, because by your mercy, or by the grace of the Holy Spirit, you have made my mind glad. “**And how splendid is your inebriating cup!**” God’s cup is understood as divine Scripture. Spiritual people are made drunk by it. For one who flees father and mother and his own home, abandons gold, silver, fields, and vineyards, puts on the meanest garments, and flees into the wilderness—does he not seem drunk to others? Many saints did this, intoxicated by such a cup.

“**And your mercy shall follow me.**” God’s mercy follows us like a guard and shepherd, lest we be snatched away by the wolf and the devil. “**All the days** [Col. 1197B] **of my life,**” that is, until the consummation of the age. And this occurs so “**that I may dwell in the house of the Lord,**” that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem, “**for length of days.**” So long, she says, as the devil ruled over me, I dwelt with him in hell; but now, because “the Lord rules me,” I shall remain forever in his wonderful house.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXIII

“**The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness.**” The Lord, says the Church, is king; let him reign. The earth is his; let no one glory in earthly rule. Or, “the earth is the Lord’s,” that is, human flesh renewed in baptism, because “sin no longer reigns in our mortal body” (Romans 6). “**The world and all** [Col. 1197C] **who dwell in it,**” that is, the whole world with its inhabitants. Or, “the earth is the Lord’s,” that is, the universal Church, which, placed as though in the midst of the sea, is shaken on every side by adversities. “**For he founded it upon the seas.**” The Church is founded upon the seas because it is situated beside the bitter surges of this world. Or, it is founded upon the seas and not beneath the sea, because it is overcome by no torments of the ungodly. Or, because vices do not rule over it, but it rules over vices. “**And he prepared it upon the rivers.**” The Lord prepared the Church upon the rivers because he appointed teachers and bishops over many peoples. We may also understand by seas and rivers the prophets and apostles, who are the foundation of the Church.

[Col. 1197D] “**Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?**” The Church has been established; the mountain of the house of the Lord has been prepared upon the summit of the mountains. But who, he says, will ascend this mountain? Who will join himself to the Church? “**Or who, after ascending, shall stand in his holy place?**” For ascending belongs to anyone whatever; standing belongs to the prudent and perfect. Judas ascended, but did not stand at all. Many others ascended, but, turning back, departed. Who then shall stand? It follows:

“**Innocent in hands and clean in heart,**” that is, one who neither does nor thinks evil; for by hands we understand deeds, and by heart thoughts. “**Who has not received his soul in vain,**” once cleansed by the font of baptism. For one receives a pure soul in vain who afterwards defiles it with vices. [Col. 1198A] “**Nor has sworn deceitfully to his neighbor,**” as to how he might deceive him. Who is this man, such as he is? “**He shall receive blessing from the Lord,**” because he will be among those to whom the Lord will say on the day of judgment: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matthew 25). “**And mercy from God, his savior;**” because he was merciful, he finds mercy. “**This is the generation of those who seek the Lord.**” From such persons, he says, the Church is constituted; these are they who seek the Lord and desire to see the face of the God of Jacob. Diapsalm.

“**Lift up your gates, O princes.**” Every person has five gates: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. Unless these gates are guarded by particular virtues, as though by individual watchmen, the devil often enters and goes out through them. But because the generation just mentioned now seeks the Lord, the devil and his gates have fled from human beings, and the eternal gates have been raised, because the senses mentioned are opened only to the eternal King. Otherwise: after the ancient enemy drew the first man out of paradise, he opened for him gates through which he might rush into hell. For some enter death and punishment through avarice, others through pride, and others through lust. These are the gates which the malignant spirit opened for us; these are what he here commands to be removed. “**And be lifted up, eternal gates:**” faith, hope, charity, and the other virtues, which are the doors of the eternal kingdom and are therefore called eternal. These are open because through them both God enters into us and we are introduced into the heavenly homeland [Col. 1198C]. Likewise: “Lift up your gates, O princes,” that is, you malignant spirits, remove the power and bonds by which you have hitherto held the saints in hell; but you, patriarchs and prophets, eternal gates, lift yourselves up and ascend into heaven. “**And the King of glory shall enter**” with you into glory.

“**Who is this King of glory?**” Do you wish to hear what he is like? “**The Lord,**” who rules all; “**strong,**” because he conquered the devil; “**mighty,**” indeed almighty. But where is he mighty? “**In battle,**” where each person’s strength is made manifest.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXIV

“**To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul.**” The voice [Col. 1198D] of the Church. We lift up the soul to the Lord when we persevere in good works. Receive, O Lord, she says, my soul, which I have raised to you and offered to you. “**My God, in you I trust,**” not in myself, not in man, not in my own powers, but in you I trust. Therefore “**I shall not be ashamed,**” like those who worshiped idols, of whom it is said: “What fruit, then, did you have in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Romans 6).

“**Nor let my enemies mock me.**” For the Gentiles mocked the saints, and, pointing with a finger at their idols, mockingly said: Where is your God, whom you believe in and await—and do so in vain? “**For all who await you shall not be confounded. Let all who act wickedly in vain be confounded.**” All indeed act wickedly, but not all do so in vain [Col. 1199A]. Whoever lies acts wickedly. “But every man is a liar” (Romans 3). Therefore every human being acts wickedly. Shall all then be confounded? Far be it! Who, then? The person who acts thus wickedly in vain—that is, who perseveres in evil.

“**Show me your ways, O Lord.**” Because, he says, one who acts wickedly will perish, show me your ways, lest, deceived by the way of error, I too be confounded and perish. “**And teach me your paths.**” I said “ways,” but now I call them paths, because “narrow is the way that leads to life” (Matthew 7).

“**Direct me in your truth.**” You, he says, are upright and true; but I am false and crooked. Therefore direct me, O Lord, that I may be able to walk according to your truth; teach me to avoid evil and choose good. [Col. 1199B] “**For you are God, my savior, and because I have waited for you all day.**” From ancient times the prophets foretold that you would come into the world; I awaited you, O Christ. Direct and teach me.

“**Remember your compassions and your mercies, which are from of old.**” You have always been merciful, he says, and so merciful that you assumed flesh and underwent the cross for us. Therefore do not forget such great mercy.

“Remember not the offenses of my youth,” which I committed through ignorance, “nor my ignorances. Remember me according to your mercy,” since I have no merits, “for the sake of your goodness, O Lord. The Lord is sweet and upright.” Sweet indeed, [Col. 1199C] because he is free from gall and bitterness, or because he promises good things to all; upright, because “he will render to each according to his works” (Rom. II).—“Therefore he will give a law to those who sin.” We are set upon the way of your commandments, and we ought to walk along this path. Yet many, turning aside and hurling themselves over the precipices of vices, sin. But because our Lord is sweet and upright, he gave to sinners upon this way a most sweet law. For this law was assigned to sinners so that they might repent, be converted, and be saved. “He will guide the meek in judgment”: when, he says, in the universal judgment the meek are to be proclaimed, the Lord will direct them to himself. Or else: those who in this world are unjustly judged by unbelievers, yet persist in patience and meekness and are not [Col. 1199D] broken by adversities, proceed by a straight road to the Lord. He also guides the meek in judgment because he grants them discernment for judging rightly. “He will teach the gentle his ways,” by which they can reach him. But what are his ways? It follows:

“All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.” For no one is chosen by God except either through mercy alone, as Jacob was, or through mercy and truth, as Job was. But for whom are these ways prepared? It follows: “For those who seek his covenant and his testimonies.” They seek the Lord’s covenant who understand spiritually the things which they say. Or, those who labor in order to become worthy of God’s covenant and adoption. And his testimonies are in the Psalms, the Prophets, and the other [Col. 1200A] Scriptures. “For your name’s sake, O Lord, you will be propitious to my sin”; because, he says, there are two ways by which one goes to you, but one of them—namely truth—is only for the perfect: for the sake of your name and mercy, be propitious to me, “for my sins are many.”

“Who is the man that fears the Lord?” The Church, rejoicing in God’s sweetness and goodness, says: “Who is the man that fears the Lord?” Let him rejoice and fear nothing; if he is a sinner, let him not despair, but repent; let him be converted, and he shall be saved. For “the Lord has established for him a law in the way which he chose”: righteousness, peace, patience, charity, and kindness are the ways through which we ought to walk. This is the way which the Lord chose. But if anyone should at some time turn aside from this way, [Col. 1200B] let him recognize the law established for him.

“His soul shall abide amid good things,” the soul of the one who enters by this way. “And his seed shall inherit the land,” because both he himself through the works which he performed, and his imitators, shall dwell in the land of the living. “The Lord is the support of those who fear him,” for in ourselves we are frail. But because we are established upon the firm rock, we do not fear the threats of the sea. “And his covenant”: he himself indeed is our support, and his covenant, by which we are strengthened through good examples, is given so that “it may be made manifest to them” who fear God; for through this covenant the Lord is manifested and known.

“My eyes are always toward the Lord.” It often happens that someone, while looking intently at something and not carefully considering where he places his foot, falls into a pit. This man, fearing this not at all, says: “My eyes are always toward the Lord,” and I shall not fear the snare, “because he will pluck my feet from the snare. Look upon me.” Look upon me, he says, because I myself look to none but you. “And have mercy on me,” as you ought, “because I am solitary and poor.” Solitary indeed, because I am alone and worship you alone; but poor because, possessing nothing, I possess all things. This may also be understood most fittingly of Christ.

“The tribulations of my heart have been multiplied,” because I am afflicted in many ways. “Deliver me from my necessities,” leading me into that kingdom in which I shall suffer no necessities.

[Col. 1200D] “See my lowliness and my labor.” See, he says, that I am in great tribulation and labor; hence it may happen that, broken at some point, I fall into sins, and therefore “forgive all my offenses. Look upon my enemies, because they have been multiplied,” and indeed they are many. “And they hate me with unjust hatred,” because they hate not the vices in me but nature itself. “Guard, therefore, my soul” from their deceits, “and deliver me, that I may not be put to shame, because I have hoped in you. The innocent and upright have clung to me”; otherwise they would not be innocent unless they clung to the Church, “because I waited for you. Deliver, O God, Israel,” that is, the Church—he speaks of himself as though of another—“from all its tribulations,” which it suffers both from vices and from men.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXV

[Col. 1201A]

“Judge me, O Lord.” The voice of the perfect. For one who asks to be judged does not fear judgment. “For I have walked in my innocence.” Therefore, he says, I do not fear judgment, because I have led an innocent life. “And hoping in the Lord, I shall not grow weak.” I shall not weaken in my work, but, as I began, so I shall labor to the end.

“Prove me, O Lord, and test me.” Prove me, he says: discover whether it is true what I said, that I have led an innocent life. And test me, that you may prove what sort of and how great a constancy I possess, since I have promised and pledged that I shall not grow weak. After you have done this, “burn my reins and my heart.” After you have proved me, he says, if you find in me any [Col. 1201B] stain of vices, burn it out; destroy it with the fire of the Holy Spirit. But if you find nothing, then kindle me toward greater love.

“For your mercy is before my eyes,” because neither do I forget mercy, nor does mercy forget me. “And” because “I have pleased” you “in your truth.” For what I say truly is yours, but what I say falsely is mine: therefore truth is yours, but falsehood is mine. Therefore you are that truth in which I have pleased you. And because “I have not sat with the council of vanity,” that is, with those who deliberate vanity; and because “I will not enter in with those who commit iniquity.” What is “I will not enter in”? That is, I will not undertake to do the same iniquity. Or else, I shall not enter death and punishment, which they have without [Col. 1201C] doubt entered. And because “I have hated the assembly of evildoers,” that is, the congregation of the wicked, “and I will not sit with the impious,” that is, I shall not persist in impiety after their likeness. Or again, I shall not be with them in torments. Because I have done this or that, therefore I do not fear judgment, but confidently say: “Judge me, O Lord.” And because “I will wash my hands among the innocent.” I dwell, he says, with the innocent, because I have hated the assembly of evildoers; being placed among them, I shall wash my works from every filth of vices—for hands signify works. And because “I will encompass your altar, O Lord.” The altar of God is the Church, or the New and Old Testaments, because in them commemoration is made of the birth, passion, resurrection, body, and blood [Col. 1201D] of the Lord. The saints surround this altar; but why do they surround it? That they may hear the voice of God’s praise, which is what follows: “That I may hear the voice of your praise.” Whoever desires to hear the praises of God should hasten to this altar and surround these two Testaments; for here they will find apostles, patriarchs, and prophets praising God. “That I may recount all your wonders.” This man does not wish to hide his Lord’s money; he does not carry a bag in which to store up treasure, but desires to share freely with all what he freely received. Because, he says, I shall do both these things and those things, therefore, hoping in the Lord, I shall not grow weak.

“O Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house,” that is, a soul adorned with virtues, chastity of mind and body. [Col. 1202A] Confirmation. “And the place where your glory dwells.”—“Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you?” (I Cor. III).

“In whose hands are iniquities.” Because all their works are unjust and wicked. “Their right hand is full of gifts,” with which they deceive the innocent. “But I have walked in my innocence,” because I have led an innocent life. “Redeem me” from all enemies, “and have mercy on me. My foot has stood in the straight way,” because I have not limped away from the straight path. And as long as I shall be, “in the churches” and holy congregations, “I shall bless you, O Lord.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXVI

“The Lord is my illumination.” The voice of the Church. Once I was in darkness and lay in blindness, but [Col. 1202B] when Christ came, “the people that sat in darkness saw a great light” (Isa. IX). The true light came, which enlightens every person coming into this world (John I). “And my salvation”: he himself enlightened me, he himself saved me; whom then shall I fear? “The Lord is the protector of my life.” The Lord, he says, redeemed my soul, enlightened it, will save and protect it lest it be lost. “From whom, therefore, shall I tremble?” I see enemies, I see malignant spirits, I see tyrants rushing upon me; but I fear no one, instructed by the Lord’s consoling admonition. For he says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. X).

“While evildoers draw near against me.” Evildoers draw near, foes attack me, enemies besiege me. To what end? “That they may eat my flesh”: that they may tear and kill me, that they may deceive the fleshly and imperfect and join them to their wicked body; for they can do nothing to the soul and bones. Or again, because they draw near, it comes about that they consume the flesh and carry away with themselves the desires of the flesh, while leaving to me a soul pure and proved. “My enemies who trouble me have themselves grown weak and fallen.” He adds the reason why he need not fear: the persecuting enemies have grown weak, or the malignant spirits were conquered, when Christ died. And they fell from dominion and power because Christ rose again. Therefore, “though camps should stand against me, my heart shall not fear.” Though, he says, an army of the impious, an assault of vices, or a host of demons should oppose me, [Col. 1202D] still I shall fear nothing; for the Lord is with me as a mighty warrior. “Though battle should rise against me” from my aforesaid enemies, “in this” helper “I shall hope.”

“One thing have I asked of the Lord.” One petition, he says, one thing have I asked of the Lord; “this I shall seek,” to this petition I shall persistently attend. But what is this petition? “That I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life,” that is, that, when the body has been put to death, I may rest forever in the heavenly Jerusalem. Hence the Apostle says: “For we know that, if our earthly house of this dwelling should be dissolved, we shall have a house not made with hands, eternal in heaven” (II Cor. V).—“That I may behold the delight of the Lord.” Therefore, [Col. 1203A] he says, I wish to dwell in the Lord’s house: that I may perfectly behold and know his delight. For now I see “through a mirror and in an enigma, but then face to face; now I know in part, but then, as I also am known” (I Cor. XIII).—“And visit his temple,” namely that ineffable and most radiant secret of the Godhead, the nature of which cannot be searched out by human intelligence.

“For he has hidden me in his tabernacle.” The order is: “I shall go around and sacrifice in his tabernacle.” What shall I go around? Myself and my soul. He follows the example of those who, guarding camps or cities, patrol by day and night lest enemies stealthily enter at any point. Likewise this man says: I shall patrol the house entrusted to me; I shall set guards at its gates, who will drive far away from it avarice, lust, pride, and all other enemies. And I shall sacrifice in his tabernacle: every believer is God’s tabernacle. But what shall I sacrifice? “A sacrifice of shouting.” Because, he says, I am God’s tabernacle, I shall sacrifice within myself a victim to him—not of goats or calves, but rather a sacrifice of praise and rejoicing, a living and immaculate victim. “I shall sing; I shall make psalm to the Lord.” I shall sing, he says: I shall preach and proclaim his praises. And I shall make psalm, because I shall fulfill words by deeds. And this deservedly, “because he has hidden me in his tabernacle.” The tabernacle itself he did not hide, but he hid me in the tabernacle, because he presented the outward person [Col. 1203C] as visible to all and allowed it to be afflicted by all. Decius saw Lawrence; he saw God’s tabernacle, violated God’s temple, and burned his house. But, as the Apostle says, “if anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him” (I Cor. III). Yet he did not see the inward person, whom God had hidden in such a tabernacle. Saints hidden in such tabernacles cannot be found by vices or malignant spirits. “In the day of evils he protected me, in the hidden place of his tabernacle.” The days of evils are called those in which evil persons exercise their wickedness. Hence the Apostle says: “For the days are evil” (Eph. V). In these days, although they might seize the tabernacle and afflict the body, they shall not be able to find me, that is, my soul.

[Col. 1203B] And because “he exalted me upon a rock,” that is, in Christ and through Christ he raised me above earthly desires. “And now he has exalted my head above my enemies.” Then our head is exalted above our enemies when the mind, considering its own dignity, yields to no adversities. “Hear, O Lord, my voice with which I cried.” Hear, he says, my prayer; grant the aforesaid petition in which I said: “One thing have I asked of the Lord.” Confirmation. “Have mercy on me, and hear me. My heart said to you.” As though he said: That prayer with which I said I had cried was not on my lips but in my heart. “My face sought you.” Explanation of the petition. I ask for nothing else, he says, except that I may see your face, know your delight, [Col. 1204A] and stand in your presence. “Do not turn your face away from me; do not turn aside in anger from your servant.” Because I, he says, your servant, seek your face, do not hide it from me; do not separate yourself from me as though angry, but do what follows: “Be my helper; do not abandon me,” either here or in the future, “nor despise me, O God,” because, although I am human and corruptible, I nevertheless seek heavenly and divine things.

“For my father and my mother have forsaken me.” Before, he says, you assumed flesh, the devil was my father, while my mother was Gentile-ness, Babylon, and confusion. But after I believed and abandoned their deeds, grieving over my salvation they forsook me. “But God,” who is the true [Col. 1204B] Father, “has received me.”—“Set a law for me in your way.” Because, he says, you have received me, give me a law of life, so that, standing firmly in your way, I may turn neither to the right nor to the left. “And guide me on the straight path,” lest I be deceived by Jews and heretics.—“Because of my enemies,” who try to deceive me, “do not hand me over to the souls of those who afflict me,” so that they may accomplish their whole intention and desire; for although they may overcome the body, they shall not overcome the soul. “For unjust witnesses rose up against me.” For false witnesses among the Jews often rose up against the apostles and called them transgressors of the law.

“And iniquity lied to itself.” Iniquity did indeed lie to itself, because their iniquity descended upon their own heads. This may also be understood of Christ, against whom unjust witnesses rose up and said: “This man said: I can destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days” (Matt. XXVI).—“I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.” How do I know that you will not hand me over to the souls of those who afflict me? The Mediator has already ascended; the Savior already prepares a place for me, because even in the holy Scriptures he daily admonishes me, saying: “Wait for the Lord,” who will both repay the reward of your labor and vindicate you against your enemies. “Act manfully”: be strengthened and be resolute—this is what he says. “Let your heart be strengthened” in good works. “And wait for the Lord,” that is, wait until he comes.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXVII

[Col. 1204B]

“To you, O Lord, I shall cry, my God.” The voice of Christ or of the Church. Christ cried on the cross when he said: “Eloi, Eloi” (Matt. XXVII). The Church too cries, because it never ceases daily to praise the Lord’s name. “Do not be silent toward me,” that is, you will not be silent toward me, because I shall always praise you. Or, do not be silent toward me, that is, answer me and hear my prayer. “Lest at any time you be silent toward me” is a confirmation. “And I shall be made like those who go down into the pit.” If I, the Church says, do not praise you, I shall be like the impious and sinners who descend into the pit and into hell. But Christ says: If you do not hear me, I shall be counted among the impious and those given over to death. Let this not happen. “Hear the voice of my supplication while [Col. 1205A] I pray to you” for the universal salvation of the whole world. “While I lift up my hands toward your holy temple,” that is, I lift up my hands on the cross so that I may build your holy temple, which is the Church. But the Church, praying to the Lord, raises its hands toward God’s temple because it sends its good works to the Lord; or because it raises itself by the steps of virtues up to God’s temple; or because, with hands uplifted, it supplicates the Lord.

“Do not deliver me together with sinners.” Do not, the Church says, hand me over together with sinners to torturers, because I have paid all that I owed and have not afflicted a fellow servant for denarii. “And do not destroy me with those who work iniquity,” because I have not worked iniquity. “Who speak peace with their neighbor,” because in words they feign friendship and peace, “but evil things are in their hearts.” In their hearts, he says, evils, snares, deceits, and betrayals lie hidden. “Give them according to their works, and according to the wickedness of their devices; give them according to the works of their hands; render their recompense to them,” that is, let them receive according to their deserts. “For they have not understood the works of the Lord,” in order to do them; “and destroy them in the works of their hands,” that is, let them perish according to the works which they have performed, “and you will not build them.” When, he says, you construct the heavenly city Jerusalem out of living stones, do not build them into its walls.

“Blessed be the Lord, because he has heard the voice of my supplication.” Knowing that the things he has requested will happen, [Col. 1205C] he blesses as though already heard and gives thanks to the Lord, because the Lord is “my helper and my protector”: a helper that we may conquer, a protector lest, wounded, we fail. “And my heart hoped in him, and I was helped. And my flesh blossomed anew.” It blossomed anew because, in baptism, having lost its old age, it was made new and youthful. Or it will blossom anew on the day of judgment, when “this corruptible shall put on incorruption” (I Cor. XV).—“And by my will I shall confess to him.” I shall confess, he says, and confess willingly, because God loves no services except those done voluntarily. “For the Lord is the strength of his people,” because through him it is strong, “and he is the protector of the salvations of his Christ.” One who gives salvation, or one to whom salvation is given, is called a savior. Therefore God is the protector of the salvations of his Christ because he protects those whom Christ has saved.

“Save your people, O Lord.” Because, he says, God protects, you, Christ, save your people, so that he may be called Protector, while you are called Jesus and Savior.

“And bless your inheritance.” God’s inheritance is the Church, of which it is said: “And I will give the nations as your inheritance.”—“And rule them with a rod of iron” (Ps. II).—“And lift them up” from virtue to virtue, “unto eternity,” that is, until they attain eternity.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXVIII

“Bring to the Lord, sons of God.” The voice of the Prophet [Col. 1206A] exhorting the nations to God’s praise. You are now, he says, sons of God and called to adoption. Therefore, “bring to the Lord.” But what ought you to bring? It follows: “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams.” Rams are called the apostles because they are teachers of the whole Church; or because they are armed, as it were, with the two horns of the New and Old Testaments. But the sons of rams are the souls of the faithful, whom the apostles begot for the Lord in baptism. Hence the Apostle says: “For in Christ Jesus I begot you” (I Cor. IV). And again: “My little children, whom I am again bringing to birth” (Gal. IV). Therefore let us bring to the Lord these sons of rams, that is, our souls, because we can bring nothing greater to God; and we bring them when we raise them through virtues.

[Col. 1206B] “Bring to the Lord glory and honor,” that is, present yourselves as such persons in whom God may be honored and glorified. Hence it was said: “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).—“Bring to the Lord glory to his name,” that is, glorify God because you are called Christians and have received his name. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs: “Your name is oil poured out; therefore young women loved you exceedingly” (Song I). Or, “glory to his name,” that is, glory for the honor of his name. “Worship the Lord in his holy court,” that is, in the newly built Church. Or in your hearts and consciences, as it is written: “Enter into your chamber, and, when the door is shut, pray to your Father” [Col. 1206C] (Matt. VI).

“The voice of the Lord is upon the waters.” Above he said: “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams,” and, “Bring to the Lord glory and honor.” But this is the voice of the Lord thundering over the waters. What are the waters but peoples? As it is written: “Many waters were multiplied.” Therefore the voice of the Lord thundered over many waters when the Apostle proclaimed the Gospel to the crowds that followed him, or when the apostles preached through all lands. The voice of the Lord also thundered over the waters, because over Christ in the Jordan the voice of the Father was heard: “This is my Son” (Matt. XVII). Even now it thunders over the waters of baptism, because priests baptize in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy [Col. 1206D] Spirit. “The God of majesty thundered.” He, he says, thundered who preached through himself, the God of majesty, power, and exalted might. “The Lord is upon many waters,” because both in person and through his disciples he proclaimed the Gospel to the whole world. “The voice of the Lord is in power; the voice of the Lord is in magnificence.” This voice, he says, is proved to be the Lord’s voice by its power and magnificence. For so great was the power of this voice that it raised the dead, gave sight to the blind, cleansed lepers (Matt. II), and healed paralytics (Mark II). It is therefore evident that such a voice is the Lord’s. But whose Lord? It follows:

“The voice of the Lord breaking cedars.” By cedars we understand the proud, rich, and powerful. The voice of the Lord [Col. 1207A] broke them, because many were humbled beneath Christ’s yoke, as it is written: “Mountains and hills shall be humbled” (Luke III). Therefore the Lord’s voice broke cedars because the Gospel humbled the proud and rich. It will also break them in judgment; for that will be the Lord’s voice which says: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV). How many are shattered by that voice cannot be said. It is therefore evident that it will break cedars. But whose cedars? It follows:

“And the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon,” because those born amid the riches of this age and the world’s brightness and prosperity he will partly convert to himself and partly hand over to eternal punishment. “And he will crush them like the calf of Lebanon.” No land, according to the interpretation of this name, can more fittingly be called Lebanon than the land of the Jews, [Col. 1207B] which flourished in the beauty of every kind of wealth and flowed with milk and honey (Deut. VI). But a calf stands for sacrifice because sacrifice was made from a calf (Lev. IV). Therefore the Lord crushed the calf of Lebanon because he destroyed the sacrifice of the Jews so thoroughly that it is said to exist nowhere. In likeness of this, therefore, the wicked shall be crushed: some shall perish altogether, like this sacrifice; others shall cease from pride and iniquity, as this land ceased from sacrifice.

“And the beloved one, like the son of unicorns.” This, like what precedes, can be applied to both the good and the bad sense; in the good sense, it is as follows. We understand the apostles as sons of unicorns [Col. 1207C] because they came forth from the Jews. They were so poor and reduced that nothing of their own remained to them, as they themselves testify: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. XIX). In comparison with them, many worldly persons have been transformed, since some become monks, others hermits, and others pilgrims, admonished by the Lord’s voice; for he says: “Whoever leaves father and mother, fields, male and female servants, shall receive a hundredfold” (ibid.). This is that voice of our Redeemer which breaks the cedars. But in the case of the wicked it is understood thus. The Jews and the sons of the Jews who crucified Christ are called unicorns; no slight punishment and fate awaits them. Therefore, whoever are condemned to eternal death, the beloved Son of God will crush them as [Col. 1207D] the sons of unicorns. But in some manuscripts there is found: “And the beloved one, like the son of unicorns.” This is interpreted thus: The beloved Son of God, who, the Prophet says, is still in every respect equal to the Father, shall in the appointed time be so crushed that, like one of the sons of the Jews, he will be believed to be wholly mere man.

“The voice of the Lord dividing the flame of fire.” This, he says, is the voice of that Lord who divides the flames of fire. For all would enter the flames of hell and unquenchable fire, had not Christ, by assuming flesh, separated hell from us and us from hell. The voice of the Lord also divides the flames [Col. 1208A] of fire because the proclamation of the Gospel cuts away from its hearers the vices and desires of the flesh.

“The voice of the Lord shaking the wilderness, and the Lord will move the desert of Kadesh.” Kadesh is interpreted “the stirring of the moth”; it signifies this world, which was formerly abandoned by the Lord. But when the Son of God came, he shook the world; he moved the desert of Kadesh, which the moth and malignant spirit had disturbed and corrupted; he shook out the moths, stirred the vices, and drove away sins. Alternatively, Kadesh signifies the Law and the Old Testament; for some interpret Kadesh as “holy.” Therefore Christ, when he came, moved the desert of Kadesh because he shook and opened the holy Law and the Prophets, which were nearly abandoned by everyone on account of their excessive obscurity; he removed the letter and made them intelligible [Col. 1208B] (Luke XXIV).

“The voice of the Lord preparing the stags.” Stags signify the apostles because they were swift in running and in announcing the Gospel, and because they made little account of the deadly poisons of the devil. “And he will reveal the thickets,” because he opened the Scriptures to them and made divine mysteries manifest. Hence the Apostle says: “I heard,” he says, “secret words which it is not permitted for a man to speak” (II Cor. XII). “And in his temple all shall speak glory,” because all in the Church praise the Lord.

“The Lord makes the flood dwell.” The flood dwells in God’s temple because prophets, apostles, bishops, and teachers are found in the holy Church. They are called a flood because they overflow with the abundance of the Holy Spirit and the fullness of all the Scriptures. [Col. 1208C] Or also because they wash people from sins. “And the Lord shall sit as king forever,” because he has always reigned in the Church and shall sit in his saints; for the saints are God’s seats. “The Lord will give strength to his people,” lest it be overcome by enemies and vices. “The Lord will bless his people” as it advances “into peace,” that is, toward himself, because “he is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. I).

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXIX

“I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have received me.” The voice of Christ: I will exalt you, Father, he says, because you received me from this world and caused me to sit at your right hand (Mark XIV). The Son exalts the Father [Col. 1208D] because the Father is praised through the Son. “And you did not delight my enemies over me.” Christ’s enemies are the Jews or malignant spirits. The Jews indeed did not delight in Christ’s death, because he rose again against their will, and because of this deed they lost their nation and place. But the malignant spirits lost both their kingdom and the souls which they held captive. “O Lord my God, I cried to you.” He cried when he said: “Father, glorify your Son.” “And you healed me,” for he was weak in respect of the flesh. Therefore the Father healed him by making that flesh immortal and incorruptible when he raised it. “O Lord, you brought my soul up from hell.” He despoiled hell and led the souls of the saints with him into heaven. “You saved me from those going down into [Col. 1209A] the pit,” that is, you freed me from the hands of the Jews, because of their own will they descend into hell, death, and the jaws of the devil.

“Sing psalms to the Lord, his saints, and confess the remembrance of his holiness.” You, his saints, he says, praise the Lord and the remembrance of his holiness, because, mindful of you, he sent his Son into the world (Gal. IV) and permitted him to die for your salvation and that of all. “For wrath is in his indignation.” Praise the Lord, he says, and do not be disobedient, lest in his indignation he be angry with you; for wrath and death occur in God’s indignation. “And life is in his will,” because whoever does his will shall live eternally.

“At evening weeping shall remain, and in the morning [Col. 1209B] joy.” An apostrophe to the apostles. O apostles, at evening weeping shall remain: for the apostles mourned and wept at the Savior’s death, when he gave up his spirit about the ninth hour (Matt. XXVI); but in the morning, once the sun had risen and Christ had risen again, immense joy arose among them. Alternatively, let us understand Adam by evening and Christ by morning. For Adam drove away day and light and brought night and darkness into the world, which is characteristic of evening. But Christ removed the night and gave the true day to humankind. Therefore for those who turn to evening and imitate the first man there shall be weeping and sadness; but for those who flee to morning and follow Christ, there shall be gladness and joy. We may also figure the day of judgment by evening and morning. [Col. 1209C] For the day of judgment shall be evening for the wicked and morning for the good. Then the wicked shall receive night and pain, but the good day and eternity. Therefore for those then coming to evening there shall be weeping, and in the morning there shall be gladness and joy.

“But I, in my abundance, shall not be moved forever.” Adam, he says, set in the abundance of eternal goods, went miserably out of paradise; but I, having returned to the Father’s right hand, shall not be moved forever, and shall say:

“O Lord, by your will you bestowed strength upon my beauty,” that is, according to your will you gave me strength by which I overcame death itself; and this befell me to my glory. “You turned your face away from me.” You gave strength to me, he says, but turned your face [Col. 1209D] from my followers, because they did not persist in the same constancy but, abandoning me, all fled (Matt. XXVI). “And I was made troubled.” This too is said of the apostles: “To you, O Lord, I shall cry, and to my God I shall pray.” I shall cry, he says, and pray to the Lord that he may turn their sadness into joy. For “what profit is there for me while I go down into corruption?” What profit, he says, will there be in the shedding of my blood if those whom I redeemed are corrupted again? The Lord “heard this voice and had mercy on me,” that is, on my followers. “He became my helper,” that is, the helper of my followers. Change of person: “You turned my mourning into joy for me,” because of the resurrection. “You tore my sackcloth,” that [Col. 1210A] is, the flesh in which the soul was wrapped. “And you girded me with joy and eternity.” Hence “my glory may sing to you.” What is the Lord’s glory except resurrection and ascension? Let it sing to the Lord, because in these he is glorified. “And I shall not be pierced” by any tribulation, because “death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI). Or again, the saints are no longer pierced because the devil’s sting has been broken. Hence the Apostle says: “Where, O death,” he says, “is your sting?” (I Cor. XV). “O Lord my God, I shall confess to you forever.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXX

“In you, O Lord, I have hoped.” The voice of the Lord’s human nature: Because I have hoped in you, he says, who are the best helper, see to it that neither I nor those who are mine are ever put to shame. [Col. 1210B] “In your righteousness deliver me.” Deliver me, he says, from the iniquity of the impious, because you are righteous and I do not depart from righteousness. “Incline your ear to me,” that is, hear my prayer. “Hasten to deliver me,” that is, quickly come to my aid. “Be to me a protecting God and a house of refuge, that you may save me.” Be, he says, my Lord and protector and the house to which I may flee, because I trust in no other protection.

“For you are my strength and my refuge.” You alone are my strength; you alone are my refuge. Therefore you alone deliver and protect me. “And for your name’s sake you will lead me.” In your name I came into the world, in the Lord’s name; I proclaimed the Lord’s name. For your name, which I shall invoke, you will lead me as I [Col. 1210C] return to you. Or, you will lead me through the apostles, so that your name may be proclaimed throughout the whole earth. And you will nourish me, namely with the sweetness of the supreme good, not with the bitterness of gall, as the Jews did (Matt. XXVII). Or, you will nourish me with the same spiritual food, my body and blood. “You will draw me out of this snare which they hid for me.” Many were the snares and many the deceits which the Jews hid for Christ; yet, always fortified by divinity, he could be deceived by none. “For you are my protector.”

“In your hands I commend my spirit.” This was fulfilled when, placed upon the cross, he said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23).—“You have redeemed me, Lord, God of truth.” A prophetic interjection. Seeing Christ’s passion, the Prophet, because the world was to be redeemed in the very departure from life of our Savior, says joyfully: “You have redeemed me, Lord, God of truth.” You have now been crucified, you have now commended your spirit to the Father, and you have redeemed the world. Thus you are proved to be the true God, because you have fulfilled what you promised.

“You have hated those who observe vain things to no purpose.” The voice of Christ. The Jews observed vanities to no purpose, because, lest Christ should rise again, they guarded the tomb (Matt. 27). Those likewise observe vanities to no purpose who cling so to earthly things that they forget heavenly ones. “But I have hoped in the Lord”; and therefore I came forth from the tomb without fear and rose according to my own will (ibid.). “I shall rejoice and be glad in your mercy” [Col. 1211A]. What was that mercy? It follows: “For you have regarded my humility; you have saved my soul from necessities.” For a human being must die. Yet Christ was delivered from this necessity, because “death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6).

“And you have not shut me up in the hands of the enemy,” because he was held neither by those guarding the tomb nor by malignant spirits in hell. “You have set my feet in a spacious place,” because the apostles preach not in Judaea alone but throughout all the kingdoms of the world (Matt. 16), although they had first been commanded to preach in Judaea alone.

“Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am troubled.” I, he says, am troubled by the Jews; but the apostles are troubled by the Gentiles to whom they preach [Col. 1211B]. Therefore, Lord, have mercy on me and on those who are mine. “My eye, my soul, and my belly are troubled in anger,” because both the perfect and the imperfect were afflicted by the wrath of evildoers. Hence he said above: “While the wicked is proud, the poor man is set on fire” (Ps. 9). For the eye and soul signify the perfect; the belly, being the better part of the body, signifies the imperfect.

“For my life fails in sorrow.” Christ’s life, indeed, ends on the cross—I speak in respect of his humanity; but the lives of the apostles failed both on the cross and amid other torments, and thus in sorrow. “And my years in groanings”: they were in adversities until life’s end. Or again, they wept for their own sins and those of others [Col. 1211C]. “My strength has been weakened in poverty.” Christ’s strength is the Gospel. Hence the Apostle: “For I am not ashamed of the Gospel, for it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes” (Rom. 1). Yet it was weakened by the poverty of believers, because the teachers themselves grew weary of preaching the Gospel, as it is written: “Lord, who has believed our report?” (Isa. 53). Or Christ’s strength was weakened in poverty because God, in a human being who is poor in himself and in need of all things, did not manifest his power, but allowed himself to be mocked and afflicted. “And my bones were troubled,” that is, the apostles, who are the Church’s support. “I have become a reproach to all my enemies, exceedingly so to my neighbours, and a terror to those who know me,” because unless they killed me, they did not think they would prevail [Col. 1211D] (John 11). Or, I became a terror to those who knew me—that is, to the apostles—because they now fear to confess my name, as the prince of the apostles himself did, who denied Christ at the word of a single maidservant (John 18). “Those who saw me outside fled from me.” For the apostles saw the Jews seize Christ and, abandoning him, all fled (Matt. 26). “I was given over to forgetfulness, as one dead from the heart.” Thus, he says, I was forgotten from the heart of the Jews, as though I were dead and should not be avenged upon them. “I became as a lost vessel,” fit for no use: robbers were lost vessels, because they were hated both by God and by human beings. Therefore Christ became as a lost vessel because he was numbered among the wicked (Matt. 15). “For I heard the reproach of many dwelling round about” [Col. 1212A]; for as robbers are reproached, so Christ too was reproached by those standing around. “While they were gathered together against me, they took counsel to take away my life.” While the wicked Jews were gathered together against me, he says, in that assembly they took counsel about nothing but destroying my life.

“But I have hoped in you, Lord; I said: You are my God. My lots are in your hands,” that is, whatever good or evil is to befall me is in your power. “For they would have had no power over me unless it had been given them by you” (John 19). Therefore, “deliver me from the hand of my enemies and from those who persecute me. Make your face shine upon your servant,” that is, glorify and reveal the divinity in your Son [Col. 1212B], lest he be understood forever as merely human—he of whom it is written: “Who, being the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance” (Heb. 3).—“And save me in your mercy. Lord, let me not be confounded, for I have called upon you. Let the ungodly be ashamed”—namely the Jews, who crucified their Lord; or the Gentiles, who worshipped idols. For they shall be ashamed at the judgment, because when they desire to enter the wedding feast they will not be permitted, but, when the door is shut, will be led down into the hell which they prepared for themselves in this age. Then at last: “Let deceitful lips be made dumb, which now speak iniquity against the just man in pride and contempt.” For the Jews spoke proudly and contemptuously—that is, contrary to the usage due from servants—against the Lord, when they said, “He is guilty of death” (Matt. 26), and “Crucify, crucify” (Luke [Col. 1212C] 23).

A prophetic interjection. Seeing through the Holy Spirit these people so miserable and cast down, and seeing the saints established in such great blessedness, he cries out: “How great is the multitude of your sweetness, Lord!” You have prepared such blessedness, such glory, such great rewards for your saints, and given them goods which can neither be spoken nor conceived (1 Cor. 2).

“Which you have hidden for those who fear you.” For we do not yet see what we shall be. *To hide* is also used in the sense of *to reserve*, so that the meaning is: How great a sweetness you have reserved for those who fear you. “Which you have perfected for those who hope in you, in the sight of the children of men.” This blessedness, he says, the Lord has perfected—that is, made complete—for those who do not hope in this world and who confessed him in the sight of the children of the ungodly [Col. 1212D]. Hence he himself says: “Whoever confesses me before men, I also will confess him before my Father” (Matt. 10).—“You shall hide them in the hiding-place of your face from the disturbance of men.” Now, he says, they shall no longer be troubled by sinners, but shall remain joyful before your face. “You shall protect them in your tabernacle,” that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem, “from the contradiction of tongues”—namely, after they have been delivered from it.

“Blessed be the Lord.” Since the Prophet saw such great divine mysteries, we give thanks to the Lord, he says. Blessed be the Lord, “because he has made his mercy wonderful to me in a fortified city.” For he could well behold the wonderful mercies of God when he saw human beings and sinners, now justified, dwelling in the heavenly Jerusalem [Col. 1213A]. He also beheld God’s wonderful mercies when he saw Christ suffering for human salvation in Jerusalem, which was very strong and fortified. Thus far the Prophet; now Christ speaks:

“But I said in the excess of my mind: I am cast away from before the face of my eyes.” The Jews, he says, spoke proudly and contemptuously against me; but in ecstasy and an excess of mind, seeing their dispersion and unbelief, I said: “I am cast away from before the face of my eyes; I am abandoned by my own people. Therefore I shall call ‘my people’ those who were not my people”: rejected by the Jews, I have been chosen by the Gentiles. “Therefore you heard the voice of my supplication when I cried to you” [Col. 1213B]. I was abandoned by the Jews, he says; I prayed for the Gentiles and was heard. “Love the Lord, all his saints, because the Lord will require truth”: he who is true, he says; whoever truly loves him shall be saved. “And he will repay abundantly those who act proudly. Act manfully” in the things you have begun. “And let your heart be strengthened,” so that you may not fear death, “all you who hope in the Lord” to receive eternal life.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXXI

“Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven.” The voice of the Church, concerning the praise of confession: Blessed are those who, confessing their sins to the Lord, have deserved to receive forgiveness. Blessed also are those “whose sins through love are covered” and forgotten by the Lord [Col. 1213C]. “For charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4).—“Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin, and in whose spirit there is no deceit.” For original sin is imputed to none who has been regenerated by the water of baptism; everyone baptized shall be blessed, provided, however, that there is no deceit in his life.

“Because I kept silence, all my bones grew old.” As though he said: Let each person confess his sins; for sins increase without confession—believe one who has experienced it. I indeed kept silence and did not confess my sins as I ought; therefore my bones grew old in sins—that is, all my strength and power was crushed and burdened by their weight. “While I cried out all day”: no cry and no prayer avails unless confession comes first.

[Col. 1213D] “But because your hand was heavy upon me day and night, I was turned in my misery while the thorn was being fixed.” Because, he says, I kept silence, therefore your hand, rod, and correction were heavy upon me; for “he who spares the rod hates his son” (Prov. 13). But immediately in that very distress or misery I turned to you, while harsh correction pressed thorns into me. “I made my offence known to you, and I did not hide my injustices.” After I discovered, he says, that you were angry with me, I no longer kept silence, but, as though compelled, said: “I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord.” I have sinned greatly, Lord; I confess my sin: let your hand now cease. This I said. But you “forgave the impiety of my sin,” because, since I confessed truly, you granted mercy [Col. 1214A]. For one confesses truly who condemns himself and speaks against himself. “For this forgiveness every saint shall pray to you.” For there is no saint who does not continually say: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6).—“In an acceptable time,” that is, in this life; hence it is said: “While we have time, let us do good to all” (Gal. 5).

“Yet in a flood of many waters they shall not come near him.” The saints indeed pray continually for forgiveness of sins; nevertheless, because they are in a flood of many waters by which they are cleansed and washed, sins cannot come near them. For they are cleansed by almsgiving, prayers, fasts, tears, and the instruction of the Scriptures. Why then [Col. 1214B] do they pray? Lest they be tempted by the devil; hence the Lord says to his disciples: “Pray that you may not enter into temptation” (Matt. 26).—“You are my refuge from the tribulation that has surrounded me”: he speaks of the adversities of this age. You are my rejoicing, because I rejoice in you. “Deliver me from those surrounding me,” that is, from all vices and evils. The Lord’s response.

“I shall give you understanding.” Do not fear, he says; I shall give you understanding, by which you may be comforted and overcome your enemies. “I shall instruct you” in good works. “In this way in which you shall walk, I shall fix my eyes upon you,” so that none may be able to harm you. “Do not become like horse and mule, in whom there is no understanding.” For the horse signifies the proud and the lustful, as it is written: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” [Col. 1214C] (Joel 1). The mule, however, signifies the sluggish and unfruitful. Thus it is as though he said: Do not be proud and lustful; do not be slothful, because the sluggard would not plough on account of the cold. Do not be empty of virtues and barren.

“With bit and bridle bind fast the jaws of those who do not draw near to you.” If, he says, there are any who refuse to receive the Gospel and to draw near to you, bind them with the bit and bridle of the Law, with the hard and threatening pronouncements of Scripture, that they may at least thus be joined to the Church. “Many are the scourges of the sinner.” Therefore cease from sinning, and do not become like horse and mule, but hope in the Lord. For “mercy shall surround the one who hopes in the Lord. Rejoice in the Lord,” not in the world, not in transitory things, “and exult, you just,” in the promised mercy; “and glory, all you upright in heart,” because “he who glories, let him glory in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10) [Col. 1214D].

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXXII

“Exult, you just, in the Lord.” The voice of the Church: Until now, he says, you exulted in gold, silver, and worldly honours; but now, because you are just, exult in the Lord and in justice. “Praise befits the upright.” Therefore, he says, exult and praise the Lord, because the Lord loves the praise of such people. “Give thanks to the Lord with the harp,” that is, with sweet speech, that you may be able to soothe Saul. “Make melody to him upon the psaltery of ten strings”: in the ten strings we understand the ten commandments of the Law. Therefore make melody to the Lord upon the psaltery [Col. 1215A] of ten strings, because he is served in these ten commandments.

“Sing to him a new song.” A new man came into the world and gave a new law to the world (Gregory, Homily 32). Therefore sing a new song: namely, his birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension; for all these things are new and unheard of by earlier generations.

“Make melody well to him with a loud cry,” that is, in the words of preaching. Those make melody well in preaching who unite deeds with words. “For the word of the Lord is right.” Therefore, he says, sing a new song because the word of the Lord is right. And make melody well to him with a loud cry, because “all his works are in faith.” Divine words are right because they proclaim truth to all; his works are faithful because they deceive no one. “He loves mercy and judgment.” Sing, he says, and declare that the Lord is both merciful and just. And because he is merciful, let no one despair; but because he is just, let all do good works, “for he will render to each according to his works” (Matt. 16). “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord.” By the earth we understand the Church, upon which the Lord had such mercy that he even delivered his Son to death for it. “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established.” Proclaim this also: that the apostles were made by the Word of the Lord and established upon the firm rock in faith in the Trinity. Or it may mean the firmament itself, because “all things were made through him” (John 1). “And by the spirit of his mouth all their power” [Col. 1215C]. For the apostles’ overcoming of vices, raising of the dead, and giving sight to the blind happened not through their own strength but through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

“Gathering the waters of the sea as into a wineskin.” He established the heavens, he says, and gathered the sinners of this world into the Church as waters into a wineskin. Or again, as waters in a wineskin, so he restrains the ungodly and sinners in his power, so that they cannot rage against the saints except when he himself permits it.

“Placing the depths in storehouses.” Because he gathers sinners into the number of the saints and into the Church, who are depths and submerged in the deeps of vices. He also places the depths in storehouses when he establishes saints in heaven [Col. 1215D]; for there is the saints’ treasure, because they lay up treasure in heaven. “Let all the earth fear the Lord.” Since the Lord is such, he says, therefore let all the earth fear him.

“Let all the inhabitants of the world be moved by him.” For they have already in part been moved, since by his counsels they have passed from unbelief to faith; but they shall be moved on the day of judgment, because he will call some to himself and send others into hell (Matt. 25). “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.” Since he made all things (John 1), all things follow his command.

“The Lord scatters the counsels of the nations,” by which they thought to destroy the Church. “But he rejects the thoughts of peoples, and rejects the counsels of princes” [Col. 1216A]. For their counsel was to destroy the Church and build temples to gods. “But the counsel of the Lord remains for ever,” because there shall always be saints delivered by his counsel. Confirmation: “The thoughts of his heart unto generation and generation,” because whatever he has said and thought shall be accomplished both in this age and in the age to come. “Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord,” and blessed is the people of the Gentiles whom this Lord “has chosen for his inheritance. The Lord looked down from heaven; he saw all the children of men.” Repetition. “From his prepared dwelling-place he looked upon all who dwell on earth.” The Lord looked, he says, from the secret place of his divinity and saw humankind grievously wounded by robbers, whom neither priest [Col. 1216B] nor Levite aided. Therefore he sent his Son; he sent the Samaritan who might have mercy on him (Luke 10). For God’s looking upon someone is his having mercy. Thus, when the Son of God came, he chose the people of the Gentiles as his inheritance.

“He fashioned their hearts individually,” because he gave to some the word of wisdom, to others interpretations of words, and to others kinds of tongues (1 Cor. 12). He also fashioned the hearts of the saints individually in this respect: some desire to become monks, others hermits; some endeavour to preserve humility, others chastity. “He understands all their works.” For the Lord knows who performs good works with a pure heart and who does so for vainglory. For one who appears chaste and humble for vainglory ought rather to be called a hypocrite than chaste and humble. “The king shall not be saved by many powers” [Col. 1216C]. The people of the Gentiles, he says, shall be saved, whom the Lord has chosen for his inheritance, because they trust not in their own strength but in mercy. But earthly kings—proud giants, mighty men trusting in themselves and in their own strength—shall not be saved. Who is more powerful than a king? Who stronger than a giant? Since these are not saved by their own power and strength, let no one seek to attain salvation except through God’s mercy.

“A horse is deceptive for salvation; in the abundance of its strength it shall not be saved.” By the horse is understood the body of the soul; it is deceptive in giving salvation, because the salvation and delight of the flesh are the death and sorrow of the soul. Therefore the horse must be restrained, lest with reins loosened it fall into a pit. We may also understand proud and recalcitrant persons by horses [Col. 1216D]. “Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him,” as though he said: Neither a king by power, nor a giant by strength, nor indeed anyone by a horse shall be saved. Who then shall be saved, and through whom? It follows: “Behold, the eyes of the Lord,” that is, the gaze of his mercy, are upon those who fear him, “and upon those who hope,” not in their own strength but “in his mercy.” For what purpose? “To deliver their souls from death,” that is, from everlasting damnation; “and to feed them in famine,” because in this life he shall refresh them with spiritual teaching and in the future fill them with highest blessedness. Hence it is said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5). Therefore “our soul waits for the Lord, because he is our helper and protector, and because our heart shall rejoice in him” [Col. 1217A], when we receive rewards according to our works. And in fear “we shall hope in his holy name.” Yet hope shall not confound. “Let your mercy, Lord, be upon us, according as we have hoped in you”: that is, because we have hoped, have mercy upon us according as we have hoped.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXXIII

“I shall bless the Lord at every time.” The voice of teachers: “His praise shall always be in my mouth.” At every time, he says, I shall bless and preach the Lord; I shall always praise him, nor shall I keep silent out of fear. “My soul shall be praised in the Lord.” It shall not be praised in itself, in the wisdom of the world, or in loftiness of speech, but in the Lord, from whom it has received both virtue and power. “Let the meek hear and rejoice” [Col. 1217B]. Let the meek hear, he says, the praise of the Lord and rejoice in his benefits.

“Magnify the Lord with me.” To you I speak, meek people, who hear the Lord’s praise and this discourse: Magnify the Lord with me—that is, praise him together with me in imitation of me. “And let us exalt his name together,” so that flocks and shepherds alike may praise and magnify the Lord harmoniously and with one voice. “I sought the Lord, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my tribulations.” It is as though he said: Learn from my example how beneficial it is to magnify and seek the Lord. I sought him, was heard, and was delivered from all tribulations. “Draw near,” therefore, you too, “to him, and be enlightened.” Draw near, he says, to the light, that you may be enlightened [Col. 1217C] by the true light. “And your faces shall not be confounded.” For those not enlightened shall be confounded, because when their lamps are extinguished and they seek oil, they shall suffer a deserved rejection.

“This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him.” Thus he speaks of himself as though of another: I cried, and the Lord heard me; therefore cry out yourselves, that you may be heard.

“The angel of the Lord shall encamp around those who fear him and shall deliver them.” An exhortation to fear and draw near to the Lord. Since, he says, the Lord loves those who fear him so greatly that an angel, guarding them with defences, delivers them from all enemies, you ought indeed to draw near to him and fear him. That saints are guarded by angels is evident; for Truth itself says: “Amen I say to you, that their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” [Col. 1217D] (Matt. 18).—“Taste and see that the Lord is sweet.” Pastors ought to admonish their subjects in many ways and with many enticements. Hence the Apostle: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke; persist in season and out of season” (2 Tim. 4). This mode of speech is discerned quite clearly in this psalm. Taste, test, see, and know the sweetness and pleasantness of the Lord, who “does not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he be converted and live” (Ezek. 33).—“Blessed is the man who hopes in him,” and not in the uncertainty of riches. “Fear the Lord, all his saints.” “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110) [Col. 1218A]. “For there is no want to those who fear him. The rich have lacked and hungered,” among whom was the man who asked Lazarus for a drop of water (Luke 16). “But those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing.” For those who possess the highest and universal Good, from whom all good things come and without whom there is nothing, will lack no good thing.

“Come, therefore, children; hear me: I shall teach you the fear of the Lord.” Since, as already said, the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, let teachers of the Church begin instruction with the fear of the Lord, so that they may introduce their children into wisdom.

“Who is the man who desires life?” Now, as though all those to whom he said above, “Come,” had gathered together, he addresses them and says: “Who is the man who desires life [Col. 1218B] and loves to see good days?” Someone answering such a question says: “I.” To him he speaks: “Therefore restrain your tongue from evil, and let not your lips speak deceit,” because it is written: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. 18). Whoever guards his tongue guards his soul as well. Likewise: “The practice of righteousness is silence” (Isa. 3). And elsewhere: “If anyone thinks himself religious while not restraining his tongue, that person’s religion is vain” (Jas. 1).—“Turn away from evil and do good.” For it is not enough to abstain from evil unless good works are performed as well. “Seek peace,” that is, Christ: “For he is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2).—“And pursue it.” To follow the Lord is to imitate him. Hence he says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up [Col. 1218C] his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16). And elsewhere: “Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness” (John 8).—“The eyes of the Lord are upon the just, and his ears are open to their prayers.” Above he said: “The angel of the Lord shall encamp around those who fear him”; but now he says that he himself looks upon and guards those who fear him. Behold how great a reward is rendered to those who flee evil and do what is right. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil. For what purpose? “To destroy their memory from the earth.” This is a deterrence, because those doing evil shall be blotted from the book of life and no remembrance of them shall arise in the land of the living. “The just cried out, and the Lord heard them.” This proves that his ears are always attentive to their prayers: whenever the just cry out, they are always heard by the Lord. “And he shall deliver them from all [Col. 1218D] their tribulations,” because, when the flesh is dissolved, they are established in heavenly kingdoms. But what wonder is it if the Lord heard them? “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart.” Because he is always near and never abandons them, he hears them when they cry out; and because “God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. 50). Those are troubled in heart whose conscience reproaches them, so that they may repent of their sins. “And he shall save the humble in spirit.” “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5); for the poor in spirit are those who presume nothing from themselves. “Many are the tribulations of the just, and from all these the Lord has delivered them. The Lord keeps all their bones,” that is, all the strength [Col. 1219A] of their virtues, because neither humility is overcome by anger nor chastity by lust. “Not one of them shall be broken,” because “to everyone who has, more shall be given, and he shall abound” (Matt. 25).

“The death of sinners is most evil,” because they shall never cease, but shall live while always dying. “And those who hate the just”—that is, Christ, who justifies the ungodly, or any one of the just. For in a just person there is nothing that ought to be hated, since both human nature and justice itself are good; but in a sinner only vices are to be hated. “They shall offend,” because they shall add iniquity to iniquity, so that whoever is filthy may become ever more filthy. “The Lord shall redeem the souls of his servants.” He has already redeemed them by his blood; he redeems them also every day when he frees them from vices and bodily necessities [Col. 1219B]; and he shall redeem them in the future, because he shall deliver them from the second death. “And all those who hope in him shall not offend,” because, always ascending from virtue to virtue, they shall trample all vices beneath their feet.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXXIV

“Judge, Lord, those who harm me.” The voice of Christ in the Passion: Judge, Lord, those who harm me; render to them according to their works. “Fight against those who fight against me,” lest they always glory in their strength. “Take up weapons” to defend me and destroy them. “And arise to help me.”

“Draw out the sword and shut them in.” Draw out, he says, the sword—Titus and Vespasian—the deserved vengeance and the swords by which they may be destroyed. “Against those [Col. 1219C] who persecute me”; and shut them in by a multitude of enemies, so that not even one may be able to leave or enter the city. “Say to my soul: I am your salvation.” Of this they themselves said: “There is no salvation for him in his God” (Ps. 3). We may also understand by the sword the Lord’s soul, by whose outpouring the Jews were shut in, because their babbling and disputation wholly ceased. “Let them be confounded and ashamed.” Let them be confounded, he says, by their falsehood when they see me risen. “And let them be afraid”: for they had no real reason to fear the Romans unless they killed Christ; but afterwards they truly feared when they saw the swords of the enemies rushing upon them. Or, let them be confounded and ashamed of their sins. Hence the Apostle: “What fruit, then, had you in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6). And let them fear, not the demon, but the Lord. “Let them be turned backward and confounded.” Let them be turned backward, he says, so that they may follow the Lord, whereas they now imitate the devil. Or let them be turned backward so that they never think of future things but desire only things present and passing, and be confounded either for the better or with everlasting shame, “who devise evils against me. Let them become as dust before the face of the wind,” so that, as dust cannot resist the wind, neither may they resist their enemies. “And let the angel of the Lord” be evil, “pursuing them,” so that wherever the Jews may be, the devil may rule over them. Or the angel of the Lord means Titus and Vespasian, whom we mentioned above. “Let their ways be darkness” [Col. 1220A], so that they may not see where they can flee; “and slippery,” so that they fall while fleeing. “And let the angel of the Lord pursue them,” so that they may easily be captured—and this deservedly. “For without cause,” that is, without any cause, Pilate himself being witness (Luke 23), “they hid destruction for me.” They hid it, indeed, because they killed him by treachery. “They reproached my soul to no purpose,” that is, without any benefit to themselves they proved that Christ could rise again; or rather, they reproached him because they inflicted many insults upon him, saying: “Hail, Rabbi” (Matt. 26), and: “You have a demon” (John 8).

“Let a snare come upon him which he does not know.” I did not indeed fail to know their snares and deceits; but they are wholly ignorant what punishment and snares await them. “And let the capture which he hid,” in order to seize me, “take hold of him”—for “with the measure with which one has measured, it shall be measured back to him” (Matt. 7)—“and let him fall into the very snare” which he prepared for me. Hence it is said: “Into the pit which you prepare for your brother, you shall fall” (Prov. 26). “But my soul,” delivered from their plots, “shall rejoice in the Lord” and delight in his salvation. Then at last “all my bones shall say: Lord, who is like you?” By the bones we understand the stronger members, that is, the apostles, who, after Christ rose, began everywhere on earth to praise and preach the Lord. “Delivering the needy from the hand of those stronger than he,” that is, Christ from the hands and power of the Jews. For Christ was needy in this world [Col. 1220C], because he possessed nothing of his own. Hence he says: “Foxes have dens and birds of the sky nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 16). And the Apostle: “Though he was rich beyond all, for us he became poor, that through his poverty he might make us rich” (2 Cor. 8). “The needy and poor from those who plunder him,” that is, from the Jews or from the princes of darkness. He called them stronger because everyone who strikes appears stronger than the one struck.

“Unjust witnesses rising up questioned me about things they did not know.” The chief priests are called unjust witnesses; questioning him, they said: “We adjure you by God, tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God.” But when Christ answered, “I am,” they cried out: “You yourselves have heard the blasphemy” [Col. 1220D] (Matt. 26). Yet this was not blasphemy but truth. Therefore they were unjust witnesses, because they testified that truth was blasphemy. They did not know whether he was the Son of God because the Holy Spirit, who might have revealed this to them, was not in them. “They repaid me evil for good,” because I thought of their salvation while they thought how they might destroy me. “The barrenness of my soul,” that is, the deprivation of life, because they killed me. Or because, when they ought to have produced grain, weeds sprang up. Moreover, the seed which I sowed upon them, as though turned upon hard stones, produced no fruit for me. O my chosen vineyard: I planted you; how have you turned to bitterness? Instead of grapes you gave wild grapes; instead of wine, vinegar to the Lord [Col. 1221A]!

“But when they troubled me,” by scourging and spitting upon me, “I put on sackcloth,” because I showed them not the power of divinity but only the weakness of the flesh. For, as though clothed with sackcloth, because he was covered with flesh, he was reckoned among sinners; sackcloth befits sinners. Hence the Apostle says: “That concerning sin he might condemn sin in the flesh” (Rom. 8).—“I humbled my soul in fasting.” In fasting, he says, I afflicted myself, because I was able to incorporate none of them into myself except one of the robbers. “And my prayer shall return into my bosom.” A prayer returns into the bosom when the same supplication is frequently turned over in the heart. Or rather [Col. 1221B], the prayer which Christ made in the secret place of his heart was turned, because, as he had formerly begun to ask God for the Jews’ salvation, so afterwards he began to ask for their confusion—and deservedly.

“As with a neighbour and as with our brother, so I pleased them.” Thus, he says, I loved the Jews as a brother and a neighbour according to the flesh. “For no one has greater love than that someone should lay down his life for his friends” (John 15).—“As one mourning and sorrowful, so I humbled myself,” either by them or for them. “And they rejoiced against me,” that is, over those things that were contrary and adverse to me. “And they gathered together.” The chief priests and Pharisees gathered, indeed, into one will and “counsel to seize and kill Christ” (Mark 14) [Col. 1221C]. “Scourges were gathered against me,” because “they came against him with swords and clubs” (Matt. 26). “And I did not know”: for there was no cause why they should crucify him (Luke 23). Hence he says: “They hated me without cause” (John 15).

“And therefore they were scattered,” that is, dispersed everywhere. Or, divided within the inward person. Or again, separated from the bond of charity. “Nor were they pierced with compunction,” because they neither repent nor believe. “They tempted me”: in many ways the Jews tempted Christ.
