Hence he himself says: “Why do you tempt me, hypocrites?” (Matt. 22). “They mocked me with mockery”—“Aha! you who destroy the temple of God” (Matt. 26)—“They gnashed their teeth at me” [Col. 1221D], crying, “Crucify, crucify” (Luke 23). “Lord, when will you look upon” their iniquity? “Restore my soul” to its former rank and to your glory. “Rescuing my only one from the lions,” from the pride and violence of the Jews. If you do this, “I shall confess you in the great Church,” that is, in the Catholic Church spread throughout the world: I shall praise you with the harmonious voice of all the saints. Confirmation. “I shall praise you among a weighty people,” that is, among the Gentiles: a people whom no wind and no doctrine can tear away from you; not among those who are fickle and readily sin, whom, like dust, “the wind casts from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1), thinking never humble things but always proud ones.

“Let not those who unjustly oppose me exult over me” [Col. 1222A]. For Christ’s adversaries would have exulted over him if he had not risen after death. “Those who hate me without cause,” that is, without fault. “And wink with their eyes”: for, signaling one another with their eyes to strike him, when the Lord Christ had been slapped they said: “Prophesy to us, Christ: who is it that struck you?” (Matt. 26). They also winked with their eyes when they showed themselves his friends to his face; this is what follows:

“For indeed they spoke peaceably to me,” saying, “Good teacher” (Matt. 19); and, “We know that you are truthful” (Matt. 22); and, “You do not regard the person of men” (ibid.). These and similar expressions are peaceful words under the guise of flattery. “And, speaking in the anger of the earth, they devised deceits”: the Pharisees and priests certainly spoke in the anger of the earth [Col. 1222B], because, pouring forth words of sedition, they provoked earthly and sinful people to anger, like him who said: “It is expedient for you that one man should die for the people, and that not the whole nation should perish” (John 11). They said this for no other reason than to seize and kill Christ by deceit (Mark 14). “And they opened their mouth wide against me”: all openly blaspheming, “they said, ‘Aha, aha!’” This is mocking praise. “Our eyes have seen”: we have seen what he was like, and at last we have recognized him. Where are the miracles he performed? Why does he who saved others not save himself? (Matt. 27). Why does he who raised Lazarus not raise himself? “You have seen, Lord,” their insults and reproaches. “Lord, do not depart from me; attend to my judgment,” that is [Col. 1222C], spread abroad and make manifest to all nations the judgment by which I was judged, so that no one may any longer despair, now that such a sacrifice has been offered. “My God and my Lord, [come] to my cause,” that is, come and distinguish my righteousness from their wickedness. “Judge me according to your righteousness, O Lord my God,” that is, since you are righteous, distinguish me as unjustly condemned and do what is just. “And let them not exult over me”—which they certainly would do unless Christ rose from death.

“Let them not say in their hearts, ‘Aha, aha, [blessed are] our souls’; nor let them say, ‘We have devoured him,’” that is, utterly destroyed him. Yet they could not do this when they heard that he had risen. “Let them blush [Col. 1222D] and be ashamed together, who rejoice at my evils.” Behold, here the prayer changes; for he no longer asks that the Father forgive them, but that they may blush and be ashamed. Let them blush, he says, for their falsehood; let them fear punishment, their own shame, and the sudden destruction that awaits those who rejoice at my evils—that is, not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them, as Pilate himself did when he said: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man” (Matt. 27). “Let those who speak evil against me be clothed with confusion and shame”: they were indeed clothed with confusion and disgrace because he rose while the guards were unwilling; and they will be so clothed at the judgment, when they see as Judge him whom they scourged as a man. Here he speaks on behalf of the Church. “Let those who desire my righteousness exult and rejoice” [Col. 1223A]. Let the Jews, he says, be clothed with confusion; but let those rejoice and be glad who desire to follow my righteousness, or who call me righteous. “And let them always say: ‘Magnified be the Lord, who desire the peace of his servant.’” For the Church always magnifies the Lord, and indeed desires to have the same peace that Christ has, who according to his flesh is the Father’s servant. “And my tongue shall meditate on your righteousness,” that is, the apostles and teachers through whom, as though by my own tongue, I proclaim to my Church my will. “And [shall meditate] your praise all day long”: for as long as time endures, the Church will always praise the Lord.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 35

“The unjust man said, that he might sin within himself.” Within himself, he says—in his heart, in his thoughts—the wicked man said: “I shall sin, steal, murder, accuse innocent persons and neighbors, and thus become rich.” Or, “within himself,” that is, against himself; for everyone who sins acts contrary to himself. “There is no fear of God before his eyes.” What wonder if he promises himself that he will sin, when he does not have the fear of God before the eyes of his heart? For the fear of God is the bridle of sin.

“For he has acted deceitfully in his sight,” that is, in the inward person whom God sees and knows; or again, the Jews acted deceitfully in Christ’s presence. Hence it comes about “that his iniquity is found unto hatred,” because, he says, he always acts deceitfully; his iniquity cannot be discovered except with hatred. “The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit”: their words are full of fraud and falsehood, because they say one thing with their mouth and turn another over in their heart [Col. 1223C]. “He would not understand, that he might do good.” Many understand good things and the Scriptures, but not in order to keep them. Hence the Apostle says: “Not the hearers of the law, but the doers, shall be justified before God” (Rom. 2). And likewise: “If you wish to be perfect, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19).

“He devised iniquity upon his bed,” that is, in the secret chamber of his heart. “He stood in every way that was not good,” because he persevered in every evil; this is what follows: “But he did not hate wickedness.” Whoever does not hate wickedness does not love mercy.

“Lord, your mercy is in heaven.” In the wicked just mentioned, he says, there is nothing but deceit, iniquity, and wickedness; but in the saints, whom we understand by “heaven,” are mercy and truth. Mercy is indeed in the saints [Col. 1223D], because they do not depart from the command of their Master, who says: “Be merciful, as I also am merciful” (Luke 6). And elsewhere: “Blessed is the man who has mercy and lends” (Ps. 111). Truth is in them because they deceive no one, unlike the man of whom we spoke above: “The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit.” In such persons there is no truth. “Unto the clouds”—understand, “reaching.” What are the clouds but apostles, teachers, and prophets? For as clouds distill rain, so these pour forth teaching. Thus the truth of God reaches as far as these, because no one has fully known the divine mysteries except one to whom the Holy Spirit has revealed them. Hence Truth itself says: “No one knows the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son shall wish to reveal him” (Matt. 11).

[Col. 1224A] “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God”: understand, “it makes men [such].” For all who imitate and cultivate God’s righteousness become like mountains; for as mountains are illumined by the sun, so the saints are always illumined by Christ. Whichever way the sun turns, it continually illuminates the mountains. “Your judgments are a great abyss,” that is, a deep and dark profundity. “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. 2). Or, “His judgments are incomprehensible” (ibid.), because by mercy he chooses some, and by truth condemns others, as it is written: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Rom. 9).

“You will save men and beasts, O Lord.” Although, he says, your mercy is in heaven, nevertheless you will save both men and beasts—that is, the wise and rational, and the brutish and unlearned; or, men and beasts, that is, the righteous and sinners. Or again, men, that is, carnal and imperfect people; and the beasts of men, that is, the apostles, who bear the burden of the whole Church [Col. 1224B]. “How you have multiplied your mercy, O God!” Seeing that the Lord has saved men and beasts, righteous and sinners, and marveling at so great a mercy, he cries: “How you have multiplied your mercy, O God!”

“But the sons of men,” that is, the entire continuation of the Church until the end of the age, “shall hope in the shelter of your wings,” that is, in your protection. Or we understand the two wings as the two arms of the cross, because, strengthened by the sign of the cross, we drive the enemy away from us. Or the two wings are the two Testaments, instructed by which we overcome heretics. We may also understand by the two wings love of God and love of neighbor; whoever lacks these has nothing by which to fly toward the kingdom of heaven.

“They shall be made drunk from the abundance of your house,” that is, from the overflowing graces of the Holy Spirit or the fullness of the Scriptures; for the apostles were full of the Holy Spirit when the Jews said that they were drunk with new wine (Acts 2). “And you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight,” that is, from the impetuosity of your mercy and the blessedness of the highest and ineffable good. You can do this indeed, “because with you is the fountain of life,” that is, Christ with the Father, as the Gospel says: “And the Word was [Col. 1224D] with God” (John 1). Christ is the fountain of life, as he himself says: “The water which I give—whoever drinks from it shall never thirst again” (John 4). “And in your light we shall see light.” Christ is light from light, who “enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). In this light we shall see light, because he is a lamp to our feet, shining before the Father’s face and glory. That this may happen, do what follows: “Extend your mercy to those who know you,” that is, your Son. Confirmation. “And your righteousness to those who are upright in heart,” so that the righteous and merciful may come to you. “Let not the foot of pride come upon me”: for the devil is the origin and support of pride. “And let not the hand of sinners move me,” that is, let diabolic suggestion and temptation not separate me from the love of God [Col. 1225A]. “There have fallen those who work iniquity,” those same evil spirits who never cease to work wickedness; for because of pride they were cast out from the seats of heaven. “They were expelled by you and could not stand.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 36

“Do not be envious of evildoers.” The voice of teachers to the Church. *Aemulari* has many meanings. Sometimes it is used for “to love,” as: “For I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God” (2 Cor. 11). Sometimes for “to imitate,” as: “Be zealous for the better gifts” (1 Cor. 12). But sometimes for “to envy,” as in this place: “Do not be envious of evildoers,” that is, do not envy those who act wickedly so as to do the same. “Neither be jealous of those who commit iniquity.” Love the person, he says; do not love the robber. Love human nature, but do not love adultery; for evil must everywhere be rejected.

“For like grass they shall quickly wither.” For a time they rejoice and flourish, but soon they dry up and are reduced to dust. “And like the green plants of the herbs,” that is, their verdure, “they shall quickly fall.” Hence Isaiah: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass. The grass has dried up, and the flower has fallen” (Isa. 40). “Hope in the Lord, and do goodness.” Do not, he says, envy evildoers, lest you too perish so swiftly. Rather, hope in the Lord—not in riches, not in beauty, not in the flower of the world. And do goodness, that is, show mercy to all [Col. 1225C]. “Inhabit the land,” that is, the holy Church, “and you shall be fed from its riches,” that is, from the sacred volumes. Or, “inhabit the land,” that is, rule over the flesh and do not permit it to wander according to its desires, and you shall be fed from its riches. “Delight in the Lord,” not in desires of the flesh or momentary goods. “And he shall give you” what these cannot give, namely, “the petitions of your heart.” For if, as is true, “the spirit desires against the flesh, and the flesh against the spirit” (Gal. 5), the petitions of the flesh are one thing, those of the spirit—that is, of the heart—another.

“Reveal your way to the Lord.” O most saving commands! The most wise and merciful teachers of the Church admonish us not to envy the wicked, not to love iniquity, to hope in the Lord, to delight in the Lord, and to confess our ways [Col. 1225D] and works to the Lord. “And hope in him, and he himself shall act.” What will he do? It follows: “And he shall bring forth your righteousness like light,” so that it may never be obscured in darkness and vices; for light is not overcome by darkness. Or, he shall bring righteousness forth like light because, raising it from this obscurity, he will make it manifest to angels and people. “For the saints shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of God” (Matt. 13). Confirmation. “And your judgment like noon”: he will make bright, free of every obscurity and darkness, that judgment by which you resolved to imitate the Lord, follow the faith, and act accordingly. This will take place on the day of judgment, when “the saints shall stand in great constancy against those who afflicted them” (Wis. 5) [Col. 1226A]. Seeing them in such glory, the wicked will say: “Behold how they have been counted among the sons of God. We fools considered their life madness” (ibid.). “Be subject to the Lord, and pray to him.” “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matt. 4).

“Do not be envious of one who prospers in his way,” that is, of a person who commits injustices. For many prosper in deceit, many in theft, many in perjury, and many in robbery; but these are not God’s ways, but human ways.

“Cease from anger.” “For the anger of a man does not work the righteousness of God” (Jas. 1). And: “Let not the sun set upon your anger” (Eph. 4). Repetition. “And abandon fury.” Or again, anger belongs to the mind, whereas fury belongs to the body; for fury is what carries people into adultery. “Do not be envious, so as to act wickedly,” but rather that you may do good.

“For those who act wickedly shall be exterminated.” They shall indeed be cut off, who remain outside the boundaries of the inheritance; or they shall soon be driven out of their bodies. “But those who wait for the Lord shall inherit the land”: those who await the Lord shall inherit the land of the living, or shall rule over their own flesh.

“And yet a little while, and the sinner shall not be.” Yet, he says, there will be a little time, and afterward the sinner shall not be, because he will be utterly destroyed. “And you shall seek his place and not find it”: that is, if you happen to seek his place, you will not be able to find it. For what does not exist cannot have a place. “But the meek shall inherit the land.” “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” (Matt. 5); for it will be their inheritance. They also possess their own flesh, lest they delight in vices. “And they shall delight in an abundance of peace.” For there will be no sedition or discord there; spirit will agree with flesh, and flesh with spirit.

Meanwhile, “the sinner watches the righteous,” in order to seize and destroy him; for thus it is read in the Gospel: “And they watched him” (Luke 14). “And he shall gnash his teeth against him,” gnashing the teeth of wickedness and impiety, by which he endeavors to devour him; for through the movement of the body we understand the disposition of the mind. “But the Lord shall laugh at him, because he foresees that his days are coming” [Col. 1226D]: for the Lord laughs at the sinner’s joy and exultation, because he knows when and what punishment will be exacted from them.

“Sinners have drawn the sword and bent their bow.” By the sword we understand open and manifest persecution; by the bow, hidden and deceitful deception, by which they lie in wait for the saints. “That they may deceive the poor and needy, that they may slay the upright in heart.” They deceive with the bow, but slay with the sword. The poor person is one who has nothing; the needy person is one who, although without resources, nevertheless possesses something. “Let their sword enter into their own hearts, and let their bow be broken.” Everyone who attempts to harm another first wounds himself with his own weapon; and the bow is broken when deceit and evil intent fail to produce their effect. “Better is a little to the righteous than the great riches of sinners” [Col. 1227A], as though he said: The poverty of the righteous is better than the riches of sinners. The one abounds with little, while the other thirsts though full; the one saves his soul, while the other hates both body and soul. But “what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world, yet suffers loss of his soul?” (Matt. 16). Better for this man is faith, which is compared to a grain of mustard seed, than for that man the faithlessness that wanders everywhere. “For the arms of sinners shall be broken,” that is, the strengths, powers, and riches in which they trust. “But the Lord strengthens the righteous” [Col. 1227B], lest they be overcome by injustice. “The Lord knows the days of the undefiled”: he knows how they lived and in what condition they ended their lives. Or, he knows because he loved them. Hence, on the contrary, he will say to the wicked: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25). “For everyone who does not know shall be unknown” (1 Cor. 14). “And their inheritance shall be forever,” that is, in Christ or in everlasting life. “They shall not be confounded in the evil time,” because to the reprobate it will be said: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire.” “And in the days of famine they shall be satisfied.” The days of famine will occur at that same time because all, whether good or evil, will desire to receive eternal joy; but when all the wicked have been expelled, a feast and wedding banquet will be prepared only for the good, while, on the contrary, “sinners alone shall perish. For the enemies of the Lord, as soon as they have been honored” [Col. 1227C] with vain and temporal glory, “and exalted” in possessions and riches, “shall fail like smoke,” because they will appear nowhere. Therefore sinners shall perish. Or they perish like smoke because the higher they rise, the more completely they vanish—and deservedly so.

“The sinner shall borrow and not repay.” For a human being has nothing that has not been received on loan, as it is written: “For what do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4). Nature created us naked. Therefore a human being has nothing that was not received on loan. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “A certain man, going abroad, called his servants and entrusted his goods to them; and to one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one” (Matt. 25). Behold, the servants received their master’s money on loan. But whoever has faithfully administered it and can repay the master on his return with interest, will hear this from his master: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your lord” (ibid.) [Col. 1227D]. The rich administer faithfully when they make alms from their wealth; teachers administer faithfully when they carry neither purse nor bag. But sinners, borrowing from the Lord riches, wisdom, virtues, and understanding, neither render him thanks nor supply the poor nor repay the money with profit. Rightly, therefore, they shall fail like smoke. “But the righteous man has mercy and gives.” He has mercy on others, he says, so that the Lord may have mercy on him also and repay the reward of mercy.

[Col. 1228A] “For those who bless him shall inherit the land.” The righteous receive this recompense because they shall inherit the land of the living. “But those who curse him shall utterly perish.” They shall truly perish, because they shall die both in soul and body. “With the Lord the steps of the man” who fears him “shall be directed,” because he shall go from strength to strength unto God. “And he shall desire his way,” because he walks according to righteousness.

“When he falls, he shall not be dashed down,” because as soon as he sins, he repents, and is strengthened by that very repentance. Or, when they fall into some adversities of this age, they shall nevertheless not be dashed down in the inward person. Why? “Because the Lord supports him with his hand,” and is never separated from the righteous. “I was young, and indeed have grown old; and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread” [Col. 1228B]. I have not seen, he says, the righteous forsaken by the Lord from the beginning of my lifetime, nor his seed lacking bread. Whoever seeks is in need; but the righteous does not seek because he is not in need. For the seed—that is, the imitators—of the righteous do not lack bread, because they always abound both in bodily and spiritual sustenance; nature is content with little and with the smallest things. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not be anxious, saying: ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’” (Matt. 6).

“All day long he has mercy and lends.” Because he has mercy on others and lends, it is thereby proved that he is not in need. For how can one who has nothing give? Therefore the righteous person has, since he is able to give; he has mercy [Col. 1228C] and lends. “And his seed shall be in blessing,” because his works, his imitators, and his exhortation are blessed by the Lord. “Therefore turn away from evil and do good,” so that the same may happen to you. Turn away from evil, turn aside from sin, flee the devil, follow good, imitate God. “And dwell for age upon age.” Where? In the Church, in the unity of faith, in the heavenly Jerusalem, in right judgment, so that you may never deviate from truth. “For the Lord loves judgment,” that is, truth. “And he will not forsake his saints”: this is the proof of one who loves truth. He does not forsake them because he preserves them forever. “The unjust shall be punished,” that is, eternally condemned, “and the seed of the wicked shall perish,” that is, their works or followers. “But the righteous shall inherit the land” of the living, not of the dead, or their own incorruptible bodies. “And they shall dwell upon it for age upon age. The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom,” both in this age and in the future. It shall not meditate injustice or deceit with which to deceive brothers, but shall always devote itself to wisdom alone. “And his tongue shall speak judgment,” that is, not pride but established truth. “The law of his God is in his heart,” which both forbids sin and teaches the doing of good. “And therefore his steps shall not be overthrown” [Col. 1228D] by the unjust and sinners. For “the sinner considers the righteous,” in order to overthrow him and turn aside his steps. “And he seeks to put him to death,” but he certainly will not do so. “But the Lord shall not forsake him in his hands,” because, although he may seize the body, he cannot seize the soul [Col. 1229A] (Matt. 10).

“Nor shall he condemn him when judgment is rendered for him,” that is, for that person’s glory and honor; this shall happen at the judgment. Therefore “wait for the Lord,” who will avenge you. Hence the Apostle says: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord” (Rom. 12). “And keep his way,” that is, keep the commandments. “And he shall exalt you” to heavenly things, “that you may receive the land as an inheritance,” namely, that land which no hostile storm can take from you. “When sinners perish, you shall see”—you shall not perish, but you shall see them perishing.

“I saw the wicked exceedingly exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon, and I passed by, and behold, he was not.” I saw, he says, wicked persons very great and lofty, endowed for a time with earthly honors [Col. 1229B]; and immediately, reflecting on eternity, I passed to the end of their lives, and behold, he was not. For if anyone passes to understanding and says in reflection, “Where is Caesar now? Where is Pompey? Where is Octavian? Where is Nero’s power?” he will certainly not find them. “And I sought him, and his place was not found”: for one who is not does not have a place. Therefore “keep innocence, and behold equity,” lest you perish after the manner of the wicked, “because there are remnants for the peaceful person.” But what remnants? Life after death. We may also understand by peaceful persons the apostles, through whose teaching the world has been made peaceful. For these there are remnants and eternal recompense. Hence the Apostle says: “If anyone’s work which he has built upon remains, he shall receive a reward” (1 Cor. 3). “The unjust shall utterly perish; together the remnants of the wicked shall perish” [Col. 1229C], because no life after death remains for them. “But the salvation of the righteous” shall be “from the Lord,” who is truly able to save. And the Lord shall be “their protector in the time of tribulation. And the Lord shall help them” amid the temptations of the age. “And he shall rescue them from sinners and save them” on the day of judgment, “because they hoped in him.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 37

“Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger.” Rebuke me, he says, but not in anger or fury; rather, in mercy and compassion. The voice of any penitent person.

[Col. 1229D] “For your arrows are fixed in me.” What are we to understand by arrows but words of correction? “And you have strengthened your hand upon me,” because you have chastised me with a master’s rod. Therefore do not scourge me further in anger and fury, because I have not forgotten your teaching, but it is fixed in my heart like a very sharp arrow. He speaks in the manner of a disciple imploring his master’s mercy. We may also understand by arrows the miseries of this age, so that this is the voice of humankind lamenting so many calamities, as though saying: Do not be angry, Lord, with your people, beset on every side by such miseries and distresses. For here your arrows—due vengeance, diseases, plagues, famine, and the other adversities of this age—wound and afflict us. Here the assaults of vices and the snares of demons disturb us. It remains, therefore, if you are angry with us, that we may not wholly perish.

“There is no health in my flesh because of your anger.” In the first root, he says, we sinned; we lost immortality, came to know your wrath, and became mortal. What health or steadfastness, then, can there be in us? “There is no peace in my bones.” My bones have been terrified. Therefore they cannot have peace. For who can have peace among enemies? By bones we understand memory, understanding, and reason; because these are disturbed by vices, they often lose peace. This may also be understood of penitents, who, recognizing God’s anger and their own sins, devote themselves continually to fasts and vigils and scarcely cling to their bones.

[Col. 1230B] “For my iniquities have gone over my head.” Therefore, he says, there is no peace in my bones, because iniquities preside over and dominate the mind; for “head” is used for the mind, which is the chief part of the soul. Hence the Gospel says: “Lift up your heads” (Luke 21). “Like a heavy burden, they have weighed upon me”: sins weigh down those who wish to lay them aside, just as, conversely, they are light to those who delight in them.

“My scars have become putrid and corrupt.” Formerly, he says, I employed the stench of vices as a sweet odor, but now my sins have begun to stink to me. This happens because my scars have become corrupt. For sores and scars become corrupt when sins are revealed. “Because of my folly,” the vices that were cut into me have become putrid and the sores have been opened, because I have recognized my folly. For who but a wise person recognizes folly?

“I have become wretched and bent down unto the end.” For the Apostle knew himself to be wretched when he said: “Unhappy man that I am, who shall free me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7). Those are bent down unto the end who, wholly humbling themselves under Christ’s yoke, perform repentance in ashes and sackcloth. “All day long I went about sorrowful,” because I continually wept for my sins. What wonder? “For my loins are filled with illusions.” He has put a part for the whole. Because, he says, my flesh was full of the illusions of demons, I could not be without sorrow [Col. 1230D], “and” because “there is no health in my flesh,” which is always wounded by vices. Hence, “I was afflicted and humbled exceedingly,” knowing that “through many tribulations I must enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Acts 14). “I roared from the groaning of my heart.” For the saints roar and weep bitterly because their hearts always groan under consciousness of sins; and you know this indeed. “Lord, all my desire is before you, and my groaning is not hidden from you.” You know, then, that I was humbled and groaned for my sins. “My heart is troubled within me,” that is, my soul. But why is it troubled? Because “my strength has forsaken me,” that is, God himself, or immortality. “And the light of my eyes—it also is not with me” [Col. 1231A], because, having lost the way of truth, I followed the devil and error.

“My friends and my neighbors drew near and stood against me.” The voice of the Head, as though saying: O human being, there is nothing you ought to complain about, nothing for which you ought to lament amid calamities. Look upon me afflicted; look upon me crucified; look upon me bearing your sins; look upon me enduring and taking away the miseries of the world. Therefore be comforted, have hope, do not be broken by adversities. “My friends”—this is irony, for he likewise called Judas friend: “Friend, for what have you come?” (Matt. 26), though he certainly was not a friend—“and my neighbors,” according to the flesh, “drew near and stood against me.” For they did not draw near in order to believe, but rather in order to kill.

[Col. 1231B] “And those who were near me stood far off,” that is, the disciples, because “all, leaving him, fled” (ibid.), as the Gospel says: “But when they had seized him, all his acquaintances stood at a distance” (Luke 23). “And those who sought my life used violence,” because they dragged me after them, and compelled James to flee naked, leaving behind his linen cloth (Mark 14). Peter too was so constrained that he denied him three times (Matt. 26).

“And those who sought evils against me spoke vanities,” because they thought to overcome me by false testimonies. “And all day long they devised deceits,” by which they might accuse me before Pilate. “But I, as though deaf, did not hear,” because I gave no answer to anyone [Col. 1231C]. Hence one of them said: “Do you not hear how many testimonies they speak against you?” (Matt. 27). “And like one mute, not opening his mouth,” as it is written: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53). “And I became like a person who does not hear and has no reproofs in his mouth.” This is an exposition of the preceding verse: “For in you, Lord, I have hoped.” Therefore, he says, I did not defend myself because I hoped not in myself but in you. Hence the Jews also said, as though reproaching him: “He trusted in God; let him deliver him if he wills” (Matt. 27). “And you will hear me, O Lord my God.” But why will you hear? It follows:

“For I said: Let not my enemies ever exult over me” [Col. 1231D]. They certainly would have done so unless I rose. “And while my feet are shaken, they spoke great things against me,” because, when the disciples’ feet were shaken into flight, they began to mock him. What wonder?

“For I am prepared for scourges.” As Peter says: “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten” (1 Pet. 2). “And my sorrow is always before me,” not only for myself, but also for my own.

“For I shall declare my iniquity.” Not because he committed iniquity, but because iniquity was done against him. “And I shall be concerned for my sin,” that is, I shall be solicitous concerning the sin the Jews committed against me. Thus we speak of “the assault of a city,” not because the city assaults someone, but because it has been assaulted by someone.

“But my enemies live.” They certainly shall not live, but shall die in death. “And they have been strengthened against me”: the Jews themselves are witnesses that, since Christ suffered, they have always been base and weak, without honor or strength. “And those who hate me unjustly have multiplied” [Col. 1232A]: they have not in fact multiplied, but have diminished both in offspring and in wealth—and deservedly so. For “those who return evil to me for good were slandering me.” Who can enumerate all the good things that the Lord did for the Jewish people? Who can set forth the mockeries and reproaches the Jews inflicted upon his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ? “Because I pursued goodness.” For this was the greater and chief reason that he died: because “he made himself the Son of God” (John 19), and because “he healed on the Sabbath” (John 9). This was nothing other than goodness. Therefore, “do not forsake me, O Lord my God; do not depart from me.” When, he says, I have despoiled hell, do not forsake me, but “attend to my help,” so that I may come to you as victor in triumph, “Lord, God of my salvation.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 38

“I said: I will guard my ways.” The voice of the Church. One guards one’s ways who protects good works from vices. “So that I may not sin with my tongue.” For those sin with the tongue who give what is holy to dogs and cast pearls before swine (Matt. 7); but this person promises so to guard his works that he may sin neither in deed nor in speech.

“**I set a guard over my mouth.**” I did not answer those who reproached me, nor did I curse those who cursed me; rather, I set a guard over my mouth, in accordance with that saying: “Bind up your silver and gold securely, and make a door and a bar for your mouth.” “**When the sinner stood against me**”—one who listened, not for edification, but in order to dispute with me and rebuke me. “**I became mute and was humbled,**” because, as though victorious, I endured their chatter. “**And I kept silence even from good things,**” because they were unwilling to obey the truth. Something similar is read in Ezekiel: when he wished to preach to the Jews, the Lord said to him: “I shall make your tongue cleave to the roof of your mouth, because they are a rebellious house” (Ezek. III).—“**And my pain was renewed,**” that is, it increased still more and became more unbearable. “**My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation fire shall blaze;**” for Isaiah too was inflamed with such anger when he said: “Lord, who has believed our report?” (Isa. LIII).

“**I spoke with my tongue,**” that is, with the tongue of the heart, in thought, which the sinner cannot refute. But what did I say? “**Make known to me, O Lord, my end.**” For no one can know his end in this life. The Apostle desired to see his end when he said: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. I).—“**And what is the number of my days;**” for those days are truly said to exist which are everlasting and have no end. “**That I may know what is lacking to me.**” No one placed in this world can fully know what he lacks; but when he has reached that heavenly and ineffable blessedness, then he will know that in this world he was wretched and in need of every good thing. “**Behold, thou hast made my days measurable.**” Each phrase answers to the other: Show me, he says, those days, because these indeed pass away and have no reckoning. Let me know what is lacking to me, because this present substance of mine is mine indeed, yet before thee it is accounted as nothing. Hence it is written: “All nations before him are as though they were not” (Isa. XL). Or again: the substance and existence even of the saints is as nothing in comparison with that Being which they shall possess before the Lord; for they “shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of God” (Matt. XIII).

[Col. 1233B] “**Yet every living human being is altogether vanity; yet man passes away in an image, and is troubled in vain.**” These two verses correspond to the preceding verse. Although, he says, days are measurable and transitory, human frailty nevertheless persists in vanity. Here he has used *man* for the sinner; and although this substance is nothing, nevertheless man passes away in an image, because in order to gather imaginary and false goods, man traverses kingdoms after kingdoms, seas, and every danger—and truly is *man*, because he seeks not heaven but earth and dust. Or: man, made in the image of God (Gen. I), passes away because he imitates not God’s likeness but the likeness of the devil. Yet he is troubled in vain.

[Col. 1233C] For he “**stores up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it.**” Therefore, he says, he is troubled in vain, because although he acquired many goods at the greatest dangers, even at the risk of death itself, he nevertheless does not know for whom he gathered them—whether for thieves, enemies, or stepchildren.

“**And now what is my expectation?**” Not gold or silver, nor the aforesaid riches, in acquiring which people sweat. “**Is it not the Lord?**” Truly the Lord: once he is received, nothing will be lacking. “**And my substance is with thee,**” which neither moth destroys nor thieves dig up or steal (Matt. VI). “**Deliver me therefore from all my iniquities,**” as thou oughtest to do, for “**thou hast made me a reproach to the foolish.**” For when he sent the disciples to preach, he gave them as a reproach to the foolish. Hence he himself says: “If they persecuted me, they will persecute you also. But they will do all these things to you on account of my name” (John XV).

“**I became mute and did not open my mouth,**” but with patience and silence I endured all the torments of my enemies, following the Master, who was led as a sheep to slaughter and did not open his mouth (Isa. LIII). “**Because thou hast done it, remove thy scourges from me.**” I am thy handiwork, thy creature; thou hast made me: have mercy upon me.

“**I have failed beneath the strength of thy hand.**” As the Lord tests his chosen ones like gold in a furnace (Wis. III), so he chastens every son whom he receives (Heb. XII); whence they fail beneath the strength of his power and lose the vigor of the flesh. Thus the Apostle says: “I have been crucified to the world” (Gal. VI). Confirmation: “**In rebukes, because of iniquity, thou hast corrected man;**” for a person is not corrected without cause.

[Col. 1234A] “**And thou hast caused his soul to waste away like a spider,**” because, weaving and spinning for itself the garment of righteousness, through devotion and diligence in the work it has wasted away from all the fatness of vices. This is that wedding garment; whoever has not put it on will not deserve Christ’s banquet. Hence Solomon says: “She sought wool and flax, and worked with the counsel of her hands” (Prov. XXXI). Likewise: “She put her hand to strong things, and her fingers grasped the distaff” (ibid.). By spinning this wool and flax for itself, the soul of the man who speaks has wasted away from every concupiscence of the flesh. “**Yet every man is troubled in vain,**” because few, imitating examples of goodness, separate themselves from the vanity of the world. “**Hear my prayer, O Lord, and receive my supplication; give ear to my tears: do not be silent,**” but answer me, “**for I am a stranger,**” dwelling in this world, “**with thee,**” because I do not depart from thy will, “**and a sojourner like all my fathers,**” because “while we are in the body, we are away from the Lord” (II Cor. V). For this psalm is made for those who pass onward, who, passing from the pilgrimage of this world to their homeland, are rightly called sojourners.

“**Forgive me, that I may be refreshed, before I depart.**” [Col. 1234C] Before I die, he says, forgive me my sins, so that in that heavenly blessedness I may have refreshment. “**And I shall be no more,**” because in hell there is no redemption; for if, my sins not having been forgiven, I arrive there, he says, I know that I shall be no more. For it is better not to be than to be unhappily.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXXIX

“**In waiting I waited for the Lord.**” The voice of the Church: Long, he says, I waited for the Lord who would deliver me from the miseries of this age. For this Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob waited; this Isaiah and Jeremiah awaited; this David himself, the composer of this utterance, awaited. “**And he inclined to me,**” that is, he came into the world for my joy and benefit. Hence the Lord himself says: “Many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Luke X). Likewise: “Abraham your father rejoiced to see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John VIII).—“**And he heard my prayers.**” He came, he says, and heard me. For no one has entreated Christ without finding mercy. “**And he drew me out of the pit of misery,**” that is, out of hell, or from the depth of vices. Confirmation: “**And from the mire of dregs,**” that is, from the error of the letter, or of paganism.

“**And he set my feet upon a rock.**” My feet, he says—my perceptions, my works—he set and established in himself and in faith in him, lest they be plunged into the pit and mire of dregs. “**And he directed my steps.**” He did not permit me, once placed upon the rock, to remain idle, but directed my feet to preach the Gospel. Or: he converted my works, which were crooked and rough, into straight and level paths. “**And he put a new song in my mouth.**” He did indeed direct my steps toward evangelizing; yet he did not wish my mouth to be empty, borrowed, and speechless, but gave me a new song, because a new man came into the world and gave a new law to the world (Gregory, Homily 32). “**A hymn to our God.**” He gave me, he says, a hymn acceptable to our God, not vain philosophy or the buffoonery of comic actors.

“**Many shall see and fear.**” For those who were blind and understood nothing about God were enlightened upon hearing this. Therefore you apostles are the light of the world (Matt. V), since you enlighten the blind. And they shall fear. What shall they fear? Certainly not their former vanity, but the Lord himself, whose “fear is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. CX).—“**And they shall hope in the Lord,**” not in the uncertainty of riches, which one possesses today and cannot find tomorrow.

“**Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord.**” They shall indeed hope in the Lord, and blessed is the man whose hope shall be the name of the Lord. The name of the Lord is Jesus, which is interpreted “Savior.” Blessed therefore is the person who hopes to be saved by Jesus.

“**And he has not looked to vanities and false insanities,**” so as to worship idols and serve avarice, or desire riches and worldly honors, which drive people mad. “**Thou, O Lord God, hast done many wonderful works.**” Seeing today many believers who yesterday worshipped idols, the preachers cried out: “Thou, O Lord God, hast done many wonderful works, **and none is like thee in thy thoughts.**” Behold, consider this.

[Col. 1235C] “**I proclaimed and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number.**” The apostles proclaimed, the nations believed, and that offspring was born which is compared to the stars of heaven, whose multitude is beyond counting.

“**Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire,**” because thou didst choose not the Jews but the people of the nations. Hence the Lord himself, questioning the Jews, says: “What is this: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice’?” (Matt. IX). In these words he indicates that he desired not the Jews, who offered sacrifices of goats and bulls (Lev. XVI), but the Gentiles, who are saved by mercy alone. “**But thou hast perfected ears for me,**” because they believed the apostles by hearing alone (Mark I). For the Jews read in the prophets, heard and saw Christ, yet did not believe (John X); the nations, however, did not see him, but believed when they heard the Gospel (Acts XIII). “**Burnt offering and sacrifice for sin thou hast not required,**” because not even for sins ought such a sacrifice to be offered. We may also understand it thus: thou didst desire neither burnt offering nor sacrifice for sin; “**then I said: Behold, I come.**” Thus far the Church speaks; now Christ speaks, answering the first verse of this psalm:

[Col. 1236A] Thou, he says, didst wait in waiting for me; but now I have said: Behold, I come, I assume flesh, and deliver thee from the mire of dregs. An apostrophe to the Father: I come, Father, as thou hast commanded me, “**that I might do thy will. And thy law is in the midst of my heart,**” which I indeed, my God, desired, just as “**in the head of the book it is written of me.**” For this is the order. But now let us unfold the meaning: in the beginning of this book it is written: “But his will is in the law of the Lord” (Ps. I). This is what is said here: “that I might do thy will”; and, “he shall meditate in his law day and night” (ibid.). Here, however, it is written: “And thy law is in the midst of my heart.” These are sufficiently equivalent.

“**I proclaimed thy righteousness in the great assembly,**” [Col. 1236B] because both in person and through the apostles he taught the universal Church (Mark XVI), gathered from every region of the world. “**Behold, I shall not restrain my lips.**” The apostles are the lips of God, because he speaks through them. For a time he restrained them, saying: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans” (Matt. X). Afterwards, however, he not only did not restrain them, but commanded them to preach to all nations. For he says: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI).—“**Lord, thou knowest.**” In this matter he calls God as witness that he commanded the apostles to preach among all nations, so that no excuse may be possible at judgment.

“**I have not hidden thy righteousness in my heart.**” [Col. 1236C] Hence he himself says to the disciples: “Whatever I heard from my Father, I have made known to you” (John XV). Therefore he also commanded the apostles not to carry with them either purse or bag (Luke X). For one carries a purse who conceals divine words in his heart. “**I have declared thy truth and thy salvation,**” because I confessed that I am thy Son (Mark XIV). “**I have not hidden thy mercy and thy truth from the great council,**” because before the Jews, before Pilate, and before rulers and priests, Christ declared himself to be the Christ (Matt. XXVI). “**But do not remove thy mercies far from me.**” He speaks this according to his humanity. “**Thy mercy and thy truth have always upheld me:**” he puts the past for the future. “**For evils without number have surrounded me,**” because he died for the sins of the whole world (II Cor. V). But what number could there be of all sins? “**My iniquities have overtaken me,**” that is, the iniquities inflicted upon me: namely, the Jews, who were so full of wickedness that they are properly called not merely wicked but iniquity itself. “**And I was unable to see.**” I did not, he says, open my eyes, nor could I open them to see anyone except enemies and those opposed to me.

“**They are multiplied beyond the hairs of my head, and my heart has forsaken me.**” Since both my own people forsook me and my enemies were innumerable, I could see none but enemies. The apostles are called Christ’s heart, because he stored in them all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge and loved them as himself (John XV). “**May it please thee, O Lord, to deliver me. O Lord, look to help me.**” Humanity asks divinity to rescue it from its enemies, because in itself it was weak and frail. “**Let those who seek my life to take it away be confounded and ashamed together. Let them be turned backward:**” either from sin to righteousness; or away from the things above, so that they may always seek the lowest things; or also because they fell upon their faces (John XVIII). “**And let those who wish evil to me fear.**” What are they to fear? Either God, or the punishment which shall suddenly come upon them.

“**Let those who say to me, ‘Well done! Well done!’ immediately bear their confusion,**” either so that, blushing for their sins, they may repent; or because they shall quickly be overthrown by their enemies. [Col. 1237B] “**Let all who seek thee rejoice and be glad in thee.**” All, he says, who seek thee through faith and love should rejoice not in themselves but in thee, so that “he who glories may glory in the Lord” (I Cor. I).—“**And let them always say: ‘Let the Lord be magnified,’**” that is, his dominion, power, and those who believe in him. “**Who love thy salvation,**” that is, Christ thy Son, through whom thou workest the salvation of all. “**But I am needy and poor.**” Rightly, he says, ought they to love me, because though I was rich over all, I became poor for them (II Cor. VIII). “**But the Lord is mindful of me,**” because he abounds in all things. “**Thou art my helper and my protector; O my God, do not delay,**” but quickly grant help by coming to my aid.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XL

[Col. 1237C]

“**Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor.**” The voice of the Prophet: I compose psalms, indeed, but they are not to be understood as referring to me. Blessed shall be the person who understands, not literally but spiritually, both the psalms and the other prophets concerning the needy and poor. By the needy and poor he signifies Christ, who, though rich over all, became poor for us (II Cor. VIII). “**In the evil day the Lord shall deliver him;**” for the day of judgment shall be evil for the wicked and good for the good. On this day the Church which believed and understood Christ shall be delivered. But you faithless Jews, await the evil day—you who understand the psalms as concerning Antichrist.

[Col. 1237D] “**May the Lord preserve him and give him life.**” I see, he says, the needy and poor man. He is now taking flesh: behold, he comes. But what is this multitude of evildoers who oppose him? O wickedness! Servants rise up against their Lord; tenant-farmers desire to kill the heir (Mark XII); mocking chief priests and priests stand around him (Matt. XXVII). May the Lord preserve him, lest the gentle Lamb be torn apart by these dogs; and give him life on the third day. “**And make him blessed in the land**” of the living, restoring to him that glory which he had with himself before the world existed (John XVII). “**Do not deliver him over to the will of his enemies.**” This indeed would have happened, had he not risen from the dead.

[Col. 1238A] “**May the Lord bring him help upon the bed of his pain.**” The bed of pain is the flesh, according to which Christ was afflicted. “**Thou hast turned all his bed in his sickness.**” Therefore, he says, I beg thee to help him upon the bed of pain, because he is wholly occupied in sickness. Hence Isaiah: “From the sole of the foot even to the crown of the head there is no soundness in him” (Isa. I). Thus his whole body was in sickness, saying:

“**I said: Lord, have mercy on me,**” that is, on those who are mine. “**Heal my soul, because I have sinned against thee.**” Did Christ commit sin? Far be it. But he calls the Church his soul, because he loved it above all things. Hence it is written: “Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his soul” (Job II). [Col. 1238B] For there was nothing that a man possessed which he would not have given for this soul. He also gave skin for skin, because for our flesh he delivered his own to death. Therefore he asks the Father to heal the Church, weakened by the multitude of sins.

“**My enemies spoke evil of me: ‘When shall he die?’**” For the Jews thought and said these evils of Christ: When will this man die, who by working miracles draws the whole world after himself? And when will “**his name perish,**” so that no one may confess him? Hence the Gospel says: “For the Jews had already agreed that, if anyone confessed him, he should be put out of the synagogue” (John IX).

“**And if he entered in, to see vanities.**” Now he turns to the chief enemy himself, who betrayed him by the most wicked treachery. And if, he says, at any time Judas—the worst of all the Jewish enemies—entered the praetorium, among the enemies and the council of the Jews, in order to see the vain things which they plotted, “**his heart spoke,**” that is, he thought what he should say and answer. “**He gathered iniquity to himself.**” To himself indeed—that is, toward his own destruction—he gathered iniquity, because “it would have been good for him if he had not been born” (Matt. XXVI).—“**And he went out,**” because, after hearing the plan, he left the praetorium. “**And he spoke to the same end,**” that is, about the same matter.

“**All my enemies whispered against me,**” that is, they busied themselves with the plan of my death. “**They devised evils against me. They established a wicked word against me,**” saying: “Crucify him, crucify him” (John XIX), as it is written: “Let us put wood into his bread, and let us erase him from the land of the living” (Isa. XV). But “**shall not one who sleeps rise again?**” Truly he shall rise. “**For the man of my peace, in whom I hoped, who ate my bread, magnified his treachery against me,**” because he betrayed him with a kiss (Luke XXII). “**But thou, have mercy on me and raise me,**” from the dead. “**And I shall repay them:**” this shall occur at judgment, when he casts them into hell.

“**By this I knew that thou hast willed me, because my enemy shall not rejoice over me.**” For neither the Jews nor the malignant spirits rejoiced in Christ’s death: the former lost both their place and their nation; the latter, their prey, whom they had held captive.

[Col. 1239A] “**But thou hast received me because of my innocence.**” Them, however, thou shalt utterly destroy because of their many iniquities. “**And thou hast established me before thee forever,**” because he sits at the Father’s right hand. Hence: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel from age unto age.” And let us answer, “Amen, Amen.”

Here ends the first book of the Psalter.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XLI

“**As the stag longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for thee, O God.**” The voice of the Church: Just as, he says, a stag touched by some poison desires to come to springs of water, so my soul longs for thee, O God—my soul which the ancient serpent has struck with deadly poison. “**My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain: when shall I come and appear before the face of God?**” The Apostle desired to come before God’s face when he said: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. I). For the saints labored for no other reason than that they might joyfully reach God’s presence.

“**My tears were my bread by day and by night.**” I have been poisoned; I thirsted for water; I desired to come to thee. In this longing I wept, I shed tears day and night, and I had tears instead of sweetest bread. But can tears become bread? They can indeed: for as the body is satisfied by bread, so the soul is refreshed by tears of compunction. “**While it was said to me daily: ‘Where is thy God?’**”

The order is this: “While it was said to me daily, ‘Where is thy God? Why art thou sorrowful, O my soul, and why dost thou trouble me?’ I remembered these things, because I shall pass to the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God, with the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting; and I poured out my soul within me, saying: ‘Hope in God, for I shall yet confess to him.’” For such is the order. Let us consider the meaning. For pagans, pointing with a finger to their gods, formerly used to say to the saints: Do you see our gods? Do you see Jupiter, Saturn, Mercury, Venus, and Diana? But tell us: where is your God? [Col. 1239D] Hearing this, the holy man, somewhat shaken, says: “Why art thou sorrowful, O my soul?” And it replies: Because I cannot see my God. And “why dost thou trouble me?” Has their persuasion prevailed? Do you think that what they say is true? Remember, I beseech thee, that thou shalt pass “to the place of the wonderful tabernacle,” even “to the house of God,” and then at last thou shalt see thy God. But how shalt thou pass? “With the voice of exultation” and ineffable joy, “and confession” and praise; a voice which shall be nothing else than “the sound of one feasting,” needing nothing and always rejoicing. “I remembered these things,” he says, “and poured out my soul within me.” Was his soul outside him? Had it already forsaken him? Truly it had forsaken him, because, deceived by the aforesaid persuasion, it already desired to follow foreign gods. Therefore he poured out his soul within himself, because he withdrew it from its perverse will, saying: “Hope in God, for I shall yet confess to him.” These things, however, are not to be understood as though one person spoke to another; rather, the soul itself exhorts and strengthens itself in God’s service. Apostrophe: “O salvation of my countenance, and my God!” See: because my soul is troubled within me, that thou mayest comfort it, I shall remember thee coming “from the land of Jordan and Hermonim, from the little mountain.” This is according to the letter. Spiritually it is understood thus: Jordan means descent or humility; Hermon means *anathema*, “a curse.” Therefore one remembers the Lord from the land of Jordan who serves the Lord in the humility of the flesh, or in the baptized body. But one who anathematizes the devil, or separates himself from vices, remembers the Lord from the land of Hermonim. The Apostle was on the little mountain when he said: “But I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle” (I Cor. XV).

[Col. 1240B] “**Deep calls to deep at the voice of thy cataracts.**” As though he said: I shall always remember thee, for whose sake deep calls to deep—that is, the New Testament hands down the Old Testament; both are called “deep” because of the profundity of their meaning. And this is “at the voice of thy cataracts.” For cataracts are said to be the windows of heaven. The apostles, however, are heavens. Therefore the mouths of the apostles are the cataracts of heaven. Through them deep calls to deep, because Gospel preaching is confirmed from the Old Testament through the apostles. Or again, deep calls to deep when the apostles announce punishment and hell to sinners. For each is called deep for different reasons. While they preach, “**all thy heights and thy waves have passed over me,**” because even the invisible things of the Creator of the world were made manifest through the preaching of the apostles. Of these waves it is elsewhere said: “The rushing of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. LXXXVI). Therefore God’s heights and waves passed over the Church, because it saw invisible things and received the inundation of the Holy Spirit.

“**By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night his song.**” What is his mercy? Christ. To whom did he command it by day? To us indeed. But to whom by night? To the Jews. For he never appeared to the Jews except in cloud and darkness (Exod. III, XIII, XIX, XXIV), signifying that, after he had assumed flesh, he would not be known by them. But he commanded it to us by day: we believe in him, know him, and venerate him. Hence it is said: “For you who believe the Son, for those who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall arise” (Mal. IV). If therefore the sun is by day, and his song by night, what does it mean that by day he commanded mercy but by night song, except that … to believers, however, he had given the law and prophets? Otherwise: By day he commanded mercy; by night the saints sang. What did the saints sing? What did they sing? His song. And what is “by night,” except among sinners, in prisons, and in adversity? Therefore “with me” is “prayer” in the heart, in the inward person, which I owe “to the God of my life,” who has given life to me already dead. “**I shall say to God: Thou art my protector,**” because thou never forsakest those who hope in thee.

[Col. 1241A] And I shall say: “**Why hast thou forgotten me?**” “I have not,” he says, “forgotten.” But he replies: “Why then do I go sorrowfully while the enemy afflicts me?” This is equivalent to saying: Why does the enemy—the malignant spirit or earthly persecutor—afflict me? Why therefore do I live without freedom from pain and sorrow?

An apostrophe to himself: “**While my bones are broken.**” This is according to the letter. And while “**my enemies who trouble me reproached me, and while it was said to me every day: ‘Where is thy God? Why art thou sorrowful, O my soul, and why dost thou trouble me?’**” Do not, he says, be troubled, but “**hope in God, for I shall yet confess to him,**” who is “**the salvation of my countenance and my God.**” *Countenance* is used for will, because the will is recognized in the countenance. He is therefore the salvation of that will, because, as we said above, he did not permit it to be separated from the good will.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XLII

“**Judge me, O God, and discern my cause.**” The voice of the faithful soul: Let not the enemy judge me, he says, nor the false opinion of men, which makes good evil and, conversely, evil good; but judge me thou, who art just and merciful. And discern my cause: if thou findest it just, “**deliver me from an unholy nation, from an unjust and deceitful man, because thou art God and my strength.**” Deliver me, he says, from my enemies, thou who art my power and strength. “**But why hast thou cast me off?**” “I have not cast thee off,” says the Lord. “Why then do I go sorrowfully while the enemy afflicts me?”—as though he said: Unless thou hadst cast me off, the enemy would not afflict me, nor, when afflicted, would I be sorrowful. That this may happen no more, do what follows:

“**Send forth thy light and thy truth.**” Remove darkness and give light; remove error and give truth, so that, enlightened, we may follow the light, and, believing, hold fast to the truth. “**They have led me.**” From where? From error and iniquity; for broad and spacious is the way which leads to death. “**And they have brought me**” where? “**To thy holy mountain and to thy tabernacles,**” that is, into the Church, into the counsel and congregation of the righteous.

[Col. 1241D] “**And I shall enter unto the altar of God.**” I shall no longer sacrifice to idols or venerate their altars, but I shall enter unto God’s altar and there offer him a living and immaculate victim. God’s altar is the Church, or faith—that is, the New and Old Testaments—or the soul of each individual; for in all these the commemoration of the Lord’s body and blood is made.

“**To God, who makes my youth glad.**” Because, having put off the old man, I have put on the new. “**I shall confess to thee on the cithara,**” that is, in sweet speech, in the torture and affliction of the flesh, in harmonious sounds. “Why then art thou sorrowful, O my soul, and why dost thou trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall yet confess to him,” both upon the cithara and psaltery and the other musical instruments, who is “the salvation of my countenance and my God.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XLIII

“**O God, we have heard with our ears.**” The voice of the martyrs: O God, we have heard with our ears. From whom? “**Our fathers have declared to us.**” What did they declare? “**The work which thou didst perform in their days, and in the days of old.**” What was it? “**Thy hand destroyed the nations, and thou didst plant them,**” our fathers, in an inheritance. “**Thou didst afflict the peoples,**” of the nations, “**and didst drive them out**” from the land flowing with milk and honey. The greatest of prophets, Moses, teaches us how the Jewish people came out from Pharaoh’s power; he declared that they came out through the immolation of a lamb (Exod. XII). Thus we too have been delivered from the devil’s power through Christ’s Passion (Col. I). They crossed the Red Sea (Exod. XIV); but to us it has been said: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III). They spent forty years in the wilderness (Exod. XVI); but we dwell far from our homeland in the pilgrimage of this world (Heb. XIII). They received manna (Exod. XVI) and water from the rock (Exod. XVII); we have received the living bread, the flesh of God’s Son (John VI), and living water from the rock. And the rock was Christ (I Cor. X). To them the law was given on Mount Sinai (Exod. XX); to us the Gospel was given on Mount Sion (Matt. V). They destroyed cities with the ark of the covenant (Josh. VI); we conquer enemies by the Lord’s cross, through which the world was reconciled. They destroyed the Hittite, Amorite, Perizzite, Jebusite, and Canaanite peoples (Josh. II); but we overthrow pride, lust, avarice, and discord. Having conquered all enemies, they entered the promised land; having overcome every vice, we shall enter the land of the living. This is what we have heard. This is what the apostles, the prophets, and our fathers declared to us. He performed this work in ancient times; the Lord performs it in our own times. “**For they did not possess the land by their own sword, nor did their arm save them, but thy right hand, thy arm, and the light of thy countenance, because thou wert pleased with them.**” All these things happened to them figuratively. Therefore let no one think that he defends his own land, flesh, body, or self from vices by his own strength, but rather by God’s right hand, God’s arm, and the illumination of his countenance. Hence the Apostle says: “Who, being the brightness of glory and the image of his substance …” (Heb. I).—“**Thou thyself art my king and my God, who commandest salvations for Jacob.**” Thou thyself, he says, through whom our fathers destroyed enemies, art my king, because sin, the devil, and pride no longer rule me; and thou art my God, because I worship no other. “Who commandest salvations for Jacob.” What is meant by Jacob except the Church? What by salvation except Christ? Therefore the Lord commanded salvation for Jacob, because through his Son he saved the Church.

“**In thee we shall scatter our enemies with the horn.**” [Col. 1243A] Therefore, because thou art our king, through thee we shall scatter and shake our enemies with the horn—with a threatening voice and martial terror. “**And in thy name,**” trusting, “**we shall despise those who rise up against us,**” namely vices, persecutors, assailants, and malignant spirits. “**For I shall not hope in my bow,**” since Jacob is rightly depicted with a bow; for Jacob is interpreted “supplanter.” “**And my sword shall not save me:**” not mine, but thine; for I fight with thy sword, and with thy sword I conquer for thee. Thy sword is the word of the Lord, which indeed is spirit (Eph. VI).

“**For thou hast saved us from those who afflict us and hast confounded those who hate us;**” therefore “**we shall praise God all day,**” so that “he who glories may glory in the Lord” (II Cor. X).—“**And in thy name we shall confess for age upon age,**” because we are called Christians from Christ.

“**But now thou hast cast us off and confounded us.**” What does it mean that above he says he has been saved, but now says he has been cast off and confounded? He speaks according to the diversity of times: the saints were sometimes in prosperity and sometimes adversity; sometimes honored by peoples, sometimes afflicted by tyrants. When he says he has been cast off, he speaks according to the judgment of the wicked. “**And thou dost not go forth with our armies,**” that is, thou dost not appear to go forth when thou permittest us to be troubled.

“**Thou hast turned us backward after our enemies,**” [Col. 1243C] so that they might drag us behind them bound with chains. Hence the Apostle says: “I beseech you, I who am bound in the Lord” (Eph. IV). Or because many, through fear of death, turned backward from the way of truth. Or again, the enemies were before them and not behind them, because they killed them no longer secretly but face to face and openly. “**And those who hated us plundered for themselves,**” scourging some, killing others, and delivering others to prison.

“Thou hast given us like sheep for food,” destined to death alone; or because, bearing the Lord’s cross and following his example, they were led like sheep to sacrifice, neither protesting nor defending themselves. “And thou hast scattered us among the nations”; for Peter was crucified at Rome, and Thomas was slain in India; and, not to seek examples far away, Blessed Secondus, author of the Astesan book, was killed in our own city of Asti.

“Thou hast sold thy people for no price.” For the saints were sold for no price when, dying for the salvation of those to whom they preached, none were converted to the Lord through their death. Lawrence, however, was not sold for no price, because in his very passion he gained for the Lord Romanus, Hippolytus, Lucillus, and many others. “And there was no multitude in exchange for them.” The saints were exchanged because they passed from death to life; but in this change there was never any multitude of believers. This may also be understood of the Jews.

[Col. 1244A] “Thou hast made us a reproach to our neighbours.” Repetition: “A mockery and derision to those who are round about us.”

“Thou hast made us a byword among the nations.” Thou hast given us, he says, as a likeness of thyself to the nations, because, “if they persecuted thee, they will persecute us also” (John XV); if they killed thee, they will kill us also. Or, he gave his saints as a byword among the nations because at one time they came to such misery that, if anyone wished evil to happen to another, he would invoke upon him the calamity of Christians. “And a shaking of the head among the peoples.” For what pagan saw saints bound, afflicted, naked, flayed, and did not immediately shake his head in derision? For the Jews are recorded to have done this also in Christ’s passion (Matt. [Col. 1244B] XXVII). Or again, when many apostles freed people from pride, luxury, and avarice—which were the head and masters of many—what else was this than a shaking of the head?

“My shame is before me all day long, and the confusion of my face has covered me.” The voice of Christ: Why, martyrs, do you lament? Why do you report your miseries to me? Do you perhaps wish to hear mine as well? For all day long—that is, throughout the whole time of the Passion—my shame, the nails, the cross, the blows, the crown of thorns, the Jews insulting me, shaking their heads, and greeting me with bent knee, are before me (Matt. XXVII). And the confusion of my face has covered not you alone but me also. “At the voice of the reproacher and slanderer,” of the Jewish [Col. 1244C] people. “At the sight of the enemy and persecutor,” the Jew.

“All these things have come upon us.” All these things, say the martyrs, which thou hast said happened to thee, have come upon us also. “Yet we have not forgotten thee,” but in all these things we overcome. “And we have not dealt unjustly” through fear of death “in thy covenant,” but have always proclaimed the truth. “And our heart has not turned back,” but we always stretch forward toward the things that lie ahead, hastening toward the promised prize. “Nor hast thou turned our paths aside from thy way”: that is, thou hast not allowed our works to depart from thy way. But, I say: why then do we complain? It follows:

“For thou hast humbled us in afflictions,” that is, in this world, in the body of our pilgrimage. “And the shadow of death has covered us,” that is, [Col. 1244D] carnal tribulations, which are not death but a kind of signification of death. “If indeed we have forgotten the name of our God, and stretched out our hands to a strange god, will not God search this out?” He certainly will search it out, “for he knows the secrets of the heart.” But because for thy sake we are put to death all day long and are counted as sheep for the slaughter: “Arise”—we are sheep and thou art the shepherd; behold the dogs, behold the wolves. Arise therefore, shepherd; guard the sheep. Why then dost thou sleep? “Arise, and do not cast us off unto the end,” that is, altogether. Or: do not cast off those who come to thee, for thou art the beginning and the end (Rev. I).

“Why dost thou turn thy face” from us? Or dost thou “forget our poverty and tribulation,” which we endure for thee? “Arise, help us, and redeem [Col. 1245A] us for thy name’s sake,” that is, freely, not because of our merits. “For our soul is humbled into the dust”: that is, we are weighed down by the ungodly and sinners. “Our belly cleaves to the earth,” because we have become more weakly and more imperfect members of the Church in earthly matters. Or again, the belly cleaves to the earth when saints prostrate themselves in prayer not merely by bending the knees, but with the whole body.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XLIV

“My heart has uttered a good word.” The voice of the teachers. What is meant by “a good word” except the Gospel? For it is interpreted as “good news.” Therefore it is a good word, since it is good news. The teachers utter this—that is, preach it abundantly and significantly. “I speak my works to the king.” Since teachers are workers of the [Col. 1245B] Gospel, their work is rightly called the Gospel. But unless they were indeed workers, it would never be said of them: “The worker is worthy of his wage” (Luke X). They speak this work to the king; they proclaim it to the praise of God. Hence the Apostle: “For we do not preach ourselves, but the Lord Jesus” (II Cor. IV).

“My tongue is the pen of a scribe.” Of what scribe? “Of one writing swiftly.” If, therefore, the tongues of the apostles are the pens of the writer, what are the tablets and parchment on which they write, except the breasts of the faithful? What then do they write, and with what ink? The Gospel indeed, and this by the divine Spirit. Hence the Apostle: “You are our epistle, written not with ink on tablets of stone, but by the Spirit of the living God [Col. 1245C] on tablets of fleshly hearts” (II Cor. III). They wrote swiftly because, as is read in the second chapter of the Acts of the Apostles, about three thousand believed in one day.

“Thou art fairer in form than the children of men.” A change of person. O Christ, who art fairer in form than the children of men, “gird thy sword upon thy thigh.” For he himself is fairer in form than the children of men because no stain of vices disfigured him. “Grace has been poured out upon thy lips.” Such grace was upon his lips that his word was regarded as a deed. For he commanded Lazarus to rise, and he rose (John II). He commanded the blind man to see, and he saw (John IX). He commanded the leper to be cleansed, and he was cleansed (Matt. VIII). “Therefore God has blessed thee [Col. 1245D] for ever”; for Christ is always praised and blessed both in heaven and on earth.

“Gird thy sword upon thy thigh.” By the sword the Gospel is understood. Hence the Apostle: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI). By the thigh, however, we understand the Lord’s body. Therefore he girded the sword upon his thigh because he preached the Gospel in the flesh which he assumed. And he did this “most mighty,” because, as the Gospel says, he preached not as the Pharisees did, but as one having authority. He also girded the sword upon his thigh because he bestowed upon the saints the steadfastness of virtues, by which they might cut off luxury, which dwells in the loins and about the thigh, and the other vices. For Christ is the head; hence the Apostle: “Christ is the head of every man” [Col. 1246A] (I Cor. II). But the Church is the body. Therefore his hand, his foot, his belly, his thigh, and likewise the rest, exist in this manner.

“In thy splendour and thy beauty, stretch thyself forth,” that is, grow in splendour and beauty. But can one be stretched forth or slackened? Certainly. How? In respect of us, who, as has been said, are his body. Therefore, when we grow in splendour and beauty, his body—and consequently he himself—is stretched forth. We may also understand it thus: Stretch thyself forth in thy splendour and beauty, so that thou mayest deign to renew and reform in thy children the image and likeness which thou gavest to our first parent (Gen. I). “Proceed prosperously.” Proceed prosperously, he says, from the Father; proceed prosperously from the virginal womb; rise prosperously from [Col. 1246B] the tomb; return prosperously from the lower world to the Father. For all these things are prosperous and blessed for us. “And reign,” having redeemed the dominion of the whole world by thy precious blood.

“Because of truth, meekness, and justice.” For all these things befit a king: reign therefore, thou who art true, meek, and just. “And thy right hand shall lead thee wonderfully,” that is, thy strength, power, and might. But where shall it lead thee? To the Father. Why wonderfully? Because in dying thou didst overcome the devil. Alternatively: because of the truth of the Gospel, the meekness of those who preach it, and the justice which they perform, they shall lead thee through all nations, so that thy name may be proclaimed everywhere. Wonderfully, by thy right hand: that is, by thine apostles, who are found to be the more eminent part of the aforesaid body, by whom the Church itself was built [Col. 1246C] up.

“Thy arrows are sharp.” Now the apostles are sent forth; now the horses are equipped, to lead the King of kings everywhere; now the arrows are sharpened; now faith will engage in battle with idolatry. But because thine apostles, thy judgments, and thy arrows are sharp, therefore “the peoples,” overcome, “shall fall under thee”; they shall adore thee and humble themselves before thee. Or, the peoples—that is, the vices—shall fall beneath thee, of which he says elsewhere: “They shall fall beneath my feet” (Ps. XVII). They are fixed “in the heart of the king’s enemies”; for these arrows are so sharp that they pierce the hard and stony hearts of the nations and, having expelled their vices, make the king’s enemies into friends.

“Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever.” O how great is God’s loving-kindness and mercy! Those who were lately enemies, etc. [Col. 1246D] The remainder is missing.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM LXXXVI

“Her foundations are in the holy mountains.” The voice of the Prophet. Whose foundations, hers?
