For he has not stated whose, and yet he says “hers.” Why does he use “hers” so absolutely, except because it is characteristic of prophets to link words with their thoughts? It is therefore as though he said: The foundations of that city of which I am always thinking, whose beauty I admire, whose towers rise to heaven, whose foundations are established not in valleys but rather upon mountains. This holy city is understood as the Church, founded upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone. These [Col. 1247A] are the lofty and holy mountains by whose faith and examples the Church has been established. “The Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the tabernacles of Jacob.” The gates of Zion are the teachers who admit others into the Church; or the virtues by which one enters from Zion into Jerusalem. The Lord loves these above all the tabernacles of Jacob, that is, above all the Jewish assemblies. Apostrophe: “Glorious things are spoken of thee, O city of God.” For the Lord says this: “I will remember Rahab and Babylon.” Rahab means pride; Babylon means confusion. What then is meant by his promise that he will remember Rahab and Babylon, especially when the former was a prostitute and the latter was always hostile to the people of God? Hear what follows: “Of those who know me.” Therefore he is not unmindful of those who know him. If anyone, then, is Rahab or Babylon, let him not despair; rather, let him strive to know the Lord, for he remembers those who know him. You have been a sinner, an adulterer, and a fornicator: remember your God, that he too may have mercy on you. You were Babylon: you lived in confusion and without discernment; therefore gain understanding, that the Lord may remember you. But what could be found more glorious than this? For if sinners are chosen for this city, what will become of the precious stones? Where will the most holy virgins be, when the Lord remembers even prostitutes?

“Behold, foreigners, and Tyre, and the people of Ethiopia: these were there.” Does not this verse also set forth something most glorious? For in the Church there are not only Jews and natives, but also foreigners, Tyrians, and Ethiopians. “There is no respect of persons [Col. 1247C] with the Lord” (Rom. II), who calls the black and the sorrowful. “For the people who sat in darkness saw a great light” (Isa. IX).

“Shall not Zion say: Man and man were born in her, and the Most High himself founded her?” For Zion alone does not say this; the Lord himself also recounts it in the writings of the peoples. Therefore the words of the apostles are true and trustworthy, not feigned and invented, as the Jews suppose. For what the apostles preach, the Lord himself affirms in both Testaments. Zion therefore does not alone say: “Man and man were born in her.” For two kinds of human beings arose in the Church, namely Jews and Gentiles. Hence the Apostle says: “Is he the God of the Jews only? Indeed, he is also the God of the Gentiles” [Col. 1247D] (Rom. III). Or: “Man and man were born in Zion,” that is, the man who is merely man, and the man who is also God—namely, the man Christ Jesus our Lord. And the Most High himself founded her. That very man who was born in her is the same Most High who founded and made her. For this is established in the writings of the peoples—that is, in the New Testament—and in the volumes of the princes and prophets who formerly were in this venerable city. “The dwelling of all of us is as that of those who rejoice in thee.” The dwelling of this city, he says, is not that of those who rejoice, but as that of those who rejoice. For now they rejoice only in hope and in the desire for the promise alone. This is not perfect joy but, as it were, joy; but when it receives the prize, then it will rejoice beyond expression.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM LXXXVII

[Col. 1248A]

“O Lord, God of my salvation.” The voice of the Head. They therefore lie who say, “There is no salvation for him in his God” (Ps. III), since thou art the God of my salvation. “In the day I cried out, and in the night before thee.” My preaching, he says, was in day and night, in prosperity and adversity, before thy sight. “Let my prayer enter into thy presence.” Formerly, he says, I cried out; now I pray. “Incline,” therefore, “thine ear to my prayer. For my soul is filled with evils,” that is, with the pain of the Passion and the bitterness of death, as he himself says: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. XXVI). “And my life drew near to hell”—not to the dead, because he went to hell and despoiled it of one [reading uncertain: *exuviis*, “spoils”] (Eph. IV).

[Col. 1248B] “I was counted with those who go down into the pit.” For the Jews thought that Christ, like other human beings, would be held by hell. “I became like a man without help.” All cried: “God has forsaken him” (Ps. LXX); no one from so great a multitude of people came to his aid. “Free among the dead,” because he who was free made free those who had been bound; he was not bound by death, but he himself bound death. John says of him: “And after a thousand years Satan shall be loosed” (Rev. XX); for by saying that he would be loosed, he proved that he had been bound.

“Like the wounded, sleeping in tombs.” They are thought to be without God’s help—supply the phrase—and so also am I. “Whom thou rememberest no more.” For the soul wounded by the devil, now sleeping as though dead in the whitened sepulchre [Col. 1248C] of flesh, is rightly said to have been forgotten by the Lord. “And they were thrust away from thy hand”: they were thrust away from God’s hand in order to be bound by the devil’s hand. “They placed me in the lowest pit,” because they supposed that he was subject to hell and death; “in dark places, and in the shadow of death,” in Tartarean places, which death darkens and overshadows.

“Thy wrath was made strong upon me, and thou hast brought all thy waves over me.” This is what he says elsewhere: “What I did not seize, then I paid” (Ps. LXVIII). For God was angry with the human race, which he would have destroyed because of one man’s offence; but he preferred that his Son should undergo the death of the cross rather than that all nations should perish. Hence the prophet says: “Because of [Col. 1248D] the sins of my people I struck him” (Isa. LIII). “Thou hast removed my acquaintances far from me”: the apostles, or the Jews. For the apostles stood afar off; but the Jews became utterly far from him. “They made me an abomination to themselves”: namely, the Jews, who did not yet wish even to hear his name.

“I was delivered up, and I did not go forth.” I was seized by a betrayer (Matt. XXVI), though I fled from no one, since I preached before them in the synagogue (Matt. IV, IX, XIII).

“My eyes languished because of poverty.” What a great eye Peter was, who languished away from God so as to deny him! (Matt. XXVI.) Others too had languished when, abandoning him, they fled (Matt. XXVI). But this was because of poverty: for they did not yet understand Scripture, because they were still carnal [Col. 1249A] and poor in divinity. You too languished, Thomas, who would not at all believe that he had risen (John XX). That they perished through poverty is shown by this: after receiving the Holy Spirit (Acts II), they could in no way be overcome. “I cried to thee, O Lord.” For he cried when he said, “Eli, Eli!” (Matt. XXVII.) “All day long I stretched out my hands to thee,” fastened to the cross. Hence it is also said elsewhere: “All day long I have stretched out my hands to a people who do not believe and contradict me” (Rom. X).

“Wilt thou perform wonders for the dead?” Why, Jews, do you think me dead? For if I were dead like others, I certainly could not perform these miracles. “Or shall physicians raise up” those whom I have not raised? “And shall they confess thee,” those who do not confess [Col. 1249B] me?

“Shall anyone declare thy mercy in the grave, and thy truth in destruction?”—“Father, preserve those whom thou hast given me” (John XVII); enlighten the eyes that languished because of poverty. For these are those who must proclaim through all lands thy mercy, thy truth, and the wonders which thou dost work; those who sleep in graves and are counted among the lost cannot tell thy works.

“Shall thy wonders be known in darkness, and thy justice in the land of forgetfulness?” For at Christ’s Passion darkness came over Judaea, along with many other wonders (Luke XXIII). Yet the Jews’ blindness was not diminished. It should be noted that at the time of the Passion darkness came, the tombs were opened, and many bodies of saints rose (ibid.). These three verses seem to have prophesied this: “Wilt thou perform wonders for the dead? Shall anyone declare thy mercy in the grave? Shall thy wonders be known in darkness?”—as though saying: What profit was there in thy raising the dead, opening the tombs, and causing darkness, when the hard hearts of the Jews were not pierced? “But I cried to thee, O Lord,” that thou mightest glorify me with my former glory. “And in the morning my prayer shall come before thee,” when I rise on the third day. “Why, O God, dost thou reject my prayer and turn thy face from me?” For he says: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from [Col. 1249D] me” (Matt. XXVI). But the Father rejected this prayer because it was made from human fear of the flesh; for perhaps martyrs might have feared the cup of death unless he had first tasted it.

“I am poor,” for obedience to thee; “and in labours from my youth,” that is, from the time I became man. “But having been exalted” upon the cross, “I was humbled” in the tomb, “and troubled” in death. “Thy wrath passed over me,” because by suffering for others I appeased thy wrath. “And thy terrors troubled me,” those which thou didst impose upon the human race. For unless Adam had sinned, we would not suffer these terrors.

“They surrounded me like water all day long; they surrounded me together. Thou hast removed friend and neighbour far from me”: the company of the apostles and Jewish kinsmen. [Col. 1250A] “And my acquaintances from misery,” because, when the shepherd was struck, the sheep of the flock were scattered. But he alone endured misery who was able to free the others from misery.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM LXXXVIII

“I will sing for ever of the mercies of the Lord.” The voice of the Church: I shall sing for ever, she says, of the mercies of the Lord, which he magnified so greatly that he did not spare his own Son, but delivered him to death for us all (Rom. VIII). “From generation to generation I will declare thy truth with my mouth.” For as long as generation succeeds generation, Christ will always be praised in the Church.

“For thou hast said: Mercy shall be built up for ever in the heavens.” For mercy is always built up in the saints, who [Col. 1250B] are called heavens, who are never separated from mercy while keeping the command of their Lord, who said: “Be merciful, as your Father also is merciful” (Luke VI). “Thy truth shall be prepared in them.” God’s truth was indeed in the Psalms and Prophets, but harsh and difficult to investigate. The apostles prepared it by expounding it spiritually and rendering it intelligible.

“And I have established a covenant with my chosen ones.” The Lord likewise established this New Covenant with his saints, in which one is commanded not to render evil for evil, but indeed good for evil (Matt. V). “I have sworn to David my servant: I will prepare thy seed for ever.” That these promises are made not to the first David, but to the second—that is, Christ—will be proved by the most certain arguments in what follows. For the seed which this David sowed shall never grow old, but shall be prepared in the Church until the consummation of the age, since the Gospel will always be read. “And I will build thy throne from generation to generation.” For Christ’s throne is the Church. It will be built better at every time through preaching, baptism, and repentance; its building was not completed by the apostles, nor indeed will it be, “until the moon is taken away” (Ps. LXXI).

“The heavens shall confess thy wonders, O Lord.” Because thou hast promised these benefits to the heavens—that is, the saints—the heavens shall therefore confess thy wonders. “And thy truth,” that is, the word of preaching, or Christ thy Son, who says: “Whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess him before my Father” (Matt. X), “in the assembly of the saints,” that is, in the congregation of the righteous. And this is fitting, since who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? For many thought John the Baptist to be Christ (John I), but neither he nor any of the prophets, who are understood by the clouds, could be made equal to him, as the Lord’s own forerunner says: “I am not the Christ, nor am I worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal” (ibid.). Yet none born of women was greater than he (Matt. II). Who, then, among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? Or who “shall be like the Lord among the sons of God?” [Col. 1251A] For all of us are sons by adoption (Rom. VIII); he, however, is the firstborn among brethren (ibid.). I shall confidently call him brother, yet as the natural Son he surpasses all.

This is that God “who is glorified, great in the council of the saints,” because he is Lord of all; “and terrible,” because he is judge of all, “above all who are around him,” whether placed at the right hand or at the left. Apostrophe:

“O Lord God of hosts, who is like thee?” Certainly none. “Thou art mighty, O Lord,” because thou hast overcome the mighty devil. “And thy truth is round about thee,” that is, the apostles, preachers of truth, of whom Truth itself said: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII).

[Col. 1251B] “Thou rulest the power of the sea,” that is, the rulers of this world. “And thou dost calm the movement of its waves,” the impulses of wrath by which they rise against the saints. “Thou hast humbled the proud one as one wounded.” The proud one was wounded, and the devil is slain by the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. VI); humbled and bound, he lies in outer darkness. “By the arm of thy justice thou hast scattered thine enemies”: in the strength of God’s power, the Jews are scattered throughout the world. “The heavens are thine, and the earth is thine.” Thine are the apostles and the Church, the righteous and sinners, the perfect and imperfect. “Thou hast founded the world and its fullness”: this literally. Or, “the world” means the solidity of the human body, and “its fullness” the constancy [Col. 1251C] of virtues. “Thou hast created the north and the sea”: Antichrist and his imitators. For although he pretends to be creator, he shall nevertheless be a creature; of him it is written: “From the north evil shall be unleashed upon all the inhabitants of the earth” (Jer. I).

“Tabor and Hermon shall rejoice in thy name.” Tabor means “coming light”; Hermon, however, means “anathema.” But what is meant by Tabor except the apostles, who are the coming light, to whom the Lord says: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V)? And what is meant by Hermon except the Church, which at the beginning of its faith, renouncing the devil and all his pomps, confesses anathema and separation? They rejoice in the Lord’s name because they are called Christians. [Col. 1251D] “Thine arm is with power,” that is, the strength by which thou hast bound the devil. “Let thy hand be strengthened, and thy right hand exalted.” For when the hand and company of the apostles had been strengthened, Christ the Lord ascended into heaven. “Justice and judgment are the preparation of thy throne”; for whoever judges himself and follows justice undoubtedly prepares a throne for the Lord. For the soul of the righteous is the throne of wisdom (Gregory, Homily 33). But that we ought to judge ourselves, hear the Apostle: “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” (I Cor. XI).

“Mercy and truth shall go before thy face.” Whoever desires, he says, to possess and behold his face must follow mercy and truth. Thus mercy and truth always go before Christ, so that none of his works is without these two. “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation,” which does not occur in voice or much speaking, but rather in the devout consciousness of mind and heart.

“O Lord, they shall walk in the light of thy countenance.” For whoever follows this torch cannot walk in darkness. Let us therefore walk in the light of the image of the Son of God, so that we may enter the heavenly home. “And in thy name they shall rejoice all day.” Who would not glory in so great a patron? Of this it is said in the Song of Songs: “Thy name is oil poured forth; therefore the young maidens loved thee” (Song I). “And in thy justice they shall be exalted.” Let the Jews, therefore, be silent, who think they are exalted by their own justice. “For thou art the glory of their strength.” The Church does not glory [Col. 1252B] in its own powers, instructed in apostolic doctrine that “he who glories, let him glory in the Lord” (II Cor. X). “And in thy good pleasure toward thy Son our horn shall be exalted,” that is, our strength and power of fighting. “For our exaltation is of the Lord. O ineffable mystery, that the Creator and Lord of the world deigned to take the flesh of a servant!” (Phil. II). “And of the Holy One of Israel, our king.” May this king live for ever, and not permit sin to reign in our mortal body.

“Then thou didst speak in a vision to thy saints.” For at the time when he assumed flesh, the Lord spoke to his saints in a vision of the Holy Spirit, as to Zechariah and Simeon (Luke I, II), who announced and awaited the consolation of Israel. Anna also, the prophetess, [Col. 1252C] confessed the same thing (Luke II). “And thou didst say: I have set help upon one who is mighty,” as though saying: No one need now be afraid, because I have placed the aid of deliverance not now in prophets, but in my own Son, who can do all things. “And I have exalted one chosen from my people,” that is, Christ the Lord, who, taking flesh from the Jewish people (ibid.), was exalted upon the cross, to the sovereignty of the kingdom, and finally also into heaven (Mark XVI).

“I have found David my servant.” I have given many helpers and defenders, he says, but none of them was able to free you from the first captivity. But now I have found David, my servant, fit to accomplish this task, who delivered the world with an outstretched arm. He is called servant in respect of his flesh. “I have anointed him with my holy oil,” for he is that flower in whom the sevenfold graces of the Holy Spirit rest. “For my hand shall help him, and my arm shall strengthen him”; for divinity, always joined to humanity, comforted it in all things. “The enemy shall profit nothing against him”: for the ancient foe tempted the Lord three times (Matt. IV), but gained nothing, because he departed defeated. “And the son of iniquity,” Judas, most wicked trafficker, “shall not add to harm him,” because, having cast away the coins, he hanged himself with a noose (Matt. XXVII). “And I shall strike down his enemies before his face.” This will occur at the judgment, when God’s enemies, slain by the sword of vengeance, shall be consigned to eternal punishment. “And I shall turn those who hate him to flight.” [Col. 1253A] The Jews shall therefore flee, never being victorious. The demons also fled from possessed bodies when, at the Lord’s command, they were compelled to depart (Matt. VIII). “And my truth and my mercy shall be with him”: for he was never able not to speak truth, never to lie in anything; he was never without mercy. “And in my name his horn shall be exalted,” when he conquered the hostile world.

“And I will set his hand in the sea and his right hand in the rivers.” Hand and right hand are rightly used for works, since works are done by hands. But we were sea and rivers, ruled by the wind of pride; now, however, we know the power and works of God. “He shall call upon me,” saying: “Thou art my Father, my God, and the defender [Col. 1253B] of my salvation.” Let the Jews, therefore, be confounded, who accused him for calling God his Father (Matt. X).

“And I will make him the firstborn, exalted above the kings of the earth.” For he is the firstborn of the dead and prince of the kings of the earth (Rev. I). All the kingdoms of the world are subject to him. “For ever I will preserve my mercy for him.” He calls the Church his mercy, since it trusts in the mercy of God alone. The Lord will preserve it for ever because of the prayer of his Son, who says: “Father, preserve those whom thou hast given me” (John XVII).

“And my covenant shall be faithful to him.” We are God’s covenant, provided we are found faithful. “And I will set his throne for ever and ever”: for the Church shall always exist. “And his throne shall be as the days of heaven,” for the saints shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of God (Matt. XIII). It shall be like the days of heaven: by heavens we understand angels, and by days their very brightness.

“If his children forsake my law,” and for a time “do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my ordinances” by some falsehood of error, “and do not keep my commandments,” I shall certainly not kill them, but “I will visit their iniquities with a rod,” that is, with the correction of repentance, “and their sins with stripes.” O most merciful Father, who does not kill us but chastises us with a light rod!

[Col. 1253D] “But my mercy I will not scatter from him, nor will I harm him.” For the Lord knows not how to harm, but to help; and in my truth let sinners repent—let no one ever despair. For behold, the Lord says not only that he will have mercy, but also: “Neither will I profane my covenant.” Exposition: “And the things that proceed from my lips I will not make void.” For he would profane his covenant if any falsehood could be found in the New or Old Testament. But, as the Lord himself says: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but his words cannot pass away” (Matt. XXIV).

“Once have I sworn by my holy one.” For we have heard one sure and firm oath, which he made by his truth, by his holy one, and by his beloved Son. What he held dearest, he made the object of his oath. “If I lie to David”: for he who cannot lie will not lie. Let us therefore believe, and believe most firmly, what is promised so steadfastly. But what is promised? It follows: “His seed shall remain for ever.” The seed is the word of God; it shall remain for ever, because “not one iota or one stroke shall pass from the law until all things are fulfilled” (Matt. V). “And his throne as the sun before me.” Let that throne rejoice which is to receive the brightness of the sun. Let the apostles rejoice, who are to be set before the Lord’s countenance. “And as the moon perfect for ever,” which can no longer diminish, nor indeed increase. For what can be increased in one who is perfectly blessed? “And the faithful witness in heaven.” For this throne, this most blessed seat, shall judge the world in true testimony. The voice of the Church:

“But thou hast cast off and despised.” What is this, Lord, she says, that thou hast promised such great benefits to thy servant David? Why didst thou above say under oath that thou wouldst have mercy upon him and his children, when we now see him cast off and despised by other nations? (Matt. XXVII.) Could there have been falsehood in thee? Far be it! “For thou hast deferred thy Christ,” to whom, in the fullness of time, thou wast to grant all these things. From here he describes the overthrow of the first David, lest anyone understand the things said above concerning him.

“Thou hast overthrown the covenant of thy servant.” For nowhere now are bull, goat, and lamb sacrificed. “Thou hast profaned his sanctuary throughout all the earth,” for everywhere he abominates the synagogue. “Thou hast destroyed all his hedges,” because it is secured by no fortifications.

“Thou hast made his stronghold a terror,” because they could be defended neither in Jerusalem nor in the citadel of Zion. Or because they feared Christ, the support of the world, should live (John XI).

“All who pass along the way have plundered him,” that is, the boundary of faith. “He has become a reproach to his neighbours,” that is, to the nations dwelling round about. “Thou hast exalted the right hand of those who oppress him; thou hast made all his enemies glad; thou hast turned away the help of his sword.” Exposition: “And thou hast not helped him in battle.”

“Thou hast destroyed him from purification.” For the Jews performed a sacrifice of purification, offering a goat for sins. But this has been annulled and destroyed. “And thou hast dashed his throne to the ground”: that high-priestly chair upon which the Scribes and Pharisees sat.

“Thou hast shortened the days of his time,” because, their expectation having been disappointed, they live without king or priest (Hos. 3). “Thou hast covered him with confusion,” temporal and eternal.

“How long, O Lord, dost thou turn away unto the end?” How long, he says, will the Lord be angry with the Jews—until the consummation of the age? But when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in, then Israel will be saved; yet until that time, “his anger shall burn like fire.”

“Remember what my substance is.” But now [Col. 1254D] [Col. 1255A] the Church speaks for herself and complains to the Lord of her own miseries: Remember, she says, O God, that I am frail and changeable; and do not allow me to be tempted beyond what I can bear. “For hast thou created all the children of men in vain?” For if we are all overcome and subject to diabolical temptations, the creation of humankind is nothing but vanity. “What man is he that shall live and not see death, and shall deliver his soul from the hand of hell?” None, he says, will escape death; none will be delivered from hell, unless thou, mindful of our weakness, protect us from our enemies.

“Where are thy former mercies, as thou didst swear to David in thy truth?” Paul is beheaded, Peter crucified; thy Church is struck on every side, though thou hadst recently promised it eternal [Col. 1255B] mercy. Where, then, are thy former mercies, O God? For to us God is not newly come. “Remember, O Lord, the reproach of thy servants, which I have borne in my bosom, from many nations.” Be mindful, I say, of that reproach which, inflicted upon thy servants by many nations, cannot slip from my memory.

“Wherewith thine enemies have reproached thee, O God; wherewith they have reproached the change of thy Christ”: that is, the death of thy Son. For God’s enemies cast this in the teeth of the saints: that they worshipped a man who had died and was subject to change. “Blessed be the Lord for ever.” Let them mock and curse; let them reproach us with the Crucified One; but let us joyfully say: “Blessed be the Lord for ever. Amen, [Col. 1255C] amen.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 89

“Lord, thou hast been a refuge to us.” The voice of the Church: We were conquered, she says, bound by enemies, handed over to prisons; but thou, Lord of highest mercy, hast become a refuge to us, from this generation of thy incarnation unto the everlasting generation.

“Before the mountains were made, and the earth and the world were formed, from age unto age thou art God”: as though he said, Thou who, by taking flesh from a virgin in time, didst become a refuge to humankind, remainest God before time and through all ages. “Turn not man away into lowliness.” Thou, he says, who art such as this, sustain and strengthen man, lest he be brought low unto death [Col. 1255D] and punishment; rather, let him be exalted above the heavens by thy mighty right hand. For thou hast said: “Return, ye children of men, and I will heal your brokenness.” Let man therefore be healed, since he has been broken.

“For a thousand years in thy sight are as yesterday, which is past, and as a watch in the night; their years, which are reckoned as nothing, shall be: in the morning he shall pass away like grass; in the morning he shall flourish and pass away; in the evening he shall fall, harden, and wither.” Man is not improperly joined to this comparison; for, since there is no comparison between the finite and the infinite, not only may our thousand years not be called a day or an hour, but they may indeed be said not to exist at all, since they wholly perish. For man quickly passes, like grass, from non-being into being; quickly [Col. 1256A] he flourishes in youth, because the flower of life is figuratively bounded; quickly he passes to evening, that is, to old age. In the evening, moreover, he falls, because old age is called the setting of life. Then he hardens, becoming wholly rough and bristling; finally he withers, and dust returns to dust. This prayer is rightly attributed to Moses, so that he who said that man was made from dry earth may confess that, returned to dryness, he withers (Gen. 3).

But “we have failed in thy anger, and in thy wrath we have been troubled”; and because “thou hast set our iniquities before thee, and our age in the light of thy countenance,” and because “all our days have failed, and in thy anger we have failed; our years shall meditate like a spider.” Our years are rightly compared to a spider, because throughout the whole time [Col. 1256B] of our life we sweat over vanities, only in the end to seem to have woven things useless, profitable neither to ourselves nor to anyone else—indeed, if one may say so, a spider’s web. But thou, Adam, root of the whole human race, hast done this to us: because, though thou wert so great and such a one as thou wert, by transgressing the Lord’s commandment (Gen. 3) thou didst incur wrath and bring failure upon thy children. This is what he says: “We have failed in thy anger, and in thy wrath we have been troubled.” We fail in the flesh; we are troubled by weakness. “Thou hast set our iniquities before thee.” Exposition: “Our age [is] in the light of thy countenance.” For the Lord has seen our age, the life we live, and whatever we do in secret. “The days of our years” are not many, because, as has already been said, all fail in swift course; “in them” perhaps there shall be “seventy [Col. 1256C] years,” for this often happens. “But if by strength [there are] eighty years” granted to someone, “and beyond these, labour and pain.” So contracted and shortened, he says, is our life that beyond eighty years we can no longer live in joy, such as it may be, and in the delights of the flesh; whatever exceeds that is labour and pain, coughing and anxiety—especially since old age itself is weakness.

“For mildness comes upon [us].” What once was impatient and strong in you, whether you will or no, old age now makes mild and humble; you no longer raise your brow, but are compelled, bent over, to look at the earth. “And we shall be corrected.” He who, he says, was proud in youth should at least be corrected in old age. “Who knoweth the power of thy anger?” Whoever has known the power [Col. 1256D] of God’s wrath is afraid to incur that wrath. And who has taken care “to number thy wrath because of fear”? The saints, fearing God, number his wrath; for they understand that the more numerous the vices that follow, the greater the multitude of wrath by which they must be condemned; and therefore they avoid such wraths.

“Make thy right hand known in this way”: as, understood, thou didst make known the wrath of transgression—so that we who through Adam have known death may through Christ receive life. Let us now know the right hand, who until now have followed the left. “And [make known] those instructed in heart in wisdom.” These, however, are the prophets, who, though deceived by vain philosophy, were filled with the Holy Spirit. The Lord made them known to us because [Col. 1257A] he disclosed their intentions and the hidden mysteries of the heart (Luke 24). “Return, O Lord; how long? And be entreated concerning thy servants”: turn wholly, he says; wholly pity the nation that is perishing; hear our prayers, with Christ interceding for us. “We have been filled in the morning with thy mercy.” “The night,” he says, “has gone before, but the day has drawn near” (Rom. 13). Therefore we give thanks to the Lord, because from the time of this light we have been filled with his mercy. “And we have exulted and delighted in all our days.” The following verse explains this.

“We rejoiced for the days wherein thou hast humbled us, and for the years wherein we have seen evils.” We no longer complain of mortality, the shortness of days, and unhappiness [Col. 1257B], because we have been filled with thy mercy; for where transgression abounded, grace abounded yet more (Rom. 5). “Look upon thy servants,” lest through some sin they may be deprived of the mercy they have received. “And upon thy works: direct their children,” that is, their souls themselves, or their succeeding posterity. “And let the brightness of the Lord our God be upon us,” so that, when the darkness of the devil’s image has been driven away, we may be re-formed into the original form and image; lest, if they are crooked, they make us limp through byways. “And direct the works of our hands.” For the works of the saints are both many and one: whatever they do is one work, because they do not differ in goodness, but tend toward one and the same purpose.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 90

[Col. 1257C]

“He that dwelleth in the help of the Most High.” The voice of the Prophet: I see, he says, that Christ will be born; I see the devil and his attendants, who will craftily lie in wait for him. But since he has dwelt in his city and in flesh assumed, not without divine help, and since he “shall abide” in the heavenly “protection of God,” he will make little of their snares. “He shall say to the Lord: Thou art my protector and my refuge, my God.” Let him who has the Lord as his refuge not fear the enemy; let him who is to be received by the Father not fear to lay down the flesh. Let him say on the cross: “My God, into thy hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23). “But I,” says the Prophet, “will hope in him, because [Col. 1257D] he has delivered me from the snare of hunters and from the harsh word.” He says that he hopes in Christ because he understood that through him the world would be saved. He has delivered, moreover, from hunters and will deliver from the harsh word. These hunters are understood as evil spirits, who pursue sinners and catch some in pride, others in avarice, others in lust, as though in separate snares. The harsh word will be that which the Lord shall utter at judgment: “Depart, ye cursed, into everlasting fire” (Matt. 25). But we have been delivered from this, because we ought to hear that most sweet word: “Come, ye blessed of my Father” (ibid.). Apostrophe.

“With his shoulders he shall overshadow thee, and under his wings thou shalt hope.” Be secure, he says, O Saviour, because, [Col. 1258A] protected by paternal power, no heat of adversity will scorch thee; the Father’s wings will sustain thee, by which, whenever thou wilt, thou shalt fly to the heavenly kingdoms. For he has one and the same power with the Father (John 16), by which he can do even impossible things. “His truth shall compass thee with a shield.” No weapons of falsehood, he says, shall prevail against thee; no testimonies of false witnesses shall overcome thee, because natural truth, invincible by the protection of a shield, shall surround thee on every side. “Thou shalt not fear the terror of the night,” when Judas the traitor comes, and with him a great crowd carrying torches, lanterns, and clubs; terrified by fear, all thy disciples shall flee, leaving thee behind (Matt. 26). But thou shalt not flee; rather, thou shalt go willingly and without fear.

“From the arrow that flieth by day.” Many arrows shall fly by day—many [Col. 1258B] openly and manifestly. Many shall cry, “Crucify, crucify” (Luke 23). “From the business that walketh in darkness”: in the darkness of the rulers and priests, the Scribes and Pharisees, schemes and wicked counsels moved about; or, because factions were formed; or, more plausibly, because they devised them in their hearts, which are the devil’s hiding places. “From the assault and the noonday demon.” Nor is it absurd for the Church to hold that, in Christ’s passion, as a multitude of angels, so also a multitude of evil spirits was present. For since they had tempted him while he fasted (Matt. 4), perhaps, on seeing him dying and hanging on the cross with thieves, they presumptuously conceived some crime, as wicked beings would. But he did not fear this, because he performed no work of fear, as he himself says: “For the prince of this world cometh, and hath nothing in me” (John 14). It may also be understood of the future judgment, when the assaults of demons, like lions ready for prey, shall cast sinners into the pit. He calls it noonday because of the exceedingly burning affliction. “A thousand shall fall at thy side.” He has used the finite for the infinite. “And ten thousand at thy right hand.” We could have understood both right and left as being at the side, had he not specified which side he meant. Therefore innumerable persons shall be cast down by thy power. “Thy right hand shall find all that hate thee” (Ps. 20). Whoever is driven by this right hand will not be able, by any strength, to stand without [Col. 1258D] falling. “But it shall not come near thee”—“for evil shall not dwell beside thee” (Ps. 5). Who then shall? “All who are upright in heart” (Ps. 93).

“Yet with thine eyes thou shalt consider.” Confirmation: “And thou shalt see the recompense of sinners,” which they gain for themselves in this world by evil works. “Because thou, O Lord, art my hope.” And because “thou hast made the Most High thy refuge, evil shall not approach thee, and the scourge shall not come near thy tabernacle,” each statement is applied to its proper subject. Thou, he says, needest not fear; evil shall not be able to approach thee, because thou hast made the Most High thy refuge. Yet neither shall the scourge approach thy tabernacle—which we are—because [Col. 1259A] thou art the hope of us all, whom none can resist (Esther 13).

“For he hath given his angels charge concerning thee, to keep thee in all thy ways.” The evil spirit himself understood this: that evil cannot approach Christ. For he says: “If thou art the Son of God, cast thyself down; for he hath given his angels charge concerning thee” (Matt. 4). “They shall bear thee up in their hands, lest perhaps thou dash thy foot against a stone.” Because thou art veiled in human form, he says, I do not know thee; but I declare these words concerning the only-begotten Son of God, that no adversity will ever harm him. Therefore, if thou confessest thyself to be the Son of God, cast thyself down, for, supported by angels, thou shalt not strike against a stone.

“Thou shalt walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and thou shalt trample [Col. 1259B] upon the lion and the dragon.” Why, devil, didst thou not also recite this verse? For thou knewest it was against thee. Thou art the asp, whose poison is incurable. Thou art the basilisk, king and prince of every vice and all wickedness. Thou art that lion which is always roaring and seeking whom thou mayest devour (1 Pet. 5). Thou art that dragon which with its tail drew down a third part of the stars from heaven (Rev. 12). Let that son of perdition perish, who is to be born at the end of the age and is called the devil’s tail. Although thou wast silent about this, devil, thy silence did thee no good, since thou hast been trampled down and crushed in baptism.

“Because he hath hoped in me, I will deliver him.” To thee, he says, it shall be said by the Father: Because he hath hoped in me, I will deliver him, “and I will protect him” with the shield of divinity, [Col. 1259C] “because he hath known my name. He shall cry to me,” while placed upon the cross, “and I will hear him,” restoring that glory which he sought from me (John 17). “I am with him in tribulation”: let those therefore be ashamed who say that God abandoned him. “I will fill him with length of days,” because he shall live for ever, and death shall no longer have dominion over him. “And I will show him my salvation”: that is, my saving power, so that he who saved others may himself also receive salvation and immortality.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 91

“It is good to confess to the Lord.” The voice of the Church: It is good for us to confess, praise, and proclaim the Lord, because “beautiful are the feet of those who preach peace, who preach good things” [Col. 1259D] (Rom. 10); “and to sing to thy name, O Most High,” that is, to rejoice in the heart: “for with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10).

“To declare thy mercy in the morning, and thy truth in the night; upon a ten-stringed psaltery, with a song upon the harp.” And this because “thou hast made me glad, O Lord, in thy creation, and I will exult in the works of thy hands.” Whatever may be the case with others, he says, I, declaring thy mercy and truth, will exult in thee alone. The apostles proclaimed God’s mercy in the morning when, in full light, openly and publicly, they preached Christ’s passion to all. But they spoke the truth in the night when, amid prisons and torments, [Col. 1260A] they confessed Christ. He praises God upon psaltery and harp because he fulfils in the ten commandments of the Law what he proclaims by mouth. This ought to be done because we delight in God’s creation. For who is not delighted by heaven and earth, sun and moon and stars, and the harmonious ordering of all other things? It is good, therefore, to praise the Creator, who is shown so wonderful in his creation; “for his invisible things,” as the Apostle says, “from the creation of the world are understood and seen through the things that are made” (Rom. 1). “How magnified are thy works, O Lord!” He delighted in the Lord’s works, which he had just been examining by subtle reflection. But because he cannot discover the reason how or whence they are, he praises the Creator in a kind of exclamation. Why does the eye, and [Col. 1260B] not the ear, see? Why does the ear, and not the eye, hear? Let whoever can answer it. Therefore God’s works are magnified when they are individually examined by anyone. Let no one, then, set his mouth against heaven, since he does not know how to account even for earth. “Thy thoughts have been made exceedingly deep.” “For who hath known the mind of the Lord?” (Rom. 11). His thoughts, therefore, are lofty, since they cannot be known by anyone.

“A senseless man shall not know, and a fool shall not understand these things: when sinners spring up like grass, and all who work iniquity appear, that they may perish for ever and ever.” Sinners arise not like the sun but like grass, because, struck by any heat or frost, they quickly fail. He who yesterday flourished is dead today; he who yesterday rejoiced now weeps; he who yesterday ran now limps. The senseless person does not know this, the fool does not understand it, and therefore works iniquity, so that, believing he shall live long in this flower of life, he may perish for ever and ever. “But thou, O Lord, art the Most High for ever,” taking vengeance from them, as is understood. “For behold thy enemies, O Lord, behold thy enemies shall perish”; and, when thou executest vengeance, “all who work iniquity shall be scattered.”

“And my horn shall be exalted like that of a unicorn.” For the Church had one horn, by which she was exalted above all enemies, concerning which the Apostle says: “The saints through faith conquered kingdoms” (Heb. 11). For the horn of the saints is faith, which is always lofty and rises above every adversity. “And my old age [Col. 1260D] in abundant mercy”: when the Church comes to old age in order to be renewed into eternal youth, and when a person has ended temporal days in order to receive eternal ones, then in abundant mercy he shall be exalted above the heavens.

“And mine eye hath looked down upon mine enemies.” I saw, he says, many enemies surrounding me; nevertheless, because I was fortified by the aforesaid horn, I despised them all as weak. “And mine ear shall hear [of] the malicious men rising up against me,” because “the righteous shall flourish like the palm tree.” I heard, he says, not the deceits, cries, and threats of malicious persons; rather, because whenever the righteous person is killed for the Lord, he begins to flourish like the palm tree, then he receives brightness [Col. 1261A] and beauty, splendour and greenness.

“He shall multiply like the cedar of Lebanon.” When the saints seem to die, then they begin to grow; for they cannot rot and perish, like the cedar, whose nature is incorruptible. “Planted in the house of the Lord, they shall flourish in the courts of the house of our God.” Now, he says, they are planted in the house of the Lord; now they are built upon the foundation of the Church. For of this planting the wise Apostle says: “I planted” (1 Cor. 3). “They shall flourish in the courts of the house of our God.” Since in this world they are seen as though a dry tree, there indeed they shall appear flourishing and shining like the sun.

“They shall still multiply in fruitful old age.” Before, he says, they flourish there, they shall multiply in fruitful old age and [Col. 1261B] in the sternness of virtues. For the saint, though a child in malice, is old in understanding at every time. “And they shall be truly wise.” For thieves also can be patient, but not rightly so: those who suffer do so not out of love but out of wickedness. “That they may declare that the Lord our God is upright, and there is no iniquity in him.” For this purpose, he says, the saints are retained in their bodies: that they may praise and proclaim Christ in the Church.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 92

“The Lord hath reigned; he is clothed with beauty.” The voice of the Church: The enemies have been conquered; the devil has been driven from the kingdom (Rev. 5). The Lord, however, has reigned, the banner of the cross raised high before the battle line. He is clothed with beauty because, rising from the dead and made immortal [Col. 1261C] (Rom. 6), he shines with his former and paternal glory. “The Lord is clothed with strength,” which can no longer be corrupted. “And he hath girded himself” with power, because he raised from the tomb above the heavens not corruptible but strong and immortal flesh (Mark 16).

“For he hath established the world, which shall not be moved.” The world is now firm, founded upon the firm rock; it is moved from the purpose of faith by no blast of winds and no storm of wicked persons. “Thy throne is prepared from then.” Apostrophe: From the time, he says, when thou didst establish the world, thy throne has been prepared; “but the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” (Gregory, Homily 38). “Thou art from everlasting.” For although, for the preparation of this throne, he was born from a Virgin [Col. 1261D] (Isa. 7), yet in the beginning and before the ages he was God (John 1).

“The rivers have lifted up, O Lord; the rivers have lifted up their voice.” By rivers are understood teachers, in whom the graces of the Holy Spirit overflow. These have raised their voice by preaching Christ the Lord and offering the drink of salvation to the thirsty.

But conversely, “the rivers have lifted up their waves.” Behold, rivers are opposed by rivers. There are four rivers of paradise (Gen. 2); the rivers of the world are innumerable. There are four Gospels; philosophers and heretics are without number. These rise against the saints with arguments, questions, and overflowing verbosity. [Col. 1262A] “From the voices of many waters, wonderful are the risings of the sea.” Many waters are many peoples. When a great multitude of Gentiles saw three or four preachers wishing to destroy the worship of the old gods, they rose against them with great roaring and brought upon them the storms of this sea and every tempest of afflictions. Then “the Lord is wonderful on high”: he seemed to be working, through his saints, so many and such great, so high and magnificent wonders. Temples were falling, idols were being broken, and tyrants at last were losing their authority, and so forth.

“Thy testimonies have become exceedingly credible.” For thou hadst permitted that they too should perform the works which thou didst perform (John 14). Nothing could be truer than this. Therefore thy testimonies are true and credible. “Holiness becometh thy house unto length of days.” For it is fitting that the Church should always be holy and pure, since thou art holy and always dwellest in her. Hence it is written: “Be holy, for I am holy” (1 Pet. 1).

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 93

“God, the Lord of vengeances.” The voice of the Church: Although God permitted his land to be ravaged for a time, although he sometimes allowed us to be crushed beneath harsh slavery, yet, born of a Virgin (Luke 2), he appeared of his own accord and brought liberty among the people. “Lift thyself up, thou who judgest the earth; render recompense to the proud.” Thou, he says, who art to judge the earth, lift thyself up and, appearing [Col. 1262C] in the exalted majesty of thy divinity, render to each according to his works (Ps. 61).

“How long shall sinners, O Lord, how long shall sinners glory?” It is not enough for them to sin; indeed, they glory in sins, namely in the slaughter of the saints. How long “shall they utter and speak iniquity?” Shall “all who work injustice” always speak thus? “Thy people, O Lord,” they have humbled by diverse kinds of torments, “and they have vexed thine inheritance.” This is injustice. “They have slain the widow and the stranger, and murdered the fatherless.” This is literally true. Spiritually, a widow is understood as anyone who dies to the Lord through some deception; a stranger, one who does not dwell firmly in the Church; and the fatherless, [Col. 1262D] those who, being sons through baptism, become orphans through evil conduct. Such persons are said to be slain by heretics and sinners when they readily assent to their inventions.

“And they said: The Lord shall not see, neither shall the God of Jacob understand.” Their deeds indeed make known what they themselves declare in heart and speech. But what answer is given them? “Understand, ye senseless among the people; and ye fools, at last be wise.” For unless they were senseless and foolish, they would by no means deprive God of sight and understanding. “He that planted the ear, shall he not hear? Or he that formed the eye, shall he not see?” Shall he not hear the righteous and the sinner, he who gave them both ear and hearing? Shall he not see, he who made sight?

[Col. 1263A] “He that correcteth the nations, shall he not rebuke? He that teacheth man knowledge?” He who corrects, teaches, and reforms the saints, he says, will he not be able to convict you of iniquity? Let people therefore cease thinking this. “For the Lord knoweth the thoughts of men, that they are vain.” To determine whether this is true, I need not seek an example outside myself: for I have thought many things which turned out otherwise. Change of speaker:

“Blessed is the man whom thou shalt instruct, O Lord, and shalt teach him out of thy law.” Miserable indeed are those who teach themselves and trust the vanities of their own thoughts. But whoever is instructed by such a teacher and nourished at the breasts of the Law is blessed with supreme blessedness. “That thou mayest make him gentle in evil days, until a pit be dug for the sinner.” Whoever is corrected [Col. 1263B] and taught in this world is not deceived by worldly wisdom and will find the Lord most gentle toward him when evil days consume the wicked. Until a pit and the due punishment are prepared for the sinner, all the saints are instructed in the ordinances of the Law.

“For the Lord will not cast off his people.” He will be gentle, he says, in evil days; he will not cast away his people from himself, “nor forsake his inheritance, until righteousness is converted into judgment, and all who are upright in heart are near it.” “Who will rise up for me against the malicious?” Thou alone, who art the best helper. It has therefore been proved that he will not forsake his inheritance. “Or who will stand with me against those who work iniquity?” Thou indeed wilt stand, since thou wilt help; for to stand is the part of one who helps (Gregory, Homily 29). Hence follows:

“Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell.” But with his help, as he himself rose again (Matt. 28), I too shall rise. “If I said, My foot is moved,” and I am about to fall from my former firmness under the assault of evils, come to the aid of one falling; hold back one slipping. “Thy mercy, O Lord, helped me. According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, thy consolations made my soul glad.” Who, therefore, would not desire many sorrows and many tribulations in this world, since in proportion to the number of sorrows he shall receive a multitude of consolations?

[Col. 1263D] “Shall the seat of iniquity cleave to thee?” For just as the saints have a seat of righteousness, so sinners have a seat of iniquity. But these shall not cleave to the Lord, because only those upright in heart shall stand near that [seat]. “Thou who fashionest labour in the commandment.” “If anyone,” says the Lord, “wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9). We have, therefore, the commandment; let us consider also the labour. What is it to follow the Lord except to imitate his works? But this does not happen without labour. Finally, to deny oneself and carry the cross is great labour. Paul denied himself when he said: “I am dead to the world” (Rom. 7): that is, I am not what I was; I am not Saul, but Paul. And he bears the cross [Col. 1264A] who both mortifies the flesh and does not hesitate to die for Christ’s name.

“They shall lie in wait for the soul of the righteous, and condemn innocent blood.” These seats of iniquity, he says, always desire to act against the souls of the righteous and condemn innocent blood to death. “But the Lord,” says the righteous man, “has become my refuge, and my God the help of my hope. And he shall repay them their iniquity”: that is, the due reward of their iniquity. “And in their malice the Lord our God shall destroy them.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 94

“Come, let us exult unto the Lord.” The voice of the Church: Flee, O nations, the worship of idols; leave [Col. 1264B] behind the works of the world; depart from iniquity; hasten to life. Why do you stand still? Come, let us exult unto the Lord; “let us make joyful noise unto God our saviour.” Let us humbly worship him who redeemed the world by his death (Gal. 3).

“Let us go before his face in confession,” lest we be found unprepared. Let us seek him with the gaze of the mind, whom we shall see “face to face” (1 Cor. 13), so that, when he comes to judge, we may not meet him as strangers. “And in psalms,” hymns, praises, and spiritual songs, “let us make joyful noise unto him. For” he is “God,” our God, “a great Lord” throughout the whole earth, “and a great King above all gods.” Let all other gods therefore be abandoned, and let this one, who alone is everywhere and encompasses all things by his greatness, [Col. 1264C] be worshipped by all. “For in his hand are all the ends of the earth.” For all the kingdoms of the world are contained in his hand and power. “And the heights of the mountains are his.” For the powers of the Apostles and their lofty understanding of all the Scriptures belong to him who is rightly called the living fountain. “For the sea is his, and he made it; and his hands formed the dry land,” for there is nothing that he did not make. “Come,” therefore, “let us worship, fall down, and weep before the Lord who made us, because he is the Lord our God.” “Blessed are ye that weep now, for ye shall laugh” (Luke 6). “And we are the people of his pasture,” because we have been placed in a place of pasture and among the riches of the Scriptures; “and the sheep of his hand,” whom one and the same [Col. 1264D] hand both made and redeemed. Whose hand? His who says: “Today, if ye hear his voice.” Since you are his sheep, “harden not your hearts,” but recognize the shepherd’s voice, “as in the provocation, according to the day of temptation in the wilderness, where your fathers tempted me, proved me, and saw my works.”

“For forty years I was offended with that generation, and I said: These always err in heart, and they have not known my ways; so I swore in my wrath: If they shall enter into my rest.” The Apostle explains this in the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying that their corpses were strewn in the wilderness (Heb. 3) and that they could not enter the land of promise. Let us therefore open [Col. 1265A] our ears, that we may understand his voice, which he daily admonishes us to heed in the Church. And let us not tempt him, lest, angered with us at some time, he cast us away from the land of the living.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 95

“Sing unto the Lord a new song.” The voice of the Prophet: A new man came into the world and gave the world a new law (Gregory the Pope, Homily 32). Therefore sing and proclaim this new law, this new song, and announce it to all nations in his praise. “Sing unto the Lord, all the earth”: Jews and Gentiles, righteous and sinners. “Sing unto the Lord, and bless his name.” His name is the Word (John 1); his utterance is Christ. We ought to bless and praise him at all times, [Col. 1265B] for he is the one of whom it is said: “Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar” (Isa. 30). “Declare his salvation from day to day”: day by day, through each day, passing from strength to strength, from the New to the Old, from the Old to the New Testament, let us proclaim his salvation. For preaching must walk upon these two feet and illumine the hearts of those subject to it by this double light. “Declare his glory among the nations.” Declare to the nations, he says, that glory which the Jews refused to receive. “His wonders among all peoples”: namely, his ineffable birth, resurrection, and ascension, saying: “For the Lord is great,” since he is Lord of all, “and exceedingly praiseworthy” in all that he has done. “He is terrible above all [Col. 1265C] gods,” because without his command they can do nothing. For “all the gods of the nations are demons; but the Lord made the heavens.”

“Confession and beauty are before him.” Whoever wishes to dwell with the Lord, he says, should confess his sins and cleanse body and soul from every crime. For confession and beauty alone are before him. “Holiness and magnificence are in his sanctification.” Whoever is sanctified by him is found pre-eminent in chastity and magnificent in virtue.

“Bring to the Lord the kindreds of the nations.” As though he said: “Bring to the Lord glory and honor; bring to the Lord glory for his name,” you who are called Christians from Christ [Col. 1265D]. “Take offerings, and enter into his courts.” For we cannot enter the courts of the Lord without offerings and hands full [of them]. But what are these courts? “In my Father’s house,” says the Lord, “there are many dwelling-places” (John 14). Now one enters the many dwelling-places by many offerings: some enter these precious houses by the offering of piety, others by the offering of humility, others by the oblation of generosity, and still others by the sacrifice of charity. But as the offerings differ, so too do the houses: for one is the brightness of the sun, another that of the moon. “Worship the Lord in his holy court.” Meanwhile, he says, worship the Lord in the Church, until, when you come to him, you offer him sheaves in your hands. “Let the whole earth be moved at his presence.” For you are, as it were, the face of God [Col. 1266A], his image and likeness. Therefore remove from yourselves whatever earthly corruption you possess, so that you may become wholly heavenly and spiritual. “And say among the nations: The Lord has reigned,” since a ruler of this kind has been conquered and hell despoiled (Eph. 4).

“For he has set the world aright.” That world, he says, which the devil had made crooked and perverse by the enticements of death, Christ set right by masterly severity. “It shall not be moved,” nor shall it any longer be separated from his faith. “He shall judge the peoples in equity”: he who set the world right will himself judge the peoples. “Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth exult.” Let the apostles rejoice, and let the Church rejoice also. “Let the sea be moved, and its fullness,” so that no little fish may be found in it which, baptized in so great a deep, does not joyfully meet its Lord [Col. 1266B]. “The fields shall rejoice, and all that is in them”: the souls and bodies of the saints shall rejoice; when thorns and briars have been uprooted from them, they themselves will be adorned with a rich harvest and the beauty of flowers. “Then all the trees of the forests shall exult”: when they have borne good fruit, they will not be cut down and thrown into the fire, but will be built into the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem. “For every tree which does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. 3).—“At the presence of the Lord,” in the Savior’s presence. “For he comes,” to redeem the time. And “because he comes” a second time, “to judge the earth.” But how will he judge?

“He will judge the world in equity, and the peoples in his truth,” humbling the proud and exalting the humble [Col. 1266C].

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XCVI

“The Lord has reigned; let the earth exult.” The Prophet’s voice: Let the earth now exult; let humanity rejoice, in which not sin but the Lord reigns. “Let the many islands rejoice.” There are many islands, many Churches dispersed in the sea of this age. Let them therefore rejoice, because, although divided by place, they are nevertheless gathered under the rule of one Emperor. “Cloud and darkness are round about him.” For the cloud which surrounded Christ may be understood either as the flesh in which he was hidden, or as the apostles full of the water of wisdom, or as that cloud which received him from their eyes (Acts 1) [Col. 1266D]. I would also call this cloud your womb, blessed Virgin, moistened by the grace of God alone. For you are that light cloud upon which the Lord came into Egypt (Luke 2). And darkness is round about him: “the Lord is in darkness” (Exod. 24); “the light shines in darkness” (John 1); and our Savior preaches in Judaea (Matt. 19), but the darkness did not comprehend it (John 1), nor did the Jews recognize their Lord. “Righteousness and judgment are the correction of his throne.” For whoever follows righteousness and judges himself corrects the throne of God. “Fire shall go before him.” He who, he says, came in cloud and darkness at his first advent, will come at his second in fire and manifest light. This fire will burn the wicked and illumine the good. This is what follows [Col. 1267A]: “And it shall set his enemies round about on fire.”

“His lightnings shone upon the world.” The very alternation of times also indicates that he now speaks of the first advent, now of the second. Because, he says, he will then come in fire, he formerly sent many lightnings beforehand. For lightnings shone throughout the world when the miracles of the apostles were declared everywhere. “The earth saw this and was moved”: some were moved toward faith, others against the saints.

“The mountains melted like wax at the presence of the Lord.” The rich, proud, and exalted, who had formerly been hard and stony, were softened by apostolic preaching and received in their breasts the evangelical words written by the divine stylus. “At the presence of the Lord, all the earth”: this, he says [Col. 1267B], the presence and knowledge of the Lord brought about in all the earth, that marble was changed into wax. “The heavens declared his righteousness.”—“The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18). The apostles preach Christ (Acts 2).

“And all peoples saw his glory”: they understood that he had now come, he who both saved the world and will give glory. “Let all who worship carved images therefore be confounded, and those who glory in their idols.” But you, “worship him, all his angels,” all preachers of the Gospel, whom they heard through your preaching. And in this “Zion rejoiced,” that is, the holy Church. “And the daughters of Judah exulted.” Zion, he says, rejoiced, and the daughters of Judah—that is, the souls of confessors—exulted, “because of your judgments, O Lord,” by keeping which they hope to be saved. “For you [Col. 1267C], O Lord, are most high over all the earth; you are exceedingly exalted above all gods.” You alone are worthy of praise and every veneration, for you surpass human beings, demons, and angels.

“You who love the Lord, hate evil.” Whoever wishes to be God’s friend must become the enemy of his enemies. “The Lord keeps the souls of his servants; he will deliver them from the hand of the sinner.”—“But, according to the Apostle, God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able” (1 Cor. 10).—“Light has risen for the righteous,” that is, Christ the Lord, for the salvation of the Church. “And joy for the upright in heart”: he whom you have long desired, behold, has come. Therefore “rejoice, you righteous, in the Lord,” not in the dignities of this age [Col. 1267D]. “And confess to the remembrance of his holiness”: confess and praise him who, mindful of you, sanctified you.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XCVII

“Sing to the Lord a new song.” The Prophet’s voice: Whoever desires to sing a new song should read what follows, so that he may find what is new. “For he has done”—is this new? For what has the Lord done that is not wonderful? It is not new, therefore, that he has done wonders, unless something else is added. But see what follows: “His right hand shall save for him.” This, however, is new and utterly unheard of before Christ’s resurrection. And what is “his right hand shall save for him,” except that he caused his Son to rise for his own praise and honor? (Mark 16). Confirmation: “And his holy arm” [Col. 1268A]. Of this arm it is said: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” “The Lord has made known his salvation.” For the Son of God, who was once wholly unknown, has now become known, and above all known to the Church. For the Apostle knew him well when he said: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2).—“Before the nations he revealed his righteousness.” Christ is called the righteousness of God, because without this righteousness no one can be justified. “He remembered his mercy and his truth,” which he promised to the house of Israel. For he says: “In those days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell securely” (Jer. 33). Therefore, mindful of this promised truth, the Lord redeemed the world by his great mercy [Col. 1268B]. “All the ends of the earth saw the salvation of our God”: the whole aforementioned new promise has now been fulfilled; but this is what is still awaited in the future. For many saw Christ at his first advent, but not all; when he comes a second time to judge, then every eye shall see him (Luke 21). Therefore rejoice in the Lord, all the earth; sing, exult, and make melody. Let us rejoice with the heart, sing with the mouth, exult in the Lord with every movement of the body; let hands, feet, and eyes make melody, serving the Lord in their respective offices. “Make melody to the Lord with the lyre, with the lyre.” For teachers possess two lyres, one in the heart and the other in the mouth. That which is in the heart plays to the Lord alone with ineffable harmony; that which is in the mouth makes the proud, the wrathful [Col. 1268C], and anyone like Saul most gentle through the sweet melody of the Scriptures. “And with the voice of a psalm”: for the voice of a psalm is made only on the psaltery; whoever sings on the psaltery serves the Lord in the ten commandments of the Law.

“With beaten trumpets and the sound of a horn-trumpet.” Beaten trumpets were made of silver, by which the Israelite people assembled as one; but horn-trumpets must not sound without silver ones, nor silver ones without horn-trumpets. In the silver trumpets is displayed purity of speech; in the horn-trumpets, the strength of virtues. Thus one must not be deceitful in speech, nor preach against heretics without horns: let him soften these with true words, but terrify those with hard horns. “Rejoice in the presence of the Lord the King.” That rejoicing takes place not in the mouth but in the heart is shown in this passage: “Man sees what is before the face, but God sees the heart” (1 Sam. 16) [Col. 1268D]. Rejoicing therefore takes place in the sight of God alone, since it is in the heart.

“Let the sea and its fullness be moved, the world and those who dwell in it.” Let all, he says, be moved; let all shake off every moth from themselves and flee to the Lord.

“The rivers shall clap their hands together.”—“If anyone thirsts,” says the Lord, “let him come and drink, and waters of life shall flow from his belly” (John 7). The saints, therefore, are rivers, since waters run forth from their belly. To clap the hands is to rejoice in the Lord. For it was the custom of the ancients to clap their hands in joy. Or rather, it is to join good works to good works without interruption [Col. 1269A]. “The mountains shall exult in the presence of the Lord, because he comes to judge the earth.” For then the saints shall rejoice, then the mountains shall exult, when it will be said: “Fall upon us” (Luke 23). Those upon whom these mountains fall cannot be found by the wrath to come. “He will judge the world in righteousness.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XCVIII

“The Lord has reigned.” The voice of the Prophet or the Church: I have said it once, I have said it again, I say it a third time: “The Lord has reigned,” so that “every word may stand in the midst of two or three witnesses” (Deut. 17). But you unbelieving Jews deny what your Prophet steadfastly affirms.

“Let the peoples be angry.” Let the Jews be angry; let them be confounded with grief, because, willing or unwilling, the Lord has reigned. Let Christians also be angry—those who were killing him whom they had once served—and, having received another King, let them no longer permit sin to reign in themselves. But where has the Lord reigned? It follows: “He who sits above the cherubim.” *Cherubim* is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” Therefore the Lord sits not only in the angels who are called by this name, but also in the saints filled with the spirit of wisdom and knowledge. “Let the earth be moved,” that is, let the peoples be angry. But this “Lord is great in Zion,” because he is praised and magnified daily in the holy Church [Col. 1269B]. “And exalted above all peoples,” though the Jews always thought that their own one slept in the tomb (Matt. 27). Apostrophe:

[Col. 1269C] “Let them confess your great name, for it is terrible and holy.” Let the name of the Lord always be praised, and let them confess to him things hidden and manifest, because it is terrible to the wicked, but holy and delightful to the righteous. “And the honor of the king loves judgment.” Whoever wishes to honor the King of kings should first judge himself, and kill and condemn to death theft, adultery, perjury, homicide, and the other evildoers of his own body; thus he will receive with honor and peace the guest coming to the seat of his own breast.

“You have prepared upright judgments.” Since all God’s judgments are prepared in uprightness and equity, let our judgments also be directed rightly. For [Col. 1269D] he does not judge rightly who, by giving life to pride within himself, kills humility. “And you have wrought righteousness in Jacob.” For when Jacob judges, he supplants (Gen. 27), and works righteousness. Yet the Lord works this righteousness when he grants the craft of supplanting. Change of person:

“Exalt the Lord our God.” So that he who is naturally great may also be held exalted in your hearts. “And worship his footstool, because it is holy.” What should we understand by the footstool except the body of the Lord? Upon this, as upon a footstool, divinity sits. All shall worship this, as he himself says: “‘As I live,’ says the Lord, ‘every knee shall bend to me’” (Isa. 45). It may also be understood of the cross, on which the Savior ended this life [Col. 1270A] (Matt. 27). “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name.” Him, he says, whom we worship as seated on the footstool, Moses, Aaron, Samuel, and all the prophets prophesied and worshiped. “They called upon the Lord”: they called upon him indeed as Lord. “But he himself heard them. And he spoke to them in a pillar of cloud.” He spoke to them in cloud and darkness because, being about to come in flesh, he would make darkness his hiding-place. “They kept his testimonies and the commandment which he gave them.” But this is said for your confusion, Jews, who insultingly said to him whom your fathers worshiped (John 4): “You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true” (John 8) [Col. 1270B]. Why, then, did Moses and Aaron keep his testimony? “O Lord our God, you heard them.” You, he says, who now, having become man, would be called a footstool, heard them formerly. “O God, you were gracious to them” in all that they asked with faith and love; “and avenging all their inventions,” as in the case of the calf which they worshiped in the wilderness. “Exalt the Lord our God.” O how great is the joy in one word: he who is God and Lord of all is called, in a special sense, our God and our Lord!

“And worship on his holy mountain,” that is, in the Church, or in your hearts, which, raised above earthly vanity, deservedly acquire the name of a mountain. And say: “For holy is the Lord [Col. 1270C] our God.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XCIX

“Rejoice in God, all the earth.” The voice of the teachers: Rejoice in God, all the earth. Paul also said this: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. 4).—“Serve the Lord in gladness.” For the Jews served not in gladness but from necessity; unless they served, they lay under the curses of the Law. But let us serve not from fear, but from love of blessing. “Enter into his presence with exultation,” for we are always in God’s presence when we perform works worthy of his sight. Whoever gives alms, prays, or preaches to others stands before God’s presence [Col. 1270D]; but unless these things are done with exultation, they seem unacceptable. “Know that he is God”: not the sun, moon, heaven, earth, or any other creature is God, but he is God who made all things (John 1). “He made us, and not we ourselves.”

“His people and the sheep of his pasture.” For all who hear his voice are his sheep (John 10). “Enter his gates in confession.” To state this briefly: I shall call him both his gate and mine who washed me in the water of baptism. Yet I could not enter it until I confessed the Lord and renounced the devil. “His courts in hymns.” To expound all this by my own example: having entered, by God’s grace, the aforementioned gate, I now utter such hymns as I can in his courts [Col. 1271A]. “Confess to him.” See how rightly the sequence proceeds: he spoke of sheep, set forth pasture, and introduced gates. Therefore, whoever enters this pasture must be a sheep; and no one is allowed to enter except through the gate, for whoever enters by another way shall be called a thief (John 10). Having entered, let him devote himself to praise and confession. “Praise his name.” Whoever is called a Christian should show himself such that Christ’s name is glorified in him. “For the Lord is sweet”: as he is sweet to the meek, so he will be harsh to the proud.

“His mercy is everlasting, and his truth unto generation and generation.” Mercy is eternal, and truth is eternal: there will always be saints who are saved by mercy, and there will always be sinners who are condemned by truth [Col. 1271B].

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM C

“I will sing to you, O Lord, mercy and judgment.” The voice of the perfect: To you, O God, I will sing both the mercy of redemption and the judgment of truth. He is merciful: let no one despair. He is true: let no one be proud. “I will sing and understand,” for many sing who do not understand; they say one thing with their tongue and think another in their heart. The tongue sings psalms, but the mind calculates the number of coins. “In the immaculate way,” I will sing, he says, but in such a way that I understand, walking in the immaculate way. There are many ways of the saints, and all are immaculate [Col. 1271C]. “When will you come to me?” Why does he say “will you come,” when the Lord is always with him? “You will come,” therefore, refers to the second advent, awaited by the saints with such longing that they seem always to say, “Come, come.”

“I walked in the innocence of my heart.” Since he had previously said that he was in the immaculate way, in this place he makes known what that way was. “I walked,” he says, “in the innocence of my heart,” which is “in the midst of my house,” that is, my body. This way is altogether immaculate: for innocence of heart, if joined with reason, is the perfection of the whole human being. “I hated those who commit transgression.” Neither, he says, did I transgress, nor did I consent to transgressors. “A perverse heart did not cling to me” [Col. 1271D]. Rather, as my heart was upright in all things, so it clung only to the upright in heart. “I did not know the evil man who turned away from me.” I did not know the evil man so as to assent to him in evil; but as he turned away from my paths, so I also turned away from him. “The one who secretly slandered his neighbor, him I persecuted,” in hope of correction, not in agreement with wickedness.

“With proud eye.” For a person’s pride is easily discerned in the eyes and brow. “And insatiable heart.” By this title the greedy person is designated. “With such a one I did not eat.” Thus the Apostle also says: “If anyone called a brother among you is a fornicator, or greedy, or a worshiper of idols, or a reviler, or [Col. 1272A] a robber, do not even take food with such a one” (1 Cor. 5). Divine response:

“My eyes are upon the faithful of the earth, that they may sit with me.” Do not regret, the Lord says, that you have done this. I saw your works, I knew your faith; I shall come to you, and place you with the other faithful in the heavenly seat. “He who walks in the immaculate way”—what you have confessed that you did—“he,” and no other, “ministered to me. He did not dwell in the midst of my house,” that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem, “who practices pride” and destroys humility. “He who speaks iniquity did not prosper before my eyes,” so as to be worthy to see my face.

“In the morning I slew all sinners of the earth.” He called the day of judgment “morning,” in which all sinners are to perish. It is called morning because it succeeds this present life, which is rightly called night [Col. 1272B].
