Finally, that day will begin to shine upon the saints, and no darkness of night shall be able to interrupt it (Rev. 21). “That I might destroy from the city of the Lord all those who work iniquity.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM CI

“O Lord, hear my prayer.” In this psalm the Church speaks first, then Christ, and afterward the Prophet. “O Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you. Do not turn your face from me; in whatever day I am troubled, incline your ear to me; in whatever day I call upon you, hear me swiftly.” With what fervor of soul the Church herself entreats the Lord is shown by the repetition of words themselves, in which the same thing is said so often: “For my days have failed like smoke.” Present life quickly slips away and vanishes; for a day gone by, like smoke that has vanished, can no longer be found. The days of the saints fail like smoke, because they cannot be without tears. Therefore the Lord must be earnestly entreated to grant us eternal days, since ours fail so swiftly, like smoke. “And my bones have dried up like a firebrand.” The bones of the Church are called the apostles, who were dried up in the frying-pan of many tribulations according to the flesh [Col. 1272C]. Whoever does not understand this should remember Lawrence’s gridiron.

“I was struck down like grass.” Formerly, he says, youth flourished in me; but when old age came, the flower of youth was immediately cut down and fell. “And my heart dried up,” because together with youth I lost all strength of body. “Because I forgot to eat my bread.” Forgetful, he says, of the bread given me, I ate that which was forbidden, because, leaving aside the other trees of paradise, I ate the forbidden tree alone (Gen. 3). For unless Adam, who was the beginning of this ecclesiastical body (Gen. 1), had forgotten his own bread, humanity would neither have been deprived of its first flower nor failed in any strength.

“Because of the sound of my groaning, my bone clung to my flesh.” When, he says, I had lost the eternity of days, the beauty of the flower, and the strength of my powers, what remained but pain and groaning? Forgetful of bread, and mindful of former happiness, I began to repent and groan and to implore the mercy of God alone [Col. 1273A]. At this groaning, flesh clung to spirit and spirit to flesh; and those which had previously opposed one another began now to be in harmony. And because, as is read in the Gospel, the two had agreed within me, the Lord heard all my petitions. The voice of Christ:

“I have become like a pelican of the wilderness.” By one and the same fault, he says, you lost both the eternity of days and God’s image and likeness; and I, for the sake of restoration, became like a pelican, who by no remedy other than his own blood gave life to his offspring. Furthermore, I brought unclean idolaters and sinners into my body, which is the Church [Col. 1273B]. There are said to be two kinds of pelicans: one in waters, the other in the wilderness. Those that inhabit the wilderness are reported to have this nature: they feed on unclean animals, such as frogs and lizards; they kill their young, and, grieving for three days and wounding themselves, restore them to life by sprinkling them with their own blood. This comparison agrees fittingly with our Savior, who, because of the transgression of the first parent, deprived us of immortality and cast us out of paradise (Gen. 3), subjecting us to the laws of death. But this our Pelican, revisiting his offspring, was grieved for three days with the sorrow of death—not so much his own death as ours—and gave them life by the shedding of his own blood. See, then, how beautifully this comparison suits what precedes [Col. 1273C]. The Church and the whole human race lamented both their expulsion from paradise, the brevity of their days, and the weakness of their powers. To this the Savior replies in most sweet consolation: “I am like the pelican; I kill and I make alive; I strike and I heal” (Deut. 32). Do not fear, therefore, human being, for I shall restore you to life.

“I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling.” Everyone knows that the night-raven, or owl, is hated by other birds, which pursue it with a certain chatter until it settles somewhere. Christ is compared to this bird: the Jews pursued him with great tumult up to the cross (John 18–19). The cross of Christ is deservedly called a dwelling, for it is imprinted upon our foreheads and upon the dwelling-place of our body [Col. 1273D]. Nor is it strange that he is likened to an owl, since he also called himself a worm (Ps. 21).

“I kept watch,” because I rose on the third day (1 Cor. 15), “and became like a sparrow,” swift in flight, “alone upon the roof,” because no one ascended to heaven with me in the flesh. “All day long my enemies reproached me,” namely the Jews, who pursued him as a night-raven. “And those who praised me,” with manifest flattery, “swore against me,” that is, conspired for his death. But for what reason?

“Because I ate ashes like bread,” that is, like the pelican, I joined the unclean and disgraceful to my body [Col. 1274A]. Hence some said that he was a drinker of wine and a friend of tax collectors (Matt. 11). “And I mixed my drink with weeping,” because he both grieved for the death of his children and shared divine and human food with those who continually wept for their sins. Among these was the sinful woman who washed his feet with tears (Luke 7). The voice of the Church:

“Because of the face of your wrath and indignation, because lifting me up you dashed me down. My days declined like a shadow.” You made me, he says, from the clay of the earth (Gen. 2), and, raising me to angelic dignity, had made me as a lord; but by transgressing the command I incurred the wrath of your indignant anger (Gen. 3) and was dashed down into earthly weakness. Thus, because of the face of your wrath and indignation [Col. 1274B], “my days declined like a shadow,” that is, they vanished with the utmost swiftness after immortality was lost. “And I dried up like grass.” Truly the people are grass: “the grass has withered and the flower has fallen” (Isa. 40); we have lost the flower and are reduced to dust. “But you, O Lord, remain forever, and your memorial unto generation and generation. You shall arise,” as you promised, “and have mercy upon Zion,” because, having taken on the likeness of the pelican, he will give us life by his own blood (Heb. 9). “For the time of showing her mercy, the time has come.” The time, he says, of our redemption and your incarnation has come.

“For her stones pleased your servants.” Living stones roll over the earth; these are those of whom it is said: “A time to gather stones, and a time to scatter” (Eccl. 3). For the Lord first gathered the apostles (Luke 6), then dispersed them to preach (Mark 16) [Col. 1274C]. Let these stones please us, and let us imitate their firmness. “And they shall have compassion upon her earth”: for that person has compassion upon his own earth who prepares an eternal dwelling for his flesh. “And the nations shall fear your name, O Lord,” so that they will not dare to swear by it in vain. “And all the kings of the earth [shall fear] your glory,” that is, your Son. “For the Lord has built Zion and shall be seen in his glory.” For, as the Apostle says, “when Christ, our life, appears, then we too shall appear with him in glory” (Col. 3).—“He looked upon the prayer of the humble and did not despise their petitions” [Col. 1274D]. The exposition of this is plain on the surface. The voice of the Prophet:

“Let these things be written for another generation,” namely the future generation, which the Lord will regard and visit through his incarnation. “And the people who shall be created” by the water of baptism and the Holy Spirit “shall praise the Lord. For he looked down from his holy height; the Lord looked from heaven upon the earth,” so that through his visitation he might have mercy upon it. “That he might hear the groaning of those in fetters.” For the patriarchs and prophets were held in chains in hell, and their groanings were heard. Those also were in chains who, bound in the chains of vices, followed the devil. “That he might loose the children of the slain.” Therefore not only our fathers [Col. 1275A], who were slain and dead, were chained, but we too were bound through them. For who is loosed unless bound? Therefore we were bound, since we were loosed by the Lord (Ps. 123). “That they might declare in Zion the name of the Lord and his praise in Jerusalem.” For this, he says, were we loosed from the devil’s snares: that we might sing the Lord’s praise in the Church.

“In gathering the peoples together as one,” that is, while all nations are assembled in the unity of one faith, “and kings, to serve the Lord. He answered him in the way of his strength,” that is, in the work of preaching, which, according to the Apostle, is called God’s power (Rom. 1). “Make known to me the fewness of my days.” To whom did he answer? Jerusalem. For when the Lord drew near to Jerusalem, as though it asked him about the fewness of its days, he answered in tears: “For if you had known—and you—that days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart,” etc. (Luke 19) [Col. 1275B]. Thus he foretells to it the fewness of its days. Apostrophe:

“Do not call me back in the midst of my days.” But allow me not merely to pass the middle, but even to continue in your service. Or: do not call me back from this life, overtaken by some judgment, before the appointed end. Fearing this, he says: “I said, in the midst of my days I shall go to the gates of hell” (Isa. 38).—“Your years are unto generation and generation.” Yours, he says, are years, days, seasons, and months; all obey your will [Col. 1275C]. “In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands.” This is true according to the letter. It may also be understood of the Church and the apostles. “They shall perish,” because they shall be changed for the better; “but you shall remain,” for you cannot change. “And all shall grow old like a garment,” when the flesh is dissolved. “And you shall change them like a covering,” so that, cleansed of the filth of vices, they may become more beautiful. “And they shall be changed,” unto eternity. “But you are the same,” altogether unchangeable. “And your years shall not fail. The children of your servants shall dwell” in the Church, the heavens having now in some manner been changed. “And their seed shall be directed forever,” for the works of the saints are never perverted.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM CII

[Col. 1275D]

“Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, his holy name.” The voice of the Church: For we ought to bless and praise the Lord not with lips only, but also with soul and heart, mind and understanding, and all our powers. “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his recompenses.” For who can count God’s benefits? He created the sun and moon, fire and water, and the other creatures for our service. Yet these are nothing when compared with future goods. “Who is gracious to all your iniquities.” Exposition: “Who heals all your infirmities,” by which either body or soul is weakened. “Who redeems your life from destruction” [Col. 1276A], which the devil oppressed. “Who crowns you in mercy,” first giving the strength of mercy, so that he may afterward grant the crown also. “Who fills your desire with good things,” though it had been emptied by evil thoughts.

“Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s.” For when an eagle reaches old age and loses its feathers through the heat of the sun, it descends into some fountain and is restored to youth. Thus too the holy Church, kindled by the heats of the Sun of righteousness and plunged into the font of baptism, puts off the old human being and puts on the youth of the new. It shall also be renewed at the judgment, when it resumes its original image.

“The Lord performs mercies and judgment for all who suffer injury; he made known his ways to Moses [Col. 1276B], his wills to the children of Israel.” He performed mercy indeed in redeeming the world (Gal. 3); he performed judgment because he will avenge the innocent. Hence the Apostle: “‘Vengeance is mine,’ he says, ‘and I will repay,’ says the Lord” (Rom. 12). Moses—that is, the apostles—knew his ways, for they were fishers in water and baptizers. But the children of Israel know his wills: that is, holy men who contemplate him with the eyes of the mind. “Will he be angry forever? For he is compassionate and merciful, patient and greatly merciful. Nor will he threaten forever,” because, as it is written, “when he suffered, he did not threaten” (1 Pet. 2).—“He did not deal with us according to our sins.” For when we deserved death, he underwent death for us [Col. 1276C]. “Nor did he repay us according to our iniquities,” when we had turned toward better things.

“Since, according to the height of heaven above earth, he has strengthened his mercy upon those who fear him.” For God’s mercy has been made firm in the saints, so that, borne above the heavens, they may be joined to the angels. “As far as east is from west, so far has he removed our iniquities from us”; for as the dead differ from the living, so the righteous differ from the unrighteous. “As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him,” chastising them with blows, not killing them with darts. “For he himself has known our frame,” which is aptly compared with that of a potter’s vessel. He knew it indeed, because he took the form of a servant (Phil. 2). “He remembered that we are dust” [Col. 1276D], which, unless he had watered it with the waters of his mercy, would be scattered by every blast of wind. Man is like grass, easily deprived of its flowers: “His days shall bloom like a flower of the field,” but not for a long space of time. “For the spirit shall pass through him, and he shall not remain; nor shall he know his place any longer,” for together with the spirit both strength and possession are lost. “But the mercy of the Lord is from everlasting, and unto everlasting, upon those who fear him; and his righteousness upon children’s children, upon those who keep his covenant.” For the children of God are all those who imitate the apostles. Hence the Apostle says: “My little children, whom I travail over again, until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4).—“And let them remember his commandments” [Col. 1277A], not merely in order to read them, but in order to do them; for, as the Apostle says, “Not the hearers of the law shall be justified before God, but the doers” (Rom. 2).

“The Lord has prepared his throne in heaven.” For, rising from the dead, he ascended into heaven (Mark 16). Or “in heaven,” that is, in the apostles, since “the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” (Gregory, Homily 33).—“And his kingdom shall rule over all.” For the apostles are the rulers of his kingdom, which is the Church, and they shall judge the other nations. “Bless the Lord, all his angels”: teachers, who proclaim him. “Mighty in strength,” because they strengthen us; “doing his word, so as to hear the voice of his utterances”: those who preach for this purpose, that his commandments may be observed.

[Col. 1277B] “Bless the Lord, all his powers,” both of angels and of men. “His ministers, who do his will.” Here, however, the blessing of the wicked is rejected. “Bless the Lord, all his works.” Can stones and wood bless the Lord? Indeed they can: stones bless the Lord when we bless the Lord in this creation. “In every place of his dominion”: the Lord is immeasurable (Ps. 112); therefore let praise and blessing be immeasurable. “Bless,” you also, “O my soul, the Lord,” that he too may reward you with everlasting blessing.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 103

“Bless the Lord, O my soul. O Lord my God, thou hast been exceedingly magnified.” The voice of the Prophet [Col. 1277C]: Since the Lord has indeed been exceedingly magnified, let him be exceedingly praised by all.

“Thou hast put on confession and beauty.” For he who was once surrounded by the Jews’ reproach and by the weakness of the flesh (Matt. 27) is now attended by the praise of angels and men, and shines with eternal beauty and brightness. “Clothed with light as with a garment.” For if the saints shine like the sun in the kingdom of God (Matt. 13), who can set forth in words the radiance of the Savior himself?

“Stretching out the heaven like a skin.” For he easily and without any difficulty stretched out and completed the lofty vault of heaven. For his speaking is doing. “Who coverest its upper parts with waters.” Hence it is written: “And he divided the waters which were above [Col. 1277D] the firmament from those which were beneath the firmament” (Gen. 1). But, if this is understood mystically, the heavens prefigured the apostles, who, because they were new wineskins, were stretched so far to receive the new wine that they themselves received the vintage of the whole vineyard (Mark 16). For whatever we possess of the New and Old Law, we have drunk through their pouring it out to us. By their upper parts he signified the prophets, who were born in an earlier age. But they were covered by such a depth of waters that no one could sail over them; yet Peter, because, as a fisherman (Matt. 4), he had been skilled in all waters, opened for us a passage across. “Who makest the cloud thy ascent.” As it is written: “And when he had said this, while they looked on, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes” [Col. 1278A] (Acts 1).—“Who walkest upon the wings of the winds”: for no wind ever ascended to where Christ was borne.

“Who makest thy angels spirits.” For when he sent Gabriel to Mary, he made an angel out of a spirit. “And thy ministers a burning fire.” For God’s ministers may be called not only angels, but also all teachers. They are called fire because they enlighten others. “Who hast founded the earth upon its stability.” The stability and foundation of the Church is Christ (Ps. 86); founded upon him, it shall not be shaken for ever and ever, but shall always ascend to higher degrees of virtues.

“The deep is his garment, his covering.” What [Col. 1278B] is meant by the deep but the understanding of the New and Old Testaments? Clothed with such a garment, the Church cannot fall to either side; for this breastplate cannot be pierced by any weapons of its adversaries (Matt. 16). “The waters shall stand above the mountains.” What do we understand by the mountains except teachers, and by the waters except sinners? The waters therefore stood above the mountains when the turbulent commotion of the wicked, driven by a diabolical storm, rose against the saints; but these, armed with the shield of both deeps and sounding the clear trumpet, calmed every threat of the sea. This is what follows:

“At thy rebuke they shall flee.” For they said: “Repent” (Matt. 3); and again: “Unless you repent, you shall die” (Luke 13); and once more: “Now the axe is laid to the root of the tree” [Col. 1278C] (Matt. 3). The waters fled from this rebuke when the nations, abandoning the vain worship of gods, submitted themselves to the Lord. “At the voice of thy thunder they shall be afraid.” The voice of thunder is the preaching of the apostles, which, bringing at once sound, lightning, and fear into human hearts, slew the devil himself with the sword of the Spirit.

“The mountains rise.” As the waters diminished: for as the crowds believed, the Churches increased. “And the plains descend,” because, abandoning the empty dignities of the world, the peoples are humbled beneath Christ’s yoke. “To the place which thou hast founded for them. Thou hast set a boundary which they shall not pass.” Whoever steals crosses the boundary laid down in the words: “Thou shalt not steal” [Col. 1278D] (Exod. 20). Hence they are called transgressors. But there is another boundary which must in no way be crossed: namely, faith in the unity and Trinity. This may also be understood of each individual’s boundary. “Neither shall they return to cover the earth,” that they might follow the pleasures of corruptible flesh; rather, they prepared for themselves only wedding garments.

“Who sendest forth springs in the valleys”: baptism and teachers in the Churches. “The waters shall pass through the midst of the mountains.” Through the midst of the Churches, the rivers of the four Gospels shall flow. “All the beasts of the field shall drink”: for all of us are God’s beasts. Let us therefore run to this water, which is freely given to all. “The wild asses shall wait in their thirst” [Col. 1279A], for this water is supplied not only to the wise but also to the foolish. Hence the Apostle says: “I am a debtor both to Jews and to Gentiles, to Greeks and barbarians, to wise and foolish” (Rom. 1).

“Above them shall the birds of heaven dwell.” The birds of heaven are the apostles, who teach others to fly by the wings of virtues. They dwell upon mountains and valleys because they hold precedence in all Churches. “From the midst of the rocks they shall give forth their voices.” In the midst of the Church they shall open their mouths (Ecclus. 15), as Paul in Corinth and Peter in Rome.

“We water the mountains from their upper parts.”—“They were all filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2).—“The earth shall be satisfied with the fruit of thy works” [Col. 1279B]. For the Church is nourished by divine benefits. “Bringing forth grass for the cattle.” Thou, he says, satisfiest the earth; it in turn brings forth grass for thy cattle, because it both feeds the apostles with bodily food and delights them with the beauty of flowers. Hence the Apostle says: “If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?” (1 Cor. 9). Confirmation: “And herb for the service of men.” Those whom he called cattle, he calls the service of men. For these cattle, given to serve us, carry provisions, food for travelers, and full baskets from the five loaves and two fishes. It is fitting, therefore, that he employ cattle who cannot live without cattle. “That thou mayest bring bread out of the earth.” For earth brought bread out of earth when the Church received from the apostles the strengthening of faith and the very living bread which came down from heaven [Col. 1279C] (John 6). “And wine which maketh glad the heart of man” signifies the deep mysteries of the Scriptures and the Savior’s own blood, consecrated by divine blessing in apostolic hands.

“That he may gladden the face with oil.” For the face and beauty of the Church are made glad by spiritual oil and healing anointing, because she believed the apostles’ words. “And bread may strengthen the heart of man.” For this reason we continually ask for daily bread: that, strengthened, our mind may yield to no temptations. “The trees of the field shall be satisfied.” This field means the Church, which the apostles cultivated and in which they planted many kinds of trees, nourished by the aforesaid bread. [Col. 1279D] Those who are lovers of the letter fail in this. “And the cedars of Lebanon, which he planted”: that is, those higher in merits, or kings and princes endowed with worldly dignities.

“There the sparrows shall make their nests.” By sparrows is denoted the multitude of poor believers. They build in the cedars when they inhabit their cells on the estates of the rich. This can most plainly be understood of monks.

“The house of the heron is their leader.” The heron is a kind of bird. Its house is the rock; and the rock is Christ (1 Cor. 10). Whoever follows him as leader “does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” (John 8).—“The high mountains” are a refuge [Col. 1280A] for the deer. The deer are the apostles, swift to run and proclaim the Gospel, who take up serpents and whom no deadly thing shall ever harm (Mark 16). For them, the mountains—the New and Old Testaments—and heaven itself are a refuge. “The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs.” The hedgehog is an animal surrounded by a dense covering of spines; for such persons that Rock is a refuge which says: “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matt. 9).

“He made the moon for seasons; the sun knew its setting.” At the time when the sun of righteousness slept upon the cross for the salvation of the whole world (1 John 2), the Church was fashioned from his side. Adam prefigured this: from the side of sleeping Adam one rib was taken, and Eve was formed (Gen. 2). Apostrophe: “Thou hast set darkness, and night was made” [Col. 1280B]. For in Christ’s passion darkness was made, when the true light set in Judaea (Matt. 27). And night was made, which blinded the peoples of the Jews. “In it all the beasts of the forest shall pass through.” They pass through Judaea, since that Jewish night has not yet been illuminated; and likewise “the lion’s whelps,” the beasts of the forest—the lion and the lion’s whelps, Beelzebub, prince of demons (Matt. 12), with all his subjects. They pass through them, because they remained in the night when Christ rose. “Roaring, and that they may seize”: as it is written, “Our enemy the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5). “And that they may seek food for themselves from God,” that is, the fulfillment of their will. They asked for Job (Job 1), but were by no means [Col. 1280C] able to devour him. Woe to thee, Judas, who wast their food (Matt. 27). This may also be understood of the apostles, who, when Christ the Lord had been crucified, were tempted by enemies in many ways, so much so that he who seemed stronger and ought to have strengthened the others denied him three times (Matt. 26). The sun rose, the Lord arose (Mark 6), and the eleven disciples gathered together in Galilee.

“And they shall be placed in their dens.” Peter in Rome, John in Ephesus, Thomas in India; or also in heavenly dwellings, not in the dens which the devil had prepared for them. “Man shall go forth to his work.” Since night has passed and the sun of righteousness has arisen, let the apostles gird themselves for the work of preaching, so that their sound may be heard through all the ends of the earth [Col. 1280D] (Mark 16). “And to his labor until evening”: that is, until the end of life or the consummation of the world. Exclamation:

“How great are thy works, O Lord!” Man, he says, has gone forth to his work: cities are taken by fishermen; kings are overcome by a rustic army. “Thou hast made all things in wisdom”: not by worldly arms, not by the multitude of tyrants, but by the death of thy Son, “through whom all things were made” (John 1), thou hast converted the world. “The earth has been filled with thy possession,” though it had lately been possessed by enemies.

“This great sea, wide in its hands.” It serves thee alone. The world is broad in its hands, that is, in the diversity of nations: one hand [Col. 1281A] belongs to the Greeks, another to the Latins. “There are creeping things without number,” where there are “small animals with great.” This is true according to the letter. Yet the small and great animals may be understood as the perfect and imperfect, wise and foolish, rich and poor. “There the ships shall pass through”: for Peter, Andrew, and the sons of Zebedee sailed here. A ship in this place means human flesh. And also, “this dragon, which thou hast formed to play with him.” This dragon is the evil spirit, cast out of paradise into this world (Rev. 12), who both deceives and is deceived, mocks and is mocked: he deceived Eve (Gen. 3), but was mocked by Mary (Luke 1). Moreover, whoever is Jacob will be able to mock him in many ways. “All things wait upon thee, that thou mayest give them food in due season” [Col. 1281B]. For he feeds all, “who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and unjust” (Matt. 5). That he does this in an ordered manner and at distinct times is known to all. He will also give food in due season, because he will render his fruit in its season. “When thou givest to them, they shall gather.”—“For every best gift and every perfect gift is from above” (Jas. 1).—“When thou openest thy hand,” that is, the abundance of thy fullness, “all shall be filled with goodness,” upon whom so great a hand has been opened. “But when thou turnest away, they shall be troubled”: namely, those from whom thou hast turned away. “Thou shalt take away their spirit, and they shall fail”: the spirit of men is life; when it is taken away, there is extinction. “And they shall return to their dust,” as it is written: “Thou art earth, and into earth thou shalt go” [Col. 1281C] (Gen. 3).—“Send forth thy Spirit,” who cannot be taken away, “and they shall be created” in firmness of faith. “And thou shalt renew the face of the earth,” that is, the image of man which had perished in Adam. But I shall say: “Let the glory of the Lord be for ever. The Lord shall rejoice in his works,” which now begin to serve him. “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble.” Blessed is the one upon whom he so looks that, pierced by compunction for his sins, he trembles. He touches the mountains, and they smoke because it is hot. Thus the mountains smoke which boil over with the burning of the Holy Spirit. “I will sing to the Lord in my life; I will sing psalms to my God as long as I am. My speech shall be pleasing and acceptable to him. Let sinners fail from the earth,” that is, from earthly desires, and let them serve the Spirit; “and the wicked, from their wickedness” [Col. 1281D], so “that they may not be” wicked, but righteous. “Bless the Lord, O my soul.” Let this psalm be sung at every time, since it cannot be ended. For where an end seems to be, there the beginning is repeated; therefore let God’s blessing roll on and never be brought to an end.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 104

“Give thanks to the Lord.” The voice of the Prophet: Confess your sins to the Lord. “And call upon his name,” that he may have mercy on you. “Declare his works among the nations,” because he is not the God of the Jews alone. “Sing to him,” with mouth and heart. “Sing psalms to him,” in action. “Relate all his wonders,” which are manifest to you. “Glory in his holy name,” not in your own works. “Let the heart [Col. 1282A] of those who seek the Lord rejoice in the Lord. Seek the Lord,” not worldly honors. “And be strengthened,” in faith and love. “Seek his face always,” that you may know how to see him. “Remember his wonders which he did” in Egypt, “and his miracles and the judgments of his mouth,” which never lie. Remember that you are “the seed of Abraham, his servants,” yet only if you do his works. “The children of Jacob, his chosen,” according to the saying: “Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated” (Mal. 1). “He himself is the Lord our God,” because we worship no other. “His judgments are in all the earth,” for he himself shall judge the living and the dead (2 Tim. 4). He who is such “was mindful for ever of his covenant,” namely, the word which he commanded for a thousand generations. Who knows the mystery of this verse [Col. 1282B]? Perhaps he said “a thousand” because in Abraham’s thousandth generation, which is separated by the greatest interval, the end of this world was established. “Which he ordained to Abraham,” saying to him: “I will make thee the father of many nations” (Gen. 17). “And his oath unto Isaac.”—“In thy seed shall all nations be blessed” (Gen. 26).—“And he established it for Jacob as a commandment, and for Israel as an everlasting covenant, saying: To thee will I give the land of Canaan.” This is what thou didst ordain to Abraham. “The line of your inheritance”: the extent of place and time. “When they were few in number, very few, and strangers therein”: though they were few and sojourners, they nevertheless believed so great a promise. “And they passed from nation to nation, and from one kingdom to another people” [Col. 1282C]. “He suffered no man to hurt them,” as he rebuked Pharaoh on Sarah’s account. “And he rebuked kings for their sakes,” saying: “Touch not my anointed, and do no evil to my prophets.” Likewise, those who advance through many tribulations into the land of the living are guarded by the Lord. “And he called for a famine upon the land, and broke all the support of bread.” “This was in the time of Jacob” (Gen. 42). “He sent a man before them,” before they reached Egypt (Gen. 46).—“Joseph was sold as a slave,” by his brothers to the Ishmaelites (Gen. 37). “They humbled his feet in fetters,” because he refused to commit adultery; “iron passed through his soul,” that is, pain and fear of death. “Until his word came,” by which he interpreted dreams [Col. 1282D]. “The utterance of the Lord inflamed him,” that is, the spirit of prophecy. “The king sent” his ministers, “and freed him” from the prison in which he was held. “The ruler of peoples, and released him. He established him lord of his house and ruler over all his possessions, that he might instruct his princes as himself and teach prudence to his elders. And Israel entered Egypt, and Jacob was a sojourner in the land of Ham. And the Lord increased his people greatly, and strengthened him above his enemies,” striking Egypt with many plagues. “He turned their heart so that they hated his people and dealt deceitfully with his servants.” These things happened so that, after tasting such bitterness, the benefits which follow might be sweeter to us [Col. 1283A]. “The Lord sent Moses his servant, and Aaron whom he chose. He placed in them the words of his signs, and their wonders in the land of Ham.” Moses and Aaron signify the apostles, whom the Lord sent to free us from our bondage, and who shone throughout the whole world by many signs and miracles. “He sent darkness and darkened them,” so that, deprived of bodily light, they might recognize the blindness of their minds. This, however, happened to those who, after being preached to by the apostles, confessed that they had erred. “And he did not embitter his words,” but acquiesced in the truth. “He turned their waters into blood,” because the wisdom of this world is reckoned by the saints as poison and sin (1 Cor. 3). “And he killed their fishes,” that, dead to the world, they might live to the Lord. “Their land [Col. 1283B] brought forth frogs,” that is, the talkativeness of heretics, who resisted the saints with voice alone and without reason, even in the inner chambers of their kings, where, as is customary, they conversed for pleasure.

“He spoke, and there came dog-flies and gnats in all their borders.” For those unwilling to believe the truth were given over by the Lord to a reprobate mind. Dog-flies and gnats pursue those continually stung by luxury and curiosity. “He made their rains hail,” because the teaching of poets brought death rather than salvation. “Burning fire in their land.” For just as the fire of the apostles enlightens, so that of the heretics burns. “And he struck their vines and their fig trees, and broke the trees of their borders. He spoke, and the locust and the caterpillar came, beyond number [Col. 1283C], and devoured all the grass in their land and all its fruit. And he struck every firstborn in their land, the firstfruits of all their labor.” These things were written so that whoever resists God’s will may know that he will perish in many afflictions.

“And he brought them forth with silver and gold.” Although we flee from Egypt, we must not disregard gold and silver. Some pagans also possess gold and silver, because they are found humble, truthful, and chaste. Yet because, lacking the knowledge of God, they worship idols, they must be avoided by us; nevertheless humility, truthfulness, and chastity are not to be despised. “And there was not one infirm among their tribes.” Therefore let us also, fleeing Egypt and hastening to the land of our promise [Col. 1283D], see to it that, burdened by infirmity, we do not die on the way. “Egypt rejoiced at their departure, because fear of them fell upon them.” This is especially to be understood of the Jewish priests, who stirred up the people until the apostles were driven from the cities. They feared them because they knew that, if the people were converted, all profit from offerings would be lost to them. “He spread a cloud for their protection, and fire to give them light by night.” By the fire and cloud he signifies the Holy Spirit, who both defended them from the heat of vices and illuminated them in the inner person. “They asked, and the quail came; and he filled them with the bread of heaven.” We too have quails [Col. 1284A], namely the flesh of our Savior; and we have the living bread which came down from heaven (John 6). “He split the rock, and waters flowed.” Our rock also, struck with a spear, brings forth blood and water for us (John 19).

“Rivers passed through the dry land.” Likewise, baptism and the Gospel pass through parched nations. But why is this? “Because he remembered his holy word, which he had spoken to Abraham his servant.”—“In thy seed shall all nations be blessed” (Gen. 26). Hence the Apostle: “He did not say, ‘and to seeds,’ as of many, but as of one: ‘and to thy seed,’ which is Christ” (Gal. 3).—“And he brought forth his people in exultation, and his chosen in joy, and gave them the regions of the nations; and they possessed the labors of peoples” [Col. 1284B]. If anyone therefore comes in joy and is not made sorrowful by any adversities of this world, that person shall dwell in those regions from which evil spirits have been expelled. “That they may keep his statutes and seek his law.” Let monks hear this, who are brought into monasteries for this reason: that, laying aside every anxiety, they may enjoy the law and service of God alone.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 105

“Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good.” The voice of the Prophet: “For his mercy is for ever.” Therefore let confession be made in this world, in which mercy can still be shown; for in hell there is no redemption (Luke 16). “Who shall declare the powers of the Lord?” Who, he says, can fully praise him? “And make all his praises heard?” For as he himself is immeasurable, so his praise cannot be ended. “Blessed are they who keep judgment and do righteousness at all times.” For the judgment of the Lord is: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and thy neighbor as thyself”; and this, as he himself says, “is the greatest and first commandment” [Col. 1284C] (Matt. 22). Whoever keeps it shall without doubt be blessed. “And do righteousness at all times,” that is, those who are never separated from his statutes.

“Remember us, O Lord, in the good pleasure of thy people.” Remember us, he says, in such a manner that we may please thy people, which we are. Or: in the good pleasure of thy people, so that I may be among those who shall please thee well in the New Testament. “Visit us in thy salvation” [Col. 1284D], that is, in thy Son. “That we may see the goodness of thy chosen,” so that we ourselves may see in the perfection in which thy chosen stand. “That we may rejoice in the joy of thy nation,” so that we, who now proclaim that he will come, may rejoice in the same joy of redemption with the renewed people when he comes; “and mayest be praised” by us also “with” the rest of “thy inheritance.”

“We have sinned with our fathers.” We confess, Lord, that “we have acted unjustly and committed iniquity. Our fathers in Egypt did not understand thy wonders”: they saw indeed (Exod. 7–11), but did not understand, for they were in Egypt and, in the blindness of their own minds, sinned. Therefore “they were not mindful of the multitude of thy mercies. And they provoked” him “as they went up to the Red Sea; and he saved them for his name’s sake, that he might make known his power. And he rebuked the Red Sea, and it was dried up; and he led them through the deep as through a wilderness. And he saved them from the hand of those who hated them, and redeemed them from the hand of the enemy. And the water covered those who troubled them; not one of them remained. And they believed his words and sang his praise.” This also happens in the Church when, as we pass through baptism, the devil perishes with all his company. “They made haste; they forgot his works” [Col. 1285A]. They made haste because they soon failed. By this manner of speech those are reproved who abandon an undertaking before its proper time. “And they did not await his counsel [Col. 1285B]; and they desired desire in the wilderness, and tempted God in a waterless place. And he gave them their request, and sent abundance into their souls. And they provoked Moses in the camp, and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord. The earth opened and swallowed Dathan, and covered the congregation of Abiram; and fire was kindled in their assembly; the flame consumed sinners.” Let no one therefore rise up against God’s priests, lest perhaps the same thing happen to him. “And they made a calf in Horeb, and worshipped a graven image; and they changed their glory into the likeness of a calf eating grass.” Those who ought, he says, to have gloried in the Lord (2 Cor. 10) gloried in the calf (Exod. 32). But if they had understood themselves to be grass, devoured by the calf, perhaps they would have [Col. 1285C] fled their enemy. “They forgot God who saved them,” who “did great things in Egypt, wonders in the land of Ham, terrible things in the Red Sea. And he said that he would destroy them, had not Moses his chosen stood in the breach before him.” Priests who can break God’s wrath must be held in great veneration. “And he turned away his wrath lest he destroy them. And they held the desirable land as nothing,” because they could not enter it (ibid.); “they did not believe his word, and murmured in their tents, and did not heed the voice of the Lord. And he lifted up his hand over them, that he might cast them down in the wilderness, and cast down their seed among the nations, and scatter them through the regions. And they were initiated into Baal-peor,” the god of the mountains, “and ate sacrifices of the dead; and provoked him by their inventions” [Col. 1285D], “and ruin was multiplied among them. And Phinehas stood and appeased him,” slaying the adulterers. “And the plague ceased.” Thus let the bishop also rise, stand, draw the sword of the Spirit—which is the word of God (Eph. 6)—and destroy fornication, that this may be reckoned to him as righteousness. “And they provoked him at the waters of contradiction, and Moses was distressed because of them, because they embittered his spirit, and he made distinctions with his lips.” He made prayer for them, he says, that they might be freed from the sin of provocation. “They did not destroy the nations which the Lord had told them”: but let us destroy pride, luxury, avarice, and the other nations which the Lord commanded us to destroy (Matt. 5). “And they mingled among the nations and learned [Col. 1286A] their works, and served their graven images; and these became a stumbling block to them. And they sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons, and shed innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters, whom they sacrificed to the graven images of Canaan. And the land was slain with blood, and defiled by their works, and they committed fornication in their inventions.” There is therefore fornication also in perverse interpretations. Hence the Apostle speaks of evil preachers as adulterating the word of God (2 Cor. 2). “And the Lord was angered with wrath against his people and abhorred his inheritance. And he gave them into the hands of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them; and their enemies afflicted them, and they were humbled beneath their hands. Many times he delivered them, but they” [Col. 1286B] “provoked him in their counsel,” devising evil things; “and they were humbled in their iniquities. And the Lord saw when they were afflicted and heard their prayers.” Sinners are never given any occasion for despair. “And he remembered his covenant,” that is, his promise to Abraham (Gen. 22), “and repented according to the multitude of his mercies.” For as he is angry with one who is angry, so he repents toward one who repents; he does not literally repent or become angry, but we find in him the operation of anger and repentance. Thus, when he punishes, he is called angry; but when he has mercy, merciful. “And he gave them into mercies in the sight of all who had taken them captive. Save us, O Lord our God,” whom thou hast redeemed at a much greater price. “And gather us from the nations,” that we may come together into one heavenly seat [Col. 1286C], or into the unity of the Church, “that we may give thanks to thy holy name and glory in thy praise. Blessed be the Lord God of Israel from everlasting and unto everlasting; and let all the people say: Be it, be it.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 106

“Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is for ever.” The voice of the Prophet: “Let those now say who have been redeemed by the Lord.” What are they to say? This confession. “Whom he has redeemed from the hand of the enemy.” For the Lord redeemed us from the devil’s power by his own blood (Col. 1). “And he gathered them from the regions.” Jews and Gentiles, Egyptians and Britons, are gathered from such diverse regions under the faith [Col. 1286D] of the one Church. This is very plainly shown in what follows.

“From the rising and the setting of the sun, from the north and the sea.” By naming these four regions of the world, he encompasses every land. For the sea, since it surrounds the whole world, is here set for the southern quarter alone. That quarter is not named because the Jewish people who inhabited it were not gathered but scattered. Yet they shall be gathered at the consummation of this world; for when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel shall be saved (Rom. 11).

“[They] wandered in the wilderness.” These generations, he says, which are gathered under one faith from all parts of the world, once wandered, because they were in a desert and solitude, in places forsaken by God. “In a waterless place.” [Col. 1287A] For this reason they wandered: they had not yet attained the water of heavenly wisdom, of which it is said: “All you who thirst, come to the water” (Isa. 55).—“They did not find the way to an inhabited city.” He had not yet come who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). Unless this way is found, not even the city of the heavenly dwelling can be found. They were “hungry and thirsty”; although they had bodily food, they were nevertheless wholly in need of spiritual food. Therefore “their soul failed within them”: the soul failed because the flesh ruled; it failed because it perished of hunger. It certainly would not have failed if it had been nourished with the living bread, since, having tasted of the tree of life, it would not die forever. “And” at last “they cried to the Lord when they were distressed.” After they had recognized, he says, hunger, tribulation, and need, [Col. 1287B] they cried to the Lord with the cry of the heart, “and the Lord delivered them from their necessities.” “And he led them forth in the right way.” This was fulfilled in the time of the apostles, when the hungry were satisfied and peoples were converted from error to the way of truth, “that they might go to the city of habitation,” that is, to the heavenly Jerusalem, the way to which they had previously been unable to find. This is rightly called the city of habitation, because its habitation shall never cease. Therefore, “let them confess the mercies of the Lord,” that is, let the Lord be praised amid the abundance of his souls, “and his wonders,” wrought “for the children of men.”

“For he satisfied the empty soul.” [Col. 1287C] The Lord satisfied empty souls because he filled them with divine bounty and heavenly grace (Acts 2). “And he satisfied the hungry soul with good things,” by which, nourished, it may never fail. The Lord delivered those “sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, bound in poverty and iron.” For the human race sat in darkness and the shadow of death, because, having lost the light of truth, it persisted in the obscurity of error. It was bound in poverty and iron because, chained by the harsh fetter of sins, it suffered lack of every good thing. This may also be understood of those whom the Lord brought up with himself from hell (Eph. 4). But why were they bound? It follows: “Because they provoked the words of the Lord.” Let divine commandments therefore be our beginnings, lest we be bound by the chain of our fathers. [Col. 1287D] “And they rejected the counsel of the Most High.” Whoever steals renders void that counsel of God by which it was said: “You shall not steal” (Matt. 19).—“And their heart was humbled in labours.” The soul is never humbled by good works; rather, as by certain steps, it always ascends to higher things. And “they were weakened, and there was none to help.” No remedy aided them, because they did not know the aid of the true physician. “And” at last “they cried to the Lord when they were distressed,” to him alone who can grant salvation. “And he delivered them from their necessities. And he brought them forth from the darkness” in which they sat, “and from the shadow of death” by which they were enveloped, “and he broke their bonds,” by which they had been entangled. Therefore, “confess the mercies of the Lord.” [Col. 1288A] “For he shattered the bronze gates,” that is, the obstacles of the devil, by which, held fast, they could not return to their homeland. Confirmation: “And he broke the iron bars; he received them from the way of their iniquity,” converting to himself those who are the way of truth and justice. “For they were humbled because of their injustices”; but this humiliation belongs not to the body, but to the soul. “Their soul abhorred every food, and they drew near even to the gates of death,” because they had abhorred every word of preaching; therefore they stood at the entrance of death. “And they cried to the Lord when they were distressed, and he delivered them from their necessities.” How did he deliver them? “He sent his Word and healed them.” Since they had rejected every food and every teaching, he therefore [Col. 1288B] sent his Son (John 3), whose words are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. Therefore, “let them confess the mercies of the Lord.”

“And let them offer the sacrifice of praise,” not of goats or bulls, nor a sacrifice liable to blame or rebuke. “And let them proclaim his works in exultation”; let them not conceal the truth through fear or favour—namely, those “who go down to the sea in ships.” These are the apostles and teachers who, seated in the little vessels of fragile flesh and sailing through the seas of this age, caught a great multitude of fish with the hook of God’s word. “Doing their works in many waters: they saw the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep.” For when they were among the impious and sinners, and were battered by various waves of tribulations, [Col. 1288C] they deserved to behold many wonders which the Lord himself worked through them (Acts 3, 13, 14).

“He spoke, and the spirit of the storm stood still.” The force of storms and the assaults of adversities, he says, stood still because he commanded whose speech is action. “And its waves were lifted up.” This is said according to the changing course of times, because the saints were at times in prosperity, at times in adversity. “They rose up to the heavens and descended to the depths.” He continues the comparison with the sea, which to those sailing upon it seems now to rise to the stars, now to descend to Tartarus; and the immensity of this terror is rightly set above all things to be feared [Col. 1288D] and avoided. “Their soul melted away in evils.” Here the measure of fear and affliction is declared. For, as the Apostle says, they were often oppressed by such great adversities that they were even weary of living (2 Cor. 2). “They were troubled and moved like a drunken man,” almost forgetting the whole faith. “And all their wisdom was swallowed up,” since they could not withstand enemies so many and so great. Or again, they were shaken like a drunken man because, although they might be killed, it was nevertheless impossible to bend them: intoxicated with heavenly wine, they had lost the wisdom of this world; and therefore he says that both their wisdom and the world’s wisdom were swallowed up. “And they cried to the Lord when they were distressed, and he brought them forth from their necessities. And he made its storm a breeze, and its waves were stilled,” so that those who had been tossed aloft by the waves of the east wind might be borne to port by the breath of the gentlest west wind. [Col. 1289A] “And they rejoiced because they were stilled, and because the Lord brought them to the harbour of their desire.” Therefore, “let them confess the mercies of the Lord and his wonders for the children of men.”

“And let them exalt him in the assembly of the people,” that is, in the gathering of the Gentiles. “And let them praise him in the seat of the elders,” that is, in the Church of apostles and prophets. He “made rivers into a wilderness”: the four Gospels among the Gentiles. Repetition: “And springs of waters into thirst,” that is, among those who suffered thirst. And “a fruitful land into salt marsh.” Into sandy and barren land, he says, the Lord sent his apostles to make it fruitful. But [Col. 1289B] why was it barren? It follows: “Because of the wickedness of those who dwell in it.” For because a multitude of vices dwells in it, it brought forth thorns and briars. “He made the wilderness into pools of water,” immersing sinners in the water of baptism. Confirmation: “And the waterless land into springs of water,” so that, irrigated by abundant waters, it might lose its barrenness. “And he placed there the hungry,” that they might be fed with spiritual foods. “And they established a city of habitation,” the holy Church, or the heavenly Jerusalem, in which they shall always dwell. “And they sowed fields and planted vineyards”: “the seed is the word of God” (Luke 8); by fields and vineyards we understand churches. “And they produced the fruit of birth,” not of death and destruction, as sinners do.

“And the Lord blessed them, and they multiplied exceedingly.” [Col. 1289C] For from the twelve apostles there grew an innumerable multitude of churches. “And he did not diminish their beasts of burden,” that is, their teachers, by whose increase the fields and vineyards might be cultivated. “And they became few.” What does it mean that he now says they were multiplied, now that they became few? They were first multiplied, then became few. For there are none now who teach the Church in comparison with the earliest ones.

“And they were afflicted by the tribulation of evils and sorrow.” Hence “contention”—wrath and indignation—“was poured out upon the princes” of this age. And their leader, the evil spirit, “made them wander in a trackless place and not in a way”; he permitted them to be led astray. “And the Lord helped the poor man out of want,” satisfying him with eternal dishes. [Col. 1289D] “And he made families like sheep,” so that each might humbly follow its own shepherd. “The upright shall see”—they shall not remain in the blindness of enemies—“and rejoice” at the sight they have found. “And all iniquity shall stop its mouth,” so that, just as the wicked man cried out in iniquity for a time, so conversely he may be mute and silent forever.

“Who is wise?” Surely the one who “will keep these things,” which have also been repeated in this Psalter. And in these things he “will understand” that the mercies of the Lord are many and great.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 107

“My heart is ready, O God.” The voice of the Church: I am ready, not only to serve, but also ready to die in your name; ready in conduct, [Col. 1290A] ready in works, ready in sense and understanding, stripped of all that is old. “I will sing and make melody in my glory.” I shall sing with my mouth; I shall make melody by my works. Yet this is not in myself, but in you, who are my glory. Whatever good we do, we do in glory and in the exultation that is our crown.

“Awake, psaltery.” Arise, perfection of action, so that I may now serve the Creator in harmony with the ten commandments. Awake, “harp”; do not sleep, sweet melody: praise the Lord, soothe Saul, put the Pythonian spirit to flight. But “I shall awake at dawn,” that is, at the consummation of this age, when the true day shall be revealed. Whoever desires to keep watch and rise at dawn should therefore first send good works before him. Meanwhile, “I shall confess you among the peoples, [Col. 1290B] O Lord, and make melody to you among the nations,” saying: “For your mercy has come great above the heavens over us, and your truth has reached in full measure unto the clouds.” Hence the Apostle says: “I heard, he says, secret words which it is not lawful for a man to utter” (2 Cor. 12). Truth therefore came unto the clouds, though it cannot descend as far as the earth. “Be exalted above the heavens, O God,” etc. What follows has been explained elsewhere and requires no elucidation here.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 108

“O God, do not be silent concerning my praise, because the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful man have opened against me.” The voice of the Head: You see, Father, that Judas, a most wicked counsellor and contriver of iniquity, [Col. 1290C] has opened his mouth against me; he presses forward to betrayal, prepares the cross for me, and strives to blot out my name (Matt. 26). But you, Father, do not be silent concerning my praise; do not conceal the resurrection. Let it become known to all nations how I rose from the dead. “They spoke deceitful things against me.” Having devised this counsel, he says, the scribes and Pharisees, high priests and priests, spoke against me with deceitful tongues, condemning me, accusing me, crying with one voice that I was guilty of death (Matt. 26). “And they surrounded me with words of hatred,” having brought false witnesses against me from every side (ibid.). “And they attacked me without cause”—without cause indeed, because without reason or justification; without cause because to no purpose and to their own dispersion.

[Col. 1290D] “In return for their love of me, they slandered me.” I bestowed many benefits upon them: I delivered them from Egypt (Exod. 14), fed them with manna in the wilderness (Gen. 18), gave them the land of promise (Josh. 14), raised their dead (Luke 7), cleansed lepers (Luke 17), and gave sight to the blind (Luke 18). Are these not causes for love rather than hatred? Yet, in return for those things by which they ought to have loved me, they slandered me. But what did I do? I prayed. O how great the mercy! How great the humility of our Redeemer! He did not curse those who cursed him, but prayed for those who slandered and persecuted him. For he said: “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23). “They set evil against me for good, and hatred in return for my love.” I offered life (John 1), they death (John 19); I medicine (Num. 21), they [Col. 1291A] poison (Rom. 3); I honey and the honeycomb (Num. 13), they offered me vinegar (John 19) mixed with gall (Matt. 27).

Therefore, “set a sinner over him.” Since they chose sinful Caesar (John 19), Barabbas (John 18), and the devil himself, the prince of all vices, let them be oppressed under his yoke and dominion. Confirmation: “And let the devil stand at his right hand.” What will his left hand do when his right hand is held by the devil? What does the left hand of that man accomplish at whose right hand the devil stands? Know, therefore, O Jews, that those things in which you especially think that you serve the Lord are diabolical.

“When he is judged, let him go forth condemned, and let his prayer become sin.” Therefore do not pray, O Jews; do not read the Psalms and prophecies, for it is sin. You offend God, and all your prayer is turned into anathema. This will be manifest when you go forth condemned from judgment (Matt. 25). “Let his days be few.” Judas’s days were few, because on that very day he hanged himself with a noose; the days of the Jews were few, because after forty-two years they lost their place and nation (Hos. 3); their days were shortened because their nights increased. [Col. 1291B] “And let another take his bishopric.” Matthias took Judas’s place (Acts 1); the Church succeeded the Synagogue. For the Synagogue lost its high priests, and the Church received apostles.

“Let his sons become orphans and his wife a widow.” This was also fulfilled literally, because in the time of Titus a great multitude of Jews perished. Spiritually, however, the sons of this people are called orphans because they crucified their Father (Matt. 27); while their mother, that is, the Synagogue, remained a widow, having received a bill of divorce and been separated from so great and such a husband. “Let his sons be driven about,” slipping and dying; let them be transferred from nation to nation, scattered, sold, and subjected to all nations. “And let them beg.” Whoever is in want is poor. Therefore the Jews are called beggars, because they are poor in the bread of heaven and spiritual riches. [Col. 1291C] “Let them be cast out of their dwellings.” Has it not happened thus? Indeed, it has.

“Let the moneylender search out all his substance.” This moneylender is understood to be the evil spirit. Let this importunate moneylender come, search out the substance of this people, and root out with him whatever is his. Explanation: “And let strangers plunder his labours,” so that whatever he has wrought may be plundered by demons. “Let there be none to help him.” For who helps the Jews? They were in Egypt and had Moses and Aaron (Exod. 7). It would take long to recount how the Lord helped them. They were also in Babylon, where Daniel comforted them. Since, therefore, they have now been in captivity for a thousand years and are not helped as formerly, what was said is fulfilled: “Let there be none to help him, nor any to have pity upon his orphans.” But do we know this to be true of visible things? What the Lord does concerning invisible things, namely souls, he himself knows better. [Col. 1292A] “Let his offspring be for destruction.” For many of them have already been killed; yet a greater destruction awaits at the judgment.

“Let his name perish in one generation,” so that they may live only in this age and have no life after death. But you, Jew, who seek the letter: do you not confess that Jerusalem was destroyed after forty-two years, in which one generation is completed? Therefore, you who seek the letter, perish according to the letter. “Let the iniquity of his fathers return to remembrance before the Lord,” so that those who were not contrite after the intervening forty years may be held under the guilt of Christ’s Passion and their fathers’ iniquity. Or, when they come to judgment, let neither original sin nor the other sins they committed be forgiven them. [Col. 1292B] “And let the sin of his mother,” namely that Jerusalem which killed the prophets (Acts 2), “not be blotted out.”

“Let them be always before the Lord.” For they were always opposed to Christ the Lord. “And let their memory perish from the earth,” lest they be written together with the saints in the book of life, “because this people did not remember to show mercy.” Because it trusts in works, it makes little of mercy. “And he persecuted the poor and needy man, and the man pierced in heart, to put him to death.” For he was poor and needy because, as the Apostle says, “though he was rich above all, he became poor for our sake” (2 Cor. 8). And he was pierced in heart when he said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26), or when he prayed to the Father for [Col. 1292C] his disciples. For he said: “Father, preserve those whom you gave me” (John 17).—“And he loved cursing,” which shall come upon the wicked. “And it shall come upon him. And he did not desire blessing,” which shall be brought into our Church. “And it shall be far from him. And he clothed himself with cursing as with a garment,” so that he might be covered by it as by an ankle-length robe. “And it entered like water into his bones,” so that those who seem stronger may not escape corruption. “Let it be to him as the garment with which he is covered, and as the belt with which he is always girded,” surrounded at all times by that with which he may be bound without end. “This is the work of those who slander me before the Lord,” whoever deny that I am the Son of God, “and who speak evils against my soul,” [Col. 1292D] saying: “God has forsaken it” (Ps. 70), and: “There is no salvation for him in his God” (Ps. 3).

“But you, O Lord, deal with me for your name’s sake,” which I have invoked, so that they may themselves be found liars. “For your mercy is sweet. Deliver me” from the weakness of this flesh. “For I am needy and poor,” so long as I am enveloped in the corruption of flesh. “And my heart is troubled within me,” as indeed the weakness of the flesh causes.

“Like a shadow when it declines, I am taken away.” Because I dwell in no part of Judaea. Or I am like a shadow because the Jews, if they wish, nevertheless cannot flee from me. “And I am shaken off like a locust,” that is, as the destroyer of people and kingdom, to whom they themselves said: “How long do you destroy our souls? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John 10).

“My knees have been weakened through fasting; my flesh has been changed because of oil.” Bones, heart, and soul are elsewhere named because of firmness in faith. In this place the knees are called the apostles because of their bending. For Peter was a knee: though he first promised, “Even if I must die with you, I shall not deny you” (Matt. 26), at the voice of one maidservant he bent lightly and said: “I do not know the man” (ibid.). [Col. 1293A] This came about through fasting, because “they did not yet understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24). With the oil gone, the flesh was changed, because, when the nourishment of the true light was extinguished, the apostles were weakened. “And I became a reproach to them,” who saw me hanging on the cross and, mocking, shook their heads, saying: “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God” (Matt. 27). [Col. 1293B]—“Help me, O Lord my God; save me according to your mercy. And let them know that this is your hand, and that you, O Lord, have done it.”—“For I have power to lay down my life and to take it up again” (John 10). It was not their power, therefore, but your hand that accomplished this: “For they would have had no power over me unless it had been given to them by you” (John 18). I do not excuse you, Jews, but proclaim God’s omnipotence; for you did what you could and willed what you could not do. “They shall curse, but you shall bless.” No human curse has any power against him. “Let those who rise against me be confounded, but your servant shall rejoice,” because “he emptied himself, taking the form [Col. 1293C] of a servant” (Phil. 2).—“Let those who slander me be clothed with shame,” so that, when I rise on the third day (Matt. 28), they may blush at the falsehood by which they slandered me before Pilate. For they said: “We remember that, while still alive, that deceiver said: After the third day I shall rise; therefore command the sepulchre to be guarded, lest he be stolen by the disciples” (Matt. 27). Let them therefore blush, because I rose. Let them be clothed with shame because they are proved liars. Yet it is not I but their prophet who testifies: “Let them be covered like a diplois with their confusion.” A *diplois* is a twofold kind of garment. The Jews’ shame is therefore rightly compared to a *diplois*, because it is twofold: it extends to soul and body, in this age and in the future. O [Col. 1293D] wretched and altogether unhappy people, who, having lost the wedding garment, are clothed with shame! But I “will confess the Lord exceedingly with my mouth, and in the midst of many I shall praise him.” For the Lord is no longer praised only in Judaea, but in all parts of the world, “because he stood at the right hand of the poor man.” Of what poor man? Of him who said: “Foxes have dens and birds of the air nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Luke 9). The Lord thus speaks of himself as if of another, as what follows teaches us. “That he might save my soul from its persecutors,” that is, from the impieties of the Jews, who surrounded the sepulchre with armed force (Matt. 27).

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 109

[Col. 1294A]

“The Lord said to my Lord.” The voice of the Prophet: “Sit at my right hand.” To my Lord returning from Edom, he says, his Father—who is both his Father and his Lord—said: Sit at my right hand. For the Father is Lord, the Son is Lord, and the Holy Spirit is Lord; yet not three Lords, but one Lord. For as Trinity abides in the persons, so truth abides in the majesty (St Athanasius, *First Creed*). Who therefore said, or to whom was it said: “Sit at my right hand”? The Father said it, and he said it to the Son. This is said according to the flesh, so that he whom the Jews humbled in the sepulchre may be understood to sit at God’s right hand.

“Until I place your enemies as the footstool of your feet.” Until all your enemies are subjected to your dominion. But whatever is here either promised or commanded must be referred to the man.

“The Lord will send forth the rod of your power out of Zion.” The Prophet is speaking. Therefore he uses the future for the past and does not observe the true order. Zion and Jerusalem are one, except that Jerusalem was the whole city, whereas Zion was a certain tower and defence of the city. From this Zion and Jerusalem came forth the law and the word of the Lord (Isa. 2), and thus also the rod of his power. [Col. 1294B] The rod of his power is understood as the Gospel, concerning which the Apostle says: “For I am not ashamed of the Gospel, for it is the power of God” (Rom. 1). By this rod those who acknowledge God’s power and omnipotence are corrected; by this venerable sceptre they are ruled. The Lord therefore sent this rod from [Col. 1294C] Zion because apostolic preaching, arising there, went forth to all ends of the earth (Ps. 18).

But “rule in the midst of your enemies.” For whoever serves the devil is an enemy of the Lord. Or, because the whole world served him before Christ assumed flesh. They were therefore his enemies, but have now become friends and rejoice in his rule and dominion.

“With you is the beginning.” You, he says, made all things with the Father; you are the beginning of every creature. “All things were made through you, and without you nothing was made” (John 1). Let the Jews therefore be confounded who cried that he had a demon, because he said that he existed before Abraham was made (John 8).

This will be manifest “in the day of your power,” [Col. 1294D] that is, “in the splendours of the saints.” When the day of your power comes, he says, on which the wicked shall perish and the saints shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of God (Prov. 8), then the Beginning and Creator of all things shall be revealed.

For you are he to whom the Father says: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” I begot you from myself before times, he says (John 1), whom I willed both to be born and to be begotten from a Virgin in time (Luke 2).

“The Lord has sworn and will not repent.” What has he sworn? It follows: “You are a priest forever.” Hence the Apostle: “Many were made priests according to the law, and therefore many, because they are prevented by death from continuing” (Heb. 7). But you, Christ, because you can no longer die, shall be a priest forever. In what order? “According to the order of Melchizedek.” Let the sacrifices of dead things therefore cease. Who is this Melchizedek, whose father, mother, and generation are unknown? Christ, indeed, had no mother according to God, nor father according to man; of him it is said: “Who has declared his generation?” (Acts 8). He is therefore without father, mother, and genealogy. [Col. 1295A] Melchizedek’s sacrifice was of bread and wine (Gen. 14), but Christ’s was of his own body and blood. Hence he himself says: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6).

“The Lord at your right hand.” He first says that the Son is at the right hand of the Father, but now that the Father is at the right hand of the Son. In this one majesty, one equality, one power, and the same might [Col. 1295B] are shown: this will crush kings and princes and tyrants of the age in judgment. It may also be understood thus: the Lord “will crush kings in the day of his wrath,” those who stand at your right hand as though girded for battle. Thus we read in Zechariah that the devil stood at the right hand of Jesus to fight against him (Zech. 3). He declared himself king because he promised the Lord all the kingdoms of the world, saying: “All these things I will give you if, falling down, you worship me” (Matt. 4). But this king shall be crushed when the day of wrath, calamity, and misery is revealed.

“He shall judge among the nations; he shall fill up the ruins.” For it is fitting that he fill up ruins who “has been set for the fall [Col. 1295C] and resurrection of many” (Luke 2). The Lord made a fall when he cast the army of evil spirits out of heaven (Rev. 12), or when he cast Adam with his wife out of paradise (Gen. 3), or when he struck down the children of Israel in the wilderness (Exod. 32). He filled it up when he delivered the devil and his angels to unquenchable fire, and thereafter no fall shall occur. He will also fill up the ruins because the saints shall ascend to the place from which angels fell. “He shall shatter heads in the land of many.” He shall shatter heads: he shall humble the proud; and this is on earth. For if they had been in heaven and spiritual, they would certainly not be shaken.

“He shall drink from the torrent on the way.” He was on the way, a pilgrim, and Christ was hastening to the Father. Therefore Christ had to drink from the torrent on this way. He drank from the torrent: he tasted the bitterness of death (Matt. 27). Of this cup he himself said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26). But what is meant by what the Gospel says: “And when he had tasted it, he would not drink” (Matt. 27), while here he is said to have drunk from the torrent? It is to show that this death was easy and swiftly passing. [Col. 1295D] “Therefore he exalted his head,” that is, he rose on the third day (Matt. 27), because he emptied himself (Phil. 2). He himself exalted his head: he did not remain in the sepulchre, but ascended mightily above the heavens (Mark 16). He lives and reigns as king and head of the whole world with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 110

[Col. 1296A]

“I will confess you, O Lord.” The voice of the Prophet: I shall praise you, I shall magnify you, not with lips only, but “with my whole heart.” Where? “In the counsel of the righteous and the congregation”; and I shall say: “The works of the Lord” will appear “great,” if they are “sought out.” For God’s wisdom, power, and operation are found most conspicuously not only in the sun, moon, and the motion of so great a firmament, but also in small things. “Confession and magnificence” attend “all his wills.” For God desires nothing else from us except confession and magnificence. Whoever therefore desires to please him should always keep confession in mind, so as both to praise the Lord and confess sins; for confession signifies both. [Col. 1296B] Let magnificence follow, so that he may always provide increase for himself. This the Lord desires: that the person who longs to come to him may continually grow and be magnified from virtue to virtue, and thus be found, like the full moon, deficient in nothing—his work.

“And his righteousness remains for ever and ever.” The works of the Lord differ from other works in this: they shall remain forever, whereas the others shall be consumed by fire. Therefore pursue that righteousness and those works which can make their imitators eternal.

“He has made a memorial of his wonders: the Lord is merciful and compassionate,” writing them down and proclaiming them through the prophets. Whoever teaches makes a remembrance; for what is wholly unknown is never held in memory. Therefore, whatever was written was written for our instruction (Rom. 15).

“He gave food to those who fear him.” For as bread is food for bodies, so the remembrance of the Scriptures is food for souls. Hence the Lord himself says: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matt. 4). He also gave another food: namely, that living bread which came down from heaven (John 6).

“He will remember his covenant forever.” For not the letter alone, but also those who observe the letter, are God’s covenant. “He shall declare to his people the power of his works.” [Col. 1296C] Justice, peace, patience, humility, and charity are works of the Lord. Under his instruction we have come to know their power. For we know that such power is present in them that [Col. 1296D] they can secure eternal life. Christ himself taught this when he proclaimed the eight beatitudes (Matt. 5).

“That he may give them the inheritance of the nations.” The nations have been expelled from the heavenly inheritance, which the Lord will give to those who labour well in the vineyard. “The works of his hands are truth and judgment,” for all that he made is true and no deceitful falsehood is found in his works. If anything is corrupt, it is no longer his work, for corruption is not good. But what belongs to God is good. Therefore things corrupted by falsehood are not his. Judgment, moreover, is in his works, because he made nothing without discernment and order.

“All his commandments are faithful.” Let all things therefore have faith, [Col. 1297A] and let all things found in either the New or Old Testament be believed by all. “Confirmed for ever and ever.” Thus Truth himself says: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Mark 13). They shall therefore be forever and ever, “made in truth and equity,” because they are true and proclaim justice; yet not everything true is also just.

“He sent redemption to his people,” that is, Christ, who redeemed the world by his blood (Heb. 9).

“He commanded his covenant forever.” [Col. 1298A] The Lord is eternal, and his covenant too is eternal. “Holy and terrible is his name.” It is holy to the holy and terrible to the wicked. “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” Whoever begins to become wise must first fear God. “Good understanding belongs to all who do it.” He therefore does not understand well who does not put into practice what he understands. Let a man then understand that fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. And, in order that his understanding may be good, let him fear the Lord as he understands; if he does this, “his praise shall remain for ever and ever.” For this is what the apostles did, whose praise comes from all.

Volume back matter

[Col. 1297]

## INDEX OF MEMORABLE SUBJECTS AND SENTENCES

The reader is referred to the numbers inserted into the text in bold type.
