[Note: [Col. 1297] This index refers to the works of Bruno of Asti. Roman numerals I and II refer to *Patrologia Latina* 164 and 165. Arabic numerals refer to column numbers printed in the text in bold type.]

[Col. 1297]

A
[Col. 1297A] **AARON** was a Levite. Because he was the firstborn brother of Moses, he was chosen by God to speak to the people and to convey to them His words and commands, I, 51. Before Pharaoh, whom he met together with Moses, the staff which he carried, when cast upon the ground, was changed into a serpent, I, 53. All the wonders by which God struck Pharaoh were performed through Aaron, because he was Moses’ minister, I, 54 and following. Aaron, together with his sons, was appointed priest and adorned with sacred garments for the administration of sacred rites, I, 102 and following, where the meanings of those garments are explained. Why Aaron was required to bear upon the breastpiece of judgment the names of the children of Israel, and bells upon the hems of his garment, I, 105 and following. All the rites and ceremonies to be observed in the exercise of the priesthood were prescribed to him by God, I, 107 and following. After Aaron, who was regarded as high priest, his sons were anointed priests and distinguished by the garments proper to their office. Urged by the Hebrews, who could not endure Moses’ delay upon Mount Sinai, he set up a golden calf, to which the frenzied people sacrificed and thereby made themselves rebellious against the true God, I, 118. Aaron is rebuked by Moses for the crime committed. Those who incited him to that wickedness and shared in the sacrilege, numbering about twenty-three thousand, were struck down by the sword and exterminated, I, 120. In Leviticus the whole order of ceremonies for the worship of the Tabernacle, for sacrifices, and for feast-days consecrated to God’s honor, is delivered and entrusted to Aaron and his sons.

**ABEL**, Adam’s younger son, is set forth as an example of righteousness and innocence. When he offered God sacrifices from the best offspring of his flock, his offerings won favor and acceptance with the Lord, I, 14. Slain through Cain’s envy, he signified Christ, who was delivered to death by the Jews, his brethren, inflamed with hatred and jealousy, I, 14. How the cry of his blood is to be understood, and how the Apostle called the voice of Christ’s blood better, I, 14.

**ABRAHAM.** Abraham, departing at the Lord’s command from the land of his birth, leaving all his kinsfolk, and setting out for the land appointed him by God, deserved to become the father of many nations, I, 22. When he believed the oracle of this promise, he won divine love for himself all the more, so that God deigned to appear to him—not in Himself, that is, in His own substance, which is ineffable and invisible, but under the appearance of three men—and to promise him and his descendants possession of the land of Canaan, I, 22. Why, in memory of so great a benefit, he there erected an altar and offered sacrifice to God, I, 22. Going down into Egypt, Abraham instructed Sarah to say, not that she was his wife, but his sister; in this he did not lie, since Sarah was indeed his sister on the father’s side, though not on the mother’s, I, 22.

[Col. 1298A] Faith justified him while he was still uncircumcised, I, 23. The captivity of the Hebrews in Egypt is foretold to Abraham, I, 25. God appeared again to Abraham and promised to give him an innumerable progeny; when he believed Him, his faith was reckoned to him as an increase of righteousness, I, 25. Abraham received God’s command to circumcise the flesh of his foreskin; circumcision of this kind was enjoined upon all male Hebrews under penalty of death, I, 25. In the vision of three Angels in human form granted to Abraham, since he saw three but worshipped only one, not a few of the Fathers held that the symbol of the most Holy Trinity was first shown to him, I, 25, in the note. Abraham had two wives, Sarah and Hagar; according to the Apostle in Galatians, they signified the two Testaments. Sarah was a figure of the Church, Hagar of the Synagogue. These matters are explained at length, I, 27. Abraham’s faith and obedience are tested in the command to sacrifice his son Isaac, I, 28. At his death Abraham made Isaac heir of his entire estate, but left movable goods to the sons of his concubines. How this is to be understood, I, 30.

**ADAM.** The first man, Adam, was formed from the clay of the earth and received the breath of God the Creator, namely the breath of life, by which he became a living and spiritual soul, so that man might consist of a twofold substance: body and spirit, I, 8. God placed him in Paradise, a place of every delight, that he might cultivate and keep it, I, 8. God gave him abundance of every fruit of the trees; nevertheless, He forbade him to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, threatening him with the penalty of death, I, 9. But since Adam was filled with the spirit of wisdom and prophecy, as soon as he saw the woman whom God had formed, while he slept, from one of his ribs, he recognized what she was and said: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh”; thus he foretold that the two would become one flesh and expressed the law of the marriage bond, I, 10. He also gave a proper name to every animal, I, 10. Through the deceit of the demon speaking in the serpent, the first parents, Adam and Eve, were deceived and ate the forbidden fruit; by transgressing that command, they learned what good they had lost and into what evil they had fallen, I, 11. After his sin Adam hid himself and feared to appear before the Lord. How could he hide himself from God, to whom all things are open? I, 12. As transgressors of the divine command, they are expelled from the Paradise of delight, I, 13, and stripped of the splendid prerogatives of their condition, I, 419. Their guilt was made still more serious because they did not humbly beg pardon for the violated command, but put forward an excuse, I, 12. In place of Abel, slain by Cain, Adam begot Seth, whose firstborn was Enosh. Since it is written of him, “This man began to call upon the name of the Lord,” it must be understood that, after Abel’s death, he called upon God more worthily and served Him, I, 16. For this reason the sons of Seth were called, above others, sons of God, I, 16. Since St. Bruno says that humankind descends from no stock other than Adam, I, 16, he refutes the opinion of those who dreamed of pre-Adamites and devised other worlds.

**ANGELS.** Almost all the Fathers think that the creation of angels is expressed by Moses in the words, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth”; that is, all the heavenly powers—namely angels, the inhabitants of heaven, prepared for His service—I, 1. By light and night we may understand good and evil angels; because they were separated on the same day, they seem to signify the sudden fall of the wicked, II, 512. One of them, lifted up in pride and striving to make himself equal to the Most High—that is, to God the Creator—was cast down from the heavenly seat with his followers. Thereafter, envying humanity’s happiness, he attempted deceitfully to cast humankind down from it. He assumed the form of the serpent, a most cunning animal; and, becoming the devil, that is, the tempter, he entered into conversation with Eve and by flattering promises induced her and Adam to violate the divine command, I, 11. A cherub armed with a fiery sword is placed before Paradise to prevent Adam’s entrance, I, 13. Three angels appeared to Abraham in human form and conversed with him; they also partook of food prepared by his wife Sarah, to whom, though afflicted with barrenness, they foretold a son. St. Bruno teaches how these things occurred, I, 25. Guardian and protecting angels are assigned by God to every people, I, 121. Through the affection and desire of seeing God, angels are said to be present before, or absent from, His sight, I, 223. Angels are called sons of God insofar as they are made like God through participation in glory, I, 223, in the note. The archangel Gabriel is sent to the Virgin Mary to announce to her divine motherhood, I, 389. Voices of angels heard in the Temple at Jerusalem foretold its destruction and utter ruin, I, 409. For since *angels* means “messengers,” those who are naturally spirits become angels when they are sent. Such is Christ’s power that, when He wills, He makes angels out of spirits and sends even the seraphim—whose name means “burning” or “setting on fire”—to minister whatever He wills, I, 520.

**SOUL.** When God had created the body of the first man, Adam, He granted him the principle of life, that is, a spiritual soul, as the words teach: “He breathed into his face the breath of life,” I, 8. Hence St. Bruno there said: “For the whole human being consists of soul and body; he set down the material of the body, but did not set down that of the soul.” By these words he acknowledged the immateriality of the soul. Although differing opinions about the soul’s origin are advanced, the view more consonant with divine revelation, and followed by St. Bruno, seems to be that, after the formation of their bodies, all other humans too are created directly by God and inspired with souls, after the likeness of the first man, I, 8. The soul is not a part of the Godhead, as certain poets and pagan philosophers taught, I, 8. Since the soul possesses understanding, counsel, and reason, which flesh does not possess, the two cannot otherwise agree together unless the flesh follows the soul, I, 28. Idleness of the soul is contrary to God’s order. As soon as the Lord formed Adam, He placed him in Paradise to work, I, 9. The mind, or thought, is the head of the soul; therefore those who exercise themselves in holy meditations aspire to perfection of life and desire with their whole longing to acquire it, I, 176. Since the souls of human beings alone cannot die, human beings alone among the animals of the earth are rightly called living beings, 13, at the end. The spirit in a human being is of a nature different from the flesh; for it is a formative spiritual substance which gives the body its principle of life. Whatever it possesses, it possesses wholly from God, I, 445. The soul of the righteous burns with desire to see and possess God, I, 424. The soul is immortal; when it sins, it dies and is separated from the true life, which is Christ, but it cannot be slain by swords. Executioners have power over the body alone; God has power over body and soul. Their punishment soon passes; His never ends, II, 55. Our soul is the image of God. Therefore let Caesar receive his own image, and God receive His own image; for man was made in God’s image. Let us render God His image; let us render God our souls: we possess nothing dearer, II, 105. The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom, II, 309.

**ANTICHRIST.** Antichrist is foretold in the sacred Scriptures and called the man of sin; he will make the Jews especially his followers and proclaimers, I, 158. The extent of his future wickedness is there described. At the consummation of this world the entire Jewish people will abandon Antichrist and, converted to the faith and reborn through the water of baptism, will join the camp of the Church, I, 158. All who perform Antichrist’s works are antichrists. For these God reserves the suffering of their father: condemned together with him, they will undergo the same torments, I, 260. His works and teaching will please all wicked persons, and all who believe him will be led with him to hell, I, 261.

[Col. 1300] It is written of this son of perdition that he will draw many people after him and countless persons before him. “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved.” For, as it is written, he will reign “for a time, times, and half a time”—that is, no more than three and a half years, I, 316. David prophesied of Antichrist in Psalm LI, calling him the most ruined of all people, because he never sought God’s help, gave himself wholly to the devil’s service, and received his name from his own impiety: since he was to be contrary in every respect to Christ the Lord, he would be called Antichrist, I, 405. The Lord Jesus will slay him with the spirit of His mouth and destroy him by the brightness of His coming, 404. His coming at the end of the age is again described, together with the great overthrow of Christians that he will cause, II, 114, etc.; II, 205. Antichrist will come in his own name, exalting himself, because he will come to preach not as one sent by God but by his own pride. The Jews will receive him and for a time will worship him as though he were God, II, 233. What devastation he will inflict upon the Church, II, 336, etc. He will overcome the prophets Enoch and Elijah and bring them to completion by martyrdom, 337.

**APOSTLES.** The twelve apostles are compared with the twelve springs of water found at Elim, from whose waters, that is, doctrines, the whole world was watered. Likewise the seventy disciples who first followed the Lord represent the seventy palm trees which the Hebrews found flourishing in the same place, I, 63. The sudden transformation of the apostles, by which they became wise and speakers of every language, could have been accomplished only by God, I, 70. The apostles deserved a double crown: the first because they overcame vices and evil spirits; the second because they spread the Word of God, namely Christ’s Gospel, throughout the whole world, I, 90. Peter and Andrew, and others after them, are called by Christ to the conversion of the world under the name of fishing. In this calling one must recognize not so much the loftiness of His purpose as their marvelous obedience, for, at the sound of one command, leaving everything, they followed Christ, II, 19. By the curtain made at the entrance of the Tabernacle is understood the company of the apostles, to whom were given the keys of heaven, the power to bind and loose, and permission to open and shut the gates of Paradise, I, 97. By their teaching and preaching, like trumpets, the apostles summoned peoples from every region of the world to the Church. By these they teach us to prepare for battles, to fight against enemies, and to overcome both vices and evil spirits, I, 179. On Pentecost, that is, the fiftieth day after Christ’s resurrection, the apostles are baptized in the Holy Spirit and fire, I, 169. Before Christ the Lord ascended into heaven, He appointed them His vicars and leaders of the whole Church, and made them partakers of His power and glory, I, 190. The heavens—that is, the holy apostles—were not yet adorned; but when the Holy Spirit came, they were immediately enriched with knowledge, diversity of languages, and the efficacy of powers, I, 267. The apostles are called at times heavens, at times cherubim, now clouds, and so forth, and by various other names suited to them for different reasons. Thus the Lord ascended above the cherubim, that is, above His apostles, to whom, as He Himself says, He had given a mouth and wisdom which their adversaries could not resist, I, 329. When the apostles preached, people recalled that blessedness which they had lost in Adam, the first man; and all the ends of the earth were converted to the Lord, I, 341. These are they who enlighten others, show the way of truth, direct them into the way of God’s commandments, and do not permit them to go astray, I, 355. One cannot reflect without the greatest wonder on how the conversion of the whole world was accomplished through simple and unlearned men, namely the apostles; how the worship of idols and the profane wisdom of philosophers, which had held sway for so many centuries, were utterly overthrown and despised as a fabrication, I, 377 and 388. Therefore, as the apostles announced the truth and preached Christ’s faith, the believers multiplied; their multitude was so great that, like the stars, it could not be numbered, I, 377 and 388. “Their sound went out into all the earth,” when the Lord commanded them to go and preach through every province, every people, and every nation, I, 437. The apostles fell away from Christ when, terrified by fear as the Jews raged against Him, they fled from Him, I, 443. The Lord gave gifts to human beings—very great gifts—when He sent the Holy Spirit to the apostles and gave them such grace that they spoke the languages of all peoples and healed every sickness and infirmity, I, 439. Therefore St. Bruno also says of the apostles that, while preaching, they performed many miracles among many peoples, I, 531. At the time of the Passion they were so weakened by fear of death that Peter himself, who was regarded as the stronger among them, denied Him three times. Indeed, through want: abundance and want are opposites. The apostles’ abundance was Christ, because in Him they had and possessed power, constancy, strength, and whatever else they needed.

[Col. 1301] Since, therefore, they fled abundance, they suffered want of every good, I, 488.

**NOAH’S ARK.** The ark which Noah built at God’s command was a figure of the Church. Those who enter it through faith are saved; those outside it perish, II, 474. It is said to have been made three hundred cubits long; divided into six parts, this measurement signified the six ages to come of the world. The first extended from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to Moses; the fourth from Moses to David; the fifth from David to Christ; the sixth from Christ to the end of the age, I, 17. Why the ark was fifty cubits broad and thirty cubits high is explained mystically, I, 17. The fact that the ark was tossed to and fro by the rising waters of the flood foreshadowed the future trials of the holy Church, which is continually shaken and disturbed by storms of adversity and waters of turmoil. Yet it will not fear to perish, since Christ the Lord promised that He would not abandon it and would preserve it to the end of the age, I, 18. Every part of the ark, like its structure, is explained mystically, II, 474 and following.

**ARK OF THE COVENANT.** In the Ark of the Covenant, made by Moses through God’s oracle and overlaid everywhere with gold, were contained a golden urn holding manna, Aaron’s rod which had budded, and the tables of the Law. It signifies the Catholic Church—not the Church which still dwells in this world and suffers many injuries, but that Church which, having passed beyond heaven’s veil, already dwells and abides in the Holy of Holies, I, 87. It was overlaid within and without with purest gold, by which are signified those who possess wisdom: they ought not to keep it inwardly alone, but show it outwardly through preaching, I, 87. The two golden cherubim placed above the ark, looking at one another, represent the two Testaments, endowed with all wisdom, full of mutual harmony, I, 89. Why this ark was called the mercy-seat is explained, I, 88.

**RAINBOW.** So that Noah and his descendants might no longer fear a flood of waters by which the human race would be exterminated from the world, God set in the sky a rainbow, formed by the refraction of light in a dewy cloud, as a sign of this promise and covenant. This testimony of divine goodness remains still and will endure to the end of the world, I, 20.

**AVARICE.** Avarice is defined as an insatiable love of possessing riches, II, 185.

## B

**BALAAM.** Although Balaam was an impious man and a priest of the gods of the nations, he prophesied, though not from himself but from the Spirit of God. He saw the whole Church, and greatly desired to die the death of the righteous and become like him. “Let my soul die the death of the righteous,” he said, I, 188. He uttered the famous prophecy concerning the Lord’s coming: “A star shall arise out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel.” He saw Christ’s coming not only as Savior but also as Judge, as he testified in these words: “I shall see him, but not now; I shall behold him, but not near,” I, 189. He caused Israel to transgress with the daughters of Moab and to sacrifice to Baal-peor, I, 189 and 528.

**BAPTISM.** Baptism does not derive its name and power from the human being who administers it, but from the Church; hence sinners and heretics administering it beget children for the Church, I, 35. We are all born infected by original sin, which Christ’s blood expiated; its power is applied in baptism, in which we are washed and recover our original righteousness, I, 60. The baptism of infants is the custom of the Church, and sponsors pledge faith on their behalf, I, 116. What catechumens ought to do when they approach baptism, I, 129. Before they are washed by the element of water, they should vow to renounce the devil, his pomps, and his works, I, 176. Those receive the baptism of blood to whom God grants strength to be purified by the fire of suffering and martyrdom, even though they have not been sanctified by the washing of water, I, 233. No one will enter the land of the living who has not first passed through baptism and received the faith and teaching of the new law, I, 211. Jesus Christ, as Joshua, opened the Jordan and taught us what the water of the Jordan signifies, since there He was baptized and commanded His disciples to baptize all nations, I, 211. Baptism makes children of God. For those are called children of men who have only one generation; but those reborn from water have deserved to have God as their Father, I, 305. What the Apostle says in I Corinthians X—“For all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea”—means from water and the Holy Spirit, so that by the sea we understand water and by the cloud the Holy Spirit, I, 526. John preached a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, but did not grant remission of sins, II, 164.

**BEATITUDES.** What are the beatitudes to which every Christian ought to aspire is explained, II, 19 and following.

**BLASPHEMY.** Every sin and every blasphemy will be forgiven human beings if they acknowledge that they have sinned and do penance; but blasphemy of the spirit will not be forgiven human beings. For that blasphemy is not forgiven which, swollen, animated, and strengthened by the spirit of pride, does not bend and humble itself toward repentance. Blasphemy is to say something against God, II, 64.

## C
CAIN, Adam’s firstborn, devoted to agriculture, envied his brother Abel because God showed that Abel’s offerings were acceptable to Him while He despised Cain’s. He learned this because he saw his brother’s sacrifice consumed by fire sent down from heaven, whereas his own was not so consumed, I, 13 and 14. By this sign holy men believed that their sacrifices had pleased God: they saw them consumed by fire sent from heaven, I, 13 and 14. Carried away by indignation against his righteous and innocent brother, he killed him in the field, same place. Cain was a figure of the Jews who conspired to kill Christ, most holy and most beneficent, I, 13 and 14. For his fratricide Cain is rebuked by God; had he asked forgiveness from Him, he would have obtained it, but by his despair he inflicted the greatest injury upon God. Therefore he was punished with temporal and eternal punishment, I, 15. He is said to have gone out from the face of God, whose mercy he entirely turned away from himself, I, 15. Yet he hears from God that his desire is subject to him: if he gives it assent, it will exercise its power over him; but if he resists it, it will withdraw, 14.

Chastity of the flesh is useless unless chastity of mind is also possessed; and it is truly excellent when neither the flesh is corrupted by fornication nor the soul by heretical perversity or love of vices, I, 111. Restraint of the eyes is especially necessary for guarding the virtue of chastity. Those who lack it shall have no share in God’s inheritance, since they easily slip into evil through depraved desires, I, 275. Every sin of lust is abominable; the crime of fornication or adultery is rightly called a fire consuming unto destruction, I, 175. Marriage is good, but continence is better, and virginity best, I, 69.

Catechumen. When a catechumen comes to the Church seeking baptism, the Creed is read to him and the Catholic faith is read to him. He is asked whether he believes thus; he answers that he believes. Then Jesus touches his eyes; then He enlightens his mind; then he is baptized; then he is enlightened, II, 51.

Charity. From the fire which, according to the rite of the old Law, was always required to burn before the tabernacle in which the divine Majesty was represented, we are taught that love of God must never be interrupted by us, 126. Priests above all must be continually kindled by this fire; for if it is absent from them, their whole office will be altogether useless. Let the priest therefore take care continually to nourish the fire of charity and day by day to lay upon it wood—that is, holy works. Let him remember the divine mercy; let him remember what God has done and what He has promised to bestow upon those who love Him, I, 136. In charity toward God and neighbor the whole Law is fulfilled, I, 232. Charity is also the discernment of good and evil. For it always burns, and is so enkindled in love of God and neighbor that it cannot be extinguished, II, 307. If, however, a priest or prelate has the care of souls, let him beware lest, because of any enmity or hatred, he neglect their salvation, I, 81. Charity nourishes, advances, and adorns all virtues, I, 81. Those who possess charity, who place their hope not in the uncertainty of riches but in God, and who devote themselves to virtue, though rich in this world, are nevertheless not lovers of the world, II, 273. Divine mysteries and sacraments are to be revealed to those whose hearts appear kindled by the fire of charity, 126. Whoever loves his neighbor loves God also, provided that he loves him with true love. For that love is not true which attends to temporal advantages and does not tend toward the glory of eternal blessedness, II, 278. The exceeding kindness and mercy of our Savior even toward His own enemies must be recalled, so that we may be ever more inflamed with the love of God and stirred to His kindness and mercy, I, 127. Not only our friends, but our very enemies, by Christ’s command, must be loved and loaded with benefits according to our means. This advancement in the Christian law is required of us; for if we loved only those who love us, we would not be unlike unbelievers, II, 26 and following. Spiritual love must be preferred to carnal love. By that love we must love our brothers and all our relatives with which Christ loved His mother and His brothers, I, 68. St. Bruno treats copiously of the command of love toward God and neighbor, II, 107. Charity is the virtue by which we love God for His own sake and our neighbor as ourselves. No virtues and no good things can profit when charity is absent, II, 491. Nothing except evil ought to be hated; for our God also loves every creature of His and hates evil alone. Whoever therefore loves God should love every creature of God, but not evil, since evil is not a creature of God, I, 503. Since whatever the world possesses and its desire pass away, we ought to delight in the Lord, since He is every good. For whoever delights in the Lord always desires to be and dwell with the Lord. This will be granted to the Saints, because they will remain with Him together without end, 369. The characteristics of charity assigned by St. Paul are explained excellently, II, 49.

CHRIST. The first human being is said to have been made even bodily in Christ’s image, I, 6. Christ is called the tree of life because He Himself says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood shall live eternally,” I, 9. Abel, innocent and pleasing to God, who was killed by his brother Cain, bore His first figure, I, 14. After the flood, Noah offers God a sacrifice from every kind of animal, and man alone is not sacrificed, because Christ, the true Lamb, was to be sacrificed in His own time in order to take away the sins of the world, I, 19. In the rite of sacrificing the Paschal lamb, the whole Passion of Christ is seen as prefigured, I, 58 and following. In Noah also, drunk with wine, there is seen a type of Christ, who, having drained the cup of His Passion, took the sleep of death. The Jews mocked Him and treated Him with insults, reckoning the cross and death which He endured to be a scandal and disgrace, I, 21. Isaac, to be sacrificed by his father Abraham, foreshadowed the image of Christ, I, 28. When the Lord was born, there was great peace everywhere, since the whole world was under Roman rule. Therefore, immediately at His birth, the voices of angels were heard crying and saying: “Glory to God in the highest,” etc., I, 451. Christ is the salvation of God, who, born of the Virgin, has been made most well known to us by many evidences, I, 503. In the maturity of His age, namely thirty years, He wished to be baptized and began His preaching, I, 17. Why He is called Mary’s firstborn Son, although she bore no other children after Christ, II, 8. The mysteries contained in the calling of the Magi to Christ’s manger, and the whole sequence of their coming to Bethlehem, are explained excellently, II, 9 and following. The day of Christ’s death is specified, I, 58. Christ blotted out our sins by His blood and reconciled the whole human race to God the Father, I, 61. The remembrance of His Passion renders every bitterness of the commandments sweet, as did the wood which Moses cast into the waters of Marah and made them, formerly bitter, sweet for the thirsty Hebrews, I, 65. He is likened to the rock to which the people of Israel came and which, struck twice, gave water; similarly, when the side of Christ hanging on the cross was struck, blood and water came forth. Therefore the Apostle rightly said that Christ is the rock by whose flowing water the whole world was restored and cleansed, I, 67. In the cloud by which the Lord was covered while speaking with Moses, the mystery of the future Incarnation was prefigured. For the divinity, veiled in flesh, could not be seen by the Jews, I, 69. Before Christ’s Passion, entrance into heaven was granted to no one, whether righteous or penitent; rather, all were received into Abraham’s bosom until Christ, the liberator of all, should come, I, 75. The impious King Herod attempted to kill Christ as an infant, I, 83. Christ’s flight into Egypt in order to escape Herod teaches us that we must flee the devil and his members, II, 11. Why Christ is called a Nazarene, II, 13. Christ is the Angel of the covenant sent by the Father, whose name is in Him; for the Father’s name is in the Son, since the Son, like the Father, is God. He goes before us, guards us, and brings us into the eternal tabernacles, I, 83. How great were the things our Lord Christ did and endured in order to open heaven’s gate to us, I, 85. The slaughter of the calf before the door of the tabernacle, performed according to the Law, was a figure of the sacrifice of Christ the Lord upon the cross for our salvation, I, 106. We ought to understand how great was Christ’s love, mercy, and kindness toward us from this: while offering Himself upon the altar of the cross, He prayed to the Father for His persecutors, same page and column. When we keep Christ’s Passion in mind, we offer God a great sacrifice for the expiation of our sins, I, 113. By His Passion Christ redeemed not only those who were beginning to believe in Him, but also all the Saints and Patriarchs of the old Law, whom faith and hope in Him had made righteous, from death, I, 132. How Christ offered Himself both by determination and freely, I, 139. The good thief, who was the first to believe in Him, gave the first fruits, as it were, of Christ’s Passion through his own offering, I, 139. Christ offered Himself both by determination and freely: by determination, because He had so disposed, ordained, and predestined this concerning Himself before the ages; freely, because He is omnipotent, I, 139. By the same most gracious will He allowed Himself to be tempted by the devil, in order to teach how we may conquer that hostile enemy, II, 17. Christ’s blood benefits the offerer himself and the universal Church, II, 141. The same blood of Christ continually intercedes for us with the Father every day until the consummation of the age, I, 157. According to the opinion of Bruno and of very many Fathers and writers, Christ the Lord was sacrificed in the thirty-third year of His age, I, 148. Before Christ’s Incarnation no one could be cleansed from original sin—that is, could of himself perform anything toward its remission, I, 161. Like Moses, Christ appointed the twelve Apostles as the leaders of His army, I, 172. He Himself was baptized in His thirtieth year, sanctifying the waters; but on the fiftieth day after His resurrection the Apostles are baptized in the Holy Spirit and fire, I, 169. The bronze serpent, which Moses caused to be raised in the wilderness by God’s command, was a figure of Christ the Lord raised up on the cross, I, 187. The sacrifice of the goat was a type of Christ, who was condemned with the ungodly and, as though a criminal, crucified with thieves, I, 191. Christ’s sacrifice is mystically renewed daily by His ministers and offered by all ministers, I, 222. In Christ’s Passion there was a great trial, so that even the disciples, struck with terror, abandoned Him, I, 224. Christ’s kingdom was established when the Synagogue—that is, Jewish dominion—fell, I, 225. After His Passion Christ descended into hell in order to rescue and free the souls of the righteous, I, 248, 295, 497; and II, 57. All the righteous of the Old Testament burned with desire to see Him and looked up to Him as the one good, I, 248. In heaven Christ is the splendor and illumination of the Saints, I, 227. Christ is God’s power and wisdom, God’s strength and prudence. Having become incarnate, He struck down the devil and expelled him from the kingdom which he had long possessed. He gathered all the nations of the world into one faith and one Church, I, 267. Although no mortal can comprehend how great Christ’s divinity is, His miracles, the holiness of His commandments, and His complete righteousness make it manifest, I, 283. Christ does not dwell in those who live softly and are given over to pleasures, I, 269. How terrible will Christ’s sentence over the impious be on the day of judgment: once uttered, they will immediately be hurled into the abyss, I, 284. Our Lord Christ is both God and man; according to His humanity He was constituted both king and Lord not only by the Father but also by Himself and by the Holy Spirit. For He who according to divinity was neither made nor created, according to humanity created and made Himself, I, 302. Against Felix and Elipandus it is asserted that Christ is not the adoptive but the substantial Son of God, begotten from eternity—that is, before the ages and without beginning; and this is the meaning of the words, “Today I have begotten you,” I, 302. If the Son of God asks anything, He asks not according to divinity but according to humanity. Moreover, He asks not only from the Father, but from Himself and from the divinity which is in Him, I, 302. The Father received the Son back to Himself, glorified Him as incarnate and made man returning to Himself, and raised Him to the seat of His Majesty, I, 303. Those things proper to God and those proper to man are distinguished in Christ, I, 324. Through the Prophet Christ says that the Father is His strength, His firm foundation, His helper, and His protector. We should believe that He said these things in His heart when He was being led to the cross, upon which He did not doubt that He would conquer all His enemies and triumph over the very enemy of the human race, I, 327. His Passion is described, in which He showed Himself to be a true human being, not phantasmal or merely apparent, as certain heretics blasphemously asserted, I, 328. On the following day, after Christ the Lord instituted the sacrament of the Eucharist, He sacrificed Himself for us upon the altar of the cross; and then He offered that rich, sweet, and acceptable burnt offering to God, by which the first and original sin was blotted out, I, 336. It was fitting, therefore, that our Savior should be crowned, whose battle and victory are recounted so gloriously. Christ’s crown is the Church, wholly constructed and built from precious stones, I, 337. Christ’s divinity is joined to His humanity in such a way that it can never depart from it; and it can assist it in all things in such a way that it needs the aid of no one. When, however, He is read to have prayed to the Father, this must be understood to have been done so that we may know that our nature is in Him, believe Him to be truly human, and understand how all things were done, I, 339. Christ cried out on the cross for the faithful whom He saw would suffer for His name, and whose cause of enduring such harsh torments would be His Passion. Moreover, He cried out also for those who, redeemed at so great a price of His blood, do not cease to sin and persist in their iniquities, I, 338. Whatever is written in both Testaments is Christ’s word, I, 340. The Lord’s name is Jesus; and Jesus means “Savior.” Thus the Lord saves, is propitious, and has mercy upon His faithful because of His name—that is, in accordance with the meaning of His name, I, 345. Let those afflicted by tribulations and adversities turn their eyes to Jesus Christ crucified, that they may be consoled, I, 373. The divinity and humanity of our Savior wonderfully concurred for us in His Passion: the former, by coming, fulfilled what it had promised; the latter, by obeying and doing His will, redeemed us by dying, I, 378.

[Col. 1305] Christ’s death was a sleep: He slept as long as He wished and rose when He wished; had He not wished it, He would never have fallen asleep, I, 380. Christ’s death was of will, not weakness. He died because He wished; had He not wished it, He could never have been killed, I, 503. Christ rose from the dead and appeared alive again to His astonished disciples, I, 405. The Lord ascended into heaven amid the greatest joy and gladness of the Apostles, who saw Him ascending in such glory and power; and likewise amid the jubilation of the angels, all of whom, we must not doubt, came to meet Him with the highest exultation. He led with Him triumphantly into heaven the souls freed from hell, I, 392, 497. Since He redeemed the world by His own blood, He restored to us our first possession and opened the gates of paradise to His faithful: this is the blessedness which the Saints will possess after this life, I, 188. When He went out to meet the Jews coming to seize Him and cast them all to the ground by a single word, He immediately showed plainly both that He did not fear and that whatever He wished was in His power. Where such power is, fear can have no place, I, 408. Our Savior is God’s mercy and truth, because He is full of all mercy and truth, and in Him and through Him the Father’s mercy and truth have been revealed to all nations, I, 414. Christ’s being presented as praying and entreating God teaches us to entreat our Lord. He Himself had no need to pray, since all things lay within His will; He gave us an example that we might follow in His footsteps, I, 416. Christ is not God only, nor man only, but at once God and man, temporal and eternal, I, 423. The year of God’s favor began from the time when the Savior came into this world, I, 430. The whole world was under a curse, but when Christ came it was granted to receive blessing, I, 434. Christ is the way to the Father because through Him one comes to the Father; He is also salvation because through Him He works salvation among the nations everywhere, I, 434. Christ’s descent into hell and liberation of all the righteous is extolled as the triumph of His victory; yet His power shines no less in freeing from the tombs of sin those who lie in them, I, 475 and following. Though Christ’s time can mean the entire time of His Incarnation, it especially means that in which He worked the greater mercy, namely the time of His Passion, I, 444. Christ’s consubstantiality with the Father as the Son of God is affirmed and expounded, I, 450. It is confirmed from the saying concerning Him: “And he shall endure with the sun, and before the moon, unto age of ages,” which signifies in the same light and the same brightness. He therefore endures with the sun unto age of ages because He never departs from the Father and always remains with the Father in the same glory and brightness, I, 450. All were captives of the devil, but many, not all, became captives of Christ; for many are still held in captivity who, if they had wished, would not be in captivity, I, 349. Why Christ is properly called the God of Christians and is God, “the Lord’s deliverances from death,” I, 439. Christ, in His gratuitous goodness, turned toward us and deigned to look upon us, though we had grievously offended Him, I, 482. No one can be saved except through Christ; no one can be saved except one who believes in Christ, I, 475. He is the one through whom we know and invoke God the Father, since He is the Word and wisdom of the Father, I, 517. The ornaments of our Savior are confession, splendor, light, charity, and beauty. To these must be added immortality, power, strength, and the other virtues, I, 519. Our Savior is God’s mercy and truth, full of every mercy and truth; in Him and through Him the Father’s mercy and truth have been revealed to all nations, I, 533. How Christ’s body was in the tomb for three days and three nights, II, 65. He came first in humility, that the Son of Man might be judged; but He will come again exalted and lofty in glory, honor, and majesty, to judge the world, II, 84. He was transfigured on Mount Tabor, and Moses and Elijah appeared with Him, II, 85. By His example He taught the faithful to pay taxes to the rulers of the world, II, 87. He enters the city of Jerusalem as a conqueror, II, 99. As often as the Lord destroys demons, so often does He take from them their powers and capacity for harm, II, 168. What is signified by that bloody sweat which Christ underwent in the garden of Gethsemane, II, 207. Notable teaching concerning Christ’s divinity is given, II, 211. He goes to the Father according to His humanity, because according to His divinity He is everywhere, II, 275.

Christians are children of Abraham, not of the flesh but of the promise. Not all Israelites are admitted to this sonship, but those who profess the faith; these properly have Abraham, the father of believers, as their father, and are counted in the seed of Jacob, I, 31. The first fruits of the harvest of the Apostles were those who believed in Christ in the primitive Church; the Apostles themselves offered these by themselves to the priest—that is, to the Lord, I, [Col. 1306] 166. Their first fruits, scarcely regenerated through baptism, are to believe, to hope, and to love God; thus faith, hope, and charity establish a new life in them, I, 83. Christians should believe not in omens or divinations, but in the precepts of the divine law and in the words of prophets and apostles, I, 161. Let them beware also of depraved thoughts; and, if any thoughts occur to a good and holy mind, let them take care to make them fruitful, I, 161. Familiar association with those who profess another law and other doctrines, or who do not think perfectly concerning Catholic truth, is very dangerous for Christians, I, 68. Christians who do not keep Christ’s commandments become despisers of His name and are therefore accounted guilty before Him, I, 71. But when the Lord’s name is entrusted to you as a pledge, remember the pledge and do not renounce what you have promised, I, 71. Those who do not conform to the Christian religion by good morals and upright faith appear in their hearts to have departed from Him, I, 74. Every faithful soul, whether in prosperity or adversity, ought to display a holy, heavenly, and angelic life, I, 174. What Christian perfection requires: one must despise the world and love God and neighbor with the whole heart, I, 201. Those who aspire to eternal life regard the days of this world as nothing, I, 237. The righteous keep their way because they always persist in the work of righteousness to which they are accustomed, I, 255. Jews, heretics, and pagans do not know the path of righteousness. It belongs to Christians alone, because they alone follow and hold the truth; they alone have been worthy to receive the Lord’s name and, deserving so great a patronymic from Christ, are called Christians, I, 341. Priestly dignity passes to Christians, while the Jews remain without law, king, or priesthood, I, 31. As many Christians as there are, so many are the branches of this vine, namely Christ. Some are good and others evil; the good are fruitful, the evil unfruitful. The unfruitful are removed and burned; the fruitful are pruned and cut with the sword of the Spirit so that they may bear more fruit. The sword of the Spirit is the word of God, II, 277.

Council. When bishops are gathered into one assembly in God’s name for matters of faith and the Church, their gathering is called a council by theologians. What do bishops and doctors of the Church do? They take up the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; they come together as one; they attack the gatherings of heretics; heresies are uncovered and pretenses laid bare. From the greatest to the least, they either seize or kill them. They kill them because, striking them with anathema, they condemn them to eternal death; but they seize those whom they are able to convert from heretical perversity to Christ’s faith, I, 38. The Arian heresy, together with its author, was condemned at the First Council of Nicaea, I, 23, 391. The Council of Rimini is counted among illicit councils, because everything in it was done by force and fraud. Many Catholic bishops were indeed deceived; nevertheless, the Nicene faith did not fail, I, 231, 441. Councils are convened for this purpose: that, errors having been condemned, the truth of doctrines may be established; and they possess the highest authority in the Church, I, 432.

Confirmation. The Mosaic rite of sprinkling a person on the third and seventh day, so that he might be cleansed after touching a dead body, and of the priest’s laying hands upon him, was a figure of the sacrament of confirmation. For after the baptized person’s threefold immersion, by which he is purified from the stain of original guilt, he is filled through the laying on of hands with the seven graces of the Holy Spirit. He is first sprinkled with water or immersed in it, because no one is confirmed by a bishop unless he has first been baptized in the Trinity, I, 186.

CONSTANTINE THE GREAT, who was the first of the emperors publicly to profess the Christian religion, recalled from exile all the saints who had been banished to islands and inhospitable places by idolatrous rulers and persecutors of the Church. Warned by a vision which washing he should use to be cleansed of leprosy, he was baptized and healed by St. Sylvester, pontiff. The same emperor granted to St. Sylvester the imperial ornaments, namely the cloak and purple, which he and his successors use at great festivals. (This opinion was commonly circulated in the time of St. Bruno.) The same emperor gave peace to the universal Church, I, 41. In the time of Constantine the Great, the Church was extended among all nations, I, 99. The same points are confirmed, II, 323.

## D
### GOD

God created all things from nothing; but at the beginning of all creatures he created heaven and earth, I, and what follows, 1. God’s speech is his will, 2. He made a twofold firmament or heaven: one in which God himself dwells with the angels; the other in which the stars and planets revolve, 3. No change took place in God when he proceeded to the creation of the world. As regards himself, God does nothing new; rather, he commands to be done those things which he disposed before time, in the manner and place or time in which they were disposed, I, 5.

[Col. 1307] He made all things in wisdom. He created man in his own image and likeness. He formed his body from the clay of the earth, but gave him a soul when he breathed into his face the breath of life. The material of the flesh was taken from muddy earth; but the soul proceeded from the very mouth of God, 8. Thus man was made into a living soul; and, lest he should be alone, he created for him a helper like himself—namely Eve—whom he made from the rib of the sleeping Adam and gave to him as wife, that she might be the mother of all living human beings, 10. Though both were endowed with singular gifts, they fell from the supreme felicity of their original condition because of their transgression of the divine command, 11.

God created the world in six days: he saw all that he had made, and behold, it was very good; on the seventh day he rested from all his work and sanctified that day—that is, he willed that it should be regarded as holy, 7. But when humankind had multiplied and their wickedness had increased upon the earth, and all flesh had corrupted its way, God repented that he had made man and resolved to destroy him, together with all things created for his sake, by sending a flood of waters upon the earth. Yet, since he wished to preserve the race of humankind and of all animals, he commanded Noah, a righteous man, to build an ark and take refuge in it with his family; he also ordered him to place in it individual kinds from every animal species, to be saved from the shipwreck, 16, 17.

After the flood Noah’s sons had multiplied; and, lest they should perish again in another flood, they planned to raise a tower reaching to heaven. To restrain their pride, God compelled them, through the confusion of languages, to abandon the work they had begun, 21, 22. Scattered therefore into different lands, they founded different peoples and cities, 22.

From Nahor, son of Shem, came Terah; and from Terah was born Abraham, who was called the father of believers. His son Isaac, called the son of promise, had by Rebekah two twin sons, Esau and Jacob. Joseph, Jacob’s son, after various misfortunes was taken into Egypt, won Pharaoh’s favor, and was appointed by him ruler of the entire kingdom. He brought his whole family—that is, his father and brothers and their wives—into Egypt. All these descendants of Abraham, to whom God had promised that his seed would be multiplied beyond the sand of the sea, multiplied wonderfully; Pharaoh, fearing them, resolved to oppress them with the harshest slavery, 28 and following.

Yet God had compassion on his people and chose Moses, fortified by heavenly power, as their deliverer, 49. Who is signified [by God], and what conception may be held concerning his essence, is described, 49. The words “I will harden his heart” are explained, 53. He foretells to Moses Pharaoh’s hardening, since Pharaoh would not permit the Hebrew people’s departure from Egypt unless repeated and most extraordinary signs compelled him, 54 and following. God, who could have crushed Pharaoh by force of arms or by a more powerful means, sends flies, gnats, frogs, hail, and the like upon him, so that it may appear what human power amounts to before him and the king’s obstinacy may be without excuse, 56.

Divine omnipotence shone forth especially in the division of the Red Sea and in the passage which the Hebrew people made through it on dry feet, 54. Another proof of divine power was the drowning and destruction of Pharaoh and his entire army in that same sea, 54. God, who is invisible by nature, in some manner permits himself to be seen when he displays his power under some kind of likeness, I, 85.

The greatness of God’s mercy toward sinners who are truly contrite and repentant is set forth, I, 115, 155, 518. God alone is able to make us clean, since we are all born unclean, 123. God is good by nature. For God is good of himself and substantially; other things, however, neither exist nor are good of themselves, but are from God whatever they are, I, 526. God looks upon the disposition of the penitent, and opens the door of forgiveness to every penitent person who wishes to make satisfaction, 170. The Lord never judges a person according to what he was or will be, but according to what he is, I, 84. What has been stolen must be given to God, to whom all things belong, if there is no proper owner to whom it may be restored, I, 84.

God is worshipped and offered sacrifice not so much by good works as by good thoughts, I, 177. So long as an idol is not within us, God is with us and does not permit us to be drawn into evil, 188. Sometimes he visits us with scourges, in order to turn from us the spirit of pride and establish us in humility, I, 233. Nevertheless, his help must be sought, so that we may bear tribulations and afflictions patiently, I, 234. If we do any good, it is from God; accordingly, let us confess that merits and the reward of merits derive from his generosity, I, 237. If we do not understand why God grants good things to the wicked and evils in this world to the good, we must nevertheless humbly submit to his providence, I, 239. At times God afflicts the righteous in this life so that they may become better; but he reserves the wicked for eternal punishments, I, and following, 240. If anyone kept in mind that he stood beneath God’s eyes, he would never turn aside from virtue, 241. Our salvation lies in God’s mercy alone, 248.

God holds all things present before him and acts in all things as Creator [Col. 1308] and Lord, 262. He knows our every way, and through temporal calamities, as gold through fire, he purifies us when it pleases him, so that nothing faulty or unclean may remain in us, 263. No created intellect can comprehend God’s eternity, 264. God is ignorant of nothing; he knows the end of every person, 296. Sometimes he does not spare for a time, in order that he may spare eternally. Blessed are those who are punished in this world in such a way that they may be saved in the other, I, 268.

To serve God is to believe in him, worship him, and adore him. But this cannot be joined with servitude to, and disordered love of, creatures, 276. God’s judgments and deeds must always be acknowledged as utterly just and wise, 279. When God sometimes does not hear prayer, this happens either because the request is not rightly made, or because he has determined to do something better for his faithful people by not granting it, 281. Many also are not heard immediately, so that they may be perfected in virtue, 281. God must not be regarded as unjust if he permits a righteous person, such as St. Job, to be afflicted; for he did not afflict him on account of his sins, but because he wished thereby to make him greater, more illustrious, and more excellent in merits, I, 281. By hidden inspiration God points out their sins to his faithful people and brings them back to their memory. He also reveals and opens the ear of their minds, I, 282.

Although the Church forgives sins—as the Lord showed when he said, “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained”—nevertheless it is God who forgives them, since he alone possesses the power and has given his Christ the power to forgive sins, II, 48. Whatever we do for God is not from our own strength but from God, I, 295. Just as we question God through desire and prayer, so he answers us by hearing and giving, I, 297. Although God is everywhere, there is nevertheless a place in which he deigns to reveal his glory more clearly and manifestly; it is called paradise, the kingdom of God, and heavenly glory, I, 304. And even if God is hidden from human wayfarers, he is readily found by those who seek him with devout desire, I, 327.

What God’s mercy is appears in the words: “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.” On this St. Bruno says: “That sinners are called and saved is mercy; but that those who unjustly consider themselves righteous are rejected is justice. The world could not be saved through sacrifice, but it was saved through mercy, because sacrifice is mercy,” II, 49. The holy Lord will not forsake the holy; and because he is innocent, he will do no harm; and because he has been chosen for his people, he will not abandon his chosen one, I, 331. Such is the mercy of our Creator that repentance and forgiveness occur in one and the same hour, I, 335.

“The counsel of the Lord remains for ever, the thoughts of his heart from age to age.” As he has disposed and predetermined before time, so—and not otherwise—it must come to pass. Both the punishment of the wicked and the glory of the righteous have been so arranged that they cannot at all be changed. Blessed, therefore, are those who believe in him and those who have been pre-elected and predestined by him, because they shall by no means lack the blessedness predestined for them, I, 300. On the same page it is explained how St. Bruno’s teaching on predestination should be understood. He raises the great question why the Lord chose some and rejected others; and gives as the greatest answer that it thus pleased the Lord, II, 60. Nothing is hidden from God; no pretense is concealed from his eyes: he sees all things and answers thought, II, 44. Although God could sometimes be seen and heard through a subjected creature, he could never be either seen or heard in his own essence, II, 233.

“God” is a common name and pertains to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit alike. But because it had previously said, “In the beginning he made,” the Father must necessarily be understood, because he worked through the Beginning, that is, through the Son. Thus the first person is the Father; the second, the Beginning, that is, the Son; and the third, the Spirit of God, who was borne over the waters, by which the Holy Spirit is most plainly indicated, II, 528.

### Devil

The names by which the devil, that ancient serpent, is called are explained, II, 334. His devices for destroying the Church and holy souls are described, 335. The devil’s food and refreshment is sin. Whoever sins more prepares greater banquets for him. Therefore none serve him as do evil kings and princes, and all the greedy and rich. For these not only sin, but compel others to sin with them, II, 522.

### Feast Days

To sanctify the Sabbath is not to cease from good works. For since the Sabbath is holy in itself, the person who works well becomes holy, I, 71. On feast days one must also refrain from lawful activities when the Church’s command requires it; that is, Christians must abstain from wedding celebrations, dances, and noisy hunts, I, 72. The seventh day, on which God rested from the work of creation that he had completed, is said to have been sanctified by him—that is, declared holy—so that it might be regarded as holy by all people and each person might cease from servile works, and still more from [Col. 1309] evil, 172. The days prescribed in the Law of Moses for solemn observance are specified, I, 84. But so that God might show how greatly the observance of the Sabbath day and abstention from every servile work mattered, he commanded Moses that the man found gathering wood in the wilderness on the Sabbath day should perish by being crushed with stones, I, 183. The Hebrews were forbidden the use of leavened bread from the first day of Passover until the seventh day. The meaning of this command is explained, I, 60. The solemn sacrifice of the Passover lamb foreshadowed Christ’s true sacrifice for the redemption of humankind, I, 58.

### Flood

Because of the sins of human beings, who had all turned to evil and corruption, God sent a flood of waters upon the earth. Rightly, all things made for man perish with man. This is what he says: “The end of all flesh has come before me”; that is, it so pleases me, it has thus been ordained by me, that all flesh should come to an end and that human beings, together with the earth, and those things which were made for humankind, should be destroyed. For in this God destroyed the earth itself, because before the flood it had been much more fertile. Hence after the flood flesh is said to have been granted for food, I, 17. What is to be understood by the fountains of the great deep and by the floodgates of heaven, which are said to have been opened in the flood, I, 18.

“And God remembered Noah,” etc. God never forgets; but he is said to remember when he has mercy upon sinners. Therefore, wishing to put an end to the flood, he brought a spirit over the earth and the waters diminished; that is, he brought a wind of serenity over the earth, and by an invisible power so great a mass of waters disappeared, and the face of the earth was again made habitable, 19. Moreover, he set a sign which should remain forever between God and humankind at all times—namely the bow, concerning which something has been said in its proper place, 20.

### Rich Person

The rich person who places hope not in God but in the riches of this world, after he has slept and closed his eyes in the sleep of death, will take nothing with him. He will open his eyes in the resurrection and find nothing. For a burning wind—that is, an evil spirit—takes him from this life; it both violently seizes souls and burns eternally those whom it seizes, I, 268. Let no one be excessively attached to riches; and still more let him beware of amassing them unjustly, I, 423. All riches are unrighteous which, when greedily retained, harm their proper owners, or which are not spent according to equity. For you spend them according to equity when you reserve for yourself only as much as may suffice and generously distribute the rest to those in need, II, 194. Evangelical teaching must be given not only in due measure but also at its proper time. For not every time is suitable for instruction; nor should one preach equally to all, nor all things to all, II, 182.

### Church

The paradise of delight which God planted in the beginning signifies the holy Church. It is rightly said to have been planted in the beginning, because God chose it before the foundation of the world, 8. Those who profess its faith belong to the Church; in it offerings are made, in it sacrifice is offered, and outside it there is no place for a true sacrifice, I, 49. The Church is born and reborn in Christ; the Church alone is founded in Christ, I, 61. At one and the same time the Church, signified by the moon, had its beginning, and Christ, the sun of righteousness, came to his setting. For as Eve was made from the side of sleeping Adam, so the Church was fashioned from the side of Christ hanging on the cross, I, 521. Those who do not remain in it until the end shall perish, I, 61 ff. Only the children of the Church are permitted to eat of the lamb; but this is forbidden to the rest, who are outside the Church, 62. Those provoke divine vengeance against themselves who ambitiously rise to ecclesiastical dignities, 69.

The primitive Church, from Christ’s Passion to the time of Emperor Constantine, was for the most part built from the holy martyrs; thereafter, until the time of Antichrist, the whole Church is called the court of the tabernacle. Hence, in an unusual manner, the court of the tabernacle is much greater than the tabernacle itself. The court of the tabernacle, therefore, is the Church of confessors, which from the time of the aforesaid prince has been extended among all nations, 49. The Church is anointed—that is, sanctified—with the oil of the Holy Spirit, so that there may be in it neither spot nor wrinkle, I, 152. Churches ought to be held in the greatest reverence because the Lord dwells in them; and while sacred rites are being performed, silence is prescribed for all who are present, I, 158. May those who love and defend the Church be strengthened in its love and defense, because the power of miracles and the grace of the Holy Spirit shall not fail it until the consummation of the age, I, 95. Not only the Church militant, but also the triumphant and glorious Church, was prefigured in the ark of the covenant, 87. Until the consummation of the age it shall not cease to offer the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, 113. For those outside the Church, no [Col. 1310] sacrifice, no abstinence, and no mortification of the flesh is of use for salvation, 130.

What the Church’s spiritual power is, I, 149. Its office is to separate harmful Christians from the good and faithful; and there are various forms of this separation, or excommunication, I, 149. Until the consummation of the age, the whole Church is cleansed and sanctified by Christ’s blood, I, 158. The goods of the Church may not be alienated, I, 169. Under the Old Law, possessions once consecrated to God could neither be sold nor redeemed, I, 171. Whoever contradicts the universal Church in its teaching is charged with great pride, I, 183. Those who refuse to keep and observe its ordinances—which are also God’s—ought to be expelled from the Church, condemned by all, and excommunicated, 183. The Church has accepted the faith of no single nation; and it itself will at last rule over all, it over which none but God shall rule, I, 167. The Church is closed to no one: whoever promises to profess the Catholic faith is admitted into it, I, 207. May the Church never be without a bishop, and may this name never fail within it, I, 210. The holy Church is constituted not only from the righteous, but also from the ungodly, sinners, and foolish, I, 212.

The faithful person ought never to cease fighting against the devil, because he continually lies in wait for him through heretics and evil Christians, I, 12. When someone is cast out of paradise—that is, from the Church—on account of sin, lest he presume to approach the tree of life, that is, to partake of Christ’s flesh, he is forbidden by its ministers, I, 13. The Church must always speak, even if it is not heard by the wicked. For then the good become better, while the wicked have no excuse for their iniquity, I, 251. Outside the Catholic Church, neither a right understanding of the sacred Scriptures nor the merit of good works can be possessed, I, 268. The pillar of truth always shines in the Church, and by its splendor all can be enlightened. For all things are made manifest to believers, I, 280.

Although the Church has suffered very many hardships and labors, it has always emerged from them, because none of its tyrants and persecutors has overstepped the limits set by God: for by death, conversion, loss of power, or some other occasion, each has ceased from madness and wickedness, I, 287. Catholic rulers have been left as guardians and protectors of the Church, so that the integrity of faith and doctrine may be preserved in it, I, 290. Many in the Church feign piety; but God looks not at words, but at hearts, I, 295. In tribulations and adversities the holy Church has been enlarged all the more. Its boundaries are from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and the sea, I, 305. The Church consists not only of the elect, but also of evil people and sinners, as of wise and foolish alike, I, 331. The praise of Christ is sung in the great Church, which is the Catholic and universal Church—not in one part of the world, but spread throughout the whole world, I, 340.

Although many churches are scattered throughout the whole world, there is nevertheless one Church, because the faith of all is one; and those who have not yet entered this holy Church are still in darkness and error, and have not yet reached light and truth, I, 384. The Church is called Christ’s inheritance, his bride, his glorious acquisition, which he purchased for himself with his blood, I, 392. It was made from Jews and Gentiles, and within it both peoples are joined under the same leader and shepherd. At the end of the age, one flock shall be made from these, I, 393. It is enough for us to preach this in the Church: that Christ is God and our king for ever; and because he himself rules and loves us, let us never depart from his rule, never pass over to another teaching, humbly do whatever he commands, accept no other ruler, and let this suffice us, I, 395. In many ways the Lord has enriched the Church, since he has endowed it with wisdom and knowledge, strength and piety, virtues and uprightness, glory and honor, and every good thing, I, 430. The Church teaches and proclaims one and the same doctrine from the beginning until now, I, 436. All churches established throughout the world are members of the one universal and Catholic Church, I, 437.

The Church is the house of God; its love consumed Christ and joined him to itself inseparably, I, 444. The whole holy Church is called a dove because it is simple and innocent. The preaching of its ministers ought not to be novel or strange, but firm and full of authority, I, 437. Therefore the Lord made for himself a way in the sea and paths in many waters, because, since this world was converted to his faith, he does not cease to walk through it invisibly and to visit his churches everywhere, I, 464. The Church has a firm foundation; therefore it fears neither rain, floods, nor wind. The Church is founded for all ages, because Christ is its foundation, I, 470. The Church is a fortress—not merely any fortress, but a strong and impregnable one—being set upon a mountain, surrounded by a wall, and armed with an army of angels and the defenses of heavenly powers. [Col. 1311] II, 177. As one house is made from many stones arranged with order and design, so one Church is established from many people united by the love of charity and brotherhood, II, 483.

### Almsgiving

How acceptable almsgiving is to God, and what reward it receives, II, 57.

### Elijah

The prophet Elijah appeared with Moses to the apostles on the mountain when Christ was transfigured before them, II, 85. At the end of the world he will come to preach Christ’s Gospel, and then the Jews will be converted, II, 86.

### Bishops

With regard to the protection of the faith, a prelate ought to have the same concern for all those subject to him as for his own children, I, 77. If a bishop knows that someone is spreading perverse doctrines among his people and does not endeavor to restrain him, the sin of seduction shall fall back upon the bishop, 77. How great the wisdom required in bishops must be, and how great the splendor of every virtue, I, 90. Unless through perfect love of God and neighbor, signified by scarlet twice dyed, and through purity and chastity of mind and body, signified by fine linen, a bishop cannot bear the burden of the office imposed upon him, I, 102. Let bishops keep before their eyes the examples of the apostles and imitate their glorious deeds, I, 103.

Therefore, says St Bruno, let a bishop always be mindful of the holy Fathers; let him always remember how they lived and served God; let him imitate their life, follow their teaching, and maintain their practice. How will he satisfy these requirements if he does not take care to read their deeds and works? Ibid. Bishops ought to possess the fullest understanding of the holy Scriptures, so that by the divine word they may instruct their people unto salvation, 103. They are compared to clouds. For they are those who rain upon the earth and water the whole earth with the showers of spiritual teaching, I, 367. The episcopal vestments are prescribed in order to show the bishop’s lofty and, as it were, heavenly dignity, I, 105. When people assemble in the Church to receive the sacraments, then especially they ought to be instructed and prepared by their pastors, I, 103. What is signified by the words *Holy to the Lord*, which the high priest bears inscribed in gold upon his forehead, I, 106. How important it is that a bishop be wise, I, 106. The book of Exodus ought especially to be read and meditated upon by bishops and priests, I, 111.

A bishop is sanctified when he receives the sacred law and divine books in order to meditate upon and teach them, and promises to observe them not merely with his lips but with his whole heart, I, 111. After St Bruno described the qualities that ought to shine forth in those chosen for the episcopate—namely, a life unstained, most pure, and never blameworthy—he says this concerning the election of a bishop: “The lamp is chosen by the people and offered to the pontiffs; but by the bishops it is consecrated, ordained, and placed in its seat.” The same holy bishop goes on thus concerning how he ought to conduct himself in the episcopate: “Let it shine before the Lord until morning; and until he departs from this miserable and dark life, let him not cease to preach to and enlighten God’s people, so that, when this night is ended, the sun of righteousness may rise for him, and he may enter that day of which the Psalmist says in Psalm LXXXIII: ‘For one day is better than thousands,’” I, 101.

Then he exhorts them thus: “Let bishops hear why they were ordained, why and by whom they were established: certainly not to exercise tyrannical and secular power, but to watch, to preach, and to fight against heretics and malignant spirits,” I, 302. Let the bishop make satisfaction to everyone, especially if he can, I, 128. It is the duty of bishops and priests to make themselves better every day, I, 137. What bishops ought to believe and undertake at their consecration, I, 141. Their office is to perform and administer the greater sacraments of the Church, I, 174. But they should not admit to holy orders those who have committed more serious crimes, in accordance with the canons forbidding this, I, 161. Therefore those who seek ordination to the sacred ministry should have testimony to their good name, establishing that they have done nothing shameful or dishonorable, I, 162.

Discipline, which may be called the teaching and training of religion, is necessary for all people, but most especially for those who ought to govern and teach others, I, 303. The agreement and uniformity of bishops in handing on the Church’s teachings produces great joy for the faithful and praise to God, I, 432. Because Christ formed the apostles by his gentleness so that they might love and heal all peoples and invite them to blessedness, bishops, who are their successors, should take care to imitate them in the same gentleness, I, 437. Their preaching should not be novel or strange, but firm and full of authority. Let them sleep between the two Testaments: on one side let them have the New, on the other the Old; from these let them receive what they preach to others, and from these take the food by which they nourish others, 437. The same is said concerning the study of sacred letters, to which bishops ought to devote themselves, II, 179.

The Church is compared to a little boat in the midst of the sea, tossed by raging winds; when the waves are stilled at the command of Christ the Lord, tranquility is restored to it, II, 45. Christ sometimes seems to sleep in it when he allows his faithful to be amid straits and afflictions; but when they implore his help, they are not abandoned by him, [Col. 1312] II, 45. A hireling bishop is one who, in feeding and ruling the sheep, seeks only temporal and passing things; who feeds the Lord’s sheep not out of love for the heavenly homeland, but for gain and the reward of temporal things, II, 251.

### Sacrament of the Eucharist

When in Eucharistic communion we receive the body and blood of Christ the Lord, we share in his Passion. For he is the true Lamb, sacrificed for us on the cross; his sacrifice is mystically renewed in the Mass and substantially and spiritually given under the appearances of bread and wine, I, 58–59. St Bruno explains why God commanded that two lambs, one in the morning and another in the evening, be sacrificed to him. “Although,” he says, “the two lambs signify one and the same thing—for they signify that Lamb who takes away the sins of the world—Christ was nevertheless sacrificed differently every day in the Church and on the cross. Here he is sacrificed by the faithful with devotion; there, by the Jews with cruelty. And indeed our Lamb was sacrificed both in the morning and in the evening: for Christ our Lord was judged and condemned by the Jews in the morning, but in the evening, hanging on the cross, he gave up his spirit,” 113.

Concerning the sacrifice of the calf, he gives the following: *A. N. on Lev., ch. I*, 125. “Moses, the Jewish people, and the Church sacrifice one and the same calf: Moses by signifying, the Jews by sinning, the Church by commemorating.” We ought to receive Christ’s body and blood not merely with the mouth but with the heart—that is, with faith and purity of soul. Those who partake unworthily, I, 59. Wicked priests are forbidden to consecrate Christ’s body and blood; likewise evil Christians are forbidden to receive them, I, 82. As the Hebrews departed from Egypt on the very day on which they ate the Passover, so those who partake of the body and blood of Christ the Lord are bound to withdraw from sins and depraved habits, I, 82.

Berengar, the arch-heretic, was the first who denied that Christ’s true body is contained in the Eucharist; he also attacked the teaching that, in the sacrifice of the Mass, bread and wine are transubstantiated into the Lord’s body and blood, I, 139. Bruno’s address to bishops and priests is notable, for in it he gives striking testimony concerning the transubstantiation of bread and wine into the Lord’s body and blood performed at the altar. “You bishops and priests,” he says, “are sons of this Aaron: therefore draw near and sacrifice; pour the blood of the calf round about. For what else do you do whenever you give us to drink the blood consecrated through your ministry, except that, after the manner of Aaron’s sons, you pour out the blood around the altar of our heart?” 126.

It is permitted to eat of the sacrifice which is wonderfully made in remembrance of Christ; but of that sacrifice which Jesus himself offered upon the altar of the cross, no one is permitted to eat it as it is in itself, I, 138. The offense taken by the disciples is mentioned: because they wrongly understood Christ when he told them that he would give them his flesh to eat, they went back, thinking that they ought to eat the flesh of Christ which they saw, not sacramentally, but cut into pieces, 138. Christ offers himself as a burnt offering, for even though it is done through the ministry of priests, he himself offers and sacrifices his flesh and blood. For it is not the priest’s voice but his own which says: “This is my body,” and, “This is the chalice of the new testament in my blood, which shall be poured out for you and for many for the remission of sins.” By this utterance the whole sacrifice is offered and sanctified, I, 141.

Here may be noted the tradition of the form of consecration both of bread and of wine in the Mass, whereby those elements become Christ’s body and blood. The same page also says that, although bishops and priests have their hands extended and raised over Christ’s body, nevertheless Jesus alone is the high priest who sanctifies and blesses, and by whose ineffable power bread and wine are converted into the substance of his body and blood. What is contained in the Eucharist, and how we ought to approach its reception, I, 157. Chastity must be especially observed by those receiving the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, 157.
