Whoever consecrates Christ’s sacrament, or approaches to receive his flesh and blood, should be fragrant with moral uprightness and the sweetness of virtues, 157.

Christ, the great priest according to the order of Melchizedek, by wonderful power changed bread and wine into the substance of his body and blood, and gave them to his disciples, saying: “Take and eat: this is my body,” etc. What those approaching the holy Eucharist ought to think of themselves: the deeper their humility, the greater will be their acquisition of grace, II, 43. No one ever ate Christ’s flesh bodily before this sacrament; no one would eat it bodily unless this sacrament were performed. Therefore in this sacrament it is eaten, yet, though eaten, is not diminished; and it would never be eaten unless this bread were substantially changed into it by Christ’s blessing. For this change is the work of the right hand of the Most High, [Col. 1313] II, 237. Whoever eats Christ’s body and drinks his blood becomes one with him, II, 238.

### Eve

From one of Adam’s ribs the divine craftsman formed Eve as a woman and gave her to him as a helper, that she might bear children and share with him an undivided manner of life, I, 10. Tempted by the devil, she tasted the forbidden fruit and offered it to her husband Adam, who likewise ate of it; and both fell into offense against God, with the greatest ruin and calamity for themselves and their descendants, I, 11. The same is confirmed, I, 457, where, as the cause of so many evils, is adduced the conversation Eve had with the serpent, whose flatteries—or rather snares—she ought to have avoided.

### Gospels

The agreement of the Gospels with the books of the Old Testament is an argument for their divine authority, I, 85. Each Gospel by itself would suffice the whole world for faith, teaching, and salvation, I, 91. The evangelists never depart from truth and never speak falsehood: whatever they say is true, just, pure, and most worthy of belief, I, 97. Since they agree fully in teaching truth, they lay claim to complete credence, I, 97. The Gospel bears witness to the Church as the Old Testament does to the Tabernacle, I, 117. The divine Scriptures must be handled only reverently and by holy people, I, 97. The glory of the New Testament is far more splendid than the Law of Moses, I, 123. The spread of the Gospel law ever flourishes and brings new nations and peoples into the Church, I, 288. The evangelists agree perfectly with the Prophets, especially David and Isaiah, in what they relate concerning Christ’s Passion; consequently there can be no doubt that their testimony is true, I, 339.

### Evangelists

The writers of the Gospels were prefigured in the four living creatures. In the first creature, described as having a human face, St Matthew the apostle is represented: beginning with Christ’s birth, he shows him to be a perfect man, born from human beings, and sets out his entire genealogy from Abraham to Christ himself. Mark appears to have the face of a lion, since at the beginning of his Gospel a voice is described as crying in the wilderness. Blessed Luke has the face of an ox, because he begins his writing with the priesthood, which was chiefly instituted for sacrifices. Among sacrificial victims, moreover, the ox is the greater offering. Why John has the face of an eagle is made most plain by the beginning of his Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” II, 525.

### Excommunication

Who has authority to excommunicate in the Church, and in what order excommunication should be imposed, II, 89–90.

### Faith

There should be no delay in receiving faith, I, 52. For faith is the firstborn of the human person, without which it is impossible to please God. It is the first of all virtues to arise in the minds of believers; it is the first to be begotten by priests in Christian hearts. But because faith without works is dead, by works it is rendered living and active, I, 63. Through the strength of faith and the grace of baptism one comes to the crown, I, 64. Faith ought to be content with revealed truth alone, and not, together with heretics, pursue curious and discordant speculations. For all their efforts are crushed and scattered by the light of the divine Scriptures, I, 66. Faith is like a door through which Christ enters the tabernacle of our breast, I, 126. What must be believed concerning Christ is explained there plainly. Errors in faith are compared to leprosy. Whoever, therefore, thinks wrongly concerning God himself and the Christian faith has leprosy in the head and bears it in the head, I, 151.

How grave the sin of unbelief is, I, 187. The works of those without faith are not reckoned as merit for eternal life, since faith is the beginning of merit, 322. Whatever is not from faith is called evil, not because all works of unbelievers are evil, but because they lack the supernatural goodness that merits eternal life and are not directed to the final end, I, 406. No faith other than that of Christians can save, I, 406. Rightly does the holy Church receive no one coming to it unless he has first been clothed with the adornment of faith, II, 487. Christ the Lord attributes the power of his virtue not to himself but to faith, and affirms that what he does, faith does, I, 487. Because of his little faith Peter sinks in the waves, II, 487. Faith is a virtue by which we most certainly believe what is told to us, even if it does not yet appear, and do not doubt that it shall come to pass, II, 488.

If the son is good, he shall not bear his father’s iniquity; but if he is evil, he shall bear the punishment of both his own and his father’s iniquity. If, moreover, the father is good and the son does not depart from his father’s goodness, he shall be enriched with far greater goods, I, 71.

### Fortitude

Fortitude is set down as the third of the cardinal virtues. [Col. 1314] Its possession is so necessary that without it wisdom and justice seem useless. This firmness or constancy resides not in the body but in the mind, by which we overcome injuries, endure every adversity, and are not uplifted by prosperity. Who they are that lack this fortitude, II, 493. The saints, however, possessed it, for they could be overcome neither by vices, torments, nor blandishments, II, 493.

### Giants

The opinion is refuted of those who have imagined that giants were begotten from intercourse between evil angels, or demons, and women. They were human beings famous not so much for exceptional height as for strength and power, I, 16.

### Grace of God

The grace of the Holy Spirit supplies us with light and protection, and abandons no one unless first abandoned. It was prefigured in the pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night which went before the people of Israel, I, 63. This pillar is the grace of the Holy Spirit, which both protects us from the heat of vices and enlightens us lest we be enveloped in the errors of vices, I, 63. Whatever the saints do holily, they perform through the power of divine grace, I, 68. The days of the saints are said to be fulfilled when, through the grace by which before the ages they were predestined for glory, they shall live eternally, I, 83. Election unto glory and mercy rest wholly in God’s will, I, 122.

We are taught how great God’s mercy is toward sinners who implore it with tears and true repentance, from the fact that Christ’s blood, full of piety and mercy and shed solely through piety and mercy, obtains for them the grace of forgiveness, even if they have been burdened with great sins, I, 155 and note. A sinner is cleansed in two ways: by penitence of contrition, and by perseverance in a good life and faithful adherence to God, I, 156. Whatever good we do we receive from God’s grace and ought to return to him, I, 177. Again we are taught that our good works are not within our own power but proceed from his Spirit breathing upon and helping us, I, 179. Likewise I, 262, 264, where it is said: it belongs to God to soften our heart and incline it to doing good. The remembrance and sorrow of one’s former life, and preparation for salvation, are God’s gift, I, 262.

God never withdraws from the righteous the eyes of his mercy—that is, the help of his grace—nor does he ever forget him, but always looks upon him. Bearing this in mind, he should not lose heart in adversity, I, 282. Remembrance of one’s former evil life, so that we may be pierced with compunction, is a gift of God and a preparation for future glory, I, 282. Although preachers of God’s word cast their nets, it is God himself who inwardly converts hearts; hence the necessity of grace is established, since it is written, John 15:6: “Without me you can do nothing,” I, 289. God’s grace is given with no preceding merits; therefore every virtue, constancy, and fortitude of the saints belongs not to themselves but to God, I, 353.

Therefore, if each saint who is in heaven, or who will be there after the judgment, were individually asked, “How did you come here?” or “How did you enter here?” what else could he answer but, “Mercy brought me,” I, 367. Blessed is the one whom the Lord has chosen in his compassion and taken to himself from so great a multitude of people: that person cannot perish, but without any doubt shall receive the good things predestined for him, I, 429. God’s grace, called the rain of heaven, is not compelled but voluntary, because it is both freely given and freely received, I, 436. God’s help must be sought everywhere and in all things, because it is necessary everywhere and in all things; for without his help we can do nothing, I, 446. All vices and sins are devices of the devil, which oppose God’s word so that it cannot penetrate the human heart. Yet God’s virtue and power prevail; and although a wretched human being is shut in and bound on the path of iniquity, God nevertheless draws him from there and recalls him to the way of truth, I, 531.

### H
Heretics are compared to frogs: by their chatter they disturb everyone, and by their foulness they defile all things. They do not come from elsewhere, but rise from the waters, because by misunderstanding the Scriptures and expounding them perversely they conceive their errors there and become heretics there, I, 54. In a manner, heretics dig cisterns for the destruction of others when, by their writings, they either attack or call into doubt the doctrines of the Church, established and confirmed from all antiquity, I, 77. Simon Magus deceived, violated, and corrupted the Roman populace, binding many to himself by magical illusions, I, 80. What ought to be done with heretics whose error admits of no doubt, I, 155. Heresy is scarcely recognized as the horrible and foul thing that must be detested; therefore those who willingly hear heretics, delight in their writings, and commend their subtleties show themselves enemies of truth and faith, I, 175. Anyone whom we consider suspect in faith must be reported to a priest or to a council of bishops, so that he may give an account of his teaching, I, 174. Together with heretics we must abominate all their perverse knowledge and doctrine, so that it may be destroyed in such a way as no longer to remain in memory, I, 196 [Col. 1315]. Heretics often pretend to sympathize with the Church and to pity her, as though she were sick in faith and had strayed from the truth. Thus, as though wishing to heal her, they preach to her the deceptions of their own error, I, 226. Luther behaved in this way when preaching the reformation of the Church. Heretics walk in darkness as though in light, since they take no less delight in the darkness of error than holy and Catholic men do in the light of truth, I, 265. Heretics overstep the bounds of faith when they persuade people to believe more or less than the Catholic Church holds. They also plunder and pasture flocks, because all the faithful whom they can steal from God and deceive, they feed and nourish with the doctrine of their error, I, 264. Heretics adulterate the sacred Scriptures, which, rightly expounded by Catholics, are turned back against them, I, 268. They are barren of good works because they suffer want and hunger for true doctrine. They gnaw in solitude because, in the thick forest of the holy Scriptures, they violently gnaw and tear apart what they cannot understand, I, 272. Sooner or later all heresies perish, and Catholic truth emerges victorious like an unconquerable wall, I, 273. Many heretics have gone out from the Church because they could not obtain greater dignities within it, I, 272. Far more dangerous is the death of the soul, which heretics inflict, than bodily death inflicted by murderers: the former is eternal, the latter temporal; the former separates the soul from God, the latter divides it only from the body. Rightly, therefore, such a man is abominated by God, being more cruel than every wild beast, I, 307. Heretics, then, are more savage than tyrants: the latter kill bodies, the former souls, I, 308. Heretics are gates of death, as are all who draw souls to death and destruction. Such a gate was Simon Magus; such were Arius and Sabellius, and many others, by whose teaching and persuasion many souls perished, I, 313. But every fraud and subtlety was exposed and confounded when their errors, and those of all others erring in faith, were proscribed and condemned in public councils, I, 370. Nestorius and Eutyches wrongly distinguished the divinity in Christ, I, 412. The Marcionites, Manichaeans, Priscillianists, and with them Simon Magus, said that Christ was not a true man, but merely appeared to be one, I, 458. All heretics, darkened by the mist of error, strive to corrupt the New Testament, same page. Those speak iniquity against God who, disputing about the Godhead itself, introduce perverse doctrines, I, 459. Heretics do not bring their doctrines from afar or receive them from the Fathers; rather, they conceive error within themselves, I, 603.

Hebrews. Israel is called the firstborn son of God, not by nature but by grace. For this nation was chosen by God and loved above the rest, I, 52. How greatly the Hebrews multiplied in Egypt is narrated in chapter 1 of Exodus: there it is said that from seventy-five persons who came forth from Jacob’s loins, the multitude of this people had increased so greatly that, when those able to go to war from the age of twenty and upward were counted, 603,566 men were found; the number of all the rest seems to have been much greater, I, 47. Fearing such a foreign nation, as it were innumerable, King Pharaoh devised a plan to oppress and exterminate it. He therefore first commanded the Hebrew midwives to kill all males by casting them into the river, while preserving only the females, I, 48. Moses is sent to them as liberator; knowing well that they were unbelieving and unteachable, he asks God that he may prove his mission by signs and miracles, I, 50. In Ishmael, who always persecuted his brother Isaac, the Hebrew people is signified: it did not cease to persecute Christ—of whom Isaac was a figure—even unto death, and it persecutes his faithful Christians with perpetual hatred, 24. Whenever the people, carried into captivity, confessed that it had sinned and, doing penance, implored God’s mercy, it was immediately heard by the most merciful Lord, I, 51. How vainly the Hebrews boasted that they were Abraham’s children when they nevertheless did not follow his works, and above all his faith, II, 14. The Hebrews’ unbelief and unrestrained impatience set up and worshipped a golden calf as the true God, I, 118. A veil was placed over their heart so that they might not understand the Scriptures, 123. How many times the Hebrews tempted God and fell away from faith, 408. The kingdom, strength, and power of the Hebrews endured, flourished, and prospered through three ages, as it were three years. The first age extended from Abraham to David; the second from David to the Babylonian deportation; the third from the Babylonian deportation to Christ, I, 23. At the time when our Savior set, darkness came to be, by which the wretched Jews were blinded both inwardly and outwardly; night and a gloom of darkness came upon them, I, 521. For this especially the Jews ought to have loved Christ: that he said he had been sent for them as lost sheep. He raised their dead, gave sight to the blind, cured paralytics, cleansed lepers, and healed dropsical persons. Yet they, on the contrary, disparaged their benefactor, I, 536.

Human Being. The creation of the human being was the work of the whole Trinity. Made in the image and likeness of God, the human being received wisdom, justice, and goodness. God, his creator, made the human being more excellent than all earthly creatures. If the human being, placed in the paradise of free will, had preserved original innocence, he would have had a blessed life on earth and, after it, eternal happiness in heaven. The words written by Moses, “He created him in the image of God,” can, according to St Bruno, be understood to mean that God also gave the human being such a bodily image as the Son—who is indeed God—had preordained before time to assume one day. Thus not only our inner but also our outer human being would in some manner be like God, I, 6. The human being is born not for rest and pleasure but for labor. Made outside paradise, he is placed in paradise. And because idleness is the enemy of the soul, he is commanded to work lest he live idly, I, 9 and 231. By eating the forbidden fruit, the first parents learned what good they had lost and into what evil they had fallen, I, 11. They lost through sin the immortality with which they had been endowed and became subject to flesh that decays and passes away, I, 16. “And Adam,” says A. N., “died as soon as he ate; not because he immediately departed this life, but because he took into himself the necessity of departing from it at some time. Had he not sinned, he would never in any way have died,” I, 10. After they sinned, Adam and Eve knew that they were naked. Although they had been naked before, they did not recognize their nakedness in themselves, because before sin their own most radiant flesh was more delightful to behold than any garment, I, 12; likewise, 389. Such, therefore, is the condition of human frailty that it needs God’s help lest it slip into sin, I, 19. Whoever does not fear to shed human blood ought at least to reverence in that person the image of God; whoever brings death upon his brother becomes guilty of death, as above, 20. In the sacred writings, “men” are very often understood as sinners, I, 116. A person sleeps if he does not serve God; and when he does not work, idleness is labor to him, not rest, I, 235. No one inhabiting the earth can protect himself from being touched by earth’s dust. Life on earth, therefore, is warfare. Each of the faithful must serve in his own condition, so as to obtain the crown of glory, same page, 2. Those devoted to idleness are afflicted by the weariness of torpor, whereas to the industrious time is always very short, I, 236. This is the condition of the human wayfarer: never to remain in the same state; but when he has attained his end, he will no longer be changed, I, 247. Constant reflection upon our condition bars the entrance to temptations, I, 248. People departing this world take with them nothing except either consolation for their good deeds or torment for the evil deeds they have done, I, 249. Perfect knowledge of all things is not granted to the human being in this life; it is reserved for us in the heavenly homeland, I, 278. When the body is destroyed by illness or old age, the mind must then be strengthened with greater vigor. Let the failing of the flesh be the soul’s strength, I, 278. Whatever a person’s race or condition, if he fears God and practices justice, he is acceptable to him, I, 180. No one knows his paths; for if he knew them, he would not be ignorant of his home. Yet that home is either hell or paradise. But how can one know the end who does not know the beginning? For in God’s ordering are arranged each person’s birth, days, years, whole life, and life’s end, I, 287. In prosperity, a person is easily separated from God, I, 300. Without innocence we are miserable; happy, however, if we possess it, I, 311. The human being was made in order to fear God and keep his commandments, I, 362. What the human condition, damaged through Adam’s sin, is, I, 376. Evil people are not written in the book of the living; rather, they are said to be erased from it because they are not permitted to be written in it. That book is nothing other than the memory of almighty God, in which all things, both first and last, are contained together, I, 445. St Bruno admirably warns people not to concern themselves excessively with earthly things, II, 33. God created no animal in this world that is of greater love and affection, greater worth and honor, in God’s sight than the human being. If, then, the almighty Lord feeds without labor and anxiety those things made for humankind and small or nothing by comparison with it, how much more will he not abandon those who, made in his image, have been reconciled to his grace. A person’s treasure is his heart: there both good and evil are stored; from it spring words of honor and disgrace, blessing and curse, II, 65.

## I

Unbelief. The reason why some Christians pass from faith into unbelief is that, puffed up with human learning, they do not keep God’s word or observe his commandments, and love the world more than God. But those who are true and faithful disciples of Christ are worthy for Christ to be revealed to them: knowing wisdom, they may be wise; knowing justice, just; knowing truth, truthful, II, 274.

Hell. Once the sinner has descended into hell, he can no longer weep for his sins. Nor is it permitted to return here to do penance again. There is nothing there but darkness and shadows; nothing but misery and the shadow of death; nothing but everlasting horror and fear, I, 243. The afflictions and torments of this life are in no way comparable to eternal punishments, I, 56. The reprobate shall forever be in hell and darkness; eternal and unquenchable fire shall torment them, their relatives, and their household, I, 250. At the last judgment, the sight of those to be condemned will shake even the saints with terror, I, 273. Would that these last things might not be erased from the minds of the faithful, I, 254. That place of punishment is deeper than both heaven and earth; rightly it is called the deepest hell, I, 254. That fire is unquenchable and, once kindled, needs not be kindled again. The condemned person, left in the tabernacle of his flesh, will always be afflicted, because flesh and soul will be tormented forever, I, 259. How great a terror the thought of hell ought to awaken in sinners, so that they may be converted, I, 283. Hell is a place which the devil himself both made and opened; for he delights only in constructing torments and places of torment. He does not cease daily to prepare a greater pit for some and a lesser one for others. But he too will fall into the pit he has made, because eternal fire is prepared for him and his angels, I, 312. The ungodly will be punished by diverse torments according to the differing character of their sins, I, 319; likewise, 396. The punishment of the wicked will have no end, I, 460. Great indeed is the mercy that frees a soul from the lower hell. As in the higher blessedness some differ from others in glory, so in hell some differ from others in torments, I, 485.

Isaac, to be sacrificed by his father Abraham, bore the figure of Christ because, on hearing God’s command, he freely gave himself to be offered, I, 28. He took Rebecca as wife; from her offspring, according to the divine promise, the Messiah—that is, Christ—was to arise, I, 29. His conception was twofold, and the mother felt in her womb sons who were to be born struggling with one another, I, 31. Rebecca consulted the Lord, who revealed to her that a division of peoples would come from the two children to be born from her, namely Jacob and Esau. The former prefigured the chosen people; the latter signified the reprobate people. “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated,” I, 31. Near death, Isaac blessed Jacob and also blessed Esau, but with different blessings, I, 32. Having completed 180 years, Isaac died and was buried by his two sons Jacob and Esau, I, 39.

## J

Jacob, younger than his brother Esau, according to God’s election receives from his father Isaac, near death, the blessing of the firstborn. He is made head of his family, from whose seed Christ, the Savior of the world, was to come. What is signified by the stone upon which Jacob slept, the ladder that appeared to him, and the angels ascending and descending by it, I, 33. Because his brother Esau hated him, Jacob departed at the command of his father and mother for Mesopotamia, to his uncle Laban, I, 33. He takes Rachel as wife; since she did not bear him children, he also married her sister Leah. These events are shown not to have occurred without figure and mystery, I, 34 and 35. As Jacob returned with all his family—namely, wives and children—to his own land, an angel met him, with whom he struggled valiantly. The same mystery is explained, 36; as are his gentleness and humility in seeking by prayers and gifts to placate Esau, lest any offense occur when they met, I, 36 and 37. When Jacob reached Bethel, which is interpreted “house of God,” he commanded his household to cast away idols, change their garments, and purify themselves. Their significance is explained, I, 37. The celebrated oracle of Jacob, “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah,” etc., is discussed at length, 43. It is explained why Jacob, blessing Ephraim, the younger in age, preferred him to Manasseh, the other of Joseph’s two sons, whom Joseph had presented to their ailing father, I, 42. There is also an excellent exposition of the individual blessings which the holy patriarch, about to die, entreated from God for each of his sons; in them the figures and mysteries of both Testaments are wonderfully outlined, I, 42 and 43, etc.

Fasting. Christ taught us fasting, since he himself, innocent and holy, spent forty days and forty nights fasting. Therefore we sinners need repentance, that we may expiate sins by fasting and imitate Christ the Lord, our teacher, II, 16, etc. Fasting from food is good, but abstaining from vices is better, 17. Our fasting must be joined with spiritual joy, so that we may seem cheerfully to give God that which is highly profitable to us and obtains for us eternal recompense, 31.

John the Baptist. This is the angel foretold by the prophets, appointed as the forerunner of Christ the restorer, who had to prepare his ways through human repentance and conversion. Who he was, he himself declared: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness,” II, 13 ff. He sent his disciples to Christ to ask whether he was the one who, according to the faith of the Fathers and the tradition of the Scriptures, was to come, II, 57. Why St John the Baptist is called more than a prophet, II, 58. Very much concerning him is found at 59. Why he was called Elijah, II, 113. He baptizes Christ the Lord in the Jordan, II, 114.

John the Evangelist. John was not killed, but was cast into a cauldron of boiling oil and exiled on the island of Patmos; he drank a cup of great affliction and bitterness, II, 97. John the Evangelist, flying higher than the others like an eagle, demonstrated that Christ, the Son of God, is God without beginning, II, 310. Blessed John wrote his Gospel and Apocalypse in Greek, II, 339.

Job. How great was his care in the upbringing of his children, I, 222. He was a type of the suffering Christ, I, 221. His unconquered patience is commended because, afflicted by great calamities, he always blessed and worshipped God, I, 225. Through the devil’s savagery, Job suffered the corruption of his entire body, I, 226. He offered many testimonies concerning Christ; he implored him as his helper and confessed that he greatly longed for him, I, 276. He calls Christ the mediator with God and the reconciler of peace, I, 279. That Job was such in holiness was ordained not by himself but by God, I, 286. All Job’s goods were restored, and, full of days and merits, he completed the course of mortal life, I, 398.

Joseph. Joseph is loved by his father Jacob above his other brothers and given a splendid garment. His brothers, envying him and regarding his visions as dreams and ravings, planned to destroy him. All this is applied as signifying Christ and the Jews, I, 39. It is shown there how great was the likeness between the Jews panting for Christ’s death and Joseph’s brothers, who conspired to destroy him. Judah sold his brother Joseph; Judas the apostle sold Christ. By Reuben, Joseph’s other brother, who sought to deliver him, may be understood that part of the people which did not consent to the Savior’s death. By the kid which they killed, Christ’s death is signified; by the tunic which they dipped in its blood, Christ’s flesh, bloodied by his own blood. Joseph is thus delivered from death if his tunic is stained with blood, because Christ suffered according to the flesh, though according to his divinity he cannot die, same page, 39. He refused to consent to evil with Potiphar’s wife; falsely accused, he was handed over to prison. His integrity was not overcome but sustained by patience and abstinence. At last, because God never allows the just to be oppressed, Pharaoh, king of Egypt, instructed of Joseph by a certain divine power, not only frees him from prison but makes him second in his kingdom and grants him full authority over all his land; Joseph thus becomes the savior of all Egypt. Pharaoh is shown to have recognized great wisdom in Joseph, whom he appointed ruler and lord of the whole land and ordered to instruct the greater and elder men, I, 525. All the sacraments contained in these events and figures are brought to light, I, 40 and 41. Jacob, or Israel, came into Egypt, and all Joseph’s brothers also came; he lived in the land of Goshen, where he died, I, 40 and 41.

Jubilee. What is to be understood concerning the jubilee of the old law, solemnly proclaimed in every fiftieth year, I, 168 ff. This year began spiritually when Christ our Lord redeemed the world from the devil’s slavery by his blood, restored to us our first possession—that is, the eternal kingdom—and opened paradise’s gates to his faithful, I, 168.

Judas Iscariot. How criminal and sacrilegious was Judas’s betrayal of Christ the Lord and his teacher, who had chosen him for the apostleship, is described in the exposition of Psalm XLV, I, 380. Again, in Psalm LIV another prophecy concerning the same traitor occurs in the words: “For if my enemy had cursed me, I would surely have endured it,” etc. Upon these words St Bruno set forth the following: “It is customary for an enemy to curse, persecute, and speak ill of an enemy. But for someone who is a friend to betray, persecute, and curse his lord and teacher is altogether absurd, unfitting, alien, and unbearable. Yet Judas was until that time of one mind with the Lord, intimate with him, and a sharer in his secrets and counsel. The Lord loved him as he loved the others, though he knew that he would one day become such a man,” I, 409 [Col. 1319].

Last Judgment. The signs that will precede the last judgment, and the great terror of the whole world, II, 113, 205, etc. The wrath of God and the time of the dead come: some are tormented and perish eternally; others, having been justly judged, receive the reward of good works; while the wicked, being destroyed, lose even the hope of being saved and returning to their homeland, II, 331.

Oath. St Bruno discusses what ought to be thought about an oath, II, 25 ff.

Justice. Among the cardinal virtues, justice is listed second; it is the constant and perpetual will to render to each person his due, II, 492. Justice must first be exercised toward God. The devil has no right in human nature. God, not the devil, made the human being. The human being belongs by right to God: he himself ought to reign in us and possess our members, II, 492. The just person is one who renders to each person his due. Therefore this name is common to all saints: all saints are called just because they work justice within themselves and, having expelled vices, render to the Lord what is his, II, 492.

## L

Lamech. Because Lamech had two wives, he is called the first bigamist. He killed Cain while hunting, and also the young man who was with him, in order to conceal his crime. He was punished by God more severely than Cain, the killer of his brother, I, 15.

The Law of the Lord. The ten commandments, given by God to the people of Israel on Mount Sinai amid thunder and lightning as a sign of the divine power to which all people must submit, were promulgated, I, 71. The first of them is that we should worship one God and set before ourselves no other god to be worshipped with him. This commandment, together with the others, is successively explained, I, 71 ff. The law of the Lord is holy and blameless: it does not overthrow, deceive, or kill souls, but rather converts, saves, and brings them to blessedness, I, 334. Every Scripture that forbids evil and commands the doing of good is the law of the Lord. Whoever obeys and believes this law is made glad and joyful according to the inner person. Conversely, the evangelical law sets forth commandments much more perfect than the Mosaic law, because Christ the Lord, its author, commands us to exercise holier virtues, II, 28. Among these, the forgetting of injuries and offenses is particularly urged, so that reconciliation may be made with those with whom one has a dispute before approaching the offering of our sacrifice, II, 24. This indeed is admirable in the Gospel: it has supplied words of life for every condition of humankind, so that everyone may attain eternal salvation in his own state, II, 62. Whoever acts otherwise is blind and walks in darkness, and great grief and sadness await him, 335.

Luxury. Although luxury is sweet to the flesh, it is poisonous and most bitter to the soul, I, 579.

## M

Manichaeans and Ebionites. The former did not accept the Old Testament; the latter accepted both Testaments, but maintained that circumcision and the remaining legal ceremonies must be observed together with baptism, I, 154.

Mary the Virgin (B. [Blessed]). The Virgin Mary, Mother of Christ, took her name from Mary, the sister of Moses; after her Son, she is the head of the whole Church, I, 65. The Blessed Virgin Mary was prefigured in the rod placed in the ark of the covenant, which, though dry, had put forth leaves, I, 88 and 184. Her inviolate virginity joined with divine motherhood is foretold in the command concerning women’s purification in Leviticus chapter XII. All women who have received human seed are subject to it, but not one who remained inviolate. This privilege was granted to the Mother of God alone, I, 147. The Blessed Virgin Mary brought Christ her Son to the temple and presented him to God, I, 81. A distinguished prophecy concerning her is found in Psalm XLIV, especially from verse 11 to the end, and is admirably explained by the commentator, I, 389 ff. There mention is made of the veneration of painted images of the Blessed Virgin Mary, from which the very ancient and praiseworthy custom of the Church of venerating them is demonstrated. The Blessed Virgin Mary is called both earth and heaven: earth by nature, heaven by grace; earth because she was made from earth, heaven because she is God’s dwelling. Truth, therefore, was made from earth because our Savior was born from the Virgin; for he himself is the way, the truth, and the life, I, 483. Reasons are given why she was betrothed to Joseph, a just man, II, 6 ff. When the most blessed Virgin departed this life, she was exalted above the choirs of angels, II, 343. Bruno, together with other Fathers, maintains that the most holy Mary was prefigured in Aaron’s rod, which, placed in the ark of the Lord, produced a flower while dry and brought forth the Savior incorruptibly, II, 476 [Col. 1320].

Marriage. The union of man and woman, in which God the supreme Creator gave woman to Adam as a companion for the propagation of humankind, entails a lifelong sharing of life between them. This is proved from woman’s creation itself: God formed her from man’s rib, and therefore she is regarded as one flesh with her husband. By God’s revelation Adam understood what Eve, his woman, would be to him, and said: “Now, bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.” Accordingly, because woman was made from man’s rib, no man is one flesh more with his wife than with every woman. Yet the two are one flesh through a certain natural mingling of pleasure and the love of unity, I, 10. Why the Apostle calls marriage a great sacrament in Christ and in the Church, same place. The reason is also given why marriages between blood relatives are prohibited, I, 159. Marriages were forbidden in the law of Moses whenever disparity of religion existed between the contracting parties; and if they married, they were punished with excommunication, I, 163.

Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, offered bread and wine to God and blessed Abraham, whose name is interpreted “exalted father” and who signifies the holy Church. Melchizedek, however, was a figure of Christ according to the Apostle Paul in Hebrews: Christ first offered himself in sacrifice to God the Father; then, having confirmed the priesthood, he does not cease daily through his servants to offer bread and wine—that is, flesh and blood—to the same God the Father, I, 23. Melchizedek’s sacrifice was bread and wine, in which Christ’s body and blood were signified. The great priest made the great sacrifice in which he reconciled the whole world to God the Father, I, 539.

Death. Adam received God’s sentence of death after he sinned, in the words: “Dust you are, and to dust you shall return.” Hence the Apostle said: “Sin entered into the world, and through sin death,” to which all people are subject, since all sinned in Adam, I, 13. Signs of death are the body’s utter weakness and the exhaustion of the spirit, 142. The brevity of life relieves and consoles the straits of tribulations. But we do not return from the path of death, since one can die only once, I, 252. Though the perverse understanding of the wicked may sometimes shine and be thought true, it will nevertheless be extinguished and scattered in his destruction, 254.

Moses was born in Egypt; cast into the river in accordance with Pharaoh’s command, he was saved by the king’s daughter and adopted as her son, I, 48. When he became an adult, he took pity on the affliction and oppression of his brothers. Seeing an Egyptian strike a Hebrew man, he killed him with his own hand and hid him in the sand. When Pharaoh learned of this, he planned to kill Moses, who fled into the land of Midian and took as wife Zipporah, daughter of the priest of Midian, I, 49. While tending the flock of his kinsman Jethro and ascending Mount Horeb, the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from the midst of a burning bush. The individual mysteries foreshadowed in this apparition are explained, I, 49. He is sent by God to Egypt to become the liberator of his people, and shares his ministry with his brother Aaron, I, 51. On the journey the Lord commands him to circumcise his son, lest he appear among his brothers as a transgressor of the divine command. This teaches us to give good example to our neighbors, I, 52. Moses and Aaron go to Pharaoh and declare God’s will to him: that he should free the Hebrews, his people, from slavery and allow them to leave Egypt, I, 52. What is to be understood in the Lord’s words to him, “Behold, I have made you a god to Pharaoh,” I, 53. God gave him power to afflict Pharaoh according to his will and humble him by signs and miracles, while the king could do nothing against him to cause him harm, I, 53. Moses was a great man in Egypt: great in words, great in miracles, great in constancy, and great because he bore the figure of Christ, I, 57. Moses, lawgiver and mediator of God’s people, signifies Jesus Christ, the mediator of God and humankind, giver of both Testaments, I, 84. Although God very often honored Moses with his sight, it must nevertheless be said that Moses saw him only through figures and appearances, according to John’s oracle: “No one has ever seen God,” I, 181. The whole land of promise was shown to him by the Lord; but, as punishment for his failure of faith when he struck the rock, he did not enter it. At the Lord’s command Moses died in the land of Moab and was buried, but God concealed his tomb, I, 220. Before dying, he blessed the children of Israel, that is, he bestowed his own blessing upon each tribe, I, 216–219.

Ages of the World. The six days in which the creation of all things was made signify the six ages of the world and foreshow the duration of the visible universe. The first age is reckoned from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the Babylonian deportation; the fifth from the Babylonian deportation to Christ; the sixth from Christ’s coming to the end of the age, I, 7.

## N

Noah was the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth, I, 16. His justice obtained from God that, in the destruction of all humanity which God had determined on account of their great wickedness, he and his family should be preserved safe. The Lord commanded him to build an ark and prescribed its height and breadth; he likewise commanded him to place within it individual kinds of every animal. Whatever was enclosed in the ark was snatched from destruction; all else perished in the common shipwreck, I, 17. When the flood ceased, Noah came out from the ark and offered to God a burnt offering from every clean living creature, because nothing but what is holy and clean ought to be offered to God. The human being alone was not offered in this sacrifice, because Christ, the true lamb who took away the sins of the world, remained to be offered in his own time, I, 19. God made this covenant with Noah and every living creature: that he would no longer bring the waters of the flood upon the earth. So that this might be believed more firmly and never doubted, he further set a sign to remain as testimony—the rainbow—which God, looking upon it, might remember his covenant, while the human being, seeing it and knowing that God had not forgotten him, might, all fear expelled, be consoled by the manifestation of so great a testimony, I, 20. How Noah represented a figure of Christ, I, 21. On account of the irreverence shown to him by his younger son Ham, Noah cursed Ham’s son Canaan and all his descendants, making him a servant of servants to his brothers, I, 21. From Shem, whose name is interpreted “renowned,” was born Abraham and the entire people of the Hebrews, from whom the Patriarchs and Prophets came. From him too, according to the flesh, our Savior and all the apostles derive their origin; and there is no doubt that not only the Canaanites but also all nations serve them. From Japheth, whose name is interpreted “breadth,” was born the Gentile people, which ruled not only over the Canaanites but over all nations, I, 21. See Ark.

Name of the Lord. Great, terrible, and holy is the name of Christ: at its invocation the dead are raised, demons driven away, lepers cleansed, and every sickness and infirmity healed. We must therefore always praise and proclaim it, I, 510.

Cloud. What the pillar of cloud from which the Lord spoke to Moses signifies, I, 511.

## O
### Death of the Righteous and the Wicked

Just as the days of the righteous are promised to be fulfilled, so the life of the wicked shall be cut short; for they will not remain alive for as long as they hope to live, I, 83. But the days of the saints shall be fulfilled, since through the predestination by which they were predestined before the ages, they shall live eternally, I, 83. Those who persevere in God’s grace until death may immediately be offered to God and received into the company of the saints; or later, if they require purgatory. Not all who are saved are received into blessedness as soon as they die, I, 164. That death is beneficial which releases a person from toil and leads him into joy and rest, I, 187.

One ought not to grieve over the death of those who live well and go to God to receive the reward of good works. Nor does he grieve rightly who grieves over the death of an unjust person: one should not grieve over the destruction of the wicked, but rejoice; rather, one ought to have grieved over his life, which was opposed to goodness and justice. Yet the saints ought to mourn and weep for such persons, in the hope that they may perhaps be converted through their prayers, I, 196. The death of the saints is the beginning of everlasting life, I, 244. They are raised by the Church to public veneration when the virtues and miracles of their life have been established; and then they are to be honored and venerated, I, 244.

The righteous person desires to be dissolved and to be with Christ; therefore he desires to see his own end. Moreover, he desires to see the number of his days—namely, that number which is, and always is, and has no end. For these days have no number, because when one is present, the other has already passed, and another is not yet. But when it is not, how can it be numbered? It may indeed be said that it was, or will be, but it cannot be said that it is, I, 375. The departure of the righteous from this life ought to be pleasant and blessed for them, I, 412. God will never again be appeased toward sinners who depart from this life, I, 436. For they will drink daily and without end the dregs of every torment. But the righteous, when they die in righteousness, shall rejoice forever and be intoxicated with the sweetness of ineffable delight, I, 460.

Who can see the powerful of this age abounding in every good thing and not judge them happy? For people are accustomed to say that such persons are loved by the Lord and could not otherwise have such great goods and possess them. Therefore only their last end must be considered. But concerning them the Prophet says in Psalm LXXII, I, 455: “Nevertheless, because of deceit, you have appointed evils for them.” What evils? “You cast them down while they were being raised up.” For suddenly, while such persons seem to be in their greatest prosperity, they fall and die, and are dragged to punishment with no regard whatever for mercy. And I came to know and see that the glory of the saints shall be eternal and that the torments of the wicked shall have no end. All the good ought to keep this consideration in mind and draw from it consolation in their distresses, I, 469.

In one way the spirit is taken from the good, so that they may rest in peace; but from the wicked, so that they may waste away, fail, be tormented, and perish, I, 522.

### Good Works Necessary for Salvation

Adam, the first man, having been made outside Paradise, was placed in Paradise in order to work there. Let his descendants take note of this, lest they give themselves to idleness or pursue deeds that do not lead to Paradise, I, 9. So long as we are in this life, we must cultivate our vineyard and olive-grove—that is, our flesh—in order that we may bear fruit for God: the grain of good work, wine that gladdens the human heart, and the oil of mercy and compassion. But in the seventh year it rests, because after this life blessedness and rest follow, I, 82.

Affection and good will make our offerings acceptable to God; without them, they rightly have no merit at all, I, 86. No one shall enter the heavenly homeland who has not performed good works, I, 207. God’s works have this power: they can grant eternal life to those who perform them, I, 541. Whoever does everything for display, so that he may be seen, praised, and honored, immediately withers away, I, 238. Even actions that are otherwise good wholly perish if they are not done chiefly for God’s honor. Therefore display and vain glory must be entirely avoided, lest at life’s end we find that we have labored in vain. Thus Christ the Lord teaches that, when you give alms, your left hand should not know what your right hand is doing, II, 26–27.

### Prayer

Christ himself taught us to pray; from him we have that best and most complete prayer which we say daily: “Our Father, who art in heaven,” etc. When our Savior taught this prayer to his disciples, I believe that from that point the prophet was present there in spirit and delighted in this prayer, so beautiful and concise. If we cannot do this with our mouths, we can nevertheless do it by desire and good intention, II, 452. St Bruno gives an excellent exposition of this Lord’s Prayer in his *Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew*, II, 29–30. He also explains, II, 29–30, how the Apostle’s words at 1 Thessalonians 5:17 are to be understood: “Pray without ceasing.”

## P

### Heavenly Paradise

Paradise is the dwelling-place of the saints in heaven, where they enjoy the vision of God. Yet the saints will not possess complete blessedness until bodies are joined with souls and their whole multitude is raised above the heavens; they shall obtain this full glorification after the judgment, I, 87. Before Christ’s Passion, no one—not even a righteous person or one who had fully completed penance—obtained entrance into the heavenly homeland, I, 195.

It is called the tabernacle of God, in which he reveals himself to his saints and his countenance is contemplated as it is in itself. There, in perfect peace and possession of every good, they shall rejoice without end with God their Creator, I, 356. Into that inheritance, or city, as Scripture says, no defiled or unclean person shall enter; therefore sins must be expiated by fitting penance before death, I, 372. In heaven reward will be rendered according to merits. Hence it is said that there are many dwellings in heaven—some higher and some lower—in which the saints shall be, I, 372.

Yet although brightness in glory will vary, blessedness itself shall not vary but will be altogether the same, since every person shall be the common joy and gladness of the glory of all. For as there is now harmony among all the members of our body, so shall there be among all the members of that heavenly city, II, 577. How great shall be the joy in heaven of those who see God, when with bodily eyes they behold Christ’s humanity remaining in one place, and with the eyes of the mind contemplate his divinity containing all things, II, 532.

### Earthly Paradise

The Lord God planted from the beginning a paradise of delight, into which he placed the man—namely Adam, whom he had formed—to cultivate and guard it, II, 472. It is interpreted “garden of delights,” where every kind of tree and fruit was found. A river went out from it and was divided into four heads: the first was called Phison, the second Gelion [Note: [Col. 1321] Vatican Codex, Geron.; Bruno’s reading, *Gyon*; Vulgate: [Col. 1322] *Gelion*], the third Tigris, and the fourth Euphrates. After Adam had been expelled from it because of his disobedience, a cherub armed with a flaming sword was stationed before it, so as to permit no human being [Col. 1323] to enter, II, 473. The four river-names—of rivers said to flow from Paradise and to water and fertilize the whole earth—are explained mystically, II, 526.

### Eternal Father

The conception of the eternal Father, as a person distinct from the other two—namely the Son and the Holy Spirit—is conveyed in Genesis chapter 1: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” In the word “God” the Father is indicated; in “beginning,” the Son eternally begotten; and in the Spirit forming the heavens, the Holy Spirit, their power, is expressed, I, 6. Faith in the Trinity—namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is the way of eternal salvation; without it no one can please God, I, 50.

Although Christ frequently taught his disciples that he had God as Father, he gave the same testimony while praying in the garden. Filled with sorrow, he said: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me.” But since his will was perfectly conformed to the will of his Father, he immediately added: “Nevertheless, not my will but yours be done,” I, 443. Although the Father is one and the Son another, the Father is not one thing and the Son another thing, since they are of the same nature and substance. The Father is said to dwell in the Son without end, because neither Father nor Son shall have an end. The Father is always in the Son, the Son always in the Father, and the Holy Spirit in both, I, 438.

### PAUL the Apostle (St)

How St Paul, most devoted lover of the Lord, fulfills what Jacob said when he blessed Benjamin, I, 217. In this Apostle Jacob’s prophecy concerning Benjamin, the last-born son, seems fulfilled: “Benjamin is a ravening wolf; in the morning he shall devour the prey, and in the evening he shall divide the spoil.” Benjamin allegorically signifies Paul the Apostle, who drew his origin from that tribe. Like a ravening wolf, he persecuted the holy Church with great fury. “Morning” and “evening” mean, as it were, “first” and “afterward.” At first he devoured the prey, persecuting, ravaging, and tearing apart the Church; afterward he divided Christ’s spoils by preaching, distributing sacred orders, and ordaining bishops and presbyters throughout bishoprics and churches, I, 46. He said that he had persecuted the Church through ignorance and therefore hoped to obtain mercy from God, I, 133.

### Original Sin

How greatly the Lord loved humanity may also be understood from this: he prepared for it such a dwelling-place that, had humanity not sinned and begotten children in the most chaste marriage without any concupiscence, then, when the number of the elect had been completed, it would have ascended to the heavenly Jerusalem without tasting any bitterness of death and, differing from the angels neither in merit nor in number, would have enjoyed eternal blessedness, I, 9. But when the first parents committed sin by eating the forbidden fruit, they immediately understood what goods they had lost and to what evils they had subjected themselves, I, 9.

It is the devil who fought and prevailed against us in the first man, and took no small spoil from us by depriving us of immortality itself, I, 187. Sin entered into the world, and death through sin. Before Christ’s incarnation no one could be cleansed from original sin—that is, could accomplish anything by himself for its remission, I, 161. When Christ the Lord was crucified, after Jesus bowed his head and gave up the spirit, all the firstborn in the land of Egypt died, because original sin throughout the whole world perished in all those who believed and were baptized, so that sin, which began through the tree of concupiscence, might be destroyed through the tree of the cross, I, 60. Both evil and good alike draw their origin from the mass of sin, I, 166. Original sin alone is sufficient for condemnation, I, 240.

Human nature, corrupted and depraved through sin from the first man, is found in all human beings; and it could be healed and liberated only by Christ’s blood, I, 547, on Psalm CXV. In the same psalm original sin is again called the bonds of the devil, which could be broken by Christ alone. In the firstborn of the Egyptians whom the Lord struck, he signified that by his blood and the water of baptism he would blot out the first and original sin in all believers, I, 173, 526. Whoever has not been freed from original sin by Christ’s blood shall undoubtedly perish eternally, I, 470.

### Causes of Sins

Lust is the foulest of all vices, and provides both an impulse and fuel for many sins, I, 65. Those who persevere in wickedness with hardened hearts, wrapped in darkness, see nothing and remain immovable like stones, I, 57. Not only a perverse interpretation of the law, but every corruption and every depravity of mind, may be called leaven, which is the cause of very many sins, I, 60. The vice of gluttony, which is the appetite for more refined foods, and intemperance oppose many virtues and drive persons into sordid depravity, I, 66. O how greatly must those abstain from what is forbidden to whom even what is permitted is forbidden! I, 69. It is a great sin to take from poor persons the things by which they sustain life, I, 80. Gifts, too, are causes of sin, because they blind and corrupt [Col. 1324] minds; therefore God commands in Exodus chapter II that they are not to be accepted, I, 81.

It is never permitted to lie; but it is sometimes not permitted to tell the truth, I, 87. A person frequently sins through ignorance, because good is easily despised and evil chosen in its place, I, 133. The soul’s impurity can arise from three sources: from the deception and suggestion of heretics and any evil persons; from oneself, when someone by his own will plunges into some heresy or grave sin; and from excessive attachment to earthly things, so that he is never raised upward by contemplating heavenly things but desires earthly things alone with all the exertion of his mind, I, 134.

Violation of a sacred thing, which is called sacrilege, occasions sin. Therefore, among the sacrilegious, the person sins more gravely who empties the divine mysteries of their force, or does not give full faith to the sacraments, or does not obtain from them the grace which he is able to obtain, and thus commits the gravest sacrilege, I, 135. To act against God’s command is sin; but not to do what the command prescribes is an offense. Hence *delictum* seems to be called, as it were, *derelictum*, “something neglected,” I, 139. Where there is no will to sin, there ought to be no penalty for sin, I, 150.

An evil habit, especially concupiscence, is overcome by fasts, vigils, almsgiving, tears, and prayers; and the flesh is cleansed from every impurity, I, 146. Although all sins inflame a person by some fire of concupiscence, it is peculiar to lust to burn through concupiscence, I, 150. Fornication contains such great depravity that it surpasses other sins in its foulness and impurity, I, 152. In recalling sins there can be a danger of pleasure, I, 153. Murder is counted among the more serious sins of action. Yet by murderers of bodies we often understand murderers of souls. Murderers of souls are understood especially to be Jews and heretics, who kill souls by separating them from Christ through false persuasion, I, 194.

A distinction is made between those who act willingly and those who act unwillingly in perpetrating evil. It is the greatest iniquity to despair of salvation, because of the injury thereby inflicted upon God; and that sin is forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come, I, 14. Because we abuse God’s gifts by sinning, we inflict a great injury upon him, I, 244. Whoever does not cease from iniquity is in some manner always fighting against God, I, 250. Sinners pass from snare to snare if they do not rise from their first fall, I, 255. The ungodly are unhappy in this age and more unhappy in the age to come, I, 259. The eternity of punishments demonstrates the wickedness of sins, I, 259.

Deliberate ignorance does not excuse from sin; it belongs to those who refuse to know the ways of the Lord. They do not walk upon the narrow path of virtues, but move toward death upon the broad ways of vices, I, 260. Evil thoughts which occur are not sins; consent is sin, I, 267. Sin reigns and rules in those who not only think and do evil but also persevere in it. This is the sin which shall be forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come, I, 335. Those who commit a crime and those who consent to it differ little in guilt, I, 400. It is worse to sin boldly than fearfully, I, 426.

Detraction is a great sin, on account of which the Church is so stirred that it institutes persecution even against detractors. The Church’s persecution is carried out through interdicts and excommunications, I, 513. To detract is to wish to diminish another’s goodness, I, 513. Sinners who refused to receive Christ the Savior shall receive Antichrist the deceiver, I, 536. Since the vice of luxury belongs to the flesh and naturally clings to it, it cannot be conquered and driven away without labor and God’s help, I, 525. Even if a person has been a sinner, once he has begun to serve God with all the powers of mind and body, with inward and outward senses, he shall no longer be called unbelieving, I, 63. One afflicted in heart is rightly said to sacrifice himself well before God; for a human being sees the face, but God looks into the heart, I, 133.

### PETER the Apostle (St)

The Apostle Peter came to Rome and took her, as a virgin free for him, as his wife; by the preaching of God’s word and the grace of the Holy Spirit he begot from her very many children of faith, I, 80. He is excused for denying Jesus Christ, his master, because he had forgotten the word spoken to him by Jesus: “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” For when Christ looked upon him, Peter remembered the word which Jesus had spoken, I, 133. Peter’s faith, upon which the Church is founded, having been confirmed by Christ the Lord, does not fail in Peter himself or in his successors, I, 122.

The words said to him, “Kill and eat,” Acts X–XI, signify that the holy Apostle was appointed for the conversion of the Gentiles. Therefore unbelievers were to be converted and brought into the Church, I, 165; likewise 444. Peter is called the greatest of all the disciples, and the one commanded to strengthen them, I, 445. The Church is asserted to be founded upon the rock chosen by Christ—that is, upon Peter; therefore the Apostle Peter must be regarded as its principal foundation, I, 485. The Church is called Peter’s wife [Col. 1325], because she was specially entrusted to him by the Lord, who said: “If you love me, feed my sheep.” Wherever the Church is, there is Peter’s house, II, 44.

What faith St Peter possessed when, at Christ the Lord’s invitation to come to him over the waters, he entrusted himself to the sea. He therefore walked upon the sea; but at the blast of the contrary wind, when his ardor of faith failed, he feared that he would sink. What this event signifies, II, 75. Peter’s primacy in the Church is discussed at length in the commentary and notes on Matthew chapter XVI, II, 82 ff. When Jesus wished to wash the feet of his disciples, he came first to Simon Peter, for he was greater than the others, II, 269. The mystery of why Peter did not wish to allow Christ to wash his feet is explained, II, 269.

### PHARAOH, King of Egypt

Pharaoh feared the Hebrew people, who had multiplied greatly in his kingdom, and devised their extermination; first he ordered their infants to be drowned in the river, I, 47. When he heard that Moses had killed an Egyptian who was quarrelling with a Hebrew, he planned to kill him. Moses, a fugitive in the land of Midian, returned to Egypt at God’s command to deliver his brethren from the king’s tyranny, becoming distinguished as the performer of many wonders by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. But Pharaoh, despising all those signs of almighty God, had his heart hardened so that nothing could soften it. How God’s words, “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart,” are to be understood, I, 52.

He is deceived by magicians who, through diabolical incantations, turn their rods into serpents before him; nor is he enlightened, although he saw Aaron’s serpents devour the dragons of the sorcerers, I, 53. The individual plagues or scourges by which Pharaoh and the Egyptians were struck are described, I, 53–57. The Lord scourged Egypt with ten plagues, by which he signified in what ways and for what reason he scourges the whole world, I, 53.

### Philosophers

The learning of those philosophers which proclaims pleasure to be the highest good, praises worldly glory, honors, and delights, and does not condemn vices and the concupiscences of the flesh, must be regarded as not so much foolish as impious, I, 54. Those who seek a rational explanation in God’s signs and wonders prepare for themselves a way to unbelief, I, 232. The Gentile philosophers, who were held to be wiser among the people, magnified their own tongue; because they erred in all matters pertaining to the worship of God, they did not all give one and the same opinion, but each gave his own separate and divergent judgments, I, 320.

### Penance

Sins are washed in the sacrament of penance, and their remission takes place through secret confession of sins to a suitable priest, to whom we open our hearts so that we may regulate our life by his counsels and instruction, I, 140. Those who recognize their conscience as infected with the leprosy of sins must be tested by a more prolonged penance and amendment, I, 150. Once penance has been completed, the sinner is absolved, because he is washed and cleansed by the priest’s absolution, I, 152. But those who neglect to repent and persevere in sins are condemned, I, 152. When the public reconciliation of sinners was performed, I, 153. True repentance is to weep over sins committed and not to commit sins that must be wept over, I, 153.

The penitent must wash his sins in living waters—that is, in spiritual works: almsgiving, fasting, prayer, and tears—living works capable of obtaining life and salvation, I, 156. Since we are images of God, we must offer ourselves to God, washing the stains of sins; for God does not receive what is unclean and stained, I, 164. The penance of one who has stolen another’s property is useless unless he makes restitution, I, 174. Penitents are bound to disclose their inner selves when questioned by confessors, I, 175. Whoever has sinned and made satisfaction through repentance ought to live innocently, so that his penance may be acceptable and fruitful to God, I, 174. Let one who was not ashamed to sin not be ashamed to repent, I, 176.

The days of righteousness perish through subsequent sins, but are restored to life by fitting repentance, I, 177. Whoever knows himself to have sinned will not be able to perform repentance in death unless he has repented before the end of his life, I, 168. One must pray to God for perfect knowledge and contrition concerning one’s sins, I, 137. Whoever has sinned, because he is uncertain of forgiveness, should grieve throughout his life so that he may deserve pardon at the end, I, 242. Let no one grieve over a man converted from the evil habit of his life to good conduct; let no one reproach him for past sins, I, 207. But unless confession of sins is complete and sorrowful, he shall not obtain forgiveness, I, 358.

Whoever knows that he has erred should practice repentance in ashes and dust—that is, burn with love for God and humble his heart before him, I, 297. As often as a person sins, so often the soul becomes weak; and as often as he returns to repentance, so often he recovers from weakness. Whoever has committed great sins should strive to erase them with great and continual weeping. Repentance must not be deferred to the end of life, since the sinner exposes himself to the danger [Col. 1326] of not obtaining forgiveness, I, 309. If anyone recovers innocence and health of soul through repentance, let him not attribute this to his own powers, but acknowledge it as the benefit of mercy alone, I, 346.

God looks not at the mouth but at the heart. Therefore repentance is in the heart, and true confession is in the heart, according to Psalm 50: “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise.” Thus he cries with the heart who is inwardly afflicted by the commission of sin and from his whole heart repels from himself the sin in which he formerly delighted, I, 357. If sinners have truly been converted and have hoped in God’s mercy, let them believe and not doubt at all that mercy shall surround those who hope in the Lord. Behold how great is the power of repentance and true confession of sins, I, 358; likewise II, 41.

Meditation upon eternal punishments is highly suitable for terrifying sinners and bringing them to repentance, I, 372. The completeness of sacramental confession is emphasized, and the fruits of true repentance are explained, I, 423. Even if someone performs harsh penance, it does not profit for salvation unless he entirely abstains from all grave sins, I, 373. Whatever a person may formerly have been—whether a prostitute or a persecutor of saints—if at last he is converted and recognizes the Lord as merciful, he shall be saved, I, 486.

There is also an excellent commentary on the words of Psalm CIII, “He touches the mountains and they smoke,” I, 523, which says the following concerning repentance: “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble” when, by his inspiration, he visits the sinner and converts him to repentance, so that he may serve him in fear and trembling. By “mountains,” moreover, the rich and powerful are signified. Although they enter the kingdom of God with difficulty, yet, touched by the Holy Spirit, they begin to smoke outwardly and burn inwardly. To smoke outwardly is to show repentance daily through tears and contrition. For unless a fire were burning within, smoke would not appear outwardly.

Christ the Lord began his preaching with repentance, in order to show sinners how supremely necessary it is, II, 18. Worthy repentance is measured not so much by mortification of the flesh or length of time as by contrition of heart, II, 64. The same is stated, II, 108. The power of absolution committed by God to the Apostles and priests is not limited to a number of sins, but is utterly extensive whenever the penitent truly grieves over sins, II, 91. The authority given by Christ to the Apostles to absolve and retain sins is understood to be exercised when sins are remitted through baptism, repentance, or holy confession; but sins are retained in some because of unbelief, an unrepentant heart, or disobedience, II, 291.

### Purgatory

One regenerated through baptism who has never departed from God, or has fully and completely expiated his guilt before death, may immediately after this life be offered to the Lord and received into the assembly of the saints; or later, if he requires purgatory. Not all who are saved are received into blessedness immediately upon death, I, 164. Every sin is forgiven to those who are to be saved, but the penalty of sin is not forgiven to all; it must be expiated in purgatory, I, 376. The Lord visits our iniquities with a rod and our sins with blows when, for sins which should be punished by most grievous penalties or even by death itself, he chastises us with mild correction, mercifully deigning to afflict and chastise us either in this life or the next, I, 493. Many sins are easily loosed, but greater sins are not forgiven without worthy repentance, II, 64.

## R

### Resurrection of the Dead

The doctrine of the resurrection of the dead is most fully affirmed by Job’s testimony, when he says that he has his hope laid up in his bosom; this is as much as if he said: “I so believe, so hope, and am so certain concerning that thing which I have in my bosom and breast,” I, 257. This truth is also demonstrated by the fact that the wicked shall be tormented eternally in their own flesh; for Job says of the condemned man: “A fire that is not quenched shall devour him; he shall be afflicted, left behind in his tent,” I, 259. Once the soul has been separated from the body, it shall never return to it again except by divine decree at the time appointed for all, I, 468. The Sadducees, who denied the resurrection of the flesh, are refuted by Christ the Lord, II, 106. At the general resurrection the bodies of all human beings, perfected and whole in every part, shall rise from the tombs at the sound of the trumpet; our author affirms this against heretics who deny it, II, 292.

## S
To keep the Sabbath holy is not to cease from good works. Since the Sabbath is holy in itself, whoever works well becomes holy, I, 71. The Jews are refuted because they reproached Christ for non-observance of the Sabbath, since he healed the sick on it, I, 71.

**Priests.** The lifting of the mind to God in contemplation of heavenly things is the priest’s proper offering, I, [Col. 1327] 137. Priests are said to offer libations before the Lord when they always stand in God’s presence and are illumined by inward enlightenment. When they distribute the word of God among the people, they disclose by preaching only those things which they recognize can suffice for the people’s understanding, I, 137. The same place also treats of the manner in which priests should handle controversies of faith. Presbyters receive the book of the Gospels from the hand of the bishop ordaining them, so that they may have authority to expound and preach God’s word, I, 144. Priests should not approach the altar unless washed—that is, cleansed from sins, I, 116. Accusations against priests are not to be accepted lightly, I, 149. Laypeople may offer victims, but to immolate the lamb at the altar belongs to the priest alone, I, 155. What distinction exists between the clerical order and the rest of the people, I, 172. Not all are permitted to evangelize, but those to whom the ministry of the word has been entrusted, I, 177. Knowledge and prudence are especially necessary for them, I, 200. Those who wished to usurp the priesthood for themselves were severely punished by God, I, 184. Criminal persons are not to be admitted to priestly order; nevertheless, they are not to be separated from the Church, I, 198. Nor are the sons of slaves received into sacred orders, because the Church of God must not violently seize what belongs to another. Yet if their masters grant permission, no one excludes them from sacred orders because of their servitude. For slavery is not a sin; moreover, as soon as they are ordained, they become free, I, 204. From the Hebrews faithful to the supreme God—who, at God’s command, slew their idolatrous brothers without sparing any—the priests of the Lord should learn, drawing the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, to spare no offender; they should prefer God’s love to every other love, I, 217. The ark of God was captured because of the insolence of Eli’s sons, who abused their priesthood, and because Eli himself neglected to correct them as he ought, I, 469. With what severity those will be punished by God who trample upon and insult the sanctuary and its ministers—that is, the priests—I, 240.

**Sacrifice.** From the beginning of the world, human beings began to worship the supreme Creator of all things and to sacrifice to him as a sign of their worship and adoration; Adam’s sons Cain and Abel did this, I, 14. Thereafter this practice spread among all nations, so that they might demonstrate inward religion also through outward acts, namely sacrifices and the like. No unclean animal was sacrificed to God, because only those who are holy and cleansed from sins please God, I, 19. He offers an immaculate lamb to the Lord who keeps himself unstained by the wickedness of sins, I, 134. Those offer incense and strange fire before God who preach contrary to the faith and promote among the people novel, false, or dangerous doctrines, I, 144. Under the old law, whether a lamb, calf, or goat was sacrificed for sin, it signified Christ’s Passion, I, 165. Nothing but what is holy may be offered to God, I, 166. The sacrifices and offerings of the old law had their appointed time until Christ, because they signified Christ’s Passion. Afterwards they were not necessary, since the shadow had to cease when the truth came, I, 378. The ancient sacrifices were accepted by God, not because of the shedding of blood, but because of what they signified, I, 399. For the sacrifice of the Mass, see under “Eucharist.”

The life of the saints is contempt for earthly things and diligent pursuit of heavenly things, I, 47. Holy men repel every assault of lust by fasts, vigils, prayers, and mortification of the flesh, I, 55. Holy men shall enter the kingdom of heaven through many tribulations, I, 87. It belongs to the righteous to will nothing except what pleases the divine will, I, 88. They meet death with a joyful heart, since they have the best hope of their salvation, I, 229. When the saints entreat God in their prayers, although they are bodily upon earth, in spirit they nevertheless fly beyond heaven itself, I, 231. The higher the saints ascend by the steps of virtues, the more they despise the adversities of the world and promise themselves hope of future prosperity, I, 19. The saints grow daily in virtue and are a terror not only to people but even to demons themselves, I, 20. The prayers of the saints have great power with God for obtaining pardon for sins, I, 297. This is no small consolation for the saints: immediately after martyrdom they will be crowned, glorified, and received into eternal blessedness, I, 303. All the righteous likewise, departing from the darkness of this life, shall enter into the blessedness of eternal light, I, 353. The saints are called the works of God’s fingers because they are formed by the grace of the Holy Spirit in such fullness that they shall shine like the sun in God’s kingdom, I, 313. The Lord alone is the inheritance of the saints, because, despising everything in the world, they have chosen the Lord alone as their portion. A good exchange: they themselves are the Lord’s inheritance, and they possess the Lord as their inheritance, I, 324. At times the saints are tested by God, as were Abraham, Job, Tobias, David himself, and many others; he visited them in the night of distress and tribulation. Yet amid tribulations they gave thanks to God, and thus no iniquity [Col. 1328] was found in them. Let those who are afflicted learn how they ought to conduct themselves, I, 325. All saints are called righteous because they do, preach, and keep righteousness. The saints suffer persecutions because they preach and defend righteousness; their affliction and persecution are nothing other than a sacrifice pleasing and acceptable to God, I, 303. The saints were needy and poor, deprived of human help, because apart from God there was no one who dared to provide them assistance, I, 447. The Son is the Father’s right hand, because through him all things are accomplished. This right hand effects all this virtue of the saints when our Savior overcame the devil by his death; there all the saints were raised in steadfastness and strength above all their enemies and delivered from the danger of eternal death, I, Psalm CXVII. The saints are called God’s altars because they are consecrated to God and God dwells in them; in them God’s holocausts and sacrifices are daily performed, I, 481. Whoever is holy is worthy to be guarded by the Lord. But I understand all those holy men who, sanctified by the sacraments of the Church, hold the faith and do not depart from the Church, I, 484. The Lord performed many signs with his saints, all for good, because the Gentiles were converted to the faith especially through the signs that occurred. On the words of Psalm LXXII, “Full days shall be found in them,” the holy Interpreter has this: “Those are full days which abound in every good thing. Such days shall the saints have after this life, when they abound beyond measure in every good thing in that blessedness,” I, 454.
