Jesus will nevertheless save and raise up all who are predestined, even if they have at some time stood as his enemies and opponents, II, 436. There is nothing which God’s saints hold more in remembrance than the remembrance of their Savior, II, 311. The saints will give glory to the God of heaven, who before the ages predestined them for life and freed them from guilt, lest they suffer the like together with sinners, II, 000.

**Wisdom.** What true wisdom is, and what use ought to be made of it, I, 572. The queen of Sheba is commended because she came to King Solomon in order to hear his wisdom. She questioned Solomon about many mysteries and attained full knowledge of all things, I, 572. Wisdom, or prudence, which precedes the other cardinal virtues and is knowledge of divine and human things, begins from knowledge and confession of God. It is therefore said to be given by God; it governs moral uprightness and pertains to the salvation of souls, I, 492. Among other virtues, wisdom is what gold is among all metals. Hence wisdom is not without reason signified by gold in Holy Scripture, I, 492.

**Scandal.** The gravity of the sin of scandal is explained, together with the punishment inflicted upon it, II, 88.

**Divine Scriptures.** By the bitter waters which the Hebrew people could not drink, and which were made sweet by the wood Moses cast into them, are to be understood the Holy Scriptures, which were not understood before Christ; but Christ’s Passion and the wood of the cross changed them from bitter to sweet—that is, opened their meaning, I, 63. How this bitterness becomes sweet is explained, I, 63. Moses wrote down the Lord’s words lest they be surrendered to oblivion through the passage of time. And since a testament is confirmed by the death of its testator, while this Testator could not die, something had to be done by which that testament might be confirmed. It was confirmed by the blood of calves until he came who was signified by the calf, I, 84. Whatever Moses wrote in the Old Testament concerning Christ in figure, the Gospels relate that Christ did in actuality; no one can doubt the truth of the deeds, II and following, 85. The Old Testament, given in a cloud, prefigured its obscurity, 86. The table which God commanded Moses to construct after the making of the ark and the cherubim signifies divine Scripture. For *cherubim*, since it signifies fullness of knowledge, flies swiftly upon certain wings and suddenly fills all things; and it is called a table because it nourishes the soul with many and varied delights, 89. There are forty-two books of the Old Testament, and six of the New; if Paul’s Epistles and the Catholic Epistles, contained in two volumes, are added, all the books become fifty. For the book of Ruth, as St Jerome says, is counted within the book of Judges, while Ezra and Nehemiah are compressed into one volume, 93. St Bruno teaches excellently what is signified by the golden rings which God commanded to be made, so that by them the curtains’ veils might be joined around the tabernacle, 93. The tablets of the law are called tablets of testimony because they testify to whatever God wills or does not will, 119. Moses breaks the tablets of the law, lest, while they remained, its rigor should utterly destroy the idolatrous people, 119. This offers those in authority an example of using indulgence lest something worse occur, 119. The breaking of the earlier tablets was a sign that the time of their end would come. God’s command that Moses make new tablets signifies that a new legislation was to replace the old, I, 122. The glory of the New [Col. 1329] Testament is far more splendid than the law of Moses, 123. Love of learning God’s wonders and investigating truth in some way overcomes the deep mysteries of Scripture and leads to ease of understanding, I, 136. Whoever searches the Holy Scriptures finds great delight in them, I, 153. Blessed are those who delight in the sacred volumes of both Testaments: they always abound in manna and never lack heavenly bread; the living bread which came down from heaven never fails them, I, 193. Divine Scripture provides us with grain, oil, and wine. In some places it is eaten with difficulty, like bread; in others it is easily drunk, like wine; everywhere, however, it heals the soul like a medicine and oil, I, 209. It happens that heretics compose books and collect testimonies from Holy Scripture in their own defense; when they bring these to councils for their defense, they are overcome by those very testimonies, as though by their own swords, I, 268. The great authority of the divine books is also inferred from this: heretics themselves, misunderstanding them, use them to defend their errors and rejoice if they seem to have discovered something new in them, I, 273. Since the Scriptures of both Testaments are obscure, they seem to be darkness and can be penetrated only by believers. Whoever therefore seeks God and desires to know him should enter this darkness; there he will find that light which enlightens every person coming into this world, I, 329. In King David’s time only the first seven books of Scripture, called the Heptateuch, were read, because the books of the Prophets had not yet been composed, I, 347. The meaning of the Old Testament must be sought in the New, for the latter is its exposition, I, 339. At the time of his Passion, the Lord spoke very few things which the Evangelists carefully relate to us. Yet in Psalm LXVIII and elsewhere the Prophet says that the Lord spoke many things not found in the Gospels. Hence it is manifest that the Prophet likewise writes those things which the Lord spoke in his heart, just as he writes those which he spoke with his mouth. He alike heard and saw both what the Lord spoke and what the Lord willed or thought, I, 444. So great is the brightness of the New Testament that the brightness of the Old Testament is reckoned darkness. Yet both Testaments are one, and both are bright and splendid if they are understood spiritually, I, 458. The Manichaeans were mad in saying that the God of the New Testament was one and the God of the Old another. The Savior was the author of both, I, 458. The fountains and streams are understood to be the law, the prophets, and the volumes of both Testaments. Those fountains had first been closed and stopped up; but the Lord opened their channels, broke the tightest bonds by which they were shut, and caused the flow of waters to issue from them, I, 457. The law given to the Jews reached even to the Gentiles and has worked, and works daily, more among this people than among that, I, 465. God willed that the Scriptures be made and the sacred volumes written in remembrance of his works, I, 541. How divine Scriptures should be read and interpreted, II, 61. The Gospels and Epistles of the Apostles, the books of Moses and the Prophets, are set before us like dishes filled with every delight, II, 186.

**Simony.** Simon deceived, violated, and corrupted the Roman people; from him the buying and selling of sacred and spiritual things is called simony, I, 80. He sought to buy from the apostles, for a price, the grace and power of the Holy Spirit, and heard from the apostle Peter that his money would turn to his perdition. Simoniacs either buy or confer sacred episcopal ordinations and other sacraments for a price; because of this crime they become outcasts from the Church, 116. Let simoniacs and invaders of the Church be deterred from so great a crime by the example of the punishment of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, 184. Since God gives only freely, he said: “Freely you have received; freely give.” Therefore those who do not confer the sacraments freely, and those who do not receive them freely, are guilty of simony, II, 53. Christ rebukes most vehemently and drives from God’s temple those buying and selling in it, by whom simoniacs are understood, II, 100.

**Hope.** Those who feign righteousness and hunt after the praise of righteousness, deservedly bestowed only upon the righteous, have no hope of eternal recompense, I, 267. Those who firmly hope in God, even if they suffer persecution, tortures, and death itself from enemies, cannot be torn away from steadfast faith and their resolve for righteousness; for God never abandons those who hope in him, I, 310. Those who, abandoning divine help, place their hope in worldly supports fall more swiftly, bound and impeded by the very source from which they expect victory. But the saints, having hope in God alone, will never lack his help and consolation, I, 336. Since whatever good we do, we do through God’s mercy preceding and assisting us, we ought to place the hope of our salvation in it, I, 342. There is nowhere room for despair, because the most sweet Lord has established for us a most sweet law. Certainly few or none could have been saved had the Lord not established this most sweet law. But he is also righteous and never departs from righteousness. He is sweet, therefore, to penitents, but righteous toward those who persevere in wickedness, I, [Col. 1330] 345. God never abandons those who hope in him; accordingly he gave the martyrs such steadfastness that, by dying, they conquered their enemies and could not be overcome by any tortures, I, 345. As nothing is worse than despair, so nothing is better than firm hope, I, 354. The hope of Christians is in the Lord’s Passion. The Church possesses this hope until the world passes away with its iniquities; thereafter hope will no longer exist, since all that can be hoped for will have been received, I, 413. Those who hope in God should have no fear of any human being. Human strength can do nothing against God’s power and will, I, 412. If divine promises are properly considered, they kindle great confidence in our salvation within us, I, 422. Those hearts fear God which are suffused with spiritual joy; and hearts suffused with spiritual joy no longer love and hope for earthly things, but heavenly things, I, 485. What may righteous men hope and confidently expect from God’s mercy, if the Lord will remember even Rahab and Babylon? I, 486. Whoever lacks hope is stripped of every good and more unhappy than every creature. Malignant spirits lack this hope, and therefore strive with all their might to lead to despair all whom they can deceive, II, 488. Apart from the sin of despair, there is no other sin which cannot be blotted out by repentance. But this is not blotted out by repentance, because it admits no repentance, II, 489. Hope is expectation of future goods. Those have this expectation who most certainly hope that they shall one day receive whatever has been promised them by God, II, 289. Distinguished righteous persons who shone in hope are enumerated in the Holy Scriptures, II, 490.

**Holy Spirit.** At the beginning of the creation of all things, God’s Spirit was manifested, of whom it is said that he moved over the waters, as co-worker with the other two persons in the creation of the whole universe, I, 2. There were heretics, namely the Macedonians, who believed in the Father and the Son but did not admit the Holy Spirit, denying that he was God; the Church condemned them at the Council of Constantinople, II, 50. His coming upon the apostles on the day of Pentecost was prefigured by God’s descent upon Sinai amid flames and resounding thunders, when he gave Moses the tablets of the law, I, 70. The procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son is affirmed, I, 114. Different names are attributed to the Holy Spirit according to the diverse bestowal of graces; yet he is one and the same Spirit, I, 402. There are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: wisdom, counsel, understanding, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of God; these are opposed to the seven unclean spirits, II, 67. He is called the Spirit of truth because he teaches nothing but truth. Therefore the sayings of the prophets, and everything composed by the Holy Spirit, are true, II, 173. Christ, when he bestowed the Holy Spirit on the apostles, breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit.” “He breathed,” says St Bruno, “so that through this we may understand and firmly believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him as from the Father,” II, 291.

**Pride.** From pride all vices take their origin. God first punished the sin of pride in the transgressing angels; secondly in Adam, who believed the serpent’s delusions promising him divinity; thirdly in people who presumed to build a tower up to heaven, I, 21. Here St Bruno says: “For God always hates pride; therefore he humbles the proud and exalts the humble. Thus also the devil, when he wished to raise his throne above the heights of heaven, was cast down. True repentance can exist in no one unless that person humbles himself before God and puts off the spirit of pride,” I, 64.

## T

**Temperance.** That virtue which does not exceed measure in its actions and seeks no superfluities is called temperance. It is so necessary that the world itself could not stand without it. Since a human being is composed of contrary elements, if there were no nature to temper things that are contrary and hostile, he could not remain long amid such discord and such immense conflict, II, 493. Temperance is useful in every undertaking; wisdom itself must keep within the bounds of temperance, II, 493. Among the wise of the world the proverb is common: “Nothing in excess.”

**The Temple of Jerusalem.** According to Christ’s prediction, the Temple and city of Jerusalem underwent final devastation and ruin by the Romans in the forty-second year after the Passion of Christ the Lord, II, 202, and in the notes.

**Temptation.** In how many ways the devil tempts us, and how his evil suggestions should be repelled. As Christ is put to death not for himself but for us, so he is tempted not for himself but for us. His temptation brought us a twofold benefit: first, that we may know how we ought to answer our tempters and those who wrong us; second, that we may place confidence in none of our virtue or wisdom, but place all our trust in God’s help, II, [Col. 1331] 16.

**The mystery of the Holy Trinity.** St Bruno teaches that the sublime and principal mystery of the Holy Trinity, professed by the Christian religion, may be drawn from the words of Genesis 1, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” Expounding them, he reasons thus: “You have, then, God—that is, the Father; and you have the beginning—that is, the Son; for he himself says: ‘I am the beginning, who also speak to you’ [John 8]. But what follows? ‘And the Spirit of God moved over the waters.’ You have also the Holy Spirit. Therefore the whole Trinity is recognized: God, his Word, and his Spirit—one God,” I, 2. Another testimony to the same truth is supplied by chapter 18 of Genesis, where it is recorded that Abraham, standing by the oak of Mamre, saw three men and worshipped one. “Behold,” says the anonymous author, “what had until then been unknown to all: he sees God in Trinity and worships him in unity. Not that he saw the Trinity itself, but because through what he saw he was granted to know God in Trinity and unity. Thus, although he saw three, he worshipped only one and called only one ‘Lord,’” I, 25; the same appears in the Commentary on Psalm XCVIII, I, 510. Furthermore, Bruno thought that David had foretold this same mystery in the words of Psalm XXXIII: “For he spoke, and they were made.” He explains them thus: “If he spoke, he spoke by the Word. But to speak was to will. The Word of God and the will of God are the Son himself. For what are the Lord, his Word, and his Spirit, but the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit? Therefore one God, by whose will the heavens were made,” I, 359. In Psalm CIX, the same Prophet declares the Son’s complete equality with the Father in the words: “With you is the beginning in the day of your power, amid the splendors of the saints; from the womb before the morning star I begot you.” And this, St Bruno adds, the Prophet says in “The Lord said to my Lord,” because the Son is with him the beginning of all creatures. In this respect he is nevertheless shown to be equal to the Father. That he is the beginning and sits at the Father’s right hand, on the day of his power and amid the splendors of the saints, will be revealed to all nations, I, 539. St Bruno also discusses the Trinity excellently, II, 60 and 273. “The Father is one [person], the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. But the Father is not one thing, the Son another thing, and the Holy Spirit another thing. For they are all one, but they are not one person. ‘One’ pertains to essence; ‘one person’ refers to person and number,” II, 529, 530 and following. The heavenly hosts never cease to cry, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty”; they indicate the mystery of the Trinity. For although “holy” is said three times, “God almighty” is said only once, so that he who is divided in persons may nevertheless be believed one in majesty, power, and substance, II, [Col. 1332] 310. On the words of Isaiah 48:11, “I am the Lord; this is my name; I will not give my glory to another,” cited in the exposition of Psalm CXII, I, 543, he says this concerning the Holy Trinity: “This is the name of the whole Trinity, because the Father is Lord, the Son is Lord, and the Holy Spirit is Lord; yet not three Lords, but one Lord.”

## U

**Usury.** Usury is forbidden by the divine writings because it is unjust. For it happens that a small sum of money lent consumes the poor person’s entire substance within a short time, I, 169. Whatever is demanded beyond the amount of gold repaid, while the debt is not extinguished by the repayment, is usury, I, 208.

## V

**Virtue.** There are four principal virtues, in which all other virtues are contained and without which they are shown to be vain and useless: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance, I, 86. Virtues acquired through labor are lost through idleness. Guarding and watching oneself are necessary for everyone at every age, I, 179. To humble oneself before God amid flourishing prosperity and fortune is virtue; amid tribulations, it may be either baseness or failure of spirit, I, 283. The tribulations of this age, when patiently endured, are expiations for sins, I, 283. This is the highest wisdom: that a person not trust in his own virtue nor glory in his riches, but love mercy, know himself, and not subject his flesh to luxuries and pleasures, I, 395. It is a beautiful way to walk from virtue to virtue: from faith to hope, from hope to charity, from charity to humility, from humility to patience, from obedience to continence, and so to pass from virtue to virtue until one comes to the highest Virtue, that is, our Savior, who is God’s virtue and patience, I, 481. Who are those who walk in innocence? I, 483.

**Vow.** Under the old law, vows which could not be fulfilled were redeemed for a price, I, 169. Whoever makes an evil vow ought to render some good thing in its place, I, 170. Alteration of a vow does not lie within the discretion of the person making it; but it may be made by one possessing authority, in the same place. The vows of those who have entered a religious order are not temporary; rather, they bind them until the end of life, I, 171. What obligation vows and oaths entail, and who may judge concerning them, I, 192. Oaths and vows contrary to justice are void, but those who thus vow and swear sin. Each person has within himself and in his heart what he can vow and render to God. Let this always be in your vow and your desire: that you praise him; and this suffices for you, I, 412.

[Col. 1331]
